This game isn't quite BattleTech and does have some balance issues. The Pay-2-Win crowd is also pretty fiece and playing a Quick Play match will drop you in a team that's a lot like the Keystone Cops. I have no interest in faction play (it gets way to Tribal in there) and without some sort of story line or AI combat; I can't justify the time I put into this title.
The game heavily favors Clan Mech over Inner Sphere Mechs (The in game meta factions) as far as build options and for a perpetual tinkerer like me, it gets frustrating to try and balance a build.
There's also a strong vein of elitism and anti-Steam user chatter that will put a lot of us on the outs. There is also no active monitoring of user age. Getting slagged by a kid is one thing, but having to listen to some 11 year old scream into the VOIP and Caps-rage about how no one will do what they're told needs to stop.
There are also legal issues at play that will continue to slow or even alter game content. I don't know enough about FASA, the old pen and paper BattleTech IP or the various people involved to make a flow chart, but there is another MechWarrior game in developement and a lot of the old 'Jocks in the Forums are still bemoaning the lack of certain Iconic Mechs in MWO.
Give this one another 2 years and another major update. If it's still up and running, go for it. For now, I'd recommend holding off.

What a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ This thing doesn't come with a proper manual that teaches you how to configure it in steam. You need to go look into their forums to get a grasp of everything or find some guides. Big picture mod is somewhat required. When configuring the controller outside of big picture mode I ran into bugs that are tedious and most of them don't occur while configuring In big picture mode.
I just use the most popular community configurations for games that have them.
The controller isn't so bad, it does have some glaring issues though.
The shoulder buttons feel very off to the position of the triggers which makes holding all four at the same time feel kind of awkward. The triggers feel ok to press but the shoulder buttons feel very stiff.
The other issues for me is the distance between the one control stick and the main four buttons. It's a little too close. I prefer the Playsation's distance they have for the dualshock. For example if I hold right on the control stick and press the X / square button my thumbs touch.
The control stick is tight though.
I prefer not to bind the buttons under the controller on each side, they seem in the way for me.
The track pads are why I bought this thing, their very interesting. I hate haptic feedback noises but these pads are fun to use in games that can use them to their full potential.
Also, if you want to use this for nonsteam games you need to add them as nonsteam games to your account to be able to set it up. There is probably other ways.
I can't recommend you buy this unless fancy hardware interests you, it's an average feeling controller with some great tech. If your still somewhat interested, wait for the revised version if one even comes out.
Maybe they'll put a rechargable battery in the next one too.

It has turn based JRPG combat without any intresting twists aside from "combos" where you can exploit a debuff on an enemy, removing the debuff but causing the exploiting attack to deal a bit more damage. Except this makes combat even more boring, as you are no longer applying debuffs for their effects but instead putting a circle through a round hole.

I played and completed the game on on "Commander" (Normal/Classic Difficulty) w/ Ironman (no rerolls of officers).
My experience of the game was of mind-numbing repetition and a frustratingly easy linear journey.
I finished the game using the same 3 officers with the same 3 variants of the 3 types of ships (appropriately upgraded to the new tiers) using the same 3-5 attack patterns for every enemy encounter regardless if the enemy were eugenics enthusiasts, pirates, bioships, terminators, or anything in between.
I couldn't call it a button masher because I still needed to choose the attack (does the most damage) I always used to attack the target (ship with the least health) I always chose.
All of the random events I encountered had obviously correct solutions and positive benefits.
All of the random traits that officers could receive were positive with no negative effects on gameplay and no interplay between officers.
All of the encounters with the alien factions were either "Please help us for little to no reward" or "You will never defeat- Please don't kill me."  They were charming at first encounter but after the 3rd or 4th time with the each race being little different from flavor text and art assets, it quickly added to the brain dead effect of the overall experience.
The resource management in the game was a joke.  I consistently had more resources than I had tech, ships, or events to spend them on and
There was no point in leveling up my other officers or using them for anytihng other than Dark Matter/Material/Crew farmers which was pointless due to the overwhelming amount of resources available just playing the game normally.
I wish tech wasn't hidden behind linear events in the story.  It would make the experience more fluid and I wouldn't have been able to over prepare for untimed events that couldn't happen without my permission.  Certain allied benefits and technologies had no use or bearing in the 3rd act of the game but could have been more fun to play with in the early 2nd act and given incentive to want to help the alien factions.
I wish that time mattered more to missions other than giving me an ordered chorelist of tasks that needed to be completed.  Maybe make completing missions earlier give more rewards or have completing missions later have stronger(more fleets have joined the fight)/weaker enemies (less HP).
I can see that the game was made to accommodate multiple fleets but I don't see how that would have made the game more fun with how tedious fleet to fleet combat was with just my one uber fleet.
I might play this game again in the future with the maximum difficulty setting to see if that might make a difference in the experience but the Classic version of the game as it is now (07/08/17) is an unrewarding and repetitive grind.

Fun game. It can be a little bit of a grind but the returns on your grind are nice and make it feel worthwhile to fly around and blow up some filthy Xenos. I'm also a bit of a min/max nut, so I tweaked on my ships and what not. In particular I enjoyed the random things that happened, Super Solder Cadet Bucky Rogers for example.  I kept yelling BUCKY IS GOING BUCKWILD AT THE BASE to my girlfriend, she wasn't particularly enthused, but it tickled me.. and I think that's what is important. There is obviously room for gameplay improvment and A LOT of room for more randomness/fun stuff/jokes, which I kind of found made the grind a lot less grindy feeling. The dev team seems pretty amped people like their game, as such the "feel" I get is we're going to see some pretty cool stuff to come. I can see how the game isn't for everyone, but if you're a bit of a sci-fi nerd I think you'll have least be able to justify what you spent on the purchase. Frankly I enjoyed it and am looking forward to the next big update, they appear to be fleshing out skill tree's and a variety of other things. If I had to have a criticism (and this may be different on higher skill settings, first playthrough was commander to figure out what was going on) I would like to know a bit more about what it is we really fought at the end and how that all came about. Also the Vo'rash ? Sup with them? In summary, I wholeheartedly endorse the game and look forward to incoming updates and  playing it on higher skill levels.

Well... It's interesting.
I can see some people's issues with there not being enough parts, but the fact that you can make (or download) parts and toss them into an Add-Ons folder kinda gets rid of that complaint.  I think the biggest failing is the fact that the tutorial is REALLY basic, expecially where the wrench is concerned.  This game looks to be extremely powerful, but withot utilizing that power it's kind of like Superman having to remain Clark Kent because the world is made of Kryptonite.
Now, that aside, I'm seeing a pretty nice game here.  The block selection is done fairly well, allowing you to customize your quick-bars to whatever parts you wish to use.  In addition you use the mouse to begin placement of a block, but then use the numberpad to fine-tune that placement.  This is great in a 3D environment, as it truly gives you easy control of your building.  It even goes so far to, when placing something wrong, tell you exactly why the placement was rejected (overlapping, etc).  Finally, there are enough DEMO worlds in this game that you can truly see all of the possibilities you can get into (as long as you know how the wrench works).
When it all comes down to it, do I recommend people play this game?  Yes I do.  THAT SAID, continue reading...
I do recommend people play this game, however I only recommend BUYING the game if you can get it at a reduced price like I did.  I got this game as part of a $2.99 bundle on Bundle Stars, and for that price this game is well worth the money.  Would I pay $10+ for it?  Absolutely not, because it doesn't have a strong dev team behind it, the developer has a really bad attitude, and I doubt it'll ever be "finished".
The most I'd ever pay is $2.99 for this game by itself...  That's a lot, considering I'm expecting the developer to see a lawsuit by Lego in the future.

you play as a character known as Pumpkin Man. Pumpkin Man is very limited in his mechanics within the control scheme. All he can do is kill enemies by launching or as the developer calls ' vomiting' candy corns until enemies vanish instantly after a certain number of hit points. There may be a story, but if there is, then I have not gotten that far in my progression of this game. There are many games out there currently in the personal computer gaming market that are now going this route. The route of re-inventing hardcore old-school platformers from the old days of the Nintendo Entertainment System, the Nintendo 64 era, Sega Genesis, Saturn, Dreamcast and the other most notable one of recreating, even some of the lovable aspects that made the Nintendo GameCube many years ago one of the best Nintendo selling systems because of its incredible array of surfeit titles and one main console exclusive,
that made it an ideal system for platformers. However, it can't compare to all the platformers that were released at the time of the Genesis and Nintendo Entertainment System's inception.
Finally, gamers, reviewers, and developers, we have a game that combines the fine details of
and
while remaining distinct from these intellectual properties (IP’s).
and
interbred and out came their baby,
or rather, Pumpkin Man. There are so many aspects to love in
from the Halloween, a dark universe with enemies that represent death such as skeleton heads, a double-headed dragon boss, the Devil, small snakes, bats, and wizards. These are only a few of the whole cast of characters that have been added to the game, while more through the later levels will arise. Alright, is this game for me?
Yes,
is worth its new price tag of $5.00. Cheaper than you can probably get into a haunted house this Halloween and later Halloweens, you get an old-school platformer that finally requires skill, patience, attention to detail, and quick reaction times. This game is separated from the majority of platformers we now have that are modern because it requires a good amount of strategy, however, most importantly, it could be counted as a side-scroller that is pattern based. Once you find the specific patterns of the bosses, the different moves that they execute, their positioning, whether they have two or three different forms, and how often these attacks occur, you will be able to defeat every single boss in the game.

The bosses in
are set up similarly to
. You go through various levels destroying normal types of enemies while you can access secret areas, hidden items that I assume will help you later on the more challenging levels, and you can regain health which is randomized, by collecting hearts which add to your health meter.
was one of the earliest games to my knowledge that came up with a specific concept, of course, they used bolts as currency and had upgrades you could buy through Dr. Wily's shop at the end of each level to prepare for other bosses. You would collect screws to be able to use at that shop. Through my experience so far (levels 1-3), I have not encountered any type of menu where you can buy upgrades nor is there any currency to collect. One of the bosses that I have encountered and beaten so far is a chainsaw man that is built like Jason Voorhees from
and reminds me of the way in which he would also kill others. It is very easy to dodge his attacks; all you must remember is to wait until he throws out his chainsaw and start jumping.
If you successfully nail this, you can at least get one shot minimum at the first boss which removes one health bar out of his full health. If you are proficient at this game, you can even go with eliminating up to two health bars at a time. The others have different moves and get progressively harder, but are relatively simple to figure out if you are one that understands simple and complex patterns in video games. One difference between this game is the excess of bosses per level. In level one, I encountered near two bosses at one time, level two also around two bosses in the level and level three I have not figured out because I am continuing my progression in it.

Hardcore mode limits you to only one hit point you can take for the whole game. This mode is for all of you, veterans if you find that earlier platformers in the 16-bit era and beyond are far too easy for you. If you are one that grew up with old-school games, spending the time to learn exact patterns, progressing faster than your average person, then give this mode a try. Standard mode has checkpoints. In the case that you die when facing a boss, it will bring you back to the start of the area you began at, but places you behind a couple or few doors before the boss will appear again. You must fight some of the same enemies you did before, but it is not difficult if you remember the exact layout of the maps in which you had run through.  I am upset that the developer did not provide any explanation behind this hardcore game mode. We don't know how fast the enemies attack, whether they take more damage to kill nor whether the bosses have more attacks and different moves than in the standard difficulty.
Although, I understand that it is not necessary but a sufficient condition that would be a nice addition for others to know before they start hardcore mode, I feel it is needed to educate all of us. When I play a platform game like this, I want to know, up front, the statistics of all of the enemies and bosses. How much health they have in quantifiable numbers, the percentage of damage that our candy corn attack does, as well as gathering an idea of the enemy types. Developer, if you get a chance to read this review, please include an update as a short ' how to play' which will describe these specific aspects I have mentioned. I believe it will be useful for every gamer that plays Halloween Forever to get a better understanding and comprehension of the game.

I have to say this game is fantastic.
First off, I don't think it's really pay to win nearly as bad as most free to play games.  I see alot of complaints about this and I don't agree. Here are my reasons:
-You start out with 4 trial mechs from each weight class (trial as in they're set loadouts, you can't customize them, that's it). So in other words, you start out with 16 mechs to try out. That's plenty for me to start with personally.
-Secondly, you can purchase and customize mechs with c-bills you earn from matches.  It's not too bad really, Ten 8 minute matches got me a good mech that I was able to deck out and start getting more kills with during matches.
-You really could not spend a dime and get a fulfilled mechwarrior experience from this game. I know I did for the first few weeks without spending anything. You can earn everything you need pretty quickly to get a handful of decent to good mechs going, and the game starts you out with some c-bills and some premium time. I only spent money because I started really getting into the game and decided I wanted to get some premium time going and to purchase a champion mech pack at some point. Plus, I honestly felt like the developers earned my money because the gameplay is that good.
OK, let's talk about the heart of the game.  How is the actual gameplay you say?  Well, as a pretty big Battletech fan and someone who played Mechcommander and Mechwarrior 3 & 4... IT'S EFFING FANTASTIC.  God, this is the best part of the game for sure.  I love the gameplay, the visuals effects, the sound effects, the tactics and potential for teamwork, everything.  The battles are how I would imaging actual Mech Combat. The autocannons roar, lasers tear, missiles swarm.  It's so good, I love it.  Even if you're not into battletech, I think most people can appreciate the realistic feel of the mechs, and the roles of the weightclasses: assault mechs brawling, heavy mechs dishing it out, and medium and light mechs supporting. It's beautiful.  I thought Piranha Games nailed mech combat.  Also, customization is awesome and relatively balanced as far as I can tell so far. I will give a fair warning that you have to use a little patience and thought when starting out.  This isn't CoD, you don't charge in and kill.  You have to stick with your team, use cover and try to use hit and run tactics.  Also, try not to drive an Assault mech first thing, you need to work up to that to utilize it properly.  If you're not a Battletech fan, I definitely recommend this game.  If you're a Battletech fan, you have to play this game!!
Alright, so I'll telly you what I think the downsides are.  The quickplay matches are a little repetitive. Not as bad as some people are saying, in my opinion the gameplay more than makes up for it.  That said, there are about 8 or so maps currently, and 3 game modes (assault, conquest, and team deathmatch). It could use a little spicing up for sure. Games typically last 5 to 15 minutes.  However - this is only the quickplay version of the game.
The main feature of the game takes place in the form of faction play, which I'm only beginning to get into and understand.  This gameplay takes place in the form of territory conquest in via assault and defence of planets.  This form of gameplay definitely has some more meat to it.  For instance one game mode takes place in the form of defending a base with friendly defense turrets and gates at the front (highly reminiscent of mechcommander i thought) which was awesome.  This is pretty cool, but my problem with faction play so far is it seems more than a little elitist (tons of premades and clans steamrolling PUGs) and not only that but it seems very difficult to break into. Like, it feels like in order to get serious about faction play, I have to prove I'm good enough to join some group that meets every Sunday, etc. Don't like that, a little too reminiscent of WoW or some other mmo for me.  This part of the game is probably a little more pay to win, or, invest a ton of time and reading online forums to win.  I don't like that too much.  The game doesn't explain the faction play very well at all, and the interface is kind of a mess and overloading the player with options.  You have to look it all up online to learn anything.
Anyways, despite a few things I don't care for, I think this game is great.  I'd give it a solid 9/10 to anyone interested in picking this game up.

[If you dislike reading seemingly irrelevant information you are free to skip to the bottom of this review. There you will find my recommendation. Thank you!]
So this game has been one of my favorite building games of all time. Starting in 2010 along with the majority of what I would say was our community, I bought the original Blockland and was having a great time. Things were getting done, updates being made. There were these classics maps I'll never forget: the Bedroom, the Kitchen, and the Slopes. I enjoyed this game, and I was estimated to be playing it about 10 hours a day or more. (Update: Many people don't believe I played this game as long as I claim. The truth is, Blockland existed before (its release on) Steam. For this reason, Steam has not registered all my hours from when I played it before. I only recently migrated to Steam Blockland from the original Vanilla Blockland. Hope that clears things up!)
It took some time but an insightful man by the name of Ephialtes in-game decided to build Blockland a new system. I believe it was around 2011-2012 that this became widely-used. It was called Return to Blockland, and was basically the Steam client for Blockland before Blockland was actually on Steam. It had a 'Workshop' (servers that hosted add-ons you could directly download from), Add-On Manager, Friends client, global IRC chat, chat rooms, easy-to-use settings system for your server, add-on preferences manager, and so much more. It was the true revelation of Blockland's existence. It brought upon a new experience for the Blockland community, and gave it a modern feel.
That officially marked the downfall of RTB, which would eventually be shut down because Steam replaced 1/3 of its functionality. There would no longer be a place to manage your add-ons, chat globally with other BL users, find your friends (since they would no longer be on RTB and you didn't know if they had Steam), and last but not least, you could no longer manage your server like you used to.
That probably drove me away the most. I stuck around for a bit, hosted a multitude of mildly popular servers as well as a 32/32 player MERP server that consisted of most of my time. After about four months, I kinda lost interest and began the process of leaving the BL community. I left a legacy, but even that would soon be forgotten...
So you know that game called Minecraft? I ended up spending almost all of my time on that. I hosted some very popular servers on Minecraft, met some great friends, and was enjoying it. I almost forgot about Blockland completely, but then my friend (who shall remain nameless) decided to get Blockland after I showed him a fun little gamemode on it called Renderman. He got it, and when I saw that he did, I decided to hop back on and play with him... but I didn't do much otherwise.
I truly came back about two months ago. I began hosting my MERP server, probably just to feel the nostalgia and see all the empires that had been built on it. A friend of mine by the name of Amir (a full-time player of my server back when it was popular) happened to stop by. We had an awesome reunion, played a bit of MERP (not really. Just remarked on how sucky our builds were), had a lot of fun. I began playing Blockland much more.
And then I stopped. Garry's Mod took up my time. I managed a community on there and couldn't depart from them. But that wasn't the only reason.
So anyways, if you got to the bottom of this review reading through an incredibly long backstory and wondering why the heck I'd write a story like that, I congratulate you. You have the patience of a... you, but none of this was really a review, was it?
So here's my take on the game.
It's a great game, don't get me wrong, but it is running on steam (get it hahahahaaha... haha. ..ha... sorry) and no longer has that spark of a game that has true potential. Maybe Badspot can turn this around one day. And maybe you can be a part of that. Me, on the other hand, have exhausted the game of Blockland. I like the game, but I can no longer play it.
Maybe it'll be different for you.

So it's not a poorly crafted game, but unfortunately, it just isn't fun.
For a game that is about base management, there is surprisingly little. There are a number of times that I just felt frustrated by lack of options when faced with an event. It's difficult to reaarange your base, which is fine, but only because it doesn't seem to matter where you put anywhere, you get no proximity bonuses for having certain types of rooms together.
The only influence you have over officer abilities is 4 rerolls each time it is time to choose a new one. After that you have to stick with the choices provided with no means to influence the spec tree of the officers. A better alternative is spending resources to alter/influence their growth.
Speaking of resources, once you figure out how to efficiently farm them, you don't have many options on how to spend what you've earned. You could build more ships, but you can't really use them without getting more officers, which has a lot of issues.
There is no fleet management screen. Well, except when you send a fleet on a mission, but you won't be able to actually call it up unless you find the fleet on the map first.
Furthermore, the combat is fun, but there is entirely too much of the same. And difficulty only really increases in terms of quantity. Kill a Big bad, your reward is to kill 4 more Big Bads.
The game will bar you from doing things in your base without actually telling you the real reason you can't take an action. I have eight officers, I got to the point where I wanted to finish off a 3rd fleet. Yet I can't for the life of me figure out, within game or without, what "traits" my current officers are missing.
The game UI needs to be redone to help provide the player with needed information. I can't easily find my ship or understand why I'm barred from taking an action, and typically I found myself going outside of the game to find answers, which there are few.
But, what made me flat out stop was that in the third Act, a bug made 3 of my officers become unavailable for anything. They exist in the roster, but I can't send them out of base or order them to perform tasks inside. And this is especially annoying since again, even when the game operates normally, it's hard to understand why you can or cannot take an action.
There's probably more, but
TL:DR - The game is frustrating, not challenging.

At a friend's suggestion I gave Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander a try. That's a really compelling game. Kind of a streamlined sci-fi 4x but with more personality than the genre generally has. I've been looking for that sort of thing for a while.
The combat system is really clever, based around setting up and then exploiting conditions on enemies, where no individual ship has both parts of that combo, so you have to set up your 3-ship fleets with some care. Feels a little like deckbuilding (though not as deep).

Not sure I'd recommend it to anyone who doesn't have that itch to scratch, but if you do, give it a look.

Helicon 6 is a lovely retro game, putting you in the position of a space station commander, and in a sense in the position of the head of humanity. The game does many things right. The graphics are very nice (for pixel graphics lovers), there is vast amount of content and the immersion is high and flawless. The concepts involved such as strategic base building, fleet management and officers training are all interesting and integrate well and at times better than X-com, which is the most natural benchmark for the strategy layer of the game.
So why a negative review? the one major and game-breaking problem of the game is gameplay. This is a grind game, not to the extent of punch club or xcom: long war, but it is still a marathon. Now, I am not against grind games, and in fact I enjoyed each of those that I have listed, but in a grinding game there has to be some element of excitement, some feeling that somthing great is about to happend and this must be accompanied by a permament sense of danger, combined with the feeling that only due to your genius you are still alive. The combat system of Halcyon is repeatative and the forces are not truely diverse. As a consequence while the long term strategy is not easy to come up with and optimize, in the tactical combat you never feel clever and gradually it turns into a chore. Over time the positive sentiments that you have developed for the story and the grand strategy aspects are diminishing. In my case I have decided that I just cannot dedicate the time to play this anymore, and I'd be better of coming back to XCom 2: long war for the grind and excitement, and to FTL for the space immersion.

I
recommend the steam controller under certain conditions.
The track-pad gives much more precise steering control than an XBox thumbstick could ever dream of doing.  If you cannot afford a racing wheel, the Steam controller is a game-changer.  The only drawback is the triggers have very little travel compared to XBox controllers.  Not as ideal for fine-grain control over breaking and acceleration.
Some motorcycle games may use one thumbstick for steering and the other for leaning the rider to keep balanced.  On the Steam controller, I like to use the track pad for steering and rotating the entire controller (gyroscope feature) to lean the rider.  This feels much more intuitive/organic.
For the twitchiest of shooters such as
, the mouse is still your best bet.  I hold the Steam Controller in my left hand and use the thumb stick for movement and use the trackpad for things like reloading.  Then I hold the mouse with my right hand.
For games where the fastest response time is not as critical such as
, the Steam Controller's gyroscopic feature feels REALLY good when aiming weapons.  Rotating the controller in your hands feels like you are aiming a gun.  It's quite amazing, really.  I know it sounds like it would be gimmicky, but it works.  For
you normally have two options..  Use your controller in one hand (limiting the number of accessible buttons), and your other hand on the mouse for aiming weapons.  Or you can use the controller to both steer and aim but this is very slow and cumbersome.  On the Steam Controller you get the best of both worlds.  Use both hands on the controller and use the gyro feature to aim your weapon.  It feels great and I feel like I would be at an advantage when multiplayer is added.
The Steam Controller's configuration system is a dream come true for tinkerers.  You can assign multiple functions to a single button.  Tap it for one command, hold it down for another.  Or double-tap it for something else.  And that is just scratching the surface of what configuration options are available.  The gyroscope function (which works really well) can either be used for moving an XBox thumbstick or moving the mouse.  Same for the track pads.
This has changed the way I game and breathed new life into old games such as
.  I bought the Steam Controller while it was on sale but after as many months as I have used it and grown dependent on it, I would now pay full price for one.  I really love this thing.
I have a flight stick and I still use it for flight games.  If I had a steering wheel I would use that instead of the Steam Controller.  But as I do not it has opened up new options for me and I love that.
As mentioned earlier the triggers squeeze a very short distance.  I wish they moved more.
The Steam Controller works by piggy-backing on the XInput API.  This means you only get full analog controls on games that normally support the XBox controller.  Older games that only support DInput will not give you access to the analog stick movements or analog triggers.  You can fake it by using the Steam controller's analog emulation.  It does an admirable job but it's not as good as true analog controls.
All configuration is done within Steam's Big Picture mode.  There is currently no interface in the standard Steam program to configure the Steam Controller.  Running your game from Big Picture mode is the only way to get Steam Controller overlay graphics for things like using the track pad as a touch menu.
On rare occasions, Big Picture (Steam) will crash while you are playing your game.  The game still functions but the controller effectively is dead.  Hopefully when this happens you are playing a game that you can save your progress using your mouse and keyboard and then quit out, restart Steam and resume your game.
So if you have the means, get the Steam Controller.  It doesn't do
, but it does do a heck of a lot of things.  And it does them better than a standard XBox controller in my opinion.

The PC Xbox controller was a great controller until I began experiencing "Controller Drift"
Controller Drift happens while playing a video game and the camera begins to drift up and all you see is the sky. Or your charater travels in one direction when you are not touching the controller. This is due to issues in the thumb controllers.
Now there are many remedies out there to correct this issue.
except for dimantling the controller and I mean DISMANTLE.
So after dealing with 3 Xbox controllers with controller drift, I vowed no more.
First off, I must say this controller will take time to get use to. However, the longer you spend with it the better the experience will become.
What makes the Steam Controller unique is its dual touchpads. On top of making the controller look like a permanently surprised owl, its dual touch pads emulate using a mouse, but not as precise. At times, it actually works. Not so good in other cases.
I have learned the touchpads do not require a firm contact. It's a slight flick. Like swiping your cell phone screen to see the next post on Instagram. That same swipe will cause a very fast 380 in a FPS like DOOM or Deus Ex: MD.
Also platformer jumping games such as Shadow Complex or a Top-Down Shooter like Neon Chrome the Steam Controller does very well.
Strategy games such as Rimworld, Ashes Of Sigularity or Total War series are another story. The controller is capable of playing those type of games. But imo they will always be played with keyboard and mouse.
And by the way, no controller drift.
A mini buffet of examples, while using The Steam Controller, has been placed before you and my final comment is this....
Like it or not, the Steam Controller is the Next Generation. Learn it.
The choice is yours.

Review:
I've never played the PS2 version in my life, so this is my very first time playing Bully. When I found out about it, people said it's like GTA. Now I have to say: I really dislike GTA myself. But looking at the screenshots for the game, I was like, this doesn't look like GTA at all. I played it for an hour, and I was really into it, and when I threw a FireCracker at someone and got busted, I laugh so hard I couldn't breath and was in tears (No joke.)
This game has a very good plot. It takes place with a kid named "Jimmy Hopkins" who got a new stepdad, and is going to BullWorth Academy for being expelled by all of the schools he has been too. BullWorth has loads of bully, and it's Jimmy's job to stop the bullies by beating them up, doing some tasks, etc. The characters are well though out, some annoying, some likable, and some dislikable. You might like Jimmy the best.
Gameplay is a bit of a key masher, and using Shift as attack is just unconformable, even running around is just awkward, and aiming is a huge pain with a mouse considering how slow the sanity is. So having Controller Support is great. The Gameplay adds more things to use in combat, which is nice so that it doesn't get repetitive. Game has Missions as well, and every single Mission is different. You can even learn new moves from Gym or the Hobo Guy. Mini-games are great as well, and though out.
Graphics are kind of Meh, but hey, it's an old game. Bugs do happen though, and some of the Physics on character can sometimes be weird, even in Cutscenes  (Example: Some guy's leg twitching, characters go through some things, etc.) The soundtrack is great, it really puts you into the mood like when getting chased by a teacher/police-men, in fights, etc. Interacting with other people in the town gives the town life, so that it doesn't feel empty, and it's open world, so that's awesome too. If you get accomplish anything, it's very rewarding, and if you get busted or fail, it feels punishing.
This game is great with humor as well, and the game is great by itself, even it's beautiful FPS.
Overall:
+Gameplay
+Story
+More weapons when playing the game more
+FPS
+Mini-games
+Great characters
+Open World
+Humor is great
+Controller Support
+Awesome Soundtrack, really puts you into the mood.
+/- Graphics are Meh
-Poor, Awkward controls with M/Keyboard
-Weird Physics that happens sometimes.
-Bugs
You should get this game. If you have the money, get it.

Firstly, this game is not a Pay to Win. For more info, scroll down to the micro-transactions section.
Mechwarrior Online is a game that (despite my hours on it so far via Steam) I have played since its open beta and friends I play with have played it since closed beta. In reality, I have around 1000 hours (maybe more, maybe less) on the game before its launch on Steam.
This game has been a rollercoaster of ups and downs as well as a game that has seen huge changes. If you were to compare the open beta and my first match with the way the game is today, it is almost completely different.
If you are looking for an honest review from an experienced mechwarrior fan (fan of the original battletech board games and of the older mechwarrior games) then look no further.
------ GRAPHICS ------
9/10
The graphics for this game have always been on point, however at times this can cause PC problems if you do not have a decent setup. It is a graphically demanding game, make no mistake. The grahpics have seen huge improvements to not only how they look but their impact on the game.  The first wave of graphical overhauls saw outrage in the community due to the bugs and lag they caused (due to the high polygon count of the textures). This has been fixed for the most part but it is still demanding on the graphics side of things.
I would recommend a GTX 650 (or AMD equivalent) or above for this kind of game if good graphics are a must for you.
------ MOVEMENT/DISPLAY MECHANICS ------
8/10
The movement mechanics of this game are complex and different from most shooters. If you are not familiar with how to steer tanks and similar vehicles in other games, then it may be tricky to begin with. Mechs essentially work like tanks in this game in that your control the lower half of the mech with WASD and you control the upper half of your mech with your mouse. In terms of jumpjets (built in jetpack devices for some mechs, to allow them some extra movement options) are a keyboard feature. The mouse is simply for aiming with.
There are also two view modes in the game: 3rd and 1st person. However you will need to know that you will be easier to see in 3rd person from the enemy's perspective. Due to 3rd person being enabled by a drone that hovers just above your mech, the enemy can see this and locate you with more ease.
For both 1st and 3rd person, the crosshair is fluid and easily seen in every environment in the game.
TIP: You may want to disable arm locking, as this will lock your arm movement with your torso movement - rectricting your firing arc.
------ MECH BUILDING MECHANICS ------
10/10
The mech building mechanics of the game are like no other game I have played. For older fans of mechwarrior, this game replicates the older games (and the board games). For the newer fans, the cusomization can be confusing at first (especially with the UI) but with practice as well as the tutorials, you will get the hang of it.
In this game you are able to customize the following:
- Armour (for specific parts of your mech, i.e legs, arms, torso etc.)
- Weapon Systems (lasers, cannons, machine guns, rockets etc.)
- Engine Size (more powerful engines = faster mech) (XL engines are lighter however span across more of your mech, however they make you more vulnerable to being destroyed.)
- Heat Sinks (for cooling systems)
- Ammo Types
- ECM (radar cloaking device), BAP (probe for countering ECM)
- Jump Jets
- Camo patterns (paint, colours etc. - however cosmetics cost money)
And other equipment (too much to list everything)
There are also four main types of mech:
- Light Mech, main roles include Scouting, Locking Targets, Capturing Bases and support of heavier mechs. (really fast, really weak armour, low DPS)
- Medium Mechs, main roles include support of heavier mechs, targeting light mechs, supporting light mechs. (moderately fast, average armour, average DPS)
- Heavy Mechs, main roles include support of assault mechs, targeting medium mechs, dealing damage. (slow, above average armour, above average DPS)
- Assult Mechs, main roles include leading a front of mechs, absorbing damage, dealing damage, need to be supported. (very slow, heavy armour, high DPS)
There are two main categories of mech:
- Inner Sphere
- Clan Mechs
Inner sphere clan mechs tend to be more robust whereas clan mechs can be brittle in comparison (depending on the mech). However Clan mechs have more powerful weaponry compared to Inner sphere. That said, Clan mechs tend to be the more favoured of the two but I am an Inner Sphere, light mech pilot.
In terms of the mechs themselves, Inner sphere tend to have better light mechs and the clans tend to have better assult mechs. The heavies and mediums being around the same.
The best part of all this is that it is true to the lore.
------ MICROTRANSACTIONS ------
5/10
The microtransations are soemthing that have always been argued about since the game's launch. Most of the cosmetic features will require you to spend real money. To own a vast collection of mechs, you need mech bays - which cost money (however you get four free mech bays to start out). Some mechs can only be bought with real money, however these mechs do not give you any advantage in a fight - they just provide you with better bonuses (such as more in game money and more XP). You can also purchase mech packages, for a collection of new mechs that come with mech bays.
This game is NOT A PAY TO WIN.
If you decide to spend money on this FREE game, you will simply skip the grind of saving in game money to buy your own mechs. I have played well over 1000 hours before it went onto Steam and only spent money on a few more mech bays and one mech.
THERE IS NO DLC.
All the maps and extra content added to the game are not DLC packs, they are added to the core game. The mechs added to the game will always have varients you can buy with in game cash. Generally, new mechs are released and for the first few months you can only aquire them via real money. After these few months, in game money varients are released for you to buy.
------ ADVANCEMENT ------
7/10
The game's grinding system can be tedious after a while but is not as long as some other games I have played (such as RPG MMOs). The grind will not be really easy but it is not so bad that you cannot get anywhere - it just takes a little time. You can put money in to skip this grind but it usually does not take long to earn enough in game money for your first mech.
The only downside is the mech bays, as you only start with four.
------ SERVERS ------
8/10
The servers are generally quite good and do not suffer lag now as much as they did. They have dedicated servers in the EU, US and in Oceania. Meaning no matter where you are in the world, there will be a server with a decent latency for your to join. You can switch where you are playing via the main hub screen.
------ USER INTERFACE ------
6/10
The user interface is a part of the game that has seen massive changes. In my own opinion, the oldest UI and original UI was the best in terms of layout as it was not complex or confusing. However the new UI is more fluid, is nt as buggy as the older UI at the cost that it is more complex than the old UI.
If you are a new player, it can be confusing at first but not too bad to get the hang of. If you are a returning player, it will be like a different game.
------ MAPS/ENVIRONMENTS ------
In the beginning, the maps were few but the quality was high. As time went on more maps were added into the map pools and (you'll be pleased to know, they do not require additonal DLC). With the advancement in graphical technology in computing and gaming in general, the older maps have been reimagined and re-released with an even higher quality than before.
You'll find yourself fighting on desert planet mech scrapyyards to swampy, steamy bogs and on moon bases in outer space.

Before I purchased Halcyon, I noticed a common thread in several of the reviews, both positive and negative, that stated that the game had a lot of ‘grinding.’  Many games have grinding as a prominent feature, but the difference between the good and bad ones is always down to the mechanics and the gameplay loop.  RPGs in particular have lived and died by the nature of ‘the grind,’ but it takes an investment of time and effort to figure that out for yourself.  Even then, the perception can be different between each player.  With Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander, I felt that the comparisons used in many descriptions (XCOM, FTL, Final Fantasy) were appealing enough when combined with the premise that I should at least give it a shot, but I ultimately found out that that the grind quickly overcame those positives.
First, let me say that the beginning of the game wasn’t wholly unpleasant.  I found the combat acceptable and assumed that a variety of enemies and scenarios would follow over a moderate span of time to keep it fresh.  I also found the base building, resource and morale management, and the general aesthetic to all be very appealing.  XCOM was the first thing I thought of in clearing out the many building areas of the Halcyon station to build up the base.  Though it may have missed an opportunity not also adopting the group synergies that XCOM made use of… which forced the player to have more foresight and potentially invest more time and resources in to expanding in certain areas for later benefit.  It also benefitted from a reasonably well designed UI, some entertaining writing, and some spectacular effects in combat, especially when you compare it to the rest of the pixel art styling.
However, as the Day timer crept higher, I began to feel the drag of the grind.   Things start blurring together as you establish a core fleet with the skills and abilities you want.  A lack of diversity in enemies, even as they get stronger, means that you rarely have to change up anything you are doing to beat them.  The constant beating back of enemies that stop your resource flow gets tiring as you simply wait for enough resources to complete a task and then wait even longer for that task to complete.  Sometimes this is a product of a game like this being either too easy or too difficult, but I left the difficulty setting on the standard recommended setting described as “classic mode,” which seemed to offer a reasonable challenge for more than half the game.  Even in doing that, I also encountered huge peaks and valleys in difficulty where certain events seemingly required you to grind for better ships and crew while other times I’d blast through the presented conflicts with hardly a scratch.  That uneven difficulty level is something I’ve noticed in Indie games much more often than games that feature dedicated QA groups.
After around 17 hours I assumed I was reaching the end of the game.  I was about to encounter some major boss fleet and figured this was the final challenge.  After beating it, the game seemed to be heading toward an ending.  I was relieved and ready to give Halcyon a somewhat negative review, but one that forgave some of the grind as perhaps poor gameplay choices that lead to a longer-than-necessary session.  Yet I was met with an expanded map and a ton of the same gameplay to look forward to.  At that point I just threw my hands up and abandoned everything.  The combat was too shallow and repetitive both in ships and on the ground.  It immediately exposed every little nitpick I had.  Like the leveling system forcing you to choose between ground and ship skills when ship battles happen exponentially more while ground battles can still have you losing officers and progress, or having to spend a good portion of the game running around collect important resources before you  can invest in automating the procedure.   Even the asinine part where your main ability to improve crew morale requires you to expend you crew resource to prevent lowered morale from continuing to make you lose crew.  Things I could easily overlook in a 10 or 15 hour full run become glaring issues when illuminated by the friction-fueled glow of the *grind*.
Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is a great concept with some well-crafted portions of the game readily apparent.  However, a needlessly long grind makes it feel padded out and forces players to become uncomfortable with other relatively minor issues.  It may be ok in short spurts over weeks where you’re less aware of the slow progress, but outside of that I can’t give this game my recommendation.

tl;dr: Solid game, good story and humor, plenty of replay value with various difficulty levels. Highly Recommend. 8.5/10.
Are we allowed to say that this is like Star Trek without getting a cease and desist by CBS..? Halcyon 6 takes influences from the ST universe and parodies them in the best way. This makes the story very enjoyable, and I find myself chuckling more than I should at some of the jokes and gags. But then I'm a ST fan and as such, this appeals to me.
The gameplay is a bit of this and a bit of that. RPG elements, base building, tactical battles, resource management, dialog options (which can have zany twists). In some places I feel that there could be a bit more, in others, a bit less. Battles for example can be a bit repetitive. ex. Hit ship with hull breach status, then the next ship's hit exploits that status and adds crew panic status, then the next ship's hit exploits that status. Combos are great, but it's a bit too simple to be really strategic and a bit too complex to make the battles quick and enjoyable. My fix would be to either make it a bit more complex or simplify it so options are quicker. Either way, there desperately needs to be some organizing to the skills and some hotkeys added (if there are hotkeys, I've yet to stumble upon them). Basically 1 for main attack, 2 for attack all ability, 3 for heal/shield, 4 for special? idk, but clicking can be tedious... but then I'm also a lazy gamer.
The difficulty to the game is about right. There are numerous settings for easier or a way tougher game. So there's something here for everyone, from us filthy casuals to those rogue-like b0ner chasers. And events can roll in or out of your favor. It helps to have an officer with a trait that gives you a special option, often gifting you bonuses on passing the event. Major plot points seem to be the same through multiple play throughs, but that doesn't mean that the game is linear. You can basically do anything you want in your somewhat little area of space.
I would highly recommend this game to people who like good games, humor, space, and Star Trek. I would not recommend this to JJ Abrams. I don't think he would get the source material. Also there's no lens flare in the game. JJ Abrams would not like this game. 8.5/10.

I think there's a lot of potential with this game.  It's very basic by nature and those who, like me, spent hours upon hours playing Championship Manager 97/98 many years ago, will recognise the likeness and the 'nod' that this game gives to the old CM series. It's clear the game is in its infancy as there is indeed some improvements needed in certain areas like searching for players more easily (i.e you cannot filter player skills at the moment) and at least having some kind of basic scouting system too. Deus Ex: Human Revolution is such a bold and a brilliant game there is nothing but praise for this game. There is just nothing like it
The plot is very well written and story is told in such a brilliant non-linear fashion it is something that is to be admired. Not only are you searching for redemption but the sub-plots which focus on darker side of technology, what it means to be human, the guilt, reason, hunger for power, manipulation, humanity, conspiracy the game tells so many things which is just brilliant.
It's not just a game where cyberpunk genre is slapped, the events that happen are actually realistic and could happen in the future. Little details about how the technology is used and is implemented is very well done and clearly the developing team paid very close detail to the actual technology and how to implement it in a realistic fashion. Dialouges are great too.
Gameplay is very unique and excellently executed, variety of weapons, the way they are handled and used in different situations is excellent.
The way you choose to progress is bloody brilliant, you may choose the stealth approach or could go guns blazing, you could explore hidden paths and reach to your destination without going through so much trouble or you could simply do a combination of both. The game looks good, the art style is well done as it gives the dark distopian tone of the near future and enhances the atmosphere, the sounds are well done and the music which is all electronic just adds more to the vibe of the distopian future they wanted to create.
Overall, a splendid game staying true to the spirit of previous games in the franchise as well as doing something different, it pays homage to it's predecessors as well as intoduces new people into the franchise. A casual gamer will love it and so will the hardcore one. It is just utter brriliance and a well executed game.

If I could only use word to describe the Steam Controller, it would be "enabler". The Steam Controller enables laziness. Do not expect to play your best playing PC games on this product. Having said that, the steam controller fulfilled all my expectations for an enabler device.
The configurations seemed overewhelming at first glance but you shouldn't have any problems understanding them after 20 minutes of browsing the config menu. I recommend searching through existing config templates made available by the community to help you with thie process of understanding the full potential of the controller.
The design of the controller is rather comfortable. While not as wellfit for my hands as the Xbox controller, the steam controller nonetheless feels like a proper controller and comfortable to handle for extended periods of time. The right analog stick, replaced with the trackpad to mimic mouse input is very accurate for those interested in playing anything that requires slow precision and is an acceptable replacement for an analog. The haptic feedback on the trackpad + D-pad is a nice touch and definitely helped with mouse movements.
You are given a wireless/wired option. The controller requres 2 AA batteries (no surprise). Software installation barely took 10 seconds.
The controller previously required that you play games on Big Picture Mode but that is no longer the case. You are still however required to add all your non-steam games to the library and launch it via steam (right click the game to edit config). For those using Origins, add the Origin.exe as a non-steam game.
So far, I've managed to successfuly play the following games to some degrees of success:
Overwatch: You can easily play any of the less demanding heroes with little aiming and movement required such as Winston.
Warhammer Total War: Took me a while to grasp troop movements and had to pause several times mid-game for attack commands.
ESO/TES/Witcher 3: Works like a charm. No complaints.
WoW: Many will find this controversial but questing as a Ret/holy paladin with the controller was VERY comfortable (granted ret rotation is like 4 buttons). I would not try or risk playing with the controller beyond questing especially as a healer main.
Diablo 3: Takes a while to get used to but works wonderfully.
Overall I was very satisfied with my purchase despite my concerns and plan to use my controller for many years to come. Do not mistake this as a KB+M alternative because it's not. The only thing this will do is enable your laziness when you don't feel like using KB+M as it can be exhausting. If that's what you're looking for and you're willing to spend 5 minutes googling then there is no other product that can fill that role better than Steam Controller.

It takes less time to open big picture and exit big picture (which turns off the controller), then it takes to hold down the button on the Steam Controller to turn it off.
Otherwise it's pretty neat. 8/10

Shows potential.
The controls are not intuitive. With a console controller you can be fairly certain that certain buttons do certain things. For example, the "B" button would mean "jump," or "back" in the same way the space bar is usually jump on a keyboard. But the Steam Controller has none of this. Instead you are expected to fit all the controls of a keyboard into a tiny controller. This works fine with most games that can be run on console (Bethesda has a official, albeit clunky, controller configuration for Fallout 4 that runs okay). But all too often I'm trapped making franken-layouts for games that were never designed with consoles in mind. And each layout takes about an hour to make, entrailing playing the game with a keyboard for a while to get a "feel" for what you'll need and then mapping and tuning it for the controller. It is a minor but annoying enough time investment that usually ends up with controls that vary wildly from game-to-game, causing you to easily forget it after not playing that game for a while. Although you can download "community made" layouts, they're usually half-functional and confusing. If you want it done right, you have to do it yourself. This may not sound bad, but multiply this with even a modest library of 20+ games and strap yourself in for one of the tedious and painful experiences of your life.
Big Picture Mode is frustrating to use, and is required to run if you want to use your controller at all. Sometimes you can't edit the controller's bindings while certain games are running due to freezing/glitches, but some are fine. Unfortunately, odds of this happening are about 50/50 with most titles. That's right, you can't use the controller with any software unless you have Steam running and have added that program to your library. This makes things like Teamspeak 3 impossible to use, as multi-window controls are near impossible. In this aspect a USB controller is better than the steam controller.
The biggest failure of the Steam Controller is that it doesn't "just work," it needs hours of fiddling and customization per game, and at that point you're better off on a $20 keyboard or even a $30 USB controller than the crime against PC gaming that is the Steam Controller. Maybe once more games support it and I won't have to look at my bindings when a game tells me to "press enter" it will be worth it, but right now it's like handing someone a bunch of random auto parts and telling them they have a "fully customizable" car.

This is my first review, please be kind.
I picked up a Steam Controller along with my Deus Ex Mankind Divided because after all of this time, I decided it was finally time to try it out.  I've been a PC Mouse/Keyboard player most of my life, but for the last 5-10 years have been playing more with gamepads and some XBox One.  After hearing about it for a while I figured I should try this out.
The touchpad was hard to get used to it, it didn't "seem" precise, and that haptic feedback was driving me nuts.  It was only my stubborness (and having spent the cash) that I continued... so for those that gave up after a few minutes I suggest you continue reading.
Seriously, I love this thing way more than my XBone controller (my previous favorite).  In fact, I WISH it was compatible with my XBox One console so I could play my XBone FPS games using THIS... I know, I know that will never happen.  It is just great all around.
The touch-pad really is great and does offer much more precision than a thumb stick.  And while it won't ever be as precise as a normal laser mouse... it is darn good.  The haptic feedback makes it easier to guage just how much you're moving during those tense moments. The touchpad IS hard to get used to, and even after you're finally loving it there are some quirks but they mostly involve "learning" how to use it better.  For example, leaving your finger on the touchpad and tapping your foot might make the screen shake. And the acceleration (swiping your finger and leaving the pad) might confuse some people at first.
The offering of the extra paddles does make life easier, though 3rd party console controllers (and the MS Elite) use those as well.  It makes it much easier to hit that X/A combo (more on that later).
The construction seems solid enough: while it doesn't feel as indestructible as some of my other controllers it feels like a good quality.
I only have 2 complaints:
The X+A buttons are replicated with the extra toggles but Y+B are not and to be honest... it's a LITTLE awkward to hit them after you've been using the touch pad for a while.  Part of this could simply be because I'm used to the position of the buttons and the right-"stick" being switched on the XBone.

While playing Mankind Divided, you can use the D-Pad to trigger 1-of-4 "augs" (powers).  Unfortuantely I'd sometimes trigger both at the same time.  I eventually got used to clicking it JUST RIGHT so that wouldn't happen but it was still annoying.
Anyway, it's a great controller and I look forward to using it more.  I'll admit, it might not be for everyone and it probably does not do great with the old emulator games and such.  But for FPS, for those that just want to play casually and non-competitively... it's great.

Keep in mind that I have not played Galactic Civilizations, which I am told this game resembles in many ways.
Endless Space is a 4x Turn-based Strategy Game in outer space.  You can choose a variety of human or alien factions, all of which each have a single defining feature as well as more general benefits and penalties.  You also have the ability to create a faction using a point buy system.
If nothing else of the gameplay is mentioned, I want to make clear that this game is a limited experience.  That is to say, unit cannot move freely around a euclidian space, but are instead limited to vertices and edges, which represent star systems and connections between star systems respectively.  What this means is, you cannot explore of the 'beaten path' so-to-speak and there isn't anything that could be reasonably called 'terrain'.  This will be important to my review later.
The game itself is pretty stable and runs smoothly even on the largest scenarios, thanks to its minimalist graphics and the system of movement I described above.  The fleet battles are pretty, run smoothly and are generally satisfying to watch.  You are allowed to free the camera to look around the battle as it happens.  However, the actual battle itself is handled automatically, with the player being allowed to simply choose a 'card' to play during each of the three phases of battle, long, medium, and short range.  More advanced tactics are earned through the use of high-level heroes in your fleet or by advancing along the science portion of the research tree.
Speaking of which, the research tree is pretty cool - it's in the fourth screenshot on the Steam preview thing.  It has four different roots, each of which allow a fair bit of leeway in choosing what to research in what order.  Each portion of research is just as important as the others, so the balance is pretty good.  The AI is quite good at putting up a formidable offense and defense when necessary and they expand well.  The best part comes when I relate the ship design suite.
In Endless Space, you are given the tools necessary to design your own fleet ships.  Research allows you to unlock new spaceframes and a wider array of equipment options as time goes on.  The most interesting part is designing your weapons and defenses to take advantage of whatever your opponents are currently equipping.  Indeed, the AI also learns from your equipment and changes their offense and defense to compensate (though their comptency at this game differs depending on their difficulty level).  All-in-all, it makes for a fun bit of customization and the meta-game of figuring out your opponents' weaknesses adds an engaging layer of gameplay.
There's really not much else to mention.  Endless Space is a simple, but decent strategy game.  My biggest gripe with it, is that it kills for me, the most important and exciting experience of any space game: the ability to explore and discover exciting  places in space.  Sure, you have to go and find out what star systems are out there.  But your ships can only fly along these strict paths and ultimately, the game wouldn't be much different if you just slapped it down on a tabletop and said it was a board game.  Whereas, games like Galactic Civs 3 and Civilization offer you the chance to explore interesting lands and terrain, to find unique places out there that energize the imagination.
I'd recommend this game, because it is fun and has a nice bit of humor here and there as well, but I wouldn't buy it if it was only ever at full price.  Honestly, $29.99 is a big asking price for this game, especially since the Disharmony expansion makes the game much better and tacks on an additional $9.99.

Bully: Scholarship Edition is a game developed and published by Rockstar Games, the same people behind the Grand Theft Auto series, Max Payne series, Manhunt series, L.A. Noire and many other games. The Scholarship Edition is an improved version from the original Playstation 2 version of Bully including updated graphics and sound and exclusive missions only found on the Scholarship Edition of the game
Bully takes place in the ficitional school known as Bullworth Academy, an academy that helps troubled children. Many people speculate that this takes place in the same universe as the Grand Theft Auto series which I highly agree on. Jimmy Hopkins is a troubled child that has been kicked out of too many schools and his only choice is now to go to Bullworth Academy which seemingly fixes troubled children like Jimmy, however something is brewing underneath the hallowed halls of this academy and a revolution may take place in this once esteemed academy
As many previous Rockstar Games, the PC version for me personally is the weakest of the bunch, however before all that, a history lesson! I love Rockstar Games and their games (whenever they get ported onto the blasted PC and are good ports!) and I love the mature controversial aspect of the games. I've played Grand Theft Auto V, I've played the Max Payne series, I've played L.A. Noire, I've tried the Manhunt series and I so desperately want Red Dead Redemption on PC (YOU BETTER PORT IT ONTO THE PC ALONG WITH ITS SEQUEL!)
So when I discovered Bully: Scholarship Edition on my friend's Nintendo Wii, I so desperately wanted a copy, originally wanting it on the Wii I moved onto the PC and now I can say that I own Bully: Scholarship Edition on the PC
The game works as a regular school/academy would work. You wake up, you go and do lessons such as English, Geography and Biology then you have enough free time to do the story missions (or extra missions however they are not forced upon you), after a select number of missions, you go onto the next chapter which usually also changes the season and opens up new parts of the school and even later on the town where Bullworth Academy is also opens up for you to explore
The missions are okay nothing special and the class too are nothing special, some are fun such as the Biology class, although you need a strong stomach to disect all the poor animals and some are really annoying such as the English and Geography class
The graphics are okay and have aged pretty well for a 2006 game and the lip syncing is some of the best I have seen from a 2006 game of the time. The music is good and I am happy that the soundtrack comes for free with the purchase of the game as I enjoy listening to them once in a while
The only issue I have is the PC port. The game is locked to 30FPS, why? You can easily unlock the game's framerate and leave it running at 60FPS with a modified version of the game, however, the game crashed so many times and I had to repeat the missions time and time again because obviously there is no autosaving, you literally have to go and find a save point and save your game manually, if your game crashes, you will have to start all the way from your last save, which can be quite a way away
Also playing the game at 30FPS made the game crash countless times and I couldn't understand as the game run perfectly fine then all of a sudden, it just crashes which made me mad as hell and not want to continue and for the length the game is I had to struggle and save often in case of a crash. Be wary especially on Windows 10!
I don't know how many times I had to tweak the controls to make them at least playable, you can easily tell that this was lazily ported from the console version, as the default controls are annoying and awkward
However, if you enjoy Rockstar Games or enjoyed the original Bully and want to play an updated version, then Bully: Scholarship Edition is the game for you, just be careful of the countless crashes!

One of Rockstar's golden gems that, sadly, has seemed to fall through the cracks.
While not as grand in scope as Grand Theft Auto or Red Dead Redemption, Bully was certainly as detailed for its time, and the PC version omits none of the finer touches. Although the interface is subpar, it is easily dealt with, and a minor hindrance at best. The combat, so to speak, is somewhat of a middle ground between Rockstar's earlier work, such as Vice City and San Andreas, and its latter work, namely Grand Theft Auto IV; while serviceable, it's not very inventive in its mechanics, per se, but rather with the imaginative weapons it puts at your disposal. Bags of marbles and stink bombs are more memorable than, say, an assault rifle and a shotgun, if purely for the novelty of their use.
To a large extent, that philosophy explains the charm of this game. While not rare for any media to take a satirical look on American schooling, Rockstar pulls it off in such a way that the plot, although unsurprising, is laced with charm. It's unique to watch a frankly idiotic protagonist emerge as a flawed hero through less-than-cliche means, and mostly for his own benefit, instead of some altruistic need to help his schoolmates. As always, the writing is truly where Rockstar shines.
I wish this game had gotten a sequel, but, as we pass the ten year anniversary of its release, that looks less and less likely. As such, Bully will have to stand on its own as a memorable critique of the farce that is the American education system.

Trap House
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Trap House is an 8-bit looking escape a house of traps and zombies type of game. I love the fact that you can make a character and that it allows LOCAL multiplayer but the game desperately needs online play. Another Great thing it has is a Level editor, this makes the game next to endless. The game has upbeat dubstep beats and a few other vintage gaming style instrumentals that arent bad. The Idea of this game was good, escape as best as you can avoiding traps, sounds fun. The game also has other game modes such as Last man standing, Murderball and Dodgesawl adding to more hours of fun.
The game has dark creepy overtones that work very well for it too.
I would say some of the menus and the way it takes forever to load the next round or restart are a downfall.
I can't stress enough how much this game needs online play.
Final Thoughts:
Overall the game is fun, I did enjoy playing it,  But due to the limitations on no online play, I see it hard for someone to pay $15 for it, If this had online play easily worth it. Without it worth maybe $10.
But Still a good game, would be 10 times better with online play.

Ok, let's just check this out quick...
*4 HOURS LATER*
Wow, where did the time go? It's late, I should be getting to bed. Ok, let's just check out one more thing quick...

Fantasitc orignal art - the backdrops are stunning for pixel art. A multitude of badass attack combinations to be strung together. And a surpisingly long and deep campaign with tons of unique events and dialog. Protecting 4 other alien races from constant raids can get annoying late game, but ultimately it doesn't make a difference if you do or don't and doesn't effect the story.
I kickstarted this game long ago, and it has changed a lot since the oringinal release. I just played through it again on a much higher difficulty, and there are a ton of new mechanics that the developers have done a great job on. Differences in enemy resistances and system modifiers makes it so you can't just use the same old attacks on different enemies, especially on higher difficulties - a welcome change from the oringal release. I remember how barren my station used to feel before the addition of many new rooms. The new mechanic of station repair and upgrades is fantastic. The satellite shuttle resource retreivement system, as well as the ability to rebuild lost resource outposts in your space, are also welcome changes. The list goes on and on.
If you enjoy FTL, and/or games with a well fleshed and balanced upgrade system, you will absoultely enjoy this game. I'd say it is worth $20 for the length, but if you can pick it up on sale for $10, even better.
Also, f*** Fluidic Clouds.

=== The Good ===
The gameplay is great: from turn based strategy, resource management, base building, to a minimal form of RPG where you name your fleet, ships, and officers - that alone deserves a recommendation.
As for the grind, I'm okay with it. It can get tedious at times, but that can be just part of the resource management.
=== The Bad ===
Music and SFX were.. weird. They were not bad or anything, just not good either. I guess it's hard to live up to the bar set by FTL.
What bugged me the most was the combat animation. Life was simply better after turning them off in the options menu. I really wish the projectiles are still shown somehow, just without the stupid ships shifting around. The only abilities I liked with combat animation that shifted the ships around were the ships Ramming into enemies, the rest are not something to write home to.
=== Suggestions ===
Maybe separate the combat animation from the ability projectiles just so they don't disappear even when combat animation is turned off.
At the same time, I hope there will be feature to left click through the combat animation to speed it up, as I really want to see the animation sometimes but not the whole thing.
I also kind of wish the game would allow some form of saving a preset of ship abilities, since different systems with different debuff resistances call for a different set of abilities.
=== Conclusion ===
Aesthetic-wise, the game is charming with its pixel art style and gory deaths. The animated characters are a nostalgic scratch on console Final Fantasy games and Day of the Tentacles style of pixel art.
The things that were let downs were the combat animations and the music/SFX for me.
Overall, it is a game I would still recommend because of its in-depth gameplay and great $$/hr ratio.
