TL;DR:
This is an *excellent* game that I highly recommend - but the presence of a few bugs dents its otherwise gleaming presentation.  They are hardly dealbreakers and shouldn't stop you from giving this game a shot - but you should know about them before you dive in so you won't get surprised or disappointed.  Pick it up on sale and enjoy many hours of stylized clandestine cyberpunk fun.  I think you'll be glad you did.
PSA WARNING:  Do not install the laser sight on the silenced sniper rifle!  You'll have a bad time.
Details:
While I DO highly recommend this game, I can only really recommend it on sale - as it has a few fairly annoying little bugs.  The game itself is worth full price - but given that the game has run its course in terms of sales and given those bugs never saw a final patch, you'll get more satisfaction picking this one up at a discount.  This Director's Cut version is made from an older, unpatched version of the game (apparently the orignal source code was lost - ouch) and while it improves some graphics like textures and tesselation, adds a couple (really cool) weapons, and improves the boss fights, it leaves out some pretty important fixes - and NO - they will never be patched.  These bugs are by no means dealbreakers for me, but they are enough that I still wish they would have just patched them.  Let's talk about the two that bug me the most:
Stutter:  Any modern rig should be able to run this game smooth as butter all day, but many users including myself experience some pretty annoying lag / jitter /stutter.  Nvidia users seem to be able to fix this with a regedit tweak (multiple guides here on steam about that) - but most AMD users like myself seem out of luck here.  I've seen a few that have managed to solve the issue, but so far none of the fixes have solved the stuttering for me and my R9 280 3gb.  It isn't terrible - the game is totally playable - but a game this old just shouldn't have it.  (The game runs pretty consistently at 60 fps, but every couple seconds there are often micro-stutters / jitters in the flow of time that can be a little distracting.  It's minor, but noticable enough to irk me at times.)  The older (non directors cut) version patched this out - but for some reason, no patch ever came along for what is now the only version available on Steam.
Sniper Rifle Aiming Bug:  Find that super awesome silenced sniper rifle?  Read the item description that says a laser sight dramatically improves accuracy?  NOPE!  Installing the laser sight will essentially break the weapon - and you can't take it off.  (Luckily, there are a few opportunities to pick up another if you mess up your first one like I did.)  It offsets the scoped aiming reticule - the bullet will hit somewhere below the crosshair.  I have found no fix for this.  There's a warning about this on the Wiki, but I don't think most players will think to check there first.
There's also a small bug with the revolver in that the ironsights aren't aligned quite right - but in this case, a laser sight is actually very helpful: having the red dot negates the need for ironsights, and makes the weapon accurate from the hip.  Fully upgraded, it's a supremely fun weapon for causing chaos.  (EXPLODING BULLETS - AW YEA)  Shooty-boom-boom.
Okay.  Ranting aside, this is a *fantastic* game that I have thoroughly enjoyed - and even with the one broken weapon and the fairly annoying stutter, I completely recommend playing through it - especially if you're the type of player that likes to investigate the details.  Taking the time to find / read everything really fleshes out the exeprience, and makes for a satisfyingly meaty game experience.  All the little emails, pda's, etc. really flesh-out the world they've created here, and it's fascinating.  The game was much longer, and with much more content than I expected from a 2010's first person game - and that was a refreshing surprise.  The gunplay is competent enough, and the weapons are super cool.  Most of those are upgradable in multiple ways - just like the original Deus Ex.  While dated nowadays, the graphics are good enough - certainly lightyears ahead of the orignal - and I really dig the art style.  The moody main character is a little angsty at times, but that's part of who he is.  Some games let you make your own character - but in this one, you step into the shoes of a person with a particular past who has been affected by it in a particular way - but you get to chose what happens from here.
The game allows for a varied approach to almost any situation, and provides multiple paths to get there - allowing the player to take advantage of various skills or upgrades.  You can hack, sneak, cloak, move through the sewers or across the rooftops - or just waltz right in the front door with machine guns and rocket launchers blazing.  Bosses aside, you can even go through the whole game without killing a soul (and get a hefty xp bonus in the process).
There are four possible endings - don't worry no spoilers here - and you essentially get to chose which one right at the end.  None of them are particularly awesome in their own right - pretty typical these days - but the game itself is so good, I ain't even mad.  (In my personal opinion, only one of the four sits well with me - but I guess that's the point of chosing!)  Now - I will say - this is one of those times where it's worth it to sit through the credits.  What would have been a slightly disappointing conclusion turns into one that sets up the next game (chronologically) and left me hyped for Deus Ex in general - and really tied the whole thing together - at least for me.
Personally, I think replay value is excellent - I just beat the game, and I'm jumping right back into New Game + on hard mode - and so far, am loving it even more the second time through.  (It's amazing what a lack of magical crosshair in the middle of the screen does for immersion.)  The variety of weapons and approaches the game offers really keeps things interesting.  While the endings themselves are multiple-choice at the end, there are various times in the game where choice / performance / path taken has an effect on the future - story and gameplay - which makes me want to go through again and try things different ways.  Lots of fun to be had here.
The people who made this game did so with a lot of passion, and it shows.  It's just a real shame that Eidos somehow lost the original source code leading to this slightly crippled final version of the game.  The Director's Cut does an otherwise great job of integrating the DLC content in a cohesive way, and I actually prefer the way it is integrated here vs having the orignal game plus the DLC.
All in all, this has become one of my favorites - flaws and all.

Pros:
-Gameplay:
The game allows you with its stealth and shooters mechanics a great varierty to deal with your missions.
Stealth and combat are equaly fun but stealth is a lot more time consuming but also way more tense.
-Leveling up, Missions and augmentations:
No matter what augs you choose it greatly changes your gameplay and the game gives you for every mission more than one way to complete it. According to your augmentations you will have to find the best solution.
Sometimes there are more answers to a problem than meets the eye. But not like many other games Deus Ex:HR doesn't present the answers to you on a silver platter. You have to think and explore and therefore the devs take the gamer seriously. A very well made addition to the game.
-Dialoge:
Deus Ex:HR is to date the best example on how you do the "Mass Effect" Conversation right. It doesn't just give you a overview of your dialoge choices. You are allowed to know the whole sentence in advance. You also have to think carefully about your next choice if you want to presuade someone.
-There are no stupid and boring "fetchquests" and busy work. Only quality missions.
Things that are okay:
-The Graphics:
Graphics are not that important to me, but the game looks fine. The lipsyncing and facial expressions could have used some additional work though
-Even though the game themes are interesting and engaging the storytelling falls short on some occasions. It is very focused on the main plot and doesn't allow you to experience the world and the setting of Deus Ex to much. It tells you things but rarely shows them. Therefore:
-The atmosphere is decent not great. The style of the graphics managed to capture a great Blader Runner like feeling but because you don't experience much of the lore firsthand it is sadly not as awesome as it could have been.
Cons:
-The Cutscences:
The cutscences per se are decent but the transition between the cinematics and gameplay is ridicolous. Almost all cutscences are dark with a specific kind of lighting and atmosphere. The scence ends and you feel like you are in a complety different world even though you are standing on the same spot. This does a lot to hurt the games atmosphere and consistency.
-It is missing something that brings a welcome chance to the gameplay. Maybe throw in a chase or a riddle/puzzle kind of quest?
-It is not a RPG.
It is a FPS/Stealth Game with RPG mechanics. Which is nothing bad but don't advertise it as a rpg. (This point doesn't affect my final rating)

Alright, I've owned it for two months now, tested it on nearly my whole Steam library; I think it's time to write a review for this.
I'll admit, when I got it, I felt a bit dumbfounded. I unplugged my trusty Xbox 360 Wired Gamepad and plugged the Steam Controller in it's place and seeing it on my tower, next to my mouse, keyboard and monitor, it just stood out so much. It looked like what all my friends and nearly the whole PC community have been calling it: a novelty item. A gimmick. A little publicity stunt from Valve so that they could make a litte bit more cash. But while the Steam Controller - at first - looks to be a novelty item in fashion, in function, I came to find that it's much much more.
First off, I should stress that the Steam Controller is the very antithesis of plug-and-play. It's number of customization options can literally reach into the thousands and no configuration is the end-all-be-all way to play for any game. It's all up to you. Will you simply use the Valve-provided generic templates for keyboard or gamepad control? Will you scourge through the Community-made configurations for your favorite game? Or will you go solo and make your own configuration for each game you own? I don't know, and maybe while you're contemplating one of these as your likely option, it's completely possible that if you do pick it up, none of them will be your option, you may go a completely different route with the controller, it's infinitely versatile! Either way, it's going to take patience, practice and a little trial-and-error to achieve your perfect configuration for any game, this isn't something for the casual consumer to pick up, this is for the handy consumer, the type of consumer that doesn't mind a little extra elbow-grease to get what they want. Experimentation is key with the Steam Controller. I could sit here and tell you what I did to get to where I am now, but that would be useless as I implied earlier, it's different for everyone. It's better that you discover these things on your own. Now don't think that using the Steam Controller to your liking is a grand task like I'm probably making it out to be. In practice, it really isn't. The UI for the Steam Controller is integrated into the Steam Overlay and is very simple to use. What's the most taxing about it is again, time. Time is what you need to sacrifice for the Steam Controller, and if you do, you'll be opening the door up to thousands of possibilities.
The Steam Controller is virtually compatible with any game. Even games that are not natively on Steam should you add them to your library. And while one could say the same thing for an Xbox or PS4 controller, there is one huge advantage (out of the 1000s) that the Steam Controller has. It can bind to keyboard controls. This basically makes any game even if it's not compatible with Direct or Xinput compatible with a controller, and that alone combined with the interchangable controls makes it definitive for PC gaming.
You know, writing this review is hard. I don't even know if this can count as a review. Maybe more a forewarning for beginners. If you were looking for a review that listed all that the Steam Controller is capable of, then I'm sorry I couldn't deliver because it's my belief that properly reviewing the Steam Controller is simply impossible to do. There's too much to say, so much to test out and do. It would take at least 100 pages or so to put it all into words. Adding to the fact is just how differently people could react to it. For me, it has basically replaced my keyboard and mouse for gaming at this point. I didn't even think it could do that, I just bought it to have a more versatile gamepad. But the Steam Controller took the extra mile with me, and was able to trump the oh so hailed way of playing computer games. Of course, I'm not a competitive player, and I'm sure a mouse would definitely beat the trackpad at a match of Counter-Strike no matter what you configured. But for the sake of conveinence, versatility, and the ability to finally sit in my chair without slouching, I can safely say that the Steam Controller is the best controller that I have ever used in my life.

"Dear Esther" is like a beautifully illustrated poem.

Important to understand: This is not a traditional video game that aims to provide a playful gameplay experience (eg. Call of Duty, Super Meat Boy, Witcher). However, while Dear Esther is experienced through the same medium containing similar and traditional game design choices (controls, movement, guided path etc.), this "game" deviates from the conventions by it being effectively just a story for the player to progress.
This does not mean that it doesn't use the video game medium to its advantage. In fact, the story becomes stronger through the immersion and the player's interactivity with the narrative. Dear Esther is a thoughtful and moving experience.
Pros: story, narrative progression and player agency, level design, audio- and visual design of the game, music
Potential cons: short (2 hours), not a game, not being able to jump can break immersion at times
Con: Achievements (not suited for this game)

Pros:
-Gameplay:
The game allows you with its stealth and shooters mechanics a great varierty to deal with your missions.
Stealth and combat are equaly fun but stealth is a lot more time consuming but also way more tense.
-Leveling up, Missions and augmentations:
No matter what augs you choose it greatly changes your gameplay and the game gives you for every mission more than one way to complete it. According to your augmentations you will have to find the best solution.
Sometimes there are more answers to a problem than meets the eye. But not like many other games Deus Ex:HR doesn't present the answers to you on a silver platter. You have to think and explore and therefore the devs take the gamer seriously. A very well made addition to the game.
-Dialoge:
Deus Ex:HR is to date the best example on how you do the "Mass Effect" Conversation right. It doesn't just give you a overview of your dialoge choices. You are allowed to know the whole sentence in advance. You also have to think carefully about your next choice if you want to presuade someone.
-There are no stupid and boring "fetchquests" and busy work. Only quality missions.
Things that are okay:
-The Graphics:
Graphics are not that important to me, but the game looks fine. The lipsyncing and facial expressions could have used some additional work though
-Even though the game themes are interesting and engaging the storytelling falls short on some occasions. It is very focused on the main plot and doesn't allow you to experience the world and the setting of Deus Ex to much. It tells you things but rarely shows them. Therefore:
-The atmosphere is decent not great. The style of the graphics managed to capture a great Blader Runner like feeling but because you don't experience much of the lore firsthand it is sadly not as awesome as it could have been.
Cons:
-The Cutscences:
The cutscences per se are decent but the transition between the cinematics and gameplay is ridicolous. Almost all cutscences are dark with a specific kind of lighting and atmosphere. The scence ends and you feel like you are in a complety different world even though you are standing on the same spot. This does a lot to hurt the games atmosphere and consistency.
-It is missing something that brings a welcome chance to the gameplay. Maybe throw in a chase or a riddle/puzzle kind of quest?
-It is not a RPG.
It is a FPS/Stealth Game with RPG mechanics. Which is nothing bad but don't advertise it as a rpg. (This point doesn't affect my final rating)
Score: 8/10

I'm not going to discuss the entire lengthy history of Mechwarrior Online it's highs and lows it's troubles and the lot. If you want that I'm sure there is a review that will or a google search. I am going to talk about the game as it is today, the 25th of December 2015.
This is a solid title faithful to Battletech/Mechwarrior franchise. There is a learning curve, some may find it steep but the first time you take down an enemy battlemech is a wonderful feeling and well worth the effort involved to get good at the game. Mech balance is overall fairly good with 30 ton light mechs able to compete against 100 ton Assaults. Weapons are actually pretty balanced and while balance is ongoing for such things the majority of mechs in the game are viable and actively used.
The F2P model is expensive but not required to have an acceptable fun time. It does speed things along but no more so then any other game title offering a "premium time" earnings. You are however limited to 4 mechbays, while more can be earned with frequent events and Community Warfare you may eventually find yourself doing the math and paying 1.50$ for a mechbay.
My biggest complaint would be Community Warfare not being in an acceptable state. The game mode is supposed to be the idea of factions facing off for galactic conquest but the way the matches play out doesn't capture that feeling at all at the moment.
Mostly you'll be hitting quick join and playing in one of the three game modes with several maps. It's fun and enjoyable if you like a sim like game vs other players.
In the end I'd suggest you try it if you have any interest at all in giant robots. It's free, the new player experience is pretty good and you can rapidly find yourself having fun if you are at all a fan of vertical tanks.

Overall, the idea behind this game is a good one, and the setting is a lot of fun. ES takes a lot of the things I love about other titles, like Master of Orion 2 and Sins of a Solar Empire, and combines them into a pretty decent 4x game. However, the game can be buggy at times, the races and techs are unbalanced, and the AI is horrible.
Computer players seems fun and interesting, at first, with a variety of reactions to your proposals and to the way you build your empire, but in the end, it's almost always the same: The other races start declaring war on you, one after the other, often seemingly out of nowhere; this is simply because (among the many factors that can influence AI attitudes)...you're doing well. Winning makes everyone hate you, apparently. Expand too much? War. Expand too quickly? War. Get too far ahead in science? War. Monopoly on valuable resources? War. Build too many ships? War. Make friends with too many other races? War. Score gets too high? War. That means, in the end, because war is pretty much inevitable, the only rewarding or realistic way to win is by determined conquest. There's a diplomacy, scientific, expansion, "supremacy," and even an economic victory option, but they're all a pain to attempt when you're constantly at war and having to account for that.
Endless Space is pretty; it's creative in a lot of ways; and it manages to hold my interest when I'm playing with humans, who are less predictable and a lot more entertaining. Overall, I recommend the game, but as a multiplayer experience: Skip the single player and don't bother with AI opponents if you want the most for your money, unless you like playing the same wargame over and over and over. Until the developer improves the AI and does some rebalancing, I can't in good consicence  really say anything positive about the single-player experience.

I played the Landmark edition, quit after reaching the third chapter.  There are two reasons I quit:
1) I have no clue what this game is trying to tell me.  The story doesn't make any sense, and there aren't enough pieces of story present to be worthwhile. Mesmerizing, beautiful, captivating
Dear Esther: Landmark Edition is a walking simulator through and through. The game is one of the progenitors of the genre that has seen many entries over the years. Dear Esther starts you off at island which you are free to explore by walking around. There are no quests, no enemies, and most of all, no running. The game is all about living in the moment while taking in the breathtaking sights and sounds of the island in all its glory.
Presentation is phenomenal all-around. Dilapitated houses, shore fronts, illuminated caves, perilous cliffsides, and watery caves all look great. Reaching and investigating such places yields commentary from the game's cryptic narrator whose garbled mumblings become more distorted as the game progresses. The player's movement is at times accompanied by musical scores which encapsulate longing, sadness, and melancholia. The end product is a beatiful and rapturous experience which is well-worth the asking price.
The game can be finished in about an hour, depending on the scope of exploration and sightseeing that you do. There hidden urns that you can look for and extra dialogue from the narrator for those who wander all over the island. Additionally, there is a director commentary option included in the options menu.
Dear Esther: Landmark Edition is nice little respite from your typical video game. It is a great experience for those who are willing to take in the slowburn gameplay. Here the journey, not the destination, is what truly matters.
Pros:
+ Hauntingly beautiful in its presentation in every sense
+ Suitable length
Cons:
- Not much replay value

Not much to say about the gameplay, as the entire game has you walking around an island as the narrator explains the events that lead to the ending. However, the melancholic music and bleak visuals keep you pushing forward, if you're into atmospheric games. Great little story. Definitely pick it up when it goes on sale.

The graphics are nice, but far from spectacular. The story - uh, what story? I suppose it's good if you are looking for mindless entertainment, but have low expectations if you do plan on playing this.

OK, first let me establish that I am in no way criticiszing the merits of the genre that has become vaugely pejoratively known as walking simulators.  I enjoyed Tacoma, Edith Finch, The Stanley Parable, Gone Home all. But this, this just doesn't do it for me.
Where the experience falls apart for me is not the aesthetics of the graphics and sound design (excellent, barring a few z-fighting issues on some of the graffiti), or the quality of the voice acting (great) or even the lack of a run button, but in the telling of the story.
This story is extremely abstract, but it is told in a heavyhanded and dense way.  The game throws whole paragraphs of voice acting at you at once.  Every once in a while doling out a line that sheds a slight amount of light on the non-abstract story but absolutely drowning it in overwrought metaphors.  Many of these paragraphs feel like pure self-indulgent fluff with nary a point to be found.
Not enough is done to flesh out the world.  The few setpieces tied to things the narrator says are the only narrative links between what is being said to the gamespace.  Without those few pieces, it may as well be an audiobook of a poem.  If there was more physical story content in the gamespace, this experience would be a lot more palatable to me.  All the structures are dull and lifeless containing next to nothing, no stories to tell, no secrets to be found.  The only color of the world is from the graffiti.  Physical storytelling by graffiti and a few odd scenes is not enough.

A beginner's review of Mech Warrior Online ---3.5 hours at the time of this review---
Common Mistakes
Hawken = Completely different game
Mech Warrior Online = Completely different game
Honestly there is no comparison between the two. You cant compare them other than it has mechs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Review
Mechwarrior online has long matches, but you have to have strategy and teamwork.
Hawken has short matches and the only way you can win is getting in a group and going around shooting enemy mechs.
Anyway the review, you can see my hours which isn't very much, but with all I know so far there is A: Steep Learning Curve (I haven't learned much because I'm busy so you may learn faster.) B: Slow starting matches that slowly go up in pace C: A load of mechs, it's a blast to try them all with different types of mechs |Light (Scouts)| |Medium mechs| |Heavy mechs| and |Assault mechs| you can equip them with all types of weapons like missiles, laser beams, gauss (Heavy kinetic weaponry etc.)
So far, that is all I have learned.
So that is a beginners review of Mech Warrior Online. So far rating it, would be a 9 out of 10.
No bugs so far, good optimization (although I have a GTX 960 so it varies)
So far so good. :D
Edit: ---10 hours played---
There are also skill trees for mechs as in you buy a mech, you play with it for some time then you use the xp gained for that mech to upgrade say movement speed, fire rate, etc. Which I think is good.

I bought this controller with a Steam Link and as a primary means of interfacing with the Steam Link device it is probably an essential device. However, as a game control device it does tend to feel somewhat less than ideal.
As a fan of the PS3 style game pads, the Steam Controller does fit my preferences better than an XboX controller which has the left stick in the wrong position IMO. However, while the Steam controller does not suffer from the XboX controller layout issues the right hand touch pad does take some getting used to and can feel too sensitive for head/look control using the default settings in games such as The Witcher 3.
If I could leave a neutral recommendation I probably would in terms of the use case as a generic Game Controller. However, in the use case of the Steam Link device I believe it is an essential thus I leave this review with an overall recommendation of yes.

This is a "tetris style" game where the blocks fall in different colours. After a few blocks you will get a block that gives you a choice of making that block a gem that will break all the blocks of that colour that are touching. Sounds simple enough and it is and often a simple concept makes for an addictive compelling game (like Tetris/bean machine, puyo pop, etc.).
The game has a zodiac theme and a small star mascot that narrates the story and shows you the game mechanics. personally I found the star and the sound it makes annoying as all hell. The "story" is forgettable and the enemies being star constellations isn't very engaging. There are no power-ups with the exception of a  "break all blocks of that colour" warp gem.
There is some fun to be had here if you really like this sort of game, which I do but this was just not fun or engaging. It seemed like luck if you got the opportunity to change a block into a gem and the game often just didn't give you the gem you needed on higher difficulties. This wasn't because you didn't place blocks right it was just you are never given the chance to break them. Which made losing feel like you were cheated rather than beaten.
Also every time you play you start from scratch. There is no save and as far as I can tell you beat the 12 zodiac signs then go around again at higher difficulty, then again, then again until the game cheats you to death.
I am not sure how they could fix this game, the main problem is with the mechanic which is the game itself. There are plenty of falling block games out there and most are better than this one. I cannot recommend I am afraid. And someone needs to kill that star (or shoot the mascot designer. Looks like one of those Milky way chocolate stars. Must have taken all of 5 seconds to draw/design. Very poor indeed).

I have to say if you enjoy sci-fi strategy games, you may like this. I've played a lot of FTL and XCOM so it fits into that bucket of game types. I enjoyed the dialog you can have with the multiple races, you really feel as if your the captain getting to make the call as to how you would respond. It doesn't really change the outcome of your diplomacy with the factions, but it was fun to feel like your a star base captain making choices. When you start you are meeting all the races, developing ships and tech to stay ahead of your enemies, and collecting resources. At the lower difficulty things are pretty manageable and its a lot of waiting for the next big event, there are ways to speed up those encounters, but I was trying to max out training on the officers that did not get used as much during the game. The final boss was hectic and even had me worried I might not make it. There is supposed to be a deeper tactical game under the hood but at the lower difficulty it is not as prevalent.
Pros:
Fun(ny) Story
Unique turn-based combat with lots of options for ships load outs
Comments(Cons sorta):
Very micro-manager in the early game with resources, but tech helps you automate much of it with planning.
End Game slows combat waiting for the bosses, but picks up the pace at the final boss phase.
I understand some of the negative reviews, that it is not as deep as many other sci-fi games, but the charm is its ability to still hold many players attention for dozens of hours and come away with an experience and a fun story of that game you played. Maybe you will find it grindy later on, but for smaller games like this I try to find that fun experience you can have and just enjoy the game for what it is. I hope this is helpful to someone that may be on the fence.

I was excited when I first heard about this game and even more excited after reading some really positive reviews, but ultimately I was left disappointed and unsatisfied.
The game itself is a walking simulator, where you as the main character are exploring a mysterious island. Why you are doing this is not clear off the bat. It has extremely limited controls, you can simply direct your character around a map with typical AWSD key functions and the mouse for view control, but other than that there is no jumping or any or movement functions. I had no problem with this, I just want to make it clear before anyone buys this game expecting more than simple movement functions that when it says this is a walking simulator it means it. This also means that the game should be heavily reliant on other features, such as the graphics and the storyline.
The graphics were the best part of the game, maybe tied with the musical score. It was simply breathtaking, with so much detail to take in. While outdoor detail was lovely and the sunset over the sea very calming, my personal favorite visuals all came from the cave later in the game (I don't consider this a spoiler because you see snippets of this in the trailer). Even with these breathtaking views, I found myself getting bored and accustomed to the scene around me. It stayed the same at any given point for way too long. You are essentially walking waiting for another note from presumably the person you are playing. These notes are few and far inbetween until the last chapter. I wish I had the option to run faster and cut out some of the monotony of the game. I tried exploring for a while and taking offshoots from the main path, but never came up upon anything super intriguing.
I typically like a lot of games like this for the combination of the ambience and the storyline. The ambience was there, but it got boring after nothing seemed to happen for a while. Like I said, you are just walking waiting for new notes from some unknown source that you eventually realize is the character you are playing. They don't really happen that often, and sometimes it's not clear what the note is related to at the current moment while other times it was tied to something you come across in your surroundings. I felt like I wasn't getting any kind of a grasp on the story until halfway through the third chapter. It just didn't make a lot of sense. I had so many questions that ended up never getting answered, and if I missed something in the narrative there was no way to go back and reread/listen to what was said at the time, making it especially hard to follow. A love story was kind of tied in near the end, and that really tugged on my heartstrings, but mainly due to the spectacular musical score.
The musical score may have been my favorite part of the whole game. It helped direct the narrative and your movement throughout the game. At times where I was struggling to understand what was going on, the music queued me in the the emotions I should be feeling and really pulled those out of me. I'm a sucker for an emotionally salient musical score.
I thought the ending was kind of anticlimactic, but that's just me. I'm sure some people loved it. I didn't even realize I had finished the game until probably the last minute of playtime. I knew I was getting somewhere, but it felt like there was more of a story to tell. And like I said, I still have a lot of unanswered questions that I am now going to Google to give me some semblance of closure.
Overall I would give this game a 6/10. It's alright. It has some things going for it, and to my understanding it spearheaded the movement of similar games, which is something to be commended. But for me, the storyline simply wasn't there and needed to be stronger. That is my main complaint. If you just want a beautiful landscape to wander around, this is the game for you. If you want an in depth storyline, I would pass on this game and go for something else like maybe What Remains of Edith Finch, a favorite of mine in the genre.

I personally love this game. I played the first Dear Esther a few years back, and now we have an updated version with higher resolution. And I know there are debates over whether or not this game even counts as one. But really, there is almost a puzzle going on in this.
As you wander the empty landscape of this desolate island, listening to the waves crashing on the shores and the narration of a man filled with melacholy and resignation for his fate, you're trying to put together the pieces of this story together. You're trying to make sense of what has happened to this man, this island, the characters in the man's books and in his life. But can you take the words of a man whose slowly giving way to insanity as truth? And is this island truly abandoned, when there is evidence that something, something is still around...
I would recommend this as an experience outside of conventional standards for both games and even novels. This feels like a playable novel, the kind that wins literary awards (or at least tries to; I do admit the writing can be somewhat sacchrine at times). But there's still something magical going on here, and it's worth checking out.

Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys first person shooters. A slower paced game, great if you want to get away from the twitchy, super competitive madness that is Halo/CoD.
Customization in the mechlab is phenomenal. Spending time in the mechlab building and tweaking mechs and testing their effectiveness is half the fun. Anything from armor values on all 8 of your different components (11 of you count the rear armor), weapons, ammo, engine size and type, and equipment, can be relocated and swapped to suit your needs.
Anyone who has played any other Mechwarrior title should feel right at home. If you haven't played/heard of Battletech before, I recommend reading up on some guides and strategies before you hop in. The learning curve is steep. You WILL lose a lot at first.
Combat is slow and methodical. Engagements will often last several minutes. The feeling of brawling with an enemy mech and having parts blasted off, will keep you on the edge of your seat; especially if it comes down to a 1v1 situation. Being '1 shotted' is very rare and is often the result of bad positioning and multiple enemy mechs focusing you down.
PROS:
-Solid game play mechanics
-The artwork and attention to detail behind the mechs and maps is visually stunning
-Mechlab/building mechs is quite fun
- Not P2W. More 'Pay to skip the grind'
-Huge selection of mechs to buy
- Encourages teamwork. Teamwork is often the deciding factor between winning and losing.
-events usually every second weekend that hand out all kinds of free goodies
-It has adhered well to the original Tabletop stats and rules, which makes balancing hard. But the game is in the best state of balance it has ever been
CONS
-The meta game Is very strict
-Development is rather slow
-Balancing tweaks are few and far between. The same meta can reign supreme for months
-The grind can feel overwhelming is you play only for Free.
-Lack of tutorials/briefing for mechlab and Faction Play
-Game mode variety is limited. Basically Team Death Match over and over again
-No real feeling of 'end game' you need 3 variants of a mech to level it up past Basic skills, then Elite, then Master. Master unlocks a module slot, but modules are basically C-bill sinks to improve your mech. A new skill tree is in the works.
All said and done, it's Free to Play, and if you enjoy the game it doesn't feel like a grind. Development has grown in leaps and bounds since the publisher broke off from the developers.

Ok. Bully. Where do I start with this game... particulary the Scholarship Edition.
Well for starters, Bully (also known as Canis Canem Edit) was first released in October 17th 2006. Damn, the game is almost 10 years old... anyway, it was released on that date and at the time, only for the Playstation 2. It was published by Rockstar Games and developed by Rockstar Games Vancouver. 2 years later, an updated version of this game was released, in March 4th 2008, with the title "Bully: Scholarship Edition". It was an updated re-release that pretty much corrected a few bugs in the game and added new content and characters.
I'll start with the story, here. The game puts you in the shoes of a 15 year-old boy named Jimmy Hopkins, who has been expelled from a lot of other schools in the United States for many reasons. We're talking about stuff like foul language, disrespecting staff, violence, etc. And as a result, Jimmy's mother and his new stepfather (whom we never really learn much about in the game) drop him at Bullworth Academy, while they go away on their honeymoon. Now, Bullworth Academy is probably the toughest school in the US, as it is full of bullies. And not just the students. Being aware of this, Jimmy prepares himself for the worst as soon as he sets foot inside the academy's grounds. From that point, you start meeting the rest of the game's character who... honestly are pretty good characters. Whether they're relevant to the story or not, you can interact with everybody. From fellow students to prefects to teachers. How you approach every single character is entirely up to you. The first three story relevant characters Jimmy meets are two fellow students named Petey and Gary, which are like... the opposite of each other. Petey's a bit of a shy kid while Gary's pretty much a sociopathic bully who wants to take over the school. The third character, who is like the very first you meet is Dr. Crabblesnitch, who is the principal at Bullworth.
Like I said before, the academy's full of bullies and the students aren't the only bullies in there. So expect crap from everyone. Even from the nerds.
Now, onto the gameplay. It's nothing different from almost every other sandbox game. Although Bully has its own unique features. But it's pretty much a huge world to explore both inside and eventually outside school grounds. Like I said, Jimmy can interact with pretty much every other NPC in the game. How do you approach people is entirely up to you. You can either try to be nice or be straight up nasty and show people who's boss.
Since this is pretty much GTA inside a school, you obviously have classes to attend to. 4 of them are part of the Scolarship Edition. There's English, Chemistry, Biology, Music, Art, Photography, Math, Shop, Geography and Gym. And some of these classes are worth attending to, for some good upgrades. I don't recommend them all, unless you're trying to go for 100% completion.
You also have lots of different collectibles spread throughout the academy and Bullworth Town, which once again you can try getting for 100% completion. I believe some of these collectibles reward you with stuff, too.
The game is also long as there are plenty of missions and side activities to do. I did a mix of both story missions and a few side activities, which caused me to have like 29 hours put into the game. But you can probably register a lot more if you complete every single side activity, attend to every single class and pass and look for every single collectible.
Last but not least, the graphics. Safe to say they did improve with the Scholarship edition, compared to the original release, back on the PS2. I personally think they look good enough for a 2008 re-release. That's all I can really say. Unfortunately I can't play the game with everything maxed out. And I'll soon explain why.
Despite Bully being a great game, the PC port has a few flaws, which can make it a little unstable. First of all, I don't think it's possible for the game to run at 60 FPS in any computer. I've seen it on my computer and on a friend's. Both decent PCs. Second, the game constantly crashes on you, making you lose progress if you haven't saved in a while or if you're in the middle of a mission or a side activity. Third, I strongly recommend playing the game with a controller, if you have one at your disposal. The game... works well with mouse and keyboard, but the controls feel a little weird. So if you can, use a controller.
Now while I may have mentioned a lot of pros about this game, the few cons I pointed out make it difficult for me to recommend this game for the PC. Since the game runs a lot more smoothly on the Xbox 360 and probably on the Wii, too. It's also available on PS3 and PS4, but it's Bully, not Bully: Scholarship Edition. So if you can, get it on console. If you're not able to, go with the PC version and do your best to be patient with the game.
And with all of that pointed out, I say it's time for the final score. I personally give Bully: Scholarship Edition a 7/10. It's a great game with a great story, great characters, plenty of stuff for you to do and a big world for you to get lost in. But it doesn't get a higher score due to its problems on PC. If it wasn't for that, I would gladly give this game an 8 or a 9.
So with that, I say go look for Bully. Hell's it's right here on Steam and it's not too expensive of a game! So go look for it, buy it and enjoy it. And don't let yourself be fooled by the title. While the game's title may sound like it's a bullying simulator, it's totally the opposite!

This is a horribly unintuitive game! The tech tree is all over the place, fleet management is clunky and the UI is so minimal that it provides no useful information at a glance. Modifying ships is nowhere near as fun as I've seen in other 4x games, yet it is pointless to click 'auto' since you get no choice of weapon range, etc. Hotkeys are either non-existant or hidden, so just trying to play this game feels odd (after having played better games). It feels to me like Endless Space goes out of its way to not be like other 4x games, even when doing so would only make it more intuitive, fun to play or easier to navigate.
I recommend Civ 5 for a streamlined 4x experience and Master of Orion 2 (still) for a fun, intuitive space 4x. Pass this one by.

**9.5/10**
HANDS DOWN!
Is the game perfect? No. Does it have some of the same issues other turn-based 4X games have? Yes. But that is where the similarities to other generic 4X games (like Civilization) end. The game occupies one of the most fascinating sci-fi settings I've seen in a strategy game, second only to Starcraft.  The gameplay is fluid, easy to pick up, but hard to master.  And as for strategy, well, let's just say even the toughest game of Risk couldn't prepare you for the decisions you have to make on the fly in this game when playing at high difficulty, both in terms of expanding to other star systems as well as micro-managing the indivudal planets and systems you already control.
Before I bought this game, I had never played an Amplitude Studios game.  "Endless Space" has single-handedly turned me into an Amplitude fanboy!
*** Also, if you enjoy "Endless Space" I HIGHLY reccommend that you also pick up their Early-Access games "Dungeon of the Endless" and "Endless Legend".  They are the most highly polished early-access games I've ever seen on Steam.  This studio knows what they're doing!

This game is a fair amount of fun.  It combines several different game elemnts into one title.  You have fleet combat, ground combat, RPG character progression, base construction, and resource management.
You are the lone survivors of the terran federation.  You run your starbase, Halcyon 6, a precursor artifact in the midst of a terrible invasion from extrea dimnesional Cruul.  To fight them you need to train officers, build better ships, and expand your base.
Space and ground combat are fairly similar.  Each character, and ship, have abilities.  Mostly to deal damage and inflict status effects on enemies.  Certain attacks exploit(which removes) certain other status effects for extra damage.  A lot of the tactical choices are trying to layer these effects and exploit them when advantageous.  For example Engines Down lowers the speed of a unit.  You may want to exploit it for damage quickly, or maybe leave it there to sneak in a few extra actions.
Ships and officers come in three specialties/classes: Science, Engineering, Tactical.  Each has a role in combat.  Science has the most debuffs and healing, Tactical has the most damaging attacks, and Engineering is a kind of mix between the two.
On your base you have to explore new rooms, and build new facilities.  Each room requires power so you have to build plenty of generators.  While some rooms are simple, like various resource multipliers, there's often story events that randomly pop up.  Like a crewman getting stuck in the dark matter multiplier, and you ahve the option to let him die, rescue him, or try and multiply him.  The outcomes are randomized.
The humor largely comes from sci-fi references, obviously a lot of things in the game are references to Star Trek(you have Green Shirts instead of Red Shirts) but other titles sprinkle in there.  The ALien races are fairly funny in and of themselves.  The merchent Yabblings are fantastically corrupt, but just see "conflicts of interest" as "business strealining"
I beat the game once.  While there's plenty of acheivements left and few little side quests I didn't get to the first playthrough, it didn't move me enough to actually play through it again, at least not right away, but there's enough meat left if you're a completionist and want to invest more time.  I would recommend this game for sci-fi fans, and those that enjoy 8-bit stylings as well as retro RPGs

Dear Esther:  A real masterpiece.  The level design, art, sound, and narrative come together better than I've seen in any other game to deliver a cohesive and brilliant work of art.  The story starts out slow but becomes trippy and exciting as you go along and if you're anything like me, you'll have to play it a few times before it really comes together for you.
This game was the father of the Walking Sim movement, and it doesn't cheap out on the premise like some other games of the genre.  The gameplay premise is entirely centered around exploration and wanting to uncover the story.
Dear Esther is certainly not for everyone, but for those who can be patient with a slow and cerebral game, you will not be disappointed.  It is a phenomenal game, and it will stick with you for a very long time.
Landmark Edition:  For those who loved the original edition, I am sure you'll play this version regardless, and the developer commentary is definitely worth the playthough.  But I did find myself disappointed by a fairly significant change in the physics.  Movement is much more constrained in Landmark, and I noticed this immediately since usually when I play the game, I climb up rocks, hills, and structures to get a good view of the landscape.  In this version, I found that I was able to climb almost none of the things that I usually do.  You might also notice that the lighting has changed fairly significantly.  So as a long time Dear Esther player, I will definitely stick to the original for future playthroughs.

I am a Tier 1 MWO veteran who has been playing this game for 2 years almost exclusively. You won't understand why until you are the last pilot alive, forced to confront five enemy Mechs with a cored centre torso, having only half your weapons at your disposal. The adrenaline rush in this game is real.
When you achieve victory on those situations, your satisfaction is immense: both intelectual and physical. You can't win at this game with just twich reflexes. You need tactical and situational awareness, teamwork (not even the best MWO players can win their matches on their own) and some serious multi-tasking skills. You need to know your Mech inside out: temperature thresholds, weapon ranges, cooldowns and projectile speeds, just to name a few, all while you aim at open components and hide yours from enemy fire.
The learning curve is steep and extremely rewarding: you learn from every defeat and victory. You hate some Mechs or weapons until you learn something new that makes you love them. You learn how to handle your legs independently from your torso, and then it's time to spread damage by torso twisting...
I have been playing this game for 2 years and every day I learn something new. And that's why I keep coming back.
The experience is so rich and engaging, you just can't get enough of it. I know I can't.

Final Score: 8/10 Very Good
Full Review:
I ended up thoroughly enjoying my time with this game. I had never played any of the Stronghold games prior to starting this one a few weeks ago. I’m not usually a fan of RTS games so I didn’t have high hopes, although I did like the premise and had heard good things. I was pleasantly surprised by Stronghold HD.
Generally most missions fall under the category of “protect your castle long enough to make n of x.” There are gradual variations in this as the game progresses and gets more complex. The game will slowly reveal more and more of itself in a way that gives you time to learn the mechanics but can at times come across as a bit too slow.
I have not yet beaten the game so I can’t speak for the entirety of the story. I am a little over halfway through and it appears the general story is that your are leading a group of patriotic rebels who are trying to restore legitimate rule in medieval England after the king was dethroned.
My two biggest complaints would be the tutorial and primitiveness.  Having never really played I game like this I first went to the tutorial where I learned all I thought I needed to know. However, the tutorial tells you nothing about combat which is perhaps half of the game. The military campaign makes up for this by going slow enough and being informative enough to function as a tutorial. Also, as previously mentioned, the game can feel somewhat repetitive at times with only slight variation in many of the missions.
Overall, I really enjoyed Stronghold HD. With only some minor faults I find this to be a very good game and definitely worth a look if you are interested in a medieval strategy game.

If you can enjoy some old school graphics, like sandbox games like Minecraft and MMORPG games then there's a good chance you'll find something to enjoy in 8BitMMO.  Unfortunately the game is not without it's issues but keep in mind this is an Early Access Game and in time some of those glaring issues will be ironed out.
Lets start with the good however.  First off this game will run on nearly any computer that's still up and running out there.  It's simple grapics style is a solid plus and you can feel confident inviting your friends to join with you no matter what kind of computer they have.  Secondly the game is free-to-play so you really have no excuse as to why you aren't at least trying this game out.  As an added bonus they currently are using what I consider one of the best free to play models out there.  There is nothing in this game, other than some cosmetic hats, that you can't get without spending money.  Other than the time things take to do your experience in this game will be no different whether you spend money or not.
So what is the gameplay like??  Well it's in part a roleplaying game.  Combat is currently limited to a small variety of mostly hand held swords that get better as you level and it is very basic but somehow enjoyable.  There are quests you can follow to recieve a nice reward in the end and different monsters to beat up.  Story wise, it's "not-so-serious" gameplay with a lot of witty humor and references to other movies, games, and so forth.  The other part of the game is very sandbox style.  Most of the world can be built up by the players which really gives you a chance to make your mark on the world, including designing dungeons and such for others to adventure in.  You buy the building blocks, monster spawners, and other building materials using in game money, which can be earned by killing monsters and completing quests, or bought with real money.  Other than a handful of hats that is the only thing that real money can buy for you.  Yes your gear is also bought with in game money however it is currently very limited and cheap enough to afford with just monster killing and questing money.  Even building materials are fairly cheap, though it will take some time saving up coins to build anything massive if your not willing to spend real money.
So what about the ugly side of the game.  Well first off the servers don't seem to currently be able to handle the load right now.  Granted there were what looked like hundreds of people playing, but I did experience quite a bit of lag that was worse in the more populated areas.  Secondly it is not at all or in any way pretty when it comes to graphics.  In some instances it can be hard to understand where you're supposed to go.  Some of this is players not being used to the building tools and thereby not building their structures in the most presentable way but some of it is simply the limitations of the graphics engine.  As far as audio goes, the sounds are extremely limited.  Start up some tunes of your own before you start the game.
Overall this is certainly a game you can and should at least try out.  While there's still a lot of things that can be ironed out there's a huge potential for this game to be massivly fun.  If you can put up with a few hiccups and bumps in the road I belive you'll find this a very enjoyable game.  It's certainly one that I will be playing from time to time and keeping an eye on.

The best controller for PC, hands down.  Or rather, without putting your hands down, on a desk - that's pretty much the point!
If you're fine with a mouse and keyboard then this isn't for you.  This is for playing on the couch when a mouse and keyboard is a crap option.
So, it has to do two things - replace a mouse and keyboard for games that don't support controllers, and replace a controller for games that do.
Replacing a mouse and keyboard: well, even with many months of practice I'm still not as precise with this (using the touchpad and gyro) as I can be with a mouse, but it's good enough.  I wouldn't be competitive, but I never was with a mouse either.  You don't have as many buttons as you do with a keyboard, but you do have sooooo many options in how you bind controls - making it depend on the type of click (quick, long, double, etc), combining buttons, creating touch menus, you can get a heck of a lot on there.  Basically, it's still not as good as a mouse and keyboard at a desk, but it's damn good, more than good enough and far better than a mouse and keyboard on the couch.
Replacing a controller, it's excellent.  Even without the configurability, dual stage triggers (pull to go to iron-sights, pull further to fire, for example) should be on all controllers, as should the rear grip buttons (left grip for reload, right for jump, for example, so you don't have to take your thumbs off movement).  With all the configuration it's a different league, especially for games with keyboard shortcuts you can bind to as well as controller inputs.  If the games natively supports Steam Controller, allowing you to directly bind to in-game actions (with situational awareness) even better.
Bottom line: to play games on the PC while sitting on the couch, this is the controller for me.
One complaints: I would like a slightly smaller one.  I have small hands, and I do find it a little less comfy to hold than the PS or X-Box controllers (although I'm not a fan of the ergonomics of the PS4 controller either).

I'm sorry to have to give this game a negative review because there a lots of positive things about it and only a small number of negative.  But one negative is a game breaker.
Bully is set in a residential school where your character is dumped by his mother and his new stepfather at the start of term.  For all the furore of the game's title the game is part of a mileu of childhood fiction - aspects of the "Just William" stories, "Tom Brown's Schooldays", "Dennis and Gnasher" "The Bash Street Kids" and "Mean Girls".
Although violence is epidemic and endemic in the school - GBH with baseball bats being regarded as "character forming" by the headmaster there's no need for your character to be a sadistic bully.  Indeed the game system, particularly at the start, favours running away from most fights and most of the missions involve helping people and pranks rather than outright sadism.
The school day breaks down into lessons (two a day) and free time where you can do various missions and favours.  Getting to class is always stressful because the game never tells you where your class is until it starts involving a mad dash to avoid hall monitors and staff to avoid truanting.  The classes themselves are mini games ranging from the very simple (music just requiring you to hit left or right trigger in reponse to the screen), to tricky (the word puzzles in English need pretty high skills), to very tricky (Biology needs you to be fast and accurate with your controls), to extremely difficult (the workshop's control tests are murderously difficult).  By the way DON'T get the game if you haven't got an X-Box for PC controller.  If you don't pass a class you keep on retaking it.
The outside class missions involve object finding, fighting, stealth and obstacle navigation.  Often you will find yourself having to run away from bullies and staff.  A skateboard may seem the better option to get away but the game has a nasty habit of flicking your perspective near objects like walls leaving you confused and trapped.  Inventory controls are clumsy with rearranging your inventory being difficult and no way to store the equipment (stink bombs, marbles, a catapult etc.) off yourperson.  Also the game bizarrely sees to lack a "Start from beginning" option so there's no way to erase a bad day without going to a previous save.
Your character sleeps but doesn't eat (a relief after the first canteen mission).
Overall the game is good fun.  The school characters and charicatures are well drawn with the language making the game unsuitable for younger, more impressionable gamers.  Also once you enter the second chaper the game world expands dramatically.  The game bumbles along whether you succeed in class or fail, succeed in missions or fail.
You can buy new items and clothing but other than mission specific items there's no indication whether these items affect gameplay at all.
Why the negative review then ?   The game crashes.  Rockstar has been aware or ought to have been aware of the problem for at least a year but the game still crashes.  There's no autosave function so since time is always ticking and is a significant limitation in the game you don't ten to go back to your bedroom (where the save ledger is) until the end of each day.  So if the game crashes late in an evening you could find yourself having to repeat two lessons and two missions you'd already completed.  On average having adjusted my setting I get about 90 minutes of play between crashes - which can then involve losing an hour of gameplay.
This would have been a strongly (but not overwhemingly) positive review without this flaw but with it the game is so annoying as to actively put you off playing.  Which is a shame because Bully is probably a better game than the first three GTAs at least.

Endless Space has you playing a turn based game very reminiscent to the final space age mode of the Maxis game ‘Spore’ along with the mapping structure of said title and others like Galactic Civilizations I and II.
Both games display forms of colonization, terra forming and research to upgrade your planets. Endless Space takes on a less direct approach than Spore however, eliminating the space to planet surfacing system that Spore displays for direct town upgrades such as turrets.
Instead Endless space gives you a huge verity of research upgrades that can benefit anything from your tech, military prowess, planet upgrades (including money, defenses, offences weapons and fleet sizes) and diplomacy.
There are 8-10 races to choose from or you can make your own race using one of the avatars provided in game, whilst picking your own pros and cons to balance said race.
The galaxy can feel empty without getting to put a face or faces to your empire, which was addressed within Endless Space. Giving you multiple heroes at your disposal, three are given to you each time you start the game, completely at random. You do need to hire them though and your max hero quota is 3 to begin with, but can be upgraded through tech.
Heroes also have classes. Multi classes can be found on each hero, but they always start with a preselected 2 that are constant for that hero in every game. Ranging from warrior types such as Spy, commander and Pilot, plus other types that benefit planets and systems more so.
I only have one thing bad to say about the game that really isn’t bad. The tutorial system in the game is vast and helps out, but only to a certain degree as it is only text based. Throughout my first 3-5 playthroughs I found myself still confused about little things that stumped me as I went along. Such as keeping my population happy, how to keep up with my fellow civilizations that were developing within the same system as myself.
All in all it is a great game; all it really needs is an upgraded tutorial system in my opinion, perhaps voiced instead of text based, or both at the same time.
Pros:
Immersive game play
extreme detailing for an indie game
Huge upgrade tree system
Wide verity of races and heroes
Bang for your buck.
Cons:
You blink and the time goes by.
Despite a vast text tutorial you’re left confused and moments that will be vital in the long run.

Summary: Easy to grasp and fun to play, guarding the stars from grotesque alien nasties is a good time. Highly recommended!
For those of you who ever wanted to see what it would be like if FTL: Faster Than Light and Final Fantasy had a baby, this is pretty much it.
Halcyon 6 presents you with a satisfying top-down management - flotillas of starships are built and dispatched by your will, and who doesn't love that? Securing and defending resource-generating colonies to support your starbase makes up a cornerstone of the gameplay, and it's a pleasingly straightforward system.
The other half of gameplay consists of a combat system reminiscent, as earlier implied, of the turn-based spellcasting and sword-swinging of the classic SNES/PS1-era Final Fantasy games. Granted, you're firing lasers and employing Star Trek-esque ship abilities rather than using swords or magic, but this combat system is simple to grasp but has enough nuance to give it an engaging level of tactical depth that keeps it from being a mere mindless shootfest.
All in all, Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is easy to get the hang of and enjoyable to play - what more could one ask from a game?

Endless Space is a complex, gorgeous and heavily emphasized on overall strategy game that changes the pace from the conventional 4X games such as Civilization. Amplitude studios have came up with a most flamboyant game that will ignite your screen with a palette of vibrant colours and one can easily spent countless hours contemplating the elegance of the endless space.
The dept of each technology trees, decisions about diplomatic relationships, positioning of fleets and planetary expansion makes the game feel alive to your every decisions, as you try to negotiate a truce to secure your stern while positioning your fleets to invade a hostile nation.
However the game is not without its shortcomings: although there are multiple ways to secure a victory the AI seems to always put an emphasis on domination victory (war), even pacifist nations such as the Sophons will eventually agress you. Furthermore, the game is axed on the overview of galatic conquest and players who are expecting an up-close and more tactical real-time strategy mechanics will be disappointed. The game does offer cinematics for space engagement only, but players will be unable to control their fleets directly, instead they will be asked to issue general commands to be used during the skirmishes and much like a rock-paper-scissor pattern some commands are superior to others and each have their own weakness.
Overall, this is a game I would only recommend to space science fiction fans who values high quality graphics and do not mind the lack of real time strategy aspect.

World of Tanks Blitz,
Is at its core nothing more than a grind arena shooter.
You're pitted against eachother in team deathmatch and capture the base modes. (Both modes active at the same time)
By doing battle you earn experience and credits. With your earned rewards you upgrade your current tank, or you purchase a new tank.
But, how does it play?
The general gameplay is solid and didn't show any real bugs. The main issue that I've got with this game is the extreme grind factor, and the very clear "Go premium to enjoy" setting.
Don't get me wrong, you don't have to go premium to enjoy the game, but it sure takes away the grind. (Or as a Brii states: "With premium you would have to grind maybe a few hours less then without premium.
But still you'd have to spend numerous hours and battles grinding.")
Did I enjoy it?
Yes I did for the first couple of rounds, Until I noticed that there's no real nation filter when it comes down what model of tank battles the other. Besides of that; the first few times things are not always as clear when it comes down to what upgrade to buy or not.
Is this a stayer?
Not for me. I like the different tank battles, but it'snothing new. There're better tank games out there, even more tactical ones. But, it's basically free and that's somewhat of a nice thing.
Still, I don't really see myself getting back into this game if they don't add some sort of single player / co-op campaign mode. Which they probably won't due to the fact that everything is geared towards PvP clashes.

The basic problems of the game is the same as with almost every free to play game on the steam marketplace: You might have some fun, but you're at a competitive disadvantage to anyone with a credit card powerup. You could have the best reflexes, great internet, great computer, intelligence and deep skill... but one swipe of the card and it's meaningless. This is a pay to win game, like all the others. Below, I'll explain the particulars of how this game executes the model.
.
Your first 25 matches give you huge amounts of 'c-bills', the main in-game currency. But after that, regardless of how good you are, you won't make more than 200k per match. Realistically, you can expect to make 50-130k, depending on skillset and build choices for your mech.  Most of the mechs you will want cost about 8-16mil for the chassis. Triple that to fit it up decently. A match will run you about 18 minutes a pop, assuming you are doing it during peak hours -- the queue times can be in the minutes range outside of that window, and 85% of the player base is N. American.  So the breakdown is, you can blow 5 hours a night and get in about 15 matches during that. That'll give you about 1.5mil. So basically, once a week you can afford to get another mech. There are about a hundred. And there are an average of about 4 variations for each. To use them well, you need to buy 3 of each chassis, and skill them up. The goal here is to get a set of 4 mechs that you can use to bring to community warfare; So you will need to grind a minimum of 12 mechs, selling 8 of them, to accomplish this. That's about 3 months of grinding every night, 5 hours a night, to be competitive in community warfare.
.
Which brings me to our next problem: Community warfare without a dozen friends is like going to a sausage party. Those few who do this make millions of c-bills an hour grinding out maps. Everyone else is just scrubs -- no matter how good you are, you're going to lose. And that's the main selling point of the game over previous mechwarrior games. So you either spend 3 months grinding so you can have a *chance* at winning -- and the load out that one of those aforementioned groups will take you in on -- or you whip out your credit card and take the express lane to the desert of community warfare.
.
By desert, I mean... there are a couple matches every hour during peak times. If you just want to play with random strangers who have no idea what they're doing, and will often suicide themselves just to get to the next match faster... you can skip community warfare. But if that kind of playstyle is aggravating to you, and teamwork is what you really want to be a part of, this is the best mechwarrior online has to offer.
.
And it ain't much.

This is a game for those who have a lot of interest in guns, as it's more a simulation of disassembly down to the tiniest parts of the gun.
The DLC and sight that it seems to be pay to win may put you off but if you're capable of remembering a gun's pieces and the order they are taken out and put back in, you can easily get many guns. Besides that you may initially think you want all of the guns and stuff like that but I'm sure if you're interested in firearms you have ones that give you a particular amount of enjoyment and as such you'll likely stick with those.
I understand that the gun you're looking for could possibly be deep within the tree of guns which would require hours of messing with the same guns over and over again but at least if you log in every day you get a slowly growing amount of exp that will definitely help you along your way, and you have to be pretty interested in firearms in order to even try out this game in the first place so you should keep calm and continue becoming better and better at disassembling and reassembling what you have at the time.
There's also cars, military vehicles, motorcycles and skeletons and such so if you're interested in those or get bored of guns you can play the game for those.
They're also still making new models of guns as far as I know so the game's still growing in size over time, which is a good thing and makes the lifetime access even more worth it for those who REALLY want to see the individual bits and pieces of every single gun they've ever seen in their lifetime.

The concept of 8BitMMO is great. A 100% player built world with combat and an infinite world? Sounds great, right?
The way it's executed, however, isn't as great.
Before I say anything else, I do /NOT/ believe that you need good graphics to make a good game. That being said, this games graphics are one of the major issues with this game. I think this game would be MUCH better if it had depth. the way it is constructed makes it difficult to tell where you are in comparison to anything. When you go under something, it dissapears, but that leads to even more confusion when trying to navigate through someones building. Furthurmore, when attenpting to build, you must puild from north to south unless using slabs. Attempting to do otherwise causes you to place the block on top of the previously placed one. Trying to build roofs or multi-story buildings is a pain, and the game doesn't tell you how to place blocks in the air without building up untill after you've placed 30 blocks. This wouldn't be an issue, except for the fact that you need gold to buy blocks. In order to get gold, you need to kill enemies, which is a good concept, but as with the rest of the game, is poorly done. The combat in this game consists of either jabbing a super-close ranged sword at the enemy, or using a pixel pistol to shoot the foes down. Aiming properly is difficult, and even if you use the swords, combat is extremely bland and difficult.
There are so many things wrong with this game, the few things it does right are not enough to counter them. Like I said before, the concept is great, but I do not recommend this game.

Background:
I've never played a Deus Ex game before but I really enjoy RPGs and have played Elder Scrolls, Final Fantasy, Knights of the Old Republic, among others.
Intro:
Deus Ex: Human Revolution gives us a perspective on a potential future for mankind where human enhancements called augments divide humanity into haves and have nots.
What I liked:
- A compelling story that kept me going until the end!
- Tough choices to make, albeit these can be a bit rare throughout the game (it's no Dragon Age).
- The game truly encourages you to think outside of the box with the choices. More often then not you can find a better alternative for the choices the game presents you.
- Arguments and conversations throughout the game are not made for the player to win. You have to be careful with what you say.
What I didn't like:
- Towards the end of the game you'll get a non optional reset of all the ability points (called praxis points) you got meaning you're back to square one and have to earn almost everything back. This is highly discouraging to continue to play the game but please don't quit. At the end of that section you'll get everything back but it still feels like the game is punishing the player unnecessarily.
- Very minor graphical glitches.
Conclusion:
In my humble opinion Deus Ex: Human Revolution has exactly what every RPG should have and should be played by any fan of the genre.
It's a game that doesn't disappoint and kept me wanting for more!

Halcyon 6 is great game to play in short bouts.  It gets a bit repetitive, but you can play it for even just 10 minutes and still make progress.
The game is basically a very light 4X mixed with JRPG-style menu driven combat.  The combat is the repetitive part, but battles are relatively quick (at least on the difficulty level I played on) and there are enough different actions and mechanics that they kept the game enjoyable and interesting for the 30 hours it took me to finish it.
Speaking of the difficulty level, there are 5 of them, and let me just say that I really, really appreciate that.  In a post-Dark Souls/Super Meat Boy world there are a lot of indie games that kind of go out of their way to be difficult and Halcyon 6 can provide that experience if you want it, but it can also provide somewhat more casual play while not being too brain dead easy.  I played on the second easiest difficulty and that was just right the right amount of challenge for the experience I wanted.
The game's writing is mostly comedic in tone and well done to that end.  There are *a lot* of sci-fi genre references and in-jokes that come off in a good way and not like the game is trying too hard to pander.  Comedy writing is very hard to do in a game and they pull it off more often than not.
Note that I didn't play the game until it reached version 1.3.1 and looking at the update history, there are some fairly extensive mechanics the developers have added to the game since its release.  It seems like it was kind of a "stealth early access" title.  I can understand why some people who played Halcyon on release might have been disappointed by a lack of variety.  However, where it stands now, I have no qualms about recommending it.  It's not a game that I'd want to play for 60 hours, but I am very satisfied by the 30 hours I got out of it.

Dear Esther is a game that tries too hard to be artsy, at great cost to gameplay and story, ironically.  You walk around an island-- just walking mind you, as there are no other game mechanics whatsoever, not so much as a puzzle to solve or an item to pick up--while your character narrates.
That would be fine, except that the narration is randomized and scrambled with no regard to making sure any actual story is conveyed.  You may get lucky on your first playthrough and get some meaningful story, but you'll probably just end up with very sparse incoherent rambling that doesn't seem to have any substance until you play through a few times and figure out what is flavor and what is central to the plot.  A plot that is deliberately written to be self-contradicting, as the devs explain in the director's commentary.  It could have been clever if it had been better executed, maybe.
That brings me to the final point: this game is short.  Absurdly short.  Between 1-3 hours for a full playthrough, depending on how thoroughly you search every nook and cranny.  Replayablility allows for about 3 playthroughs before you're pretty done with this.

overall, i think i enjoyed my time with dear esther. sure, the walking pace is god awful, but the art is stunning, the voice acting is compelling and wondrous, and the music and aura of the game exudes beauty. it's not everyone's cup of tea, but i thoroughly enjoyed my time with it.
(the only problem you might have with this game are the achievements?? if you fail to initiate an achievement on your first playthrough, you'll have to do another, plus one more for the director's commentary. so be warned.)
