I played this game since it appeared as early alpha access up until sometime after full release, but before Disharmony.  I can tell you without a shred of doubt that it had great potential in alpha.  I was rather blown away by the amount of polish and content already in the game, as well as the ease of the interface.
Endless Space is a fantastic single player game, if it was only that, I would have been clamoring for multiplayer but satisfied to play alone vs AI (although AI was never brilliant).  As far as space 4x goes, the exploration and expansion aspect was very nice. The combat tries mix being quick with some player choices so its not purely predetermined who would win. I found I could win a military victory extremely fast and easily. As a normally aggressive player, I liked this. And here comes why I hate this game...
It is because after this game, I hate amplitude studios. Bugs. Extremely buggy alpha. Buggy multiplayer, buggy beta, buggy release, buggy dlc. I remember at one point they announced that they had hired more programmers or some such to fix the various bugs of the game. They did fix some things, semi-quickly.  Going back to why I played aggressively, it was because a multiplayer game reliably crashed around turn 30. I could kill someone by turn 22. So this was the only way I could finish a game. In this I found enjoyment, but it does not by any means make it a good product. After they fixed some bugs, turn 40 became the new life expectancy.  Also, in addition to that, multiplayer games had a host, and the game was reliant on the host. So if you kill the host, or he quits, every one gets booted to the title screen. Someone has to load the autosave, and get everyone to rejoin, which hardly happened. Most of the time the save file was corrupted anyways.
Let's insert a small note about amplitudes voting process for their games.  You get forum points of some sort for various reasons, and that is your voting power. They will give you choices of what to vote on to implement next in the game, and you vote. The problem here is the majority of players just play single player or co-op, so they aren't usually looking to balance the game for multiplayer, they just want aesthetic things. Fix the games bugs was never a vote option, mind you. Keep in mind, all these things will be added at some point, you are just voting on the priority project. It's all well and fine, but trivial.
So lets fast forward to Disharmony DLC. A guy on my steam friend list still played the game and would periodically invite his entire list, i presumed. I said oh, Disharmony is out and a lot changed, ok, maybe its all better now. So i picked it up. NOPE, still buggy for multiplayer.  Expect to crash sometime after turn 60.  Additionally, they slowed the pace of the game, by nerfing nearly everything.  I was immediately reminded why I hate them, which was amplified by the fact that it had been HOW LONG???? since the game was in alpha and the same game crashing bugs still existed. This was made worse since even though now the game won't crash as early, the pace of the game was slowed so much that it didn't matter.
So any "Endless" Title I expect the same garbage to happen. I wanted so bad to give this game around a 8/10 initially, but the studio seemed to not really care much about polishing it, that I really give it a 4/10.  I was recommending it in alpha, I was telling people to never get it ever after release. That is backwards, in case you were wondering.

Being a fan of Science Fiction and Strategy games, I was intrigued when I saw Endless Space on Steam. Not only did it combine both of my favorite genres, but it was an indie game as well. So I decided to take it for a spin. Little did I realize that I would be sucked into a vibrant universe and asking my wife to allow me "Just one more turn!"
Endless Space plays like a standard 4X game. The player guides his race in gathering resources, researching technologies, building up a military force, and managing star systems in an attempt to conquer the galaxy. What sets this title apart from its peers is how it combines these elements together. First off, the game is easy to learn. This is because the interface is clean and very intuitive. Gone are the days of sifting through various menus to find out what something is and what you are working on. For example, if you want to see what you are researching, just click on the research button. You are then presented with an easy to read research tree with the current project highlighted. Also, if you are unsure what something is or does, just mouse over the item and it will tell you what it is. As with any game of this type, managing your far flung empire later in the game can get tedious. Amplitude Studios combats this problem in a unique way. When an event happens you are notified by a pop-up that will take you to the event when you click on it. If multiple events are present, this pop-up will remain until the player dismisses it or has addressed all the events listed. While this goes a long way to ease empire management, it does not totally resolve the problem. Later turns can still be long and drawn out while you deal with these events.
The combat in Endless Space is where the game excels. The player can either have the computer resolve the battle automatically, or the player can take control and fight the battle. It is one of the few titles that I have played where tactics are essential. Do I send my fighters in first or do I bombard the enemy from a distance. Each choice affects not only if you are successful, but how many losses one sustains. The game also rewards players for using a mix of ship types. While yes, one could win a battle with a battle group composed of only battleships, but a "combined arms" battle group will make the battles quicker with less losses. This creates a world where each battle is different, and sometimes the "weaker" side will win.
The only problem with Endless Space is that the factions are balanced too well. No matter what faction you play, you have some sort of built in counter that negates the other faction's abilities. At first this made the game really easy to play and but soon it can become monotonous. Most of the balance issues have been addressed with the Disharmony DLC and patches, but some of them still remain.
Overall, I have to give Endless Space 9 out of 10 stars. This highly polished and easy to learn game has raised the standard for not only games from the 4X genre, but indie games as well. I highly recommend it to not only fans of the 4X genre, but new players as well. Just make sure to say goodbye to your friends and family before you play!

I've played World of Tanks, World of Warplanes, World of Warships and World of Tanks Blitz, and WoT is my favorite out of them all. A cool, fast paced game. Great for a quick arcade-style game of action. This coming from a dedicated War Thunder player. Though WoT may not be the mose realistic game, it is definetley very fun. No, War Thunder isn't all that realistic either, but it has a more relistic feel to it. While most people don't consider HP bars and health points realistic, it gives WoT predictable gameplay. I stopped playing WoT after a few months, as I play the majority of my games on a crappy toaster, so it could barley run even the most simple games. About a year after, War Gaming came out with World of Tanks Blitz. At this time, War Gaming had a fairly bad reputation because of War Thunder. I decided to try it out. It was awesome. WG kept pumping out interesting and stable updates, keeping the game alive. Although it had the extreme P2P feel and grind, it was still loads of fun. I still play WoTB mobile today, and the release of WoTB on Steam was pretty cool. While Steam isn't the ideal place to put a MOBILE BASED game on, it did prove quite good. I expected my "toaster" to not be able to run it even on minimum graphics, but it proved very smooth and playable. After all, they probably just did a copy/paste of the game engine from a phone to a PC. Though I did find a few flaws: frame rates may be good, but it is very unstable. Controls have not fully adapted from mobile to PC. Mouse sensitivity is very sluggish, even when bringing it up. if you are familiar with mouse acceleration, this is exactly the problem. For those who don't know, mouse acceleration is the speed at which your cursor moves dependent on how fast you physically move your mouse. For example, if you physically move use slowly, the cursor will move slowly, and if you move your mouse fast, your cursor will move fast. And for a fast-paced game like WoTB, where multiple swipes/movements are required to keep up with your aim, this makes aiming very hard as it is very slow and unpredictable.
Another problame I found was when launching the game. The game hasn't been out on Steam long so there are bound to be bugs, specifically game launch bugs. Every time I launch the game via Steam, it says it needs to do the "First Time Launch" stuff with the "Windows bla bla bla step 1 4908134" or some crazy thing like that. (It's really just 3 steps) It took the game over half an hour to complete 2 steps and took another 20 mins to finish and launch the game. This does this every time. I was actually waiting for the game to load and decided to write this long♥♥♥♥♥review. It almost an hour for it to boot up for the second time. In fact, in the middle of writing this paragraph the game decided to load up and interrupt me mid-sentence... :,(
Other than that, WoTB PC is exactly the same as the mobile version. I like it, but that's just my opinion.

A long, long time ago, in a galaxy far away, Eric "Badspot" Hartman casually experimented with the idea of making a lego-oriented game with the Torque Engine. You place lego bricks in a voxel world, drive brick cars, shoot weapons, destroy bricks with hammers, ski down slopes, etc... The kinds of things most kids like to imagine doing with legos.
Today, the game has reached new heights compared to its early years. The creative side of Blockland has gone to new extremes with their endeavors. When you first enter the game, you might be disoriented at first. There is no direction; you just place and edit bricks, among other things. But stick around and explore, and the rewards will be greater every time. Build a house or other structure of your choice. Then build another; then another, and another. Improve your technique, and watch your skills improve as your builds become more elaborate and more detailed, realistic, and higher quality.
Make the bricks do things with the Wrench Event system, whereupon you might begin crafting brick-event computers and contraptions, sci fi setups, RP games, and countless other possibilities yet to be explored...
Explore online servers and see what the other players are doing; of all the things you might find, locally famous examples include: A 1:1 scale exact detail replica of the RMS Titanic, giant six-story spaceships, high-detailed yachts, realistic houses both vintage and modernesque, science labs, roleplay worlds, giant dragonflies, arenas, etc...  you'll find many visual examples of Blockland creations through this link:
, the Blockland trailor, and of course on online servers.
The game's add-on system is among the most prominent features of the game. You might consider searching out and downloading custom bricks, vehicles, tools, gamemodes, events, etc as well to enhance your potential. Most add-ons may be found in the Add-ons section of the Blockland forums.
In all, this game will be well worth the money if you stick around and explore the possibilities. The game's path is yours.
-----
PS: Before you step in, beware: The Blockland community is, in general, exceptionally... er... badly influenced. There are nice people out there, but it is advised that you use your own judgement to find them, and beware that dwelling too long in the general sea of the Blockland Forum and many Blockland internet servers, your sanity may be at risk. I urge you not to let this effect your impression of the game itself.

I am on the fence on this one.  It has so much potential and can be very fun at times.  However, a lot of work still needs to be done to balance the mechs and the matchups.  It seemed well balanced in the first couple matches I played, then all of a sudden the difficulty in opponents just ramped through the roof.  I lose 3 out of 4 games played and by large margins.  They need to work on the team match making.  Balance the good ( or experienced ) players with the not so good ( new players, or just those of us that are casual ).  Until that time I can't recommend the game as no one wants to keep playing a game where they just get stomped on by the hardcore players on the vast majority of matches.
I love the cockpit, mech selection, customization, and nostalgia it brings from the days of Mechwarrior 2, Mercenaries, etc.  They just need to work on balance to make it fun for everyone and not just for the hardcore players to pick on the beginners and casual players.
++Update++ - I gave the game another month of additional play for a full shakedown.  After such, I will revise my recommendation from a "No" to "Yes".  There are still two big negatives, the matchmaking mentioned earlier, and the cost of the microtransactions.  Or in this case macro transactions based on the cost.
League of Legends, while a different type of game, IMO manages both of these two aspects of the game far better.  My hope with a good matchmaking system is to eventually end up with a 50/50 split of wins to losses.  That just has not been my experience so far, even after the extended play time.  It is my fear that the current system will scare away the casual players and beginners making this a hardcore only game.  This can hurt the commercial success of any title.  This is especially noticeable when teaming up with a friend.  I tried playing with a friend and we lost almost every match we played but two.  This is no where near a 50/50 split.  Almost all of the games put us up against entire teams of "clan" players.
Micro transactions should be just that, micro, not starting at a price point greater than most games and soaring to levels that can buy you a gaming system.
However, what really pushed me to a "Yes" is the customization and difference between the mechs.  They nailed this aspect of the game and I actually enjoy building and tweaking the mech as much as playing it.  Gaining extra chassis and leveling up the 3 variants forces me to customize weapons outside of my play style and adapt to new ways to play.  I think this part of the game is brilliant.
Summary:  So while it has a couple of major flaws, further play has revealed a depth to the game that can be enjoyed when trying to master multiple chassis.

One of the best castle management games I've ever played. I've beat it twice before, ages ago, and once again when I got it on steam.
The game holds up very well despite it's age. The maps come to life with wildlife like wolfs, rabbits, deer, bears and birds like eagles and seaguls. Trees move in the wind and water flows in the river. The sound effects are also really good and differs depending on what you focus your screen on. Scroll over the forrest an you'll hear the wind in the trees, over rivers you'll hear the water flow and over the ocean you'll hear the waves and the seagulls. If you scroll over buildings you'll hear the sound of work going on inside. Building walls and roofs also becomes transparent when work is going on, showing animations of workers/weapon makers (and in the case of inn's: drunkards) inside.
All of the inhabitants in your castle deliver some simple dialogue when selected, reflecting what they think of the imminent situation and about you as their lord. When attacked women and children scream as they run for their homes to take cover.
All of this makes the landscape and the castle come to life. Everything is littered with small details adding to the visual and audible appeal.
As for gameplay there's a main military campaign with 21 separate missions, as well as a shorter Economic Campaign. In the military campaing focus lies on training units and defeating your enemy or successfully defend against enemy attack, while the economic campaign focus on gathering specific supplies.
There are also stand alone missions like historically inspired sieges feauturing game renderings of real life castles.
You don't control your peasants but only your military units. Peasants moves to your castle if you have housing for them and provide them with food. You'll have to balance the amount of food you hand out and your tax rate to keep people happy. If they are unhappy they will leave your castle.
You can also manage your peasants by placing "good" or "bad" things. Placing ponds and gardens increase happiness and gives your soldiers bonuses in a fight, but your peasants will work slower strolling in the park now and then. Placing chopping blocks or skulls on spikes will do the opposite. It will lower happiness and give soldiers penalties in battles but increase output from your buildings.
The crafting tree is has multiple tiers. To make bread you first need a wheat farm, then a wind mill and last a bakery. All goods go through the stockpile beside your Keep/Stronghold, except bread that goes to the granary. If either the granary or the stockpile gets full they will need to be expanded or production will halt. Have this in mind when placing buildings.
Weapons follow the same rules: you need wood to make bows, crossbows and spears, iron to make platemale, swords and maces, and leather to make leather armour. To get wood you need woodchoppers, to get iron you need mines and to get leather you need a farm and a tanner.
Many production lines cross, and you'll have to plan what to build based on the land available (apples and wheat don't grow in any soil, and cows need to grace) and the threat you are facing. You have to protect your lord or you will be immediatly defeated, but leave your farms unprotected and they will likely all be destroyed in the event of an attack.
There is also a freebuild mode where you build and manage your castle on a map of your choice without intervention. Build the castle of your dreams!
A map editor is available where you can edit the terrain of your map and build castles and place buildings. Make your own scenario, stand alone mission or freebuild map.
The editor is also very fun to play around in. No buildings will function in this mode but you don't need resources as everything is placed for free. You can build castles, place units from different factions and have them fight eachother.
One negative aspect of the game is that the isometric view sometimes makes it hard to tell the elevation of different points on the map, and it's possible for characters to get stuck on terrain. Another problem is the path tracing. The enemy will always, immediatly find a hole in your wall but if your wall is intact they seem to attack the part closest to them. They do this even if that part is made up of 5 layers of stone wall and another section is made of fragile wooden wall.
This makes it quite easy to lure the enemie through deathtraps like making them run back an forth through a maze of stone walls with archers on them. You don't have to exploit it ofcourse but it can be hard to resist :p
In conclusion, it's a solid game and I've had a hard time finding anything with the same feel as Stronghold. The HD edition makes much more playable on modern screens as you can zoom out and see almost the entire map at once. I defenitly recommend this to anyone interested in strategy games. It will run on practically any computer and offer hours of fun, and I haven't even tried the multiplayer.

Won't lie. One of the best JRPGs I played, and if you look at my Library, all the ones I own I hardly play.
So why is it good? First off the quirky humor in the text is pretty nice, it plays homage to the old 70s-90s sci fi genres, such as Star Trek and really that's all I can say in terms of that. It has base management similar to that of Xcom, though I wish they added the system in which if you have power rooms next to power rooms, workshops next workshops, etc. they would get buffs.
It also has the similar space exploration to that of FTL, however, its not the main focus. Combat, resource gathering, and base management are its focus. There is a permadeath system set in the game, however, later on there is a building you can research and construct that'll help render that bit out. Though lets say your officer dies in space combat, you can revive the officer and his/her traits, but the ship itself, and its crew, will be lost.
Yes, the ship. Not only will you be leveling up your officers, you'll be leveling up the ship and its crew. You'll get better and stronger cadets which'll apply small, passive buffs which'll help you tremoundsly in later combat scenarios.
How's the combat? Its typical JRPG combat with a new quirk, at least new to me, which makes it so you can basically do combos. Oh you panicked a pirate ships crew, cool, now teleport a bomb into the engine bay and blow them hell. That sorta stuff. It makes it really fun to play and try out different combos which can either win or lose you the battle. However, don't get cocky because on harder difficulties the A.I. will start comboing you as well and seriously ♥♥♥♥ you up.
The animations in the combat portions are really fun and nice to watch, the death animations in the ground scenarios are really brutal, poor cadets. I don't get annoyed due to the animations being fast and tolerable, however since the devs are awesome and are constantly updating the game you can now turn them off in the options menu.
The combat can be kinda grindy and the game sorta slows down after you get tier 2 ships and the pacing just face plants. Thankfully they added the new drone system into the game where you can build automated drones at certain colonys who'll construct shipping lanes back to your base, so you aren't needed to go out every five ♥♥♥♥ing seconds to get some new cadets.
Overall the game is fun, and since the DEVs haven't let us down yet and are constantly updating it, I'm sure it'll become a lot better in the future!.

Background:
I've never played a Deus Ex game before but I really enjoy RPGs and have played Elder Scrolls, Final Fantasy, Knights of the Old Republic, among others.
Intro:
Deus Ex: Human Revolution gives us a perspective on a potential future for mankind where human enhancements called augments divide humanity into haves and have nots.
What I liked:
- A compelling story that kept me going until the end!
- Tough choices to make, albeit these can be a bit rare throughout the game (it's no Dragon Age).
- The game truly encourages you to think outside of the box with the choices. More often then not you can find a better alternative for the choices the game presents you.
- Arguments and conversations throughout the game are not made for the player to win. You have to be careful with what you say.
What I didn't like:
- Towards the end of the game you'll get a non optional reset of all the ability points (called praxis points) you got meaning you're back to square one and have to earn almost everything back. This is highly discouraging to continue to play the game but please don't quit. At the end of that section you'll get everything back but it still feels like the game is punishing the player unnecessarily.
- Very minor graphical glitches.
Conclusion:
In my humble opinion Deus Ex: Human Revolution has exactly what every RPG should have and should be played by any fan of the genre.
It's a game that doesn't disappoint and kept me wanting for more!
The issues I had with this game are truly minor compared to everything this game does right!

While reading my review, please keep in mind that I never played the original Deus Ex games.
I went into this game thinking it would be your every day shooter game with average story and decent game mechanics. What I got was something much more pleasing. Deus Ex: Human Revolution has got to be one of my most favorite games of all time. Every penny I spent on this game was well worth it and I will never forget the experience Human Revolution has given me.
The game takes place in the future where robotic limbs and augmentation is possible. A lot of thought went into this concept as you've got the pro-life supporters stating that augmentation is wrong and that you shouldn't do anything to your body. On the other hand you've got those who support human augmentation stating that this is how the human race will evolve. You play as Adam Jensen- a security guard. You used to be "fully human" without any augmentations until a day came where you were attacked by an augmented human and left nearly for dead. Practically every limb in Jensen's body has been replaced due to the severity of the attack he barely lived through.
6 months fly by and you are called in again to help stop those responsible for the attack on Serif Industries and get revenge on those that made you what you are. The story is rich and deep- and the characters are very memorable. Adam questions if he is still human, or something more. As mentioned- the developers put a lot of thought into the story of this game and it stands out. I haven't played the game in months and I still remember the story as if I played the game yesterday.
The game mechanics are wonderful. It's more of stealth game or taking enemies out one by one than anything. Adam is not a Call of Duty soldier by any means and can't step into a middle of a room unprotected. The game requires strategy. You can tackle a level in several different way whether you try and go in fully stealthy or take out enemies every time they are encountered. You are rewarded in XP for exploring or not being seen at all or not killing enemies but rather, knocking them out. The more you level or find certain collectibles to upgrade your augments, the more you can do with them. For instance, you couldn't fall from a certain height without dying unless you got enough XP to purchase the Icarus upgrade which would allow you to fall from any height and not be hurt let alone die. Or you can't lift anything with the exception of like a remote unless you put XP into an upgrade that would allow you to move heavy things such as dumpsters. A great concept that makes the game challenging or sometimes making you wish you put your upgrade into some other augmentation based on the current situation you are in.
The game has branching paths. You can choose certain dialogue options and some of these options do have an impact on how the mission progresses or ends. You'll have speech checks that if you fail- could be the death of a hostage or information being withheld from you. Speaking certain things or asking questions helps you understand the story more. I've never been more interest in doing side quests and reading emails and everything as I have with Human Revolution. This game makes you want to complete the side quests. This game makes you want to explore and find out every little secret that you can find out about. And if that wasn't enough, the soundtrack to this game is beautiful and well compose and fits Human Revolution perfectly.
Don't go into this game thinking you are a super soldier who can soak up bullets. You might be a very augmented individual- but you are still human and can take damage like crazy if you are careless. The best strategy of this game is to go in stealthy or taking enemies out one by one when necessary. Strategy is going to be your best friend in this game. If this is not your play style or you aren't willing to play that kind of play style, don't get this game. However- if you are looking for a great story with lots of lore to get into along with great game mechanics, I cannot recommend this game enough.

Recommended: An exceedingly well-executed and designed space 4X strategy game that stumbles a bit with a lack of personality that typically characterises its predecessors such as Star Control 2 or even newer competitors such as Stardrive.  It's much more Master of Orion-esque in that, but if you liked that kind of game, then you will certainly enjoy Endless Space.
Endless Space is a space 4X strategy game developed and published by AMPLITUDE Studios.  It's a sleekly presented 4X game that's something of a wonder child for the UNITY engine, and certainly proof that more complex games can be made with the engine, although it certainly also highlights some of the flaws in the engine.
The presentation is both the strongest suit of the game and also what puts some people off.  It's presented in a very clear and logical format, with items presented in a logical selection of sub-screens.  It's very clean, and that's also the crux of why it puts some people off.  Unlike Star Control 2 that had some great personality to the different races available, the presentation of racial interaction and diplomacy is just as sterile as the rest of Endless Spaces' interface.  It's unfortunate.  For some people this sinks the game.  Personally, I would say that it is certainly say what has kept a good game from being a great game, but it is still a good game regardless.  It just has an unrealised potential that could have been tapped to make it better.
Graphically, the game is indeed pretty impressive for a UNITY engine game.  Together with the polish in the interface and the gorgeous loading screen art its graphically rather impressive.  The camera view in the combat sections makes for some sweeping shots of starship combat that are quite nice.  There's certainly shinier games out there, don't get me wrong, but the game has a careful attention to the production values all the way through that shows.  The music that accompanies the game is likewise quite good.
I spend as much time on the presentation as I do because the mechanics are bog standard.  They're done competently but there's nothing particularly new to the genre here.  The one thing that is done differently from the genre standard is the combat.  It's kind of a halfway between tactical combat and simply ordering a unit to attack and getting an auto-calculated result.  Instead, you choose tactic at long range, medium range, and close range.  There are a variety of different categorizations of tactics and each tactic is strong against one category and weak against another.  So essentially it creates a paper scissors stone game in the mechanics that is kind of simplistic.  Some of them don't seem very balanced though.  There's a few you'll be to unlock after some time in the game that are just objectively better than any other tactic in the category.  Nonetheless it does add a small amount of depth to combat that is otherwise auto-calculated.
At the end of the day its a well-executed game that does the genre pretty well but doesn't have anything that really sets it apart other than the high production values.  It's certainly well-made and a good entry into the genre, however.  It just isn't going to set the world on fire.

For some reason, I thought I liked this lite RPG back when it was on iOS. I'm not really sure why that was, because playing through the PC version revealed it to be a relatively brainless and lackluster experience.
Gameplay-wise, playing a warrior class is a rather easy and boring experience, with the only interesting parts of the game being your first campaign or so, when you still have to trade off between trying to hit enemies in the head for high damage but only a 25-35% chance to hit, or hitting them in the body for normal damage 100% of the time. Quickly, however, you reach the point where your equipped weapon is good enough that you kill most enemies before they get a chance to attack you, and after that the only real threat comes from enemies who can do hundreds of damage if they get a turn. "Fortunately", though probably not for game balance, this is a game with purchasable invincibility potions that last an entire fight (or five!), making even those a fairly easy task. I can't say how it'd have been if I picked a class that focused on spellcasting, however.
The game also generally lacks in interesting loot until the last campaign, with almost everything being buyable in the store rather than being found in a dungeon, which ends up adding to the mediocre feeling, especially since the majority of the armor items only have two or three varieties, meaning that the only items that even really drop are weapons and potions. The main exception is the final campaign, which adds a bunch of weapons stronger than the previous best weapons near the end of the game... as well as a limited-use weapon called the Soul Eater that kills anything in one shot, but only has five uses. Fortunately, the blacksmith in town will repair it infinitely for free, so it really has infinite uses once you get it back to town.
Engine-wise, the game also is rather lackluster, suffering from notable slowdown if the game is left open for a while, slowing down when I attempt to purchase toolkits, having some issues with line-of-sight being drawn through solid stone blockades or other walls at times, and the last campaign giving me several crash-like bugs, where nothing in the game would respond to clicking any more, as well as outright crashes in the last mission. Also, once a mission's requirements are complete, all of the enemies get random-seeming stat boosts, making them much harder than they would be. As a result, it's almost always good to kill everything in a mission before you complete the requirements for it, which can be awkward and appears to be the result of either a bug or an undocumented (at least, so far as I could see) feature.
The story is also lacking in most places, mostly being mission descriptions that give an excuse for why you're hacking up monsters in nearly identical-looking dungeons and short in-mission blurbs often riddled with typos. The only obnoxious bit I really remember is that the final campaign ends with a cultist saying their dark god(dess?) will soon revive... and, well, that's the end of the last campaign. That said, story is clearly not supposed to be the draw of this game.
Graphically, the game is rather boring and repetitive... until the last campaign, which has some issues with the tileset at times (external walls not being visible until the inside of the building is visible in the town maps, for instance) as well as some minor issues with how tightly-packed some of the maps are, but which is way more visually impressive than the rest of the game. Unfortunately, the seven campaigns before the Black Sheep campaign have you basically going into areas that all look the same again and again. While some of this is clearly due to the HeroQuest inspiration, HeroQuest was working with the limitations of a physical board and still included custom tiles for every expansion.
Last but not least, this game loves hilariously blatant copyright violations, which I found kind of amusing - the hidden campaign is almost exactly the original 12 missions from HeroQuest translated to the game's format, and there are cameo appearances by Drizzt do'Urden, Raistlin Majere, Liliana Vess, and Sephiroth. A bunch of other stuff in the game also uses names and terms (like deity names and locations) from Dungeons & Dragons. While Hasbro/Games Workshop might frown at the Origins campaign if they knew about it, I still felt it was a cool addition. The other stuff just seems silly and unnecessary.
All in all, I can't recommend this game, mostly because almost all of the game is combat but it doesn't have a very solid combat system, instead having one that quickly devolves into "hit attack until the enemy dies, or drink a potion of invulnerability at the start of combat if it's really nasty and then hit attack until the enemy dies." The bug-ridden engine, lack of interesting loot, and general bland and repetitive feeling of 7/8 of the campaigns are also issues, but the core gameplay not being fun is the main reason this is a thumbs-down.

I began playing Dear Esther with low expectations. Even friends of mine who typically enjoy so-called "walking sims" have disliked this game, For the first 15 to 20 minutes these expectations were seemingly proving true. I began asking myself questions such as "Why am I here?" and "Who is this guy talking to me?" It didn't help that before playing Dear Esther, I had already enjoyed other, better-received "walking sims" like Edith Finch and Gone Home.
It wasn't until the second chapter that I began to appreciate the game and the third chapter loving the game. By then I realized what the game's intentions were and that they were succeeding in a very unique fashion. Dear Esther is a very unique game, and I recommend it to a certain crowds. Dear Esther's target audience seems to not be any broad group. Not even many narrative gamers would necessarily appreciate Dear Esther, as it is an art game at its core. Those who look for the art in gaming - those inspired by poetry and subtlety in design will likely appreciate this game as I have.
It helps to mention that I played the landmark edition. The environments portrayed in this edition are breathtakingly beautiful, and it's not simply because of crisp textures, but simply the lighting and colors. Yet the game succeeds in not portraying a pretty environment, but telling the story with its environment. I feel it needs to be said that I do not offer this compliment often. People praising environmental storytelling in AAA games because there are two skeletons laying on a bed together with bullets on the floor, or a diary laying around for the player to read are very direct and apparent to anyone actually paying attention to the game. Contrarily, Dear Esther has little that is obvious. While there is a narrator reading the story, the player still has to parse through his words to understand the real meaning behind what he says. The environment often serves to add to these details and even make important plot developments that aren't directly states by the narrator.
Dear Esther is a game I am certain most gamers will not enjoy. Gameplay enthusiasts will be bored. Many narrative gamers may not get into a game with a story not directly told to them. Yet I still recommend Dear Esther to most gamers as a litmus test for what gaming has the potential to be. I would certainly prefer gaming to go in the direction of Dear Esther than most AAA games. It is unique even among other walking sims, so that alone warrants a look.

After logging in about 120 hours in a little under 2 weeks, I think I can safely say I am addicted to this game.
Being a long-time fan of BattleTech and MechWarior games in the past, I was very excited when I found out about this game a few years back. I tried it then, but it failed to catch my interest. I think this was mostly due to the lack of classic mechs from those earlier games, mechs like the: Marauder, Archer, Crusader, Phoenix Hawk, Locust, Wasp, Stinger, Rifleman, and WarHammer.
Here we are a few years later and I decide to give it another chance when I see it become available on Steam. The game play is fun and the graphics are really good. There are strategic and tactical elements to the game. There are advancements for both the pilot and the mechs. Between the large variety of chassis and the numerous variations of each chassis, plus the ability to customize your builds and looks, there are a huge number of options available.
The one major thing that this game has done to capture my interest this time around is to include classic mechs from the early days of BattleTech. The Locust and Marauder are already in the game. The WarHammer, Rifleman and Archer are all on the release schedule with confirmed delivery dates. I still hope to see other classics like the Phoenix Hawk, Crusader, Wasp and Stinger eventually, but at least they now have some of the most important classic mechs available in the game.
There is a lot to grind in this game, but that is a good thing. It means you will have plenty of work to keep you motivated for the long haul. You have the option to grind any mech you want in whatever order you want. Nothing is time-gated or level-gated. If you want to pilot an Assault mech from the start you have that option without having to work your way through Light, Medium and Heavy mechs first. The boosters and bonuses you receive during your first 25 missions are more than enough to help any new player get into whatever mech they are interested in. The company also seems to do a lot of promotions offering free in-game currency and gear. I come from War Thunder, where it took me over a year of playing to unlock top tier aircraft and max out aircrews in just one of five countries. The grind in this game seems like nothing compared to that. At least with MWO you have access to everything right from the beginning.
MWO is a free to play game, but like with other such games, they do need a source of revenue. They earn this by selling early access to new content, cosmetic options, subscription time, etc. None of that is mandatory. The early access to new content is for things like new mechs, which everybody gets access to eventually anyways. The cosmetic options are nice to have, but are completely optional, and they let you earn some options during events. The subscription options are actually very beneficial if you are at all bothered by "The Grind", and give you a +50% bonus to XP and C-Bills. If you don't mind grinding content like me then you can just enjoy the journey and feel good when you complete your goals on your own merit.
In addition to your normal quick-play modes of Capture, Assault and Skirmish on numerous unique maps, there is a more advanced mode called Community Warfare. This is the mode for experienced players that have built up a collection of fully loaded mechs, understand tactics and strategy, and work together in teams. This mode is about capturing and defending planets while fulfilling contracts for the Houses of the Inner Sphere or the invading Clans. The stakes are much greater, but so too are the rewards. It will be quite a while before I am capable of participating in Community Warfare, but this seems like a excellent mode for extending a player's interest in the game. I look forward to getting involved in this mode.
I am very happy with the progress I have seen in this game since I first tried it a few years ago. It is much improved, and definitely worth playing for anybody interested in mech combat or fans of BattleTech.

Since going on Steam, I have noticed a definet lowering of skill in the player base. Namely in the Community Warfare games. I have witnessed many people shooting the gates themselves, rather than the power generator. I have seen them run off to do their own thing and get killed for it. The old problem of being shot in the back by teammates at the start of a match is back because people want to test fire.
If you want to play this game then I suggest you read the forums first. There is a wonderful section for new players. If you cannot be arsed to do that much, there is an in game tutorial about handling your mech, firing weapons and generally how to not get popped shortly after your mech is dropped on the planet. It rewards you with in game currency for doing the tutorial. Sadly, there is no tutorial covering Community Warfare, but is it really so difficult to watch what all of the other pilots are doing before rushing off to do your own thing? More importantly, is it really so important that you ignore what other pilots are telling you? Many times I have attempted to direct my team, or even just make a suggestion like "stick together, fire on the same target." I get it, I am a veteran and therefore exude some kind of aura that says "do the opposite, ignore them, blame them if it goes wrong and argue with them about their expeirence." I would think that it would not be so hard to fight against that aura, but recent evidence is proving me wrong.
Are there problems with this game? Sure, it has glitches. Namely, I find that I crash when I play it through Steam. Sometimes there are problems with the maps and I get stuck with certain chassis in particular spots, or I get stuck rubber banding. These things happen. But worse than any glitches, is the new player base. Learn to pilot your multi-ton death machine to the benefit of your team, or take off the neuro-helm and find something else.

I've played World Of Tanks Blitz (WoT Blitz) since the Beta on my tablet. It was great, I got far enough to have a Tier X heavy tank.
Many are criticizing Wargaming for not giving them the PC version on Steam. Fair enough. But the reviews should be about THIS VERSION, not about some other game.
I think bringing WoT Blitz to Windows and OS X is a fantastic idea. Controlling the tanks with the keyboard and mouse is an improvement over the touch controls of the mobile version. By making the game cross-platform, it's really easy to continue your progress either on your computer, or on your tablet or phone.
One other major benefit of bringing the mobile game on the computers and not the other way around is that the game is very optimized to work on low powered low performance devices, so the game runs very smooth on pretty old computers and on laptops with sub-standard video cards for today's power-hungry games.
One other thing I like about this version is the game dynamics. With smaller maps and smaller number of players per match than WoT, the matches are shorter, but with more action (there's a lower level of camping than in WoT).
The development of new tank trees is pretty slow, and nowhere near the WoT Version.
The devs don't solve bugs very fast. I remember I stopped playing the mobile version for about six months or more, because they had a bug (which I reported on their forums) where every time you'd enter the game you'd be spam with friend invites from people you have blocked. :) On this version I found that, even though it says that a person is blocked, I can still see the spammer's/troll's messages on chat. :) The idea is not to expect for bugs to be fixed rapidly.
Some UI things are akward or lacking functionality: upside down chat history, friends can be seen somewhere in the chat page, no action on people directly from the chat (like friend invites).
There is still no Linux version, even though there is a OS X version (meaning there's somekind of openGL code that should work perfectly fine on Linux).
Also, they could improve the graphics options for computers. For example, on the iPad everything looks much better than on my PC, because it's rendering at a higher resolution. They could add an option to render at 2x, 3x the resolution, so the visuals look way better, even on low ress screens.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who wants almost the same fun that WoT offers, but in smaller chunks. It's great for people that are on the move, which may play on their gaming PC at home, but also on their laptop or mobile devices.

A retro themed speed runner which all from Casuals to Pros can enjoy, Flem is an interesting, chirpy, level-based platformer with an occasional cold heart.
✓ Nice amount of levels with varying difficulties each with a good level flow for speed running
✓ Fast deaths, resets and a stable framerate ensure the game doesn't hold you back when you're speed running
✓ Challenging gold medal times keep the game challenging while remaining fair, realistic and achievable even for casual players
✓ Level by level global leaderboards to fuel competition
✓ Nostalgic platforming gameplay with interesting power ups providing some neat and fun areas
✓ Music fits the gameplay nicely and doesn't draw too much attention
✓ Has good controller support with easy to pick up controls
✗ Some levels have projectiles spawning off screen which make it difficult to dodge when they appear, this happens in the first set of levels and made me hate that certain type of enemy pretty quickly.
✗ Difficulty spikes throughout, nothing too huge until the Fall season where it seems to skyrocket at a certain point.
✗ The game doesn't teach the player much at all, the game is easy to pick up but there are some parts not so clear.
✗ Sound was rather quiet by default
~ Considering there are 40 levels over 4 Seasons and I’m towards the end of the third season (when writing this), I can say the game is rather short to play through. That being said, the game is highly re-playable and being a speed runner you'll be back improving on your previous times to get the gold medal or place in the leaderboards which will extend the games length by quite some time.
~ Visuals can be repetitive but it adds to the retro style
~ Doesn't make use of the analog stick - DPad only for movement. Having analog support would be nice but I don't believe it's required, I never felt like the Dpad was holding me back.
~ Keyboard controls are odd at first honestly but can be rebinded in the menu if needed.

For Gameplay and First Impressions:
+:
-The visuals pass in terms of at least being doable to a certain extent.
-The basics are there at least. The very basics.
-:
-Control implementation is a problem, with only the dpad being available for the controller, in a game that needs precision.
-Level design includes leaps of faith and off screen projectiles that will frustrate.
-Not enough Variety leadss to boring missions.
-Weird spikes in difficulty curve happen and don't naturally teach and progress the player.
-Blending blue and green that naturally blend into each other makes it an odd choice for the base color of the protagonist, as he blends into the background. Green's complement, something like Magenta, would have made a lot more sense.
-Doesn't really offer anything substanial. Nothing new or interesting, or solid in nature.
Flem does attempt to be a speedrunner, but basic elements of level design and layout show a game that doesn't have the elements to appeal to its core audience. Leap of Faith gameplay combined with off screen projectiles can frustrate the player, while precision with jumping due to using the dpad with a controller for an example hinders the experience. Not enough variety occurs within the first hour and a half and made me want to play a game like JumpJet Rex for a speedrunner fix.

I unfortunately have to change my Recommended to a Not Recommended given an announcement for the game's future that just happened today.
I didn't mind Unbound being added to the game at all because it was giving Hirez the opportunity to make more money from the game while also expanding the playerbase. I don't have to play in the one mode that is Unbound only. I can play in all the other modes that offer Bound, or are Bound only. Again, OB64, which introduced Unbound, also gave all cards to all players, which made all Bound modes more fair than they've ever been, since prior you had to grind or buy those cards.  Now the card system is only unfair (barring all the huge balance issues, that is) if you choose to play in Unbound modes.  Hence, I didn't have an issue with the OB64 changes.
But, the current game modes still need a lot of attention for proper balance to occur.  Not only that, but there are plenty of unaddressed bugs in all existing game modes that have yet to be addressed, and bugs in general seem to be getting addressed at a snail's pace.  Now they have announced that they are removing Payload to replace with a Team Deathmatch mode, and they are also adding a PUBG style "Battleground" mode.
So now instead of having a lot of work to be done to balance three game modes (King of the Hill [Onslaught], Unbound Siege, Classic Siege/Ranked), we have five. And the two new additions aren't just slight spins on the existing modes. This is a game that was designed from the ground up to be a Overwatch style game (though before Overwatch was known to the Hirez team), a team MOBA FPS capture-and-push game. Team Deathmatch and especially a "Battlegrounds" mode are entirely different gamestyles that this game just isn't going to fit naturally into. So they will need even more work to balance for, than the existing modes do that are still a far cry from being balanced.  And if you balance the game for a Battlegrounds mode, it's not going to be balanced for "Capture and Push" modes.  And if you balance for "Capture and Push", is isn't  going to be balanced in a Battlegrounds mode.
They already have a lot of difficulty balancing since the card system makes this virtually impossible given all the possible combinations for loadouts people can have.  But they could have focused and eventually had something that worked.  Now they're putting the game in an impossible spot as far as balance goes.  It's never going to work now.
I don't understand what it is they're trying to do with the game anymore. This gives me the impression they aren't certain either, like they're throwing more on the wall (and taking Payload off of it, by the way) to see what sticks, because they're deciding to reduce focus on what's already there for some reason.
This late in an Open Beta, it's a pretty huge shift to suddenly be throwing in a Battlegrounds mode especially.  Imagine if 65% of the way through development, PUBG decided to become an Overwatch-style shooter. The inverse is what's happening here, except since they're going to continue to develop for all existing modes in the process, like, this is impossible!  I don't know what happened, but this game was already... it was already being built towards something great.  It was going to take time but this is it's like a bipolar development mentality.  I can't wrap my head around this.

I tried this out for a while and didn't enjoy it.  The controls for placing and orienting blocks are very clumsy, and to build anything above chest height you typically need to use the awkward jetpack.  It's very difficult to orient and snap things in place when you're trying to fly with the jetpack or balance on a wall while placing lego blocks, and I grew to hate the process.    Frankly, it's difficult and awkward even while standing still on ground level, and very time-consuming.  It's especially frustrating that you're limited to working with a single block at a time -- you can't grab a group of blocks and move them like you could with real blocks, and the tedium of aligning and placing each block with the really unreliable controls just sucked.
After making a small room-sized building, I realized just how limited the blocks really are.  There's not a lot of interesting pieces, and it takes forever to work with even the pieces you're given to make anything.  Making even basic stuff takes an unreasonably long time because of the unreliable alignment and orientation (requiring very specific adjustments to camera angle with each block placed).  If you want to spend time creatively crafting a world, I recommend Minecraft instead as it's a lot more streamlined and there are a lot more block types and effects.  If you love legos, go buy some real ones, because this clumsy game just doesn't have the satisfying feeling of playing with legos in real life, and the process is so awkward and slow it will take you an unreasonably long time to do anything.
The cart racing was mildly interesting for a round or two, but lag was crippling and the game became rapidly un-fun and un-playable, even on a low-lag server.  Once you fall into one of the many instant-death traps or pits, you have to sit and wait for the round to end (and lag usually makes sure you die sooner than later, but even without lag, the controls are terrible).  Also, you can't really do much with your cart -- building cool custom stuff on wheels just isn't available, and you apparently only get to select from pre-designed carts each round.  You appear to be able to make custom levels, and a few people have gone to the trouble, but the cart game itself is so clunky that the environments don't add much.  And most of the environments I saw were pretty boring and undetailed, which isn't surprising given the work it takes to do basic stuff.
Frankly, I have trouble taking the preview images on the store page seriously.  To do that in minecraft would take a few hours; to do it in blockland would take a few weeks.  It makes me wonder if the people making those images used external tools to build the worlds, instead of the clunky in-game process.
Last of all... the community is unpleasant.  There were a few nice people, but many people on multiplayer servers devote every second of their day to harassing other players, and this appeared to be actively encouraged.  They picked the most spammy, disruptive weapons and a victim and fired at him nonstop.  The super-spammer rocket launcher didn't destroy what I was trying to build, but it made progressing further impossible because my screen shook like crazy and the effects blinded me.  I felt that I was wasting my time playing on a server where someone can just hop on and start harassing me without reason, and it's not fun playing alone.  It takes too long to build anything, and you walk away feeling like the time you spent was wasted.  There are a lot of builder games out there, including early access stuff that's much more advanced than this (e.g. Space Engineers & Minecraft).
Give this one a pass.  I wasted time trying it, I wasted friends' time trying it.  We all walked away disappointed and feeling cheated.  Ignore the pretty advertisement pictures; even if you had the patience to someday craft that with the bad controls and obnoxious griefers, you won't walk away satisfied or having enjoyed the process.  Game is not as advertised.

Interesting, fun, and relaxing. That's how I'd describe this dungeon crawler.
I love dungeon crawlers but sometimes don't like to stress out over the layers of complexity that many DC'ers (Dungeon Crawlers) use to flesh out the basic concept of the game.
This one, on the other hand, is a relaxful, stress-free dungeon crawler that can be played just for a few minutes to many hours. A good game to de-stress with after work or school or just for some no brain drain relaxful dungeon crawling.
Especially good since most dungeons are a single layer/screen size. So they're nice "bite-sized" chunks that can be done in 15 minutes or so.
All-in-all, a good non-pretentious game for those who enjoy dungeon crawlers but don't want to spend a lot of time micro-managing.

This game has received many negative reviews – mostly because the graphics are old, and the base game doesn't have much if you don't like building. Some points to know if you want this game:
1. This game is old. And I mean really old – it started back around '02. It's changed tremendously since then, but it's no longer receiving updates. This means that the community os slowly dying.
2. This game doesn't run too well on iMacs. You can play it fine, without any lag, as long as all the settings are turned down, which hinders the already-not-so-great graphics.
3. The community isn't too great. Eventually, the game is gonna die, which is a sad thought, but it will last for some years yet.
Now, that being said, I love this game. It's like being turned into a Lego Man and thrown into a pile of bricks. In fact, that's the whole premise of the game! You can build anything you want – and trust me, the community has done some awesome things – and it's not too difficult to get your head around.
Not only that, but the addon (a form of mod that is official) library for this game is MASSIVE!
Hop on over to
for the best ones, and they're easy to install. This makes an already huge game massive. The many servers (some of the best being Boss Battles and Tez's Prison Escape) have taken advantage of these addons to make some very enjoyable experiences.
I would recommend this game to anyone who loves being creative. You'll spend countless hours on this game, even though the developer has moved on.
That's the 'official' sounding review.
My personal view?
It makes me feel like I'm a Lego Man, and I can make castles, battle arenas, ships, cities - anything.
I love this game with all my heart - I'll not stop playing it for some time.
One little warning:
The community isn't too great. Be careful where you go. :)
Have fun, and don't stop building.

I can't with good conscience recommend this game to anyone. It's a straight mobile port. It does well to adapt to different resolutions but the art used in the game really doesn't stand up to being brought up to HD. The asthetics the art goes for though are pretty lovely, I have to admit. It evokes the themes of the old HeroQuest boardgame mixed in with the classic old fantasy art tropes of that era, which I think looks fantastic. A little silly, but there's nothing wrong with light hearted fun!
Fun though is something this game lacks. The primary gameplay is wandering through a tile-based dungeon, bumping into enemies and then fighting them one on one. No matter how many enemies are in a room, you will never face them at the same time. They'll get in line and take turns being beaten up by you. What groups of monsters do is give something they call a 'gang' buff; when you get into a fight with a monster that has other monsters close by, it gets a +50% buff. I'm not sure what exactly gets buffed, if it's a specific stat or just straight up all of them, but they do get noticably tougher.
Dealing with them doesn't change, however. You just click until they die. You drink a potion every once in a while if you're taking damage, or you can use a spell charge if you're feeling fancy, but that's really it. Whether you play the Assassin, the Water Demon or the Ninja, you'll be doing the same exact thing, using the same tactics. All that changes between them is that some have access to different types of gear from shops, but even then the gear doesn't add anything but flavour. It's all just pure stat bonuses; a bonus to attack or a bonus to defense.
If you play this game for more than five to ten minutes it quickly becomes terribly boring. The game is best enjoyed, I believe, in short bursts on a cellphone or a tablet, where it shines. There the lack of tactics don't mean much because you're just grabbing it for a tiny bit. Kill a few monsters, do a quest, get some gold and get a little tougher. The utter lack of depth is completely fine in that setting. It's ironic then that the cellphone version is less than half the current price (at the time of writing) than the PC version.
Right now the game is being sold for $5.99 with a -15% special promotion that drops it down to $5.09. Meanwhile you can get the game for your Android at $1.99. No joke. You're paying $3 extra ($4 after the sale ends on March 10th) for a far inferior experience, which I find terribly dishonest. I don't know why mobile ports feel like they have to charge double or triple or quadruple the mobile prices. Oh well!
All in all, I suggest you give this a pass. If you're a fan of boardgames, this does not invoke any of the old joys of HeroQuest or its ilk. It's not a good RPG, or adventure, or a good exploration. Check out the mobile version instead.

It's been an old school dungeon delving feast of late with the release of Warhammer Quest, Dark
Quest, Runers, Darkest Dungeon, continuous updates of Desktop Dungeons and so many other ways to punch and be punched by monsters it drives a grizzled veteran to  glorious distraction. Right before turning last night at 5 AM I decided to check Steam one more time.  And what do I fnd but a glorious gem called Mighty Dungeons! As one old wizard once said, "stay awhile and listen." [NOTE: Sorry Blizzard, I'm dead broke so even if you do try to sue me for using a line, you won't get a cent. Besides, I'm protected by the academic fair use clause AND the Malodorous Ring of Power Against Megacorporations so, bite me].
Wow, where to begin? I don't write reviews as a sort of list as I am too addle pated so intead I'll
write a review. [Get on with it! - ed.].What we have here intrepid Steamers is an unabashed love letter to boardgame classics like the legendary Heroquest and that is a Very Good Thing (TM). Veterans know the ropes of course: complete quests by punching monsters and finding Important Stuff (TM). The game comes with 8 campaigns each with 8 to 12 quests per campaign. It's Heroquest mashed together with Dungeonmaster and apologies to you young'uns out there that have the addled notion that Skyrim is the only game in town.
You want heroes? You got 'em with a bucketload of choices from warriors and elves to murderin' maulin' minotaurs (I love alliteration), and if you are feeling especially murderous you can be a demon and almost anything else in between. Each hero has her/his strengths and weaknesses and because there are so many choices, replayability is high out of the gate. Additionally, you can repeat quests as often as you like but with each repeat the monsters get significantly tougher and the rewards diminish to prevent over farming for gold runs. Of course in gamer speak that means that one MUST repeat quests because the developer has thrown down the proverbial gauntlet. ;)
The game started life in iOS land. But wait, don't run away! This version has been made PC worthy by ramping up the difficulty, full screen resolution support AND the ability to create new content for the game! I should state that there is no level editor per se included but creating content is VERY easy and if you visit
you will find all kids of guides. That said, the developer indicated that he is working on uploading some tools to Steam Workshop. I can only imagine what twisted mightiness will emerge from the sick.. errrr.. I mean BRILLIANT minds that haunt Steam.
You can make this game play as you like it. Do you want to play it as a roguelike with all the odds against you an permadeath? Tick off the appropriate boxes and die - a lot. It could be however that you had a really crappy day at work or you want to punch your professor for assigning a 50 page paper on Hegel's Reason in History that's due in two days. Well then, tick off the godlike option and slay all in your path. You won't get your paper done but at least you won't be jailed for trying to faceroll your professor.
Do not let the games iOS looks deceive you. The boardgame style serves a purpose in that it focuses on the most important component in any game, namely, game play.
Quite a long review for a game that only costs a fiver but this game is so very content rich and I haven't even scratched the surface. It costs less than a Starbuck's coffee and you don't have to deal with a cranky barista. The developer is VERY active on the community hub and get this: there was a gamer who couldn't choose between this or Dark Quest. The developer told the gamer to buy Dark Quest to support a fellow indie developer THEN e-mail him and he would give the gamer a free Steam key for Mighty Dungeons.
This my friends is the kind of developer that deserves support. He releases a wonderful game for a song, helps out a competing developer, and a member of the community.
May the fleas of a thousand camels infest your [insert area here] if you don't buy this.

________________________________________________________________________________
Endless Space is a game by AMPLITUDE Studios were you start as an empire in space with a single planet, and your goals are either to become the strongest nation and conquer everything, become scientifically advanced that you reach the Endless stage and win, or colonize a ton of the galaxy so no one else has a chance. This game requires a ton of thought. I'm going to put it plainly, it really does require a large amount of thought with it, but let's not start the review there. Let's start at the learning curve, and the fact that if you were to graph it that it would be a steep climb, then a flat line. When you first start the game, you don't get a tutorial, all you get is tool tips. These wont help you any because they barely explain anything at all so it will take you, depending on the type of gamer you are, anywhere from 30 minutes to a few hours. This can push a few people away, but after you get past that you will love the game for what it is possibly. Key word being possibly. +6 Rating
________________________________________________________________________________
Lets move on to the games factions. There are several factions in game that you can play as, or if you get Disharmony you can create your own faction. These factions are; United Empire, Sophons, Hissho, Amoeba, Cravers, Horatio, Sowers, Pilgrims, Sheredyn, Automatons, and Harmony.
The United Empire is a faction that just loves to expand and attack the weaker. They love to expand, but they don't expand quickly. If you're playing against them I would recommend you quickly grab your border systems so that they can't push in. U.E. can gather a military at a moderate place, but doesn't have the strongest military. The U.E. gets its military from its economy, and the economy from its colonies so if you want to destroy them quickly, don't allow them the colonies they want. If the U.E. sees a faction weaker than it that has a small military, and it doesn't think it would be able to defend itself well they will attack so be prepared.
The Sophons are a scientific faction that prefers Isolation unlike the U.E. counterparts. If you play as a nation that focuses almost entirely on your military you should make these people part of your alliance as they will give you some things they research for your dust.
The Hissho are a big problem when it comes to military as they don't like anyone most of the time. The Hissho will have a strong military that will become a pest if you don't try to get rid of it quickly, but they do research slowly. If you play a scientific nation become allies with these people. They will protect you for what you research.
The Amoeba are a faction of peace, but they colonize extremely quickly. Their people are happier whenever they are at peace with a faction, or a few factions. The Amoeba can quickly gather the Dust to prepare for war. If you are in need of dust, make sure you're on these guys good side, as they are very nice about giving it to you if you are.
The Cravers are a war monging, money hogging, system conquering faction. They are fun to play as, but they can not be in any alliances. Period. Don't even try to be nice with them.
The Horatio like to expand, and go to war when it comes to defense, or if they feel provoked. There isn't much to be said about them besides what I just said here.
The Sowers are an odd nation to say the least. They are a machine race that will either build a wonder to victory, or just attempt to conquer everyone else. This is literally all I can say for them until I get a better notice of how they play.
The Pilgrims are like the Horatio, and like to expand. They are a bit more like America in a sense though, they can be a bit unpredictable in some games as they have a good research rate, a good military, and a good ability to colonize systems. With all of this though comes the odd economy, it's definitely an interesting faction to play as, or with.
The Sheredyn is very likely to make an alliance with the United Empire, as according to lore they were at first the United Empires body guards for the Emporer. They are a very strong nation for military as they make it impossible for an enemy to retreat. They also have a pretty good economy at times. This is possibly one of the easiest factions to play as, but one of the harder ones to play against. That is my own opinion though.
The Automatons are a nation of building. Just building. They can do a weird resource gather thing if they aren't building anything, and if something large comes along to build that would take any other nation about 10-15 Turns the Automatons can likely do it 5-10 turns. This also gives them the ability to spam ships out sometimes.
Lastly the Harmony. They don't have an economy, and can populate systems rather quickly. They don't believe in using money because it can supossedly corrupt them. This means if you want to build anything you can't buy it out. Ever. They require patience when it comes to military. Calling them odd is the nicest thing to say as I could go even farther than calling the "Exuberantly weird" +15 Rating

The game starts out as one of the many free-to-play games that you are interested by, and decide "why the hell not" and download. It's fun, for a bit, once you start getting angel investors you really start to take the game seriously and play to great extents.
Through the many upgrades, resetting to claim the investors, and launching to the moon and mars, the game always finds a new way to try to hook you in. And it worked for me, for a little while at least.
There comes a point in AdVenture Capitalist that it just isn't fun anymore. It's basically a cycle of resetting, buying back everything, unlocking new "unlocks" and repeating. There isn't any variety, unless you decide to do one of the 3-day events (which are pretty much the exact same way, and they don't happen often) or you buy gold to speed up the processes.
The game is designed for profit, and once there's no fun in the game and it's very slow to unlock new things, they know that you will be forced to buy gold or pretty much just leave the game on your computer until you come back a month later and have a ton of profits. These gold upgrades cost real money, and it's going to drain your wallet if you're impatient for upgrades- like many people are that have probably purchased gold or wanted to get ahead on the leaderboards in events.
If you're looking for a tycoon-style game, don't go with Adventure Capitalist. There are many more, as well as free, options on the Steam market that are more focused on the player experience. I'll only play until I have all the achievements, then another game thrown into the virtual game recycle bin.

Well, I personally don't really like shooter games in general (as a matter of fact this is the only one I play regularly) but this is a lot of fun. The game claims there are billions of possible guns, but of course the obvious response is "oh yeah I bet most of them are useless". However, there are probably around 30 viable types of gun, each with plenty of possible tweaks and variations. In total, there are probably around 1,000 different combinations that are used by most players. The game is surprisingly well balanced considering the level of possible customisation, and it offers really unusual options depending on how you want to play. For instance, I once played a game where someone on my team had a sniper rifle that fired healing rounds, and just looked around for any skirmishes going on and made sure nobody on our team died.
The gameplay and art style can best be described as TF2 on lots of crack. Firefights are very fast, characters are very mobile and many of the maps are quite enclosed. By way of gamemodes, Loadout takes standard shooter ideas and tweaks them slightly. The mode Jackhammer, for instance, is based on capture the flag, but this time the flag is a giant hammer, and the more kills you get using it before bringing it to your base, the more points you score. There are 5 gamemodes for normal matches, ranked matches feature a special gamemode which is effectively the all the other gamemodes mashed together.
As a free-to-play, there are plenty of purchasable cosmetic items, however all gun parts can be obtained fairly quickly using earnable currency. Weapon saveslots are limited however, and while considerable grind is needed to unlock more than 3, there are only 5 that can be unlocked without resorting to purchases. That said, at no stage have I ever felt as if I was being put at a disadvantage against other players by not spending money, and I was able to obtain parts for the guns I wanted to use after around 6 games. Also, there is a rare chance once per day that you may get a cosmetic item for free, which is nice.
The only real issue I have regarding this game is the slightly worrying privacy policy. I made a new gmail address to create my account with, as I'm not completely sure what the game is capable of doing. I've not noticed anything untoward since downloading the game, but I think it's reasonable to make people aware of this.

Dear Esther is certainly not a game for everyone, but I feel like it’s very transparent about who will like it and who should rather play something else. It takes less than two hours to complete, goes out of its way to obfuscate its (not overly complicated) story, and offers no gameplay mechanics outside of walking and an option to slightly zoom in. Nevertheless, the game's landscape is picturesque, I found the story compelling enough to not lose interest within the first fifteen minutes, and even if you should at some point wonder why in the world you would continue slouching around the island at the speed of a drowsy tortoise, Jessica Curry's hauntingly beautiful soundtrack will probably pull you right back in. If you can accept the slow pace and will accept the fact that Dear Esther asks more questions than it answers, I think it’s very much worth your time.

First off this is a walking simulator and the only thing you can do is walk around and explore the island. If this does not sound like your type of game, then I would not recommend playing it. However, I enjoyed this game because the atmosphere was captivating, the voiceover was great, and the music was beautiful and fit the game perfectly. It took me 3 playthroughs to complete the story, developer's commentary, and all the achievements. Each time you play the voiceovers may be different, which adds some replay value. I would recommend playing this game for the story and atmosphere.
