Disregard my time played: I've been with this game since launch about 2 years ago, and have sunk hundreds of hours into it.
Right, so, where to begin...
As soon as the game came out, I was instantaneously disappointed. I, and a lot of other fans of the BattleTek and MW franchise wanted Mechwarrior 5.
This is, by no means, Mechwarrior 5.
Go google Mechwarrior: Living Legends. THAT, is what MW5 should have been like.
*Ahem*
Anywho, so, yes, this is not the game we wanted, however it is a pretty decent game in it's own rights.
Prior to the steam release, the game was much, much more P2W.
You used to make 20-30k cbills a match, maybe 50k if you were good. That meant it took eons to save up for mechs you could "easily" just buy with cash. There were also a lot of mech variants that were marginally better, that were only available for cash. I played it anyway cause, hey, Mechwarrior.
Now that it's on steam, it's roughly 200% better in my opinion. I get minimum 100k cbills a match (even if I lose), and up to 400k if I have a good run. That's quite a bit more, and allows me to play around with my loadouts, and get more mechs sooner. Makes the game much less of a grind.
So, would I recommend?
6 months ago: No.
Now: YES.
Here's some tips for new players:
DO NOT WASTE YOUR STARTING CBILLS ON AN 11MIL ASSAULT MECH. Go for something cheaper, so you still have room to mess with the loadout. People always choose the assault mechs, such as the Atlas, because they look bada$$, are freakin huge, and look like they could just tank and destroy everyone.
If you believe that, prepare to be let down. Even the mighty Atlas or Direwolf are not tanks. Go with a light mech if you prefer a faster, hit and run/bugger the heck out of the enemy playstyle, or a medium or possibly heavy if you prefer more of a DPS/somewhat-tanking role.
DO YOUR RESEARCH
The first mech I bought was a Banshee variant. Was about 8mil cbills if I recall. Thing looked like it could pack quite a bit of power in and seemed well armoured.
After purchasing, I realized it only had Laser hardpoints. Not  bad thing in of itself, but for a tanking mech like that, all-laser builds do not fare very well. No matter what build I tried, I never found one that i was satisfyed with. So I sold it.
SELLING A MECH GETS YOU ROUGHLY 1/4-1/2 THE CBILLS BACK. So make sure you research the mech you're interested in, look up builds, because choosing the wrong mech can be costly.
DON'T EVERYONE BE AN LRM BOAT. An LRM boat is a mech that holds only, or mostly LRM's (long-range missiles). Yes, they're fantastic for surpressing the enemy or providing extra support to the front line mechs, but I've been seeing more and more matches recently with 6-7 (out of 12 total teammates) Maddogs or Catapults (clan and IS lrm boats). As you can imagine, having the majority of your team be artillary does not work very well.
PICK A MECH AND STICK WITH IT. This goes along with what I said earlier, but it adds more. Staying with one mech will benefit you much more than having a load of them. Once you learn how to play a mech, and play it well, and create your perfect loadout, the game gets 1000% more fun. Seriously. Once you get your insanely fast light mech and start running around the enemies shredding the armour and destroying them, or once you get your beefy assault/heavy mech and partake in glorious close-mid range all out brawls? That's where this game shines. I found my perfect mech a couple weeks ago, the Arctic Cheeta ACH-B.
Got my perfect loadout, and I've maxed out it's efficiencies. Even though I've now nothing to work towards with it (nothing to unlock for it), just messing about with different loadouts is fun. And playing the thing? It's fantastic, I love the hit and run style it allows for.
GAME DOESN'T RUN WELL? You see those minimum specs down there? Disregard them. You see those recommended specs down there? Disregard them too. I run an FX-6300, 6 core, OC'd to 4.1ghz, R9 270x 2gb (slightly better than a GTX 750ti), 16 gb 1600mhz ram, and an SSD, displaying to a 1920x1080 monitor. I average 50-60 fps, drop down to 30-40 when it hits the fan. On low graphics. Now, imo, the game looks the same on all graphic settings, so I highly suggest you just go with minimal graphics. This is one of those games where 30 and sometimes even sub 30 FPS is playable, however, if you play a light mech, you need the fastest response time you can get, so 60 FPS would be best.
USE VOICE COMMS. AGAIN, USE. VOICE. COMMS.
Play a match where your team just communicates with text chat, or not at all, to a game where your team talks with VOIP, and you'll see a large difference. When VOIP comes in to play, that's when the real fun happens. Tactics, strategy, mid-game banter with your 'mates. The community is quite friendly from what I've seen too, I've never had a bad 'mate on VOIP. Even if only to say "Assault lance advanding delta 6" or such every so often, use voice comms. It makes the match so, so much better.
I hope this review and some of these tips helped you, and I'm glad to see new players to this game from steam!

--- Your torso moves separate from legs, and some Mechs have Jump Jets, which allow short flight depending on the number of JJ's equipped.
--- Stay with the pack, especially when you first start. Don't be the only Mech the enemy sees.
In standard "Quick Play" game you drop in one Mech, after you die, you will have to wait until that game is finished before you can play that Mech again. In Faction Play (Clan Warfare) you get to drop with 4 Mechs.
--- Movement and turn speeds are based on the Mech you are in, not the speed you set your mouse to.
---The speed difference alone between the fastest and slowest Mech is over 100kph, leading to huge variations in play style. Aside from this, Lasers, Ballistics/PPCs, Long Range Missiles (LRMs), and Short Range Missiles (SRMs) all have different methods to success.
---  If you "spray and pray", you will get damage in, but fail to kill your opponent. Targeting vital spots is key to putting the enemy down. Let your lasers burn the whole duration into your opponent to get full damage. The opposite is true if you are getting shot, make sure to turn your torso to spread damage.
--- Almost all weapons create heat on use, and if not managed will put you into a shutdown state, or if you override the shutdown, do extreme internal damage.
--- Setting your Mech up with weapons and armor of your choosing is the one of the best parts of the game, but you don't get to do that until you buy your own Mech. This does not mean you have to spend real money however, as they give you large bonuses for the first 20 or so matches. Do make your first choice wisely, the forums are a good place to get suggestions.
--- You can get a lot out of this game for free. The way you earn money (C-bills) to buy Mechs is by playing more matches, so I can't really consider it a grind. You do need to have Mech Bays in order to buy Mechs however, and these cost MC, which is real money currency.  If you are patient PGI does give away MC and Mech Bays during special events for participation, and task competition. Some Mechs, called Hero Mechs can only be purchased with MC, the only thing that makes them worthwhile is a bonus to C-bill earning, otherwise they are mostly just novelty paint, on a somewhat unique loadout, however never really better than what you can buy normally. If you do want to spend money, I suggest buying MC in a quantity that gets a good discount and buying Mech Bays when they go on sale.
--- The Match Maker works fairly well, though it is population dependent. If you are new, you will start at the bottom "Tier" which is 5. As you move up, not only does individual skill ramp up, but so does group cooperation.
NGNG has a good youtube channel if you want to see some gameplay.

I really wanted to like this game. The art is beautiful. I'm a sucker for space. The trailer captivated me. The game seemed to scratch all the right issues, but it's not enough. After 20 hours, I found myself bored.
The game has variable difficulty, but even the normal difficulty is really difficult and incredibly grindy.  The combat just gets old. Everynow and then you get a new power or something, and it's neat for a bit, but this ultimately feels like a game of cat and mouse. This colony is being attacked. Send your ship. Defeat the intruders. Repeat until a plot point happens. The plot point will just be going to attack somebody. The combat is just kind of dull after a bit. It's not that there's no strategy, it's that the strategy is obvious. One ship is vulnerable to x or y and resistant to everything else, so that's what it gets hit with. There's just not enough choice.
In combat, you have three ships. They do too. Each of your ships has between 3 and 6 different attacks that will do some combination of damaging the enemy, healing/protecting your allies, and inflicting statuses on the enemy. What the statuses do is never really well defined. I still don't know what "Crew panic" does. If these battles seemed consequential, it might be okay, butt he biggest thing about this game is that so few of the battles seem consequential. It's whack-a-mole, but each whack takes 5-10 minutes.
In the midst of this, you'll do some improvements to your base, but the improvements are less choice and more following directions. You're free to explore the tech tree, but doing so resulted in not having enough resources when the plot dictates you research something else.
Sometimes there are cool sectors that pop up with story events, but it's not at all uncommon to never be able to explore them because if you do, you'll lose several colonies.
Ultimately, this game doesn't feel like it's something you're intended to win. If you fall behind, it's game over, and you know it's game over, but the game doesn't. You can either start over, again, or play for a couple extra hours hoping to squeeze out one more plot point before the game tells you it's over. Halcyon 6 a castle defense game that's trying to be a 4x game, and it doesn't excel at either.

I never write reviews but this game deserved one. I picked this game up this morning and finally put it down 9 hours later after what amounts to the opening chapter. It's exactly what it wants to be, an amazing blend of FTL, Star Trek, Xcom and large scale space sims, with none of the depth of any one of these things, but fusing them together into one epic space story.
The combat, a classic final-fantasy style system, is based around managing debuffs on enemies to combo for maximum damage. It's simple on the surface, with enough depth that most fights aren't dull grinds and require some careful teambuilding to work around the RNG of weapon disruptions, for example.
The space management is simpler still, with a basic array of resources spots you can place or recover colonies from, and a few upgrades for each. I would say this is the weakest part of the game, but it lends context to everything else. When you lose a ship it hurts making tough fights intensely stressful. The big bad aliens continually sends waves to harass your colonies, forcing you to manage your defensive and offensive groups carefully, or be stretched too thin with one group.
One of my favorite moments,
Finally the story. The diplomatic relations between races are inventive, funny and bring you into the world. The missions are given a lot of context, even if the core combat gameplay is generally go here, kill that. It feeds new characters, stories and neat missions at a great pace, and I hope the well animated characters and little plotlines don't slow down as I go further into the game.
All in all, if you enjoyed FTL, I think this is a must buy. It's the first single-player game to capture my attention for a very long time and it brings back memories of all the final fantasy games I loved. Get it, have fun.
I'm not a shill, but will gladly accept a huge payment from the developers, or anyone.

Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander (2016) is a retro space strategy RPG developed and published by Massive Damage, Inc. for the PC, Mac OS X, Linux, and SteamOS.
Humanity has become an advanced space-faring race united under The New Terran Federation and plays an important economic, military, and political role in the galaxy (sounds familiar).  One day, however, the Federation establishes contact with a mysterious alien race.  Soon after, almost all colonies and fleets across Federation space drop out of contact.  Only “Halcyon 6,” an ancient alien station, remains as the sole known operational Federation facility.  You are left as the ranking officer in charge of the station and all remaining Federation forces.  You must maintain diplomatic relations with other sentient spacefaring species, reestablish contact with any remaining Federation outposts, and unearth the true nature of this mysterious race.
The plot has a simple premise, and the game typically does not obsess over providing intricate backstories for every faction.  In fact, the game’s writers seem keen on poking light fun at several tropes in sci-fi shows and RPGs.  Nonetheless, it offers ample choice regarding which factions to befriend, which events in space to partake in, which battles to fight, and etc.  Your decisions will have positive or negative consequences for your relationships with other factions.  Push a faction’s anger over the limit, and you may find yourself fighting a new enemy.  You must decide how to proceed as Halcyon 6’s starbase commander, and the game’s multiple endings reflect your decisions’ impacts on the future of the Federation and other factions.
Rating: fair
The gameplay combines simple territorial expansion aspects, traditional turn-based battle mechanics, and base management.  Multitasking is CRUCIAL to creating a thriving Federation network that will support you in the battles to come.  It is therefore wise to increase your team of officers, important personnel for commanding warships and directing various tasks on- and off-base.
Halcyon 6 is situated on the edge of Federation space, close to the edges of other factions’ zones of control.  Factions can request for aid, assault the station, or even attack one another, letting you decide where and when to intervene.  Within Federation space, you manage several sectors by recommissioning abandoned/ruined sectors, retrieving resources, and improving facilities to increase resource production.  Sectors may fall under attack, and you’ll have to decide whether to repel the assailants or evacuate the sectors.  In addition, the Halcyon 6 station comes with its own events and research/construction projects that can provide various benefits when completed.  The station contains several sections can be fitted with various facilities for power, ship construction, ship repairs, officer training, and etc.  Planning facility construction beforehand can help you streamline the base expansion process and allow you to make use of your initially limited construction space.
The key to success in Halcyon 6 is learning to pick your battles and time your fleet deployments while keeping up-to-date with ships and research.  Some enemy groups are tough and require some preparation before combat, while other enemies are easily brushed over.  Getting into the habit of checking enemy fleet strengths/weaknesses and environmental traits will go a long way towards ensuring success in space battles.  Likewise, investing in certain skills for each officer can make space and/or ground combat easier.  By understanding your enemies beforehand, you can chain together combos by applying and detonating status effects for massive damage.
The fairly multilayered gameplay offers hours of replayability.  I did run into a few bugs where quest markers on sectors would not always clear from the map even after completing all quest stages, but those did not prevent me from completing the game.  Some folks have pointed out that the game’s pacing slows a bit near the end, although I personally didn’t find that too off-putting.  I used that time to improve my fleets.  In the end, I believe the gameplay has substantial merit.
Rating: good
The graphic designers opted for a pixelated style that works fairly well for characterizing the in-game factions.  Each faction has its own predominant color scheme and artwork that permeates ship aesthetics, sprite appearance, base interiors, home planet design, certain weapon effects, and etc.  Factions such as the fleshy hive-like Chruul, the treacherous space pirates, the paranoid and mutagenic Xlar-Yanthu, and others end up having their own distinct “personalities.”  Combined with some of the writing and music, the artwork can also enhance some of the goofier aspects of the narrative and dialogue when dealing with some groups.
The artwork does well in delivering very atmospheric vibes to various areas of the game, serving both aesthetic and functional roles.  There are several background slides for each sector of space you encounter, each denoting predominant resource types or environmental conditions in the area.  Planets you land down on will also have different types of surface environments, ranging from tropical beaches to barren canyons.  When navigating the various levels of Halcyon 6, you’ll get an overview of the base’s separate compartments.  Each compartment can house either facilities with distinct structural designs and color palettes or run-down ruins with ample loose scrap metal.
Rating: good
On average, I felt the music was alright.  I loved the ambient music and found each faction’s theme music fitting, but felt some of the combat tracks were about “average.”  The sound effects are okay but don’t deliver anything I don’t already expect from traditional turn-based battle scenarios in other games.
Rating: fair/good
I really enjoyed my time with this game and consider it a nice gem in my Steam library.  It’s a cute, endearing, silly romp through space in what could be a somewhat goofy sci-fi show.  If the blend of gameplay elements here sounds interesting to you, then I recommend giving this game a shot.

TL:DR All in all it's a good game for the price point. Fun for both longer sit downs, and quick diversions. 9/10
Edit: More time with this game has seen me upgrade it from my initial 7.5 to a 9. I've also added a bit more to the review to reflect that change. Being a port from another platform should not be held agaisnt a game, unless it was ported poorly. Looking at you Dynasty Warriors 8   ;...;
It's a good budget dungeon crawler. It sticks to the roots of dungeon crawling; explore dungeon, search rooms, kill mosnters, complete quests, collect booty, upgrade hero stats and equipment. I good selection of starting characters should  provide you with one to fit your play style. There really isn't much room for play style though- kill monsters, collect loot. The upgrade system is pretty flexible and allows you to customize as you see fit. You earn achievments by clearing dungeons, and killing things. You can then spend these points to upgrade your heros stats. Money and loot can be exchanged in town at the shop to allow further customization. Strategy comes into play when deciding to tank it up with more armor, go for more damage to kill the baddies faster, more spells to upgrade your arsenal, or the ever important potions. From the basic and essential healing potions, to the stat and combat buff potions.  It's fun and satisfying to see your potion guzziling whelp, evolve into a dungeon destroying machine.
Being able to pick any dungeon you want from the start, is a nice feature. Sucking down too many potions as you progress up the chain in a quest line? Try moving to the lower tiers of another dungeon to help you farm those achivment points, and much sought after gold!
Visuals are very basic, but do not detract from the dungeon crawling experience. The simplistic icons fit into the Hero Quest/Board Game feel quite nicely. Audio is adequate in giving you some olde timey, or darker dungeon crawly music and fight sound effects, but is nothing to make you beg for the OST.
Comabat is a little lacking, but fun in it's own way. A simplistic "click&kill" interface can be nice sometimes. You can gamble on aiming for a critical location. I find aiming for the arm on a monster with high HP can make all the difference in the long hall. Monsters get a bonus for other monters in the area with them. A pathetic goblin provides the same bonus as a fearsome dark knight. Even when you try to use the narrow hallways to your advantage to fight them 1v1, somehow the monsters in the back are still able to provide support. They don't have to be adjacent either. It seems any baddie within a couple squares can lend a hand. The only real tactics I've found are to engage the weaklings before the biggers ones, and kite down hallways trying to lose the others. Thus removing the "gang bonus" before fighting the more powerfull things.
There's no hidden costs, or microtransaction store. The game is fully accessible from the start.
If you're into old school dungeon crawlers, give this a try. It's good at scratching that itch. If you want a fast paced, bloody, immersive 3D, visceral dismemberment orgy... this might not be the game for you.

Preface: I've had this game since 2010 back in v16 and it has changed a LOT since then.  I've watched the community grow and change and I've probably spent several hundred hours on the game before it came to Steam.
Blockland is a creative sandbox game created in 2004 by Badspot.  A lot of people say it's kind of like Lego Garry's Mod, which isn't far from the truth.  I love this game to pieces and always have, but it does have certain flaws that can seriously hinder the experience at times.
The game is great because you can do nearly anything, but the community is a bit... strange, at times.  There are two groups of people in the game: the noobs that don't know how anything works, and the old-timers that are either very supportive of newcomers or are spiteful towards them.  There's not much middle ground between these groups and quite a lot of the veteran players have left the game since v21 was released, a few months before the game came to Steam.
The biggest actual gameplay drawbacks will be very obvious within the first couple hours of playing: a bad physics engine and subpar graphics.  The physics engine has been buggy and unpredictable since the game's creation, although the graphics are actually substantially better now than before.
Possibly the only thing that has really kept me playing the game this long is the giant amount of user-made content that can be found on the official forums.  The custom add-ons really bring the game to life and it's somewhat bland without them.  Nearly every popular server runs many add-ons, allowing for an even more custom and unique experience.
Due to its Garry's Mod-like sandbox nature, Blockland has also inspired several notable video makers on YouTube, including Teneksi, Filipe1020, 8bitcube, Flubbman97, SirHerg1, and others.

Before I start with this review, Let me just say this.
This is a fun colorful game that I recommend for the RPG, Turn-based type fans out there, Otherwise you might not like it very much, Because the game's focus is pretty much on that.
So to begin.
Mighty Dungeons is a really fun game, It is very customize-able so gives you more choices to go with your adventure.
As you can see in the screenshots, Your character and enemies are icons moving across the map, Which is not really a bad thing it gives the game a more (strategic) feeling.
The game is fast, You don't feel that (Come on just move already) part, Because everything goes by fast.
I am not a fan of phone ports (Ios/android) But this one was built again for pc to suit it better, And the devs are doing a great job with it so far.
A feature I like about the game, All those customizing features in it, When creating a new character you choose the game difficulty, Character buffs ( making it stronger ) Enemy buffs ( making them also stronger).
You also choose if the fights are turn-based or with a 5 second timer, Also while making a new character you can choose if Perma-Death is enabled or disabled for it, For a stronger challenge to some.
With more than 10 characters to choose from, All can equip certain types of Weapons, Armor, Spells, And more.
And they all look very good in design gotta hand it to them.
About 7 Campaigns, Each having 8 levels becomes harder as you progress through, And also a great feature which is workshop, So you can create more Quests, Campaigns, Characters, Weapons, And steam community is very creative, Hoping to see some good stuff.
I like the old-school Rpg style in battles, Nothing too complicated just the basic Rpg type.
The map design is splendid, Gives you a path to follow and to reach the destination, And with every quest and campaigns it gets bigger and better with new designs and layouts, Chests and Cabinet and more to loot, Monsters everywhere, Traps to disarm and Secret paths to find.
The quests are easy, Find the thing, Rescue this guy, Kill the Dungeon master and a lot more.
A shop to buy all sort of stuff from, A tavern to reach after finishing a quest, A training area to test your power, And after every quest and achievement you get points to spend to upgrade your hero.
Oh yeah also Achievements, There's a huge pack of them in this game.
What I disliked so far is the game's balance, I feel like certain characters are overpowered ( Fire demon ) On nightmare mode, Your hp becomes much lower but damage gets higher, So becomes easy to 1 hit monsters before they get the chance to attack you.
So I don't suggest going Nightmare mode, I highly recommend going with the original mode.
Lets go to the pros and cons.
1 - Fast paced battles and movement to explore dungeons faster.
2 - Many characters with different builds, A lot of levels to play, And customize-able features.
3 - Great level design and characters that was built by the dev and the community.
4 - Good soundeffects and soundtracks, Suits the game just right.
5 - Equip weapons, Repair them, Use spells, Heal with potions and more Rpg-styled features.
6 - Loot loot and loot, For some reason we gamers really like looting and this game has it.
7 - I found a few bugs and errors, After reporting it to the developer they were fixed within the day, So huge thumbs up here.
8 - It sure takes a long time to finish, 6 hours in and still climbing up the way to the end, And With achievements I'm sure it will take much more time.
1 - The matter of balance, Some characters feels much stronger than the rest, But I guess that's because of the (Nightmare) Mode, Which makes the character's damage much higher but with less health, So just go with original mode.
2 - After a while the game feels kinda repetitive, But to turn-based dungeon crawler fans, That shouldn't be an issue.
I am not being generous here the game has a lot more Pros than cons, The repetitive one is just my own opinion, To some others who gets addicted to this type of game, They would feel different about it.
But the balance is still an issue if you want a very hardcore challenge, You can choose perma-death or just click the option that makes the monsters crazier and go with Original mode to have a more balanced experience.
TL;DR
Recommended to people who'd enjoy this type of game, An rpg dungeon crawler type of game, That focuses mainly on that while ignoring some visual features, It gives a lot of hours and a lot of fun.
I wouldn't really recommend this for people who are not really into this genre and would like to try it, Just see a few videos before deciding who knows, You might end up liking it.
Overall
Had some real fun playing this game, Kudos to you devs good job on this.

Purchased: Humble Indie Bundle 8
Probably the pioneer of the walking around genre of games. I can't recommend it.
Unlike The Stanley Parable which had choices, or The Beginner's Guide which had interactive and engaging moments, there's no player action in Dear Esther besides walking.
And you walk very slowly.
The game is meant to be played slowly and thoughtfully, but it ended up being really frustrating simply because the walking speed discourages exploration. There's one moment where I saw something interesting in the distance, took an annoyingly long time to walk there and then found out there was no interaction possible with what looked like someplace where a secret should be.
Then I walked slowly back to the main road so I could continue listening to the narration.
The game is also very short. The story is conveyed in an esoteric fashion. The music was not very memorable but the ambiance fit the mood. There are some interesting moments in the level design, but for the most part it's far too ordinary to warrent slowly walking through.
I don't like it.
This is truly a "walking simulator". There is nothing you can do except walking. So is it boring? Yes, it is boring. Also beautiful and sad. But mostly boring.
I didn't think I would enjoy a game like this, but when the setting is done so well, so gorgeous...    the backgrounds become the foreground characters 90 minutes well spent.

I'm not sure I fully understand exactly what happened from the narration (but I get the gist) and I'm not compelled to replay or search to find out more, but I definitely enjoyed the ride. The art direction is incredible, and the narrator's delivery is great. The music did get a little obnoxious once or twice, though.
Fun facts about the making of game added to the great story for this game. Worth the time!

This is only a game in so much that there isn't really another thing to call it.  Interactive story?  It's not really interactive, but it's all story...kind of.  I played through the previous version many times, and each time you get a different set of snippets of the narrative and dialogue.  The visuals and environments are fantastic, and the atmosphere is captivating if, and that's a big "if", this kind of storytelling is interesting to you.  If you are expecting a large, open-world exploration game, or a point-and-click adventure, you're going to have a bad time.  If you are only interested in FPS games, you are going to have an even worse time.  This is pure story, the story is somewhat ambiguous at times given that it's broken into so many bits and pieces, and the pace is intentionally slow to try to force you to digest every little bit that you get.
I found the way to "play" this is to sit with a good drink and something to nibble on, and take it a piece at a time with nothing else going on in your mind.  If you find you are getting tired or distracted, leave and come back later with an empty head.  You can run through it end-to-end in one go without stopping, but you won't "get" it, and you probably won't enjoy it.  Patience, patience, always patience with this title.
[Edit: I don't know whether to say I got the game for free or not because I paid for the previous version, which got me the new version free...so "maybe"?]

Still one of the most hauntingly beautiful and immersive games ever made. But what about its substance? How does the "gameplay" hold up after all these years?
Suffice it to say, Dear Esther - in any version - is not a "game" for anyone who believes that the definition of such things requires a great deal of action, or skill. It's perfectly true that there's no skill required to "beat" this game. It's the game that virtually coined the term "walking simulator", for ♥♥♥♥'s sake. Yes, you mostly just hold down W and steer with the mouse. Yes, your grandmother could probably finish it, in under two hours no less. So perhaps the more important question here is...how does the Dear Esther: Landmark Edition stand up against not only the OLD version of the game, but the wave of walking sims which have appeared in its wake?
I'm pleased to announce that Dear Esther holds up every bit as well as the day it was released, and while I'm not sure I fully appreciated whatever "improvements" have been made to this new version, I can only assume they were for the better and not the worse! (Gimme a break, I only played the old version once, alright?) All owners of the original got this one for free anyway, and given that said original can no longer be bought in the Steam Store, there's definitely no dilemma about which version to shell out for.
Personally, I just took the opportunity to re-experience the game in as definitive a form as possible, and if the good people at The Chinese Room believe this is the Real McCoy, then I'm happy to go along with them. Simply put, one of the classiest walking simulators ever made, and a game arguably deserving of both its cult status and gaming industry infamy in equal measure. A purchase not liable to be regretted by existing fans of this genre, and as good a place as any for newbies to start. (Basically: if you hate this game, you'll probably hate every other walking sim ever made. Life sucks, get a helmet.)
Verdict: 9/10.
(PS Again, I managed to miss almost all of the ghosts on the island. But they're there, apparently. And a fond screw-you to The Chinese Room for nearly making me cry at the end there again, even if I don't yet fully understand the story which precedes it. Truly a thing of beauty, whatever the heck this "game" is.)

Let me make it clear to the boozos who stupidly bash this game without playing or spending any form of time in game. I have played this game on mobile for well above a year and played it on Steam after 126+ hours and the PCMR & Steam community decides to listen to chumps who play less than an hour in the game. Shame on you.
World Of Tanks Blitz is essentially a CASUAL WoT intended to BRING potential newcomers to the PC brother. It can never compete against it's older brother anyways.
For players like me who enjoy World Of Tank's mechanics and core gameplay but HATE the EXTREMELY LONG AND EXPENSIVE grind in WoT, Blitz is a GODSENT.
What more, there is 0 Artillery. ZERO.
Games span for about 6 minutes, maps are smaller, faster thinking and quick mm is, to me, a better way to play. If you get matchmaked with idiots, you don't have to play with them for a long time and queue's are quick, making it far better than WoT.
In Blitz, there is a LARGE FOCUS ON QUICK THINKING AND SKILL. Sure, WoT has it's more highly skilled mechanics but Blitz places you into more pressuring fights that forces players to be on their feet and respond quickly. Hitpoints, speed, alpha, dpm, aiming, auto-aim, everything matters more in Blitz where you are limited to only 7 people to juggle around with.
Not to mention, tanks don't cost $100+ and are much cheaper on the Blitz version
That is not to say this game is without its flaws.
Heavier tanks don't matter as much as in WoT, Tank Destroyers are much more difficult to play in, Servers are unreliable after every update, graphics are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ some unbalanced tanks (Looking at you, Keni Otsu) and much easier prammo spam.
Say what you want to say about Wargaming not putting WoT on steam but tell me, which company in the right mind would spend YEARS developing their own client only to have it placed on steam?

Deus Ex is a game which I didn't pay much attention to at release, however everyone was talking about it so I gave it a try, and I loved almost everything about it! I highly recommend playing it, I feel it's one of few games which really delivers a solid all round experience.
I ended up playing this game through twice on console, once on PC and then again when the Directors Cut was released. I enjoyed every single playthrough.
Liked:
- The number of gameplay choices you have as a player is great, there are many different ways to approach a mission and the skills you choose can create different experiences which may vary from your friends.
- Initially I didn't like the visual style from the promo shots, but once I started playing I started to really like it.
- The story is well done and the main character Adam Jenson is very likeable. Good voice acting too.
- The soundtrack by Michael McCann is outstanding.
- Visually the game is pretty impressive, some locations are beautiful.
Disliked:
- Not much to dislike really!
The game is almost always on sale and well worth the money.

Halcyon 6 was an extremely successful mix of several different game types. The combat is turn-based RPG, there is RTS resource collecting and management, a very basic Diplomacy system, and a bunch of little guys to click to make their numbers get bigger. The "Starbase" has some rooms to explore and upgrades to give your crew members (kind of like XCom, I don't know what 'type' of game that is).
They tied together really well, right up until you say "Alright. I get it. I fly the ship and fight the guy and do the thing." That was around hour 17; I had another 10 to go.
I can't really recommend this game past the halfway point of the story. One playthrough was more than enough. The gameplay gets very repetitive very quickly. Every quest is a fetch quest where you read something and click a button, and maybe fight someone.
It's one of those games that says "BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE!" and you don't really want any more, you just want to beat the thing and save the galaxy.

A fun mix of JRP and XCOM.  The game still has its fair share of bugs, but none of them are game breaking and the combat itself is really fun.  There's some cool alien designs and humorous interactions.  It can get a bit frustrating mid to late game because of resource management, but you can automate that, which improves the game ALOT.  Interesting mix of starship and ground combat, all built around an ailment, exploit RPG system.

The most ballanced Mechwarrior/Battletech game yet, lacking the insane legging issues of Mechwarrior 3 (where losing one leg would take you out of the match) and the poptarting meta-game of Mechwarrior 4 (hiding behind a hill then jumping up for fire and letting the hill protect you as your weapons reloaded)
The ever changing nature of an MMO, and Free-to-play games in general however, does mean that today's best mechs, can be tomorrow's garbage - and then back again.
Case in point, since open beta, I have watched the Hunchback chassis travel from "Best medium chassis in the game, and nothing can change that" to "worthless garbage, and nothing can change that" and back at least twice.
Now for a comparison of sorts...
As far as most free-to-play issues (IE, is it REALLY free?)
Absolutely no money needs to be spent to do well, or to do ANYTHING in the game.
What mechs there are that cost real-world money to buy, can be bought with patience and timing.
MC (The real-world-money equivalent) is given for playing the Faction Warfare mode (also known as Community Warfare) as are Mechbays - arguably the one thing you would need to actually buy.
In the end, knowing your mech, and how to play, is far more important than anything else.

As someone who has supported and played this game from closed beta I can honestly say that this game is good.  Not amazing, not superb, but good.  It is by no means an easy game to jump into and pick up, but they are slowly improving and making steps in the right direction.  It has a lot of potential, and for a relatively small dev group it is a solid game.  The current biggest drawbacks for me are the long queue times, broken ELO/BR, and heavy-handed "balancing" that is doled out on the regular.  It should still be in beta with the amount of changes they make with each patch and their pricing is definitely not on the cheap side, but the content is good and if you can get a group of friends to play with you regularly this game can be very satisfying.  If you have the time and effort to really learn the game, research, make new friends who can help you learn the ins and outs, or even have a group of friends who are interested in playing, then by all means, pick this game up.  If you're a casual gamer who likes the idea of mech combat and isn't interested in team play, tactics, or focus firing then do us all a favor and skip this game.  Perhaps check out hawken or some other cod-style twitch shooter, MWO is definitely not all about 360 no scoping.

I've been playing from alpha.
If you are looking for great team based mech combat based in the battletech franchise - this IS it.
If you are looking for the above coupled within the battletech social/political space - this is NOT it.
I had a much longer review typed out and accidentaly hit the back key on my mouse button, so I'll summarize...
The game is fun, and only a few of your L337 FPS skills are going to transfer over. Its going to take a great deal of time to master your piloting and build your arsenal al la carte.
Have fun, but remember that the game will be pretty stagnant within a years time if the developers don't pull yon head from dark hole and make faction/house/clan/merc warfare a MEANINGFUL part of the game. Right now its just a short lobby-drop grind for c-bills and xp (quick match) or a little longer grind for c-bills and xp (faction warfare) and thats absolutely it. The social aspect of the game is completely non-existant except for calling out spotting intel and coordination while in combat. Yes you can group with friends - no you can't do anything meaningful within a company or within the faction warfare system. Again, there are no in-game tools or perks to promote anything within this games socio-political space.
There are no tools in game that would support a player driven company be it mercs/clans or house military. There is no trading of mechs or c-bills. There are no decisions on repair costs. Your only decision is how to outfit your mech, who to group up with, and how to click the ready button.
Now thats not to say the devs have not been working on improving the game beyond what we have now. Hopefully we'll get some perks for faction warfare as it relates to taking defending and holding territory at the faction level (including merc allegiances). Hopefully we get some social tools to promote clan/guild/merc/house military development. Hopefully at some point I can promote or demote someone within my company and set their weekly pay accordingly, which is not tied to some silly rank/achievment system. hopefully we get an ARENA with some commentator tools along with prizes and ladders.
However I won't hold my breath on that last block of text. I will however pony up 25k in real hard cash for the first mechwarrior 12 vs 12 tournament in the Solaris arena and get my buddy Deman to commentate the ladder match during a live stream. We need commentator spectator tools/cameras though.

The universe.
Created in 1984, the BattleTech universe is one of the best know science fiction settings for my generation. It is in no small part thanks to the computer games, titled MechWarrior, which popularised this setting and a concept of a BattleMech – a bipedal behemoth powered by a fusion engine fitted into a skeletal frame moved by strands of myomer (artificial muscles), clad in tons of armour, armed with lasers, missiles and guns striders the battlefields of the XXXI century raining death on everything that stands in its way. And each of these mighty engines of destruction is piloted by a single individual, a MechWarrior. There are no aliens, no supernatural powers, just humans and their never ending conflicts.
What is MechWarrior Online?
In essence its a free to play game that is designed to simulate the clashes of teams of 12 MechWarriors piloting their Mechs on various battlegrounds of the future. Compared to other F2P games I played (mainly World of Tank and Warthunder) I find MechWarrior Online (MWO) a much better experience. First one - there is not tech tree. This means that you can buy whatever Mechs you want as long as you can afford them. Secondly - the business model. You REALLY ONLY NEED to spend money in this game to buy new mechbays for your Mechs. And even those can be earned through playing Community Warfare mode or achieving goals at special events that are run several times a year. But if you want to have access to certain stuff quicker or buy premium time you can. It is entirely up to you.
Preparations.
As mentioned before the game plays like a simulator. Each of the several dozen Mechs available in it pilots differently, has different stats such as top speed, acceleration/deceleration, max yawn and pitch angles of the torso and arms, maximum tonnage, number, location and type of weapons mounts, amount of armour on different section of the Mech, ammo and heat sinks capacity and so on. This allows for a very wide customisation of a Mech in terms of armament, speed, protection and heat dissipation, which is important. If you overheat, your Mech powers down for a few seconds and becomes a sitting duck. On top of that it can take some damage to is power core which in term can lead to the Mech’s destruction. ALWAYS WATCH THE HEAT METER.
New players won’t have to bother themselves with all that customisation bit. You will have no in game cash (CBills) to buy Mechs and will have to rely in “trial” ones which cannot be customised. Yet during your first 25 matches you will be rewarded extra CBills, so after those games you will probably by able to buy even the most expensive Mech.
Furthermore, You should really look through the key bindings and either learn the setup or rebind it to you preferences. The most important ones are Target Lock, Full Stop and Push to Talk (cooperation with others is key to victory). And finally - PLAY THE TUTORIAL – most of the game mechanics are  explained there + you get 2,500,000 CBills which a beginner really needs.
The battlefield.
Once you hit the button to search for game and be paired with other players, you will be thrown into battlefields rendered with the CryEngine 3. Depending on your setting they will look from plain to gorgeous. Each map is different, some have a few variations depending on the weather conditions or day/night time. You get deserts, canyons, forests, cities, snow and ice, volcanoes, swamps, you name it. Getting to know the maps helps a lot as you know the possible enemy approaches, ambush spots and best firing positions.
Regular games have one of three objectives – destroy the enemy team (skirmish), cap their base or kill them (assault), gather 750 resource points by controlling key areas on the map or kill them (conquest). Simple but fun. Community warfare is another cup of tea and I will try to cover it in a guide at a later date.
When the shooting starts it can be very organized of completely frantic. It all depends on the teams you are in. Fortunately you usually play with players with similar experience level so its happens very really that you are thrown against really good players or teams of such, which can literally obliterate an entire enemy team in 5 min. The clashes themselves look fantastic – lasers firing, bullets and missiles flying around, lots of sparks and explosions. After a few minutes of fighting most Mechs show signs of damage, from bullet/laser holes to missing limbs and weapon mounts. All in all it is simply enjoyable to watch. And also to hear. Though the in game music is nothing special the SFX are simply a blast. Each individual sound, from the hum of the fusion engines, which is different in every Mech, to the sounds of various actuators, the stomping of Mech legs, sounds of being hit, hitting obstacles to very distinguishable weapon sounds make this game a very immersive experience.
The Mechs and balance.
As mentioned before MWO doesn’t use a tech tree. Instead the balance is done by allowing a specified number of Mechs from each of the 4 classes to enter a match. The classes are as follows:
LIGHTS – 20 to 35 tons. Role – scout, sniper, assassin, harasser.
Pros – very fast, small targets, manoeuvrable, low purchase cost, most have ECM which makes them hard to detect at a distance (you can still fire at them when you have visual contact).
Cons – low armour, few weapons mounts, low ammo space, will overheat quickly when weapons are fired continuously.
MEDIUMS - 40 to 55 tons. Role – second line Mechs, flanking, sniping, brawling, support (with LRMs).
Pros – quite fast and manoeuvrable, reasonable cost, considerable amount of weapon mounts, ammo space, quite good armour
Cons – yet not good enough to be in the first line of an assault, need to rely on heavier Mechs to spearhead it.
HEAVIES - 60 to 75 tons. Role – first line Mechs, flanking, sniping, brawling, support (with LRMs).
Pros – some can be still quite fast, numerous weapon mounts, good armour, loads of space for ammo, survivability under fire.
Cons – costly to purchase, big targets, not as manoeuvrable as lights and mediums.
ASSAULTS - 80 to 100 tons. Role – spearheading assaults, sniping, support (with LRMs, which is a wastes in this case).
Pros – can take absurd punishment compared to other Mechs, numerous weapon mounts, very good armour, loads of space for ammo.
Cons – very expensive to purchase, very big targets, slow to move and turn, die quickly without support, vulnerable to assassin light Mechs.
Then come the weapons:
Lasers, Pulse Lasers and PPCs– don’t use ammo but generate the most heat so cannot be shot for too long without pause. Come in different sizes with their own pros and cons.
Ballistic weapons – MG and various Auto Cannons, have limited ammo but generate little heat, used correctly can really shred Mechs to pieces.
LMRs – used as fire support, some love them some hate them. Just remember to have your talget constantly locked on so that the missiles hit.
SRMs – act more or less like a shotgun with 270m max range. Very nice for brawling but generates considerable heat.
Considering all of the above, the combinations are numerous and it will often happen that your Mech will be very good in one combat scenario and completely useless in another. Just bare in mind that the most powerful and game breaking weapon is TEAM WORK ;)
Final thoughts.
For me MWO is currently the best F2P game out there and one of the very few that lets you bash it out against gigantic robots. So if you are bored with the setting of WOT, WarThunder and Armoured Warfare, want to try something new or just like SF themed game – jump right in. It will just cost you some of your time and who knows, maybe we will meat on the battlefield in the same team or in my Tiberwolfe’s crosshair ;P

What is Mechwarrior? Briefly, it's a PVP Shooter where you are inside a building tall robot, with several sets of weapons and you fire them at the group of 3/5 enemy mechs that seem to want to kill YOU first than the rest of your team...
There are several ways to play it, but there are no classes, its your speed, choice of weapons and team behaviour that determines what you'll be that game. But keep in mind this is a TEAM game, lone wolfs dont last long.
Customizing your mech will take your time but not at first, take one of the trial mechs, I recommend a "Heavy" for decent armor and firepower.
Despite the flaws, (loadings, crashes) there are some things that make this a different game. No other "fps" moves like this, torso and legs are independent, the speeds, the vision angle limits, the arms range, everything matters. The weapons feel good and you can for example have an arm destroyed, or a leg and still carry on fighting as long as the Center Torso is intact and you can walk.
As a game engine (graphics/gameplay) its awesome, how it plays and also the visuals. It is demanding and seems to be getting more, you might need a powerful PC to run medium/high.
But, comparing to MW4, the mechs and fights are fantastic.
Finally, MWO has a very decent player base so you'll get in a game fast by clicking quickplay and can try against other starting Tier 5 players.
In the end spending money might give you a little advantage but you still need to know how to make it count. It's mostly for cosmetics. And with the regular weekly events you can get all that for free.

I so want to love this game as it was my favourite show as a kid, the cut scenes are a fantastic update to the original show and the voices are close enough even if it starts too far into the story, but the controls and lack of full controller support is simply unforgivable. A simple mapping of menu buttons could have address this, instead it smacks of cheaply done mobile port with a high price tag. If you decide to use the controller, you'll have to get off the couch to reach for the keyboard and mouse at the end of each level. Trying to use the default mouse control is worse, as you won't be able to interact with most objects no matter how hard you try. The puzzles seem a bit simple and a little repetitive. All sadly makes for a frustrating, if briefly entertaining, experience.

The Mysterious Cities of Gold was probably among the cartoons I was watching when I was a kid. I don't remember well the story in itself but the main song yeah.
So, I'm glad to have that game in my library. Esteban, Zia and Tao learn about a possible City of Gold in China and go there.  But once there, between pirates, bandits and several puzzles, how will they manage?
The story is told also with cinematics that gives you the feeling that you're watching an episode of the series, though I must say that some sequences didn't really make sense at all.
The gameplay makes you take control of the three characters, with their own special tricks: Esteban can activate special pillars as the chosen one, Zia can get through small cracks and Tao can read every inscription you'll find so that you can solve the puzzle without forgetting that the parrot, Pichu, that is hanging with Tao, can steal keys.
The game is mainly about that: finding dragon stones, use them either to solve a riddle needing 4 people for plates that are activated when there is a weight on them or to open doors, sneak out areas with enemies (and trying not to get captured), etc.. It's true that for an adult, the game may be seen very very repetitive and very easy to manage (though some puzzles are kinda hard) but the game is pleasant, mainly because of challenges (time, captures, scrolls to collect and even a treasure chest with pictures to unlock).
Anyway, you can retry a level as you want and with achievements to unlock, you'll have to negociate some levels very very well to earn them. It's not always easy to do a speedrun by collecting all scrolls and avoiding captures when enemies's patterns are letting you only a small frame of time to act.

Endless Space is a 4X game in every way, shape, and form, all presented in a beautiful science fiction setting. As per usual, you'll gather resrouces, expand your empire, and try to rule the galaxy in a variety of ways.
What I love most about Endless Space:
1. One of the most impressive UIs I've ever used in a game of this kind. Seamless controls, intuitive, easy to learn. The design of the UI is just flat-out brilliant.
2. The variety of ships and combat strategies separate this game from most 4X games. Instead of just a results screen, you can watch combat unfold in epic real-time, even controlling the camera in any way you want. So combat, while still essentially all based on mathematical values, is visually stunning and fun.
Where I think Endless Space lacks:
1. As with most 4X games, diplomacy is weird and factions can do some very random things. For instance, a faction offered me a Cooperative Alliance which I accepted. I hit "end turn" and they declared war on me. Strange, but common to me in my experience playing these types of games.
2. More of personal hope, more compatibility between Mac and PC, so that my brother and I don't have to try several times to get a multiplayer match going. :)
All in all, if you are a fan of 4X games and want a scifi themed one, look no further. Endless Space is beautiful to look at, a breeze to control while playing, and a very in-depth game experience.

This is it. The final part of Naruto Shippuden translated into gameplay, something which the anime still hasn't delivered to us. Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 4 or NUNS4 starts off with some backstory on who is fighting against who and for what cause which provides some great fights with a fun combat style and a interactive cinematic quick time event finish for most of them that both Naruto fans new and old can enjoy. Other than the main story mode the game has other modes as well which I'll go explain based on how they appear on the main menu (You could also skip to the conclusion if you don't want a detailed explanation of what each game mode has to offer)
STORY
The story mode covers both backstory for some of the main key characters in the 4th great ninja war as well as everything from when the ten tails is first summoned all the way up to the "final fight" as well as a nice ending cutscene.
ADVENTURE
Adventure is a more open-world take on story telling covering a mini arc that happens in between the ending of Shippuden and The Last: Naruto the Movie. To me it felt more like a filler episode but enjoyable nonetheless. In this story Naruto reminiscences of stories dating back from when he was a kid up until this point serving as memorable battles that are a blast from the past. Also mentioned before you can roam around the ninja world just as the after game in Naruto Ultimate Ninja Storm 3 (Full Burst) but other than completing some of the side quests there isn't that much to explore.
*There are also extra DLC stories of which 2 are out right now featuring Shikamaru and Gaara as the main characters.
COLLECTION
As always there is a lot to collect, some of which you can buy here ranging from voice clips to costumes for characters. You should have enough money to buy what you want after play through the story once. I never felt like I had to grind to get more money.
ONLINE BATTLE
As I am not a competitive or "pvp" player I cannot accurately review this game mode however I do know that if you're into online pvp and ranked systems this mode will probably satisfy your needs.
FREE BATTLE
I feel like the name for this mode does not do the actual content justice. There are so many extra game modes hidden away in this non-descriptive name that I could probably split this part up by itself. I'll try to keep it short though. Free battle contains a training mode where you can just test out various characters/teams against a npc as well as a Survival and League mode which mode add a new twist to the regular matches and are definitely worth checking out.
CONCLUSION
NUNS4 is THE ending I wanted for this amazing franchise. With a giant roster of countless memorable characters and adding on to the gameplay showing that the Ultimate Ninja Storm series has an ever evolving combat system by now giving you abilities like switching character mid fight or breaking the weapons/armour of your opponent. The game looks even more stunning whilst still maintaining the same style as previous titles in the franchise HOWEVER this comes with a cost, the system requirements have been boosted up so I did have to play on low settings to achieve a stable fps count. Anyways if you are a fan of Naruto you really gotta pick up this game as it is the epic conclusion to an epic story as I hope this is not the end but a standard that should be achieved once again as I hope for a Boruto: Ultimate Ninja Storm 5.

I did this after finishing all of the achievements and purely out of the love for the game/franchise and as such this review is kinda biased(Believe it!).

I received the Steam Controller along with the Link for my birthday and so far I am having a great time with it but it isn't without quirks and flaws. Hopefully this review will help people out who are undecided.
Before I made the decision to get the controller I did a lot of research in the form of checking reviews on Steam as well as reading reviews and watching videos. The main thing that I learned is that a lot of the negative comments come from people saying it isn't like a traditional gamepad - and they aren't wrong, this thing is nothing like an Xbox or PS4 controller, that isn't a bad thing however. When I finally got mine and opened it up the controller definitely feels alien at first, the buttons aren't where you expect them to be (resulting in a frustrating initial gaming sessions) and the track pads are weird.
Once I got a better feel for the controller and started messing around with configurations, that is when the strengths of the controller really shines through. Absolutely everything is customisable and not only can you share these but you can download other people's set-ups if you'd prefer - I would however recommend playing around with configurations as it is very satisfying when it all comes together.
The biggest thing I feel that the Steam Controller has going against it is that it may be too different for people who just want to pick up a controller and play. Stick with it however and you definitely won't regret it. I am considering picking up a 2nd controller to go with it for multiplayer.

The Steam Controller is a weird but surprisingly functional controller, and for some games it's even quite useful. The biggest distinction between this and most standard USB controllers is obvious just from looking at it: the two touch pads it uses in place of a d-pad on the left and a control stick on the right. This is both a benefit and a hindrance. It is surprisingly decent at emulating mouse controls. Although I haven't tested that functionality extensively, it will definitely open more possibilities for games that would traditionally require a mouse and a keyboard. On the other hand, the touch pads aren't very precise, so if you want to use the left touch pad as a d-pad, you'll really have to practice at it, and even once you get experienced, you'll still be better off using another controller. The other main difference is the addition of two additional buttons on the back of the controller, although these have not been heavily utilized in control schemes that I've used. Other than these differences, it's a good device that is similar to your standard device. The form factor is good, fitting well in my hands and being well sized, and the buttons all feel good to use. It's well manufactured. Ultimately, the deciding factor in making your purchase should be how much you play games on Steam, as that's where it's most useful. It may have limited compatibility with other platforms, but on Steam it makes things so easy. Nearly every game is compatible right out of the box, and thanks to the Steam community, the rare games that don't natively support gamepads usually have community configurations ready to go, and you can create your own custom configs as well. Using configurations has a bit of a learning curve, and there are some titles that just won't work right no matter your configs, but with a bit of practice, it becomes easy. If you don't play on Steam much, then I'm surprised you're here at all, and I can't recommend the controller, but it's great for use on Steam, and if you have a Steam connected TV, it's ability to mimic a mouse and keyboard might even be essential.

This game is a free fast-paced FPS with mostly ballistic weapons and awesome movement mechanics including jetpacks and a complete friction loss from the ground. And because gliding + hills + speed + ballistic weapons = hard to hit, this game is difficult. And awesome.
Now to get a little more precise, the movement can be compared with the little iOS game tiny wings, where you slide through the little gaps between round hills and fly around as fast as you can, but this is 3D. The weapons are mostly in one of these 3 categories: Explosive weapons fire slowly, have rather slowly flying projectiles with splash damage and extreme damage on a direct hit, while bullet based guns (autos) fire rather fast flying little projectiles dealing high damage per second if you manage to hit all shots and the usually weakest but easy to aim hitscan weapons, which work as all guns do in "modern shooters". You point at an enemy and when you click, they die.
As you may have guessed, to be good at the game you should be able to handle guns from the first category, which are the way it's meant to be played and the only real honorable option (Debatable, I know, discuss it on reddit or whatever). The fast movement is hard to control in the beginning and hitting fast people with ballistic weapons can be extremely hard. This is what puts game's skill ceiling so high.
The community is not as big as it used to be, by now the game is slowly dying (
). Still, there's always enough EU servers filled to join in a suitable game for me, so I will be enjoying the game for a long time. The good players are friendly to each other, the few toxic parts of the community are found in low-level servers and quit plaing sooner or later. Your first matches will be on these novice servers, although you will soon reach level 10 just to be thrown into games with the seasoned veterans when you know little about the game but the basics. This makes it even harder for new players.
So, to come to a conclusion:
The game is awesome, but difficult.
We can use more new players learning with each other instead of getting wrecked by pros, so give it a try.
What you can have for free is one of the best multiplayer shooters out there.
Prepare to get owned! Don't be frustrated, it's bound to happen.
Continue playing and think about what you do, learn from the enemy and you will get better.
Have fun!

This isn't a bad game. I feel a little bad giving it a thumbs down, but I wouldn't recommend it. The problem is that they stretched about 4 hours of content into a 16 hour (my playthrough time) game. That means you get in a lot of fights that are just pure grinding. There is zero threat of losing these fights, they're just waste time. But you have to do them.
People have said this game is like XCOM and FTL. That's completely untrue. Both of those games are much better. The combat in this game is more like Final Fantasy 7. You just take turns using abilities on each other. The ground battles are exactly the same as the space battles, but with different abilities. There are like 5 challenging fights in the whole game, out of hundreds.
It's also buggy. Sometimes you have to click a button multiple times before it registers a click. Other times buttons just don't work. I had a quest stuck in my quest log for like 14 of the 16 hours that I couldn't complete due to a problem with a scripted event.
There are some positives. The combat is fun in those few challenging fights. The progression is decent. The other alien races are fairly interesting.
If you want to play a game like this try The Ur-Quan Masters. It's from 1992, but it's a much better game. The combat is real-time and more fun. There are way more alien races and they're more interesting. Resource collection is better. It's free. It's just an all around better game.
Why are you reading these reviews? Just do it.

There is a nice addition to being able to unlock upgrades for weapons if that is your thing. Also there is a perk system there for those that like that sort of thing. Plus I just don’t have the time for it with so many games filling up in my library. However I could be tempted to do some COOP stuff, now that would be cool.
If this was my first experience of DOOM as it was all those years ago then I would have been blown away, as I was back then.

Blockland has been around for a long time, and has sadly been burried. People still play, but it lost so much popularity. It's a fun sandbox building game where you can build and program anything. The way you build stuff is very similar to real-life LEGOs, where you are not allowed to have floating bricks. The law of gravity is impossible to break. You can still make bricks float by making invisible and walk through towers under a brick. You can press the left mouse button to activate your jets so you can fly around. There's a spray can that allows you to not only paint bricks, but give them special effects such as rainbows and also make bricks transparent. You start with three tools; a hammer, a wrench, and a printing gun. The hammer lets you break bricks you put, but you can't break bricks under another brick unless the brick you want to destroy won't cause the other bricks above to float in the air. You can type /wand to get a wand that acts just like a hammer, but if you destroy a brick that would cause any bricks above it to float, everything above it breaks also. The wrench lets you do many different things with your bricks. While holding the wrench, you can click on a brick to view its properties. You can make your brick emit fire, or smoke, or any other particle that's in the game. You can spawn more tools, like a sword or a gun, or something that'll help you build better things. You can also program your bricks with events. Events are super easy to learn. I made a basic Windows XP computer with very little knowledge of events when I was a noob, and the results were satisfactory! The properties will be different depending on the brick you select. For example, if I use the wrench on a vehicle spawner, I won't have the ability to make it into a spear giver. I can only select from a list of rideable objects. If I use the wrench on a music brick, I will be able to choose from a list of music for it to play. The printer gun lets you put pictures on printer bricks. It's useful for making signs for things like stores, or for cooler security systems. Building in Blockland is lots of fun! You can also download add-ons that other users made from other websites so you can get more content such as more guns and swords to blow up everyone, or tools to help you build better things. I hope Steam workshop comes out for this game soon so it'll be quicker to download and find add-ons. Blockland also has a minigame feature which lets you disable and enable certain fuctions such as building or jets and allow players to get points for doing certain tasks. With add-ons, you can enhance your minigames and make them even more fun to play with your friends. You could make a futuristic team deathmatch minigame, or a survival horror game using the popular Renderman add-on based on the legendary Renderman! This game has endless possibilities, and I am really sad to see it die like this. I mean it. I am literally sad. After the extremely popular Return to Blockland add-on was gone, many people started to give up on this game. Return to Blockland made Blockland more social by adding private chat (much like Steam's chat), friends, and the ability to join your friend in a server they are playing. It didn't just make Blockland a better game to play it friends. It gave you better admin tools. It allowed you to download add-ons very similar to how Steam workshop works. Many add-ons lost some functions because they depended on RTB. The Renderman add-on was one of them. You can't control when he spawns anymore. I will always remember how much fun Blockland was. R.I.P. one of my favorite sandbox games ever.

(This following is copy-pasted from my original Dear Esther review. The Landmark Edition contains a few improvements to the visuals and a developer commentary, but my opinion of the game is more or less identical to before. If you do plan on buying Dear Esther, then the Landmark Edition is the version to get.)
Dear Esther is beautifully designed, hauntingly atmospheric and splendidly narrated. It also has a couple of very big problems...
<Contains minor spoilers>
...but funnily enough, the question of whether or not Dear Esther is a game isn't one that bothers me. Gaming is still a relatively young medium, and writing off a game just because it doesn't meet the traditional definition can only stifle innovation and discourage others from experimenting. Ultimately, I'm more interested in the question: did Dear Esther succeed in what it set out to do? Well, allow me to elaborate on what I think.
Dear Esther is a so-called "walking simulator" (i.e. has very little gameplay besides walking and looking) set on a bleak Hebridian island. This island is perhaps the most compelling character in the entire story: it is nothing short of breathtaking. I regularly visit these islands in real life, and Dear Esther succeeds magnificently in capturing their bleak magnificence. Coastal winds whistle through rusted chain-link fences, smoky clouds hug towering cliffs, bothies speckle the terrain and rocky bays with rotten wooden structures dominate the landscape. Both the visual (spinning 2D plants aside) and the sound design are spot-on in establishing the atmosphere, which in turn is helped by the superb soundtrack. There were some moments that left me literally stunned at what I was witnessing on my screen, that's a rare achievement for any video game.
Anywho, you play as a nameless, voiceless, faceless protagonist shipwrecked on a harsh Scottish island, who must make their way towards the radio tower on the horizon. It's not really clear what you intend to do once you get there, but never mind. Interaction is limited to walking around the island and sometimes poking your head into forlorn buildings, only to find them empty and long-abandoned. The lion's share of the game is spent listening to a well-spoken narrator reading a series of letters written to the eponymous Esther. The narrator himself is another highlight of the game; speaking in a deliberately monotone voice to start with, but rising to passionate speeches as you approach the game's climax.
So I like everything so far, and I don't mind the bare-bones gameplay, so why a No?
Because of the limited interactivity, the narration pretty much forms the crux of the entire experience. Sadly, I found the quality of the writing in Dear Esther to be wanting.
If ever there was a walking definition of purple prose, this would be it. Although it contains a handful of reasonably well-written lines, the core parts of the narrative are so cluttered with flowery dialogue that it repeatedly draws attention to itself with how ridiculous it sounds. I admit to not being the smartest when it comes to analyzing good writing, but I can usually get invested in a well-told story even if I don't fully understand everything behind it. But Dear Esther is so full of itself and so utterly pretentious that I found myself getting frustrated rather than intrigued by the story. Here are a couple excerpts from the game:
Perhaps my experience with human beings is limited, but this sounds like it was written by a teenager in English class trying to sound far cleverer than he actually is (this I can speak from experience though, because it sounds like one of my old essays). This is the only story I've experienced that somehow manages to be both frustratingly vague and tiresomely heavy-handed at the same time. Not sure how they did that, but that's the thought that kept crossing my mind as I listened to it.
Then we come to the second problem: the player. The fact that Dear Esther may not be a 'real' game isn't what bothers me. What does bother me is that the player is completely amputated from the story being told. We're not here to partake in a moving tale of human loss, instead we're merely treated as a vehicle for the narrator to force flowery nonsense down our throats without getting to experience or even influence any of it. In fact, we're almost a hindrance to the game for our mere presence. This makes me wonder why Dear Esther is even a game in the first place, especially since it wrestles control from you during the ending (the only time something of note actually happens). The only benefit from it being a game is that I get to hold down W for 90 minutes, so it's essentially like watching a film on a DVD player with a broken pause button. On top of that, the walking speed is painfully slow:
This is what admirers of the game often tell me when I bring this up. Fair enough, I like immersing myself in a slow-burner, if anything I prefer a slower-paced story. But more often than not you'll wander down rather lengthy corridors, find nothing of interest, not even a bit of narration, and then have to slowly plod all the way back again. At this point, all the carefully planned pacing in the game comes to a crashing halt. Then there are other times when you have to traverse fairly featureless expanses all the while sliding along at the speed of a Peugeot driver on the Edinburgh bypass. This is not good pacing, this is just time wasting.
Some might say that I've simply missed the point of the game, and that I'm too thick or impatient to fully appreciate Dear Esther's strengths. In all honestly, there's a good chance that you're correct in saying that. However, this game did not engage me on any level. I never felt invested in any of the character shells we're given a vague description of, and its eagerness to be intellectual and thought-provoking just came across as pretentious and condescending. I can give it credit for trying, but not for failing in its primary purpose. For that reason, I cannot recommend Dear Esther as a video game.
(But I do recommend buying the soundtrack. Seriously, go get it, it really is that good)

Dear Esther is the precursor of walking simulators and the remake Dear Esther: Landmark Edition is an homage to the genre and even more worth the experience.
The beautiful landscape, even if littered and bleak, sets the atmosphere to the gloomy thoughts, possibly depressed mind of the protagonist and his journey through a desolate island. The music is melancholic and thoughtfully distributed throughout the scenes, equally as recognizable as the visuals and the wonderfully heartfelt narration. As the randomized voice-overs play while exploring the environment, the player is invited to construct his own story with hints from the writing or bits and pieces found in the vicinity.
With respect to the five to ten years older originals, the quality of the graphics and audio have been improved and enhanced. With a few more options and additional directors' commentary, the Landmark Edition is true to its name in that it's the definitive version of the first walking simulator. The commentary offers interesting insights into the thought process behind the literally game-changing decisions made in Dear Esther and moreover shows, that the game is a true labour of love.
For anyone undeterred by the genre, Dear Esther: Landmark Edition deserves a playthrough.
