This game is stunning.
Dear Esther is a game changer- literally; it essentially founded and defined the 'walking simulator' genre. Starting as a Half-Life mod and progressing to full game and now the beautiful landmark edition. As the protagonist you wander a Hebridean island piecing together bits of your past through triggered voice overs, scenery and items; all of which are randomly generated and non-linear, ensuring every player has a unique experience!
The narration is fairly sparse and the story is left intentionally vague and open to interpretation without being unsatisfying or feeling incomplete; it held my interest and I was intrigued throughout. The voice acting is perfectly suited to the rest of the game; I found it emotive but calm and with an air of distance reminding you that is in an inner monologue. Visually the game is beautiful (I took SO many screenshots!) and Jessica Curry's soundtrack, especially recorded with live musicians, is mesmerising- I often fall asleep listening to the soundtrack to this or Everybody's Gone to the Rapture on Spotify! Every aspect of the game comes together seamlessly to gradually build the overall atmosphere and reach its crescendo.
You get a real sense of the dedication, work and love that went into this game when you play it and is even more evident if you then play with the developers' commentary as I did. It provides some really interesting insight into both the game and the process of producing it.
Overall, it is well made, emotive, relaxing, and beautiful game and even though it may not be to everyone's tastes I think it is a relatively unique and beautiful experience that I would happily recommend it.

I've finally finished the story for this game and as far as how it tells the tale is pretty good, much better than usual anyways. I think it does an excellent job of delivering plenty of story content and any who enjoys the series should definitely grab the game, some of the specialized fights are extremely fun and creative. The only real con I have is that the characters are completely without balance at all, I understand it isn't exactly an E-sport game but many of the characters just have blatantly unfair advantages compared to most characters. It isn't like you'll be unable to beat story mode but you'll definitely find yourself throwing the controller from a BS combo or CPU specific ability getting an insanely lucky combo on you that ruins your S rank attempt or even drops you to B. I have to say that it does suck that the best way to obtain rank S in story is basically just spam your regular ninjutsu (not your special one) and hope for a lucky streak usually you can recover most of the chakra used before they get up, and if you have most of your substitutions the CPU generally won't rush you to stop it either. This is especially effective with characters like Senjutsu Naruto who has a thrown Ninjutsu with extreme range. Otherwise you'll find yourself restarting fights dozens of times each, the boss battles are very very unbalanced as well, the ones with the gigantic fighting or non-character players are generally way too easy, you can get S in these AND do the extra objectives almost accidentally. But the boss battles with regular characters seem overtuned, their ability to spam jutsu and substitution will have you screaming at your screen, yet again the best thing to do is spam single load ninjutsu (they almost always dodge/block double load with insanely inhuman speed). Overall the AI for this game is completely out of whack, at first it seems like a good challenge but it is realistically just their reflexes turned up to insane levels.
Besides the bad character balance and the overtuned AI, the design of the characters is very fluid, some of them have abilities that are blatantly ridiculous of course (pretty much any character that teleports will be easy to win S ranks with). But besides that they look and feel great to play, probably their least balanced game ever but out of the ultimate ninja series their story-telling and design level is out of this world this time around.

Rating: 8/10
Replayability: Low

Length: Takes a few days to beat.
Pros:
Great story, decent engine, good graphics (even by today's standards, the game is decent enough to play), the game has a sequel coming up soon, choices and consequences - The game actively makes you reap what you sow, great dialogue system on par with other RPGs from that time, and even some today - fully voice acted, great story.
Cons:
Human Revolution is optimized for console, which can seem like a big minus, unless you own a controller for your PC, which seriously smoothens the experience.
Somewhat confusing inventory system.
Very harsh gameplay where you get severely punished for missing minor details early in the game.
Very confusing endings (to the point where beating the game actually seems pointless compared to simply playing it).
Whether you're new to the Deus Ex series, or this is your first attempt, this game is a good place to start. The older games certainly hold good memories for those who played them when they came out, but due to possitively ancient gameplay - many people simply will not consider them playable anymore.
Story-wise, there doesn't seem to be anything you explicitly have to know from the previous games, in order to enjoy Human Revolution, so it's not really a sequel, but just another game in the series.

I started this game 100% fresh to MechWarrior and BattleTech in general and am loving every minute of it. I don't feel as though it's pay to win, I'm no stranger to tactical shooters so maybe that helps.
After my first 25 Cadet games I had ~20 mill C-bills which seemed to be enough to get either a few IS mechs or a single clan mech and completely kit them out with a custom loadout. Which may not seem like alot, considering the vast variety of mech choices there are, but for the most part it's a solid starting point.
I will argue that c-bill gain without premium time after those 25 cadet games can be very slow, but just like any similar game to this (World of Tanks, War Thunder, etc) it's just a grind, and for the most part the mechs are fairly well balanced at the moment. Some mechs are argueably just flat out worse than others, but if you learn the game mechanics and play properly any mech can work in the right pilots hands. So far I've spent very little money on this game and I have played it for a solid 2-4 hours minimum per day since I downloaded it and it's still a blast.
So far I have had very little problems with the community, the occasional salty teammate in chat, but what game doesn't have that. Not alot of people use the in game VOIP which is relatively disappointing considering the game revolves aren't alot of focus firing and communication, but it hasn't seemed to dictate the overall results of my matches (though the matches go much smoother when communication is present). There is tons of useful information for new and verteran players alike on the forums, pretty much anything I've wanted to learn about the game has been readily available via a simple google search.
Being new to MechWarrior the gameplay mechanics at first were a little overwhelming but even the most average of gamers can readily grasp how to play the game and even more advanced mechanics like shielding and such. The introduction tutorial isn't anything incredible but it does give a fairly solid overview of the basics of the game such as targetting components, firegroups, and mech movement. Alright, where do I start?
Also this review is written on 12/21/2015, so some information may change.
- F2P -
The game is a free-to-play game, so give it a shot. The grind in-game isn't as bad as it used to be. You can now gain in-game currency at a reasonable rate whether you do well or not. There is some content that's locked behind a paywall. There's some stuff you can purchase with the premium currency (MC) and some stuff you can purchase with cash directly from the
website.The premium currency stuff is mostly cosmetics. You can purchase mechs and stuff with the premium currency, but that's a waste. There are some premium only mechs with unique hardpoint configurations.Thankfully, PGI is rather generous, as there are ways to gather the premium currency in-game. As for the direct cash purchase items, they are typical pre-order mechs that'll eventually get released for
purchase via the in-game currency. Some of them have special stuff that's exclusive to the purchase, so if you're a sucker for some of those aesthetics, feel free to purchase?
- Gameplay -
As for the gameplay, its a more tactical shooter, with a simulation game feel. It significantly slower than most shooters in the market, so don't try to play it like those other games. You get to pilot some stompy robots and shoot some lasers, ballistics, missiles and stuff at each other. And you get to fully customize their loadouts and such. It's rather entertaining.
There are 4 weight classes of mechs you get to pick from. Lights: Played fast and twitchy. They typically have little armor and weaponry, but they get to run all over and wreck heavier mechs in various situations. If you have a twitch shooter background, playing lights may help you ease into the game. Mediums: Relatively nimble and armed. I recommend playing mediums if you have no clue where to start. They have enough tools to show you the range of what mechs can do. Heavys: Well armored and armed. Heavies are the bread and butter of the team, as they have the mobility and firepower to influence a match greatly. Most players play heavies for that purpose. Assaults: Heavily armored, and armed to the teeth. Playing a assault makes you a walking turret. You're supposed to tank damage and push for your team, as most players will follow you. If you get cold feet or are indecisive, don't play an assault. There's a ridiculous amount of awareness you need to play an assault well.
- Learning Curve -
The learning curve is steep. There are a ridiculous number of mechanics to keep note of. And a lot of them aren't explained at all in the game. I could type endlessly about it and probably not cover it all. But thankfully, there are various external informational outlets you can find to tell you about those. But for the most part, there's a lot to take in. So don't be intimidated by that fact. Just play and learn from your mistakes. Also, big tip: use the minimap and don't use 3rd-person view.
Give the game a shot, its a genre that's been overshadowed, and who doesn't like robots?
Also on a side note: PGI has done some shady stuff, so keep note of that if anything seems to be going south.

Edit: While I still would recommend the game to anyone with a passing interest in mech combat the lethargic pace of development has just got me really down on actually wanting to play this continuously. A mech is announced months before it comes out, and then it goes out to the pre-orderers, then a month later it comes out for cbills. It just fosters this environment of staleness, perhaps this will be fixed this coming summer with the addition of new weapons and tech, but until then me picking the game up since i stopped playing months ago feels exactly the same.
I feel PGI could learn a lot about improving their model from other games such as WarFrame, I understand there's limitations for a niche game like MWO that wouldn't necessarily work like that, but the annoyance I get out of not wanting to get new mechs outweighs that heavily. The new skill tree system helps alleviate that now that players do not need 3 variants of a chassis to master it.
=========

Overall I don't like this controller. The thumbs down should give that away, but let me go into detail about what is good and what is bad. The overall theme of this controller is that everything it tries to do unique causes it to be bad.
The controller is mostly comfortable. The only thing uncomfortable about this controller is the two pads on the bottom that act as extra buttons. I'll elaborate on the pads down the line. But yeah, the controller feels fine to hold as a whole, and the buttons are (mostly) placed in good spots that are easy to reach.
The battery? I couldn't really tell you. I always hated the idea of using batteries to keep a controller going, so I always plugged it in to play. But I don't like having a controller that can only be used wireless by shoving disposable batteries into it now and then.
The biggest problem in this controller is the main feature. The circle pad. This feature was meant to make the controller more precise and feel more like a mouse. It does not. It feels more like trying to use the trackpad on a laptop. Have you ever tried playing a shooter on a laptop trackpad? Yeah, it's pretty awful. There's always RTS games, but because you're on a controller, hotkeys are extremely limited, and the precision is still lacking. It's just... bad. And this is the selling point of the controller! Why bother getting it then, when you can just get a double j-stick controller?
Now we get to the buttons on the back. You might think "Cool, now I get two extra buttons on my controller!" You're wrong! These buttons are just rebinds of other buttons on the controller. All they do is save you a tiny bit of reaching around, while posing a risk of accidentally pressing them, and making the controller less comfortable. Yet another feature working against the controller.

Tribes, the definition of what I want to see in a game. The unique mechanics in this game are so original and flawless that it makes me weep for everyone who think each new call of duty is revolutionizing the FPS genre, or nearly any shooter for that matter. With tribes you need true skill to do almost anything in this beautiful game unlike some other shooters I know where spray and pray is just the norm. While that could mean a bit of a steep learning curve I guarantee you that your time will not be wasted learning this game, and you will surely understand from this from the brilliant "cha-ching" of your very first blueplate. This game is also very pretty if you can run it on the higher settings (unlike me) and the sense of speed as you fly through the terrain is unreal. Sadly though as I wright this review the developer, Hi-Rez, have completely dropped this game from their radar. It is no longer being looked after and the community is very small which is a shame with how magnificent this game is. Even though there is no campaign, no developer oversight, and hardly any people playing it this still remains to this day my #1 favorite game simply because of how perfect the core gameplay experience is and how unique this game is among the vast array of shooter that, to be honest, all feel exactly the same. Hopefully in the future there will be another addition to the tribes series and I sincerely hope that Hi-Rez will do it great justice and now that the company is out of its infancy will understand how to keep a game thriving. This game deserves so much more credit then it recieves, even if it recieved some form of GOTY award, it deserves even more attention. It saddens me that good games like this get shoved to the side and forgotten while every "new" COD gets so much attention even when it is doing the same thing over and over.
What makes me most sad though is to anyone who would pick up this game today would not understand the impact this game had to some people in its prime, all they would see is hundreds of empty servers with what seems like 50 people online at any one time. Even though this game has admittedly gone downhill it will still remain as my favorite game of all time.

I highly recommend this game, but there's a slight warning there.  This game outlives its content in its current iteration.
I'm not going into the detail others have writen, because what exists in the game is great, but the game stops evolving far before it finishes.  I'm pretty sure the game could have ended at about 25% the length it is, because nothing new mechanically happens in the last 75%.  You start the game with a bunch of research, and the foundation is great.  There's a soft cap on what you can research until you reach a certain plot point, but once you reach that point, you unlock tier 4 ships, and that's it.  You can easily have 100% of the research unlocked before said plot point, and that composes rouhghly 90% of the entire game's research tree.
That, in of itself, is not terrible, but the rest of the game past the plot point becomes "wait 180 days for the next trigger to occur," which is then repeated 4 more times.  I got out of the first phase at about day 200, with all the tech researched, so that left me a very large amount of game time twiddling my thumbs, grinding pointless resources, and maxing out every unit I had.
But the devs have plans to add a lot to this game.  Hopefully that will fill the massive, achingly painful gap that is the latter end of the game, which is made even more awkward when compared to the incredibly strong start of the game.  The actual end is also really good, it just takes traveling through dead space for a dozen or so irl hours to get there.

A Strong start and a Poor Ending.
I had real enthusiasm for this game.  It starts off very well, interesting set up, bleak future and silly humor.  It comes off as a very basic but cheeky satire on Star Trek.  The game play is simple enough, but it was engaging to start, and easy to pick up.  It was engaging and made me want to play more, even when I needed to start over to get farther.
Unfortunately, this does not last.  The game starts to bog down relentless enemy power climb that your always struggling to stay at par with.  Random events that at first add depth to multiple playthroughs or dull sections lose their charm when you realize almost all of them are bad.  The real problem starts to creep up with ship tiers and officers.  Lower tier ships can stand against higher ones if there is only 1 higher enemy in a fight but as soon as the enemy is sending in groups of higher tier ships your lower ones are cannon fodder.  As you can't send out ships without an officer (why?) you end up with a problem.  You either don't have enough officer to send out more than a single strong battle group, or you end up with a single strong battle group backed by a bunch of low level officers flying outclassed ships.  Your officers are often under leveled save for your battle group, meaning the tasks they can engage in are limited, the low-level stuff already gone.
I ran into brick walls several times during game play, and restarted 3 times to get around those walls, as there was no way to recover once they happened.  The final time I made it to a boss monster attacking the station, I had made it 250+ turns, had 8 officers (main and 1st officer +4 from academy, the rescue from new terra and "Bucky") and enough high end ships to equip 5 of them.  The boss on arrival suddenly pull a new wall out of his rear and I just wanted to stop playing.  Even with help from the pirates this just wasn’t fun anymore.  I spent the better part if day replaying to this point and i was left with squads of tier 3 enemies everywhere (which are no fun to fight even in tier 3), a boss with that surprise at my door, and a portal guarded by a tier 4. And I have had enough.
This game starts well, it drew me in, but the end game is awful.  If you’re ok with knowing you will encounter that just for the fun of the early game, go for it, pick this game up and have at it.  Anyone who wants to actually finish this game...forget it

This game had the potential to be really fun to play. It has an interesting art style, amazing cutscenes, puzzle solving with multiple characters and the potential for a great story.
However it suffers from some terrible design decisions. The puzzles are really simple and require next to no thinking to figure out, which makes it obvious that this game is intended for the younger audiences. The stealth system is very simplistic, enemies have no recollection of you and all you have to do is stay out of the line of sight and hide in a bush or a vase or something like that if you are spotted. Managing the playable characters is extremely tedious and it would help a lot if the developers added some simple commands such as follow, as it stands right now you have to move each character individually through the whole map. The levels are short, but they feel extremely long because of the aforementioned difficulty with controlling the playable characters.
And the absolute biggest problem with the game is how the story is presented. Mysterious Cities of Gold is based on a cartoon and also copies the story from it, including the cutscenes which are taken from the cartoon. This makes the game not suitable to play for anyone who isn't familiar with the cartoon, because all you get from the story are gorgeously animated short cutscenes which skip ahead a lot, because the game is trying to present the story of the full run of the cartoon within a small number of short cutscenes..
Do not play this game if you are not either familiar with the story or a preteen. If you are at least one of those, they you will likely enjoy the game. However I am neither one, so I simply got frustrated and bored with it.

Eric "Badspot" Hartman, the modern day Pablo Picasso and creator of this masterpiece obviously knows how to create new, fresh, original content, and not take the ideas of others and put them into a subpar game, in a genre controlled by a single giant game. Minecraft, on the other hand, attempts to rip off a game such as this, to a lesser quality. Does minecraft have a destruction engine? Nope, but this mona lisa of games does. The Steam controller is probably one of the most controversial controllers for the PC. Some people like it and some people hate it. I personally bought this controller when it was on sale for $35 and I think it is worth that. Honestly it's not a bad buy for $50, but it seems to be going on sale often enough and it's worth the wait. I bought this controller as kind of a novelty. I thought it was cool that it had the steam logo on it and I liked the back paddles. I tried out a friends before I bought mine and I decided to get one not really knowing what I am going to use it for. I wouldn't use this to replace a controller that you use for a competitive game (such as Rocket League) or something that you are already comfortable using a different controller for. This is my fourth PC compatible controller and I think its a great additition to my collection. I will now go over some pros and cons.
Pros.
-Cool Looking
-Back paddles offer a faster way to perform an action
-YOU CAN USE THE TRACKPADS TO CONTROL YOUR PC!!! The controller can act like a mouse and you can use the trackpads for moving and scrolling and the triggers for left and right click.
-THIS CONTROLLER CAN BE USED ON BASICALLY ANY GAME!!! This means you can use a controller for a game without any controller support. Believe it or not this works very well for some games.
-Vastly different from, but at the same time still similar to other controllers
-Comfortable Weight
-You can set custom startup sounds
-Comes with a long micro SD card
-Fairly Inexpensive and good quality
Cons:
-There is no place on the back of the controller for the usb connector
-It can be weird to hold at times
-Will NOT work well for all games
-An Xbox 360 or Xbox One Controller is better in a lot of cases
Overall I would reccomend this controller. This is my fourth PC compatible controller and I think its a great additition to my collection.

For the longest time, I've struggled with pain in my wrists and hands from the conventional mouse and keyboard gaming. I've tried various types of keyboards and mouse combinations, and while some helped, I still continued to suffer from the same problem. When I saw this go on sale a few months back, I decided to give it a go. I have been using it for about 2 months now, and after 100+ hours of gameplay, and some getting used to, here is my review.
+ fully able to customize the controler to make it function how you want it to
+ able to use for pretty much every type of game
+ much easier on the hands and wrists than playing with a keyboard and mouse
+ the butterfly trigger buttons on the back of the controller really are a great addition
+ the controller really ties in great with Steam's Big Picture Mode
+ eliminates me from going back and forth between mouse and controller while in game - I LOVE THAT
- while playing games with free movement, I noticed the left joystick sometimes does not always return to center mass when I release it, causing my character to continue on without me touching the controller (very annoying while playing FPS games)
- the button layout took me a lot of getting used to. A common problem I'm having is while using the A,B,X,Y buttons, I will often times brush the right trackpad causing unwanted camera movement
All in all, regardless of the few small issues I have, I'm still very satisfied with this product. I would highly recommend this to my fellow gamers who struggle with wrist and hand pain.

Tribes, the definition of what I want to see in a game. The unique mechanics in this game are so original and flawless that it makes me weep for everyone who think each new call of duty is revolutionizing the FPS genre, or nearly any shooter for that matter. With tribes you need true skill to do almost anything in this beautiful game unlike some other shooters I know where spray and pray is just the norm. While that could mean a bit of a steep learning curve I guarantee you that your time will not be wasted learning this game, and you will surely understand from this from the brilliant "cha-ching" of your very first blueplate. This game is also very pretty if you can run it on the higher settings (unlike me) and the sense of speed as you fly through the terrain is unreal. Sadly though as I wright this review the developer, Hi-Rez, have completely dropped this game from their radar. It is no longer being looked after and the community is very small which is a shame with how magnificent this game is. Even though there is no campaign, no developer oversight, and hardly any people playing it this still remains to this day my #1 favorite game simply because of how perfect the core gameplay experience is and how unique this game is among the vast array of shooter that, to be honest, all feel exactly the same. Hopefully in the future there will be another addition to the tribes series and I sincerely hope that Hi-Rez will do it great justice and now that the company is out of its infancy will understand how to keep a game thriving. This game deserves so much more credit then it recieves, even if it recieved some form of GOTY award, it deserves even more attention. It saddens me that good games like this get shoved to the side and forgotten while every "new" COD gets so much attention even when it is doing the same thing over and over.
What makes me most sad though is to anyone who would pick up this game today would not understand the impact this game had to some people in its prime, all they would see is hundreds of empty servers with what seems like 50 people online at any one time. Even though this game has admittedly gone downhill it will still remain as my favorite game of all time.

Halycon 6 has a lot of things going for it, but as an actual game it is a bit lacklustre. The art style is cute and very much along the lines of FTL or Shovel Knight, the sound design is fanastic with the music being both amusing and extremely fitting and the gameplay is both functional and easy to understand while still presenting a challenge to the player. That all said, despite what the marketing might say about this game being 'the next FTL' or 'the next XCOM', it fails to outshine either of those games. Halycon 6 is by no means a bad game, I've had a lot of fun playing it. It just happens to not be the longest living of games. All in all, Haylcon 6 ticks all the right boxes, but you should maybe hold off getting it until it goes on sale.

People love FTL because of it's challanging yet rewarding gameplay with interesting RPG elements and fighting mechanics.
Halcyon 6 didn't manage to accomplish it, Firstly, fighting is unreasonably slow, not challenging and not rewarding even at higher difficulty levels than normal. Secondly, leveling up characters isn't satisfying, because nothing really changes except for you get a few more abilities and then you upgrade them.
Before you say "well, getting more abilities and upgrading them is character progression by definition". Yes, but in practice, it doesn't matter here. Game bugged out for me once and I entered a fight without my character, so I only had my ship's basic abilities (as if, the ship was flying by itself). And I won, and it was an easy win. See my point? Character progression, while being a neccessary element of the game, remains pointless in practice.
People love XCOM because of squad customisation, base development and interesting tactical turn-based fighting.
In Halcyon 6 base-building Is good, actually, no major complaints. A bit tedious to navigate through at times, but nothing game-breaking.
Squad customisation and tactical fighting is not present though. I played with 2 ships for 5 hours straight because frankly, getting more characteres to run new ships (as well as building those new ships) is resource-consuming and there is no real need for it in the first place since fights are very easy anyway.
In XCOM you just cannot get by with a small group of troops: you constantly need more, you want to upgrade your squad, you want to try different combinations and see what works best. In Halcyon 6 rolling with Engineer + Scientist + Tactician is your best bet and it's obvious even before you get into your first fight (3 classes - 3 available slots... hmm what do I choose?)
And once you get in a fight, you don't need to plan out your actions, because, for starters, it's not really possible due to RNG and enemies acting in an unpredictable fashion. And secondly, you will win the fight easily anyway so why bother.
If you've played Darkest Dungeon, you probably know that it starts fantastic, addicting and all-around fun only to turn into a grindfest after the first 20-30 hours of gameplay. Well, that's actually pretty much how Halcyon 6 is like, except for instead of 20-30 hours of fun you get around 2-3 hours of fun.
In Darkest Dungeon you upgrade your base and your "squad" inbetween going to various missions similarly to what Halcyon 6 is all about. Except for, in Darkest Dungeon you have way more classes to choose from and you have various dungeons with different enemies to explore and loot.
Instead of various dungeons Halcyon 6 offers you to fight off same goddamn aliens that keep swarming your colonies over and over again. And they don't even drop loot! It is a chore and the game doesn't even try to make it fun. You also have Pirates attacking your base from time to time, which is not really that different from aliens though.
It gets a bit different when you get onto story quests, but the proportion between fights with aliens / pirates / other factions is ridiculous. I remember only 1 fight with another faction from my 6 hours of playtime. ONE. I wish I could go off and explore other factions more, but upon return I would have found half my colonies to be destroyed or occupied by aliens, so that wasn't an option.
Alien invasions are simple: they open up a portal, immideately send one or two fleets to a local colony and then they keep doing that until you destroy the portal. So you fly over, destroy the portal, then fly around cleaning up the mess they've made, then fly back to base only to realise they have opened yet another damn portal and, yet again, are already swarming your colonies.
It's so sad. The game has great promise to it. Most flaws I described when comparing Halcyon 6 to FTL or XCOM are completely fine because regardless of them the game has it's own charm.
Aliens though.
I hate aliens. I wish there was a mod that allows you to tweak the time inbetween alien attacks because it's just unbearable. You keep flying around your Faction cleaning up alien fleets over and over again. Fighting them takes a load of time and gives completely zero joy.
The game is not terrible, in fact, it could be great!
I really liked that you can have different characters of the
and they would have different backstories, different unique abilities and personal traits. You have a wide variety of ships to choose from, which is also great.
There is a number of factions/races that you get in contact with, they all have their own style of comunication and actually say interesting stuff followed by well drawn animated portraits you see on the telecomunication screen. You can choose how to answer to them and from what it seems, this impacts on how they treat you in the future.
After you've developed your base enough, you can actually automate the resource gathering process using drones (many people complained about having to manually gather resources over and over again). I wish, you didn't have to manually install drones though, makes zero sense, but that's besides the point.
It saddens me that developers put so much time into the game to recieve so many bad reviews by unsatisfied players, because the game actually could be truly amazing.
Halcyon 6  just needed a bit more polish before release or a nice patch that fixes game-breaking flaws. The basis for a great game is there, too bad it was ruined by simpliest things. There really are not too many major issues in the game.
Unfortunate part is, even though the number of said issues is not great, their impact on the gameplay is.

I've got to echo other negative reviews in that I *really* want to love this game, but it just falls flat in some really basic areas that I can't look past. First and foremost, to me at least, is the interface. I don't understand some of the design decisions here. For example, if I have a fleet already in space and I want to send another fleet out I can't just select those ships and go. You have to click the destination , click send fleet, click to remove the ships from your first fleet that are inexplicably auto-filled into the "new fleet" screen despite being lightyears away, then click launch.
Similarly travel is counter-intuitive. Certain systems generate "fuel" that is a universal resource used any time any fleet goes anywhere. The costs are fairly high and if you're out of fuel you must "return to base" which does not, somehow, cost any fuel at all. On the return flight you might pass right over an asteroid that has more fuel but you can't stop, so if a distant fleet needs fuel you can only fix it by sending a different fleet to collect fuel near your starbase which somehow allows the other fleets to move. If my description is confusing it's because so is the mechanic.
I considered refunding, but I decided against it because in the end I do see a tremendous amount of promise in this game. It needs polish, some direction and a hard look at the interface. With some changes, including an auto-resolve function, it could be a real cult hit.
I hope I can recommend this game one day, but as it stands I've got to give this one a thumbs down.

Landmark Edition is the remastered version of Dear Esther, adding achievements, Director's Commentary, and somewhat improving the visuals. Director's Commentary is by far the best addition and is definitely worth listening to, although the execution could have been better. Unlike the perfectly timed narration, commentary runs too long and forces frequent stops to allow the recording to finish before triggering the next one. It does create pauses where you can just stand and take in the landscape though, so perhaps it was intentional. (I still think these should have been rehearsed a bit to cut down on babble and repetition). Achievements are a dubious addition and usually distract from the story and ruin immersion, so whether or not these add value is up to you. Visually, Landmark Edition is definitely an improvement with sharper textures and thicker grass, but does this drastically improve the game? I don't think it does, and since, for some strange reason, the remaster does not support ultrawide resolutions, I would say it is a step backwards where it counts and you should try to get your hands on the regular edition instead.

Dear Esther had an impact on me, and I found myself ruminating on it a long time after I had completed it.
First off, I should state, that Dear Esther is more of an
than a traditional game.  The only action you can take as the player is to walk and zoom in.  There is nothing to interact with, nothing to fight, and nothing to do except to explore.  If this doesn't appeal to you, then you won't enjoy Dear Esther.
However, the experience of Dear Esther is a powerful one.  The island is gorgeous, particularly when you visit the island's cave system.  The story is told through voiceover narration, assumedly from your character.  The voiceovers take the form of short little snippets (sometimes, in a way that seems overly grandiloquent) from letters the narrator has written to Esther.  These snippets are, overall, very interesting, and feed into the mysterious feel of the game.  Something has happened on this island and to the narrator, and it becomes a intriguing little diversion as you explore the island to try and peice together the puzzle of the events.  However, while you can a get a broad picture of what happened, many details are obscured or contradicted as the narrator reads these snippets - and you eventually discover that the narrator is likely unreliable.
It should be noted, that if you play through the game again (I have not done this), that you get randomized snippets, which may reveal more of the mystery of what has happened.  However, I am not compelled to do this.  Dear Esther, while having a real impact on me, is not something I will likely play again.  This should not be considered a mark against the game - I just know that the impact of the experience will be much less than the first time around.
Dear Esther is a short game, I took my time exploring the island and I spent almost 2 hours with it.  During this 2 hours, I thoroughly experienced Dear Esther - I triggered all the voiceovers (seemingly triggered by reaching certain points of the island), I found all the collectibles, and I explored every interesting nook and cranny of the island.  If the value proposition of a game is important to you, this will likely feed into your decision to buy it.  I bought the original game on sale for a few bucks, and recieved the Landmark edition free when it was released.  If the value proposition is important to you, but you still think you would enjoy experiencing Dear Esther, I would recommend waiting for it to go on sale.
: Dear Esther is a game that will appeal to a certain type of person.  If you enjoy reading and do not necessarily need your video games to be action packed, you will probably enjoy this game.  It should also be noted, that while Dear Esther is, of course, a video game, I think it could easily also be classified as an
.  For my part, over the 2 hours I spent exploring Dear Esther, I felt intrigued, mesmerized, relaxed, and a little depressed.  I can heartily recommend Dear Esther to a certain type of gamer (on sale, for the budget conscious gamer).  While short, it will leave a mark on you, and you will be thinking about it a long time after you finish.

Arguably the first of its kind and quite polarizing because of its unique nature,
pushes the boundaries of games as an artistic medium to the extreme and revolutionizes as genre defining phenomenon .
I'm gonna say that I've played the original game a few years ago but when we got the free upgrade of the
which includes a free directors commentary, I couldn't miss the opportunity of re-experiencing this fantastic game with the added bonus of listening to the insight of the game's creators.
Dear Esther can claim to be the very first
, a polarizing genre which over the past few years managed to create a lot of attention and grow exponentially. The genre has produced masterpieces and at the same time lazy cash grabs and truth be told that was to be expected. In its core, Dear Esther and other walking simulator offer the player minimal gameplay. Understandably this will create a gap between gamers who want to experience something different and people who take the word 'game' quite more literally than others.
I'm not gonna insult or demean people who consider Dear Esther and other walking simulators, less of a game and more like a semi-interactive movie or novel. Despite all the (sometimes necessary) labels, Dear Esther has a big heart underneath and I believe even if you might feel dismissive because of preconceived false stigma which the game bares, I recommend opening your heart and mind and soul for just two hours and see what Dear Esther has to offer.
It is thanks to Dear Esther that I managed to mature more as a gamer and appreciate games more than just killing time and having fun. Becoming emotionally invested in the story/characters, breathing and taking in the scenery and atmosphere a game has to offer, read between the lines for underlying themes, give your own interpretation and meaning on how the game unfolds and finishes and so much more.
Walking simulators are by nature more prone to evoke said emotions and tantalize the mind of the player albeit such feats are neither frequent nor easy. You'd think that making a game of this genre is easy work but you'd be wrong. As mentioned in the directors commentary, games like Dear Esther are naked for the player to scrutinize; they are exposed and their flaws are easily identified. It is therefore a much harder task to completely enthrall the player into their world.
So if you're one of the privileged few who haven't experienced the game before, what can you expect from Dear Esther? Well be prepared for a short but powerful experience. A bleak, dreary, melancholic but ultimately hopeful journey through an uninhabited Hebridean island, listening to a series of letters which provide a unique way to let the story unravel in front your mind's eye. All of this is accompanied by a beautifully fitting soundtrack, some stunningly magnificent visuals for a
game and an eerie yet breathtaking atmosphere which will almost overwhelm you at certain parts of the game.
The story and the ending are open to many interpretations and I believe that's also one of the main strengths of Dear Esther. There's an element of ambiguity yet at the same time certainty of the imagery you'll see, the soundtrack you'll hear, the echoing words of the narrator, everything blends together and blurs the line between what's real and what's not.
Even if you've played the game before, I strongly recommend a replay with the director's commentary ON so you'll get more information on the creative process from the developers who offer a fantastic insight on how the game came to be.
I'd dare call this game a masterpiece in my book but at the same I understand people who might want to pass on this one. It's not for everyone but I firmly believe that you should give yourself a couple of hours and delve deep into an one-of-kind gaming experience. An absolute recommendation.

Full review:
I’ll start off by saying, I’ve never seen the original anime that this game is based on. I actually did not know of its existence until I stumbled onto this interesting game. I might actually want to watch the 80′s anime, the game made it seem quite interesting. Because of this, I’ll be unaffected by the “nostalgia factor” that many people had when they saw this game. Anyways, I’ve seen a lot of people purchasing this purely out of nostalgia, and learned about the show because of it; now, onto the review!
I was slightly disappointing by how the game played out. The game essentially combines puzzle elements with some scavenger hunting mechanics. That’s the entire game in a nutshell. The basic concept of the game is not that hard to understand. You’ll find yourself switching between the three main characters, Esteban, Tau, and Zia. Each character has their own special ability used for certain puzzle mechanics found scattered throughout the levels of the game. Each of these skills will have to be used in a certain pattern in order to complete a level. This ultimately results in the player wandering around looking for an object that pertains to a character’s ability, like a crack in a wall, which Zia can slip through.
The levels can easily be traversed with a free-roaming camera, marking each character with an icon and allowing you to figure out the solution to a puzzle from an easier perspective. The problem with this style of gameplay is that switching between the characters feels like a chore. You have to operate all three characters separately, each being used for their ability. Throughout the game, you pick up these “parchments”, which act as collectibles scattered throughout a level. Collecting them all gives you a gold medal at the end of the level for finding them all. The problem with this is that some of the parchments are color-coded, allowing only certain characters to pick them up. This can be a nuisance when you have one character standing on these parchments, unable to pick them up, and the actual character needed to pick them up on the opposite side of the level, awaiting their orders from the player.
The puzzles can be a bit shallow sometimes. There was one instance where a series of pressure plates were laid out in front of me, and three of them had to be activated to open the next door. Above these plates was a plaque that only Tao could read. Reading it tells you what plates to stand on, usually in the form of a riddle, which is nice, but some of them were a little too easy for my tastes. Along with the parchments that can be collected, there is a treasure chest hidden in each level. Finding the chest unlocks an illustration, just another bonus collectible to find.
It’s also worth mentioning that I ran into a game-breaking bug twice. I had to press a button to open a door, and upon pressing the button, it showed the door opening, then immediately closing. I thought I had messed up somewhere, but upon exiting and restarting the game, the door stayed open and I could continue with the game. This happened to me in the first and third worlds. Both occurring near the end of the level, which was quite annoying, having to restart the level.
The game’s graphics were awesome. In-between levels, cutscenes would play with the style of the original anime and leaves me wondering if these cutscenes were actually in the anime themselves. I’m sure fans of the original show would appreciate that. The animation for the characters was smooth, but could be clunky at times, especially when walking across platforms that can be turned with a lever. Overall, the art style was very charming and I really liked it. Although not memorable, the music was great and fit the theme of the game well.

Nostalgia obviously plays a huge role when it comes to such a classic license but this game is good enough to stand out on its own. The basic gameplay is engaging but with a gentle difficulty curve that makes it suitable for younger players. Experienced players can aim for all the optional goals to up the challenge. After spending many hours with this title, the best I can say is that is about one third complete. The mechanics are so rigid as to prevent any real play variance. For example, you are compelled into a strict regimen of  play - as any variance either too far ahead or behind results in being attacked. There is no real diplomatic and trade based approach. IN the same way, if you want to pursue a science theme, forget it - as the game is designed to "reward" following a path that essentially linear across the whole possible range of improvements. The time to discover items becomes so distorted if you try to follow a "theme", with turn times blowing out from 2-5 as an average to 30 plus if you try to go a specific route.
The planet developments consist of just letting it be automated - trying to decipher half the meanings of some improvements is both frustrating and pointless - there is no visual or other queues to show what you need to stop youe empire constantly going into near revolt, with half of your systems "on strike" - even at the easiest settings. As an example, at the lowest setting, playing the Empire, every system has to be set at "approval enhancements" for it to work at all.
This may sound harsh, but this was NOT a $10 game - and having played MOO II 10 tens ago, which absolutely blows this away, I expected far more than I got.

Endless Space has Endless Playability and can be enjoyed as long as you continue to enjoy games of its type. You start with one planet and must slowly spread through any means required to take as many systems as you can and push back your enemies. You can form alliances, design your warships, and conquer any opponent foolish enough to oppose you. Through careful trading and taking resources for yourself, you can make a monopoly on them, generating bonuses for your empire. All the while, take over star systems and the planets inside them, building upgrades to increase your peoples loyalty and the resources they generate. Multiple races and map types allow variety and then you can create customized versions of the races too, creating your own custom faction. If you love turn based strategy and sci-fi action, this is one of the best games of its style that I have ever played!

Doomguy is back (this time, you're called the Doom Slayer, which is even cooler), and you're at it again.
You remember the saying that the demons should be terrified of you?
Well, in this game, they canonically are.
The demons know of you.
They are terrified of you.
And you make their fears of you real.
Being the monster that demons are afraid of is awesome.
The Glory Kills, which are the unique melee kills you can execute, remains fun and satisfying from start to finish.
Mowing everything down with your bullets, swimming in the blood of demons without uttering a single word, not even a grunt, is such an amazing experience.
One thing that I was afraid of was the repetition.
I mean, you can only shoot and melee demons in so many ways, right?
Well, yeah, but it never gets old.
Bethesda has somehow made the repeated massacres of hordes of demons enjoyable the whole way; which is impressive if you think about it.
Graphically, amazing.
You can see 1 map before and after being corrupted by Hell, and it adds a lot of flavor.
Mars and Hell itself has fantastic landscapes; especially Hell.
The sound effects is so satisfying.
Gauss Canon on Siege Mode; everytime you ready this beast, you feel like a badass.
Every time you fire it, you get the oh-so-satisfying feeling of power.
The music is amazing.
Just listen to the music in the menu alone and you'd understand.
If fits the game perfectly.
Story wise, it's quite minimal if you just go at the demons with nothing but murder in mind.
You will get some story, but it's super straightforward, and just plain Doom.
Go find demons, kill demons, close down Hell portal; same old wonderful plot. xD
But if you are interested you can read the flavor texts, and they are plentiful.
This is game that revels in what it does best.
Doom; it's where you go kill demons, and everything else is secondary to that.
Bethesda, you've outdone yourselves with this.
Bravo.

I both love and hate Naruto Shippuden: Ultimate Ninja Storm 4. As a fan of the anime and manga, I expected lots of intense action from what’s been presented as the final game of the Ultimate Ninja Storm series, and to its credit, Storm 4 delivers. The characters and over-the-top battles look and feel great, and the story pays off in a satisfying way. On the other hand, even the best combat system in the world would be wasted if there are no worthy opponents to be found.
That's not to say that this combat is the best, but it is pretty strong. Fights are fast and fierce, and are treated like major events by way of plenty of cinematic camera angles and powerful jutsu moves at your disposal. The controls are simple and the most responsive of the Storm games to date. What I liked most, however, was the ability to switch between your active fighter and two support characters on the fly by moving the right analog stick. This let me use my characters for both active and support roles, and didn’t limit them to one task in a fight. In one battle, I was able launch a series of punches with Hinata before calling for an assist from Naruto to deal more damage, and then switching to Hashirama Senju to recharge my energy fast for a  follow-up jutsu attack.

At first I liked Human Revolution. The atmosphere is wonderful and it really feels true to the original. However once you start getting into the game, you encounter horrific bugs that detract from the game experience.
I'm an explorer. I like looking for all the little nooks and crannies where the hidden items are. I climb fire escapes, jump from ledges, find all the vents, and hack into rooms that are locked. This is just how I like playing the game. Which is why the Icarus mod has so soured the game for me. Icarus lets you fall safely from any height. When it detects you are falling, it kicks in and slows your descent so you safely fall straight down.

Being one of the gems of my childhood, you can imagine how surprised and excited I was to see this series pop up in the steam store. For those unfarmiliar, Stronghold is a sort of economy based midevail RTS. Esentially, you are given a set of different scenarios in which you have to use the resources in the varying enviorments you are given. Sometimes, these enviornments will help you get an advantage to your enemy - you may be located close to trees, which will allow you to get a quick start on building many essential things, such as food and weapon producing buildings. Otherwise, you may be given a disadvantage at times and being able to make do with what you have can make victory all the more satisfying.
In Stronghold, you need to think carefully about how you spend your resources. On one hand, it will be important to build a barracks so you can hold a strong and ready militia to defend against your enemy's forces. On the other hand, in order to raise a decent army, you need to keep your peasants happy and in your castle. This requires keeping your grainary stocked with food, being able to have enough industrial buildings to build farms to keep peasants fed, and other mechanics.
To be victorious, you have to carefully plan out your divison of resources - it is equally important to keep your peasants populous and happy and to have a strong defence to wane off enemy attacks, as one good strike can land a once prosperous land in ruins, and you very vulnerable to further attacks. All in all, I would strongly recommend Stronghold to anybody new to the RTS genre. RTS veterans would probably enjoy playing this one, too. There's nothing quite as satisfying as surviving a seige and being able to crush your enemy in a few swift blows.

Would enjoy multiplayer more if they allowed for bigger maps than 400x400, but overall this game was my childhood.

After using the Steam Controller for a couple of months, I have quite a few words to describe it. Its functionality is quite limited when you're playing FPS titles, or anything fast-paced in general.  The touchpad that's meant to replace the thumbstick is quite awful when you're fully engaged playing your favorite games. GTA V, for example, didn't work for me, at all. Even at the highest sensitivity settings, and toying around with the different options for the gamepad, I couldn't really play comfortably... it felt like I was playing on a laptop touchpad, with the added benefits of being on a controller.
I did feel the Steam Controller shone in other places, like laid back RTS titles and with games like Cities: Skylines.  Though it is better to use a mouse and keyboard for these types of titles, I did appreciate the comfort of sitting back in my preferred chair, letting the controller do the work for me.  This gamepad was not meant for every game in my opinion, but it was still an awesome experience experimenting with the different ones in my library.
It also has the additional use as being a "remote" of sorts.  I hooked up a laptop, with Steam installed, and connected it to the living room television. I could actually fully use my computer from the couch  with my Steam Controller.  I watched a variety of videos on Youtube and Netflix with utter ease and simplicity. The typing feature that utilizes both of the touchpads is painless and intuitive to use, not even taking that long to search for whatever your heart desires.
I really can recommend the Steam Controller if you often partake in any of the activities above. It truly is a handy tool for me, and possibly can be for you, too.

The unique mechanics in this game are so original and flawless that it makes me weep for everyone who think each new call of duty is revolutionizing the FPS genre, or nearly any shooter for that matter. With tribes you need true skill to do almost anything in this beautiful game unlike some other shooters I know where spray and pray is just the norm. While that could mean a bit of a steep learning curve I guarantee you that your time will not be wasted learning this game, and you will surely understand from this from the brilliant "cha-ching" of your very first blueplate. This game is also very pretty if you can run it on the higher settings (unlike me) and the sense of speed as you fly through the terrain is unreal. Sadly though as I wright this review the developer, Hi-Rez, have completely dropped this game from their radar. It is no longer being looked after and the community is very small which is a shame with how magnificent this game is. As a long time veteran player, fan of the mechwarrior series and a general lover of big stompy robots. I would seriously recommend giving the game a try.
Unlike most shooters a mech has legs and a torso that you have to control seperately.  A mech plays like a giant walking tank. However unlike a tank the mech consists of independent body parts. You can lose arms, a leg or shoulders and still keep on going. When you lose a body part, you also lose the weapons in that body part. This adds an extra layer of tactics on top of normal shooter gameplay. By twisting away you can choose which body part will take the damage.
Also unlike most shooters a mech also has two cross-hairs, one for the weapons in the torso and one for the weapons in the arms (you do need to turn arm lock off). You control both with the mouse at the same time, one just moves a bit slower then the other. The weapons located in the arms can aim much higher and lower and move faster. They are however less protected then the weapons in the torso. This means that you have to think about your position on the battlefield. You want to move so all your weapons can shoot while your opponent won't be able to shoot back at all or atleast with all his weapons.
You are also able to customize your mech. Change the weapons, the speed at which the mech moves and a few other things. Because you're able to control which body part will take most of the damage and because the location of the weapons in the body matters this allows for allot of interesting choices and gameplay.
That said. Buying mechs and upgrading mechs is expensive. As new player you won't notice right away. Completing the tutorial, mechwarrior academy and the first two dozen of games will shower you with C-Bills. After that it takes some serious grinding. Pick your first purcachse wisely.
The gameplay is still that of an Arena shooter, two teams of 12 players face off one of 13 maps. In quick play there is no respawn and fight last usually about 7-8 minutes. After that it is mopping up for the victor. In quickplay there are three game modes. Though on most maps the winner is usually decided by which side wins the big fight in the middle. The objectives don't matter much here. There are other strategies but those require a coordinated team which you won't find in quick play.
For coordinated teams there is faction warefare. Two teams of 12 players either try to asault or defend a base. Each team has 4 respawns. A good game usually last between 30 and 45 minutes. Paladins WAS an amazing FPS MOBA game that gave you Overwatch-esc gameplay, with a twist.
The best part of Paladins was you could customize the champions to YOUR play style using cards and loadouts. I always hated how Overwatch made you bend to the style of the character you were playing.
Paladins was a game I would consider my personal favorite, It was my goto game to play with friends. It was free to play without any pay to win garbage thrown in....Notice how I said was.
OB64 is a way for Hi-rez to give Paladins the Star Wars BattleFront 2 treatment, except Disney isn't here to slap Hi-rez on the wrist for screwing up.
OB64 Takes the customization I praised so highly before and asks "How can we earn more money from that?"
Prior to OB64 loadouts had a limited number of points you could give to your cards per loadout. Cards had a maximum of 5 levels and you had 5 cards per loadout. It was easy and fair, everyone had the same amount of points to dedicate to a loadout and no loadouts were objectively better just because you gave Hi-rez a little more ca$h.
Cards were obtained using Essence which you got by logging in, completing quests and getting duplicates which was a very easy task.
In OB64 each card has a Max level of 10 and the level is no longer determined on a per-loadout basis, now cards are always the same level nomatter what loadout they're in. How do you level up cards? Why duplicates ofcourse! How do you get duplicates? by opening radiant chests (Lootboxes), which you obtain by playing the game...or by paying some extra $$$ for some chest keys to speed up the process. The grind is rediculous and it's very unbalanced. Radiant chests contain 3 items per chest (4 if you purchase a boost...ofcourse) there are over 20 champions each of them having an equal amount of cards so it'd impossible to focus on leveling up a specific champion...well sorta.
Champion chests are a thing, which are chests that will only give you items for 1 specific champion which decreases the grind..slightly, you can purchase these chests with gold or by playing a bunch with one champion in the UNBOUND mode.
Paladins now has 2 modes Unbound (Pay 2 Win) and Classic (The old game but stripped to it's core.)
Unbound mode gives you 3 gamemode options Seige, Onslaught and Payload.
Unbound players can have card levels ranging from level 1 - 10 (fair right?)
Classic Mode gives you 1 gamemode with 2 flavors. Siege, Competitive Seige.
Forces all cards to Level 4.
Competitive mode is ranked..obviously.
It's sad that Hi-rez has gone down this Pay-To-Win road.
Hi-rez doesn't listen to the community backlash and overall would sacrifice fan loyalty for a few extra dollars.
This game is now a game for the whales. The only thing we can hope for now is for Paladins to recieve a "Mostly Negative" on steam and let it die.
Honestly If Hi-rez came to me and said they reverted back all the changes they made in OB64 and begged me to come back, I wouldn't. If they'll do this once they'll do it again, thats the end of that.
It pains me to give what once was my favorite game a bad review, but I have to try and spread the word to potential new players. If you're new and looking for a good fun game to play with your mates, Paladins is not the game for you.

Having played all the previous incarnations of DOOM all those years ago on pc then on the greystation. I can’t say I’m one of those who dislikes this version. I love it! It is fast paced and optimised very very well. I run it with all the bells and whistles on and get solid frames on an ageing i7 2600k GTX 980ti system @ 1440p. It looks and sounds amazing. It is a visceral heart pounding experience, visually it is an eye busting feast. The sound is crisp and full of depth the ambient sounds really immerse you. I really don’t think there is much in this game that you cannot and should not enjoy.
Haven’t delved into multiplayer but did finish the SP campaign and thoroughly enjoyed it, if you are in it for an intellectual plot and depth then look elsewhere but if you want hoards of demonic creatures to blow holes in then this is the game for you. I think it is faithful to the original DOOM to some degree but you don’t play it for that right? You wanna shred demons and feel overwhelmingly powerful. There is a nice addition to being able to unlock upgrades for weapons if that is your thing. Also there is a perk system there for those that like that sort of thing. I’m aware some people criticised this but I guess this is the way games are going these days. There is the usual Bestiary there too. I though t some of the boss fights were a bit naff and where more about systematic timing and jumping than anything.
I’m not sure I would do another play through, not because it is a bad game but I don’t usually do that unless a game offers me something that drives me too. Plus I just don’t have the time for it with so many games filling up in my library. However I could be tempted to do some COOP stuff, now that would be cool.
If this was my first experience of DOOM as it was all those years ago then I would have been blown away, as I was back then.
Rip and tear. That's all I have to say.

This game is like an attractive girl with some very bad habits and/or attitudes. I tried to love this game, I tried to overlook the bugs, but I can't, they are too obvious. It is a good game, but sometimes, I cannot tell if some of the stuff they have are supposed to be features or bugs. For example, enemies can move during MY turn. If I wanted my enemies to move at the same time as me, I would go back to Sins of a Solar Empire.
Another frustrating thing is that my main fleet was trapped in a star system for X amount of turns because the AI, for whatever reason, decided to send 10 individual ships to that same system and set them on blockade mode. I can only kill 1 at a time so the chances of that fleet leaving on its own was close to zero, unless I mount a rescue.
The diplomacy is broken beyond believe. AIs often offer star systems and resources as part of their Cease Fire agreements. However, these agreements would be undone next turn, because the systems they surrendered contain the same resources in the agreement, so they have no more resources to pay me. Another thing that is annoying is that I do not understand why "create alliance", "cease fire" and such needed to be researched. When someone is beating your @$$, you would instinctively yell 'stop', not to these advance space beings apparently.
The tutorial is inadequate at best. After going through the whole tutorial, I still don't grasp the important points of the game such as battles and ship designs until I googled them. I figured the rest out because of my past experience with Alpha Centauri and Civ.
The AIs are dumb and overly aggressive. By 20-30 turns, my closest neighbour declared war on me for absolutely no reason at all. At least in AC or Civ, they would give you some sort of warning, but not Endless Space! It will f--k you when it feels like f--king you up, regardless of their capabilities. And they refuse to make peace when they just lost all their ships. Based on my reading on multiplayers, it seems that it is buggy as hell online as well. So this game doesn't have much going for it, since you can't play with the AIs and you can't play with other people.
In Civ V, they have a nice range of difficulties, ranging from settler to deity (8 levels). In ES, they have something similar too. However, the problem is that the gaps between each is as wide as the Grand Canyon. Say, ES's normal is like Civ's Chieftain or Warlord, its hard mode is like Deity. So either the game is too easy for you to learn from, or it is so hard that you just can't survive past the 100th turn. I was either bored or frustrated.
Regardless of your fraction, you almost always research the same techs every time. Colonize planets, Enhances weapons, Make ships bigger, Enhances more weapons, Make ships even bigger, with the occasional resource unlocking, incoming increasing, happiness inducing tech here and there.
While I appreciate the game for telling me that the AIs are winning, it doesn't need to start reminding me when they are only 10-20% complete toward certain victories. A even more ridiculous example is when I am at 60% completion, they warn me of this AI who is close to winning the game at 20%. Very helpful indeed.
I paid around $15 in Nov of 2013 for both Endless Space and Disharmony. I want my money back and I am trying to save yours here. This game is great in the sense that it is like Alpha Centauri but on a galactic scale. It's like Civ 5 with levelable heroes. The management/production system is nice. But everything else is not. The concept is great but it is very poorly executed or maintained (based on my investigation, a lot of bugs seemed to stem from Disharmony).
I have uninstalled this game after close to 100hours of play and it will take a major cleansing for me to reinstall it and give it another go. This game as it stands is worth $5 at best, anymore, you are getting ripped off. Spend your money elsewhere. Thanks for reading.

Pros and Cons, need to be broken up into 2 sets, Hardware and Operations, and actual game perferences:

This game's fantastic. It's also a bit hard to describe, the game's picture describes it as XCOM meets FTL, but more appropriately I think it's XCOM meets FTL meets Child of Light meets Knights of Pen and Paper, maybe?
The XCOM gameplay elements are it's base building aspects, the resource management, and the way missions work. Also, the game has a pretty steep difficulty curve on the Normal difficulty mode. No idea about the more advanced ones.
FTL is pretty obvious right? Space combat/exploration/fuel management/all that stuff.
You can replace Child of Light with any turn-based combat game, the game's combat system functions like that. Only instead of all of your units going and then all of theirs going, every unit has a speed value that they have which goes along a line of time, and this can be increased with abilities and stuff, hence the Child of Light comparison.
Knights of Pen and Paper because of the combat abilities. You can pick and choose from different ones, but when you first start up your ships will have three abilities you can use in combat. I think you have six you can choose from, and they all do different things to add into the combo system. You get additional abilities as your captain's level up (which are seperate from your general ship abilities), and more advanced ships can have more general ship abilities with the second tier ships having I think five slots with nine abilities you can use.
Then there's the combo system. Not technically called that, but whatever. Like, two-thirds of every combat ability gives the enemy some kinda status effect. Every combat ability has a special ability where if an enemy has status effect X, then that combat ability does bonus damage. As you get better ships and more "officers", you can obviously get some pretty nice combos going off. Personally, I love it. It's a neat little feature.
The game also has a suprisingly complex tech tree for what it is.
But, onto the difficulty curve I mentioned before. So, for the first uhhh...let's say hour and a half on Normal difficulty, the game will be pretty evenly balanced. After you reach that point the enemies will start to spawn faster, and in tougher groups. Bit more of a challenge, but still no big problem. The next difficulty increase isn't until you decide to upgrade your ships to Tier II, after which all of the enemies start to do the same. It's around this point they get champion variants. Still no biggie. Right up until you complete a certain mission that causes a certain structure to spawn right beside your base.
After which point in time Tier III enemy ships start spawning from said structure, and their Tier III ships rip through your pathetic Tier II ships as if they were made of paper. This is about when I took a break from the game to write this review, so I don't know much more about it.
All in all, I'd most definetly recommend this game, and if I had to rate it, I'd probably give it a 7/10.

After getting denied a refund request for this game, I decided to actually play and complete it. I thought that it gets better later on but boy I was wrong. Do note that I played it on lieutenant difficulty.
For starters, the music is your generically "epic" battle music which near instantly switches to overworld's generically calm music. 3 hours into the game I got bored with it and turned it down in favor of current top musicians like DJ Khaled and Lazytown's "We are number one" which eventually autoplayed to Katy Perry and even then they served as better background noise than garbage you find in this game.
Graphics are your usual sprites that pretend to be pixelated. It tries to bring some nostalgia from DOS era but ultimately fails, as nowadays every indie video game artist pulls this out of under the table claiming "We're totally doing it better, guys! Promise! *wink*" and people fall for it every time. Personally I'd love a change of pace, like vectorized sprites or even downscaled bitmaps.
Gameplay is something out of this world. The first two ship tiers are you trying to meet ends together as THE ♥♥♥♥ING SATELLITE DRONE SYSTEM IS NOT AVAILABLE SINCE START OF THE GAME EVEN IF YOU'RE REPLAYING IT AND YOU SPEND THE FIRST TWO HOURS MICROMANAGING YOUR TWO SHIPS TO FETCH YOU ALL THE RESOURCES, while the rest of the game is just one giant chore. "GO HERE. DO THIS. KICK HIM IN THE NUTS. KICK HIM IN THE NUTS AS WELL" Huh. I guess that's where my rights to refund went. Well played Massive Damage Inc. You jewed me out of probably 10 euros during the christmas sale.
Meanwhile the combat is all about chaining your status ailments. That's really it. It could've been drastically improved if "All enemies" skills skipped targeting phase and went on with it but nope, gotta get them extra minutes to prevent them from refunding.
The skill descriptions are really scarce and half of them barely tell you what it does. Even if the descriptions said "THIS SKILL IS DAMAGE PER TURN AND DOES X" it would've been much more informative instead "THIS SKILL CAUSES X". What is X? What does it do? Why is it here? Is it also here to prevent me from refunding?
Diplomacy is non-existent. I guess if you made aliens upset they would attack you more often, but up until that point you barely interact with them. They occasionally drop in to drop you a quest but all in all it doesn't even matter. In fact it feels like another time waster to get those refund rights away from you.
Skill leveling system is awful. You really don't need additional buttons to show that there are more levels to them than one. All you had to do was CHANGE THE DESCRIPTION. But that would make the screen as empty as a blank sheet of paper.
Ground combat is tier 1 combat: repeat. At some point you start having more officers that are just sitting in your base, making the whole "upgrade cadets" thing redundant. I'd assume that in harder difficulties there are more enemies flying around thus having 2-3 fleets flying around is mandatory, but that would end up getting too micromanagy as well.
I seriously want to beat the guy responsible for controls. Mouse wheel barely scrolls and the whole control scheme feels like everything was made with tablets in mind. Wait a minute. It all makes sense now. The terrible UI, the terrible controls, the awful gameplay and constant requirement of confirmation to do things. All of this is literally a tablet game you'd find in google store under paid shovelware category.
All in all, this game does not belong on steam. Developer steals your refunds and makes them their own. Perhaps the same could be said about all indie games, but it is as empty as any other artsy indie game. PC ill needs such game. But what is a game? A miserable pile of code and entertainment. But enough talk. Get a refund now.

I've been a fan of MechWarrior since I was a kid. This game seriously delivers and feels like a true expansion on the universe. Although I recommend the game, I would like to point out some weakpoints.
1. The tutorial falls short. It takes you through the basics but the customization in MechWarrior Online is immense and the sheer number of buttons that work in game is on par with a good flight simulator. There is a learning curve and you will have to figure out the intricacies yourself.
2. The in-game currency is earned slowly and the purchased currency is expensive. This is the case with most free to play games, but MechWarrior Online is a little steep even by these standards. A single assault mech can cost upwards of $30. You'll need to earn experience on 3 variants of the same mech to maximize your perks, do the math.
3. Waiting. You only get one life in a normal game and four lives in a Faction based game. After your lives are expended, you have to wait for the match to expire before you can begin again. I normally enjoy this style of play but I have found myself in a match with an AFK player that forces everyone to wait for the 15 minuite match timer to expire before play can begin again (the maps can get pretty big, and AFK/disconnected players are not always found).
