I wanted to like Endless Space so badly. I love 4x space games, and like a lot of us am still waiting for the successor to Master of Orion 2 to come along. I'd been hoping ES would finally succeed where so many others had failed. In fact, I periodically download and play it again hoping that maybe I was wrong and there's a good game buried in there somewhere.
There's not.
As many people have written the biggest problem is combat. There's nothing interesting about it. There are three types of weapons and three types of defenses. Each gets linearly more powerful as you tech up, and each defense stops one type of weapon and is useless against the other two. If you have the right defense against an enemy ship you win. If you don't, they win. There's a system where you play three cards to influence the battle, but it moves too slowly and has too little impact to make any difference.
There's no diversity of units like in Civilization nor tactical combat like in Master of Orion (or the brilliant Total War series). There's just a big game of rock, paper, scissors. One side wins, the other side loses, you rebuild and repeat. Don't bother with any other type of victory either. There's no room for cleverness in a rocks/paper/scissors system and no stationary defenses, so if you don't put everything into your military the player who did will crush you every time.
It's the same with domestic policy. Your systems have to specialize, so you pick whether a system will produce money, tech or industry, plug in all the appropriate buildings and then auto build cash, science or ships. You don't really decide which to do, because each planet is good for one particular thing so the system composition pretty much decides this for you. There's nothing interesting happening in the galaxy or territory uniquely worth fighting over, no external threat or game changing discoveries. Even the little tactical interest that comes from star lanes and wormholes is gone shortly into the game once ships can fly through open space.
By the mid-game your empire is pretty much running on autopilot. Cash and science systems tick away and your only interaction is to build fleets and throw them at the enemy. Periodically you upgrade the design of your ships for new science or if the enemy switches to a different weapon.
Most of the problem came from the developers' focus on making a multiplayer game. They stripped the mechanics down in order to keep them balanced, and that ultimately made the game *much* less interesting. The wonders, for example, confer system bonuses instead of being big, powerful icons that can change the course of play. System bonuses aren't interesting. I can catch up to that with a few extra factories and don't even need to if they show up on a lousy planet. But the multiplayer would be unbalanced if one person could, by random chance, stumble across a game changer.
It's the same with everything else. There are no weird discoveries to make in the galaxy or overpowered planets, like MOO2's gaians, because that would advantage one player too much. Military tech marches up rails up three branches and that's it, no clever or assymetrical weapons or decisions to make for fear of breaking things. Even the races are just a collection of relatively minor statistical differences from each other, nothiing that feels truly different or unique.
There are a lot of little things wrong with Endless Space and a couple of big ones, but ultimately the game just isn't that much fun. It feels flat and lifeless. One play through is pretty much exactly like every other and by midway through your second game you'll get bored.

Deus Ex is a very polished FPS with RPG elemtns, boasting a moderate amount of replayability depending on your interests. The Director's Cut edition offers an extra set of missions in the middle of the original story.
8/10
- Polished gameplay, very few bugs
- Visuals are nice
- Content-rich world
- Fun storyline and side-missions
- A wide range of useful and interesting character upgrades
- Reasonably good AI
- Well-designed environments and levels
- A somewhat limited amount of weapons and weapon upgrades
- Not quite a true open-world experience due to the storyline, which hurts the replayability a bit
- The director's cut story can be frustrating to play as you temporarily lose your character's weaponry and hard-earned upgrades.
Deus Ex is a FPS with an RPG element where in you unlock and upgrade an array of built-in cyborg capabilities. You can even upgrade your weapons with modifications like laser sights, ammo capacity increases and explosive rounds just to name a few. This aspect stays somewhat true to the original.
Gameplay is smooth, but may feel a little clumsy at times when aiming with guns. Sometimes in the heat of a shootout it can feel a bit sluggish trying to gun down enemies whilst strafing around. So keep in mind this is not a shooter like Halo or CoD where you can move around very quickly dodging fire. You need to pick your positions carefully to ensure a clear shot and safe cover.
The way Deus Ex is meant to be played is taking cover behind objects in your environment, and either gunning down your enemies - or stealth. The stealth mechanics of the game are brilliant. Enemies are very aware of noise and are smart enough to check areas thoroughly if they suspect an intruder is there. If you accidentally alert enemies to your presence, you often have to back out of the whole area unnoticed if you want to remain hidden.
Not only is stealth fun, but the game is highly rewarding of stealth tactics. Enemies are typically easier to kill if you can sneak up on them, you can slip through areas quickly if you plan your movement correctly, and you get bonus experience points for stealth kills and mission objectives. This allows for faster character levelling.
If you prefer to empty your guns in each room, that's also very fun, but the enemies don't make it easy. Very rarely can you pull a rambo in this game and get away with it. Enemies shoot accurately and will quickly make easy work of you if you are not adequately positioned or equipped with sufficient firepower.
The visuals are great and most elements in the game are nicely detailed. The environments are awesomely put together. The atmospheric places of America, China and the fictional Panchea create an immersive experience which feels exciting, disturbing, suspenseful and curious all at the same time. In addition to the graphical detail, the areas have many avenues for exploring which can reward you with hidden items, such as powerful weapons and bonus upgrades. Many areas are only accessible after acquiring certain upgrades to your character (e.g. jumping higher and withstandning electrical damage) which adds another entertaining level of complexity to the game.
It is led by an in-depth storyline with many twists and turns. The main storyline involves hunting down several super-powered soldiers, using similar technology to yourself, in an attempt to find the protagonist's girlfriend (ex... sorta... you'll see) as well as following the suspicious orders of his boss. There are plenty of side-missions which are a good source for extra content and bonus experience and cash.
Overall, Deus Ex: HR - DC is worth the current price of $20 as it does provide some good replayability. You can play through the game using different styles and upgrades and it provides a different experience with each way. If it goes on sale, it is definitely worth picking up to play through at least once.

BOY, do I have A LOT to say about this game. After purchasing and finishing The Stanley Parable, (it's awesome, check it out) I wanted to play related games to it. I browsed through various titles, but eventually settled on this one. I was excited to play as a dying explorer, and listen to his descent into madness. I wanted multiple choices, exploration. This was not what I got. Instead, a 16th century explorer rambled on about "Esther" and "Paul", while I simply just walked around. The story is great, the visuals are amazing, but there is no choice. No exploration. The questions are never answered. No mysteries await. This game had so much potential, but used none of it. I WISH it had used its potential. It would have turned out so amazing. But no. However, despite my criticism, I am fairly split towards this game. The scenery is beautiful, there are SOME strange symbols and mysteries, the story is great, I like the narrator, if only I could understand him, but there is no choice. There is no exploration. Cons of Dear Esther:
-No choice
-No exploration of your own
-Short, too short
-You are literally just walking
-Somewhat expensive

All in all, I'm kinda split with this game. Of course, I do have to choose if I want to reccomend it or not. is one of my favourite games of all time. The reasons for that are twofold, but they both start with 'B': it's because this game is both
and
. How so? Let's find out!
Over the years, there's been many a game creator whose only real desire was to tell a story—and nothing more. With truly Procrustean enthusiasm they shoehorned their ideas into various genres, be it FPSs, stealth games, adventures, or RPGs. These alliances weren't necessarily bad, of course; but adding elements to the game simply because it's traditional and you feel like you must is bad design, even if this element is challenge.
Just think about how simple it would have been to throw a puzzle or two into
—and avoid all the vitriolic comments calling it a non-game.
But it didn't.
is precisely what it wants to be: an almost non-interactive audiovisual experience aimed at movie geeks or exhibition visitors rather than typical gamers. It was the first game of this type that boldly announced that it's okay to have no puzzles or challenge. Come to think of it, there are an awful lot of "real" adventure games that pose no challenge either and can be solved through sheer trial and error or are deliberately simple. Yet dropping the pretence of having a challenge was shocking to many people—possibly because they were used to being concentrated and alert when playing a game and didn't know where to redirect their focus when told that there absolutely, positively,
was no reason to expect any kind of challenge.
Which is, of course, the point: you're supposed to focus on the artistic side of things. And
is not a mindless meditative experience either: it does require some brain-racking.
You'll have to concentrate on figuring out the story, delivered in a feverish and hard-to-parse way.
The visuals and the music of
are almost universaly praised: the stark Scottish island and the melancholy tunes have impressed many players. It's the dialogue and the story that have people divided. Some call the dialogue poetic; others, overwritten. To some, the story is appropriately fractured; to others, it's incoherent.
The game was devised as a narrative experiment: while some bits of dialogue are fixed, many are randomised and mutually exclusive—meaning each playthrough ends up having its own unique story. (This is supported by some assets also being randomised.) So instead of a plain narrative
opts for a much more poetic structure, with verbal imagery interconnecting the broken pieces of dialogue.
It is indeed structured like a poem. For example, it's hard to say where the number twenty one, that much of the dialogue revolves around, comes from; is it Esther's age? Indeed the number of circuits in car brakes? The length of the road they still had left ahead of them?
The thing is, it doesn't matter all that much. What matters is that when the narrator begins seeing the number everywhere, it comes across as true obsession—and the obscurity of the object the narrator obsesses over only makes it more poignant.
Creating an open-ended story is a treacherous goal, of course. I think
works so well because, while it goes into pure ravings sometimes, the imagery of the game, both visual and verbal, is so grounded in reality. The island it takes place upon is real, the bits of its history are either real or very plain and realistic. It's so mundane and detailed, with only sprinkles of magic realism, that it actally honestly allows for the ambiguity regarding whether the journey is real or metaphorical (usually, when such ambiguity is claimed, you just know it's all a ham-fisted metaphor).
And if you take the island as a metaphor, the whole thing becomes arguably even more compelling, with the metaphor (the island and what we see in the game) being logical, simple, and mundane and the reality behind it (that we glean through the narration) feeling broken, insane, and sometimes even self-contradictory.
This is a far cry from many other walking simulators that bathe us in superfluous metaphoric surrealism that sometimes only highlights how mundane the story is (yeah, someone probably died, possibly you).
In the directors' commentary Dan Pinchback notes that while games venture into audiovisual poetry more boldly these days, for some reason the actual texts they offer are rarely structured as such. It's actually not that simple to even remember a game that would feature poetry—not the rhyming kind, I mean, but the kind that relies on rhythm and strong imagery rather than functionality in delivering explainations or instructions to the player.
offers just that: poetry.
It's a game that pioneered many things and remains unsurpassed in some areas. Whether you like it or not, it's pivotal to the modern gaming scene. I
with its style, presentation, imagery, and mood to an almost obscene degree.
But even if you dont—even if you don't like it at all—I think it's hard not to agree that
is a game that deserves an awful lot of respect.

Dear Esther is a narrative driven adventure game on a deserted island. This Landmark Edition is remake of the original game/mod in Unity, with remastered visuals and audio.
The remastered visuals look decent enough and some sections (like the caves) are quite beautiful. However, the game is also full of dated 3D models and low resolution textures.
The game has a nice sound track and the sound effects are reasonably well done too. The voice acting is passable but not great.
The gameplay in Dear Esther is truly terrible. You just wander around pointlessly through the fairly linear levels and trigger audio monologs along the way. There's zero interactivity and even your movement is rather restricted. The tiniest obstacle will block your movement and you can't jump or even run.
Dear Esther is an extremely easy game, there's absolutely no challenge.
The controls are passable enough but the game could have really used a run key.
The writing is quite pretentious and pretty poor in general. The story is rather heavy-handed as well and not particularly interesting. You are just listening to pieces of someone else's story and there's no real immersion.
I found Dear Esther a fairly terrible experience. There's no real gameplay and the writing is pretty dreadful. Even if you are interested in the so-called walking simulators there are far better examples of the genre available on Steam. Not recommended.
It took me around one hour to finish the game.

I received this product as a free upgrade for owning the original Dear Esther.
One of the classic "walking simulators," and one of the first, Dear Esther retains its wind-swept, desolate fascination in the Landmark Edition remastering. If you were a fan of the original or enjoy vague, fragmented story-telling, Dear Esther is still one of the best of its genre. The soundtrack (now recorded with real instruments) is superb, and the story bits change from playthrough to playthrough; the plot will remain similar, but who exactly is speaking is never clearly established. The graphics still look impressive, too. Worth a purchase at the asking price if you're a fan of the genre.
That said, there are some issues:
- Broken V-sync. It will not work, not through the game's settings, or through my graphics card driver settings (hello, screen-tearing!). In the original game, there was a Triple Buffering option in the settings that fixed the issue; the Triple Buffering option has been removed from the Landmark Edition.
- The soundtrack has some amazing moments, but is poorly balanced at times (especially in the beginning of Chapter 4). The mid-range and upper frequencies are generally over-saturated, creating a shrill, brittle audio ambiance that wasn't present in the original version of the game.
- Not all voice-over triggers as it is supposed to. I've played the Dear Esther several times, I knew there was a voice-over before the ending cave in Chapter 2, but it took 4 playthroughs of the chapter before it triggered.
Not much to do, story wise it's very cryptic. But it's enjoyable.

I was a huge fan of Dear Esther back when it was a humble Source mod, and I bought the standalone version as soon as it came out several years back.  It was a beautiful and thought-provoking experience.  That is still true today, to some extent, but time and aging has been very good to the narrative-driven walking simulator genre and very bad for Dear Esther.  We've seen better, and we know what these kinds of games are capable of now.
As an owner of the first commercial release, I received the Landmark Edition for free.  It was a slog to get through again.  The visuals have held up well, if not perfectly, and the music is still great.  The story is slow, the walking speed is slow, and the emotional impact is quite shallow compared to the likes of Dr. Langeskov, Firewatch, and other similar works.  The prevalence of loops, dead ends, and repeated sections is also aggravating.  Such devices are fine in most games, but they actively detract from the experience here.  Overall, Dear Esther is unsatisfying to play and not worth your money.  It fails to stand up against similar games on the market, many of which cost nothing at all.
That being said, Dear Esther's role in formalizing the genre and its position as one of the first games of its kind makes it worth remembering, if just for posterity's sake.  The Chinese Room made their contribution to history with this, and I wish them well on their future endeavors.

Dropping my "Not Recommended" here. Hi-Rez has a history of killing games with greed. Paladins is not an exception.
I stopped playing after 330 hours. I had a LOT of fun... for a while, with the game in the state it was in 20+ patches ago, but the trends were already clear: Simple fixes to polish the game were being ignored, champions were becoming more unbalanced, in-game currency grinding was becoming more of a chore (and was HARDER ON NEW PLAYERS ESPECIALLY - accessibility to new players [i.e. your friends] was one of the best things Paladins previously had going for it), the minimum requirements to experiment with gameplay in new and exciting ways were being pushed further out of reach, community feedback was being ignored, and unique core aspects of the game that made it what it was - that made it *fun* - were being eroded bit by bit.
... and let's not even get into the bugs - actually, a bug with mouse input (which probably still hasn't been acknowledged) made the game unplayable for me, and that's why I really quit. By the way, mouse sensitivity options were *awful* last I played, where 0 was no movement, 1 was sluggish, and 2 was out of control for me. You don't get to enter a decimal, like in certain other games, like a thriving, polished hero shooter that gives me far fewer reasons to complain. The name starts with Overwat. anyway.
I haven't opened the game for any reason since May, but I've paid attention to patch notes, and occasionally watched gameplay. It's clear that all of these trends have been spiraling out of control, and testing the patience of the community more and more. This last update should be the nail in its coffin: The previous, relatively balanced loadout system NO LONGER EXISTS - BOUND MODE IS NOT THE SAME. Unbound mode - which seems to be the new focus for development - NUMERICALLY PUTS NEW PLAYERS AND FREE-TO-PLAY PLAYERS AT A DISADVANTAGE AGAINST VETERANS AND BIG SPENDERS. If someone were to spend LITERAL THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS to have their champion builds maxed today, the grind for a free player to catch up before facing them would be INSURMOUNTABLE.
What's left of [the backbone of what was once a promising game worth sinking hundreds of hours into] may lure in and briefly entertain new players. Loyal players may want to believe this isn't a big deal. Hi-Rez may offer the equivalent of lots of expired candies with pocket lint stuck to them to keep the above groups from immediately escaping their grasp. But if you're looking for a game that is either currently or foreseeably polished and fair for everyone, don't let anyone convince you that this is it.

I'm sure there's been everything I've written down already said, and I'll also point out that I put in time since the closed beta, got the Atlas Founder's Pack and Overlord Phoenix pack (both of which I regret to this day), so I'll basically sum up first, and explain my biggest (not the only ones, just the biggest) beefs with this game. If you like Battletech/Mechwarrior,
. It's not Mechwarrior, it's some sort of terrible World of Tanks clone wearing Battletech's skin. Don't even download the installer, just pop in that Mechwarrior 4: Mercenaries disc that I know you have, and play that until Jordan Weisman's real Battletech game comes out.
Let's put down some details.
- The 'Mechs, and about 2 maps are real pretty. End of list.
- The development of this game has honestly been a fantastic, 3-year long trainwreck in slow motion with 3-D effects. Although I'll mention that deciding to use Cryengine (an engine that is poorly optimized, and completely miserable to work with) is typically a good indicator that the developer has no clue what they're doing, they just want it to look pretty, that's not even the main problem.
The first biggest issue is they absolutely have no idea how to balance their game. Endless Space is one of the best 4X game i have ever played. The game mechanics are quite simple to understand but they are also deep and polished, and the graphic aspect is great for this kind of game, with a lot of beautiful planets and some nice explosion during space fights! The random galaxy generation, the huge amount of special features that planets can have (for example anomalies, strategic resource or luxury resource) and the random events that can occasionally occur make every game unique. Endless Space also offers great customization options (pirates, game speed, events, galaxy size and shape...) and a lot of interesting features such as heroes, that can be assigned to fleets or systems to upgrade them, planet production customization, moon exploration, which can lead to important and powerful discoveries, and a fantastic tech tree with interesting and funny descriptions for every single technology!
Endless Space isn't surely perfect, beacuse some technologies are definitely too powerful and unbalanced, the combat system (real time combat divided into 3 parts with a card strategy system) may not appeal to everyone, and some annoying bugs still afflict the game, but it has been created with a lot of attention for details and is a great title for everyone who's looking for a solid yet not too difficult and extremely addicting 4X Sci-fi experience.

I highly recommend this game to 4x fans. I think I can sum up the review more quickly than most.
Endless Space is GalCiv 2.5. It's a spiritual successor and good in its own right. The gameplay is exactly what you'd expect, the graphics are nice, the soundtrack is solid. It's just.. a great game.
Pros:
Cheap - especially with a coupon or sale.
Seriously fun.
Replayable... one of those games I actually wanted to get achievements for.
Great moments of triumph - see the cons.
Cons:
The learning curve is a touch steep if you haven't touched GalCiv, but if you have it's old hat.
The AI - many people complain that its too difficult... I haven't really experienced that. yes, some play throughs you will have terrible luck, but that's not a huge deal - it's random. My advice if you're frustrated - lower the difficulty until you understand the game mechanics. HUGE AI fleets can be overcome and you can retake your system and start steamrolling them by outthinking the AI. Tons of ships with lasers? Build yours with shields and guns... They use missiles? Use flak and guns. I heart guns.
Which is the other con. Once you master beating the AI, you have..well... done that. You'll be able to do it on every play through. Occassionally though there are terrible situations that will actually make you figure out a solution that might not be apparent and will require experimentation and thinking laterally. (Ex; Fighting the Amoeba in the end game can be a nightmare... an absolute nightmare, but when you crack that nut you will feel genuinely awesome.)
Totally recommend.

It's been a while since I last played this game. I was hooked on this game when I was 10. I'm now 20, and Stronghold is still one of my favourite games. I definitely recommend it.
9.5/10

I first bought a CD-ROM copy of Stronghold in 2001. I'd already developed a taste for strategy games playing Age of Empires and its sequel Age of Empires II: Age of Kings, so I was more than willing to give this one a try as well. And I have never regretted it. 13 years later I still play Stronghold on a regular basis. I lost my CD-ROM copy years ago, and when I saw that Stronghold was available on Steam I bought it instantly - I doubt I even looked at the price. Stronghold's two campaigns are both compelling and challenging, and its various stand-alone missions are equally enjoyable. The map editor in this first installment is, in my opinion, easier to work and more accessible than the map editors of later games (indeed, I don't think any subsequent game has quite matched the overall quality of the original title, much as I enjoy Stronghold Crusader and Stronghold 2 .... the less said of Stronghold Legends and Stronghold 3 the better). I would highly recommend Stronghold to any fan of RTS or Simulator games and know that I shall be playing it for years to come.

PROS:
+Fantastic maps; YES there are indeed a lot less then in Crusader, but the maps that are here are not only balanced but unlike Crusader I like playing all of them instead of there only being a few that I like to play.
+Great music; this game and Crusader have indeed some of the most atmosphereic pieces of music in any game. From slow mandaline as you begin to create your kingdom, to the fan favorite Stcks and Stones which is a huge 10 minute battle melody that changes depending on how the battle is progressing!

The graphical style is outdated by today's 3D graphics, but unlike today's 3D graphics the pixel based sprites look vibrant, crisp, and colorful. And holy crap, seeing your castle go from just a small camp to becoming a military power house with industrailzation and over population of people and having to build hundreds of farms just to get enough food is insane to watch.
CONS:
+No Skirmish; Crusader fixes this problem but there is no way to play the game against AI so if you want to play a Skirmish type mode you are forced to play Multiplayer.

+The FPS halves when you attempt to zoom all the way out (Also in Crusader) which is odd and very noticable)
OVERALL:

Dear Esther is much slower paced than most games, it's about exploring the beautiful world that is provided to you and trying to make sense of the story. This game is unique as it actually gets you thinking on the first playthrough about if the island is real or whether it's just clever symbology and the dialogue can keep you guessing. It's not a long story but there's multiple paths so it's always worth going back through to try and get some more pieces of the story.
There's also an element of different paths and randomisation (which I won't spoil as it's pretty key to the story) and that's something that really makes this seemingly linear game actually quite complex.
In terms of graphics, the island is absolutely beautiful, this is one of the nicest looking games that I've played in a while. It's not because of raw texture sizes or anything like that but the use of colours and landmarks in combination with some fantastic weather effects. Combined with the music this creates a really amazing atmosphere when playing through the game, quite unlike anything you normally get with Steam games.
Overall I'd say if you're after some fast paced, action heavy game... this isn't for you. If you want a game that leans much more heavily on atmosphere and narrative adventure then this is one that you should certainly have a look at!

The original Dear Esther mod for Half-Life 2 was one of the first games to ever garner the often maligned genre of "walking simulator." I've never played the mod version or the first incarnation of the standalone game of this game. I don't necessarily like these types of games, but I went into playing this one with an open mind and while there are a lot of things to like about this game there are definitely more to not like.
To start, I'm pretty sure this game is universally praised for its fantastic score. The landmark edition's introduction of a live orchestra really brings life to the soundtrack. Jessica Curry's themes really resonate with the tone of game and tracks like "I Have Begun my Ascent" and "Remember" will haunt me for years to come. Curry creates a phenomenal auditory landscape that really fits in with the narrative of the game.
There is a story here, but its definitely not easy or straightforward. Dan Pinchbeck's story of a man who's lost his love is intriguing, but the kicker is that nothing seems to be resolved. The narration is packed to the brim with metaphors and symbolism that would make an english major proud, but the story doesn't really solidify. To be frank, the poetic nature of the narration really makes it feel borderline pretentious. The writing is not subtle about how it wants to be preceived. I will say that the whole design with which the story is delivered is truly refreshing. The script that is delivered to the player is based on their actions and what they decided to explore in the game. Two different players could have completely different interpretations of the game's story simply based on where they went on the island. The design of this game is really what impresses me the most.
The whole game kind of feels like a hallucintory experience with barren landscapes that seemed to stretch on forever, insane drawings and symbols that don't quite make sense, and landmarks that feel like they're from civilizations long gone. Having never played the original mod or the initial version of the standalone game, I can't say how the graphics have improved, but this game is gorgeous. The attention to detail is mentioned extensively in the commentary for this game and it really shows. Each chapter of this game is surpringly unique looking plays so well into the story of depression and loneliness.
This game is about as non-interactive as they come and for me as a player that really lessens the draw this game has over me. I'm a sucker for a good story and there is one here, but it takes a lot of digging through symbolism and psychological riddles and maybe that's the point because the story is a sad one of loss and regret and how it affects a person mentally and emotionally. I think complex human emotions and especially unhappy ones should be explored more in games, but I don't think Dear Esther quite hits the mark with this. I wouldn't recommend playing this game unless you are deeply interested in the genre.
However, I do believe that the effort and creativity of Thechineseroom is well worth praise here. This game has really opened the door for more games of this nature (Gone Home) and I look forward to what they release next.

As a developer for a "walking simulator" studio myself (Not going to mention that again) I would like to say that I crossed paths with Dear Esther lifetimes ago during it's run on Moddb. My opinion of it has changed very little over the course of time, and ultimately I still cannot wholly recommend this narrative due to its obtuse structure and vague, meandering thread of dialog that does little to pull the heart strings or strike at the core issues the protagonist faces.
Why would you want to play this game?
It advertises itself as a walking simulator that is story first, bringing you to heel in an island forlorn and somber with a narrative and musical composition to boot. Ultimately, you progress in one direction through various environments while the game procedurally generates the order in which (important to remember) you find out "what happened." Final lines can be near the middle, the beginning lines could be the last you hear. Knowing you need to piece things together as you go, is this a cerebral and captivating experience, or a wet thud of an attempt? Let's explore onward to decide together.
Dear Esther LM: 2.5/5 - Thumbs sideways. Worth it under $10.
Pros:
*Some truly astonishing visuals, most notably the ending chapter and the cavern sequences.
*An award winning soundtrack that cannot be missed for anything. Captures the mood of the local more than the story does.
*Gentle, relaxing, peaceful and well paced levels that don't stretch on too long.
*A few vocalisms are stunningly written. Namely, when he mentions all the letters to Esther he put out to sea. Unbelievably emotive.
Cons:
*Literally nothing to do but walk forward.
*Disconnected storyline is randomly drip fed to the player, with numerous connotations to Christianity, predestination of fate, chemistry, mental illness and various diseases.
*Story never reaches any emotional heights. We never feel for the character, Donnelley, Esther, etc. The story evokes almost a stoic retrospective about circumstances it never fully explains, and paces itself like an elderly man on a rocking chair loosely recounting things that mattered but can't wholly remember.
*The environment is a living metaphor for the narration, or perhaps, your body. If so, any challenges, puzzles, stealth, enemies, or even diary pages would have done a lot to capture this.
Dear Esther finds you awakening on the shores of an Irish/English channel island and roaming around while a narrator recalls... a lot of exposition. This hook is interesting because it feels like a eulogy, ghost story, theater play, broken diary entries and mournful recollections woven into one. But shortly after reaching the second or even third 'acts' you'll realize this yarn is tumbling off the needles. There are no visceral revelations, sad twists, moments of clarity in the otherwise mentally ill narration, and so on. There is no reward or resolution for actually playing it -- in fact, things get more and more cloudy as the narrator appears to grow delirious and sick as you waddle onward.
Graphically, the game is servicable. It runs at a million FPS on low hardware and provides occasionally extraordinary level design to sit back and take in. Mountain views, the ocean, the caverns, the moon on the horizon at the end, etc. Texture work can be bland, especially near the beaches, and decals are in short supply on anything not a building. No real weather effects to speak of, would have adored storms.
The soundtrack is probably the best part of the game. Like the narration it, too, is randomized. And it is haunting and ethereal and in this version of the game, was composed live I suppose, so it sounds even better.
Alright. Let me distill my thoughts and stop catalogging the list above. Ultimately as a story, you can find better in this genre. Ethan Carter and SOMA come to mind immediately. Dear Esther doesn't really tell any kind of story, it tells an intangible series of emotions that are letterboxed within a car crash and a relationship. It's like reading the apendices of a novel you love and someone is commenting on bits and pieces, without properly framing the narration from A to Z. It is confusing, a little irritating, a little boring, but occasionally hits the right notes to make this worth a sale for /fans/ of walking simulators.
Although this game was interesting, overall I'd give it a dislike. While the graphics and imagery were nice and intriguing, the storyline was was melodramatic and self-defeating; would not recommend.

I think it's safe to say that Dear Esther is a divisive game. Its reputation generally tends to precede it, and while some revel in its slow pacing, short play-time and disjointed narrative, others despise everything about it and all that it represents. But after several hours in its company (both here and in its originally release) I can easily say I fall comfortably into the former camp of admirers and enthusiasts.
My very first review on Steam was written over three years ago for the initial retail version of the game, and was actually what inspired me to start writing in the first place as I was so moved and compelled to share my thoughts on it. So it seemed only fitting that, for my one-hundredth review, I should come back full circle and revisit my old friend in the form of its upgraded re-release. Thankfully, time hasn't dulled its impact or significance, and I still love this game now as much as the day I first played it, possibly even more so, in fact.
Back then I described Dear Esther as a form of interactive art, like a painting you are able to step into and explore rather than merely admire from one set perspective, and I still stand by that now. For the two hours or so it'll take for you to see the end credits, your whole experience will consist solely of walking around and observing your surroundings while accompanied by a mesmerising soundtrack and occasional doses of ponderous dialogue. There's nothing to collect, hit or jump over, nothing to interact with or even any real obstacles to overcome or fail state to end the game or undo your progress. It's a true walking simulator, and everything that term now encompasses (thanks largely to this game in the first place). It's bleak, it's trudging, it's confusing and highfalutin, but it's also entirely knowing in those facts and absolutely intentional.
There have been various graphical and technical improvements made to the game, but to be completely honest, I can't say I noticed them. But then again, I'm really not the person to ask about such things. Instead, the addition I really got the most out of here was the developers' commentary. In fact, I'd go so far as to say I genuinely believe this is a must-listen for anyone who wishes to have any kind of truly meaningful understanding of the game. It's hugely revealing and insightful, and helped me discover all kinds of hidden depths that had previously been lost on me.
I learned things like, as well as dialogue being partially random, so too are some of the items strewn around the island you explore, potentially giving each player a very different view on their journey; or how the timing of musical notes in one section contains a secret message in the form of Morse code; or the symbolism that surrounds you everywhere, even in the very shapes of the landscape around you. Though, the biggest surprise was probably learning that there actually is no set, definitive story, but rather there are fragments of information imparted to the player for them to then construct their own narrative and draw their own conclusions. There really is so much more going on than I ever gave it credit for, and I'd urge every player to revisit the game with the commentary active just to see all these things for themselves and gain their own newfound appreciation for the creative processes that went into realising this.
As I said, this game is divisive. I already know that simply calling it a game is enough to rile some feathers. But I honestly don't know why people take umbrage with its mere existence or what difference a label on something makes to the actual content of an experience. Is anyone really going to sleep any better at night if the status of game is taken away from every title that falls under the genre of walking simulator, or if other people are enjoying these games even if they're not? Another thing I learned from the commentary was the intent behind this slow-paced approach. They considered a faster pace but settled on a brisk walk, and ultimately decided they wanted to give the player "space to dream", moments of quiet to allow the player to ruminate on everything they were seeing and hearing, having faith in them to allow for moments of consideration and draw their own conclusions. Maybe it's just me, but I think it's a really brave move to trust an audience to think for themselves and discover how they feel about something under their own influence, rather than
them what they should think or feel.
And this is what I feel is Dear Esther's greatest triumph - to have such courage and try to do so many things differently; to be deliberately restrained and oblique and not give a clear story, but still trust us to find something just as meaningful and impactful all the same... to actually respect us and our ability to think for ourselves.

I'm gonna be honest: I tried to hate this game. As a loving fan of the original Doom, I really wanted to hate this game, but goddamn did ID manage to pull this off.
Pros:
+Gameplay is viscerally fun without the feel of repetitiveness, each encounter giving you something fun to play with to make every battle a blast.
+Nice and fast paced, a breath of fresh air considering how slow many shooters seem to be these days.
+The maps in the game are large, expansive, and fun to roam around in, fighting demons around every corner (at least after the first couple of levels).
+Love the verticality added to the maps. Jumping seems a little weird at first, but the platforming is nice and the battlefield uses of the double jump are great, helping the feeling of chaotic fun.
+Lots of secrets to find, including the ability to unlock classic levels.
+Weapons are a blast to use, especially when upgraded with some of the attachments (looking at you, Super Shotgun and Mobile Turret Chaingun).
+The upgrade system is fine as it all goes back into the combat, adding more enjoyment while the game treats you with enough respect that you can make any choice in upgrades and still beat the game.
+The weapon attachments honestly feel like a perfect addition to each of the weapons, most of them feeling like they make each weapon more fun to use.
+Classic weapons make a return and are as fun to use as they were before (except the pistol, which was honestly always kinda ♥♥♥♥♥♥), but the new weapons all feel fun to use and like natural addons to your arsenal.
+Enemies are varied, old and new alike with some old enemies getting a redesign in how they're fought and some of them being way better to fight than their older counterparts.
+Powerups are really damn fun to use, being both varied and a natural addition to your abilities. Its a good thing when I find the invincibility powerup to be the most dull.
+LOTS of lore if that's your thing with lots of little bits of info to find on characters, enemies, enviornments, and more. Really nice to read if that's your bag.
+Snapmap, while not a proper replacement for actual modding tools, is a nice way to get more bang for your buck, including official maps.
Cons:
-Music is REALLY hit and miss. Some of the tracks pump the blood while others feel like they just make my eyes glaze over. I'm particularly fond of the tracks you hear in Hell, but the rest are kind of a techno/metal mess compared to iconic music of the past.
-The game kinda feels a bit easier towards the end as it seems to run out of creativity in the challenges it throws at you, being particularly fond of sending a couple barons of hell or hell knights at you rather than throwing more meaty challenges at you. I'd recommend a higher difficulty if you're at all familiar with the series.
-Glory Kills (what this game calls finishing moves) get really repetitive after a while. Its useful for getting back health, but it breaks flow after so many.
-This game has a bit of a bad habit of turning enemies into supply pinatas whenever you're low on health or a common type of ammo, leading to the game feeling a bit easy at times with how you never seem to really be short on health when they should really reserve that for those glory kills or something.
-The Chainsaw and BFG are really kinda situational. The Chainsaw isn't infinite use anymore and turns enemies into ammo dispensers when you get a kill with it and the BFG's ammo is so scarce that I didn't find a time I could really let loose with it. And don't even get me started on the grenades, the things I found, used once, then never touched again.
-The story is kinda bothersome. Its too generic to be worth paying attention to, but with all the jokes the story seems to make with how the player character doesn't care about the plot, there seems to be too many times where we just are told to sit and let plot happen.
-Ends on what seems to be a pretty big sequel hook. Wouldn't be such a problem if all the DLC time that was spend on this game wasn't spent on the ♥♥♥♥ing multiplayer.
-Oh, and the Multiplayer sucks too.
8/10

This game at first may appear like a turn-based RPG, but it is actually only like that during combat and some mild leveling). Overall, this game actually plays more like a real time strategy... just, without the real time and more actual strategy. That might seem confusing, but hear me out. It's actually really smart and makes for an extremely enjoyable game.
A majority of this game is recourse gathering and management/base building. Sounds like an RTS, right? Just replace constructing buildings with construsting rooms inside your mothership, and that's what this game is. You build units (granted, a much smaller number of units than in a typical RTS) to farm recourses so you can build more units (captains and ships), contruct more rooms on your mothership and purchase upgrades. The only catch is, time isn't always moving. Whenever you're in your base looking at upgrades to buy, rooms to build or ships to construct, time stops. Then once you've done your maitence, you manually unpause time to resume progress. You can pause time anytime you like as well, so can do things like select each of your ships and tell them what to do while time is frozen, then unpause and have all of them begin their tasks at once. Most things take time to complate - a ship moving from planet to planet, an upgrade being research, a ship being built - so these things will only progress while time is unpaused. The result is a game that plays very similarly to an RTS, but gives you time to plan, breathe, and strategize. So, this game can ultimately be described as an RTS with less RT and more S.
The only part of this game that is truly a turn-based RPG is the combat. When your ship or fleet of ships enters an area with an emeny it, time pauses an it takes you to a battle screen, RPG style. This ties in nicely to what the rest of the game is like - less RT and more S. The turn based battles allow for some real strategy on all levels of the game, from the battles themselves to which units you send into which battles to which upgrades you research back at the base.
There's also some mild leveling machanics. Your units kind of come in two parts - ships and captains. Ships need to have a captain assigned to them. Ships can be upgraded, and better ships are unlocked throughout the game. Captains, however, cannot be upgraded and there are no "better captains" you can buy(train?) later. Instead, captains will level up, and with each level up you'll get to pick an ability from one of a few abilities trees to unlock/upgrade. As you get better ships, you can move the captain from an old ship to the new bigger ship (in fact, you'll probably have to, because better ships require higher-leve captains to comand them). This gives the game an interesting mix of RTS (getting better units to outclass the old ones) and RPG (watching your units grow stronger over time). It's a really nice touch, and feels very cohesive with the world of space combat.
Speaking of world, quick tanget - the writing in the game is very good, although not very serious-toned. It's like Star Trek except if every race was a sitcom character (and I mean that as a good thing). There are several races you'll interact with, each one having their own quirks, and most of them are rather amusing. It's not trying to be to be a comedy or anything, it's just open to having fun with the writing and characters. It makes the diolauge fun to read and makes each race very likeable (even though ethically speaking, none of them are good people). This game knows that the story is just reason/excuse to get player from point A to point B, so they don't try and play it up an amazingly deep and spectacular literary work, instead just letting it be silly interactions between fun characters. It really works in this game's benifit, I think, but I can see how someone may be disapointed.
Anyways, beyond just the intruge of it being a not-quite-RTS (and the lovable characters), this game is really solid from every angle. As a strategy game, it is very well done.  Visually impressive as well, with great pixel art, cool ship and alien desgins and flashy animations. I mostly wanted to write this review to point out how intruiging the gameplay machanics are. I haven't seen another game quite like it. This is a truly unique sci-fi strtegy experience I recomend to RTS fans, RPG fans, and turn-based strategy (TBS?) fans.
Incredibly fun, worth your time and money.  Similar in style to Knights of Pen and Paper and X-Com.

Now that I've played through the campaign, I'm very happy that I kickstarted this game. I tried it for a bit in the beta, and it has come a
way since then regarding variety, substance, and polish. Since it's been said so many times, it's largely a blend of XCOM and FTL, with a turn-based instead of tactical combat system. It isn't entirely borrowed ideas, but the ones the designers selected work well together.
Bear in mind I played at the recommended difficulty.
+ Highly thematic
+ Soundtrack has some really strong tracks
+ Solid sense of progression through ship tiers
+ Early chapters have decent challenge and have the appropriate amount of pressure
+ The combat exploit system adds enough complexity without being fiddly
+ Some of the space combat looks and feels very satisfying
+ The writing is loaded with bits of [contemporary] humor (e.g. one mission with The Collective was "No Puppet, You're the Puppet!")
+ Factions feel distinct from writing to ships to abilities
- Ground combat feels a little neglected
- Difficulty curve isn't particularly smooth
- Officer powers have
different power levels. Unlucky re-rolls can wind you up with a crap officer (you can always send them to their death to get a new one... but that doesn't feel too good).
- End game was a bit too grindy (XP gain past level 10 is slow)
- A few visuals and sounds feel off
- "Protagonist-itis" (aliens are helpless as allies)
- *spoilers* story feels a little unresolved, as you
.
Despite a few shortcomings I thoroughly enjoyed this game and would recommend it to anyone who likes sci-fi, strategy, or old school RPGs. There's a lot of game in here for $20, and as of today, even more features are on the way!

This game has come a LONG way since it's humble beta back in ~2013, when I last played. There's still work to be done, but the developers continually endeavor to squash bugs, improve balancing (an endless battle in and of itself) and add new content.
As a "new" player coming into a game that's been out for a while, I didn't feel hamstrung by my lack of kit versus the more established players. I was able to drop right in and make a difference. As a "free to play" game, there are of course microtransactions - but I feel it is very well balanced and not at all pay to win. While you can skip ahead to the best mechs and fitments by throwing money around, winning will always come down to player experience and teamwork in the field. You don't have to spend a single dime to be effective. If you like it, you can always throw them a few bucks towards "premium" game time, which grants bigger rewards at the end of each battle, similar to how World of Tanks handles it.
If you're a fan of BattleTech or have played any of the previous MechWarrior games, much of the gameplay will be familiar to you. You purchase BattleMechs ('Mechs for short), outfit them in the MechLab, and go to battle. You control the torso with the mouse, much like any shooter, but you control the legs independently from the torso with the keyboard (you can also use a joystick, gamepad, etc. for both). This allows you to shoot on the move, as well as dance around your target while continually pouring hellfire into them. If you've ever played World of Tanks, or used vehicles in Battlefield, you'll be familiar with the feel of this already.
The developers have recently included a galaxy-spanning metagame, where the outcome of your battles have real consequences. Groups of players can fight for control of individual planets in the name of their faction (of which there are several to choose from), and the map is updated to reflect the ebb and flow of the battle lines as the campaign progresses. The closest existing example for this that comes to mind is WW2Online (Battleground Europe).
Anyway, the game has a lot to offer and it gets my recommendation!

I haven't played since the Disharmony expansion came out, but this is a very nice
game.  I rate it as the best space-themed
game (of course, it's also among the newest) and second only to Sid Meier's Civilization games for best
overall.  It would be tempting to call this Civ2 in Space, but that's not quite accurate.  Certainly, if you've played Civilization or any other
game you'll recognize that the basic ideas and goals are the same - learning the /massive/ tech tree, manipulating heroes, and mastering the nuances of unit behavior will still take some time, however.  The interface is, unfortunately, clunky and hard to read in the same way that the old Civ games were.  The presentation problems are primarily related to the tiny fonts that don't seem to scale with screen resolution and the amazing complexity of the game.  Here, each hero has multiple disciplines with unique talent trees for each.  Deep options for ship customization almost make for a game within itself, as much time can be spent min/max optimizing weight budget by rotating out varying armaments, engines, colonization pods, hulls, and more.  Planetary systems are similarly complex, and require a fair amount of micromanagement for min/max players - it's a lot like the way it was necessary to position each villager for each town in old Civilization games at harder difficulties.  Unfortunately, it's also rather tedious.
If you're a fan of Civilization and the idea of Civ in space sounds enticing, then this is the game you should be looking at.  It's not perfect and the learning curve is substantial, but there's a lot of promise here.  I'm not sure if there is a follow-up in the works or not, but this is an amazing first effort and I can absolutely see the potential for successive versions to challenge Sid Meier's lordship over the
genre.

If you are from South America, you might want to give this game a try. For the most part, I think the community is from BR. The game is for the most part dead. It averages 100 players.
If you want to know what happened you can ask some devs or read what I think happened below.
Beta Players were in love with this game and it had a following. Loadout made the decision to release and the players thought it was way to early. Although they probably did this due to lack of funds.
At launch there was no competitive mode but youtubers covered this game like pigs to a bucket. The art style and gameplay fit perfect for a quick one of video for youtubers. The game was downlaoded and played successfully by many. However, the hype slowly died. The game had no real thing making you want to play. I loved this game, but my friends didn't have the same drive to play it. A lot of gamers now days like comeptitive modes and I think this was its first fault.
The playerbase was still plentiful at this point. I think it was averaging 5k players. Since there was no real rank system you would get matched up to anyone and everyone. This game has a STEEP skill curve, but you can do just fine without being the best at aiming a sniper or laser.
When competitive mode came out the playerbase starting to fall a bit already. I think it was around 3k players. However, this didn't really head the game int he right direction. This is what it eventually came.
Overall the game wasn't getting money and it was slowly failing. It wasn't that no one bought their stuff. I bought every bundle they ever had and spent probably $300-400. Most player just didn't buy anything. The community even wanted them to release bundles and more skins and do weekly sales to give us a reason to buy stuff. I know this because I asked on the forums and people supported this idea. The community really loved this game and it was fantastic.
The company needed money and they went with Ps4 I think to try and get it out there. We know they made a deal and had obligations but we don't know what they were. During this time the community got split. There was the Beta Testers for the PS4 version that the PC was suppose to become. Then there was the PC players playing the current PC build. The PS4 version never made it to the PC version past the beta test version. Sorry If I confused you there. So the PC version never converted like it was suppose to due to the PS4 version not getting the in game purcahes they needed to keep it going.
Overall, money killed this game. The devs did what they could with the community while dealing with financial problems. It is a shame the game ended how it did but the game is still fun. If you have a group of friends give it a try.

I'll be very simple with the review since it's not a game that you need to over-complicate or go too in-depth with the details of. Blockland is a lego-like sandbox game in which you can create and design any kind of world or server you could ever desire. The game can be compared to the sandbox "Garry's Mod", which also centers on a player-driven system.
Like Garry's Mod, this game is somewhat of a niche, yet because of it's marketed open-endedness and scope, as well as low price and system requirements has been marketed to mass public. And like Garry's Mod, this is a game for specific people, and not the mass market.
The community has been accused of being focuses of drama and controversy and the forum and game policing has said to be flimsy at best, but this is a community driven game, again, like Garry's Mod. And on top of that, this game was developed in a time period in which indie games struggled quite a bit to get on their feet. This combined with the rare lifespan that this game has exhibbited has picked up a lot of baggage over the years, just like anything would. And the high social learning curve that comes with this game isn't exactly friendly to new players. What I mean is that each server is maintained and controlled be either a board of admins that the host has chosen to moderate and maintain the server, or a singular admin. How that admin wants to host and represent that server is up to them. People who like the hosts ideals will likely drift towards the servers with those admins, making sub-cultures in the game world.
The best thing for a new player to do is find a server with friendly new players and slowly intigrate into the community, otherwise you will most likely irritate the sometimes easily irritatable inhabitance of the game.
All in all, coming from a "veteran" player that watched this game grow and grow over the years, I'd say that it is enjoyable, so long as you can find a server community that you can intigrate with, you will have no problem with the community. As for the game, it's a high customisable sandbox game. That's pretty much the depth of it.

Dear Esther is a game developed and published by The Chinese Room. Dear Esther is hard to categorize. It is a beautiful piece of interactive, melancholy art. It is a profoundly moving game with randomised elements that change the story subtly each time you play
This 'landmark edition' improves the graphics of the game considerably and adds an informative commentary from the game makers and the composer who produced the iconic music for this title. If you're looking to try the game or replay it then this is the version to go for
You play a man traversing a beautiful, semi-linear island toward a radio tower far off in the distance. The narrative is delivered in the form of gorgeous, disembodied prose. These small anecdotes are often triggered out of order, depending on which path you take, creating a tragic jigsaw of a story that gradually becomes clearer as you progress
The most interesting mystery, however, is your location, and even your state of being. While the island has a distinct geographic location, it is covered in crypic paintings depicting anything from bacteria to circuitry
There are horror elements, ghosts in the periphery of your vision. There are vague mathematical concepts, and subtle religious imagery, yet somehow it manages to not come off as pretentious. Items from the narrator's memories are scattered about, often in out-of-the-way places
Regardless, the island is staggering to behold, with perhaps the most incredible level of environmental detail ever put into a game. You feel like you are in a real place, full of real history, real weather, and real imperfection. The textures, while kind of medium-quality, get the job done
However, the real hero here is the soundtrack by Jessica Curry, which is worth buying the game alone. Dear Esther is chock full of design choices carefully crafted to make you experience your journey a particular way, no matter how you choose to interpret the message, and the love that went into it clearly shows
As I mentioned at the beginning, this is a deliberately slow game. There is no run button. You have to put yourself in the right frame of mind. Slow your heartbeat and take it all in

pros :

-ingame currencies are easier and cheaper to acquire
-less painful spotting system
-small memory size

-tier difference per match is only +1-1, compared to wot pc's +2-2, and on some tanks even +3-2
cons :
-harder to grind tanks, since the xp distribution per kills, caps, etc are the same (so killing the entire enemy here is just a regular 7 kills on wot pc looking by the xp gains)
-far less tanks than the original wot pc
-since almost every tank is used rather frequently by other players due to the limitations of tank choice, ace tankers are far harder to gain
-on wot pc rarely AFKers and wallet warriors make a difference, in here 1 tank makes all the difference in the world. (get the reference?)
neutral :
-no artilleries. if you like to play artilleries then wanky♥♥♥♥shitdipshit, if you play heavy tanks than this is a real nice stuff to hear
-armor thickness indicators. it's good to have armor penetration indicators so you can easily see if it's a fight or if it's a flight situation, but since the enemy can use the same armor thickness indicators on you you better play it smart. rip AT-2
-less players per team, per match. if you're the type of player that can bring strategies and tactics for your teammate to achieve victory then this is a real good stuff to hear, but on the other side less teammates means less chance of victory when your team unluckily died.
-somewhat arcadish style of gameplay, also quicker matches. if you're the type of player who likes to play a quick game before switching to another one then this is for you, 7 minutes MAX per match, usually it's done in 4-5 minutes. on the other side, if you're the one who likes to take time doing damages little by little then it's a big problem for you, since the match would be over in no time.

The premist of the game looks very promising; both ship and soldier combat, upgrading a starbase, research options, a story, exploration, but after playing for a while this game becomes a tedious grind. It basically comes down to waiting for enough resources so you can advance to the next tier of ships, wait for more resources to buy those new ships, then kill the current "boss" which will trigger the next stage of the "story" where you do everything all over again.
Exploration is non-existent, there literary is nothing to explore. Maybe they are referring to the neutral NPC factions but those you cannot interact with unless the game wants you to.
Base management has no tactical aspect and just means building everything the game allows you to build at your current stage in the game. The same with the "research tree"; there are no choices, no tactics, just get all of them asap.
Other notes:
Lastly, the comparison to FTL is just wrong. FTL is much better and way more detailed. This game has no rogue-like aspects to it, and the combat in FTL allows for way more strategy.
TLDR conclusion; play FTL if you want a rogue-like with tactical combat. Play GalCiv II if you want to build a space empire. Play XCOM if you want to upgrade / reseach from a base. Only buy this game if you don't mind tedious grinding and it on a serious discount.

I feel that this game had a pretty good plotline and excellent character options. I especially appreciated being able to decide on focusing on stealth or being more frontal assault oriented, or somewhere in between. Also, the fact that I could be entirely non-lethal (with the exception of the boss battles of course) was a cool feature. I thought that certain time critical moments without an actual timer component were well done. How the game presented the consequences of success or failure of theses critical moments as a part of the story were handled seamlessly. It came as a very big surprise to find out later that certain parts could have had a different outcome based on my actions. While I did enjoy this game immensely, it did have its flaws. The biggest flaw to me was the inventory system. I was OK with needing upgrades to expand my inventory, that at least made some sense. What didn't however was which items stacked and which did not. It was just confounding to me that items such as mines stacked, but mine templates didn't, or that grenades didn't either. Plus the auto-arrangement code seemed slightly bugged when inventory was near full (like it wouldn't always rotate ammo stacks to accomodate fitting in bigger items). I felt like I had to spend too much time managing inventory just to be able to pick up upgrades or spare weapons to sell for money. Added to this was the lack of being able to rotate items manually if necessary. Another disappointment was that during certain conversations, if you don't have the social influencer module, certain dialog options aren't present to the point that the character is made to look less observant or more obtuse than is truly accurate. Lastly, there is a point in the game where the character's enhancements get wiped clean. You are credited with some points to re-upgrade, but only partially. This causes the following section of the game to be potentially way more challenging than it needs to be, since the player is forced to re-allocate those points in an expedient time frame without knowing anything about any of the upcoming challenges. Even on the normal difficultly I cannot recall how many times I was killed because I didn't have certain abilities that I had before the forced reset and either didn't or couldn't re-allocate points into those abilities. It made for a rather frustrating mission that almost killed the game for me. Overall, this game was still fun to play and I would recommend it for at least one good play through.

Best controller for PC gaming.
It was around August 2nd when my urge for a new controller rised. I had been using my PS1 Dualshock with an adapter to play games for 11 years before that. Mainly it is because I found it highly comfortable to use with emulators and most of the PC games feel better with Keyboard and Mouse.
And then companies began to port games to PC more often with enhanced experience features. X360ce doesn't work so well without massive hassles or compromises.
In my mind, I wanted a wireless controller to rid me off the chunk of wires beneath my desk. The DS4 looks really nice and the unofficial driver to make it work with PC adds some cool touch to it, but its battery life (8hrs) pushed me to the Xbox One S controller. I had read plenty of news about its new bluetooth and it sounded like a step up from DS4 with 20hrs replacable AA batteries. A week went by and it was still not on sale in my country.
I couldn't put my gaming on hold any longer so that's how I came to know this Steam Controller.
Gotta say it was the best choice that I've made.
Indeed it felt strange. The layout was confusing. At first I thought I got a bad product but turned out there are 2 extra triggers at the back of the controller.
Took me a good 30 minutes to get used to the new layout and button configurations but from then, pure bliss.
Pros:
-80 hrs long battery life with replacable AA batteries.
-Constantly supported.
-Cheap ( compared to using DS4 or XBox One S controller )
-Plenty of freedom in mapping inputs/outputs with very active community's templates.
-Works with many emulators.
Cons:
-Takes time to remember the new layout.
-Takes time to get used to the configuration steps.

Back when I first got my Steam controller, I hated the damn thing.
It took an inordinate amount of faff to get Steam to download driver updates and firmware patches.  The design felt clunky and un-ergonomic, support for non-Windows OSs was limited (no support for gamepad functionality on OSX at all) and to make matters worse, most of the features of the controller beyond basic functionality were reserved for Steam Beta participants in spite of this not being advertised on the store-page.
Fast forward to today, and I have nothing but praise for the thing.  You get all the remapping functionality you could possibly want, all the important features have made it into the mainline Steam client, and most importantly, it feels
once you get used to the layout.  You'll be surprised how quickly it replaces keyboard-and-mouse in a
of games, and not just the ones you'd expect.
Valve have done a lot in recent months to make the experience better, and I would have no trouble recommending it to anybody except maybe hardcore sim fans or esports players - it's not going to replace a keyboard / mouse or HOTAS setup for these players, but for everybody else you'll be surprised at how close it comes to doing couch PC gaming right.

The build quality on the controller is nice, and the flaps on the back can come in handy. The customization options are immense. So much so that I hesitate to get into all of them here. I think most people already have a 360 controller that they're happy with, and with that comes the only real reason to not have the controller. It simply doesn't outshine the Microsoft controllers.
The true utility of the controller comes when you are without a mouse, but you can't use a stick. If you're partnering the controller and the link in your living from your couch, they work great together.
The complaints I have aren't dealbreaking. I mostly just find the trackpads hard to use in some instances, and usually those come when the design is centered around having a stick. Selecting weapons/radio stations in GTAV comes to mind. The selections just kind of jump around, making quick actions extremely infuriating. Similarly, trying to work the left "dpad" trackpad like an actual dpad is a pain. Trying to select quick chat in Rocket League was about like flipping a coin as to whether or not you would actually register the one you wanted or one beside it. This might be remedied after more time with the pads.
If you're already really satisfied with your Microsoft controller, then you probably won't be blown away by the Steam controller. That said, if you wish for something more, something different, or if you're just curious, then pull the trigger!

I have stubbornly been a traditional mouse/keyboard player, but decided to give the Steam Controller a try because Valve.
It takes some getting used to at first; after playing through Bastion and Super Meatboy, I am very happy with the look, feel, and performance. I do wonder how it will hold up after extended use.
The Steam Controller + Big Picture Mode is a seamless combo, and if I had a TV I would probably get a Link as well.
I am using it for controller supported games, and found it convenient and functional for spectating Dota2.
I have not dived into custom controls for keyboard/mouse centric games, but have gotten comfortable utilizing it for short bursts of Windows navigation and web browsing in Chrome.
Very happy having spent full price; pondering if a second controller would ever be necessary, to take advantage of the weekend deal.

Lots of options for input binding. You can do practically anything short of macros with these.
Big grudge though: it likes to change the Steam Overlay to the Big Picture one, and the only reliable solution I've found to solve this is to restart Steam.

Look at the Windows Steam Client.
Now imagine if Valve made a controller.
The controller is slightly worse than my XBOX 360 or PS 4 controllers for PC games that have full controller support (e.g., Rocket League); for XCOM 2, a game that the controller actually came bundled with, it's annoying to the point where I'd rather use keyboard and mouse. I played XCOM EU and EW on my XBOX 360 console, XCOM works great with controllers. XCOM 2, with no native controller support, does not, and the Steam controller is not a solution.
Being forced to run Big Picture on a desktop PC in order to use the controller is also rather annoying.
Not being able to use rechargeable batteries is pretty sad (although, to be fair, regular batteries do last a long time).
I've had the controller since it was launched in the UK, so it's not like it's just taking me a while to get used to it:/
Edit: In fact, it's mostly garbage. It won't work at all with several Steam games that work fine with my XBOX 360 controller. I'd refund it if I somehow magically could. I've only still got this because my son likes it for Rocket League.

World of Guns:Gun Disassembly, as its title suggests, is a game where you disassemble guns.
Initially, there are very few guns accessable to the players, but with the hourly quiz you should be able to unlock the models you want. Alternatively all guns currently available and to be added will be unlocked for you at the price of $50. Not cheap, but you want to skip straight to your favourite guns, that's the way to go. The developers interact with the community to get guns people want added, so go tell them about what you want.
As for actual game play, some of the achievements are rather difficult and not all that fun to do. Especially Sniper achievements. I suppose you can disassemble a gun a lot and remember the thing or just use a youtube video or something if you really wanted it, but that's not fun is it?
Paint mode could still use some work, as of right now you can only paint over the metal texture like a monkey, which means you have to mess with transparency to preserve some of the metal texture if you want to change a standard black painted part to a polished stainless look. However it is rather effortless.
As for the weapon models themselves, they are decently done, not 100% perfect and you won't get you choice of Type-56, AKM, Zastava M70, WASR-10, various VEPRs, Saiga-12, Vityaz and Bizon all together for the AK family, but given the fact that we are not talking about a game with infinite budget and man power, a few key variants like the AKS-74U and AK47 is good enough. Although it is odd as to why developers decided to add optics and rails and other crap to some guns while neglecting others. And thankfully nobody has called a magazine a clip yet.
Actual game modes come in field stripe, disassembly and reassembly, game mode (previous modes with no hints), and harder variations of game modes.
The paint mode is also linked to the workshop, and you can upload your ugly vomit of Counter-Strike style gun painting all over the Internet to ruin our eyes.
While the game is rough around the edges, it is free, and for a free game you are getting a lot of content. Get it.

World of Tanks Blitz is at the forefront of future gaming : crossplatform (PC / Smartphone / Tablet, Windows / Mac OS / Android / IOS). This already exists for turn based genres such as card game but Wot Blitz is one of the first in real time games.
World of Tanks (PC) has been enjoying a huge success since 2010. It is the 5th best-selling PC digital game of 2015. Why play Wot Blitz on PC ?
Graphics: granted, Wot Blitz is a step behind regular Wot. But many successful games have proven that graphics are not the main point: Minecraft, Unturned, League of Legends, DFO in Asia, TF2, you name it…
Gameplay: Wot Blitz is similar to Wot except for 2 main points. First point: no artillery. Artillery prevents camping. But in an objective based game, camping is detrimental. Second point: team size (7 vs 7) is significantly smaller. This is a major improvement for 2 reasons. It is impossible to coordinate 15 players in regular World of Tanks. And in a smaller team each player is more important and can really impact the game and carry.
Overall, after many years of experience, Wot Blitz is an updated and improved version of Wot.
F2P: if you want immediately all the new toys, Wot Blitz is very expensive. One premium tank costs the price of a full game ! Don’t go that way. This is true for every F2P game: if you want all items it becomes the most expensive game of the world.
You are given some gold at the beginning. Don’t waste it ! Save it for buying slots at discounted price during an event.
The grinding process to buy and improve free tanks is slow. But patience is required in any F2P. More importantly, by grinding you improve your player skill. Moving up the tiers with real money is detrimental because you will face new maps and good players will crush you.
Overall Wot Blitz is a worthy product full of fun and of challenges. It takes time and patience to become a skilled tank pilot !
