This game is a mixed bag. This game does not bring any new innovation to this genere/game type. This game had so much potentional of being good but failed upon that. This game does not look anything that the thumbnail of this game suggested, it looked like more of a "sci-fi tank genre" in the thumbnail then modern. Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying modern is bad, all I'm saying is, many other companies like "War Gaming" has already done this type of game and theirs is much better in terms of effects and whatnot. There's frankly nothing exciting or new here. I do understand that this is a BETA game, and I may change my review if the following changes:
- More detailed maps--->better graphics (I don't mention on improving graphics in many reviews, because I get the target auidence that the company is trying to fullfill, but I believe the target auidence for this game are for those who want immersion and a better graphical experince. I understand that this is a free to play game, but on that same note, "World of Tanks" is also free to play with much better graphics.
- Better physics--->I'm not sure what is off with the physics, but I do detect something is dull about it. I think the explosion of the projectiles upon impact needs improvement as well as mechnics of the tank itself.
- Needs more gamemodes, not just elimination, the gamemodes are crazy fast; needs to be gamemodes where you can select what you wish to play *(Although I suspect that they will be adding this feature later on)
- The 60FPS cap needs to be removed. I could not find such way to remove it in the settings tab. Let the users decide if they wish to have a 60FPS or not, I have a 140Hz monitor with dual 1080's in SLI, and I wanted to get above 60FPS, and I was not able to.
- The above point is making me lead into my second point, they should support multiple GPU setups for those who have such luxary to do so.
- I also notice those lines on the edges of objects (e.i tanks, boxes, battlefield decor, etc.)--this is a result of having limited graphical settings with no AA option. Please fix this too.
- Give incentives to players who are not "premium" users (so all the free users.)--->let's not forget that the free users make up majority of this game, and there should be more incentives (WITHOUT making the premium feel uneeded, but have the less "pay to win" vibe going on.)
If these are fixed, I may give the game a second go, but for now I cannot recommend the game in its current state. It is, however, a good time killer, I suppose, and that's what it'll ever be until they make more improvements which give players incentives to keep coming back and playing more.

It started when I was playing along the peaceful economic single-player campaign having a tranquil time completing my little castle. I was supposed to make a bunch of bread and weapons, so I knew that I would have to create an efficient castle to be able to complete my task in the time limit. I first tried building a solid base of wood and food production to allow the construction of an array of weapon/bread facilities. But I slightly miscalculated causing starvation to the point everyone abandoned my city and before I could recover fires broke out in the farms and destroyed any hope of repopulating in time. So I restarted, and this time made sure that I would have ample production of food early on. However when I built my iron mines I didn't accompany them with enough hauler oxen so my miners were carrying each ingot back to my stockpile individually.
So I restarted, and this time I was going to get it right. I built an efficient layout of early game farms, with a proper number of accompanying lumberjacks. I expanded to iron production and wheat farms early enough to get plenty of resources for weapon production. I even laid out a grid of wells to quench any fires that would start and fought off the occasional bandit raid without harm coming to my people. Soon I had a bustling little burb, but upon creating a few new buildings the scribe informed me that I had no new workers available and I needed to build a new hut. While I was building a few new houses, the scribe again popped up telling me that a fire had started in the baker's quarter. I had no worries since there were wells everywhere...until I realized that I hadn't put wells around my new baker shoppes. In a panic I watched as the new baker shoppes caught fire while the bakers were trying in vain to escape the flames. Soon my firemen were on top of things throwing pails of water on the problem, but the fire was spreading and jumping from building to building faster then the pails could be delivered. It took a long time before the firemen from the farms arrived to lend a hand dousing the final flames. I looked around my smoking castle and realized I had not lost a single building. Not one. My firemen had put out every building before it burned down. Then it dawned on me, none of my buildings were being worked. The fire had lasted so long that all of my workers had burned to death, and all my farmers, and all my miners, and anyone not carrying a bucket of water. But hope remained! I had a small remnant of food left in my granary to get going and maybe I could get my castle running again. And then a theif stole most of what was left.
So now I am restarting.

I don't write many reviews but this game is AMAZING and well worth $15!  It's like FTL, XCOM and Master of Orion had a baby.  It has combined some great elements from many different games.  The base management is a lot like XCOM, but then there is a 4X space element like Master of Orion and Star Control.  And then sometimes you have ground combat which has an old school RPG feel to it like Final Fantasy.  The space combat is like that too.
I'm a little biased, I love turn-based combat but there is something really unique to how they did turn-based combat.  Different types of attacks have a chance to cause an affliction to the enemy ship/monster.  If another member of your fleet/party has a skill that exploits that weakness, it does increased damage.  That makes it so if you are good at micro-managing your parties/fleets and chain their attacks together you will be more effective.  Very rewarding!
There is also this resource management component where at the beginning you have actually use your ships to transport resources to and from your base and then later on you can launch satellites to auto-transfer resources at a certain rate.  There is a very deep tech tree.
All I can say is: WELL DONE!

Very nice title. Well worth at least its sale price.
Base building is pretty straightforward. Reminds me a lot of XCOM. But instead of excavating spots, you commit an officer to clear it out. Maybe nothing happens. Maybe he runs into hostiles. I like it. I also like that once you build facilities you can order your officers to perform various tasks within. You need an officer to train new crew, or run a materials fabricator, or develop ship upgrades.
As you can probably tell by now, a lot revolves around your officers. They don't just command your ships. They explore parts of the alien starbase. They run most facilities. They establish new resource collectors, as well as build upgrades to them. And if they are doing one thing, they cannot be doing anything else. As a fan of RPGs, I love it. It is like I have my own little collection of heroes to manage. You can even rename them.. which I do. :)
Combat is more Final Fantasy style. Line up and hurl skills at one another. Pretty easy to understand. And it doesn't take much to realize how you can stack attacks for maximum effect. I like that there is ground combat as well as space. Though mechanically they are the same, just with different sets of skills used.
Resource gathering is a bit of a nuisance. You gotta fly out to the collector, load it, then return home. When you only have a couple of ships, that is a real pain. Means you cannot do the fun stuff, like combat or exploration. There is a way to automate, but I feel it comes way later in the game than it should.
Which gets me to another gripe: when things are secretly locked behind specific missions or events. I don't like it when seemingly-open games do this. I'm fine with locking tasks behind an officer-level wall. But don't hide parts of the game behind specific missions. If you do, at least mark these tasks as more important than the rest. "Primary Task" or "Campaign Mission" or something.
Really, these gripes don't take away too much from the game. Once you get near a half-dozen officers, things really take off. More officers, more fun things to do.

This is actually a great game. Turn based combat. Overall resource management. It's a great strategy game. Actual enemy progression scales pretty nicely as you go on. It's exciting to play and you never quite know what might happen next, so you have to be prepared for anything.

This has the same 3 on 3 battle system that started with Final Fantasy, with a very small twist: combos can be set up by using attacks that create vulnerabilities in the enemy.  So the combos are only available if you arrange the attacks correctly.
Still, I was a little turned off by the 3 on 3 fighting before I bought the game.  But it plays out really well and speeds up the game.
The XCOM comparisons are mostly (though not completely) "dig out the basement to build office space" part of the game.  Research allows certain rooms to be built out.  This adds nicely to the gameplay especially weighing out how to spend resources.  Research is paid for with the same resources used to make ships and upgrades, so its a big balancing act, with some dead ends on first play-throughs.
Officers can have one of 3 careeers: engineers, scientists or tacticians, and they each have a skill tree.  They have a choice of 2 or 3 different ships for each career type, and each ship can have allocated attack build-outs.  How a ship is built out, and how an officer is built out for ground or space attacks determines which attacks or specials can be used in a fight.  Higher tiers of ships are eventually available.
I just bought the game, and proceeded to play a solid 3 hours nonstop, with no desire to stop other than I'm tired.  But the game has the right stuff -- and there is some good light humor in flavor events.  "Take that stool sample to the lab and spare no expense!"
The game does feel a little grindy - which I've read other reviews saying to up the difficulty to get around that.  There is a good feeling of accomplishment beating higher level enemies.
Lag?  I haven't encountered any and my laptop is not very high end.  This seems to have very low demands on a system, nor can I see any way the game would increase that demand the way the gameplay is set up.
I wholeheartedly recommend this for anyone who likes 4X space games.  Even though this plays like a 4x - technically it is not.  There are heavy storyline components and timed or triggered events, and the map seems to be static.  But the same logistics and decision-making apply.  Compared to a pure 4x - this is more interesting, because the pressure to resolve conflicts begins immediately, rather than many turns in.

Slower paced than hawken, much more unforgiving.  This is a thinking man's shooter; if you want to mindlessly kill things without any real skill involved, CoD is probably more up your ally.  Basically, you play a big♥♥♥♥♥stompy robot, loaded for bare and ready to ♥♥♥♥ up the nearest scrub to cross your path.  Think Gundam.
There are 4 mech weight classes in the game, Light, Medium, Heavy, and Assault.  There are many mechs of each weight class, just pick one that fits your playstyle.  Each weight class has a different purpose.
Lights act as nimble scouts/Assault killers/Fire support.  Lights are typically fast moving, highly mobile, low damage mechs.  GOTTA GO FAST!!!!
Mediums act as nimble fire support.  Mediums have a nice balance of weapons and speed to out manouver your enemies while still putting decent fire down range.
Heavies are your fairly hard to kill well armed mechs.  Heavies act as moderately mobile weapon platforms that you dont want to get in front of in a light.
Assaults are your heavily armored slow moving death machines that can kill you in a couple volleys, but get shreaded if a light gets behind them.
Pick a mech and and stick to your team like a sad lost puppy (especially if your buddies are bigger than you, give those ♥♥♥♥ers a hug).  If you're in a light/medium, use your heavy/assault buddies as human shields while plinking the enemies in their weak points (which vary).  Shoot anything that gets near your heavy/assault buddy  If you're in a heavy/assault, pick the nearest/most damaged enemy mech and pull all your triggers (plural ♥♥♥♥ing triggers).
When you shoot, your weapons ganerate heat (IT'S JUST LIKE REAL LIFE!).  Therefore you have to watch your heat generation and not just mindlessly fire your weapons into the abyss, you'll overheat.  Much like a computer when it overheats, you shut-the-♥♥♥♥ down, and damage your internal componets, leaving you vulnerable to enemy fire (as you cant dodge/shield the damage).  So, check yourself before you wreck yourself.  Lasers generate a lot of heat, but have infinite ammo.  Missiles generate moderate heat, but have limited ammo.  Ballistics generate low heat, but have very limited ammo.
Credentials:  I'm a veteran player (since beta) and I love this game from a PvP persepctive, it forces team cohesion and team play.  I almost always have a good time, even in defeat.  I have 1749 games on record (quick play games, not CW), given that ever match is about 10 minutes, that's 291 hours on record (just in match time, double/tripple that time if you count the time i've spent in the mechlab and CW).

Short explanation of some bad reviews:  Lots of the bad reviews come from unfulfilled promised of what the game was supposed to be.  The old publisher IGP (Infinite Game Publishing) was ruining what the devs PGI (Piranha Games Incorporated) was setting out to do.  This caused IGP to see the game as a flop and return the game rights to PGI.  Many of this game's founders and vereran players felt wronged by some of the actions forced upon PGI via IGP.  Since PGI broke away from IGP, the geme has been on an upward spiral in every respect.  IGP was a group of money grubbing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that wanted a flow of income from the game they had the rights to (to an extreme degree).  Many people are still butthurt over these things.
Intense Con:  Mechs are expencive with IRL money, keep in mind, this is a small developer making a very high quality game, and they have to eat too  (plus the Mechwarrior Community is a niche with many whales who will throw money at a develpower willing to make a game in the nearly dead franchise)
Potential Pros:  With the influx of new players from the Steam release, prices of things in game (IRL money) may become cheaper due to the larger player base.
PGI has hired many more people to work on the game (i caught this bit of info from on of the devs in a twitch stream chat)
The free to play model is actually not too bad, with 16 trial mechs each on rotation (that actually have good loadouts).  Back in beta, and early release, there were only 4 trial mechs with garbage♥♥♥♥♥loadouts.
You don't need to put any money into this game to have a good time, but hell, if you find that you're having lots of fun just with the trial mechs, toss $20 at the game, and get a mech or two.  If you enjoyed the game for many hours already, it's probably worth atleast a couple dollars.
TL;DR:  New players, give it a shot, it's free.  Old players, give it another shot, it WILL surprise you with all the improvements made since beta.

Deus Ex Human Revolution is a solid game on a technical point. Having beaten it numerous times in the past, it seems quite obvious that I did enjoy the title.
However, after replaying the classic Deus Ex, it clicked in my mind that Human Revolution is quite poorly developed Deus Ex title, albeit solid game on its own.
It is centered around conspiracy, new technology for betterment of human life & its abuse by hidden society lusting for global power.
It's not that the story itself is the issue. I love the idea of augmented people struggling in the streets & being discriminated. It's how it
&

It feels like a detective game. Find a clue, this clue leads to this culprit, then the culprit directs you to yet ANOTHER culprit & it repeats till you finally discover the location of the kidnapped scientists. After that, the finale is a very short portion of not-being-a-detective-game anymore, with a lame "boss" fight & cut and dry ending choices due to time restraints in development process.
Let's compare it to original Deus Ex story flow. You stop terrorism, blow up Universal Constructor that manufactures a virus & its vaccine, you meet members of the old hidden nearly powerless society group & join them, you sink the super-freighter, get components for the new UC, redirect nuke's target...
See the variety? THIS is what HR lacks & it's a major blow for me. It felt great weakening Majestic 12's globalistic plans after every major goal was completed. HR offered no satisfactory of that kind.
After credits dialog seems to me that the entire game was quite pointless to go through. You are in the mission to save five scientist, including Jensen ex, Megan & after you do, Megan straight joins Illuminati?! For what?!
It's so boring & in the end, not worth your time. Even side quests were more fun. They had a variety in them. In fact, reading news was more interesting.
Speaking of news, apparently newspapers were abandoned & replaced by some electronic device.
Ok, so the game takes place in 2027, which is 25 years before original Deus Ex, yet in the latter, news are actually on the paper?!
Heck, everything is futuristic in HR compare to the original. Makes no sense at all.
Well, since it's a 2011 title, this already can tell you it is a consolized mess, extremely dumbed down compare to the original with its more complicated system. Though, it did improve in some places, like the ability to loot what you want instead of just right-clicking a body to get what fits in your coat, the upgrade system is what fails.
Let's put weapon upgrades aside because it's no different from each other.
For augs to be installed, you need to find an aug. canister & a medical bot.
In order to upgrade them, you need to find an aug. upgrade canister, though bot is no needed.
You receive exp. points for skills via completing goals & exploring the areas.
Each new potential upgrade raises its cost.
Praxis points - Via exp. points, LIMB clinics & exploring.
Unlocking takes 2 points, each upgrade takes 1.
An upgrade difference example:
The aug. that lets you run silent in HR, it's just 1 praxis point till it becomes fully effective after you unlock it. In the original Deus Ex, you need to upgrade it 3 times for it to become fully efficient & you need to find specific items to upgrade it.
Another one I know of is Vision Enhancement. Same exact thing.
One-press-button takedowns is an absolute ridiculous system. If you played original, you know how careful you have to be to knock out a person in that game.
Casualized gameplay, samey story flow & non-sensical futuristic setting between games is what killed it for me to play it ever again.
Solid game on it's own but as a prequel to the classic, quite poor with "modern shooter" stigma slapped on it.

I love it. If you want controller for PC get it.

PROs
Feels like a good quality build - it's lightweight yet durable.
Extremely customizable - you can map pretty much anything anywhere. Have your joystick send d-pad commands or key(board) presses, it doesn't freaking care. You can also set a hotkey that changes what inputs will be sent (e.g. holding the left grip could turn your d-pad into a joystick input if you wanted). There are also community templates that are uploaded, and generic templates you can customize yourself. Lastly, you can save your configurations to your steam cloud so you won't need to worry about losing them.
Grips - Two buttons where your fingers already are. This is super convenient for many reasons (easy reloading, jumping, mode switching, etc)
Gyro (physically turning the controller to send input) - I'd never used one on a controller before and it is just an awesome thing. With a small amount of tinkering with the settings, I immediately noticed how much easier it was to aim precisely. I couldn't imagine a first person game (or anything that involves aiming really) without it now.
Touchpads - Relatively precise, but mainly good for swiping and getting the general angle of things. I did notice that after using them for a little while now I can navigate my computer using the controller fairly easily. In game however, combine a touchpad with the gyro to be golden.
Haptic Feedback - It's pretty much everywhere. But in a good way. The gyro gives you haptic feedback so you know how much input you're sending, the touchpad does the same, the d-pad can also do the same, the joystick can "click" (haptic feedback) when you set certain thresholds, and you can set how much haptic feedback you want from each thing (or none if you hate it). It goes on. Moral = easy to feel how much input you're sending.
How it holds - I personally like how it fits in the hand. My hand's are probably between small and medium closer to medium, but some controllers make my hands feel jammed up especially when my fingers are touching and it's just weird. But more of this will be in the cons.
CONs
This list probably isn't going to be as long but overall I like the controller so that makes sense right?
Physical Button Layout (personal con) - The d-pad/touchpad thing is on the outside, and the joystick is on the inside. This is inconvenient for me, because typically you use a joystick to move, and for many games I can usually handle most of the other inputs with my right-thumb (including d-pad), depending on the game obviously.
With the dpad being on the outer edge my thumb can't get to it, so I'm currently trying to get used to having the left touchpad act as a joystick while treating the joystick as a dpad. The main problem is, without this setup, it's difficult to keep moving while continually sending inputs from both the d-pad and buttonpad. TLDR this con = the button layout is a mind  to my playstyle Edit Note: This isn't an issue with most games, and there are other solutions you can come up with yourself (e.g. hold a grip to have the buttonpad send d-pad input, or even something more complex)
Customization - I saw someone post it as a con in some other review that too much customization was bad because it takes time to fine tune each configuration. I agree to an extent, it can be tedious to get that layout and you may spend a decent chunk of time just trying to get the controls how you want them, but you may also end up with very intuitive controls.
Force Big Picture Mode - I like big picture mode when I'm just finna chill n game n sh, but this may be a turnoff to people. However, I did just run the Witcher 3 from .. not... big picture mode... and it auto overlayed the ... big picture mode... overlay... without having to turn on big picture mode. So you'll be forced to use the overlay but at least you won't have to enable it before entering a game. Or something. This was a grammatical disaster, sorry?
Overall
I would recommend this to anyone who games often with a controller. If you, like, occasionally sit down on the couch to play... Plants Vs. Zombies? or something, this may not be for you, as it will definitely take getting used to.
Congratulations if you made it through this review, I'm surprised I did. I'll update this if my opinion changes.

Very nice experience. Not so much a game as an interactive movie. By exploring the environment you get to unravel what's going on with the protagonists past, present and future. Although the genre of "walking simulator" is an acquired taste, Dear Esther is one of the best. One caveat: the game is rather short, but then again, it is ample enough to tell the engaging story.

While the Landmark Edition is certainly noticeably prettier than the original with enhanced textures, it still doesn't make up for the game's numerous other flaws.  For starters, there is still no sprint button.  The pacing for Dear Esther is unbearably slow despite the fact that I understand developers want the player to soak in the environments and everything.  Like others have said, there is only so much you can actually look at considering your snail pace.
Voice acting is excellent but that does very little when there is essentially nothing in the way of meaningful and constructive storytelling.  The narrative or lack thereof didn't sit well with me.  It lacked substance.  Some people loved it, others could have passed on it.  I am the latter.   Esther's soundtrack is fitting however, especially with the environments you travel through.  Controls are about as basic as a game can get.  You can only walk.  People have called Dear Esther a walking simulator and with good reason.  It is literally all you can do.  You can't interact with anything.  The most you can do is zoom in and occasionally in dark areas the character will turn on his flashlight, which you have zero control over.  There are other games similar to this genre that are more engrossing and engaging.  Take for example Mind: Path to Thalamus which adds puzzles into the game.
Overall, I can't recommend Dear Esther especially not for its asking price of $10.  It is a relaxing and short (~2 hours if you take your time) experience at most and calling it a game simply doesn't feel appropriate.  But to each their own; the game has a sizeable fanbase for what it is and they love it.  To me though, this just wasn't my cup of tea.

A Preface: As someone who never actually played Stronghold "back in the day" I'm hoping that this review might be of help for others like me. That is, folks for whom this game pulls no nostalgic heartstrings but might still be interested in playing it.
A Review:
After the last season of Game of Thrones ended, I began looking for a game that would satisfy my Medieval itch, but wouldn't be as complicated as something like Crusader Kings. Stronghold HD is the game I settled on checking out and I couldn't be more satisfied with it (though there is a severe lack of assassins for my taste, maybe I'll check out Stronghold Crusader).
The basic premise of most of the game's levels is classic Rampart from the NES days: either build from scratch or take over a castle, then defend it from waves of invaders with breaks in between to rebuild and refortify your defenses and replenish your troops until you clear the level. There are plenty of variations to this premise as the game's campaign goes on, and you're ever so slowly advanced up the tech tree, but that's generally the gist for most of the game as far as I can tell (I'm not quite finished with the main campaign yet, but I'm doubting a big turnaround at this point).
There's a lot of Age of Empires 2 in not only the controls, but the game's graphical and audio stylings, but that really isn't a bad thing, as well designed pre-rendered 3D as seen here turns out to be quite timeless, and even the most amateurish British voice over sounds pretty classy.
So yeah, it's a High Medieval RTS/City Builder/Castle Builder with a lot of elements of what would eventually be tower defense in it for good measure . . . that's the game, and there really isn't more to it than that. Fairly uncomplicated really, and that's a good thing, as it leads to a very polished and enjoyable experience for when you're in the mood to put on your Lordly crown, and order some peasants to toil in the fields or add more mortar to the walls.
Oh and since it is a classic retro game, there's a LOT of content. I mean, the multiple campaigns (There's an economic mode I haven't even tried yet) have a ton of levels (replete with a silly little story and characters) and that's on top of a map editor and an MP mode! Seriously, on content alone you're going to get your money's worth.
Still, if you're more into leading an army rather than manning the walls, this isn't going to be the game for you. For that, I'll say to check out Medieval Total War (1 or 2, both are good). And if you want to focus more on the city building, Banished will probably be more to your tastes. And if you want a mix of both but a still more offensive based game, there's always Age of Empires.
But if you're like me, and just want a game that:
A) Stays in the Middle Ages rather than hopping around time
B) Let's you boss a bunch of peasants around while you sit at your computer drinking red wine from your goblet, and
C) Lets you focus on designing your dream castle in intricate detail
. . . then this is the game for you milord!

MW:O was my first contact with the Battletech universe.
I started playing around october 2014 and did enjoy the game from the beginning. Although, at this time, there was almost no help for new players and the whole game was quite confusing.
But I kept playing and with the help of some other players I got the hang out of it and since then I just love the game (and the whole universe, which I learend about after getting both legs in the game).
You have endless combinations of 'Mechs to build, tons of different 'Mechs, with tons of different variants. Every variant can be customised with a lot of weapons and equipments. You don't need to take "meta" builds and you don't have something like "the OP super cool" 'Mech. More importantly than the meta is, that you find a 'Mech and a fitting, which suits your very own playstile.
Although, of course, some people would disagree: I would say the game is balanced good and you can have a lot of fun with every 'Mech.
There is absolutly NO need to pay money, if you don't want to.
You won't get an advantage ingame, for paying real money. But there are some variants, which can only be achieved via real money (or premium currency won by events). But these 'Mechs (called "Hero" and "Champion" 'Mechs) aren't better than their ingame-currency-variants. They "only" give you the ability to gain more income or more XP from battles (30%).
Real money can only be used to lessen the "grind", but if you play regularily, you won't need to spend money, you can get enough income over time to afford your own hangar full of 'Mechs :)
The game is developed further, every two weeks there is an update on tuesday, which provides new content, or updated game aspects.
You should try MW:O and make a decision for yourself :)

The steam controller is the best controller I have ever used. It's not perfect, but it's pretty close.
I have used this to great effect in older games with some pretty backwards control schemes since every button, touchpad, and trigger is fully customizable.
The main thing I like about this controller that would be good even without the ability to customize is the fact that it has 3 triggers per side, which opens up two whole new buttons to use with video games. Should be an industry standard as far as I'm concerned, same with layout customization.
However, while this controller mostly excels at everything you could want a controller to do a quantum leap above a dual analog when it comes to PC gaming, it is actually pretty bad at emulating a dual analog itself. I have been at some things for hours trying to find a configuration for a dual analog emulation that is comfortable, using everything from the gyro to switching up sensitivity and deadzone and I have not been able to find something that accurately emulates the feel and responsiveness of a twin stick setup for controller only games. I've come extremely close, but not close enough to be as comfortable. This is a non issue if you are using a mouse and keyboard emulation since using the right touchpad for wide turns and the gyro for fine tune aim provides near the same level of accuracy of a mouse, but when you do this same setup with a gamepad emulation it's floaty and always goes just off from where you want it to. I'm sure a software update or just simply more configuration will fix this issue in the future.
This issue aside, I do highly recommend this controller, as it's constantly being updated with new features software side and feels good to use after configuring it and getting used to it. It also is incredibly versatile, I love how I can even use it as a makeshift steering wheel controller thanks to the gyro, and it's especially nice for character action games like Metal Gear Rising and Devil May Cry where you can macro bind just guards and other important maneuvers to the back triggers, and never have to take your finger off of a dodge button to block.
Be warned, you must be okay with configuring things to like this controller. It's something you will have to acquire a taste for because of just how different it is from other controllers, but once I acclimated myself to this new kind of control, for everything except stuff that can only be used with a controller, I'd take this over a dual analog any day. In fact sometimes I look for excuses to use this over mouse and keyboard so I can just lay down and play my games without the compromise of a dual analog aim. Another thing to be weary about is the absolutely
shipping cost of getting this from steam, it's a whopping 8 dollars if I recall correctly and as such I would only recommend this on sale, especially because you may not love this controller as I do.
In short, this is a criminally underrated controller because it's just so different. But there are loads of things about this that I consider should be industry standard rather than an outlying experiment like haptic vibrations, customizability, and 3 triggers per side. But that's just my opinion. I can see why people won't like it, it does require you to customize it to your liking. But when you do, I think this beats dual analog. However, it doesn't replace your dual analog, it merely compliments your options greatly. I still recommend having a regular controller nearby just in case you want a twin stick experience with a game, but this is good for the other 75% of things you would use a controller for.

Dear Esther is either the sort of game you'll love, or hate, and you'll know exactly which before you the play the game. I am a lover.
It's a walking simulator, in fact, I think it is one of the first walking simulators. Started a Half-Life 2 mod. There isn't much interaction, you walk. You are exploring an island, and your path isn't completely locked on rails, but there isn't a lot of choice. There is a story, but it isn't much, and it takes awhile to sew together the narration with the visual clues you find.
So why do I love this game? It's an emotion. When you add together the sounds of the narrator, the music, the wind, and the sea, plus the rocky landscape, I feel a certain type of way. The island is rocky, and cold. The sky is overcast. The buildings are ruined relics. There are no people, but our trash has found a home on the island. There is a bleakness to it. And yet, there is the occasional gull, and wildflowers. I can zoom in and watch them sway in the breeze, or zoom out and admire the field. Clear water flows through phospherescent caves. The narrators voice is soothing, the music is often beautiful, with just a touch of dissonance. The whole game has the depth and richness of a minor key. So the real life me can sit in a chair, push the W button on my keyboard, and just be for two hours.

Dear Esther is hard to categorize. Plebs would call it a "walking simulator"-- the first ever-- though this label is painfully regressive. In reality, it is a beautiful piece of interactive, melancholy art. You play a man traversing a beautiful, semi-linear island toward a radio tower far off in the distance. The narrative is delivered in the form of gorgeous, disembodied prose. These small anecdotes are often triggered out of order, depending on which path you take, creating a tragic jigsaw of a story that gradually becomes clearer as you progress.
The most interesting mystery, however, is your location, and even your state of being. While the island has a distinct geographic location, it is covered in crypic paintings depicting anything from bacteria to circuitry. There are horror elements-- ghosts in the periphery of your vision. There are vague mathematical concepts, and subtle religious imagery, yet somehow it manages to not come off as pretentious. Items from the narrator's memories are scattered about, often in out-of-the-way places. Where are you, really? A physical place, or a metaphor for transcendence? Purgatory? Coma? The developers intentionally leave this open to interpretation.
Regardless, the island is staggering to behold, with perhaps the most incredible level of environmental detail ever put into a game. You feel like you are in a real place, full of real history, real weather, and real imperfection. The textures, while kind of medium-quality, get the job done. However, the real hero here is the soundtrack by Jessica Curry, which is worth buying the game alone. Dear Esther is chock full of design choices carefully crafted to make you experience your journey a particular way, no matter how you choose to interpret the message, and the love that went into it clearly shows.
As I mentioned at the beginning, this is a deliberately slow game. There is no run button. You have to put yourself in the right frame of mind, like you would when watching a Tarkovsky film. Slow your heartbeat and take it all in. While I had no problem progressing the roughly two-hour play time (for the third time since it was a Half-Life 2 mod), others might find it easier to digest while bedridden with the flu, or suffering / enjoying some other form of mild hallucinatory / altered state.
If you are looking for great storytelling with great presentation and killer visuals and don't mind your input being limited to ASDF and mouse look, you're in for a real treat.

This game is pretty great.
Take an XCOM reboot style overall strategy system, right? There's a map, there are things on the map. You have dudes with semirandom skills and abilities as well as skills and abilities determined by their equipment (spaceships) who level up.
Your job, much like XCOM2 is as the last living commander after the end of civilization as you know it. Kinda. A mysterious alien race has wiped out all of your space empire's communications and military, and plunged said space federation in to chaos overnight. You are battlefield promoted to commander of the titular Halcyon 6, an ancient alien space station and the last fortified position of the federation.
In the early game you'll spend a lot of time flying around your busted empire, closing portals, making contact with scattered colonists, and deal with 'sorry but not sorry' neighboring races. You'll have to manage your officers and spaceships to find a balance between expansing your sphere of incluence and space, exploring your alien station, building things, training things, etc.
Imagine, basically, XCOM2's grand strategy, only that there are more choices to make on the map and that your combat troops are also your engineers so you need to balance where you use them. One thing that's refreshing is that most research is completed instantly, and the time sinks in the base are much more repeatable and varied choice wise s things are more balanced around resource acquisition and interative stat upgrades in stead of taking a long time to unlock new research. It feels much more deterministic than the XCOM model for this reason, with lots of valuable options that don't feel like they make each other worthless choices.
Combat is handled in a 3-on-3 turn based affair reminiscent of old school JRPGs but with a much higher stakes tactical twist that revolves around applying and "exploiting" various debuffs. Space combat is the most common (and for this reason there are more stat levers to play with, including two ship types at each tier, a random upgrade bonus system for the crew of the ships and their capitains, and a large selection of ship and pilot abilities to fine tune your fleets and synergise their abilities for combat. In a nice touch, most star systems have an environmental effect that makes participants in the battle, both enemy and ally, immune to a certain status effect, which can really change how your fight plays out. For instance, if the drawback to a skill is vulnerable on self, and you're in a system that makes everyone immune to vuln, then you can use that skill without the drawback. On the flip side, if your fleet relies on a status effect like stun or weapon disruption to defend itself of pull off damage combos then you may have to use a second fleet or change your strategy for that fight.
The ground combat uses mostly the same fomula, but the abilities are limited to what the officers know. There's no equipment or research choices for this part of the game, but you'll do probably 1/5 as much ground ifghting as in space. I do hope in future iterations they expand the ground game with some equipment similar to what ships do for the space combat.
As the game goes on a lighthearted and sort of tongue in cheek space opera ensues, complete with well animated and written envoys from your standard space trope alien races including the totally-not-borg, totally-not-klingons, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ space traders, space psychics, and some others as well as the incomprehensible main antagonist the Chrull.
In later stages you'll be required to deftly manage multiple fleets as well as various station systems to keep your resources going and begin to unlock the mysterious relationship between your station and the invading enemy, as well as make besties with your alien neighbors (or just demand they give you the GDP of entire planets as protection money.)
It can be a slow starter early on when you're constantly running out of fuel and resources, but if you enter with a mindset toward expansion you'll find a very fun, funny, and meaty strategy game here that's not too punishing, but not too forgiving either.
I highly reccommend this game.

Ahh, Stronghold... A slice of nostalgia, and a damn fun game to boot. I'm going to go on a bit of a rant here, to be perfectly honest, so for anyone remotely interested in this game I'll give you a quick overview right now. Stronghold is a classic real time strategy game with a focus on replayability, base building/management and careful positioning over the micromanaging tactics that tend to dominate many RTS games today. If that sounds up your street, I'd buy it at full price. The game is WELL worth £3.50 and I must have sunk at least 40 hours into creating new and interesting siege maps and swapping them with my friends to challenge one another alone.

There's no reworking of the graphics or anything like that, and the opening cinematic still plays in a hilariously tiny box in the middle of a great big black void. Fortunately, in-game itself is treated very nicely indeed with the new resolutions... There's definitely a charm to the animations, and the little details like the cinematics that play out on your minimap when you select certain buildings or to mark events are welcome... But there's not much here to recommend beyond the rustic medieval design of the game's interface as a whole, which still stands up to some degree despite the game's age. I suppose one bonus of this is that you certainly won't have to worry about upgrading your rig to meet any requirements...
3/10

Particularly on returning to it, I'm surprised at how good the campaign story gets once you get into later sections. This is a simple story of revenge and honour in a historically ambigious version of England. And yet the game does manage to go beyond a simple framework that leads your nameless character from point A to point B to fight Lord C because... Well because Daddy issues. No, it actually manages to create something that you can invest in to an odd degree. Mostly though it's use of larger than life, fun characters.
Your two main advisors are a fun pair of Lords that bounce off each other in a way that's mildly amusing, but it's primarily the villains of the game that get the best moments. The four lords, The Rat, The Snake, The Pig and The Wolf (going by their nicknames) are each clearly defined, given backgrounds and range from freaking hilarious to pathetic to loathsome. The game does a great job throughout of giving you great reason to want to crush these four villains both in and out of gameplay itself, with the dialogue not stopping once your in-game itself. (Apparently medieval Skype calls were a thing. Who knew?)
The voice acting for these parts is... Well, this is going to be the divisive bit. It works for me, in an odd way. But if you've got any kind of ear for actors, you're quickly going to pick up on the fact that there's basically one, maybe two (three at a push) guys voicing EVERYTHING IN THE GAME. And yes, I said guys quite intentionally, as this includes the women. The game, however, appears to be well aware of this deficiency and plays it up for all it's worth (Most notably in the case of the mother's wondering around your keep who let you know how lovely the morning is in their best Monty Python impersonation) with some success. It's a matter of taste, but I find it pretty entertaining, and within the campaign itself it does add a kind of charm to the whole proceedings in regards to the storytelling nature of it's plot.
7/10 (6/10 if you don't appreciate hilarious voice acting.)
Ah. Here we go. This is what it's all about. Simply put, Stronghold is a fantasticly fun RTS. There are a variety of units that serve basic purposes, but the game knows not to go too far with it. When the time of a siege is approaching fast and you only have limited moments to decide whether to split your resources between your economy, your castle walls or your military, it's important that you know exactly what every soldier is there to do. The game does an excellent job of setting up a simple, but useful roster of troops to choose from. Without going into extreme detail here, just be aware that this is one game where zerg swarming the weakest units isn't going to get you very far if you're trying to siege anything beyond a very basic wooden set-up... Not if the defender is at all smart with their pitch and engineer set up, that is...
There are counters to pretty much any unit type, and as of such this often becomes a game of out manouvering your opponent or careful planning rather than sudden quick decisions. The siege mode which is entirely focused on the combat and a single siege (obviously) is certainly more exciting in that sense, but even during battles the game is not a fast-paced affair. It is exciting primarily in the scale and degree of strategy you must deploy to break through seemingly impregnable sets of walls and defences, or ensure that those damn trebutchet don't get set up out of your archers and crossbowmen's range... And if they do, whether it's worth sacrificing your precious few knights in a charge to try and destroy them this early on. All in all, Stronghold is an oddly relaxing game inbetween battles. Every decision matters, but the game's soothing soundtrack and charming graphics, combined with the focus on placement and management over micromanaging and quick reflexes gives it a very laidback feeling compared to a lot of modern RTS installments. If you haven't played a game like this before, this may seem a bit 'off' to begin with, but give it some time and I think you'll soon grow to appreciate it. Unless, of course, you're a twitch gaming junkee that just needs his next fix, in which case why are you even looking at an RTS review? You weirdo. Sheesh.
Oh and I suppose we should talk about replayability. You want to talk about replayability? This game comes out, walks up to most games that talk about replayability and just slaps them across the face and then suplexes them into the corner, screaming like it's Hulk Hogan and the Ultimate Warrior's unholy love child. Stronghold's map creator is probably one of it's best features. The base maps themselves within the siege and invasion modes are already great fun, but the map creator allows you to basically do whatever you like, however. It's a standard other RTS games should look to achieve.
If I were to lay any complaints at the floor of Stronghold's gameplay, they would all come from dated limitations. It is possible to flatten the world and look at structure layout by pressing spacebar, which helps make sure that you haven't missed any gaps but camera positioning IS an issue. For the most part, it's fine, but I am now spoilt by modern games that give full use of a camera that allows seemless positioning and zooming. This game allows you to switch between looking at the map from four different directions when you hold down right click and select a compass. And yes, I know that I've been particularly fair on the game given it's age before this point, but this IS the game's one major failing. It's not a big one, honestly, but it's one that should be mentioned. All I can say is, thank god they thought to add in the spacebar option.
8/10

It's a great customizable controller which I recommend for most games. Games that work with a regular xbox controller are playable with the Steam controller, most will benefit from the extra features or offer an equivalent experience to a regular controller but some will be slightly downgraded because of the lack of a proper d-pad and a second stick. Some games will not work great without some experimenting with configurations and settings.
It's great for third person action-games like Witcher 3 or the recent Batman games where one of the sticks is mainly for controlling a camera and the d-pad is not used that often and not used in any precision/fidelity ways, for games like that you get the benefits of two mouse-like surfaces and two extra buttons under the controller. You can map a bunch of buttons two one of the pads and get an awesome camera for the other.
If you really need two sticks, for example you need both to control individual characters like in brothers then I don't recommend it. Use a two stick controller for that, you can emulate a stick using one of the pads but a real stick will always be better for controlling a platforming character with analog movement for example. If you need a d-pad for fighting games then it probably won't be enough either. You still have the regular stick but some people want a d-pad and the stick is a bit small.
First person and third person shooters games all depends on how customizable the games options are, how good steam controller configurations you can get for the game and how open to new control methods you are. The steam controller is probably more capable and the closest you can get to a mouse level of precision with a controller thanks to the mouse and the gyro. I have been playing Overwatch using the controller and use the gyro for main aiming and the pad for some aiming and I can get pretty close to regular scores using it, however I'm not some pro fps player. The main flaw is close quarters combat with quick precision aiming but overall it works surprisingly well. I will always do better at my desk however, still fun to play from the couch. Other FPS games have different sensitivity and your mileage may vary but if you do some testing with configs you can get it to work in an acceptable way.
The biggest unsung feature of this controller is the gyro. It's crazy how good it can be for aiming when you need your thumb to do something else like hitting reload or you need to do some twitch aiming, if you have played Splatoon on the Wii U then you know how gyro controls will always beat stick aiming despite how crazy it sounds.
The last thing it does is just act as a keyboard and mouse for games like civ5 or just doing stuff on your desktop from the couch, this can be very convenient.
Not a controller for everyone or a better controller for everything but still a good controller and awesome controller if you like to change how stuff works and are willing to learn to try stuff a new way.
Versatile, ergonomic, all-round a good controler.

General points:
- The game is not Pay-To-Win in any way, shape, or form.  Everything can be purchased with Cbills, which are rewarded at the end of games.
- The game has a very rough learning curve.  Those who do not know how to look one way while moving another are going to have problems here.
- No, seriously, learning curve.  Additionally you have two crosshairs - one for your arms, the other for all torso-mounted weapons.  They will not necessarily be pointing at the same thing at any given point in time.
- Most customization of a giant robot outside of the Armored Core series of games.
- A-symmetrical warfare.  There are two sides to every conflict.  In this game it's the Inner Sphere vs the Clan.  Inner Sphere pilot mechs that are centuries old - clan mechs are the latest and greatest.  PGI has done a very good job keeping these concepts without overpowering one side or the other.
- About that learning curve... There are mechanics that are not readily apparent.  When constructing your mech, look for a red 'yield' sign and mouse over it for further information.
- The game really is free, and there's literally no reason not to try it.
General review:  In no other game on the market can you play as a robot the size of a building, slinging shells the size of volkswagens to shear off plates of titanium, ceramic, steel, AND DIAMOND from other robots the size of buildings.  Mechwarrior Online is a Moba in the truest sense of the acronym - Multiplayer Online Battle Arena.  Select and customize your mech to take part in a 12 on 12 battle royales against other players and their unique snowflake mechs to see who will come out on top.  Ultimately, Mechwarrior Online is a very challenging slow-paced first person shooter that plays a lot like a simulation.  Moving your mech is increasing the throttle, and you accelerate to your top speed which not only varies from mech class to mech class (Light, Medium, Heavy, Assault) but from mech to mech (depending on the engine that you choose to bring).  Mechwarrior Online definitely isn't for everyone, but with a Free to Play model that isn't pay to win - you lose nothing for giving it a try.  6/10.
Review for those who have played Mechwarrior Online since Beta (Founders):  The game has come a long way from when there were four mechs.  All told, the game still isn't everything that was asked for, but despite that, it's a game that after YEARS of play, we keep coming back to it.  Giving PGI credit where it's due 7/10.
Review for those who have played other Mechwarrior Titles (MW 2,3,4):  Mechwarrior Online plays a lot different from the game you remember.  This is mostly because the game is a multiplayer experience only based on the World of Tanks gameplay and monitization system.  Matches were desinged to be played in 15 minutes or less, so there is definitely an arcade feel here.  As the most recent Mechwarrior title, its looks are far better than the previous titles (as it should), and the redesigns of the mech models are quite superb.  Mechbay is much different from what you would be used to - instead of swapping out weapons of a type to fill the slots available, mech customization is deeper, while similarly limited.  MWO has a steep learning curve, but as a Mechwarrior veteran you should be able to catch up quick.  7/10
Review for those who play fast-paced mech titles (Armored Core series):  You aren't going to be impressed with this title as the gameplay is not what you are looking for.  Armored Core, while similar in the level of customization, also is far more fast paced.  Control over an Normal or Next is far less like operating a machine of war, and far more like playing a FPS where you look like a mech.  In AC, your mech has a total hitpoint value based on your  components, while in MWO your mech's health is determined by component.  This means you can be killed when your mech is at 65% simply by taking damage to your center torso and losing it, or having your cockpit destroyed (headshots), wheras AC doesn't have these distinctions.  AC's gameplay is a fast-paced gundam style while MWO is more like if you were trying to drive a World War 2 tank.  It's a free game so give it a shot, but you will be better served by playing Hawken.  4/10

Dear Esther is not as much a game as it is an experience, and it has a special connection for me personally.
I first played the original Dear Esther mod for Half-Life 2. At that time, I was playing a lot of different Half-life 2 mods and I was mostly out for quick-paced-action-intense mods, but Dear Esther offered something completely different. It was a slow burn and with its eerie atmosphere towering with dread and ill omens I played it through and wasn't really sure what to make of it. But I was quiet young as well. When the full version came out I picked it up at a sale some time after the release. Once again, the dread of the island haunted me and the very beautiful graphics intrigued me. Having also experience the island once before, this time I was more prepared for what exactly Dear Esther was and what it would offer me.
So this brings us up to speed, I received this product for free, benefiting from already owning the original edition. This version is more beautiful than the others, it includes developer commentary which was a nice touch and gave some insight into the development and also adding more to the eeriness of the island and clearing up some mysteries, such as that the audio commentary and visuals are randomized for each playthrough, offering a nice garnish to your playthrough.
Dear Esther offers you a very unique experience that I think most people would appreciate, but you must know what to expect when you go in. Set aside 2 hours (you'll probably need less), make yourself a nice cup of tea, sit down and enjoy the experience all at once. Then a couple of years later, play it again, I'll wager you'll like it even more.
It's cheap as it is but if you're hesitant, pick it up at a sale, you'll pay less for it than a beer at a pub and it deserves to be played more than once. Just make sure you let some time elapse before you boot it up for a second run. I'd recommend it to anyone with some patience and over the age of 18, you'll need some life experience and heart ache to truly appreciate it.

I wanted to love this game and honestly, it's ok.
But.
It feels dated.
I played the first Deus Ex when it first came out. DXHR is a neat hommage to the first one. Actually, it feels too close to the original one for me : the world is very schematic. The story, the characters, the theme, everything feels one dimensional. The so called "depth" of the Deus Ex games comes solely from exposition and logs that are firstly very boring to read and secondly not interesting. I'm an avid SciFi reader and DXHR feels older than anything written in the 1970's. DXHR's SciFi layer is essentially chrome for a power fantasy. At least, a game like Crysis aknowlegdes this aspect and focuses on the gameplay. Here, it's really a mixed bag.
The only aspect I really enjoyed (or at least that intrigued me) was the "social enhancement" or whatever they call it. In some (rare) dialogues, you can evaluate the person you're talking with, diffuse pheromones and either charm or pressure the persons depending on their personality type. It's still schematic but the creators clearly put a lot of thought into it. You actually have to read them, and it's not as obvious (and stupid) as LA Noire where a liar will have a forced "liar's face". For me, it was the only occurence where the characters in DXHR felt like there was some depth to them.
The graphics feel already old. At every step, you feel the walls of the world. And it's ugly.
Every quest, even the main one, feel like uninsteresting fetch quests. Go here, get this, get that, go there, bla bla.
Gameplay is ok but really not that engaging. Just compare it to Styx, a humble yet rigorous stealth game with real challenge, wonderful level design and you'll understand what I miss here.
A good game may have good gameplay and a mediocre story. I can even accept an uninteresting gameplay with an excellent story. But a mediocre gameplay with a mediocre story make a mediocre game.
Sure, the stealth aspect of the game can be quite exciting. But DXHR is one of those games where everything is obvious. Air vents are just waiting for you everywhere. You can snipe anyone and carry their bodies at will. And if anything gets a bit difficult, you can save and reload endlessly.
It feels like work.

If Civilization, Sim City and Age of Empires had a baby it would be this game. It's a reasonably difficult RTS with some really neat ideas in all aspects of the game. Its original release was back in ye olden times when all RTSes were sprite-based isometric affairs, and this one pulls it off in a brilliant fashion and rather ahead of its time. You can rotate the camera in the four cardinal directions to get a better view, flatten the terrain dynamically, and there's even a plan view.
The resource aspect is incredibly granular and adds a lot of flavour and its own brand of difficulty to the game by not only managing your population to grow your army, but also the different workers you need for each resource. Chopping wood, mining stone, farming, crafting each type of weapon, as well as managing the food resource drain as well as taxes and natural disasters sets it very much apart from the standard 2-3 resource affairs like StarCraft, Command and Conquer, and the like.
Nearly every aspect of the game has been crafted with care, and it shows. There's several nice nuances in this lovably cheesy and self-aware game, my favorite of which is easily the Scribe. Quick little messages like "It's very late, me lord, aren't you tired?" or "How about a snack, me lord?" are really quite super, and only increase both the immersion and show the care that the developers had for both the game and the player.
TL;DR - Buy this game, especially if you like Strategy titles. It's a perfect example of an "oldie but a goodie" and the HD resolution is a welcome addition for today's systems.

This game surprised me; in a good way.
It's an unapologetic, almost retro FPS.  Crazy power-ups; a protagonist that carries an entire arsenal of weapons; ammo ammo, health and armour litter the ground; keycards unlock doors to progress to the next area etc etc.  The graphics are excellent, the sound design and music really add to the experience and the storyline is actually a lot more involved than it needs to be.  There's loads of flavour-text in collectible data logs too and a dark sense of humour running through it.
The violence is horrendously over-the-top, but as you're blasting apart demons from hell rather than humans, the absurdity of tearing an imp in half with your bare hands becomes quite cathartic rather than disturbing.
The level design is good, the guns are all unique enough to have their own uses and iconic weapons from the series make a welcome return.  Collectibles and secrets provide replay value and the length of the single player campaign is generous.  The difficulty seems about right (a few boss battles took more than one attempt to clear, but that's fine really).  The autosave checkpoints are just frequent enough to save substantial repetition if you do die (sometimes accidentally by mis-timing a jump or due to environmental hazards).
All in all, it is a very polished product that it is a lot better than it really has a right to be (being a remake/reboot of probably one of the most iconic gaming franchise ever made).  By sticking to its roots and avoiding a lot of the pitfalls of modern games (microtransactions, day-one DLC, under-developed single player campaign etc.) it is a stronger product for it.
I don't play multiplayer so I can't comment on that aspect of it, but the single player campaign was excellent and I'd definitely recommend this to any fans of the FPS genre, or anyone that's nostalgic for the original Doom but wants something with a more modern feel to it.

Most of the action is done through your Officers who are leveled up and upgraded throughout the game.  The officers captain your ships, research upgrades at various rooms you build unto the station, and go on away missions.
Combat is similar to Final Fantasy and other Eastern RPGs, which works surprising well in a game of a much different nature.
Along the way, you meet various alien and pirate factions and have the opporunity to befriend some and make enemies of others, depending on your actions.  The aliens are dripping with personality and remind me of the acclaimed aliens from the Star Control series more than anything else.
All in all this a fun, different game full of personality and originality.  HIghly recommended.

Anyone who owned a copy of 'Dear Esther' when the Landmark Edition came out last month had a free copy of the Landmark Edition added to their library (So owners of the original have both the 'original' and 'Dear Esther: Landmark Edition' versions in their libraries).
Dear Esther will be one of those games that you either really like, or think it's really boring. I belong to the first group. I personally love the music in this game, and have the whole soundtrack added to my Spotify playlist. The graphics in the Landmark Edition are amazing for being a $10 indie game.
The game is considered a "walking simulator", similar to the games 'Proteus' and 'Eidolon'. You explore a 'Hebridean Island', and during the exploration, the 'narrator' - who I at first thought was voiced by Bill Nighy (the guy from "Underworld", "Pirates of the Caribbean", and "Shaun of the Dead"), and at times seems like he's delusional and rambling nonsense - discusses his life story.
Where you come in is how you interpret the story he's telling. How many people are a part of the story he's telling? 2? 4? Was he one of the victims of the accident, or the one who caused it? And what significance does the number 21 have? These are questions you'll (hopefully) find the answers to as you explore the island.

The Landmark Edition changes very little in terms of graphics/audio (although the audio is remastered) but adds a Director's Commentary function that lets you delve into the minds of the writer, game designer/artist and composer. There are 59 commentary nodes covering inspiration behind the game, difficult design decisions etc. This edition also includes fun achievements like falling off a cliff, drowning yourself or walking 5000 steps. I must confess I didn't understand the precise meaning of half of the narration but like the developers explain in the commentary, the game is poetic, focuses on emotions and deliberately befuddles the player, so it's no shame if you don't get it all because this game is designed specifically that way. And from what I've heard, even the developers still find new interpretations of the symbolism every now and then. So wander and wonder on.

Mechwarrior has been a fantastic series of games, but in the past, the multiplayer options never even began to capture the feel of the old pen and paper.  It was always a race to the top.  Run the biggest mech or die!
MWO has fixed that.  This is a tactics game.  This is a game where how you play your role is REWARDING.  This is a game where two large teams enter, but every player counts.
And this game rewards you for finding your favorite balance of speed, armor, firepower, and battle field enduance (heat and quantity of ammo).
This is a game about trading blows, taking risks, and defining the envelope.
And the best thing about this game, is it truly is free to play.  The light mechs are cheap, but POWERFUL in skilled hands.  The medium mechs are affordable and are the standard battlefield units.  The expensive assault, though expansive, may have a role to play, and are worth every penny, but they do NOT own the battlefield.
And every patch rewards people who play their role more and more.

Long do 4x space TBS fans await for a true worthy successor of Master of Orion I & 2, and like few decent iterations that spawned over the last 15 years, Endless Space can be .....  ' close to Orion, but not quite '...
For an indie production value however, this game shows remarkable efforts put to the overall artistic eye candy, for probably the best looking game of the genre at its release. Micromanagement exhibits several similarities with MoO and various clones, decent throughout but space combat remains shallow despite what the developers wanted to bring with their card system ( long/medium/short range ). Ship design could have been more flexible, few customisable options buried within an unintuitive user interface. Though the AI performs surprisingly well at a strategic level, signs of coding flaws at some tactical level like invasion or ship upgrades offset ( a bit ) an otherwise challenging game even for experienced players. It may be intentional or not, yet the game has a plethora of hidden features and buried formulae that even a ' galactic pedia' from AAA games couldn't cover entirely.
Pros: artistic direction; galactic settings; strategic planning; rightly paced micromanagemnt; some specific factions coerce the player to rethink whole new strategy and ways to expand ( namely Harmony, Cravers ); soothing audio track.
Mixed bag: AI ( like the vast majority of strategy games anyway ).
Cons: generic combat system; user interface ( many fonts too small also ); ship design needs more work; too many ways to win FOR the few ones that really matter for both AI and player; lack of some value to colonizing & terraforming ( untapped potential here ).
Bottom line: recommended to hardcore fans of the genre.

This is by far the best Storm game in my opinion. Naturally, it would make it better if developers could listen to fans and bring back such features as 4th combo, jutsu clashes, wall running, Storm 1 free roam, etc.. However, they're known for doing it in their own way..
● Storyline picks up from where Storm 3 left off and covers everything what's left. It's amazing as always: beautiful visuals, stunning boss battles.
● Biggest roster yet (over a hundred) with the ability to choose between several jutsu for your character. Some old characters got rebalanced or slightly changed.
● Leader switch system. It changed the game drastically. The transition is very smooth, fluid and accessible almost anytime.
● Rounds (best of 3). Matches are longer, therefore,  you gain a chance to analyze your opponent and perform huge comebacks in the rounds to come.
● Elemental effects: ability to set players on fire with jutsus and explosive tags, bigger water and lightning attacks on water.
● Charged chakra dash.
● Reworked counter which helps to balance the game out.
● Upgraded visuals (more sparkles, particles), some objects and buildings can be destroyed on stage.
● Faster loading screens. (almost instant)
● Better online experience: smoother battles, fixed ranked system, matching voices, character usage top.
● Better in-game settings regarding visual effects and resolutions.
+- Now in 60 fps, however, substitution bars are regenerating 2x times faster making it impossible to punish players who waste their subs mindlessly. Furthermore, 60 frames slowed down jutsu and customization selection.
● Ugh.. Adventure mode. Boring and unnecessary like in previous games.
● Frame drops during certain moves.
● A few stages have been removed.
● Character accessories are gone.
● Frequent disconnections while in the middle of the match.
● Lack of important characters and updates to old ones.
● Still images taken from the anime (with added effects like water splash or camera shake) during the first half of the storyline. All the other cutscenes are pre-rendered. Thus, their quality is pretty low.
● Bingo book and friends' leaderboard freezes or crashes the game.
● No microphone mute option (even for your opponents that play while their mom yells at them in Russian)
● Multiple exploits, bugs, lack of balance.

World of Guns: Gun Disassembly is a free gun puzzle game. It lets you disassemble and assemble firearms. Moreover, you can also see how a gun works and, albeit in a few cases only, visit a shooting range and put your aiming skills to test.
The gameplay is centred around, you guessed it, assembling and disassembling weaponry. It relies mostly on memorising which parts to move and when to do that. You can move single parts and the whole assemblies. The downside associated with it is that the moveable parts vary from weapon to weapon and it is very easy to make mistakes when disassembling/assembling. Who said that gun assembly was easy?
Apart from the clue of the game, you can also examine how a firearm works. There are some features which come in handy, including x-ray vision and slow-motion. During the "Operation", you perform many actions with the gun, such as fire, reload, attaching accessories (flashlights, scopes, etc.), changing the fire mode, and so on.
The weaponry ranges from historical (Winchester 1887) to modern-day rifles (TAR-21) and everything in-between. There are well-over 100 guns, including pistols, machine guns, and even artillery. To access them, however, you have to earn it the hard way. You start with the AK-47 and unlock other weapons by spending either experience points or credits. The former are earned by completing the weapon tasks (field strip, disassembly, assembly, operation, normal game, super game, and hardcore game) and completing quizzes (one quiz per hour). The latter are either bought or earned by topping the scoreboard in normal, super, or hardcore games (one credit per weapon). Getting all the guns requires a lot of grinding, but that is to be expected from a free game.
To sum up, I recommend this game not only to firearm fans but also to people playing casually. Despite being an unforgiving and sometimes frustrating game, it is still tons of fun to play and discover. Furthermore, it can be ran on pretty much any PC. Beware though: a wise man once said that this game should not be played at an airport. Mark his words, for you might miss your flight!

Dear Esther is the title that defined the Walking Simulator genre. This Landmark Edition is the remake of the original commercial release that came out in 2012 (which was initially a Half-Life 2 mod). It's now based on the Unity engine instead of Valve's Source and therefore looks really great (although the original still doesn't look bad in my opinion). Developer's commentary from creaters Jessica Curry, Rob Briscoe and Dan Pinchbeck has been added and the amazing audio has been remastered as well.
It's not everyone's cup of tea, but if you haven't played it before you should definitely check it out. It's short (1 to 1.5 hours), but it's a game that leaves an impression for a much longer time.
+ Artistically impressive
+ Amazing soundtrack
+ Developer's commentary
+ Genre-defining
- Limited gameplay
- Very short (1-1.5 hours)
Score: 85

Looking back at my review written about the first edition of this game makes me perplexed. Perplexed as to how unappreciative I was regarding the game and, naturally, its genre. This was back in 2014 and playing a walking sim at that time was a lot different.
You investigate an island in this game where our protagonist can only walk. The creators deliberately removed the option of running - I remember this being one of the major issues reported by players especially regarding their later product (Everybody's Gone to the Rapture). This is, however, not an actual problem as only by walking can you appreciate the surrounding area and notice how varied the game's soundtrack is.
This so-called landmark edition includes achievements and a developer's commentary option that is similar to the one we've already seen in Half Life 2. Text bubbles can be interacted with so that the creators can not only tell us the background of the making of the game but also what their opinion is about a particular area. It is my understanding that this is a redone version of the original edition - regardless, this is just as good looking and while it is not on par with the current generation of AAA games Dear Esther is still a visually stunning video game.
It lets you ponder at the end only for you to start your journey of walking once more and, eventually, meditate further on the events that transpire. The real question is: What exactly did transpire? I think this game is on par with the Vanishing of Ethan Carter and Leviathan and is a must when it comes to the world of walking sims.

Dear Esther is far removed from what the standard 'gamer' would understand as a game. This isn't a first person shooter, action adventure or any other simple genre. This game is better understood as an interactive story with elements of game play. Having removed all but the movement and sight controls, Dear Esther removes the aspect of the 'interaction hunt' that many modern games use. Dear Esther has areas with featured dialog that a player can visit, so that allows you to focus on exploration. Players are invited to explore beautifully detailed hills,caves, beaches and open grass lands. The sound design helps reinforce what the player is seeing, for example, the cave environments feature soft dripping sounds and running water in the distance. Grasslands and hills have a sparse, windblown feel and sound. Dear Esther's main draw is the spoken narrative, softly spoken lines from a dairy of a forlorn lover. While piecing together the story and diaries from the narrator,  delivered through wonderful voice over work, the player has to interpret what is happening around them on the seemingly deserted island.
During your play through, you wont be directed through the landscape with glowing arrows or objective markers as we are now so used to seeing. Your direction is earned from listening to the narration and the masterful level design. Soft lights, like that of a candle or the large pulsing light a top an aerial sitting on a mountain, offer distant markers for exploration. Water will also, at times, help guide you when you feel lost with its flow having opened paths and small accesses. Open landscapes often drive the player forward with the use of points of interest in the distance. The narration will also offer insight as to where you might want to explore.
To explore the mind of someone else, and to experience their life, is a hard thing to master when it comes to video games. However, the makers of Dear Esther have accomplished this, as you are invited into the dairies of a man that has lost a loved one. You experience how this loss has affected him, you will question whether this lose has effected his mind as you see ghostly figures and shapes hiding around the island. Hallucinations of the event that has lead the narrator to his island will haunt you as you explore the landscape. You are left to make sense of the story as you explore the mysterious island and venture deeper into the narrators dairies. All over the island, you will find items scattered in almost ritualistic graves or shrines. For an added experience, each item will change depending on the play through. What I saw and took away from what was shown to me may be different for you. This doesn't completely change the story, but offers different insights into what has happened to the narrator and to the island.
