Don't judge a book by it's cover.
When I first saw this, I thought it was going to be one of those games. How wrong I was. It's a beautiful blast of sprites, waves of bullets, and what-the-heck-are-you-wearing.
First things first. The gameplay  could be summed up like this: 'Imagine if Cave Story and Touhou got spliced together by some mad scientist.' Because that's Rabi-Ribi for you. It combines brilliant platforming with relentless bullet-hell patterns in a way that I really haven't seen before. The last time someone made a game this ingeniously unique was, as much as I fear to say the name, Undertale. It takes two completely different genres and smashes them together into something completely new. And it works like a freaking charm.
The graphics next. (hoo boy.) The sprites are brilliantly made and fit the game perfectly. Joining this is some interesting art that, while initially a bit pervy, mocks this aspect at every opportunity, with people saying that main-lead bunny should reallyu wear more and sidekick Ribbon telling gawking nerds to sod off, saying that this isn't some kind of R-rated game. Yes, this game gets a bit meta at times and I love it for that very reason, but I digress.
The music is downright incredible. Harking to its Touhou genes, it churns out masterpieces at every turn. From upbeat tunes like Adventure Starts Here, to the sombre Floating Graveyard, to the relaxing Unfamiliar Place,  to every one of its battle themes (go play the game, don't spoil yourself. It's infinitely more epic when you don't know what's coming.) every note is beautiful, and always sets the perfect atmosphere for what it's used for.
In all, this is easily one of the best, most beautiful, most fun games I've played in a long while. I would definitely recommend that you go play this already.
Oh, yeah, its utterly brutal when you're playing on any mode other than casual. Just thought I'd point that out before you snap a keyboard or two.

Overall having a lot of fun with this one.  Metroidvania formula is intact, but it's pretty tight so I don't expect any skill-based sequence breaks.  Bosses are as numerous as they are varied, which is a huge plus for me.
The only turn-off is the sheer amount of exposition - I expected a fair amount in the prologue, but it has been a drag clear into 2nd chapter.  It has not made me care about supporting characters at all, and I just mash the start button to skip - it's a real shame.  Some focus could have made the game better, but it ends up hurting it instead.

Cute girls, metroidvania with COMPLETE non-linearity (In fact there are achievements for sequence breaking, and even for beating the game with no upgrades at all, including movement ones).
Difficult bosses, or not so difficult bosses, depends on what you want from the game when choosing difficulty. The overworld is pretty big as well, but there are teleporters everywhere so it's not bad.
The writing is also witty and humorous, though sometimes it seems a bit forced to make you fight someone, but fightings the point anyway so I'll give it a pass.
As for the story, even after the post game there are still some unanswered questions. I have not yet gotten the DLC yet, and that presumably answers them. Other than that, the main story is rather simple.
All in all, a wonderful game with tons of polish that WANTS you to try to break it. And I believe the dev is still updating it, so even better!

To truly enjoy MWO:
1) Get a microphone
2) Get used to team work
3) Remember that FF is on and to not overheat because you will damage yourself and you will kill yourself.
-
Short Review: It's a good game that is very addictive, very fun and very team oriented. If you're a lone-wolf type prepare to be disappointed because this game isn't for you.  MWO uses a number of effects that you rarely see in FPS shooters and requires more thought to kill one mech than I have ever seen in any game before.
Things that I liked about the game:
+ HEAT: Mechs don't just fire lazers endlessly, you have a certain amount of HEAT before you pass the thresh-hold and just shut down. This makes firing something as unlimited as lazers tricky. HEAT is effective by the ambient temperature as well as other enviornmental quirks. What I liked about HEAT is that it balances the fire-power within mechs.
+A lot of variants: MWO has tons of variants and classes of mechs to choose from. Don't like being a big clunky and slow target? Pick a light class mech. Don't like using only lazers? Well there's different variants for different chasis. Because the variants are so easy to get and the upgrades for them are cheap this makes experimenting with the bots less costly and more fun.
+FACTIONS: This conquer and defend style of factions kept me in a very happy mood. Loads of banners to cast your loyalty to and loads of perks and rewards for siding with those factions. FACTION PLAY is the big leagues for MWO. With thousands of planets and maps to explore you will be occupied with more than just the DM style of quickplay. Not only does FACTION demand a sense of loyalty but a sense of tactical approach I have never seen in an FPS. You will find that players are actively trying to call out and use plans to thwart their enemy combatants. From defending a planet you own to attacking another to increase your factions control of the galaxy this is something that I really enjoyed!
-
What I didn't like:
-Mech Bays: Mech bays limit the amount of mechs that you can buy and add to your MECHLAB. This doesn't seem like much of a big deal but the SKILLS for certain variants of mechs require you to buy and maximum level 3 variants. You only get 4 empty mech bays at the start and you can only aquire more by either paying real money or by earning them through faction promotions. This makes it difficult to get EXPERT into mechs and limits your choice of weight class if you're interested in experting in a certain chasis.
----
That's all I feel about MWO. The content is grand and the players are fun.

Have you played Call of Duty, or Battlefield and had a great time?  Are you prone to lone wolf tactics?  Can you take down the entire enemy team on your own armed with nothing but a knife?  Then this is not the game for you.
Mechwarrior is for thinkers, not twich gamers.  Gamers who need to consider everything around them, and take decisive action.  Mistakes are very costly, losing armor, or weapons systems can break you.  You have to consider your role, and work well with a team in order to succeed.
The team at Pirhana Games has created a wonderful interpretation of the Battletech universe.  No, it's not much like the tabletop, but it's certainly no HAWKEN.  MWO is closer to a mech sim than a FPS, with localized damage, tonnage and ammo requirements, no respawning, and slow paced tactical combat.  Driving these mechs makes you feel the weight of a multi ton killing machine.  The impact of missiles and autocannon rounds is visceral and makes you seek cover when they hit.  The victories are sweet, just as the defeats can be crushing, but always satisfying and fun.  If you like World of Tanks, you'll like MWO.  If you like COD, go play HAWKEN or Titanfall for some sweet mech action.

Let me start off by saying that I don't write reviews.
MechWarrior Online, though, I am writing one for.
I really, really love this game. It really allows you to cater to nearly every playstyle with a high level of customization (with the right mech chassis, of course, which will likely be your hardest choice).
The game is NOT pay to win, you can only pay for cosmetic items and shortcut items so you don't have to grind so hard. However, I find buying it discouraging to buy anything in the store, because the price points are much higher than the majority of other games I've played involving in-game transactions. For example, a premium assault mech (heaviest and hardest-hitting class) Stalker Misery (top of my wishlist) is roughly $40 - for ONE mech. You don't find many people in this game who just throw that kind of money at one item just to win. Even then, it's more skill and team-based than anything, and those who do pay for primo features are often targeted and taken down first.
Big thumbs up to the devs, this game is a breath of fresh air in every way. Keep doing what you're doing.

It really does give this game that extra edge, the core gameplay itself is perfectly enjoyable of course, but this title is a good example of the paradigm that attention to detail is what can turn a solid title into an excellent one.
For those that missed out on it in the early 2000s - get it. It's a landmark title, defined a good few concepts and mechanics that were used by later RTS & City-building sim titles, and the latest HD version brings full support for modern OSs and widescreen resolutions.

Again, you're never too old for Lego. This is a fantastic game.
This game is all about building. Minecraft can hardly touch this. Why? Minecraft is limited to the simple one size blocks. Blockland however is like LEGO. There are plates, rounds, poles and much more. Building in this game gives your a lot of freedom.
Besides the building of the house, you are able to use the wrench to make "events". Think of light switches, automatic garage doors and much more. It's a bit like redstone in Minecraft or wire in Garry's Mod. It is not as advanced as GMOD's Wire, but you're still able to do a hell lot of fun stuff with it. Fantastic to make the perfect haunted house!
There's items and vehicles; check out all the add-ons too. There's lots of them. If you've always wanted a LEGO Delorian; they're out there.
The game is however quite dated. The menus feel and are old. The controls are hard to get used to. There's nothing wrong with the graphics though; it's LEGO. The worst part of the game must be the physics. They are implemented, but the collisions between vehicles are as unreal as Kim Kardashian's behind. The multiplayer is good fun; it's sad there are few good dedicated servers out there. This game could and should have a reboot in community; it still has so much potential.
Verdict; if you love(d) Minecraft, but you'd like some more advanced building options such as in Garry's Mod, this is your game. It's worth the price without a doubt; I bought it myself in the Steam Summer Sale for just 2 euros.

Picked this up on a whim and thought it would be a gimmick or uninteresting, especially being free.  I was wrong.
The developers put a lot of work into this game.  The models in-game are based on real world models.  Every part is labeled with it's correct name, down to the smallest pins, rollers and springs.  If you are detail oriented, mechanically-minded, or simply curious, this will be up your alley!
Whether you are a firearm enthusiast or simply wondered how firearms function, check this "game" out.  I don't even consider this to be a game, but more of a fun educational tool with games on the side.
There are "pay" aspects, but only if you want to progress faster or move onto a subject other than guns, such as military vehicles, race cars, even skeletons, etc.  As for progression within the "gun" world, it's free.
The game consists of assembly, dis assembly, function, games (including a firing range) and even painting the firearms.  You can try to disassemble then reassemble as fast as you can, without "hasty" clicks, and without errors for extra points.  It's very challenging (and I'm adept at this using actual firearms).
The X-ray feature allows the player to see inside a firearm, even while firing, reloading, safety on-off, etc.  This is what I liked the most about it.
In the real world, one can take apart an actual gun, learn the names of the parts, and understand the basic functions; but to see the pieces in action (while inside the gun) gives us a better understanding of how all the parts work together.
The models are pretty good looking too.  They aren't super high res, but they aren't low-res either.
My only two complaints with this game:
- The way one moves around the gun/parts to get a different angle is awkward, sometimes frustrating, but it's not game-breaking bad...not by any means; just an annoyance at times.
- Some areas of the breakdown and assembly are draconian when it shouldn't be.  For example:  the AK-47, one does not have to remove the accessories pouch from the rifle-butt BEFORE removing the rifle-butt (in real life).  The game penalizes the player if the pouch isn't removed first though.
This problem is more of a developer's attitude of "You have to follow MY procedure, even if it's not necessary in the real world".  This is not game-breaking either, but VERY frustrating when trying to go from start to finish with zero errors.
Overall, I would recommend this game, 100%.

Dear Esther: Landmark Edition
Dear Esther: Landmark Edition is a remaster of an older version, titled more simply as: Dear Esther. Because I have not played the original version of the game, and as such cannot compare the two, I will not be covering the differences between them, and I'll be reviewing Dear Esther: Landmark Edition, as if there were no previous release.
Dear Esther: Landmark Edition, is a First-Person Exploration / Narrative experience. Do not play this game expecting any particular type of gameplay: While you technically 'play' the game, it's clearly not supposed to compete in a similar way to games that don the genre 'RPG,' or 'FPS.'
The narrative and scenery is beautifully designed, if not great graphics-wise. If you're patient and willing to give the game the time it needs to deliver the experience to you, you'll find yourself listening to a reasonably voice-acted string of lines, that play when you reach a certain place on the island. The story it tells is dark, and vague at times, but still at the very least interesting to listen to. (I personally enjoyed the story this game told.)
Unfortunately, with good comes the bad, and there's plenty in Dear Esther: Landmark Edition. Firstly, while you may not realize this immediately, the game forces you into a linear pathway, allowing practically no exploration of the island you're on. This is done in a few ways: Not granting a 'jump' button to the player (this one can be particularly annoying at times, but is not a game-killer,) and, particularly immersion-breaking, the infamous invisible wall. Invisible walls line the path you take at all times, and often disallow backtracking of any kind. Later in the game, backtracking is shown to be clearly logically impossible, but is inexcusable earlier in the game. At times, it can feel like you're fighting with the controls to get where you want to go; inevitably leading to the game forcing you down the route it wants you to take. I can't help but think that there was a better way to present a funneled experience; perhaps giving visual cues to the player, to imply that the player should go to that spot? Making the rest of the landscape unremarkable, and adding a particular structure to draw the player's eye? At times, the experience does this, and at times, it does it very well - I found myself completing the entire experience in about an hour. At times, it fails to do this well, and you're left with an utterly immersion-killing segment of the experience.
In conclusion, this game has a great experience, IF you're patient enough to travel slowly through it, and if you're patient enough with the design of the game, to excuse its immersion-breaking walls. The game has no discernable type of 'gameplay', and should truly don the proposed title, 'interactive experience' over 'game.'
I recommend this game for the people who are interested in dark narrative, and who are patient enough to travel slowly through the story. People who play games largely for gameplay and who enjoy narrative as a bonus, or perhaps not at all, I highly advise against playing this game.

The notion whether Dear Esther is a game or not has been under debate since its release. Many people see this game as just a walking simulator without any gameplay, however, having played through it myself, it doesn't appear to be the case. This game like many others, tells a story, however where it differs is that while the majority of other games tell the story through some form of gameplay, Dear Esther tells it through exploration. As you explore the beautifully designed environments, progressing through the game, you build the story from the narrative, where the environment is used to reinforce those ideas.
I have has my hands on the original Dear Esther for years, where it had stayed on the tail-end of my backlog of games. Seeing the Dear Esther: Landmark Edition pop-up in my library piqued my interest. I had no idea what the game was about before I played it, the only thing that I heard was that it was short. So one evening, I decided to sit down and play though it one sitting. A certainly wasn't disappointed. Although this is a short game, it definitely tells a powerful story. Playing through a second time to listen to the director's commentary was also thoroughly enjoyable, and it was very interesting to hear how the game was designed to reinforce the story.

The last Naruto game from the Storm series! Feels great and sad at the same time. I'll try to be as honest as possible in my review.
- Premise: Its a arcady fighting game duh! In spite of all the "new features" they added, it feels largely the same as previous reiterations of the series. Which ISN'T a bad thing per se. Some people enjoy this 3D oriented fighting style, some don't. It's not the deepest fighting game. You won't find the complexity of say Mortal Kombat or Tekken, but it IS a visually appealing game that won't fail to surprise you. With the fact that now you can switch up your support characters as you main characters, essentially you get to play as 3 characters every match!
- Story/Singleplayer: Ah, the meat of the game, well atleast for me. This marks the FINAL game of the Naruto Shippuden manga. That's right all the way up to **SPOILERS**  .... Naruto vs Sasuke heh :) Seriously though, the cutscenes, the visual set-pieces....if you have decent graphics, it'll blow your mind. The action is vibrant. Every wanted to know how it felt to be Hashirama riding on your Turtle/Tree/Dragon thingamajig all the while throwing Kamehameha waves that render the earth as it flies off towards Madara and his Susan'o? No? Well I did and I got it in this game.
Basically if you loved the story-telling aspects of the previous Storm games, then think of this as that times 10! No really, the single player itself is worth the price you pay for this game (which I'll get to later)
- Graphics: I'm not a huge sucker for graphics in an anime-based game, still I was blown away by how good it looked and played. No complaints there.
- Sound: Eargasm
- Online: Ugh, here we come to the part of the review where I get to butcher this game's reputation, don't worry I won't be too harsh.......STAY AWAY! Now I don't speak for everyone. If you got this thing to run and play fine online, and you're having a blast playing, then all the power to you my friend :)
BUT...if you're me or any number of people I've met you for the love of all things sane couldn't bear the lag, then hop on board. I don't know what it is. Netcode? Connection issues? I can run all games and play them online but not this. It either times out while searching for a match or disconnects in the middle of one. Ugh. Bad, Very bad.
- DLC content: Meh. It's good if you're a completionist. I rarely, if at all, use all and every item from DLC purchases. That and the fact that these DLCs are basically reskins of characters....no thanks. As for the additional story modes, I'm not really interested in knowing about the great and might Shikamaru haha. I'll just wait until a couple of mods drop :)
- Price: This was an issue for me. Being in Canada, I would NOT want to pay $69.99 for this title. Yes the game is awesome but lets also not forget that these games REALLY haven't changed much in the 3-4 years that the series has been running. Get it on sale.
VERDICT: If you liked the previous titles, this one if a must-have. If you're a single player junky like me then this is a love letter to you. Why kill yourself by watching filler anime episodes when you can just kill your wallet and watch all the awesome parts in full HD?! Boasting the largest roster of characters too. There is no reason NOT to have this title. Plus this being the last game in the series, only time will tell what "new" game CC2 will have in store.
BTW I own this on PS4 as well, so I didn't really put a lot of time into the PC version, but as you can see, I loved it enough to get it a second time. I'm horrible with my money. Bye,

MWO is simply a great game that has improved tremendously over the years.  I've been playing MWO since its closed beta, and it has always had great combat and customization.  In the beginning there were a very limited amount of mechs to play, but over the last few years they have increased it to the point where there is a huge selection of mechs available for every role and tonnage.  If you have ever wanted to play a game where you controlled a walking tank with huge firepower in PvP, this is your game.  Regardless of your play style, whether it be fast twitch or slow tanky, this game has you covered.
A few small tips for new players:
1. Use the new tutorial!  Seriously, this game has a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of buttons and complexity.  HIGHLY recommended!  PGI has outdone themselves making it as well.
2. If you ignored No. 1, use R to spot targets for your team.  If the triangle is full, you are sharing that info with your team.  Hollow triangles mean nobody has them locked!
3. TORSO TWIST.  Seriously, try to spread the damage you are taking as much as possible.  Not only does it keep you alive, but it also stops you from having parts of your mech blown off.
4. If playing a light mech, NEVER STOP MOVING.  The only exception is if you are behind an enemy mech lining up a shot and NOBODY knows you are there.  Seriously, your armor is made of paper, so speed is your only defense.  That being said, light mechs are still ridiculously good.
5. For the first 25 games you play or so, you will earn a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of cbills.  I highly suggest that you try to figure out what your play style is with the trial mechs before you buy anything.  As far as your first purchase, I personally feel that the clan "omni-mechs" are the best investment.  You can outfit a single omni-mech for pretty much any type of weapon mix because you can change their weapon hardpoints by swapping torso pieces.   I  suggest the Arctic Chetah, Stormcrow, Timberwolf, or Dire Wolf as a beginner omni-mech for those respective classes.  For non-omni mechs I suggest the Jenner / Raven, Hunchback / Crab, Grasshopper / Cataphract, or King Crab / Atlas.
Keep up the great work PGI,

Oh Mechwarrior Online... What can I say, I've had a love hate relationship with this game for quite sometime. Playing as far back as open beta, this game never lived up to what Mechwarrior 5 could have been (at least in my opinion). However, playing on and off all these years, it slowly but surely did get a place in my heart and hopefully I can persuade you into playing this rather unique multiplayer game.
Pros:
-Giant, beautifully detailed, engines of destruction, Alex Iglesias has done a superbe job revitalising these old mech designs.
-Exillerating combat, when you engage in a so called death circle where both pilots are moving in a circle shooting at critical points until one of you is left standing
-Slow paced, now this is subjective, but to me its nice to play a slower multiplayer game when most multiplayer shooters are fast paced and twichy.
-Decent maps and design
-Customization has always been a strong point of Mechwarrior or any battletech game and MWO does not fail to deliver on that front
-Regular content influx by the devs with tons of content on the way
- Reworked old maps with time of day added
-Reworked Tutorial that goes much more indepth
-Two main factions with their own unique mechs that work differently
-A ♥♥♥♥ton of mechs to choose from, all with unique cockpits (however, it's worth mentioning that mechs have chassis and variants i.e. the Raven mech is the chassis but it had 3 variants of it which look exactly the same but have different potential loadouts, basically, even though there are a lot of mechs, some are "repeats" of the same mech)
-Private lobbies
-Good matchmaking done by rank and also by weight type i.e. the matchmaker will alwasys try to creat matches with 3 assaults, 3 heavies, 3 mediums and 3 lights
-F2P model that is pretty fair, you can't buy power, only mechs with unique skins and extra income potential.
-Servers on NA, EU and Oceanic
Cons:
-Sound assets could really use some work, Autocannons, lasers, missles don't sound pleasant
-Multiple gamemodes that all boil down to Deathmatch in a huge deathball formation (i.e. all mechs just cluster together and slug it out)
-Community Warfare (this is the one gamemode that doesn't always degenerate into deathmatch, but even then counterattacks are essentially deathmatches, it's only attack/defend where you have to option to destroy the generators and the huge orbital gun to win instead of killing everyone) that has been in beta for eons, it has tons of promise but the development for it should have started way back in open beta imho, not 1 year into the release. As it currently stands it's alright, but nothing to write home about.
-Killing a mech isn't satisfiying, no huge explosion sounds or a fireball exploding from the cockpit as the pilot ejects, just a puff of black smoke with the mech slowly falling down to the ground, ragdoll style, the explosion sounding more like a television frying out, not particularly impressive
-Mech immersion isn't the greatest, you can run over trees on certain maps, but buildings, vehicles and terrain are all indestructable
-The leveling up of mechs isn't really the best as it is very time consuming (ofc it's probably due to it being F2P), basically you have to buy 3 variants of the same mech(which is long in it of itself) and unlock basic skills, etlie skills and master skills for each of the 3 mech variants. However, it is worth mentioning that the skills themselves aren't game breaking, they make your mech handle better and move slightly faster than it otherwise would.
-Preordering mechs is an alright way for PGI to make money, but the in-game rewards you get for prepurchase generally aren't worth the price they ask for.
-Speaking of prices, the price for buying mechs with irl cash is pretty crazy going anywhere from 20-100+$ granted those 100+$ ones usually come with multiple mechs, but still, one mech costing 20$ is pretty expensive.
In the end MWO is one of those games you have to try for yourself, it's F2P so there's not much to lose, and all things considered, it's a pretty good one at that.

Addictive. REALLY addictive.
To compare this to any kind of tank battle game is somewhat an injustice. I mean, tanks are tanks, and these mechs are 100 tons of ♥♥♥♥ YOU. This game requires several times more thinking power than any other FPS I've played.
Excellent team communication, strategy and execution are all part of the formula that makes a match a victory.
You can easily spend HOURS tinkering with the settings to optimize your mech, and there's SO MANY mechs to play with.
With such a vast variety of weapons and ways to set up your mech, there is a plethura of tactics and playstyles to learn and utilize (i.e. Light and fast to flank the enemy team, and sunder their defenses while your team rolls over them like the extremely overweight freight-trains-on-legs that they are, or Heavy and kitted with the firepower to tear asunder any unfortunate soul to turn the corner to greet you).
Oh, good lord.. the combat. While sometimes it can be frustrating, it's quite apparent that PGI has worked to balance everything carefully so that each mech, each weapon and each player has its place on the battlefield. And, you have to be careful how you go about things. Being careless could give the enemy team the opportunity to destroy one of your components. When I started, I carelessly peeked around a corner and moved out into the open without looking around. Within a second, I had my right torso -- which held the ammo for my ballistic weapons, along with my right arm (where half of my weapons were set) -- destroyed. It's things like that which can turn the tide of battle, when a mech has its firepower crippled or completely neutralized.
While I'm sure there are some negative aspects to the game, I simply cannot see them from my perspective. Keep in mind, I wasn't around pre steam release, but since I picked it up less than a week ago, I've already logged 43 hours (since the time of this post) of constant gameplay. If a game is good enough that my family will probably need to schedule an intervention to make me stop, then I'm not sure what else needs to be said.

I am a new player of this game in the past week and have already sunk about 60 hours into it. I'm enjoying every minute. I'm going to present some PROS and CONS that I've encountered in my first almost-week of playing, as well as some TIPS for enjoying yourself if you decide to give this game a try.
PROS:
-Tactical shooter/mech simulation with a surprisingly high "realism" factor which enhances gameplay; Is someone killing you with the lasers on their right arm? Simple: shoot their right arm off! Are you overheating? Simple: run in the water so the heatsinks you put in your mech's legs can be more efficient.
-Community seems mostly friendly toward newbies. In team-versus-team games, rage and salt are usually everywhere. Especially when you are new and don't know how to play. I've had some mixed experiences, but for the most part the veterans seem willing to help the newbies learn the mechanics.
-Different "weight classes" and varieties of mechs provide different playstyles. Want to dart in and out of enemy lines, drawing fire away from your allies? Play a Light mech. Want to lead a push and pack lots of firepower? Play an Assault mech.
-Customization system for "bought" (in-game currency or premium currency) mechs adds to replayability, and allows a single mech to be played many different ways.
-It is truly Free-to-Play. There are some mechs which you can only buy with premium currency, however the benefits they provide are being able to grind faster and having different weapon slots. Both of these are things F2P players can thrive without. I will provide a DISCLAIMER and say that Mech Bays (ability to buy and store more mechs), while something F2P players can absolutely live without, will be very very tempting to buy. You can buy and store 4 mechs (enough for Faction Play) without buying any additional Mech Bays.
CONS
-Steep learning curve, especially for FPS newbies.
-It is a team-versus-team game. There are always going to be toxic people who will tell you "ur bad, git good, ur a♥♥♥♥♥ go back to the kitchen where u belong," etc. etc.
-It's a Grind. Depending on what you want to do with your mechs, you might end up spending a lot of time grinding in-game currency and XP to upgrade them. This may or may not be a CON for you.
-Mech Bays, while not necessary to play the game and not giving any gameplay benefits to players who own them, will be tempting to buy. (With premium currency.) They allow you to buy and store extra mechs, so if you get addicted to this game like I am and want ALL THE MECHS... you are going to have to buy some with premium currency.
TIPS:
-If at all possible, use VOIP! Your team will love you for it. You won't be expected to lead the team as a newbie; calling out enemy locations (using the
to make sure you're understood) when they are first spotted and when a Light is skittering around the back line will earn you brownie points, and maybe help you win.
-Don't spend your in-game currency right away. Most people recommend waiting until your Cadet Bonus (first 25 games) has expired until you buy your first custom mech from the Store; that way you can get an idea of what does what. Of course, if you see something out in the field and say "I want THAT one!," I wouldn't stop you.
-Don't be intimidated by the tutorials! Your best tutorial is out in the field--in other words, your first few Quick Play matches getting exploded. You will get oriented, but not without dying horribly. Ask for advice on team chat (Y) or VOIP (CAPS Lock) if you need to.
-Make friends with other newbies. You're most likely to get matched with your peers, so if someone friendly is on VOIP or team chat, don't be afraid to reach out. (Heck, make friends with veterans!)
Give this game a try if you think it looks like your thing. Be patient with yourself if the mechanics are giving you trouble. Enjoy yourself.

When first seeing the product and seeing what it was possible of doing with the two pads I thought to myself "yeah, but it won't work like that at all". I was very cynical and my thinking was "if it aint broke, don't fix it". I used an xbox 360 controller before buying a steam controller which i love, It's got a great weight to it. It's a nice size, the buttons feel sturdy and it's hard to accidentally hit a command, having said this about the 360 controller, the steam controller is better and should now be considered the standard with consoles.
It was a hard transition to go from 360 Controller to steam controller because of the different layout, but once you get past that you realise how much of a beast the controller is and how useful it is for gaming and gamers. The control scheme is COMPLETELY customisable, to the point where I can even control how the input on the pad is registered in game which is something that I can't do with my 360 controller or even on the native console its from.
Lets get into buttons; so the SC (Steam Controller - Tired of writing Steam Controller already) has 22 Buttons. 2 triggers, 2 shoulder pads, 2 center buttons in each pad, 4 buttons as a D pad in one pad, ABXY buttons, Back and Start, an analogue stick button and a steam button. which adds up to 18 buttons. I only mention these because they are the standard. The SC adds 4 more, in each trigger there is a separate button at the end of pushing it which is pressed by applying extra pressure to the triggers. there are also 2 buttons under where you hold the controller by where you third, fourth and pinkie finger would sit. I LOVE these additions, It means I have absolute control over my triggers and I have two extra buttons which might make certain games feel better, for instance, in Batman Arkham Knight I can use the two back and set them as attack and counter attack, It means I still have a thumb free to look around the room and am able to press the shoulder or trigger buttons whilst I look around.
Not only is this an amazing piece of hardware, but the software used for mapping the buttons is quite a pleasure to use. it's fast, changes the configuration the instant you change it. has so many options to change that I couldn't list them. One option i did notice however was something called "mode switching". This option means whilst this button is pressed you can set other buttons to do different actions which is also great for games such as Batman Arkham Knight because I really like the "trackpad" mode on the SC, but trackpad mode doesn't work with the hacking system because it will always revert to center, so I can set one of the back buttons or perhaps the analogue stick button to mode switch the right pad so it will work like an analogue stick for the period you are using the two pads to hack. If someone had told me a week before i bought the steam controller "hey, imagine a controller better than the xbox 360 controller" I would've had a very hard time visualising a concept, but Valve have nailed it.
Time to stop giving virtual handjobs to valve engineers and tell you the very few flaws I think this device has.
It runs on batteries. Not THAT big an issue but i'm trying to nitpick this because most controllers are wireless without batteries (I bought a battery pack for the 360, but I know there are others I can buy that don't use batteries and are wireless)
Another small issue I have is that the back buttons in a time of excitement or panic can be pressed accidentally when you squeeze the controller. Since the back buttons aren't particularly useful unless you've set them to be useful it's not that big an issue unless you've made it one.
Overall, this incredible controller should be a standard across consoles and everyone should migrate to this controller. It feels well built, engineered incredibly well that even the battery compartments feel great when putting batteries in and the software is incredible too.
If you were having doubts before, you shouldn't be now. buy it!
9.5/10 (knocked 0.5 because of the back buttons accidentally pressed, maybe i need to control myself more when playing games)

My recommendation to anyone thinking about playing the updated version of this game (as well as the original) is to go into it with the proper mindset. It is not so much a game in the traditionally understood sense of the word. Rather, “Dear Esther” is an almost entirely cerebral experience. It works on the player in much the same way a good painting will effect an observer who sees in the art not merely a window looking out on our own world, but that same world slightly altered by the surreal, and thus bringing to light things about ourselves we might not otherwise see. That said, “Dear Esther”, by it's very poetic nature, is one of the most immediately captivating games I have encountered; I do not believe it should be overlooked simply because it does not conform to the usual way in which people have come to view video games.
Overwhelming is the sense of solitude on this gloomy, desolate Hebridean island. Heavier still is the desperately sorrowful soundtrack, by Jessica Curry. In style, it is similar to film composer Christopher Young's most sparsely written music, and perhaps plays as an even more effective voice in this introspective journey than does the admittedly remarkable, potent narrator, Nigel Carrington. I often find game music lacking in its ability to plunge beneath the fabric of a game and tug to light its individual and vibrantly beating heart, but this is a rare instance where such a feat is accomplished. Haunting as any chamber music has ever been, the score to “Dear Esther” will probe the emptiness within each of us, and get us contemplating questions most prefer to ignore.
The original version of “Dear Esther” already offered up a treasure trove of stunning and beautiful visuals; the “Landmark Edition”, remade using the Unity engine, effectively enhances all of its former glory. Although the surroundings are sparse and desolate, the amazing visuals cause exploration to become somewhat compulsory. And the thorough and thoughtful gamer will be rewarded by a number of sightings (such as photographs, books, etchings and other items) which enhance the deeply psychological underpinnings of the narrative.
While the extras featured in the “Landmark Edition” add some time to this game over the original version, “Dear Esther” is still a relatively short journey, requiring the gamer to simply progress across the island until they have reached a lone radio mast. The “Landmark Edition" adds ten achievements, and a director's commentary which is absolutely fascinating to listen to—especially once you have played the game a few times and have settled on your own personal interpretation of it's story. There are no in-game decisions to be made beyond deciding whether or not to do a little extra exploration of the island, no objects to interact with (besides the four urns you can find for an achievement), and the fragmented and slightly randomized narration of the main character plays out as you progress. A fair portion of the narration is not activated along the main path of the game, so there is an added incentive to do some deeper looking around. The epistolary narrative renders the intent of the story in a vague light, like a sequence of events seen through shimmering tears. It is debatable what “Dear Esther” is actually trying to say (and according to some of the game's commentary that was a deliberate choice), but anyone willing to open themselves to the voices haunting this Scottish island are certain to draw some very strong conclusions.
To me, the story deals primarily with unspeakable loss, and how we set ourselves up for even greater heartache (potentially leading even to madness) if God is not our anchor in all things. I, for one, see the issue of personal transcendence (as it is articulated at the end of the game by the main character's leap from the radio tower, who then begins a flight of rebirth across the moon-dappled sea, followed by a black fade) to be illustrative not of our ability to achieve any kind of positive spiritual shift on our own, but exactly the opposite: There exists within fallen humanity a perpetual, aching cry to be delivered, redeemed--to transcend the shattering effects of our sinful natures.... But humanism cannot accomplish this miracle, nor any form of man-centered religion focusing on personal moral performance or upon the sincerity of their emotions as they are connected to a certain belief system. The blood of the Lord Jesus Christ is the only atonement by which we can be saved from all this death. He is the only peace, the only Truth. The end result of all other efforts at redemption lead only to chilly shadows and vacuous spaces brimming with regret.
Hopefully sharing my personal interpretation of “Dear Esther” does not come across as a clumsy effort to proselytize (if that were the case, I would certainly have given the Gospel in its fullness), but rather illustrates the power and versatility the player can expect to experience by such an unconventional game as this.
For anyone looking to plunge beneath the surface within themselves as they embark upon the solitary journey to the radio tower, “Dear Esther” offers surprising treasures that periodically flash their brilliance even years after the experience has ended. And here, years after it's initial release in 2014, it proves to continue to do just that.

The Landmark Edition is a full remake of the original Source game, rebuilt in Unity. The journey of a poetically delirious man through a desolate island remains intact, but the feeling left behind by each edition has altered with its assets. The terrain is of course more detailed, but it is also darker, richer, and smoother in this new edition. The original was full of sharper angles and was brighter - and lonelier because of it.
The sound design has shifted entirely. The mixing of the musical tracks and the narrative is indisputably better, and the narration has stayed mostly the same, but the musical choices are so different they seem to be from different games. Gone are the strange, unexplained hints of radio or whispers hidden under the incidental themes. Those themes have now become - like the island - deeper and richer as well as twisted, taking into themselves the strangeness of those previous hints.
The Landmark Edition also includes developer commentary and achievements. The commentary provides insights into the founding of the 'walking simulator' genre and pulls back the curtain on the development of the game, for good or ill. The achievements add a valuable means of tracking how much of what the game has to offer you've discovered and little else of worth.
Dear Esther's Landmark Edition both shares enough in common with and has changed enough to warrant a playthrough if you happen to discover this game suddenly in your library due purchasing the original before February. And, if choosing between the two editions available on Steam at the moment, this new edition - with its updates and additions - likely presents the better option.

Best shooter in recent memory. Has the chaotic Doom feel and tons of little in-game extras to make you smile in between demonic genocide runs. The visuals are stunning, and overall the game is just FUN to play. There are plenty of difficulty settings for everyone, and the multiplayer mode holds it's own as well. I spent most of my time with this game on the campaign, which was very Doom-like, plus a little extra. Lots of hidden features, in-game-minigames and throwbacks to the original series.
The only problem I had with this is that the arena-based combat format was predictable and a bit repetitive, and the game is super-linear (which works well for this format). Once you realize that you're going from one circular arena to the other, and the only thing which changes is the scenery and the number/level of monsters spawned, the game can feel a bit repetitive, although each arena does present a unique challenge, so you can't just use the same tactics from arena to arena and expect to survive. Additionally, there isn't a lot of randomization in the game, monster spawns are almost always pre-determined and don't change much between replays. This is good for speed-runners and OCD Steve Wiebe type completionists, bad for providing a feeling of a unique experience between playthroughs.
Overall I highly recommend this game, it's just FUN to play!

As I've been playing through Rabi-Ribi I've wondered why, despite having been out for a while and the Overwhelmingly Positive Steam rating, none of the major review sites have ever had anything to say about it. I can only assume that they've eyeballed some of the art and instantly dismissed it as "weeb game for neckbeard pervs" or, if the Cuphead tutorial debacle's anything to go by, none of them could get far enough to pass any kind of comment at all.
Either way they're fools, because they've missed out on a real treat.
The marriage of metroidvania and bullet hell works so well that in retrospect I'm surprised it's not been done more. It's rare to see sequence-breaking and skipping as actively encouraged as it is here, with a wide variety of achievements on offer for deliberately missing what you thought were key items. Even then there's a lot to see, with 22 areas on offer it's not a small game by any means.
With such heavy danmaku roots it'd be so easy for the bosses' bullet patterns to descend into maddening walls of relentless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and it's to the designers' immense credit that not only is that never the case, but each fight is unique and memorable. That's not to say there are any gimmes; even on Normal you won't be in for an easy ride and if you're not well prepared you're going to get tonked seven ways from Sunday, but you'll rarely feel like a fight's completely beyond your ability if only you can sharpen up your concentration.
For me personally, getting value for money from my games is a massive plus point, and at £9.10 I feel like I've robbed the devs blind. Even without the POST-post-game bosses (because the game insists on continuing to throw out things for you to do!) and any of the DLC, the wealth of options that unlock after your first playthrough mean you'll always have a reason to come back. Multiple higher difficulties, a speedrun mode, a boss rush mode, and the achievements for no-damage boss fights and sequence breaks mean that although my time spent is currently 27 hours, there's going to be a damn sight more than that by the time I'm through with it.
If I had one tiny issue with the game it'd be with the character conversations. I get that if you're buying a game with bunny girls in it weird plot is going to come with the territory but my efforts at trying to make any sense out of it were consistently hampered by characters, in the middle of discussing what I assumed to be story, spiralling off into meaningless asides about day-to-day life, or their relationships with each other. Rather than give up the game or try to keep track I just decided I'd have more fun if I simply didn't bother, and that's how it proved.
Rabi-Ribi is a deeply mature game, wrapped inside a deeply childish one. If bunny girls and nonsensical plots are your bag then fair enough, but don't give it a go for those reasons. Give it a go because you almost certainly haven't played anything quite like it before; a tight, finely crafted fusion of two great genres into one superb product that ends up becoming far more than the sum of its parts.

The last Naruto game from the Storm series! Feels great and sad at the same time. I'll try to be as honest as possible in my review.
- Premise: Its a arcady fighting game duh! In spite of all the "new features" they added, it feels largely the same as previous reiterations of the series. Which ISN'T a bad thing per se. Some people enjoy this 3D oriented fighting style, some don't. It's not the deepest fighting game. You won't find the complexity of say Mortal Kombat or Tekken, but it IS a visually appealing game that won't fail to surprise you. With the fact that now you can switch up your support characters as you main characters, essentially you get to play as 3 characters every match!
- Story/Singleplayer: Ah, the meat of the game, well atleast for me. This marks the FINAL game of the Naruto Shippuden manga. That's right all the way up to **SPOILERS**  .... Naruto vs Sasuke heh :) Seriously though, the cutscenes, the visual set-pieces....if you have decent graphics, it'll blow your mind. The action is vibrant. Every wanted to know how it felt to be Hashirama riding on your Turtle/Tree/Dragon thingamajig all the while throwing Kamehameha waves that render the earth as it flies off towards Madara and his Susan'o? No? Well I did and I got it in this game.
Basically if you loved the story-telling aspects of the previous Storm games, then think of this as that times 10! No really, the single player itself is worth the price you pay for this game (which I'll get to later)
- Graphics: I'm not a huge sucker for graphics in an anime-based game, still I was blown away by how good it looked and played. No complaints there.
- Sound: Eargasm
- Online: Ugh, here we come to the part of the review where I get to butcher this game's reputation, don't worry I won't be too harsh.......STAY AWAY! Now I don't speak for everyone. If you got this thing to run and play fine online, and you're having a blast playing, then all the power to you my friend :)
BUT...if you're me or any number of people I've met you for the love of all things sane couldn't bear the lag, then hop on board. I don't know what it is. Netcode? Connection issues? I can run all games and play them online but not this. It either times out while searching for a match or disconnects in the middle of one. Ugh. Bad, Very bad.
- DLC content: Meh. It's good if you're a completionist. I rarely, if at all, use all and every item from DLC purchases. That and the fact that these DLCs are basically reskins of characters....no thanks. As for the additional story modes, I'm not really interested in knowing about the great and might Shikamaru haha. I'll just wait until a couple of mods drop :)
- Price: This was an issue for me. Being in Canada, I would NOT want to pay $69.99 for this title. Yes the game is awesome but lets also not forget that these games REALLY haven't changed much in the 3-4 years that the series has been running. Get it on sale.
VERDICT: If you liked the previous titles, this one if a must-have. If you're a single player junky like me then this is a love letter to you. Why kill yourself by watching filler anime episodes when you can just kill your wallet and watch all the awesome parts in full HD?! Boasting the largest roster of characters too. There is no reason NOT to have this title. Plus this being the last game in the series, only time will tell what "new" game CC2 will have in store.
BTW I own this on PS4 as well, so I didn't really put a lot of time into the PC version, but as you can see, I loved it enough to get it a second time. I'm horrible with my money. Bye,

I love my Steam Controller, but it wasn't always that way. When I first got one (near launch) there was a definite learning curve that was hard to get over - having one analog stick felt wrong, and emulating one with the touchpad felt unorthodox at first. The firmware for the first few updates was fairly miserable - controllers could only be configured in Big Picture Mode, lotta Steam overlay glitches, etc. Most of these issues have improved over time - firmware has been updated, and I've grown used to the controller layout, but my initial reception was certainly only slightly positive at best.
Fast forward to late May of this year. I injured my all-important left hand while moving into a new apartment, and the fracture had my pinky and ring fingers left in a cast for about a month. No more FPS, ARPG, or any other fast moving games while injured right? No way I'd be hitting WASD with a hand in a cast after all.
ENTER THE STEAM CONTROLLER --
I was able to quickly create configurations using my Steam Controller AND mouse that were adequate enough for me to continue playing FPS games and others without the usual loss of precision that accompanies controller use in kb+m settings. I was able to game with a setup where my left hand, still in-cast, would control my movement with the analog stick and back pad/triggers while I aimed and used abilities as normal with my right hand on my mouse.
That's when the sheer awesomeness of this controller really hit me. The ease of configuring a setup, and integrating it even with standard kb+m play makes video gaming more accessible for those of us who may not always have full use of our hands. Joy2Key exists for other controller setups, sure, but in all my years messing around with various controllers to try and find a set up that makes kb + m gaming really 'work' (I don't have chronic hand problems, just a lot of time on them) only the Steam Controller has really stuck around as anything more than a novelty.
There are some issues with the layout of the controller, and hopefully future iterations improve upon the flaws others have highlighted here in these reviews (perhaps a smaller version sold alongside this one, maybe another model with two analog sticks, etc.)
For starters, the bigger your hands, the better this controller will feel. It's not a situation like with the original Xbox controllers where they were just too damn big for anybody but Barry Bonds and the Jolly Green Giant, rather, the button/touchpad layout on the front is infinitely more comfortable if you have the extra length in your digits to operate the front face of the controller with thumbs only, or thumbs and index finger(s) alone. There are enough buttons in the back of the controller to make the traditional 'claw' hold a lot of controller users have adopted fairly unviable - I personally use my two thumbs, and OCCASIONALLY my left index finger on the front face of the controller and have all my other digits dedicated to triggers, shoulder buttons, and the back pads respectively. I also often rebind some of the face buttons (ABXY) to the back pad buttons just for ease of access, which I guess cuts into the number of unique bindings available on the controller at any given time.
I think your mileage may vary depending on the game genres you frequently play, as well as your willingness to adjust to a new controller style; however, if you can get over the initial 'learning curve' and really start to dive deep into the customization features, this controller truly starts to feel like the 'One Controller to Rule them All' it's supposed to be.
Valve is definitely onto something here. I have no regrets purchasing my controllers (I now own 2!) but definitely see why some may want to wait for a second iteration. If you are on the fence and aren't averse to reprogramming some of your controller muscle memory I would urge you to pick up one of the bundles Steam has going, or just get it on sale, and give this thing a go.

While it's not quite the replacement for a mouse and keyboard you might hope, it's easily the closest any controller I've used has come, and will let you play nearly any non-competitive Steam game you fancy from the comfort of your couch.
Getting set up is trivial: plug in the receiver and it just works. Firmware updates are also quick and easy: your controller powers off for a few seconds and then comes right back. The integration with Big Picture is great: you can launch it straight from the controller and when you turn your PC off the controller shuts itself down automatically.
The trackpad is excellent and is the best part of the controller. You've got a choice of haptic feedback, it's very responsive, and you can set it to work in several different modes, from mimicing a classic joystick to being a normal trackpad to simulating a trackball with weight and acceleration. If the sensitivity isn't quite what you want you can set one of the other controller buttons to act as a modifier so when you hold that button down the trackpad sensitivity completely changes (sniper mode!). The flexibility you have in setting this up should let you do whatever you want. I used this with (single-player) FPS games very successfully.
The other buttons on the controller are also quite good. Feedback is solid and the buttons feel nice. They're not quite as good as a classic XBox controller but close enough that it doesn't matter.
Many games support the Steam controller and will swap the key shortcuts you see on the screen to those on the controller instead. The integration is quite good. In addition, there are loads of public controller profiles for any game you choose to play, so you can start with a very good setup and then modify it if you need to.
The customizability is a great selling point for me. Like changing your mouse sensitivity or adjusting your keybindings, you can start with a good profile for a game that will work for most people but then dive in and adjust everything in great detail if you'd rather have more control. If you don't want to deal with this then using one of the public profiles should get you through just fine, but having the option to tweak your settings and the huge range of options available is amazing.
In short, while I wouldn't go so far as to say you could use this to the same level as a mouse and keyboard (and thus I'd shy away from using it for anything competitive), you can play pretty much anything from the comfort of your couch quickly and easily.

Before you buy the Steam Controller read some of the negative reviews.  There is one great review by a guy named “Fortyseven” that I agree with 100 per cent.  This controller is not for gamers like me.  I only bought it to try it out.  After 5 minutes of playing "Doom" I don't like it and put it away.  I will never use all the different ways to configure it so it is not for me.
Besides what “Fortyseven” states there are two big reasons I don’t like this controller.
First:  it is missing a right thumb controller stick and instead has a touch pad.  If I want to do a 180 degree turn in “Doom” I have to repeatedly slide my right thumb on the touch pad which causes erratic control unless you precisely slide it horizontally (your thumb naturally makes an arch which causes erratic control).  On a normal controller you simply hold the right thumb controller stick to the left and you spin around.
Second:  the X Y B and A buttons are too far toward the left.  I have to make a stretch to reach the X button.  This is a bad design.
One other thing to add:  Steam states:  “The Steam Controller lets you play your entire collection of Steam games on your TV……”  This implies that if you buy the controller you can now play your games on your TV.  This is not what they mean.  The only way to play your computer games on a TV screen is to use your flat screen TV as a monitor.  This has nothing to do with the Steam Controller.  This is a deceptive statement from Steam.  The controller does not in any way connect your TV to your computer.

Is this a good or a bad game? Well unfortunately it's not about the game. It's about the developing company, PGI. A case of a bad company stumbling on a good idea.
I returned to this game after a year or so to find out what had changed. The thing that matter to me have not. Let's start with the simple things. They have implemented an arrow to help new players realize where their feet were pointing to. Good idea right? Well it's working only if you 're moving on straight ground or downhill. If you 're going uphill, the arrow dives into the ground, unseen. Expect a simple bug like that to never be addressed. So let's move on to the serious stuff.
Back in closed beta, Catapult K2 came out. That variant was supposed to be able to pack 2 mgs, but ppl found out you could put 2 gauss rifles, with enough ammo. Some suggested that, like previous Mechwarrior titles, mechs should have slot sizes. The response we got was that they wanted us to be able to customize our mechs in any way we wanted. Then the Stalker came out. Ppl would install 6 Ppcs and one shot enemies. To cut a long story short, Pgi took the path of least effort giving us “ghost heat”. Firing a set amount of weapons  in the same time, gave you more heat. But they didn't stop here. They razed heat and/or cd times in weapons, making a single weapon bad. You had to boat them in order to be effective.
Then we started getting maps with hot ambient temperature, then we got “coolshot”. Originally the one purchased with real cash was the better one. An outrage by the community forced them to make the in game money versions to be upgraded, through grind.
There were long periods of time when new light mechs would be invunurable due to bad hit boxes and the, still present to a point, bad netcode. When the spider was introduced, it was always the last mech standing on the enemy team. Same with the raven and ppl call the arctic cheetah as “arctic cheater” for a reason.
And then it was time for the clans. Clanmechs are supposed to be harder shooting, have better ranges, be faster but be way hotter. The original idea for balancing them was to drop 12 inner sphere mechs vs 10 clan mechs. Again PGI was unable or unwilling to do it, so they nerfed clan weapons but not the heat. Of cource the nerf happened after ppl had bought the early access clan mechs with real cash and was time to release them for in game currency.
We now have regional servers but most of the balancing work have been done with ppl playing on the Canadian servers. That means they were trying to balance a person playing with 20 ping in Canada, with a player playing with 350 ping from Australia. And there were times that ppl could not have their hits register, mech rubberbanding all over the place from midround on. We never got a response for it and they refused to stop premium time ticking for those who asked.
So, your welcome to try this game, but think twice before giving money to them.

If the answer is yes to those F2P titles, Mechwarrior is another entry to the genre of tatical, partial-simulator FPS. Slower than your average FPS, grindy as any other, with a skill curve sure to be steep.
It is much simplier sim/combat than Arma or OF, harder than your average FPS. It is more Battlefield than COD, with the team depedancy of TF2. And even a good team can end a game in a crushing defeat.
It is slow to release actual features but mechs are frequent, and I would consider maps release acceptable. Early access to mechs cost money like the recent trend of games. Weapons are tweaked like all good F2P games despite the whinge.
The most efficient use of money is mechbays. Or if you want to spend less time grinding then premium time and mechbays. No purchase will guarrentee you victory (although may increase your odds). Time spent learning the pace of the game, learning your mech, observing when your team mates are aggressive or hesitant; these are a few points of focus in the first 10 hours of gameplay (I'm a slow learner).
It was my lifestyle game, I'd play it every day for 2 years. According to my madstats I have clocked 528 hours of in-match game time (tinkering not included). If you think it mech combat might tickle your fancy and don't mind F2P, you have nothing to lose. If you only have time for AAA games, you probably want to give it a miss.
All that being said I stopped playing a while ago as the F2P Moba-like (character release) loop was getting boring. I haven't seen anything to bring me back yet.

This game is basically a gun deconstruction and reconstruction simulator. The game works by you hovering around a 3d model of a gun and clicking on the individual bits after which an animation plays where the bit in question is either removed or put back into the gun, however you must do so in order. As a bonus you may interact with the gun by operating it including firing, reloading, activating the safety, etc. and you may do so in either an Xray mode, a slow motion mode, both at the same time, or niether. The game could a fairly decent educational aid if you have a gun and want to understand how it works and need something that will keep pace with you while you take it apart.
The problem I have with this game is something very common to "free to play" games. The game forces you to unlock new guns by following a vast web of unlocks instead of a simple search feature. The game takes the opprotunity to become a very tedious expierence. Every gun has a series of acheivements relating to it which allow you to unlock in game currency, however as you progess further down the web guns get progressively more expensive while the rewards fail to scale. The game features a "quiz" mode which allows you to earn some extra points by answering a series of questions but you may only do so once every hour and the awards are fairly petty soon in. Even then some guns are simply real-money-only deals and some of these block of the path to other guns.
This game is very good for those in it's niche auidence once you actually get to the guns but the unlock system makes this game very tedious and it feels like the developers are holding certain guns hostage from you. You may be willing to pay a dollar or two to see a Desert Eagle model or an WW2 AT gun disassembly but having to pay for a dozen other models or endure possibly weeks of grinding to get to that point simply makes this game a tainted experince.
And even with the sheer number of avaiblie models the 50 dollar asking price for full access is well below what I feel is delivered.

I bought the closed beta in October 2011, and having never played any of the original tribes I was hooked. The game was a whole different ballgame than what I've played in the last 15 years. Having come from military shooters, with the exception of some co-op and TF2, I was looking forward to the projectile game as that's all I cared for in TF2 and I never got big in to quake either back in the day.
When T:A went F2P I -- like most closed beta -- had high hopes it would be 'the next big thing' but boy we were wrong. As time went on and the game expanded you realized the developers had no idea about anything at all. Map Designers had no logic in their design, no maps made sense as to where you may find assets / repair guns / vehicle pads / inventory stations. Some maps do not even offer vehicles (not talking ones with them disabled). While it's not terribly hard to play the maps a few times and learn them you'll find yourself irritated so much with the fact there's no standardized design for maps. Suiciding will become your friend.
After you make peace with terrible map design (to be fair 20-33% aren't too bad, but all lack consistancy you'll find in every major fps) you'll come to realize that the weapons are super inbalanced. The game started off with pretty much projectiles, save the inf (no one used it) and soldier AR. As time moved on everyone got machine guns. This was a big blow to the game in term of longetivity and probably is the main reason it's died. Not only were none of the maps designed with such weapons in everyones hands (no cover to hide from the literal 1-5k bullet spam per 20 seconds) but using a [timed] health regen system on top makes regending impossible unless you camp your base (which is why all pub games are defense).
Anyone who has time logged knows autos are super easy to use, because they have no recoil, no spread. The only one which is implemented in a great way is the pathfinder lar -- because it's limited to 3 shot burst , and with a from-beta-possibly-alpha bug of dry firing you can bank on the person missing a few shots from it not actually firing.
So on top of horrible map design, and imbalanced/spam weapons not compatable with map terrain or the health system you'll find a few other things that are a bit messed up like the snipers. You'll come to find out about this game there's a few things: Hi-Rez thinks the 2% of people who pug (or "compete" if you want to call it that) are the only people who play here. if you've ever seen a 'competitive' tribes game you'll see 2 things: endless auto spam, and cappers so terrible that the best strategy is to 'punt the flag'. It's why competitve t:a never took off and the only people who play(ed) it are people who can't let go of the game.
Oh yes, back to the pug voice dictacting the game flow. So one thing you'll know if you've been around a long time is that snipers are terrible. Terribly easy to play, terribly imbalanced, and have absolutely no place in this game as it sits. They, like most things, were added because 'chasing is too hard for the autospam/flag punting 2%'. I put only a few dozen hours in to sentinel if that and I could consistantly hit the top 5 clans in the game (s1-2) @ 300-400 sanics no problem. The problem with the sniper isn't the 1-3 shot ability; it's that the class generally isn't in any danger because they camp far back. T:A was supposed to be about action, not d stacks and sent camps because no one can catch the flag guy (too logical to fix cap speeds). On top of this, you have numerous bugs still existing from beta, and many of the glitches such as rock bounces added as 'features' due to , again, the 2%. -- This was when I quit.
Now, 3 weeks ago I started playing again with a friend. Sad to say, it got worse. If you're lucky you'll find 5-10 servers with people on them, only to find 1/2 of them are level restricted to 1-10. So you fight over queueing in to 1 of 3-4 servers with the same people. All of them spamming automatics endlessly and spamming the VGS system. You'll see pubstar cappers ending games in 5-0s trying to look good but failing to realize the entire t:a population of < 500 people aren't too interested in capping a flag. Yes, I know, it's CTF. But that's because no other servers exist, and the only TDM I saw was 1-10 restricted.
So, that about sums up this game. It's totally fun to tinker with casually, but it's never anything to take seriously. The developers used it as a cash cow to fund their next game then dumped it, no mod support even as a thank you. They quit supporting it in June 2013 so it is what it is and that's not much.
I still enjoy tanking auto noobs and blue plating people but you'll find yourself wondering why the same people you see in every server haven't learned how to shoot a projectile well by now.

Dear Esther seems to strive for the whole “video games are art” thing. Effectively, it is a walking simulator. A pretty one, sure, but a walking simulator nonetheless.
The story in the game is told via narration. There are no characters to interact with, no literature to read… you walk along your path and listen to the voice of the narrator (who is presumably yourself) as he speaks about some part of his life.
The problem with the story was I found it incredibly hard to follow. Perhaps I was too easily distracted by the environment. Perhaps I lack the focus to pay enough attention. But I simply could not grasp the overarching plot - assuming there was one.
There are many points in the game that are breathtakingly beautiful, especially for a game this old. On the flip side, there are many points in this game that are bland and uninteresting. I think the third chapter had the most captivating scenery, for sure.
The choppiness and stuttering were incredibly frustrating. As I was walking along, the game would skip frames every few seconds. The graphics settings are limited in what can be changed, so I had to deal with that as there seemed to be no fix.
The music in this game was the most enjoyable aspect. I found myself paying more attention to the song than anything else in the game (which certainly did not help my ability to grasp the story).
Usually I turn off the music in a game, because I get too easily engrossed in the soundtrack and lose interest in the rest of the game. Alas, that was not an option here.
It was… boring. Sure, the graphics were nice, and the soundtrack was solid, but overall the game was just uninteresting. Was something to do between catching Pokemon, I suppose.
Don’t go into this expecting a game, per se. Just enjoy the journey it takes you on.

It doesn't have as interesting of a storyline as Grand Theft Auto series and does at times feel a bit repetitive (beat up bullies earn respect, beat up greasers earn respect, beat up preppies earn respect etc) and also gets a bit annoying having to always be running away from prefects, teachers or police for being out after curfew or skipping school, but that's life being a kid at Bullworth.
The open world map isn't the biggest and not surprising as you don't have a vehicle to explore too far except your skateboard and a bike which do make getting around a lot easier and are very handy on missions where there is a time limit.
With quite a few weapons at your disposal from slingshot, potato canon, bottle rockets, bangers, stink bombs, itching powder, marbles, eggs and not forgetting any item you find on the floor like a brick, apples or even snow, you have plenty to chose from to fight back against your enemies or your "friends"
The missions are spread across the school and the town and the further you get in to the game the more the town will unlock and just like Grand Theft Auto, will generally have two different missions on map at a time. The missions aren't too hard and see you move through the school from one group to the next earning respect by doing tasks or beating people up. It's fun and the stories are humorous.
As well as this are side missions and classes which are not mandatory but can help. For example "A Little Help" requires you to take transistors to a homeless person in exchange for him teaching you fighting moves. Six Transistors in total brought to the homeless man will allow Jimmy to learn six new moves and aid in keeping the rest of the school in line. The classes also teach new tricks to Jimmy like how to apologise to police or prefects to remove wanted level or taunt a bully to get rid of them (English) where as others (Art) teach Jimmy how to be a ladies' man and by kissing the girls can give him up to 100% extra health.
The lessons can be a bit tedious at times and is one of the reasons I gave up with this game when it first came out. But as they're not essential to completing the story you can skip them although if you are seen and caught out of class you will be forced to attend it. Basically if you don't want to go to class then don't get caught.
Classes are all mini games like QTE (Chemistry, Music, Shop), word jumble (English), matching flags with locations (Geography), dissecting an animal (Biology),actual maths (Math), dodge ball/ wrestling(Gym).
Not being from America, when the geography class asked me to match state flags with the states was a bit annoying but google was helpful for that and after completing marked locations of collectible rubber bands on the map.
Overall this is still a really good game. Not brilliant, as the story I felt could have been better and not so repetitive but I still liked it and a lot of parts in the story cut scenes reminded me of Grand Theft with its witty dialogue which was a good thing.
The controls (X Box 360 controller) where fine and worked really well with movement, combat and targeting. Graphics is still decent for now and if you wanted to, there are high resolution textures out there you can download, but I thought as it is, at 1080p was fine.
