After reading the other reviews and the preview images, I thought this game would be a fun jRPG with a modern twist. I love games published by Aldorlea, as well.
However, this game, I can not say in good faith I reccomend to anyone. I bought it for 1.99 and I still think it was too much. I spent the first hour, tirelessly grinding through uninspiring dungeons before I realized that, no, it wasn't going to get better.
The only positive to this game is the turn based combat system, but you can find that in any jRPG.
Pros-
Some of the character facesets are appealing
Cons-
Where do I begin?
The game starts off making absolute zero sense. The comic cut ins were neat, but I had no idea what was going on. First off, the game is about finding your 'girlfriend', um. no. The guy in the game hasn't even talked to the girl before, but somehow he's going around risking life and limb for someone he's never even talked to.
Somehow you're supposed to believe in broad daylight, a man waltzes into a heavy populated area in a large city, throws a woman over his shoulder like a sack of potatoes, and runs off with no motive, or obstacles.
The party members make zero sense. You have a choice of taking 3 with you on your journey, but they, like the 'girlfriend' have never interacted with the party member before. If they did, it's not shown very well.
One of the party member's faceset is completely identical to the girl being kidnapped, and I was completely confused and thought they were the same person!
Onto the game, there *is* none. The game is dungeon after dungeon. Once you clear a dungeon, you're transported to another dungeon. There is no progression in the story or explanation for what you're doing or why. You have no option of going back. It's grinding, without an end goal.
The dungeons are the most uninspiring dungeons I've ever seen, and for the first dungeon, the battlers don't even make any sense. Why am I fighting samurais and a midieval knight in an office complex? The same battlers are used over and over, there is no variety or method to why they are where they are. You just fight. This isn't even explained.
And can I mention the party member that you pick up when starting the game you can't control? He's COMPLETELY overpowered and makes the battle system completely unbalanced. All of my characters were KO'd yet this unwanted dude took on 4 battlers by himself. WHY? Who wants that? I'd rather die and figure out what I did wrong than have the game essentially play itself.
I played this for about 2 hours thinking the game would get better, but the more I played it, the worse it became. The dialogue between the characters is terrible at worst, immature at best. The characters swear, but instead of using actual words, the game uses symbols. And these characters swear A LOT. When the dialogue is nothing but symbols, it's time to forfeit the symbols, or better yet, think of more productive dialogue.
Also, the characters have bars abbreviated as "TP" but the items regenerating it call it "SP". Unless I'm completely missing something, I feel they both should be abbreviated the same way to explain to the player what they're regenerating when they're using an item.
There's no explanation on what the characters stats are or what they do, it's assumed the player already knows. It should not be the players job to correctly assume what the stats on the characters do.
As I said before, the dungeons look depressing. I get that the developer is going for a retro vibe, but it's 2017. Just because you CAN put in less effort doesn't mean you SHOULD. If the game is going to be nothing but dungeons I feel like it should be changed up a bit. The last dungeon I played before quitting was nothing but white walls and blue pipes. This is what you're looking at for a good hour, only to be rewarded with dialogue that adds completely nothing to the story.
IE:
Villain: "I don't know anything about where the girl is. Why do you care so much?"
Main character: "I just do!"
Yeah, I'm not even exaggerating on that.
I know this is harsh, but the truth is the game is boring, unbalanced, nonsensical, and amateur. I feel like the developer should practice way more before trying to release a full game like this and asking for money. Truth be told, I feel like this was a quick way to get a couple dollars because I truly feel absolutely no effort was put into this.
I can't reccomend this game in good faith, even at sale price. This game looks and feels like a first project.
The save points are very infrequent. It was almost a half hour to an hour between save points for me.
A much better indie JRPG is Moonchild, it is also published by Aldorlea Games and was also made in RPG Maker.

This game is... very different from Ultimate Ninja Storm 3.
Whilst 3 had overworlds where you had to run to your next mission, and many animated and text based cutscenes, 4 takes a more... straighforward approach. You are given a tree with nodes to choose from. These nodes are your cutscenes and missions, and will branch off to show the story for different characters.
The cutscenes are also static pictures taken from the anime with small animation thrown in, like water dripping in the backround, or shaking the screen during a cave collapse. A bit of a downgrade, and kinda kills the intense immersion 3 had.
Whilst 3 also had mostly similar battles between characters throughout the campaign, spicing it up with unique bosses or mob battles, 4 has many, many unique fights. Giant monsters fighting. Dynasty Warrior-esque fights. Etc. Kinda neat, honestly.
Also, there seem to be a lot less cinamatic QTEs, which is rather disappointing, considering how intense they made certain situations.
Graphics are pretty great, overall.
Multiplayer servers are lacking. Expect Lag. Can't mute other players. Bad skill matching.
Expect crashes. Plenty of crashes.
Overall, if you can deal with the downsides, a pretty solid game.

A multi-layered cooperative tactical first person shooter. Your skill matters, but so do your choices regarding what weapons and equipment to put on your battlemech. Instead of being able to respawn, you have a durable giant stompy robot. Armor protects your internal structures (legs, arms, torsos, head) and components, and 'mechs are often able to stay in the fight with multiple destroyed sections. There are a variety of weapon systems, covering short & long range, and burst or steady damage -- with a cooldown & heat management system to keep you from firing all the weapons all the time. Battle awareness and communication play are crucial, as you work with 11 other players to encounter and destroy a roughly even opposing force of 12 rival pilots. There is a full spectrum of mech sizes (20 ton "light 'mechs" to 100 ton "assault 'mechs") that slot into a variety of roles (scout, close range brawler, mid range fire support, indirect long range fire support, long range sniper) that are needed in every battle, and rewarded for doing the job well.
This game can be frustrating at time, and seems to have a fairly steep learning curve, but rewards strategic (loadout, map & mech knowledge) and tactical (positioning, targeting, communication) skills and keeps me coming back for the challenge and variety.
Big robots, big guns, what more do you want?

Never has picking yes or no on a recommendation been more difficult than with this thing. It needs a big logical diagram of decisions to make any kind of sense.
1. Do you own a steam link, or do you game on a tv and want to play PC games in the living room? Yes (2) No (3)
2. Do your games require keyboard and mouse? Yes (4) No (3)
3. You don't need this
4. Get one if you've disposable income
There is basically zero reason to buy this if you plan on using it in a context where you have a mouse and keyboard available, because it does not improve on that experience in the least. Neither does it improve on games that have controller support if you've a dual stick 360 pad style controller available, because it's just not that great. It's clicky, noisy, feels sort of cheap, and generally just serves as a decent patch solution to a logistical problem. Exactly zero games are improved by this thing. The button layouts are not great, the stick isn't great, the bumpers feel like the Wii U bumpers in that they're always too far away for comfort, and the whole thing is so clicky and loud it fills the room with clatter.
As a general thing, I just can't recommend buying this unless you've a very specific living room setup. Paired with the clunky config UI, the crashiness of steam streaming, and the number of pc/keyboard games that don't support the steam overlay (and thus not the steam controller in a good way), it's just really hard to recommend.
On the flipside, it's an interesting object. If you're a collector and want a look at what is still the best attempt at replicating keyboard/mouse in a joypad form factor while innovating in some modestly successful ways (the depth of reprogrammability here is impressive, as is the wildly enthusiastic haptic feedback) it's worth having just to have a look at what Valve has wrought.

Girlfriend Rescue.  Well this game was something to experience, that’s for sure.  I need to start by saying that this review is, unfortunately, personally biased.  No, not because I received a copy of the game for free (although I did that didn’t affect my review).  No, I found myself personally biased because quite frankly I love RPG maker games.  As a man very close to his 40s at the time of writing this, I grew up playing Final Fantasy on my NES, and consuming every RPG I could get my hand on.  RPG maker games often evoke a feeling of nostalgia in me that takes me back to the late 80s and early 90s.  Boy, let me tell you… Girlfriend Rescue triggers that sentimentality, and triggers it hard, in all the right ways.
So, the store page claims that “Girlfriend Rescue is a thrilling adventure where the gameplay of "Dragon Quest" meets the atmosphere of "Streets of Rage".”  One word, yup.  I get it, I totally get it.  Playing Girlfriend Rescue absolutely reminded me of the game play of the old Dragon Quest style JRPGs and had the pointless, often campy, story reminiscent of games like Streets of Rage or Bad Dudes.  First of all, hilariously, this game isn’t about rescuing your ‘girlfriend’ it’s about trying to rescue some chick the main character has a crush on.  A girl that likely has no idea the hero even exists.  You’re less a boyfriend and more a stalker to be honest.  The inclusion of choice of gender of both the protagonist and the ‘crush’ was a nice touch.  It felt unnecessary to me, but it was one of those choices that was simple to include in the game and some players will probably appreciate.  So you set off on a quest with three of your ‘gang’ to try to rescue your crush.
This is one of the game’s interesting points, you choose three members of your gang with very little information about what they are going to bring to the party.  There were several times that I wanted to restart just to see what the other gang members would have done because I ended up with a melee heavy party with no healing.  Still I found the game not too difficult, even on normal.  Though I was searching every square inch possible for every scrap of food, healing medicine, or coin to make sure I could keep my party healthy and satiated.  Oh, yeah, because hunger is a thing.  A thing that actually adds a little depth to the game in fact, you might not want to use all your healing items if they are also the only food you have, because someone might get hungry soon.
Actually there’s a lot of different status effects in this game.  Almost too many, and I couldn’t tell you after playing for three hours if I’d seen them all, and I certainly couldn’t tell you what most of them did.  But in the end that doesn’t really matter too much, as you get the idea that good status effects are good, and bad ones are bad.  It’s not required to know that one lowers strength by 10% and defense by 30% while another one lowers strength by 30% and defense by 10%.  Just keep smashing in the faces of bad guys.
The game isn’t without it’s faults of course.  The music is a bit repetitive and I found myself turning it off after not too long.  Likewise the graphics are quite underwhelming.  I’m sure that the idea was to go for a retro feel.  But somehow it doesn’t work out quite as well as other RPG maker games I’ve played.  The in game sprites feel very flat, and the levels all just feel like cookie cutter layouts.
But in the end, I find that I don’t mind this too much and they are more minor points when it comes to the story and the game.  I’ve found myself quite pleased with the time I’ve put into this one.  Comparing it against other RPG maker games, this one comes out very well.  But you have to get into the campy feel that they are throwing down.  Throw yourself back to 1990 and you’ll get it, but if you look at this and compare it to modern RPGs you’ll be disappointed.  So caveat emptor I suppose, but for me, I’ve enjoyed it quite a bit and recommend it to anyone, who like myself, is old enough to recognize what the developers were going for with this campy beat em up RPGMaker game.
NOTE - I was given a free copy of this game in exchange for an honest and unbiased review.

Girlfriend Rescue is a very well thought out story, as well as beautiful with it's hand drawn artwork used for all the scenes and character portraits. While I've only played the game for a short amount of time, I do plan on finishing it and delivering a much more detailed review.
So far, it's worth every cent.

is a turn/round-based RPG through and through which starts out with a conversation among friends about approaching your crush, but you find out that some recently escaped prisoner has taken her!  You have to form a party to find a way to save her.  You start out with choices you can make about your gender, name, crush’s name, and once you can move around, you have a selection of up to two other members you are friendly with that can help you out as you start your quest to get your girl back.  I would have liked to have been able to try them all to find out what each possible party member could do, but I would not really know future abilities as they leveled up anyway, so it is probably not a very important issue.
As you begin, you get a lot of nice tips from the local police NPCs on various aspects of play.  This was helpful for me as I began journeying around.  There are a lot of various original things about this RPG game that I like, such as the various debuffs and what can change when things happen.  They are atypical to what I am used to seeing, which is pretty interesting and refreshing to me.  I mean, a lot of it involves various stats, so it’s not too different, but the way it is done is not the typical type of stuff.  I like what I’ve encountered so far in this game.  The combat system is a standard turn-based style where you have attack and defend commands along with special moves you can learn as you level up, which you pick for the next round, and watch the round unfold.
The actual gameplay outside of combat is roaming around a map, trying to find X amount of enemies on the area you explore, and taking out the last guy on the map.  I have not tried finishing an area with less than the target number, but I am guessing your bonus reward at the end would change if you got less than the number it shows, which finalizes after the last “boss” character on the map, as far as I can tell, ever since the first area I explored fully.
The plot is different, and I find the initial gameplay and overall setting nicely done.
The look of the areas so far work with what’s going on at the paticular time.  Fits in nicely.
Since you can only pick limited characters for each run through the game, there is some replay value with this to find out what other characters are about, and which combinations might work the best on a harder difficulty, for instance.  I haven’t finished to see if there is a new game plus, and what that entails exactly, but there is definitely some replay value here in some way shape or form, which I always like!
I am always happy when I can be rewarded with items for exploring around.  Most stuff seems to be added to inventory automatically when you are on the proper square or area, so it makes it a bit easier not having to mindlessly press buttons to click each spot.  Some boxes do require a click, but they are usually obvious.
The various combat mechanics in the special moves are very different than the standard RPG type of moves.  I really like the originality that is put into many of my party’s special techniques.
The status effects are not standard to RPGs either, and the originality is nice to see.  While most just lower stats in a few areas or stop you from moving, etc. they are not your typical “paralyze” or whatever.  Some will have a chance to go away after a turn or so, while others can last a bit longer.  They have interesting debuff names and the debuffs are generally not the typical types of effects.  Usually seems to be a series of stats that are lowered for most I have encountered so far.  Some will persist until you cure it, like hunger for instance.  There are a good many battle stat debuffs, and they have various different things they change or lower on your characters.
By clearing areas and dispatching every enemy there, you gain a special bonus, which carries over to the next areas.  You also get several items, which I haven’t tried comparing yet to unfinished area bonuses.
Autosaves after five battles have gone by.
While it doesn’t affect things too terribly much, the hunger aspect lowers stats a bit in certain areas.  I like the addition of needing to eat as you travel.
Very linear gameplay.  While I don’t expect anything like a total open world experience, I would like more choice, and the possibility of returning enemies to grind if I wanted to do so.  One aspect I enjoy on RPGs that I miss here.
If I level up with items, I am unable to see what improves.  I can only see this directly when I win battles and level up.
Some of the items are not very clear as to what they do, or are buggy.  Some don’t seem to work the way they should.  The Red Toro is supposed to counter Tired status, but it remains on the alien I try to use it on, but works on other characters.  Another character was Infected, and Cortisol never works for removal of this.  It might only work when actually in battle, but I haven’t really tried and compared this to being out of battle, where it doesn’t change the status effect while on characters.
Near the beginning, when I am first able to choose my party, it would be nice to be able to see what each one is capable of.  Maybe being able to switch out at various times if I wanted to just try others instead of needing to start over and try them a while.  Of course, with no grinding, this would probably not be advantageous unless they took the same level as the character they were switched out for, since you wouldn’t get as many experience points for the three you would mainly use, and they would be spread out too much, which would cause an imbalance in the parity that exists in a limited battle grind-free style environment..
I love a good map, even on something I consider a bit linear.  Good to know where I am.
Is the game worth the $4.99 USD price tag to pick up?  Probably.  I think with the replay value, and the decent length of the game so far among other things, that alone is worth it.  The combat has some interesting abilities and the buffs and debuffs are not your ordinary stuff, for the most part.  I’m the type that likes to get games on sale, so I’d pick it up on a deal, but saying that, this game is definitely worth the price it is at, and I am surprised it does not carry a higher base price, honestly.  It’s a good one for the RPGMaker style engine.  I can highly recommend this game after my fairly limited gameplay thus far.

This is an extreme change to the game, but its one of the first major defining features of Paladins, and helps distance the game from Overwatch.

TL;DR and background: I was around for the closed beta of this game and have followed the development for the last 4 years up until the steam release. This is an average arena shooter made by a mediocre developer with 4 years of bad history behind them.
Pros:
- Art design is good.
- On an extremely basic level, the gameplay feels about what a mechwarrior game should feel like.
Cons:
- Glacial development pace.
- Balance and metagame are in a constant state of tail chasing. Instead of fixing a specific issue that causes some undesired meta, PGI makes broad sweeping changes that may or may not fix the original problem while causing more problems of their own.
- Game mechanics are simplistic and often counter-intuitive. Nowhere near something deserving of the mechwarrior franchise.
- Grind is bad. In order to max out a mech, you need to purchase and max out 3 different variants. Each varriant costs between 5-12 million cbills to buy, and then another 4-10 million to equip effectively. An average new player can expect to earn about 100-120k cbills per match. Do the math.
- PGI has a rich history of releasing mechs for real money in a horribly overpowered state, denying that said mechs are overpowered, then nerfing them shortly before they become availible for ingame currency. When asked about this, the CEO of the company made a joke likening people who found that to be sketchy to 9/11 conspiracy theorists.
- Gameplay gets boring and repetitive after about 15 hours of play.
- Playing solo has fairly low wait times and passable matchmaking. Add a single friend to the mix and you get put in group queue, where you'll get roflstomped repeatedly by organized deathballs of 12 mechs.
In summary, if you want to play and have fun for a week or two, go for it. Just don't expect any great improvements or groundbreaking new innovation.

I recommend Dear Esther, but not as a 'game'.  It isn't a game.  It's more of a walk-through novel and 'experience'.  Other than walking and exploring, there isn't much to actually do except wander and admire the scenery and voiceover work.  And that's the whole point.   The plot is designed to leave a lot to your imagination, the scenery designed to give ambiguous hints as to what is really going on, and only towards the end does it become clear what you're really doing.
As this 'experience' is highly dependent on the graphic and audio detail, you're going to want the best version, and this Unity remake is the one to get here and now.  The lack of any antagonists, characters or threats (other than the odd bit of water or steep drop) is such that there's so much more opporutnity to let your GPU focus on fine details.  The director commentary on this version is also a major plus, it gives away just enough to give a little bit of context.  The commentary also explained that this style of game is actually a genre now, so off to the store to find some more, then.

I've finally finished the game. It took me about 80 minutes, and now it's time to review it. Do know that I haven't played the original Dear Esther game. I do own the original game and the Chinese Room gave me this remastered edition for free.
I wouldn't really consider this a game. It's more an experience, a bedtime story that you can listen to at your own pace. It's not interactive or anything. There're no puzzles, no buttons to be pressed, levers to be pulled. You can't in any way interact with you environment. All you can do is walk, enjoy your surroundings and listen to the story. The game has 4 chapters, each lasting about 20-ish minutes. The game itself doesn't last long (around 80+ -ish minutes) and has no real replayability, unless you want to hear the story again.
Let's start with the good bits. The environment is beautiful and the textures are amazing. The music is also very emotional and it fits the mood of the game well. The voice acting is great as well.
Now to the bad parts of the game. I've read many reviews and a lot of them referred to this game as a walking simulator. At first, before I played the game, I thought they were overreacting, but they weren't. All you can do is walk. You can't jump, you can't crouch and you can't even sprint. If you'd check the key binding options, there're only 5 keys needed. Four keys are for walking (wasd / zqsd) and one is for zooming in (mouse button).
Besides the fact that you can't sprint, you walk slow. I understand that this gives the player more time to enjoy the surroundings and gives the game more time to play the storytexts, but it is really slow when there's very little to look at (especially the first part of the game). The game wants you to explore the map, but since you walk this slow and there're multiple dead ends, you probably don't want to waste your time trying to explore every corner of every chapter. Also, when you walk up (as in you walk up a hill or walk up stairs), you walk even slower. Although I applaud the game makers for thinking about a small detail like this, I don't think gamers really needed it and it's another thing that slows down the game.
During the 3rd chapter
, there's a bug that makes your walking really weird. At some points, you seem to get launched to a wall at the other side of the room. It seems like you sometimes, accidentally, enter god mode, which speeds up your walking, gives you some limited flying abilities and sometimes allows you to pass through walls.
My last complaint is the save-feature. There's an auto-save feature, which I generally like, but it only saves after each chapter. A chapter takes about 20 minutes to complete, so you can't stop mid-chapter.
That what could be improved:
Story-wise, I can't really say if it's good or bad. The monologues trigger automatically and are voiced, but not subtitled which makes it hard to follow the story. I wish The Chinese Room
would add a feature that allows you to read the discovered story, so it makes it easier to follow. Since I didn't really follow the story, I haven't commented on the story. (EDIT: Apparently, there're subtitles available.)
The environments are gorgeous, but dark at some times. The game gives you a flashlight, but you don't have any control over it. Your character automatically takes out its flashlight when it enters certain dark places, but not for all places. I think it would be better to give the player control of when he wants the flashlight.
All in all, this kind of experience isn't really for me. This game is aimed at a niche audience. Not everyone will like this game, but if you do enjoy these kind of games, then you should go for it. Although I think $10 for 80 minutes of entertainment might be a bit much, so buy when on sale.

This seems very much like an original, high-quality anime franchise, encapsulated within a very particular type of Metroidvania! You play as the rabbit-person Erina, who somehow makes friends with the fairy Ribbon, and they have somewhat weird adventures together as they meet other women who seem either fascinated with the fact a rabbit has turned into a not-unattractive woman, or somewhat repulsed by the idea. Or else, they want to capture her and do God knows what to her.
Gameplay more or less follows the basic scheme of a Metroidvania; get powers to get further in the world, but with twists all involving the introduction of Bullet Hell elements! That's right, you're on foot pretty much all the time and you have to constantly dodge everything that your enemies throw at you. It's not especially difficult, but it can be frustrating. Also you can add badges to get various effects like more attack power, more defense, the ability to see your enemies' health upon attacking them, and much more!
The story is so delightfully bizarre I find it hard to wrap my head around sometimes, so I will leave you to discover it! I recommend the game to all who like Metroidvania and quirky anime themes.

CONS:

OVERVIEW:
I have played games like Roblox, Minecraft and Ace of Spades, and find joy in those games because of the community's creative standpoint, and Blockland is no exception. This game is the easiest one to pick up because it ACTUALLY HAS A TUTORIAL! (Which is still dumb because you have to load it up, there is no "Tutorial" button anywhere so you're left to find it yourself.) The controls are easy AND difficult. If you're used to FPS controls of switching through your weapons using 1, 2,  etc. Then prepare to be tricked as your bricks are assigned to your number keys while your weapons are located in your tools inventory by pressing Q (Or binded key). The numbpad can be used to move your bricks along a grid before placing them, which helps A LOT. Not a lot of sandbox, blocky games have this kind of feature and just makes Blockland much easier to play and enjoy. As for bricks, THIS GAME HAS A TON and more can even be added as add-ons, which by the way, is simple and easy to understand so you can install a plethora of mods made by the community. The Multiplayer in this game is really fun and most likely the only way you will play. The community is thriving through servers so meeting people in one place and finding them in another is pretty common and honestly feels nice because it feels like you are really getting to know the community and its players. As for Multiplayer gameplay, expect the normal Call of Duty like feedback from players. The occasional "OMG stop playing like that!" does turn up and its just as annoying. But if you're a troll and like screwing with players, then it should be no different than from how you troll on any other game. For the cons listed, I feel really upset that these are actually issues, because most of it can be easily simplified and fixed, fun-wise. The graphics are really up there in terms of quality. High graphics means your computer is somehow a beast because most high-end graphic cards can't run this game to its full potential. As for Singleplayer gameplay. Its just a simple complaint. This may be more of a personal standpoint so understand that this is mainly just a suggestion if anything. Singleplayer is NOT fun. It doesn't matter if you nuke entire maps of zombie NPCs. You will get bored of playing alone EASILY, and it is only because there isn't any actual user-friendly feedback coming from the game. I understand it's a singleplayer mode in a sandbox game, but even Gmod has a way of communicating with the player to make them seem like they are a part of the games world, immersing them into the game and grabbing their attention to want to continue playing.
This game is not bad, but your own fun has to be found in it, especially in the Multiplayer which can still give you a great taste of the game's actual feel. I do recommend this game, but it does feel like it can easily be put down.
Very bad camera work, hard control of charackter, supid physics... Brick placing system is hard to control too. In one word: annoying  :( Not recommending for anyone

Anyway, onto the review. Girlfriend Rescue was developed by Aldorlea Games, was released on July 10th 2015 Girlfriend rescue is an indie RPG, which describes itself as a cross between Dragon Quest and Streets of Rage, however, my experience with the game feels more like diluted gameplay of Final Fantasy mixed with the urban setting of Streets of Rage. Girlfriend Rescue is an RPGMaker game, and those familiar with RPG Maker games know that they are not always the highest quality of games, for obvious reasons. Girlfriend Rescue is not an exception, however, compared to some of the other RPGMaker games I have played in the past, I quite enjoyed Girlfriend Maker.
The story to Girlfriend Rescue is about how the love of your life is kidnapped by a crime syndicate, and it’s up to you, and your friends, to save her.
The gameplay is my favorite part of the game. The combat is very enjoyable, and for casual RPG players, or those looking to spark an interest in the JRPG, or perhaps even seasoned JRPG enthusiasts looking for something a bit easier to play or to 100% achieve the achievements. Those looking for replay value Should not turn away from Girlfriend Rescue, since every playthrough you can choose A different party of characters, or equip different items and utilities.
The graphics for Girlfriend Rescue aren’t the greatest, however, they are decent and not too hard on the eyes. There are many hand drawn scenes in Girlfriend Rescue which are very visually pleasing. However, like every game, there are cons. One downside to Girlfriend Rescue which I Immediately noticed was the music.
The soundtrack to the game is composed solely of creative commons music. Now, you might be thinking, “Hey Deviation! You use NoCopyrightSounds in your videos, how does that make you any better?” Well, the simple truth is, I don’t make anyone pay to watch my videos, however, to play Girlfriend Rescue, you’re going to have to fork over some of your hard earned money.
Another downside to Girlfriend Rescue is the illusion of choice at the very beginning. Similar to Pokemon Mystery Dungeon: Red Rescue Team, although there are probably a lot more games that have the same beginning, Girlfriend Rescue will ask you a few questions. What’s your name, what sexuality are you, what gender, and if you have a crush or whatever you want to call it. However, after answering all of those questions, it does not have an outcome on your game. For example, me, being the funny guy I am, chose the option that I’m gay at the beginning of the game
, however, it still said that I was in love with the damsel in distress (Laura). I’m pretty sure that those who are homosexual only like those of the same gender, and since I was a male and homosexual, doesn’t that mean I’m only attracted to men? Yeah, I thought so. Check mate, game.
The final downside to the game is the odd theme. The first few levels make since, you're in an urban setting fighting off thugs and rats, however, as soon as you go into a very modern apartment building, you’re greeted by ninjas, samurai, and other Oriental themed enemies. Very strange, but not a huge downside.
If you are a fan of old school JRPGs with an odd story, or if you are interested in indie games in general, I would recommend Girlfriend Rescue, however strange it may be, however, I would suggest you mute the audio and play whatever music you like, as I did.
Rating:
Graphics: 7.2/10
Audio: 3/10
Gameplay: 7.6/10
Overall: 5.9/10

When I first saw this game, I was a bit doubtful; story didn't interest me too much and I used to play medieval/fantasy or sci-fi rpgs and this was (kinda) present time in normal world. But I decided give it a try, and glad I did that! Game was hilarious and I kept laughing thro playtime. (It could had something to do late hours I played tho) Character's classes were silly and their skills were ridiculous, suited users perfectly.
And overall, I enjoyed this game, more than I thought I would.  It was very linear, different from most games I've played, not much room to exploring (and getting lost) but its fine once in a while. Game also was challenging at some parts, due no item-, money- or levelgrinding and NPC heals weren't available so often. And you couldn't save when you wanted, if you didn't feel like backtracking a lot. I got couple close-calls, and one wipe at boss fights ("Just one more hit, I don't have to heal yet, just one more hit and.. oh, thats a critical hit.. daymmmn.), even when I was playing easy mode. Annoying healing items and dots were difficult to handle in some fights. Luckily stuns, blocks, charms etc. worked quite well with +SKI gear, it did take some points from damage output and defence tho, but at least I wasn't wiped out on first turn.
Music was nice, nothing mindblowing or epic, but it suited stage themes pretty well and gladly it was playing whole time, not just short moments. Story, what I didn't feel from beginning, began interest me after a while. Why would one kidnap a normal girl who is not a princess, lost heir of great mage or something like that. Had to know!
Looting wihtout key was refreshing and I kept finding new items almost all the time, when I just stumbled to wall or something and DING find a new item.
Game had few downsides tho, it was a bit disappointing that you couldn't turn story to girl saves her boyfriend, even when I got that impression when game asked name and sex. But it wasn't any gamebreaking ragecausing thing. Mobs didn't respwan at all and since I am a bit (well maybe more than just a bit..) levelgrinding fanatic who could spend hours and hours to overleveling characters, a brief moment I was disapointed about that. But that was just minor setback and I'm pretty sure thats just my personal crazyness in my playingstyle. And it was meant to be that way for various reasons.
Perhaps artwork wasn't best what Aldorlea can offer but it wasn't too bad. I have seen much worst. *brrrrrh*. Hunger factor of game was most annoying thing in game, in my opinion. Had to waste healing items, because guys wanted a pizza. And speaking of the devil; healing overall was annoying as hell. Most items healed only xx% and maybe I didn't really get how it should work. Sometimes when my guys had only 11 hp left, healing back to surviving range was a pain, because all items seems to heal only xx% from remaining HP. There were couple items what restored some amount of hit points, but in my game those were precious and pretty rare. Or maybe I just didn't check every levels closely enough. Due lack of healing some levels were really challenging, had to do some wipe-grinding leveling once because I got defeated all the time and I just didn't have enough items to heal or satisfy characters hunger. I hate dots.
But yes, I did enjoy this game, it was funny, sweet and different what I've been playing before. Somehow whole game felt very.. well, that the creator really put heart to make this game. I think that is one reason why people likes Aldorlea games, including myself.
And ps. please forgive my grammar and spelling mistakes, this is first review I write in English.

If only Steam would let me call it "mediocre" or "almost Yes Recommend."  I expected to write Yes without reservation after the first few days.
I like the graphics.  I like the set-up. It borrows from some other nostalgic games, notably Star Control 2 -- in a good way. Had me hooked for a couple days, ferrying human surivivors to the station.  Romantic last stand vs. the darkness.
Some X-Com base building and management sort of, away missions with Greenshirts.  A couple things could have used more polish, like zooming to officers.  I like that you can rename ships, officers.  Star system object renaming would have been nice, would have made it easier to keep track, but over time I got to not care about that.
I played on "Normal" difficulty.  That probably ruined the game for me.  You are constantly at a disadvantage, the pacing is messed up.  Even when I had a big advanced fleet, I was way behind the curve.  I didn't realize I should go to dead worlds to fix them up (as there isn't enough of a tutorial), but I doubt it would have mattered.  You are constantly bombarded with space battles to deal with, but the catch-22 comes in that I only had 3 useful level 13 officers and a bunch of basically useless lower level ones.  I needed Level 13s to upgrade various things in my fleet, but they never had a week off from being able to fight to do that.  The lower level officers couldn't pilot cutting edge ships.  After while I realize I could go with an L10 science officer and try to get luckier in combat, but by then two races had been wiped out.  I saw a couple of mission related bugs, one related to rescuing an officer that I did twice, getting two copies of them.  The gamebreaker bug came in recovering an artifact from a race that had been wiped out.  I wiped out the defenders, went to the planet, and I can't interact with it to recover it.  I went to the forums and the best answer is loading a game before they got wiped out and saving them.  Not sure if I could do that even if I loaded, because I was waiting for upgrades at the time, but more importantly you are in SOOOO many space combats that it means like wiping out 50 combats.  Too tedious to consider.
So I'm waiting maybe for a patch and if I replay again it'll be on easiest difficulty.

I started a new game after Loot DLC.  The loot DLC itself I wasn't that impressed with, but the game is clearly quite a bit more polished.  I only had one minor bug, and the pacing seemed a little better.  Towards the last 1/3 of the game the combat got especially tedious, and again I had an issue with not being able to have more than one fleet with top tier ships.  I was in the process of getting XP on the backup fleet (because I got a new officer with a superpower) when I triggered the endgame battles.
I would recommend they build a room that lets you gain experience for officers, to avoid making so many of them basically useless -- and leaving with you with A-team fleet that can't be everywhere at once.
Anyway, you can tell the folks that made the game are sci-fi lovers, there's alot of craft that went into the game.  It's not perfect but after the update I think it was worth the money, a worthy effort.

Decent overall. I enjoyed most aspects of it, but the game seems to be still devloping features, and there are areas that need some more work. Don't get me wrong, it's a complete game, but it's in a phase where the it's final form is yet to be revealed.
Needless to say, the art style, storytelling and music are great, but some mechanical aspects need some more polish.
There's not a lot of an incentive to host multiple fleets. Experience is hard enough to come by and you need your officers to be of a certain level to be able to do certain tasks. I'm not sure if it was messing with the pacing or difficulty curve, but I ended up sticking to one crew the entire game.
The ground combat is a bit of a gimmick right now. It seldom happens, it's generally easy and it's usually not very rewarding.
The spaceship combat is engaging to a good extent, but can get a bit repetitive. It would be nice to have an autoresolve option for easier encounters.
Mothership construction and customisation don't seem very fleshed out, at least on the normal diffictuly. It felt I can excavate way more room than I can possibly have any use for and there wasn't any planning really involved. No synergy between the rooms, no great benefit in building multiple rooms of the same type and no real choice in development path. The technology tree is pretty straigtforward and basically comes down to building the next level of the port when your captains are high enough level to take advantage of the new ships.
There are a few minor issues with the achivements, like completing the game on Normal not unlocking similar achievements for Easy and Very Easy.
Overall, still a pretty good experience and I would recommend giving it a shot.

Human Revolution, like its predecessors in this line of popular first person role playing stealth games, offers freedom in almost every aspect to fit any play style. As far as multiplatform games go, this is probably the best you can get to recreate the old Deus Ex atmosphere.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the third instalment in the Deus Ex series, and it’s also the prequel and the spiritual successor of the highly acclaimed first game from 2000– mostly disregarding the existence of the not-so-popular second game.
Deus Ex always liked to promote freedom in play styles. All missions, be it plot-critical or just a side quest, have at least two solutions: go in guns blazing, or be sneaky. Although there is a decent arsenal in the game, and a few lethal augmentations (this franchise’s version of spells), the designers clearly favour the latter: there are hidden routes everywhere, you can bypass security systems, and there are several ways to dispose of the guards in a non-lethal, silent manner. You even get a large praxis (experience) boost when choosing these solutions.
The story involves yet another conspiracy, but without any clandestine organisations secretly trying to topple the current society. The scale is smaller: you deal with corporate espionage and political movements resenting the human augmentation technology. You will still encounter soldiers working for the secret government, but the most common enemies are thugs and private security.
The Director’s Cut, the only version available now, integrates the formerly separate expansion into the storyline, which unbalances the endgame, but creates a more coherent narrative. The boss fights, the bane of the original edition, also got revamped, but they are only slightly better now. Still, all and all, this is the superior version (despite some technical issues), the one recommended for all cRPG fans, be them new or old.

I remember playing this many, many years ago, when it was only just a free mod for a little game called Half-Life 2. "Oh, I'll crack it open again, only a half-hour of game, something I can cross off of my game list." For I had taken to categorizing them chiefly into such plain categories as "in progress", "complete", and "unopened". Certainly, a short time later and I would be done, crossing another game off with satisfaction.
It was only a short time later I realized I had walked the wrong way. Oh, certainly, I had gotten a bit of gab for my efforts, but only silence greeted me as I turned back, holding the W key in a devil's grip, not even the cries of gulls to greet me on my return. I went and checked the options, but there was no auto-walk key to be found. "Even upon the release of this Landmark Edition, I have to hold the W key all the way through?" Dissapointment stabbed at my soul like fallen icicles. Still, I continued on. This game would end up in the "complete" category, I swore to myself.
At one point I found my walking halted, only to look down upon a small, tiny stone wall, no higher than a cat's tail might rise. "Oh, I have to walk around it. It's like a little maze.", I said, puzzled that I had to do that. Still, I continued on. I had felt this more eerie my first time, the paintings on the cliff walls more stark. "It is a pretty game.", I thought as I continued on. "The textures haven't aged at all well, though. That garbage? Just a bit of color scattered across the ground. No bump mapping to be found at all, there." Looking at things in the distance was surely more rewarding. There was lots of fog around. Had that been there before, I wondered? It was nice.
The caves were different this time. I had remembered fearing for myself the first time in their dark expanses, knowing a game like this surely wouldn't kill me or deliver up a monster from the depths, but they were eerie. Now, they felt well-lit by convenient glowing mushrooms. "So many well-lit caverns in video games.", I thought. "I had even thoughtfully brought a flashlight which gets used in buildings, but I never needed it the caves. A bit odd, that." Still, I took some screenshots. They were pretty caves. I guess the narrative was continuing on, but I'd already heard it all, hadn't I? Oh, there were achievements now. "Very artistic.", I thought to myself as another popped up. "That's what literature has been missing all this time, getting a pat on the back every fifty pages I can show off to my friends. 'Look, I held down the W key for a half-hour and wiggled a mouse! I even drowned myself once, even though the game certainly didn't want me to!'", I can now proclaim to them proudly.
As I came to the end of the story, I mused back upon it. It was all very poetic, but I realized with a slight discomfort that the narrative struck me in a way I hadn't realized. "Is this romanticizing what I think it is?", I thought. "Or is a narrative about taking control of one's destiny?" I thought on it as the game took control from me to deliver its final wistful words and force my viewpoint into its final act. "I realize this is probably a limitation of the engine at the time, they probably had difficulty rendering- hm. Still, the player ought to be guiding this final act. They could have done more with it." And I'm not sure I'm so keen on the themes, as I think more on them. I'm not sure I like the ugly task it tries to paint a pretty picture over. I have no problem just guiding a viewpoint and getting to see some nice sights and play out a narrative, but I'm not sure I like the story, in the end. It's well enough written, I supposed. But at times the experience becomes disconnected from the narrative, severed and floating free like a lost leaf from a tree. At one point I was supposed to be injured, but if so, there was no sign of it. I'm not sure that story beat was entirely necessary, given it just reminded me of the disconnect. Part of it is the age of the thing, of course, but all the new edition delivered was these little medals coined "achievements" and a bit of nattering on by the director. I was left with a singular, burning decision: do I recommend this?
Mmm.
"Nah.", I thought aloud. "But you'll probably get it in a Humble Bundle at some point anyway."

I did not recommend the original game in my 2014 review, and I do not recommend Landmark Edition because it's basically identical. However, I can say that lines like the above have stuck with me for several years. There's no doubt this game contains some deep and poetic writing, some brilliant voice acting, nice visuals, atmosphere and musical cues.
I think the story is worth telling, and I love the concept of wandering an island while this tower looms in the background, luring you to your destiny. But for the most part, I was bored. There just wasn't enough in this package or the way it was presented for me to find it appealing enough to genuinely recommend to others. There could have been more ambient sounds for a stronger atmosphere, there could have been optional documents or artifacts to pick up and examine in detail. The visuals as I said are "nice", but nothing blew me away. A game as slow and non-interactive as this needs visuals which blow you away.
The developer commentary says the game is "made in an impressionist style" and that "the scenery is too grand to actually exist". I didn't get a sense of these at all. I think I've seen too many games which accidentally look like this while trying to look realistic for it to occur to me Dear Esther's art is stylised. I think the artist was being too subtle if he was going for impressionism or surrealism, and something grander would have wowed me.
Landmark Edition is an excellent port of Dear Esther from the Source engine to Unity. It looks better technically, and the developer commentary offers some interesting insights. But the commentary is quite a slow ordeal as the markers are too close together (or the commentary wasn't planned or edited down enough) to prevent them overlapping. So I found myself running in circles waiting for each commentary track to finish until I became dizzy.
I would recommend only if you're an aspiring writer or game designer.

Very fun game. It's an *extremely* open-ended metroidvania that generally lets you proceed in any direction you want, intended order or not. The levels are well-designed and fun, and items are hidden everywhere. The bullet-hell bosses are all very well designed and fun to fight. You're eventually given a wide, wide variety of abilities you can use in combat, and a decent number for exploration.
As for replay value, the game has tons of acheivements for stuff like skipping key items or doing things out of order. And like I said, you can pursue most of the bosses and items in any order. And yes, there's selectable difficulty levels. My first run lasted ~14 hours to see the credit roll on normal, but there's still another chapter and at least half a dozen more bosses, so this is a pretty long game to start with.
Art is good but notexceptional, music is quite good. The plot is mostly an excuse to fight people but that's ok.
Bottom line: This game is very good at all the things it tries to be. Would recommend.

When I first picked up this game I was a bit hesitant due to the artstyle and gamplay photos. Sometimes boobs are put on mediocre games to make them sell just a little bit. This game however, is far from mediocre.
The particle effects in game makes every attack feel interesting and fair. Never have I wondered what I took damage from during a boss fight, and every time I attempted the same boss again I felt like I was ready to put my skills and knowledge about its attack patterns to the test.
The controls feel responsive, and movement and attack choices unlock in a pace that makes you feel like you always have quite a bit of options without being overwhelmed.
The game offers a bit of replayability due to its different difficulty options, and its different modes that changes the gamplay a bit. And since it will be your second or third time playing, you will aready know where certain key items and bosses are on the map, allowing you to choose your own path through the game (you can even chose to play the game without any items). More so if you master the reverse wall jump and wall kick techniques.
The story is interesting and the characters are cute, and unless you have a problem with the fact that it is an all female cast, you will find yourself quite invested in the world and everyone in it.
The soundtrack is one of the best ones I have heard, and helps create the atmosphere for each area.

While there is definitely some fanservice, there is no H-Content, and the game even actually jokes about it at one point in a scene that would make the people that are actually into H-games look bad.
But with that minirant done with, this is a very well made Metroidvania with a very balanced level of challenge. The platforming is not really difficult in most areas and gets harder near the end of the postgame areas, but it's nothing too unreasonable. The main strength of the game is in the boss fights where you will need to learn how to deal with all sorts of patterns.
There are lots of hidden items to find. Sequence Breaking is encouraged and sometimes even rewarded(there's even an achievement for doing some of them). Most bosses can be fought in whatever order you like, but there are some cases where you have to beat certain bosses to access some parts of the game or other bosses. While glitches do get patched out, there is an option in game to reenable them, so that speedruns can still use them.
The game has many difficulty options. From easy modes that anyone who just cares about the story to get through to ones that should satisfy hardcore players. The only downside with this is that the harder ones have to be unlocked. Patterns get more bullets and get faster with increasing difficulty, but at least up to the game's standard highest difficulty of Bunny Extinction, the game is for the most part completely fair. At least during what comes in the game without DLC, if you get hit, it pretty much is always your fault in some way. Some of the DLC content may not necessarily be fully balanced, but I haven't spent as much time on that to see if I'm just missing stuff that would make things fair. There are higher difficulties than Bunny Extinction in the artbook DLC, but they were cut for a reason, there's lots of unfair stuff in those ones, but some people do enjoy that as well.
The achievements in this will also be a decent challenge if you're looking for a difficult game to 100%. Not only do you have to beat almost every standard game boss without getting hit(though final and postgame bosses do allow some hits), you will have to get through a boss rush of 28 bosses in a row, no heals between rounds, and if you die you will go right back to round 1, on Bunny Extinction or harder(The artbook's Unknown and Impossible do let you have 3 of the healing items compared to BEX cap of 1, but everything else about those probably makes it actually harder than BEX even with more healing available, but I have not finished the game on Impossible yet to be able to check that)

Girlfriend Rescue is perhaps one of the dumbest and most simple RPGs ever. It has nothing particularly special about it – it's made with RPG Maker, the story is laughably silly, and the gameplay is pretty much what you'd expect from a typical turn-based RPG. So, why am I recommending it? Well, read on and find out!
The game “combines the atmosphere of Streets of Rage with the gameplay of Dragon Quest”, according to the store page at least. The gameplay might be a little different than Dragon Quest, but the bit about Streets of Rage is pretty much spot on – this is clearly a silly game with a silly premise. I mean, the name says it all!
Perhaps one of the funniest parts about the story though is that the girl you're trying to rescue from the bad guys (ninjas, of course!) isn't actually the main character's girlfriend. Instead, she's just some random girl that the guy has a crush on. He decides to team up with 3 of 13 (4 of those are unlockables)  characters/friends to stop the bad guys. Personally, I found the character designs for the party members to be pretty amusing. My party consisted of the main dude, a shady-looking “dealer” character, a little boy, and a frog. Yep, a frog. Each of the characters have amusing dialogue occasionally, yet what truly sets them apart from each other is their strategies during battles.
See, the gameplay of Girlfriend Rescue basically consists of a series of battles in a set area. The game throws you into a series of areas linked together by an overall location (like say, a line of train cars in a train). In these, you fight a variety of enemies, collect items by walking into objects (yeah, it's weird), and manage your party through equipping gear or using consumables like pizza, drugs, or “red toro” (Red Bull). The battles themselves are pretty much what you'd expect: turn-based attacks, skills, defending, and whatnot. Each character has their own special skills (sometimes with silly names) that sometimes apply status effects to enemies; certain weapons can also do this.
Now, a somewhat minor complaint I had is that it was a bit difficult to remember what most of these status effects actually do. There's a LOT of them – quite a bit more than most RPGs – and it became tough to try and remember what would happen if an enemy “infected” one of my party members, made them “tired”, “doomed”, etc. There's police officers NPCs that can be found every once in a while and explain about a few status effects, but it would be nice to have a help section or even just an item that gives little text blurbs about each status effect as a quick refesher.
Another part that bugged me about Girlfriend Rescue was how repetitive it got after a while. Each “world” was basically the exact same – slap on a fresh new coat of paint for the scenery and enemies, fight a bunch of enemies in a mostly linear path, then rinse and repeat. There wasn't a lot of variety besides the pixel art, different songs for different worlds, enemy designs, and bosses. Speaking of bosses, they were pretty much incredibly easy, or at least all the ones that I fought were. I would have gotten farther, but.....well......
….the difficulty. This game has really strange difficulty spikes. At the beginning of the game, it recommends you play on Easy for a first playthrough, which I found a bit odd, so I decided to be rebellious and pick Normal. Now, for most of the game I had a good challenge, but it was nothing too tough. For the first few worlds, my characters rarely died at all. Yet, when I reached the 4th world, I kept dying to the enemies of that area, zombies. It wasn't too much, but it was definitely a noticeable difference in difficulty from the previous areas. The weird part though is that the 5th area was one of the easiest for me – I beat the boss (or rather 2 bosses) quite quickly and the enemies were similarly a breeze. However, the 6th location......oh jeez. It began simple enough: a town with snakes. So what? Well, it turned out to be extremely difficult, to the point that my characters were all either dying or nearly dying after every battle. Those damn snakes were crazy hard, and the weird part is that the difficulty spike sort of came out of nowhere – I had great equipment and a decent combo of powerful fighters and spell casters at that point. So, I don't really understand why that area was so incredibly challenging for pretty much no reason. Eh, oh well.
Anyway, why might I be recommending this game then? To be honest, I think a lot of it was how charming I found the game to be. The story made me laugh at its silliness, and pretty much everything about the game was dumb. Yet, the game embraced its stupidity and just sort of went with it. I love it for that. Yeah, it's clearly not amazing – the repetitive nature of the gameplay limits it quite a bit. For a silly little RPG Maker game though? Not bad, not bad at all!
Girlfriend Rescue is a strange mix of a charming and silly atmosphere mixed with slightly repetitive "beat up all the bad guys" turn-based gameplay. Sure, it has its fair share of problems, but overall this is a great addition to anyone's library. If you're not a fan of RPGs or RPG Maker games, it may not appeal to you, but for those who enjoy a silly story and a good ol' fun RPG, I think you may quite like this one.

I really don't like giving any video game thumbs down...but this is just not good. You spawn in a city and choose players, then you just go. No explanation. You just go. This is a flawed game, that said, it's also pretty fun. The battling in this game can get tedious, and the writing isn't particularly good, but those problems aren't so problematic that they ruin the experience. In my playthorugh I have enjoyed myself fighting the varied enemies, using the skills unique to each character, searching items for loot, and customizing my character's gear. The two biggest problems I have with the game is that combat grows repeteitive and boring if you play for more than an hour or two, and the fact that regardless of whether you put down your gender as male, female, gay or straight, you are always playing as a male character trying to save a woman, since the main character has no personality beyond wanting to save a the girl
I don't understand why your can't play as a female trying to rescue a man, or a homosexual female, or a male trying to rescue a male, all that it would have required was a skin change for the main character and a couple of alternate pieces of still art, if there was any animation or voice acting in the game then I would understand, but there isn't and the game asks you your gender and sexual preference at the beggining so I don't understand this decision. And as I mentioned, the main character has almost literally no personality, though the supporting party members make up for that somewhat, they actually have personalities, though those are all hilariously one dimensional. In the party from my playthough, I had a guy who kept on talking about working out, a girl who kept talking about cosplay, and a different guy who only ever talked about his "informants." there is something kind of funny about these characters, since none of them are actually crucial to the "plot" they can say whatever the writers wanted them to, and it shows. But in my opinion that just gives the game a bit of charm. The supporting party is also an interesting and unique take, at the beggining you chose three party members out of (I believe) nine who will be with you for the whole game. Each possible party member has their own completely unique collection of special attacks, which encourages replays to see all the different attacks. This might be more effective if there was any kind of animation in for the attacks, but there isn't any animation for any attacks. But the different special moves feel very different from each other, so this is forgivable. Visually the game is fine, it's got a cool retro thing going, and the colors in each level work well with each other, but overall it's boring. Nice looking, but boring. The soundtrack is nothing special either, most of the time it's inoffensive (althought the soudntrack in the first level got on my nerves really fast) so I wouldn't recommend it on that criteria. Overall this game is slightly above average, it's better than a lot of indie retro RPGs that get put out, but at the same time there are much better titles out there. If you find this on sale, or if you just want the indie game equivalent of a B-Movie revenge flick then this probably worth checking out.

Streets of Rage and similar brawlers have nothing to do with it, this is just your average RPG with pills and drugs instead of potions and magic. As for the “real world” setting, the contrived yet paper-thin plot gives several excuses to throw among enemies random stuff like zombies, medieval knights and Taoist monks just to recycle sprites presumably from other titles.
The combat itself quickly becomes a chore and most of the levels are particularly uninspired and repetitive (especially areas 4 & 5), with lame graphics and no different things to do other than fight. The characters are not interesting at all, and the writing is amusing in places, but substitutes the wittiness and charm from TBOL with slang and memes that quickly get old.
I don't recommend buying this at full price, and even then just if you're a JRPG fanatic.

NOTE: I have NOT played MWO before it entered Steam and hence will not take into the account of what the company has done BEFORE it's release onto Steam. This will be a first-impression of the game without any prior knowledge of the company, community and their actions.
So is MechWarrior Online worth playing?
Hell yes.
Is it worth paying the premium for?
Let's start with the overall basics of the game, it's the closest you can get for a latest-generation MechWarrior game. Being a Mechwarrior fan since the 1995 MechWarrior 2, I felt an extreme sense of nostalgia while playing the game. Launch PPCs using a TimberWolf from far has never felt better. However, the P2Win element, as per all F2P games, is obviously there. And the game IS shoving that right into your face. Despite that flaw, I'd say that MechWarrior Online is worth playing, but not worth paying for.
Here's why.
Gameplay Wise, the game is as solid as a MechWarrior game can get. You pick a mech, you drop into the landing zone, and you blow everything up. It isn't as fast paced as the spin-offs such as MechAssault, and stays true to the classic, oversized, clunky mechs that stomp around blasting each other with lasers. Newbies to the series will HAVE to play through the tutorial before going into matchmaking or risk getting stomped. Older Veterans from past MechWarriors should have little to no trouble getting familar with the game's controls asa in my opinion, the game plays very similar to MechWarrior 4 Vengence.
You pick a mech, you click on matchmake, and you're off to blow stuff up. There's several game modes, but most of them just consists of blowing up the enemy team, because it's THAT fun to blow up mechs. There's also a more serious matchmaking called Faction Play, where you team up with people on your selected Faction, and work together to win--imagine ranked play or ELO, or comp, you get the point.
The sound?
I'm using a subwoofer below my desktop, when my mech fires it's weapons, it's amazing. The lasers, rockets and autocannons are amazing for a F2P game. Or it could just be my childhood nostalgia kicking in.
The P2Win Element?
Yes, it's there, RIGHT SMACK IN YOUR FACE. As a newbie, your first mech is free, after about 25 games. However, you only have enough money to buy 1 Mech and equip it with decent weapons. Make a mistake in your mech purchase and you're outta luck. A typical matchmaking game would land you about 100-300k credits (or so). A new, stock mech, should you choose to buy a second (which you will), can easily go for 15M credits. Do the maths. Yes, it is a huge grind to get to your second stock mech, and the cost of equipping it with decent weapons? Ugh.
Matchs end with credits and how well you've scored, also, a screen which says how much YOU COULD HAVE EARNT if you've played on premium time. Yes, you can buy bonus credits using real money.
Stock Mechs for real cash? Yeah sure, just hand over $30, and they'll give you a stock mech, which you could have bought for 15M worth of grinding. The amount you hand them is NOT, in my opinion, worth the amount you receive. For instance, other F2P games such as Dota, LoL or heck, even MapleStory gets you decent items with say, $6?. That amount here gets you nothing close. Skins for a single type of Mech would hit insane prices of $10 and above. So imagine you have 3 mechs, you'll have to spend $30 just for skins themselves!
No, they're not marketable like CS:GO skins. Don't bother talking about reselling.
Also, Faction Play normally consists of players with insane mech build ups, most of which can outgun, and outclass you. So I'd personally advise for one to play normal matchmaking, get a nice mech collection THEN jump into Faction Play.
The Community?
2 game modes - Normal play and Faction Play. Normal play matches you with just about anyone, no coordination most of the time--it's essentially a 12 v 12 deathmatch. Faction Play, people get more serious, they use mics, they use fully equipped mechs, all the good stuff--Essentially, most of the guys here have played for a long time. They can be extremely elitist, or, welcoming to new players. For my time spent in Faction Play, the people that I've been matched with were really friend, save for a few exceptions.
Overall
This game plays ALOT of nostalgia for old MechWarrior fans, it might be fun for a while, but you'll begin to notice the grind element creeping in. Personally, as a fan of the series, I don't mind sitting at my desk, spending an hour or two a day on normal matchmaking and doing other stuff later.
TL:DR?
It's worth playing for FREE.
The premium content is ridiculous in pricing. Absolutely ridiculous.

Hello mechwarriors, and potential mechwarriors.
I'am a long time player, original founder, and competitive team vet. I also played ALL the previous iterations of this franchise, going all the way back to the beginning. For what it's worth. I have played in well over 5000 drops, own 200+ mechs.

Oh I have spent money, but mostly, because I wanted to, I buy mech bays, and premium time mostly and up until recently every mech pack they sold. You can play the game as a solo participant or as a group participant, here is the divide, teamwork is OP, and always will be in a game that boasts a 12v12 atmosphere.
Many people are reviewing this game, and many giove it negative reviews, mostly, because they are now, or at least were at some point, very passionate about this game, this is the common theme you will in reviews on steam for MWO, passion, it makes for a diverse and interesting commentary on how this game effects  the people who play it. Dear Esther. I have now walked the stretch of the island between the lighthouse and the aerial over twenty-one times, but although I have all the reports and all the witnesses and have cross-referenced them within a millimetre using my ordnance survey maps, I still find new things each and every playthrough.
I was an active member of Moddb back in 2008 when a strange and experimental mod called Dear Esther released for the first time. For '08 Source modding, it was game changing. Then in 2011 they announced they were going indie and released a stunning Source game in 2012. Now, in 2017, here I am walking these familiar cliff faces once more.
This game is hands-down one of the most emotional, engrossing journeys I have ever gone on. Thank you chineseroom for letting me explore the island with the narrator once more.

“Give sorrow words; the grief that does not speak knits up the o-er wrought heart and bids it break.”
William Shakespeare
Ready the whole bag of Kleenex tissues and make sure you’re alone when tears start falling, for another version of Dear Esther is upon us. Heralded as the first game in the “Walking Simulator” genre, Dear Esther still stands as the best of the bunch, with captivating visuals and artistic direction, outstanding music and voice over, and the gut-wrenching and mesmerizing story that will stay with you and haunt you long after you are done playing. And if you are like me, you will fall in love with this game. Dear Esther is a story about the loss, inevitability and acceptance; it is a timeless masterpiece that, even if it’s dark and sorrowful experience, will never lose its meaning and importance in the history of video games and in your heart. And if you’ve got one, you owe it to yourself to play Dear Esther!

My review of the original Dear Esther, posted January 10th, 2013:
Spot on, younger Dewie, spot on.
This game is not for everyone, admittingly. There are no enemies. There's nothing to blow up. Nothing is chasing you. There is no time limit or things to collect, nor are there awesome outer space battles (missed opportunity imo). Dear Esther not only started Walking Simulators, it remains the poster boy for the genre.
However, those (like myself) that enjoy and appreciate artsy games that have a story to tell and emotions to convey rather than objectives to complete will find something special here. My first trip across the island was a huge eye opener for me, a glimpse of what games could be. The (then) stunning visuals; the slow-burn of a tragic tale through narration by the absurdly talented Nigel Carrington; a masterfully crafted path across littered shorelines, winding cliffside paths, and through graffitied caves -- it all blended together to not only convey a story, but to show video games are as much art as any medium.
The 'are walking simulators actually games' argument might still be up for debate, but the impact of this game isn't, and for good reason. Put aside your expectations for a game, kick back, and get immersed. It's f^&k'n great, and worth your money.

Girlfriend Rescue is a game in the genre of RPG Maker. I met before the game in this genre, but never played like that. I will say that I really liked this game, did not know that the game is in two-dimensional graphics can be delayed for long. As for the plot - it is and it is cool :). A typical day at the cafe. She sat a girl who you liked, and then directly from the cafe it kidnaps the monster, you get up and go look for her slowly, fighting on the road against the infidels. Then I will not spoil :)

POSITIVES:
+ Absurd concept which throws you right into action (I'll go talk to my crush over ther- KIDNAPPED BY A NINJA)
+ Cheesy setting (let's say this lasts for the first 3 chapters out of 8)
+ Renaming your protagonist/girlfriend/party members. Allows some chuckles when you name them after friends or such.
+ I wanted to say "choices", but...
NEGATIVES:
- The *illusion* of choices. Game starts with asking for both your own and your crush's gender, seemingly allowing any combination. Straight/gay dude/chick? Technically you can choose whatever - but no matter what you pick, you will be playing a dude rescuing a girl.
Similarly, at the team-collecting stage you are asked if you want to go on the adventure alone - but when you pick the "yes" for that, you character goes "nah" and you are forced to gather a party anyway. This wouldn't be in negatives if these questions were never present, but the illusion of choice here is more disappointing than the lack of it would be.
- That cheesy setting from positives? Eventually goes stale when the game apparently gives up half-way and instead of being creative with enemies, it just keeps throwing more variants of Asian warriors at you and calls it a day.
- Lack of manual or a way to rebind keys. This results in having to go through trial-and-error to figure out all keys, some of which aren't the most obvious (like in party creation renaming your characters from the default name requires a backspace - which is bound to the Insert key of all things).
No manual means you'll also have a limited idea of how in-game stats work and affect your effectivity. This can be "fixed" with getting the paid guide dlc - which isn't exactly a thing one would give a Plus for.
- Annoying mechanics in the quality-of-life department.
Example 1) With hunger, game doesn't check when you last ate, but rather when you last stopped being hungry. This makes it common to heal a character with 3 pizzas, only to a few moments later hear him say "I'm hungry bro, got any pizza?"
Example 2) Red toros are a +50exp consumable. You find dozens and hundreds of them, but can only consume one at a time, each requiring the "worldmap -> menu -> items -> ok -> scroll down to toro -> pick toro -> pick party member -> ok -> automatic return to worldmap" sequence.
- Questionable difficulty, aka the reason I gave up and dropped the game. The game saves every 5 fights, and my party is currectly encountering ninjas in packs of few per fight. Each ninja takes 1-2 rounds to be taken down, and each can one-hit kill a party member if he feels like it. All that despite having my party members using best weapons and armor I could find and buy, actively trying to play the game in a smart way, and all this on "easy mode" (!) at that.

Recently finished, so here's my 2 cents:
Girlfriend Rescue is your standard issue RPG Maker game, both developed and published by Aldorlea Games (notorious developer of many RPG Maker games). Its a JRPG that handles similar to old school Dragon Warrior or Final Fantasy, but with a bit more room for strategy in both building your party and combat. The story itself takes place in a modern, urban setting which is a breath of fresh air (ironically) as opposed to your typical medieval fantasies. There's an interesting variety of characters to construct your party with, to which you will use to trudge through the 8 different scenarios. Explore a bit, loot things, fight baddies, and continue onwards. At the end of each scenario you get a little piece of story that serves as a reminder in case you forgot what the game was all about (see: title), and then you go back to walking and mashing the X button.
Its not the most fun I've had with one of these kinds of games, in fact I'm a bit disappointed in Aldorlea Games. After playing Deadly Sin 2 and Skyborn, I really expected more from this title. I only recommend it if you have absolutely no other RPGs to play.. or just really need that old school RPG fix, even then wait for a sale.
Pros:
+ Interesting variety of characters
+ Fresh, urban setting
+ Fast paced combat
+ Colorful visuals
Cons:
- Mediocre story
- Poorly written dialogue
- Repetitive battles
- Ugly enemy artwork
- Vague character/skill descriptions
- Messed up controls with my X360 gamepad
- Lack of settings (volume, controls, etc)
