When Loadout first appeared, it had a great deal of promise:
- Good graphics
- Campy animation
- Interesting weaponry possibilities
- An in-game store where you spend real money on things like apparel (i.e. you can't directly "buy" your way to upgrades) that still forced you to grind your characters up the levels (which is good).
Sure, there were bugs:
- Bot logic allows bots to shoot through walls, mountains, around corners, etc.
- Bot accuracy logic is cranked way to high.  They rarely miss.
- Some of the weapon combos create guns that are nearly impossible to beat ... or survive (get hit by a flame-based pulse shot and you're essentially done).
- Leveling up is maxed at level 40.  Not a bad thing, except that after that, you gain no more experience points, so you can't continue to unlock new weapon parts.  Once you roll Lvl40, you're stuck with that you have.
Still, it had potential.  The version 5.0 public beta previewed a new angle that looked even more promising:  multiple alien types with different behaviors and skills.  It definitely added to the play ... for the duration of the beta, which was shut down in January and not a peep has been heard since.  Come to think of it, communications from EoR essentially vanished after they announced the release of the PS4 version of Loadout, possibly implying that EoR isn't interested in supporting/upgrading/fixing any other platform.
This could have been a great game.  It still is fun from time to time, even though you can only play version 4.0 (though the images of v5 still haunt me as the game I wish I could play).  Yes, I do return to it from time to time, more from wishful thinking than anything else (I'm still hopeful, but that hope is fading fast).
With no news from EoR (apart form "thank you for participatiung in the beta ... we'll let you know if/when we ever upgrade the game"), there's no point is spending time on this game.  And there's DEFINITELY no point in spending money on this.
If EoR ever gets their head(s) out of wherever they are, I'm happy to revisit this review and change my opinion but, at this point, I'm not holding my breath as simply rolling out v5.0 isn't going to be enough to salvage this in the long run.
This is one of those cases where instead of "yes/no" for "Do you recommend this game?" there should be a "yes, but..." category.  My advice:  If you're into FPS games, and can tolerate some questionable NPC behavior, check it out.  But, don't waste your money in the game.
Once you hit Lvl40, delete it and move on.  It appears EoR already has.

Firefly Studios makes a brilliant castle simulator game, Stronghold. Then over ten years later they bring it back in HD, finally you can play this epic on modern machines. For those who never played a Stronghold game and for veterans alike this is a great game to get into.
This game is based on its campaign; a very interesting story involving you, a young man, bringing down the monstrous villains who murdered your father in cold blood. You embark on this quest with a small band of soldiers still loyal to your father to retake the kingdom. With a few allies along the way you vanquish the foes of the king one by one. In this epic campaign you meet series’ most notorious villains The Rat, The Snake, The Pig, and The Wolf; each one of these criminals crueler than the last.
This game introduces basic elements of castle simulation, mostly focusing on combat. You construct a castle, manage taxes, harvest resources, and construct weapons. In order to bring about this balance you must maintain popularity and income within your castle. Villagers will move in until your houses are full and you've got to make sure you can support them.
Some of the missions are near impossible even on the easiest difficulty. On the other hand some missions are so mind-numbingly easy even on the hardest difficulty. There are no achievements for this game and cheating is always an option. In order to beat the Pigs Castle the second time I had to use cheats (the gold cheat) so I keep building new catapults with my Engineers. The map took me for ages to beat, but other than that one mission the rest of the game was rather simple.
I would recommend shifting the game speed throughout missions. When you start each missions putting it at the lowest speed, 10. Then once you've got all your buildings in place raise the speed up to 30 or 40. When you know you have won the map move the speed up to 90 again in order to speed up the victory process.
If you like city builders, enjoy real time strategy combat, and prefer macro-managing to micromanaging then this is the game for you. I would recommend this game regardless of whether it is on sale or not, its a great game and you can easily get 12-hours out of the campaign alone. For an older generation game Stronghold is leaps and bounds beyond its competition.
Pros:
+You not only build a castle, but you also manage it politically.
+Military units require villagers as well as weapons/armor in your armory.
+The campaign offers a very riveting story that takes you across the Great Britain.
+The combat is rather intense and can require the usage of multiple siege tools.
+The market allows you to buy and sell goods in order to meet tough deadlines.
Cons:
-Sieging a castle can be near impossible unless you outnumber your enemy 100:1
-Some missions basically require you to cheat in order to win.
-Building an army quickly can be ridiculously hard because of the prerequisites (most missions I built a market and bought weapons rather than building them myself).
-No skirmish mode
-Poor unit mapping, many times units will spread out rather than clump causing enemy archers to shoot them (units hit by arrows will stand in position until they die rather than move themselves to avoid being hit).

Some people just dismiss this as being worse than WoT but Blitz does have some advantages and I do enjoy a few odd games of this:
Pros:
- Games are quicker and more action packed
-  No arty ( kinda pro )
- You don't lose credits in higher tier tanks ( big plus )
- Multiplatform game ( your account is carried over to the mobile app )
Cons:
- The game feels implified i.e. pennitration chances are marked on tanks
- Mobile grade graphics
- Not integrated with the other war gaming titles
- Currently a smaller selection of tanks than WoT
Overall this game has more of an arcady feel than World of Tanks would. The maps are smaller, games feel less tactical but the games are just quicker overall ideal if you're in a rush and don't have a huge amount of time to stay around for some possible 15minute games.

World of Tanks: Blitz is a backport of the same game on mobile devices running iOS, Android or Windows 10. It plays great and while it's easy to learn, it is very hard to master.
I'd say this is a game for those who already have some tanks unlocked in the mobile version and would like to play some WoT on Mac/PC. If you want to pick up a _new_ tank game, this game probably is not for you, you'll be better off trying normal WoT.
The game is not an exact 1-to-1 port from PC. Game rules and the content are a little different:
+1/-1 matchmaking
quick fix games (7 minutes max)
smaller teams (7 vs 7)
plays smooth 60fps even on old PCs
Visuals are a little different, too. WoT: Blitz looks much like older version of WoT, but considering this game was targeted mainly on mobile devices, visuals are excellent for a mobile game.
Progress you make on tablet or phone is synced with PC/Mac, so you can play either on the go, or in your cozy gaming den.

Years ago when TA was first released to the public I would have told you that it wasn't worth your time. Since I stopped playing however the game has significantly improved! For instance, loadouts are back! While the weapons and a few items are restricted to the bodytype now this is still a vast improvement, when I was playing regularly. Light bodytypes cannot equip chainguns, as an example. :P It's still possible to alter ones course while skiing, without aid from a jetpack, but at higher speeds this is more difficult. I believe hit-scan weapons are still a thing, but TA now has an option to simulate projectiles - which I assume means you have to lead your targets. Keep in mind, however, that this is an option and not a requirement - I'm also unaware if this can be forced via server options. The maps have also been updated, and are far superior to their original designs. All in all Tribes Ascend finally feels complete. TA had a rough start but it's finally made it, to that Tribes game status. That may not sound like much of an achievement, but when you're talking about a game like Tribes, it means a lot. Hardcore fans might still enjoy the older games, TA is not 100% like them after all - given the tech and design choices. With what is present in Tribes Ascend though, you won't be disappointed. Do you like chainwh*ring? Do you like abandonning any weapon that needs predictive aiming skill to use? Do you like spamming stupid autokill orbital strikes for a cheap kill?
This game is for you then.
Graphics. For very well done graphics and visuals. Unfortunantly this is not what makes a good person shooter. In fact the visual crap and doo-dads actually got on my way in combat. We know everyone ignores visual effects after about 10 minutes into the game anyways.
Level design. Most of the levels are too close together. I suppose they HAD to do this since a larger map on high graphics would bring most pre-2010 video cards to their knees.
Balance and gameplay. The weapons are ALL over the place and the discfuser and showcklance are on the back burner in leu of the plethera of submachineguns and assualt rifles. This is not Call of Duty, this is Tribes where aiming is HARD and predicting where you target is - is paramount. Did not seem a Tribes game to me at all. What happens when you make certain weapons really easy to use and really easy to get kills with is that the hard core, GOOD players leave the game entirely and the inexerienced kiddies and man-children move in. Then they brag about how they so owned you with a SMG from 130 meters. Yeah, it's like that.
Beta Tester support. Let's face it, Hi-Res spent most of their time on Smite and left Tribes:Ascend out in the cold. When Beta Testers spent up to $50-$60 on buying suits and weapons (something that should have been FREE), one year later Hi-Res crapped on them when they said "Everything unlocked! Sale for $20!". Yeah, I felt cheated after spending $50 in Beta unlocking HALF THE STUFF.
Final note:
I LOVE the Tribes game series. Starsiege, Tribes 2 and maybe even Tribes Veangeance (if only for the really single player campaign) are close to my gaming heart. What Hi-Res did this franchise put the nail in the coffin of this game concept that had so much promise.
Hi-Res did to Tribes what George Lucas did to Star Wars.

These sorts of 'ode to old school' type games I generally enjoy and Halcyon 6 is no different. It is a turn-based rpg that doesn't require any sort of high end system, so older, lesser laptops I suspect will run it fine. The game also provides a fair amount of variety of enemies and tactics.
I would hope however for the future perhaps a 2 dimensional board will be employed to also provide positioning strategy as well as the skill-based rpg aspect. I may be a bit biased though, I never got into any of the Final Fantasy type games unless it involved more depthy strategy.
In addition I will also hope for bigger fleets and larger fights. A proper space fleet, such as it is in naval combat, would offer a variety of roles to fill, for individuals fleets as well as individual ships. But, I understand I may be barking up the wrong tree here, this game is more of a 'pure' turn based rpg.
I would also hope for wider ranges of combat options and weaponry. Perhaps an option to customize your own class of ship? Or put more control into the classes available. Star Ruler spoiled me a bit with some of that, designing my own ships/classes to suit an intended and sometimes specialized role of my own design, every single attribute, strength and weakness, weapon, defense and any other goodie under my control.
It's probably a little overpriced for the content and depth of gameplay, but it is a fun game and suitable for probably the vast, vast majority of pc's still running today. If you don't mind the price or are patient enough to wait for a sale again it's a nice addition for the turn-based 'old school' 'Final Fantasy' style in space with pixelated, detailed gore and crafty, stylish artistry enthusiast.

The Steam Controller doesn't lack behind in quality and is as sturdy and well built as my previous xbox360 controller from what I can see and feel. The only complain I would have is that you can hear the modules behind the touch pads if you shake the controller but I guess they have to be somewhat loose.
Before I go too deeply into this topic it would be appropriate for me to mention that I have big hands and therefore favour big controller. Exactly that is the Steam Controller, big. It grips are bigger than your mundain xbox or ps controller which seemed weird at first but it's actually a pretty clever design choice. When I hold the controller my thumps automatically rest between the touchpads and the buttons on the right side and the control stick on the left side with both thumps pointung towards the pause and select button.
Which brings me to my next step the buttons. I really like the L/R 2 trigger and the control stick. Both are very responsive but yet not so sensitive that you have to be careful. The L/R 1 trigger on the other hand are comparably hard to press and loud which is annyoing and quickly exhausting for games that utilize them all the time like Dark Souls. The A,B,Y and X buttons are standard and the layout is borrowed from the xbox controller which is a nice thing for me since I was used to that one anyway.
It feels like the controller was made just for this game. The right pad emulates the mouse, the L/R 2 are the mouse buttons and every button on the controller corresponds to a function within the game, be it end the turn, quick save or simply pause.
It is possible to play Dark Souls 3 with the Steam Controller, although  I will probably stick to the xbox controller with this one. I could put the functions of the L/R 1 triggers to the triggers of the back or anywhere else but I am a man of habbit. :P
Works as you would expect for a racing game. Nothing fancy to see here.
After you memorized the layout of the controller and what which button does it's actually not bad and for casual play on the couch it's definitiey an option.
Most games I played weren't utilizing the pads from the Steam Controller as good as they could but thanks to the steam community and the houndreds of configs that you can chose from there will always be one that fits your taste or you just make one your own.

This is review of DOOM multiplayer mostly, if you're not planning to play online - consider this review positive and move on.
I'm a guy who spent lots of time on multiplayer shooters. 4k hours in l4d2 and 4k hours in TF2, hundreds in Quake Live. But singleplayer was always less important to me.

Ok, so let me begin
Mulitplayer engine is horrible let me point out stuff:
* everyrone is playing with >150ms ping what seems really strange for not that complex multiplayer game. Also it's hard to modify UI so you can see number instead of symbols.
* It auto selects region as america each time you restart game, even tho you leave in Europe.
* You spend so much time waiting for round to begin. It's like driving sport car in city while having red light each intersection.
* HUD might work in single, but i'm excepting something else for multi. It was really hard for me to tell if my equipment was ready to use - it was just so small i had to change focus from crosshair to bottom of the screen. Same goes for health and ammo.
* Incoming damage visuals aren't clealry noticable to which was pain.
* No balance system so you very often play 5v2.

This is a pretty awesome alternative to Overwatch. Many of the characters have similar gimmicks to the overwatch characters, but usually with a nice and fun twist to their gameplay. For example, Makoa has a similar weapon and abilities to Roadhog, even with the chain, however he is a better tank because he can create a powerful mobile shield. My favorite thing about this game is the creativity you get with each character, you can create a loadout for each character, which is made of 6 unique perks, buffing certain abilities of that character. There are plenty of perks to choose from, giving you a lot of experimentation. Not only that but in each match you get a bit of a DoTa 2 style upgrade system, where you can spend points earned during the match to upgrade your character even more. You can make your character build up their ult faster, or make your character have shorter cooldowns on their abilities, deal more damage to opponents shields, and so on. I do think Overwatch is a bit more balanced, but this game is overall more fun imo. I also feel that with the daily challenges & rewards, plus the in-game award system, it is fairly easy to earn enough currency to unlock the characters that you want. It is great fun to play with friends as well.

So yeah, I heartily recommend this game! :D

Dear Esther is the game that created the "walking simulator" genre, and for that I am eternally grateful. I first played Dear Esther as a Source mod way back in 2008, and immediately fell in love with it. It's a game that's much more about evoking emotions rather than telling a concrete story (though there is a concrete story there if you dig far enough), which was and still is pretty unique in the gaming world. Dear Esther is a poem in game form.
As far as upgrades from the Source remake, the biggest addition is the new developer commentary, which I greatly enjoyed listening through with the devs talking about their experiences and thoughts on the game. Graphically it still looks as good as I remember it. I'm sure it's been graphically improved, but I think it's a testament to the beautiful art style that it's still pretty much just like I remember it.
As always, Dear Esther (and walking simulators in general) aren't going to be everyone's cup of tea. But for me personally, I enjoy just chilling out after a long day and letting the dulcet tones of Nigel Carrington's narration and Jessica Curry's music wash over me.

Once again, after all these years, people come back to this pretentious pile of excrement masquerading as a game, and yet somehow it still doesn’t get the scorn it deserves. How anyone could possibly give this a positive rating is beyond me. These people must be the same ones who think a canvas composed of different coloured squares are art, or 4 minutes and 30 seconds of silence can be music.
Graphics are at least average; there are some nice models and textures, but the main problem is that everything is so monotonous and grey (with the exception of a relatively nice luminescent cave system about half way through the game). Everything from the lighting, to the textures, to the colour scheme is flat and dull.
Music is relatively nice, but it’s not the nicest I’ve heard in a walking sim. Some of it comes across quite pleasant, other times it can screech into your ear. The narrator’s speech drones on, as if his voice itself is dragging its feet, completely uninterested in what he’s even saying himself.
The dialogue and story is boll*cks; a relatively simple, grey, soulless tale, elevated into pretentious grandeur by bohemian-level writing. Poetry comes in many forms, but this writing doesn’t feel smart, it feels like someone just got out a thesaurus and tried to include as many words as he can.
Lastly, the gameplay. Or lack-thereof, I should say. I’m sure you’ve heard it before, but blimey. No interaction, other than walking forward and looking around. You can’t even sprint, which is horrible when you find yourself walking down a long section, only to find out it leads nowhere and having to backtrack all the way back.
There is no room for joy in this game. If you hate fun and have poor taste in art, then sure, try this out. I would say the game is too short, clocking in at an hour long, but frankly I was glad it was over with by the time I reached the end. At the very least, the most positive thing I can say about this is that it started the Walking Sim genre, which has spurred on other, more intelligent, interesting and – most importantly – more enjoyable games.

This "game" is a bit of a rollarcoaster. There are some positive things, but unfortunately it's just another free to play game ruined by a lack of focus, and a scarcely concealed paywall.
Positive:
- The gun models are beautifully made, and a lot of care has been taken to model every little pin and bolt on each of them. If you are into guns, or just want to learn about the mechanics that makes a gun or rifle work, then this is most likely going to be very exciting for you.
- As the game is fond of pointing out in the screenshots, there really are a lot of both handguns and rifles. For each gun you unlock, two more potential unlocks appear.
- There are multiple different modes of working with the gun, such as field stripping, complete dissasembly/assembly, taking it apart without selecting the wrong parts, etc. So if you like a particular gun, you're not gonna be done with it in 2 minutes.
Negative:
- Above all else, the biggest issue is the abuse of the free to play model. This game is free to try, and free to grind while loosing the will to live. Completing each mode gives you exp, and you use said exp to unlock new guns. However, the exp needed to unlock guns rise for each gun unlocked, and the exp gains from completing the modes do not. After unlocking your third gun, you will need to go back and grind the previous modes (which give ridiculously low exp after the first completion) to earn enough points to unlock more.
Furthermore, you have to grind even more exp to unlock shooting ranges, which are separate unlocks (without which you cannot try shooting the guns). There is also bonus content, such as cars and skeletons, which cannot be unlocked with exp at all.
Of course everything can be unlocked with cash, and the game is quick to remind you every time you get exp, that you could have had more if you had only bought an exp boost.
- Secondly, the reason I put game in quotation marks up above, is that this is barely a game. It's a gun simulator with a few challenges. There are only two gameplay elements: Stripping down guns on time, and the memory game of not clicking the wrong parts in a single mode. Add to that, that the timed play is pointless as it just compares you on a gigantic highscore list with tens of thousands of other players that you will never be as fast as. There is no local highscore list, no competing against friends, etc. It's pretty dull.
So for my part, this is unfortunately a bit of a disappointment. The idea of stripping down guns is fun, and I'd love to see it brought to other devices too. Unfortunately the lack of gameplay, and especially the consumer-unfriendly use of micropayments, completely destroys it.

Edit:  I am adding/removing things as I'm going through.  As a result, I don't consider this to be a full review.
It's possible that my review will change as I progress further into the game, but so far I'm not impressed.  Before I continue, a little about me.  I've been working with different versions of RPG Maker since the late 90s.  In fact, even now I'm working on an RPG Maker VX title that I will hopefully submit on Steam at some point, though that is easily months away from now.  That said, I have a number of issues with this title.
Almost everything reeks of generic.  The main character is not interesting, nor are any of the side characters.  The dialogue really needs to be entirely redone as it's very amateurish and riddled with multiple grammatical errors that I would overlook if they were attempting to parody other grammatical errors from other games, but clearly they are not.  There are a lot of subtle issues with the game as well.
For starters, barely pressing in one direction in a menu will often cause my cursor to go crazy and skip several lines or just straight up go into hyperdrive.  This has caused me to run from battles where I meant to go into rush instead.  While the graphics are entirely custom, the characters and environments are pretty terrible and low res in general, which makes the game feel that even further cheapened.
I mean, I get it...the sheer number of normal Steam users that complain and drone on about default RTP for RPG Maker more or less forces you to use custom everything and that's fine, but at least make it something halfway appealing and BETTER than the default.  It also doesn't help that certain things went unchecked.  For example, when you stumble upon a merchant, you have the option to deal or not.  If you select not to, it still brings up the shop menu.
These are things that should have been ironed out WAY before release.  As I said, it's possible that I will enjoy it more as time goes on (the opening cutscene was pretty nice for example), but as it stands this comes off more bland and unappealing than I had anticipated.

This RPG game is a nice change up from storming castles and dungeon crawlers.  Takes place in unique settings from planes, to trains, and city streets for example. Levels all have unique monsters that fit the level.  There are unlockable characters by beating different modes in different ways.  With the levels just the right size this game is great to speedrun, even better on higher difficulties where the characters move speed becomes super fast!  Great replay value!
There is no manual for the game that explains ANYTHING in the game or what skills do, or describes any of the stats.  Apparently some of that info is in a separate guide players can buy somewhere online, but even that doesnt include the details of what party members do what people say.  Only way to find a good party is to experiment around and see what works best, or just charge in blindly!   There is also no way to play full screen, hitting alt enter leaves those annoying black bars on every side meaning 30-40% of the screen is just black.  Its un noticable as the heat of battle kicks in though.  WIthout a manual its not a perfect 10 but its so close otherwise from great music to great replay value its a fun RPG to kill time with and change things up from the usual.

At first glance, and from it's straightforward name "Girlfriend Rescue" looks to be a fairly easy or casual sort of game ---- but not too long into the very first world you will find that it is full of intricacies, assorted choices, and complex decisions that reveal a great story that is very difficult to take a break from.
The story told is solid and good fun, the characters are very well developed and likable, and the action/exploration is virtually non-stop.
As the title reveals, your girlfriend has been kidnapped for unknown nefarious reasons in worn down Detroit, and you and your friends immediately set out to rescue her. A big part of the game is the creation of your party from the available characters since each character has different attributes which will change the way you approach the game ---- so the replay value is very high. (especially if you are wanting to unlock all the achievements.)
The artwork is beautifully done, the music adds a lot to the atmosphere of the game, and the gameplay itself is flawless.
There are a great many items to find and spells to use and learn so you need to explore the game very carefully to find everything. Each world (presented in a maze like style) will tell you how many enemies need to be defeated, and once defeated, they do not reappear. Defeat them all for big bonuses.
So there is great fun to be had here with lots of replay that will keep you busy for many hours. Give this one a try, and you will be drawn into a game that is a bit of a variation on the old style rpg experience that is familiar, and very appealing.

Inaccurate. Too many compromises.
Being a Nintendo DS player and loving the controls of Metroid (with the thumb stylus), I was actually quite hyped for this controller. It didn't take long though to realize capacitive touchpads will never work as well: while the resistive screen of the DS registers an exact touch point on the screen, capacitive ones keep track of the whole blob that is your thumb. The problem with the latter is that even tiny movement can result in huge input distances (e.g. when you press another button), due to the center changing. So theoretically touching the pad with as little skin as possible would help, but the concave nature of the pad counteracts this, even my phone is more accurate in shooters.
A bigger touchpad would somewhat fix this, but here comes my second point: ABXY had to go somewhere. A tiny version of them, though. Instead of going with a huge trackpad and covering one genre well, they tried to go with all of them. This results in quite an awkward layout. I have quite large fingers, and it is still uncomfortable to hit the shoulder button and touch A with my thumb tip at the same time, unless I hold the damn thing with just my fingertips.
I would use it if I had nothing else, but that's not the case.

This is the Linux of gamepads. If you're willing to put the time into setting it up for EACH game, and you're playing in Steam, you'll probably enjoy it. Only time will tell if I wind up using this more often.

Observations from the first couple hours of use:
PROS:
- Feels good in the hand, overall.
- The single analog stick feels great. Grippy.
- Wireless is optional. I wasn't sure about that going in, but sure enough, you can play it wired, without batteries.
- The right touchpad uses a clever combination of tactile haptics, and input behavior to simulate a trackball... and it really feels like one. Bravo to whoever got this going. The best part of this thing.
- Adorable, configurable musical ditty on power on/off.
- When the stars align, and you get a great config... it can be a really decent alternative to a traditional gamepad.
CONS:
- Solid, except for the triggers. They're easily the weakest part.
- The XYAB buttons are positioned very poorly. Unless you have much larger hands, they're far too much left for comfortable use. Which is why I said this isn't a 360 replacement -- it feels more focused on being an FPS/mouse replacement, where it generally excels.
- Can't use rechargeable AA batteries that are charged via the USB port. (So I've heard, at least.)
- Out of the box, every game, you'll almost certainly be A) picking an input config from the community, B) tweaking that config, C) wondering why the ♥♥♥♥ it's not working, D) fiddling with♥♥♥♥♥♥everywhere, E) giving up OR finally playing. Or if you're adventurous, F) hunkering down for a bit and creating your own config.

So I've been thinking about this recently, and I think this game might be evil. Not just Adventure Capitalist, but the entire clicker / incremental game genre.
While this is not the only genre that makes use of the Skinner Box to keep players going, it may be the only one to use it to the exclusivity of everything else (such as, for instance, a game). Some RPGs push their Skinner Box rewards to the point where it is debatably the only reason anyone plays the game, but even those maintain some semblance of a game build around their pellet dispenser.
At its heart, Adventure Capitalist is a game about watching bars fill up, with associated values increasing each time the bar reaches its apex. I say heart, but that's the only organ this game has. You watch bars fill up. Ostensibly each bar represents the dividends from different businesses, but in the end they are just identical bars with a different icon next to each. Other planets and holidays offer bars that fill at different speeds or have some kind of gimmick, but they too are just non-interactive bars.
If I were just reviewing this game in comparison to others in the genre, I might be tempted to throw a thumbs up at it. The aesthetic is fairly charming, the pacing of the bars is relatively well-thought out, and it doesn't feel as outwardly cynical as a lot of these clicker games. However, this genre as a whole should be avoided at all cost. It eats time that you will never get back, and at the end you were not so much a participant as an addict. It is possible to take the general premise of this genre and do something worthwhile with it, but this game doesn't even come close to that.
For your own sake, avoid this and any other clicker game. I'm a little sickened that I fell for it for so long.

This is a clicker game.  You buy assets, make money, buy more assets, then sell off all for angel investors.  In a nutshell, that's the game.
There is strategy in finding the right combinations, knowing when to reset angel investors, which upgrades to buy when, and what the best buys are at the right time, but ultimately, this game comes down to patience and patience.  Mid, late, and end game can take weeks between when you can progress between steps on the way up the ladder to fortune.
There are some laughs in the game, through references or the absurdity of the cash flows.  The game can also take some thought, with lots of need to consider long term moves (days to weeks in advance irl).
The game is free to play and pretty fun to play around with.  I'd recommend giving it a try.

Each time your mastery goes up a level you get a chest for that character, containing only cards and items for that character. I feel that by maximum mastery you can undoubtedly have max level on most if not all your cards for that character. As for the unbalanced feel because of this system, cards do not determine the outcome of the game. Non-legendary cards provide slight augmentation to abilities, and legendary cards just give your favorite thing more useability, meaning they are purely for making the character more playable for you, more thn powering up the hero. In the end the game is purely skill based and I am 100% certain that even without using any cards a lot of people could still make an impact in their games. therefore I highly recomend this game to anyone wanting an awesome and slightly more casual fps.

There are only three things I don't like about this game, and they're pretty minor:
1. Absolutely no cosmetic customization options are currently available (15December2015) without paying some real money. You can't so much as change your paint job without spending real money. Not a big deal to me, but not something I feel like spending real dough on, you know?
2. The pricing is a little predatory. You don't get a lot of virtual currency for your real cash - it's like Zynga designed their pricing scheme.
3. I don't feel like this is a pay to win game. I've won plenty without spending a dime! However, the people who are willing to dish out real money can get a definite advantage if they want it, loading themselves out with premier mechs and equipment. Skill is still a huge factor, and a good "free" player will still usually do fine, but it can be a little annoying watching a Hero-level Timber Wolf walking around the map... it's like watching that guy who got into a prestigious college because his dad bought them a new library.

Once upon a time in the late 20th Century, in an era of vintage classics, the great Lords of Gaming bestowed upon their subjects a series called MechWarrior. Those were good times indeed.
In those days I had happened upon a copy of MechWarrior 2, after being an obsessive fan of sci-fi simulation games like X-Wing, and strapped in to my first Mech Simulator and powered up - "All Systems Nominal." Everything got better from there that is until the Golden Century of Gaming had ended and the Great League of Publishers fell into dissarray (or were destroyed by the Word of EA and Microsoft).
After a decade or so of players keeping MW alive, with the franchise having fallen into the dusbtin of history, and MW5 being destroyed by the evil of publishers a kickstarter-like (but not really a kickstarter) declared MW was back in 2012, and with promises that it would be "awesome."
Was it in fact awesome? Let's see.
As most people may be aware, the first games in this unique series were made with a quality standard for premium type games. However, MW had been reborn, as a Freemium in 2012, made by developer Piranha known for classic games like Duke Nukem Forever Multiplayer and Bass Fish Gaming? Where is Jordan Weisman? No clue. The Nostalgia Was Strong and I threw my money into the 5 million dollar pile and be a glorified Beta Tester for 2 years.
For those that know me, I have a love-hate relationship and low tolerance for plenty of OTHER F2P type games and approached this game with trepidation. I gave it my best shot. A series, once based on the old BattleTech franchise, and doing the bidding of Space Lords from your Cockpit with detailed, branching Single-Player with an addictive, bonus Multiplayer - became
. I'll get to that at the end, but firstly what to expect out of this review:  My honest take on the game and what you can expect, either as someone brand new to this series or those who were aware of the original franchise.
The game overall left me simply wanting MORE out of it. Sort of 'ok' for a time until it set in how much it lacks in true content, depth, and a boatload of features compared with even the tacked on Multiplayer of previous games alone, let alone SP.
, but if you're like me where certain F2Ps just rub you wrong way with aggressive grinds and pay2notgrind nonsense or want a TRUE MechWarrior5, this just doesn't cut it. Frankly it saddens me that THIS is all that's left of the rich MW series. This is it? A shallow husk that feels 'average.'  It would be great if someone just makes MW5, but frankly perhaps MechWarrior should just be drug out back and buried.  All in all the type of f2p design decisions in this game holds it back from being truly great.

Besides all these funny things you can do at any time in this game, I wish to list all the pros and cons so you could understand what the game is realy about;
Pros:
+ An open world to explore, a BIG one, with 2 main environments - The school to which the main charachter goes, and the town around the school. Both of them are filled with side missions and main missions keeping you entertained for along time.
+ Flawless storyline built around the environments mentioned above with a lots of diversed missions, unlike most open world games.
+ Brilliant humor, mainly coming up through dialogs between the charachters but also from all the things you can do as part of the interaction with the world, and that would be the next on the list:
+ The interaction and possabilities in the open world - things such as smooching girls on a way to the class, running around doing wicked stupid things (such as mentioned in the beginning of the review!)
+ Great soundtrack
+ Long story/'campaign' - I played 15-20 hours and ony finished 1/3 of the game. There is a count of your progress by percantage that you can see everytime you save your game.
+ Fun/Dicking around factor is super high. If you love that kind of stuff this is the game for you.
Cons:
- Crashes Often on late versions of Microsoft Windows (8 or 10) - I'm playing this on a windows 10 laptop and this problem is fixable but the common solutions often do not work. Take this in to consideration if you want to buy this game
- The game wasn't designed for PC, therefore some of the QTE missions are annoying to do due to high fail rate (not optimal PC port)
- You have to save your progress manualy which can be annoing at first, although to me it's not even a con anymore (just get used to it and it won't bother you)
That's all I can think of, as a general opinion I would say this is an excellant game, even a brilliancy at some level.

A visual trip down memory lane.
This game was a feat that pushed Source to it's visual limits and birthed the modern "walking simulator" genre. And you really do JUST walk here, that cannot be understated. You just walk. There are sights to behold though. An average, vague narrative offers just enough to tie things together and a drop of original music completes the amazing atmosphere. I think the genre has improved in the years since but Dear Esther has moments. Moments are important in games. The lack of writing doesn't mean you won't find something here. For me it was simply walking up a narrow canyon and the trail crisscrossing over a creek. I felt immersed in a game for that moment thanks to a familiar feel. And it was fun to revisit the spot after all these years. Screenshots of the cave sections were my desktop background for weeks. Really, the level/environment design is what you're here for with this game. Some people find far deeper meaning in every bit of the game and whether from the get go or with hindsight, the developers agree. Though I might laugh and groan at the self congratulatory self confident artsy-fartsy stuff spilling out of mouths, I can still appreciate and enjoy the art.  Even marvel at it. I'm not buying what you're selling for a second but I'm buying what you're making so to speak. Dear Esther is a game and is whatever art is. But no more so than any other complete game.

If ever there was a product on Steam that didn't need to be re-made again, it's Dear Esther.
Dear Esther is a walking simulator. The most basic one there is since all you do is walk. There is ZERO interactivity otherwise. You're meant to just press 'w' and listen to the narrator drone on and on about the island he's on, lost love, and death. There is no running or jumping and no puzzles to solve. Just walking. Literally.
At least Gone Home had some puzzles. At least The Stanley Parable had a humourous narrator and situations. At least both of those weren't completely linear. Listening to the "story" the narrator told in this "interactive" fiction was boring at first and unbearable by the end of it.
As bad as the narrator is, turning on developer commentary (unfortunately required for an achievement) is much worse. Listening to three people refer to this thing as a "game" is farcical. This is not a game. Not in the slightest.
I really cannot recommend this thing. Not at all. Your time is better spent elsewhere. With actual games.

As for my Dislikes of the game there are a few things, most notably being the adventure mode. While the adventure mode of previous installments was nothing to brag about (excluding storm 2 and 1) this seems to be the worst so far. There is no advantage in playing it unless you are trying to get all the achievements in which case it ends up being a long drawn out farming session, going around, doing mundane tasks for people and then fighting normaly enemies with boosts to their defense and attack (basically a handicap for free battle). The one good thing about the adventure mode is that it does give a bit of insight into naruto: the last.
The second and last of my dislikes is the sometimes bad, other times downright awful connection you will have with other people. I find this most often comes when playing against people from other regions and other than that there may be  a short lag, but if you have a good gaming computer you shouldn't have a whole lot to worry about and I'm still hopeful that they will patch it. But besides playing against others in different regions, the game, as stated before, feels moderately fluid, even moreso than previous installments in my opinion.
The game overall feels fluid and is most definetely better than the last installment.

This was originally a mobile port of World of Tanks, now available to play on PC! Many original WoT players may wonder why one would want this game for the PC, considering PC WoT is much bigger and has a lot more content than Blitz. As a veteran of both games, there is a specific niche for both of these games.
The main plus for Blitz is the fact that you can play on both the PC and your phone, letting you continue your progress from the PC to your phone and vice versa. By the way, you can log in using your WoT account, but none of your tanks will progress from your original WoT account to Blitz.
Blitz is structured quite differently from PC WoT. There are different mechanics to ammo switching (you do not need to unload your gun to switch ammo, you simply choose and you shoot that ammo automatically) as well as different game modes.
I find Blitz a lot less stressful than PC WoT, I'm quite a tryhard in WoT but I find that I don't get as frustrated in Blitz as I do in PC WoT. The game is also a lot easier to play than PC WoT, so if you're a veteran of PC WoT you will do very (VERY) well in Blitz.

I'll get this out of the way: the Steam Controller is one of the greatest things to ever happen to me. It changed the way I approach gaming, and singlehandedly sucked me back onto the Steam platform in a big way.
That out of the way, some things you should know:
1. It works best with games already designed for controllers, but makes the experience much, much better. Simply put, look/aim with traditional analog sticks always sucked. Being able to couch potato while controlling my "mouse look" with a flick of the thumb is a complete revelation, and is the heart of the controller's user experience. That was the first eureka moment. First games I played with the Steam Controller were Dishonored and BioShock Infinite. Those titles + Steam Controller = perfection.
2. Easy to learn, difficult to master. I got the hang of the trackball in a few minutes. Then I spent hours upon hours digging through all of the customization menus. Tweaking every little sensitivity. You'll never see anything this deep on consoles--this is pure PC gamer menu-hell nerd bliss.
3. But crucially, the controller is *not* a no-brainer replacement for all FPS keyboard/mouse play. No, you're not going to be competitive on Counter-Strike with the Steam Controller any time soon. If ever. (Some guys on YouTube claim they are, and god bless 'em because I will never have that level of skill.)
4. That said, games that were previously keyboard/mouse only are now at least approachable with a controller. I played BioShock 1 with the Steam Controller--the experience was far from perfect, and I had to play on Easy. But it was doable.
5. Customization. Game doesn't allow controller remapping? Steam controller gets around that. It's also really nice to tweak customizations in order to play rando games that previously had rando controller showstoppers (I'm looking at you, Monkey Island 2).
6. It introduces some new concepts. Like the paddle buttons, which are my new "sprint" go-to. Or, have you ever used gyro controls to fine-tune your crosshair aiming or spill suppression? Me neither, but those were some more eureka moments.
TL;DR - even if you only use the Steam Controller for action, stealth, and games generally designed with controllers in mind, the trackball at your thumb immediately makes those 100x more enjoyable than playing with your trusty old XBox controller. Mouse Look without a mouse: that right there is worth the price of admission. The other pros, like customization and accessibility, are icing on the cake.

One of the best controllers I've every tried.
I've always been a PC gamer, and a blind supporter of KB/M over controllers, but some recent titles and actually using a few controllers slightly tilted me towards controllers.
The first game I ever played on a controller was "The Witcher 3", which I bought my XBox 360 controller for. After that, I really felt like using controllers are actually really comfortable.
After Witcher 3, I tried a few other games with my XBox 360 controller, like Metal Gear Solid V. It was good, but aiming was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ And being a PC gamer used to mouse aiming, I gave up and went back to using KB/M.
Mad Max went great with controllers so did Batman Arkham City, and both was very fun.
I also got Forza 6 from the windows store, didn't even bother trying it with KB/M.
I tried playing GTA V with a controller too, but you guessed it, aiming prevented me from playing for too long.
In the summer sale, I saw this the Steam Controller was on sale for 35$. I decided to try it. It arrived about 2 weeks ago. Using it at first was a bit uncomfortable, being used to Xbox button layout, but I got used to it fast enough.
In short, I loved it. The XYAB buttons are a bit too small, but other than that, the controller itself is fantastic. Aiming? I won't say it as good as aiming with a KB/M, but it's close. Very close. Specially if spend a bit of time tweaking it to your liking. I no longer play GTA V with KB/M, only with my Steam Controller.
On other games, well, The Witcher 3 is best played with the controller and this one doesn't change that, but because of the grip buttons you can have more controll. Quicksaving? Just a grip button click away.
I also got Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor in the summer sale, and played it only with this controller. It was amazing. I had trouble executing combos with the 360, and this cotnroller fixed that. I just remapped grip buttons to Y+B or others, and it's no longer a hassle.
Do I recommend it? Of course. Specially if it's your first time getting into conrollers, you'll get used to it easily and won't have the "adjusting time" I had, coming from a 360 controller.
Highly recommended, for any game.

I did not like this game. Theoretically it has everything it takes to make a great strategy game. It's stable and not buggy. What it's missing is colour. Flavour. Spice. Endless Space is, like outer space, boring.
The science research is generally pretty boring. Either it adds a point to this or that stat, or lets you build a new building that enhances a stat. There's nothing that feels fun, where you anticipate getting a research item because it opens up cool new possibilities in strategic depth. It's more like, "Oh now my fleets can have 6 ships instead of 5... wow..." Compare and contrast with Master of Orion, where you could have black hole weapons and teleporters, cool stuff that change how the game plays.
Combat is worse. There is only one (possibly 2) viable strategy and a dumb card mechanic and super boring non-interactive combat scenes. I started reading something else while the combat scenes were going, because they're so long and uninteresting. As a game design mechanic they have you play cards during the battle. I believe they did this to encourage people to watch the combat, but all it does is force you to sit through the combat if you want to play the game optimally. Bad design. Compare with Master of Magic's highly tactical combat, or Civ 5's simple and quick combat, either style of which is much better.
I think Endless Space 2, where they've retooled everything and made it fun, would be great. Endless Space the original, however, I don't recommend.

A friend got me into this game quite some time ago, and I had a blast with it.  Don't let the time on steam fool you since I've been playing for 50 to 100hrs of game time, potentially more.
In short, MechWarrior Online (MWO) is an interesting game where you get to pilot your own X ton robot to blow the crap out of other people piloting their own X ton robot.  The game can be fast or slow, depending upon what type of team you get into.  Members of the community can be a mixed bag where you'll get some helpful veteran players or jerks.
What drew me into MWO wasn't the aspect of it being free, but the depth to which you can customize your playthrough.  Mechs that have light tonnage can be extremly fast and agile.  This lends itself to a quick playthrough, but you're a walking target since armor is quite limited.  On the other end of the spectrum would be Heavy/Assault.  Do NOT confuse the two as Assault mechs are the heaviest class of mechs (the Atlas being a primary example), and these boys do some serious damage with heavier firepower.
Overall, I would give the game a shot, however, I will give some word of caution.  This isn't an FPS game where you run in guns blazing to take down every single enemy in sight.  It's a more tactical approach where you have to isolate targets and attack as a coordinated group.

Add a turn-based battle system like a Mana Khemia or Atelier game ( in which the turns are visible as a timeline on the screen ), and a complex set of status afflictions.  Now give it a pixel graphics look and the twisted sense of humor of Star Control 2 (AKA the Ur-Quan Masters ), and you've got one Hell of a space game.

This game is basically pokemon with spaceships. No, wait, it's like Pokemon FTL!
When you first start up the game, the tutorial shows you everything at once, and you may feel a little overwhelmed. However, after a few hours, it all starts to make sense. You are running a starbase, and in some ways the tech and structure building is like Civ, or even XCOM, though much simpler. Research is done the moment you can afford to click it. The further into the game you get, the more things open up. Your only military units are your officers, kind of like a team of pokemon, or your main cast of an RPG. You'll want to spread out your cast, and have as much variety in abilities as possible.
While some may not like how slow it starts you off, it's for the best. The first few hours will have you fighting simple battles and leveling up your first few officers. What you'll soon learn is that battles are decided by how you use your special abilities. Most abilities do both damage and give your enemy a debuff. For example, your cannot may doo 100 damage, but also disable the ship's engines. This will make your enemy slower, sure. You can cast ability after ability to make your enemy slower, weaker, poisoned, etc. There are dozens of buffs and debuffs, and it's impossible to remember them all, so don't even bother.
However, a better way to think of that attack you just pulled off is that you just turned your enemy into a water type pokemon. He may be slower, but he's also weak to electric attacks. And your fellow officer just happens to have a electric attack, baby. Now your second officer's ability, which is extra effective against enemies with the engines down debuff, suddenly does double damage, AND turns your enemy into a grass type Pokemon. What you want to do is figure out ways for your teams to synergise, because if you can manage to have teams that take advantage of each others' attacks, your team becomes very powerful.
By the time you've figured all of this out, the story will have ramped up, enemies will become tougher, and you'll have enough officers for 2 fleets. And then you'll realize one of two things: 1) This game is freaking awsome! 2) This game is shallow as hell! Honestly, I fall somewhere in the middle, a little closer to the freaking awesome end of the spectrum. The art style is great, and everything is intuitive enough, but resource gathering can be a little tedius. There aren't many bugs left at this point, but the music can start to get a little repetetive.
All in all, it's Pokemon is space. Seriously, if you like RPGs or Strategy games, and you like games like FTL or XCOM, then this game might be right up your alley. I recommend it.

I have to say I agree with other negative reviews on this game. I really liked this game at first, but it has some serious flaws in it.
First, and most importantly, this game simply has no balance. Resources, especially crew, can stretch very thin very quickly. When you lose a game, it will be because of one mistake. The game will punish you for making one.
The space combat is interesting at first, and the ideas seem clever, but at times they simply make no sense. Your damage overtime abilities suffer because of this. If you use a skill that causes damage over time, then use another skill that combos with it, the damage over time stops. You think the damage would get worse. If you cause a hull breach, for example, and use a skill that exploits it, the hull breach is magically healed, along with your damage over time. This is flawed logic and makes zero sense.
The space combat is servicable, but eventually devolves into simply doing the right things in a proper order. It's also hard to tell if a fleet of ships will do well in combat without actually trying them out. I've had one fleet be quite devastating, and then another be completely worthless.
The ground combat goes from incredibly easy to hopeless disasters at a microsecond's notice. It's just plain poor game design.
Also be aware of other things that make no sense. An example is my level 10 ships being stuck at level 10. In my research projects, it says something about having to be an admiral at level 13 to do that advance. I could not figure out how to unlock the next levels, or perhaps my game is bugged.  There are a lot of things you are left in the dark about.
Don't worry about replay. New games have little difference from the last one.

Drowning in an ocean of pretention deeper than the water surrounding Dear Esther's island, DE: Landmark Edition is a remaster of the original nominee for "Most Dull and Boring Game Ever, Please Do Not Let This Become A Thing". It, however, did become a thing, as Dear Esther paved the way for an influx of walking simulators. Whatever your opinion is of the genre, I am not the biggest fan, but I can be privy to some. This is what frustrates me about Dear Esther--it frustrated me 3 years ago, and it does now, too.
There is absolutely zero interactivity in this game. You walk. That's it. There is no jumping, there is no action or activation or what have you, and there is certainly no mechanic at all beyond walking and falling. You must be the sole witness to a narrator reading off line after line of flowery poetry disguised as a letter to "Esther". When you're not listening to him drone on and on, there is nothing but absolute silence as you crawl (I say crawl because that's how slow you move) across the linear paths on the island.
Why mention other walking simulators? Because they do so much more. Games likeThe Stanley Parable or Gone Home offer interactivity, clever thinking, physics, just--SOMETHING besides walking. Despite being walking simulators, they still offered so much more than Dear Esther did. While these games came out after DE, this is currently a review for a remastered edition in 2017, which means we should look at it as a piece that has released in our current time and not so many years ago--which means I absolutely cannot recommend something so heinously dull and unexciting when there are better walking simulators--or actually, better games, than this drivel.
I got as far as I could (not long at all) because I wanted to give it another shot. But if you know the story already, no amount of pretty visuals can hide the sheer tedium of the slow crawl narrated by some pretentious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There's just so many better ways to spend your time, and I encourage you to do so.

Besides all these funny things you can do at any time in this game, I wish to list all the pros and cons so you could understand what the game is realy about;
Pros:
+ An open world to explore, a BIG one, with 2 main environments - The school to which the main charachter goes, and the town around the school. Both of them are filled with side missions and main missions keeping you entertained for along time.
+ Flawless storyline built around the environments mentioned above with a lots of diversed missions, unlike most open world games.
+ Brilliant humor, mainly coming up through dialogs between the charachters but also from all the things you can do as part of the interaction with the world, and that would be the next on the list:

+ Fun/Dicking around factor is super high. If you love that kind of stuff this is the game for you.
Cons:
- Crashes Often on late versions of Microsoft Windows (8 or 10) - I'm playing this on a windows 10 laptop and this problem is fixable but the common solutions often do not work. Take this in to consideration if you want to buy this game
- The game wasn't designed for PC, therefore some of the QTE missions are annoying to do due to high fail rate (not optimal PC port)
- You have to save your progress manualy which can be annoing at first, although to me it's not even a con anymore (just get used to it and it won't bother you)
That's all I can think of, as a general opinion I would say this is an excellant game, even a brilliancy at some level.

Paladins is a great game with some balancing issues (as there is expected to be from an early access game) and although many may call it a knockoff version of Overwatch, it really isn't.
But why am I giving Paladins a negative review despite all of this? Simple.
HiRez does not care about their community. At all.
When the developers of a game receive backlash from a large majority of their community for their "fun and innovative" ideas as well as a post on the frontpage of IGN centered around players against the Paladins OB64 update, you would think that the developers would think twice and revert the changes or at least consider changing the parts about the update that nobody wants to see come to public release.
Don't talk about this situation as if it's a matter of pride; the Paladins developer team has reverted an update before after everyone critisized it, and even so with the amount of community backlash they've gotten with the OB64 update you would think that they would at the very least swallow up their pride and admit their faults with the update. The fact that the Paladins developer team has pushed yet another update that nearly no one wanted even while the game has hit a record low in players online proves that quite simply put, the developers are not interested in your feedback, and nor are they interested in keeping Paladins alive.
One more thing you might want to note is that a lot of the games HiRez has spat out in the past were fairly popular and fun to play, but the only one that still thrives to this day apart from Paladins is Smite, so I guess fool me once, shame on you, fool me twice, shame on me, and fool me a third time and it's about time I clean my slate of HiRez games.
If you are coming to enjoy a brief time with a game similar to Overwatch but free, download Paladins.
If you are downloading the game to stick with it for a long while, then you are taking a gamble.
That gamble is not one I am willing to take.

Halcyon 6 is a pretty damn fun game, with some flaws. The game takes RPG elements and combines it with strategy and management genres and molds it into a smooth adventure, for the first few hours at least. Halcyon 6 starts off amazing, everything is fresh, the options you have seem vast and exciting and you ruin into a lot of different scenarios. However, as the game goes on things start to become a little tedious. Missions become the same thing painted differently, and resource management becomes a chore.
Lets talk artwork. Its good, great even. I like pixelated graphics but I always am a little held back by the animations that usually go hand in hand with them. Halcyon 6 has some fantastic visuals though. Attacks in battles are appealing and explosive, the background images of space are captivated, characters are well made and their animations flow smoothly. It's very easy on the eyes, and very cool to experience.
As far as story goes, its a pretty simple concept. I wont spoil much, but lets just say theres not a whole lot to spoil. Things are exciting but after a while the excitement begins to fade, but I'll get to that in...
Gameplay. Freaaaaaking sweet. You start out small feeling like most everyone is a threat and you have to play smart to become victorious, then as you progress you get bigger and bigger ships making yourself feel like a hulking force to be reckoned with. But after a few hours of doing missions over and over, enjoying them mind you, you start to lose your sense of accomplishment because enemies and missions just because the same thing but with enemies with slightly higher HP and slightly higher damage. It's really not game breaking but its still noticeable.
The big thing that frustrated me most was how resources worked. It becomes a chore to visit each and every system to get resources over and over again, because if you dont you can't do a whole lot. You need resources to research, repair, build rooms, hire officers, everything. WHICH IS EXPECTED. But you are constantly going back and forth between the system and your base because even traveling to collect resources costs resources. It's just plain annoying. This is one of those games that is a really good idea, and has some really good mechanics, but in its current state I just can't recommend this. The basic premise is a solid one: you manage a starbase in the midst of an invasion by a species of very hostile aliens. You have to manage your starbase a la XCOM, do turn-based combat with the alien invaders both in space and on the ground, and manage your various officers.
Some of it is very good; some of it is very bad. Combat isn't too bad; most of your damage-causing abilities can be enhanced by status ailments the enemy receives, so you want to synergize them. But it means most fights proceed the exact same way: tag with blindness, tag with engine damage, exploit, stun when needed, heal when needed, win. In and of itself, it's not bad; at least the difficult boss fights require some careful strategy about timing. But there are SO MANY fights that it often feels like wave attacks of fights that mostly happen the exact same way each time, and they rapidly become boring.
Pacing is also a serious issue with this game, because you need to sit back and consolidate resources. It's sort of counter-intuitive; you want to delay progressing with the plot for as long as possible. But some thing will force your hand, whether it's the wave of enemy ships or other encounters. And God help you if you haven't set up an efficient collection system.
Speaking of resources, they're kind of broken. Dark matter always seems to be a real bottleneck in this game, so the first infrastructure you should invest in is improving the production of dark matter facilities (which costs dark matter) and then building satellite drones to automate their collection (which also costs dark matter). Ships cost dark matter, research costs dark matter, repairs cost dark matter...Materials, by contrast, feel kind of useless and unloved, and even on commander I had an enormous surplus of them. The devs made the good decision of implementing the satellites; prior to that, you had to (constantly) send out fleets to pick up resources.
Base management is pretty dull. You don't really make decisions because there's only one correct way of doing things. For some reason, you can't demolish rooms and rebuild new things there, so that's a frustrating design decision. Some rooms also seem to have absolutely no purpose; the Chruul Lab is used for one thing in Act I and then serves no function in Act II. Ships can be researched for improvements, but guess what, that costs dark matter, and it's better to rush development of the next tier of ships.
On the higher difficulties, leveling up multiple fleets is also far too difficult. The resources are too limited to build the most advanced ships for all of your people, and as the enemy ships become more powerful it's suicide to send less-leveled officers and weaker ships up against them. But then you get caught in a Catch-22: it takes high-level officers to pilot high-level ships, but you don't have them because you can't level them up in fights. Base activities can theoretically give them XP, but it happens too slowly to stay competitive. In effect, you'll be stuck with one fleet until Act III, when if you've made allies with the NPC factions, they'll give you high-level officers (on the higher difficulties).
But those allies are a tremendous pain in the♥♥♥♥♥until then. They contribute nothing and constantly ask for assistance, especially in Act II. Your own colonies are vulnerable to invasion, but in addition to protecting them you need to safeguard these allied factions' colonies or your reputation will suffer. Yet it's just that many more fights you have to deal with in a game where there are already far too many. I actually hoped the aliens would just wipe them out and make it easier for me. Those pirates who I helped, and helped, and helped again, what did the do for me in Act III? Nothing. Good God, their pirates kept attacking me even after I rescued them. I should have saved the resources and let them die.
The game also feels frustratingly incomplete for a game supposedly not in Early Access. They're promising more random encounters (they happen, but I swear in hundred-day stretches) and all of these other upgrades, but the game is supposed to be complete. It doesn't feel that way. With that, I just have to say that this isn't worh the money at present.

World of Guns is an interesting game in which you get to disassemble, and reassemble guns. At first, I looked at it and thought "There is no way I'll like this.", but then I started playing it. I thought, 'Why would I want to do that?' almost every step of the way, after all, it's just taking bits out of a model and then putting it back together.
Well, it turns out that if you have a few minutes to spare while a friend is off doing something, or half an hour before going to work with only boredom to keep you company, the prospect of a gun model to pull apart and put back together is pretty pleasing.
Most things appear at first to be accessible with no payment needed, and a few that you can get by being the daily top score on a gun. It's free, so that's great value already, and you get hourly quizzes for bonus exp(Used to unlock more guns).
So then, how does it play?
You can field strip a gun, taking apart only bits of it, and then putting it back together
You can disassemble and reassemble a gun, which is doing the obvious
There is a simulation of how the guns work, with slow down, x-ray vision, and multiple magazines and assesories you can use
After you completed those, you will unlock the 'game', 'supergame', and 'hardore game' modes.
Game is a time attack, you have to disassemble and then reassemble your model as fast as possible, with bonusses for not clicking too fast and not clicking any part that you aren't going to activate. (Hint: Spacebar activates whatever you have selected, this will help your time a lot. You can also turn off the auto-zoom to selected parts in the options)
Supergame is also a timed mode, but now you get to time your activation a second time on some parts. If on time, the part moves out faster. If not on time, it's slower. You get a bonus for not clicking too much.
Hardcore game automatically activates any part you click on, and you can activate multiple at once. This is where things get fast, with large amounts of bits, pins, screws, and all sorts of springs flying all over, you'll get a bonus if you don't click anything you can't activate
And in all this, you will become very familiar with what I have called the "Ikea effect". Namely, there will be one or two little screws or pins somewhere that you can't find, possibly having vanished into the ether when you weren't looking. Luckily it isn't modeled on reassembly, so you won't have to worry about a spring rolling under somewhere and disappearing into an alternate plane of existence
Gun enthusiasts, you probably already have this. But if not, I recommend it to you.
Others, if you enjoy score-based or slightly competitive - With the whole playerbase or just between you and friends, this may be a good choice
But aside from that, if you just want to grab something simple to spend some time on between things you're doing, this is a great choice. The small size means its a fast download and the short gamemodes means you can spend as long as you want on this. But I'll warn you, perfection on a model may take a lot of time
(I would also recommend a youtube search for LethalFeline, he has videos up of him playing if you still aren't sure)

Mechwarrior Online is a fun game.   There's very little like it - most mech games tend toward the anime super robot genre - lighting quick maneuvers, rapid fire, and a fast pace. MWO bills itself a 'thinking man's shooter' because it's pedegree has been real robot from the beginning. The mechs drive like tanks - legs independent of torso twist, and the largest and toughest of them are slow and ponderous.  Some weapons have extremely long reload times between firing - Gauss Rifles have a five second reload time as of writing this, plus a .75 second charge time before firing - nearly six second between shots.
If you've played any of the old Mechwarrior games, it feels very similar in terms of gameplay - the visuals are great, as is the soundscape of lasers and missiles firing.  Like all Mechwarrior games, there's a sort of sub-game in the customization and weapon loadout you choose to fit your mech with, balancing the internal space available in your mech with the amount of tonnage your machine can carry.  Getting your machine just right for your preferred playstyle is an accomplishment which is always enjoyable.
The Quick Play tab is great and matchmaking generally only takes a minute or two at the longest.  With the current matchmaker, the matches tend to be pretty close and it's largely fun - drop into a team of 12 to blow up another team of 12.  Matches take an average of 6-9 minutes, and cap at 15 minutes. It's a fun arena shooter, with some maps being enormous and some more intimate.  Map repetition is a bit of an issue - you vote on maps before a match starts and the community has certain maps they don't like, so you may not play on Terra Therma or Forest Colony very much.
That said there are some downsides - at the moment the Community Warfare/Faction Play is terribly barebones, and dominated by large units that organize thier drop decks and plans.  A new player attempting Faction Play is not likely to have a fun time, which is a shame, because Faction Play is one of the few ways a new player has to reliably gain more mech bays - the slots needed to own mechs.  You start with 4, but need to master three variants of a single mech in order to get beyond basic pilot Efficiencies with it.  The monetization scheme is a little unfair as well - mechbays are reasonably priced, but mechs may cost up to $45 or $50 for a single mech if purchased with MC. The packages offered on MWO's website are a better value, costing $7-10 per mech or so, but that's still very expensive compared to many F2P games.
Overall, I reccomend it, as it's fun to play, but I'd be careful about spending your money on it.

Endless space is a 4x strategy game.  Set in a galaxy populated by strange, diverse races, you must expand throughout the galaxy, with the goal of dominating the galaxy through many different way, ranging from very peaceful to military subjugation.  In my time playing it, I was quickly grabbed by its clear mechanics and an awesome interface.  It wasn't until playing this that I realized what a big difference the UI made in the enjoyment of complex strategy titles.  The game is clearly inspired by the Master of Orion series, though for my money it's actually better than them.
As a 4x game, it has several features of the genre: expanding, researching, ship building/war, and diplomacy.  I'll talk a bit about each.
Each 'star system' in this game functions similarly to a single city, in thats its production, food, science, dust (the game's currency), and approval is bound to that one system.  Each system contains up to 6 planets, of different types, that the player expands to once a planet in the system has been settled.  I found this to be an elegant middle ground that allows for a galaxy full of planets, but without the need to tediously micromanage each planet.  The different planet types range from comfortable earth-like landmasses to inhospitable lava planets.  The more difficult to settle planets offer substantial bonuses things like industry or science, but cause unhappiness and lack food of their own.   Later on, players gain the power to play god and terraform planets to suit their strategy.  Managing how to best exploit these systems is a great part of the appeal to me.
Star systems are linked in a node system, though later technologies loosen things up.  I felt this provided much needed structure to the systems, and allows for strategic placing of outposts and fleets.
The game constantly presents the player with difficult choices.  I always feel pulled by several extremely useful technologies, not to mention each race's custom technologies. It always feels like there are many viable strategies to pursue, and the tech trees allow numerous ways to meet challenges.
I've often found the ship building to be too complex for my tastes in other games, but everything here was straightforward for me, there were still difficult choices between weapon types and the balance between defensive and offensive units.
While most of the game is told from a crisp overhead view of a galaxy, combat will happen (though it's possible to play very peacefully).  Fortunately, the combat is gorgeous.  Ships for each race are diverse and detailed.  Combat moves through three main phases, with each phase allowing combatants to play a 'card' that grants specific offensive or defensive bonuses.  While it cannot totally turn around lost battle, clever usage of them can enable you to overcome superior foes.
The diplomacy is simpler than I'd prefer, as is the lack of a leader screen.  It feels like an opportunity to add more personality to the game was lost.  You can set up all sorts of trade deals and alliances, but it lacks some of the more sophisticated elements that a series like Civ has.
Fortunately, some personality is added to the game through random events, ancient relics found on planets, and heroes which can be recruited to you empire, each with their own backstory.  Each hero can be assigned to a fleet or system, potentially making it much more powerful.
There is a satisfying snowball effect as your empire becomes more powerful.  In fact, with proper terraforming manipulation, you can easily quadruple a particular type of output across your whole empire in less than 15 turns.  It's hard to see this game reaching over 200 turns.  My first win came at 165 turns, and my third and most recent clocked in at 112.
As a nitpick, there are some mechanics for the game that I wanted a deeper explanation of.  While there is a tooltip for almost everything, I wished there was something in the game like a Civilopedia that catalogued every mechanic in depth.  It's really only need for min/maxing, but it would save having to dive into the wiki many times.
Overall, this is a 4x game that I highly recommend. I've tried many, but few ever interest me like this.  It's mechanics are simple to grasp, but there's enough depth to allow for interesting strategies.  The 8 different races for the game each feel liek the bring a very unique playstyle, and if that's not enough, there's the option to create your own.
Two final notes: I've not tried the multiplayer, but I've heard it's perfectly functional.  Also, some new users find the game very difficult, but that has not been my experience at all.  Holding out a planet against the AI can be done with ease, and the AI seems to always accept lengthy ceasefires. There are plenty of helpful guides out there that teach the fundamentals.
5/5 Ebin
