While i have only played 30 minutes on the steam version, i have already clocked in a good 70 hours on the original World of Tanks on pc and another 40 or so on the mobile version of World of Tanks Blitz and another 10 on the newly released World of Tanks Blitz on the Windows store. The game is great, it's basically a downscaled and simplified version of the original World of Tanks, it has less tanks than the original, and less maps. it still has micro-transactions in it that is available in most free-to-play games. However, micro-transactions only allow you to progress faster in the tech tree, the further you are on it, the tougher your enemies. The micro-transactions are not pay-to-win
The gameplay isn't very different from the original World of Tanks, only that it's faster, the maps are smaller, and matches generally last less than 5 minutes. a new armor highlighter system has been added for this version of the game, letting players see which parts of the armor are easier to penetrate. this however, may turn off some of the more hardcore players, you must understand however, that World of Tanks Blitz is designed as a casual game, not a heavily competitive one.
progression is somewhat of a grind, where you have to collect xp coins to upgrade your tanks, and to progress in the tech tree. as mentioned earlier, there are less tanks in the Blitz version of the game, however, regular updates every month or so add more tanks and armored vehicles into the game.
graphics is as previously said, the same as the original world of tanks, but downscaled. the textures are not as sharp, and the models are simplified.
overall, it is in my opinion that it's a great game and worth a try for anyone who likes simple and fast tank combat. if the beta is closed on steam but you still want to play this game, you are able to download it on your mobile phone or from the Windows store

I've read a lot of the reviews and I think most of them focus on the fact that the steam controller is not better than a keyboard/mouse. Yes, a keyboard and mouse are better than a steam controller, but the real question comes down to wether or not a steam controller is better than a classic controller (360,ps3,etc). Here is my opinion on that.
The steam controller is great if you are looking for an alternative to a classic controller for FPS games, or games where aiming in general is required. It is also great for games that would normally require a mouse, because the right touch pad can be configured to be exactly the same as a mouse.
The downside to the steam controller is honestly just it's button design. The touchpad that is supposed to be a D-Pad on the left would be better suited just as a normal D-Pad in my opinion, and the buttons for A,B,X, and Y are just too darn small.
The right touchpad as a replacement as a joystick is the best part about the controller though in my opinion. Having a touchpad as a poor-man's mouse instead of using a joystick is a godsend in any FPS. If you are someone who is tired after work and doesn't want to sit up at their desk and would rather sit back in their recliner or couch to play a game, the steam controller opens up more for you. FPS shooters are more of an option than they otherwise would be.
So honestly, it really depends on what you are using it for. I think ultimately Steam is on the right track with this controller. If you can find one on sale (I found mine for 25 bucks at a local retailer), it is a great alternative to a classic controller if yours is starting to get old.
TL;DR - Touchpad on right is boss. Other buttons 2 small. Better than classic controller for FPS.

8/10
Pros:
*Easy, intuitive base management
*Engaging space combat
*Game atmosphere (Setting/Story/Visuals)
*Detailed unit management and team building
Cons:
*Unsightly, but not gamebreaking bugs (Mission tracker not clearing completed missions, graphic glitches, etc.)
*Lackluster ground combat
*Game pacing (No time to enjoy your triumphs while the universe is in peril!)
*Difficulty design
Definitely a diamond in the rough undergoing continuous improvements and updates. If you ever wanted to scratch the itch of steering a loose federation of interstellar races against a galactic enemy then you'll need not look any further than Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander. It does Star Trek better than the Star Trek franchise has in recent (and sadly, distant) memory. The story fits the setting and the dialogue invoked fond memories of the Star Control series.
The game's systems develop naturally and each challenge seemlessly draws you into the next phase of the game. Although I thoroughly enjoyed myself, I was unable to shake the feeling that the game's pacing eventually became frenetic as time drew on and I was unable to enjoy any of my newfound game options. I all but abandoned the ship upgrade research tree until the final boss because the game outpaced it. Also, the game has a system to keep your pilots relatively even in level, but even that fell short for me which regulated me to having an "A" team and then a "C"-ish team (at best).
Massive Damage, Inc. has stated that they are committed to the game and so far they have eagerly accepted feedback and issued updates containing bugfixes and gameplay improvements. I have no doubt that this game will receive the polish it needs to become a true gem.

This is an amazing JRPG/Management game. Its basically Admiral of Starfleet Simulator 2016. Its not a rouge-like and its definately not FTL. Non-combat aspects, such as research, resource collection, and base building, allow you to build up your fleet's strength. A great castle building and strategy simulation.  I'm glad to see this in an HD remake for modern systems.  I just really enjoy this game a lot and it i definitely one that I keep coming back to several years after its initial publish.
The game plays a lot like any other "simulation" game in that you don't have direct control over the minions you have available.  Rather, you make buildings that provide jobs for your minions.  This creates chains of industry.  For example, you spot a woodworker's hut to gather wood.  Then spot a Fletcher's workshop to create bows.  Supplement this with a cow farm/tanner's facility to provide leather armor and now your fletcher can begin making crossbows (or it could be iron...haven't played in a while!).
Strategy comes in laying out your castle defenses or siege equipment, depending on the mission.  Sighting walls, towers, and gates can provide almost god-like advantages in holding off massive sieges.  On the other side, deciding where to send your tunnelers and siege equipment while covering them with archers can open holes in the most vulnerable of positions.
If you're looking for the latest graphics, or expecting something visually spectacular, pass up this game for something else.  Stronghold HD is just a resolution update for a game that came out in 2001.  Also, the AI can be downright predictable as it tends to want to assemble in the same place and wait for a while before beginning its siege phase.  This makes some missions laughably easy as you're able to set up traps in this assembly area and slaughter the AI army long before they begin to make their first moves.
Altogether, though, it's a fun game.  Definitely a must-play if you're a thinking type person who likes a bare minimum of city planning.

I am a huge fan of Masters of Orion 2.  I eagerly anticipated Masters of Orion 3, but it left me disappointed.  In many ways, Endless Space is what Masters of Orion 3 should have been.  The graphic are very visually appealing.  I sometimes find myself just gazing upon my planets when I zoom into a system because they are so pretty.  Another plus is that you manage your empire primarily at the system level, rather than the planetary level, so you don't get bogged down managing build queues for several dozen planets.  However, despite this system focus, each planet does offer unique contributions to your empire.  The game allows you to create customer races in a manner similar to MOO2.  You also have the ability to create customer starships, although not at the same level of detail as MOO2.
One of the games drawbacks is the combat.  You control combat at a very high strategic level, issuing just a few commands each round, and then twidding your thumbs and hoping for the best as the battle plays out in front of you.  There is a skill element to it, in that you have to try to pick a strategy that complements your fleet but also counters your opponent's strategy.  But often times this ends up feeling like a flashy game of rock/paper/scissors.
Another drawback is that the victory methods seem very mathmatical.  For example, you win a diplomatic victory by making deals throughout the game.  Each deal contributes to a percentage that adds up over time.  Once you reach 100%, you win.  To me, this makes victory feel anti-climactic.  I can't help comparing it to games like Civilization V or even Masters of Orion 2, where a diplomatic victory can become a very exciting effort to accumulate enough votes to win an election.
Ultimately, I would recommend this game, with two caveats.  1)  Unless you're super impatient, this game isn't so great that it's not worth waiting for a 50% or 75% off deal.  2)  If you are going to get it, buy it with the Disharmony expansion, which improves upon the base game a bit.

TL;DR at bottom
Dungeons 3 is most definitely a parody game, riffing on Lord of the Rings, Warcraft, Diablo, Star Wars, and more.  It's narrated by the brilliant Richard Ridings, who also did Dungeons 2 and The Stanley Parable.  The gameplay, like Dungeons 2, is a mix between RTS and Dungeon Managment with an overworld/underworld dual map setup, respectively.  While I do feel like the overworld is a little shallow, it's done well enough that it's a good compliment to the dungeon management aspect.
While playing as the [adjective/descriptive phrase] Evil, you have access to 3 separate races: Horde, Undead, and Demons.
Horde have a very straight-forward, Hulk Smash, A-move play style, along with the ability to be healed during combat.  They are also the race that does most of the engineering, so if you want to go for fast traps, you'll need to tech down the Horde tree.
Undead are more fragile, but they don't permanently die upon, well, dying.  Instead, they teleport back to their tomb to regenerate.  They've got some powerful support abilities, such as the Banshee's ability to Slow targets in a cone in front of her, or the Lich's ability to do AOE slow damage.  Additionally, the Undead are responsible for resurrecting fallen Horde members with the right tech tree and construction requirements.
The Demons are more ranged, with even their tank unit being a mid-line attacker.  There's a good mix of abilities and DOTs they do, and the ability to convert enemy units to your side.  They will generate mana for you, so dipping a few points into their tech tree early on is not a bad idea, as it allows you to more frequently cast spells.  Similar to Undead, Demons return to their portals when they die, allowing wave-based tactics.
I got about 30-35 hours of gameplay out of it, and I enjoyed most of it.  There were times I felt like the game just wouldn't end, and several missions took me over an hour to play, as they were challenging and kept me on my toes.  The last several missions, once you have all the tech trees unlocked, are easily the best designed.  I enjoyed this game, and I gladly give it a recommendation.
TL;DR:  Overall, if you like Dungeon Management games, I recommend Dungeons 3.  If you're a hardcore RTS player, this will be a light snack before moving on to something like Starcraft, but it's definitely fun.

I had been thinking about buying a new controller and I saw this on sale a little while back and said sure, yolo.
Initially I was mixed between disappointed and impressed by the dual touch pads. I really liked the idea of two touch pads so I wanted to like the controller even though it felt really weird in my hands. It certainly took time to get used to, but I'm glad I did, because I tend to have a much more enjoyable gaming experience because of it (and notice the word tend).
Feels like a good quality build - it's lightweight yet durable.
Extremely customizable - you can map pretty much anything anywhere. Have your joystick send d-pad commands or key(board) presses, it doesn't freaking care. You can also set a hotkey that changes what inputs will be sent (e.g. holding the left grip could turn your d-pad into a joystick input if you wanted). There are also community templates that are uploaded, and generic templates you can customize yourself. Lastly, you can save your configurations to your steam cloud so you won't need to worry about losing them.
Grips - Two buttons where your fingers already are. This is super convenient for many reasons (easy reloading, jumping, mode switching, etc)
Gyro (physically turning the controller to send input) - I'd never used one on a controller before and it is just an awesome thing. With a small amount of tinkering with the settings, I immediately noticed how much easier it was to aim precisely. I couldn't imagine a first person game (or anything that involves aiming really) without it now.
Touchpads - Relatively precise, but mainly good for swiping and getting the general angle of things. I did notice that after using them for a little while now I can navigate my computer using the controller fairly easily. In game however, combine a touchpad with the gyro to be golden.
Haptic Feedback - It's pretty much everywhere. But in a good way. The gyro gives you haptic feedback so you know how much input you're sending, the touchpad does the same, the d-pad can also do the same, the joystick can "click" (haptic feedback) when you set certain thresholds, and you can set how much haptic feedback you want from each thing (or none if you hate it). It goes on. Moral = easy to feel how much input you're sending.
How it holds - I personally like how it fits in the hand. My hand's are probably between small and medium closer to medium, but some controllers make my hands feel jammed up especially when my fingers are touching and it's just weird. But more of this will be in the cons.
This list probably isn't going to be as long but overall I like the controller so that makes sense right?
Physical Button Layout (personal con) - The d-pad/touchpad thing is on the outside, and the joystick is on the inside. This is inconvenient for me, because typically you use a joystick to move, and for many games I can usually handle
of the other inputs with my right-thumb (including d-pad), depending on the game obviously.
With the dpad being on the outer edge my thumb can't get to it, so I'm currently trying to get used to having the left touchpad act as a joystick while treating the joystick as a dpad. The main problem is, without this setup, it's difficult to keep moving while continually sending inputs from both the d-pad and buttonpad.
Edit Note: This isn't an issue with most games, and there are other solutions you can come up with yourself (e.g. hold a grip to have the buttonpad send d-pad input, or even something more complex)
--update: upon getting used to this I now prefer to use the d-pad as a joystick (for movement) and the joystick as a d-pad.
Customization - I saw someone post it as a con in some other review that too much customization was bad because it takes time to fine tune each configuration. I agree to an extent, it can be tedious to get that layout and you may spend a decent chunk of time just trying to get the controls how you want them, but you may also end up with very intuitive controls.
Force Big Picture Mode - I like big picture mode when I'm just finna chill n game n sh
, but this may be a turnoff to people. However, I did just run the Witcher 3 from .. not... big picture mode... and it auto overlayed the ... big picture mode... overlay... without having to turn on big picture mode. So you'll be forced to use the overlay but at least you won't have to enable it before entering a game. Or something. This was a grammatical disaster, sorry?
I would recommend this to anyone who games often with a controller. If you, like, occasionally sit down on the couch to play... Plants Vs. Zombies? or something, this may not be for you, as it will definitely take getting used to.
Congratulations if you made it through this review, I'm surprised I did. I'll update this if my opinion changes.
EDITS: Clarity, Updates, Grammar

First impressions after around 1 hour of gameplay:
- The sound effects are awful. Either too low, or so loud that it gets completely distorted.
- There is no music.
- Most of the time, the game is silent. When it is not silent, there is some explosion or some loud sound.
- The graphics don't look good. Specifically, the lighting effects and the particles look awful.
- Building blocks is not as fun because it requires both clicking and using the keyboard numpad. Minecraft got it right, putting blocks in Minecraft is fun and intuitive. Putting blocks in Blockland is not.
- The physics engine is weird and bad. I started up a new single-player kart racing game, drove for a few seconds, and accidentally hit a wall. The next second I was flying across the map.
- Multiplayer kart racing is not fun. At one moment I'm driving, at the next moment I'm flying across the map because someone hit me.
- Due to poor car handling, I have not managed to finish any kart racing. Neither in single-player, nor in multiplayer.
- I don't know if it is triple-buffering or something else, but I feel there is some input lag in the game.
- It has an achievement called "Gay Pirate". I guess the author thought it would have been funny, but it is not. In fact, it is completely out-of-place, and some people might view it as offensive.
After 1 hour of gameplay, I'm wondering why I bought this game. Well, it was because it cost me 2 dollars. But now I wonder if I will ever play it again.
Then I come back to Steam Community and look at the developer response to some reviews. I'm really starting to regret buying this game.
Note: Using keyboard to place blocks can be very handy sometimes. However, requiring it all the time is not practical, as it means I need to move my hand away from WASD or from the mouse. Not fun.
Note 2: At least the game has a borderless mode (besides the windowed mode and fullscreen mode).
Note 3: The entire game has less than 100MB when installed.
Bottom line: I had more fun exploring worlds of Second Life, playing the single-player survival mode of Minecraft, and building levels in Cube Engine and Sauerbraten.

Now, to be fair, I'm a BT/MW self confessed fanboy, so PGI had a big head start in gaining a seal of approval! That being said, I highly recommend giving MWO a look. On condition that you don't want a game where you're instantly godlike in terms of skill. There's a bit of a learning curve, but if you put a bit of time in and accept initially you may well have terrible matches initially whilst you learn the basics, you'll be well rewarded. My suggestion - watch streams, I learnt a huge amnount when I first started (twitch is a good place to start), and ask questions of the streamers and the viewers. 99% of the MWO community are great guys and girls who will be more than happy to help.
MWO is a true free to play game. You can be successful and have fun without spending a single penny. At most you used to have to admit, well, you do need to buy mechbays at a buck or two a pop, but PGI give so many away these days (via Faction Play achievements for example) that even this isn't necessary any more. Mechs come out in packages for real world monies with some extra swag (if you pre-order early enough) several months before they're available for in game currency. But that extra swag is mainly cosmetic, nothing in there gives you an ingame advantage. However, those exact mechs will be available for free eventually. There are no 'you must buy this to win' mechs. Hero and special mechs come with a boost to the earnings you can make in in game currency per match, at 30%. However, those mechs don't garauntee you will have a good match, they're no better than the standard variants available. Champion mechs give a boost in a similar way but to XP earned. In all honesty, champion versions of the standard variants aren't something that's ever appealed to me.
When you have a mech, you need to 'level it up' through basic, elite and master skills. This slightly improves things such as it's heat efficiency, maneuverability, speed etc. Which is where the XP comes in. XP is earned in matches along with CBills (currency). You have to have 3 variants of a mech at full basic level before you can work on elite skills. Once elite skills are done, you can then complete the master skills. Once one mech is mastered for a weight class, you only have to basic three variants of a new mech, from there you can if you choose elite and master a single variant. This levelling of mechs is where some folks say it's a bit of a grind, along with earning cbills to buy new mechs, but I've never found it to be too big of an issue personally.
There are also mastery packs available which give you several variants of a mech chassis that are available for cash, at big savings if you bought them separately (plus some extras I think but I'm not too sure on that). I'm not going to comment on the value of the mastery packs, after 3 years and 150 or so mechs in the garage, they're not something I've had a need to look at, so I'll just make you aware they're there if you want to take a look at them. But at a glance, to me they seem good value if you want to spend real money on something which largely (but not everything) consists of content available for in game currency. Value is subjective, if you have the cash avaialble, it's your choice!
Anyway, personally I love the game, when balance issues arise PGI are usually pretty quick to change things, content is free flowing, and quite simply the game is a hell of a lot of fun! And the great thing is, there's much more content to come from PGI and MWO!
This is the game where I have spent the most money and also the one I've played the most. And will play :)

Full disclosure, I'm a founder that's been playing since closed beta.
Even if you ignore all the controversey including PGI selling a bill of goods and then pulling a bait & switch, most of which is detailed in this article

-addition of real money consumeables(buying power)
-addition of 3rd Person View allowing players to peek over ridges
-addition of ghost heat limiting viable builds that are already limited by a chassis weight class, number of critical slots, number of hardpoints and their locations to discourage laser/PPC boating due totheir pinpoint accuracy. Resulting in players being cored within seconds of a match. This resulted in lasers and PPC's being suboptimal as they were never buffed after the devs limited how many could be viably equipped relegating them to supplementary weapons because of high heat output, delay between shots on standard lasers or reduced range on pulse lasers.
it doesn't change that the game itself isn't for casual Battletech fans. Especially with mech pack pre-orders in the hundreds of dollars that are withheld as timed exclusives until an arbitrary date after they are released. 'Whales' are willing to pay which is why the pricing structure hasn't changed since the beta.
Virtually everything in the game besides non-hero mechs carry a premium real money price in the form of MC(MechCredits), including literally paint, none of which can be unlocked over time via the in-game currency you accumulate through normal play(c-bills).
One of the biggest problems is the mechbay gating system. Each mech you own artbitrarily requires an available corresponding mechbay. If you have 10 mechbays and 10 mechs, you cannot unlock an additional mech until you either sell at a loss that you've already spent time leveling up, or you purchase an additional mechbay which can also only be purchased with MC. Effectively, you will always be spending money on the game. It fails as an F2P title because you cannot unlock using time as a currency by simply grinding out enough in-game currency through nomral play.
TL:DR
Bottomline, I love Mechwarrior, I've been a fan since the 90's. Even in MWO I love tweaking the mechs, the combat is fun even with the flaws and I like being able setup various weapon groups to control which weapons fire independently of others. It's been proposed in the past that they offer a VIP system where once you've spent a combined minimum total on the game, you would unlock VIP status that would remove the Mechbay system and give you a permanent XP/C-bill bonus and maybe even a permanent 10-15% discount on premium items that would stack with sales promotions, if not also unlock the all the paints. I would gladly spend another $50 or $60 on the game if it granted those benefits. Sadly, however, I cannot recommend the game in its current incarnation. Hopefully we will eventually get a proper Mechwarrior 5.

I can recommend this game if you meet these two reasons:
1. You love Battletech.
2. You don't mind a Free to Play setup for your Battletech game. (Free to Play being Pay to Win)
Now with that being said I downloaded this for free realizing it was Free to Play from the description. No harm there since I want to look things over. I tried it out and the test range tutorals and it feels like a mix between Mechwarrior 2, 3, and 4. The mechs handle nicely and the graphics are very nice during game play.
The interface for creating custom mechs is there but it's somewhat limited to the hard point concept setup I'm guessing in started in Mechwarrior 4. That's the first time I remember seeing something like that which limited choices on mech/omni-mech designs. I hate that part of the game since I used to be a big time pen and papper battletech player and loved creating mech designs just to try out. So in that respect the game is limiting for me and puts a dampener on my interest in playing. The other aspect that contributes to this is the Free to Play model limitations.
Personally I wish this wasn't an MMO Free to Play setup. The game is good but I think it would have been better if it were more like the Mechwarrior series before it in that there's a single player campaign but with a more robust multiplayer setup. This is basically a big cash grab using Battletech. Nice if you have the cash to blow on it but not so much if you want more then just that.
Update 01/14/2016 - I put some time in to this and some money. The barrier for entry in to this game is dependant by the choice of grinding out tons of C-Bills for mech and equipment purchases which is perfectly fine. The other aspect is the fast track to buying mechs with real money. That being said the prices for some of those add-ons is really high when you look at the mech bundles.
In game mech purchases provide a wide variety of choices but there are some limited to the Pay to Play credits or Mech Credits which you buy for real cash. Also expanding your garage for more mechs requires you to put real cash in which seems fine to me really for a pay to play system as well as the certain mechs requiring paying cash to get.
A big downer I've had playing however is that in order to get better mastery of a mech you like you must purchase other variants of that mech and pilot those. So basically to level up your favorite mech you have to pilot other mechs to unlock the higher progression trees. I think that stinks in that if you are going to master something you don't practice with something else to master it.
I feel this was put in to push people towards paying to buy mechs more frequently. The game itself isn't fun when you have to pilot something else to level and play the one mech you enjoy most.
There is an instant messaging system in the game for when you aren't in matches so don't expect to find many social areas in the game itself like chat rooms or something. I've yet to find them myself in there. Really it's like paying WoW's BG system with Battletech and not having any place to socialize afterwards. I'm guessing you are limited to game forums and steam forums for that.
Final thoughts: Don't spend any money till after your first 25 bonus matches are completed. Stick with the trial mechs and use them to get your initial C-Bill boost. It'll go a long way to saving up for a mech you find fun to pilot unless the trial mech is a Mech Credit only mech where you have to pay real money for.
Final Final Thoughts: No Linux client is a real downer for this game. But that's OK since Battletech coming out in 2017 will have a Linux client.

I Beta Tested. I Backed it. I left it a long time ago.
It was refreshing abit to come back, but the core issues on the game keep coming back to me on this, and as such - I just cannot reccomend it.
There is so much in this that "isn't" how it should feel to me, making this off-putting, at least as it is for this specific game/goal.
It is not Mechwarrior. It isn't anywhere close to BattleTech. That much makes the naming only for the looks - but I have to admit, it looks great. Its just not the same in either the lines of the old Mechwarrior games, and the translation of the numbers from BattleTech makes this feel choopy.
The gameplay is much the same as it was. It feels "floaty" in a way that can only be described as this is a FPS with a mech-skin. Think Modern Warfare or Call of Duty and the gameplay makes so much more sense.
The biggest issue for me is the mechs have no weight. They feel light as a feather, responsive as any twitch-shooter, and as such breaks the immersion of the idea - you forget you are driving 100-ton mechs when the respond like a sports car.
That to me is why this doesn't feel right. But that's my feelings on it.
The game itself, the way it plays, the intent the devs have put into this is... alright, but its just not how I would think the game should be. It doesn't strike me as Mechwarrior outside the appearance. And that's it.
The other major reason I gotta complain? When I backed this in its beta the cost for mechs and parts were reasonable. Cheap, effective - now? Its like pulling teeth through your toenails. They bleed you dry in this Pay 2 Win. And it is P2W. You need to grind for perks, grind for credits, grind for that mech - until you grind to the parts that work and eventually the neigh-broken Clan equip. All the while others are standing on the top of that shooting you back down to the ground.
It just doesn't feel right. The MM is dodgy that way, often placing vets against newbies, slanting the games into a slaughtering ground.
All and all.. it feels much the same it was back in the day. With a direction that just doesn't feel like it should. Not Great by any means - but also not horrible.
So long as you get into it knowing and understanding its P2W, grinding, and its somewhat off-kilter approach to featherweight mechs you'll probably enjoy it - but don't expect much more from it.

Adorable. Deadly. Hectic. Challenging. A bundle of many unusual elements together to form one of the most fun games I've played.
Rabi Ribi is a game that surprises me with how much it has to offer for a single playthrough and beyond, offering a main playthrough that will last most players around at least a couple of hours. In addition to this, there is a lot of incentive to replay the game with ng+, post-game bosses/content, a free Halloween themed DLC with a hell of a fight, and many ways of rewarding players who wish to go the extra mile of challenging yourself via silly handicaps, speedruns, no items, etc. Non-linearity is embraced throughout a majority of the game with only gradual bits of the story restricting you from particular areas. You can determine how difficult bosses become via scaling with story progress or on the area by choice when you start off your playthrough, the first being more friendly for beginners doing mainly story progress and the latter being for those going off the course exploring to your liking.
Gameplay consists of a chaotic and fun mix of action, platforming, and shmup/bullet-hell elements while navigating a Metroidvania-esque world map with lots of exploration, hidden items, secret spots, and more. While navigating through areas is interesting enough clearing a variety of enemies while looking for fake walls or breakable surfaces, the real meat and bones of how it plays comes together well bundled in the game's many many boss fights, with all having unique patterns that keep you on the edge and get gradually tougher and complex as your difficulty increases. No need to fear though, Erina has an arsenal of different shot types, a hammer to melee with, several unlockable items, and many techniques and tricks up her sleeve to reward skilled players, several which are related to hidden achievements so I will not discuss them here.
If you feel intimidated by the difficulty or are having a hard time progressing, no need to fear. The game offers easier difficulties, a continue system that offers a special buff to reduce damage taken (not avaliable on hard or higher), and there are healing items avaliable. If you are still struggling with the difficulty you chose, shortly early on in the game is access to an NPC that offers to make the game easier.
On a final note, I wanted to discuss the art style if it is a concern for those who are not generally a fan of anime styled art, chibis, or any of that. I'd implore for you to look past the looks as it more focused on gameplay while not burdened with excessive fan service despite appearances or preconceptions you might have about the looks of this game.
Still doing post-game as of this review and enjoying it. Highly recommend this game to anyone.

CONS:
1. Its achievements are cookie cutter for each item...Ex: A bonus game is available were you disassemble a human skeleton. Successful dismssemble of the skeleton awards "technician," successful reassemble awards, "armouer"...thats just lazy programing..at least change the names.
2. Muisc is horrible...its is a 1 minute loop of bad WWF/WWE theme music from 1994...over and over and over and over.
3. Game lags between mouse clicks, which in accuracy drills like "hardcore" cost you the game. Example: You know a weapon system like the back of your hand, and you dont click in very precise spot, the game registers it as a miss (as attributed to #4 below).
4. The camera system in the game auto swings, depending on what part you click, many times causing you to miss a click on an object, or waste a split second where you know what you need to click on, but cant because the camera is swinging around (of course you are penalized in xp for a mis-click, or for slow speed...all a ploy for you to pay $$...more on that later).
5. Very repetative actions kill the game when forced to go through so many motions on weapons you have no interest in. The whole game is based on XP gained from successfull guided assemble and disassemble , then unassisted assemble and dissassemble, and then timed assemble and disassemble, etc....see the pattern.
6. Game doesn't always record your stats after each round, or occassional "erases" all of your stats "temporarly." This can be fixed by going into an already completed gun, and redoing a portion. Again...wasting my time.
7. No ability to see ahead, and plan towards unlocking a weapon YOU want to unlock. Unfortunately, all but the next possible unlock tier is visable, so you dont know which tree to begin unlocking in order to make progress towards the weapons you want to unlock until you have already wasted the xp (which is NOT that easy to get once you have "mastered" gun).
This all leads to to my biggest gripe...
8. Of course if you actually want to play the game as advertized ("Assemble and disassemble your favorite guns!") or put an end to the infinite "whats behind door #2" game where you blindly waste xp that took you an hour earning taking apart and reassembling a gun you didnt care about....just to find out that you also dont care about the next unlocked gun either....
YOU CAN GIVE THEM $49.99 to unlock it all.....
Conclusion:

At least call it what it is...its a Demo. NOT free...

Shame on the developers to think they could charge as much for this game as full release of Skyrim, CoD, or Battlefield 4. This game has way to many bugs and glitches and feels way to unpolished...
Wait until the summer and it goes on sale for $6.49...then think about it.

My review is based in the rose tinted machinations of nostalgia having played both Warhammer III and Dungeon Keeper (1 & 2).
Based on that rose tinted knowledge, I would happily give this game a thumbs up, and i'll summarise the reasons why you might want to buy this game:
- Developers are good at adding new content and updating.
- Dungeon building is always easy and the option to replace dirt will help those with OCD like tendencies.
- Easy to understand mechanics, and the balance between overworld and dungeon play is well put together.
- Nice variety of units
- Story mode was pretty good for helping get used to the gameplay.
- The game pacing is much better than Dungeons 2
- Addition of evil points is a nice touch (research menu is much better).
Some things that gave me a headache.
- Once you reach a certain point in a game it becomes boring, if you set up a certain trap combo, nothing can get through.
- Whilst unit variety is nice, i always end up building the same dungeon over and over again.
- The humour is good, but you don't need to break the fourth wall every ten seconds, it just makes for elongated and pointless dialogue.

Elizabeth Find M.D. - Diagnosis Mystery - Season 2 is a hidden-object puzzle game, where you uncover clues to diagnose and treat patients by playing through hidden-object puzzles at various locations. In between these patient scenario's, a storyline develops regarding Doctor Find, her relationships with coworkers, and her employment at the hospital.

All in all I had fun with it. It is a decent hidden-object puzzle game.

The only problem with the last system was that F2P players may not have the cards that they want, but opening loot chests gave them a chance, and if they got a card for a character they didn't care about they could sell it for essence and duplicates aslo rewasr essence to buy the cards you want, not completely terrible, but does favor P2W.
The way it works now is every cards is unlocked from the beginning, and you can upgrade your cards by opening chests. There is no level cap for a loadout, and the max level for a card is 10. You can't buy chests, unless I'm mistaken, making the game now Grind2Win, as you get a chests for every level, and gold for every match which now has a cap per day, which is used to buy chests, not the buyable crystals. Hi-Rez has shown that they don't listen to their fans because there was a lot of backlash while this patch was in the testing phase, and they went through with it anyways.

This is a very enjoyable and a great bang for your buck game!  It takes just enough of the right mechanics from  other games you loves and melds them into its own cohesive style.
It has just enough space exploration and star system management to peak interest but keeps is simple and manageable as to not run into micro-management tediousness.
The story is thoughtful and enough to get you to want to see it through.  The random event are often humorous and a welcome distraction from your current goal.
Then there is the combat which, of course, is the main and best mechanic.  Done in a traditional 3 on 3 turn base style it utilizes debuffs you inflict to later exploit with other attacks at the expense of losing that debuff.  For instance one ship and inflict a sensor down debuff that will decrease  an enemy chance to hit, and another ship will have an attack that can exploit sensor down to do greater damage but will remove the debuff.  It’s this inflict and exploit tactic that really gets you thinking from fight to fight.
I also like how the officers you get have randomized abilities so it’s very hard to ever assemble a “perfect” team of usable abilities, you generally look for 1 or 2 traits that work well and build your squad around it.
Again this is a great game in the $10-15 range and you can easily expect to  clock a few dozen hours into it.  Don’t expect anything ground breaking or genre changing but a great game to fill in those gaps of time between major production games.

Halcyon is a sort of rogue like strategy RPG. You play a starbase commander, who is just a small part of a much larger federation of starbases and fleets. Only♥♥♥♥♥♥goes super wrong and you end up being the last guy standing, suddenly in charge of the whole schebang. It's a fun premise and managing a galaxy of colonies and interacting with other factions is a great experience. The visuals are mostly 2-d 16 bit sprites, which I'm a big fan of, but it's not an artstyle that works for everyone. The music is great as well.
The combat is interesting, but somewhat shallow at the moment. There are three kinds of characters you can use, Engineers, Scientists and Tactical officers. Each has a different set of moves, but it mostly comes down to one character applying a debuff and the next using that debuff to do bonus damage. It's an interesting concept, but I find that most of my choices are made for me before the turn starts. Just do the thing that does bonus damage. It can make battles tedious at times. There are both ship and ground battles, but they're functionally very similar, with slightly different moves.
I think the biggest problem with Halcyon right now is the metagame. Like many rogue-likes, Halcyon employs a game timer of sorts. There's a ton of weird bio alien ships invading your galaxy and you're constantly sending out fleets to secure your colonies. The problem is, that's 95% of the game. Just putting out fires over and over again. And eventually a mega fleet comes to crush you. It feels very heavy handed and the game doesn't do near enough to prepare you for the impending hulk sized leap in difficulty. Expect to run face first into this brickwall, and don't be shy about completely restarting your game. It'll become clear that there's no way to win at times. I've found this to be a common problem with Rogue-like game design. By relegating much of the game's difficulty to RNG, the player is often exposed to preposterously difficult or laughably easy scenarios, without enough of the rewardingly challenging situations that feel much better for the player.
I think Halcyon has a lot of potential, and none of the problems I have with the game can't be solved by some light balance changes and redesign. If you're a fan of FTL, Star Trek, or X-com, give Halcyon a shot and I think you'll enjoy it.

Halcyon 6 has a lot of great hooks right from the get-go, where XCOM meets Deep Space 9 and Battlestar Galactica. After a mysterious and endless alien race wipes out most of humanity, you're tasked with rebuilding humanity's last remaining forces and halting the tide of these new aggressive, organic enemies.
As you slowly explore and unlock new chambers of your space station, new modules can be built and slotted into them, allowing you to expand the amount of fuel your produce, or open up new options in upgrading your officers, building ships, etc.
After you construct a fleet of three ships, you'll be able to explore the surrounding galaxies and fight against both former friend and enemy alike. This is where the main gameplay comes in, with a turn based, JRPG-esque combat. The turn order is displayed at the bottom and when I first heard of all the different genres and inspirations H6 borrows from, I was pumped to play it.
However, this game may borrow from the greats, but it is merely a pale imitation of them. Combat quickly devolves into clicking the same commands over and over again and the sheer number of encounters and the amount of attacks to get through them makes fighting a boring and tedious affair.
Tedious is the word I would use to describe most of the underlying facets of gameplay here. Navigating the galaxy takes two to three times as many clicks as you'd want, as does combat, and base building. There's a really wonderful game hiding underneath bad UI and the grind.
There's a general unpolishedness in most areas of the game that you will discover with time. Prepare for unfair difficulty spikes and glitches where completed quests don't disappear or quests have vague descriptions that send you heading to message boards in the hope of deciphering them. When you upgrade your ship, you should feel powerful and excited, but in reality, you just have a little more HP and you do more damage. Enemies quickly upgrade with you, leading to it feeling like a pallete swap more than a real upgrade.
While this is not an Early Access title, it sure feels like one. Come back in 6 months to a year.

This game is simply the best and probably loved by the fans and maybe the devs themselves alike. A great platformer, bullet hell featuring cutesy characters and great graphical artwork
Updates, guides, and DLC's still pouring in even after it's initial release a year ago, and with each passing update, makes the game more fun as it is!
For the initial game it can literally be described in a LOT of words, which is probably why reviews here are so short, but here's what I think about it :
The visuals are AMAZING. I love how the backgrounds in each levels are thought out really well and immerses you in the environment. Character artwork and sprites complement each other, accurate that their pixel-y selves are distinct even without even seeing their artwork. And the generous use of light colors in its UI, characters, and environment gives the game it's cute, soft, and adorable charm.
The story is okay, not bad but not that great either. The initial game doesn't tell anything too much about the lore of the island you play on. It does tell you a bit about all the characters and the island itself, along with it's background fairly well. Thanks to that, you might feel attached to one of the characters since all of them have different personalities. (And it might want you to play the game twice or more >:o)
The gameplay itself is extremely diverse... Able to captivate new-comers to the bullet hell genre to hardcore players thriving for the records in really unforgiving scales of difficulties. I'd let you find out what works best for you in there, there's literally a tons of things to beat if you're up for a challenge!
The controls? Simple and straightforward. I've only used a keyboard and it's the only thing you'd ever need playing this game (except when you prefer a controller :L). It might seem alienating at first, but trust me, you'd get fitted into it in no time. Even the devs anticipated this and made it so that boss encounters are events in which even the newest player of this genre can easily overcome thanks to their gradual difficulty increase.
Overall, this game is a great all rounder, considering the price (It lowers to being literally almost free during sales), this game is too much to pass on. Try it, I think you'll really like it if you want to try an entirely different game from what you're playing now!

With about another 1000+ hours dedicated using the MWO standalone launcher, I can safely say that people should not invest their time, but more importantly their money, into this F2P game.
I say this with sadness, given that I have been a Battletech fan since I was a wee-lad. MechWarrior: Online is fun game on the surface level, however that enjoyment soon fades as you start to realize the actual state it's in. Last year in 2016, the game could've been considered at its "height" during the summer. It has since became a sad shell of its former self.
The developers for the game, Piranha Games, are by far one of the most incompetent and least transparent developers in the gaming industry. Continually screwing up the balance of the game, leading the game to never feel at equilibrium, and just when you are used to one certain playstyle, the developers screw the balance up again to keep you on your toes and make you leave any sort of comfort zone you knew.
The only form of communication that Piranha Games utilizes to get in touch with their MWO playerbase is through Twitter, and this is through a single person. You are more likely to be struck by lightning than see a PGI employee communicating with players on the OFFICIAL MWO forums.
Since the game is F2P, the developers have made everything else ridiculously expensive in the game itself... Even here on Steam there is evidence of this. $30-$60 for Steam bundles that only add two Mechs to your arsenal? These packs are meant to fool new players into buying them thinking they are getting a good deal, when in reality they are actually being conned for a ridiculous sum that adds so little. The in-game currency itself is a slow grind to accumulate, unless you have "Premium Time," and you guessed it, that costs money to use. However I will give PGI credit, the tutorial for the game gives a new player up to 18 million C-Bills, which is quite a lot for a new player.
The game itself is lacking in content as well. Besides the dozens of Mechs in the game, the map selection to fight on is very limited, and you'll find yourself playing the same rotation of maps in a single sitting. As of September 2017, PGI has not added in a single map in a full calender year. However, they continually add in new Mechs on a monthly basis that are only available to be purchased with money, and not in-game currency. Where exactly is all this money going to? That's up for debate.
tl;dr - MWO is a shallow arena shooter with a shrinking playerbase ran by incompetent developers who don't communicate with their playerbase, screw up the balance of the game, and pump out Mechs that add little to the game other than add cosmetics and worsen the powercreep - whilst ignoring adding any real content such as maps, Inverse Kinematics (Even MechWarrior 4 in '00 had this implimented), realistic in-game economy to go with Faction Warfare, etc.
This is an excellent game!  75% of the nay sayers are trolls or old players that have a vendetta against PGI.

"Transhumanism (abbreviated as H+ or h+) is an international cultural and intellectual movement with the goal of fundamentally transforming the human condition by eventually developing and making widely available technologies to greatly enhance human intellectual, physical, and psychological capacities."
The 3rd entry to the Deus Ex franchise, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a cyberpunk themed stealth RPG. Developed by Eidos Montreal, the original Deus Ex is considered one of the most influential games of all time, pioneering on player choice, RPG mechanics and stealth. With all this said, Human Revolution has quite a bit to live up to as part of the Deus Ex series. Prior knowledge to the Deus Ex series is not required to play Human Revolution, apart from a few nods and easter eggs to the original game, you can safely play Human Revolution without knowledge of the first. So how does Human Revolution stand on its own?
Set in 2027, 25 years before the events of the first game, the world is on the brink of a human revolution. Augmentations, human enhancements that allow people to improve themselves through the use of cybernetic limbs, neuroenhancements bionic eyes. Humans are now able to improve themselves through augmentation technology, some simply using it to replace a lost leg or fading vision, while some augment themselves into super-humans, replacing their limbs with cybernetic ones, turning themselves into more machine than man. Multinational corporations now have more control over the people than their governments (sounds like the world today), from the rise of augmentation technology. But not all organizations support the notion of humanity reaching beyond their limits through augmentation technology.
One one side there are those who see augmentation as the next step for humanity, allowing mankind to break free of their natural limits and using augmentation as the next step for human evolution. On the other side are the "anti-aug" or "pro-human" groups, who fear the ethics of augmentation, and the power it can give to augmented individuals, believing humanity should never have that power. Deus Ex: Human Revolution has done an excellent job of presenting the augmentation debate into a coherent and believable story. The game presents many overarching themes, such as the ethics of transhumanism, human survival, poverty, the power organizations have over people, and most importantly, questioning what it means to be human. It can sound all pretentious on paper, but Human Revolution at no point feels like it is trying to be more than it is not. Do humans lose part of themselves when they replace their limbs with cybernetic prosthetics, even when it may give them a better life? Is a person that is more machine than man still a human being? The game asks these questions but does not give any answers, instead allowing the player to form their own opinion.
This cannot all have been done without the fantastic effort gone into the world building of Deus Ex. All characters you meet have something to say on the argument, whether they are for or against augmentation. You find newspapers scattered across the game, with stories ranging from anti-augmentation protests, a fully-augmented pop-star winning at an awards ceremony, the next games for the "National Enhanced Hockey League." You hear a husband and wife arguing with each other, upset that they no longer love each other because one had become augmented, less human in the others eyes. News reports coming from the television talk of U.N debates on whether to regulate augmentation. These are all such small details, but it makes the world of Deus Ex: Human Revolution so much more than just an open world to explore.
You play as Adam Jensen, a private security officer for Sarif Industries, one of the worlds leading biotech corporations. After an attack on the company, Jensen is severely injured, forced to go through augmentations throughout his entire body to survive. Throughout the game, you can upgrade your augments through XP, which is awarded for completing quests, eliminating enemies, successfully hacking an object, finding hidden paths and areas or sneaking through an entire area undetected. The progression system is extremely well done, with all augments being extremely different from the other. There are several "paths" in which augmentations are categorized, namely "combat," "stealth," "hacking," and "social." All of these offer different playstyles in which the player has the option of customizing as they please. Combat augments are as expected, allowing maximized armor, less weapon recoil. Stealth augments range from cloaking, to silent footsteps, to seeing enemies and objects through walls. Hacking augments allow players to hack doors, sentry turrents, cameras and robots, allowing players to find new hidden areas or potentially disabling/turning robots and turrents on the enemy. The social is the most interesting augment. and one that is extremely well done. Throughout the game, you can engage in "dialogue battles," and "boss conversations." With the social augments, these allow you to see the personality of the person (Alpha, Beta, Omega), and a psychological profile listing that persons psychological traits and personality, which give hints to how the person may react to certain dialogue options. Using the information given and paying attention to the reactions of the person, you are able to "win" these dialogue battles.
Level and art design is masterfully handled. You have several open hub areas, namely Detroit and Hengsha, where you can explore the city, get side-quests, find hidden areas and buy equipment from merchants. In both side-quests and the main story, you are given a free reign on how you wish to approach it and get from point A to B. All missions in the game have various direct and hidden routes, such as entering a guarded complex from the sewers below, approaching it straight from the front, or climbing the roof and entering from a neighboring building. This freedom allows all players, no matter what style of play they chose to make their own decisions on how to complete an objective, and one of the games best features. Art design in the game is aesthetically appropriate to the games cyberpunk theme. Both Detroit and Hengsha are filled by towering buildings with large electronic billboard advertisements, neon signs pointing to the nearest attractions, the slums and sewers below filled with the homeless and those who have chosen to reject augmentation. The black and gold hue of the game suits it well, being able to evoke the futuristic atmosphere of the game very well.
Despite all this, there are a few flaws in Human Revolution that deserve mentioning. While the progression system is generally well done, it is a little imbalanced, favoring the "stealth-hacker." Throughout a level you can find pocket secretaries in drawers or hidden elsewhere, which often contain passcodes or passwords for computers in the level. However even with this information, the same result can be achieved by simply hacking into the computer or door, which can give both XP and cash/credits, while entering the passcode/password does not. Finding hidden paths and alternative routes to the objective is one of the main elements of the game and is one of the best, however it is unbalanced by the XP reward given by finding these areas. Finding a hidden area is always rewarded in giving 100-300 XP, a huge amount relative to the other alternatives. Lastly, the boss battles feel out of place, despite the Director's Cut allowing hacker oriented players to beat the bulletsponge bosses by hacking nearby computers to turn the robots against the enemy. That being said, these a minor aspects which do not detract from the larger game itself.

- Gameplay is objectivley geared towards stealth approach, rewarding those who think and plan ahead.
- Story is compelling until it falls flat on it's♥♥♥♥♥right at the end.
- Mediocre character development.
- Best Deus Ex game since the original, though still lacking the same open ended potential of it's year 2000 predecessor.

- Use a SweetFX/ ReShade preset if you are getting sick of the yellow tint on EVERYTHING.
- Gameplay best enjoyed if approached with a keen sense of detail and patience.

Excellent game all around with a lot to offer for fans of games like Civilization. The strategic gameplay is great, with a smoothly streamlined colony management system and an interesting tech tree. AI is, as always, a crapshoot. 'Diplomatic' factions will wage all out war while all-out war factions will attempt to broker peace treaties, but there are at least benefits to playing the diplomatic game in the form of trade and unique faction traits that give benefits for treaties.
That said though, the tactical side is a little wonky, with an over-emphasis on symmetry on paper getting in the way of actual balance. Some features are useless or counter-productive *coughfighterscough*, while others are massively overpowered, and learning which is which is the key to playing well rather than actually gaining skill. The difficulty curve is also stupid, with higher difficulty levels simply ratcheting up the ratios by which the AI is cheating. All levels play with the same AI, harder ones simply have to spend less time and money on ships and upgrades, have a bonus to empire approval, move faster, hit harder, have more health, expand more easily, research faster, get better heroes sooner, and can rush production for less money.
My recommendation? Play a game or two against AIs and then find a few friends to play with. The single player game is frustrating once you're better than a novice, as all games are either a cakewalk or an endless parade of superior vessels crushing your holdings. There's a ton of game here to enjoy if you can get past the flaws, so definitely pick it up.

Despite how it looks, Halcyon 6 is a (J)RPG with a dash of time/resource management mixed in. If you're looking for a strategy game where you need to carefully calculate the tradeoff of your every move or consider your every action against another faction, I highly doubt this game is for you. But if you're like me, someone who enjoyed RPG (especially turn based one), then you're in for a treat and I cannot recommend this game enough for you.
Anyway, my biggest complaint about the game is probably how pointless the ground combat is. There are barely any upgrade for the ground combat and they happen pretty rarely too. It just feels like the ground combat is added simply for the sake of being able to say "there is combat on the ground too!" on the feature list. My suggestion? Just remove the damn thing.
Other than that, I really enjoyed my almost-30 hours with the game =3

At first, Halcyon 6's mix of so many sub-genres is a little daunting and feels maybe a little watered down. There are elements of JRPG, ship building, character and ship leveling. You have all of these different factions coming at you and resources to gather and it's hard to really see the point when you begin playing.
After a game or two, though, for me, the game really shined and seemed a lot simpler in scope. I'd suggest playing on an easier difficulty your first play-through, but then putting on the suggested difficulty after that. The game gets a lot easier and you start gaining confidence, then BAM, you're all messed up and watching your hard work come crashing down.
It reminds me of FTL in that sense, but instead of suddenly watching your ship get demolished, you watch your little empire slowly crumble.
I'm really enjoying this game now, as simplistic and low-key as it is for such a giant concept.

If you're a fan of real-time strategy games like I am, you're going to love this.
I bought this game back when it was new for my old computer and played it
for hours on end. It has a very beginner-friendly introductory to all of the
game's mechanics and techniques to play it and along the way you'll surely
forge your own strategies and methods to solve problems.
Stronghold keeps the traditional way of gathering resources to build up
an army to defeat your enemy, but it also adds a couple of new things to
stir it up a bit. You have a whole variety of different kinds of resources
and materials you can gather that all has a different impact on your
people and economy. You can create churches where people can marry,
taverns for people to get drunk in, flowers and parks where people can
hang-out but you can also place gruesome torture machines if you feel
a little.. 'mischevious'. You can even decide how many rations of food
you allow your people to take aswell as bribing them or making them
pay taxes so that you, in return, can buy certain things to further improve
military or your town's economy. I think all of this gives limitless possibilities
in how to play the game and complete campaigns and levels and it's very
smart, in my opinion.
Whilst the game's graphics may be somewhat dated by today's standards
it still holds up pretty well and the HD release on Steam makes it look
a little better than it would if you'd have gotten it to work using the
original game CD.
The game's soundtrack is filled with atmospheric sound and beautiful
compositions to really set the tone of whatever situation you're in
and truly gives the game a medieval! Some of the game's tracks
will have you feeling rather peaceful and relaxed as you improve
the lifestyle of your town and others will have you bravely striking
back against your foes to drive them away from your kingdom.
As mentioned before the gameplay is smooth and still holds up
great today and if you got a few bucks to spend and you got a
couple hours to kill then i'd strongly recommend this game to anyone
who likes strategy games.

Halcyon 6 is an interesting indie game in the mold of X-Com, with some glorious pixel art and JRPG style combat, but some seriously dodgy design decisions and a slew of bugs. Combat itself plays out like in Final Fantasy, or any other classical JRPG, but with a twist. All attacks either inflict, or gain bonus damage from status effects, making exploiting status effects critical to battle. Unfortunately, combined with the lack of enemy diversity, this leads to combat being monotonous and repetitive, forcing you to chain the same attacks over and over again.
Much worse is the game's strategic management. You build your space station in an X-Com style ant farm, but the size and shape of the station prevent you from seeing all of it at the same time, making managing it a chore. Also, due to the extremely fast ramp up in difficulty, you cannot build many facilities or get many upgrades, as you need absolutely all of your resources to build higher level shipyards and ships. However, once you have gotten to higher level buildings and the old ones become useless, you cannot dissasemble them.
Bugs and poor interface design hampers things greatly. For example, there is no way to see your standing with all of the other factions. Instead you need to click on their (unmarked) homeworlds. Quests outside of your own territory do not appear to clear correctly, making it extremely difficult to find planets that are still under attack, and plotline quests that have to be completed.
These are only the worst of the issues that I have encountered, it is by no means an exhaustive list. The game has potential, some bugfixes and changes would greatly improve matters. Until then, stay away.

Guide to fix all possible crashes ( i can run it despite my processor being below the requirements ):
1- go to Nvidia Geforce control panel, set every thing to run automatically on Nvidia.
2- go to the config file in naruto folder and type the following in it:
iMaxdecalsperscale=100
FrameLimit=999
Framerate=60
3- set the .exe to run in compatable mode for windows 7 despite the version u are using.
4- disable shadows, vsync and all the useless settings and keep the game it 1280x720 so it doesnt crash midgame.
5- if it still doesnt run properly then make sure all your drivers are updated.
6- restart your computer and run the game.

This review will probably not be long. Words simply cannot express how good this game is. It is a masterpiece that can be shown to people while teaching them how do one makes a video game. This game will still be good even after 20 years or more pass. It seems that CreSpirit, the developer, understands what a good game is, and not just that – they can also make one!
Rabi-Ribi is essentially a game, in which the player controls a character and explore areas, looking for items, hidden routes and fights with enemies. The game mixes these elements with a bullet hell shooter. It comes out they go with each other really well, although it takes some time to become used to it. The bullet hell elements are present pimarily with boss fights. Regular enemies also attack using bullet patterns, but these are not complex and high in number enough to qualify as bullet hell.
The difficulty lies in that bullet hells are normally shooters, in which you control a flying object and can move in all directions. In Rabi-Ribi, you control a character which moves left and right, and can jump off the ground. Learning how to avoid bullets with this limited movement takes some time. It is an ‘easy to learn, hard to master’ type of game.
The game engine pre-loads a lot of things, so the start-up is slow, but there no loadings later whatoever. If you fail, which you will a lot, even on Casual difficulty, restart happens fast so that you may try again almost instantly. There is plenty of checkpoints and they are in places and times that you would want them to be in and at.
This game has a story, but it is not really significant. It can be completely ignored and the experience will still be as good. The story is actually a right kind of story for this time of game. The story is a mystery one, which invites and motivates the player to explore the island the story takes place on some more.
In such a game, as a player, you want there to be well-designed levels. This game have very good level design. It is really fun to explore the maps. At first, you don’t know about there being hidden passages, but the areas are structured so that you would eventually find them. The game guides the player with an invisible hand. You learn things in a way that you may not even notice that the game has told your about something. For example, the player finds a Carrot Bomb item. One of usages of a Carrot Bomb is that it can destory specific blocks of terrain and open up hidden passages. While playing the game, you learn which areas might be destroyable. You almost never look for things aimlessly without cues.
The game is filled with content and things to do, mainly communicated through the achievement system. It is split into what is referred to as the ‘main game,’ which is the first five chapters and the ‘post game,’ which is the remaining five. There are achievements for simply clearing the game. There are achievements for clearing the game in different difficulties. There are achievements for clearing the game in another mode. There is a speedrun mode. There is a boss rush mode, in which you fight all bosses in turn. There is an Artbook DLC, accessible through the game, which inludes some Beta Content which is playable. You can even try to finish the game without collecting any items or not touching any spikes and there are achievements for that, too. These are actual achievements which encourage players to try different ways and styles of play that the game offers.
The 0% items run is doable, because with the Standard Rule settings, the level of bosses is determined by what you have. In this mode, when one has 0% items, the last boss of the main game is at level 11, which is low. For comparision, in warawaras first playthough it was around 65. The game is also prepared for ‘breaking it’ by doing things out of order by using Hidden Tech moves and hidden passages you have learnt about. There is a harder New Game+, which starts another loop. If you did not obtain an item that increases jump or a weapon, the system adapts to this situation so that you can finish the game, for example, the height of a pillar of bullets changes in a boss fight. As a player, you will certainly spend a lot of time with this product as it is solid like a rock and polished like a diamond.
The game is presented with pixel art graphics. These are very good pixel art graphics. They use pastel colours that introduces to you to a world full of love. There is plenty of animation in the spirtes. They move, jump and do things that brings a smile to one’s face. It is co cute and charming you simply want it to play it some more.
The game is essentially a collection of connected rooms, which are viewed from the side, but – even with this presentation – when in a boss fight, there is actually some camera movement like close-ups! It happens so naturally that you may not even notice it happening.
The background music is simply perfect. It fits really well with all the places on the map and the fights. Actually, warawara bought this game through Steam primarily to get the OST, because the music by Tridust, 3R2 and few others is so great warawara had to own a copy of it. Warawara cannot find the words to describe how the experience of fighing a boss with ‘Get On With It’ or ‘The Truth Never Spoken’ (by 3R2) playing in the background feels like. The right music plays at the right times. Simply hearing some of the pieces and watching the trailer for the console version bought warawara instantly. It is simply amazing how well is goes along with the rest of the game. There are also touches like lowering and increasing the speed of music when you gain status effects that alter the player’s movement speed.
To sum it up, warawara highly recommends this game.

Rabi-Ribi is a Bunny Exploration Bullet Hell Action game and the best (only?) of its kind.  It bears many gameplay similarities to Super Metroid, like the exploration aspect, and hidden abilities, upgrades, and items, so if that's your thing, you'll probably love this game.  Beyond the core gameplay though, Rabi-Ribi is quite different, and something very special and unique.  This game is all about cute girls, a beautiful world with colourful environments, lighthearted characters, and nice upbeat music.
The world in this game is so beautifully designed and makes you want to keep coming back to spend time in it.  The visuals are lovely and I really could not ask for more there.  The artists did a really good job with the visual presentation for the game.  The areas, artwork, and sprites are all really nice, and all the small details like the characters' facial expressions are really great and add so much to the game.  The characters in this game are an absolute joy to be around and they really make the game.  The interactions are cute and fun and it feels great meeting and getting to know each character.  I don't know what it is, but there's just something special about these characters that makes me really feel attached to them.  They really bring a smile to my face and I can really feel the love that GemaYue put into creating them, and the artists put into drawing them.
The soundtrack is really fantastic as well.  Everything works out really well and fits in with the spirit of the game.  Most of the music is quite cheerful and nice to listen to casually as well.  All of the composers did an amazing job and I'm really happy with the music in this game.  It was also really cool to see 3R2 on the team for the game music, since I've been a fan of his music for years and this was actually part of what got me interested in this game in the first place.
Also there's a ton of content and replay value with this game, with are 6 difficulties (excluding DLC), 5 main game modes, a speedrun mode, and multiple boss rush modes.  Overall this game is a must-play and I would recommend it to anyone who likes games (that means you!).  I came in expecting a pretty good action-platformer Metroid-style game and ended up with what is easily one of my favorite games of all time.  Definitely grab this game whenever you can.  It's wonderful.  I'd say it's easily worth paying full price even, and I'm a pretty cheap person, so there's not many games I say that about!
As a side note, since it isn't obvious from the title, I also want to mention the artbook DLC includes various beta version gameplay content (which is described in the artbook DLC page).  If you're just buying the main game now and thinking about DLC later, then it's something to keep in mind, and if you're on the fence on whether or not to get the full package, then I'd say just go for it.

First off it is a free to play model game.  Knowing that if you are patient you can quite feasably never spend real money on anything in this game and be competitive and slowly grow your stable of mechs.  There are always events going on that have various rewards: in game currency(CBills), mechbays (which you need to stable more mechs), cosmetics and even small amounts of MC( purchased currency used to buy hero mechs, mech bays camo patterns etc etc.)
The game has a pretty steep learning curve, learning maps, heat, weapon ranges etc all while staying alive, but the community is friendly, the forums are a great resource for any questions and plenty of helpful people to ask questions.
Now this being a f2p game if you want to play more than the 4 mechs your initial 4 bays alllow the best place to drop some money on the game is for mechbays. a few dollars will get you a good number of bays.
The important thing to note about this game is buying a "hero" mech does not give you a competitive advantage and in most cases the "hero" mech is no better and sometimes has a worse layout over a standard mech varient.  The only big thing a "hero" mech will give you is a 30% bonus to CBills when you complete a match which cuts the grind for in game currency before you can purchase that next mech, weapon, module.
Other thing of note is that unlike call of duty type game there is no respawn, your mech has a set amount of armor and structure it can use to absorb incoming damage before you are destroyed, and friendly fire isn't very friendly in MWO.  Watch you fire lines, stay with the team and manage your heat.

A fun strategy game, akin to Space Empires or Civilization in space. In other words it is not a game focused mainly on the action or combat, the fun comes in managing and upgrading your empire and ships. The combat itself is interesting, you don't control the ships directly but rather issue up to 3 commands using command cards. You do get to customize and name your own ship builds, and there are 4 huge branches of research to explore. The graphics and UI are nice as well.

The appeal of Endless Space is simple but beautiful. Overall, it feels like some sort of Civilization Light (in space). It is not as good as Civ, because both diplomacy and battles are by far too simple. However, I consider these two points to be the only week spots of ES. Overall, it's more than just a solid 4x game. Faction creation, tech tree, colonozing, heroes - all these things are expertly balanced and carefully considering your next steps is just as much fun as it is in Total War or Civilization. Anyway, if you like 4x space games, you probably already bought this, right?

Endless Space is a space 4X game with a notably well-designed expansion mechanic. Unfortunately, the smaller details of this game's mechanics are not well-documented; while the mechanics overall are easy to understand, there are many sneaky factors that can cause a large impact on the game. For example, a star system outside your colored influence circles generate only HALF the science and money - but nowhere is this mentioned, save for a small "distance from empire" factor when you examine your science output in detail.
The military system in Endless Space is often criticized. Indeed, space battles quickly devolve into mashing the auto button over and over, as you watch your indestructible ships blow up the AI's endless stream of useless fodder. Because of the common rebalances and redesigns of ship-building, it is extremely difficult to reason about the effectiveness of ship designs. Additionally, capturing star systems is less than glamorous, with bombardment reduced to watching a colored circle fill up and a turns left icon count down.
Despite its flaws, Endless Space is in the end still a strong 4X game. Strategy in general remains the same no matter what race or victory type you play, but the game mechanics' nuances and relative importance of timing make mastering this strategy a great challenge.

ES is a great game, but you definitely need to do some research before playing or while you are playing the first time. It is complicated and deep, but the manual and forums will help sort things out. I would recommend to anyone who likes turn-based strategy games.
