The first time you play Endless Space, the task seems daunting. The learning curve is not easy and the tutorial is long and filled with walls of text. This, however, does not make Endless Space a bad game. Endless Space is in fact one of the best, if not THE best, strategy games I have ever played in my life.
Gameplay in Endless Space is extremely rewarding, helping you set goals and manage your start systems. When these goals are met they make you feel pretty awesome. Being able to play and do it well are skills that take time to develop through the playing of the game. You will find that playing online with friends is an extremely fun experience and the game allows you to save online games for the host to continue later. You will NEED the save function as games will take MANY HOURS to complete. You're in this for the long haul, and because of this, menus for online play are very easy to use and allow easy access to continue previously begun games.
I find that the menus and UI for Endless space are very intuitive and provide a lot of need-to-know information to you instantly. Everything can be explained further through a quick mouseover as well, and this will also give you loads of interesting lore and scientific information that helps to build a really fun level of immersion that a lot of people (like myself) look for in games. You really feel like you're doing something important and executing very strategic moves and decisions that help you win something as important as an entire galaxy.
The two negative things I have to say about this game are:
1) The AI doesn't know how to handle deals very well and opt to create extremely one-sided deals instead of a deal that mutually benefits both races.
2) It can be a bit buggy at times and after many hours of play you may need to verify your game cache to make sure all files are working fine.
Endless Space is well worth the buy as one really sweet strategy game.

This may well be a better XCOM 2 than XCOM 2.
It definitely feels like an XCOM game; there's the pausable realtime overworld where you handle the big picture stuff like resource management and base building, while combat is handled in more confined, turn-based encounters. The core difference is mainly that while there was an exploratory phase to XCOM's combat, battles in Halcyon 6 are handled like something in the vein of Final Fantasy combat encounters. I never really was too keen on those, and that's the largest worry I had going in. Instead, I found the combat refreshingly cerebral.
Simply hammering away with any old ability will be far less effective than having your characters work together to perform devestating combos. Admittedly, the combos themselves seem to be relatively simple to execute (at least where I am in the game) but the sheer variety of status effects and ship abilities keeps it feeling fresh. Land combat is also satisfyingly visceral; slain enemies and allies alike die in horribly violent ways, though the pixel art makes it seem charming rather than gratuitous.
I have no real complaints about the game so far, though I'll update this review if that changes. The game is rather difficult though, and for your first few attempts you should expect to fail until you've nailed down some of the finer points. I can see why some people may be put off by that, but at least in my experience the time from start to restart was relatively short and the events in each game unfolded differently enough each time to keep me intrigued. Once you're over that bump, the difficulty curve is still steep, but the game is pretty fair with how it approaches it.
In short, if you're willing to invest an hour or two into losing and learning before you really jump in, this seems like a solid choice. Replayability is high and the amount of content is pretty impressive.

After a decade of this game, Stronghold STILL is one of the most accurate and beautiful medieval castle management simulators out there. Even after like, what, 12 years from this game's release the graphics, gameplay and experience are still awesome for me. After a few years of not playing it, nostalgia kicks back in and thank goodness Steam has it when I decided to install Steam as one of my game hubs to base my games on. Even though it's has no flashy graphics like Starcraft: Wings of Liberty or Call of Duty, the graphics have most certainly endured. Even I don't know why. Maybe it's because the experience made up for it, or maybe the detail that goes to each building and terrain defies ravages of time. The gameplay, especially if you're into management and simulators like let's say Age of Empires and its similar counterparts like Warcraft, this will DEFINITELY be a breath of fresh air for you. I guarantee it!! After actually playing this game, I couldn't go back to Age of Empires II because as great as Age of Empires is, it simply became lackluster and it's like you had your fill of it and there's nothing new, you know? But Stronghold. It's amazing after a decade I still can replay a game and still feel like I've never played it. Maybe it's because the game as a whole actually FEELS REAL. You see little people, doing their merry little jobs, greeting you if you click on them, and every single one of the living creature has their own name. The logic in this game is absolutely fantastic; it gets you to think how content the people are, how fast the jobs' going to be done, how soon do you need to consider managing the food rations......It feels REAL.
The campaigns are great with a good pace of difficulty, and one of the most amazing trait of this game that amuses me and still makes me smile to this day is how every single character with a voice seems to be voiced by the same guy - and all of them still sounds so different!! Of course they could have added more kinds of dialogues or add even more stuff to make the game more difficult and more real now that I've played it for so long. But then it'll be too hard for the starters, wouldn't it?
This game may not be for everybody, but I strongly suggest anyone, especially ANYONE who's played Age of Empires, Starcraft, Warcraft; BUY THIS GAME. PLAY THIS GAME. It will refresh your dull old expectations for a strategy game of that nature. The price on Steam is not bad either, even without the discounts. I usually just go pirated but it's an insult not to support Firefly Studios for this classic, so I bought it! Just try it out. You won't be disappointed!!

Alright, my first review on steam, bear with me.
Unclaimed World shows great promise, vast replayability, and an intriguing concept, which is that you are kind of like management, and you create orders and such, then it's up to the A.I., (read: your colonists). You will be in turns proud and irritated by them, just like if they were employees, and not fighting for their independence and survival.
Most of the time, the game is quite addictive, especially as you begin to actually have structures up that are more advanced, and create production lines for food, and the colonists stop complaining. But that's usually where the frustration begins for me, as it seems as though the colonists start to get what I call 'Lazy, and definately human', LoL.
They begin to do less and less work and more time lollygagging. Don't know if that's a bug or if the developer was aiming to make it as 'realistic' as possible.
Either way, it makes for a challenge as you begin to think of new ways to improve the time colonists spend actually doing task; obtaining tools and weapons or creating them, using several means of obtaining fuels, and building more than one structure of each type, so more can be done at once. This is where you get to steer your outpost, or settlement, in the direction you choose
Trade is quite important as well, because sometimes it's cheaper and quicker to buy basic materials or tools than to attempt the time required to make them. Now with the addition of being able to buy dogs and robots, perhaps this will get your colonists in line once and for all!
Okay, gripe done. The artwork is beautifully rendered, and a wonderful change from the simplistic terrains offered in other games of this genre, and yes, there is ALWAYS a dendrot hiding in those Spoak jungles. Creature and characters are a nice change as well, they look more realistic in my opinion. Kudos to the dev on that point.
As for problems with the game, I have been playing this game for over a year now. The forums may show a lot of threads concerning bugs, but I've found that though dev is somewhat spotty in replying, they do pay attention and try to stamp out those problems fairly quickly. Perhaps patches can be rolled out quicker, but maybe the code is such that it may create problems in other areas if hotfixes were used instead. No idea, but I usually see major issues resolved very quickly.
All in all, this game is a good value, and I can honestly say the dev picked a heck of an idea, the problem is that it's a very BIG, and multi-threaded idea. There is just sooo much that can be done with this game, and if it ever gets to the mod-able state, possibilities are endless! Perhaps rebuilding the actual technology lost by the former colonists? Paving the way for a 4X? Bwaha, I'll buy that one!

MWO has come a long way from where it was when I started playing it in January of 2015. PGI has made great strides at improving MWO.
Now how is the game itself now? Pretty darn good. The game is easier to get into than say World of Tanks or WarThunder as everyone has access to to pretty much everything from the start. With the playingfield far more level you also do not get oneshotted as easily making MWO far more forgiving to the new player.
When trying to learn MWO do the tutorial, do the optional parts of the tutorial not just for the bonus Cbills but also to get a better idea of how mechs handle. Learn how each weapon system handles, look up some guides, and if you are in doubt, suck up the high price tag of clan mechs and get one with your cadet bonus. Trust me it is worth it, use it to learn how heat works, how to torso twist, get yourself a Hunchback, Stormcrow or Timberwolf and go to town.
Seriously go grab a Stormcrow it is one of the most forgiving medium mechs in the game. If you want to get an Inner Sphere mech? Hunchback, any of them, but, best would be the one with the AC/10 which is the Hunchback HBK-4H. The Hunchback and Stormcrow are very, very forgiving and flexible mechs. Also everyone wants to pilot a heavy mech as well, so a medium mech will help with queue times.
Another advantage of grabbing a clan mech first is that when building your mech you have far less things that you can do wrong, like under-engining your mech and making you an easy target. Get to also know what the various upgrades do for your mechs, get to know how much ammo you use.
Reading guides on the meta is a good idea, it will give you an idea of what you will be fighting, it will also give you an idea of the weaknesses of each weapon system is and strengths. You do not, and I stress this, and should not blindly follow the meta, learn why the meta is the way it is so you can tune your mechs to capitalize on how the game works.
Most of all, find what you enjoy to run in your mechs and run it. Also don't forget to find some friends, look up the faction team speak servers and do group queue drops. Trust me, working with friends or just communicating in general will do more for your match score, cbills, and exp gains than any metamech build.
Before getting into Faction play, otherwise known as Community Warfare you should get a good grasp of how your mechs work and get four of them that add up to 240 tons. Make certain they are all basiced.

I played this a bunch when it was new. It recently arrived on Steam and I elected to pick it up again to see if it had changed any over the years.
On a technical level, the game is pretty decent. It's visually pleasing, plays smooth, has excellent balance and controls that can be picked up quickly. THere are a few bugs that pop up from time to time, but mostly they are contained to the tutorials and control mapping. Joystick support seems like a cruelly halfwitted afterthought due to how much more simplified and twitch-response oriented the game has become over the years, but the game otherwise plays like a slightly clumsy FPS with a usual mouse and keyboard.
But there's something significant that it's missing. I can't quite put my finger on it, but allow me to try to explain.
The whole thing consists of nothing but an endless series of pick-up fights lasting less than 10 minutes each on average, with exactly zero control over the scenario beyond "Which chassis do I want to use (which you pick before you know where and what you're going to play) and do I want to be a commander or not".  Game types are semi-randomized, as are maps. You play for hours on end and the only thing you feel is fatigue; you don't really feel like you've accomplished anything.
The devs have done an acceptable job of keeping the game off of a pay-to-win scale, which has really become more of a pay-to-not-grind system. WHile this is an improvement, to be certain, it still feels hollow.
I used to play MechWarrior 4 competitively. This was obviously a long time ago, and the game feels less like a simulator now and more like a MOBA with robots.
If youy are among the multitudes who love MOBAs, you should give it a try. It's free, it's easy and quick to pick up, and certainly offers a huge number of possibilities.
It's just that, like DotA, like Smite, like LoL, there's no story to speak of and none of those possibilities really feels even remotely meaningful.

I have been playing MechWarrior Online since closed beta (summer 2012) and have to say that this is one of the most gratifying and addictive games... once you climb the learning curve. The gameplay is unique in that you can customize your 'Mechs with a very wide variety of weapons. There are no re-spawns in 2 of the 3 game modes, which forces you to play smart rather than run and gun, like most FPS games. It can be frustrating to die in the first few minutes of a game (solo and group queue matches are a maximum 15 minutes, but usually average about 10 minutes, while Community Warfare matches typically last 20-30 mins).
If you are an FPS gamer, you will appreciate the higher level of tactical play and it rewards good aim and movement. In fact, the component/hitbox design of the 'Mechs really rewards players who have precision aiming. Headshots (cockpit kills) are extremely difficult, but highly satisfying in this game... more so than any other FPS I have played.
There are 4 weight classes of'Mechs, ranging from Light through to Assault, and offer you different roles to play within a team and changes your playstyle. Some people specialize in one or 2 roles/weight classes because it suits their playstyle and others are flex players who like variety.
Team Damage: Yes, it is a real thing and it is annoying as hell to be on the receiving end from trolls (which are few and far between, I might add). Thankfully, you can monitor your team damage at the end of round info screen. Do keep your firing lanes clear and apologize to your teammates if you accidentally shoot them in the back (where there is MUCH less armour and can destroy weapons or even kill them in one full volley of your weapons if placed in one spot). If you are tabbed out of the game and click back in with your mouse, you will fire your weapons, so please alt-tab back into the game instead.
Interface: The out of game user interface in the game has changed a lot over the past couple of years and it still isn't perfect, but it MUCH better than older ones. The lack of customizable UI is understandable, due to the sheer volume of parts that make up the info needed and it still can't all fit on one screen. This is a game that is very complex when played to its fullest potential, yet offers instant action once you become familiar with the ideal builds for each 'Mech. Expect to spend a lot of time initially tinkering with Mechs and unlocking skills and items (modules that enhance your weapons, movement or ability to gather info). The in-game interface is pretty cool and has recently introducted additional info within the cockpit (you can also play in 3rd person view, but it highly affects your aiming for precision shots and people can see you are in 3PV because a drone flies above your Mech... you may get a bit flamed for it, as it can also be a visual cheat due to terrain design).
Team-Play/Communications: As with any team-based game, you are highly recommended to find a unit and utilize voice comms, but you can play strictly in the solo queue to build your experience, level up your 'Mechs (skill trees take about 30-40 matches to complete for one Mech chassis), or experiment with different weapon loadouts and heat management. Voice comms are available in game, but not used by everyone. You can mute annoying players quite easily. Clans, House Units or Merc Units (aka guilds) are constantly looking for players and have their tag displayed in game next to their name. If you start to see players with a given tag and like your cohesion (and win rate!) with them, I advise you find out their voice comms info and play with them in a group. Just request to join them in chat or add them as a friend and use the in-game messaging feature.
Heat?: Ah yes, heat management... this is a layer of complexity that requires you to really be aware of your heat production caused by weapon use and movement. Learning to squeeze out the most of your Mech takes a lot of time and understanding, but there are some great community resources out there. You eventually can do it by feel, but there are visual and audio cues to help. Overheating causes damage to your internals and you can even blow yourself up by riding in the red too long. In those last ditch attempts to squeeze off a final kill, you can choose to override your auto shutdown when past 100%, but do so wisely! Suiciding due to overheat can still reward the kill to a player shooting at you.
Community: there are always toxic players or trolls, but you will find an overall very nurturing community. The game is no doubt a niche game, but has a very, very loyal following with some very big whales who love the BattleTech universe. There is no other multiplayer game on the market quite like this one and it induces a lot of passion within the MWO forums and MWO sub-reddits.
eSports: There is a budding attempt to turn MWO into an eSport with a $100K prize pool world tournament starting in Q1 2016. Those in the competitive-minded community hope that enough new players with great skills enter MWO to spawn new teams or revive some old ones that have felt that the competitive scene is stale. Most competitive play is accomplished via community-run leagues (MRBC, RHoD, and a few 8/12/16 team invitationals). The publisher did host one official beta tournament, which brought out a lot of new names to the competitive scene and we hope that will be the case in the near future with the influx of new players from Steam.
Pay Model: The game is F2P and used to be very limited in this regard, but has opened up widely since Community Warfare started. Initially you begin with 4 Mech Bays. You had to buy additional ones in the past, but now you can earn them through in-game rewards and special events. There are some Hero and Champion Mechs that are only purchasable with real money (MC), but they are not mandatory to buy. They do offer enhanced XP or C-Bill (in-game currency) bonuses, so it can be a good way to farm cash to buy additional 'Mechs. As with most F2P games, you will end up paying more for this game than a retail box model should you get into it... and there is nothing wrong with that at all! Mech Packs are pricey, but it is more of a pay to early access feature rather than a Pay 2 Play/Win model. There are only a few Hero Mechs that you may want to buy should you wish to get into competitive play. Wait for paid items to go on sale at 50% off to get the best value, which happens often.
Matchmaking: There are 5 skill tiers and that is how the base matchmaker tries to pair up players. Sometimes you will be matched with players a tier higher or lower, but the idea is that both sides are matched as evenly as possible. There are also weight and chassis limits per side, so as to maintain some degree of balance of teams. The past saw some issues with queue times due to lower populations, which has been less of an issue since Steam release. However, the Community Warfare (CW) mode still suffers from a lack of popluation due to lack of real incentives to play that game mode vs time per match. We hope that an increased CW population will reduce the wait times and increases the potential of this game mode. More on CW below.
End Game: Community Warfare is the persistent universe game mode and is not based on any matchmaking at all, but a specific weight tolerance of the 4 Mechs you can bring to each match. Yes, this is the only game mode where you have respawns, but you still need to use each Mech wisely, as matches are more prolonged with different phases to the fight. There is a defense and an offense mode to each map and new game modes are going to be introduced to increase playability of CW during off-peak times. Here is where you can unlock in-game rewards and also earn MC, the real money currency that can unlock more Mech Bays (character slots, per say), cosmetic items, or even Champion or Hero Mechs, if you grind it out.

Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
DISCLAIMER: Please do not be fooled by my amount of time played on Steam. I have been playing this game since Beta 2012, so I assure you I have many, many hours logged on this game. More hours logged then all other games I own combined for that matter!
Review:
This is an excellent game with great potential and a bright future ahead! I recommend this game for anyone looking for more tactical gameplay in their FPS gaming.
Last year, the devs introduced Community Warfar, a gamemode targeted at hardcore players with an entire star map and several factions to fight for. If you decide to give this game a shot, I recommend shying away from this gamemode for the first while until you get a grasp of the main concepts of combat roles and loadouts, and decide this is a game you want to continue with. If you make it to ComWar, you will enjoy increased rewards, frequent events, and the final end-all Battle for Tukayyid Tournament to end each season of ComWar. ComWar is currently in Beta II, with Beta III just around the corner. In Beta III, players will be able to choose from several unique Career paths, vote on planets to attack, pool C-bills for tactical bonuses & ordinance (TACTICAL NUKE CONFIRMED), and perform either full out planetary Assault or planetary Scouting missions to collect intel for additional bonuses.
The devs are continuously pumping out new content in the form of Battlemechs, Camo, (coming soon) Decals and Maps. They are also dedicated to perfecting player balance as much as possible, so one can expect one or two updates to gameplay mechanics every month, on top of new content updates.
MechWarrior Online got off to a rough start in 2012. Whether you talk to the haters or the lovers, everyone can admit this fact. This was largely due to the now defunct company Infinite Games Publishing (IGP) and its control over the project. The good news is that since its departure, progress on this game has been swift and positive. The game's 'mech concepts are lauded as one of its strongest points, with much of the beautiful 'mech designs now slated for use in the upcoming turn-strategy game Battletech (if you don't know about this game, also worth a look!
.
The game's UI has been improved frequently, but new players will still have some difficulty navigating some tabs. Notably, new players may struggle with customizing loadouts. My best recommendation for this is to visit the game's forums
and get advice from the playerbase, most of whom are very helpful.
The game's Tutorial zone has been revamped recently! All new players should visit this zone first, because this is not a game that you can simply skip the tutorial unless you are a returning player (the tutorial even has in-game rewards for completing challenges). As a veteran player, I still use this zone to practice with new 'mechs.
Some may get turned off buy the game's MC currency (money purchasable currency) that allows players to skip a lot of the grind and get the good stuff. While this game may seem Pay-To-Win, this is certainly not the case, as virtually all chassis, weapons, equipment and upgrades are purchasable with C-bills (gameplay generated/earned currency). The only things unobtainable without MC are vanity items & a select group of 'Hero' mechs that come with unique camo patterns and weapon hardpoints (which are arguably no better or worse in performance when compared to their standard counterpart). Also purchaseable with MC-only are designated 'Champion' 'mechs, but do not be fooled! These mechs are simply optimized versions of standard C-bill purchasable mechs, they do not differ at all in performance potential!
In summary, this is a great tactical shooter with very unique gameplay concepts. As such, the learning curve can be rather steep for some, and there are still a few rough spots that require development. The future of this game is bright, however, with constant updates and some really exciting new content lined up for spring. In the words of the game's devs, they are "far from finished" with this game!

This is a Phoenix from a failed Kicktarted campaign. You can disassemble/reassemble guns mainly. As you finish one weapon, you are allowed to unlock adjacent weapons in a map, so there's some progression. If you pay extra you can also disassemble cars, skeletons and etc.... You can also pay more to get to certain weapons sooner, but it's not required. The business model here is a very fair one! You can even skip segments of the map progression, although it costs more of the game's monopoly money which is earned by completing challanges and beating weapon disassemblies/assemblies.
What I find most interesting is the operations mode where you can seen the gun in action and it's inner workings in great detail. Recently, a painting mode was also added, so you can create your own skins for your favourite guns. I've painted my FP-45 pink for giggles.
For a small selection of guns, you can even walk through a shooting gallery in the style of an FPS. Although, Metro Last Light did this way better...
Some of the animations aren't the best and sometimes I scratch my head at the hierarchy of actions that the game forces you to use during disassembly/assembly. Yet, the catalog of guns keeps growing each month. At the end of the day, this is a great game which could use some more polish.

Halcyon 6, as of the date of this review (9/26/16), gets a conditional reccomendation.  It has fully occupied my gaming for the past week, and I can say I definately had fun with it.
Grindy, mindless, but fun, JRPG combat is combined with amazing pixel art and a moderately deep resource management system to produce a game with great potential.  The excessive Act 1 micro required for resourse harvesting in the 1.0 release has been addressed with the latest patch, so that particular grind is much less of an issue now.
Resource/risk management games are my thing, and this aspect of Halcyon 6 is competently implemented.  Your most limiting resourse are your officers' time.  They are required for both commanding the starships that fight the aliens, and completing tasks at planets and the starbase.  They can only do one or the other at one time.  The player will find themselves juggling their officers' taskings to hold the enemy at bay while at the same time improving their position.  I strongly reccomend that new players get both an A and B team up and running quickly, otherwise they will be overwhelmed.
Do not be mistaken: there is a
grind to get to the top tiers of equipment.  If nearly endless space battles don't sound like fun, or at least tolerable, I'd steer away.  IMO, they are done well enough; I enjoyed this aspect of the game.  So if you like dealing with the alien menace while desprately trying to find the time to level up your logistics, this is a very good game as is.

TLDR:
Until they make the interface much more coherent, I cannot recommend this. Maybe a year from now when all that gets worked out... but not right now. Unless you like menus. Lots and lots of menus. Underlying game is decent... but those damn menus.
REVIEW:
Played through the game once, and it is way too long for the content it provides.  Not a bad game overall, but very lacking in polish, full of bugs, and the gameplay itself is repetitive.
The 'flow' of the UI is easily the worst offender here. You really have to micromanage a lot of stuff like 'routes to collect resources', but there is no waypoint system and managing your fleet is a nightmare. Honestly, I felt like I was fighting the interface more than playing the game.
Devs, please make it much easier to see which officer is assigned to which ship and which ship is in what fleet, and where each fleet is at. The game desparately needs a way to manage that in a unified manner, preferably from one or two screens only! As it is, it's a nightmare of oddly linked menus screens. You're constantly traversing  up to the starmap, down to the ships, down into the officers, out into the station, back to the starmap,  wait... that guys in a different fleet and I just sent it away! Damn it! and round and round in goes... clicking in circles trying to figure out where everyones at and re-assigning them to where they need to be.
Despite all that, there is a decent underlying game here... a little too focused on the space battles though. The away missions feel like an afterthought... but still the game itself was decent.
Final Verdict:
Until they make the interface much more coherent, I would not recommend this. Maybe a year from now when all that gets worked out, it'll be good. But not right now. Unless you like menus. Lots and lots menus.

Halcyon 6 is a marriage of an X-Com-ish strategic layer to early-JRPG style combat.  It's dead addictive from the start, with a constant series of missions that need completing, base upgrades to build, and progression to aim for.  Ultimately, however, it ends up feeling like a bunch of easy and unsatisfying busiwork.
On the world map, you complete missions, defend your colonies, and collect supplies.  This consists of dispatching some of your officers in their ships somewhere and then- except for supply gathering runs- completing one of the aforementioned JRPG-style combats.
Theoretically, there are decisions to be made here.  The missions can mostly be skipped with negative consequences if you don't want to or can't do them, and colonies can be evacuated when visiting which grants you an influx of crew but shuts down a resource faucet.
Five hours in, however, I've never once found myself wanting to skip or been unable to complete a mission.  Likewise, I've never had to evacuate a colony.  The game claims you would want to to evacuate "vulnerable" colonies, but except for saving me a bit of travel time if I shut down the colonies I'm not sure how it would.  There's no indication that doing so would reduce the number of incoming attacks I would face, the colonies are all equally defensible (save travel time), and I've had no difficulty defending them.  If I were to evacuate a colony- and I have- it's just because I'm sick of having to manually find a free crew member and dispatch them to pick stuff up from it every few minutes when its storage capacity tops off.
You also have some discretion in completing strategic objectives.  For example, there are space pirates to be delt with, shutting off periodic attacks on your bases, which basically works as advetised but doesn't really matter since the attacks were never threatening.  As another example, there's an enemy gateway spawning periodic attacks on my colonies that I can attack to shut down, but this appears entirely pointless as killing it just causes it to almost immediately pop up somewhere else and resume its work.  In one case I shut down a gate, and before my fleet completed a meandering supply-harvesting path home the gate popped up exactly where it was before and the nearest colony was already under attack again.
There's a tech tree, but it's not particularly interesting and impactful.  Your base consists of many rooms in a new-X-Com style ant farm.  You'll clear out each room by assigning an officer to de-rubble it for a few days, sometimes resulting in another JRPG fight.  With this space, you can build rooms that either passively provide bonuses or that you can actively assign workers to to research new technologies and gather resources.
These rooms offer many options, but they're not really game changers.   You can research alternate ships for each of your classes of ships which give you a different set of attacks in combat, which is one of the more interesting options.  You can construct workshops that give you +15% income to the resources and allow an officer to work there to directly harvest the resource, get +10% strategic speed or fuel efficiency, give a ships category +10% damage and HP, etc, etc.  It all feels pretty minor and incremental and won't change how you play.
The biggest jumps are increasing your officer pool and going up ship tiers, but it doesn't feel like a huge game changer or a challenging strategic decision to make.
Upgrading your officer pool is a huge boost and doesn't cost much, so it's pretty much just a matter of waiting until you have an officer of a high enough level to do so.  When you do it, you get more officers (units) to command, which lets you do more stuff but doesn't much change what or how you do it.
Upgrading to higher tiers ships does require enough resources that it'll take some saving up to get to, but it's still essentially an automatic decision to do so because you've got no other dire threats or especially compelling upgrades tugging you to put those resources in another direction.  When you do complete the upgrade you get a slightly different set of attacks on your combatants, and a bigger jump in HP and damage, which will let you deal with the next tier of enemies but still doesn't really change how you're playing much.
You're also occasionally presented with decisions.  Aliens will offer you quests, and you can say yes or no- I'm not really sure why you would say no after five hours of gameplay.  Frequently there will be a threat or opportunity, and you'll have two options to pick from.  For example "this person accidentally fell into the matter replicator- try to clone them?" or "the cadets accidentally blew a hole in the wall- yell at them or praise them?"  This is flavorful, but doesn't really add much- I've never been in dire enough straights to care about the outcome, and were I then I would be frustrated that I don't have the information to make a good decision.
That's the strategic layer.  The other bit of the game is the combat, which is broken up into ground and space combat but plays similarly in both.  You and the enemy have up to three units each.  Units queue up according to speed initially, and then act one-by-one, falling back into the queue based upon thier speed after acting.  When your turn is up you select a single attack, buff, or heal action and a target, and then the action is resolved and the next unit up at bat takes their swing.
The combat has a bunch of vulnerabilities, weaknesses, and status effects going on, but it's a pretty rote affair.  Stun and debuff the most threatening enemies, use attacks that have synergizing effects (apply bleed, use attack that exploits bleed), focus targets down, throw out heals to keep the enemy from knocking any of you down.  It's not a particularly difficult decision tree.  Most of the time I can't be bothered to even look up the enemy's vulnerabilities and resistances.
After five hours I only saw a character die once, and that wasn't as much a matter of difficulty as a mix of apathy and because it wasn't clear when in the combat the "round" border was when damage-over-time effects applied.
There's also some minor UI complaints and bugs on both the map and in combat, such as ship orders sometimes causing time to pass without issuing the order, or unhelpful DoT mouse-overs telling you an enemy is suffering "35% base damage" per turn instead of something useful like "20 damage per turn".  (without telling you what skill the base damage is from, either)
Even if more difficult- and there are two difficulty levels above the default one I played- I have a hard time imagining Halcyon 6 being an interesting game.  There's just not many meaningful decisions or trade offs involved in any of the component systems of the game, and they don't really come together in a compelling way.
Halcyon 6 has some nice art in it- I particularly like the death animations and the alien portraits during conversations.  The writing's can be amusing.  It's got a ton of things for you to do and creates an addictive one-more-turn environment where there's always one more mission, progression objective, or task you want to complete to keep you from shutting it down.  If the idea of doing tons and tons of early-JRPG style combat while handling your levelling up via a strategic layer appeals to you, and you're not looking for a lot of depth or challenge, it might very well be for you.
For me, however, I quickly ended up feeling like I'd grasped and mastered what the game offered and found myself looking a shopping list of story progression to end the game by completing the same fetch quests and Final Fantasy random monster encounters over and over again for many hours to come, and uninstalled.

I've had this controller for a few months now and I feel like I can finally give a review on it... it really is an awesome piece to have, however, it is not a replacement for the Xbox 360 controller.  It's just easier to use the 360 controller with games that were designed to use it. Where this thing really shines is when you want to play your older games or titles that were never designed for controller support. I still play my original copy of doom 3 with the steam controller and I love it! Also call of duty games come to mind. It does take a bit of setup for each game, but everything on this game pad is completely customisable to get the feel you are looking for while playing. It's also very helpful that a press of the steam button pulls up the overlay where things can be changed quite quickly.  Targeting with the track pad is difficult at first, but so was a joystick when that was new back in the ps1 days. With a little practice it becomes second nature. Overall it is worth getting if you still play your old titles (which is kind of the big reason I choose pc over consoles). Just add them to your steam library and you're good. I have noticed that with some games you must launch stem as administrator for it to work. Big picture mode is nice with it as well, but as others have stated, the on screen keyboard can sometimes get in the way. Once again, not a replacement for the 360 controller, but a solution to a problem with older or mouse and keyboard only games.

First off the overall design is tremendously off-putting and the feel in-hand is uncomfortable. The functionality was also terrible. It's clearly designed to be used with Steam OS and nothing else. Using it properly on any real OS is a struggle and requires that Steam Big Picture mode be minimized in order to get your personalized keybindings to work or to use the keyboard which in and of itself is also tremendously buggy. (Often appearing over the area you're trying to type in or even on occasion full screening itself for no purpose) In fact, far too frequently the controller would just stop working altogether. (Still on and giving haptic feedback, but resulting in no actual input being registered by the computer.)
Many people say that it's better once you get used to it, but after trying my best to like it I realized that I wasn't getting used to how great it was, I was getting used to it being inferior. For my HTPC I now use an Xbox controller along with Controller Companion. ($2.99 on Steam) You can save yourself some time and skip to that part.

World of Guns is a great game if you just want to kill a couple of minutes at a time, but it can still hold up extended sessions too. It's very interesting to see the workings of all the models without having to own them and get a reputation as a murderous lunatic. That, and actually since you can hide parts and slow down time while watching the weapons operate, it gives some insights into the gun that most people wouldn't be able to uncover with equipment they have at home even if they owned it.
The biggest problem for me is that the game is ever so slightly skittish on the virtual currency and clearly tries to goad the player into forking out some cash. This would be no problem otherwise, but I don't want to buy the exp straight out as it's the pacing that keeps the game interesting, nor do I want to unlock weapons directly, for the same reason. The boosters are cheaply done; they only last an hour and are much too expensive. The only real incentive to spend money I see here is stickers and other cosmetics for the guns, which I'm not all that interested in. In fact I find the ability to customize the guns with bright colors, animal prints and stick-on pictures a bit tacky.
Something I could see myself pay for would be a premium version where I can take apart all the weapon accessories I normally only get to see attached in operation mode. The differences between skeleton, wooden and synthetic stocks could be interesting, for example. Or maybe being able to operate weapons with parts taken off (and getting to see malfunctions, dry fire, etc). For the right price I could pay for these features even gun by gun.

I wanted to like this controller. I really did! Sadly, I tried it out for a week and it has since sat in the closet of my game room collecting dust. The real downfall of this controller was supposed to be its big selling point: the touch track pad. I'm sure that there are some games that it works well with. Unfortunately, FPS games and any other games that require quick responses are not among those. Targeting in particular is difficult if not impossible except when a single-player game is on the easiest setting. DO NOT try to use this controller in a live match. You will die. A lot.
On the plus side, I did like the responsiveness of the triggers and the paddles underneath are a welcome addition to the modern controller setup. And using this in "Big Screen" mode did make Steam feel more like a console while still retaining all the power of the PC (PC master race for life!).
Still, you don't realize how much you miss the secondary joystick until it's gone.
Edit: packed it away right after writing this review. It's a good thing it's in a closet or it would probably have a layer of dust on it by now.

Overall Rating: 8.5 / 10
DISCLAIMER: Please do not be fooled by my amount of time played on Steam. I have been playing this game since Beta 2012, so I assure you I have many, many hours logged on this game. More hours logged then all other games I own combined for that matter!
Review:
This is an excellent game with great potential and a bright future ahead! I recommend this game for anyone looking for more tactical gameplay in their FPS gaming.
Last year, the devs introduced Community Warfar, a gamemode targeted at hardcore players with an entire star map and several factions to fight for. If you decide to give this game a shot, I recommend shying away from this gamemode for the first while until you get a grasp of the main concepts of combat roles and loadouts, and decide this is a game you want to continue with. If you make it to ComWar, you will enjoy increased rewards, frequent events, and the final end-all Battle for Tukayyid Tournament to end each season of ComWar. ComWar is currently in Beta II, with Beta III just around the corner. In Beta III, players will be able to choose from several unique Career paths, vote on planets to attack, pool C-bills for tactical bonuses & ordinance (TACTICAL NUKE CONFIRMED), and perform either full out planetary Assault or planetary Scouting missions to collect intel for additional bonuses.
The devs are continuously pumping out new content in the form of Battlemechs, Camo, (coming soon) Decals and Maps. They are also dedicated to perfecting player balance as much as possible, so one can expect one or two updates to gameplay mechanics every month, on top of new content updates.
MechWarrior Online got off to a rough start in 2012. Whether you talk to the haters or the lovers, everyone can admit this fact. This was largely due to the now defunct company Infinite Games Publishing (IGP) and its control over the project. The good news is that since its departure, progress on this game has been swift and positive. The game's 'mech concepts are lauded as one of its strongest points, with much of the beautiful 'mech designs now slated for use in the upcoming turn-strategy game Battletech (if you don't know about this game, also worth a look!
.
The game's UI has been improved frequently, but new players will still have some difficulty navigating some tabs. Notably, new players may struggle with customizing loadouts. My best recommendation for this is to visit the game's forums
and get advice from the playerbase, most of whom are very helpful.
The game's Tutorial zone has been revamped recently! All new players should visit this zone first, because this is not a game that you can simply skip the tutorial unless you are a returning player (the tutorial even has in-game rewards for completing challenges). As a veteran player, I still use this zone to practice with new 'mechs.
Some may get turned off buy the game's MC currency (money purchasable currency) that allows players to skip a lot of the grind and get the good stuff. While this game may seem Pay-To-Win, this is certainly not the case, as virtually all chassis, weapons, equipment and upgrades are purchasable with C-bills (gameplay generated/earned currency). The only things unobtainable without MC are vanity items & a select group of 'Hero' mechs that come with unique camo patterns and weapon hardpoints (which are arguably no better or worse in performance when compared to their standard counterpart). Also purchaseable with MC-only are designated 'Champion' 'mechs, but do not be fooled! These mechs are simply optimized versions of standard C-bill purchasable mechs, they do not differ at all in performance potential!
In summary, this is a great tactical shooter with very unique gameplay concepts. As such, the learning curve can be rather steep for some, and there are still a few rough spots that require development. The future of this game is bright, however, with constant updates and some really exciting new content lined up for spring. In the words of the game's devs, they are "far from finished" with this game!

I find it a little difficult not to recommend a free to play game, especially one that has the polished look that MWO has. One that has the look/feel of a complete pay to play game. That being the case I won't say - no, I don't recommend it.
Instead I will say don't get into this free to play game expecting great things. As some reviewers have mentioned the grind is real. I don't really care about comparisons of other games and how much you have to grind on them to get anywhere. From my personal experience I have probably in the neighborhood of 75 hours into this game. I also have well over $80 into this game. If the cost of MC is the same it has been for a couple years then I have $95 into the game. So that's nearly 80 hours and $95... Know what I have? Ten mechs currently. I believe I have sold one that I decided I'd never use again, and it was a mech that I had won. Also one of the mechs I currently have I won as well. Three of the mechs I have I bought with real money essentially. So that means I've been able to afford to buy six mechs in the game with nearly 80 hours worth of grinding. And this includes using "Hero" mechs that net you more c-bills per match.
If you spend real money on this game know that the "value" simply will not be there. I have never spent $95 on a single stand alone game. A full copy of a game, then DLC that comes out later, yes. But $95 for a game that completely lacks any kind of story mode, only allows for online multiplayer and last I knew in order to "host" a game yourself with buddies that cost real money.
Bottom line is if you put any kind of money into the game you're essentially paying for - at best half a game depending on how you want to look at it. Because real money doesn't even come close to unlocking or allowing one to use all of the mechs in the game. Worst case scenario dropping $50 on the game has the potential to allow you to play with... 5% of the game, at best? I think that's pretty fair. And if you're one those that doesn't spend any money on the game be prepared for some major grinding. And if the grind wasn't bad enough the game becomes very monotonous because of the underwhemling gameplay.

I recommend this game if you're a fan of MechWarrior or if you're looking for something unique amongst the F2P catalogue.
MechWarrior Online is definately a game worth trying simply because it is free. But be warned: the game is very grindy and difficult. Matches will seem unfair to someone new. This game is slow paced, which is different from other shooters.
This game is also very niche. Even if the game was perfect, most will not like it because it's only fun for certain people.
The main issue this game faces is the grindy nature of the game. You will spend a lot of time playing to get the end game stuff, which is acceptable. However, you have to specialize in a mech (buying three varients of the same mech) in order to get high-level "masteries." If you make the wrong choice, you could find that you just wasted millions of C-Bills (in-game currency) trying to play.
Real-money prices are also high. So expect to drop serious coin if you want a small advantage. Like with everything in this game, you have to educate yourself before you buy. You might not like that sweet mech you just spent 10 dollars for. Personally, I don't mind throwing a little money here and there to stack up my real-money currency, because it adds up fast. To cut on the grind, you can throw some money for an XP and C-bill boost, which is nice and adds 50% to all earnings. Certain mechs that cost real money also carry a XP or C-BIll bonus when using them. You could be earning upwards to 70% extra money and XP due to these mechs.
Overall, try this game out. I love it, but it's still a work in progress. The say it's released, but they need to address some things.

I absolutely love this game. Looks and sounds great, but the strongest point is the diversity of gameplay. You start out a lowly human, but by the end you will be diving off rooftops and punching through walls thanks to your cybernetic upgrades. Combat is very diverse. You can choose to dive in with guns blazing and blades flying (the takedowns can be very satisfying) or quietly creep from room to room dropping enemies like the cyber-ninja that you are. You can even take on a real challenge and leave (almost) everyone still breathing. Conversations with NPCs take varying paths and the things you say can shape your next move. In all, a strong entry in the Deus Ex universe. If I have one complaint it's that the game can develop very bad lag in certain places. Deus Ex games always seems to have lag problems around fires and this one is no exception. As a final note, your best bet is to disable DirectX 11 right from the start. It seems to solve most of any graphics issues that I found.

This is probably the closest you will get to having a Dungeon Keeper 1/2.  However, there are some downsides to this game.
Pros:
Great flexibility.  For the most part I beat the game with mostly naga healers.  I used some risen undead and converted heroes, but my main pack were the naga.  It was a lot of fun to play how I wanted.  I dabbled in some of the others and saw my viable builds.
Dungeon design.  It was being able to design a nice looking dungeon and seeing all of the parts work.  The decor was nice for each of the races and room types.
Mission variety.  Decent mission variety for the most part.  The early missions add new items bit by bit, while the later missions get progressively harder.
The overworld.  Neat take on the battles.  Pull your unit in the overworld to attack and find evilness, which is like a resource to spend on the research tree.  I enjoyed that part quite a lot, but it's not a true RTS.
Cons:
The narrator.  Sorry, he was grating on me.
The jokes.  Eventually the puns wear thin.  I started to skip scenes or ignore what was being said.  I get it, make jokes of WoW or LotR.  Eventually it just wasn't funny and was more annoying.
The sound bugs.  Sometimes my sound effecits and/or the music would just cut out, for no reason at all.
The shortcuts.  Casting spells was a pain.  It was hard to remember the shortcuts to hit on a keyboard to cast a spell.  This could have been part of the UI, however thet brings me to the next con...
The UI.  It wasn't that great.  Some elements got in the way, such as the HUGE boss health bars on the screen at all times.
Overall:
Great game if it's on sale, I think.  I think I spent $30 on it, but it's not worth more than that.  However, I still enjoyed it.  As there is neutral option, I do recommend it, but again, only if on sale.
Also, for those who are a fan of Dungeons 1 - this game is nothing like it.  I enjoyed Dungeons 1, but they moved away from that formula.

Finally, my itch has been scratched. I remember seeing a demo of the original dungeon keeper in the mall back in the 90's. Thanks for bringing back all to good times. After playing this game for weeks, I've come to love it.  At the start, it throws a curve ball in that if you expand too fast you end up crippling your entire empire via low morale.  Once you get used to this, the game becomes quite fun.  I highly recommend you start on the Newbie difficulty first and then move from there.
The AI is good early on, but it ends up not doing well vs. humans in the end.  Even on the hardest difficulty, the AI doesn't take the initiative and attack you.  Also, towards the end, the AI's ships will just not compare to your own.  They seem to ignore the special modules that can greatly increase your effectiveness.
The actual battles themselves are not the greatest.  You have rock-scissor-paper type cards to play that will somewhat change the outcome.  You can watch the battle live, but it becomes simply a waste of time.  You cannot speed it up, you can't skip it if you accidently go into it, and the camera constantly changes on you.  It is a bit sad because the graphics are quite good in the battle...  They could have done more with it.
The colony management and tech tree are superb.  Once you get used to the interface, everything feels it was put there for a reason.  While there are automatic planet managers, I would not use them.  They do not do a good job of maximizing your potential.  Many times, I end up changing Desert planets to Lava for the huge increase in production (at the cost of morale) later in the game for huge production systems.  Plus, all you are truely doing in this game is building up colonies with tech you picked out in order to build ships to fight.
There is a ship design screen, but it is extremely basic.  It is essentially like Master of Orion 2.

Do you enjoy a challenge?  Then this is the game for you.
10 Second Ninja has fairly simple controls: move, jump, throw a shuriken, and katana slash.  But don't let that sort of simplicity fool you because this game offers a very infuriating yet exhilerating challenge with every level.  The goal?  Complete each stage in under 10 seconds - and if your performance is ranked on a 3-star rating.  The challenge of obtaining 3 stars on each level is - to me - the most fun quality of 10 Second Ninja.
So if you're a completionist, enjoy games where you experience an infuriating challenge but feel absolutely ecstatic once you accomplish your goal, and you also enjoy the idea of destroying Nazi robots, then I highly recommend this game!

Unclaimed World is an awesome game. The colony system is quite deep and it has a more relatable feeling that the Fantasy colony management games out there. I like the attemps to give the colonists personality, but their AI leaves some space for improvements: it frustrates me when they drop tasks halfway, leaving all the tools behind. Otherwise, this is a relaxing game with a complicated system where you construct a nice village. You'll be choosing new goals for your colony, pinning them to the UI to keep track of them, feeling great when they are achieved.
There are some draw-backs, however. In 10 hours of gametime, I've crashed twice and I feel that the character AI could be optimized.

I think that the game is fun and pretty complex in a good way. I have recently started it and there is a lot to learn in the start but it is easy to learn. I like that there is wide crafting with a control of a colony. It has not bugged out or crashed yet and has good music. I hope that you get the game and see for your self but, it is complex. Have fun!

I've recently started playing and am finding the game to have a lot more depth than similar titles (like world of tanks, world of warships etc.), with just as much if not more room for progression. Certainly mastering every mech chassis and finding optimal builds that work for you on all of them would take a long time.
From what I've seen the c-bill (currency earned in game) variants of mechs are at least competitive with, if not better than the mechs you can only buy with real money. As such the only thing you ever 'need' to buy are mech bays, though if you're putting in enough time to get the c-bills for that many mechs (and equiprment) then putting a little money in is fairly reasonable. If you are going to spend real money then the steam dlc 'mech performance packs' aren't the best idea - you only get one mech chassis variant of each type so you'd need to spend quite a lot of time getting the money for two more variants as you need to own three in order to master a chassis, which you'd definitely want to be doing. For my money I'd get a mastery pack for MC (the premium currency) which you can see in-game.
Certainly the game is worth downloading and trying; there's a whole lot of content on offer, most of which you can get without spending anything if you're willing to put in the time.

The Steam controller. It's built well and looks nice. I've thrown it around and so far don't hear any plastic rattling around inside. I like that's it's wireless and you can program it to function however you please with ANY game. However, there are some points that can be improved upon.
There really should be a right analog stick to accurately play FPS games. The trackpad is accurate but feels odd when you're trying to make quick gun aiming movements by sliding your thumb across the trackpad's semi-slick plastic. There needs be actual rumble motors too, not just the haptic motors with their very light and squeeky rumble "emulation". The triggers should have more pressure resistance so you can accurately modulate gas and brake when racing as opposed to flooring it all the time. Additionally, the wireless dongle should be much smaller, like that of a wireless work mouse. The current dongle is about half the length of an old USB stick, which can get bumped and wear out the USB ports, at least when using with a laptop. I also want to safely keep the dongle plugged into my laptop when I move it around and put it in it's travel bag.
Other then many small points that need improvement, I like the controller a lot and have been using it almost daily. I feel like the main point of the Steam controller was to bring PC gaming to the couch and it has suceeded physically, and on the software side with the community made custom bindings. I'm looking forward to a revised Steam controller which addresses my points.

An essential addition for anyone who enjoys 2D action games and gets a thrill from persevering against insanely difficult bosses for hours on end, Rabi-Ribi is at its best when it's testing you to dodge a swarm of bullets (with gravity, no less) in its over 30 boss fights, but is also an enjoyable platforming and exploration game that offers tons of replayablity due to its extremely non-linear design.
First thing's first: This game is fanservice-y, but that's not the focus of the game. It's aware enough of this to lampshade Ribbon's skimpy outfit at times. Don't be turned off by the Steam store page description about a bunny-girl costume, because I would not have sunk 200 hours into this game if I just wanted to look at ecchi. You'll see some humorous dialogue teasing at yuri themes as well, but overall, the story of the game is an actual story about Erina, Rabi-Rabi Island, and some of its inhabitants, though it doesn't truly begin to unfold until halfway through the game. The initial premise is that Erina, formerly a pet rabbit of Rumi but turned human by unknown means, is tasked with trying to track down Rumi's sister Miru, who has been magicked away by a stone tablet, and Erina needs the help of other magic-users on the island to power this tablet and follow Miru. But there's a much more interesting story that you'll uncover about the island's origins and a figure from its past as you progress--though it remains bunny-themed to the end.
Progression in Rabi-Ribi is similar to other Metroidvania games in that you start with just a basic jumping ability and go on to acquire myriad upgrades to your attacks, mobility, and statistics hidden throughout the world. In the prologue, you are railroaded towards the town at the island's center, but afterwards you are free to explore almost the entirety of the fairly large overworld, with just a few areas locked behind certain events. Two big twists that delighted me as I played this game: one, every single item, even Erina's primary attack, is optional, if you look hard enough for alternate routes and can wrap your head around the island's layout; two, while the game explicitly guides you (with waypoints and objectives, even) towards a smoothly curved difficulty progression that will help you pick up important items early, you are free to utterly ignore this and go virtually anywhere in any order. One achievement, for example, requires you to traverse the entire world "backwards" from the start to avoid meeting a boss just outside of town for most of the game.
In addition to simple stat ups and new movement and attack abilities, you will find badges tied to the game's nicely tuned badge system, allowing you to equip a limited point value of badges you've found to tweak your stats, gain immunity to various statuses, earn more currency, and the like. It's a fun system that allows you to heavily prioritize offense or defense, as several badges trade one for the other.
The major attraction in Rabi-Ribi is the boss fights, however. After a few easy bosses in the opening sequence, the game quickly ramps up to a brutal difficulty; outside of the lowest difficulties (which are fairly easy as long as you pick up a few items), this is a game where you will not beat many, if any, bosses on the first attempt. Most fights are fairly short, about five minutes in length, but some late-game bosses can exceed ten or fifteen minutes. If you love the feeling of gradual improvement, learning how to deal with various patterns, progressing farther each time only to be faced with an even more brutal attack, then this game will be a great fit for you. If this is a turn-off, and you're only looking to coast through, it's still a decent game, but you won't get the same sort of value. Those who want to challenge themselves get the option of six difficulties, each of which scales up in difficulty nigh-endlessly with repeated loops of New Game+ (though the actual dodging mechanic starts to fall apart around four or five loops and it just turns into a battle of overpowered offenses). Challenge aside, each boss has their own unique theme (with the exception of two pairs of siblings who have variants of the other's attacks), and it's wonderfully illustrated in their attack patterns. Cocoa, the penniless inventor, fights using an assortment of automated bombs; Pandora, the ancient princess(?) waiting inside a tricky pyramid, can slow your movement and fights with several puzzle- and trap-like attacks; Ashuri feels like a classical Ordinary Magician and takes to her broomstick for several fly-by attacks.
On top of the story mode, Rabi-Ribi offers a speedrun mode which skips the intro segment and all cutscenes automatically and has a frame-accurate timer plus leaderboards for all difficulties, any%, 0%, and 100%, plus an absolutely brutal Boss Rush mode that places you against absurd odds (the "True Boss Rush" mode will easily take over 90 minutes to finish, for perspective).
The game does have a history of technical issues on some PCs due to its requirement of running at 60 FPS (and no more). However, a late 2017 patch seems to have addressed this.
Rabi-Ribi was easily my favorite game of 2016, and continues to occupy me periodically nearing the end of 2017. There is simply so much to do here, especially if you follow the achievement list for ideas for your next challenge, that you are pretty much certain to get insane value from the purchase if the genre is at all to your liking. Please, don't pass on this hidden gem just because the outfits or bunny-girl theme turn you off.

You, the world-conquering-and-now-slightly-bored-evil, set out to conquer a new land. Fighting and destroying those tree-hugging, fairy loving cretin do-gooders you embark on an epic story, narrated brilliantly and smothered in references anyone should recognize. The humor in this game is fantastic, especially for a Lord of the Rings fan and World of Warcraft player, and the gameplay reminds of the good old Dungeon Keeper series.
While the whole process of rebuilding your base gets a little repetitive (like with any strategy game where you start (most of the time) from scratch each mission), the game has a fast enough pace that it's not bothersome. The narrative to this game is simply amazing and will have you laughing out loud often and the art work is simply lovely while running smoothly on even a mid-tier gaming rig.
I don't tend to write reviews, but this game simply warrants one. If this is not already in your library .. it should be. Recommended. Very much so.

I first played MechWarrior Online way back during beta years ago, and honestly I had not touched it since. Now that MechWarrior Online is on Steam I have been playing it at least a little bit every day with friends. I have to say, I have been having a good time! While this is not hte first MechWarrior game I have ever played, that title being taken by MechWarrior 2 for the playstation, i've got to say MechWarrior Online is probably one of my favorite modern mech war games, along with Hawken and the Armored Core series.
In MechWarrior Online you customize your mech with weapons and equipment and then take them into battle against other players. There are a  variety of weapons from ballistic, energy, and missile based weapons. Its not just a mech based shooter though, you will have to manage armour, ammunition and most importantly heat generation on your mech. If you overheat mid fight your a goner.
There are a pretty decent variety of maps, each changing gameplay up in different ways. Some maps will have extremely high or low ambient temperature, affecting the heat generation of the mech, some maps will even have higher or lower gravity, or more noticeable higher or lower light levels. If it gets too dark you may have to fight the rest of the match in night vision, or thermal!
MechWarrior Online has a handful of game modes I have played so far, you have Conquest, a standard capture the points for resource tickets type of game mode, Assault a game mode where your objective is to capture the enemy base and Skirmish, the standard TDM of MechWarrior. There are also more complicated game modes apart of "Faction Play" I have not played any of these yet but from what I can tell you have Invasion an attack and defense game mode, and invasion counter attack, another attack and defense game mode.  The one thing all of these game modes have in common from what I can tell is there are no respawns in any of them. No respawns means dont run off alone and try to solo multiple enemy mechs. This is not your average shooter, if you play it like one you will probably get wrecked really quick.
I have to say, I definitely recommend MechWarrior Online. I thought it died a while ago but it seems to be going pretty strong at least for now. I would say anyone who is a fan of mech games would want to try MechWarrior Online. It has its own feeling that I am sure lots of people enjoy.

I have been playing since March 2015 (long after all the IGP/ PGI stuff).  I play may be an hour a day at most on average through the week.
Overview:
At the moment the game consists of 2 main aspects; the mech battles (game play) and the mechlab (customisation).  There should be more but outside those areas the game feels less than fully developed
What's good.
Mech battles are either through, solo (quick play), group queue or Community Warfare (CW).  The fights are fun and last about 5minutes (except CW which is about 30 mins).  In quick drop there is no messing about it's pick a mech and hit the play button then into a 12 v 12 match.
The fights are fun and as a general rule when you die you don't feel it is because of anything other than your own mistakes.  The game has a steep learning curve, expect to die and die quickly until you learn and understand what is going on.
The mech lab is where you customise your mech.  Generally when you first buy a mech it does not have a good load out and so you'll be spending more money to fit it out with better stuff.  You however have the use of trial mechs which have a good loadout so no need even to buy your own mech straight away.  The mechlab is now well laid out and generally easy to understand (although again there is a learning curve).  I would like to see improvements to the lab including better information on heat management.
What's lacking:
CW at the moment lacks any real reason to  play it other than the free mech bays it gives out.  They have indicated that they are adding to CW by Spring 2016, hopefully this will improve.
The LFG and in game chat is basic and could do with some improvement.
the various game modes all work out as kill the enemy team as quickly as possible and play out in a reasonably similar way.  Again a new game mode on CW might make this better.  in part however this a design decision that no team has respawns (or only 4 in CW) therefore logically killing the other team is the logical way to play.  This I can over look because the Mech on Mech combat is great.
The "skill tree" is little more than an xp bucket with an upper limit.  there is no "tree" and they provide a reasonable bonus for having 3 variants of the same mech with all the basics unlocked (which can be annoying and only there to encourage you to have 3 of each mech).  There have been comments by PGI that they are looking to change this and that would be welcomed and well over due.
How PGi makes its money:
There is no pay to win in this game.  Everyone gets one mech (or 4 in CW) and therefore if you own a 100 you're in no better position than someone that owns 4.  The only mechs that are cash only are Hero mechs (unique variants and c-bill bonus) and Champ Mechs (which have an xp bonus on a standard variant).
To get a mech or buy anything in the game you have to earn c-bills by playing.  Yes this is a grind and that is added too by the fact to get all the "skill tree" bonuses.
In order to own a mech (which allows you to customise it) you have to not only pay c-bills for it but have a spare mech bay.  Mech bays cost real world money (you can earn some in CW or events but if you play for a while that will not be enough) they are however not expensive about $7 will get you 4 mech bays (or more if mech bays are on sale).  Also you start out with 4 mech bays so no need to  spend money on these for some time.
If you want a mech fast you can just pay real world money for it.  The best value is usually a mastery pack of 3 variants of the same mech with the mech bays and premium time.  I am of the view that the prices are at the top end of what PGI can get away with, they can be eye wateringly expensive (I think they would make more money by dropping the prices).
Premium time is also a means of making money.  you can buy premium time and whilst it is active (it runs even when not in game) you get a bonus to xp and c-bills.
Also when releasing a new mech it will be sold on pre-order (early orders also get additional bonus goodies) and released to the pre-orders for a few weeks before being made available for the MC (bought with real world money to spend in game) only for a period before being made available for c-bills.
So they get you to spend the money on getting things faster or because you want to have a wider variety of mechs available.  In a match though none of that makes any difference to how you play and who wins.
Summary:
The game needs improving in lots of aspects to add depth (hopefully those will come with time).
The main headline has to be however that the game play is good and fun and different.  It is a game that keeps you coming back regularly because there is no game play like it at the moment.  Over the past 9 months I have spent too many hours happily destroying mechs in this game and I don't have time to waste on things that are not enjoyable.
I know that people have been playing the game for 3 years now and that in and of its self says a lot.  Not many games are played for that length of time.
All in all it's fun to play and a good game.  It however could easily be a great game (if they fix some of the placeholders)!

I recommend this game highly.
Don't be fooled by the negative reviews, this game has a lot of variety available and can be made as easy or as difficult as you want.  It just takes a little tinkering with the inital settings to create endless possible ways to play this game.  The developers may have mis-labeled the difficulty settings, but they do start you off in an easy version by choosing a small universe with two players.  The difficulty settings start with the rating of Newby, where most people want to start on Normal.  Normal setting gives a significant advantage to the AI, which may seem like Cheating, but Newby is set as an even game.  So, there is no advantage to the AI in Newby, and I recommend players start from this setting. Even though most advanced or experienced gamers want to play Normal and Newby seems like too easy, all new players to this game should start on Newby.
You can add difficulty, even on the Newby setting by increasing the number of other species in the game, changing the species that you use, and changing the layout, size, and planet types (content) of the universe.  I recommend doing all these things before upping the difficulty level.  There is plenty to do at the Newby level before making the game too difficult on oneself.
The mechanics are very intuitive once you start playing the game and should be picked up quickly by most players. Although at first, things might not be well explained in the tutorial, I found all the answers to my questions in the steam community.  The tutorial could have been done a little better, but I usually enjoy jumping in and playing from the start anyway.
There are a lot of good elements to this game and the computer system does a lot of work correctly to make this game less tedius and more enjoyable than games like Civ.  I have always found Civ too click intensive. It is not simply, build a lot of high level ships and destroy everything either.  There are a lot of ways to win and destruction is not required.  And even with the high level ships, taking over other systems takes time and rebuilding them takes more time.  You have to slowly get the approval of those citizens living on conquered worlds.  So, it is not easy to simply blitz through a lot of systems quickly.  Even the AI usually only takes one or two systems when they attack you before seeking peace. They will not usually (in my experience) try to conquer you outright, even if they are fighting a war against you.  They will stop, and you can rebuild.
Overall, there is a lot of good variation in this game and a lot of good game play.  It will give you long hours of playability.

Having just finished Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's cut i thought it would be the perfect time to write a review on it!
Deus Ex is a first person shooter with third person elements and a strong stealth vibe. Throughout the game you make your way through non-linear but more open-ended missions with multiple paths other than the standard "Run n Gun" style of most first person shooters out there. The third person section of the game is stricly when using cover, doing a stealth takedown and during cutscenes.
The Gameplay is very fun and fairly streamlined. While not as polished to perfection like some other firstperson shooters, it still was very playable and the mix of stealth and action was very well done. I especially liked the takedown animations.  Which ranged from very stylized martial arts, to a very blunt and powerful punch right to the face. I personaly never got tired of watching the spit go flying out an unsuspecting Bad-Guys face after my powerful augmented fist meet his jaw.
The Story implements RPG like chracter progression and story plot choices. Which also helps add to the feeling that this is no ordinary shooter. The story follows a newly augmented Adam Jenson whom after being involved in a brutal attack must start an investigation for his boss. Of course many things are going on the Adam dosn't know about and discovers through the games missions. There are around 16 story missions to go through and a handful or two of side missions. The side missions actually are quite interesting and feel like a standard story mission due to general relevency and interesting objectives. I would strongly suggest any player to play as many side missions as they can and make sure to explore for that ammo or praxis kits!
The graphics are slighlty dated but if you have a modern PC of normal quality than you should not have many problems running this on the max settings. I personaly liked the art style but not everyone may be so inclined. On my gaming rig i was running this game mostly 60FPS. Although i noticed when i transitioned from a loading screen into another area, for about 2 seconds my framerate would drop to the 40's range. But that is still better than those X-Box 360 and Playstation 3 versions that are out there.
I really would suggest this game to almost any gamer who likes these styles of games: Shooter, Stealth, Action, Story-Driven, Interesting, etc.
