Many will look at this game and be ready to dismiss it because it looks like a fanservice laden h-game. Those people are fools.
For one, despite some ecchi-ish CG art, nothing's flat out NC-18 (No nudity, certainly no lewd acts), this ends up being one of the most solid Metroidvania titles in a long time. Why? It embraces the non-linearity that makes a good Metroidvania. This is a Metroidvania where you can literally go "Y'know what? I don't WANT my primary weapon. I'm gonna run the game without it." And you can challenge the game with just Ribbon (Your 'gun' of sorts). Sequence breaking isn't actively blocked, in fact it's outright encouraged. Some achievements even *REQUIRE* you to sequence break, playing the game out of the "intended" order of progression. This right here is what makes me love this game so much. A lot of Metroidvanias will try to prevent you from breaking sequences or doing things out of order. You might be able to get one or two items out of order now and then, but nothing hugely game breaking. This on the other hand, is a game that *wants* you to break it. And for the skilled player, it will reward you for doing so.
Oh right, some people may not know what a Metroidvania is. I should clarify that. It's a game where you basically explore a large, interconnected world. More of it becomes available to explore as you find upgrades to traverse more of it.  There's a lot of platforming, as well as fighting. And both are fun as heck here.
On top of this you have a fun bullet-hell esque form of boss fighting that keeps things quite intense, but due to the upgrade nature of the game, you can always snag more health and attack power to get the advantage in a tougher boss fight whose patterns you haven't quite nailed yet.
This is a Metroidvania that gets so much right where other games in the genre get it wrong. Virtually the entire world map is accessible to you from the getgo if you know how to bypass certain obstacles with Erina's hidden techs. If you were the type of person who loved being able to go out of order in Super Metroid via walljumps and Machballs, you are going to love the way this game encourages more of the same.

Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja Storm 4, in a nutshell, is simply the best of all from the series.
PROS
1. Graphic (only if your specs allows)
Compared to the previous few, NSUNS4 has terrific graphic even at 1280x800. The cut-scenes, jutsu and fight scenes makes it almost close to watching the anime.
2. Controls
Simple combinations of buttons on controller just like the previous series. Nothing much to explain on it other than the fact that even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ can easily pull off an ultimate jutsu
3. Story mode
While I personally do not really like the previous one with mecha-naruto, this story mode simply blows your mind off.
It makes you feel as if you are watching the anime, only that you get to control the characters of the scene to do your bidding. My personal favourite would be the Naruto and Sasuke episode. Naruto and Hinata from The Last. still a better love story than Twilight.

In conclusion, I would rate the game 9/10 and recommend anybody who is interested, to definitely get the game. (do check your PC specs first)

Unclaimed World is about humans trying to survive on an alien world. Different scenarios take place at different points in the history of the world, so you see the people of the planet at different times from early in the colonization to generations later. The alien world itself has lots of strange and new species of plants and creatures, and the look of the settings is interesting and beautiful.
Gameplay revolves around managing the actions of your community of colonists by giving them tasks and prioritizing. A lot of the colony management is zone-based, where you drag and create zones and indicate the actions the colonists should take within that zone - scouting out new locations, gathering resources, patrolling for dangerous creatures, etc. You also manage the production of tools, buildings, food, etc. through a production menu that has an extensive technology tree. The developers have done a great job of making it easy to click through and access information which is great because the technology of the world is well-realized, you need the right materials and tools to gather or build things, and for the more complex technologies it's relatively easy to click through the different menus to see what you might be missing.
Using all this you manage the colonist's needs for food, comfort, and security. To begin with you start off with basic hunter-gatherer technologies to establish a foundation for your colony, and as you accumulate food, dwellings for your settlers, and defenses, your colonists can vote to establish new policies that simultaneously give you access to more advanced technologies but also increase your colonists' expectations of each category, which means you can't rush farming without first getting a good amount of food stocked up from fishing, berrypicking, hunting, etc. I feel like this helps to realize the technology of the world and state of the settlement - your colonists will get upset if you look to set up farms where fields will yield crops month from now, but they need food
If colonists get unhappy enough, they'll leave for a neighboring settlement.
Which brings up another important aspect of the game - trade. You can establish trade with neighboring settlements in order to get access to tools and resources you need, and also you can entice new people with new skillsets to your settlement. This is often necessary as your small hunter-gatherer village will probably not start off with a blacksmith, so in order to advance your technology and create new tools and buildings you'll need to find a blacksmith and ask them to join you.
The game has come a long way and the developers have been great about continuing to improve on and develop the game. They're extremely responsive to questions and bug reports, and it's been a pleasure seeing this game make its journey from vision of a strange alien planet to released game. If you're interested in city building sims, survival sims, or colony management sims (e.g. Banished) you'll probably enjoy this game.
As a last note, I want to point out that many of the negative reviews of this game have come from early in Early Access and the complaints are regarding problems that have since been resolved or the absence of features that have since been added to the game. If you feel this review isn't helpful, feel free to ask any questions and I'll respond in the comments and amend my review to include the information. Thanks for reading.

Many reviews and ratings for this game are really out of date. I am writing this review as of version 0.9, have been playing since early Alpha, and have logged 80hrs on this game. I will say that a lot of those hours were very frustrating and felt like a slog BUT - the game is really improving.
:
Thankfully it's mostly stuff that's still in progress!
* Finicky system for harvesting resources; sometimes they're visible but not harvesting
* Balance still needed for food production and how the colonists perceive their level of supply and comfort
* Lots of time waiting for colonists to finish tasks
* No randomized maps
* Sometimes difficulty is frustrating rather than challenging
* Still has some instability/crashes
:
* Maps are handcrafted and beautiful, and highly dynamic and interactive
* Feels like a fleshed out eco-system into which your colonists are intruding (not just hey there are rabbits and also wolves)
* Highly varied animal species which each play unique role
* TONNES of things to harvest, which can be over-harvested and lead to realistic resource scarcity, forcing your colonists to wait for them to regrow! You have to plan your settlement strategically
* Cobbling together buildings and tools from realistic ingredients (not oh hey I need 5 wood and now magically have a workbench - you can see the ingredients in the design of each structure: i.e., this simple workbench has a big purple leaf as its awning, and this could break and need to be replaced)
* Highly stratified task-management system to juggle priority of specific tasks and task categories
* Each colonist has not just specific skill sets but different priorities for the colony (some want better food, others can live off survival rations but want more comfortable living arrangements)
* Different scenarios in different timelines give different blends of survival/advanced technology perfect for a Space Western kind of genre.
* Slowly and deliberately build from a collection of tents and eating fish to a developed industry town producing machine parts, finished rubber products, bombs, or moonshine!
Overall the game really is a
to play, and I wait with baited breath for each content release. It feels very distinct from other similar games, such as Stonehearth, Rim World, and Clockwork Empires and has a lot to recommend it!

'Mech Warrior Online is an incredible shooter that, while not as 'simulation' heavy as the older titles in the series, still ends up coming out feeling like the only decent 'Mech Simulator on the market for the last 10 years. Forget that Hawken junk.
'Mech Warrior Online is set in the battletech universe and as such brings 30 years worth of history and lore with it, though admittedly most of is left on the table and instead you're given a solid, action packed shooter that focuses on what matters: The 'Mechs. And it pulls the combat off excellently. No absured spotting mechanic that plagues these kind of games, no stupid dice rolls and 24% deviance on impact, no sloping and facing that unrealistically bounces shots (Thoug this skill is replaces with your own skills at spreading damage) and of course, no Russian Bias.
BALANCE, as with most shooters is a hard thing to talk about. It's constantly in flux and tryhards always use the current meta builds that weild the most damage in a single strike and nothing else. However saying that, balance is in the best place it's ever been for a long long time. Sure there are still some usless weapons (Flame throwerers) but now it's more about what works on your 'Mech rather than how many of weapon X you can squeeze on. I have never once found a death in MWO to be annoying or 'cheap' in MWO. Something I don't think any other game can claim.
'Mechs themselves are also generally well balanced however there are 'Mechs that are simply better than others in certain weight catagories. They usually have tradeoffs, and many of the "Worse" Inner Sphere 'Mechs have "Quirks" to make them more appealing, like better refire rate on a weapon, more range, more damage, etc. You'll never disregard a 'Mech as fodder when it runs at you, but there are certainly others you'll back away from while calling to your team for help.
MAPS are generally all good in the regular queue. The maps that the community dislikes are being remade with new features added to them and old design issues ironed out and the rest of the maps are for the most part perfectly fine. Everyone has their own favorites but there are no maps that are beyond unplayable and straight up unfair . You'll never find yourself spawning in and thinking "Oh no I'm at this side of the map" at least.
And the big one: MICRO TRANSACTIONS\PAY WAL. Long and short there ain't one. It can be a bit grindy to get up to speed, it can feel like a chore to master a 'Mech you've grown to dislike and it can feel like you're so far away from earning that next 'Mech, but it certainly achivable and easily done for free. I have been playing this as a Legendary Founder since day 1 with a friend, who has never every, beyond that first payment put a further penny into the game and he currently has around 80+ 'Mechs.
If you do pay, it's going to make your life easier, wether it be getting 'Mechs from packs or enjoying the benifits of premium time or perhaps a hero 'Mech (A middling 'Mech on a partcular chassis, only used because they generate 30% more C-bills.) but there are no guns or 'Mechs that you can never have sooner or later.
Pay responsibly!
And now a little newbie guide:
A new player should hop in the tutorial and complete that, trying to score gold in the movement challenge before moving on to the main game. In the game you'll now get 25 matches that will grant bonus C-Bills known as a cadet bonus. Use these 25 games to get a feel for movment, positioning and managing heat in a range of chassis weights but do not spend a penny of your C-Bills until you get all 25 games done. You should come out with between 15-19 million depending on how well you did. This will let you get pretty much anything you like and I personally would recommend either the Timberwolf or Stormcrow, two very forgiving and powerful units.
A new player should stay _far_ away from Assault 'Mechs and should really really think about if they can handle a light before jumping on it. From here you can now customise your 'Mechs though it's likely going to take a handful of games to earn enough money to do that. Be sure to spend your 'Mech XP in the Skills tab after each game and then use that 'Mech to build up a large stockpile of cash, once you've got three of the same Chassis (But different Mechs, so like TBR-Prime, TBR-C and TBR-D) all skilled up you'll be able to do the Elite catagory of skills and from here you should be able to fend for yourself.
Now find a unit!
Good luck, 'Mech Warriors!!

This is less a game and more a simulator, and I feel that the sim in its entirety is easily worth the $50 lifetime purchase. The game is simply as advertised: disassembling and reassembling firearms. If you want to shoot firearms, this isn't the game for you. Yes, there are a few shooting ranges, and you do get to watch the gun fire in x50 slo-mo while x-rayed, which is freaking awesome, but you don't get to watch the bullet leave the chamber, much less impact on the target. The shooting range is just like target shooting in any other FPS, not much to write home about there. The real reason to play this game is to learn about the internal workings of over 100 models of firearms without having to buy them personally and risk messing up and not being able to fix them.
However, the pay model and unlocking system leaves a bad taste in my mouth. For someone who doesn't have $50 to blow on a sim that I would thoughouly enjoy, I downloaded the free version and started in on unlocking new models. I quickly realized that this was a microtransaction model GAME when played in this way, focusing on high scores and achievements to unlock new weapons... all of which can by bypassed incrementally by small XP boosts. I personally got the $10 Starter Pack, believing that this gave me enough of a boost to unlock what I wanted to shortly (all I really want is to unlock the Glock 19- the gun I personally own).
For someone just casually interested in the internal workings of guns, this game will satisfy that by giving you a Colt 1911 and an AK47 to play with for free, which you should be able to quickly unlock your next gun with. For someone who really wants to study firearms and get to see every model in the game right off the bat, go ahead and pay the full price. It is easily up there with some of those car mechanic simulators.
Either way, it's worth the download. Don't put money into it until you know exactly how much you're willing to spend, and if the full purchase is possibly a better buy for you. Even then, you have to put down money for the car and Humvee disassembly if you want those.

It's not bad. I've also played Galactic Civilisations 2 and I was looking for something equally awesome. Diplomacy is better than is generally the case in this genre (I'm looking at you, Civ 5) and the AI isn't completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. As always, rushing superior weaponry is a winning strategy - but not ridiculously so. If you sit on your laurels for too long even on normal (I enjoy building a lot more than fighting, so I tend to make a deterrent fleet and just swallow up the universe) the AI will come back with weapons built to counter everything you have and roflstomp you. If that fails to work, it's generally *also* pursuing alternate victory paths (getting owned, winning and still being defeated by a wonder victory is kind of nice).
The endgame *does* tend to drag a bit, especially if you're winning very badly. The AI will fight you until the last breath, and always seems to be spawning ships from every single planet that could conceivably build them. This isn't bad, but if you're looking for a quick game (quick being less than 8-9 hours on a medium map with two opponents) you're probably not going to like this.
All in all I'd get it if you enjoy the genre. There's no terribly obvious flaws and the AI is reasonably crafty.

Blockland describes itself as 'that game where you build stuff'. That's actually pretty accurate!
Blockland runs on an older version of the Torque Game Engine. It revolves around what are essentially legos, as the title implies. You control a small plastic figure called a 'blockhead', and the core element of the game involves placing bricks (with very intuitive controls) and then changing them with paint, emitters, or a simple programming system to create pretty much anything. There's support for add-ons and a weapon system, which opens possibilities for team deathmatches and any number of other gamemodes.
The controls. Blockland's movement and view controls are similar to any other 3D game - WASD to move, mouse to look, space to jump, so on, so forth. The build controls are almost as easy to use. Pressing a numpad key moves the brick in that direction, just like WASD; the corner keys move up and down or rotate the brick, and numpad 0 clears your 'ghost' brick (which shows where you're going to place it). This does take a day or two to learn well, but once you figure it out it's hard to think of a better way.
Blockland also has decent multiplayer features, and involves a player-hosted server system. One of the core elements of the game is the fact that you're not just building stuff - you're
building stuff together. Servers can, by default, support up to 32 players; a workaround has been used to increase this to 99. The fact that servers are player-hosted removes most problems with lag; each individual server has to have a poor connection to be affected, instead of just one master server (there is, in fact, a master server, but it only keeps a list of all the servers players are hosting; IP connections can still be used).
Bricks can be 'evented', or programmed, to do a number of things. The events system acts on a per-brick basis and is actually very easy to understand. You choose an input from a drop-down box - like onActivate (when the brick is clicked) or onPlayerTouch (more self-explanatory), then a target (Player, Client, Brick, Named Brick, etc.), then an action (setColor, Kill, playSound). For example -
would make a ladder rung, when clicked, give the player a boost up. More than one event can be placed on a brick, and they can be delayed or even chained together with something called a relay.
Finally, Blockland has an extensive add-on system that can be used to change almost any part of the game. New bricks can be added, or emitters, or colors, or events, or any other number of things. Even the GUI is open for change; the only rules are those that the programming language sets. The programming language is, however, slightly limited by the game's creator; this is mostly to avoid hacking or cheating, which are nigh-impossible without illegally modifying the game.
First - the game carries the potential for what I call
. You buy the game and just LOVE it; then you play it for several weeks or months and abruptly lose all interest. I first encountered this effect while playing Minecraft, hence the name; I used to play both games constantly, and now I haven't touched either of them for months for no apparent reason.
Secondly, the game's community can be picky. Just mentioning Minecraft as above might get me some insults and complaints; half of Blockland's community is notorious for their hate of the games Minecraft and Roblox, the sole reason appearing to be that they're similar to Blockland (or vice verse). Also, the game has a website with a forum; there's a good share of good people as well as an impressive number of idiots that can be found there. The community isn't horrible, but it isn't the greatest I've seen, either.
Finally, the game lost some of its former value with the v21 update. This update removed terrains and interiors - excellent parts of the game that allowed landscapes and buildings to be used as the scene for construction - in favor of shaders (like you might find in any other game) and bots (what it says on the tin). The game wasn't
, but it was definitely made worse. Terrains and interiors may return, and I hope they do, but having to build on an infinite flat plane shouldn't hinder your creativity!
Blockland's features outweigh its flaws - while the community could be nicer and some recent updates are questionable, the game has a solid base and a good number of features to support it. Its support for add-ons and mods make almost anything possible, and there's already a great number of these out there. If you enjoyed building with legos as a kid, consider yourself a decent artist, need practice with programming, or just want a good way to have fun with your friends - this game is for you.

I like the art style and I really appreciated the humor of the last two but this game kinda falls flat. The punchline to every joke is a reference to some fantasy trope. The game even makes fun of itself for making these references too much. You can't use the 'the punchline is that this joke is bad' card too many times without it becoming overused and lazy. Maybe as someone who played Dungeons 2, it just feels like the same joke told with a different character... or the same really because the only real 'character' between each game is the Narrator.
It's nice to see that the developer is listening to feedback, I can definitely feel a marked improvement over Dungeons 2: The evil hand is still there, but you have your own cursor that the evil hand follows rather than forcing you to have this GIANT guantlet as your cursor. They also took a page from Starcraft in that you can only rotate the maps 45 degrees in either direction but the camera goes back to default when you let go of the button, Dungeons 2 you could rotate 360 and with the two maps orientation got really hard to keep track of. I look forward to the future of this game.
However, this game suffers from the same core problem that plagued it's predecessor:  you are forced to play two different games at once that are incompatible with each other. A dungeon management sim, and a real time strategy. I want to play a modern version of the classic Dungeon Keeper, not Warcraft. It sounds good on paper, right? But the execution is the problem. There's this new resource called 'Evilness'. It's used to unlock tech in the tech tree. The only way to get Evilness is by going to the above ground and attacking people. You do this by commanding your troops just like an RTS, i.e. the only thing they will do on their own is attack nearby enemies. The game has boss fights too, which have you moving your cluster of troops out of telegraphed AOE attacks. Cool idea for a RTS game but kinda dumb for a management sim. Every RTS moment is kinda slow and not very engaging. You just move your guys when you see the circles on the ground.
In the original dungeon keeper, the only way to directly control a unit was to posess it and control it FPS style, you gave your units order, but if they were angry for whatever reason, they wouldn't do as you told them to. I'm not asking for that FPS mode to be added it just seems really dumb that your minions are autonomous, for the most part, in your dungeon and will heal/feed/guard without you telling them anything, but above ground their AI is non-existant.
My suggestion to the dev is to create a mode where the above ground is part of it but you have two different types of minions: Defenders and Invaders. Defenders live in the dungeon, Invaders periodically go loot and pillage. Maybe you have the ability to throw a boon/buff to your invaders every once in awhile in the heat of battle but you don't have direct control of them. Everytime they go on a raiding party, some die and some come back with loot and XP. Failure to send out enough invaders limits your Evilness production and eventually the Townsfolk build up to a point where you can keep them back.

- You have to manually send out a ship to each resource planet/location to gather resources and return them to base
- You must continually level up your officers in order to train additional officers
- Go here, kill X, repeat pattern
- Use skills in this order for each enemy you fight (the order rarely changes)

Halcyon 6 is an RPG with some obvious flaws obscuring a basically fun and ambitious design.
Most of the time, you're moving fleets around on the map to pick up materials, or fighting. The fleet-moving is busywork because you keep visiting the same stars, where "visiting" consists entirely of entering a menu that asks if you want to pick up the latest batch of resources (answer: yes).
Fighting is where this game shines. It's superficially Final Fantasy with starships, if SquareEnix had had an ounce of creativity in the 1990s. You're constantly trying to inflict status effects and exploiting them with attacks that do extra damage based on what you've already inflicted. Ground-based battles are less fun, because you're often saddled with worthless "greenshirt" cadets and one real character.
How about the space diplomacy? There basically isn't any. I was expecting long, elaborate conversations in the style of the now-free "Star Control 2/The Ur-Quan Masters", but despite the screenshots the conversations are very short monologues with your choice of snappy comeback. You don't learn much about the aliens or make plot decisions about them, so far as I can tell.
Lately I'm having trouble with the pacing. Certain random events get frantic once you've done certain story events. Playing medium difficulty, I just killed off a Chruul fleet, chased another fleet home and killed it, only to find there are three urgent colony-saving missions and probably another fleet about to attack my station, and I can't make headway on an optional quest because every one of those requires the attention of my one top-tier fleet. Can't level up my second-rate officers because there're no challenges suited to them and I can't afford the increasingly ludicrous costs to research, then build, then use the latest shipyard. There's no empire management either, despite appearances, because you can never build a new colony to speed up future resource returns.
So, overall I would give this game a neutral rating, and am voting yes only because I must pick up/down and I've gotten some hours of fun out of it. If the game added an attempt at richer conversation with the aliens, and a balance tweak at medium level to reduce prices and slow the madness a bit, and fixed the UI, I'd go to a clear yes vote. Good work by the developers but this game isn't quite what it has the potential to be, yet.
Edit: Changed to a No vote after trying to play again and finding the play balance so broken I can't proceed. Also noting some buggy interface parts and two quests that're never marked as done when completed.

I have to say this is an actually interesting concept - things happening, aliens you build relationships with, all of it. I didn't see anything related to xcom except basebuilding - but i did get a nice SC2 memory trigger, twice. First when i met aliens and then when i thought about the ending
. It's very enjoyable and has a sense of meaning. While sure as hell i'm not fond of hipster graphics, it is distinctive, enjoyable and most importantly doesn't feel tacked on to justify inept and basic design and absence of complexity. The game is not a classic. Yet. There are downsides.
- Aliens have unique interactions only in the first third of the game, and generally could use more personality and fleshing out. Despite revisited memories this is not SC2. It's going in the right direction though in the beginning - and that should DAMN DEFINITELY be built upon.
- Grind. I don't like formulaic replicas of things and i don't. ♥♥♥♥ing. like. mindless. grind.  as we know there are exactly two JRPGs, FF6 - and the other one everybody is remaking (ah yes, possibly there is also a third, Dragon Knight 1-4, which is The Other One with porn, the number denotes one of 4 distinct porn sets incorporated into The Other One). Halcyon 6 has lots of elements from The Other One (no porn). Not encouraging. The part where you have to grind from lvl 10 - 13 is particularly sinful.

- Lack of things to interact with, explore and do - the game would be so much more wonderful if there were more random quests and places like Xiao quest, changing from playthrough to playthrough.
These three things fixed (first and third fix the second obviously) would make it a true, magnificent classic imo. Thankfully this is what devs are mostly promising with the updates.
Overall 7/10 with a potential to be 9/10. Give it a spin, definitely later when there are more updates if not now - whoever is making it has actually done something beautiful and has created a story you want to play a part in, instead of a hollow-feeling shell that goes through the motions of being a game. This controller is great, for some games. For other games it's awful. However I do recommend this controller because for those games, it's worth it. I pre ordered this controller back in 2015 so I got the controller early. I tested this controller on a few games in my library so I'll go in order.
I'll start with the good
The Evil Within: If you get a good config, the controller for this game is great! The trackpad makes it easy to shoot and aim. I had almost no problem using this controller with The Evil Within. So yes, great controller for a great game.
Alien Isolation: Default config for this game is great, although you might have to turn the sensitivity up a bit. But the overall controls are good. The trackpad makes a first person experience easy, so this makes it a great controller to play with.
Rocket League: You don't need to use the trackpad that much for the core gameplay that much, but the controller works perfectly for the game. Not much else to say really.
Before I move onto the bad I want to write about the feel of the controller. At first grip, it will feel awkward if you use the standard Xbox One or Playstation 4 controller, like really strange. After a little while you start to get used to it, so don't feel bad about your purchase if you don't like it at first, it'll start to grow on you. For this controller, it's not for console users. I've showed my brothers that play on Xbox this controller and they didn't have a good first impression. Other console users have said that they also have mixed reviews on this controller, so keep that in mind. For the games I'm about to list make sure to have a standard Xbox One controller or PS4 controller just in case.
Max Payne 3: Awful. I spent an hour and a half trying to find a good config and tweaking it myself for it to work. Just too difficult to play with this controller. It's really difficult trying to get the perfect shot. So I recommend using a mouse and keyboard or a standard XOne or PS4 controller for this game.
Grand Theft Auto V: Same problem with Max Payne 3, the aim was too hard to manage, strange though I thought this device would be perfect for it but I guess not. You absolutely need aim assist on or otherwise you're going to be a horrible shooter for the job. Disapointing because I do play this game a lot.
Fallout 4: I couldn't aim for♥♥♥♥♥♥in this game, I play this game with a mouse and keyboard (as well as all the other games I listed) but this time I was playing it on my TV so I had to use a controller and the Steam controller was in my reach. Unfortunately this device didn't live up to my expectations. The aim was so difficult that I just switched to the Xbox controller for the duration of that session. I was happy to return to my mouse and keyboard after that.
Those are the games I've tested so far and I might update the list but for now, this is what I'll write. Overall I'd rate this controller 7/10. For some first person games I'd definietly recommend this controller but for some I'd go against. Same with Third Person games. Depends on what you like, but if you are buying for the wireless sake, there's a wireless receiver for Xbox One controllers that work with Windows 10.

I recommend if your looking to play Rocket League and maybe some other racing games. Its also nice to be able to control your desktop and surf the web with it. This game is an absolutely amazing concept for an economic/town management type simulator. I love how the game combines advanced technologies with very low level primitive technologies to give an exciting twist on economic and town management in a futuristic sci-fi setting.
If you enjoyed playing the old Caesar 3, Emperor and Pharoah games then then this is your type of simulation game but it is however much more than these games because it combines other aspects into the settlement running that make it a lot less mechanical and requires a lot more input from the player, it really pulls the aspects of building a town that will thrive while ensuring that you survive together into one continuous journey. You will constantly be tested by dangerous beasts that try to eat your settlers and plagued by vermin who steal your food stores.
I bought this game at a very early stage of development and was very disappointed with the lack of features in the game but since the release of a lot more content it has started to become the simulator/town management game that I have dreamed of playing for so long and has really in my opinion become money well spent on a game under development even though I didn't initially feel this way.
Be advised that the game is still in a very early stage of development and there does tend to be a long wait time on updates to the game but when an update is released it tends to add a whole new level of depth to the game which really makes it worth playing which is why I have recently logged so many hours playing this game.
I would like to see a lot more content added to this game both in the world variety (fauna, flora and environment) as well as different scenario types each with their own unique challenges. Unfortunately there is only a single player mode so there is no intertribal warring and there is currently no sandbox mode.

This game has given me hours of enjoyment before the release on Steam, and since it's release on Steam some of my friends were more willing to pick it up and play as well.  I've probably played most of the games set in the BattleTech universe as my dad showed me the series and it has kept me entertained even in it's worst moments.  MechWarrior Online has gotten better, it can still use a lot of development but it is a pretty solid experience overall.

There are plenty of things I don't like about MWO. The fact that the canon is treated too lightly would be an example. I do not mean balance-related things like Clan Mechs being severely inferior to their BT originals. This is quite understandable in an online PvP game. Lazy execution of many gameplay aspects, however, is much harder to excuse.
Pinpoint convergence makes everyone boat the same or very similar kinds of weapons, because bringing as much of them to the battlefield as possible allows unleashing a lot of punishment precisely into a single component. This makes diversifying your Mech’s loadout meaningless and even detrimental to performance. This also created all kinds of paradoxes. You would think that AC/20 would be the king of brawling and you would be wrong. Small pulse lasers get you more damage, more DPS and require no ammo for the same short-range pinpoint effect. Many weapon systems are similarly flawed, and while there is some kind of balance it is achieved primarily by nerfing whatever is the king of the hill weapon system of the day.
Furthermore, despite the game not being pay to win, you would definitely need to pay if you don't want to be bored to death grinding c-bills in the same Mech for hundreds of matches. Grinding for a fully customized (i.e. competitive) heavy or assault Mech variant (looking at 13-14 million c-bills) can easily take 100 matches. You will need 3 of these variants to master a single chassis and skill up all of your variants. You would also be looking at up to another 100 games just to outfit one of your Mech variants with suitable modules. These modules are not just gimmicks either, they enhance performance immensely. So, sure, you do not HAVE to spend money on this game, but if you have a life in addition to gaming you WILL have to do it at one point or another. The amount of money you are going to spend can be easily equivalent or greater than the price of a brand spanking new AAA title.
But as Canada Bill Jones famously said, "I know it's crooked, but it's the only game in town." MechWarrior Online is the only MechWarrior game that came out in the last 15 years (except for other titles now dead and gone). It is hardly a "MechWarrior simulator" as it has been once advertised, but the game is serviceable. It is true enough to the BattleTech universe that you actually feel like a Mech pilot when playing it. It also has a large emphasis on tactics and a notable absense of cheap P2W which plagues similar titles (I am looking at you, WOT). Despite what many people say the community is pretty decent. Bickering kids and elitist jerks are few and quite easily ignored.
In the end if piloting a BattleMech is something you are after, then I would definitely recommend trying MWO out. If you aren't completely sure about, then I would recommend trying MWO out. If you want an online game that could help you relieve stress in just 10-15 minutes, I would recommend trying MWO just for that purpose.

Hello potential MechWarriors,
I am Khan CoffiNail Tseng a unit leader of the Clan Faction loyalist unit Clan Ghost Bear International. I have been on and off heavily active in MechWarrior since May 2010, a year before MWO was even announced playing in a MechWarrior mod for the game Crysis. I was a zealous fan of MWO from the start of announcements for MechWarrior Online using a daily puzzle of the Atlas concept artwork and twitter to stir a buzz felt around the net. I was so crazy in love with this game I ended being the 25th register forum member. I still play this game and am more a grey knight than a zealous fan for various reasons, but I am a die-hard Mechhead and love to see MechWarrior in the spotlight it had back in the 90s. The game has its flaws, but so does any game that is in development still, it may be out but it is a perpetually in development game. So the MWO you play today, will not be the same one in a year, as content is continuously coming out and being teased with.
It is a great game. It has very well done artwork, and the Mechs are extremely well done. Animation is great as most mechs feel weighty and others make you jump if you run in to them around a corner and you skid to a stop to try and get back around your corner. Scale could be considered a little off by some, but with the addition half a year ago with destructible light posts, knockdown trees, etc the scale seems fairly well for Machines only a dozen meters tall. The environments are beautiful and I still find myself getting lost in them at times.
Do you want a game that can be both twitch and slow, where good aim pays off to take down critical components, but someone who’s aim is mediocre can still do decent damage and have a great time doing it? MWO is a good FREE game to add to your library. If you want a game with a lot of weapons fire going off and an often chaotic battlefield or something to get a fill of stompy big robots this game is a great FREE addition to your library. You are someone who just loves to tinker with things until they are just right, shedding armour off this leg to add a bit more armour or heat sinks, crafting the perfect build and playstyle this would be a great FREE addition to your library. Honestly, it is free, so give it a try and do not take my word for it but experience the battlefield of 1980’s 31st Century Battlefield Technology.
This game has had its ups and downs much like any develop game and the fact their game has been in a large sense open to the public since November 1st 2011 and the very start of their development, now this means they have had a lot of scrutiny and under the microscope. They have been developing a nestablished universe with a fairly strong fanbase. These fans have not had a game since early 2002 in MechWarrior 4. Of course these loyal crowd, to which I am one love the core universe MechWarrior Online was place in, Battletech. It has a deep and rich backstory that is the effect of an alternate history starting in the 1980s.
PGI’s announcement of MechWarrior Online had a very exciting start. With a twitter feed giving daily in universe news written by the current developer of the tabletop, backstory universe Randall Bills. It had hints of the setting, a puzzle of concept art. The month of October 2011 was fairly amazing from a Mechwarrior fan’s point
This is getting to be a very balanced game. No longer do you have a arms race to the largest Mechs with the most advanced tech. Every mech in the right hands could be a very deadly opponent. Like in this universe the elite skilled were some of the deadliest pilots, who could operate their machines like and extension of themselves. A green and fresh pilot in a Atlas, should come down to a veteran in a light Mech Jenner.
The Customization of Mechs via the Mechlab. Giving you hours of lost time playing around to get your warmachine just the way you like it, with the weapons you like. The deeper meta of the mechlab is an art all in itself and is a core aspect to master in competitive scenes.
Role Warfare: Where your Assault Mechs going in force alone would mean nothing, but a well-coordinated team, mixed with different weight classes and loadouts could crush a more numerous opponents. Your Heavy Mechs were the support and the force going in with the assaults and crushing the opposition. Medium Mechs the backbone of the game, your go to for price and power. The light Mechs of your team were experts as going in behind enemy lines and at using Electronic Counter Measures (ECM) to shield your team from enemy sensors.
Intelligence Warfare: From the above lights, to other, heavier chassis with ECM and other electronics of the battlefield. Using your gear to assist in spotting for you Long Range Missiles allies in the rear or to jam the ECM of your foe.
Community Warfare: The creation of units in-game. Guilds, clans, communities. The larger picture of the glory that is a game set in the war torn Inner Sphere of the Battletech Universe. There is always war, and this give the community as deeper meta game to bring to the table.
Something always feels great about piloting 20-100 ton Bipedal Warmachine of destruction and smashing them around a forest or city. The rush you can have being the last pilot in a match, or as you take on a mech in a higher weight class, or even as that Assault crashing in to wreak havoc with your team.
Thanks for reading. I hope I have given a bit of sway for you to try MechWarrior Online, or at least to keep it on your scope to try soon. We see the same games in different forms, and MWO has a bit of a different take on the FPS. I hope to see you on the battlefield MechWarrior.
-Khan CoffiNail Tseng, Clan Ghost Bear International

The idea that the latest patch, OB64, ruined the game with pay to win mechanics is honestly absurd. There are separate game modes for casual gameplay that allow you to choose between an admittedly pay to win system that's more meant to be "silly" than serious and then there's the other version where every card is locked to level 4 which requires no grinding for literally anything. You get all of the cards for free and all of the cards are locked at level 4 no matter whether you've upgraded your cards or not. Upgrading your cards only affects the "silly" game mode. Queue times for locked game mode are pretty reasonable and ranked is entirely set to the locked game mode. Basically, if you don't like the "silly" game mode then you have no obligation to ever play it in your life if you so chose not to play it.
That being said, balancing lately has been entirely wrecked because of this latest change but that his been managed over time and bugs have been getting fixed. One should expect even more balance changes and bug fixes in the near future. I'm not going to go too deep into the meta because I could go on about it for paragraphs, but basically it's not where it should be at the moment. I still enjoy the game and I would recommend it casually for sure. Competitively, the game is constantly undergoing changes that affect the meta entirely. Some people might like that, if you're coming from DotA 2 you are probably already used to it. If you don't like a meta that can completely change and negatively affect your style of gameplay, you might not want to play this game. Right now, frontlines and flanks are having a hard time because of nerfs and direct damages (and Bomb King) run the game.
Basically, if you can't handle change or if you can't use your brain to determine what is a good change or isn't one then you won't like this game at all. If you think change is refreshing, give it a shot. I've had a great time with this game and I've felt negatively and positively about this game. I would recommend it until Hi-Rez gives us the big dong.

Okay, so I put off playing Deus Ex Human Revolution for a very long time, and I am perhaps a fool for doing it. What we have here is a finely crafted First Person, Role Playing hybrid without the complexities of a full on RPG like Fallout, or not quite as simple as Call of Duty or Battlefield.
I am sorry to say that having owned it on both PS3/Xbox 360 and now PC, I played it a little but I was initially put off by the games visuals on the console version of the game. This stigma would keep me away from this startlingly well realised Sci-Fi future for several years. Though I was disappointed that the visuals were not of the Cut Scene quality on PC, like one might have expected when the visuals at first glance appear quite basic too (or at least, appeared to be the same as the consoles on my laptop).
Where do I begin. The visuals take a while to get used to, but while seeming dated initially, do a fine job of telling the story and showcasing the action that is on offer here. This is not an open world game, but gives you a sense of freedom that games of the Call of Duty ilk just do not do.
Initially after playing an hour or so I was aliking the game to a quasi-Mass Effect in First Person Shooter format, though perhaps not as complex in it's story telling at first glance; as the game progresses how you interact with those you meet, and perhaps how you approach certain situations can have wildly different effects.
Early on in the game, when you are finally given a little free time and the ability to persue some side-quests, you can run into Adams past so-to-speak (his ex-colleagues), how you treat them can have very different effects on your personal story and the way others might percieve you later.
Jerky character animations for NPCs when you interact with them can sometimes make you feel odd as they talk to you, but if you ignore this, then no problems here. The game is visually striking, with and structure and setting that harkens back to Perfect Dark on the N64 for myself. The game gives you the freedom to tackle objectives however you want, and does require a little thought, and caution. Go guns blazing if that is your thing, take the non-lethal approach, or dismember your opponents in a gruesome (for this kind of game) hand-to-bladed-arm-hand combat, or take the stealthy long distance or just pain sneaky approach, it's all available.
I have only scratched the surface of this game and will continue to play it till the end as I haven't finished the game yet.

Greetings as always!  Today I’m reviewing Dungeons 3 the latest game in a trilogy that started out disappointing and with every consecutive release has continued to impress and scratch that dungeon building itch.  With that said it should be no surprise of my thoughts but read on if you need specifics.
Parody of a bad game:  This is the third game (as the title says) and continues the theme from the last game of a pure dungeon building / management game but with a nice RTS element where your monsters are sent to the surface to take the fight to the enemy.  There are a lot of improvements here however; to begin with one of the big frustrating components was dropping your units into the ‘overworld’ which has been resolved and no longer an issue of mine.  The map itself is much easier to read where the entrances line up with the exits.   I especially love the addition of the corrupted heroes, it’s a simple addition and I love the skin swaps and names they give them.  I was hoping to see the return of a ‘banner’ spell that would gather your army without having to plop them down in the path of the invaders but that was not to be.  The combat is much improved, as there are methods to see what health your units are at and though the units sometimes handle sluggishly this helped a great deal.
Building Boats:  The story continues off from the previous game and unlike most games of this type nothing happens where you have to ‘start over’  but this time you are simply invading a far away land.  There are amusing quips and some cringe moments but the overall story is really by the numbers for these types of games and what really keeps you interested is the game play.  With that said I did have a few laugh out loud moments.  The graphics have improved as well and the audio is nothing to sneer at, though there is this one issue that many (myself included) seem to have where the audio cuts out and you have to load the game to reset it.
Aside from the mentioning of the audio issues and a missing spell the game didn’t have much wrong with it.  I never experienced any screen tears, crashes though I did have a common problem with Frame Rate during large battles or dropping off huge armies (really, I don’t consider this unacceptable).  I did occasionally have issues with my units not listening to me or the collision causing weird issues where one wouldn’t attack because it was trying to move but couldn’t.  Overall, the game is otherwise so improved that I really can’t complain about any of these and the development staff seems to be releasing patches frequently. I have always been on the lookout for a good space strategy game.  The previous winner for this category that a few friends and I would play a lot was Sins of a Solar Empire.  If that game was say, a 6/10 on the space strategy scale, I'd have to put this at 9.5/10 at least.  If you were a fan of Sins, you gotta check this game out.
At first I was a little hesitant to get it when it was on sale for $9.99 because one of the buddies who I played Sins with already had it and said it was rather boring.  I checked out other reviews from critics and players and decided to give it a shot.  Best decision I could have made.  I talked my buddy into playing a game with me just to give it another chance.  Half way through our first game, he admits he had misunderstood this game and that it was significantly better than he'd given it credit for.
I've heard people compare this game to Civ V in space, and I actually have to agree with them.  Before playing Civ V, I hated turn based strategy games.  I was an Age of Empires fan down to the core and any game like that.  Civ V changed my opinion on that and opened the door for more turn based games.  This game is turn based and is actually extremely similar to Civ V with gameplay and mechanics.
The game may seem a bit overwhelming at first, but in my opinion, that's a good thing.  I'd much rather play a game that takes a half hour to an hour to learn over a game that dumbs it all down for you anyday.  Alright, enough of my opinion, I'll give you an idea of the mechanics now so you can decide if this game is truly all I'm making it out to be.
Before you even start the game, you have several options to set in the lobby.  You can change the size and shape of the galaxy, number of players, age of the galaxy ( similar to Civ V's world age option ), your faction, roughly how many star systems will be in, how far apart, difficulty, gamespeed, and whether you want the game to be private, private multiplayer, or public multiplayer.  There are a few more options, but they're not as important.
Press start game and you're on your way to galactic domination.  Once in game, you are provided with a very useful tutorial.  The tutorial in this game is especially well done because it doesn't spring it all on you at once.  Instead, it slowly walks through each part as you come to it.  It won't talk about diplomacy on turn one because there's no need for it and it will only add a bit of confusion.  Instead they have it so that when you click on one of the 5 tabs that display information - Empire Overview, Research Overview, Fleet Overview, Diplomatic Overview, and Hero Overview.
Each turn can take a little bit of time.  Usually they're medium slow in the beginning because you have to set everything up for the first time.  Early to mid game things speed up because you're waiting for research to get done and exploring which isn't a big time consumer.  Mid game to early late game things tend to slow down a lot.  In my experience, after I have a stable empire foundation, I'm ready to expand.  This can vary based on your faction because some factions expand like crazy as soon as possible, but I usually pick a more casual and slower expanding faction.  There is an empire approval meter that you have to watch out for.  It's not hard to keep it very high, however, it can also easly slip if you're not paying attention.  Towards the end things pick up again as you wrap things up.
One thing to note is exactly what a star system is.  Essentially, they're just pre-built Civ V cities.  You go in, colonize one planet in the system, and then build things in that system.  There are things to build that act exactly alike a granery, library, workshop, etc from Civ V.  Each system has it's own income, production, science, approval, and food.  You also build fleets out of systems.  You have to take the time to stop building improvements in a system and build a military unit instead - just like Civ.  You can also use the money in the game ( which is Dust ) to buy upgrades to have them built in 1 turn rather than waiting 2, 10, or even 20 turns for them.  This is extremely useful when you have a new system that has next to no production and would take forever to get it started.
One of the coolest features that I've found to be incredibly useful is the management system in the Empire Overview.  Specifically, you have the ability to tell the computer that you want it to take over control of a system.  You can tell it what you want it to focus on, be it food, science, approval, diplomacy, balanced, whatever.  You can set it, change it, and remove it with 2 clicks at any time you choose.  If you have a large empire of even just 15+ systems, this is invaluable as it keeps everything in order for you.  Even when you let the AI govern it, you can still go in a tweak the build order or rush something important when ever you need.  This was made in such a way that it is 100% useful and 0% restrictive or in the way.
Another note about star systems is that you will fine strategic and luxury resources ( very similar to Civ V ) within star systems.  They are clearly marked on a very simple gui.  Strategic resources appear as purple while luxury are white.  You cannot access them for your empire until have have researched sufficient technology.  They also offer bonuses if you can get a monopoly on them ( which simply means have access to 3 for the normal game I believe, or 4 for Disharmony ).  They're not totally game changing, but they can be nice, for example, +20% approval across your empire.
Similar to Civ V, there are numerous roads to victory.  To me, this is one of the biggest selling points - that you don't always have to bash everyone else's face in to win the game.  I'm a big fan of the science focused faction because I prefer building my own empire over destroying other empires.  The different roads to victory are as follows: Score, Supremacy, Wonder, Expansion, Diplomatic, Scientific, and Economic.  You can play the game your way!  As I've mentioned before, I usually prefer to achieve scientific victory because I enjoy have a technological advantage over my opponents as opposed to numbers.
Other things worth mentioning include the hero system.  Can hire heroes that have different attributes.  They come with 2 specialties to them ( administration, corporate, pilot, commander, spy, etc ) and you either assign them to govern a star system or as an admiral in a fleet.  Where ever you put them, they always have very positive effects.  The diplomacy system is great when dealing with other people because once you research it, you will have the ability to trade money ( flat or per turn ), research, star systems, and luxury or strategic resources.
As for complaints, my only one thus far would be AI logic when dealing with diplomacy.  Unfortunately, if you try to make deals with them, even something as little as offer peace, they tend to demand all of your strategic resources to even consider it.  This is a common problem I've seen in many games, including Civ V.  Deals have to be unbelievably skewed in the bot's favor for them to accept it as 'fair'.  However, if you wait long enough, they will often propose a deal to you which is in your favor ( such as offer peace and give you a luxury resource ).
Overall, I'd say this game is definitely worth $30.  The average game length is comparable to a Civ V game so expect to spread it out over multiple days.  Not counting sales, Civ V Gold costs $49.99.  If you get your money's worth from Civ V, you'll definitely get the same value from this game.  As for space based strategy games, I've never seen one do what this game does.

I recently picked up Endless Space on sale and was pleasantly surprised that I found it to be a much better game than I had expected.  If you enjoy space 4X games like GalCiv2 or you wanted to try one out, I think this is a good pick. Overall it is well designed in all areas and a lot of thought has been put into both the UI and the game play mechanics.
One highlight of the game is the depth of the star system development systems. There are a lot of different planet types (about 11) with different and plausible characteristics, moons and bonus resources and there up to six planets per system which are dealt out randomly for each new game. There are also a lot of different techs to research related to colony development that significantly affect what planets you can colonise and how you can develop them. This adds up to a richer experience in this area than,say, GalCiv2, and also sets up a different challenge and opportunity set for each new game since easily colonisable planets are rare and you can't colonise difficult ones willy-nilly until teched up to do so.
You do need to do a fair bit of micromanagement to develop your empire as specific build orders and priority choices are necessary for effective play. The game allows you to set an AI helper to devop a system for you but this is mostly not recommended because it tends to colonise new planets in a system too early leading to a big drop in approval (probably becasue they use the same algorythms the AI factions use and they do not suffer the same level of approval hits as you do).
The fleet combat system is surprisingly fun and exiting IMO. Getting attacked (and you will be) is an adrenalin-fueled experience because unlike GalCiv2 you do not know the strength of configuration of enemy ships except when in actual battle so you can easily find youself on the receiving end of a nasty butt-kicking and enemy ships crawling all over your systems. Unlike many 4X and strategy games in Endless Space there are several things you can do about this, it's not necessarily game over.
Firstly you can play the rock-paper-scissors ship design game which follows GalCiv's system of mass driver/beam/missile countered by armour/shield/point defence repectively. The key mechanic is that unlike most games you can instantly retrofit your existing ships if you have the money to do so, so one key military tech and a refit can turn the tables very quickly (and of course the enemy can do that to you too). Secondly you can deploy heroes (with combat bonuses) and play the second level rock-paper-scissors game of tactical battle cards to win crucial fights against the odds. Thirdly you can build defence structures in your systems that can massively slow down attempts to invade them, much more so than in , say, GalCiv giving you time to up-tech and refit. It becomes apparent as you play that a lot of thought has gone into this and it works surprisingly well IMO.
The diplomacy systems are well presented but I have not played long enough to evaluate how good the the diplomacy AI (including victim selection) systems really are. It seems to be pretty good and sensible at certain things, but be unable to adapt its strategy if what its trying to do diplomatically doen't work.  For example my neighbour is the strongest faction in the game and gets into a war on three fronts. He desparatly wants an alliance with me and keeps asking for one (which is a sensible goal) but I won't play ball becasue I want to cut him down to size and steal some of his juicy systems. What he couldn't do was realise this was the case and cosy up to someone else to before attacking me instead, he couldn't interpret my actions as the threat they were it seems.  However diplomacy AI is extremely difficult to do given it has to compete with human capabilities of averice, treachery and cunning honed over millions of years of evolution: I rate it as above average at the moment, some way behind Paradox's CK2 and EUIV but ahead of GalCiv2.
In summary I think this game is well designed and fun to play so long as you enjoy tinkering with star system development and ship designs over time between adrenalin fueled war episodes. Not ground-breaking, not a classic, but above average.

Next to the controller itself it includes:
As a 'hardcore' keyboard & mouse (K&M) user (never owned any of the consoles) getting any controller in my hands is always something I need to get used to. Some games are easier than others, like platformers. But more sophisticated games are always a handful for me. Nevertheless the first thing that struck me was how it's an easy and intuitive replacement of K&M in mouse oriented games and could easily function as a "remote" outside of any game or Steam Big Picture. The right touch pad is by default set up like a tracker ball. If only I could use the Steam Controller on-screen keyboard outside games. Once I got used to that it's pretty easy to type with it!
The Steam Controller is certainly no heavy one and is kept relitively light. This in turn may make the controller feel 'cheap', as by some button presses, like those under the touch pads, it sounds somewhat hollow. Putting sound dampening material inside so that it would sound/feel more 'solid' would take away some of that illusion, I think. Since I do not own any other controllers myself, I cannot do any direct comparison, but to me this controller does not experience as something cheaper than the Sony and Microsoft counterparts outside of that. The only thing I've found slightly uncomfortable is the weight behind the shoulder buttons (those highest up on the back side). They feel a bit heavy to press, compared to the other buttons.
Since most of the games released on Steam are mainly developed with a PC in mind and no Steam Controller not all games may be (fully) compatible. While some games will recognise the controller straight out of the box and support it completely as if it was built around it, others will need to set up a profile where it will simulate K&M presses. However some games may need some extra fiddeling in the game itself to make it work like it should.
If you need to set up profiles for certain games, then they can easily be saved, shared and downloaded through Steam Workshop, and since the specific controller can be registered to your account specifically you can take your controller to someone else's place, connect with it to his or her Steam and still get your own set up personal profiles. I personally have not yet tried this feature, as I haven't had the opportunity yet.
When you dive further into the customisation of these profiles, you can easily be a bit overwhelmed by the sheer amount of 'micro-management' that you can put into it. The controller even features a gyriscope that next to gravity also works on compass readings. Seriously, it kinda feels like ploughing through a flight simulator manual when you seriously look into it for the first time. SO MANY OPTIONS!


All-in-all I think this controller has enormous potential and diversity, but really needs some getting used to. What to some may feel cheaply built, feels fine to me personally. Hopefully (more) game developers will try to support it to its full potential, as right now you may risk that it may still be bumpy ride to make it work comfortably for your favourite game.

Insanity: doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results”
When Albert Einstein gave the definition of insanity, he most certainly could not account for video games and most certainly a jewel as ’10 second ninja’.
10 Second Ninja is a marvelous precision platformer where timing matters the most. I could argue that there is the puzzle element in it as well, as to finding the optimal route in each level, however, I find the precision element to be the main feature of the game. You are the ninja, the one and only, and robot Hitler must destroy you because you are awesome! Seriously, that’s it! The game has some awesomely made basic story that will give you the giggles or even make you get that 6 pack you always dreamed about, with all the laughter it will cause!
The purpose of the game is beating each level in less than 10 seconds. While that sounds easy at first, as the levels progress and become more complex you’ll see that you will have to strategize a bit more, find the perfect route and even do combo kills. After you beat each level you are awarded 1 to 3 stars, depending on how fast you did it, with 1 star just beating the level with at least 1 millisecond left and 3 beating its preset times, usually 3 sec! The catch? The game is split into areas, each area has it’s own boss level that you’ll need to unlock by getting a set number of stars, usually 2 per level. This means that you will replay the majority of the game again and again and again and… well, you get the picture. Eventually, you’ll mechanically press the restart button after 1 sec in the level and ragequit so you ‘reset’ your nerves! Super Meat Boy lovers and such, rejoice! There are also in-game leaderboards to make you feel bad for your performance!
A great addition to this is the achievement system, that compliments the humor of the story! While there are the generic achievements, like beat X area or beat X area with all stars, there are also many funny ones that require you to do something silly in game, like canceling a cinematic or the credits, to be precise there is no credits option but a button labeled ‘The morons who made this’.
While the graphics aren’t something special are just what this time of game needs. However, the music and sounds are great. The music in the menu gives the ninja-y meditation dojo theme (take your pick) but in-game, it’s fast paced and accompanies the gameplay perfectly! The game supports both keyboard and controller inputs, with the keyboard being completely customizable.
While at first, I didn’t give much value to this title in order to try it, while I generally love platformers like S.M.B. or Fenix Rage, I now know that I have never been more wrong! And as a great bonus to all this, this, epically made with love, 1 sec restart simulator has a sequel, that for the time being resides at my wishlist.
Overall, if you are a precision platformer fun this game will easily be a 9/10, due to the attention to detail its developers had. However a more realistic score considering more current games would probably be along 8/10, simply because I do have to take into account it’s graphics and given all the humor it provides up front, it will dry out, as the achievements are 1 time only.

Handsome Mr. Frog is an excellent single screen arcade game based around the premise of using your tongue to eat enemies and then spit them at enemies. The game plays in four waves per room. Each wave has several enemies and when you get down to the last enemy there's always an object in the room to eat and spit at the last foe. There's no way to digest the enemies. Completing every few rooms will send you to the next theme. Swamp goes to ice, goes to something else, goes to the spooky haunted realm and then the game loops to the beginning.
The art is great and fits with an 8-bit style, the soundtrack is barely noticeable. Controls are easy to master, left, right, tongue and jump. There is even controller support which is always a plus.
The tongue mechanic is simple, it will extend out and return. If it catches an enemy it returns instantly. Using the tongue in mid air will freeze Handsome Mr. Toad hovering until the tongue returns. You can keep using it and just stay in the air. Its a good mechanic even with its flaws. Sometimes I managed to catch an enemy behind me while extending the tongue in the opposite direction.
After a few enemies get disposed of and fall into the drink, bubbles with collectables appear and float up. These collectables are 1-ups, treats that result in points and hot tamales. These hot tamales let you spit a single burst of three fireballs that bounce around objects and melt through enemies. Its a fun addition to an already good tongue mechanic.
Your foes get into the room by in from ceiling holes. When they walk off screen a new enemy spawns to take its place. You however can run laps around the environment. Go out the left side of the screen and appear on the right. There is a bit of a safe spot as you can completely disappear from the screen.
Each theme has two different enemies: The swamp has birds that run at you and gators that move forward at a slow pace. The ice theme has penguins that dive at you and something a bit slower. In the aquatic realm, octopi will shower you with water that can push you out of the way as well as kongs that run about. The spooky haunted realm has bone throwing skeletons and ghosts that can go through solid objects. The diversity keeps the entertainment factor up.
Some of the rooms feel a bit unfair as some have no safe spots to stand from quick dropping enemies. Well you can always stand off to the side between the left and right of the screen. Other rooms are well designed and make things easier. Each theme has a mixed bag of rooms from easy to challenging.

Troubleshooting Advice for Mac Users
I want to point out that I had serious problems running this game after selecting the Full Screen setting under the options.  It crashed the application.  I ended up having to hit "Command" & "Q" to exit the application on my iMac.  After that, the application kept crashing and wouldn't boot anymore.
I had to delete the application's preferences file to get it to boot up in the default settings again.  I had to keep doing this until I got the game working in the desired resolution and video settings.  Below is the location of the Blockland prefs.cs file in OS X version 10.6.8, in case you run into this problem:
username/Library/Application Support/ Steam/SteamApps/common/Blockland/config/client/prefs.cs
The game is running fine now in window mode only though…  I believe the only thing that actually crashed the application was trying to run it in Full Screen mode.  I have everything turned up as high as I can.  The games graphics are a little dated, but they still look okay.
Again, you only need to either rename or trash the Blockland prefs.cs file to get the game to launch again in the default settings mode.  After you get the game settings the way you want them and it's not crashing anymore you can safely play the game.  Just do not try running it in Full Screen mode again.

Good game. Decent amount of customization, maybe even too much for some people. It takes some time to learn how to properly outfit a mech.
Heavy emphasis on teamplay. 12v12 matches, elimination style.
Not pay to win. No magic ammo, and best mechs are available for in-game currency. There are consumables for UAV, airstrike, artillery strike, and cooldown. They are a waste of money imo, but those who bother buying them will have an advantage. These are available for in-game cbills and can be bought with real money.
While there is no traditional tech tree to grind, getting enough money for your mechs, engines, weapons, and modules can be quite a grind. To 'master' a mech (unlock performance bonuses), you must own 3 variants of that mech and grind their xp to unlock the bonuses. You might get tired of the game before you have enough mechs or equpiment to try something new. Really it's just the same fights over and over again. If you don't have a wide selection of mechs and equipment to keep things interesting, it gets incredibly stale. And to reiterate, it will take you a long time to have a decent selection. By the way you only get 4 mech bays. Additional bays cost actual money.
edit.. I should mention that there are 'trial mechs', that is, you can play with pre-made mechs that you don't actually own. You can still earn cbills with them too, but you can't customize them.
They frequently hold events. These are awesome and have actually been getting a lot better. Participation can get you quite a bit of Cbills (even MC sometimes), cosmetic items,mechs, and mechbays. Sales turn up quite often as well. Personally, I don't bother buying anything unless it's on discount. I suggest you wait for sales if you can; stuff is overpriced imo.
There are essentially 3 modes of play; solo queue, group queue, and Community Warfare. Solo queue is just you queuing up to be matched up with other random people who did the same for a battle. Group queue is what happens when you try to play with a friend; You have to play against other people who have grouped. This means you and your one friend could be on a motley team of other small groups against an entire 12-man clan group who will wreck your♥♥♥♥♥♥ These modes are supposed to match players according to skill, but really it just matches vets with vets and noobs with noobs. There doesn't seem to be anything inbetween, and group queue......just seems to match whatever it can find tbh. Also,  you will drag your lower ranked friend into higher rank play and they might hate the game for it. If you are both same rank, congrats.
Community Warfare is just horrible. It can take forever to find people to play with, and the maps are♥♥♥♥♥♥ Don't bother with it unless you have a good (exceedingly good) group of people to play with. THERE IS NO RANKED MATCHMAKING, you will fight the best of the best and hate it; you will often be placed against a badass 12-man group who will annihilate you, and even worse be horrible sports about it. That said, this mode inexplicably allows solo players to participate. You've been warned!
I should tell you that it's more than just team deathmatch, but it's basically just team deathmatch no matter what mode you select.
The balance of the game is ...... odd. It goes through huge changes every year, dramatically shifting the meta. They have come up with all sorts of convoluted ideas to try to shift the meta and avoid actually balancing the game. That's an entire subject of it's own and I really shouldn't get into it. That said, 'clan' mechs tend to be best, and pay attention to those 'quirks' that each mech has. Be sure to take advantage of their magical bonus strengths (these can be pretty overpowered). Don't get too comfortable with your mech and it's loadout. They will change the rules again. and again.
By the way, the game runs like garbage. I hope you have a hell of a computer.

First of all as a long-time player before the steam release, my hours clock in at around 300. If you don't believe me and you're one of the 2 other people who use the Raptr gaming client, go look me up there.
Mechwarrior Online is a shooter that brings a lot of unique things to the table, and while I could tote the customizibility and unique feel of each chassis that makes owning over 60 mechs feel insufficient, I'd rather just explain the main reason I love this game so much. Not only is this a "thinking man's shooter", rewarding tactical thought and teamplay to a far greater degree than most others, Mechwarrior Online also has an immense skill-cap. Pilot skill has more to do with the effectiveness of any given build than any other factor. The game is well balanced in the sense that everybody has access to the same tools to make their mech perfectly suit them, and once you find those builds that just feel right, you can take on a 100 ton direwolf in a 35 ton panther with nothing but 4 lasers and come out with a solo kill as long as you know what you're doing. But this game doesn't only reward individual skill: far more valueable is your ability to position and work with your team. That's what makes the release of this game to the broad audience of steam so exciting. Players who are used to voice chatting with random strangers (hint: the current community does not utilize the built-in VOIP at all) and who can breathe some life into this stale yet unusally friendly and passionate community. The learning curve is steep, but at its peak lies a game that you can sink just as many hours into as TF2 and CS:GO only with a kind of gameplay you won't find anywhere else. And ignore those people who complain about "paywalls"; the developers frequently hold challenges where everybody can earn rewards such as the paid currency (in good amounts, too), mechs, mechbays, and colors, as well as a ton of in-game currency.
