This game is a fantastic combination of teamwork, 3 dimensional movement, precision aiming, and skill. It is exciting and worth a try as a free game. Be mindful that you will probably get wrecked for your first few matches until you develop a sense of how to move, shoot, and be aware of others.
It is very high skillcap and enjoyed an eSports following after launch. However, the skillcap also makes it very frustrating to learn and requires a lot of practice (and innate skill) to become truely exceptional. The community, more often than not, can be harsh and critical of new players, even in the low rank servers.
Despite the tag, the game is not "Pay 2 Win". Every weapon, kit, and class is unlockable and upgradeable through XP earned during play. It will take a long time, but the 3 initial classes (Pathfinder, Solider, and Juggernaut) are the most effective once you learn to play them. Paying money for Tribes gold is really only necessary if you want special skins or voice packs.
Unfortunately the game is "abandonware" and won't continue to see the developer support. Hi-Rez has moved on to their new MOBA game Smite in search of microtransaction profit and has minimal staff overseeing this game.
Be warned that the developer's customer service has a poor track record, even for loyal players. HiRez runs an anticheat program as long as the service as up that will detect "undesireable software" running on your computer such as Cheat Engine. Even if that program is not affecting/injecting code into Tribes, it will be sent to the servers for a very quick IP ban and permanent ban on your account. These false positives are almost never reviewed seriously and bans are maintained indefinitely with curt/generic responses to your complaints. The "undesired software" is not explicitly defined and you should use caution when playing while running any software that may affect your game (or any other game - example: ENBInjector for Skyrim originally caused false positives).
I recommend this game as a free diversion and exposure to my favorite style of FPS, but caution you not to spend money on it. This game is unlikely to see any major support from Hi-Rez Studios.

Another thing I like about this game is that it requires skill and practice to master. As the "skiing" mechanic allows for you to go very fast, and as most of the weapons fire slow projectiles, it is difficult to land hits with the weapons. Nearly every aspect of this game requires time and effort to master, making this game fairly well balanced.
Not everything about this game is GREAT, though. A few weapons seem slightly over-powered, such as the fractal grenade for the brute and the SMGs for the raider. This may be frustrating at times, but it's nothing horrible. Also, this game is way past its prime, and new players may find it difficult to find a server with lots of people to play with. Hi-Rez studios has also stopped updating the game, and seemingly has abandoned it, and there are still some issues worth fixing, such as the over-powered weapons as mentioned above. I think this game would be much more popular if the developers still seemed to care.
Overall though, I recommend this game. It's a very unique FPS that is definitely worth trying. After all, it is free.

After 16,5 hours I finished this game on the easiest difficulty. I wanted to try out the space strategy genre with this one, but did not have experience with FTL, Xcom or similar, yet.
+ Lovely and detailed pixel art
+ Really good soundtrack and sound effects
+ Creative Final Fantasy combat fit to the space genre
+ It feels good to gain a new starship and own aliens with them
+ Many starships / officers to choose from, each with own abilities
+ Gameplay overall
(+/- No way of automating resource gathering in the beginning) EDIT:FIXED
+/- Several bugs (I didn't have any gamebreaking though)
+/- Story
+/- Some raids to your starbases occure so often, it just gets annoying
- Tech-tree is not as complex as it looks (pretty linear)
- Some repetetive gameplay from mid to endgame
There are 3 classes of starships, 2 types for each one (=6) and five tiers for each one (=30). PLUS some extras I won't spoil. That's 30 times more the shiptypes you can get compared to No Man's Sky (sorry had to bring in that one). Each starship needs to be commanded by a fitting officer and has it's class specific abilites.
Combat is about 90% in space and 10% in ground. Both are basically the same and turn based. At first it seems complex, but after a while you realize, that you will be spamming the same combos until you upgrade your ships. Nevertheless it's still pretty fun even though it get's repetetive.

This may sound a little boring, but it's hella fun especially when you start! Even though a little bit more tactical aspect and complexity would've been great.
I played it on the easiest one, because I never played a space game like this, and never were stuck at some point (duh). But that doesn't mean it's a piece of cake. Especially in the endgame were some encounters I barely survived. So I guess it can be pretty challenging if you play it on the higher ones.
Not the jaw dropping story you'd expect, but a rock solid one which fits perfectly to the gameplay.
The devs are active in the steam community forums (which I really love) and are constantly working on some bug fixes, which are still in the game (Sept. 2016). Also they announced some free gameplay updates for the future to widen up the overall expierence, which I'm really lookin' forward to!
A really solid indie-space-combat game, with base building and upgrade system. I had fun from the beginning 'til the end, even though it had some repetetive aspects.

DE:HR is a fantastic experience with enjoyable writing and acting, mature themes and some of the coolest art direction I’ve seen. My main disappointment is how it motivates you to play in a very narrow way (a certain stealth approach); rendering all of the cool gadgets you collect null. I’ll explain later.
The game throws you right into the middle of things, and you need to pay attention to understand who’s who and what’s what. There’s no slow prologue telling how the world came to be in the state it is and how you find yourself there. It's something I like, because it helps establish this sense of realism that sticks throughout the entire game - that this is an actual world, not dependent on your existence to continue moving. You are part of it, not the center of it. Still, I’ll help you with the basic orientation.
You’re Adam Jensen, former SWAT and currently chief of security at a biotech company, that is at the forefront of human augmentation (mechanical upgrades to humans) research and development. You are an existing and set character, not a blank slate, so the choices you make are limited to what is reasonable for Adam to do. Many people enjoy creating their characters out of scratch. This is not that kind of game. Personally, I prefer this format. It’s a fine balance that offers some amount of input, but not too much to the point that it sacrifices the depth of the story just to give you more choices that end up being shallow. Speaking of which, the consequences of your decisions are also pleasantly felt later on. I didn't find them to be too drastic, but the small nods were satisfying nevertheless.
Augmentation is the main topic the world is embroiled in at 2027, and the debate about its pros and cons extends to ethical, political, economical and social aspects. It’s a nice take on sci-fi that manages to keep things still relatively grounded and credible, while also enjoying some creative liberties where the developers wanted to emphasize the subject. Suspension of disbelief is required in some places more than others, but overall the game manages to sell a believable, alternate world. And it’s a bleak one. Earth is in the midst of a cyber renaissance, but once you move away from the socialites to the streets and alleyways, you will feel an atmosphere that is opposite from the optimistic aura of revolution that is present among the upper class. The change the world is going through isn’t embraced by all, doesn’t grace all, and there is an obvious tension in the air. The title of the next game is Mankind Divided, but the hints and seeds of that segregation are already found here.
The progression through levels is linear. While you revisit some of them, they’re in a changed state, and you can never go back to a level you’ve finished. They’re divided into the regular hub areas you know from most RPGs – open areas for your exploration to restock, talk with people, do side quests, etc – and the hostile levels that are much more fight or stealth oriented. Less talk, more action.
Augmentations are the source of your abilities, and they’re varied enough to make leveling up an exciting occurrence. DE:HR isn't plagued by endless passive upgrades (e.g. 4% damage increase) that leave you with nothing to look forward to. You have plenty of enhancements that are new abilities, which allow you to do things you couldn’t previously achieve. There’s an interesting dialogue system that triggers with certain, important NPCs. One augmentation helps you better analyze these key figures to find the correct answer. Hacking is everywhere, and the mini-game that seems confusing at first turns out to be simple and fun. You can choose to jump higher to reach new areas, punch through weak walls or move heavy objects to open additional routes. And on the RPG note, you even have an old-school inventory system that forces you to choose what to take and what to ditch. Weapons or stealth equipment? You can't have everything.
All these abilities and gadgets have their uses thanks to great level design. Stealth games can be compared to puzzles, and each room in DE:HR has multiple solutions to it. You can crawl through vents around your enemies, hack into the security system and turn turrets or robots against them, move huge crates that offer you a shortcut or jump up high to snipe them. You also have some cool tactical augmentations that make things easier and allow you to better plan or execute your actions. You can see through walls, turn invisible or run silently without alerting enemies. It’s all very fun, and part of the reason for my inflated play time – other than just enjoying the stroll slowly and taking in all the details of this beautifully crafted world (or, uh, alt-tabbing) – is because I always wanted to explore each region to its fullest after I cleared it of enemies, in order to see all the alternate routes I didn’t utilize.
You can also just shoot your way through, but here is my main complaint about the game, and it’s a fairly big one. DE:HR, strangely, offers you a huge array of tools, from lethal to non-lethal, loud or silent, but doesn’t encourage their use. You can silently kill people with your crossbow, loudly blast them with a rocket launcher, tranquilize them, stun them, throw grenades, set mines, use robots, or just engage in massive gunfights with several fun options in weaponry. And while the fighting mechanics aren’t top of the end, from what I toyed around with, they’re still fun. On the hardest difficulty you die very quickly if you’re reckless, but your enemies aren’t bullet sponges, either – and that makes for intense battles. The problem with all of this is that DE:HR rewards an extremely specific game style. It’s not even that it’s just stealth – it’s stealth takedowns (melee). Meaning that even all your stealth equipment might go unused.
If you don’t care about min-maxing, this won’t matter to you. But I have this suspicion that most gamers do want to unlock more powers, and when you get 10 XP for shooting down an enemy from afar, or 50 for taking them down in a non-lethal manner from up close, I imagine you’ll be inclined to do the latter. That 50 piles up in the long run. You also get bonuses at the end of the mission, depending on whether or not you were spotted, and whether an alarm was raised. Together, these bonuses amount to a huge sum that you’ll never enjoy in an aggressive approach, since it doesn’t offer some alternate reward for different achievements. This also caused me to quick-load over and over, since letting things develop dynamically felt more like a punishment. By the end of the game, a non-lethal, melee takedown playstyle will end up rewarding the player significantly more, mechanically, but will also become very repetitive. It’s disappointing that the game offers so many fun instruments, but motivates you with its XP distribution to use one single function alone throughout the entire playthrough. There’s an NG+ option in the director’s cut, and I might do a second run sometime in the future with my developed build, so I can enjoy fighting my enemies guilt-free and without that fear of missing out. But for a single playthrough, it ends up feeling like wasted potential. The gameplay offers you many options but draws a thick, red circle around a very specific one with a big smiley above it.
It’s a major complaint from my perspective, but regardless, as a whole, the experience remains terrific. For anyone interested in a stealth-oriented game with a mature and interesting story and awesome setting, DE:HR is highly recommended. For those who want a sci-fi action game, you can find it here too, albeit discriminated against. You need to approach it with a mentality that doesn’t fret about receiving the bare minimum XP.

After reading the reviews of Deus Ex HR in the summer of 2011, I instantly paid $50 USD on Steam. Before that, the most I'd ever paid for a new Steam game was $20 USD. I did not regret my purchase - this game was a true "Revolution" that was worth every penny I paid. After two memorable playthroughs, I forked out another $15 for the also-excellent Missing Link DLC upon release. I have now beaten the game NINE times to date, with my most recent playthrough being on the Director's Cut version - which Square Enix generously discounted to $5 USD for those who already owned the base game and the DLC.
I'll start by reviewing the game as a game, ignoring the Director's Cut aspect for the time being.
The sandbox RPG nature of the gameplay is exemplary. The worlds are all much smaller than, say, the Elder Scrolls or Mass Effect, and that's a good thing, because exploring every nook and cranny to find every little secret and side-mission is actually loads of fun and doesn't feel repetitive at all. The progression for your augmentations and weapons is well balanced. It's not ridiculously easy to level up, not does it feel like a mindless grind.
There are enough augmentations to suit both the run-and-gun and stealth-it playstyles (I much prefer the latter). Stealthy players can also choose between kill-everyone or be-merciful, and the augmentations also suit both attitudes really well. The powers are just ridiculously cool, from the swords-coming-out-of-arms takedowns to the Icarus Landing System to the door/computer hacking minigame.
Somewhat unfortunately, the focus on cool augmentations came at the expense of gunplay. As a primarily stealth player, I didn't really mind, but the flaws did not go unnoticed. At the beginning, gunplay is actually quite frustrating. Enemies drop very little ammo, the guns are inaccurate if aimed from behind cover, and you just feel like a weakling rather than a trained ex-SWAT officer. It's simply easier and more entertaining to stealth it and take down everyone with your augs. If you wait it out and save every bullet you find and spend your money wisely on upgrades, then the gunplay improves quite a bit. Invest in laser sights for any gun you think you'll use regularly - this will relieve a LOT of frustration when firing from cover. Silencers and damage upgrades (especially the pistol's armour piercing upgrade) will make you feel like a true badass.
The non-lethal weapons are also fun to use, especially the tranquilizer rifle with the target-homing upgrade. They were implemented much better than the guns.
When you're not snooping around and killing/KOing enemies, you'll be doing a lot of talking, and this is one of the aspects of Deus Ex that seriously encourages a second and third playthrough. You're given multiple options in most conversations and what you say can please or ♥♥♥♥ off the other guy, and often your choices have real repercussions in future events in the game. Some of your choices will unlock side missions that are otherwise impossible to know about. If you want the other guy to give you something that helps you in the game, you'll also have to think carefully about what you want to say. Deus Ex HR was actually my very first introduction to this sort of gameplay mechanic (I only started Fallout, Mass Effect, etc around 2012), and I absolutely loved it.
The real downers were the boss fights, which were outsourced for some reason... they were completely unnecessary and sometimes even made the game unnecessarily difficult for stealth players.
The game was also amazingly well optimized at the time, thanks to Nixxes Software which has done the PC ports for many Square Enix games. The control scheme is completely revamped for a mouse-and-keyboard (thankfully, because the controller scheme would be HORRIBLE on a mouse and keyboard), taking full advantage of the many keys, i.e. using the number keys to quick-equip up to 10 items, separating actions between different keys, etc. The graphics options are extensive, as good as any self respecting PC game would offer. The performance was highly scalable. At the time, I only had a laptop with a Core i3 2.4Ghz and 4GB RAM and an ATI Mobility Radeon HD 5650 GPU, and I was able to get great fps at 720p on medium details. I've long since switched to a desktop which of course blows the game away at 1080p max. So Deus Ex HR is not just a good game, but also a good PC game.
Now, on to the Director's Cut specific aspects that made it well worth $5.
The awful boss fights are still there but the levels were redesigned to give players a proper stealth-only option, which I appreciated.
The Missing Link DLC is properly integrated into the main story, as it should have been, because it takes place between two levels in the main game, not before or after the main game. At first I was worried that I would truly lose all my augmentations and not have enough powers for the Singapore and Panchea levels, but fortunately the ending of the Missing Link will restore ALL the Praxis kits that you had before starting the Missing Link. This means you also have a chance to re-spec your augmentation tree if you regretted any previous choices.
The preorder bonuses from the base game are all present, including Tong's mission.
There's a cool New Game Plus option that will allow you to use powerful augmentations earlier than normal when you start a new game, since it carries over what you had at the end of your last playthrough. Want to use the CASIE aug on Zeke Sanders but don't want to waste praxis kits at the beginning? Start a New Game Plus and see how it works out for you!
Sadly, the Second Screen capability found on the console versions didn't make it to the PC. Given the absurdly low price, that's not a big deal, but it's disappointing especially when the technical capabilities do exist, and most players already have a smartphone and/or tablet.
I just cannot recommend this game enough. If you like story-driven RPGs, PLAY THIS GAME. It will suck you back in for a second and third playthrough. I'm absolutely excited for Mankind Divided. Also, the devs are Canadian and the voice cast is Canadian talent including Elias Toufexis.
I'll finish off with a few suggestions for the sequel:
- Hacking is fun and a great way to get cheap XP. However, players also should be properly rewarded if they find the password themselves, i.e. through a pocket secretary nabbed off a dead/unconscious guard. I think awarding the same XP that otherwise would've gone to hacking would be fair. Also, if the player has already found the password, then disable the hacking option when interacting with the lock, to prevent gaining double XP.
- No boss fights. Look at the ending of the Missing Link for a way to implement a good showdown with a main villain.
- If you're going to feature a level set in Canada, let us explore outside of a single building! (national pride here)
- No pre-rendered cutscenes please. If you must have them, don't make them look low-res and blurry. Think of Halo 2's remaster - the prerendered cutscenes actually looked BETTER than the main game!
- Don't be lazy with the character model in third person view. I like it when I can see what gear my character has equipped in third person, instead of magically producing gear out of thin air.
- Let us open doors while dragging bodies.
- Pretend that Deus Ex The Fall never existed and do not get any ideas from the team that made that game!

This game has a lot of potential but is seriously flawed at present. However, it sucked me in and I've racked up 24 hours of playing time, so there must be something about it.
It is advertised as a 'a retro space strategy RPG with base building, deep tactical combat, crew management and emergent storytelling', so let's take a look at those claims.
Retro space strategy RPG. That it certainly is. The graphics are dire. If you like Commodore graphics, fine.
Base building? I've yet to see any evidence but perhaps I haven't got far enough into the game.
Deep tactical combat. What? So much of the game is spent running around killing Space Aliens that little time can be spent planning any deep tactical moves.
Emergent StoryTellinging is supposed to reflect complex situations in gameplay that emerge from the interaction of game mechanics. Every time I've played this game I've seen the same old storyline so there's nothing emergent about it.
Battle gets a little tedious. It is turn based zap em fare and takes little thought. You build big enough ships, that have the ability to heal themselves or each other, and you can bully your way around the star system beating up aliens and collecting HP and resources.
A huge complaint I have is that Halcyon 6 itself, which builds these ships, has no way of healing itself. Indeed, until it blows up in your face, you have no idea of the health of the most important part of your game.
I doubt I'll ever be drawn back into this game.

>>TL;DR
It's a nice and casual replacement for mouse + keyboard that'll be worth your time and money once, or rather if, a second revision is ever released that would make the controller work as an actual controller. It's not bad so I don't really want to give it a thumbs-down, however it neither truly works as a console-style controller nor as a mouse replacement and most definitely not the "one controller to play them all" kind of thing many had hoped it would be.
Waste your time on my wall of text to find out why.
>THE HARDWARE
You won't feel like you completely wasted your money on the controller. The hardware is nicely built, solid and is rugged enough to take a plunge off your desk. It features 2 touchpads, 1 stick, a standard 4-button pad, double shoulder buttons, and unusually 2 grip buttons on the backside. It lies comfortably in your hands assuming you're a grown person with grown hands. All in all very comparable to modern console controllers though with a few twists and a definite focus on the touchpads.
Those pads are very similar to touchpads you find on laptops. And though they're not equal in fidelity compared to a gamer mouse with high DPI, they are pretty accurate and tactile. Using the controller's pads feels more responsive than using the average touchscreen anyway, possibly because of the faint haptic feedback the controller gives off (more on that in a bit). The other components are also well produced, buttons don't get stuck in the controller's case, the stick moves smoothly in place, it feels good in your hands and doesn't falter under your fingers either.
One of the bigger changes when compared to normal controllers is the haptic feedback. Rather than having the classic rumble feature where the controller shakes around in your hand, it features a very slight feedback, half sound - half haptics, which accompanies most touchpad inputs. The sound can be roughly described as a cat sharpening its claws on a rug, not loud or obnoxious but definitely audible. It seems off-putting at first but since the feedback comes in proportion to how fast you move across the touchpads, using the pads becomes a very natural mouse-like input over time.
Another big change compared to normal controllers is the layout of the Steam controller - and that is where most of my praise ends.
The button pad and the movement stick are both placed fairly inward on the controller and take some effort to reach, which makes the controller feel unnatural when playing console-style games.
Now, the controller is designed for touchpad use however a lot of games are built natively around classic (console-style) controller input, any Dark Souls for example. Native double stick inputs and strong use of the button pad will leave you unhappy with the controller's layout, guaranteed.
The touchpads (and everything else) can be configured to act as virtual sticks, d-pads and buttons to make up for that.
However, like trying to ride a kid's bicycle as an adult, emulating inputs onto virtual sticks and d-pads feels wobbly and unresponsive at times, for example adjusting the camera in Dark Souls III. Using the right touchpad as a virtual stick felt so consistently wrong, no matter what the config, I had to change back to my X360 controller.
On the other hand: playing games made for mouse + keyboard can work better than you'd think. I've enjoyed hours and hours of Civ with this controller, as most of Civ can be controlled with just a mouse. I can see other games work rather well in much the same way but in the end it really depends on how casually the game can be controlled; don't expect to do well in FPS games with this controller!
Oh yea, it can play sounds from some sort of internal speaker as well, though you really only notice that when booting it up or shutting it down.
>THE SOFTWARE
The software IN the controller (the firmware) works just fine however a lot of the software AROUND it does not. Having the controller connected to your computer means every Steam game will launch in Big Picture mode. All the controller configuration options are found exclusively in Big Picture mode. I understand the controller is meant to be a companion to Steam machines and HTPCs and the like but it could have worked just fine without Big Picture mode. Big Picture wouldn't even be a problem if it didn't regularly fail or freeze when Alt+Tabbing or if it weren't so sluggish for the little it actually does or if the games recognized it as well as they do the normal Steam game overlay. Alas...
The configuration process can take anywhere from 10 seconds to literally hours (per game). Really depends on whether you use a pre-made config compiled by someone else or sit down and fine-tune every last aspect of the controller yourself. When I first tried to configure the controller I was positively surprised by how much you can actually configure and emulate. Want the buttons to translate into literally any other Direct-X input? You can! Wanna set deadzones and even cheaty fast triggers? No problem!
But then it hit me: I'd have to repeat this mildly arduous process for every game I'd ever play with a Steam controller, not just the general setup process but all the fine-tuning like deadzones, special button combos, etc. There really is no fast way to compile a config completely to your own liking. You'll have to download someone else's config and play around with that instead, slowly building a config that suits you OK.
Luckily most games will have at least one config scheme made by other players, so it's likely you'll not start at 0. Many games even feature a number of schemes for you to play around with.
>SUMMARY
It's nicely made and the hardware is of high quality. It's made for adult hands and doesn't make your fingers hurt even after longer play sessions (for me at least).
It's definitely NOT the controller to rule all controllers as many had hoped it to be. Instead it's a considerable contender to those weird keyboards with integrated touchpads. Because that's pretty much what it is: a compromise between PC configurability and console feeling presumably made as a companion to "entertainment station" PCs. Sadly though it doesn't excel in either regard nor does it make for a must have hybrid.
Most of that comes from the layout. It's just not compatible to today's controller layouts and you'll quickly notice that when trying to play console-style games that make use of the full controller. Casual PC-style games can work very well but don't expect it to work with very fast games or games that require high accuracy.
They should have shipped the thing with 2 touchpads, 2 d-pads, 2 sticks and a button pad, all the exact same size so you can modularly interchange them; set the layout of the controller as you please, not just in software but in hardware as well.
I feel like the configuration process should have been more modular as well, allowing you to quickly configure one of your pads, no matter which one, with config archetypes or some config snippets of sorts. As it is right now you'll either have someone else configure the controller for you or you'll go crazy setting everything up yourself.
Wait for a hopefully modular revision 2 (when/if ever) and get that instead.

Regarding the performance, this game is solid, it runs absolutely smooth, I did not have any frame drops and the 30FPS-Lock did not bother me actually, because it somehow did not feel like 30FPS... Maybe I got used to it quick, don't know.

PROS:

NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 - the first game in years that I paid full price for.
Story:
There are two "story modes" in the game. The first one is "Story Mode" where you play through the story from the manga/anime starting with
. If you, like me, haven't read the manga and only watch the anime, I see nothing wrong with seeing how it ends by playing this game. The fights in this game felt
more epic than they did in the anime. The fight between
felt a bit meh in the anime, but in this game the fight just blew me away. The Naruto-story is way too long to summarize in a short paragraph like this, and if you're new to Naruto I recommend catching up on the story up until the
.
However, if you don't feel like reading up on Naruto before playing the game, you might want to play "Adventure Mode" first. In this mode you control Naruto, and you run around in the ninja world doing simple quest and collecting "memory fragments". The story in this mode takes place after the end of Story Mode, so there might be some slight spoilers, but there are also a lot of flashbacks which is a nice way of catching up with all the past events. To me this mode felt a bit superfluous, but it is a nice bonus. Also, Hinata is great as always.
Gameplay:
I am enjoying the gameplay a lot. The fights feel smooth, and being able to switch between the leader and the supports mid-combo is awesome. Some of the ultimate jutsus feel a bit overpowered, especially against the AI, and during some fights if I were having a hard time I could just spam my ultimate jutsu. There are ways to counter it however, and being able to win using regular attacks and combos feels even better than winning using the (great-looking) ultimate jutsus.
In addition to the regular fights, in the Story mode you also have "boss fights" and quick-time events. I didn't really enjoy the boss fights at first, since I had a hard time controlling the huge characters and dodging the enemy attacks, but as soon as I got used to the controls the fights became a lot more fun. The quick-time events were pretty much like that as well. At first I had a pretty hard time, but after some trial and error it became pretty easy to get a perfect score.
The online worked fine for me, however there should be some sort of punishment for people who ragequit when they are about to lose. I only played non-ranked, and people were still ragequitting.  Why would you ragequit from a non-ranked game!? If you are considering buying the game mainly for the online multiplayer, then you might want to re-think your purchase.
And honestly, what is the point of those ninja tools? I don't think I used them even once.
Graphics:
Yes, this game is locked at 30 fps. Some people seem to have an issue with this, but honestly I couldn't care less. To me it looks pretty damn good. When the game was released a lot of people, including me, were having performance issues despite having a computer above the minimum requirements. Personally I wasn't able to play the game for a few days until a fanmade patch was released. However, within two weeks of the release of the game two official patches were released, and this fixed all the problems I was having. I am now able to run the game at max settings with only some minor drops in fps, which is more than good enough seeing as my specs are not that high.
Music:
The game looks, sounds and feels just like a Naruto-game should. All the music and voices are pulled straight from the anime, which means that they match the world and the characters perfectly. And the opening theme is awesome. Seriously, they should use this opening as the last opening for the anime.
Overall:
Overall I loved this game, and I'm sure that any fan of the manga/anime will be able to enjoy it as well. Even people who are not familiar with the Narutoverse will most likely enjoy it if they enjoy fighting games, although they might have a slightly hard time following the story. And to the people who whine about the 30 fps lock or the graphics or whatever: is that
what is most important?
I got the game at full price, and I don't regret doing so. I pre-ordered it to receive the Boruto and Sarada characters, which are now unobtainable, but honestly I have only used those characters one time each, so if not being able to get those characters is putting you off then I wouldn't worry about it too much. There are plenty of great characters to choose from. (My most played character is Minato (4th Hokage), followed by Rin and Hanabi). Rin sure brings out the feels. Her regular moves are so cheerful, but then you see her ultimate jutsu...
Anyhow, I definitely recommend this game. Even at full price.

The game has just gone live as version 1.0 so I thought I'd take another look at it. The developers have put effort into polishing it, and there have definitely been some optimizations, however I'm still not very impressed and I won't be playing this very much if at all.
The isometric view of the game is frustrating. I keep wanting to zoom in on what is happening, but you only ever have the one fixed distance and it is from a long way out. You end up peering at the map to try and find details like plants etc that should be easy to identify.
The control interface is not intuitive. Everything feels clumsy and wrongly done. Too many complicated menus, with information and controls in unlikely places. The game itself is not that complex, but learning the interface is.  I can't help but feel that a more experienced team might have designed this differently and more effectively.
The pace is not well balanced, and the game drags. The first tutorial takes about 15 minutes to play through, even if you speed up time x4, however what happens feels like it should take 5 minutes. I always feel like I'm waiting for the game to catch up. That's the real killer for me, I find the game is tedious to play, and plain not entertaining.
I wish I could support this small indy team more, but to be honest I'd never recommend this game to a friend.

<edit> Unclaimed World seems to have been dumped out of Early Access unfinshed.  All the potential I hoped for never materialised.  Do not buy.  </edit>
Unclaimed World has oodles of potential oozing out from between the flaws.  But don't be tempted, the flaws are terrible and many.  After playing 0.1.2.1 in January 2015. I'm going to probably give this game a year or more before trying again.  And now I have given it a year - it's January 2016 - and things have changed but not drastically.
First off, the good stuff.  Unclaimed World is like Majesty and Dwarf Fortress at it's core.  You designate tasks and one or more of your free-willed plebs will undertake them.  There is no mico-managing workers.  The banter between the various colonists is the perfect way to introduce the new world.  The scenarios are not random so after a couple of tries you'll know which colonists you get and what their skills are.
I like the graphical style and the smooth character animations, they give a good sense of pioneering on an alien planet.  The character portraits, whilst somewhat caricatured, make knowing and empathising with said characters much easier.
But.
That's where the good stops.
There are currently only three stages, the tutorial which is so hand-holdy it's a chore; and not one I've forced myself to complete.  The first stage which is impossible to lose unless you try really, really had to get your colonists killed.  And lastly the second stage which crashes fairly early in.  Don't expect content, it's not here.
The user interface is bad - but vastly impoved from when it was first released.  And as things start to take shape it's now possible to see higher level issues with interface.  Right click context sensitive menus have been a 'thing' for a very, very long time now.  Unfortunately the devs have ignored years of progress and have a wierd left click, bring up a small box with an arrow, left click the arrow, bring up the context sensitive menu.  Right clicking hides the interface but doesn't close anything.  Left clicking brings back all the menus as they were.
Unclaimed World is SLOW.  The characters idle along at maybe 5 to 10 pixels a seond but have to traverse areas that are thousands of pixels across.  Leaving the game to run whilst doing other things seems to be the only meaningful way to play.  Even after three version bumps this is still a problem and I suspect it's a fatal one.  I've added more detail in my first comment.
And the speed gets worse on the (previously mentioned) second stage.  The characters still move at about the same rate but the screen refreshes at less than a frame a second until eventually it becomes a slide show and crashes.  I'm sure a simple 2D game should run better than this.
The artificial intelligence in a game where units can't be directly controlled has to be good.  But in Unclaimed World it's not.  It's awful.  I can't seem to prioritise tasks. Gathering seems to take precedence over everything.  So if there are a couple of construction projects going on and I set a new gather task then everyone drops what they're doing and rushes (relatively) to all gather the same stick of firewood.  Practicaly this means as long as there are gather tasks construcion tasks will not finish.
Furthermore the AI in combat is even more deficient, with the characters commenting that they must attack as a group and then walking in one at a time; and only after the previous character has been killed.  It's horrible.  They also seem to get lost and will wander backwards and forwards through an enemy nest despite there not being any tasks near it.  I still haven't found a good way to get the colonist to move and work as a unit.
In closing, Unclaimed World has a lot of potential with a good exploration and command vibe but it is so far from being completed that it's barely even a tech demo - let alone a full game.  Avoid.

Rabi Rabi does itself no favours. Going by the art and reviews you’d assume that it was one of the seemingly endless not quite pornographic visual novels being inserted every which way into steam. Look, there’s a bunny girl and a fairy with no clothes! 10/10 would disappoint family again. Guffaw. It’s worth enduring the beady eyed judgemental stares of your awful friends though, as Rabi Rabi is actually one of the best Metroidvanias on steam.
While it’s not as beautiful as something like Ori, Rabi Rabi has very slick presentation with excellent spritework, animation and music, even if the art itself might be more divisive. Rabi Rabi’s big selling point is its non-linearity – this is probably the most open game of its type I’ve ever played, with an expectation that you will explore as signposting is deliberately vague. Like most metroidvanias mobility options increase the speed at which you can traverse and backtrack and encourage doing so with an enormous number of hidden pickups, and the game opens up very organically. Rabi Rabi is absolutely massive as well – even a normal runthrough will take 10-12 hours, and a 100% run could easily double that.
Your basic goal is to recruit characters (in largely any order), a certain number of which will allow you to move onto the next story event. You recruit characters, naturally, by beating them up. There’s a lot of boss fights in this game, and even on normal difficulty they’re no slouch, especially early on. This is where the other selling point of Rabi Rabi comes up - it’s also a bullet hell game, with every boss vomiting forth endless patterns of glowing blobs. Even with your tiny hitbox it will test your platforming and fighting skills – there’s no shame in starting on novice if you’re not a veteran of these genres, whatever the internet might say.
The boss fights end up being both some of the best and worst aspects of Rabi Rabi – at their best they’re tense and challenging, at their worst they’re tiresome slogs through seemingly endless HP bars where you inevitably end up dying five minutes in to a ridiculous super attack right at the end of the fight. The open nature of the game means that there’s always a chance you’ll bite off more than you can chew, though the difficulty of the preceding area gives a pretty good indication of whether or not the boss will thoroughly bum you.
In spite of these flaws Rabi Rabi represents the very best of a crowded genre on steam( alongside Axiom Verge) – it would be a shame if prospective players were put off by the theme, if only because Rabi Rabi could be the gateway to the world of waifus they secretly crave.

So... I don't like FPS games in general. Hey - come to think of it, I barely like any games.
But, I like this one. I've played it for nearly two years, practically every day.
Two reasons:
1) You are part of a team.
Sometime your team is a blessing, sometime it's a curse. The game is unforgiving and does not keep tabs - make the wrong choice of 'mech or loadout, forget about where the team is and what they're doing, play in a match of random players doing all kinds of funny (bad) stuff - one misstake (yours or a team mate's) and you're out. Cry and moan every way you want about the outcome of the match or the performance of your team, but there's always something YOU could have done better  or better communicated with someone else about.
Every now and again you have nothing to do with the outcome of a match - learn to live with it!
2) It's Battletech(tm).
Yes - It lacks some of the elements seen in previous titles in the franchise. It also is better than previous titles at other things. The last year, I've seen improvements in development I never would have thought possible when I started playing. There's also a lot of great improvements in the roadmaps, which I hope will adress many of the current shortcomings.
I know many care about what have been and what will come. Me, I just play the hand I was dealt - Adopt, and have fun.

The interface is messy, the battles are mundane and outside of combat the game is mostly busy work.  Don't get me wrong, what the game HAS is personality, and I really, really want to like it for that.  The aliens and humor are just right and make me want to like it more, but I don't because the rest of the gameplay offers bland repetition.
I can't quite place it, because I'm not willing to play enough to figure it out, but it's one of those games where nothing I do 'clicks'.  It's not satisfying like blowing a demon away in Doom or researching Plasma weaponry in XCOM.  I don't feel the joy of pulling off an insane combo in Mortal Kombat X or surviving a harrowing fight in FTL.  Hell, even Papers Please feels more engaging to me.  I just do not find it fun, and I'm not lying when I say I want to.  I want to run a starbase and send ships out to explore the void, but not like this.  My hopes lie with Lightspeed edition, and hoping the new streamlined gameplay makes for a more entertaining game.  However, Halcyon 6 "Classic" is not a game I recommend.

If you are new to the game, you will probably fail at least one or two runs, just to adjust and get used to a certain difficulty spike that only those who have experienced it will know how best to prepare. The game doesn't let up towards the end either, and that final boss is... Well. I will probably have to celeberate with a coffee for beating it on my second try. And I'm a non-coffee drinker who gets headaches after drinking.
The gameplay is definitely the strongest point of the game however. Despite the fact that it keeps the player suspiciously busy if not outright frantic (refer next point), 3v3 turn-based ship combat never goes stale and is ridiculously satisfying. Each faction's fleet has their own unique attributes - The Xlaar can buff their damage when damaged, the Yab is really fast, the Chruul has EVERY kind of ships and is infinitely more OP. Ground combat isn't boring either. They've beefed up the difficulty quite a bit from last time, and now you have every reason to train up Officers asap (P.S: You won't have enough time when Act 3 starts) and specialize a few in ground combat. Skills are simple but well designed; ships variety and combos will make you wanna jot down specifics, compare before reloading and get the right tech. Resource management and stuff.
A question though: I've seen screenshots of ground combat on a beach background, but despite having played through the entire game I've never seen that background. Was it a red herring? Just concept art stuff?
Also, during Act 3 the notification made me thought I would be gathering legendary officer(s) for the final act. There was in fact only 1; a total of 2 legendary officers you can pick up by doing events. I must have missed something, haven't I?"
Story-wise and events, it isn't much. You know just enough to appreciate the plot and that subtle breaking-the-4th-wall hint, 'Hey you're in desperate times you don't have time for plot ya know?' At least a third of the game's difficulty is due to the fact that the pacing is so crazy frantic that you almost never have time to leisure about and do stuff that you really want to do. It's also used to keep you busy and hide the fact that there really aren't as many events as you hope for.
The characters are entertaining, if not a bit too much of a joke and stereotypical for my taste. Faction interaction and events are strictly minimal; if you would believe it the pirate event chain is probably three times longer than anything you'll get with the factions. There is probably a way to make friends with the new faction since there's that achievement, but you are too busy fending off endless hordes of Chruul that when you at last have an opening to drop by their home planet the only available choice yet is to commit geonocide - Which funnily enough, makes for a more serious storyline than anything else you share with the other factions despite having zero interaction whatsoever (plot related reasons).
Combat animations are awesome; with the newly updated 'Unlock Framerate' option it is now actually a TREAT to watch the colors explode, and god damn do they explode. Really, really satisfying. Same goes with music - it's the same tunes over and over and yet despite 30+ hours of gameplay it never gets too stale. Too focused on the combat to really notice it for long, really.
There are some bugs, but not game breaking. If you didn't save the colonies in time and they get destroyed, the 'Under Attack' notice remain in the Quest log. I'm pretty sure my entire Pirate segment was bugged after Act 1 or 2, after I've taken down the Admirax save for that chosen one (Wraithers!). The faction showed Korpsers and the numbers shown are... well bugged basically.
All in all, this is a fantastic game. I can't wait to see it flesh out and have another go.

The game has some good ideas, maybe eventually it'll get polished enough to warrant a "buy".

SUMMARY: An effective and clever fusion of JRPG, basebuilding, research, light 4x, and diplomacy gives us Halcyon 6, which is "Babylon 5 the game."  A mix of simple to play with complex interactions makes this a game fans of space-and-base strategy should look at.
Halcyon 6 is a game where you, a space commander assigned to an unexplored ancient alien starbase, have your day get worse when mysterious aliens overrun your part of the universe.  Left with an unexplored home, a few personnel, and an unknown threat, assorted alien races and factions, you get figure out what's up and save the day.  Good luck with that.
The game itself consists of mechanics we've all seen before, making it easy to pick up, but giving it a depth that encourages exploration - and brings challenge.  Just because you've seen this before doesn't mean the game goes easy on you:
* You have a space station to manage, clearing rooms, building facilities, and researching new technologies.  Of course each room might reveal some unexpected secrets or trigger an event . .
* You have your officers, who can run starbase facilities, command starships, clear rooms in your base, or explore alien worlds.  Each of them is different in skills and personality, so figuring out how they work together with each other and technology is important . . .
* You have your ships.  Ships are needed to explore and gather resources.  Each ship type is different, types can be improved, and types provide their own special abilities.  Your officers and the ships they command form unique combinations of abilities, which is good as . . .
* Space combat is pure JRPG as well, heavy on interacting status effects.  The right officer in the right ship on the right team is a powerful force.  A mismatched team is space dust.  Of course it's not any different as . . .
* Combat in rooms and on planets is also JRPG style, with different character abilities, combos, and a variety of enemies.  The right team of officers can clean up, the wrong team gets taken to the cleaners, and your resources are limited . . .
* In fact, you'll have to be scavenging for resources across the galaxies, sending ships to and fro, fighting enemies, landing on planets to protect people and more.  You'll need all of that to keep your base and fleets going.  Of course you're doing it all yourself, but you aren't alone . . .
* Several factions are in the game, each with their own personalities, history, ships, and habits.  You'll have to work with them or work against them.  Make choices carefully, because the value in some decisions isn't always immediately obvious.
The game's different levels, interacting, make every choice vital, ever decision important, and give the game real depth.  A bad choice can haunt you, a good choice benefit you, and everything interacts.  The game is a rich tapestry woven of simple threads.
However despite the challenge and grim theme, the game's pixel aesthetics and writing are more lighthearted.  There's a charm to the whole affair that make it even more enjoyable, and show great thought and design.
Halcyon 6 is really the whole package for someone who wants a good space adventure, and the relatively simple mechanics in complex combinations make it accessible and challenging at the same time.
Who's this for?
* If the above review made you go "wow" you'll want to buy it.
* If you're on the fence, watch some videos and read a few reviews.  That should easily let you make up your mind.
* If you want to give a gift to someone you know likes space-management-4X sims, this is probably a good choice - and its quirky nature makes it endearing.
* If you don't want to do careful management and planning, its probably not for you, despite the easy of access.  This is a fun game, but I find it's not necessarily relaxing - it challenges you, but in a friendly way.
A great game, and I'd consider it an achievement in fusing game elements together.  It reminds me of Massive Chalice in the way it fuses concepts and creates long-range repercussions for choices - something I enjoyed a lot.

Disclaimer: I've just completed act 1. I hear this means I am halfway through the game.
A science fiction RPG for lovers of science fiction, and quite obviously written by lovers of science fiction. Blends ideas from Babylon 5 (obviously), Star Trek, Mass Effect, Star Control, and probably quite a few other places. The music couldn't be any more Bablyon 5 without ripping off the sound track. The graphics get the job done. The combat system... eh. Let's talk about that.
I've seen people mention FTL or even X-Com in reference to this game, but I don't see any influence at all. The combat is turn based JRPG style either with starships or with officer (and cadet) combat. The combat system seems shallow at first. Attacks do damage, and can either add a status effect, or consume a status effect for extra damage. It's obvious that you want to chain attacks together to stick status effects on enemies, then consume those effects with your next attack, but sometimes the status effect is too useful to consume for added damage output. I found that sticking to the same combos was usually not a great idea. One size doesn't fit all, and changing up your fleet and officer compositions will create new, useful combos. The combat system isn't anything really special, but it works and it doesn't feel too repetitive.
The thing is I'm not playing for the combat system. The feel is top notch and I can't help but imagine I'm controlling some sort of Babylon 5 offshoot story. If that appeals, then pick this up in a heartbeat. If not, then wait for a sale.

May (insert your deity or non-deity here) bless this controller - and its creators! This controller is imperfect - it does have its flaws, like so many other things do (Wish it had a better "feel" and better reach of the physical buttons, though time helps with this). However, the things you can make this controller do FAR outweigh the cons. The customization of this device is rivaled by no other controller. The responsiveness of the controller feels good, and the feedback it sends is accurate.
Combined with the Steam Link, the world of PC gaming from the distant past until now has been brought to the living room about as seamlessly as possible. With the practically endless amounts of customization this device has, it will only become better.
For a solution to bringing the PC gaming world to the living room without the limitations of a traditional controller and the awkwardness of a mouse/keyboard setup on your lap, the Steam Controller handles this wonderfully.
9/10

I have yet to find a game where I'd rather use the Steam Controller over a PS4 one. The vague hope that some community would make the best settings for every game is a flop. Not much about making a config is amenable to a Wiki-style development [citation needed].
So you're stuck making some settings by yourself, for yourself. It's all BIG PICTURE only, mushroom stick only, no mouse, you can't even use the Steam Controller's own trackball pad to navigate the highly WIMP inspired controller editor. Every sensitivity point, transition ring etc is a blind slider, the only way to know their effect is to try them in-game. And oh boy, the cycle of launching a game to try stuff out, watching the Nvidia™ graphic, loading your game, and quitting back out again will drive you nuts.
In conclusion: it's a revolution of different, not better. And the software lets it down.

Boss fights for this game are everything I've heard...and less. But other than that, I find this game really enjoyable. The world is extensively fleshed out, with the ebooks providing even more lore, and I'm constantly exploring every little alleyway hunting for secret passages and hidden items.The combat shines in some areas, and is just plain confusing in others. If there's an achievement for getting zero kills, then why is non-lethal ammunition so few and far between? I got 8 tranquilizer rounds at the beginning of the game (which in itself was too little) and I was always having to scrounge for more ammo, and when I did find some, it was usually just one dart.
The keyboard controls work very well for this game, I haven't had many problems with them. They're a lot more conducive to stealth gameplay than, say, the Hitman: Absolution controls.
All in all, this game was well worth the buy.

This game... wow, how to describe it?
Well, for those of you who care, my favorite singleplayer game in recent years was Dishonored. I liked the decision-based semi-RPG feel, combined with the richly detailed universe. This game delivers that same atmosphere.
At first, I was frustrated by the gunplay. It seemed woefully inconsistant, but... I actually enjoy it. Headshots are headshots, whether on you or an enemy.
The universe has depth. I spent a good half-hour hacking into e-mail accounts just for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles.
The action bar is weird. Some things equip themselves, some things consume themselves, others equip as secondary gear that just confuses me.
However, I don't know why, but Adam Jensen seems to capture a depth of character Corvo Attano lacked. Perhaps it's the fact that he has voice lines.
All in all, I think this game is the cyberpunk counterpart to the steampunk Dishonored.

I was very sceptical at first seeing that this is an early access game, and I have considered for awhile now if I should buy it.  The graphics didn’t seem to be worth a mention … I mean you’re playing with midgets 
Well two days ago I though what the heck, seeing as the devs are not going to drop the price I just get it over with and buy it. They’ll probably reduce the price now that I’ve bought the game (Murphy’s Law).
I have only 90 minutes on record with this game and I must admit, its 90 minutes that went by very quickly. The reason being that I started enjoying these midgets’ tasks to complete. They seem a bit lazy because they move very slow, but hey their going through a tough time right. And they seem reluctant to start working on tasks that are urgent, but that’s the rebellious nature of man. As mentioned the time spent on playing this game went buy very quickly and that is because I found it to be a very enjoyable experience. Its one of those games where you say “I just want them to build this before I quit”, and after that its one more thing and the process just keep on repeating itself until you see the night is gone and you need to get ready for school or work, or even worse you’re totally late for your date with the girl of your dreams. O well, you’re now learning how to survive, so you’ll probably get a new girl. Maybe not your dream girl but hey, if you play sports you have to live with the injuries.
I can appreciate the fact that the game is still in early access therefor a lot of work still needs to be done. So I think the end product should be very good. The idea of starting with nothing, salvaging, gathering and surviving is a very intriguing idea and I think there is a level of satisfaction to make these guys do stuff in order to survive.
So do I recommend buying Unclaimed World in its early access state? Yes I do.

Note:  This is a review of the Early Access version of the game as of Aug 24, 2014.
The game is virtually unplayable because of the incredibly frustrating, unintuitive, unfinished, and buggy interface.
I fought with the interface for at least half an hour, but anyone without a lot of patience and determination will probably give up on the game in a few minutes.
I'm not sorry I paid for this game, despite its unplayability, because I do think the game has a lot of potential and I want to give its developers a chance, but it's got a LONG way to go before it even becomes remotely playable, much less fun or interesting.
Right now it's nothing but an exercise in frustration.  Did I mention the game was frustrating?  Frustration, frustration, frustration.  Nothing but frustration.  Actually, that's not true.  As you can see from the screenshots, the art is beautiful, and so is the music, and it's got an interesting concept... but it's all overshadowed by how awful the interface is.
I hope this game gets better, I really do.  But right now I can't help but recommend that you stay away unless you want to contribute some money to its development without expecting to get any gameplay out of it at all.

Graphics:
Who thought that OpenGL is a good idea for a fast shooter game like this? (other modern games plays fine with this hardware setup) Leveldesign is pretty okay but not as good as in doom 3.
Sound:
The soundtrack is great but becomes annoying as hell when you progress in the game. Every time, when enemies spawn, the soundtrack changes to a more agressive combat style until you killed the last enemy from said spawn. This is exactly the same as in painkiller or serious sam but they did it right and doom sadly did not. noises from enemies feel like they are played directly infront of you. I had trouble seeing enemies because the sound indicated a whole other direction than the enemies are actually standing.
Gameplay:
I had a very bad feeling about the "glory kill" moves at first but they are pretty okay. there are just a few problems with it. first of all, you're not invincible during glory kills.. at least not for the whole kill move wich leads often to death after glory kill animation because you can't move until the animation is fully played. If you try to avoid the glory kills, you often end up shooting more than enough bullets till an enemy gets down without glory kill... I think without the kill moves you need 3 times more bullets then with a glory kill.
next thing I'll have to cover is the fact, that this game playes almost exactly like serious sam or painkiller. you enter an area, all doors get locked, a fixed amount of enemies spawn and after you killed them all you can continue to the next area. and with the changig sound, you always know when an enemy is still alive. this ruins the whole scary part that doom3 had. areas with enemies are mostly build in a circle and play like multiplayer maps. enemies spawn in almost every spot at almost the same time so that you end up running in said circles untill every enemy is down.
weapon upgrades are just there to make the s*** look a bit better. they're nearly useless in my opinion because the secondary firemode of the weapons do not enough damage to be usefull, I almost never used them.
the game offers ingame challanges to unlock some sort of talisman which makes enemies stay longer in the tumbling glory kill state or increases the radius in which items get collected but like the weapon upgrades, they're more or less useless because you just stand right next to the items, when enmies drop them (f.e.)
Story and Playtrough:
the story feels pretty rushed. you get the chainsaw and I believe the first 4 weapons in the 2nd level of the game. and thats almost everything you need to complete the game (I never used the gatling gun or the bfg which you'll get later) while doom 3 took care of slowly getting into something like a story, the new doom just throws you in hell and then you're back on the mars base and that was it. I knew hardly what I was doing besides clearing areas and walking to the next ones. At certain points you'll have to find a keycard or a switch which is pretty boring depending that this game wants to be an arcade game. I guess they tried to make something like doom 1 but horribly failed. The only good thing is, that the checkpoints are decent placed and there was never a situation where I had no idea what to do next.
If you want to play a creepy horror game with some action: play doom 3
if you want to play an arcade game like the good old dooms, just play painkiller or seriouse sam instead.

Rabi Rabi does itself no favours. Going by the art and reviews you’d assume that it was one of the seemingly endless not quite pornographic visual novels being inserted every which way into steam. Look, there’s a bunny girl and a fairy with no clothes! 10/10 would disappoint family again. Guffaw. It’s worth enduring the beady eyed judgemental stares of your awful friends though, as Rabi Rabi is actually one of the best Metroidvanias on steam.
While it’s not as beautiful as something like Ori, Rabi Rabi has very slick presentation with excellent spritework, animation and music, even if the art itself might be more divisive. Rabi Rabi’s big selling point is its non-linearity – this is probably the most open game of its type I’ve ever played, with an expectation that you will explore as signposting is deliberately vague. Like most metroidvanias mobility options increase the speed at which you can traverse and backtrack and encourage doing so with an enormous number of hidden pickups, and the game opens up very organically. Rabi Rabi is absolutely massive as well – even a normal runthrough will take 10-12 hours, and a 100% run could easily double that.
Your basic goal is to recruit characters (in largely any order), a certain number of which will allow you to move onto the next story event. You recruit characters, naturally, by beating them up. There’s a lot of boss fights in this game, and even on normal difficulty they’re no slouch, especially early on. This is where the other selling point of Rabi Rabi comes up - it’s also a bullet hell game, with every boss vomiting forth endless patterns of glowing blobs. Even with your tiny hitbox it will test your platforming and fighting skills – there’s no shame in starting on novice if you’re not a veteran of these genres, whatever the internet might say.
The boss fights end up being both some of the best and worst aspects of Rabi Rabi – at their best they’re tense and challenging, at their worst they’re tiresome slogs through seemingly endless HP bars where you inevitably end up dying five minutes in to a ridiculous super attack right at the end of the fight. The open nature of the game means that there’s always a chance you’ll bite off more than you can chew, though the difficulty of the preceding area gives a pretty good indication of whether or not the boss will thoroughly bum you.
In spite of these flaws Rabi Rabi represents the very best of a crowded genre on steam( alongside Axiom Verge) – it would be a shame if prospective players were put off by the theme, if only because Rabi Rabi could be the gateway to the world of waifus they secretly crave.

I went into this game skeptical. It's usually my experience that bunny girls and sexy-lolita-pixies are a sign that someone's trying to distract from their deficiencies. That was not the case here.
Rabi-Ribi is an intense Metroidvania bullet-hell, and it handles both genres marvelously. The game has multiple difficulty options, each of which seems to be balanced meticulously. Read the descriptions of the difficulties because they're accurate, and if you find yourself going in blind on Hard mode you ARE going to see the Game Over screen more than once per boss fight on average. There are a
of boss fights.
Normally with a Metroidvania, boss fights at some difficulty start to feel like stat checks. "Did I go find the ____ beam?" "Oh, guess I don't have the ____ armor yet." "I probably need better bombs." And some of those moments do happen here, but more often the conversation you have with yourself goes "OH! So I need to dodge over her and attack her from behind because that attack only hits to the right" or "Damn! I really need to get better at using my invulnerability frames."
It's intense, it's rewarding, and it's going to leave you wanting more. So long as you don't have someone else in the house who you have to justify the groped bunny-woman to, this game is absolutely best-in-class.

I have played MWO extensively for 2 years. In those 2 years I have spent close to $1,000 on this game, so if you're looking for an inexpensive game, this isn't the game for you. Since I started playing the game, there has always been a struggle with the same set of issues which PGI can never seem to fix, which is why I left a negative review. Heres the bad and good.
The Bad:
1) Balance-be prepared to hear about non stop whinig about this topic and it's well deserved. Meta is always flip flopping and PGI constantly nerfs/buffs mechs. You buy a mech, its sweet and kicks♥♥♥♥♥ people cry and your sweet mech becomes obsolete. New mechs get relased and its the same pattern, so you'll always have to buy the new stuff or play whats broken at the time. Weapons mechanics always changing along with movement/speed of your mech. Match balance is also an issue, games are always lopsided and short. PGI doesnt tier mechs in the MM like other games so your so-so mech will be tossed into matches w/ top tier mechs, yay! It's a headache.
2) New content-just a general lack thereof. We waited about 3 years for CW, it was cool for awhile then became boring as all hell, because theres just not much there. They're releasing CW 3.0 which will likely have same effect. New Maps, maybe 2-3 a year or so. They do however release new mech packs constantly for you to buy. When you browse the website you'll see most of the highlights are new things to buy and maybe one about an event or something, like I said $1000.
3) Hit Registration/Bugs-always a problem. Constant bugs, glitches, etc. Not such a big deal but everytime they relase a patch theres an immediate hot fix. Hit Reg is still a problem and will likely always be one. It took 2 years to fix the SRM hit reg issue.
4) Things take forever-you'll wait a long time for small changes.
5) General game play-this and number one are the big ones. Game play is monotonous, maps always play the same way and stratagies are all similar from map to map. A lot of Nascar tactics or camping.
Some good things:
1) Customization-no other game offers better customization, you'll spend hours in the mechlab which is nicely laid out.
2) Good rewards-Pays well especially CW if you farm pugs :-P
3) PGI communicates-Russ is active on twitter and generally will respond to you if you're nice. Kind of cool but I dont like his answers much!
4) High learning curve-a plus for me, you'll spend months/years to master this game and it is more of a thinking mans shooter then say BF or Halo.
5) Always new mechs to buy-get your wallet out. Good and Bad.

I've played MWO since closed Beta, over 3 years, and I love it. After playing for all this time, I can easily say that MWO has had better staying power than nearly any other computer game I've ever played. I also, for the most part, like the MWO community. I've met some great friends and have a lot of fun playing with them. Although, you don't have to join a group to have fun. I've had hundreds of great games playing solo.
The ability to customize your mech to fit your chosen game style is great. Scout, brawler, sniper, missile boat, leader or follower. Fast mechs, slow mechs, big mechs or small mechs. Lasers, canons, missiles, or support roles like NARC, ECM, and tag. The game has some real depth to it, and the developers continually work to make it better. My experience with the support team has been good (and I really have had to work with them on some connection issues).
It's not like most shooters, where your life span is measured in seconds. In games like Halo and COD, I always disliked that the average life span seemed to be 10 seconds or less. In MWO you can live for several minutes while taking fire and get into some insane brawls with opposing mechs. Minor mistakes can be overcome (provided your mistake isn't walking smack into the middle of the opposing team) and you can really make a difference to your side's success even after half your mech is blown off.
Having said that, the game does have a learning curve. There can be real depth to the gameplay. Teamwork is very key. You have to watch your position relative to your team, your enemy, and the map itself. Some locations on the maps are better than others, and you'll have to discover them. You have to pay attention to your heat, your mechs armor and internal structure, your weapon status, and to be a good player you also have to pay close attention to your opponents status and aim with precision at where they are weakest; all the while maneuvering as best you can to absorb incoming fire while delivering your own.
The tutorial is pretty good and a must for new players. Several of the existing player groups will also welcome new players and help you learn. I know mine will. If you can, get into one of the teamspeak rooms and ask around, or look at the gaming fourms in the faction groups. Most players are helpful in answering honest questions.
I would recommend premium time at a minimum if you're serious about playing. The 50% boost to Cbills and expierence really add a great deal over time and let you customize your mechs in a relatively short time. I would also recommend you find what kind of mech you like and then give a Hero Mech a try. The Hero Mechs give Cbill and experience bonuses that stack with the premium time. Make money with a Hero Mech and you can purchase and kit out your garage nicely without having to pay a dime more. I have way over a hundred mechs, and most of them were purchased for free, with Cbills earned in the game (or even given away by the developers during special weekend events!).
Of course, some mechs are better than others, and there's always going to be "meta" mechs and builds that are at the top, but the developers really have done a pretty good job of balancing the mechs. The game is definitely NOT pay to win. The Hero Mechs and Premium time ease the grind, but they are not an "I win button." I love that it doesn't matter so much if you are in a light, heavy, or assault mech, if you are a good pilot and play it right, you can beat your opponent regardless of what they are driving. So long as you don't take yourself too seriously (remember, it's a game!) you can have fun with all of the mechs, and there are a ton of them to choose from.
So what don't I like? I wish the game had better visuals and sound effects for internal ammo explosions (basically the MWO version of a critical hit where ammunication inside a mech starts to explode). I wish some of the original iconic mechs, like the capapult, looked and played like they did in closed Beta (give me back that torso twist and the monster PPC barrels!). I also wish that scouting and support roles gave more rewards than they do now. Oh, and I hate how the gauss rifle works. Other than that, I'd say I'm extremely satisfied in my experience with the game.
One other point to add is that this game is pretty sanitary for a young person if you are a parent and concerned about your kids watching and/or playing violent games. There's no blood; no humans with guns killing other humans with guns (or worse). It's giant stompy robots blowing up other giant stompy robots, so the sense of human on human violence is much less than other first person shooters.
So, if you like first person shooters and are looking for a game with great gameplay, good graphics and more than the ten second life-span of HALO and COD, the game is one you should give a chance. It's free to try, so you have nothing to lose, and alot to gain. Good luck, and see you in the next drop!

I have been playing this game on and off since the closed beta, it is true that its not the greatest game in the world and that there is a heafty price on some mechs if you dont want to grind and want everything now. The actual gameplay of the battles and customization of the mechs in the mechbay is where this game is great.
The battles are fought as 3 4 mech lances (squads) so to get the best out of the game you need to work together and support your team (it only takes 1 mech to run off by themselves to turn a garanteed victory into a defeat) each mech class has its own advantages and uses that you will find out from playing.
The grind in the game isn't to reach the biggest mechs as you can pretty much get these from the get go and each class plays verry differently suiting different people, if you like to run and gun darting from cover to cover in hit and run tactics then a light mech is your thing, if you like heavy firepower and the armour to stand your ground (because you are not moving very fast) then assault mechs might be your thing but remember even in the biggest baddest looking mech you can still be turned into a smoking wreck in a matter of seconds by light mechs without the support of your team.
So I will leave with this, the game is f2p you have nothing to lose so give it ago, compleet the tutorial, use the trial mechs to get a feel for the different classes and find the class that suits you then once you have finished 25 matches and earned all the cadet bonus you should have a fair amount of credits to get a mech of your choice all without spending any real money.
So have fun and I may see you on the field of battle mechwarrior.
