I really wanted to like this game.  I love difficult platformers like Super Meat Boy, N+ and Electronic Super Joy so I figured adding in a 10 second time limit would make it interesting.  Unfortunately, poorly designed levels and a lack of purposeful progression holds the game back.  While most of the other games start out with a steady increase in difficulty while using clevel level design to teach and refine certain game mechanics, this one just tosses you into the fray with little structure.  Typically I would run through a game and not get A+ type scores/times, but would complete them to learn the game and get some practice time, while here, you're shoehorned into rehashing the same levels for high scores (not just completion) before you can unlock the next tier.  It's just tedious for the sake of being tedious and I can't see any real purpose.  If you're the type of person that likes hard platformers and doesn't mind a grind on single level before moving to the next, then you'd like this, but if you're a more gradual gamer that goes back for polish, then this one isn't for you.

Incredibly fun, fast paced game perfect for completionists, as well as those looking for a difficult race against the clock. Most of this game is not in completing the levels, but instead in perfecting them to achieve the fastest time possible.

The game is
short, but has replayability in the form of some 'bonus levels' after game completion.
If you're not worried about 3-starring every single level you're probably looking at 2 hours of gameplay, including cutscenes.
Having said that, it's definitely 2 hours of good fun.
Killing the robots and 3-starring a level feels nicely satisfying and is complimented by
sleek simplistic graphics and a fun short story presented in little animations inbetween worlds.
The game introduces few new mechanics along the way, but just enough to keep me interested.
The progression curve could've been a lot better. Especially the final world seemed to be much easier then some of the previous levels.
Although I've only ran into a couple minor issues with the game (had to restart the game once), I've seen many people with unresolved bugs in the discussions. It's definitely something to note.
PROS:
+ Pleasing simplistic graphics
+ Controller support
+ Quick satisfying gameplay
+ Fun story
CONS:
- Very short
- Unfixed Bugs
- Flawed progression Curve
- Probably overpriced
I'd recommend picking it up during a sale or in a bundle; I don't think it's worth full price.

RIP Mastertronic. In November of 2015, the stalwart game publisher entered administration. As of 7 months later, it remains to be seen whether they will resurface.
I actually used to have a somewhat negative impression of the publisher at first, due to what I perceived were their misses (
and
come to mind). But as time passed, I gradually grew to really appreciate their catalogue, and they had published a few impressive games mere months before they went into administration. From the outside, who would have thought that would happen, coming 7 months after
, 2 after
and 1 after
?
But enough of that, into the review proper. 10 Second Ninja, compared to the other Mastertronic titles mentioned above, is one of the relatively older games from the publisher released on Steam.  Good news if you take game titles at face value - this one is exactly what it says. You're a ninja (check) who has to complete levels and kill Nazi (wait, what? I'll explain later) robots...within 10 seconds (check).
The controls felt very satisfying and easy to learn. I did often get confused though whenever I had to use the shurikens or sword slash for some reason - probably bad muscle memory. I'd often use the other attack instead of what I intended to use. No biggie.
Each level must be completed in a maximum of 10 seconds, and with there being 40 levels, that means you can theoretically breeze through the whole game in about 7 minutes. However, you'll normally find yourself taking longer than that. This is because some levels are gated by the number of stars you have earned from completing the levels. You'll thus end up spending the bulk of your time on replaying these levels - failing repeatedly multiple times as you attempt to shave milliseconds off your best records just to get 3 stars on each level.
While the joy and exhilaration from finally 3-starring the levels does make up for the flaws I've observed, that is not to say they aren't noticeable, however.
The aforementioned Nazi robots can be seen as a rather offensive joke by some people (though I personally have no problems and find the cutscenes featuring Robot Hitler rather hilarious) - turning on the censor filter will remove the symbols, but also removes the cutscenes as well.
As mentioned earlier, the maximum time restriction imposed on each level ultimately makes this a rather fast game to complete - too fast, maybe. The implication is that this might be a bad game to pick up if you are concerned about the cost to time-spent ratio. In fairness though, I got this game from a bundle in January 2015 (and ended up playing it 1 and a half years later!) so that definitely took the sting out of my wallet slightly.
And lastly, a few bugs are still apparent with no hope of them being resolved - sometimes my ninja runs to the side without me pressing (this usually happens after I restart while I'm moving though I'm not sure of the specifics), and sometimes after I get a new record it lags for no apparent reason. When it lags, it lags really bad, and even upon restarting the game it persists. It does go away after a while though I have no idea how to consistently remove the lag.
Still, for a game that is the very embodiment of the joy of pure speedrunning, this is a really solid effort and will definitely appeal to platformer lovers looking to get some speedrunning in. Oh, and the soundtrack with its layered touch (a more barebones version in the menu compared to much more instrumentation in the levels) is really neat and groovy too.
And for added challenge, after three-starring all the levels you get a Hard mode where you speedrun the entire game in 4 minutes maximum for the ultimate challenge. Restarts and deaths will prove very costly.
With the seeming lack of support for this title as the developers have already moved on to the sequel, get this only if it's on sale. Or, better yet, save your money and get the sequel instead. It contains remastered versions of the 40 levels in this game, thus rendering this almost obsolete - unless some relatively easy achievements are your thing.

Great idea, poor implementation...
1) You will enjoy "time managment" related to manually harvesting resources from "colonies".
Sadly, unlike random web milkers, you can't just click everywhere, you have only one "fleet".
Also there is no "donate" button and you can't skip it, get ready for "fun".
Later in game you will face constant raids on colonies that never stop and cannot be prevented.
2) You MUST ran 3 ship party at all time, ever on very easy, you will be chewed if try to solo random pirate fleet.
3) ALL combat is about using skill A after skill B, no other options.
One ship down engines, second one "exploit" vulnerability, repeat N time.
4) Major slot machine simulator is included, in some cases, you have 75% chance to win and 25% chance to lose, have fun.
5) Due to resource costs of everything, harsh penalty on "death" and stupid limits on officers and ship levels, losing ship is reload, zero replayability and zero ways to recover.
6) oh god "ground combat", fighting without ship is mandatory in many cases, if you can't beat ground combat - --restart game-- uninstall, there is no way to "improve" your officers.
7) There is hidden and obscure time limit that prevent you from leaving rails, it will punish if you are "too slow" without any kind of warning.
Too slow? well, we will spawn 6 fleets of high level ships and wipe your sector, without warning.
With few modifications related to complete removal of all "time managment" features, level locks and adjustments of loot and prices, game will be fun, currently it is tedious, slow, boring and single timed.

Like many others have said before me, "I really wanted to like this game". I love the pixel art, the soundtrack is decent, combat is okay although a bit too simple, the factions are fun, and I was interested in where the story was going.
However, the brutal difficulty is killing the game for me. Now I'm not a strategy expert, but even on easy this game can be relentlessly cruel. The problem is that the balance has no consistency. You'll be breezing through ground and fleet battles one moment, and then ridiculous difficulty spikes blindside you.
I tend not to shy away from difficult games if it's a fair sort of difficulty with a pattern to learn and better yourself from, but there is so much RNG in Halcyon 6 that all you can do sometimes is cross your fingers and hope for the best. Even enemies that are supposedly the same "Tier" as you can often dish out more than twice as much damage as you're capable of.
I get that crew and officer death is sort of meant to be a regular thing and I'm okay with that, but you might want to pass on that memo to the game. If you ever lose one of your best ships or, god forbid, a top officer, you'll be at a significant disadvantage as the game gives you little to no time to recover from mistakes.
I felt like I had been on top of crisis events for most of the game and even then I had no time to breathe. No time to explore or test strategies, no time to get a proper secondary fleet up and running, no time to research much of anything beyond what the main missions were telling me to research.
To top it all off, Halcyon outright fails to mention EXTREMELY important information on a regular basis. There are plot developments that, if you're not aware of them or if you're not prepared, it's an unavoidable game over. "10 hours down the drain, restart your playthrough please. Bet you didn't see that coming, eh? Funny stuff."
As it currently stands, I cannot recommend this game. If the balance is ever fixed, or if the easy modes ever actually become easy, I will change my rating.

fun, challenging and charming game with a lot of great systems and replayability.
the game starts off with a core loop that revolves around building up your base, researching technology, defeating enemies with your fleet(s) and gathering resources. things get more and more intense in the 2nd and 3rd acts and towards the end you're just trying to survive against ever-increasing odds.
i beat the game on commander difficulty by the skin of my teeth and i'm looking forward to jumping back in on a harder difficulty and trying out some different combinations of ships and skills.
some negative criticisms:
- the ground combat isn't all that compelling
- some of the end game goals aren't immediately made clear to the player. what is diplomacy? why does it matter? which races should i ally with and why?
all in all, it's a very unique game that's both challenging and fun. definitely looking forward to what's coming next!

Amazing controller, coming from a mousepad user the mouse control and scroll pad instantly feel natural. Very sturdy as well I accidentally dropped it multiple times yet it still works fine. Setting up controls for different games and even non steam games is very easy. I think this controller is essential for certain games like Dark Souls while not as viable in others. Living in the EU it was delived quite quickly as well (within aprox 48 hours (?).

The controller itself, in terms of actual use in-game, is great. The controller configuration schema, big picture mode, and everything else you need to deal with to use the controller is absolute crap.
There does not seem to be any way to set a global configuration (ie, I will never want haptic feedback on button press or joystick movement, but I have to disable that for every game individually... and when I change it in desktop mode, it never sticks). Big Picture Mode turns on automatically if you're using the controller, so instead of getting the normal steam overlay, you instead get a laggy and less-functional overlay that you cannot interact with EXCEPT through the controller... which is great fun when the battery is dying and literally the only thing you can do is alt-f4 out of the game and lose your progress.
Overall, it's great when I actually get to use it to play games; however, the frequency with which I DON'T is enough that I just don't want to deal with its crap any more. Get a wired 360 controller and use that instead, it'll work out of the box and not mess up Steam.

It's a fun game with a well-developed storyline and packed with a dystopian, creepy atmosphere of crime and secrets. I played the first Deus Ex game and absolutely loved it, although by today's standards that game is kind of a lackluster game (crappy graphics, dumb NPCs and whatnot).
If you've never played a Deus Ex game before, they play similar to Metal Gear Solid but with a different atmosphere and different plots/locations (however from a primarily 1st-person perspective).
However, this game is really neat, but it's also full of bugs, and has a good deal of gameplay/design issues. However, most of these issues almost completely disappear from gameplay for some reason by the time you get about halfway done with the game, so that's a plus.
.      1) Sometimes your left-click ability will break for all menus in the game; this makes it impossible to save your progress any further and so you have to exit the entire game and restart it in order to fix it, until it happens again.
.      2) You are limited to only 100 save file slots. This can be extremely annoying if you are someone like me who prefers to save frequently. For comparison, I have over 1,800 save files on Skyrim. I ran out of slots to save my game in by the time I got to the 1st boss fight (not gonna say what the boss is for those who havent played yet).
.      3) Sometimes the HUD will be slid all the way across the screen from the corner, making it impossible to see any of your vital information you need to see. This is a huge graphical problem and can only be fixed by restarting the game.
.      4) When you are visibly armed in public areas, most of the dialogue from people when they tell you "please put the weapon away", etc. is severely muffled and low-quality, in contrast to all other dialogue in the game. Some sort of audio bug I guess.
.      5) The brightness setting/slider in the video options is broken, it doesn't work and you can't change the brightness of the game as a result. I've confirmed that my friends who also play this game have the same problem.
.      6) Some map parts are not designed well, and as a result, you can see wall parts that clip through each other, or wall parts that expose "the void" (the empty space of nothingness outside the map).
.      7) When dragging bodies around the corner of a room, half the time they will clip through the corner of the floor and disappear into nowhere. Some real half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥collision work there.
.      8) Emitters/effects from explosions clip through cielings and can be seen from the floor above.
.      9) Half the textures on objects and in the environment are very low-quality, almost same LoD as most textures were from the first Deus Ex game from (now) 15 years ago. The only difference is that the new textures in this game have normal maps applied to them.
.      10) You cannot carry multiple guns of the same type (eg. carrying two combat rifles at the same time). This can be frustrating if you've got a lot of loot to grab and want to resell it, because if you try to pick up other guns of the same type if you've already picked up one, it just grabs the ammo from that extra gun and removes that extra gun entirely.
.      11) The levels that take place in China and other non-American places have a lot of racial stereotypes forced into the portrayals of the people that live in these areas.
I'm not one to care much about political correction, but you'd think that the Deus Ex team would've figured out by now, after a decade, that it's not okay to portray entire races this way in video games.
.      12) The game is quite easy to beat even on the highest difficulty. There is not much challenge involved, it's mostly just a matter of waiting for the NPCs to do something stupid so you can take them down with a quick shot in the head, hide the body, then repeat with all the other NPCs until there are no enemies between you and your objective. That's not my idea of a challenge. The boss fights are the only parts of the game that are actually difficult.
.      13) The mouse cursor is offset upwards from what it's actually meaning to point at; this can be frustrating when trying to play the hacking minigames because you will frequently accidentally use a nuke virus when you just wanted to capture a node, forcing you to reload your save file if you want to recover that accidentally-used virus.
.      14) The environments in the game are, for the most part, extremely "cookie-cutter" style, as in lots of parts, room designs and props are CONSTANTLY reused, like how it is on MMO's or games with procedurally generated environments (eg. Star Trek Online or SCP Containment Breach). To me this kind of shows a bit of laziness and lack of effort on the game developer's part, and it also makes exploration a lot less rewarding, because you know you're gonna generally find the same exact stuff everywhere you go.
.      15) When you go to exit the game to desktop, the game just freezes as soon as you click "yes", and won't unfreeze unless you deliberately end the game's processes via the windows task manager, or else wait until it registers as having crashed/not responding.
.      16) Early on into my playthrough of the game, the firing sounds for the combat rifle broke and so I have a totally silent rifle that's not silent at all. It never went back to the way it originally was again. I have googled this issue and apparently it's a bug that was in the original console versions, and was well-known, yet Eidos did not fix it when they ported the game to PC. Lazy♥♥♥♥♥devs. GG
.      17) The "Talion A.D." sidequest is annoyingly difficult to complete due to a lack of a normal game feature: the map marker. Once you get to the part of the quest where you're supposed to read the dead guard's pocket secretary, you can read it but you will not be given any more map markers after reading it, so you have NO idea where to go to complete the mission. It took me two hours of combing around Lower Heng-Sha to finally discover that the next step of the sidequest took place in a remote sewer area on the very edge of the map. Utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
.      18) There is a serious bug where for most of the Hengsha Dock level, it is impossible to save the game, seriously hindering progress. The save feature started working again for me after I completed the level.
.      19) It's interesting how a Detroit police station, an abandoned old Chinese noodle factory, a military cargo ship, and a top-secret Illuminati facility all have the exact same kind and look of air duct systems. In a nutshell, all the air vents in the game look EXACTLY the same.
That said, this game was hounded over and developed meticulously by the hardworking staff at Eidos Montreal (this was their first game that they have ever made, being a new game studio), and though Deus Ex HR still has all these bugs, it's still pretty good, and pretty fun to play.
However, similar to the first Deus Ex game, Human Revolution suffers from a ridiculous/overpowering ending game segment. I like to think of this as the "Gunbuster" effect: Start out with a plot that's understandable, reasonable and small, then start exponentially ramping it up until the point where it's no longer believable or is just obnoxious in its scale/implications/complexity.
The same stupid plot ideas about the Illuminati and god-like transcendence crap that ruined the original Deus Ex's plot are back again in this game, only this time in a fortunately more believable/understandable way. The Deus Ex franchise's theme is all about the effects and consequences of advanced technology on mankind, and they definitely did a better job of showing that in this game than they did on the first.
All in all, this game is still really good despite its flaws, and you should definitely get it.
One last note: Some like Angry Joe have said it's only got 20 hours worth of gameplay, but I can testify that I got over 80 out of it.

Handsome Mr. Frog is an arcade styled game in the same type as classics like Donkey Kong, BurgerTime, or Mario Bros. arcade games. It is a single screen, two dimensional, platforming game. In this game, you play through wave after wave of various enemy types on each stage. There are a few stages in each world. The worlds have different settings, including the basic starting world, an icy world, a horror world, and a world with water hazards. The gameplay consists of jumping and eating enemies as an attack. You are a frog and use your tongue to grab enemies and spit them at other enemies to destroy them both. To clear a wave of enemies you must defeat them all. You also have a box or two to help you out as you can throw that at enemies as well. The controls are simple, just jump button, eat button, pause, and movement, and it can be played well with keyboard or Steam Controller setups. There are items like extra lives, points powerups, and a chili pepper that lets you shoot fire. You also have a leaderboards system to see your online rank. One of the best parts of this game is collecting hats for Mr. Frog. The hats appear randomly in game, and once restarted you can choose one to wear throughout the gameplay. The game is a lot of fun, just like an arcade game, it kept me coming back to it on a weekly basis but usually for short plays at a time. I definitely recommend it to fans of the arcade classics.

You play as Erina, a bunny who wakes up a human (the "Rabi"). Her partner-in-crime is a fairy named Ribbon (the "Ribi") who shoots magic. Together they combine to form Rabi-Ribi, and set out on a quest to find a bunch of people, none of whom are wearing pants.
The overworld is metroidvania, the boss battles are bullet hells, the music is pretty good, the gameplay is very nicely polished, packaged in a whimsical anime skin.
+ Excellent gameplay. Knocked it out of the park here. This is just one line here, but so hugely important to this game, that any detractor seems like a nitpick.
+ Lots of stuff to do. Lots of bosses, lots of settings, tons of collectibles for the 100% nutters, speedrun timers for the speedrunners, 0% item mode run for the people who think the ground is too soft, casual mode for the babbies, and several harder difficulty modes for the people who wish more of their bones were broken. Erina has a hammer for melee attacks, and Ribbon has ranged attacks, and there's an achievement for playing through the game without picking up the hammer at the start.
+ Challenging, especially if you want it to be. Are you a bad enough dude to get the "complete all bosses in MAX rank mode" and "complete all bosses without taking any damage" achievements? Get ready to work for them and git gud or die trying.
+ Not linear, do things in whatever order you like. You can get a few achievements for non-standard sequences.
+ Has an atmosphere the polar opposite of Grimdark, Noblebright. There's the smell of a lazy vacation day, where the worst conflicts are just misunderstandings, suffering is a temporary step before a lesson is learned, and everyone is generally content. All the elements of the game combine to a kind of pleasant and carefree feeling.
+ Music is good. Most of it is forgettable, but there's a few catchy tunes, and the music sets the mood well, which is what it needs to do.
? Art is very anime. I feel like I shouldn't need to point this out since it's so obvious, but if this is a dealbraker for you, why did you get this far in considering if you're going to buy this? While I'm talking about it, there's nothing more sexualized here than what you can see in the trailer.
? Writing is also very anime. I can appreciate that this game really rolls with the whole "most characters are incapable of understanding innuendo" thing because on some level it's innocent and endearing, but I can also see it becoming grating.
? Characters. A well-executed combination of the above two points, if you like them or not will be up to your tolerance for anime tropes.
? The island is experiencing a drastic shortage of pants.
- The story. The characters really drive the story along, but there's nothing outstanding to see here. Each boss battle is framed with some dialogue, but most of the reasons for fighting are contrived, and the game knows it. This kind of goes back to the whole Noblebright thing. There's generally the impression that anything bad is just temporary and things will just work out eventually, so there doesn't really feel like there's too much at stake. Ribbon and Erina really care about the main story line, but the way the world is framed makes me think it would have all worked out on its own.
A very solid, thorough, and challenging game in its genres.
. Basically the only reason not to get this is if you are allergic to anime, have no interest in platforming gameplay, or are playing video games for their deep and compelling stories instead of reading a book.

Long before this game started on Steam, or was even talked about being a part of the Steam Community, I've played since Beta, back in 2010. For close two and half years, PGI struggled under the yoke of Infinite Game Publishing, And much to Russ Bullock and Company's credit, they have done a superb job. By first, buying themselves out from under IGP and going on their own. It's Piranha Games is a small company with little or no experience, and for most companies, that's a death's knell. Most would close their doors and fade off into the gaming world sunset, but PGI has prevailed.
MechWarrior has a long standing tradition of rich gameplay and diverse community. Small that it may be, but even the smallest game can be the biggest of giants. And MechWarrior is no exception. I can still recall playing NetMech and going head to head with people using a dial up internet system, where the computers were as big as coffee table books and games were played from a Floppy disc. Yes, it shows my age, but still I have played this game since that time and its many titles: MechWarrior 2, MechWarrior 2: Mercenaries, and MechWarrior 2: Ghost Bears Legacy; MechWarrior 3 and MechWarrior 3: Pirates Moon; MechWarrior 4: Vengeance, Black Knight and Mercenaries, and now a total, but competely new version of the Franchise- MechWarrior Online.
I have loved this game since I first played the Table top version, where I chose the BattleMaster to play with using nothing but dice and paper and paperboard cutouts to simulate warfare in the 31st Century. Too many times in the past with those that I mentioned above I wondered. . . when? When will I see those legends again: the Marauder, Archer, WarHammer, Rifleman, Stinger, Wasp, my BattleMaster, my Executioner [Gladiator]. When will they return? My faith in both Russ and PGI as well as patience has paid off.
The Legends are returning, first with Project Phoenix `Mech Package, consisting of: BattleMaster, Thunderbolt, Griffin, Wolverine, Locust, and Shadow Hawk have returned to the honored faithful, and soon, the other legends of the BattleTech World will make their debut. The Marauder released on Dec. 1, has become a steady favorite to the new players. The WarHammer will see its release on January 16th, and the Rifleman will soon follow it on Feb. 16, and the Archer is set for release some time in March [this is just a guess. Nothing is set as of my writing this review]/ But what a great time to join! Soon on Dec. 15th, Origins IIC package will see a full release of all four Clan Second-Line `Mechs: Highlander, Hunchback, Jenner and Orion `Mechs, will be getting the Clan Treatment. How can one not want to join?! I ask this time and time again.
As for those out there whom have said that MechWarrior is a dying game. One might want to rethink that. For no one person can foresee the future, and tell the demise of another. MechWarrior will come to its end when the time and effort have all but gone. When that will be is anyone's guess. As for me, I will continue to play till time has called me to go home and leave this plane of existence.
There are many reasons in why someone would want to play this game. I'll start with these:
COMMUNITY
As I said above, there are many games that come and go, and few stay the test of time. What sets them apart from those that do last a lifetime like MechWarrior, is the following they garner over that time. Thirty years is a long time for one game. And yes, it's a lifetime of years. And yet, with a Community like MechWarrior has, the game still exists. True. League of Legends, War Craft, Star Craft, and even EVEOnline have great communities, but none of them have garnered a lifetime of fans and player like MechWarrior. Except for Star Trek and Star Wars, both which have their fandom and support, they are the only games I know of that comes close, or even better than, MechWarrior. I'm not bad mouthing the game. Rather, I'm only comparing them to this game. Those games, War Craft/Star Craft, have only been around for a few years, and maybe more than ten at best. Star Wars, Star Trek, and MechWarrior have been around a lot longer, and all three have their fans to their credit. It would not suprise me in the least if Robotech jumped on board and entered the Online Gaming World. Cause like MechWarrior/BattleTech, and many know the history between the two properties, it too has a large majority of support.
CUSTOMIZATION
Another reason for joining this: Customizing A Machine of War. Not many games have this ability, and many have tried to copy what MechWarrior has to offer when it comes to gigantic machines of war. And yet, they failed to live up to that promise. Think of it this way: if one has played BattleTech, then one will know where I coming from with this. No other game I know of allows for changing out weapons to fit ones play style or fits into their idea of fun. MechWarrior offers that. We all have our favorites, and mine I stated above. For the Inner Sphere: it's the BattleMaster. For the Clans: No doubt, the Gladiator. Between the two, the Gladiator affords me more of opportunity to make a machine that'll make Russ lose his knickers in a less than a heartbeat. True. I can switch weapons on the BattleMaster, but with Galdiator, aka Executioner, it gives me tens tons more and has a pod space of 26.5 tons. Which is not too shabby. I can make a war machine with Autocannons and Lasers.
That's makes this game so unique. It gives players a chance to make any combination of weapons, even with Meta builds, and then take said machine into the playing, and own or get owned by another with the same concept. Not many games I know of can do this, except EVEOnline, but it's not MechWarrior. True. EVEOnline offers the opportunity to make a machine of war. However, it's not a game of gigantic war machines with a massive chip on their shoulders looking to kick someone's metallic♥♥♥♥♥♥straight to hades and back again. If one wants to build a ship with long research and skill training over a long period of time. . . EVE Online is the game for that someone. If one wants to go out in a simulated blaze of glory and owning someone else's♥♥♥♥♥♥with a machine that has a massive chip on its shoulder. . . then one has found it in MechWarrior.
PLAY ABILITY
As I said Before, not many games stand the test of time, and few have lasted as long as MechWarrior has. Not even World of Tanks can compare itself to MechWarrior. Even though, like MechWarrior, the game has the same play ability and fun aspect as MechWarrior, it can't allow one to customize a machine the way MechWarrior can. That's the attraction for this game is the play ability, and that lies in the means to make and change around the weapons to fit any and all situations that one may find themselves in. Sure EVE offers that, but going around space looking for action, mining one asteroid after another, researching and earning skills, and droning about from one of space to another, is not the same as MechWarrior.
Only MechWarrior offers the means to go and get into the action quickly, and yes, World of Tanks has this as well. Yet ask this: can you switch our a 122mm D-25T gun off an IS-3? Sure, but if one grinds the points necessary to get another gun. Here, one does not need to research anything or make a character, and go mine, build, and claim a part of space as their own. Or drive some tank into a battle and hope that one does better than the other players. Plus one does not need to use a Mod of any sort to become a better player.
Now all I ask is this: what are you waiting for? JOIN UP. Make this legendary game come to life, and enjoy the time of playing a great and wholesome game.
I am James Edward Crego, aka Hawk819 of the Second Federated Suns Armored Cavalry, and I and my unit, invite any and all players to join this game, and have a great time playing it. Take care, and Godspeed. <Salute>

There continues to be a dedicated community around this game. For better or worse, their love of what this game "could be" keeps them both playing and being positive about the game as a whole.
As far as positives there are some great members of the MWO community, and early on that kept me playing this game. As a founder unfortunately I don't have similiar feelings about the developers but my feelings are less important then the facts.
When advertising for the game began several promises were made about the type of game being delievered. Mech warrior online would be a "....the Mechwarrior you know. It's a fully first-person. It's not a new interpretation."  "Players will be able to band together in the format of a lance..... they'll be able to band together as a mercnary coporation for hire.... to customize the look and feel ..... how they enter battle, the lances, their names, ranks, and all kinds of things."
"Anything that would affect or give you a tactical advantage, you can't purchase with real cash."
I could continue quoting unrealized promises and quickly run over the character limit for reviews so I will sumarize.
Of the "four pillars" of gameplay (mech, role, community, information) at best two are fully realized.
You can both purchase mechs/items with real money and some of the meta (most useful in the current game) mechs can not be purchased without a cash purchase.
The idea of community warfare and therefore the ability to act as a "mercenary" is completely non-existant even though it was heavily talked about.
News/lore relevant to actual gameplay (arguably another part of community warfare, but still missing)
A single player campaign, PVE, the explicit statement that there would be no 3rd person, coolant flush/shots, priority strikes (improved usuables only available with real money).
The devs also had several at best insulting statements to large portions of the community on multiple occasions, claiming that same old "small vocal minority".
There are multiple instances of employees acting out towards individuals in the mwo community, there are certainly claims on both sides, but several instances of them acting out without just cause, including the entire banning of huge groups of players, then later saying they would unban anyone who asked nicely. Theres no doubt they unjustly banned players to ever make such an offer.
On top of this the game has only gotten more punishing for new players with hard to understand hidden mechanics, the worst example being "ghost heat".
On all of these, simply google them, no need to take my word. Theres more to be found.
tl:dr Game with potential and amazing community members ruined by the developer and employees.

I have been playing MWO off and on for about 3 years now. I highly reccommend it if you favor strategy and team play over a lone wolf, arcade style shooter. As far as Battletech fans from the table-top or past MechWarrior games, this is probably not for you, but as it is free-to-play, I would at least give it a try. It is a solid game with TONS of customization and it still feels great getting into those mechs and bringing the pain. It's very possible to have fun playing the game solo but the most fun I've ever had playing this game has been joining up with a full drop team and communicating strategy and tactics during tournaments and scheduled team vs team skirmishes.
One thing I will say about the game as a negative, it has a rather large learning curve. The new in-game tutorial is great and a significant improvement for welcoming new players, but I would still definitely recommend trying to join a MWO clan or group that is willing to teach you the game or at least give you some tips. At the very least maybe watch a tutorial video guide about weapon systems and loadouts. As an example, overall, the premade load-outs for the mechs you use are decent but definitely not the most optimal. Learning which weapons, engines, armor, etc, work best in your mech of choice and which role you should be playing on the battlefield with that loadout, is imperative to your (and your team's) success and overall enjoyment in the game.

Very interesting game!
It's free, so there's absolutely no reason for anybody to not try it - obviously, yeah, you can buy things in-game with real money, but it's not necessary unless you want to unlock more things/get more EXP faster (which, again - without paying a dime, you get a ton of content, so it's not necessary).
If you're interested in guns at all, even just a little bit, then this game is for you.  The graphics, while not necessarily impressive, are nice, and the "Operation" mode is just outstanding.  Every working part of the gun is shown to you - be it in varying levels of X-ray mode, and/or in slow motion, you can see how a gun operates from the inside out.  This isn't just limited to one weapon, either - every gun you unlock, you can watch how all of the parts interact to fire a bullet.
As well, the disassembly/assembly modes are pretty cool, and the "game" and "super game", and "hardcore game" modes are really fun.  You're not just racing the clock or grinding for EXP, you're learning how a gun is constructed at the same time.  I've field stripped a Colt 1911 in real life before, and this game has it down to a T.  I haven't fully disassembled one before, but I'm assuming they got that right, as well.
All in all, really fun, sort of niche game that you should definitely go for.  It takes about 10 minutes to install, and is literally an educational time waster (for free!).

I'm writing this review from the perspective of someone who's never touched the first game.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution, to me, is the pinnacle of modern RPG games. It has super satisfying gunplay and extremely tense stealth moments when playing on the hardest difficulty. The areas are incredibly detailed and you are rewarded greatly for not barging though every room. Around every corner there's some kind of secret, a piece of lore in the form of an eBook, Email, Newspaper, etc., and there's always multiple ways to attack any given situation (With some exception to scripted boss fights, which still can technically be taken down any way you please, I took out the first boss with sniper headshots instead of using the explosives in the room)
The hub areas are massive and filled with unique stories and side quests to be done. The world is alive with police, gang members, and civilians, all able to share specifically two pieces of dialogue with you.
The combat in this game is extremely satisfying, as is the stealth, as are the persuasion moments, as are the non-lethal takedowns, as are the lethal takedowns. This game lets you approach in any way you choose and you can have a good time doing it.
That's being said, this game obviously is not without it's faults, and here's a quick pro/con list to help sort some of these things out.
PROS:
Stealth and Combat are equally satisfying:  Though one option is technically better, and I'll get to that in a moment, neither is more satisfying than the other. The stealth mechanics work really well, where if one enemy thinks he sees you the others aren't immediatly alerted. They'll question whether the guy who saw you is going crazy or drunk or something before searching for you, if they even do. Enemies don't just instantly drop what they're doing, they go through a few stages of detection. Oblivious, Suspicious, Alterted, and Hostile. At each stage it will take longer for them to ignore you, and they will be more and more alert. The gunplay is also extremely well put together, with the guns feeling satisfying and being extremely fun to use effectively. So in the event you're caught, you won't feel dissatisfied (Other than with your lack of ability to stay hidden)
The areas are extremely detailed: There's something unique around every corner, and if you pay close enough attention you can find terminals to hack that lead to weapon mods, money, and ammo. This game rewards you for not rushing it, it rewards you for thinking, and it rewards exploration in a really nice way.
These are really the two main pros, obviously there's the interesting story backed with gamey voice acting that we're all used to. Some of the voice acting is pretty good, but most of it is pretty corny and obviously read from a script, but that's okay. Now onto the con.
Con:
Stealth is clearly the superior way to play. Non-lethal takedowns and hacking reward extremely highly. Normal kills get you 10 whatever points, headshots get you 20, while non-lethal takedowns always get you 30 or more. Hacking also gives you points, so even if you know the code to a door or computer, you might as well just hack it for the extra points and upgrades. Using stealth you can easily unlock every augment in the game, which breaks a lot of replay value. The only reason not to use stealth would be to see how the story changes when you kill everyone, which is extremely difficult on the hardest setting. I wish that it wasn't such a clear choice to go for stealth if you're looking for all the money and upgrades, but it is.
Anyways, this game is extremely fun, and very deep. There's tons of content and i've barely scratched the surface of the game 12 hours into it, because I can't stop finding new places to go and new areas to explore. This game does exploration and discovery in a uniquely satsisfying way and I highly recommend picking it up.

I didn't quite realize I needed a game quite like this until I played it.  It's a fun romp through space with some JRPG combat, base building, and space flight mixed in, and its suprisingly challenging all the way through.
First off, I really love the pixel graphics.  Pixels are hardly uncommon in the indie scene, but there's a lot of life to the creatures and characters in here.  The various alien races are nice and distinct.
As a fan of games like Shin Megami Tensei, I really liked a battle system built around the exploitation of status effects.  It required me to put a lot of thought into my fleet builds as the game progressed to make sure every ship complemented the others in the fleet.
The soundtrack is bloody amazing and I feel lame for not having the scratch to have bought it, but its nice and epic for the universe.
The storyline of being attacked by a mysterious outer space C'thulu like race is pretty simple, but the game is good at making you feel like you really are largely on your own.  On my first playthrough (where I died :( ), I had almost no allies save for one, and even as I scrambled to try and protect my spacestation from a monstrous fleet, I realized the end had come and it was all on me.
Now, the cons.  I'll be cliche'd and point out the current system for gathering resources in the early game is painful.  I get the idea of it trying to encourage the player to prioritize what they need to gather, but it's cumberous and tedious instead of fun.  A lot of the later upgrades are hard to predict what resources you need - my first campaign ended in defeat because I had only 50 days to build a Tier 3 starship bay, then a starship, then kill FIVE other ships before my space station was blown up.  Not shockingly, this wasn't nearly enough time to get everything I needed together.
The space combat is, frankly, more fun than the ground combat.  Since there's more space combat than ground combat, I found myself trying to pick officers that could survive space battles but then my ground teams were just plain underpowered.
While the combination of genres made a full experience for me (at this price point), it's hard not to note how simple they feel.  The research tree simply requires that you save up the resources and buy the next level - instantly.  Rather anti-climactic.
Overall though, I'm still working my way through this game and hoping to get better.  The dev has promised updates to address some of my cons, so if you're on the fence, maybe wait to see how those future patches turn out.

Hey Naruto fans,
I've never written a review for a game before but I felt like I needed to for NS4. I'm a huge Naruto fan, and I've spent hundreds of hours playing Ninja Storm 3 on my 360. I'm writing this review to inform you, a fellow leaf village ninja, on the positives and negatives of this game, the aspects that need to be worked on, and whether or not I think you should buy it right now.
Tournaments, endless mode, and ranked were what made NS3 so addicting. I've never focused too much on the campaign's quality or any of the side quests. I already read the manga and watched the anime so I didn't care too much about watching it all over again. The same applies to NS4 - I skipped through most of the cutscenes of the story mode because it was stuff I already knew, but the missions were definitely way more fun than NS3 were. They don't have a lot of walking around, it's strictly fighting, the boss fights were fun, and the ending of the game was superb. But the slideshow style cutscenes seemed like a lazy drawback. The adventure mode is dumb and collections are also a waste of time.
The fighting mechanics are amazing. I love the new round system and I really enjoy the way the supports have evolved. The characters are fun to play, some are a bit overpowered but balancing doesn't seem like a huge issue at the moment. The new maps are refreshing, and the wall running doesn't seem too useful.
I want to remind you that I did not play Revolutions, so I didn't know that spectator mode had already been removed somewhat from that game. It wasn't until buying NS4 that I realized that they took out the ability to watch your friends play in Endless or in tournaments. That is the biggest flaw with the game right now besides the terrible servers that constantly disconnect you from matches and pit you up against laggy players. CC2 also halved the size of the tournaments and endless matches from 8 players to 4 players. I couldn't believe it when I fought in my first tournament tonight. I immediately went out to see if CC2 planned on fixing this soon and had announced an upcoming patch, but no, apparently Revolutions had already removed spectator mode somewhat and many people had already made a petition to bring it back.
3000 people to be exact. You can sign this petition too here:
Despite that, I do recommend this game to naruto fans. It's fun to play with your friends for a little bit, but can get repetitive and boring without spectator mode. You're stuck watching a screen that says "Other players are fighting right now. Please wait." The campaign was good, not amazing, but it did have a solid ending. If you have people over often, or have siblings or friends you can play this with, it's a great deal of fun.
Overall, if I had to give it a rating, it'd be a 7/10. Please watch ShikasCloud's review if you're planning on buying the game:

Storyline/ Plot
The story is fairly simple and straight to the point. Nazis are taking over the world led by a robot Hitler and his army of nazi robots. Fortunately for you (or not), you are the only person capable of stopping them because of your abilities as a ninja. This makes you their principal target.
Gameplay
The game was originally made for xbox360 and we can strongly feel it through the controls. After multiple attempts at configuring my keyboard and mouse to find a comfortable way of playing the game, I simply decided to plug in my xbox360 controller and everything was better. The time attack aspect of the game requires some kind of eye to hand coordination as well as quick reflexes. If you lack these qualities, chances are, that the game will seem overly difficult.
Graphics
Like everything else in this game, the graphics are fairly simple and straight to the point. It is a 2D platformer with a single camera shot that means that there is no camera movement. The overall look of the game is cartoony and simple, nothing too flashy or disturbing.
Music & Sound
The soundtrack complements well the rest of the game, creating a homogenous overall. However, the repetitive aspect of the soundtrack can become quickly annoying after an extensive amount of gameplay. The sound on the other hand offers and crispy, enjoyable sound to hear, whenever you slash a nazi robot.
Special Feature
The game’s simple gameplay, yields no revolutionary special feature but still allows us to battle with friends for those lacking milliseconds.
Conclusion
Pros
- simple but addictive concept
- fast paced and fun to play
- great sense of achievement when finishing a level
- cheap price !
Cons
- repetitive
- only 40 levels
- might induce rage
Final impression
10 Second Ninja is a great game to play when you don’t have much time and you are looking to relax a bit after having worked ten hours on your dissertation.  Also, fans of Super Meat Boy will be served in this game. The only criticism that I could address a game of this standing is its short life as there are only 40 levels.

This is one of the most dangerous time sinks I have run into since Minecraft.
I managed to unlock the Colt 1911, the MP5 and the Intratec Tec-9.  After a few hours turning them around seeing how everything works I went for the DLC with the unlimited guns. The M-16 A1 model brought back not-so-fond memories of skinning my knuckles trying to pull out the handguards. I also noticed that the o-rings in the bolt are stacked exactly like in real life, it's obvious that these models went through an insane amount of scrutiny.
What's good:
1. You get to see how most of everything inside works.
2. You get to fire the weapons.
What's not so good:
1. The full weapons unlock should allow hiding all new guns and click to show/hide guns as needed so it is not so damn hard to navigate. It is overwhelming when you see all of the guns up to date displayed in one shot.
2. I wish I could use my controller in the shooting games.
3. The game doesn't explain things, it just walks you through. And sometimes the safeties can't be engaged by clicking on the weapon, you have to click a menu button.
4. Sometimes the fire selectors don't allow all positions, so you are also stuck using a menu button to select fire modes.
5. The only adjustable sight post that moves at all so far is the AK-47. The M16-A1s front post doesn't turn, unless I am doing something wrong.
6. Some weapons should allow movement of the hammer but the model only allows to pull back the slide.
Wish list for the developers:
1. Allow show/hide of items already purchased/unlocked/etc.
2. Allow a visualization of the return mechanism, for example the M16-A1 should show me the gas blow back, etc.
3. Allow sights to move if/when the originals do.
4. Explain a little bit more of what's going on.
5. All safeties, fire selectors, de-cocking levers, etc. should be movable from the model, not from menu buttons.
BTW, hats off to the parties responsible for the game mode achievement for doing things in the right order. It's frustrating as hell, but these being dangerous machines it makes sense to force people to learn an assembly sequence. I have been busting my♥♥♥♥♥for two long miserable days trying to do the Colt 1911 in order and I keep screwing up because I pick the main spring out of sequence or I click the recoil spring plug when I wanted to click on the recoil spring, that kind of thing.
Overall:
A complete absolute win for anyone that is curious about how machines work. The first time you dig into that AK-47 and you figure out on your own why the auto mode works, you'll feel like a rocket scientist.

I've been playing MechWarrior Online since open Beta (August 2013) and the road has been a bumpy one since the original release. Though, it has come a long way in terms of user friendlyness and content. It's at the point between "it could be better" and "just right" for a multiplayer only game.
MWO was once only 8 versus 8 deathmatch early in development, then became 12 vs. 12 with team play queue. Now, we have tutorials, ease of 'Mech customization, and Community Warfare (still in Beta, but can participate to gain the highest rewards) with more in production. So, content is slowly being added, but the speed of release can be a turn off to some. There are plans for PvE, co-op, and smaller 4 vs. 4 events in 2016.
This is a fun game if you do not take it seriously and would rather role-play a Clammer (Clan pilot) with 11 other drunk, uncoordinated players. The PuG games will make you rage quit if you have a nack for skill and winning, so it is wise to pick up a team or join a faction and use TeamSpeak/Ventrillo to better your chances and reap greater rewards.
I recommend this game to any true die-hard MechWarrior fan, as it is the only MW game availalbe (until Hairbrain Scheme's BattleTech in 2017) that has a resemblence of MW4's multiplayer. It's still a decent simulator/shooter despite most of its flaws.
MWO is one of those games you can splurge for a month, drop it for a while, and come back and enjoy relearning after some major content patches. It's easy to pick up for the price of free-to-play.
However, MWO does suffer from poor optimization with many players crashing and disconnecting at the beginning or mid match, which is another off-putting minus to the game. Especialy, since loosing an Assault in a critical point can make battle exchanges lopsided before they rejoin.
I hope to see some of you on the battlefield and as they say: "Die well" (because you will die a lot).

A totally solid Mechwarrior game.  While it does have issues such as a limited number of maps and game modes, it is clear that the developers want to expand the game greatly in terms of content and game experience.  There is already robust support for multiple playstyles.
The need to balance player experience with sellable content is obvious in a F2P game, and I feel the developers are making a fair and earnest effort to provide a great game for those on a budget while offering the big spender ways to part with their money without completely breaking the balance of the game.
All in all, the game art is beautiful and the game tries to adhere to Battletech lore insofar as is possible, so fans of "armored combat" style shooters and Battletech fans alike should all be able to find something that keeps them coming back.

Taking out three or four opponents with a light mech dancing between laser fire or watching arms and legs fly off your Centurion as you grind your way through the shattered remains of your enemy never fails to put a smile on my face.
The key thing with Mechwarrior is patience, it's not a simple game to pickup but it's a rewarding game, there's lots of subtle nuances you can pickup that makes a skillful player vastly better than his opponent (of which I have yet to pickup half of them years later).Take your time and learn the game, do not be disheartened and remember that you WILL get better through practice.
I'd reccomend this game for anyone willing to invest a bit of time in picking up a slower paced F2P shooter.

It's not quite terrible, but Halcyon 6 leaves much to be desired. It's got influences from various games, but still manages to stand out from other ones, unfortunately in a bad way.
Let's get the premise out of the way. The federation is crippled, and you're the last commanding officer in charge of the
Halycon 6. It's archeotech with the ability to make ships out of basically nothing but energy. You have to build up a roster of officers, and take back the galaxy from all aliens who would oppose you. The station and map is a bit like x-com. You have to clear out limited space on your station to build more rooms on it, generators, research buildings, etc. On the space map you can see incoming attacks and various resource outposts which you need to protect.
This is where problem #1 starts. Resource collection
You have to lead to manually order a fleet around to pick up resources on each outpost. There's no way to set up a patrol routes leading you to constantly reroute fleet(s) around the map. Admittedly this ends in the second half of the game, but that was already at least 6 hours. I can't fathom why this was in the game. The only thing I can think of was to make you have to chose decisions on how to use your available resources, but it's really nothing to send out 1 or 2 ships and have them pick up supplies, it was the tedium of moving them around that stopped me, not because of lack of resources. Which leads me into problem #2
Problem #2: Resource Management
I feel like this was another part of the game that instead of being a challenge, just ended up detracting from it. There are three resources and not once have I ever thought to myself "man should I buy this upgrade or that one? Save up for a ship or get a bunch of upgrades?" It's never like this. Progression is so linear and the best options are so obvious that there is never a moment where I had to step back and think on my ultimate strategy. You'll always want to prioritize ships first, officers next, ship battle upgrades third. Everything else is either minor or so cheap it makes no sense not to get it. You'll never get an FTL flashback playing this game, wondering if you should use your scrap for an upgrade or save it and possibly die in order to get a great crewmember, or a dank weapon at a later shop. At some points at the game you'll just be twiddling your thumbs as you slowly produce more materials to get up a tier.
Problem #3: Combat
Ugh. Where do I begin? The combat sucks. The easiest way to show that is the repition and lack of counterplay. Aside from maybe the few hardest boss ships in the game, every battle will play out the same way. You'll cast the same buffs, use the same debuffs, and use the same damage skills. If you're unlucky and get hit a lot you'll heal. This isn't exaggeration that no matter what the enemy fleet compisition is you'll use the same skills. Supposedly each ship has it's own weaknesses and resistances, but they're so minor that they're often not worth exploiting. Part of this because of the three ship classes. There's Tactical ships, Engineer, and science ships. Tacitcal ships are the only ships that can actually do any sort of damage in a reasonable time frame. Science ships tend to have the best buffs and heals, while engineer ships are just kind of there. Some of them can do a little more damage than science ships, and tend to have more damage reducton skills, but ultimately they're the worst class. Because healing skills are limited per battle the only real way fleet compisitions are either 1 / 1 / 1 , 2 / 1 / 0 , 2 / 0 / 1.  Unless your tactical ship(s) can exploit the weakness (with a strong attack) or avoid the resistance just ignore them. Another thing are status effects. A lot of attacks can apply them, and many more can 'exploit them' meaning that the status effect is wiped out and your attack damage increased. This system is broken. Unless your tactical ship can exploit one of the status effects, or MAYBE a level 3 high damage skill, it's pointless to wipe out a beneifical debuff on an enemy for a paltry damage increase on your science or engineer ship.  At higher tiers enemy damage starts increasing at a much higher rate than your hull points, leading your ships to flunctate wildly on hp, leading to x-com rng syndrome.
The music is alright, doesn't hold a candle to FTL's beats, and while the graphics are solid enough, the battle sound effects and visual effects are so overdone and lazily added you'll just want to skip them all. I kept playing this game thinking that at maybe higher tiers strategy would have to be involved, but it's just not there.
I didn't even mention ground combat earlier but it's just awful, unlike space combat which combines your ship skills and officer skills, ground combat is entirely reliant on officer skills, leading to a new batch of problems, and hit rates on both sides are much much lower.
This is a hidden gem; I'd really recommend picking it up if you like these sorts of games and/or you're on the fence. For the price, it's really worth it.

Paladins is a First/Third Person Shooter in a Multiplayer Online Battle Arena setting, where with a team of mates you have to push an objective towards the enemy base to win points in a round.
I waited with my review for the last big patch to hit to see the progress of the game and sadly, if before the patch I would have recommended this game, after the patch I sadly can not. The gameplay consisting of you hitting the enemy quicker than he hits you, using abilities at the right time and individualising your character the way you enjoy it most, has been quite "broken" by the patch. Getting Master rank in competetive in just few weeks, I can tell, that even though Hi-Rez states they are knowing what they are doing with the game, the feedback they receive from players after this patch definetely shows they do not. Introducing card levels also introduced "Pay2Win" elements to the game (outside of ranked mode), the last patch hit tons of bugs effecting all the modes, like players disappearing under the floor, objectives no getting counted while you stand on the payload or the point, players doing damage after they died, cards not working properly, etc. Most of my friends and clan members quit the game and I trying to wait for fixes, there is nothing left but follow them.
The competetive side of the game being playing ranked in team of 5 players or alone has been also destroyed by the patch. The balance shifted heavily in favour of some champions, but the real problem of ranked is more the bugs and cheats currently abused in even high ranked matches. And even though the combat itself still stayed fun, there is no purpose behind it anymore, so if you are only for a quick fun shooting some people in the faces, you might enjoy it but long term the drive for becoming high ranked is destroyed since it is all about which side gets most game-breaking bugs and champions.
The graphic in Paladins is definetely likable and is not effected by the negative touch for the last patch brought live. The characters are fun, animations fluid and all abilities are recognisable. What still is on a level of a year 2010 multiplayer game is the interface in main menu and game mode selection. The whole interface is looking clunky and takes a while getting used to aswell the store feels clunky. The game selection mode hides behind multiple buttons, while in ranked the champion selection could be improved by a lot, even if they would take examples on competitor games like LoL.
The progress of buying more champions and unlocking the cards has also been broken by the patch. Now you have to either farm months to get the cards leveled up on a champion you want to play, or you will get stomped in unranked matches. Obviously, there is a possibility to buy them through the cash shop...The progress in ranked has been destroyed by the bugs and at the moment not good balance. There are no mini-games in Paladins, so not much to value more in this section besides the summary: unranked = P2W or grind for months, while ranked = broken due to bugs and unbalance.
The audio is something well done in this game, since every hero has a recognisable ability sounds and especially ultimates let you hear who is using theirs. The voice packs give a nice touch to the character and the emotes are sounding fun. Some random chatter the champions are doing is fun to listen to. Audio was and definetely is currently the more qualitatively made part of this game.
Paladins, that was a decent alternative to Blizzards Overwatch, being a fun MOBA with nice competetive scene has been "broken" by Hi-Rez last patch. Sadly, most players were warning the developer not to bring out the patch to live servers but they still did and it shows their attitude towards their players base. As you can see on recent ratings and reviews, such attitude should be the death of an online game developer/publisher. If the player base starts to dwindle to a matter where they start to listen to a community again remains to be seen.
In the current state I can not recommend Paladins to anyone due to technical issues the game experiences, disbalancing in terms of cash shop in unranked modes aswell the attitude of the publisher towards its customers.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

Paladins is in open beta, but it's promoted and monetized as if it has been released, yet it's balanced as if it was in closed alpha. Over the course of a year or so, the game has had 3 EXTREMELY sweeping systems changes that basically broke the balance of the game. Balance issues have been addressed since these changes (except the most recent one as of this review), but it's just annoying playing a game that will change fundamentals so frequently. Characters have also been released at a ridiculous pace, at one point 3 characters in 2 months, and some lazy design choices are obvious.
It also took me a while to realize that this game was clearly moving in a P2W direction for some time, and recent changes have cemented that.
Once upon a time, I found Paladins to have better core gameplay than Overwatch. It's always been inferior in every other way. Now, I'm pretty sick of the way the balance in this game is being handled. If you're OK playing a very unpolished game that is supposedly in early access, but monetizes as if it were released, I suppose Paladins might be worth a shot. Otherwise stay away.

A perfect example how to NOT make a game. 2/10
Graphics:
Who thought that OpenGL is a good idea for a fast shooter game like this? The over-colored envirements look like extracted from a childs book. textures pop up as you look at them because of that useless "prerender" option that just make the game unplayable at nearly 18fps with a gtx 750 and an i7. (other modern games plays fine with this hardware setup) Leveldesign is pretty okay but not as good as in doom 3.
Sound:
The soundtrack is great but becomes annoying as hell when you progress in the game. Every time, when enemies spawn, the soundtrack changes to a more agressive combat style until you killed the last enemy from said spawn. This is exactly the same as in painkiller or serious sam but they did it right and doom sadly did not. noises from enemies feel like they are played directly infront of you. I had trouble seeing enemies because the sound indicated a whole other direction than the enemies are actually standing.
Gameplay:
I had a very bad feeling about the "glory kill" moves at first but they are pretty okay. there are just a few problems with it. first of all, you're not invincible during glory kills.. at least not for the whole kill move wich leads often to death after glory kill animation because you can't move until the animation is fully played. If you try to avoid the glory kills, you often end up shooting more than enough bullets till an enemy gets down without glory kill... I think without the kill moves you need 3 times more bullets then with a glory kill.
next thing I'll have to cover is the fact, that this game playes almost exactly like serious sam or painkiller. you enter an area, all doors get locked, a fixed amount of enemies spawn and after you killed them all you can continue to the next area. and with the changig sound, you always know when an enemy is still alive. this ruins the whole scary part that doom3 had. areas with enemies are mostly build in a circle and play like multiplayer maps. enemies spawn in almost every spot at almost the same time so that you end up running in said circles untill every enemy is down.
weapon upgrades are just there to make the s*** look a bit better. they're nearly useless in my opinion because the secondary firemode of the weapons do not enough damage to be usefull, I almost never used them.
the game offers ingame challanges to unlock some sort of talisman which makes enemies stay longer in the tumbling glory kill state or increases the radius in which items get collected but like the weapon upgrades, they're more or less useless because you just stand right next to the items, when enmies drop them (f.e.)
Story and Playtrough:
the story feels pretty rushed. you get the chainsaw and I believe the first 4 weapons in the 2nd level of the game. and thats almost everything you need to complete the game (I never used the gatling gun or the bfg which you'll get later) while doom 3 took care of slowly getting into something like a story, the new doom just throws you in hell and then you're back on the mars base and that was it. I knew hardly what I was doing besides clearing areas and walking to the next ones. At certain points you'll have to find a keycard or a switch which is pretty boring depending that this game wants to be an arcade game. I guess they tried to make something like doom 1 but horribly failed. The only good thing is, that the checkpoints are decent placed and there was never a situation where I had no idea what to do next.
If you want to play a creepy horror game with some action: play doom 3
if you want to play an arcade game like the good old dooms, just play painkiller or seriouse sam instead.

Wanted to like this game, but really felt it was nothing new in the end.
Although the game appears like you're a bad guy defending a dungeon against do-gooders in a RTS, it's really just a base with ___# of access points, and the adventure takes place on the surface. The game makes it more economical to defend your base in other ways than traps (I only built traps in the entire campaign as a luxury, something if I had resources to waste. It was far more economical to build a strong army and use a portal spell to recall them if attacked).

The game is best described as a platforming arcade score chaser. Its developer, Cowboy Color, was the team behind
, so it's no surprise that this game looks and plays so well. The premise of the game is that you are the titular handsome frog whose hat has been stolen by thieving animals, and you go on a vengeful rampage. It's pretty great.
The gameplay is simple but fluid. You can grab onto enemies or blocks with your long tongue and then launch them into others to knock them out. The game spans across 4 different worlds with 3 levels each, drawing from a pool of randomized room designs. Each world has 2 types of different enemies with separate behaviors, giving you a new challenge to adapt to as you progress. Along the way, you can pick up items in bubbles to increase your score, spit fireballs, or even unlock cute hats! Getting hit once will knock you out, but you start with 10 lives that can be replenished through pickups, so the game feels forgiving. All of this helps the game feel fast and fun.
The look of the game clearly draws from a retro aesthetic, but it's so charming that it stands apart from other indie games that use the gimmick. Most importantly, all of the art is clear and easy to read. You can always find yourself on the screen, and all of the enemies and items are easy to spot. The sound design is also hilarious. Mr. Frog always sounds like a robot with a sore throat when he talks. On death, I swear he sounds like he's saying "Donald Trump". I'm not kidding. Plus, you're playing along to sweet, catchy tunes. It sounds like you're playing on an old arcade machine; it's such a great
.
All in all, I love this game. The controls feel tight and responsive, and it's easy to pick up and learn. Others might feel like it's too simple, but that doesn't mean it's bad. It's a great game to pick up and play, and it's easily addictive enough to keep you entertained for as long as you want to be. Besides, anybody who'd give a negative review to this game is probably a killjoy, anyway. The game is well worth its $0.99 asking price, and I definitely got what I wanted out of it. #worthit

10 Second Ninja is a game that is reminicent of the quick and easy flash games on the internet and it doesn't disappoint. You will be hopping around slashing at Nazi robots and a big robot Hitler, while laughing at the weird cutscenes.
Controls: They are pretty simplistic. Arrow Keys to move around and you can slash with you sword/throw ninja stars with X and Z. The game is really responsive to the control input, which is great. I played a bit on the steam controller and its just as good. I used the analog stick instead of arrow keys, with X and B as the sword and ninja stars, and the A as jump.
Graphics: It's not too great, but that isn't the purpose. The purpose is suppose to similar to the internet flash games. Simplistic and easy on the computer.
Music: Not really that prominent. It's not really that bad but it's not really that good either.
Overall: 10 Seconds Ninja is a great game, and I would recommend the game to anybody, but I don't think that it is worth the full price and wouldn't be a bad buy on a sale. You don't need godlike reflexes, but the game instead relys on you being able to break through the puzzles and see which is the best route to beat the level and then practice it to perfection.

Note: I've played and finished this game long before I got another Steam copy for myself to unlock the achievements.
This is a brilliant platformer with some of the craziest challenges I've ever seen. You are essentially playing as a superfast ninja who has to destroy a certain number of enemies in 10 seconds in every level.
That includes bosses and some of the ridiculously hard to reach enemies as well, which of course means you will struggle with every 10 second level for up to 10 hours.
But it is SO MUCH FUN! I recorded myself doing this once and it was fun to watch the frustration built up until that final moment when you get it just right.
The levels are well thought out and you are essentially competing with yourself for the best possible scores.
There are also ridiculous bosses that add a bit of flavor as well.
All in all, an amazing title with great music, gameplay and overall feel to the game.
Must play for fans of challenging platformers

Ill honestly say it puts in perspective the level of skill that I totally don’t have anymore, as I struggle to repeat the same actions over and over with little success.  My only gripe about this game is the price -- at ten dollars, I feel like the game doesnt quite offer enough to be worth the investment.  That being said, I know it does go on sale often, so keep an eye out for a sale, and snatch it up for a nice little side project.
Game’s Fate: Kept. A quick little time waster that's worth keeping around.

The premise is simple:  Destroy all robots as rapidly as possible using your sword and 3 throwing stars.  This requires discovering the ideal/shortest path through many, many deaths.  While each level has a 10 second limit, you'll quickly learn that you'll need to complete a level in just a few seconds if you want to receive full marks (3 star rating).  Before you can move on to the next world (of a set of levels), you must earn so many stars in the current world.  Thus, while you can complete a level and move on with a single star, earning a single star on multiple levels of that world will not be enough to move you on to the next world; so you replay the levels you did poory at and replay them, and replay them, until you can get ~ a 2 star or more average on all that world's levels.
The game in itself seems to be pretty well done -- the minimal graphics, style, and humor all work together nicely, and I love the leaderboard to see where you stack up against your friends and the world; both per level rankings and per world.  That did motivate me to press on just a little bit more and shave a few more hundredths of a second off my time.  :-)
The only minor downside I have with this game is the high level of difficulty required in order to progress to the next world.  I want to play to have fun; not to be nearly perfect.
