Loadout matches unfold like demented, R-rated cartoons. Players jump and dodge around an interstellar trailer park with the mobility of a platformer, unloading a rainbow of munitions from guns of their own design, no one quite like the other.
It's completely over-the-top and embraces the inherent comedy in multiplayer shooters. Though the presentation seems simple, it's very well thought-out, with complex hit maps and animations that click together to create hilarious and disgusting surprises—sometimes I survive a rocket to the head, leaving only a brain and two eyeballs poking out of my neck.
The same is true of Loadout's defining feature: a gun crafting system, which allows me to be creative and spotlight my greatest strengths as a player. It's fun to tinker with weapons between matches, mixing and matching guns that I recognize from other shooters. It's a system that encourages open-ended creativity and experimentation but doesn't break Loadout's balance.

There are four gun types: rifle, launcher, beam, and pulse, each with four or five customizable parts and different kinds of ammo. The standard assault rifle becomes a sniper rifle with the addition of a long barrel and scope. A scatter barrel will just as easily turn it into a shotgun, and a beam weapon with a healing mod into a healing tool.
Officer Winslow keeps the peace, a rocket launcher for when I'm cool and collected enough make use of its laser-guidance system.
I can also exchange my grenades for a deployable turret or a cloaking device that makes me look like a member of the opposing team. Since I can choose from any of these tools, I can easily create a medic who's also great at laying suppressive fire, a spy who can sneak behind enemy lines for the perfect sniping position, and other hybrids.
Experimentation can result in simple, obvious adjustments at first. A sniper rifle with a bolt loading mechanism does extra damage, while a clip increases its rate of fire. A rocket launcher can shoot three small rockets quickly, or maybe one big cluster bomb. Loadout is well-balanced, so every configuration is viable, but it was most entertaining and rewarding to dig as deep as possible to find the right gun for me.
I like Loadout's third-person perspective and agility. Jumping, dodging and sprinting in and out of encounters, so a shotgun suits me well; I don't have to slow down as much to aim. I add shell loading, which allows me to load rounds one at a time when I reload instead of committing to the time it takes to swap a whole magazine. Electrically charged ammo, which can damage multiple enemies standing together, is the final piece of the puzzle. Using it improves my odds when outnumbered, and makes me more confident charging in head first.

When I found the right formula, everything clicked. In the game's capture point mode, I'm a menace with my electric shotgun. But all someone has to do to keep me in check is set up far enough away and put me down with one or two powerful sniper shots. They can take their sweet time too, as my electric shots can't reach them.
All shooters are Darwinistic in the sense that the most lethal strategies rise to the top. Loadout capitalizes on this. Rather than nerfing annoying, overpowered builds, it empowers players to come up with counters. It was fantastic when a gun I created made me feel invincible, but it was also satisfying to go after the player who proved me wrong, pick up his gun (usually named “DooDoo Launcher,” or something equally humiliating), and figure out his build.
Bringing the Jackhammer down on poor carebear90.
Strangely, my favorite Loadout mode, Jackhammer, takes attention away from the guns. Jackhammer is capture the flag, only the flag is giant hammer that can kill any player in a small radius with one strike. It makes everyone play more aggressively in a mode that can usually cause stalemates because there's immediate, selfish benefit to picking it up. In other games, carrying the flag made me an easy target. When players saw me with the Jackhammer in Loadout, they usually ran in the opposite direction. It's a brilliant addition to an old formula.
Unfortunately, Loadout lacks more modes of the same quality, and with its simple mechanics, matches start to feel the same after only a few hours, even with the complex gun customization at play. Its ambitious “Competitive” Annihilation mode is muddled with too many ideas, causing matches to drag on aimlessly.
Testing fire ammo on my assault rifle.
Loadout lacks long-term appeal, but it's worth the fun of its best mode and the gun customization, and that I barely feel the need to mention that it's free-to-play is the biggest compliment I can give it. I can buy XP and currency multipliers to unlock things faster, but the free alternative isn't punishing. Amazingly, Loadout also made me want to spend money on cosmetic items because I liked the character design enough to want to make mine unique. It's not necessary, but the $20 Starter Pack allowed me to do that, as well get gun components faster. It's a fair deal.
I'm not going to obsess over Loadout like I did Battlefield 3—there just aren't as many stories to tell through Loadout's matches—but it's different, does a few things very well, and is super fun to play casually, a match here, a match there.

I've loved MechWarrior ever since MechWarrior 2 back in the day. MWO improves much of the gameplay aspects (espectially the multiplayer balance) over the past games, and despite other big name shooters - Titanfall, Battlefield, Battlefront - I still come back to MWO. There is no other equivalent to customizing your mech, taking into account each chassis' quirks, weapon types and equipment, and having that all play out in real time during a match.
For instance, did you store ammo in your leg? Well, if someone strips your leg armor, there's a chance that the ammo will explode and take your leg with it. How about a heat sink instead? On certain maps, there are large pools of water; submerging your legs in them will make those heat sinks work more efficiently. On top of all this, you can pick your opponents apart piece by piece; or opt to try and core them out and take them down as quickly as possible.
Now, the drawbacks: Visually, the mech designs are awesome (and by far the best this franchise has seen). However, the actual art direction (coloring, textures, map design) are only just adequate. Colors are often over-saturated, bloom is used too much, and texture resolution is hit and miss (mostly due to the complexity of having so many patterns and giant vehicles to cover, which can wreak havoc on install size if not toned down). The other drawback is the lack of a single-player component, which is probably my favorite part of the series. The devs have it as a future goal (and have started to implement AI) but it will likely be a year before we see the beginnings of that coming to fruition.
Overall, I've sunk more hours into this game than any other in recent memory, so if you've got a stompy robot addiction like me, then this should provide your fix. Plus it's free and has no equivalent to 'gold ammo' or other pay2win mechanics (hero mechs generally range from terrible to just ok, anyway) so there's no hurt in giving it a try. Just be sure to go through the Mechwarrior Academy training mode first.

is what you'd call a modern classic. It's one of the greatest games of our time, and will most likely stand the test of time. I've bought and played through it twice to completion, once on PS3 and now on PC, and the Director's Cut includes the fun and story-adding Missing Link DLC. This game is a worthy addition to any gamer's library, and now I think it's time to explain why.
Surveying the warehouse floor, you see five guards patrolling. You could snatch the shotgun that lies, unattended, in the office, or you could hack the security system that will turn the turret systems against the guards. You could cloak and move silently past them. You could choke or stab each one, dragging them away from sight and picking them off one by one. You could unlock the doors, sneak through the vent, throw a concussion grenade, drop a box on their head... the possibilities are essentially endless. You want to try an approach in this game, go ahead. Sure, the pure combat approach may not be the most fun shooter you've ever played, but the stealth system in this game is great, and the free-form missions enable you to play multiple saves and never have the same experience twice.
You can augment your character with a large variety of different augmentations, which all have practical use in many instances throughout the game. There isn't really one that you will regret buying, though, still, spend wisely! The only thing that lets this section down are still the iffy boss fights. There still isn't a true stealth option, at least not to my knowledge.
You play Adam Jensen, security chief of one of America's largest biotech industries. One day, before going to present a new technology to the world, your offices are attacked, and you left for dead. Resurrected by the very biotechnology you protected, Adam now investigates the biggest conspiracy of the 2020s in an effort to bring justice to the people who murdered his friends and coworkers. It's a very good story and excellent mystery. Well worth playing just for the story.
The graphics are, perhaps, slightly dated, but still look crisp enough that you'll enjoy it.
The atmosphere of the game is spot on. Deus Ex paints a future that is worrying, but you'll still think that Adam Jensen looks damned awesome in those augmented shades. The gritty, cyberpunk world is well worth exploring every nook and cranny for.
The sound of the game is also spot on. The rattle of the combat rifle, the hiss as you reload the magazine, the subtle footsteps, the idle chatter of the enemies, and who can forget the incredible theme song, Icarus. Another great element to a great game.
An rollicking mystery with intriguing plot twists and interesting characters who you can't trust 100%, this game is most definitely worth playing twice, even more than twice... This game isn't perfect, but after all, it was only made by humans...

So disappointed by this game, and after such a bright start, too.
The early game is full of personality and promise. Interesting choices are offered up in side-missions, often funny encounters with alien races occur and the combat seems to warrant a faith it will build into a satisfying, tactical experience. But all this quickly dries up and the brilliant art-style, the fantastic music and quirky humour is not enough to cover the widening cracks that reveal themselves in the mid and late game.
Resource collection is incredibly tedious throughout. It moves from laboriously visiting facilities for materials/crew etc into repeatedly assigning officers to the same task through a series of clicks you will come to loathe. The latter tasks also seem to be heavily bugged, with the game telling you an officer will take 8 days of game time to complete a resource gathering task when it in fact takes roughly as little as 2. Leading my play-through to have a big surplus of resources. Not only that but the starbase structures you are encouraged to build in order to supplement your resources (by increasing mission rewards) are rendered half-useless by an apparent bug which occurs after a certain point in the game, when rewards simply cease to appear in the rewards box you are presented with after each successfully completed mission.
Story and side-missions seem to evaporate entirely as the game progresses. Instead you are faced with hours of rinse and repeat space battles that at points never seem to end. The ground-combat occurs so rarely compared to ship-combat that you lose all incentive to allocate officer skill points to ground focussed abilities. And when it does occur it's either hopelessly easy or depressingly difficult, mainly as a result of the game not encouraging any development of your officers' ground skills.
The combat also quickly becomes tired and doesn't develop any further depth after the early game. It's based on a system of inflicting debuffs on your opponents, which you then "exploit" for extra damage. And because this is really the only mechanic to use and the most effective action you can take, you find yourself feeling like you are fighting the same battle over and over again. I think this is also a symptom of having your maximum fleet compliment limited to only three ships, with no mechanics in place to exploit positioning or formations, there is no wiggle room for tactical substance. Unfortunately the brilliantly distinctive ship design for each alien race does little to disguise this feeling and cements the combat as an initially enticing but essentially superficial affair.
Balance is an issue as well. Difficulty see-saws from trivial to impossible. With certain enemy ship combinations just one-shotting your whole fleet. This mainly seemed to happen when fighting the Xlar (an ancillary cast member), who buff their damage to absurd degrees making destruction of your whole fleet possible in one round of attacks. While your arch enemy and ‘deadliest threat to humankind’, The Chruul, don't seem to offer nearly the same challenge.
Tooltips and information about skills seem to be either desperately inaccurate or overly vague, making it tricky to gauge how you should act in fights. Skills touted as having a 75% chance to inflict a status effect used against a ship with a listed 50% resistance to that skill will mysteriously have 0% chance of hitting, when you could intuitively assume that chance should be 25%. This vagueness in the tooltip information often impacts the amount of expected damage ships do to each other as well, with abilities doing  as much as double what you would assume was possible from the information you are given. The aggregate effect of this cloudy information makes you feel out of touch with the combat and eliminates any sense of satisfaction.
The diplomacy between races is pretty empty, to the point you could argue there isn't any. The only feature here (apart from the rare but excellent hypercasts you receive from other races) is a bar under each races' home planet that represents your favour with that race. Their opinion of you seems to only be affected by the identical missions each of them gives you. And as you quickly discover the distinctive personality of each race only stretches as far as their initial communication with you, having no influence on the style, theme or parameters of the missions themselves. Then once you jump through their banal hoops and max out your favour with another race, it seems to have no effect on the way they act towards you. Instead you are met with the same script and the same response each time you encounter them (at least to the point in the game I played to: level 5 ships and level 13 officers).
Of particular note areThe Voraash: A hostile race that appear out of nowhere without introduction or warning, which initially seems exciting and intriguing. Until you realise their silence is probably not intentional. They never appear as the other races do on your station bridge view screen, and do nothing but attack you. Yet the game seems to expect you to save their facilities when they are attacked (facilities that enter the game, appearing as they do on the starmap, as though they have already been destroyed) and treat them as you do the other races. For me there was an inescapable sense that these guys were unfinished, that there was a mistake in the way they are introduced to the player or that there was nothing there to introduce at the point of release.
It's disingenuous to mention this game in the same breath as X-Com or Master of Orion II. It has none of the meat those games possess. It's clear that a lot of care and talent has been poured into certain areas, but the parts that matter, the ones that will give this title longevity, have been neglected. Like many new releases these days, this game trades on the reputation of better games in the same genre. It’s unfair to do so and just leaves me with a bad taste in my mouth. Perhaps there’s hope for it, but it lies many patches into the future.

Could have been a fun game, but below are the serious deal-breakers for me.  I gladly spend money in Steam (100+ games, DLC, hats, etc.) and this is the first time I am asking for a refund.  The game needed to stay in alpha/beta longer -- there are just such major problems with its interface and it's basic gameplay loop.
1. There are many interface problems.
1a. You can't zoom out far enough on the starmap and it's a major pain and waste of time to scroll around to find your fleets and look at the status of the points of interest. If you have played other space games like Stellaris, Sins of a Solar Empire, etc. -- you will understand how much of a pain you are in for if you can imagine in those games you did not have a fleet management overlay to use, and you could not zoom out at all on the starmap. Similarly for managing your base, the zoom is constrained and the text labels for the rooms are tiny. One is forced to click-drag and hunt for your rooms, and the rooms that have special statuses, you don't see the status until you click on the room.
1b. Also, the "deep tactical combat" relies on you chaining and comboing moves together between your ships and officers. However, at the point where you need to choose a new officer, YOU ARE INEXPLICABLY NOT ABLE TO SEE YOUR EXISTING OFFICERS AND SHIPS TO MAKE AN INFORMED DECISION -- WTF? Thus I am forced to record on paper what skills my officers and ships have.  Similarly during combat, the skills are not display unless you hover or right-click -- so you have to keep clicking on them to see, and you can't really memorize them because your officers skills are randomized (basically) from game to game.
1c. Various other annoyances, mostly things that waste your time, makes it difficult for you to plan your "deep tactics", for makes it tedious to see the information that you need to make decisions.  There is no overview where you can see all your ships and their stats/skills at once -- you have to click one-by-one and memorize them to keep track.  Ditto for your officers -- you can only look at one officer at a time and there is no way for you to see them all at once to plan your skill builds, combos, etc.  The "deep tactical combat" depends on this planning, but the interface sucks for allowing you to do it.
2. To collect resources, it's essentially a cow-clicking game. I'm told that changes in mid-game, but I've just spent the last 16 hours learning the game, spending it in the early game cow-clicking.  I have  better things to do with my life than to grind through the cow-clicking in the early game.  What is the point of cow-clicking resource collection? Especially if the game is already coded not to require it later in the game.

TL;DR: DOOM is probably one of the better triple A single-player shooters that's come out in a long time, but as an actual DOOM title, despite being a little better than Doom 3, still doesn't feel like a DOOM game.
First off, let me point out that I have religiously played the original Doom games a hell of a lot (No pun intended) and when the initial teasers for Doom 4 actually came out, it looked impressive. Much more so than Doom 3 did which tried for a more spooky approach to what Doom in the current era should feel like. I watched a few e-celebs play it, and in all fairness, it looked fun. Emphasis on, 'looked' fun.
To start with, the game is a WHOPPING 58GB. For real? How ♥♥♥♥ing unoptimised is your game, id software? Compared to other shooters that have more content and, arguably, look better, where did all of those extra gigabytes get thrown in? Are you seriously telling me you couldn't compress any of your textures or audio, especially considering most of the audio spoken in game is all crackly and filtered through to make it sound like it's come out of some bad signal radio.
On to the gameplay now, within the first hour or so I already knew where I stood on this game. Picking up the starting pistol, it was nice to see it take out the first sets of enemies in single headshots, I thought 'Oh, hey! This game's going to be quite fast paced then?'. But as I picked up the initial shotgun and the first 'imp' spawned in, I could feel my childhood almost disappear. Not only does it have a puny capacity and power, but the range on it was attrocious! All of the enemies feel like enormous bullet sponges, and the guns you get near the start feel pathetic. After slogging through even further, I started to see this big emphasis on using these 'equipment items' like grenades, and altfire upgrades to existing weapons that you could utilise, and even these felt very weak. Why couldn't you have just, you know, made the actual shotgun decent to use in the first place instead of making the player rely on extras to use? None of the weapons were satisfying to use at all. It doesn't help the fact that there are so few enemies during combat, and how slow the player's speed is compared to the original games. It actually feels slower paced and more sluggish than the originals, which, for a supposed reboot, is despicable.
I've seen a lot of people praise DOOM for it's core focus on the gameplay with few cutscenes, with the game poking fun at this by the Doomguy throwing away a monitor as it tries to spout exposition at him. But seemingly everything the Doomguy does has some kind of cutscene to it, for instance, pressing a button, finding a keycard or secret collectible, picking up a new weapon, pushing open a jammed door, all tiny little cutscenes that add pointless padding. Beating the second area, for instance, the game locked me into some unskippable cutscene full of filler that I couldn't skip through that lasted a good minute or two. So much for fast paced, high octane action. The glory kill system is also a big example of this as well, with the combat actually taking a heavy reliance to using it when you play on the hardest difficulties (Which I did, I ran through the first two levels on Nightmare) and the game simply does not give you much of anything. Ammo and health are scarce and you're pretty much forced to use these slow, boring glory kills to take out enemies for the extra health they drop. The chainsaw is also relegated to a 'get your ammo back' tool for this very purpose, being a cutscene only weapon that shows the Doomguy cutting an enemy to pieces instead of, you know, the player actually skillfully dodging enemy fire to dance around the enemy with the chainsaw like in the original games. The game just feels so... sluggish.
And it's a disappointment, really. As a big Doom fan I wanted to love this game. Compared to most shooters released today, it's a step up. But it's still not saying much. For a revival of the franchise you could have done so much more with this. The music is perhaps one of the best factors of this game, with Mick Gordon of Killer Instinct fame doing the soundtrack he really hit home what a gory, action-filled romp through hell should sound like. The game's just not Doom enough for me. Considering how much this game costs, as well, you'd get much more bang for your buck buying the original two Doom games than buying this.

From the developers of the original Doom and Wolfenstein, who tried to revive their creations for the last 10+ years, here comes the game, that should have been their last attempt to ressurect franchise long dead and forgotten. But instead, DOOM(4) became exactly what we needed - one of few reboots, that was done right.
Returning to basics was refreshing:
+ Health and armor pickups without regeneration
+ Almost 0% of cover on every level
+ Wide areas, where you get shot from all directions, filled with secrets
+ Arsenal of our very familiar weapons
+ Sprint is always on
+ No reload
+ Multiplayer that looks almost like Quake 3 Arena.
+ And very-very-very familiar demons, that demand our close attention.
Nevertheless it brings just the right amount of modern touch:
+ Collectibles
+ Codex entries
+ Rune challenges
+ Upgrade system for both SP and MP
+ Epic story of vengeance
+ Bloody fatalities to finish critically wounded demons. They are impressive until you pick up the Berserk power up - that`s where they were hiding the real stuff.
Minuses:
- I need MOAR!!!

So this game started with a bit of a rocky release. That said, the patches have been major helps and there is far more consistent support for this game on PC than I personally expected and I have been pleasantly surprised with the game as a whole.
The game is what you would expect. The Story mode finishes off the series decently well. Some scenes are animated and some are stills. The best scenes were done very well (the last ones) and it was definitely an enjoyable experience. The adventure mode offers the ability to run around and see the areas (fighting arenas mostly) and talk with significant people. Definitely worth doing! It also gives you different "memory" scenarios to relive all of the major fights in the original series and Shippuden.
The versus is great and the online is fun. Don't be off put by the overwhelming entrance punishment you'll likely receive your first trip to the online lobby. You'll do well in time and it makes the game all the more fun and challenging, further increasing the potential lifespan.
Also, the character roster is overwhelming in a good way. A decent amount of the moves are recycled from past games but the new additions are fun and worth playing for/with every time.
If you're a Naruto fan, this game is definitely for you. If you're interested in an anime fighting game, this game is for you. If you want 60 fps precision fighting, maybe look elsewhere. This does offer a ton of fun and a flashy experience.
I definitely recommend this game.

This is a really cute, and nice game, reminiscent of arcade games from years before, or, at least it channels that sort of charm--it's fairly fun, but, a few nitpicks have kept it from being very fun, and more along the lines of frustrating, at least to me. For one, when you jump, and move backwards of the direction you're currently facing, Mr. Frog keeps facing the same direction; so if you jump, and try to turn around to fire something at an enemy right behind you, you're going to fire in the other direction, leaving you quite vulnerable to being hit, ergo, losing one of ten lives you start with. Second, there isn't a pause feature of any kind, so if you need a break at some point, you aren't going to be able to get one until all waves of enemies are cleared, giving you a little breather. Overall, it's a charming, and adorable game, but these two issues are quite off-putting to me, since I'm used to fluid reactions in my video games. Mr. Frog feels as though he's slippery in mid-air, and doesn't react very quickly.

It's a less fun Super Mario, the one where enemies come from pipes near the top of the screen. Because the controlls aren't fluid and the levels are designed poorly the optimum strategy is to sit in one place and spam the "x" button. Also, Super Mario was good because you had to voluntarily be in harm's way in order to hit the enemies, whereas this game allows you to stay completely safe while killing things.

Handsome Mr. Frog is an adorable and entertaining retro-arcade styled game that is pure fun! Completely different from Cowboy Color's first and also addicting game ChargeShot, Handsome Mr. Frog serves as a delightful homage to those quarter-gobbling time wasters you'd find from the golden age of arcade video games.
Controls are simple, all you do is jump with your squishy froggy self, lick and gobble up enemies and other stage props, and spit them back at colorful foes who try to ruin your day. As you clear each wave, more new stages and enemies appear to test your survival accompanied with catchy tunes. Along the way, you can pop bubbles that float up the screen and collect candies and fruit to raise your score, hot chili peppers that allow you to spit flames, and different hats for Handsome Mr. Frog to wear to become even more handsome.

It's clear from the getgo that Cowboy Color pays attention to little details that help the player immerse themselves within the quirky little world. From the quick yet implicit little tutorial at the startup that teaches you how to jump and move to the adorable Ribs and Bits of the titular frog gulping and spitting various objects out, Handsome Mr. Frog brings a lot of character to the indie game community. My personal favorite details are the beads of sweat that pour off of the character after he eats a chili pepper and the squishiness of his body as he bumps against the ceilings and lands on the ground.
The 8-bit soundtrack is extremely well done and great to hum along to, as well as being inexpensive to purchase along with the game! Shouts out to @zbwmusic for influencing me to buy a video game OST!
The integrated Steam leaderboards help add to the addicting and competitive replay value of this game!

On first impression I initially thought less of Rabi-Ribi, primarily due to the sexual content present in the trailer.
Yet when I actually caved in and bought the game, I discovered that the hype was real. This is by far one of the best metroidvania titles I've ever played. The combat system is decent, the world feels huge and the characters are surprisingly well-written - even if the story often goes crazy at times.
Boss battles are also really tough, especially if you decide to slide the difficulty up. When the developers described their game as 'bullet hell', they were not kidding. There are times when your screen will fill with loads of projectiles which you have to dodge. Thankfully, Erina has a surprisingly small hitbox for her size, so it is possible to dodge.
There is a surprising amount of hand-holding at the start and there are some places that are pretty much inaccessible until after you've beaten the game. Other than tthat, you are often given the freedom to explore.
Be warned, however. If you don't like fanservice in anime or manga, this game is filled with it.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! The only Deus Ex sequel which is worthy of bearing the title (so far). Having played through the vanilla DX:HR four times before playing this and loving every second, I still wish I could have played the DC first time around.

Secondly, the Missing Link DLC has been properly incorporated into the storyline, allowing you to reset your augmentations mid-game incase you've invested points in stuff you don't use.

Even if I weren't a rabid Deus Ex fanboy, I'd still regard this game as one of the best of the past decade. Absolutely essential.

Closed Beta player, so I have been there from the beginning in 2012. The game has substantially evolved since that time period, from 5 'Mechs and a single map with 8 vs 8 and one game mode (Assault), to 3 Quick Play modes, 2 Faction Play modes, 12 Quick Play maps, 7 Faction Play maps, over 60 'Mech chassis (totalling 300 variants), 12 v 12, and a host of other improvements.
But this review isn't about a chronological list of stuff that happened, you wanna know how the game plays, right?
The new Player Experience is still a little rough. Once you've gone through the MechWarrior Academy (a welcome recent addition), there's no real tutorials on proper teamplay with other players, as well as any information on customizing your own BattleMech. However, the pace that PGI has been going at of late, this stuff may all come soon.
Once you've actually learned basic and advanced tactics, it is a proper BattleMech simulator; your 'Mech has a limited pivoting torso, you have loads of weapons on your 'Mech that can make you overheat if you're not careful, and of course, speed is still life. Assault 'Mechs, the biggest of them all, do indeed struggle with much smaller 'Mechs (such as almost all Light 'Mechs, and the Cicada and Ice Ferret), because of the much slower pace of the lumbering giant compared to the relative agility of the gnats surrounding it. This sort of inherent balance, coupled with different scouting mechanics that feel closer to World of Tanks than previous MechWarrior games (a good thing) already makes this feel more balanced and visceral than those earlier MechWarrior games.
Maps can and do restrict tactics in places, and many  of these maps can also change up the gameplay or make it stale. They're not quite as pretty or realistic as some of today's AAA titles, but I think they're very much sufficient for what they're trying to do, especially for trying to realize BattleTech's universe.
All this and I forgot about the pricing model. 'Mechs are EXPENSIVE when paid for with real money. If you want to build a collection, you will have to fork over a little money for MechWarrior Credits [MC] and buy some bays, and if you're not patient enough to accrue C-Bills (keep in mind that your first 25 matches, you get a major bonus to get you your first couple 'Mechs sooner), you can buy 'Mechs with MC, too. Fortunately, PGI runs sales and events rather regularly, so you may be gifted with some scraps of MC or some free 'Mech Bays, and rarely, even a new 'Mech! Keep an eye on their website for more information!
Give Piranha Games some patience, the greatest has yet to come. They are overhauling Faction Play a bit, and someone's pet project is proper Single Player/Cooperative.
TD;DR: This isn't your father's MechWarrior. It comes with its ups and downs but it is very much worth a play. Just be mindful of your wallet, 'Mechs are not cheap.

The core game play experience is well worth people trying it out and seeing for themselves if they like it or not.  The game is fun and deep compared to many other games out in the F2P space and well worth the time of anyone to download for free and try it out to see if they like it or not. Particularly of note for those that do play other F2P games that will make this game more appealing:
- No tier system.  If you grind your cadet bonus' in trial mechs, by the end of your cadet period you can buy literally any non-pre-order mech in the game to start out with.
- No golden ammo or boosters that directly affect the game matches. (Only booster is premium time that boosts earnings and experience grind.
- In general no P2W mechs.  The "hero" mechs are fairly different but not inherently better then their counterparts. (No boosted weapon damage etc.) And the company sells mech packs under a "pre-order" moetization system that as a generalization isn't pay to win.  Full disclosure though, every now and then one or two mechs defiantly creeps over the power scale before being nerfed leading up to a more general release. But for every mech that tends to break this curb on release ends up being about 3-4 mechs that are either mediocre or under-powered during their pre-order access and are buffed at a later time so it does even out in the grand scheme of things.
The game isn't perfect, but trying it out for yourself and let you form your own opinion of it. Its good enough to at least give it a try on your own. Of particular note is that MWO has been getting better with every patch, and in particular the past year of development has really stepped up the pace when it comes to meaningful changes made to the game.  If they continue the pace of development they have been maintaining up to this point, the game will only get better in the long run.

I, personally, love this game. Take a look at that word there, "personally".
I say that because this game isn't for everyone. It's not CoD, it's not Battlefield, it's not even Hawken. It's a robot simulator with 30+ years of Lore, books, and other games behind it. It's slow, it's grindy (when leveling up new mechs, when you choose to do that), it's got it's own share of problems constantly popping up, or constantly being fixed and hammered out.
Don't come in to MW:O looking for your next singleplayer robot game, or come in expecting to kill everyone forever, or expecting your robots to fly around the maps while doing backflips.
Come into this game looking for a unique, fun, slower paced game. Come into MW:O looking for kick♥♥♥♥♥robot battles, missiles flying overhead, lasers everywhere. Come for the giant land-slide games where you and your team crushes 12 other robots into the ground with giant guns... stay for the games that drag on.
Stay for the games that come down to the wire, with a panicking Light mech falling apart while darting around the map to spot the last few guys on the other team, so your last few nearly-exploded friendly mechs don't walk into a trap. Stay for the games where you're the last-mech-standing on your team, going full Rambo on the last lance of enemy mechs.
Yes, the game has its flaws, but it's a free-2-play game that's actually fair and paying money gives no in-combat advantage. Give it a try, just understand this isn't your average robot shoot-em-up.

This game has a JRPG combat system, portions of xcom's base building/research/production, and resource stations scattered around the federation's former territory.  In act 1 resource collection is manual, meaning a ship must visit each station to pick up its production.  once you defeat the boss in act 1 (you will know it when you see it, and it comes to you) stations send their own shuttles to your mega station.  this frees up the player to focus on the many large attacks happening between the other alien nations and your main threat.
Officers Crew a ship, which add their ship abilities to ship based combat.  each ship type has 2 static upgrades that can be researched.  Officers can level up, and have one skill point per level to enable a new ability from a limited list viewable when you recruit that officer, or improve an existing skill to a maximum of level 3.
there are so many things to juggle and most combat attacks either inflict status conditions or exploit those conditions for bonus damage.  once upgraded at the cadet barraks, the cadets can contribute to a fight on the station, just remember to use an officer if available.
this game was intense at times, and may be outright brutal on higher difficulties.  i recommend this game for anyone who likes both JRPG's and Xcom enemy unknown.

My original review can be seen here:
I gave it a 7.9 back then and thing have changed quite a bit since.
So, for my personnal satisfaction and to help people around steam here is a new look at the game. Several months later.
I want to start by saying that F2P games are usualy a gamble.
Some games will go out and shine and others will die a few seasons after it's initial release.
I've supported MWO since the alpha and beta by purchasingthe Legendary Founder pack for a roughly 120$
I've since invested around 650$ more in Pirhana's game and so far, I haven't been desapointed.
Mechwarrior Online is first and foremost a thinking shooter.
It relies heavily on situation awareness and chassis build rather than quick reflexes and headshot.
You still need to be quite good at aiming to hit the important and damaged componenet of your enemy but overall it's not as big of a factor as for say Counter Strike, Hawken or Battlefield.
That being said, since MWO is a f2p game, you will start with 4 mech bays for you to fill with your own mech you will purchase and 20 matches of "recruit" that will give you around 10 000 000 cbills that you can invest in chassis and customizing them. So far so good. However, some of the heavier mechs are worth up to 33 000 000 cbills. Calculate that matches give you around 80 000 to 200 000 per match without premium, you will have to play a lot before getting you hand on them.
That being said, investing on a 33 000 000 cbill mech doesnt give you an instant victory machine. Since mechs are seperated in 3 classes, light, medium, heavy and assault. They all have purpose and are fairly balanced. I'm saying fairly because some mechs are obviously better than others. Depending on their loadout, profile size, armor, speed and weapon mounting point. Overall thou, it's quite balance and once you know the chassis strength and weakness you will know what battle is worth fighting.
The game sets two teams of 12 players against each other. Quickplay allows you to jump directly on the battlefield and gives the players a quick vote on which map and playstyle to fight for. It works well and makes the game a lot more viable than the old imposing system. There is also 3 main server around the world so you shouldn't have problems of connectivity as well. Community Warfare is the second part of the game, you can choose a faction and fight for them on a galactic space map. It works well and gives you 4 mechs to bring on a single battlefield. It's intense, relies heavily on teamplay for success. A victory will give you reputation points toward the chosen faction as well as a considerable amount of cash. The game will however average 25 to 30 minutes.
Mechs are fun to play with and works mainly like tanks. Which means the legs and torso can turn seperatly from one another. Arms also have free movement compared to the mounted weapons. It gives MWO a special type of gameplay that ask for more thoughtfull movement.
Weapons varies from small machine guns, lasers, long range missiles and automatic AC 20. They all have different type of attacks, heat displacement and damage output. Half of the game is centered around cusotmizing the mech and fortunately it's very enjoyable. Experimenting around and just going all gooffing around gives the game deep possibilities and management that is rare for any other game.
Graphics have nice textures but overall effects are OKAY at best. The cryengine is demanding but models are sweet looking. Better yet is the animation and the waight of the mechs that gives the immersive sense of huge humanoid robot combat pleasant.
Sound is again, adequate but the music is boring and some gun sounds cheap. Some great moment arrives thou when in space and the echoes of explosion on the cockpit shakes about and ♥♥♥♥♥ing betty is telling you that you are about to die in agony.
MWO is fun, but it's more a love or hate relationship. Try it, you have nothing to lose. It's best played in team and there is no pay 2 win mentality. If you play for a while, buy yourself some pack and help Pirhana invest back in the community.
Board a nice Timber Wolft, Equip some LRM's and Medium Pulser laser and deliver death and destruction.
Take care!

Halcyon 6 is nearly brilliant.
The writing is funny, the pixel art is luscious and expressive, the combat is chunky and satisfying. It's quite hard at times, and like XCOM (which it structurally resembles) you need to swallow a few seemingly insurmountable defeats to proceed. But it's flexible enough to allow different approaches if you persevere, and enormously satisfying to overcome the occasionally overwhelming odds.
The combat system is tremendous fun at first, but needs a little more complexity - battles will get repetitous down the line. They look gorgeous though, and as an unashamed fan of pixelly spaceships blatting each other I love the juicy death rays.
Where it suffers slightly is in little things - the bar at the bottom of the screen that tells you the order of combat gives away the result of your attack way before the animation has played out, removing the tense wait to see if your all-or-nothing gambit has paid off. The collection of resources in the early game is pure tiresome busywork. There's no way to see what skills you will get in a new ship without spending a lot of scarce resources to research it. And the synergies between different classes (which are central to the combat systems) are a little cumbersome to navigate, especially in ground combat where it seems particularly hard to link your attacks effectively.
Those are polish issues though and the devs have committed to adding depth and extra systems so they're still honing it.
Really enjoyed it - well worth a look for the fantastic pixel spaceships alone.
PS The soundtrack is marvellous - James Horner has had Ben Prunty's lovechild.

Back in the 90's there was this little show called Star Trek: Deep Space Nine.  It was a heavily narrative driven show about a space station and the many alien denizens and factions that the commanding officer Sisko had to deal with.(Also Sisko was the most bad♥♥♥♥♥commander, ever but that's another article) See where I am going with this? Halcyon 6 takes that formula and does it justice in a dynamic and fun pixeled RPG way. You are the commander of Halcyon 6,  a strange alien space station that the Terran Federation(coughStarfleetcough) are excavating.
The game starts with a distress call and everything going to hell in about 60 seconds. I don't wanna spoil anything for you but things go bad, REAL bad. Suddenly you are thrusted into command of the station and must battle for survival and make key decisions as to how to deal with different species, factions, construction, exploration, recruitment, and the over all looming threat of annihaltion. Needless to say there is quite a bit of customization for how you craft your fleet, its officers, and starbase itself. The over all UI and interaction of the game is very reminicent to XCOM in style. That isn't to say that this is EXACTLY like XCOM as many seem quick to point at.
After choosing your starting commander (and naming him Sisko), you are shown an assortment of abilites that are split between space and ground combat. Yes there are away missions baby! Every officer has a set of random skills depending on their profiency, science, tactical, and engineering. All of which can be upgraded as your officers progress.
To simplify: its DPS(Tactical/Red), Support (Science/Blue), Tank(Engineering/Yellow) and this reflects in the ground/space combat as well. Enemies have their own profiency but you can expect more or less the same idea.
Now I could go into the nitty gritty of all the game mechanics and tell you my thoughts on them but Halcyon 6 has quite a few in-depth systems. There is a research tree, ship contruction, base construction,  resource management, and much more that I could write forever about. All of them are very well crafted and pretty easy to figure out.
One issue I did have is the games tutorial is very bare bones, only teaching you the very, very basics of what to do and how things work. Another thing I did notice where the UI fails is letting you access all of the games research rooms. You have to manually enter your Starbase and seek the room out by clicking around. Some of the rooms are similar looking and this becomes a little bit of a nusance.
Halcyon 6 primarily wants you to do things at your own pace, that is if you can handle constant invading attacks. There is a huge starmap that does change between campaigns and displays your missions and other factions. Now where I feel the game is extremely different from XCOM is in its sense of  urgency and obviously combat. XCOM made you feel like time was running out and you needed to make quick decisions. Halcyon doesn't really have that feeling, there are events that happen over time, but for the most part the game gives you the time you need to get your crap together. In comparison, I felt XCOM just threw me in the deep end of the pool and I struggled to float. Losing a high level officer was devastating, where in Halcyon, it just kinda sucks, but oh well.
The combat is the standard turn based RPG style combat, where buffs and debuffs are the primary way to achieve victory in combat.  Every ability has a affect and an exploitation, your torpedos might cause a hull breach and exploits crew panic, where lasers might cause crew panic and exploit a hull breach. Exploitations usually increase damage by 100% of base damage.
It's this buff/debuff system that gives you the statistical advantage with the combination of your officers abilities and how well they work together. Combat itself does look rather pleasing as ships blast each apart and the ships appearance begins to degrade as damage occurs. Ground combat is more or less the same idea, but I found these situations very rare and mostly on Starbase exploration. I wish away missions were more in-depth and unique as it almost kinda feels tacked on and not fully thought out. Overall though combat works well and is easy to understand, it becomes very underwhelming as battles become a rinse and repeat situation of using the same abilites in combination to win. This doesn't make them boring, just repetitive.
One area that the game does shine is its length. I played the game for about 8 hours and felt like there was still more to unlock, and more to see. Your campaign to save the Terrans is going to be a long one, so you're going to get that bang for your buck even if you play it once. If you play it twice, even more, as the game does feature many levels of difficulty. The game is full of charm with its dialogue, alien species, and even a light bit of decision making. I wish this area was more expanded upon with more in game politics but thats just my personal opinion. The graphics are pixeled but abilites and ship combat does have nice animations that have some oomph to them.
Halcyon 6 is very unique, I wish there were more games like this in general, so for that alone I would highly recommend the title to anyone who enjoys strategy games or RPG's in general. The game lets you live out your sci-fi fantasy of running a space station and kicking some alien booty. Now if only the game would let me punch John De Lancie in the face.

Very addicting and lots of fun, but not without its flaws. Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander brings a lot of potential to the table, and really delivers with a lot of it.
The turn-based combat is very reminiscent of Darkest Dungeon, where your fleet will have to work together to debuff and exploit weakness in your opponent in order to prevail, rather than just spamming one or two moves. Every battle can be a legitimate threat, with no typical RPG random encounters of weak enemies only designed for grinding.
The base management is comparable to X-COM/XCOM, where you need to excavate and explore your base in order to expand. The problem I found with this is that you really have to compete to get time to expand your base, as any time spent by an officer exploring the base is time lost defending the sector or gathering resources. Once you get more officers this problem resolves, somewhat, but it definitely makes it harder to have enough room to build everything you need.
As for defending and gathering resources, the game does a very good job of overwhelming you, yet still keeping it reasonable. You need to keep your fleet patrolling the sector whenever possible to oust any incursions of pirates, Chruul (the main enemy race), or any other potential invading race. Your colonies will be raided frequently, and if you don't defend them efficiently, you're going to lose a lot of resource income. The game handles this very well, but there have been times that I've felt completely swamped by how much is going on, especially later on in the game.
I felt the game shined the most in the second part of the game, as after a point in the initial invasion the game will expand to you not only having to manage your own large sector of space, but also having to help the various other races that will either reward you for helping them or lash out in anger for leaving them. This is the point where I started to feel too overwhelmed, and started losing more colonies than I had lost in the first part almost immediately. I was playing on the second of five difficulties for my first run, so I would have appreciated if the difficulty didn't ramp up so immensely.
Overall, the game is fantastic, and I'm looking forward to finishing my first run along with playing again, though I don't know how replayable the game is going to be. It definitely has some issues in terms of difficulty, but those familiar with the type of challenge games like X-COM will throw at you should feel right at home with Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander.
UPDATE: Just finished the game, so I have a little more to say.
Towards the end of the game the difficulty ramps up quite a bit as the Chruul incursions in the other races' space got more and more overwhelming. However, I just started ignoring them and found no penalty in doing so. You don't really get any bonus or penalty for allying with or making an enemy of any of the races, so you can mostly just ignore them. You get small rewards for directly responding to incursions, but that's about it, there's no real diplomacy involved. There was some diplomacy going on near the beginning of the game as the other races will sometimes contact you, but it seems those contacts are only meant to address some new plot development and don't actually bear any change on how they think of you. In the end credits the developers mention that there will still be more content to be added to the base game, so what I would like to see is more depth to the other races. An example would be receiving random gifts or help from allied races, or occasionally finding yourself under attack from enemy races.

Halcyon 6 is absolutely worth playing if you generally enjoy turn-based combat design. Some reviewers are putting forth that the game, though worthwhile, can become tedious. Though this can be said for all lengthy play sessions of essentially pouring through menus of one sort or another, figuring building timers versus quest timers, random uncontrolled events, etc.
Really, all I'm saying is know what you're getting into and it's unlikely you'll be disappointed. However, it is possible, like I'm sure reviewers have experienced, even knowing beforehand the gist of the game did not prevent their overall disappointment. Completely valid.
Everything considered, I continue to have a far more positive than negative experience with Halcyon 6. I'd provide information on the game's mechanics, storytelling/humor, build progressions and such, but that is easily available in more entertaining fashion on any popular gameplay or review site. For the price of admission, considering you generally enjoy turn-based RPGs with some tactics/stategy thrown in, Halcyon 6 offers up very absorbing gameplay.

A perfect example how to NOT make a game. 2/10
Graphics:
Who thought that OpenGL is a good idea for a fast shooter game like this? The over-colored envirements look like extracted from a childs book. textures pop up as you look at them because of that useless "prerender" option that just make the game unplayable at nearly 18fps with a gtx 750 and an i7. (other modern games plays fine with this hardware setup) Leveldesign is pretty okay but not as good as in doom 3.
Sound:
The soundtrack is great but becomes annoying as hell when you progress in the game. Every time, when enemies spawn, the soundtrack changes to a more agressive combat style until you killed the last enemy from said spawn. This is exactly the same as in painkiller or serious sam but they did it right and doom sadly did not. noises from enemies feel like they are played directly infront of you. I had trouble seeing enemies because the sound indicated a whole other direction than the enemies are actually standing.
Gameplay:
I had a very bad feeling about the "glory kill" moves at first but they are pretty okay. there are just a few problems with it. first of all, you're not invincible during glory kills.. at least not for the whole kill move wich leads often to death after glory kill animation because you can't move until the animation is fully played. If you try to avoid the glory kills, you often end up shooting more than enough bullets till an enemy gets down without glory kill... I think without the kill moves you need 3 times more bullets then with a glory kill.
next thing I'll have to cover is the fact, that this game playes almost exactly like serious sam or painkiller. you enter an area, all doors get locked, a fixed amount of enemies spawn and after you killed them all you can continue to the next area. and with the changig sound, you always know when an enemy is still alive. this ruins the whole scary part that doom3 had. areas with enemies are mostly build in a circle and play like multiplayer maps. enemies spawn in almost every spot at almost the same time so that you end up running in said circles untill every enemy is down.
weapon upgrades are just there to make the s*** look a bit better. they're nearly useless in my opinion because the secondary firemode of the weapons do not enough damage to be usefull, I almost never used them.
the game offers ingame challanges to unlock some sort of talisman which makes enemies stay longer in the tumbling glory kill state or increases the radius in which items get collected but like the weapon upgrades, they're more or less useless because you just stand right next to the items, when enmies drop them (f.e.)
Story and Playtrough:
the story feels pretty rushed. you get the chainsaw and I believe the first 4 weapons in the 2nd level of the game. and thats almost everything you need to complete the game (I never used the gatling gun or the bfg which you'll get later) while doom 3 took care of slowly getting into something like a story, the new doom just throws you in hell and then you're back on the mars base and that was it. I knew hardly what I was doing besides clearing areas and walking to the next ones. At certain points you'll have to find a keycard or a switch which is pretty boring depending that this game wants to be an arcade game. I guess they tried to make something like doom 1 but horribly failed. The only good thing is, that the checkpoints are decent placed and there was never a situation where I had no idea what to do next.
If you want to play a creepy horror game with some action: play doom 3
if you want to play an arcade game like the good old dooms, just play painkiller or seriouse sam instead.

Tl:dr A decent game, fun to play with some new elements to the dungeon keeper genre. Dont expect a compelling story though.  7.5/10 Recommended only if you got spare cash.
Dungeons 3 is one of the newest addition to the Dungeon Keeper genre. It plays similar to its brothers in that you have to manage a dungeon in order to complete an objective. Dungeons 3 does this in a similar way except that you send your troops to the surface where it becomes a Warcraft style RTS. While this is a intresting concept you will find that you are more than likely to just wad your minions into a death ball until the enemy is dead or your death ball is. Monsters do have abilities but most are passive rather than activatable further enforcing the death ball strategy. While the game states that it has created a breakthrough in the genre its more of a small gimmick.
The asthetics of the game are done quite well. While cartoony it does have enough grit to satisfy the dark and broody dungeon lords. Its appealing to the eye and the animations run smoothly.
The story writing is the biggest killer of this game. The game is extremly self aware, so much so that I feared it was secretly sky net planning to obtain control of my computer. Every sentence comes with fourth wall breaks and lamp shading. The game prides itself in its "clever and witty" self examination so much so that it becomes rather annoying. You arn't clever if it becomes redudant, your just making me want to scoop out my ear lobes with rusty spoons. They have some very talented voice actors as well which saddens me when they have waste thier time on such drivel. The game just can't seem to take itself seriously for more than a minute. Although the occasional wise crack may give you a chuckle you will find yourself groaning more than laughing.
The game runs rather smoothly with a few bugs. At times AI decide to have a fit, which is understandable for this genre. One time my army of banshess decided they wished to become sychronized dancers and all spin circles while fighting a boss. The game did become unresponsive when alt tabbing, but no major crashes.
Notable Points
The concept of the races are done rather well. Horde, Demons, and Undead have a nice individual feel to them.
Limited to ONLY 8 zombies. How can I be an evil necromancer with only 4 zombies?
The main character emits a EAR PIERCING scream when dropped occasionally.
The slap is is unsatisfying. I want to hear a loud smack rather than a gentle love tap.
A full price game where its competitors are cheap.

I have played 64 hours of this game and can say this is a safe purchase. Not knowing what to expect I really enjoyed the game a lot; there are 20+ campaign levels that follow the absolute evil and a dark elf named Thalya. The tutorial was adequate although I didn't find out you could recycle units until I completed the game so theres room for improvement. The story was comical however I found the humour (humor for my American speaking friends) to be a bit over the top as they tried to spit a joke out every second.
The campaign levels have a good variety slowly introducing you to the mechanics of the game, after completing a level you are rewarded with a simple and silly short animation that is definitely entertaining. The objective of pretty much all the campaign and skirmish is to build a dungeon and army to annihilate the enemy, you start by tunneling out rooms before outfitting them for purpose using gold and tool boxes. You gather evil alongside gold to research new rooms, units, spells and traps.
As you progress through a game your units needs get a bit more complex and if they go unfulfilled can and will lead to creatures going strikes. There are three creature factions you can use (four if you count the heroes) with four different units each. Horde creatures are easy to obtain and recruit but die permanently (until you research the crypt that is) while the demons and undead can be resurrected (the undead cannot be healed however). Each faction also possesses titan unit with its own flare for combat and these units along with the creatures and Thalya can be given tomes to grant them special boons.
Creatures do level up after gaining experience but most likely won't survive long enough without researching new buildings, power-ups and spells. If they die your dungeon can still be defended with a variety of traps (like the boulder or thrasher in my case) and spells (like magical barrier and tentacle). If your dungeon heart is destroyed you are history, so you better make sure you are prepared and make sure to recruit heroes via the torture chamber.
The graphics are decent but not the greatest, the music however is very well put together and very iconic and the narrator acts as your advisor (and game master). You can do an evil laugh while you do evil things but I mostly forget it is there; all of these things come together to make an epic, one the bards frequently sing (before you kill them that is).
If I had any complaints it would be that the research takes a while, especially if the enemy heroes keep claiming Evil Isle' TM which leads to a hasty mobilization to eradicate the heroes leading to early victories (mostly in skirmish) before you bring the cool stuff to bear. Another flaw in my opinion would be the population total adding up to TWENTY WHOLE UNITS!!
You can exceed this with zombies, skeletons, titans and dark heroes. Unfortunately the zombies and skeletons are tough as paper while the titans and dark heroes take time to acquire as previously mentioned; I know it has something to do with balance and game stability however, I feel that you are not properly simulating a villain if your not outnumbering like villains usually do... oh well *sighs*
Despite those grievances, this game has a solid recommendation from me.

*Revisited*
My initial review a few years ago, was rather critical of this 'app' as it incorporates payment methods to advance, and long termed playtime in order to unlock more items.
I wasn't a big fan of this, as i had hoped it would come with everything. Of course, seeing how much content is there now, i must of been naive.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This is a great little(big) application, that offers a wide variaty of different firearms models, ranging from pistols to automatic rifles, all at your disposal to be dissasembled, reassembled, and operated.
If you've looked at the screenshots and thought "Can all guns really be taken this much apart?" the answer would be "Yes" they pretty much can.
While going directly to dissasembling a gun looks confusing, this app offers easy to follow instructions on how to do so. It's also possible to do dissasemble, and reassemble a gun without instructions, if you'd like to do so. However, all guns must be "field stripped" with instructions, before this mode can be unlocked.
3 gamemodes are also available for all guns, in these you can dissasemble, and ressamble guns on time, or with 'instant death' (if you fail to select the right part for fitting) and compete with others, to reach the top of the high score boards.
After having mastered assembly of a specific firearm, you can 'operate' it. Here you get a very detailed insight into how a gun mechanically works, it will answer alot of questions regarding gun functionality, aswell as other mysteries. (I always wondered how catridges are eject from the bolt after being fired, now i know)
I was however dissapointed to see, that not all weapons has a 'cut away' option, as otherwise you have to manually hide certain pieces to view the gun insights. This is however only a minor annoyance.
The app also offers shooting ranges, where you can test your guns and skills. This however only counts for certain guns, and i have hopes that more will be introduced as time carriers on.
Overall, this is a great application that i would recommend to anyone who is interested in firearms as a whole, gun mechanics, or wants to become a gun smith.
It must however be said, that if you are not interested in the above subjects at all, this app may be somewhat of a bore for you.
Personally i would recommend getting the "Guns Lifetime Access" DLC, as it unlocks every firing range, and available firearm, aswell as future firearms.
However, before doing so, it would be wise to play alittle around with the app, before you decide to drop 36€

10 Second Ninja! If blowing up masses of nazi robots in 10 seconds of ninja action sounds like a good way to blow the afternoon, this game is for you. Not for the clinically serious gamer. Let's take a look
The graphics are pixelated, but look well enough. You'll find most of the enemies look the same, but the graphics are not the main point. The music is fine enough, but you'll be heading to the options to turn it off after half an hour or so, as the track can get repetitive.
The gameplay is the real action here. Your task is to destroy all the ninja nazis in your vicinity within ten seconds. This can become quite easy, but when you realize that for all three stars you need to do that in what is about one-third of this time, strategies begin to develop. It can be quite fun to find new ways to go around a level faster to defeat all of those pesky nazi robots. However, some levels begin to boil down to simple quick reactions, which can easily become frustrating after retrying a level ten times because you're one-tenth of a second short each time. However, the sense of accomplishment after finally winning is great.
There is no story other than the fact that you are a ninja and there are evil nazi robots and you must kill them.
So would I recommend it? If you haven't seen the big blue thumbs-up, then I would say yes. The gameplay is fun, as you feel great after defeating five nazi robots in three seconds. The music is no problem, and neither are the graphics. If you're looking for a quick, humerous, reaction-based puzzle game, then this is for you.

This game, man. This game is just absolutely fantastic. If you like metroidvania-type games and bullet hells, you will most likely love this game. It's by far
, and that's not just in gameplay. Ignoring the story itself (which is probably mediocre at best, but charming nonetheless), there are so many ways that you can play and explore this colorful world. Want to complete the entire game without collecting any item whatsoever? You can do that. Want to break the order of which the story progresses? Well, you can do that too.
Rabi-Ribi is the very definition of non-linear. You can do what you want, when you want, and in any order that you want. There's a plethora of hidden passageways and secrets. Some of these things also only appear depending on how you're currently playing. For example: if you are going through the game without collecting items, there is a part where you normally would not be able to progress without some specific items (e.g. double jump), but upon reaching this area on a 0% item run, a spring will appear and you'll be able to move forward. And to be crystal clear, this spring will not appear if you have collected any item at all (except rainbow eggs and three other things that are forced onto you), so you wouldn't be able to abuse this. In that aspect, it's appearent that the developers really put a lot of thought into the game's structure, and I think that that should be respected because, nowadays, you just don't see things like this in games.
The game has eight (six + two DLC) different difficulty levels. Hard and above are there to provide a challenge to those that want it, but those that don't can opt to play on an easier difficulty that is closer to their own skill level.
Casual
Novice
Normal
Hard
Hell (Unlocked after clearing Hard)
Bunny Extinction (Unlocked after clearing Hell)
Unknown (DLC)
Impossible (DLC)
Now, going back to the word 'colorful': Rabi-Ribi is beautiful for a pixelated world. It's very eye-catching and relaxing to look at. Not to mention that the soundtrack is quite fitting for the overall atmosphere of the game. But although the soundtrack is nice, I don't think that it's anything mindblowing and I can see it being repetitive for some people after a while. There could stand to be more tracks for boss fights, as well, because as of right now it's very limited. But that's just a minor complaint for me, as after the 80 hours that I've played so far, I am still enjoying it.
Actually, I think that words cannot accurately express how much I am enjoying this game as a whole. I'm not even good enough at it to do things like True Boss Rush on Hell difficulty or above. In fact, I had some trouble just completing the game on Hard (though, to be fair, I didn't use buffs or consumables). But that doesn't, and never did, take away from the fun that I am having with the game. There are plenty of other things for me to do, and if I ever feel like hating myself, I can just practice until I'm good enough to complete Impossible mode.
Also, to be honest, I feel like the $17.99 price tag is pretty low (I'd gladly pay at least $40) for how many hours one can get out of it. The game itself is not that long and can be beaten in just a few hours or less (if you know what you're doing), but its replay value is off the charts. I mean, just check out those achievements. And although it's not terribly long, the first playthrough for most people, on average, will probably take 15-20 hours. Personally, it took me between 40-50 hours for my first playthrough because I played on Hard and went around collecting all items without using a guide.
... Anyway. TLDR; Rabi-Ribi provides a challenge for players of all skill levels in a way that almost no other game does, and that's letting you, the player, go at your own discretion. It's also pretty spectacular, and if you love the metroidvania/bullet hell genres, you owe it to yourself to buy this game. Don't even think about it--just do it. I can guarantee that you won't regret it.
(Also, the art is very cute and has some ecchi bits to it. If you're not into that, please don't let it turn you off of buying the game. You'll be missing out, greatly.)

This is a game that I played briefly about 6-7 years ago that I never completed, which is strange because I usually obsessively play the story in Rockstar games to completion. Chances are if you wanted to play this game at some point you have by now. Coming back to this in 2016 was rough graphically and gameplay-wise. However, once you get past the rough edges, this is a game where the sheer lunacy of the tasks you are completing (such as beating up midgets dressed like Christmas elves, helping a drunk santa find his drugs, collecting panties for the peverted gym teacher) still makes this game playable. The story has major holes and meanders throughout, but the characters and setup for missions remain entertaining. The combat and skateboard/bike are fun if at times a little clunky. Last but not least, the soundtrack is pretty incredible (no hyperbole), though you'll hear the main theme over and over again. The only way I  can recommend this game in 2016 is if you somehow missed it in years past and care more about atmosphere and mood of a game than the mechanics itself. This is a really cool little offshoot that Rockstar has done aside from the GTA games. At the price you're likely to get it at nowadays, it's a cheap, laid back time if you missed out on this little piece of Rockstar's history. The obvious downside is the graphical fidelity that really makes you appreciate how good games look nowadays, in addition to audio bugs that take away from the overall presentation. If you don't play it, at least give the soundtrack a listen.

A lot like some of my other favorite games of all time Deus-Ex Human Revolution started out as one of those games I had heard of, but had never gotten why people loved them so much. I picked the game up along with the original and the two other games for around $7, a pretty good deal considering how amazing I consider this game to be.
22 years in the future from right now mankind has created augmentations, essentially robotic limbs and prostetics, a field we are actually exploring right now for birth defects, veterans, and work place injuries. With the creation of more and more advanced augmentations the public starts to worry that with the steady increase of aug users, will people begin to abuse it? The actual game story (and not the backstory) starts after waking up from a 6 month coma, where you wake up heavily augmented as to save your life. You play as Adam Jensen, the head of security of Serif industries. After an attack on your company which was the cause of your coma, your new augmentations, and the supposed death of your girlfriend and 5 other scientists. As you systematically track down the perpetrators of the attack it leads you into an even bigger bunnyhole on a global scale.
The cover system and stealth mechanics feel a lot like the Metal Gear Solid series. With guards and enemies responding to every noise and thing they see. If you're jumping around trying to find a route past them, they're going to check it out. If you leave a body laying around by another guards patrol area they're going to call it in and raise the alarm. Actual combat is a bit lacking though, if you want to go all in and just shoot everything you're just going to get holes shot in you as you die in about 10 shots. Boss battles, (excluding the last one) are a bit lacking, as one battle just has you shoot the guy in the head and that's it. He taunts you for a good 30 minutes and once you get to him, bang, zoom, 6ft under. While silencers for your pistol and assault rifle are rather hard to find in the beginning, they come around later along with damage, reload, target seeking, lasers, armor piercing, and even magazine upgrades. You can even upgrade your augmentations to be able to carry more items (the inventory has a set size which is kind of BS), be able to punch through walls, be able to takedown multiple enemies, fire explosive ball bearings out of your chest and more.
