If you have been reading the reviews, then you will notice a trend of either bitter long time players, or veteran players with a new hope for this game. These view points are obscured in broken promises, gameplay features, or the feeling that a childhood game is not what they wanted it to be. However, this review should be based on the game in question and not the previous titles, or the best laid plans of a company that has never developed a title like this before. If you take this game as a stand alone product and review it fairly based off its production, content, and concept, their is really nothing like it in the gaming community. However, players that have played Battletech games in the past, or played table top versions of this game, and use that as a back drop to compare this game are always going to have problems with what the developers do to this game.
The truth is the player base is much older in this game and most are not skilled FPS gamers like in other titles. So the great whole of the communty wants balance to the game and often blames a lot of their own inadequacies on the developers rather than holding themselves acountable. While, the small percentage of gamers with skill in the game are left unsatisfied because their is not enough competition in the game. This is where the Steam launch means everything and where players thinking about trying this game should really give it a chance. This game came out in 2011 (Beta) and I started playing early on in 2013, but to many people this game is just now being released. If the player base expanded, with the current opportunities in this game, as well as the improvements PGI has been making in the past year, then this game could become truly great. However, players that have been here since 2011 have lost faith and are a little burnt out with the process. The bottom line if you like big stompy robots, and a thinking man shooter, then Mechwarrior Online is the game for you.
My advice is check out the reddit pages, use the
website, watch streamers on Twitch, and try to find a unit in game so you can ask questions. Take this game as a stand alone product and have fun, as someone who plays it everyday I recommend it. See you on the battlefield!

TL;DR = Game is still good, pretty much still the same as the last patch in terms of gameplay, balance changes will come eventually, Stop whining about an unbound system when the game has given you the choice to play a bound mode.
A lot of people are saying the game has become unplayable because of OB64 but when I and my friends play it, I can barely feel any difference between this and the last patches. It's pretty much the same game.
The main drive for criticism right now is the cards unbound system which to me is fine now, they've seperated the queues for unbound and bound cards so that you can choose to play either old Paladins where everyone has equal card levels or the newly implemented cards unbound system. It's your choice, you can choose whether to play a game mode almost identical to the last patch or play the newer game mode that everyone apparently hates. If you choose to continue complaining then maybe the problem lies within you because I dont see any with the game right now.
Yes there are a lot of balance changes that still need to be made, yes the game has changed drastically in it's card building mechanic, yes there are a lot of new bugs with the new updates. But this is all that will eventually be fixed over time, I dont expect Hi rez to have an immediately balanced game after such big changes at the get go and neither should you. This is a process that's going to take a lot of time and community feedback in order find the sweet spot.
And while I may not agree with all of what Hi rez has done I understand their motive and why they decided to implement the cards unbound system.  The old card system was unbalanced and inhererntly favored other cards over others, it's obvious that there's always going to be one superior loadout that outshines any other kind of loadout and Hi rez wants to solve this issue by trying out something new, in other words cards unbound. All this "Hi rez are only doing it for money" ordeal is nothing but a theory, there is no solid proof that they are doing this purely for money and should only be taken by a grain of salt.
This mob of hate against OB64 has reached a point where its pretty much becoming more about whining then it is about giving constructive criticism. If I were looking to play the game in it's current state I'd say ignore the crowd and give it a go, just be sure to play classic siege which is the mode everyone likes.

Dungeons 3 is the third game in which you play the Evil side and give the goody good-shoes a rumbling! For people known to the old Dungeons games, the gameplay is very similar to Dungeons 2. The story takes place after the DLC  of Dungeons 2 in which, the Ultimate Evil reigned surpeme. The story now takes you further to new lands, a new evil hero and more heroes which may  sound very familiar to you. Packed of course with the lovely narrator from Dungeons 2 who you either love or hate. As any Dungeons game, the game is packed with humors and puns.
The biggest improvement is that you don't just control one 'faction'. This allows for more combinations and army setups. Besides that a lot of spells on the Overworld from troops and heroes  now can work automatically. This avoids the hassle of having to micro-manage everything in a large fight. The new research systems also brings an unique flavor as you can choose which upgrades you exactly want, allowing you to specialise in what you think is best.
The only thing I expected a bit more from is the difficulty. From my experience the difficulty takes a bit of a leap back to the original Dungeons 2 difficulty while I hoped for a difficulty closer to the Dungeons 2 DLC. But there is a voluntarily hellish mode to cover that problem.
Technically speaking I could discover no problems in this game. No unexplainable disconnects, crashes or low FPS drops.
All in all, it really feels like the developers listened well to the weaker points of Dungeons 2 and did their best to fix these points for Dungeons 3. Anyone who enjoyed Dungeons 2 will defintely love this game as well. Due to the normal difficulty being close to the original Dungeons 2, it's defintely also recommendable to players new to strategy games and the Dungeons serie.

I've had this controller since the original early release last year, and I've had mixed feelings about it since then. Some games it works like a dream, and it fun to use, but others it can be an absolute nightmare to control; shooters in particular can be annoying.
Pros:
Size - I love the size of the controller. I have big hands and so its nice to have a controller than fits to my hands so well.
Buttons - The triggers and bumpers are much bigger than the Xbox One, and so its easier to use from my experience. The back buttons are very useful as well. I don't use them as often as I should, but they do come in handy as useful tools for stuff like pulling up maps or quick saving.
Customization - There is no equal when it comes to customization. You can change everything about this controller in the options menu, which is great if you don't like a control scheme, or if the you need the to change stuff like sensitivity. You can even change your on and off noises.
Cons:
Right Track Pad - This is my biggest and longest problem with the controller. The right pad, or camera pad, can be very tricky to use. Depending on how you make it in the options menu, it can alter your style. While this level of options are nice to have, at the same time, it can be infuriatingly annoying to get it to your liking. I've tinkered with the right camera for up to 30 mins before trying to get it to work for the specific game I want. I love and I hate this thing. I like it cause it gives you better precision sometimes, but I hate the amount of work you have to do in order to get that.
Overall, I think the controller is worth getting if you want an alternative to the Xbox controller. But if you aren't looking for a controller than you can customize, and just want to plug and play, then this is not what you want. But if you're tired of always using a M/K and want a controller than you can play almost any game with, then this is your best bet.

10 Second Ninja is caught in a strange position for me. At first glance (as well as when you play it) the concept seems more geared to be a mobile game than a PC game. However, the pacing is more fitting of a PC/console game. Completing each level in 10 seconds or less is not hard at all, even if you aren't used to fast paced games. With practice, avoiding spikes and falling objects becomes easy. The real challenge is getting 3 stars on every level, which can take some time.
If you are considering buying it, ask yourself this: "Am I going to try to 100% it?" If the answer is no, you aren't going to get much out of the game. Playing through each level only once won't take much time, and is especially not worth $9.99 in that regard. If you are a completionist (or are for just this game), definitely pick up the game, but still at a discounted price. I only heard about it and bought it because I crafted a 90% off coupon for it (s***, it was 99 cents!). At that price, it was definitely worth it.
Of course, getting 3 stars on every level is often brutally difficult, and at times frustrating. You will have to time your jumps and attacks perfectly , which will take loads of trial and error (and error and error and error). This is a turn-off for a lot of people, but a selling point for others. It is entirely dependent on whether you enjoy fast-paced games or not. Completing each level with 3 stars left me saying "Damn, I can't believe I just did that, let's do the bonus levels!" and not "Wow, I just wasted 5.8 hours on that?".
In the end, the question I ask myself is "Did I have fun?". Yes. A lot of it. There were some levels that were just frustrating (I'm looking at you Deathcube Level 1), but most of them were a blast to complete. Definitely pick it up when it is discounted if you enjoy fast-paced games or are looking for something new to try.

WAR ON FOLVOS is not a bad game. It is your standard hexagonal turn-base strategy, that tries to port to a fiction future the  tactics of today (tanks, infantry, long range artillery, air units for both air combat and ground attack etc.). I detect no groundbreaking evolution whatsoever in this game. But it must be said that, although 'more of the same', that is not grounds for dismissing the game. The stats of the units and the maps in which the scenarios unfold are well balanced, the scenarios are challenging, there is an interesting story (once again, too much reminiscent of 'dune' but interesting nonetheless).
So though not revolutionary, it is a good hex-TBS game. Actually, if I have never seen PG or Dune I would have found this game excellent. It just isn't because of the formula being so overextended by now. Still, it satisfied me because I do like the genre and so I welcome new installments of the same game-type. It would have deserved a bad review if the game was flat-out bad, but the thing is it isn't.
So it's more like having a new, good expansion to something you already know and like. If hex-TBS is your cup of tea, buy it, you won't regret it.

War on Folvos is a simple turn based hex-grid strategy with simple mechanics, though I still found it fairly satisfying. Each unit gets two action points per turn and you can use those to move or fire as you wish. With effective scouting, rotating your armour units and pumelling your enemy with artillery the invader campaign becomes very easy. The rebel campaign is a bit more challenging with its weaker units. New objectives given to you part way through a mission can catch you offguard.
You can right click on units to view their more detailed stats and descriptions, however I feel key information was missing there such as weapon range. Speed and range need to be learned the hard way.
Each campaign's story complements the other and they fit together reasonably well. Overall the story is a bit back and forth across the map with somewhat poorly translated (or written?) conversations between the characters.
No skirmish mode, so after the two campaigns there's no replay value. For its low price it'll keep you entertained for a few hours on the cheap if this is your genre. On this basis I recommend it. Credits lists a very small indie team, so good going to them for a reasonably well polished release.
There's a bit of an early Dune vibe to it, and I half expected to retreat into the desert to tame sandworms. Maybe in a sequel?

Call it "PlanetXistan, the latest game from Avalon Hill."
As a turn-bsed tactical game on a hexagonal map, War on Folvos is something of a throwback to the wargaming boardgames of the 1970's and 80's. It's like taking an ancient Avalon Hill game like Afrika Corps or a *very* simplified version of Squad Leader and animating it with 1990's-era graphics. The game has the same deliberate pace and slow thought demands of one of those old games with the little cardboard chits. You can almost see little tufts of pixelated cardboard sticking out of the corners of the units.
The story is minimal and easily ignored. The setting is sci-fi, but the tactics are really not much more futuristic than with present-day technology. It's kind of a WWII tactical game disguised as a sci-fi TBS game, although the storyline, scenery, and color calls to mind Afghanistan or the current Syrian civil war.
The pace and deliberateness is its strength and its weakness. It's decently entertaining for nostalgic types like me who want to play something like an old wargame without needing to find a opponent or setting up a board. What would have been great is a feature that would allow you to speed up the housekeeping of each turn, instead of having to wait a few seconds for each unit to get into position.
This game will not blow you away nor keep you replaying it over and over again. Nothing more or less than a good two days' worth of fairly old-fashioned gaming for only a few dollars.

Halcyon 6 wants to be a good game. And somewhere inside what you can buy right now, a good game no doubt exists. Unfortunately, minor annoyances, tedius gameplay, and an inexplicably sharp difficulty curve bring down what is otherwise an entertaining experience.
-------
1. Base Management
The game draws parallels to XCOM with its ant-farm base building. You clear rooms. You put stuff in the rooms. You research new stuff. You clear new rooms. You put new stuff in new rooms. With rare exception, you can assign officers to the rooms to generate resources, conduct research, or upgrade ships.
Unfortunately, this devolves into a click-fest micromanagement hell. Officers assigned to generate resources must be reassigned every few days -- a minute or so, real time -- with each assignment dragging you away from whatever you were doing to click through four layers of menus. Want more dark matter? Click the base menu. Click the dark matter converter. Click the mission. Assign the officer. Click to confirm. Click back out of the base menu. Go back to what you were doing. Then repeat this process every 60-90 seconds, multiplied by the number of dark matter/mineral/crew missions you want to run concurrently.
I'm not sure why the designers didn't allow for an auto-repeat option, or set rooms to passively generate resources if an officer is assigned. Instead, base management feels like a grindy clicker game.
2. The Galaxy Map
Your station sits in a neat galaxy, populated with a few different factions and colonies that can provide resources if you keep them alive. The Big Bad occasionally sends monsters to eat your colonies; fight off the monsters or lose the colonies. Here again, the game descends into tedium. Different colonies generate different resources, and each has a storage cap. Collecting them means sending a fleet to each colony, every time they're full. Click to send fleet. Click to collect resource. Click to confirm collecting. Click to return to galaxy map. Click to send fleet. Repeat up to a dozen times, depending on how many colonies are alive.
The caps are small enough that you lose significant production by not constantly circling through your delivery route. The cap for crew colonies is around two dozen, and they generate two per day. Every five minutes, go and pick up your crew. And your dark matter. And your materials. And also fight off the 3-5 enemy fleets that appear semi-regularly.
Manual harvesting doesn't add anything to the experience. An automated system, even if it meant investing in shuttles or whatever in-universe gimmick would explain it, would remove the tedium but allow the player to choose and manage. Instead, it's like playing an iOS game; better log in every ten minutes to tap the farm, or else it's not going to generate any more melons!
3. Combat
Both ground and space combat are turn-based JRPG style. The primary mechanic is applying and exploiting different effects for bonus damage. Knock out an enemy's sensors by uploading a virus from your science ship, and your tactical ship's next hasass attack hits twice as hard. Effectively executing this cycle is mandatory: you will lose battles if you mash attacks without planning. Pulling off combos feels good, and reward smart play.
Unfortunately, there are only so many workable combos. Each ship type has a pre-set list of attacks; each officer has a randomly generated list of attacks. Once you've figured out which combination the random character generator has blessed you with, every battle plays out in the same loop. After your 50th round of (breach hull) + (portal gun) = damage, it stops feeling fun.
Critical hits and dodges mix things up, but not in a good way. In more difficult fights, an early crit from the enemy means saving and reloading. Resources are too tight to spam ships, and experienced officers cannot be easily replaced. God forbid you lose a Legendary Officer -- who have special, extremely powerful skills -- because that's gone forever now. Moreover, retreating from a losing battle applies permanent debuffs to the survivors. It feels like a squad-wipe in XCOM: it's not worth fighting forward.
4. Difficulty Curve
This deserves special mention. Through the first few hours, the game is tough but fair. At a certain point, doing thing X will trigger event Y and summon boss Z. You'll get a 50-day warning until Boss Z arrives at your station and murderates everyone. Fighting Boss Z requires fully-upgraded T3 ships, though, which isn't mentioned at any point along the way. If you don't have them when you trigger the event, stop your game and start over.
It's a bizarre punishment. The game actively encourages you to do Thing X, which can be accomplished easily with T2 ships. Then, presumably with a cruel smirk on its face, the game mentions you should spend thousands of units of resources building and upgrading a proper defense fleet within a strict time limit, or lose.
-------
I don't want to sound too down on the game, because I enjoyed large parts of it. The story is fairly generic but well-written and engaging, the NPC races are fun to interact with, and the combat feels tense but (minus absurd crits) skill-based. If the developer patches in some kind of automation and softens the difficult curve, Halcyon 6 will be the great game it so desperately wants to be.
Until then? I'd recommend buying something else.

This game is definitely not for everyone. personally, i love some of its features; unlocking techs, new ships (stuck at tier 3 currently), unlocking officers, more ships. There are definitely twists as the game forces you to move forward down the story (more of a phase i guess as there is really not much of a story tbh); i've tried to stall the game by not completing key quest and suddenly the quest is replaced (i assume its because ive already research/build higher tier ships; whenever i upgrade my ships to story seems to move on itself without requiring us to complete any quest). Resource management is definitely one if not the most important aspect in this game but it will change after you finish the tutorial/first phase of the story.
Battle is repetitive and yes, lots of grinding, like most JRPG. I find the battle system challenging enough as you cant go auto-pilot and wish it will turn out okay, even at the lowest difficulty, well at least until you unlock tier 3 and everyhting is pretty much cannon fodder.  Leveling up your chars doesnt really reward them with anything but minor stat upgrade. The ONLY way to prevail (or survive in my first few tries) in this game is to research higher tier ships BEFORE the story or the in-game development actually requires you to do so.
Now dont listen to those crybabies in their reviews who only spent like 20 minutes in-game and barely scratch the mid-part of tutorial. This game is tricky, if youre not careful, youll be crushed, FROM TUTORIAL. Once you have cleared the first phase and *SPOILER* killed the first boss *SPOILER* then you can actually enjoy it in your own phase.
I do recommend this game for those used to strategy-resource management, grinding and repetitive action; learning curve is low but if you prefer FPS or action games, this might not be the game for you. Would i recommend this to JRPG fans? No. This is not JRPG, the battle system and grind part is, but nothing else is. If you're a hardcore Civs or alike game fans, its tech tree might be too simple for your liking.

I absolutely love this game.
It's been a while since I've actually enjoyed a decent platformer with a great story and this game personally takes the cake for being an excellent adventure game. The story itself is great and the characters are adorable and loveable. There is so much to interact with and explore. The artwork of the game itself is colorful and attractive.
The game mechanics and difficulty are top notch. The game allows the players to cater the level of difficulty towards their preference. This goes beyond the standard "easy", "normal", and "hard" difficulties. If things get too hard, the game offers aid which helps the player may accept or decline. This helps the player not feel frustrated or stuck (especially on boss levels).
Being a bullet hell game, true skill comes from mastering the art of movements. Since Rabi-Ribi also has platformer mechanics, not only do you have to deal with gravity and an onslaught of projectiles, you also have to deal with the enemy you're fighting and successfully chain attacks to defeat them. This definitely ups the learning curve but is super rewarding when mastered.
This game definitely provides a challenge when set right.
The soundtrack of the game is very well done and I highly recommend getting the UPRPRC edition which comes with the game OST in FLAC. With the UPRPRC, you can also enjoy the digital artbook.
Overall, this game holds a special place in my heart and I highly recommend this game.

When the game first showed up couple of years ago, I tried it out with high expectations as a big BattleTech fan, and fan of massive robots in general. It didn't work out. Game was removed within few weeks.
Then, about two months ago, I saw someone streaming it on Twitch (thanks Gimpy21!), and decided to give it one more shot - it's been a long time. And oh boy, did things change (for the better).
TL;DR - This is as much fun with 'mechs as one could have at the moment, and that says a lot.
Mind you, this game does require you to think more than rely on your reflexes and mouse DPI, and is most definitely not your regular FPS. Each mech is special, and it might take a long time to get accustomed to various options, loadouts - even before digging into what's meta. Experiment, have fun with stompy mechs, and know that your mechs WILL get killed MANY times. However, each time you get to learn what went wrong, and you can't wait to begin firing alphas again (no, seriously, don't do that as a newbie ;)).
I encourage new players to visit official forums for incredibly helpful guides, and aside from written stuff there are plenty of embedded YouTube tutorials to help anyone and everyone - if you decide to dive in. Ignore the toxic comments, and enjoy many mature players who are there to help you out and have fun with mechs.
Highly recommended title - feel free to ask for any details I might be able to answer.
Tip: As a newbie and without a group of teammates, avoid playing Faction portion of the game (Community Warfare) at the very start. Also avoid buying mechs/mech packs with real money until you've gotten a good grip of what style and chassis you like to play.
Also bear in mind that you really don't have to pay a single cent of the real money to progress in this game and buy mechs, nor does paying real money for mechs make you play better in any way.

First things first: I'm reviewing this game based on what it its now, not on what happened in the past or what it could have been.
Be aware the devs made quite a few mistakes in the past and didn't hit all the goals they set when pitching the game for crowdfunding (which was to be expected, since the goals were quite exorbitant for such a small studio). They made mistakes in their communication with the playerbase. There is a vocal part of the (former) community which is "very" disgruntled over these mistakes (and decisions they didn't like), so take reviews with a grain of salt. When reading reviews or discussions be aware that there are some guys on a crusade to make this game fail. Furthermore many guys are wearing the thickest rose-tinted nostalgia glasses I have ever seen in any game series (regarding previous Mechwarrior games).
I'm recommending this game. It isn't perfect, but it is better than many games on the F2P market. Take it for what it is: a tactical, slow paced, vehicle combat arena shooter. As of now, it doesn't have an evolving endgame, but Community Warfare Phase 3 has recently been announced to be released around spring 2016, which looks like it will add long term goals.
The game always had balance issues to some extents, but since the last balance overhaul it's the best it has ever been. The devs recently fixed some issues that plagued the game for a long time, and the overall state of the game is better than ever.
Pros:
- The core gameplay (mech combat) is really good, probably best of any Mechwarrior title
- Lots of customization
- All mech classes play differently but fun
- IT IS NOT P2W
- Graphics are above average for a F2P game
- You can play this game without ever spending money (mechbays can be obtained in CW)
- Devs frequently give away ingame and real money currency through events
- Overall a really good community
Mixed:
- The maps swing between really good and bad
- Balance still not where it could be
- Game is not easy to learn
- It seems to be pretty grindy in the beginning but it gets alot less once you understand the game better
Cons:
- Community has some self-proclaimed gamedesigners who depreciate all but their own opinion and constantly bash the devs for not designing the game after their (often terrible) ideas
- Community Warfare is not where it should be
- Prices are pretty high (don't buy at full price, there are plenty of sales)
- Game is not optimized well (hardware)
- The 3 gamemodes in quickplay play pretty similar
Verdict:
Try it, it's free. If you are looking for rock solid mech combat, this is your game.  You currently won't find a better one. Don't decide based on reviews, give it a shot.
Ps: Don't buy stuff without reading a guide or asking the forum. You "really" don't want to waste  your cadet bonus on things you don't need.

First thing: I only recomment if it's in a bundle or a good sale. $9.99 is way to high for for this game in my opinion. The most I would be willing to pay is $4.99, and that's only if I really liked speed run games, which I don't, so the most I'd personally be willing to pay is $1.99. Thankfully, I got it in a good bundle.
The concept if fun and interesting, but it doesn't give any reason for the 10 second time limit that I saw, but since I don't really care for speed run games, I quit trying shortly after the first boss. I did kill some time betting some non-completion or score based achievements while waiting for cards to drop.
The artwork and audio is decent and fits the game fairly well. Some of the graphical mechanics were odd, but didn't effect gameplay at all... do ninjas really bounce excessively when they die?
The levels have some real challenge to them if to care about the stars. Although, you do need to get 2 stars on each level of a world before you can move on to the boss fight, so casual play will keep you from progressing.
If you are using a controller and aiming for best time with 3 stars, you should definitely enable clutch mode, which remaps the restart function from RB to BACK. After restarting 100 times, sick of being 0.08 second away from 3 stars, you will probably already have your finger on the restart button and accidentally restart early... repeatedly. Additionally, if you are using a keyboard, stop. Use a responsive controller that you are comfortable with.
Overall, if you like speed running, get it. If you don't like speed running, only get it if it's dirt cheap: 80% off or better.

Being a decades-long veteran of space empire-building games, and having followed and supported the development of this game since beta, I can honestly say that I am fairly well-acquainted with the goals and motivations that drove Endless Space to be what it has become. While it definitely follows in the footsteps of many of the games that have preceded it in its genre, the developers at Amplitude have succeeded quite well in creating a unique game with its own vision and theme.
At a basic level, Endless Space takes inspiration from classic games like Master of Orion, Stars! and Spaceward Ho! The interfaces are clean, simple, and intuitive, controls are easy and responsive to use and useful information that the player requires to make good decisions is presented in a straightforward and organized manner. Easily navigable menus, well-labeled buttons and a handful of sliders ensure that any function or command is no more than two or three clicks away at all times. Empire management, ship design, diplomacy, and research all blend seamlessly together, enabling a player to manage even a fairly large empire relatively quickly, keeping turns short and the game moving at a solid pace.
While Endless Space does contain all of the standard space empire-builder conventions, they are generally presented in a very flavorful way. Like Master of Orion and its sequel, Endless Space has a rich and lore-heavy backstory behind it; the difference is that this lore permeates the gameplay itself in a much more extensive way. It also takes a page from the Civ series of games by introducing strategic resources that can provide bonuses to players that control them, as well as limiting the availability of certain technologies by requiring them as prerequisites for ship components and even some facilities. Many planets possess unique features, of which there are many, which will provide specific bonuses (or penalties) depending on the technology the player has at hand.
Ship design is easy but broad in scope; there are six different size classes for hulls, each of which is better suited to fulfilling certain roles. Even the largest hulls cannot hope to carry much of everything, forcing you to design specialized vessels and build mixed fleets to deal with specific scenarios. Space combat is a real-time, strategic experience that rewards good planning and recon, rather than reflexes. Much like in GalCiv2, starship weapons and defenses utilize a rock/paper/scissors approach; care must be taken to balance your ships to match an enemy's strengths and exploit their weaknesses. Each weapon type has a specific range where it is the most effective, and specific tactics must be chosen to maximize the effectiveness of weapons fire as well as counter the enemy's plans.
Diplomacy is not given short shrift, either; a detailed counter keeps a record of all the different factors influencing your relationship with the other factions and gives you a comprehensive breakdown of why they like (or hate) you. There are extensive options for signing agreements and making trades, as well as a number of potential relationship states, and access to all of these depends on how many xenocultural techs you have researched as well. (The only weakness in this area is the lack of a detailed espionage system). The tech tree itself is extensive and provides a wealth of options depending on your preferred playstyle, with several of the victory conditions tied directly to tech tree items
The game has changed considerably in the time since it was first released; the developers have shown great interaction with the community and have responded directly to player feedback in shaping the content provided by each new update. Players who have bought the game and joined the community gained the ability to cast votes for what they prefer to see next; we have seen the inclusion of entire new races, an updated tech tree with more race-specific techs, an overhaul to the ship design system, the addition of strike craft and improved invasion and siege mechanics, and exploration-related random events. Planetary wonders, unique planets, and an array of powerful leaders who can be hired and gain experience levels from governing planets or leading fleets add a deep level of strategy. Add all of this to a wealth of options when setting up a new game, and Endless Space allows for literally 'endless' replayability for hundreds (if not thousands) of hours of deep strategic gameplay.

I've played it for several hours now, and it remains addicting and difficult fun. You can probably get a better idea of how it plays by going onto YouTube than by reading a review, but all I'll say is that with the caveat of having no prior experience in 'space strategy' games, Halcyon feels unique, expansive, and makes it easy to lose track of time while playing it. There might be plenty of fans more familiar with this genre than I, though, so this review won't apply to everyone equally; anybody like me, with exclusive experience in blockbusters like XCOM, will find this experience new.
What I haven't noticed other reviewers mention yet, though, is how many science fiction TV shows are paid homages to or parodied in this game or the work that's gone into the art. There are side quests that parody the 'O'Brien Must Suffer' trope in DS9. There are little pixel characters for John Crichton and Aeryn Sun, among a LOT of other familiar sci fi characters, that make cameos as crew members on your warships. The atmosphere of the game feels like Star Trek as written by Douglas Adams, and for me at least, there were a lot of laugh-out-loud moments. The music and art have a depth to them that I hadn't seen in some relatively well-received $60 Kickstarter games.
There are some issues that make it less compelling; basically, the user interface and the way the game presents information to you is a little bit less well organized than in games like XCOM (which, let's not forget, is 3x the price at least and isn't a Kickstarter game). Clearing space in your base requires higher level crewmen the deeper you go, but the game never actually tells you that beyond a little fine print in the corner of the screen and instead just says 'crewmen unavailable', instead of explaining more clearly that high-level crewmen are required. There could be more visible reminders or notifications when colonies are about to fall (proportional to the time required to get there, maybe, which also isn't readily available information) or Chruul portals appear. Clicking ships back and forth between colonies to collect resources gets tedious after a few hours, let alone over longer periods. But these are niggling issues that don't, for me, detract from the best parts of the experience.
If you're only familiar with turn-based strategy from blockbusters like XCOM and you feel like you'd enjoy humorous references to late 90's sci fi TV coupled with compelling pixel art, I can definitely say Halcyon is well worth $20.

Great game. Easily one of my new favorites.

Tl;dr: Awesome game that could use a few small improvements
Pros:
-Fun gameplay.
-Exploring and building the base is satisfying.
-The game is about much more than your starbase! That's part of the story, but even when you're doing stuff in your starbase it's so you can go out and do more awesome stuff.

-The learning curve is not steep. It took only a short time to get the hang of it, and the more officers I get the more combos I figure out. I haven't figured the whole thing out but it's actually fun to do.
-The choices make it so it doesn't feel so linear, and you can attack problems in the order you choose, and the quests that have expirations make sense.
-It is its own game. It's not FTL, Final Fantasy, XCOM, etc, and that's a good thing. You can find similarities but my favorite thing is that it's something different, in a good way.
Suggestions:
-Automate resource gathering.
-The economy gets a tad overpriced the further you get, to the point where I have found myself waiting a couple times just to have the resources to continue, when I've never stopped doing everything I could to gather resources.
-Maybe I just haven't seen it yet, but some kind of sensor warning as soon as ships start approaching the starbase would be amazing, instead of scouring the entire map every once in a while to see if something is coming. Yes, it tells you when something has reached one of your planets or your starbase, but by then it's probably too late to recall a fleet, especially when defending your starbase.
-Drop "Starbase Commander" from the title for two reasons. 1) It sounds over the top, and 2) I know it's part of the 5 second pitch to show people what your game is and get them interested, but I wasn't interested in commanding a starbase and I passed after checking the game out. Then, only because of a recommendation from my brother and finding out what it's really about, I got it. XCOM! Master of Orion! Civilization! FTL! I love all of those games, and having them as inspirations gave me great hopes for the game.
And, in the beginning, it was good. For a while.
There's a science system with a tech tree!
There is a base that you get to build up (fun!) that looks (and feels) suspiciously similar to the one from XCOM2!
There are battle tactics that you can use to "exploit" your enemies' weaknesses!
There is a wide(-ish) universe just waiting to be explored!
There's some sort of story going on that you get to slowly learn about!
But then... it became tedious.
The tech tree is 100% linear and gives very few (no?) options, since you'll probably just research everything. Research itself seems tacked on - you simply "buy" the techs (instantly) with the exact same resources you use for everything else.
The buildings you can build in the starbase are extremely limited, and they sometimes produce unexpected results. (For example, you can build two Dark Matter Multipliers, but if you assign an officer to one, both get locked out.)
Tactics become "solved" pretty quickly - you find a good rotation of "inflict status condition, exploit status condition, utility skill, repeat" and I never had to change it. Imagine doing the same skills over and over again for 20 hours. Awful. I wished I could have put the battles on fast-forward.
There isn't actually anything to _do_ in the universe except battles (boring, as per above) and resource gathering (even more boring, but thankfully you only have to do that for the first few hours).
The story has few details, is very linear, and fairly forgettable. Interactions with AI groups seemed meaningless. :/
In fact, after the first two hours, after I had learned all the systems... there wasn't anything else new in the game. It was the same things, over and over again. Tech up, build some very similar but now larger ships, fight enemies with the same strategies except their hit points are higher and so is my damage output. But because I'm a completionist (gotta finish!), I spent an addition 25 hours grinding through it, hoping for more.
Unlimited re-playability? Not at this point. I could not play this game again, as it is clear from the mid-late game that there wasn't anything more to it.
I really want to like this game. And it deserves somewhat decent, but not amazing, reviews. If I had stopped after 2 hours, I would have also given it a great review. But I have to not recommend this game as it does not actually fulfill its promises past the first hour or two.
There's room to grow. There's lots of promise. It's just not there yet. It's a good start, but it's like being promised a trilogy and only getting half of the first book. I think this will get there, someday, but it's just not there yet.

If you're expecting a carbon copy of the original Doom games (I and II), you won't be happy.
This game is fast paced, immensely fun, and differs greatly from the original Doom games. It has a perk/skill system, weapon upgrades, glory kills, and a few other "new style" game additions. Coming from an old school gamer who has been gaming for about thirty years, this may seem like a bad thing.
It's not. This game is a sequel done right. They have made changes to increase the replayability, and ensure the pace of the game is kept up. They nailed it.
The controls are on point, it runs well on moderate systems, and it will keep you wanting more. This is a fantastic game, and I would recommend it to anyone who is into a fast paced, single player FPS game.

Updated 10/31/17 *Covered Multiplayer now*
DOOM (2016)
Great shooter, probably the best I've played in the last 4 years. But the platforming makes me wanna tear my hair out! The way the game registers whether you've grabbed onto a ledge, or not is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and has probably caused most of my death's so far on any difficulty mode. Advanced platforming in a first person shooter just doesn't work Half-Life already proved this decades ago.
Rant aside though this is a pure-blooded shooter at it's core and a darn good one at that. Wide-variety of weapons to take on a variety of enemies. Combat stress's reflex's, and movement control over sheer aim like CS:GO for example. Level design is constantly changing from wide open arena's to claustrophobic environment's forcing you to adapt or die. The  story is understated, subtle environmental narration is what pulls you in to read codex entries that flesh out the lore. It's a wonderful balance that doesn't hinder gameplay, or ever pull control away from the player.
Sound design is top-notch, surround directional audio could've been better, but the raw quality of FX captured is phenomenal. Demons are harrowing, and voice actor's for characters like Samuel Hayden demand authority. Weapons are punchy focusing on the mid-low to low frequencies, basshead's will get a kick out of this.
Visuals strike a perfect balance between looks, and performance with plenty of scalability. The implementation of Vulkan is a godsend in a sea of DirectX title's, offering better overall performance for the majority of graphics card's. Ton's of beautiful post-processing effects with standout's being depth-of-field, motion blur, and high-quality bloom.  I tested Doom on a GTX 660ti (2GB Vram), and an R9 390 (8GB Vram). Both scaled superbly with settings being appropriately placed at low, 900p, on the former, and medium-high, 1080p, for the latter. Managing to hit an average of 100fps on both card's.
I invested about 13 hours into the multiplayer until I reached LVL 50, 1st prestige, or equivalent of it in Doom. Multiplayer is definiately an after thought, it's not balanced, some loadouts are more versatile and better than others, it's not a good competitive game mode either, but it is a fun casual experience. A large variety of maps, demon power-ups are great until your on the receiving end, it remind's me of COD killstreaks to a certain extent in which an already good player only get's more assistance to streamroll you even harder. As it stands I would consider it a poor man's Unreal Tournament, doesn't come close to being as fast as Quake for example. Ultimately your mileage may vary when it comes to enjoyment of mp.
All in all Doom (2016) proves that late 90's shooters are the apex of the genre, which since then have been bogged, padded, or distilled with silly mechanics and mediocre level design. It is the essence of what makes a great shooter, and is captured in a bloody bottle.
Final Score: 9/10

I finally got around to playing doom.  After 25 years of waiting, I'm blown away by what people could do in the 90s with graphics technology at the time.
Oh of course this isn't the original doom, and of course I've played Doom MANY times on many different systems.  But I also did grow up in the 80s and 90s and gave Doom to me as an impressionable child of only 12.   And ignoring what Jack Thompson would spout for years later I grew up to be a game developer and not a murderer.   Doom was one of those revolutionary games.
24 years later, Doom came out again, the original team is no longer at ID but... if we grabbed that team and transported magically through time, Doom would probably look, play, and perhaps feel the same as this game.  And it's really DAMN brilliant.
If I tried to sell a company on "DOOM" as it is, and called it anything else, I think I would be laughed out of an office.  A FPS where the story isn't the focus.  Where it's just room after room of fighting the same enemies, simple weapons that were made 20 years ago, and just the most ultra violence I could make.
The thing is, DOOM is a game you can't make any more for all those reasons, it's probably TOO violent, it's mostly simplistic, and it's repetitive.    But this isn't any game, this is a vitalization of a franchise that started the genre and honestly anything but what this game is, would be a crime.
There's really too many brilliant things to mention.  There is a story, but it's clear through action (not words) the main character isn't having any of it.  There's repetation but my god the action is INTENSE that even going through the same enemies thirty or forty times is intense.  Even the gameplay is run and gun, not "War run and gun" But this is DOOM classic run and gun.  An attack is coming at you?  Move out of the way.  Do that again and again and return fire and that's honestly a bit of brilliance in the modern era.  Raycasted bullets are the standard, but dear god, this breaks that mold.
Then there's the violence, and it's QUITE over the top, but you know what? You're fighting demons from hell, using all sorts of weapons on them, and while the violence is visceral and in your face, it fits with the game's themes.
There's the fact you fight enemies over and over, but this is a masterclass in level design.  The enemies have a good variety, but change slowly, the locations though are always epic, and you feel awesome ducking behind different areas, and seeing different elements of level design come into play, like the verticality and circular levels.   It's really exceptionally well done, something Romero would only have been able to dream of all those years ago.
There's just a solo problem with the entire game, and that's the music.   E1M1 (At Doom's gate) is a masterpiece of audio that may not have been topped in video games, it gets you ready, puts you in the fight and gets your blood pumping, just listening to is just so awesome.
New Doom however.  The music isn't "bad" but there's definitely a lacking edge to this music and it's the single area that the game hasn't topped the original, but being unable to top a masterpiece isn't a horrible problem.  And while the music might not live up to it, the entire rest of the game gives with both barrels.
There's Snapmap, and multiplayer and while snap map is interesting as an experiment, and multiplayer is decent, I didn't really feel a reason to return to either of them even with the improvements.  What you want to do here is play Doom, the most excellent of retro shooters, perhaps the only game that should be this retro and does so with the perfect style.
But to be honest, this is a game that's going to be retro, and I really wish everyone could and would enjoy it.  The fact is much of this game is a return to form of a 25 year old game, however gaming has moved on in those 25 years, yet every "return to form" is exactly that.  It's returning to the great old days, not the rose tinted nostalgia days that were "better back then" but it returns us to what was great about those days and makes us glory in it.
So while not every single person will like it (Some people will never be able to accept the super fast pace action), I can't do anything BUT recommend this game as to me I'd call it the perfect sequel to Doom.    And god I can't wait for the next one.
Just please don't call the next one Doom 2, it's confusing enough calling this one DOOM.

So I've been playing this game for a few weeks (I think), I wake up in the morning, and I'm thinking hey, I'll check my progress on Adventure Capitalist before I go to work. And so I stare into those progress bars for a while. And then the thought passes through my mind. The thought that started it all. The thought that should not be.
What if I just stayed here? What if I didn't even go to work?
And then, in thinking that thought, I was struck with a sudden realisation.
I hate my job so much that I would rather watch a bunch of progress bars earn me fake money than go to my real job and do whatever it is I even do and earn real money.
But yet, I have to. I'm not even human anymore. I'm just a slave. I don't even know who I am anymore, because slaves don't get to have identities. I can't do it. I'd rather kill myself than go to my real job. But I have to go there. The only reason I haven't killed myself is because I'm afraid of death and I don't want to leave people behind. This isn't a meme review. I seriously want to commit suicide. It's better than suffering through the daily grind. And this? This game? This is just an abstract representation of the daily grind.
The only difference, really, between this game and a job is that you become homeless and die if you don't have a job. With this game there's no commitment. You can quit whenever you want. But if that's the only difference, is that the sole reason why you don't quit? Because you can? And yet when there's a job that you can't quit, you want to. But you can't, so you quit life.
Nothing makes sense. It took this game to make me realise that. This game made me realise that I wish I was dead.

But I mean, whatever. Does it even matter anymore? This game could be the best thing ever, it could be a load of garbage, in the end I still have to get up and go to work the next day. It makes no difference.

This is a good modern/futuristic turn based strategy game, in the likes of Panzer General, that went completely under the radar.
War on Folvos is set in a modern/future setting, the game has a decent storyline about a nation that gets invaded and 'rises up' against the invaders. War on Folvos offers players the chance to play as either side, the invaders, or the rebels. Each side has an interesting mix of units - some based off of real-world vehicles.
The combat mechancis are good, with units having a set number of 'action points' per turn that allows them to maneuver or shoot - or both. Additionally, there is a logistical layer that limits fuel and ammunition per unit. Both sides have repair/resupply vehicles that keep units supplied and repaired.
Overall fun game. Good price. Pick it up.

This was my second playthrough of Deus Ex: HR. It was just as entertaining as the first one.
There's a lot of bad ratings for this game and I don't know why. Haven't encountered any bugs, crashes or anything like that to merit a negative rating.
What struck me most during my second playthrough is how actually average the game looks. I know graphics are not the only factor in a game but it always helps when it looks good. It's a game from 2011 and it hasn't aged well. I'm currently playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R Clear Sky and even though it's a game from 2008 it looks way better - higher resolution textures, better lighting effects and so on.
Story wise it's an ok game. If you like conspiracies and stuff, you'll like the plot of the game. If you don't, well it's still enjoyable and engaging.
The strength of the game lays in how it reacts to your choices. It's not just some key moments in the game like dialogs and stuff. The way you augment your character will have a huge impact on how you can approach/reach your goals. Same goes for your equipment and how you choose to upgrade it. Everything has a bigger or smaller impact on gameplay. Sure there are lots of games with skill trees, abilities, guns and such, but Deus Ex HR is designed in a way that makes you feel your choices leading you on a certain path. If you augment your hacking skills you'll be able to bypass security easily without detection. If you get cloak, you can sneak into heavily patroled areas. If you don't, you'll have to figure out another way or go guns blazing. With each decision the game locks some doors and opens others. That is why it has replay value as you can test different kinds of approaches, different augmentations etc.
It's a fun game worth trying. Even if you don't like the plot, there's still a solid FPS game in there. You can stealth it or go berserk. How you play is your choice.

I'm a strategic player that adores strategy games, especially when they have deep customizations systems and base building.
I've played this game over 12 hours, out of those I enjoyed the first 1-2 and the rest have been tedious and have been spent more or less farming. I played this game on normal difficulty but regardless of difficulty I can sadly not recommed this game.
Firstly I will say this game is 90% gameplay it lacks story and other elements to make it interesting therefore I will heavily focus on gameplay in this review.
This game consists of mainly two gameplay parts:
-The "space map" part were you spend all your time focusing on where to allocate your resources. For example, where will your manpower go, will they explore, fight, upgrade or farm resources. You think this will be interesting and engaging with all the different choices to make on what to upgrades and what to build and especially with where you will send your space fleet. However because you basically have tons of free time you feel like you can do everything and you are always in control therefore this mode feels superflous. I go into more details on this later
-The "fight" part, this is classic final fantasy style turn based combat. There are two different kinds, space combat and land combat and they both work similary but slightly different and with wholley different skills and different settings. The fight part of this game is too hard and too easy at the same time. I mentioned in the previous segment that the game gives you a lot of time to do whatever you which during "space time", the thing is the enemy that attacks you are always pretty weak. You can defeat them fairly easily if you are a decent strategy player and plan so you fight with full HP. I say the fights are fairly easy but the game keeps throwing these easy enemies your way, all the time and the thing is the combat is very slow. You keep defeating enemy after enemy, but every battle(even if you vastly outpower your enemies) takes 5-10 minutes. But what about the bosses you say, yeah they are hard, they are definitely challening but not only in a good way. The boss battles are hard and also very random, sometimes there are nothing you can do, you were just simply unlucky and that is even more annoying when you need to win several battles in a row(which many boss battles do).
The summary of this game is weird, its too easy and too hard at the same time. The battles are normally easy but they are always time consuming resulting in tedium and you farming. Since the bosses are hard you need to farm even more to defeat them and advance the story which results in even more tedium. The bosses are the fun part but they feel very reliant on RNG and the time it takes to get to a point were you can take on a boss is not fun. Its bizarre really. The "space map" part is easy as pie, the battles are easy but time consuming and you need to spend tons of time doing these easy boring parts because they bosses are hard and depending on your luck frustrating. Highering the difficulty would not help this since it would just make the bosses even more hard and the time consuming battles even more tedious even if they might get more fun because they would be more challenging.
This game had tons of potential but sadly they have totally botched the balance and pacing in this game.

This game is a great platform for all kinds of amazing content and feature expansions down the road. However, it is just too simple and deterministic right now. There needs to be more risk, emergent elements, and tactical depth before it can reach a level of engagement on par with comperable games like FTL or Darkest Dungeon.
In short, after only a few hours, I felt like this game had nothing more to offer me.
In terms of tactics, I cant put my finger on exactly what is missing because I am not a game designer, but all of the combat seems very simple and static compared to games like Darkest Dungeon -- which is a game that has basically the same turn based mechanics, but is still somehow more challenging and dynamic.
I will definitely revisit this game after a few patches, content updates, or DLC purchases -- but until then I can't recommend it.

Highly addictive 4X game. Like Civilization in space. A little rough around the edges in terms of the user interface but lots of fun. If you don't build lots of ships and wage lots of war it can get pretty monotonous. The introductory tutorial was so complicated I almost stopped playing but I really got into it after that.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS: it has one of the best interfaces I've seen in a 4X game in a long (long!) time. Streamlined, polished, modern... whatever action/item you want access to is usually no farther than 2 clicks away. This is not a minor feat, since interface is what you are constantly interacting with in these kind of games. Combat system, with its "card game" mechanics, is a mixed bag -I liked so far, but I can undersand people reacting negatively to it. I think I will have a more educated opinion with a couple of dozen hours of gamplay under my belt, but as I said, so far combat is working for me. Tech tree is comprehensive and intrincate, nothing to envy of Galactic Civilizations or Sid Meier's Civilization itself. Exploring is compelling and empire management hits the right balance between being detailed but not overwhelming.
As I said, these are just FIRST IMPRESSIONS, with only around 5 hours of gameplay. Most important feature yet to evaluate is AI; too litlle interaction yet. So far, I recommend this game as a true succesor of GalCivII. I will update further down the road.

Outstanding game! This truelly is a gem for all who love fast pase, thinking 2 steps ahead, cute cartoony character beat em up games... BUT! This game have a slight twist then the normal beat em up game...
There are no direct control of your hero's movement, they taking turns jump into then fight then withdraw when the next hero enter the battle, and the control have been split for both left and right hand...
Left hand WASD = Controlls the roaster of heroes in your team, game will auto rotate your heroes if no extra command was given, but you can use WASD keys to force select a hero from your roaster so you can unleash one of his skill that is not in cooldown.
Right hand IHJK = Controlls the 4 skills of each hero. J is the basic attack, that every heroes start with at lv1. K is advanced tier attack, and H is higher tier attack, Heroes unlock this 2 at higher level. I is ultimate attack, and also the last skill to be unlocked, they are not just dealing large amount of damage, they also laster way longer then any other attacks, and the lasting effect extend into 1-2 more heroes's turn.
The goal of this game is to plan and form combos with the attacks of your heroes, and use those attack to ether stunlock or push back waves of enemy, but enemy do have special ability or will be located at areas that some attacks just won't be able to touch them, so it will be up to the player to form up a team of heroes to bring down those annony buggers.
This game have a really fast gaming pace, really nice graphic for an indie game, funky cartoony design... It is fun to play, and even the music make me want to record it for my MP3 player!!
Okie.. I forgot to mention the down side... Due to this is a Chinese indie game, so far only some of the dialogues (most of them) and menus were translated into English, other in-game signs like "Let The Battle Begin!", "Show them what you can do!" and "Victory!" are still in Chinese... So it might be eyesore for some Internet Nazi, but not a big issue for normal game player. :P

Blockland is that game where you build "stuff". offten accused of being a copy of Roblox or Minecraft, Blockland is in fact it's own genre. its more of a Garrys Mod with blocks than a Minecraft clone. in fact Blockland came out in 2007 compared to Mincrafts 2010 release.
Anyways like i said in Blockland you can build whatever you can image and build with blocks. i am not very good myself at building and creating but even then Blockland is fun. you can play gamemodes like Deathmatch using any weapon you want. even better Blockland has an "event" system that allows players to make extreme almost script like content.
The best part of Blockland has to be the thousands of mods you can get for it on Return to Blockland, a mod within itself that lets you easily download addons for Blockland all most like Steam Workshop. what kind of addons? well all most anything, there are addons that add new bricks, addons that give you more weapons, addons that give you new things to drive, addons that give you different colors to use in builds, and addons that add gamemodes. some modders have added zombies and left for dead like gamemodes. there are racing game modes and plan old sandbox gamemodes.
Blockland is uber fun with people online or even a LAN game. the problem is that Blockland seems to have network issues. regularly kicking you from games or even just not letting you join them. and as with Garry's mod if you join a server with addons that you don't have, getting them from the server will be a pain. i also wish Blockland had a voice talk ability in Multiplayer but that can be solved by using TeamSpeak or some such service.
Blockland suffers from an outdated game engine know as Torque 3D. while the newest version of Torque itself is not bad Blockland uses the older version.the game did just get Shader support it came at the cost of Blockland maps. Maps had terrain and objects that where not made out of blocks. but because the Shader system could not support the maps they where removed. meaning the only way you can get terrain is if you build it out of blocks. not a problem for people good with the blocks and those with a good computer. because having that many blocks hits the Frame Rate pretty bad.
In the end Blockland is a fun sandbox game that lets you do a lot of epic stuff. as long as your comptuer can handle it. it is in NO WAY a clone of Mincraft, Roblox, or any other block like game. if you enjoy games like Garry's Mod then Blockland will be perfect for you.

This is a very awesome and accurate 3d representation of guns and how they break down piece for piece. There are several modes of play from a basic field strip to a full on disassembly of the gun right down to the last screw and spring. There is a reassmebly mode and then there are 3 different game modes that require you to do a full disassemble and reassemble while being timed with bonuses for not clicking any of the wrong pieces among others. This game has a large and beautiful catalog of guns to choose from. Everything from Mauser to Glock as well as Beretta, Colt, AK variants, Heckler and Koch, Fabrique Nationale, Walther and many others.
This is a fantastic game for any gun enthusiast. It will make you a lot more knowledgeable about the guns and how they break down. You can also see an x-ray view of how the gun works in real time or slow motion while it is in operation.
If that isn't enough you can also fire guns off at firing ranges as you unlock them. (You must unlock guns as well as ranges) One downfall to this is that it doesn't let you choose which gun to use at the range. The ranges have 4 games which are preset to certain guns.
In the end I don't think there is much to complain about. The game is free, and it has tons of guns. You can compete for high scores with other players and friends. You can learn about all of the parts of the guns, and you can even select an option that allows you to see the names of each and every part.
If you love guns, get this game. You won't regret it.
I own a beretta 92FS and I will say the break down of the gun in the game is 100% accurate to the real thing. Every spring, every pin, every screw. Perfect to a fault.
Rating: 10/10

My xbox 360 controller 1500 hours of Rocket League, I needed a new one. I DID NOT want a steam controller but I decided to try something different for a change. Most people who posted about the Steam Controller, did not recommend it for Rocket League however once I got it I was surprised with the results.
Pros (for me personally)

The size - I have big hands, I feel like I could crush a xbox 360 controller if I grip it. The Steam Controller is bulky but it fits my hands perfectly.
The back paddles - I knew alot of controllers were coming out with this feature but I did not think it would be so useful, I dont have to try and move my trigger finger to the buttons when I need to press 2 buttons at a time, I can program the back to be any controller I desire.
Customization - When moving from Console to PC alot of people are often concered with how to build the pc, they find it too hard because there's so much that can be customized. The Steam Controller is the embodiment of that same idea, you can customize your pc anyway possible the same goes for this controller. There's so much that be achieved by using the Steam Controller's custom settings, It's up to you to decide how you want it.
Cons (for me personally)
Cheap material - When putting in the batteries my finger nails at some point were able to dig into the back leaving marks, they wernt even that long.
Price - I paid $50 for this controller, I missed the summer sale deal by a couple hours. I did not want to pay $50 for it, but I had the money in my steam funds already, and I don't buy games very often. I still do not think it's worth the $50 despite how much iv'e enjoyed it so far, I wish I could've gotten it for the summer price, because now I want to return it for a refund.
I do like the Steam Controller, I just don't like the price for it, despite what It's capable of I think it's too cheaply made. I don't think It'll last me very long.

Nothing I have done has worked, and the worst part is that this is apparently an issue people have been having since an update that came out in the spring of 2016. The fact that ID and Bethesda haven't fixed this issue after over 18 months is nothing less than unforgivable and I cannot in good conscious recommend anyone buy this off of steam. If you absolutely MUST get it, I highly suggest either getting the console version, since that won't run into any sort of issues when trying to run it, or better yet, pirate it first to make sure you can actually play the game before you spend any money on a game that doesn't work.

This review comes after a Hard Playthrough on Alternative Rule.
Rabi Ribi is a Metroidvania style 2d platform game with a focus on Bullet Hell.  You play as Erina, a rabbit turned human, with her friend Ribbon the fairy, on a journey to discover why Erina became a human.
The gameplay is incredibly fluid. Most of the bullet hell sections are found in the form of Boss Battles, of which there are tons. The premise of a boss fight is to usually learn their patterns and get better at them over multiple tries, although some will be easily conquerable in one attempt. Erina's hitbox is quite forgiving, but you'll still find yourself being hit over and over if you can't react fast enough. Bullet Hell is a very particular type of genre, one not everyone enjoys, but Rabi Ribi tries its best to be appealing to everyone by offering multiple game difficulties from the get go, from masochistic (for people like me), to, 'I'm just here for the 'story''.
Combat itself is simple, you have your main attack, the hammer, which you use for the bulk of close combat damage andRibbon attacks using spells which are very useful for long range combat and keeping up a combo, Erina controls very tightly and very rarely will you take damage out of fault other than your own. There are a multitude of powerups that affect combat, and each makes combat more interesting and fun.
The game, as a 2D platformer, of course offers ton to explore and discover. You can completely bypass some powerups in your first playthrough, and there are tons of upgrades hidden across the map, some in plain sight, others very well hidden. The game also offers multiple ways to play, such as speedruns, boss rushes, and 0% item runs.
Rabi Ribi's main flaw is its story. Its very simple and, while that's not inherently a downside by itself, you won't find any grand tale in this game. It usually just comes down to 'we need helpers, go find some' do a plot point 'we need more helpers'. There are some good moments here and there, and an anime fan would definitely enjoy the entire thing, but its definitely not my cup of tea.
As many others have said before me, do not judge this game before you have played it. The game looks like a girly anime game that should be written off before even being played, but if you're a fan of Metroidvania games like Shantae or Dust, or a fan of Bullet Hell games such as Touhou or Nuclear Throne, you'll find yourself enjoying Rabi Ribi a great bunch.

I won't really be able to add a lot that hasn't already been said in other reviews, but here's my 2 cents...
I've been playing MWO since early 2013. I know there are many players who've played from the start, but this is the only "MMO" game I've stuck with. EVE online is the only other one that compelled me to really gave it a chance with, but after a month I was done for several reasons. Mostly, I just wasn't having fun.
MWO on the other hand has been my go to game since I started playing it. I don't play daily(except during my vacations), but I do play several hours a day on my weekends. and more importantly, I look forward to playing every single week. The only other game that can say that for me is XCOM(and hopefully XCOM 2). I can either sit down and play 3 hours of matches without a break, or play 1-2, take a break/eat/deal with the kids/etc.. the play some more. Or, I can just spend time in the mech lab trying out different configs and builds.
voice/text chat during matches is, for the vast majority of the time, pleasant and good natured. Of course there is always "that guy" on occasion, but that's the exception, not the rule. forum wise, the community is VERY passionate. the can and will debate over what to an outsider seems like a very trivial matter to someone outside the community. size of hit boxes, XL vs standard engines in certain mechs, scale, the merit of weapon types, and on and on and on... Is there toxic players/posters? yes. just like in all games. and unfortunately that passion the community has can make for some very disgruntled players who are upset over things that happened long ago. sometimes they have a valid point. too often a minor thing is turned into a conspiracy theory based on nothing but their feels.
which brings me to PGI. stellar company? no. to be frank, they REALLY messed up and tripped coming out of the gate at the start of development. VERY bad balance choices that took them far too long to correct. poor communication. poor feed back. over promising. unrealistic  release dates. poor marketing choices. rushed clan mechs. and so on. having said that, ditching IGP really helped clear up a lot of those problems. and in the last year and a half VAST improvements in those categories have been made. My only real issue at the moment is that it still feels like new features are talking too long to implement(looking at you CW phase 3).
But having said all that, the important thing is gameplay. gameplay trumps all else in my opinion, and as I said, this is the game I keep coming back to week after week. and that's all that matters to me.
so to sum up my opinion on MWO...It's a F2P game, that's not pay to win, has a pretty decent community barring a few individuals, is still being developed(even if I wish it was quicker about that) good graphics for what it is, immersive, and most importantly...it's fun.
I recommend you give it a shot and see if you like it. after all, it's free.
A good game, I'd give it a solid 7/10. It has the potential to be a great game, and while it has a steep learning curve it's worth the time.

Let's just get this out of the way right here, right now: this game is *hard.* Hard to understand for most folks, hard to play by the same, and most definitely hard to fully and truly master. If you love giant freakin' robots with lasers, giant guns, and rockets pouring out the ears, this'll be your cup of tea for sure.
But if you're going the free-to-play route, you're going to have an uphill slog ahead.
See, buying any pack of 'mechs whatsoever gives you a leg-up on getting the purchased 'mechs mastered. If you've read the reviews of some other players, you'll know what this means: getting three variants of the same 'mech chassis, just to grind experience on them so you can unlock all their upgrades on the skill tree in order to up their performance in the field. And MWO is going to be one hell of a grindfest; you'll be grinding for C-Bills to purchase new 'mechs, grinding those 'mechs in the field so you can get their performance upped, and grinding General XP so you can unlock beneficial modules that'll keep you on the game and competitive.
Trust me when I say that just cause' my record *says* so many hours, it's oh so much more than that. And let's just say that I was on well before they introduced Trial 'mechs that were "optimized" (read: upgraded and given a weapons loadout that compliments them).
All in all you really should go in loving giant stompy war machines in order to get any mileage out of this game. And start learning to be sociable too: you'll want to be in a group of players you trust and play beside frequently in order to pierce the heavy metal veil that is Community Warfare. To those of you interested and playing; keep at it and don't give up. Bite the bullet and keep at the controls. Oh, and hit the academy, the lessons'll help a lot. Because after all this struggle, the first time you core an enemy Assault 'mech after a hard fight against it? It's likely gonna feel like an accomplishment, like you yourself managed to bring down a titanic 80+ ton bipedal war machine of death and destruction. Yes, even if you had help from your teammates!
Now for the record: I recommend you *try* MWO at least before you judge it, as in *really* try it. Don't just struggle through a few matches, give up, and delete it from your Steam library either; like I said, it takes time to get used to this circus and the troupe of monkeys (BattleMechs) you need to train.

10 Second Ninja is a really cool little platformer aimed for speedrunners! It's more of an initiation to speedrunning than a game tailored for experienced speedrunners, but it's probably enjoyable to both sides!
Each level has a 10 second limit, taking some of Super Meat Boy's standards to the extreme, with quick restarts and keeping the player in the action at all times.
I've 100% the game a bit after 4 hours, which includes beating the game in 4 minutes.
The level themselves are pretty easy to beat, but getting the 3 stars (for time) can be infuriating! In a good way, though. Missing the mark for 0.02 seconds is tough, but finally getting the 3 stars is really rewarding as well!
The boss fights were rather uninspired, but it's easy to overlook that.
There are several worlds, each introducing a small mechanic and making use of it.
It might be a bit price-y for its content, but the game itself is pretty good! The short length fits nicely, and it's a nice game to start up once in a while to make a quick <5 minutes speedrun. I like it.
The humour in the game was a bit of a flop to me, but hey... the level design was nice and the game felt responsive most of the time.
If you can get it cheap and the idea of speedrunning attracts you, give it a go! Some games can be overwhelming but 10 Second Ninja may just be the byte-sized introduction you're looking for.

So, I haven't played the game long, and already I love it. I am fairly certain that I am going to "die horribly" my first time through, and fail to save the Galaxy, because I picked the standard difficulty level. I will say that the tutorial is bare bones at best, and doesn't teach you how to do many of the things that will be essential to figure out. That said, the game is not so punishing as to crush you for a tiny mistake (or in my case, three lost days because I didn't understand why it wasn't letting me explore farther reaches of the station).
The game is a mix of RPG, base builder, and strategy game. Plus some diplomacy thrown in. Use your fleet to guard those bases you can, evacuate the ones you can't. Both help you out. You get more crew from evacuating bases, but you get more resources from agreeing to protect them from the big bads.
With all these elements the game is complex, but not complicated. And the tutorial does cover most of the essential stuff, space combat, building ships, researching technologies, etc.  Ground combat is not covered, which seems an odd ommission, but it works more or less the same as space combat.
