I must say that I am not even a fan of metroidvanias or even bullet hell games. Yet, Rabi-Ribi managed to be one of my favorite games all the time.
Definitely worth the price!
Rabi-Ribi is an action platformer game in which the player explore a massive metroidvania-like map. There are lots of bosses to beat, attacking the player using swarms of bullets which create a pattern (hence the bullet hell).
I am not an expert of bullet hell games myself, but I believe a good bullet hell game involves "readable" patterns (both bullets and attack patterns). By this, I don't mean an easy-to-read patterns. At least the player needs to be able to figure out how to dodge any kind of bullet patterns. Rabi-Ribi has them. They may seem overwhelming at first, but after several trials and errors you will eventually figure them out. That said, there may be times when you just can't dodge the bullets no matter what. But not to worry, the game provides a workaround for this. You can enter invincibility mode for several seconds just by a mere button push, but the amount is kinda limited. If you got hit it's not the end of the world either, so you should not worry about dodging every single bullet. Just don't get hit too much.
The combat mechanic is fluid enough. Hammer attacks may seem like a single button push at first, but as you advance the game a whole bunch of attacks to build your combo will be added. Uppercut, sliding attack, aerial rolling attack, air dash, carrot bomb, drill attack, etc. Your partner Ribbon covers your weakness in attack range by giving you a wide range of ranged attacks (pun intended) and some nukes.
Tons of upgrades also included in form of badges, items, and power-ups. Badges are meant to be used in a certain situation, while the power-ups are just straightforward buffs. But you should be aware that using them means fighting more advanced enemies. So they should be used sparingly.
Also, secrets. The game has lots of them secret contents. On your first playthrough it may be hard to get 100% of the items since many of them are hidden.
And the most interesting of all, you can even beat the game without any items–including the hammer!
Do you think the term "bullet hell" is an abomination created by a cultist who worships satan for them hardcore masochists? Well... fear not! Rabi-Ribi includes seven types of difficulty for any kind of player. If you haven't played any bullet hell games before, you may try the casual difficulty first. But IMO the novice one provides more suitable challenge while also forgiving at the same time.
For those who are familiar with the bullet hell genre but finds touhou games too challenging, there is normal difficulty. It is a perfect difficulty for starters before you tackle the higher ones: Hard or Hell.
But maybe you're THE masochist, aren't you? Then step up to the challenge. Clear the impossible or even bunny extinction mode! Also don't forget that there are speedrun and boss rush mode. In addition, the game has a huge amount of achievements but around 50% of them are either challenging or need a lot of effort to achieve. For instance, the dodge masters (Take 0 damage while fighting a decent boss), Sequence-breaking, 100%-ing, and speedrunning achievements. And did I mention no-items run?
Lots of other reviewers said the story is "meh". While I understand this point of view, I don't think it is all that bad. It may not have deep or intriguing plot points, and sometimes the plot doesn't even make sense. But for me it's entertaining enough to make me wanting to know more about the plot. It fits the theme (Cute magical girls in a magical world) and the gameplay (another day, another boss fight) too. I think the story feels like those moe slice-of-life animes. No depth, no plot twists, no sense made, just moe girls (and some humor).
The characters' role needs a rework, though. So many characters in this game, but they lack purpose. They exist only for the sake of... existing. While having distinctive character design and backstory, many side characters contribute almost nothing to the plot, making you question whether they are relevant to the story or not.
Oooh, boy! I love the aesthetics. The characters are so adorable, suitable to my taste. Call me a moefag if you want :p
On a serious note, if you like moe anime-styled games, then you may like this game. One may even say that it's the art that keeps you playing the game. And not to mention the design of the world. Both of them synergically creates an experience: Being in a cute, colorful world.
However, the pixel art style feels kinda off to me. This may be my personal opinion, but consistent anime style for both the characters and the world will fit better. Not saying that it's a bad design choice, though. At least it's not cancerous.
While the art is good and all, the only thing that hooked me up is the music. I once thought this game is just like some other anime games, cute anime girls but no engaging gameplay. Once I heard the music on that trailer, I bought it almost instantly. And I'm still glad that I did. The music fits the mood, theme, and world perfectly. Some tracks felt bland however, but it's not much.
Rabi-Ribi has controller support, and I believe it works best with controllers. That said, I'm a keyboard player, and the controls for keyboard are easy to master. The bunny amulet invincibility buff needs two keys to activate, though, which may be annoying if you want to release it in less than a second. Thankfully the game lets you define one shortcut key for not only the bunny amulet but also the air dash attack.
You can remap the keys if you don't like the default setting. I don't know about controllers, but one thing I don't like about this is that you have to remap ALL of the keys even though you just want one and only one. This is a chore even for me.
Well, it's a 2D platformer game, so it should not have any issues on a laptop using integrated graphics card, right? Well, that's not the case for Rabi-Ribi. The game did run well in 60FPS on my rig. But I had huge FPS drop on my Pentium 2.13GHz laptop with Intel HD Graphics, resulting in slow-motion gameplay. My other laptop (Pentium 1.9GHz, also Intel HD) had the same problem. Those laptops run 2D and 3D games with DirectX 9.0 just fine, though. So I think those system requirements are pretty much underestimated... or this game just hates onboard graphics.
In short, I recommend this game for the fans of bullet hell or anime-styled games, no matter your skills. I don't play metroidvania that much, but I think metroidvania fans will like it too. Don't expect engaging story, since you won't find it here. And if you think anime is cancer then it would be best if you just move along and find other games that are not cancerous for you.
Final verdict: 8.5/10

Good game. You manage, expand, and secure an underground base before moving into an overworld and attack-moving through groups of enemies. The base management is a cycle of digging to make space for rooms/to look for gold veins for money and building rooms in order to get access to a huge variety unit/trap/spell tech or upgrades. There's little-to-no APM requirement for the overworld battles or base-building, so you can plow your deathball into some bad guys and return to tinkering with your base while the battle rages.
The one issue I have experienced with the game is that traps and spells are almost useless compared to the sheer cost-effectiveness of combat units. There's one spell that's essential, which is a portal that allows your forces to teleport back to the underground or directly into the overworld, which combined with the fact that you can grab and drop units at will in the underground, eliminates the need for traps to defend from enemy incursions. In addition, spells are very weak compared to your deathball's DPS, and there's no hotkeying spells, so you're better off managing your dungeon or even microing back wounded units during battles.
Although I would much prefer that spells and traps have more to them than fun factor, I enjoyed my time with Dungeons 3. There's something about carving out an underground labryinth and smashing through enemies that never gets old.

I really like the Overlord series, as well as dungeon building, and Dungeons 2 was my first entry into this series.
The previous game had a lot of fun stuff, but some of it felt a little unbalanced.
Those issues are solved in Dungeons 3. I had enough confidence in the developer that I pre-purchased and stayed up all night to make sure I could play the first second I could when it released.
The demo isn't pointless- I don't think you can get 90% (or any) of the achievements, but you CAN play some missions that show the story between the end of Dungeons 2 and beginning of Dungeons 3, so I'd suggest playing that.
The main character and narrator are frenemies, and the two of them have a sarcastic humor that feels somewhere in between Monty Python and Bard's Tale (which they make references to). There's a lot of fourth-wall breaking jokes, which is good for an eye-rolling laugh or two (per mission, at least).
The tech UI for Dungeons 2 was wonky, but not in Dungeons 3. Just click the icons on the left panel to bring up things like recruitment, unit overview, spells, and tech (such as troop count/availability/quality, room/trap availability, and various upgrades).
There are very few missions that offer a challenge, but there is always "hellish" mode! Nice way to learn the story ASAP and then if you want a challenge do it again (or hellish to begin with).
Another upgrade from Dungeons 2 is the Infinite Gold tiles. In the first game, if you took too long or goofed around with mazes or got your units killed a lot, then you'd run out of gold and you couldn't do anything- not that it ever happened to me. The infinite gold spots in Dungeons 3 counter this easily- each dungeon has a couple, so you'll find them if you dig around enough. You'll probably find it anyway when making a trap maze.
There are benefits to all 3 of the themes:
-Horde-
1. Orcs do average damage, have high armor and health, and are good tanks because of it.
2. Naga do okay damage, but usually are too busy healing orcs.
3. Goblins don't usually get targeted if there's something else to hit, and do nice damage. Their gob-o-bot upgrade isn't as good as it was in Dungeons 2, and they lose their 'naturally not attacked' trait, but if their damage goes way up. If the mech gets destroyed then they get their ignore trait back. Kind of like an extra life for your damage dealer.
You need a Crypt in order to resurrect Horde troops.
-Demon-
1. Imps have excellent range and their magic not only penetrates armor, but does a lot of damage.
2. Succubi can charm stuff in combat, and out-of-combat can turn unconscious heroes into evil heroes that you control.
3. Spider demons don't have as good of range as an imp, but aren't melee either. They're a mid-range fighter that can slow an area.
All demons can meditate and generate mana which is used to cast spells and resurrect themselves. Demons also have low health and armor.
-Undead-
1. Banshees are very useful en-masse because of their debuff when they attack in melee.
2. Vampires naturally life-leech when killing heroes (or other things you find).
3. Liches have excellent damage with their ice magic, but imp fire and lich ice counter each other.
4. Zombies are free units! Killing heroes inside your dungeon (with a Cemetary) will get you up to 4 (4 per 'pack')
5. Skeletons are free units! Knocking heroes unconscious and making them starve to death in your Prison will get you up to 4 (4 per 'pack')
Undead come back to life on their own. Also, they don't eat, drink, or sleep.
There are 8 other troops that I won't describe. You might not even get them all through the game. Find that out yourself. However, I think you can see that the themes are balanced both within themselves and with each other.
My favorite thing in Dungeons 3? The Temple of the Dark Gods. If you're lucky, you can get a hundred packs of zombies even though you can normally only have 2 packs at most with all techs researched (or so, have to check map size). How fun would that be? Answer: very!

I have played a lot of Mechwarrior Online. To qualify that: I was one of the first 500 invited into the closed beta in 2012. I have also played community warfare (CW) with some of the best players in the game since that game mode was added over a year ago.
In 2011 I bought a 60 (Canadian) dollar founders pack for this game, because I feel that is a sane and reasonable limit to spend for a quality videogame product. And, despite the thumbs down on this review, at the time I was completely happy with my purchase. That 60 dollar founders pack came with an exclusive mech, 30 days of premium time, and 20 000 MC (the paid for currency of this game).
Today to buy the same collection of things in mechwarrior will cost you over 100 American dollars, and brings up the real issue I have with this game: The fun you will have is a byproduct of a gaming experience that has been designed from the ground up to take from you.
If you decide to play this game, you will face an extremely punishing grind. "Mastering" a mech involves grinding out three tiers of skills with xp, which unlocks various bonuses that are straight upgrades. If you want that 7.5% faster run speed (huge) you will need to basic out all the elite skills on 3 mechs of the same chassis, essentially slightly different versions of the same mech. This is assuming that you have ground out enough cash to purchase the 3 mechs, and outfit them with good weapons, and upgrade them properly. It goes without saying that all of this takes a significant amount of time.
The classic rebuttal to this is the argument that this is a free to play game, and people are free to pay to bypass the grind. That fails to denude the fact that this game will either take a lot of your time, or a lot of your money, or sometimes both (you can't buy those mastery skills but you can buy premium to help you grind faster). The carrot of mech stomping laser blasting fun lies at the top of a steep greasy hill, and the people on that hill will be firing at you the whole time you're climbing up.
This is the price you are expected to pay as a new player, and it is why I cannot recommend this game to any of my friends or you.
"review the game play" - Man in comments section
The basic controls and movement in MWO are actually pretty solid, it's probably the thing this game does the best. You feel like a big heavy mech, your arm weapons can track different target than your torso weapons, you get stuck on tiny rocks a LOT. That last item was sarcasm. You will constantly be clipping up against small pieces of terrain that don't really serve a purpose and can't be destroyed or crushed like a proper mech should be able to do. Also, as a related issue, there are problems with the hitboxes on a lot of terrain. You will often see your lasers and autocanons impact a rock that is visually several feet to the side. Also, there are no targets in this game other than enemy mechs. There are no tanks, vehicles, helicopters, or infantry to give you a sense of scale to undercut how much psychotic power you should be feeling while driving a multi story killing machine. The hitboxes on mechs also suffer a lot of problems related to their geometry. You can take damage on your back armour when being shot from the front sometimes for no reason.
The weapon balance in this game is atrocious, but I'm not going to be able to talk about balance in this game without incurring a LOT of vitriol from old timey mechwarrior fans who's deluded iron grip on a tabletop game that ceased to be relevant 20 years ago turns every rational discussion about balance in this game into a horde of mewling cries of "th th thats not like the tabletop!" So I expect to have a lot of fun with the comments section after this edit.
The battletech tabletop game doesn't let players control which part of the enemy mech they shoot, it's decided with 2d6 instead. In the land of first person shooters, you get to decide how you want to click on the screen, which is something a lot of the diehard tabletop crew isn't very good at and doesn't understand. In MWO, the best builds are the ones that do a ton of alpha damage to a concentrated specific part of the enemy mech, usually center torso or legs. That is just objectively the fastest way to kill someone. The best weapons for this are lasers, because they are hitscan, have decent range, and also weigh much less than their counterparts, ballistic and missile weapons. For the most part, there is no reason to use anything else. On the other end of the spectrum, you have long range missiles (LRMs) which are laughably useless. They require a target lock, and then you need to wait for a long arcing travel time while maintaining that lock for the missiles to connect. They hit in a spread pattern which doesn't synergize with the whole "kill them quickly" plan. They also have a minimum range, where the missiles just impact and do nothing. Also, the expensive and costly "target deprivation" pilot module breaks target lock as soon as you break line of sight. Experienced players who know how to position themselves almost never get hit.
Clan vs Inner Sphere is also a big problem. In Battletech lore, the clans are a seperate faction of militant space facists who show up halfway into the timeline so FASA could make some more money. Clan mechs run faster, carry more weapons for less weight, have improved cooling, carry more armour, and take more internal damage before being destroyed. They also have the only mechs in the game with MASC at the moment, which is basically a sprint button. The developers initially added clans into the game with the same values they had on the tabletop without really any balance considerations. Whoever had spent real money on a clan mech was god for several months. The developers tried to bring Inner Sphere mechs up to par by giving them "quirks" internal perks that are bound to specific chassis that do things like increase heat dissipation or decrease cooldown on specific types of weapons. This system works but only for a small handful inner sphere mechs out of hundreds of possible choices, the rest of them have mostly useless quirks, like increased range on anti missile systems (nobody uses these).
The reality of this is mostly ignored by a huge section of the community. You will rarely see good builds, even at the highest matchmaking tier. You will also run into a lot of people who call themselves "support players" which is just another way of saying that they will be the last on your team to die hiding behind a hill because they only brought LRMs. If you ask for advice, most of the time that advice will be wrong. I can honestly say that this is one of the most fanatically ignorant gaming communities that I have ever born witness to.
If you plan to play with anything less than 11 other friends this game is miserable to play from a team co-ordination perspective. Most solo queue matches involve teams milling around aimlessly until one of them is dead. If you queue up with a buddy, you will end up in the group queue with a bunch of other small un-cordinated teams usually sided against a full 12 man most of the time. If you queue up for CW by yourself things only get worse, because those games take longer, usually end up more lopsided, and have no actual matchmaking to determine who plays who.

I am giving this game a "do not recommend" due to the bugs I've experienced, the poor UI design, and tedious nature of the game.  This game could really be great with some more development time, but as of now it objectively isn't.  A common complaint that you'll see in other reviews is that 90% of your time in combat you're just setting up the exact same combos.  Yes, as your officers level up they get 3-4 new powers, but by level 7 you have all the good ones.  After that you're just spending points on abilities you'll never use.
Halcyon 6 has two very high quality elements, the art and the writing.  Thematically, its setting and pixel-art characters with unique names and abilities, as well as permadeath, draw similarities to FTL.  Comparisons to XCOM are generally only accurate in that there is a base with lots of rectangular rooms.
The positive elements keep the game fun enough at first, but it shows less polish the longer you play.  Accordingly, many of the positive reviews have very little playtime.  I have played two games, one in early access before deciding to wait for the full release, then 33hrs on a single Commander difficulty play through in full release (until the game broke).  Only 0.3% of players as of now have beaten this game on any difficulty, so I'd take reviews with shorter play times with some skepticism.
The game has a lot of bugs.  Not to the point that it's falling apart, but the bugs leech some of the fun out of the game.  A non-comprehensive list of the bugs I remember are:
-Game locks up at boss fight (obviously)
-At some point, my ships started failing to reroute without first visiting their original destination, retrying always costs fuel even though it never works, can cause unintended battles and delays in getting to desired destination.
-Officer got "stuck" and could not be assigned even though he was available, had to fly him out on a ship then bring him back.
-Tier 5 hangar says level 10 officer needed for task, but only accepts level 13 (probably a typo).
-Time does not always correlate to tasks correctly.  For example, I am rich because at some point my material multiplier broke and it completes at 400% speed (varies).
-Clicking the magnifying glass in the notification screen just deletes the notification.
Much worse than the bugs is the lack of many basic features you'd expect from a well-made game, and the elements that are objectively wrong.  Again, most of these aren't a huge deal in the first couple of hours, but by the latter half of the game I questioned if it had been play tested at all.
Ships:
-No fleet management screen, you have to start sending a fleet somewhere in order to adjust your fleet
-Ship management screen has no sorting methods.  Can't sort by captain rank, can't sort by ship tier, can't sort by anything.
-No idea what a ship can do until you pay to research it, so to formulate your best strategy you need to research all the available ships before you pick one, but you don't have that kind of money so you just pick one and hope it all works out.
Officers:
-Officer icons at the bottom of the screen indicate if they are flying, available, or doing a task.  But not where they are, where they are going, or time remaining on a task.  Clicking on their icon takes you to the officer's lounge, not the officer's actual location.  In the late game, the map gets much bigger, your base gets bigger, and there are dozens of active fleets.  Have fun searching for you ships and officers when you continue a game after being away for more than an hour.
-No text indication of experience gained or needed for officer level up.  Your ability to perform tasks and fly ships is tied to officer level, but you can't plan best strategies for gaining without knowing how you gain XP.
Map:
-Hitting "return home" always starts the clock, even though you can disable this in other places.  Again, when you have two fleets to deal with 30+ enemy fleets, time is of the essence.
-If an enemy is flying to "planet x," you have to search for it by hand or wait for the enemy to get there. Would a simple dotted line be too much to ask?
-"Days remaining" is meaningless.  If it says "29 day left" in a colony attack, that colony could be dead in 1 day.  Might be a bug?
-No way to jump to fleet location.
-No estimate for travel time of your ships, making strategy difficult.
Base:
-Often no visual indicator of an event taking place on base.  For example, a room was attacked in my base while my officers were away.  Later, I sent a fleet to the base to address it.  Which room was it again?  I just had to open and close each one.
-No way to take down a room you've built, so good luck if you get to the end game and want one of the newly available rooms.
-There's no queue for base tasks, so if you have an officer dedicated to mining resources, get ready for a clicker mini-game.
Combat:
-Can't skip a turn.
-Can't review what powers your ships have available for use, such as "did I use stasis lock with my other ship yet?"
-Some powers have no clear explanation until used in combat.
-Selecting officers for ground combat previews their ability icons only, no explanation until the battle starts.
Tech Tree:
-Looks like a napkin sketch of a tech tree, used to explain what tech trees are to someone who's never seen one before.
Fuel:
-Fuel costs make no sense.  If a fleet is away from base and wants to go directly to Starbase Approach, it will cost fuel.  If the fleet returns to base first, then goes to the Approach, it will cost no fuel.
-Fuel cost really makes no sense.  Stopping at a planet on your way back from another often costs more fuel than going back to base first.
-Seriously, though, fuel?  Sending a shuttle costs the same fuel as three Tier 5 ships.
AI:
-The combat AI is stupid.  It's intentionally stupid, and it's not trying to win.  For example, rather than finishing off a ship that is in critical condition, it will fire on a ship with thousands of hit points
-The turn order at the bottom of the combat screen does not reflect "ship disabled" correctly.  If you disable an enemy ship, they are removed from the turn queue for the duration of the effect.  When the ship is not longer disabled, it doesn't start at the end of the queue, it jumps in wherever the game thinks it fits, meaning you can't use the queue for strategizing.
-Even as a race is being destroyed, it still sends fleets to attack other races.  Ships, mind you, that could crush the ships that are decimating their homeworlds.
Story:
-I owed a race some money.  I thought that was a fun little story element.  They kept collecting it after they were dead.
-In the endgame, it says "you can finish this whenever you want," but if you wait for a few extra days, everyone on base will be killed.
-For about 100 game days I had no idea how to end the game.  Then something happened out of the blue and I thought maybe I could do it again.  I did, and suddenly a base destroying something (no spoilers) appeared.  Had I simply waited, I could have (theoretically) built up several fleets and tons of resources, so the trigger for the end game was unclear, but by figuring it out, I was at a disadvantage.
Gameplay:
-It's unlikely that you'll ever recover from losing a ship in your primary fleet.  I hadn't lost a ship in 600 days, but when I did I knew there was absolutely no way of beating the game without that ship and officer, and loaded a save.
-Resource mining in the early game takes several unnecessary steps, which compounds horribly as you mine more planets.
Conclusion:  As a fan of FTL and XCOM I wanted to like this game, and I have enjoyed some percentage of my play time due to the writing, art, and setting.  But the game feels like it hasn't been fully play tested.  I hold onto hope for Halcyon 6 v2.0.

I must say that I am not even a fan of metroidvanias or even bullet hell games. Yet, Rabi-Ribi managed to be one of my favorite games all the time.
Definitely worth the price!
Rabi-Ribi is an action platformer game in which the player explore a massive metroidvania-like map. There are lots of bosses to beat, attacking the player using swarms of bullets which create a pattern (hence the bullet hell).
I am not an expert of bullet hell games myself, but I believe a good bullet hell game involves "readable" patterns (both bullets and attack patterns). By this, I don't mean an easy-to-read patterns. At least the player needs to be able to figure out how to dodge any kind of bullet patterns. Rabi-Ribi has them. They may seem overwhelming at first, but after several trials and errors you will eventually figure them out. That said, there may be times when you just can't dodge the bullets no matter what. But not to worry, the game provides a workaround for this. You can enter invincibility mode for several seconds just by a mere button push, but the amount is kinda limited. If you got hit it's not the end of the world either, so you should not worry about dodging every single bullet. Just don't get hit too much.
The combat mechanic is fluid enough. Hammer attacks may seem like a single button push at first, but as you advance the game a whole bunch of attacks to build your combo will be added. Uppercut, sliding attack, aerial rolling attack, air dash, carrot bomb, drill attack, etc. Your partner Ribbon covers your weakness in attack range by giving you a wide range of ranged attacks (pun intended) and some nukes.
Tons of upgrades also included in form of badges, items, and power-ups. Badges are meant to be used in a certain situation, while the power-ups are just straightforward buffs. But you should be aware that using them means fighting more advanced enemies. So they should be used sparingly.
Also, secrets. The game has lots of them secret contents. On your first playthrough it may be hard to get 100% of the items since many of them are hidden.
And the most interesting of all, you can even beat the game without any items–including the hammer!
Do you think the term "bullet hell" is an abomination created by a cultist who worships satan for them hardcore masochists? Well... fear not! Rabi-Ribi includes seven types of difficulty for any kind of player. If you haven't played any bullet hell games before, you may try the casual difficulty first. But IMO the novice one provides more suitable challenge while also forgiving at the same time.
For those who are familiar with the bullet hell genre but finds touhou games too challenging, there is normal difficulty. It is a perfect difficulty for starters before you tackle the higher ones: Hard or Hell.
But maybe you're THE masochist, aren't you? Then step up to the challenge. Clear the impossible or even bunny extinction mode! Also don't forget that there are speedrun and boss rush mode. In addition, the game has a huge amount of achievements but around 50% of them are either challenging or need a lot of effort to achieve. For instance, the dodge masters (Take 0 damage while fighting a decent boss), Sequence-breaking, 100%-ing, and speedrunning achievements. And did I mention no-items run?
Lots of other reviewers said the story is "meh". While I understand this point of view, I don't think it is all that bad. It may not have deep or intriguing plot points, and sometimes the plot doesn't even make sense. But for me it's entertaining enough to make me wanting to know more about the plot. It fits the theme (Cute magical girls in a magical world) and the gameplay (another day, another boss fight) too. I think the story feels like those moe slice-of-life animes. No depth, no plot twists, no sense made, just moe girls (and some humor).
The characters' role needs a rework, though. So many characters in this game, but they lack purpose. They exist only for the sake of... existing. While having distinctive character design and backstory, many side characters contribute almost nothing to the plot, making you question whether they are relevant to the story or not.
Oooh, boy! I love the aesthetics. The characters are so adorable, suitable to my taste. Call me a moefag if you want :p
On a serious note, if you like moe anime-styled games, then you may like this game. One may even say that it's the art that keeps you playing the game. And not to mention the design of the world. Both of them synergically creates an experience: Being in a cute, colorful world.
However, the pixel art style feels kinda off to me. This may be my personal opinion, but consistent anime style for both the characters and the world will fit better. Not saying that it's a bad design choice, though. At least it's not cancerous.
While the art is good and all, the only thing that hooked me up is the music. I once thought this game is just like some other anime games, cute anime girls but no engaging gameplay. Once I heard the music on that trailer, I bought it almost instantly. And I'm still glad that I did. The music fits the mood, theme, and world perfectly. Some tracks felt bland however, but it's not much.
Rabi-Ribi has controller support, and I believe it works best with controllers. That said, I'm a keyboard player, and the controls for keyboard are easy to master. The bunny amulet invincibility buff needs two keys to activate, though, which may be annoying if you want to release it in less than a second. Thankfully the game lets you define one shortcut key for not only the bunny amulet but also the air dash attack.
You can remap the keys if you don't like the default setting. I don't know about controllers, but one thing I don't like about this is that you have to remap ALL of the keys even though you just want one and only one. This is a chore even for me.
Well, it's a 2D platformer game, so it should not have any issues on a laptop using integrated graphics card, right? Well, that's not the case for Rabi-Ribi. The game did run well in 60FPS on my rig. But I had huge FPS drop on my Pentium 2.13GHz laptop with Intel HD Graphics, resulting in slow-motion gameplay. My other laptop (Pentium 1.9GHz, also Intel HD) had the same problem. Those laptops run 2D and 3D games with DirectX 9.0 just fine, though. So I think those system requirements are pretty much underestimated... or this game just hates onboard graphics.
In short, I recommend this game for the fans of bullet hell or anime-styled games, no matter your skills. I don't play metroidvania that much, but I think metroidvania fans will like it too. Don't expect engaging story, since you won't find it here. And if you think anime is cancer then it would be best if you just move along and find other games that are not cancerous for you.
Final verdict: 8.5/10

My experience with this game over the last three years has been akin to watching a car crash in slow motion. At first you see a pristine great concept, and original design, then gradually watch in horror as it is torn to crumpled shreds by the oaf at the wheel, reducing it to a mangled ruin bereft of any former glory.
This is not a good game for many reasons, the first being that the developers have burned every bridge imaginable. PGI is infmaous for throwing community managers under the proverbial bus to shirk responsibility for unpopular additions, censorship is rampant on their forums, the community is ignored or shunned at every turn, players are repeatedly outright lied to by the developers and balance is a joke.
Over the years we have seen massive knee jerk reactions over and over again by the PGI, going for the quick and easy solutions to problems over retaining actual balance. This resulted in nightmares like the Jenner being an unstoppable god-slaying machine for the early months of the closed beta. With every new patch there was some new horror which stripped away at the game’s integrity, from the disastrous implementation of ECM and the poor handling of ghost heat, to the mishandled inclusion clan mechs and the developer’s sheer inability to pay even the vaguest hint of attention to BattleTech lore.
If you want a good tactical combat game in this style, look into World of Tanks or War Thunder. Sure, they might not have big stomping mechs, but they're well-rounded in terms of balance and have a developer who sees their game as a product rather than a glorified premium milking machine.

In all you will either love or hate the Steam controller but I would suggest giving it a try.

A great game so far, it will satisfy your Dungeon Keeper itch for sure.
The Dungeons series brings it's own unique twists to the dungeon management genre. The first game flipped the script and focused more on satisfying heroes who visit the dungeon rather than building a satisfying dungeon and making your own creatures happy. While I enjoyed it's novel approach, I still haven't finished it and likely never will. The second Dungeons game was more faithful to the genre and returned to the traditional dungeon experience, but added a different twist that helped it stand out: the Overworld. Now, instead of building your dungeon and raising your army to simply defend against and attack heroes that have invaded the underground, you could take your army topside and bring the battle to them with a system that incorporated Real Time Strategy elements. While both the Underworld dungeon mechanics and the Overworld RTS mechanics were simpler than other games in both genres, the gamble on combining the two paid off and made for an enjoyable game experience. This entry also introduced us to the top-tier comedic stylings of the Narrator, whose witty commentary, fantasy pop culture references and puns, and annoyed banter with the game's characters helped make this game truly stand out as the funniest in the genre.
This third entry keeps to the formula of the second game, combing dungeon management with RTS combat and topping it off with the ever funny narrator. It combines the best aspects from the three playable armies in the second game to keep things fresh and simple, and also refines the mechanics of both the dungeon and the Overworld. The game adopts the playable protagonist feature that was added in the second game's DLC campaign and centers the story around her and her struggle with good and evil. New types of challenges and objectives are added to keep things interesting, and a ton of objective based achievements are included as well. The Narrator returns with his tongue-in-cheek commentary to tell the story as well as ridicule the protagonist and the player alike. Overall the game is a good improvement on the previous entries in the series while staying true to form. I'm clocking an average of 2 hours per level (though your own play time may very depending on your playstyle), so this is definitely a good purchase for anyone who enjoys dungeon management games, even at the full release price of $40.

Tribes ascend is a rare jewel of a game that most people don't know about, and unfortunately will never really have the recognition it deserves.  Set in the distant future, T:A is a FPS that utilizes a mechanic called "skiiing" along with jetpacks to result in a 3d shooting experience where most firefights occur at while moving faster than you usually drive on the way to work.  A good pathfinder in T:A can move in excess of 200mph.  Pretty much every weapon in the game has a projectile with a travel speed, causing you to have to lead your target in order to hit it.  There are multiple game modes, but unfortunately only three are played any more.  There is a stardard team deathmatch where a flag is dropped by the first player to die.  The team controlling the flag drains the enemy's reinforcement counter twice as fast for every kill.  There is an arena mode, which is similar to TDM without a flag, usually on a small map, and is 5v5.  Finally, the main game mode is capture the flag.  CTF has so many aspects it is difficult to explain everything in a relatively short review.  In addition to grabbing the flag and taking it back to your stand, each team has a generator which powers all things on their team.  Turrets, sensors, dropped packs, shields, etc. are all disabled when a generator is destroyed.  There are vehicles in the game, but they are not very commonly used in PUB CTF games.  As with any game, there are downsides.  Depending on your location, it can be difficult to find a server with a ping under 100 with a bunch of players.  The game model is F2P, and you really don't need to buy anything to be competitve with a few classes, but if you want to play all of the classes with weapons that appeal to you, you will either have to play a LONG time or shell out some cash.  If you do this, the GotY edition is the best deal.  Morale of the story is: T:A is a great game, and it is free to try out.  At the very least download it and play a few matches.  If it doesn't interest you after three or four games, you aren't out any cash.  Make sure you try to do a couple of tutorials before you jump right into a game though.

Naruto Shippuden Ultimate Ninja STORM 4 is the final game in the Naruto franchise and it's the perfect way to end the series. A great game that I'll never forget, but it has some draw backs that stops it from being the best in the series.
Pros: Naruto STORM 4 has one of the best story modes in the series. It covers the most episodes out of any STORM game. It covers from where Storm 3 left off to the end of the show. We get the English Dub from start to finish which I love since it hasn't even come out in the anime yet. It's gameplay is the best in the series. The exact same as Storm 3 but refined perfectly. Runs great, I've never had any FPS issues. The way the story mode is shown with pictures in half of the cutscenes makes you feel like you're watching the actual anime. Also it has new ultimate jutsu's and more characters so that's good.
Cons: The story mode covers the most in the series yet I can finish it in half the time it takes me to finish Storm 2 or Storm 3. Because of the way it doesn't have you going through a hub world it's scripted. I don't know if it's just me but I almost always get lag in online mode so I never play against people online. The adventure mode really was a let down. It's way shorter than any game in the series and after I finished it and all of the side missions I screamed "WTF THAT'S IT!?!?!"
8.5 A great game and one of the best in the series but those cons stop it from being the best. I think Storm 2 and 3 are better.

Here's my review after 940 hours of gameplay.
Although lots might say the game is pay to win, it isn't fully P2W. There are 2 different Siege modes in the game, one is Bound and one Unbound (Reason of P2W), Bound Siege sets all of your cards at lvl 4 and works the same for all others in the match.
Paladins is still fun, but not as fun as it once was. The TTK (Time to Kill) in the game is lowering in each patch, and players can easily get melted in 2 seconds because Low-Rez basically threw the balance out the window. They've made several changes to the once balanced champions that now have incredibly low skill floor and ceiling, making them overpowered even for newbies to deal insane amount of damage.
Low-Rez also balances the PC patch alongside with the console version, in one patch they doubled the speed of all projectiles just to suit consoles but resulting in some champions becoming way overpowered on PC. Some high damage projectiles were supposed to be slow and to require more skills and timing to perform well, that's not the case anymore.
Try the game at your own risk, you might or might not like the game but it's free, so it's worth a try.

I've been playing this game since beta.
At first, I was somewhat hesitant about MWO. You see, I’m not all that into PvP games. And, when I learned that MWO was all PvP, I really wasn’t interested at first. But, the lure of Big Stompy Robots eventually dragged me into trying it.
So, there I was grinding out my twenty five cadet bonus matches in a Trial JM-6 Jagermech. My first mech purchase was a Blackjack as they were first released. I realized that this was a different kind of PvP game- it was slower, the concept of walking tanks did a good job of mitigating the twitch play that I didn’t like. Sure there was still twitch play with light mechs, but it was still a little slower and methodical that other FPS games I played.
Now, a few years (and a bunch of mech packs) later, I find I truly do love this game.
What I like most about this game, compared to other tank games, is the method in which you get your vehicles. See, in other tank games, you have to contend with tech/progression trees- forcing you to drive or fly equipment you don’t like in order to work your way into gear that you do.
Not so with this game. If I want to drive a Timberwolf, I can either grind the CBills to get them, buy the MC to get it or buy it straight away from the gift store. Can’t do that with an M1 Abrams, German Tiger or P-51.
I love how customizable the game is. Much of the fun of the game is spending time in the mechlab finding that perfect build that synergizes my playstyle with the mechs quirks and hardpoint arrangement. See not all build fit all, some build that work great for one guy may not work so well for other. But, finding that great build that works for you is truly satisfying.
Another thing I love about this game is the regular events that PGI holds. Grab bag events, Leaderboard events, Faction play events and Cumulative stretch goal events, there’s always something going on.
There’s a lot of good stuff on the horizon for this game-
The fabled Unseens are being released on a monthly basis as we speak.  If you’re a Battletech aficionado, you can truly appreciate the return of these classics.
PvE is coming; we already see glimpses of PvE in the Mechwarrior Academy.
A large update is coming to Faction Warfare that will appeal to small groups (4v4) as well as large.
If you’re new to the game, do check out the Spike Brave tutorials on youtube. Also, play the Mechwarrior Academy, play it a lot, play it some more. The Mechwarrior Acandemy is a great resource.
Give the game its fair shake, just like I did, and I think you will be impressed with it, just like I am.

As a veteran player, this game is a substantial letdown.
Gone are the mechanics and thrill of piloting a mech that was present in Mechwarrior 2, Ghost Bear's Legacy, and so forth. The game itself is graphically beautiful and may take a recent graphics card to handle it at a good frame-rate. Sadly, this is the only real good thing going for it.
Much of the control system has been entirely removed, opting for an extremely "streamlined" method of play. This is to such an extent that one wonders if a keyboard is really necessary anymore. The sheer amount of customisation that was in previous entries is vastly reduced. While the predecessors gave the feel of a simulator, this rendition feels more like an arcade game.
Although the publisher claims the game to be free, it is instead paid through numerous, pricey "microtransactions". It would be far, far cheaper to just buy a game outright. There is no option for that here (it would be significantly cheaper).
As a note to those who have played MechWarrior Online in the past, you will be forced to play through a tutorial before you can return to active multiplayer gaming.
If one is completely new to the genre, they may enjoy it. For others, I strongly recommend running the older games or looking for an open-source game that competes with this.

EDIT: The Out of the Blue patch has improved this game immensely, bringing it more in line with Tribes and Tribes 2. However, there still are some balance issues, but much more concerning is the still-dwindling player base. Hi Rez has shown they've not completely forgotten about the game, but now they need to show they're commited to actually making it a good one. Check out all the new changes, and keep an eye on the game. Hopefully things continue to improve.
An interesting title that's more a mixed bag than anything. Flashy graphics and unique mechanics provide lots of fun, but the massive xp costs for the countless amount of unlocks turns what would be a solid FPS into a frustrating grind fest. Not to mention, the learning curve is extremely steep; between learning all the weapon behaviors and skiing, there's a rather large barrier of entry for a newcomer. However, the DOTA- and CS-like difficulty is compounded by the xp grind and feeling of helplessness against those who have arguably "better" unlocks and more time with the game. Granted, mastering skiing and grinding for the unlocks will certainly keep you coming back, the former being genuinely fun and the latter having the same addictiveness for completionists.
The classic F2P microtransation system really forces you to start pumping money in to bolster your arsenal. You'll have so little if you solely unlock through grinding that you're likely to never know what you actually prefer otherwise. For those inclined to do so can use Steam Wallet funds to purchase Tribes Gold in-game. This allows you to unlock weapons, classes and perks much faster than by grinding alone.
However, putting money into this does leave a bad taste in your mouth. The game does feel like it's slowly expiring, so spending money on the myriad of arguably better and/or necessary unlocks also quickly kills the desire to play. Having dropped $20 in my 30 hours of play has left me little fulfillment. More often than not, I'll want to play, but the sense of aversion due to the xp grind and complete chaos in pubs keeps me from hitting the play button now.
Hackers are both stupidly obvious and game breaking. One will ruin a game entirely; ironically, this is usually the best way to grind xp. Furthermore, despite the potential for large and hectic matches, even the normal 12vs12 games feel sparsely populated, every player preferring to go at it lone-wolf. This frequently results in both team having one or two players with better unlocks capping uninterrupted or camping your generator. The only time it feels like people are truly working together is when it's hardcore players stomping your team.
Vehicles also don't seem to be touched at all, another disappointment considering the amazing potential they can have. The vehicle pad screams for more attention. Of the three (yes, only three - that doesn't even fill the list space!) vehicles you can purchase during a match, two are bland, expected additions that most games in this genre will have. The Grav Cycle is the best of the three, but still pales compared to other vehicles seen in FPS games in the past decade.
I find myself picking it up every so often because despite its issues I really do want to enjoy this game. As you perfect your skiing and get better at predicting shots, there is some degree of redemption afforded the game? Those one-in-a-million shots are extremely gratifying, and high-speed chases are thrilling. Unfortunately, for a game so young, it seems to be suffering from the same fate many significantly older games are: a dwindling player base and no new official content. While Tribes fans may be able to look past the flaws to play a game bearing the series name with a modern paintjob, after a certain point the enjoyment of mid-air spinfusor directs simply can't produce enough draw to boot the game again. Whether that's after 5, 50, or 500 hours is dependent on how much you like the franchise.
Sadly, Tribes: Ascend is only really recommendable to the intensely curious who won't mind the grinding and frustration or the long-time fans who'll buy the GOTY version. For a game with so much potential, it really feels the weight of its awards have crushed it. It's had its 15 minutes of fame and has ceased being profitable for the developer. Without a support team to keep it patched, hacker free, and fresh with new content, Tribes: Ascend is simply crumbling under its own weight.
I love this game but it hates me. The Tribes franchise deserved better.

The Steam Controller (for me and others around the web at least) requires you to launch Steam in administrator mode.
This is a security hole as the Steam client also acts as a web browser, and if that part of the steam client were to be compromised (through viewing a malformed page (or even advertisement)), your computer is much easier to compromise in that mode.
Some people don’t seem to have this problem, others do. Your call.
Valve would be better to have a standard driver for this piece of hardware, but I guess in their wisdom, they wish for the steam client to be able to handle driver updates for feeble minded people.

A throw-back to the classic shooters of the 90's, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is more about story and exploration than it is about actually shooting things.
The game is partly a stealth shooter, with many ways of approaching a series of rooms full of armed guards, giving options such as: sniping from the rafters, cloaking and hacking the turrets, quietly picking them off with hand to hand combat, or just nuking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of anything that moves with a rocket launcher.  Though some may wish that therewere more options to choose from, anything is much better than the linear shooters we have come to know, where all one has to do is hold a button, run down a hallway. and aim for the head.
The other part of this is game is heavily plot driven, giving ~40 hours of story which is very engaging, but unfortunatly a little predictable.  Dealing with the morallity and ethics of cybernetic enhancement, the true meaning of freedom, and the role of corporate greed in both, the game provides thought provoking scenarios and opens up many topics that humanity should probably start thinking about in the near future.  Personally, I found that the only setback story-wise was the inability to roleplay, or even feel like your character is developing with the information you are discovering.  Many times in the game I found that my natural reactions to events were not presented by the games main character, who tends to be either extremely sassy, or just ignorant and impatient.
This game is a great play and definetly worth checking out, and I would recommend it to anyone that isn't deterred by the fact that it is ~40 hour game about sneaking around with robot limbs trying to stop the ILLOOMINAUGHTY.

The Steam Controller isn't really meant to be the ultimate choice for using a gamepad on PC games but it might as well be for me, not just because I picked this up during the summer sales. Works with all my Steam games as well as non-Steam titles added to the Steam client but be warned you're gonna need a decent amount of time to set the controls up right to how you want them due to the many ways you can route game controls to the Steam Controller, especially with the touchpads adding more options to that. Hell, I don't really miss the right thumb stick as I'm more of a kb+m guy and while the Steam Controller isn't a substitute for a mouse, it's close enough to be one and offers better accuracy overall.
The only downsides I'm seeing with this controller is the battery mechanism as it can't accept certain batteries due to length and many rechargeable batteries are longer than the standard alkaline batteries, not to mention you can't charge batteries through the controller with the cable either so you'll have to wait and pop them into a charger then use a cable while you wait. Also, teardowns I've seen for this controller shows that the left thumbstick is soldered right onto the board and knowing how thumbsticks are more often than not the part to fail first, the Steam controller's longevity might actually be shorter. It feels sturdy enough though where it won't feel like a problem but I'd imagine it to be one later down the road.
Either way, really great controller from Valve despite the weird learning curve required due to its versatility and shape. Best used with a Steam Link.........and a lot of patience.

Massive Damage have done massive damage to their reputation in my book.
I really wanted to like this game. It was on sale, so I thought I'd give it a try. So far, I've played for 22 hours (pretty constantly in 5 hour sessions over about 3 days), and am a fan of strategic 4X games.
+ Creative skills combination system (think Xenogears in space)
+ Base-building,
+ Familiar ground and space combat system
+ Multiple ship designs
+ Non-irritating music
- Game-breaking bugs (see below)
- Gameplay at mid-game feels like a tedious game of whack-a-mole. You send the same fleet around to do the same sequence of tactical actions - rock, paper, scissors style. Oh, and the lovely RNG makes it so that if your disable ship tactic doesn't work you're in for a heal-a-thon. This serves to only extend the length of the tedious battles.
- Not fun
- Never get to enjoy the full game because bugs choke it to death prematurely
The game is broken. I can handle (and even welcome) games that force you to make tough decisions. I can handle games that pit you against overwhelming odds. I can handle resource challenges that force you to do the best with what you've got.
What I can't handle is bugs that fundamentally break the game and ruin a system of well-established rules arbitrarily. Those kind of games aren't fun and are a betrayal of the gamer's trust, rendering the time and effort he or she has invested into a game moot.
Some background: I'm still on my first playthrough winning battles against any fleet in the game, even though I'm still using Tier 2 ships (with Tier 3 ships on the way once I get the resources). My officers are almost all around level 7. I made an early mistake and so I am missing a tactical officer (have 2 Eng, 2 Science, 1 Tactical Officer so I don't have two sets of 1 of each officer/ship in my fleets).
Example 1: I had a settlement 20 days away from falling. I scoot over there and while en route I get a notification it had fallen to the Chruul. I arrived, killed the enemy, and the screen showed the same fleet there and my ship was in the position it had been when I got the notification. WTF?!
Example 2: In the most egregious bug (and the subject of a lot of discussion) is when the first Spire arrives. It seems to appear based on time. I killed the fleet guarding it, and then it gave me the message I needed more research back at the Starbase. I acknowlege that screen and indicate for my fleet to go to another system. It shows that message again. I dismiss it again.
I go back to the base and there is no relevant research. I checked the OFficer Training area and not even the biowarfare upgrade was the one. So this is a terribly bad quest with zero in-game clues as to how to obtain this research. I did a google search and found how, but triggering this condition (
) brings about the arrival of the Chimera, which would exacerbate an already bad situation.
Example 3: Main quest "Expand the Starbase" missions is bugged and never progresses even though it is checked.
The bottom line is: you cannot have a plot-based, branching campaign with these kinds of debilitating bugs- especially when there is no way to recoup resources once a system is (unfairly) conquered. In the end, every victory I win is a Phyyric one, which only delays the inevitable due to these massive bugs. When it slowly dawns on you that the game becomes a series of Sisyphean tasks, it's just not worth playing any more.
Right now, I've stopped playing and won't play again until these issues are dispositively fixed.
I'm extremely disappointed, and was very angry when my colony (which again had 20 days to go) was instantly killed because of a damn bug.

So I have just beaten this game on Cadet to try it out and experience what they have created. Now I'm going to do my best to express what I have experienced and hopefully help everyone out on whether to buy this or not.
Let's start with the Pro's and Con's shall we?!
Con's: Oooo doing this first....
Recourses - Are a bit tedious at first, I mean, I was getting a bit annoyed that I had to send a fleet to every single facility manned by survivors of the Federation to gather recourses, even to the point where I had about 4 Officers, which equals to 4 ships, one ship to a fleet so 4 fleets, all flying out to four different facilities and gathering resources as quickly as possible before another Chruul portal and Chruul assault on another facility of mine. I even got as far as 6 officers, 6 ships, 6 fleets and...yeah you get the point.
Battles - Both ground and space battles can take a bit of time at first, because you are limited to a number of skills at the beginning, so you have to be creative to annihilate the enemy fleet without getting a single ship of yours destroyed. (I simply despise replacing officers, especially if they are so high in level.)
Frequencies of Attacks - Now this one bothered me the most. Chruul's, Voraash and Pirate frequency of attacks, especially after the 2nd part of the game where Chruul has their own section of space, you would have to go save other race's butts from Chruul attacks almost all the time. Especially when the Chruul takes over said Race's fleet and have to defend against that Fleet before it does any harm to your Starbase. So I send my two fleets out there to fend off Chruul attack and Chruul possessed (Race Name) Fleet, only to be notified...Hey, this OTHER race is under Chruul attack too!! And OH, one of your facilities is being attacked by Rogue Pirates and... OH YEAH!! This OTHER- Race is being attacked by the Voraash!! Have fun :D!! ... At least they give you 30+ days to each attack to react and destroy those attacking Fleets though...that does help.
Okay done with the Con's, On to the Pro's!
Pro's - Yaaay!
Recourses - Say what? Yup! Recourses. Because once you get to the 2nd part of the game, after pretty much shoving the Chruul back through their ars...eerr Portal Hole in space or whatever, and free Federation Space from any Chruul assaults, every facility you saved (do try to explore every system in Federation Territory AND save them as well from Chruul attacks. Trust me, I had a few wiped out on my end D: ) will become AUTOMATED!! YES! Auto-mated. They will send all their recourses to YOU!! At this point, I dismantled my Resource Collecting Fleets...had like 6 of them... And reassignd ships to more attacking Fleets to fend off raids and assaults from other races, Voraash, rogue pirates and Chruul.
Battles - Oh really? Yup. Higher Tier ships you research, unlock, build and such, adds more useful skills. And plus your officers have reached the level to command those higher tier ships, so if you don't already, you have more skills, your skills are stronger, and the skills the higher tier ships provide also make battles much easier. I have even tried all ships of all tier levels, One fleet was specific ships all the way to Tier 5, and same for the second fleet. No fleet had the same ship as the other fleet. So I have tried all the ships and all the skills they had to offer, and I believe I have found a decent ship/skill combo to use. That's another thing, once you discover the best ships to have in your fleet, very specific ships too, you will find certain combos and chain attacks that will be VERY EFFECTIVE! And will make battles quite quick. Most battles with the Chruul I've had still took a bit, but every battle with the Voraash, Pirates, and Raiding Fleets from all the races, were pieces of cake. Especially if you send your main fleet with the 3 Legendary Officers with their Epic Skills ready to go...maaaaan it is sooo much fun to use those Epic Skills.
Races - I found some of the races to be rather humorous. Especially the Yablings and their way of thinking. But when you save the races from an attack on one of their planets/facilities, you have the option to take No recourse or as much recourse as you want! Except, taking none gives +10 Diplo and taking all gives -10 Diplo. So most of the time I chose none, and then I started taking some that offered +5 Diplo, and then just took more and more that didn't add or subtract any Diplo. Basically it got to the point that the more you helped your friends, the more recourses you got!! YAY MORE RECOURSES!!
This game has an FTL and XCom feel to it. You're fending off an unknown number and unreasonable enemy, in a space and ground combat environment with skills that can often be usefull or on rare occasions, useless, and you're unlocking and building more and more facilities on your Starbase to better your Fleet, obtain more recourses, train your Cadets and Officers, and be ready to face the mother of all mothers...Mother Chruul. Which happens to be a ... Naaaah, you'll find out when you beat the game :D.
I am hoping for a Conquest Mode to be added. Something similar to Star Wars: Empires at War or Star Trek: Starfleet Command 1, 2, and 3. Hexagon space map or galactic map like EaW, sending fleets to sieze and capture planets to obtain more and more recourses. Just something to add a twist to the game but then again that's a whole other developing there.
I am most eager to play the game again on a higher difficulty and see what kind of sacrifices I have to make in order to survive :P.
And most eager for the updates to come! Can't wait to see what they do to make this game better!
I'm also a big space game gamer, Star Trek, Star Wars, Elite Dangerous, etc. So this game hits home right to my space gaming heart. If you're a big space gamer, and like RPG style games of survival and watching aliens die at your feet...or get sucked out into space or blown up in front of your face by your fleet's mighty weapons...okay maybe getting carried away BUT, THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU!
And definitely a game to try out. I'm pretty sure the videos, pictures, all the GOOD reviews and the fact that overall, Very Positive...should be more than enough to convince anyone to play this game! So don't just take my word for it, take your own! If you have the slightest, inklist thought of 'Ohhhh maybe I should give it a try' then DO IT! If this game hits you home to the kind of game and style that you love most, what are you waiting for?

After OB64, the game has turned very pay to win with the ridiculous amount of grinding that goes into making loadouts worth using unless you buy chests, which are still RNG, so even if you do pay, you still probably don't get what you want.

This game used to be a fantastic and unique standout in the hero shooter genre. After having put several hundred hours into this game and slowly watching it go downhill from what it used to be the OB64 patch finally put the nail in the coffin for me. HiRez decided to implement a system that vastly reduced hero customization and locked higher levels of cards that were previously available at any level behind chests extremely similar to the horrendous Star Wars Battlefront II lootboxes. requiring you to open duplicates of cards to level up the ones you currently have.
This patch has been absolutely blasted by the community and is widely regarded by the vocal players online as the death of the game (which based on the fact that me and everybody I know that used to play it has uninstalled might be true). Despite the MASSIVE amount of negative feedback HiRez stated that they are standing by this update, completely disregarding whether or not the playerbase wants it. They have stated that the game will not be pay to win because they won't allow the purchase of chests with premium currency AT THIS TIME but then stated that it's a possibility in the future which, given the fact that this game just released in China where players are very much used to and willing to put money into pay to win games, makes the whole update seem like a giant cash grab and a slap in the face for existing players. Also while the chests are not directly purchasable right now the game still contains pay to win elements after the update do to account/xp/gold boosters that can be bought, reducing the grind and giving an in game advantage to people willing to shell out the money
All in all with the copious amount of bugs, horrible optimization, rapidly decreasing TTK, constantly dumbing down characters by nerfing mobility and adding more damage, increasingly boring characters being added into the game, and overall disregard that HiRez seems to be having towards the community I can't in good concience recommend anyone to play this game. Save your time and go play TF2, Overwatch, Battlerite, or any number of games that will be much more enjoyable than the ♥♥♥♥♥how this game has become.
TLDR; HiRez got greedy and instead of fixing their game decided to milk people for as much money as possible in a free to play game, effectively killing it.

So many mechs!
My background:  I haven't played tabletop, nor a huge Battletech fan.  I have played previous titles.  I don't normally play Shooters.  That said, here is an honest review...
PROS:
*Maps look great (graphics tend to the more "real" feel)
*Good tutorial (Mechwarrior Academy)
*Can run around solo on the multiplayer maps in Trainings Grounds
*Almost unlimited configuations (once you can afford to buy mechs)
*Earning in-game currency is easy at first
*Mechs look amazing and there are plenty
*Lots of weapons to choose from
*Map voting
*VOIP
*Slower, more time to think than a Shooter
*Simulation feel of being in the cockpit of a giant mech (has both 1st and 3rd Person available views)
*Community Warfare shows initial signs of being a cornerstone of the Great Houses/Clans conflict
*Matchmaker seems to generally do ok pairing players together
*Excellent sound effects for weapons
*3 Quick Play game modes plus Faction Play
CONS:
*Navigating the UI can be a challenge.
*Steep learning curve (previous titles in the franchise were just as difficult)
*Only trial mechs to start out with
*No tutorial on how to build a decent mech
*Game mechanics seem complicated
*No respawn (although limited in Faction Play)
*No matchmaking in Faction Play
*Game modes seem similar
*Minimal destrucible environment
GRAPHICS: 8/10 (tend toward realism, uses CryEngine)
GAMEPLAY: 7.5/10 (mainly Deathmatch/Destruction, with an occasional base cap)
MUSIC/SOUND: 8.5/10 (Music decent, sound effects awesome, no music during matches)
UI: 6.5/10 (it's pretty, but overly complicated)
MAPS: 7.5/10 (13? distinct maps.  They recently reworked 3 that come with some destructible terrain, dropship, and time of day changes)
MECHLAB: 7/10 (Building a mech itself is as deep as any previous title, but no tutorial and overly complicated at first)
COMMUNITY: 7/10 (Most are friendly, some very sour apples...forums at
REPLAY VALUE: 8/10 (Enough maps, mechs, weapons, and game modes to replay, but can get repetitive.  At that point might be a good time to switch over to Faction Play)
PRICE: 9/10.  It is totally F2P. Biggest complaint I've heard is that there are mechs P2W.  Not true.  Can buy any mech except Hero mechs with in-game currency.  Only about 10% of the mechs are Hero and do have different hardpoints, but they are rarely seen on the battlefield because they are not any better than others in the associated chassis.  They do receive a 30% Cbill boost which is why pilots buy them - to earn cash and not to dominate the battlefield.  If you are going to buy a mech I would suggest looking at the in-game store first.  A $14.95 MC package can get you 2 Medium mechs (Cicadas), or it could get you 4 Light mechs (2 Commandos, 2 Locusts).  Obviously Heavies and Assaults are more expensive.
TLDR:  8.5/10.  Game is a blast, needs work, but bi-monthly patches introduce regular new content and fixes. (34 patches in the last 1 1/2 years alone...view them here

Can't say I can recommend the Steam Controller at all.
Right out of the box, I played around with it for a bit and it seemed to feel pretty alright. It was interesting exploring the vast number of buttons on the controller and imagining the unlimited possibilities.
Plugged in the wireless adapter, which was nifty, and gave it a try with a few games. In Mega Man 5 (Legacy Collection), I first attempted to play using the D-Pad for movement, and soon realize how terrible the D-Pad is on this thing. Trying to quickly shift from one direction on the D-Pad to another was not at all like I've felt it on other controllers and just didn't work. I played with the control stick instead which worked pretty well, but even then, shooting and jumping with A and X didn't feel right at all. Like the Wii U Pro Controller, the face buttons are simply set way too low on the controller. However, it's much worse on the Steam Controller because they are also too far inwards. I have to physically move my thumb inwards on the face of the controller to hit any face button other than B.
...Maybe a bad choice for a game. So, I decided to jump the gun and try a few non-controller games. Maybe adapting KBM controls to a controller might work out alright.
In Final Fantasy XIII, the game played just as it did when I played the game on Xbox 360. However, using the right touchpad to simulate mouse camera movement worked at a grandmothers' pace. No matter how many user-submitted presets I used or tweaks I made to the controls myself, I couldn't get the controls to feel right at all. I also happened to notice how thin and hard to push the Start and Select/Back buttons were, much like the PlayStation Vita 1000.
I even attempted a few more games like Bully: Scholarship Edition and it turned out the same way. Mind you, Bully is a game I love playing with an Xbox 360 controller, but I simply can't get around this Steam Controller at all with this game. Or any game.
The build quality seems pretty good, but the ergonomics of the controller baffle me. This thing wasn't designed for human hands at all. It felt alright out of the box, but once I was playing games with it, my hands (particularly my left hand) starting getting cramped up and uncomfortable like you wouldn't believe. It's just simply not a comfortable controller to use for long periods of time.
Using it to browse webpages is a neat novelty, but like using a PS2 controller with Joy2Key, the novelty soon wore off as I went back to my comfortable KBM. Even getting batteries in and out of this controller is like pulling teeth.
I'll keep the controller around in the rare event that I find a game that works well with it. The idea of being able to take my controller to my couch and route my computer to my TV is amazing, but if I'm gonna go that route, I'm not using the Steam Controller. Back to my trusty Xbox 360 controller.

The Steam Controller takes some getting used to, but not much.  Out of the box, you get everything you need to get started, even batteries.  To be sure, the Steam Controller is priced fairly.
What really separates the Steam Controller from others is the nearly endless options for customization.  Everything, from trackpad sensitivity to the brightness of the steam button, right down to turn on/off sounds, can be fine-tuned to your preference.
That said, while it is a great controller, it will not replace your mouse and keyboard for games where they are needed, despite what the advertising says.  Therefore, bear in mind that you're buying a controller, not a replacement for your mouse & keyboard.
All in all, I would definitely recommend this controller.

Well-made remix of the original Deus Ex, presenting beautifully crafted backstory and solid, entertaining gameplay. It is wise, it is made of nothing but best efforts and good intentions. A brilliant of the game. I see truth in every sane positive review, in every high mark that title got. Superb stuff, which is worth every penny.
Yet, I’m not satisfied with it. For some reason, I feel that game is too tied to the past, to be something I call cyberpunk.
Deus Ex Human Revolution has everything I could only ask from cyberpunk game. It calls itself so. But that’s a lie. Not completely, of course. You know, the standard definition for cyberpunk sounds like “Hi tech. Low life”, and that’s that we see a plenty in our game. But I’ve got another quote for you, from our precious W. Gibson: “The world has never had so many moving particles and so few labels for them”.
I think the label “cyberpunk” is not fitting Deus Ex HR completely, because it is way too caring about what’s going on, in a global meaning. It is way too conscious for an action game. And it is praising a human life so high, that it makes me sick sometimes. In Hengsha events, to be precise. And even worse – in that embedded, crushed into the flesh of the original game, DLC Missed Link. I know I’m facing the bad guys, who are not caring about human lives at all. Why should I care for their lives? I don’t know. But all those bonuses to Exp points, all those achievements like Pacifist or Factory Zero, all the given pre-history of my protagonist Adam Jensen, insisting I should leave them be. And that leaves a mark.
Okay, I know that does not convince you about my point. Have another: the creators of Deus Ex HR were too attached to the original Deus Ex of the year 2000, to create really new game. I understand them, surely: were they too innovative, and all those fans would destroy a game’s name in the media, made a lower metacritic score, and that would be a disaster, of course. But again, cutting off  something new and of hi tech because someone cares and could dislike you – does it sounds cyberpunk to you? For me, it’s  plain and pure conservatism there.
So many good things in this game:
1) brilliant level design, there you always have the choice of routes, for every tactic you would like, would that be stealth, assault, some kind of “social engineering”, or mix of those.
2) Delightful hacking mini game and all interactions with computers in general. It is certainly quite natural and adding much of context in the game. Wish we had something like that in the new Shadowrun series...
3) Speaking of context, I also enjoyed the level of detail through all the game. For example, when I suddenly decided to kill some merks on my second walkthrough, I couldn’t find their leader later in the game. Because he was expecting me, for one, and was feared that I won’t spare him, secondly. Damn right he was! Funny thing was  that I remember in my first trip when I knocked him off, I was deciding, whether to kill him, or leave him be… and obeyed the Pacifist rule, to get an achievement.

4) Not only every situation in the game could be untied in various styles. There are some options which I believe was not even predicted by the designers! Like: there are two guards and turret. I can crouch behind guards, but if I want to deal with them, to have clear backside, I need to deal with turret first. I can switch it off, but guards will notice me doing so. I can sneak behind the turret and shove her into a corner, where it can’t be a problem anymore. But once I just picked that turret and threw it into the guards. And knocked them both by that throw! Pure luck, I guess.
5) Music is nice, I still have some of soundtrack in my playlist. Voicing is gorgeous, can’t wish for better. All the visuals part is good, even if some details are look exactly like in the first Deus Ex.
Bads list is small:
1) Even with all good effort on details, there are some very generic elements which I can’t tolerate, like the looks of offices, office decks and, worst of all, damned faxes everywhere! Oh, why?
2) Implementation of the “Missing Link” dlc in the middle of the base game is furies me. I really don’t think this was a good idea, and good implementation. I like that dlc the way it was. It reminds me of the Sleeping Dogs Definitive edition, where they messed all the fun both from the game AND dlc stuff by implementing it.
3) That game takes too much effort “to make it right”, in Pacifist way. It is so persistent with that “what’s right” thing, even (especially) in the endings… I can’t bear it. The game supposed to be multiplexed, fit every approach… but no, all that freedom of choice is something of illusion. I know people who like Dishonored more, for their choices make a bigger difference in the end. Me? I prefer Alpha Protocol.
Overall mark 8.99/10, for the amount of work, and with handsel to the next game, which, as I knew already, will do better.
