A brief review: it's fun enough to play, especially at first, but could be much better.
Core gameplay: we're constantly moving our ships across the map to get resources and fighting aliens in space and on the ground. Resources are used to unlock new techs and upgrade ships\crew, and to build new, better ships. From time to time we encounter random events, complete story or side missions, and also nursing our crew.
But 90% of time we are grinding resources and fighting aliens. Grinding is the dumbest part of the game, mostly due to an idiotic decisions in UI design. Click-click-click-click-click-click-click-click-click! Clicker games idiocy came even to a space strategies! I found no way to automate this process. Waypoints? Automatic gathering at approach? No! Each time you'll need to get a resource from another planet, you'll have to travel through several menus. Click a planet, click to select a proper fleet, click "Redirect fleet", wait a few secs while your fleet travels to its destination, at a planetary menu click an option to get resources, and then click "Leave planet". Repeat 20 times to empty all planets, and then start over again. And things will get even more complicated as soon as you'll have two or more fleets in space. Dear sir, I clicked less while playing Diablo 3!
And combat system... Well, it's quite repetitive. As soon as you'll get a proper combination of ships and abilities, in most cases you'll use the same combination of actions to defeat each enemy. Boring. And also there's almost no gameplay difference between ground and space battles.
I had lots of doubts deciding what option to choose: to recommend or not, but finally used "thumbs up". A few hours of fun exploring game features is guaranteed, and only then the game will show you its gameplay impotency.  The price of this game is about 5 bucks in my region, and it surely worth it.
P.s. I've played about 7 hours before I wrote this review, I haven't completed the game yet and I'm already tired of fighting game's interfaces and taking part in numerous repetitive battles, but I still hope to see if there are a few more secrets in pockets.

Now that we got that out of the way, Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is a difficult turn based space RPG.
You are the reminants of an alliance that was all but destroyed by an unkown foe. Tasked with survivng and eliminating this unkown foe, you upgrade your starbase (Halcyon 6), train crew, gather resources and build ships to pilot in your strugle.
Gameplay revolves around a time system. Activities outside of combat take X amount of days to complete, meaning time management is a core part of gameplay. The 3 resources that the game has you gather are mainly gained by visiting locations around the map by sending a fleet to retrieve them (there is travel time in days), winning battles, and finishing quests. These resources are used to upgrade your tech and build new ships.
Combat is done in an old school turn based system akin to early Final Fantasy games, be it ground or space combat. Turn order is displayed for you to use for planning out your combat. However, the main flavor of combat comes from combos. Attacks can have two types of modifiers to them that enhance it beyond doing damage to add a status effect on your foe. Some attacks can be used to exploit a particular status effect to do bonus damage and remove said status effect. For example causing a hull breach (light DoT) then attacking with a skill that exploits it, will cause the hull breach to expire immediatly, but the attack will do more damage in return.
All in all, its a fun, albeit stressful, game of time and resources management with the flavor of old school turn based combat. If that sounds fun, pick Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander up.

While the premise of Halcyon 6 feels relatively fresh, mixing elements of FTL, XCOM and the JRPG genre, the game falls short very soon after you familiarize yourself with its mechanics.
I feel kinda bad saying this, because the game has potential. The art style is great, and the writing is really entertaining, with each alien race having its own quirks. as well as your officers, which blurt out some snappy lines after a well placed shot (or their ship exploding).
The main problem? Repetitiveness.
The most common way to gather resources to develop your base is utilizing outposts scattered throughout space, from which you have to periodically collect resources. This wouldn't be so bad if you didn't have to physically send a ship to get them, one by one.
What makes it worse is that these colonies cap out their goodies very fast, meaning you have to ferry around a ship every 5 minutes or so. It really gets under your skin after a while.
The number of available abilities for each ship (or officer) is another hurdle, as the battle system relies on a series of combos done by sequencing the abilities of different ships to do the maximum possible damage.
After having discovered the best combinations of powers, you are basically forced to keep spamming the same combos fight after fight, adding to the already prominent monotony of the game.

To sum it up, Halcyon 6 feels like a huge missed opportunity. But who knows, the devs gave the impression they wanted to keep working on the game post launch. They might fix some, if not all, of these issues. Until then, if you're looking for a game to invest a lot of time in, I'd think twice about buying this one.
TL,DR: Great retro graphics and fun dialogues aren't enough to save an extremely repetitive and grindy game.

Do you like Sci-Fi? Do you hate Aliens? Have you ever desired to send waves of Greenshirts to their deaths?
Halcyon 6 is primarily Star Trek combined with FTL, Final Fantasy and a flavour of XCOM.
You have base, which you explore and develop. You enlist hero Star Fleet Officers and train them, love them and become sad when they die. Combat is turn based with each Officer bringing a unique skill set. Ship combat is a dazzling affair but it's the ground combat which is my favourite. Watching 5ft 1' Lt. O'Hara perform a Khirklee Death Punch on a 7ft alien will live with me forever. If your Officer was exploring solo then he/she beams in lightly armed Greenshirts to support, who tragically die.
Actually there is a strong Star Trek story theme throughout the narrative. You are managing a federation disaster and you have to choose how to interact with the myriad alien races who seek to undermine humanity during their moment of weakness. There are multiple outcomes to each diplomatic event, an ally in one game might be a bitter enemy in the next.
The art style is gorgeous and the music is very much FTL. My only negative point for the game is it's lack of in-game help - there are many features which are never explained and which you discover by accident. For example I had no idea how to upgrade my ships Tiers for ages. It was 8 hours before I realised I could visit unmarked systems to trigger random events. It's as if the game needs a little bit more polish and direction at times.
For a fun Sci-fi flick, this game ticks all the boxes. Now, Warp speed Mr Sulu.

This game is absolutely AMAZING.
I'm not particularly a fan of platformers (burned out mostly), metroidvanias, or bullet hells, but Rabi Ribi pulls them all into a very satisfying (and very challenging) mix that'll keep you hooked for hours on end. Don't be fooled by its cuteness! It WILL make you git gud. Thankfully there's difficulty options for those who need or want it.
Character design is cute, the world is huge, there's a ton of power-ups to find and buy (in 20hs I only mapped 60% of the map and found 55% of the items, and I didn't even fight all the bosses).
The gameplay is really a lot of fun, you have many different moves to find and upgrade, the soundtrack is really catchy and amazing, each boss fight is unique and challenging with their own mesmerizing movesets.
You can sequence break very hard, you might stumble upon later bosses by chance near the start of the game, there's all sorts of achievements related to sequence breaking, the game can be played very non-linearly which adds to the replayability, but don't worry, bosses scale based on your items.
If you're an achievement collector you probably don't want to play this game for those though, since it has very hard achievements, some of which include speedrunning.
The game is also still getting updated with many free patches and it even got a free DLC for halloween that I haven't gotten around to playing.
If Rabi Ribi has any weak spots I'd say the translation is a bit clumsy, but there aren't any real errors in it that I noticed, it just fumbles a bit when telling the story, but I haven't cleared the postgame content yet which looks like it'll have some answers so maybe I'll update on that one. Other than that it's mostly lighthearted and funny.
I've seen some people ignorantly pass this up due to the way it looks, but rest assured there's no real fanservice, and I'm sure all the girls are old enough anyways.
Definitely a must-buy. 10/10.

As a Doom player and fan since Doom 1 on PC and SNES i feel bad for buying this at release.
Why? I will explain because i am 30+, have played hundreds of games now in my lifetime and for my taste new AAA game releases are getting worse and worse every year.
Good looking? Mostly yes! All the other stuff is mostly mediocre or worse.
Gameplay is way to casual these days, not challenging at all, repetitive and shallow.
So let's start this and i know a lot will disagree because they enjoyed the game BUT i don't care - i try to be as honest as i can.
The good:
Graphics are good, performance and optimization is nice and rare these days.
Sound design and soundtrack is nice too - no question.
The maps design is ok, but i wish there was some more "material" or "reference" to the first two Doom games.
Enemies are nice designed but it gets boring after the third time killinge the same enemy - AI is not that great.
The bad:
Only 10 hours of gamesplay in singleplayer and i wasn't even fast.
It's boring and - to be honest - i had to force myself to play it till the end.
It was fun for like 1-3 hours, following 3 hours were ok but i thought every hour "hell, i hope there is something new coming soon - this game is so repetitive and i am bored!". But there wasn't. So i forced myself to finish it the last 3-4 hours. And there is no way i would replay this again.
It was so boring and i don't know. Lack of everything Doom has been for me up to now.
The "new" mechanics killed it totally for me - simply some "OH WOW!"-stuff to get some casual kids buying and playing it, nothing else.
Multiplayer is nothing to talk about - it's not worth any minute.
Maps are boring, map editor is again a thing i would like to forget as fast as possible.
So - now let's come to my decission why i can not recommend this game for 30€ or even 20€. At 10€ maybe worth a look.
I do compare price and playtime for myself.
If a game totally blows your mind in 10 hours for 30-40 hours - i'm ok with that. ( Hellblade: Senuas Sacrifice )
But such shallow gameplay with lack of everything Doom has been before ( because it was something new back then ) is not worth 30 or 20 bucks.
Grab it at 10 $/€ - that's ok.

Since I've made it near the end, it's time for a more serious review.
The Neptunia franchise is the first anime franchise that I ever got into. The quirkyness, the overall theme and plot were among the most interesting to me at the time. But... We're not here to talk about the entire franchise.
What can I say about Megadimension Neptunia VII? It's enjoyable, it's lengthy, it can be challenging at points. It has everything you need for a good JRPG. The combat system isn't the greatest, as sometimes it seems a bit rigged. For example, enemies will target a very specific character from your party, even though it seems like the opposite would be logical. Sometimes certain characters and/or enemies will gain extra turns for seemingly no reason. It's not perfect, but it's enjoyable at the least.
The story - or rather, storieS - are what sold this game for me. There's always a twist around every corner, for example
. And when you least expect it, there's always a boss battle.
Speaking of bosses, I heavily enjoy the new Parts system. If an enemy has certain defensive parts, you can perform a Parts Break on them. That is, attacking said parts enough to the point where they will shatter, leaving the enemy vulnerable. The only area I found this mechanic to be an issue is during
. It felt like it was put in to create a false sense of difficulty -
.
The quests system has stayed the same throughout the franchise, giving the players optional side-quests to perform for Shares, extra items, EXP, etc. It's useful if you want to grind the game to hell, I suppose.
Speaking of grinding, I found this installment to be far less grindy than previous ones. I only had to go grinding for one or two levels per character every now and then, which is extremely welcome for someone like me who hates the idea of grinding for hours on end.
The route system. Sometimes the route system felt like an unnecessary nuisance to pad the game for length at certain points
.
Now on to probably the best part about the game: The soundtrack. God damn, I LOVE Neptunia's soundtrack. Kenji Kaneko and all the other composers did an excellent job in making music for these games, and I applaud them a million times over. My favourite track out of this game would probably have to be "Absolute."
Overall, I really enjoyed this game. I feel like I got my money's worth, given the 50+ hour length and the sheer amount of content within. The story was great, the gameplay was solid. I have few bad things to say about this game.
Pros and Cons time, folks!
Pros:
-Great story.
-♥♥♥♥ing amazing soundtrack.
-Great mechanics.
-Great combat system.
-Minimal grinding (At least for me).
-It's Neptunia. What more could you want?
Cons:
-Combat seemed to be rigged at points.
-Route system seemed unnecessary.
-Enemies and Characters alike seemed to gain extra turns for no reason.
All in all, this game is great. I highly recommend it to any Neptunia fan, or for anyone who enjoys a good JRPG.
I give Megadimension Neptunia VII a 10/10.

They are slowly turning the table from the close disaster that IGP got unto them, heck we might even get a proper CW, and Solaris free for all arena, cash prize kinda tournament feature (MIGHT get, take it with a bit of salt). Give them a chance, with an open mind.
NOW! Pros and cons from my experience so far.
PROS:
1: Alot of mech varity and more to come.
2: As good as balance can get so far between Clan and IS mech and tech. Balancing lore and gameplay priorities are difficult, understand that.
3: No, no Pay 2 Play! It got his Paywall for preorders, but that will ever be a short term "cash-grab".

To claim the prizes by clicking greish tabs.

CONS:

2: Lacks a bit of optimiation, might be a bit laggy even with super computer.

I'm an old-school gamer, gaming since I was in my early teens (13-14) and a veteran of MechWarrior 4 (Mercenaries + Vengeance). I played competitive CS and Battlefield most recently at a high level. My usertag back then was "3N3RGY".
I have friends from MechWarrior 4 that have been waiting for the newest installment of MechWarrior since 2003. I, myself, and others, literally built PCs (computers) for this game when it was announced. Everyone had VERY high expectations. I played the game in beta and upon release.
The game had numerous drama since, and if I talked about it all, I could write a 100 page paper. I'll try to keep it short. I'm stll a bit salty because I feel this game, MWO, has a lower skill-cap than MechWarrior 4, but there are simply NO mech games on the market. Thus, if one is looking for a "mech" fps game, then this is it.
I still wish the game implemented suicide options for the mech, crouch ability, active/passive radar ability, and more freedom with movement, as-well as bigger maps and weapons with longer ranges with high skill cap to allow more elite/skilled players to master that have more hours in the game, to show their expertise over more novice gamers. I feel currently with the way the game is setup, a good player can peak at 100hours, and there wouldn't be THAT much difference with someone at 1000hours, but this skill cap just isn't that high (i.e. CS:GO).
Anyway, as mentioned before, there are simply no other mech games that compare, thus I have to recommend. I guess I also have immense nostalgia from MechWarrior 4, and I truly have not met, not in Battlefield or Counter-strike or ANY game I played, as many DEDICATED, DIE-HARD battletech fans as you find in MechWarrior. There has been a lot of critiscim on PGI and Russ Bullock, but they have made efforts thus far and I have to support though (Though I am still banned on MWO Forums and they refuse to change my ingame name, "ENERGY").
Nevertheless, try the game, love or hate it, it is one of the best if not best mech game on the market currently. I would love to write a more comprehensive review, since the drama around this game has been insane, but instead I recommend new players log-on to HPG outreach on reddit, as it's a very good MWO resource.

The gameplay it self is fun while you level up your armor and weapons.  In the game they have classes for pretty much anyone.  The Pathfinder for those who like a fast hard to hit class.  The Sentinel for those of us who like sniping (this class is hard at first but don't give up right away on it.). The Infiltrator whose main job is stealth and powerful weapons to blow stuff up.
These classes are the light classes who are fast but fragile like Master Chief.  The Soldier is the middlle ground class has a little bit of everything (start with this class first to get the hang of the game.). The Raider is a tougher kind of soldier which likes explosions (good for players that like the explosion guy with good armor and weapons)  The Technician is the class that knows engineering and fixes the base up. Those are the middle classes that have a little bit of everything in them.
For those of you who like the big tough guys these next 3 classes are for you.  The Juggernaut is the light heavy with good powerful weapns ( if you like heavys but want to move at good speed choose this class.). The Doom Bringer speacalizes in rocket launchers and chain guns. The brute is the most dominant class with hard hitting weapons that pack a punch ( only downside is your slow.)
Each class has a jetpack which helps you get around. Its a fast pace game with tons of killing.  If you read this review I hope it was helpful.

The Steam Controller takes some getting used to, but not much.  Out of the box, you get everything you need to get started, even batteries.  To be sure, the Steam Controller is priced fairly.
What really separates the Steam Controller from others is the nearly endless options for customization.  Everything, from trackpad sensitivity to the brightness of the steam button, right down to turn on/off sounds, can be fine-tuned to your preference.
That said, while it is a great controller, it will not replace your mouse and keyboard for games where they are needed, despite what the advertising says.  Therefore, bear in mind that you're buying a controller, not a replacement for your mouse & keyboard.
All in all, I would definitely recommend this controller.

The setup process for each game is outrageous. For example I used the Game FTL, a strategy game  that required constant mouse movement and several inputs that could also use keyboard inputs. After spending roughly an hour going through all the commands and tweaking the controller to my liking I found myself running out of room. Going deep into the button layout resolved this, at the cost of having to hold the paddles to make the joystick act as 8 buttons instead of just 4. That would have been fine until I realized this created the arduous process of remembering the keys for each button on the controller. That might not seem like a big issue for just this one game, but changing from game to game creates the issues of re learning the custom controller youve created for each of the games.
Alternativley? you can run a Usb extension cable (I took the time to create a wall mount and convert the USB to CAT5 so I can extend the range even further) and plugged in a cheap keyboard and mouse and put them next to my couch. No need to re learn inputs, just as confortable, works as intended.
Thinking of picking up 4 of these for coop couch games? Just get the 360 wireless a receiver and you can use any game that supports 360 controllers, which at this point is s pretty large selection. In the box you get the Controller, a USB dongle, 2 batteries for the controller, a USB 2 wire (the controller is wired) and what I assume is an external USB port for the dongle (Can also be used with the wire to move the dongle away from your machine)

*** Review in progress, need more testing time.  ***trackpad review for FPS and strategy games will come soon.  This is a basic review of the Steam Controller.
I’m currently testing the Steam controller with Spelunky, Talos Principle, and Civ 5.  I bought the Steam controller as a substitution to KB+M because my right wrist hurts sometimes.

In terms of hardware
Build quality: The Steam controller doesn’t feel as cheap as some users have said.  The buttons and trackpads don’t feel cheap.  But the plastic casing of the body of the controller could be improved because it doesn’t feel as smooth as the 360 controller.
Weight: Without batteries the Steam controller feels about as heavy as a 360 controller.  So the heavier feel while playing wireless might be an issue for long gameplay.
***Shape: The bottom half of the 360 controller has a downward curve which gives the user a nice comfortable grip. The bottom half of the Steam controller has an upward curve and feels awkward and uncomfortable for your palms.
Size of buttons:  The buttons are smaller than the 360 controller which currently gives me less precision in platforming games like Spelunky, but maybe I’ll get used to it over time.
In terms of software
It currently feels like I’m in a beta test because there are few games with full support so you do have to do some configurations, but fortunately Steam users have set up configurations for most programs.  And it’s pretty cool that users have configured hotkeys in non Steam programs like Itunes.
Overall
I appreciate the innovation the Steam controller brings to gaming.  I recommend it to people who want to play KB+M games on the couch.  For non couch gamers, the controller does not feel necessary.

This has to be one of the most complete and enjoyable Metroidvania's i've played in a long time.
Let me discuss some strong selling points for it.
Pros
- It's massive. Bursting with content that will keep you busy for ages and that's not including the FREE DLC.
- Combat is flexable and interesting with the idea of building up a combo meter and avoiding hits (this is a bullet hell game as well ;3). Plenty of tools to use and lots of upgrades to expand on your mobility.
- The ability to sequence break and take the game at your leasiure. You can go in any direction and most of the time keep going, being able to cheat around things that would require upgrades (or at the very least a long detour).
- Plenty of boss fights with a crap ton of challenge. Don't let the cute looks of the visuals turn you off. Behind their moe is a terminator ready to murder you after a wrong step or even a funny look.
- Great music. Each tune suits the area and the music often gets distorted when you're affected with status effects (slow down and instant death are a great example of this).
Cons (minor grips in the long scheme of things)
- Events are funneled in to a singlar area at times in which afterwards triggers the ability to get powerful mobility upgrades. It's rather inorganic and kinda disrupts the design of such a free flowing game.
- Story is a tad weak. Alot of the story resolves things purely in to 'excuse to fight things'. I guess that's a weakness of giving players such freedom. They still have to fight things.
All in all it's some of the best 18 bucks i've spent in a long time for a game. (not including the OST/artbook buy. The artbook is totally worth a buy btw).

Rabi-Ribi is, in a word, delightful.
The game is simply wonderful to play and experience. For something I picked up on a whim while it was on sale, I can easily see myself playing this game again and again in the future. For people who love a good, classic-feeling Metroidvania game with an intense bullet-hell twist that is both fun and challenging, this is a knock-out.
The story of Rabi-Ribi is fairly simple, all things considered, and it very rarely takes itself too seriously. This is by no means a bad thing. If anything, it helps make the game very easy to dive into. It's cute and fun, but never makes you feel like what you're doing in the game is pointless, and there's enough of a mystery here and there to make you want to press forward so you can solve it. There are a slew of interesting and unique characters in the game that you run into (and often fight) multiple times, and between their design, dialogue, and battles, each one feels as new and as fresh as the first, and never suffer from a feeling of repetition. If I had to find one complaint with the characters, it's that even though there are dozens of well-designed and fun characters in the game, I feel like there could stand to be a little bit more interaction between the supporting cast as a whole, not just with the main character. That's not to say that there isn't any interaction at all, though! Several characters often have other characters and the relationships they share as some of their motivations, and they never feel trite or "shoehorned." I just wish that there had been a little more.
The controls are solid and smooth. There were very few, if any, points in the game where I felt like I was suffering difficulties because of the controls as opposed to the intended challenge at that point. They made perfect sense, too; it felt no different than playing Super Metroid or Castlevania: SotN, controls-wise. My only nitpick with the controls is that as you progress through the game and unlock more attacks and movement abilities, there were some moments where I found myself accidentally triggering one when I intended to trigger the other (e.g., Fast-falling when I intended to do a downward aerial-strike). However, these moments were extremely few and far between, and I'm more likely to chalk them up to getting panicked in difficult situations as opposed to any flaw of the controls themselves.
Rabi-Ribi has a wonderful, retro-esque appeal with its graphics. Characters and backgrounds look as if they fell right out of a Super Nintendo game, which helps lend and even greater "classic" feel to its Metroidvania-style gameplay. One thing I found very pleasing, though, is that while the backgrounds and characters have a 16-bit feel to them, the danmaku patterns that bosses throw out generally appear a little more "higher-def," for lack of a better word. Far from being jarring or disruptive, it definitely helps you understand exactly where the threat of an enemy attack is, making it easier to approach and render the feeling of an attack to be more fair of a challenge, without being any less difficult.
The soundtrack of Rabi-Ribi is phenomenal. The background music for each area fits perfectly and each track helps pile even more charm on top of the already wonderful appearance and "feeling" of all of them. From quiet, explorative tunes to intense, pulse-pounding boss tracks, the music just helped pull me even deeper into the game as a whole.
Heaps of it! There are not only multiple difficulty levels, ranging from "Novice" to "Bunny Extinction," there's also New Game+ mode and several (!) different Boss Rush challenges, as well as a Speedrun mode. On top of the standard difficulty settings, there are also some options that change how the game's difficulty scales with your progress. Normally, the bosses' difficulties scale with both how far you've progressed in the story
how many items and powerups you've collected. However, there's also an Alternate mode that causes bosses to scale only with story progress, and much more strongly at that. This mode encourages players to spend as much time as they can exploring, backtracking, and using new  abilities they've unlocked to power up and prepare for the bosses. Between the different scaling modes (some of which I haven't unlocked!) and the multiple difficulties, the main story alone can be experienced multiple times with a different feeling each time, to say nothing of the bonus Boss Rush modes!
I enjoyed the heck out of Rabi-Ribi. It's an absolutely wonderful game to play and experience, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who enjoys Metroidvania-style games with a challenge.

8BitMMO in my opinion seems to be a game where building a community is key. You don't get handed your materials and get sent out to mine and craft them though like several other games out there. Instead you have two systems working and playing off of each other. On one hand you have the RPG section. Here the system handles your characters progression, shop system, quests, economey and the most importing thing, FIGHTING THE BAD GUYS! On the other hand you have have the Building system that directly feeds off of the RPG system. You fight monsters which nets you gold and expierence which can net you more expierence and gold from a quest but most importantly it lets you get your materials to build. The shop is tiered in such a way that your level dictates what you can buy in the various sections of the shop and you use the gold you gain to purchase the items. You can then take the materials you purchase to your own Pocket Dimension. Here you can build what you want then invite people to visit or open it up to the public. The game has heart behind it. I can clearly see inspirations, aspirations and a future for this game, if it can quickly evolve and try to weather the storm.

If you enjoyed Faster Than Light this is the game for you. Everything is randomized so no game is the same. For example a faction in the game I have never met before was infected with nanites and began raiding my territories forcing me to destroy them. Even though an achievement says that I can ally with them.
The game's story is pretty much mass effect meets star trek where an all powerful alien race invades the galaxy and it's up to you to rally all factions under your banner to fight them.
Pros:
-Your choices matter somewhat usually when you take the risky route or invest it comes out positive instead of there being a chance of explosion in your starbase. Diplomacy usually concerns which faction you protect from the main antagonist and which side you support when two factions begin attacking each other.
-The graphics do have their own charm in a way that it's very high quality despite being pixels. you can see the bits of spacecraft fly off as it explodes or the pixelated blood from your crew members as they get their heads blown off.
-Combat is great using a combo system, knowing when to exploit them to cause extra damage or not exploting them so their status effect can stay on the enemy is key to winning a space battle.
-Game features a somewhat complex tech web.
-Many pop culture references are in the game including Buck Rogers and the amount of red shirts that die in Star Trek. In the game however the green shirts fill this role.
Cons:
-The beginning of the game is very tedious as you constantly have to send out fleets to pick up supplies from your systems; however this is remedied when you push the antagonist out of your systems then all of your territories automatically send resources to you. People who do not finish the game and write a review misinterpret an actual part of the story with a permanent game mechanic. Your territories do not send you resources at the beginning of the game due to the antagonist destroying the main terran fleet along with their home planet.
-The ground combat however is very dry and a waste of time. There is no point to leveling ground combat skills and it is only related mission wise at one point in the game.
-The game has the occasional glitch that usually has to be fixed by restarting the game.
-The other factions tend to be useless other than providing an artifact for your starbase and one subpar ship for the final battle. Instead of a 3 ship fleet or at least a powerful flagship that is seen in game on occasion. These are entire races with multiple solar systems under their control and they cannot afford to give you more. They also do not fight the antagonist either, they more or less do the opposite where their fleets are constantly taken over and just sent straight to your starbase to attack you. Even after saving their homeworld they still raid other factions as if there are no other areas in their territory being taken by the antagonist.
-Only two ships for each officer type exists so six different ships in total where they are split in half for synergy. So only 2 types of fleets are viable or else you cannot combo and do large amounts of damage.
-Cut content: I looked at the Wiki page and even the photos on this store page show ships or content that are not in the game. For example the Targe and Stiletto class ships are not in game. Officer traits are also not in the game nor ship customization. Reading the Halcyon 6 wikipedia pages will give a lot more on this. Those photos of faction leaders are also never seen in game.
Overall what was included is very good and when I beat the game the creators left a message saying that a lot of improvements will be coming to the game. Hopefully the DLC will be free because all of the evidence is here that these things are or were in the game already. Then again, supporting an indie developer that gives a reasonable price for DLC will work for me as well.
Edit: It's been several months since this review and the creators have already taken all feedback and fixed most problems for free. With the ship customization currently in beta it will break the last con I have where you are forced into a mold.
Drone construction is now available for the first part of the game to gather resources.
Factions now send flagships for the end game along with expert pilots

Playing this game since beginning of open beta, but let's get straight to the interesting part, shall we?
+ Almost 0 pay to win
+ Rewards twitchy skills AND strategic thinking in combat
+ Sophisticated hitzone system
+ Rewards experimenting through customization (half the battle is fought, before it even began)
+ Customization is HUGE (for combat and aesthetics)
+ Many, very different, mechs and designs to choose from
+ No negative incomes -> never worry about losing money for bad matches
+ Rewards Teamplay
+ Pretty unique experience
+ It's big stompy robots!
- Ingame earnings aren't very high (recently buffed, so its better now)
- Some optional, but helpful stuff takes rather long to get
- Balance could absolutely be better (though not horrible)
- Learning curve is steep and acquired skill vanishes quickly when not played for a while
- There could be more maps
- Too many "spend your money on this" events, which distracts even if optional
Overall a very unique game among all those twitch heavy shooters and hectic arena games out there. I especially love how it combines these elements with a very tactical, slower paced environment. The mechs and their designs are really cool and add a lot to the game, even more so for mechwarrior fans. Take into account the steep learning curve though and don't give up if piloting seems hard at first.
If you love experimenting with many different builds and having a lot of options, this is also a game for you.

If you like arena shooters, but wish there was some more thinking and strategy involved, this is a game for you. The goal is the destroy the enemy, but whether or not you're successful depends not just on your accuracy with a mouse, but how well you can build your mech, and how well you can manage your systems mid-battle.
There are a variety of mechs and weapons to choose from, and you can endlessly customize them with numerous paint schemes and colors. Decals are coming soon. You can choose from several factions, each on either side of a galactic war.
There's a built-in VOIP, but many people have their own team speak servers. I would recommend getting on one or the other because team coordination is the most powerful tool in this game.
Wait on trying the Community Warfare (Faction tab) until you're experienced and own your own customized mechs. It is absolutely a Hardcore mode, and you don't want to try it with the free trial mechs.
Don't worry, you can buy everything you need with in-game currency. There is no P2W here, and the 1-2% of items locked behind a paywall do not confer any advantages, they are just unique items.
I have been playing since before Steam, and I'd recommend this to any Steam players that want to think when they shoot and engage with a more mature community.

As a Doom player and fan since Doom 1 on PC and SNES i feel bad for buying this at release.
Why? I will explain because i am 30+, have played hundreds of games now in my lifetime and for my taste new AAA game releases are getting worse and worse every year.
Good looking? Mostly yes! All the other stuff is mostly mediocre or worse.
Gameplay is way to casual these days, not challenging at all, repetitive and shallow.
So let's start this and i know a lot will disagree because they enjoyed the game BUT i don't care - i try to be as honest as i can.
The good:
Graphics are good, performance and optimization is nice and rare these days.
Sound design and soundtrack is nice too - no question.
The maps design is ok, but i wish there was some more "material" or "reference" to the first two Doom games.
Enemies are nice designed but it gets boring after the third time killinge the same enemy - AI is not that great.
The bad:
Only 10 hours of gamesplay in singleplayer and i wasn't even fast.
It's boring and - to be honest - i had to force myself to play it till the end.
It was fun for like 1-3 hours, following 3 hours were ok but i thought every hour "hell, i hope there is something new coming soon - this game is so repetitive and i am bored!". But there wasn't. So i forced myself to finish it the last 3-4 hours. And there is no way i would replay this again.
It was so boring and i don't know. Lack of everything Doom has been for me up to now.
The "new" mechanics killed it totally for me - simply some "OH WOW!"-stuff to get some casual kids buying and playing it, nothing else.
Multiplayer is nothing to talk about - it's not worth any minute.
Maps are boring, map editor is again a thing i would like to forget as fast as possible.
So - now let's come to my decission why i can not recommend this game for 30€ or even 20€. At 10€ maybe worth a look.
I do compare price and playtime for myself.
If a game totally blows your mind in 10 hours for 30-40 hours - i'm ok with that. ( Hellblade: Senuas Sacrifice )
But such shallow gameplay with lack of everything Doom has been before ( because it was something new back then ) is not worth 30 or 20 bucks.
Grab it at 10 $/€ - that's ok.

First, let me get this out of the way:  Don't buy this if it'll be your only controller.  Some games flat do not work with this controller, and I'm not sure if it works at all with games that aren't on Steam.
Now, to the meat of the review:  This is an amazing controller.  Yes, it feels cheap, but the amount of customization in the controls and the fact that it has haptics and a gyro more than make up for it.  The right touchpad is awesome as an analog stick, and the fact that you can remap the stick button gives you unlimited options for customization.  You can even use macros on any button you please.  Way more options than the Xbox controller I was using.  The fact that the stick behavior can be customized helps too.  The buttons on the back are really handy for FPS games, I like mine set to Sneak and Reload.  The interface for customizing controls is pretty straightforward, but you may have to play with it to get the buttons the way you like them.  I don't really like the fact that the D-pad is a touchpad too, but if you set it to touch sensitive with maximum haptic feedback, it feels like you're pushing a button when you're really just touching it.
TL;dr:  This controller is for you if you don't really feel that Xbox controllers give you enough buttons to control your games (or you want to remap controls in a way that makes more sense to you) but it's a little plasticky.  Battery life is great (for the amount of gaming I do anyway) and it works well on the Steam Link.  All in all, I have no complaints about spending what I did for it, and I'd recommend it as a great step between kb+m and xbox controllers, with the caveat that you may need to fiddle with the mappings on some non-controller optimized games.

In short, it was difficult getting used to it at first - specifically the trac pads, but it is an excellent controller.
Pros:
o It allows you to play games that don't have controller support with a controller
o You can assign any keyboard key to any button and have a mix between game pad buttons + keyboard/mouse functionality, eg - using A, B, Y, X game pad functionality but having right trigger act as RMB
o There is mode shifting, giving even more functionality to the controller
o Works extremelly well with Steam Link
o The right Trac Pad (where there would normally be a second stick) gives almost mouse accuracy
o The amount of customizations is excellent
o You can set the Trac Pads to bring up in-game radial overlays that can activate any mouse/keyboard/gamepad button
Cons:
o Takes some getting used to using the Trac Pads
o No Macro programming, but you can set a single button to activate multiple buttons at the same time
o It would be cool if there was a headphone slot
Highly recommended for use with Steam Link/Couch gaming.

, it is the third game in the Deus Ex series, and a prequel to the original game released in 2000.
As Adam Jensen, you are taking main, missions and side missions, if you choose (you can’t get back to finish side quest if you already finished the main missions). Missions allow you the freedom to complete them according to your preferences: You can choose to infiltrate a building with lethal or non-lethal means, to sneak around and never engage the enemy or to use hacking and turn existing security features to your side. From the outset, you're given all of the tools — guns, a takedown move (in both lethal and non-lethal flavors) and the skills to hack into systems — and let loose into the world.
You also have choices when it comes to your skills and abilities. You earn "praxis points" by gaining XP from main quests and side quests, which are good for spending on the "augmentations" you'd like. Earning XP has a lot more different minor ways — you’ll be more interested to explore more through secret paths to gain traveler/explorer/pathfinder XP and using non-lethal take down to your enemies to earn expedient and merciful XP really brings this game to the more maximum stealth game. There are abilities associated with each kind of play style — stealthy upgrades like a limited-time invisibility cloak (which I think is the most important skill that is super helpful to pass through guards waves, lasers, cameras, robots and etc. like a ghost if you like to play with non-lethal style), thicker skin for the pugilistic, hacking skills and etc.
This emphasis on choice — along with often brilliant level and mission design — makes playing Human Revolution a powerful experience. I went into missions tense, worked my way through waves of guards, talk and investigating people with people like a detective and challenges methodically and always felt satisfied by my progress. Human Revolution made me feel like a smart genius resourceful spy.
The game draws remarkable atmosphere between the sterility of the corporate world and the grit of the city with its cyberpunk, transhumanism, futuristic style. Office interiors feature clean lines and metallic surfaces; in trash-street corners, the sewer, the homeless huddle around flaming barrels for warmth.  It all comes back to that gold and that black. The color combination rivals teal and orange for its known visual appeal, but the color palette's impact goes beyond its attractiveness. In China, the term "black gold" refers to political corruption and corporate greed, key narrative elements in Human Revolution. The colors recall the brightness of modern machinery and the darkness of Detroit's alleyways, and evoke the works of Botticelli and Da Vinci, who ushered in a renaissance, just as David Sarif hopes to lead the world into a new era of enlightenment. There is so much meaning in this single detail.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a story-driven action adventure RPG, taking place in a cyberpunk future ruled by scientific breakthroughs and corporate greed. You play as Adam Jenson, an ex-cop turned fully-augmented head of security for one of the worldwide leading companies in technological advancement, Sarif Industries. You'll travel the globe, sneak into top-secret enemy facilities, and eventually unearth a conspiracy hidden to the public eye. Needless to say, the story of Human Revolution is very deep; the game deals heavily with themes regarding humanity, freedom, and limitation, and has you questioning the morality of scientific advancement in post-modern society. While it takes a while to set up an engaging story, the game keeps you playing based simply on its fascinating vision of the not-too-far-off future. The choices you encounter along the way effect the story in meaninful ways as well. In short, Human Revolution may not feature the most emotionally compelling story ever in a video game, but easily one of the most intriguing.
Human Revolution can be completed in two differing ways; by sneaking past all your enemies stealthily, or going guns-blazing into every encounter. Because the level design is incredibly well done, both approaches are commendable. I usually prefer the stealthy approach, but only because it's more rewarding and has more features available. As you level up, you'll earn Praxis Kits, which  upgrade your augmentations. Let me just say that no game I've played has offered as many useful upgrades as are available here. The game also has a hacking element, which is basically a simple minigame. However, hacking also acts as one of the unsung approaches of Human Revolution; you can disable cameras, gain access to secret files, and even turn programmed turrets on your enemies. Enemy AI as well is usually pretty intelligent. Any time that I think I've been spotted while stealthing, enemies will most definitely have spotted me. Overall, the gameplay here is fairly well thought-out and challenging.
Overall, Deus Ex is the cyberpunk game that I've always wanted, but never had the chance to play. While it's definitely built as a stealth title, players used to the combat approach will still have a fun time. The soundtrack might I add is also amazingly good. On a final note, the Director's Cut merely includes a DLC expansion into the main story, adding about an hour or two of additional gameplay, though it's still worth it. If you're into conspiracy-heavy plots, cyberpunk settings, or just a well-built stealth game, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the ideal game for you.

If I had to describe this strategy RPG in a sentence it would be something like "Darkest Dungeon's combat and X-COM's management gameplay had a baby in a FTL themed universe." Massive Damage made a great game that tries to do a lot of different things: from turn based ground and space combat to managing a base, resources, research, and construction; and even a bit of faction management and exploration thrown in there as well.
Combat is turn based, and in order to beat the enemy fleet as quickly and painlessly as possible you have to learn how your officers and their ships abilities best synergize. For example, a science ship attack may put a debuff on an enemy that causes a tactical ship attack to do extra damage. When not in combat, you have to make sure that you are gathering resources in order to research and build new and higher level ships. Outside of combat the game has a real time mode similar to X-COM. While the game is paused you build, assign officers to projects, order fleets around, then press play and watch stuff happen. While at the start you have to micromanage gathering resources by sending fleets to gather them, at the end of the first part of the game this becomes automated. You can also have officers use rooms in your base to generate small lump sums of resources and a bit of xp.
While this game offers a lot, it's not really a complex game. I would say one of the biggest strengths of this game is that it combines a lot of good parts of other games into a simple and fun whole. This is also its weakness as some might see the game as "dumbing down" these aspects. For example, ship choices are fairly simple. Besides faction ships that you can get from befriending the factions (and any secrets I don't know about yet) there are only 2 ship choices per officer type per level, and each higher level ship is a direct upgrade from its lower level counterpart. There are 3 officer types, and 5 levels, so there are 30 primary ships; and instead of mixing and matching, you will probably want to just go for the higher level ships rather than experiment as the higher level ships have much better stats.
Halcyon 6 takes the management aspects of X-COM, the combat elements of Darkest Dungeon, streamlines them, adds an FTL art style and feel, stirs in some faction management, pokes some fun at Star Trek, and calls it a day. If you want a fun game that makes a lot of different parts work as a fun and engaging strategy RPG, I'd highly recommend it.

Mechwarrior Online continues the tradition of a proud franchise. This is a sim-light shooter that maintains all the greatness of the previous versions while also providing a fantastic community of people to play with in a simulated galactic war that, while still in development, is shaping up to be a very unique experience.
Most importantly this "freemium" game has a very reasonable grind and practically no "pay to win" elements. The Hero mechs are a nice way to ease the grind, but after playing 2 years I can honestly say that most of my best mechs were purchased with the in-game currency - "C-Bills", which are earned by simply playing the game. There is no "gold ammo" or any other such pay to win devices here. The only thing that costs money that is essential are mech-bays, but these are frequently rewarded in weekend spanning "events" that offer many prizes for scoring "points" for game play. Many of these prizes are "real money" items and PGI has proven very generous.
That's not to say that there isn't a reason to spend money. There is plenty of "swag" that can be purchased to deck out your favorite mechs, such as - War Horns, Camo Patterns, Paints and cockpit items. You can also purchase mech packs or if you want the hot new thing, you can pay for early access to new mechs before they are available for C-Bills. Last but most importantly there is "premium time" which increases the XP and C-bills earned during matches. This decreases the grind and when coupled with Hero 'Mechs practically removes the grind completely. I have spent more money on this game than any other in my life, and I will continue to do so, simply because I don't feel I have to.. There is no extortion here, no "pay to win". The grind is hardly a grind at all. If you enjoy playing the game, forget about your bank account and check on it occassionally and be surprised by how fast it grows.
To sum up, MWO is perhaps the best "free to play" game on the market. It hits that perfect balance of "free" and "grind" without aggravating "pay to win" mechanics. I have been playing it solidly for over 2 years now and still play it more than any other game I own. Be warned though. The learning curve here is very steep (2-3 months). Don't be surprised if you go a week before getting a legitmate kill. But in return MWO offers an incredibly deep and diverse "thinking man's shooter" experience unlike any other.

Read on, I've got the goods on this one: Ignore the time Steam says I have invested. My forum profile tells me I have over 6000 regular matches and I know I have a couple thousand at least before they put that counter in. I'm pretty sure that doesn't even include my community warfare drops either. I presently own 254 mechs (all mastered but the newest 4) and I had never heard of Battletech or MechWarrior before trying this game. I still don't know jack about the lore, I make my own stories up thank ya very much. Only thing you need to learn is how to point and shoot while running for your life.
The good: This game is completely 100% free to play. No BS money sinks, you don't have to put in one single cent to play or be amongst the elite. The weekend (or weeklong) challenges will give you all the MC or mechbays you will need to keep growing your army (community warfare alone allows you to unlock a bunch of mechbays just for playing). Real money buys paint, cockpit items, warhorns and hero mechs (which are not as good as regular variants in nearly 100% of chassis). Even my $500 Gold Direwolf is only a fancy paint job; it's the same Direwolf Prime you can buy yourself with in-game currency. You can make an argument that premium time is essential - I am never without it or my glass of wine - as it cuts down on the grind a lot. I have never not had premium time up so I can't speak to the wasted sober hours some go through.
Game play is addicting and can swing between exhilarating and infuriating because all your pug team mates are idiots, right? What you will eventually do is join a community. Then you will find out those guys are annoying and lose every second match and you will move on and find another one. They will be a little better but you'll still be bouncing around like Tigger at a swingers club until you find that sweet spot where those guys who know how to carry a team play. If you're lucky you will pick up a trick or two. I won't tell you who the elite groups are but you'll figure that out.
The bad: Bad is a strong word. Work-in-progress is more apt. Community warfare is leaving beta 2 and beta 3 is right around the corner and this game is by no means finished as it is constantly evolving with an ever-changing meta but this is not an early access game. At least you'll be learning about the new features and game modes at the same time as all the vets and won't be at too much of a disadvantage there. Some of the maps are weak and we still need more. In my opinion map making is PGI's greatest weakness but a couple of them are great so that saved their goat. What on earth possessed them to make so many maps that require night vision and heat vision for targeting when you are trying to sell paint jobs to make all your mechs look cool is beyond me. My $500 (HUNDRED!!) Direwolf is Gold and you dummies can't see it cuz you are in heat vision. Look at me dammit, Im gold!!  You can now vote for maps and game modes so the terra-bad (pun!) ones hardly ever come up.
I would be remiss without a little word about the griefers. Oh-my-god-some-kids-won't-take-it-like-a-man saga is alive and well. So many people can't handle FPS games and being shot in a pretend world. It's amazing how fragile they are. You will see people have complete public meltdowns. I find alcohol helps, maybe you like pills, I don't judge. Want my advice? Ignore the forums too. It's just a whine and rant-fest. Get TeamSpeak and join a team and ask your questions there. The community is huge. The PGI hate-train is always up and running but I have no issues with MechWarrior at all and I have given them well over a thousand bucks for paint and warhorns. And even though I have given them a ridiculous amount of money they have no issues telling me to go pound sand when I send in my own little rant. Money can't buy you love here, just paint. Lots of paint.
Gotta wrap this up cuz the wife is wearing something hot. No-time-to-spell/grammar-check-this-hot, you feel me?. This game rocks. You will go on epic winning and losing streaks, theory craft until your 6am morning alarm goes off, and find a nemesis who you will go to the ends of the earth to kill (I'm looking at you H8Wine). It's run by a North American company so any money you spend here isn't going to some dodgy 3rd world country like some if it's competitors. Go find your fortune, I'll be waiting for you with guns loaded. And kill that H8Wine guy and tell him I sent you.

text:
There's little more for me to say when so many other reviews have aptly described the issues with this game, so I'll be blunt:
Try it if you really, really want to. There's no loss involved. But expect to be punished unless you're a veteran coming back or you've already spent money on the game.
Since other users have already thoroughly warned you about PGI's track record (and if you haven't seen that yet, you should glance through a few negative reviews, because they're valid,) I'll focus instead on warning you on what you, as a new player, should expect to see starting out.
The community is insular. They'll go on for hours and hours about how they want to be inviting and friendly, but their behavior and conduct don't reflect this. Teamplay is important, so pugs are referred to disparagingly by even the most polite of players. Most people still playing are still playing because they have intimate ties to the Battletech or Mechwarrior licenses; the game preys on their nostalgia and they in turn feed the machine and defend it from disparaging remarks. If you play other video games, expect to hear players lamenting about the "call of duty" crowd or other such stupid garbage - further distancing themselves from the general community of online PC gamers at large.
The grind is deceptively monumental: you get a massive boost in cbills (ingame currency) via your first 25 matches and by completing the tutorial, which is generally enough to purchase (though not properly outfit) a single inner sphere mech. If you want to be on even remotely even footing with anyone else, you will need to do this three times: purchase three variants of a single mech, outfit those three variants so they're viable enough to play (stock builds are enormous garbage,) and then play them until you rack up enough experience points to grind out all their "basic skills," which are flat percentage increases to your mech's performance (reduced heat generation, increased acceleration and deceleration, the works.) This will allow you access to a chassis' "elite skills," which are even more powerful advantages afforded to you for greater XP cost (including increased top speed.) Unlocking all four on a variant will literally
all bonuses conferred from basic skills. Yes, you read that right. Grinding obscene amounts of experience into a mech makes it infinitely superior to the same variant, same build, piloted by a new player, regardless of player skill.
After your cadet bonuses are gone, your average income per match as a new player may run anywhere from 50,000 cbills (on a loss) to 300,000 cbills (on a well-played win. You will not see this much money as a new player, as the game's mechanics are relatively complicated, poorly explained, and map design is extremely unforgiving to inexperienced players.) You can probably expect about 100k to 150k per match if you're new. Mech prices vary wildly depending on tonnage, stock loadout, and technology (a clan heavy omnimech with a gauss rifle is going to be much more expensive than an inner sphere light mech with medium lasers and machine guns.) You can expect a decent IS heavy to run you about 7-8 million cbills, then outfitting it with decent weapons, upgraded systems (endo-steel and double heat sinks are generally a must) and a good engine may cost you as much as 7 million more. You can expect a decent clan mech (the stormcrow and timber wolf, both clan mechs, are still bar-none the best vehicles in the game) to run you anywhere from 10 million to 14 million cbills, but luckily there's less to upgrade. Sure hope you know what actually performs well, though, because if you ♥♥♥♥ up and build something ♥♥♥♥♥♥, you'll be selling it back for a fraction of what it cost you.
Weapon balance is comical. There exist entire weapons systems in the game that are completely useless, including machineguns and flamers. No one will tell you this, because A) PGI doesn't understand their own game and balances around a meta they know nothing about, B) the game is loaded with whales who believe themselves to be experts on the game's balance who will tout that you can pilot anything and perform well, as long as you know what you're doing (they don't.) and C) knowledge is steeply guarded by anyone who actually knows how to play the game. "Comp" teams are fiercely protective of their strategies and aren't about to share tips and tricks with every Tom,♥♥♥♥♥♥ and Harry fresh off of steam. There was a line from the old Battletech cartoon that the players think is a hilarious meme: "Information is ammunition." Well it's true, and ammunition is both in shortage and at a premium.
Suffice it to say that lasers are almost universally better than any other weapon.
Map design and the existence of 12v12 matches also have a massive impact on weapon balance, and very few players seem to understand this. Small arenas defined by chokepoints, DotA lanes, massive sight lines, and confusing geometry are the order of the day. Scale is confusing and map geometry frequently makes little sense (why are there rocks in the middle of river city if they offer poor protection from literally any angle? Why is forest colony so huge when there's no objective but to head straight for the middle and fight with the enemy?) Because teams are composed of 12 mechs, the key to victory is focusing targets. Even a premade composed of 12 clown-shoed morons like NKVA can stomp all over the game's population (which is likely to include you, new steam user.) The community will frequently lament the TTK (time to kill) being much too fast, blaming this on the weapons systems and completely disregarding that despite the game's glacial pace for an arena shooter, their woes can be attributed to the fact that the Smart Strategy is to move in a big blob and shoot the same target. These are the same people who sarcastically remark that "teamwork is OP" if you try to bring up disparities in the weapon and technology balance department.
TL;DR the game is stupid, the devs are stupid, and the community is either stupid or uninterested in sharing with you how to get good. The game is enormously rewarding to those who have invested ungodly hours into it, and severely punishing of those who have not. The players and devs alike are confused at how this formula continues to drive away new blood, which the game desperately needs to survive, and don't understand why it leads to a mind-bogglingly steep pricing scheme, like paying 120 US dollars for a mech pack. But they totally want you to come revitalize their game. Because it
their game, after all. Not yours.

Let me say first that I started playing MWO about a year or so ago, and so far I got roughly 80 hourse playtime.
Let's start with the two most common points of criticism for the game:
1. MWO get's much hate because the developers did some really bad things in the past and were inconsistent about their development.
2. MWO is based on the "BattleTech" book series. Many people expected (as was initially promised as far as I know) a game that is very similar to the mech battles in the books. That didn't completely work out though.
So let's address these points:
1. That was the past. Nowadays the developers are very open about the development, posting a kind of status report and roadmap monthly on the forums. They are listening more to what the players want now too. The development as it is now is quite good. As said, it's consistent, the devs aren't acting too much against the players desires and we get two patches, one a bit lighter and one more content-heavy, each month, steadily improving the game. PGI, the developers, are also not afraid to revisit and redo many ingame mechanics.
2. If you don't expect this game to be like the books or didn't even knew about the franchise before, you won't have any problems with this. I actually can't tell how different this is to the books as I simply don't think about it. I recognize BattleTech in this game, but there are also some differences to be noticed.
In conclusion, development is fine today, and if you don't care about the books that's not a point of criticism either.
No. You can only use the premium currency MC to buy cosmetics, mechs and garage slots to have more mechs at the same time. Regarding the mech buying:
You can buy every mech that is availabe for C-Bills, the ingame currency, with MC too to skip the grind.
When new mechs are released, the first month or so they are available for MC only, after that for C-Bills too.
But then, there are also hero mechs. Hero mechs can only ever be bought for MC. They are specially colored and maybe uniquely equipped variants of "regular" mechs. They have unique names and are well known from the books, but they aren't in any way OP. If you want to play an OP mech (lol) you will definitely find one available for C-Bills too.
In the beginning you only have the trial mechs, which change every few weeks or months or so. Trial mechs are regular mechs which you can play without buying, but can't customize, so you're stuck with the standard loadout. As you don't own a mech yet, you have to play some trial-mech matches. The game will support you financially in the beginning by giving you extra money for every battle fought, for the first 25 battles or so. This will make you able to buy your own mech quickly. With the money earned in your next matches you will buy and try different kinds of equipment for your mech. After said first 25 matches though, money earning slows down a lot. You will get up to 200k C-Bills for very good matches and roughly 20k from bad ones. The cheapest mechs cost 1,5 mil, the most expensive ones cost 16 mil. Note that this is not just the chassis, but also motor, weapons, ammo, armor etc. so you can reuse most of the stuff you buy, but it still takes quite some time to make enough money to afford a new mech. Additionally, you will probably spend some millions on buying upgrades and equipment for your new mech.
If you're like me, you will feel a bit shocked when you used up all of the initial money boost and begin to realize how much you actually need to buy a mech. This feeling will however go away after some time and it will feel really rewarding when you can finally buy a new mech or an expensive upgrade. Also, cheap mechs aren't bad. The price of a mech is just the sum of all of the equipment included in the initial loadout plus a bit extra for the chassis. Cheap mechs are light mechs. Light mechs can be just as enjoyable as the huge, hard-hitting but slow assault mechs, it's just personal preference and playstyle.
Graphics are good, not staggering but a sudden laser cutting through the darkness looks really neat. Also, you really feel like in a mechpilots cockpit because of screen shake, red alarm lights and stuff.
Sound is very good, each weapon type has it's own sounds and you can really feel the impacts of attacks on your armor. There's even a map without atmosphere where you can only hear your own movement and impacts on your armor, but nothing else from outside.
.. most of the criticism can be ignored, that really depends on yourself. As always with F2P games, just try it out. If you can get behind the initial confusion about the quite complex MWO and behind the trial mechs, get a mech you like and equip it how you want, you will have a really good time.
Game is incredibly fun.

I am a founder.  I bought the mid-tier founders pack and have not regretted it.  The first year was a bit rocky, but through it all, PGI has done all it can to bring the best sim game the Mechwarrior franchise has seen.  I loved all the other titles, but this is the closest to balanced as any Mechwarrior has been.  PGI has not taken all the suggestions they have received and implemented them (the other founders that are crying and putting up negative reviews are doing so because of this.  Entitlement at it's finest lol), but they have implemented many of them, and even improved on some of those recommendations.  Overall, the game has been good enough for me to buy well over $1000 on mech packs and MC, and there are many many others out there that are like me. MWO is a very teamplay focused 12v12 tactical shooter. Teamwork and good positioning including good use of cover are key to winning. It is free to play and there is no pay to win. Definitely worth to download and give it a try.
There is a nice, short ingame tutorial that teaches you how to move and kill stuff.
Beyond that there is the mechlab, where you can customize your mechs and adjust their loadout to their playstyle. It's easy to spend more hours in the mechlab than in the matches themselves.
In higher tier matches, even the geometry of the mechs and placement of weapons on them become important. The higher the weapon mounts, the less you have to expose yourself from cover to shoot your enemies. In short: There is a lot of depth to the gameplay to explore.
The usual MWO Quick Play match lasts for about 10-15 minutes. Faction Play matches last longer, usually about 20-30 minutes. MWO is perfect for one to three hours of gameplay in the evening and a ton of fun. For longer playing sessions, it feels a bit too repetetive, but that's just my personal experience.
Quick note for newcomers:
If you are new to the game, you should finish the tutorial first and complete the callenges in the Mechwarrior Academy for extra CBills (ingame currency). Try out the different trial mechs available to you in Quick Matches, until you know which kind of mech suits your playstyle best. Once you earned your complete cadet bonus (you get extra CBills in your 25 first Quick Matches), you will have gathered more than enough money to buy your first mech and start to customize it.
That's about it. Good hunting mechwarrior!

I did a total 180 within the first hour of owning it. When I first turned it on, it felt pretty bad, but as I played with it more I realized how much I appreciated the controller and the advantages it had over my standard Xbox controller.
The first game I tried was Dark Souls 3. The default configuration for the game had the right thumbpad open this on-screen menu for various actions.  Now, on the Xbox controller  I am used to the right thumbstick click being used to lock onto enemies. Not so with the default steam controller configuration. On the Steam controller clicking would produce various actions, depending on the position of my thumb. So if I clicked in the middle, lock on worked as expected, if I was ever so slightly off, my character would instead do something like drink estus. The camera movement also felt strange.
Slightly disappointed I decided to try another game on a whim. This time I booted up Dark Souls 2. Now the default DS2 config was much better. The camera worked well, and the right click worked exactly as expected. I did some more research and realized just how customizable the controller is. I was able to export the configurations and use it in Dark Souls 3.
You can also download user premades, so downloading some highly rated preset usually yields great results, and if not, it's very easy to customize it to your liking.
What I'm saying is, much like all "PC Gamer' things, this thing benefits heavily from being configurable and customizable and that's what made me prefer it to my old Xbox controller setup. Most powerful of all though is the ability to use this controller for playing games that normally don't have controller support. Every function of the controller can be mapped to whatever keyboard button you like. In addition, the touchpads are highly customizable to emulate something like mouse movement, thumbtricks, trackpads, and trackbals.  If you bought this and feel like it's not working out, try the customization options, they really make a huge difference.

Honestly can say this pad trumps my 360 so much in my opinion, removing the clunky analogue sticks for smooth touches from your fingers.  This control glides and can work just as much as a mouse on your desktop as it can play on games. Down to some specifics:
Fit:
When first holding this controller I was very weary as didn't feel right.  Both me and my partner held it and both felt it didn't feel great.  On using this however, it works beautifully and I have never actually felt the feeling of the pad is bad whilst using it.  The touchpads are so sensitive that the balls at the bottom help rest your fingers just over the touch pad, taking a more traditional design (e.g. the curve upwards to the analogue sticks on the 360 controller) would actually make this pad difficult to use.  After using this on a few hours on Dark Souls I honestly love the fit now.
Weight:
With batteries the weight of the controller feels slightly heavier than the 360 controller however it isn't bad.  Decent weight overall and, although not tested, believe you might be able yo use this pad on a wired connection if you wish.
Future developments would be nice if you could add and remove weights but it's not an issue.
Responsiveness:
This is the most responsive pad I have ever own.  Everything about it feels slick and the right touch pad has gentle clicking feedback to make it clear when your cursor should move.  I feel in complete control when I hold this pad, the only issue is knowing what each button does, however you can view and change these through using Big Picture mode.
Software and features:
Customising the buttons for games would be better if this was a seperate programme as it is awkward going into big picture mode.  Features overall however are great.  You have more buttons and appears you can match them up however you like.  There are different profiles you can set and when to trigger them.  I couldn't work out what the targetting button was for Dark Souls however was able to customise this easily and now it is actually easier to do this on my pad (as it is a button on the back where my fingers generally rest).  To top it all off, there are a couple of wake up and shut down noises you can give it.
Conclusion:
There are improvements that can be made, but this pad has lived up to the expectations I gave it.  I no longer use my 360 pad as having no wires, more responsiveness and customisation to assign controller buttons on all Steam games is great.  Would hust love one that made it easier for all games, including those not in your Steam library (not explored this much but not found any way of doing this easily so far)

Did you ever dream about being a cashier? Me neither. Yet, this game attracted me because I may have seen an educational side to it. That's why I activated the link offered in a bundle on itch.io and that's why the game is in my steam library too.
So, you bet that your job is to scan products and to put them in the bag while making sure that nothing get crushed because of the weight. Also, you greet people, you take their Shoppy Mart card if they have one, coupons if they have one, etc.. And for fruit and vegetable and seasonal items (Halloween, Christmas for now, I suppose we'll get Easter and bunny chocolate), you have to enter a product code that you can see by pressing SHIFT and your numpad.
That's the core of the game: the more you do levels the more xp you collect and you can unlock new customers like the Stoner, the Pringles look-a-like, the Hobo, etc... Besides, thanks to the weight now shown on the cash register, you can finally avoid more crushing bags and loose a customer. Because after 5 lost, you're fired and you're going to start again the game at first day.
Anyway, don't worry for the money you need to give back to the customer if they're paying with money instead of a credit card, you have the right number shown and what you still have to give.
And the game is mainly put into a world where everything is a parody: from the credit cards, to the memo given by your boss to the customers.
Another little thing: I've spoken about the game as if you had your time for each customer.... because I played it in Easy and that I'll wait until launching me in Normal where you have a timer and that greeting, asking for the card, coupons, scanning them, etc.., is buying you time.
Shoppy Mart is a fun game, even if in the end, the educational side isn't present (unless to see the difference between weights or if giving back money is also interesting). Pezomi, the developer, is present and answering you when you have bugs (like I had with achievements unlocking out of the blue, the game freezing because of a disappearing receipt or money or game that didn't launch anymore correctly).
So yeah, for the price, you have a little good game!
