I'm a big fan of any well executed TBS game. Played all of them and enjoyed most.
This one just doesn't do it for me, I'll tell you why:
-Base building is a bit boring and simplistic
-The interface and gameflow gets very tedious quite quick
-Despite being well-crafted many things are unclear
-It lacks depth and there is no sense of real progress
-Not enough choice, three base commander/ship types, that's it, they do get better but that's all
-Map management becomes very tedious very quick
-Skills don't feel differentiated enough
-Choices don't really have consequence or affect gameplay significantly
-It doesn't reward well, everything is incremental and slow, just a bit more of the same in every aspect
-Battles are boring, the first battle feels exactly the same as your last battle
-Interface could be better streamlined
-The tutorial is tedious, it overstates simple gameplay mechanics and fails to explain some advanced
To sum it up, it is just not fleshed out enough. It feels like the developers had a few good ideas and some nice pixel art to go with it and thought that would be enough. To me there is just no feeling of accomplishment, progress and the crucial just-one-more-day-addiction.
This game feels like the steam edition of 'Knights of pen and paper' another hailed pixel art TBS game, for mobile users, that just didn't do it for me either. Maybe that's my main problem, it feels like a simplistic, albeit good looking, mobile game. For a serious contender on steam it just lacks depth and immersion.
It becomes a boring clickfest way too soon. Developers of indie games need to learn that a few good ideas and some "cool" pixel art doesn't make a good game.
The people hailing this in the reviews as original and creative just haven't played the genre properly:
This game literally does nothing that hasn't been done befoe.
This game doesn't combine anything that hasn't been combined before.
This game doesn't execute it nearly as good as has been done before.
No it just doesn't, I wish it did, really wanted to like it but it's just not there.

Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander brings back fond memories of the old Microprose game Lightspeed. It's a single player game with a single story, and a kind of FTL meets Master of Orion. When there is a single storyline, the last thing you want is to encounter (as I have) a game-breaking bug that kills the immersion and means your only option is: to begin the story again from the beginning in the hope of not hitting the same bug again. Or another one.
At launch, Lightspeed was complete. It had no game-breaking bugs. I guess we've come a long way since then. NOT.
Nevertheless, I'll still give this game a thumbs-up, because if the bug(s) can be fixed then it has a lot of promise for an old Star Trek fan like me :)

So I've finally had the chance the see the ending of the Manga animated in some way (Game came out before the Anime finished the story) and I'm pretty happy how they ended the story in the game. At first I was suprised that the story mode was so short, since it started in midst of the 4th great ninja war. But they implemented the story prior to the war into the adventure mode. I disliked the "diashows" of anime screenshots they used to tell parts of the story, some of those screenshots were definitely not suited to be used in the game. Other that that the animation was nice and the last fight of Naruto and Sasuke was very well done.
In the adventure mode you're able to carry out different type of missions and replay old events of the story. You can travel between different locations and decide whether you want to follow the main events or carry out the side quests.
In addition to the story and adventure mode, the game offers a survival and a tournament mode.
The fighting system is similar to previous Storm titles and is pretty straightforward. You can fight alone or in a team of two/three people. I liked the addition of character swapping while fighting, it added more diversity to the fights. Most of the Manga/Anime characters are among the playable characters and we'll get more in later DLCs. Every character has it's own skillset and awakening mode.
I had no problems regarding resolution, performance and settings.
All in all I really liked the game and would recommend it, but if you own the previous storm titles, wait til this game is on sale, since there aren't huge differences between those games. 8/10

Looking for the honest opinion of a veteran of big stompy robot goodness?  Someone with an intimate understanding of even the smallest game mechanics, and who can give an objective review for all of MWO's features without sugar-coating them?  Well sit back and read on potential mechwarrior.  I, the venerable Carchemish (in-game name) do kinda sorta fit that description.  Mostly.
I'll break this down into what MWO is, and what it is not.  First the 'is':
-  Mechwarrior Online is a player vs player, team arena style game set in the venerable Battletech universe.
-  It is a beautifully rendered game, both in the landscapes and of course the mechs.  PGI has done a fantastic job making the mechs look amazing, especially given the awful source material. Anyone familiar with the old crappy Battletech "artwork" knows what I mean.  I really can’t say enough about this.  I’m always blown away by how they continue to make such gorgeous mechs from such bad original art
-  It is a great blend of slow, build-up-to-the-fight, and then fast paced action.
-  You’ll have a huge mech variety to explore.  Want to race across the map in a fast, agile scout?  Done.  Want to slowly lumber into the battle in a behemoth carrying a blistering array of guns?  Make it happen.
-  MWO is well balanced across the two opposing factions, the Inner Sphere and the Clans.  Those familiar with the BT lore will know how insanely strong Clan tech was compared to the Inner Sphere.  PGI has done a very good job of balancing the two sides without entirely neutering the Clans.
-  MWO has an appreciable learning curve, and will take some time to fully absorb.  The actual gameplay is essentially point and shoot, but the mech and weapon variety will take a while to get used to.
Now for the 'is not':
-  MWO has no PVE content (yet).  If you prefer a story-driven game with missions and NPCs and such, this may not be the game for you.
-  MWO is not a ‘fast action all the time’ game.  Players will have to scout, find the enemy, set themselves up in the best positions they can, maneuver on the fly, and duke it out with the other team.  Planning and forethought will help you win games. Which brings me to my next point.
-  Mechwarrior Online is NOT a single player game.  It is a team effort which rewards players for working with their cohorts.  Running off by yourself (with few exceptions) will likely get you and your team murdered.
-  It is by no means a perfect game.  It has bugs, though they are few in number.  The mech balancing isn’t complete, though they continue to work on that.
-  It is not “pay to win”.  This one deserves some attention.  Yes, there are some mechs (the so-called “hero” variants) which can only be purchased with real cash, but in most cases they are actually inferior to the standard variants!  So why would you buy them in the first place, you ask?  Hero mechs provide a c-bill (in game currency) boost when playing them, so they’re a good way to earn more money to buy more mechs!  And when I say “inferior”, I mean marginally so in most cases.  Sometimes they are just as good.   And yes you can purchase mech packages with real money, but they offer no advantage over other players who choose to grind out the in-game money!
-  It is not World of Tanks!
All in all, MWO is a solid game with a lot of playability and huge potential for even more features in the future.  If you enjoy the PvP experience, and are into the mech genre, this one won’t disappoint.  I fully recommend it, so long as you know what you’re getting into.  Last thing…getting a hold of a decent headset/mic and Teamspeak will make your mech life much easier.
Hope to see you on the battlefield!

Just typing these words will inspire emotion in several of us older "kids" who may well be pusing our 40's. I have been playing and collecting stuff from this universe since the 1980's when I was in grade school. To put it lightly PGI has an oppurtunity to cash in on my nostalgia and sell a piece of my childhood back to me.
Many of you are younger. You may never have heard of this title, or the previous games. The idea of little me sitting with a friend and nervously moving cardboard cut outs on a hex map could be hilarious.
The question is, is there something here for both of us? I say yes. PGI has made several choices that take the game away from a direct port of the old table top rules. This is good, those rules were not well balanced and the mechs there were not able to face each other with anything like parity. In table top bigger was better.
Here in MWO each weight class, there are four, is played by a single individual. Unlike previous titles all are viable in the battlefield. The little mechs can take on the big ones and win. Similatly Clan versus Inner Sphere balance is better on this platform than in any other location. In table top the balance was performed with points and Clans got fewer mechs. That does not work in an online enviroment. In MWO Clan mechs are situationally better than Inner Sphere mechs, and IS mechs are situationally better in others. In any situation pilot skill and teamwork are more important than loadout.
Pilot Skill and Teamwork. These are the hallmarks of this game. Battles can be as deep or shallow as your interaction with the other players. If you are looking to be a lone rambo, try light mechs, but this is probably not the game for you.
If you like working with others for a common goal, and you like big robots killing each other, this is definately the game for you.

Caesar 3 is the first of a quartet of city builders made my Impressions Studios, the successors being Pharaoh, Zeus and Emperor. The four are set to the Roman Empire, the many Egyptian kingdoms, the Greek city states and the long history of China respectively, each depicting the prosperity - and decline - of dynasties and cities.
In many ways, Caesar 3 was the 'prototype' that the other three were built upon, and as you play the latter titles, this shows. The backdrop and intermixing of history is a bit shallow in Caesar 3 compared to the latter titles, and though this game pioneered the 'walker' system of distributing goods and services, it lacks the basic tools of controlling said distribution that its sequels wisely got. While you can substitute the basic roadblock with a massive gatehouse building and thus somewhat control where your citizens patrol, you'll very much miss the better controls of markets, warehouses and granaries that's been present from Pharaoh onward. The only way to micromanage this is by sheer distance; markets won't fetch goods that are some sixty tiles away - good to know when you want to deny your plebs wine or fine dining.
You might also find it a bit odd that Romans speak in cockney accent (click on your citizens, they'll tell you) - but that's also somewhat charming. Indeed, consulting your citizens on how the city is faring is a favorite passtime of mine when playing Caesar 3.
I have many fond memories of Caesar 3, and it's a good game - but its successors give a far better experience as they introduce the tools you need to properly control the flow of goods and services. I highly recommend buying them bundled when possible; as they share the basic architecture you pretty much learn them all by learning any one of them. Fortunately, Steam seems to have a big Sierra bundle that contains the first three games (and expansions). Emperor is not available on Steam as of this review, but can be bought over at GoodOldGames.
Building a better Rome is great fun - as long as you can keep the pesky barbarians at bay. There's always that one little village out by the sea that refuses to submit to Roman rule, after all.
I've been playing the game on Windows 10 and I've had no issues save two annoyances; occasionally the music track will stutter and begin to loop endlessly (which can be solved by getting the proper dll files from IndirectSound), and the fact that the in-game video clips do NOT adjust audio according to the game's volume setting. If you play with greatly lowered game volume for whatever reason, the videos might bust your ear drums.
I'd heartily recommend any of Impressions' classic city builders - just keep in mind that they refined the product as they advanced the series. That said, there's something very special about building a Roman settlement, with all the fineries of the burgeoning empire. Caesar 3 definitely brings this to the table, and is well worth the pittance it now costs.

Pros: Extremely detailed. Very relaxing. The actual process is exhaustively accurate (or at least aspires to be - I don't own a gun myself that I can cross-check their work with.) If a given part could not be removed in reality without removing another part, the game makes you do it in the correct order. It also forces you to deal with parts so small that they don't initially seem to be there even on a close examination. "Plastic" mode colors all the parts differently in bright neon colors to make them stand out more, useful in these cases. A competitive element that you can engage or ignore freely - each gun has leaderboards you can compare yourself against. There's also cars and skeletons to disassemble, although only a handful of each, and a motorcycle and two military vehicles. The game includes shooting ranges and challenges to allow you to play with the guns as well as just examine them, but it appears that not all guns have corresponding ranges. Out of the five I've unlocked, only two have such levels.
Cons: You start with only three models - AK-47. 1911, and a human skeleton (under bonus models.) To unlock more guns, you have to either save up experience points or spend real-world money. If you're willing to spend money, you unlock guns quite quickly. To do it through XP, you have to grind. That's slow - I'm seven hours in, and have unlocked just three additional guns. (Keep in mind that each gun I have encountered so far takes no more than ten minutes to completely disassemble and re-assemble - and that's the first time attacking a relatively complex gun like the AK. The TEC-9, clocking in at less than forty parts, took just five minutes total, and judging by the leaderboards, I'm slow.)
What's more, guns unlock in a specific order along a tree like a Civ V tech tree, except that it goes in multiple directions. You have to unlock eight guns to get to the Garand, for instance, and those eight guns take you in the opposite direction from the Desert Eagle, for another example. You cannot actually see the whole tree to begin with, either. You see the next guns available to unlock, and you can see vague outlines of the ones after that with no names or detail. After that, nothing. You have to consult charts made by other players to plan your unlocks more than two steps ahead. There's also a handful of guns that can be unlocked only with purchased credits. There are often  guns beyond these that can only be accessed by getting through that one gun - so while they're "free," you can't get at them without having paid. Virtually all of the respectable handful of non-gun models are paid-credits only, as well.
Conclusion: It's good for killing a few hours here or there, but completionists should be aware that it is impossible to 100 percent this title without paying, and everyone should be aware that what progress you can make is made only at a comparative crawl.

Now this is a pretty unique offering! Less game and more simulator and infodex, World of Guns offers the opportunity to explore, in considerable depth, the construction and functionality of real life firearms. Want to understand exactly what happens when an AK trigger is pulled? Think you'd enjoy practicing field strip and full disassembly of a sizeable and growing range of primarily modern combat arms? If so, then WoG provides a high resolution 3D environment with a high emphasis on technical accuracy that you'll find worth your time. It breaks new ground for a number of niche audiences, and shines light on a path that has "AAA and beyond" written all over it.
A few features I'd like to see: user remappable keys, more sandbox-y physics, greater depth around materials, and support for swappable parts and user part mods.

It's going to be awkward reviewing this game while avoiding what Steam considers "inappropriate language" so bear with me.
There are a lot of things about this DOOM that are very different from classic DOOM. There are more things, however, in my opinion, that resonate with old school DOOM than there are things that don't fit with it. It especially feels like a return to "real" DOOM compared to Doom 3. The biggest difference though, between this and classic DOOM, is that this time around, the Doom Marine is definitely more of an agressor. You kick the unholy crap out of the demonic horde in this DOOM. Sometimes the Imps even flee from you.
The violence in this game can be best described, I think, as brutal to the point of being horribly comical. When using the new "glory kill" feature, where you hit the melee button(yeah, it has one now) when close enough to a staggered enemy, you proceed to beat them to death in horriffic fashion. Its even badder when you are under the effects of berserk. Maybe it's just me having a twisted sense of humor, but during this game I often was reminded of Bart and Lisa Simpson laughing at "Itchy and Scratchy" by my own laughter while brutalizing the demons. Seriously, you really rip 'em a new one in this game, like few others. Try using the chainsaw on the mancubus.
Unlike old DOOM, there's not a constant background music for each level. Instead, heavy metal begins to play when you get into a big fight. There's also some atmoshperic music in hell.
The weapons in this DOOM are pretty good. Like Doom 3, there's an assault rifle class weapon before you get the bigger chaingun, and there's a new, additional energy weapon that offers power and accuracy instead of the plasma rifle's better rate of fire. I found myself using all the weapons at different points, but felt like the maximum ammo capacity could have been higher. There are also grenades, and, conveniently enough, a grenade button.
The bottom line is, I thought this game was cool, and it felt right for a DOOM game. I recommend it.

I somehow completely missed both the Kickstarter and all pre-release hype for Halcyon 6. That's both a shame and a pleasure because this game not only surprised me greatly, I've been glued to it since well after I did my video.
Halcyon 6 is basically a combination of Master of Orion II, Star Control II and adds in JRPG combat but with spaceships. The former two games are in my top three of all-time so that is very high praise. The story is fairly simple: You and a group of scientists found this ancient alien space station and while you were away, most of humanity got wiped out by some nasty aliens. Your goal is to rebuild humanity and ultimately, fight off this invading force while also balancing relations with the other colourful alien races you share the galaxy with.
You have to spin many plates in Halcyon 6. You have to expand and develop your base, train and foster a good officer group, maintain multiple fleets of ships, pick up supplies from colonies, do missions for the various alien factions and fight back the invaders, all at the same time. The game isn't turn-based per ce but you can pause it at any time to stack up commands and when time is running, it runs very fast on purpose. You'll always have multiple tasks to think about and you will quickly learn that it's not within your power to accomplish them all. Sacrifices will be necessary and which ones you choose to make will greatly affect your path forward. Choices have weight and many of them are not easy ones to make.
As you gain experience, the officers in your fleet will level up and you can spend those upgrades on different offensive and defensive abilities. The abilities vary a fair bit and you'll want to find the combination that works best for you. There are three classes of officers, all of whom operate in different ways. As you recruit more officers later, you're given pre-rolled options to choose from but will always have one from each category. You'll also need various resources found on colonies and which you can also produce on your base to a degree in order to build upgrades, new ships and take care of other tasks. Colonies will produce these for you but you have to do supply runs to pick them up and colonies left unprotected are vulnerable to enemy attack and destruction.
Combat plays very similar to a JRPG. Everything is turn based and your officers have different abilities and classes that need to be used in combination to both hurt the enemies and keep your fleet intact. If a ship takes too much damage, it doesn't immediately die but enters into "Critical State", which is basically a grace period that allows you to heal it or hopefully take out the rest of the enemies before it self-destructs. However, if it dies, it's dead and that officer and all their experience upgrades are gone for good. The combat is tense but also gives you a lot of time to plan.
I've absolutely adored what I've played of Halcyon 6 so far. It mashes up some of my favourite games ever in a fantastic way that hearkens back to some of the best gaming I had as a kid. There's a very good chance this game I'd never heard of until a couple of weeks ago will make my top 10 list this year. If you liked Master of Orion or Star Control at all, get this.

Deus Ex is an interesting game.
Sure, the mechanics are solid. The AI is built well enough to make the difficulty in stealth a fair one, and your character's RPG-like "Augmentation" tree is dynamic and intersting. Unlike, say, borderlands upgrades, most of the upgrades of your Augments are based on utility instead of small boosts. You might find an Icarus system that lets you fall great hights, or a cloak system that makes you briefly invisible, etc. and you have many choices in combat. Kill, or incapacitate? Stealth, or a more aggressive approach? You have options in how you'd like to play.
Even so, the mechanics aren't what makes this game so interesting. The politics surrounding human augmentation of very controversial and interesting. Questions arise like, "Do augments make natural humans outdated? Does that impede human rights?" and "Are these implants a risk to security?" are some of the biggest, and you will meet the dissenting factions on both sides. The future of this world is at stake, and you slowly unravel the true nature of Augmentations.
[SPOILER PARAGRAPH] The only concern I have with the game is the ending. It's just 3 choices with simple narrations. Nothing interesting and none of the answers were ones I agreed with.
Overall, it can get a little frustrating to people, like me, who don't excell at stealth games. Even so, it was very fun to play and I would definitely recommend to anyone who wants real sustenance out of their games.

As you all can see from the trailer and screenshots, Rabi-Ribi is set in an overwhelmingly cute and colorful world full of anime chicks with magic powers. The main character (Erina) seems to be a rabbit who for some odd reason gets transformed into human-like. After very little progress in the game Erina partners up with Ribbon, a small fairy that will help Erina on fulfilling her mission, etc, etc, etc.
The plot of the game is stupid as hell and it is meant to be so. If you're here for an epic storyline or an intriguing playthrough, look elsewhere. Plot is like the most secondary thing in Rabi-Ribi and there are many dialogue lines doing fun of topics. And some lines are even cringy.
Behind this land of cuteness, Rabi-Ribi hides one of the most polished and complete metroidvanias I've played. Once again from the trailer you can get a notion of it, but that just reflects a small portion of what this game truly uncovers.
Rabi-Ribi is a unique metroidvania game that is carefully mixed with the shmup/bullet-hell genre. The fastest comparison you can get are with Touhou games, which is also full of chicks with magic powers. Rabi-Ribi takes that but into platforming.
If well boss fights are the main core of this game, there's also a huge world to explore. Tons of secrets, tons of upgrades, tons of stuff to do. And of course, tons of ways to play this game. Now onto section to section:
: The combat system in Rabi-Ribi is pretty special. Erina takes care of all melee-related attacks (with her...big...hammer. Kek.), including many sets of movements such as uppercats, quint-combos, dashes and so on. Ribbon takes part of the ranged-related attacks, with different types of magic (consider them as "guns" to make it more understandable) that can be unlocked through game progress. Learning how to combine both is extremely important if you wanna deal good amounts of damage. And depending on what you are playing, you definately want that. The game also features "badges" which can be considered as the passive skills (such as getting more attack for the price of defense, smaller hitbox, etc.) and that allows more space to strategize your fights. You can choose how you wanna play this game, if either aggressive or defensive.
: The map in Rabi-Ribi is pretty big and it should take you good amounts of hours on your first playthrough to unlock everything from it. Tons of secrets are hidden for you to discover them. Map is, like in many metroidvanias, set in gridblocks and there's over 800 of them. For reference, it took me 30h in my first playthrough to get 100% of map and collectibles.
: It is hard to tell how leveling up goes in Rabi-Ribi. Pretty much almost whatever item you find makes Erina keep leveling up. This includes new skills (i.e. Double Jump), upgrades (ATK UP, MANA UP, HP UP, REGEN UP), badges... Also, many of the items found in map can be upgraded through the store. All that affects the level of not only Erina, but also bosses. Bosses scale with how many items you have, and it's really hard to tell how will this affect to the difficulty of fights.
: You basically choose it. Rabi-Ribi can be either a walk in the park or a brutal experience. Difficulties availables are Casual, Novice, Normal, Hard, Hell and Bunny Extinction. Different difficulties not only greatly affect on how much hits you can take, or how much health bosses have, but also at bullet patterns' complexity.
: Eargasm. Go check yourself.
: Just insane. You can play this game at so many ways: Full items run, 0% items run, speedrunning, New Game+ loops, alternative way of boss leveling... The game is also extremely non-linear, so you can just do whatever the hell you want. Devs keep adding content to the game (many of it for free) so just keep checking from time to time because it just never stops.
: Are you here dragged by the huge quantity of achievements? Good luck then. Completing this game is insanely hard and you better know where you're stepping if you're that challenge-seeker/completionist guy. Among many hard stuff (like of course, completing the game at the highest difficulty), you are meant to clear a Boss Rush that includes 28 bosses, at the highest difficulty as well (and nope, you don't get heal between rounds). You better have some experience with these genres or you'll have a bad time!
: Rabi-Ribi is a huge, incredible and detailed piece that should be played. Don't judge the kawaii aura the game has; it's a mask. This game is just unreally good and I'm so glad I didn't ignore this game for that. This is not a VN, this is my GOTY 2016.

Rabi-Ribi is a metroidvania game with bullet hell patterns, and it's probably my favorite metroidvania ever. The combat may feel shallow at first, but as you pick up more and more items, you end up with a variety of options for any situation and can freeform combos. Make no mistake, this game is hard and with a variety of difficulties, can get even harder. But like Ys and like good hard games in general, theres almost no bs, you can always improve and you'll eventually beat that annoying boss, even if it does take a few tries.
What makes it really special in my eyes is that like metroid, its designed with exploraiton in mind. You can go pretty much anywhere once you're out of the very short prologue. The game does suggest places to go, but if you see a path to somewhere else, you can take it and the game will (mostly) not stop you. Theres only two places where you can't, and thats due to plot relevance. But even then, this game was designed with sequence breaking in mind. You can beat the game without picking up a single item! That's super cool!
Rabi Ribi is great, give it a shot!

Been playing this game for years, now it is out on steam! Huge community, very active. Devs are greedy money ♥♥♥♥♥s, but that means new mechs to buy on a constant (every month or two) basis. This game can be pay-to-easymode but not pay to win. Constant updates, more maps, more modes, everything is getting slowly improved but it feels only 80% done right now. I highly recommend if you like giant stompy robots.
Gameplay consists of you buying your mech chassis, outfitting it with the engine, weapons, ammo, heatsinks, armor, etc. You then que up for a match and wait to be paired with 24 people (12v12) in your skill catagory. You all vote on the map and mode (Skirmish, assault, conquest etc). Then you play as a team to smash your opponents in stategic and skill-based combat.
There are "skills" to unlock as you gain XP in your played mech. This makes your mech a bit faster, more agile, etc. There are various (3-8) variant of each mech chassis, 3 need to be purchased and leveled up individually if you want maximum skill level, because there's a bonus if you max level 3 variants of 1 chassis.
Some mech variants can only be bought with MC (Mechwarrior Credits) which you only get through events or buying with money.
It is very fun to buy your favorite chassis and variants, then outfit them with just the loadout you like, then either brawl (close combat fighting) or long-range snipe. Missiles, lasers, guns, flamethrowers, PPCs, it's all there to play with! Try it out, but give it 5-10 hours to fully appreciate the fun this game offers!

This is an old school strategy city builder. There's a lot to be said for the fun and nostalgia value wrapped up in the game. I didn't own it in the 90's so picked it up on Steam as I always wanted to give it a go. If you're not sure about whether you should pick it up then perhaps have a look at some of the old Caesar 3 forum comments to get a feel of what sort of experience you're likely to have. The game has some real design issues. Services need to be provided by walkers who apparently randomly traverse the streets and intersections in your cities, meaning that it could be a toss-up as to whether they would actually reach their intended destination to provide the service needed in your city. The workaround for this apparently is to create a long winding snake of a street with no intersections, which is pretty artificial and makes the playing the game a bit contrived. However there are also real glitches in the game. In playing it I noted that changes to remuneration and tax had a negligible effect on gameplay, and reordering priorities for worker assignment (food gathering vs working in the entertainment industry) appeared not to work at all, with many otherwise fine farms remaining unstaffed while the interface indicates that all needed farmworkers are on the job. This can make it fairly frustrating to play, even for a seasoned old school strategy player like myself. Bear in mind that this game is also available form GOG for about the same price but I am not sure whether their version runs any better. Enjoy the nostalgia, but if you haven't played it before lower your expectations. There are vastly better city builder strategy games like Tropico 3 for the same price but offering much better enjoyment.

Works in Windows 10. Caesar III is from the moment you start playing a captivating game. It's difficulty curve allows for both beginner and veteran citybuilder sim enthusiasts to enjoy the game. Despite this it is still a thoroughly complex and challenging game. It appeases both the general and the city planner in all of us through it's 'peaceful/aggressive' design of level selection. This same design also allows for a degree of replayability in a game. Although even without that aspect, the game is so entertaining and provides so much choice in how to design and manage your city that it would still manage to keep me immersed for far longer than most citybuilders. A feature which I believe is often underrepresented by game critics is that of music, and in this area, as well as any other, Caesar III excels. The music doesn't distract, keeping a largely ambient feel; yet it is sufficiently 'epic' to give to the experience of being a general/governor and eventually Emperor. I feel that Caesar III can unquestionably be called the Citybuilder upon which all future Citybuilers should be measured. The game is a city building classics. Even after so many years it offers finely tuned gameplay, cute graphics, memorable soundtrack... I install it every few years when I look for some modern city building game but find none this good.

Let me just say that this is the first time I am writing a review for the game, and I am writing this because I genuinely cared for this game.
Paladins has quite a history for a game that is still in beta. It went through a lot of changes. The current iteration of the game is only slightly similar to what it looked like in the early alpha stages, and it even differs quite a lot from it's closed beta stage.
Some of these changes benefited the game. Back then, when the game wasn't yet on Steam, the setting was on a large map and the game was advanced by killing off your opponents to get to the enemy gates, while escorting a siege engine to help crash these gates down.
The game received a major overhaul, bringing the current siege mode which consists of capturing a center point and then escorting a payload to the enemy base, resulting in much smaller maps. This iteration of Paladins earned it an infamous Overwatch clone status, seeing how similar was to Overwatch after these changes, but Paladins still retained their uniqueness in form of deep character customization via cards and an in game item shop where you upgrade your character during the game with credits you earn by doing stuff (capturing an objective, eliminating opponents, healing, dealing damage etc).
This customization was a selling point of Paladins, and by the opinion of many, and including myself, this character customization was the reason why would we choose Paladins over other games of the same genre.
Around March 2017. Hi Rez introduced essence to Paladins ,however. Another ingame currency that was used to specifically craft cards for these loadouts. Before that, you could get the cards easily with gold which you get by playing the game, but to get essence you had to earn gold to open chests which then get you essence but only if you get duplicates of the cards. Expectedly many people were unhappy about this, because it increased the grind by a huge margin, and getting stuff that affected the gameplay was harder. Hi Rez did some tweaks on it, making it somewhat manageable, but addition of essence left a bitter taste in the community.
Then the December of 2017 arrived. The patch titled OB64 was introduced with removal of essence, and now you can get all of your cards for free. Great, right. Except... Not really.
Previously, each non legendary card had 4 levels total. You would choose 5 cards, and put points into the cards from lvl1 to lvl4 all 5 cards totaling into a maximum of 12 points, and this allowed for some great customization and creating of your own playstyles.
However, with OB64 Hi Rez completely removed this system, and now all cards have 10 levels. The cards you are given, as a new player start on level 1, and you level up those cards by getting duplicates from Radiant Chests or Champion Chests which you grind gold for. Except, you will have to grind hours and hours (someone calculated it would take over 2500 hours) if you want to get all the cards to level 10. Or you could commit to one champion and level his cards to level 10, and play only that champion. The fact that duplicates you get from chests are completely at the mercy of RNG, it is going to be the challenge to level up cards you actually want.
There is a game mode, which locks all of your cards at level 4, but it is only limited to one game mode and a ranked mode. You can't play gamemodes such as Payload and Onslaught and Test Maps in this, so you are stuck with siege only, and the cards that really aren't that great, and veteran players who played a lot during the old system, now find champions with current card system underwhelming and not as fun to play with. Not to mention that the current card system is seemingly a nightmare to balance.
All of these series of events and extremely questionable choices by Hi Rez, made me, and many others quit the game, and being unable to recommend this game to new players. If you love endless grinding for gameplay content, then... You will probably love this, I guess? But unfortunately, this game gets a thumbs down from me.

This game used to be fun.  Then OB64 happened.
With the old 12-point loadout system, everyone was pretty much balanced.  The way it worked was each character had 20 regular cards and 3 legendaries, and you would make a loadout by selecting one legendary and five cards.  Legendary cards would significantly change one of your champion's abilities which would change your playstyle and the role your character could fill.  The other five cards would give further buffs to particular skills.  You could then distribute 12 points among your five cards, with a max of 4 points in any one card, to make that card stronger.  The nice thing about this system is that unlocking new cards didn't strictly make you more powerful, because the cards were pretty balanced.  It just allowed for a wider variety of play styles, which didn't give you a bigger advantage, it only made the game more fun.
Now, we have Cards Unbound.  Everyone has every card unlocked at the start, but they're all at level 1.  To level them up, you have to find duplicates in loot boxes.  Gone are the days when everyone would have some strong cards and some weak ones, depending on how they spend their 12 points.  Now, whoever has the most money to spend on lootboxes to level up their cards is going to have the advantage, plain and simple.
Just don't waste your time with this game.  I used to love it but it has since been uninstalled.

Frankly I was dissappointed with this game. Navigating the menus and gathering your resourses is just so unintuitive and boring to do. It takes way to many imputs to do something that should be simple since in my nearly two hours of play accounts for 80% of it.
You're basically playing as a working in an RTS, you go to a resourse and then you return to a base. Sometimes you fight using one of 3 classes. And as far as I can tell there no variation in the classes themselves. All engineers are (ultimately) the same as the rest. The ships are where you get more "variety" but even then combat all plays out the same, the slight variety in skills isn't all the noticable.
I'd also like to mention how unpolished a lot of the game feels. There's next to no feedback on a lot of things that shoulds have it. For example I had a mission pop up on a pirate planet for a distress signal. I sent a ship there, and nothing. Did I do it wrong? Is there something I have to do first? Why does this mission randomly not work the same as the others? Looking at the mission just tells me to go there. There's just so many little things like that that pop up and feel like it just isn't quite working right and that I need to do some many extra steps just to get it to work.
Also the fuel system is a joke. Litterally uses the designated amount of fuel to travel right at the start of movement. So if you have to suddenly change where you move your fleet then all the fuel for the first movement is just gone. (You can litterally use all your fuel by just redirecting your ships and not actually having them move...I mean, why?)
RNG is also "Hey, this happened! Keep going about your day." and you lose a few resourses or crew. Or you're just presented with an option to basically choose what resourse to lose. Maybe later on it changes, but for now it's just kinda...there.

My experience has been nothing but negative.

- Trackpad will also act up a lot during playing, sticking in certain directions etc
- You need to use big picture. This is fine if you could use it with a keyboard and mouse to chat with friends, but your more or less locked in the controller interface when playing with one.
- FPS's are pretty unplayable with the track pad.

- You have to add all your non steam games to steam to use the controller with them.
At the end of the day, if you want a controller,  buy one elsewhere with a more traditional design. The next generation of steam controllers will hopefully be more robust with better designed and responsive tracking, and hopefully they will have sorted out the big picture system too.

I absolutely adore this thing. There's a lot of great things to mention about the controller considering its price (seriously, some pro-controllers that do marginally less than this thing are within double the price range)
Pros:
Works with almost every single game available on steam,
make the controls as you see fit.
Controller itself is sturdy and can take a nasty drop to the floor (I still shriek no less whenever it falls off my desk)
Touchpads are oddly easy to pick up on quickly.
It will more than likely replace that old wired Xbox 360 controller you have sitting in front of you on your desk.
Wireless (comes with an adapter, uses USB 1.0 for wired connection.)
Plenty of customization options for the controller itself (Boot up sound, shutdown sound, center button brightness, name of the controller)
Usable outside of steam.
Gyro controls are
from being half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Valve really put heart into making sure motion control was functional and viable for competitive and casual gaming.
Touchpads are located to where your thumbs will naturally rest on them so they're always comfortable and ready for use.
Wireless connection range is more than plenty for couch or across the room gaming.
-
And as great as this controller is, there are some rather nasty drawbacks to this things as well...
Cons:
This is a problem on Steam's end, which the only remedy to it is unfortunately, rebooting your computer. Every once in a blue moon, gyro controls will become ungodly spazzy, looking as if you were throwing your mouse all over the place and causing jagged movement inside the games you're playing them (this is very obvious to notice, and it
drive you to insanity if you don't know to fix it.
The wireless adapter must
be abused.
when extending it with the USB cable. Over time of careless incidents of it hitting the floor, it will cease to properly function and will require you to fiddle with it for minutes, leaving you in a heap of frustration until you can get it to work. It will happen often and lead you to almost not want to use the controller anymore. However, according to the steam community, Valve will replace your wireless adapter for you free of charge if it breaks given you can prove evidence that it's broken and that you have your box, serial number, and the controller (duh).
The facebuttons (A B Y X) are rather difficult to get used to if you are switching from a traditional controller. They are smaller than Xbox/PS3 facebuttons and are located lower than normal. You will often be pressing "Y" thinking it's "B" until your brain recognizes the layout of the controller. It's an odd learning curve as everything else on the controller feels natural. The reason of this is because of the right touchpad, there wasn't enough room on the controller to put the facebuttons in a more familiar area. It is a small annoyance at first, but you will get used to it eventually.
-
In the end, I can definitely suggest purchasing this controller. It is very reliable and
my controller of choice when I'm feeling too lazy to operate my keyboard. It's not a must, but it's definitely something to consider.

General - 9,0
The game allows you to do almost everything the leftists in your country won't (in my country PT - Partido dos Trabalhadores/Worker's Party). As a gun enthusiast I can say it's the best simulator in the genre that I've seen, it's an almost real experience. If you're looking for a random FPS don't download it, probably you'll find it boring, but if you wanna learn the mechanics or practise the disassembly of some of the most known and reliable weapons it's a must in your library. It has a greater educational value than entertainment value, however I do find pleasure on this kind of knowledge.
Content - 9,5
There are several models of handguns, assault rifles, sniper rifles, SMG's, etc. You start with an AK-47 and afterwards a Colt 1911, the other guns you will have to buy, but you can unlock many more with your exp. points. You get exp. completing achievements and logging in everyday. As if it wasn't good enough, you can also disassemble skeletons (got the highest score of the day :D) and vehicles, which I find amusing. In addition there are shooting ranges, quiz and information about the weapons. Models are downloaded the first time they're used.
Gameplay - 7.5
Modes are: field strip, disassembly, assembly, operation, game, super game and hardcore game, each has a description at the beginning. There are also achievements for each mode and world leaderboards for all 3 game modes. If you liked in the first 10 minutes, chances are you'll play for 10 hours in the first day, so I don't have to say it's replayable and addictive. You use the mouse to interact with parts and control the camera, you can also use keyboard for some actions but I don't recommend. Sometimes a different part is selected in game mode and in some modes the camera moves against your will. In most modes you have to wait for the end of the animation to perform an action, that's annoying in timed modes. RMB is a good and quick way to zoom a specific part. Controls could be more precise.
Graphics - 7.5
Models are very precise and some even include a bit of visual external wear (mechanic wear would make a nice DLC), however they only look like plastic. Options are very limited, but they're not very relevant on this game, you can identify any part at all times, and if you don't, there's a caption in the lower centre of the screen for each part selected. There's native AA support and fixed frame rate at 60fps. The game is windowed by default. In general the models look like any good directx 9 game, I believe it's playable even with integrated video cards. Menus could look better. The game hasn't crashed yet.
Overall - 8.4

I'll keep this short and simple. Endless Space is a breath of fresh air in the 4X genre that has been limping along for so many years.
The UI in particular shines in this game and it's about time someone made a 4X game that doesn't drown you in useless information and complex controls you never wanted in the first place.
The biggest downside however is combat, it's not tactical. It's a rock-paper-scissors style game and you have very little control over the outcome of battles. You can play 'cards' to modify certain values but they rarely make that large of a difference. There are only three weapon types in the game, so not much in the way of customizing your fleet.
Put a real turn-based tactical combat system, yes from the champion of the genre Masters of Orion 2, into this game and it would be perfect.
So in short, the system management end of the game is perfect, but the combat end of it is overly simplistic and unsatisfying. Still, it is one of the best 4X games to come out in years and the one I've enjoyed most since Masters of Orion II and Imperium Galactica II.

I played this game for about 2 weeks back in OB40~ something. It was a great deal of fun and I really did enjoy the game during that time. I have, however, returned to Team Fortress 2; because I started noticing some problems with how the game handled monetization. I must credit this game for getting me back into TF2, without having played my time in here, I'm not sure if I would've returned to TF2 just in time for the Pyro Update.
This is a review for this game, all though I brought up TF2 quite a bit now. They are different games, although similar in some ways. The reason I liked Paladins so much was that there were specs for heroes -- so a hero you saw could be fundamentally be different from the same hero from previous experiences. It was also great to feel and know, that the hero I chose could also be fundamentally different from the one on the opposing team. My Skye, for instance, was all burst and reset based on her stealth ability -- but another viable loadout for her was to sink in points into her Poison Dart which causes a DOT (Damage over Time) and does relatively high sustain damage and rewards hitting your poison shot ability. There was a depth to this system that not only did you choose cards to go with a spec/build -- you would choose the level or tier that would be allocated to that specific build.
This is where OB64 has come in -- although there have been slight changes to the original preview of OB64 -- the "Cards Unbound" system removes the kind of depth I just wrote about. It also divides the casual community into 2 divisions. A division that is relatively similar to the "competitive" format -- and that which uses the new "Cards Unbound" system.
For balancing purposes, I understand how Hi-Rez capped and standardized cards for competitive/bound formats of the game -- however it has reduced the customizability of a hero and in that loses the charm that the old "12-Point System" gave the game some needed depth to differentiate itself from it's competitor Overwatch.
The other format for casual -- "Unbound" -- is where the game has become truly flawed. It is a "casual" game format that emphasises a Pay 2 Win mentality, where players start with all cards but must level them up by buying up duplicates through Loot Boxes that can be bought with real money. These loot boxes are also controlled by RNG which results in leveling up/getting duplicates of cards for heroes you may not or even never use. There are instances where characters can become so broken when specific cards are maxed out. It means those who dump money to build up level 10 cards have a vastly superior advantage to those who are just getting those loot boxes through quests and in-game currency.
Further more, I'd like to touch upon my experiences before with the cash shop within the game. Before this debacle with a new fundamentally Pay 2 Win situation. Paladins was a game that had great cosmetics that rivaled other F2P hero arena games. Which was great until -- I realized that before the game fixes/patches -- the devs put so much devtime into outputing cosmetics and premium cash shop items that are on monthly rotations to further entice players to "Buy Now" or get screwed with their RNG loot boxes later -- as a lot of their monthly cosmetic bundles eventually make it in the game as loot boxes in which you will have to piece together set at the mercy of the RNG gods.
It honestly wouldn't have been so bad if it wasn't so blatantly cornering consumers a 1-month limit to get their goodies at a guaranteed discount, else be screwed spending cash for loot boxes. They kept doing this every couple or so updates where really cool item bundles would be phased out as they rolled in new cosmetics for said month -- and in which case -- it became apparent that their focus was more on pumping out premium skins and microtransactions to maximize revenue at the cost of actually balancing and fixing the game first.
The game is of course still in Beta -- and so bugs and fixes are expected to come and go -- but with their focus on microtransaction revenue -- I can not recommend this game. I originally loved it -- but their in-game economy just isn't as new player friendly as per say -- Team Fortress 2 and/or Overwatch.
Good luck and Have fun!

I have over 11,000 matches played in this game, and way too many hours invested. I obviously enjoy it.
The pros of this game? You get to run big stompy robots. I love the history and background of this game. I enjoy the fact that the meta has shifted now and then, it makes me relearn various aspects. The mechbay and design of mechs, the optimizing of builds, understanding weapon ranges and timing, all of it is enjoyable. The marketing says thinking man's shooter. People that are not terrible at this game know that to be true. That said, there are plenty of dumbasses with terrible builds as well..
The cons? This game is developed by a small company. They have limited resources. Promised additions and fixes come slowly. They have to focus attention on money making content to keep their business open, and sometimes that trumps adding fun content like game modes or user interface improvements.
The neutral? Game balance has been a rocky road. The tabletop game this adapts was balanced in a way that didn't translate to a real time shooter. They have made slow akward attempts at balance, and the game is in a decent state at the moment. The developers of this game have been historically really bad at their own game, and hesitant to listen to the top tier players. They recently have been playing more in queue, and have joined some tournaments. Their game knowlege in the real playerbase is growing, and I believe that is helping the balance work.
The future? With hopes that we can grow this community via new steam users, I hope that this game can make some money so that staff can be added, and playing modes expanded. I really want to see Faction Warfare fleshed out, and a campaign mode added, and player base expansion will support that. The game desperately needs some more good players. Hopefully the balance is decent enough to retain those type of people at this point.
I'll be here shooting stompy robots for a long time. Hopefully you will be too.

Veteran pilot here, back from closed beta days until now.  My review of Mechwarrior Online is not going to be any polarized PGI aft kissing or hyperbolic salt dripping.  No, I'm going to be honest and as neutral as I can be.  I'm not going to overly delve into the history of the game.  I'll simply state what my thoughts on the game are.
Mechwarrior Online offers some of the best arena shooting Mechwarrior combat that I have experienced.  The actual combat is good.  The map variety is solid.  Balance is... acceptable, and certainly more even between Clan and IS tech trees than its predecesors.  The attention to detail in the art department, the visual customization based on loadouts, is heads and tails above all others, with the possible exception of MWLL.  The degree of customization is positively immense!
However, not everything is perfect, either.  Development is slow, rocky, and far too often follows illogical decision making.  There is a lack of transparency from the developers, and they do have a nasty habit of ignoring the experienced community's input.  The current, as of this writing, game modes are just variations of team deathmatch and absolutely need expansion in their mechanics as it can get stale playing the same thing over and over again.  Community Warfare matches, while soon(tm) due to have a significant update, currently is of questionable enjoyment and of zero consequence to the overall big picture.
Yet it is a game I keep coming back to.
Why?  Because the game is still loads of fun.  The core experience is just plain enjoyable (teams permitting), and I can play the game, get my top tier mech experience, eventually get burnt out or tired of the issues that still haunt the game, set it down, and return to it with fresh eyes a couple months later.  That PGI managed to avoid a P2W situation is a fantastic perk that should not be undervalued - nothing you can buy with money is any more competitive than anything you can (eventually) get out of playing the game.  It is pay for convenience, though without the grind can be a little excessive.  Also, while I often disagree with the developers' methods, they work hard.  Not necessarily working smart, but they do work hard at their product.
Would I recommend the game?  Absolutely.  Would I recommend spending money on it?  Well... YMMV, and that's just something you'll need to decide on your own.

You are a ninja, and you have to go through 5 worlds with the ability to double jump, your katana and shurikens. Here is how the game works : for each level, you have 10 seconds to kill all of the nazi robots, and for each world, the last level relies on killing a boss which is a Hitler robot.

Here goes my first Steam review! I have only been playing the campgain so far, so this review is mostly based on that.
I feel slightly conflicted. As pointed out by many, this game is like a combination of both Dungeo Keeper 2 and Warcraft 3. DK 2 beats this game in dungeon management, WC 3 beats it in RTS, both by miles. But is that a fair comparison? I don't think so. This is a game of its brand (of course, with borrowed elements), and I think it's doing pretty OK in that.
A few minor suggestions for the game:
1. Having a confirmation button after loading screen, so the player doesn't get thrown right into the game after waiting for arbitruarity many seconds.
2. When underground, I feel like 10% of the time I have no idea where I am going to click on, or what action I am performing: deselection/reselection of action isn't always smooth, and the acted square isn't always the one the hand is hovering over. It feels worse when the dungeon is under attack (my own stress problem).
3. Ctrl+# works fine above ground to group minions. It would be awesome if it also worked underground for the minions that I picked up.
4. Would be cool to add dungeon faction war into the campgain, rather than only fighting against human. This is a new contenient, of course there can be other evil warlords to conquer! (Feel free to use this idea for expansion! :))
I see that there are many complaining about the level of humor (or bad joke) in the narriation. First of all, there is an option to reduce the chattiness. Secondly, I think it is part of this brand of game. The developers have chosen this to be part of the game's theme, spamming multiple titles. It would be weird for this title to all the sudden become more serious. I don't want to say "go find a dungeon management game with a tone suiting your style", but I can't phrase it better. :P
Overall, would recommend. Would strongly recommend if the price is lower (from current $40 to $30), or if the control is smoother.

Under linux, you may have to modify some udev settings to get the controller to work for games (rather than just for steam big picture), but when you do, you'll find out what an amazing device this is.
The trackpad doesn't just function as a mouse or joystick, it actually feels them too, thanks to the haptics. The same goes for the DPAD, which is technically a trackpad that has a pressure switch, just like the actual trackpad, but manages to feel like a dpad. Another innovative feature is the grip switches: squeezing your hand a little harder is also a button!
You likely will have to customize the controller configuration for many games, which takes a bit of getting used to, but that does mean you get to setup your controller just the way you want it. If you take it with you to someone else's house, the controller configuration is supposed to come with it, which should be great, but I haven't actually tested that yet.

This controller has a very interesting/unique design, layout, and build. Works to PERFECTION with games SPECIFICALLY DESIGNED to utilize the Steam Controller. Unfortunately, only a very few games take full advantage of the Steam Controller's  design. For ALL games NOT tailored to the Steam Controller (99%+ of Steam Games at present), I MUCH PREFER XBOX CONTROLLERS. That said, I am still recommending this hardware... Acceptance & integration of the Steam Controller is a work in progress. Not to mention the fact that there is no such thing as "too many controllers"!! I suggest you purchase a Steam Controller, but make sure you get it on sale or from an authorized reseller. There is no reason to pay more than $35(US) for it.

The touch controls work great and are easy to use. The triggers and grip buttons are great. The bumpers are a tad hard to reach. The face buttons are a tiny bit mushy but not bad. The analog stick is very good. The customization is a tad annoying but still pretty good. So what's the problem?
Or, more improtantly, the tops of the grips curve
from the face in defiance of 25 years of controller design. Now that might works somewhere, this controller isn't exactly orthodox anyway. It makes the touchpads a bit easier to reach, but at a huge cost: the face buttons and especially the analog stick are a massive pain to use.
I have medium sized hands for an American according to the last pair of gloves I bought. I prefered The Duke to the Controller S on the original Xbox. PlayStation contollers (at least up to the PS3) always felt like the grips were way too small for me. This is not me hating controllers with bigger grips in general.
Hold a 360 (or presumably almost any other) controller in your right hand and the Steam contoller in your left and try to use the thumbsticks and the problem quickly becomes obvious: the grip on a steam controller presses on the inner muscles of your thumb if you try to use the thumbstick with
grip on the controller.
The idea of the grips curving forward was almost certianly to make the touchpads easier to use, which it does. If just the thumbstick were hard to reach that might have been an acceptable compromise, but the face buttons are equally affected.
For some hard data, the thickest point on a 360 controller grip (meaused with calipers) is 38.5mm or 1.52 inches. the thickest point on the steam controller is slightly harder to measure due to the uneven curve but 48.5mm or 1.91 inches. The distance from the center of the thumbstick to the parallel edge of the controller is about 60mm or 2.36 inches compared to the 360's (right, to keep the comparison even) thumbstick being about 50mm or 1.97 inches away.
I will continue to use it for things were I don't need the thumbstick or the face buttons, because the touchpads are good, but there are not that many places where this is the case.

- The Swiss Army Knife-
+ Good joystick
+ Lot of buttons
+ lot of custom configuration possible.
+ has gyro functions (very precise, fun for FPS)
+ very long battery life
+ replacable standard batteries (AA, you can use rechargebles if you like)
- Button placement is not optimal due to having big touchpad (vingers get tired fairly quick)
- up,down, left, right buttons missing (platformers are less fun to play with this gamepad)
- complicated to configure for some people (mostly the older and younger people)
- controller is big,
- not suitable for kids (my kids get tired of this controller after 30 to 40 minutes. Never happend with other controllers)
Conclussion: any controller these days wil be compared to the xbox and playstation controllers, this controller has some benefits but also major downsides. Its like having a Swiss Army Knife, while it can do everything its not fun to work with. Everything is much harder to do and sometimes even less fun.

Overall I've very impressed, I've been using an Xbox Elite Controller for a long time - it's a very nice refined controller and "just works" but I found in many games there was always a couple of essential buttons that just weren't on the pad and there was no way around it so I had to keep a keyboard near by just to press 1 or 2 keys on occasion - I was curious about the steam controller but was worried by its "cheap" look but as it was on sale I decided to have a punt & buy a Steam Controller (Ps - The £7.50 UK Shipping from Steam was very offputting) but after a week it arrived.
The moment unboxed it I was pretty impressed by how well thought out it was, with a button to eject the battery cover then buttons inside the compartment to eject the batteries it was clearly well thought out - then I turned it on I was shocked at just how much haptic feedback there was (everything can vibrate!) & how Incredibly configurable controller is, you can assign any mouse (5) buttons / keyboard button / Xbox controller buttons from 1 menu and it's possible to have different inputs for a quick press & a long press. (including Turbo toggles, which helps a lot for games that have you spamming 1 key to farm) with different inputs for a soft pull of the trigger and a hard pull etc and as for the touchpads don't even get me started they have so many options I never even knew existed or even thought were even possible.

It still has some room for improvement I think the face buttons are maybe too small or not quite in an optimal position as I find myself hitting Y instead of X very frequently & Steam is required to be open in order to use the controller profiles which is an issue as personally I use my controller on the desktop etc as well & should steam want to update / close / crash etc and the controller loses its settings until Steam is restored - so it would be nice if it had a standalone light weight application or if Steam could build it into a background service even if Steam's closed.... but all in all its a very impressive bit of kit with enough technology inside it to justify the price tag.
Ps, - Buy rechargable batteries... as I use my controller for games + desktop on my HTPC I get a full days heavy usable comfortably from a set of batteries but a set of batteries every couple of days would be very expensive if your just buying normal batteries.

This review is more for people who are on the fence for purchasing this game, and are looking to get more insight from the reviews.  There are a load of reviews comparing this to FTL, but the only similarities that these two games have is that they're both in the space genre.
Don't get me wrong - this game mixes the base-building of X-Com with the encounter RNG of Darkest Dungeon.  You get to expand your starbase out, while dealing with random encounters of other alien races, pirates, space monsters, etc.  It's exciting because even as you're going through the tutorial, you can see the potential for a great game to unfold.  Unfortunately, this excitement dries up after an hour of grinding the same planets and battles.
The FIRST problem is that the combat in this game is a turn-based JRPG style - not the real-time, systems-based battles of FTL or the tactical RPG of X-Com.  Unlike most JRPGs that sport an expansive selection of actions, you have a very limited number of attacks/buffs per character or ship, which means you're spamming the same attack combos each battle.  And you will spam these combos many, many times.
The SECOND problem is this game is similar to a "clicker" farming genre of mobile app games, because you're stuck shuttling resources between the starbase and systems ALL THE TIME.  A system will generate one type of resource, and once it reaches capacity for that resource, an indicator will signify that it's ready for you to send a fleet over to pick it up.  You're basically just clicking systems and ferrying resources around for about 1/3 of the game.
This sucks! because they've managed to make a compelling character generator (complete with backstories), interesting aliens, dialogue, and mixed it with fantastic music and graphics.  Unfortunately, the game falls short of being fun and lands in being super tedious.
It reminds me of Cosmonautica - another highly polished space game that at it's core just isn't very fun to play.

But later in the game it mixes it up a bit with having to hold over cubes that are moving in the way, to slow them down, then quickly switching back to your cube and launching it again, which calls for some skill, speed and precision.

I think the thing i liked the most about this game, and the most surprising thing was the boss battles at the end of every world. These are really off from the game, but in a good way. The first worlds boss is a circle in the middle that shoots lazers towards you that you have to dodge while bouncing into the circle twenty times. It added quite a few fun mechanics and was a really fun challenge. Now the second boss was even more impressive, as it wasn't really a boss at all. It was a game of asteroids where you had to hit at least 60 asteroids while dodging exploding circles, it took me several tries on this one, but it was a fun challenge. As i said before, i haven't gotten to boss three yet, but i bet that one will also be as interesting.

Poorly developed for PC: There are still incredible lag issues. The devs didn't really optimize it properly for PC. When you go wandering around (most of the lag issues stem from here) or in battle, that's when it happens. FPS drops to around 10-15. Another thing to note is that all the controls are based on the PS4 controls when playing on PC. You basically have to jumble your fingers around the keyboard as you struggle to find the correct controls. It was very difficult to search the controls to find the correct buttons. Plus it demands the most expensive upgrades to your PC to play it.
Ridiculous price: The rest of the Megadimension series is priced at $30 and this one is priced at $40. Even when the entire series goes on sale at a reasonable price, this episode is still ridiculously fahking expensive at $14. It just isn't sensible for such a good series. I get the PS4 price and it’s legit for the PS4 version but not for PC.
Devs not listening: The devs don't really take the time to listen to concerns. Valvo, 2K, Firaxis, Psyonix and other game devs of similar strategy and turn-based games actually take the time to listen to concerns and address them. IF Int'l doesn't really communicate effectively and that's why some issues haven't been fixed.
Lack of effective updates: When was the last effective update for this game? Over a fahking year ago when it initially came out. One year later, they left Uzume to disappear with Zero dimension.
Game engine: No one knows the unfamiliar game engine. Rather it would have been better to use Unreal or Source engine which are much more user friendly.
Oversexualization: Some characters are somewhat oversexualized. Cases of bouncing b**bs (particularly Vert's for example) and whatever, I mean I understand that could be typical of anime, but it goes a little too far. It happens way too much and should be cut down somewhat.
This game is really fun, fellow denizens of Zero Dimension, and I would recommend it all the way ONLY if you buy on PS4, not PC unless your PC supports the game smoothly.

I have played MWO a lot in the last two years. I find the gameplay is good, the maps are fun, and the variety in the mechs adds a lot of flavor, strategy and planning that needs to be done before a match even starts.
Is the game perfect? Definitely not. There is a steep initial learning curve, the matchmaker can sometimes take a while to find a match, and with all the customization it's easy to bring something to the battle that is very sub-optimal. On the flip side, I really enjoy the high skill ceiling, the high level of customization, the intense matches, and that good strategy/tactics pay off in the field.
Would I recommend this to anyone? Absolutely. Is everyone going to find something to like about the game? Absolutely not. If the theme or style appeals to you at all, there is a lot of stompy robot goodness to love in the game. If you like shooters, I'd say give it a try and see if it's your thing. I'd still recommend anyone slightly interested give it a try, as the game is great for a free game. I continue to get a lot of enjoyment and entertainment from it.
If you try it out and don't like it, then I wish you luck on finding your next game.
If you try it out and do like it, you are in for a lot of fun! I'll look forward to dropping with you in the near future. :)
Cheers!

Overall, the Steam controller is the best gamepad for tinkering with controls. If you want to use your device as a steering wheel, you can set it up in 10 seconds, then tweak it from its haptic feedback to its acceleration. You can branch your configurations off of popular ones, those which have advanced functionality added (e.g. In L4D2, the D-Pad touchpad maps to virtual button pad for selecting weapon), and have controller that is perfectly tailored to YOUR needs.
As for the quality of the physical hardware, I was pleasantly surprised, as some negative reviews seemed to look disfavorably thereon. Yes, it is made of hard plastic, but it feels just as uncomfortable as any mouse or keyboard out there. How else can it cost the small sum of $30?
My performance in first-person shooters is sub-optimal, as I prefer the mouse and keyboard. However, I prefer the controller in non-competitive games like Portal 2 Euro Truck Simulator 2, and even RuneScape.
This is a controller that puts the power in the user, and is a perfect example of the customizability of PC gaming and the true glory of the PC Master Race.

First let me say that I played the hell out of this game as a teenager and loved it. Relative to the time of release, it was held in very high regard as being one of the best CB's of all time.
Let's be realistic though, nobody should expect a game this old to stand the test of time without a little smoothing of it's innately rough edges, And therein lies the problem.
Sure, the gameplay is fun and addictive, the nostalgic juices are flowing,  but the game is severely hampered by the cobweb's of it's era. Now I don't blame the game, but rather time itself. Over the years we gamer's have been conditioned to expect higher standards both in playability and functionality than what was on offer 20 odd years ago.
Playing this in 2016 I found it really hard to ignore some of the grossly unrefined technical aspects of the game, so much so that it completely overshadowed the feelings of nostalgia and joy I used to get from playing it. These are only minor things, but when you add them up it really hinders the fun-factor.
Things such as:
Stretched and grainy 2D textures
Extremely limited game resolution
Severe lack or absence of Game options/Display settings/Key Mapping
2D map that seemingly shifts at 5fps while scrolling
Some Audio distortion
The game really is fantastic, but I just can't bring myself to recommend it in 2016, at least until a little effort goes into cleaning out those cobweb's, perhaps in a "Remastered" version hint hint!
No I'm not going for a refund because I feel I owe it to Sierra as a tribute for giving me many good memories and joy-filled hours a young lad.
TLDR:
Great City-builder but extremely dated.

Wanna simulate a modern city? Get SimCity
Wanna simulate a theme-park? Get Rollercoaster Tycoon
Wanna simulate a roman historical civilization? GET THIS GAME!

First of all, you shouldn't buy this game if you do not like outdatet graphics and a game that has many minor issues to deal with, like a sound bug (just type in Caesar 3 sound loop in google and you should find help), a game that won't let you tab out unless you close it, that has no steam overlay and that will change the resolution of your screen (will set back automatically once you close it), aswell as some random crashes (I played for 6 hours straigt while the game was still smoothly working, but I heared about some crashes).
Well, you have to keep in mind that this game is 17 years old and if you are unwillingly to give up some comfort or to look for a fix or two, than this game is definitively nothing for you.
If you are still eager to buy this game after my warning, then you definitively should, because this game offers:
- A immense population system: you might be familiar to games like SimCity or City:Skylines, where your Houses grow based on ratings like education, healthcare, attractivity and many more. Well, a simular system will await you in C3. While this game lacks in the variety of different houses (all houses on one tier look like eachother), there are plenty of different tiers. Your citizens will move in as simple tent-dewellers, but their houses can evolve over more than a dozen of different tiers, until they might live in the finest palace you've ever seen.
-  A career mode and freeplay mode: There is a career mode in the game serving as tutoral, while you can also select up to ten maps (google Caesar 3 maps to get much more) to play a endless game.
- A complex demand system: In order to grow your houses you need to fullfill different requirements like Entertainment, water, healthcare and goods. Goods are either Food or luxuriers. The game offers 4 types of food (fish, vegetables, wheat and fruits) and 4 different luxuriers ( Furniture, Oil, Wine, Pottery). Food does not have to be refines (e.g. you won't need a mill and bakery to turn wheat into bread), while to acquire luxuries you have to gather the raw materials first (In order to get some furniture you have to build a woodcutter hood for the wood and a sawmill to turn the wood into furniture)
- Beware of the warth of the gods: There are 5 gods (Neptune, Ceres, Mars, Mercury and Venus), who demand you to build temples. Don't make them mad, if you don't want to suffer.
- Work and Unemployment: Every of your citizens wants to work. High unemployment leads to riots or emmigration. High demand of workers will leave some buildings infunctional (you can set a list which sector (like healthcare) has the highest priority). Your citizens also need to be close enough to reach their workplace.
- Disasters: There are 2 core buildings you should have on every corner: The praefecture and the engineers office. The Praefect will walk around to lower the fire-risk, while the engineer cares about the risk of collapse. If you fail to have enough from these you city will soon turn into a burning pile of rubble (there are a few more important buildings like the doctor to prevent the plage)
- War: If you choose to play on a rather troubled provice you will have to face enemies sooner than later. In oder to keep these nasty guys out of your city, you will have to care for city defenses like walls and towers as well as you have to build some legions to deal with the barbarian hordes. There isn't much depth in strategy or tactics of your troops, but it still offers a decent diversity to the building.
For newcommers this game might feel a bit rushed, thus i recommend the career mode, but rather than this Caesar 3 offers you a nice, flawless game expieriece with plenty to do.
