For modern gamers, this is where to start in the Deus Ex franchise.
For old school gamers, maybe you can do the original, but it will feel dated and I'd still recommend starting with Human Revolution.
For those who don't know, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an open-world sci-fi dystopian first-person RPG. The world is fighting for about the augmented and the purists, who don't believe in augmentation. Human Revolution puts you in the shoes of Adam Jensen, a man forced with no choice to be augmented to save his life.
You use Praxis Kits as a way to unlock augmentations, which allow you to have new abilities, such as cloak and no fall damage. This makes it so much more different than your average shooter. You will have to think tactically, as this is a resourceful game. You got a limited amount of Praxis Kits and money, so use it wisely! Sometimes you might be out of ammo and will have to use stealth and/or scavenge the area.
The story is great and will keep you invested throughout the entire campaign. The characters are memorable and you'll remember their (first) names and a little bit about them, even after it ends.

Good Old School fun really.
There is not a massive amount happening here, but having played a few games that required you to juggle 10 or so different resources while trying to remember the micro bonus difference of every single building and upgrade, having a game that is simple is actually a Good Thing(tm).
Learning curve seems about right, allowing you to keep feeling like you are progressing without being smothered by the enemies. True, I am currently playing on only the second level of difficulty but in my defence, (a) this is my very first play through and (b) if I wanted to be constantly crushed down by problems I have no ability to counter then I would simply spend more time at work.
Space combat is easy enough to get your head around and start developing your own combat style. For the most part you are the attacker and can pick the fights you believe you can win, letting you carefully level up your officers before taking on some of the more difficult enemy fleets.
Ground combat seems to be less common, but unlike space combat where you are restricted in your fleet size by the ammount of ships you have already built and crewed with officers (each ship needs an officer, meaning increasing your fleet size requires you to recruit more officers first), ground combat fleshes out your away team with 'Green Shirts' who are amusingly useless and die rather easily.
Currently I believe I am about 1/3rd of the way through the game. How long the interest is sustained I cannot yet say, nor can I tell if the game has any more twists to add plot wise apart from the enemies gradually levelling up as you do.
I am also not sure that this is a game for massive replayability. Unlike other 4X types games there is only one 'nation/race' so there isn't the replay choice variation on offer. Instead I see this more as a game I play through, enjoy, put aside for several weeks and then, with fond memories and knowing just what I am getting back into, playing again a few months later.
Either way, well worth the money spent.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut took me 62 hours according to Steam. Deus Ex Human Revolution "directors cut" is the best video game I've ever played. I'll never play it again and it wouldn't make a list of my favorite games. But, Deus Ex is still the best game I've ever played.
Storytelling is far and away the best I've encountered in a video game. I felt like I was experiencing a science fiction blockbuster film. You're thrown into controlling Keanu Reeves and you get to experience this near-future in which rapidly up-scaling technology has led to severe classism and an imminent singularity. Everything is packaged as a corporate espionage themed thriller as Keanu plays the head of security for a large bio-tech company.
Game play is great. It's like Gears of War meets a FPS version of Metal Gear Solid. DXHR has designed encounters and levels where there are countless ways to approach each scenario, it's not simply stealth or guns-a-blazing. It's ten different ways to approach it stealthily and ten different ways to approach an encounter like a face-smasher. The mechanics are familiar and there is no reinventing the wheel here. Everything comes down to level design, the different approaches to encounters is moreso about how you move about the level than about how you kill/incapacitate. DXHR is the first game where I felt like I could pick and choose my battles and have that really be true. Best way to describe is that there is always twenty different ways to move from A to B, but it's still just stealth or non-stealth. Same ole', same ole', just presented flawlessly. There are also some RPG elements where you can spend sill point things and upgrade weapons. The story of the game is about bio-tech so it lends itself well to the whole upgrading element. Certain choices impact gameplay and will allow you to tailor to your playstyle. However, by the end you'll have purchased almost everything, in the early parts of the game the decisions matter though.
Controls are awesome. I played on PC with Xbox 360 controller and everything felt responsive. Inventory management, weapons swapping, aiming, sneaking - it all feels good. I like the gameplay mechanic where you can use things for cover and change your stance to aim, take cover, sneak, etc, DXHR has a lot of that.
My two biggest complaints with DXHR are both environment issues: There are so many destructible containers to interact with in the game world and the majority of them are empty and serve no purpose. I smashed so many cardboard boxes and eventually gave up. Some containers and movable objects do lead to alternate passages and ways to complete objectives, I found it rare though. Second, is that the game world doesn't refresh itself. There are hundreds of NPCs running around the game in each area and yet only a handful of them actually interact with the environment. Anything you do, stays did and most NPCs are indifferent to what you do. The game is so detailed and vibrant, yet you're limited in how you can impact your surroundings. Leave a body in the streets it will be there later on despite literally a hundred people waking by it. Yet one of those same people is literally sweeping the streets.
I don't want to seem like I wanted a more open world game. As DXHR does a masterful job of creating the cities you travel between throughout the game. They are in my opinion the perfect size and are designed intuitively. It was fun learning my way around the cities. I just simply wish I could do more to impact the environment besides smash things and hide bodies. Like I can make a permanent imprint on the game world, but, it doesn't change the way anyone interacts.
I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes sci-fi, stealth games, or shooters. Best gave I've ever played, but, one play through is enough for me. I say buy that game at any price point.

If you aren't a speedrunner, I wouldn't consider 10 Second Ninja. I decided to buckle down and really work at the game after a frustrating introduction, and quickly completed it with some effort. The full content is around 4
long, with later levels only adding portals and enemies that take
hits to kill. The only appeal of the game is finding routes to optimize times, but other games do so much more in the genre.
The game is built on Game Maker, I only knew this after the 2nd cutscene gave up a Game Maker error report and crashed the game when an image couldn't be found. The program seems to take process priority along with nearly 500MB of RAM, slowing the Desktop and all other activities if you want to Alt-Tab. FPS is good, and I assume the high priority is to make sure the clock is accurate.
Controls are simple but inconsistent, not really fitting for a precision platformer. The sword hitbox can be gigantic at times, even allowing some kills through walls. Normal ground behaves more like Ice, while Ice really didn't give me much issue. Sometimes the ninja would run with no buttons pressed after restarting, while other times it would ignore my inputs (mostly in the Hard mode 100% run, wasting precious time). The 10-second max means most levels are very limited, with only 4 of the 40 levels spanning beyond the screen. I'm kinda shocked a ninja in a platforming game can't wall-jump, while a famous cube of meat puts this ninja to shame.
The game requires Stars to progress in the game, so expect to repeat and perfect levels from the start. Beginners will get trapped in the first world until they can improve times for Stars. At least the community seems friendly, with some helpful strategy videos to complete the game. I don't know if the developer cleans time records, but there's a cheater with a 100% time under 5 seconds that needs wiped. At least the music in the Bonus area was really good.
Overall, the game is too one-dimensional. Super Meat Boy, Stealth Bast Deluxe, and other platformers allow speedrunning without limiting level design and cutting mechanics. 40 short levels, no variety in traps or enemies, and no included level editor means content is slim. It's bundle fodder, which is where I got it, and the store price is insane. There's nothing really unique here. If you're a speedrunner that has exhausted every other game, you could still find other games with more content. The cutscenes may be longer than the gameplay, but they try too hard to be memetic and get tweets. A hashtag in a cutscene, yuck. Considering all the levels can be reasonably completed in 240 seconds, you must see the cost-per-hour here is awful. It had potential, but the title restricted the gameplay far too much.

10 Second Ninja moves so fast that it's over almost before you realize it's begun, but its brief length is used so effectively as a tool to making a blisteringly precise, difficult platformer accessible that it's actually the better for it.
Designed as a series of miniature speedruns, you're given but 10 seconds to complete a given level, jumping, slicing, and throwing shurikens to clear out Robot Hitler's mechanical army as quickly as possible. It might sound like a gimmick, but levels are designed in such a way as to be almost puzzle like in execution, requiring not only brute reflexes but also an understanding of how to best make use of your limited repertoire to shave off every tenth of a second you can manage.
Naturally, this causes the game to move at a ridiculous pace, but unlike a lot of hyper challenging platformers 10 Second Ninja avoided ever becoming overwhelming. Its basic mechanics give you just enough leeway to experiment within levels so as to keep them from feeling too linear or restricting their design, while being entirely understandable and intuitive to execute, and the necessarily small size of each level keeps the experience easily digestible but not to the detriment of a satisfying challenge. 10 Second Ninja isn't an easy game, but it always feels surmountable, if only you could find the perfect strategy or go a little faster.
And then an hour later you're through, perhaps having missed a few perfect level ratings but for the most part seeing what the game has to offer. And surprisingly I was entirely OK with that. 10 Second Ninja for as short as it is makes every moment engaging, each level offering its own twist on mechanics that never change because they don't need to, and finding time for some humorous dialogue in between smashing up Robot Hitler's disembodied head. There's just something inherently entertaining here, and it all comes together into a tightly condensed package that understands it doesn't need to be hundreds of hours long. It just needs to be fun.

A brief but enjoyable speedrunning/optimization kind of hit-the-targets game. Good move speed and jump height, sword attack has nice range, shruikens are decently fast, double jump really helps out, and each area has a few gimmicks of its own to keep things fresh.
The main problem is that, well, the game is super short. Let's put it in perspective; "hard mode" has  you play through the entire game in under four minutes. So yeah... not a massive amount of content in all, especially for $10. And that's, really, the sticking point for me. I quite enjoyed my time with this game, it was a ton of fun. This kind of thing is right up my alley. But for the asking price, combined with the presentation equivalent to a flash game, I would *not* recommend this game at its full price. Half off, maybe. 66% off is what I got it for and even that feels a bit too high for me, but considering that I did enjoy most every moment I spent with the game I suppose I can't complain too much. It's designed well, the 3 star times are fairly realistic when you figure out the expected route, and the fact that everything is so quick helps too since you're never losing more than a few seconds of progress with every failure (or a few minutes in hard mode, but that's usually more than one failure to fail the target time...)
So yeah, if you want a good fast-paced platformer with an emphasis on speedrunning, and you don't care about the price, pick it up for sure. If money is a factor, wait for a sale. I do enjoy this game a lot, so it's a bit disappointing that it's as short as it is, really.

As a tiny blue ninja, you're mankind's last hope against the mischievous Robot Hitler and his robot army. In this fast-paced platformer, your aim is to clear every single level in less than ten seconds - that is, kill every robot on the screen, using your weaponry and triggering environmental hazards. Aim for the lowest possible time to earn a three-star rating!
The concept is really nice, and the par times are very tightly balanced. Finding the optimal route for each level will require meticulous planning, and the execution leaves no room for error.
when you nail your inputs perfectly and maximize a route's potential, and deeply unnerving when even then, you're still half a second too slow; reconsider what seems obvious, think outside the box and, most of all, keep optimizing your inputs. The original core concept, the precise controls and meticulously balanced level design are the game's main strenghts.
Now for the cons. The visuals and cutscenes are entirely forgettable, which can be excused in a low-budget indie game such as this. The soundtrack, albeit repetitive, serves its purpose but isn't particularly memorable either. My main criticism would be that
, and perhaps not quite as "hardcore" as it may appear at first. I was a little disappointed to hit the ending credits after only a few hours (plus maybe an extra half hour on the bonus world), with all the three-star ratings earned and without hitting any major roadblocks.
I would have loved more content, and I felt that certain ideas in the level design could have been further developped (portals, falling/crumbling blocks, etc). As it is, I can't say that the game has exploited its potential to the fullest; nevertheless, it remains a solid puzzle platformer and one of the most execution-intensive games I have played in a while, with relatively fair content for its price. A shame that such an interesting challenge turned out so short.

So here we go.
MechWarrior Online is an MMO sequel to the rather well known MechWarrior series set in the BattleTech universe created by FASA in 1984.
While most of the MechWarrior games were good (sans MechAssault 1, 2, and Phantom War), this one started out... horrible. So I have been around this game since basically it came out, but I didn't play it until December of 2012. Since then I have watched it at its peaks, and at its worst. The game started out little more than Hawken, just slower paced. It was generic and not worth a dime. Now however it is really good.
The game features very good mechanics to improve the experience (such as arms move separate of the torso which moves separate of the legs), and the maps are exponentially better. The game is still working on balance though.
If you are familiar with the BT universe you know that the Clans were like... over powered gorillas in a house full of chimpanzees (kind of how they viewed the Inner Sphere philosophically too haha). They are like that here too. The weapons are extremely good, and just way better than anything the Inner Sphere can match. But in Community Warfare there is one thing that the Inner Sphere has on their side. Higher Tonnage rates which gives them the advantage of having more large mechs than the Clans. Now straight Clan mechs can't upgrade engines either. So there is some balance but unfortunately the Clans still are severely over powered at times.
Overall the game is pretty decent. This community is newbie friendly (look up the B33f on the forums if you want training videos, or find me on occasion under the name Marack Drock), the game plays nicely, and there is a lot of content now. If this was 1.5 years ago I wouldn't have suggested this, but I do now.

High/dynamic difficulty danmaku platforming metroidvania with the vast majority of obstacles being waifus and miscellaneous cute things. While the fodder is just there for filler and rarely provide much of a challenge (As at Hard Post-Game Boss Rush), bosses always require active play and thought.
The combat system is based around being able to attack with both melee and ranged attacks simultaneously, doing so is incentivised by the combo meter which increases your attack output as it it gets higher, incentivising risky play to get more hits in to reach multipliers over 50%.
For those more partial to masochism than general challenge there are many parts of the game built around sequence breaking and conquering areas that no sane person should be able to beat, let alone attempt. Another encouraged self-imposed challenge is the 0% items run for those who truly hate themselves, relying solely on the pea shooter and level management to get through the metroidvania experience, taking non-linearity to its logical conclusion.
My only real complaints are the lack of analogue movement for controllers, meaning one can never have total control over their high-speed dodging, and a lack of the option to always have a visible hitbox, although it isn't hard to approximate with the overlay at the start of the boss fight. The developer is constantly adding quality of life improvements, so it’s very possible that these critiques could be irrelevant in a few months’ time.
Objectively, the gratuitous art style may put a good amount of people off of the game, but it is evident through playing Rabi Ribi, that it knows exactly what audience it wants to target

Summary:
I tried out the steam controller across several different games spanning many genres (include platformers, FPS, strategy, racing/sport, and puzzle games). It is a very impressive first showing by Valve in the controller market, and I'm excited about what Valve can do in the future to build off this foundation. However, despite it's thoughtful design and inclusion in the steam ecosystem, it is just too foreign in comparison to the controller showcase of the last decade to be deemed a worthwhile purchase. The Steam Controller is ideal for people who want couch PC play but cannot use a regular controller nor a mouse and keyboard. It is a decent compromise, but not an ideal replacement for either.
Pros:
-Very easy to connect to a PC or other steam-capable hardware. Connects via micro USB cable or an included wireless dongle, and can then be powered by two easy to pop-in AA batteries.
-Rear grip (paddle) buttons add extra possibilities for button mapping and are surprisingly convenient. I wish more controllers had them. They make certain controls, especially ones tied to movement, feel very natural.
-Very affordable price and lightweight.
-Customizability has potential to be in a class of it's own.
Cons:
-Steam Big Picture Mode required. Not all PC games fall under steams umbrella, and so varying degrees of hoops are needed to use the controller. Steam BPM also isn't great.
-It's just not easy to plug and play. Too much time spent to configure the controller for each game you'd want to use it with. Some games with adequate community support make this issue negligable.
-Feels cheap and fragile at times, and the haptic pads emit a low, disturbing sound when tracking thumb movements.
-Haptic touch pads don't feel as responsive as they need to be, in comparison to thumbsticks or traditional D-pads.
-Huge learning curve necessary to get over the odd layout and concave shape. The face buttons in particular are oddly placed and much of the customization is needed to compensate for their bad placement.
Details:
On a whim I bought a Steam Controller to see just what might be hiding in the currently lush controller market. I use controllers only to play controller supported games that feel light and simple to enjoy with thumbstics vs mouse input. In the past I've used Xbox 360 controllers and Dualshock 4s for this purpose, and while those are perfectly great options themselves I was really just too curious about Valve's prideful contraption.
It was very easy to plug in and get started, and the included dongle is a tempting option when I want to sit comfortably farther away from the rig. It greeted me with a delightful little tune from Portal that I adored. The initial impressions flooded me - fantastic customization, steam support, and was easily playable on supported games like Rocket League. However, over time and through testing with many different games, the frustrations began to pile on.
Not all PC games are steam supported, meaning that you'll have to jump through some hoops (small and large, depending) to get non-steam games to accept a steam overlay. This is so you can use Steam's Big Picture Mode, which is needed to configure buttons and layouts and install templates for (hopefully) quick and easy setup. At first, it feels fine to take a moment to get your controller ready for play, but not all games are made equal. Furthermore, Steam BPM is clunky, obtrusive, and frustrating to navigate on occasion. This meant that across multiple titles, I was spending more time fiddling with the controller and settings menus in order to play the game, rather than PLAYING the game. At one point I unplugged the steam controller and plugged in a DS4 out of sheer annoyance, and was so relieved that the Dualshock was operating perfectly without any hand-holding.
The device also does not perform equally well across games even after it's been configured properly.  Non-steam FPS games in particular were annoying to arrive at a comfortable composition due to the interactivity of sensitivity controls between Steams settings and the game defaults. The haptic pad, for example, might be great for camera control in rocket league, but become spotty in a top-down shooter, or even flat out unreliable in an FPS. This lead me to understand that games which were bundled in support of the Steam controller of course fit with it  seemlessly, but that case does not expand to all controller-supported PC  gaming.
The controller felt very cheap and awkward to handle. I've read many other reviews stating that it just "takes getting used to" which I can believe but not enough to live with it for any amount longer. The face buttons are placed strangely far away from the thumbs, which makes for an uncomfortable stretch to reach the A and X buttons. I found this particularly funny considering that the (excellent) grip buttons are, by default, bound to A and X. While I love the rear paddle buttons, it's a shame their existence is probably partly due to the poor decision of placing the face buttons in inconvenient places. Despite the extra buttons, the odd layout leads to varied and strange button mapping in general.
This product is definitely not meant for me. It can be used, and it can be a decent option. It is probably best suited to someone who wants to play Steam supported PC games from their couch, and they cannot use any other kind of input device (gamepad nor mouse and keyboard). In that situation, the Steam Controller is your lifeline. It can navigate PC menus, the web, and Steams infrastructure pretty well. The onscreen controls and keyboard are workable. However, at no point did I ever feel that the Steam Controller was a replacement for anything. It lacked the ease and comfort of many competing gamepads, and it lacked the precision of a mouse and keyboard. That leaves it in some loathsome middle ground where maybe someone can be happy, but that person isn't me.
I leave this review with a sincere thanks to Valve for the attempt. The controller is an excellent start into the input hardware market and it shows plenty of good ideas and thoughtful design. Hopefully, after many years of software support and technical innovation, we can see evolutions of the steam controller that can really be something special along with being better than it's class. This, right here, right now, though...just isn't worth it.
P.S. Please put more Portal jingles in things. It makes life more delightful :D

Megadimension Neptunia VII (Victory II). I got to admit, this game is brilliant for both people who are new and experienced with the Hyperdimension Neptunia series. It'll probably provide you upwards of 50 hours of unadulterated gameplay and story through it's unique trilogy based structure with 2(3) seperate endings and Visual Novel styled story telling.
The enemies aren't all that difficult most of the time, but the bosses make up for that. On my first playthrough many bosses I only survived by the skin of my teeth. The post-game content and DLC (Which isn't needed at all to enjoy the game) provides quite a bit of gameplay for anyone looking to get the most out of the game.
Many dungeons, enemies, backgrounds/assets, etc are commonly reused with minor modifications, especially in post game content or further into the story. (This is common in JRPGs)
I personally enjoyed the story and would recommend it to anyone who wants a darker more serious theme from the Neptunia series. The comedic moments were abundant and well placed. (I'll admit, I smiled more than I should've), the story wasn't too predictable and the self-aware nature (Like the rest of the Neptunia series) that many games with bad stories try to use as a coverup was actually executed well and bought everything together. It's definitely a step up from other Neptunia games.
The fan service ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) is less frequent but still strongly present in the game in some scenes (As expected of a Hyperdimension game) if you like fan service you'll be rewarded quite well in the "True Ending"! (Which I only reccomend doing on your 2nd run of the game!)
The combat system is interesting, the skills and the combo attacks aren't always scaled together correctly, and DLC weapons almost "break" the game at some points (Which is your choice to buy and enable anyway). Apart from this I'd say its pretty good for a turned based combat system. The skill animations are interesting, comedic and full of energy until you end up skipping all of them the 10th time you've seen them but you always end up taking a peek every so often especially on that last finishing blow.
Overall, if you're a Neptunia fan why haven't you bought this yet, seriously? If you've played other JRPGs and Visual novels before I'd also reccomend this, it has it all. If you're new to eastern games you might be put off by the hyperbolic nature (anime), post-game grinding and fan-service :^).

This is one of my favorite games. It's simple, takes little time to learn, has cute graphics, and runs flawlessly. The game entirely faces entirely fictional nazi robots , but if you don't even want that you can censor it with a simple visit to the settings. It's in a cute art style that's entirely appropriate for the game.
The mechanics are perfect. Due to little your computer needs to process, there will be no lag. Like, ever. Also the character always does what you'd expect him to do according to what you did, and overall just really tight controls.
The game is a kind of speed-running one in which you try and map out the perfect route to remove a series of robots in an area. The games last no more than 10 seconds (Thus, 10 Second Ninja) and you can instantly restart the round with a quick tap of the R key. The maps are easy to complete but it has you coming back for a 3 star rating which you do, because there's nothing more satisfying than achieving it, and you invest little time in going back to it.
Overall, it's a quick game if you don't care about stars. If you do, it'll last another few hours. It's not a large or long-lasting treat, but a very tasty one at that.

If you are a gun enthusiast or just like constructing stuff, this game is for you. What you see in the videos and screenshots is more or less what you get. You can disassemble and assemble different weapons; you can see their inner workings during operation; and you can also shoot a few of them at one of the firing ranges for a number of challenges.
There are quite a few different guns in the game but for some reason, at the moment of writing this review, every gun range is locked to a specific weapon. I find this strange considering that there is already a mode in the game that allows the gun to be fired so the animations are already there. What's the problem with adding an option to use each weapon at each firing range? Anyway, as you can see from the screenshots and videos, the gameplay at the range is simple and looks bad. The ranges are not what this game is about.
There are several game modes for each weapon. You start with only the field stripping mode and proceed to more complex ones by unlocking the previous one. As you finish each mode you get experience points, which you can use to unlock all modes for a particular weapon (instead of having to unlock each mode by playing). I have not seen any other use for the experience points  besides this.
In certain modes your speed and accuracy at assembly and disassembly or firing of weapons is recorded and added to the public leaderboards. Special credits are awarded to the player with the best daily score, which can be spent to unlock the locked models. I think the way it works is that if you don't buy lifetime access (which I did) then a lot of the guns will be locked but if you buy the lifetime access then only the bonus items like cars are locked. This is not a particularly nice system unless you are really competitive. Of course someone is going to be better than you, so everyone but the best are left with having to buy credits with real money if they want to play the locked content.
You can also find some information on each weapon, with images. This information is just the stuff you can read on wikipedia but it is still a nice touch.
This is not a very extensive or high quality game, but it is definitely educational and the assembly of weapons is actually surprisingly fun. It is like building Legos.

I've been playing MWO for around three years now. During that period it would be fair to say that the game has seen some ups and downs. However, over the last year or so, the game has got noticably better and it seems this trend is likely to continue.
The things are like about it are
*The combat is extremely deep, and tactical. The ability to specifically target different components to destroy or disable a mech is absolutely brilliantly done
*The building of mechs. You can totally customise every single mech to your playstyle and liking
*Balance. This game was horribly unbalanced between Clan Mechs and IS for a long time, but its better than it has ever been before currently
*Strategy and teamwork. This game rewards intelligence and teamwork over quick reflexes and lone wolfing.
The things I think could use some work are:
*Maps. I'd like to see more maps
*Community Warfare. Currently is too complicated and takes too long to find a game for casuals
*The graphics. Some parts of the game look great, some like dire. Needs more polish overall.
*There are still some terrible bugs that need fixing (like the stairs on Viridian bog)
But overall, the game is great fun, and probably my most consistantly played game of the last few years. The learning curve is steep, but I urge anyone with an interest in big stompy mechs exploding to give it a go.

Update: After so many years and destroying so many mechs....its still one of my top all time mutiplayer game. With the current rewards system and weekly events, game just got better both visually and total satisfaction in completing event objectives.
I welcome those who are new to this game and I recommend them to fully read this to both understand what to expect and what to do.
A little background on my self with this game, I've been on this game non-stop 3-5 times weekly for teh past 2 years since the founding times so I know what I'm taking about. Also I'm playing all the way from Malaysia in Asia with my buddies/unit based in the US/UK regions and I have like over 120 mechs of both IS and Clan. I'm a Corporal rank in my unit, 1st Crucis Recon and previously we were from Head Hunters of Davion (Davion Faction's largest unit).
What to expect:
1) Light/Medium mechs are fast while Heavy/Assault mechs are slow but powerful (slow as in, you can time and see em turn like how an elephant turns it's body, so basically Light mechs run circles around the bigger guys literally).
2) Mechs are expensive since it's Free To Play, but not impossible to achieve (when I started; with 0 mech of my own, I used the free trail version Hunchback for a week).
3) Don't expect head shots every time, it's super hard to do and very rare (to date I've done less than 50).
4) Grinding/making cash is faster with certain methods (I'll explain later).
Very Important:
For those starting, the first thing I recommend is to go setup your VOIP setting in game to ecnable radio communications.
This game is all about teamwork with your teammates in every match.
Read the guides/manuals/FAQ of the game when you progress further.
And most important, play the tutorials to get a hang of things.
Gameplay:
For starters, there are 2 types of game; quickplay and Faction-play.
Quickplay is a 12vs12 match in either Assault/Conquest/Skirmish mode.
Faction-play is choosing a Faction to support by taking a contract (you can select how long; weeks/months/permanent), and playing either defense/attack of planets in a big war of 12vs12 (with each warrior respawn of 4 times/ 4 mechs each).
Faction-play although slow and hard for beginners, is quite rewarding in it's faction rewards; some being in game c-bills, free mech bay, gxp, xp and more.
I suggest doing some faction games done when you can to at least reach tier 3 of a faction's loyalty rewards programme, you need those free mech bays.
So How Make C-Bills/More Mechs Fast?
Play quickplay a lot. As a newbie/PUG, select trail mechs, run in groups with other veteran mechs (mechs with lots of custom paint jobs is a very clear sign) and help them in game. Don't run out alone to just die fast tot eh enemy, it has very little rewards given as c-bills. Doing more of teamwork during games gives you more rewards when you either win/lose the match.
Keeping this in mind, it's best to stay alive with the team and if you die, just quit match, reselect another trail mech and find another match. Doing this method could easily see you making about 1million C-Bills within 1 hour. I got my first Hunchback (50 ton medium mech) within a day, so yeah, it's not that tough a grind.
Keep playing this way to amke more money and soon you will pick up things like cutomization of your mech weapons, skills and how to use GXP, don't worry; the learning curve is not as hard as some might say, you just need to do some reading like I did.
Gameplay Pros:
1) Awesome graphics, details and effects
2) Cutomizable mechs galore
3) Nice flow of game play and one of the best times I had playing in groups/with teammates
4) Rewards progression of skills, c-bills, game performance per match
Cons:
1) Like all Free To Play, you need to pay some to get to some more mechbays or cumization options like color and patterns.
2) If your teammates don't know what they are doing, the match ends very quickly.

Do you like a seemingly normal game that quickly descends into raving conspiracies?
Do you like finely-crafted stealth gameplay that allows you to take on the level as you see fit?
Do you like an overabundance of detail and world-building which makes the world feel more lively?
Do you like having lots of optional objectives and having freedom over how you'll build your character?
Do you want to presented with a realistic conflict over the control of human revolution, where the game will sit back and let you follow your own views on the matter?
Probably, in which case, you should get Deus Ex: Human Revolution.
And in chronological order, the game. Firstly, raving conspiracies. Deus Ex is a series known for involving deep, winding conspiracies that get more and more far-fetched as the game goes on. Human Revolution is no different. You start off innocently, as a Security Chief working for a biotech company named "Sarif Industries". After an attack on your company, you, being the security chief, end up tracking down a few leads on your attackers, and then it just goes down into the rabbit hole from there. Some of the characters felt bland, which made the storytelling feel out of place at times.
The gameplay. My god, the gameplay. When I said you were working for a biotech company, I mean that they're in the business of making augmentations. Augmentations are essentially devices like basic prosthetics, ranging to full-fledged cerebral modifications that alter how an individual would think. Well, your character is ♥♥♥♥in' laced with the things, and they all serve to give you plenty of powers and abilities to upgrade and play with. You can enhance the stealth gameplay by upgrading your augmentations and tailoring your character to whichever type of stealth you want to use. If you plan on knocking everyone out, you can invest in augmentations that allow you to silently knock out two enemies at once. Or perhaps you just wanna sneak past people, in which case you could upgrade your cloaking augmentation to allow you to slip past people with invisibility. The augmentation system allows you to spec your character for stealth and proritize your gameplay preference.
When I talk about taking on the levels however you see fit, I mean through a number of ways. At one point, I found a guard all alone, easily beaten, but instead of just knocking him out, I decided to take another solution. I brutally beat the ♥♥♥♥o to death by throwing a ♥♥♥♥ing photocopier at him repeatedly, and the game let me do that. If I wanted, I could have just passed by that guard, or choked him out, or killed him, or lured him out of the room.
And my god, is Human Revolution detailed. The world itself is littered with side quests, providing a load of extra content and adding some interesting side stories to the game. But then comes the even more hidden storylines. If one goes off track for a while and reads a few emails, they uncover all kinds off things going on between employees and guards. I once stumbled upon a "Dwayne Crosby" sending a threatening email to his subordinates after he found his screensaver and desktop background had been replaced by images of animal porn. After that, I hacked a few more PCs in the area and eventually found the culprits, all secretly conspiring over email in a dastardly attempt to ♥♥♥♥ with their boss.
Once again, augmentations and side objectives. You can spec your character for all kinds of stealth, or for combat, or to even just talk his way through everything. You can decide what objectives you want to take on and whether they're really necessary.
And then the augmentation crisis. To provide a little more backstory here, an augmentation blurs the lines between human and machine. They had sparked endless debate in the world of Deus Ex, with the "purists", Humanity Front, being the anti-augs, and the pro-augs, being biotech companies. Human Revolution presents you with a very realistic conflict, with people arguing many different points about augmentations, their advantages and disadvantages. These arguments become very important later on in the game.
You see, when it finally comes down to it, Human Revolution asks you to make a choice on what you think is right. Are you a pro-aug or anti-aug? And believe me, it's not simple decision. I don't think I've ever been more conflicted on a decision like this in a video game. The beauty of the whole system is that the game never stresses either viewpoint. It will never make pro-augs or anti-augs out to be the bad guys, or try to influence your decision in the end. In the end, you decide for yourself, based around your own views of the matter. The game doesn't provide benefits for either choice and remains mostly unbiased. I started the game off being pro-aug, but by the end of it, I felt like my opinion had been changed completely.
It feels like an actual, real-life conflict happening, and although augmentation technology doesn't exist yet, I can imagine that a situation like Human Revolution's wouldn't be far from the truth. On one hand, it's about preserving humanity, and on the other, it's about achieving new heights for humanity.

A simple but ingenious idea for a game. The controls are extremely fluent, and the game takes about 10 seconds to pick up and play, and perhaps 10 minutes to get the hang of it. It combines puzzle with speedrunning in the most fundamental kind of way. The fact that each level is about 5 seconds long and restarting is instant means it's not frustrating or off-putting. This is perhaps its greatest strength - that by having extremely short levels, the execution becomes much more important. Timing jumps and movement perfectly to shave off milliseconds is something you'll be doing a lot right from the beggining - and this is, in essense, what speedrunning is all about. Games with longer levels and deeper mechanics are so complex that most players never really reach the point of searching for an extra few milliseconds to hit the target time because most players don't have the time to practice perfecting their run of a level longer than a minute - and thus, they lose out on the excitement of time trials. This game is extremely accessible and fun to play, and clearly demonstrates the appeal of speedrunning to any non-gamer. Would highly recommend for perfectionists. Also, the ahcievements are awesome.

I normally dislike platformers - I bought this on impulse and now I'm slowly becoming addicted.

The game is divided up into worlds, each with several standard levels that lead up to a 'world boss' fight which must be unlocked by achieving enough stars on the previous levels. Every level, including boss fights, must be completed in under ten seconds, hence the name.
This isn't normally too taxing - the difficulty comes when attempting to either gain stars or to achieve a better time in order to get into the top 50 leaderboards.
The comedy in the cutscenes is fantastic - the premise being that 'Robot Hitler' and a legion of baddies are planning world domination and one little ninja is all that stands in his way.
Easy to pick up and put down. An extremely fun distraction. Great as a tool for reaction speed training, too.
Highly recommended.

I've been playing MWO since early 2013 and while it's had it's ups and downs (mostly due to over-entitled, unrealistic expectations on the part of some parts of the community), it's still a brilliant Mechwarrior game, if you're into PvP. If you've played other Mechwarrior games, you will easily pick this up - to me it felt like coming home to an old friend.
Getting to used to playing against real humans tho', takes some time - anyone can pilot and fire a 'mech, but the true art of war is required here, including an understanding of tactics, customisation etc. You need a deep understanding of the game mechanics to really do well at the game. But that doesn't mean you can't just jump in a mech and have a go - just don't expect to win or do much damage and win big spacebucks.
The choice and range of mechs is mind-blowing, the graphics are great, the game modes are fun (though they could expand them). The end-game content if you're into the serious group co-ordination required (and yes, group co-ordination *IS* required for CW to make it fun) is rewarding - the time invested is rewarded very well in that mode and the more strategic aspect of when to use what mech, on what map, against what skill level opponent is the true challenge.
And more importantly, the game is still under development - great big new things are being added every quarter.

Great game but has some serious flaws.
Firstly is the misconception that Clan 'mechs are vastly superior to IS mechs.  When quirks are considered this is completely false, a lot of 'mechs from the Inner Sphere out perform their Clan counterparts.  A good example is the Blackjack that can actually tank more damage than some Assault mechs.  This misconception seriously infringes on game balance as the Inner Sphere community constantly cries out "Clan is OP", mistaking coordination and pilot skill for over powered 'mech chassis.
Secondly is the game engine itself, it's not very well optimized and is prone to crashes.
Lastly is the fact they charge ridiculous prices for 'mech packs and Mech Credits aka MC, sometimes asking for more than $200 (Clan Masakari Pack for example).
Despite that the game is really good, especially if you join a unit and start dropping in full 12 man organized groups.  The mech customization offers a lot of variety (less so for Inner Sphere due to relying on Quirks).  You have to manage your heat which adds an element not seen in most 'mech games or FPS's.
Overall I recommend this game and not just for the die hard Battletech fan.  It's a great game for anyone who enjoys FPS's, just don't expect another CoD like title where player skill is literally non-existant.  You will die, you will die horribly at times, especially if you participate in Community Warfare but once you start to master the gameplay you'll see exactly why this is a great game.  It's a game where you actually have to think, you can't just go running in guns blazing and kill everyone, it'll get you killed.  You need to communicate and coordinate with your team mates, more so than most other FPS titles.

No time to read: 12 vs 12 robot combat (no respawns), with great weapon and mech customization options. Plays similar to (but not exactly lilke) tank games such as Warthunder, but with more of a sci-fi bent, a more 'gamey' damage system, and a lot more customization options. Not pay to win, but the grind can be pretty hard for new players, and paying for mech content can be expensive.
I played Mechwarrior 1, Mechwarrior 4 (plus the Black Knight expansion) and Mechwarrior 4 Mercs back in the day, and their style of Mech vs Mech combat hasn't really been equalled by any other game. Customizing your mech's weapons, then going into combat with your lance (a unit of 4 mechs) and seeing all your customization pay off in the battlefield was the biggest draw of those games for me. It's a bit sad really that there hasn't been any Mechwarrior games since Mechwarrior 4 Mercenaries release in 2002.
Enter Mechwarrior Online. I found this game about 3 months after its launch in September 2013 and have been playing it since. It captures the flavor of the combat in the old Mechwarrior games and updates it to use a modern graphics engine, as well as adding its own innovations to the mech's various weapon systems.
First about the combat. The combat itself is a lot more hectic compared to tank games. Games focus more on maneuvering to get an advantage on your enemy, as opposed to taking and holding good sniping positions in other tank games. There's a lot more movement and frantic close range fights as you try to take out your enemy. Because of the game's damage system, there's also skill involved in the fights, where you target specific components of the enemy mech to take it down faster. There are very few one-hit kills (even for the biggest mechs it's not easy to one shot kill even the lightest mechs), so it gives you time to react to getting shot (which is very good because the fights have no respawns). If you've played the previous Mechwarrior games and liked their style of combat, chances are you'll like Mechwarrior Online's combat as well.
Fights are 12 vs 12, with no respawns. After the fight, you earn CBills (the game's non-premium currency), which you can then use to buy new mechs or weapons.
The damage system is relatively simple. Each mech has 8 components (head, left/right arms/legs, center and left/right torso) and each component can be damaged separately. To take out an enemy mech you have to destroy its center torso*, head or both its legs. Each component has external armor and internal structure, and once internal structure is reduced to zero, the component is destroyed, taking out any weapons or ammo that are mounted on that component. Weapons do a set amount of damage, when they hit a component they reduce that components armor/structure by that amount (you don't have to worry about penetration values or hit angles as in other tank games).
In contrast to other tank games, Mechwarrior online has a large variety of weapons and gives you great leeway in customizing your mech to use these weapons. There are 6 kinds of lasers**, 3 types of ballistic weapons each type having further subtypes with different ranges***, 3 kinds of missiles**** and a particle projection cannon (basically a long range lightning gun). All these weapons behave differently from each other and have advantages and disadvantages that would affect your playstyle if you want to use them effectively. It's not just a matter of getting a bigger main gun as in other tank games.
The game also has a lot of mechs (over 100 variants in total). While each mech is not totally different from another, there's enough difference in armor, firepower and speed that you definitely will feel the difference when piloting different mech variants.
All this variety is really what makes Mechwarrior Online stand out from other tank games. In Warthunder for example, its usually just a race to get the biggest gun and the thickest armor. In Mechwarrior Online you can have a small, fast mech armed with lasers designed to shoot larger mechs in the back, or a giant hulking mech armed with lasers, ballistics and missiles to handle different types of threats, and both mechs would remain viable (even necessary) in high level play.
Now lets talk about the bad stuff. The grind for getting enough in-game currency to buy new mechs can be pretty tough, especially when you're starting out. Once you've gotten out of your cadet period, it can take upwards of 30 games (at about 10-15 minutes each) to earn enough currency to buy and fully outfit one of the smaller mechs. The game does allow you to use pre-configured trial mechs for free, but since you can't modify them you won't be able to enjoy the game's wonderful customization options. You can buy premium time with real money to boost your in-game currency income by 50% to the tune of about $12 US a month. You can also buy mechs outright with real money, but they are pricey (to the tune of around US$10 to US$30 for one mech).
The game's customization options are not very well tutorialized in the game either. There's also relatively few in-game tools outside of combat for players to interact with each other. Fortunately there's a lot of resources made by the community to help out in this regard.
In the end, its the combat and customization that makes Mechwarrior Online worth it. Its outfitting your mech with the right weapons, and then using them with skill in the battlefield that keeps me coming back to play time after time.

This game was originally released on the PS4 as opposed to the Vita Re;Birth series, and it really shows. The models are nicer, the UI cleaner, the framerates smoother, the animations crisper, everything just looks and feels better. The sound design's a very notable example of this: weapons hit with just enough of an edge to feel ♥♥♥♥ing glorious and the soundtrack's got some pretty great tunes that go beyond the "fantasy with electronic" tunes of the original series.

They're really, really small. They do make a pretty damn big difference, though. The game's been turned into somewhat more of a strategy game- weapons have their own combo slot now and combos their own crits activated by certain criteria, so there's no more just hitting away at enemies with the latest weapon you grab- you have to think about if the extra damage would outweigh the advantages of the current combo setup, and if your new combo setup would be better, and if you'd be better off with the rush attacks instead of the power, and-where am I going with this?
The EXE gauge has been heavily nerfed. That thing was basically a "im bored kill it now just lets get it over with" button. Neat. Luckily, the gauge fills up much faster, so that's nice. Also, some of the EXE skills involve having the characters arrange themselves in a certain formation, so there's a bit of planning on "should i move my character there and risk being targeted and hit by an attack so i can use this skill" or some nonsense like that...I don't really know what to say. Barring some port issues like the capped framerate and others, the game runs damn well perfectly on my system (i5 4460, MSI GTX 970 and 8GB DDR3 Ram).
Now there are some other issues I'd like to adress.
1) The game did not seem to want to work with my Logitech F710 gamepad. Why this was, I have no clue. The gamepad works fine on other games such as GTA V.
2) The voiced dialogue in cutscenes in the story mode played only in the left channel. Headphone only users were shafted in this regard, I avoided the issue by using speakers. As of the latest patch this issue has been resolved, however.
3) The story mode was short. All In all I'd clock it to around 8-9 hours. I, having watched the anime and read the manga past the point the anime is at right now, finished it in 7 hours by skipping some cutscenes.
4) The adventure mode feels lackluster and pointless. About as dumb as Storm Revolution's open world mode, if you've played it.
5) There's some amount of latency in online. I've found that if you're playing against somebody that's in a different region to you, you'd get considerable input lag. It cripples the online fights quite badly.
I've got no other complaints though. The story mode was fantastic and the new additions (being able to switch to your support characters) was refreshing to the gameplay that's been largely the same since the first Storm game.

The game may have a couple bugs, but I don't mind the bugs, genuinely because they are mainly launch bugs, that will and can be fixed.
This game is easily my favourite, I thoroughly enjoyed Storm 3 and Revolution personally, and this tops even Storm 3, in my personal opinion.
The games visuals are beautiful.
The Jutsus look fantastic.
The game has added some amazing mechanics, mainly being the Leader Switch system, being able to play as 3 different characters in 1 game makes the game itself so much more enjoyable.
I see a lot of people giving this game a bad review based on the bugs etc. and not the gameplay, which IS UNDERSTANDABLE considering the game is unrunnable for some users, which is sure going to get patched, and allow these people to play.
My Specs are:
MSI GeForce GTX970 Twin Frozr
i7 4790K
16GB RAM
and runs this game with my PC basically producing ICE.
I've only had the 1 or 2 FPS drops where i've tabbed out a couple times causing it to drop, and when I accidentally loaded the game and had CSGO also running in the background (closed it, and it ran it again) the bugs WILL get patched, and i'd like to see a lot more positive feedback on this game when it happens, because the game is fantastic.
The story, it ends the franchise brilliantly, the last fight (if you've read the manga you'll know... but I mean, who hasn't by now... come on.) is great, it's superbly done. The story mode in general is incredibly fun, just like the game itself.
Yet to play online mode, but i'll be sure to check it out sooner or later atleast.
Adventure is fun in it's own way, I enjoyed it a lot, the tournament is a nice addition (don't sell the Five Kage Kunai, nerd.) and the Memory Fragments are a really nice addition as well, being able to play historic fights over again, why not?!
I definitely reccomend the game, whether you buy it now, or wait for a few more updates it's your choice, but this game is easily worth buying.

I'd like to review this game in the form of a short story, if it's alright with you.
A warped floating cluster of rock and dust, bathed for an instant in a waterfall of every conceivable color, shot back to a pale grey as part of the mind which held it released.
"At times we wonder about the value of this work," thought the Menos aspect.
As far as was possible for a living star being to turn, the Fera aspect looked back into space and fully joined Menos' thought stream.
"Menos, such doubt is most surprising. Surely the importance of what we're doing is clear. While all of the worlds age, their inhabitants at last meeting an unenlightened end, we are the final constant that preserves their memories. What greater duty or honor is there?"
Menos' glow dimmed gently with affection. Fera was right, of course. Their species, the Denethi, was privileged to see what lesser beings called "history" unfold countless times, from the most humble beginnings to unexpected yet beautiful ends. But still, how difficult it was to watch so many species destroy one another, having lived all their lives in complete isolation and with no true fulfillment...
They were so fundamentally different. The Denethi knew no "I" or true separation of selves, for a continuum of flowing minds recognizes such distinction only with great effort. All Denethi loved being aspects of a great, abstract whole and gladly reached out to see if other minds were capable of the same. The effort had not been fruitful practically from the beginning, though - it seemed as though these minds were so accustomed to division that only the merging process of the Denethi after death could bring them together. And in that merging, poignant artifacts always remained.
"There can be no greater honor. Anyway, these appear to be some of the last memories. What was the species called again?"
"That was dependent on the language each subgroup used. Many of them agreed on the descriptor of 'Homo Sapien', or colloquially, 'human'," reflected Fera.
"Let us take inventory again. Have the wars been resolved? All fears, conflicts, disagreements, misunderstandings been eradicated from the final product?"
"All but one, it would seem, and it is most puzzling..."
Menos knew in an instant what had confused Fera.
"How... How can such a trivial distraction remain a regret for so long?"
"Such matters are not for us to judge, Menos. We only know that they valued this, and it tormented them until the last. Remember that their memories still live. As far as any of them know, they are alive in their own time, suffering as always, until we bring them some resolution."
Menos couldn't help but hesitate.
Fera's rays gave a reassuring caress.
"Beloved, we shall set them free. Come now, it is time."
The light between them waxed brighter with Fera's insistence, and Menos slowly offered strength to the bond. Once again the kaleidoscope of colors found their way to the surface, and the few quanta of collective consciousness that remained there buzzed and crackled with energy.
Then the deed was done, and it was as though the consciousness breathed a sigh of relief.
"At last," its final thoughtful intonation echoed.
"I have won AdVenture Capitalist."

After a few hours, you'll find Endless Space a bit simple compared to many other modern civ games, but you'll know why that's not a bad thing. This is a very well polished and balanced game, and stands out for its focus on straight-forward design choices.
Where many civ games take weeks of play to get a handle on good practices, where war or other ends will have you dreading their management, Endless Space provides easy terms and informative tooltips for what you're looking at, or looking to accomplish.
The most significant difference in Endless Space compared to other games is the method of exploration: hex-tiles these are not. Each system is connected to others in spokes of preset flight paths, which are traveled in warp according to the speed you equipped your ships with, and movement cannot be changed once a fleet leaves for another system. This makes strategy in movement much different, and often results in simpler movement tactics than in hex or territory-based games, but you will find that simple doesn't mean easy, especially once you or your neighbors research the ability to forego these causeways and launch scouts or invasions deep within your territory. Hope you've got long-ranged scanners.
Scattered throughout the galaxies will be ruins left by the mysterious and ironically named Endless, which directly or indirectly placed many of the races on their paths to meet. These relics provide unique modifiers available on certain planets, and often require certain technological ability to take advantage of. The result is mostly in the numbers, but the wonderfully written tooltips put you right on the ground--or gas giant, as it were.
Tech trees are an important factor for any civ lover, and Endless Space understands this. The trees are split into four paths which each interweave with themselves, providing nonlinear expansion options. The trees are fun to explore as they open up new exploration options for your galaxy both abroad and within your borders such as scanning moons, colonizing new planet types, unlocking new resources, travel options, and new ship customizations, all which drastically change the game as you advance. Even with a strong focus on research, the game has a way of coaxing you into keeping to one or two limbs in each main branch, which can feel limiting, but makes for a unique playthrough each time, and some adaptability is always available as the sub-branches intersect as they fan out. You will often need to ponder various coinciding tech tree plans to accomplish your longterm goals, and will juggle each main branch to satisfy these needs. These research options really do feel like research.
The exhaustive customization options for your ships will keep you on your toes as your foes will eventually adapt to your fleet tactics, and you must try to do the same. In that sense, ship design can tip too heavily toward one of the three RPS-style offensive or defensive types in short-term, but over the lifetime of a game, you'll find things mixing up more as your saved ship designs join mixed-tactic fleets, especially as you engage other factions which have advanced in their own way. Once in battle, the unique three-stage combat system adds another level of elegant complexity with long range, medium range, and melee range, with each three weapon systems available for each range. The tactical cards used to change battle tactics in the fray add yet another level of choice, and you can unlock more of them, making combat more engaging than in other games without going full turn-based tactical battles. These choices focus on a few factors at a time, made dynamic through the quantity of subsequent choices you'll have to make, without overwhelming you, which is a design philosophy you'll notice throughout the game.
The game allows open hostilities in colonized systems that have not yet reached the level of stability to project influence, which provides for an interesting expansion era before things go diplomatic on you. The inability to effectively siege planets early on is also a deciding factor for how you will make you first moves, perhaps containing expansion by force rather than rushing to meet it with your own. You'll need good engines, and may regret holding them back from too far. Every turn will have you planning your expansion, research, and system improvements in sync, and dynamic events and AI will both keep you shifting priority.
The races are unique and well-written, and can be customized. The lore of the game is overall much more engaging and easily apparent than most games of this type. You are not simply given bonuses or penalties for a race with a loose archetypal flavor, but are given a sort of gameplay philosophy that establishes itself as the natural choice to adhere to, which fits with the often compelling story of the race's origin. Unique technology choices support this, but they often blend in as they simply replace research nodes in the existing tree. If you enjoy reading lore tooltips, Endless Space is full of them. Other than in battle sequences and in diplomacy, you may not get much else differentiating the races than tooltips and relevant playstyle.
The hero system is engaging, but not quite as fun as one would perhaps hope it to be, since other than unlocking unique tactical card choices in combat, their uses only amount to stat bonuses, which are traded around like any other resource. Their leveling options quickly become old hat. Clearly this was not a strong focus in the game's design as much as it was a meeting of contemporary standards.
The interface is practically a marvel of elegance. I can hardly remember a time I was searching for any piece of information I needed, which can be credited to the design choice of keeping as few primary variables as is necessary.
Galactic Civilizations II is probably the richer, more complex version of Endless Space, but Endless Space has a natural simplicity and polish that makes for a fun and balanced game without significant investment in learning curve or playtime. Most importantly, Endless Space succeeds in the illusion of exploring and colonizing a galaxy of hidden wonders, while vying for your race's idea of supremacy.

There are only two difficulty game modes to choose from: Easy and Expert.
Notebook keep tracks of the game's story and clues. Most of the clues are used to solve of the puzzles in the game.
Task Objective panel can be brought up by clicking on the notepad paper.
The inventory panel doesn't have an option to lock it in place to keep it stationary. But it does slides up when being mouse over.
There's no interactive map provided in this game. The individual player must remember where to go within the game.
All of the game's hidden object scenes consists of traditional word lists with some or no interaction.
Most of the game's puzzles are fairly easy to solve without having the need to skip any of them.
There are collectible morphing objects, twenty-two in total, but they're scattered throughout the game to find.
There twenty-seven different achievements to earn from playing the game. Only five achievements are tied to hidden object scenes, puzzles and completing the game. The remainder of the achievements are tied to finding all of the changing items in the game.
Final thoughts, I've found this game enjoyable to certain extend. The replay value for this game is low. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

Let’s start with the fact that this game was made by these people
who mainly have created hidden object games since 2007 and have just over a dozen of them under their belt. I'm not sure where this one falls in place in that timeline of creation and for their sake I hope it was one of their earlier attempts as this game seems rather crude in comparison to the HOG genre we've recently become accustomed to.
This really barely scrapes a thumbs up from me, and like its title you may wish to keep this asylum abandoned. While there are several steam reviews that state that this game has an interesting story, ITS A LIE! Seriously I've seen a better story content come out of my handkerchief after blowing my nose. Maybe they should make a game out of that and start looking for hidden objects...
One of the biggest problems with the game is that there are only two characters you ever come across and both of them are just lucky that my in game sledgehammer was missing by the time i found them. Both of them together seem to have an IQ lower than what might come out of my handkerchief. First there is a young boy which blurts out that he has done something wrong and runs away the second you get there and the second is a shivering policeman who swears that he left the crime scene of a similar boy who was dead at the bottom of an elevator shaft to have some coffee with his partner and upon his return the boy was gone. Is this really to be considered riveting story telling?
Granted this is only a red herring side plot as the main plot is about you a person who wakes up every night in a cold sweat after a nightmare where you’re running down the asylum corridor being chased by an unknown entity. While it might sound supernatural, it isn't. In fact it's rather nothing at all. There are hardly any documents that tell you anything other than the fact of obvious things like your standing in an asylum. There are six skeletons that you will eventually discover and all that they will tell you is that they are dead. In fact a half-eaten chicken leg on one of the asylum dinner tables probably told me a better story than the six skeletons combined did. As you venture to the top floor you will find 7 torture rooms each with their own cut scene animation. None of which make any sense either.
The whole game is so illogical and the worst part is, it doesn’t do a good job in attempting to properly answer everything. Why was the policeman there in the first place? Don't know. Who is the kid and who are his parents? Don't know. Did the skeletons really kill themselves or were they murdered? Don't know. Who are you? Don't know. What happened to the previous mental patients that escaped? Don't know. Why do you have dreams of falling down the elevator shaft when you never actually did that in the past? Don't know. Who the hell is feeding the dog since everyone has been long dead? Don't know. Why the hell are their puzzles on every bleeding door? Don't know. Why are their fresh brains in the bin? Don't know. Why am I searching for other things that I don't need such as a bowling pin, a camel, a penguin, even after I have found the item I need to progress the game? Don't know. Why can't i pick up other objects that seem more useful such as a gun in the hidden object scene instead of just boring stuff like an empty glass? Don't know. I've played for a few years now and have my share of achieves, own about 100 or so mechs, and a little over 4,000 matches under my belt. I started out, like most noobs not knowing my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from my elbow.  Overall the game is a decent game, not great, but getting there. What makes it better are the squads. Some of the best team play you will ever find can be found in any number of the squads that float around. The community is very active about filling in gaps that the develpoer hasn't quite stepped up to filling yet. Though, to their credit, they seem to actually be -trying- to improve the product even if they sometimes fall short. There are multiple tournament ladders, for both solo drop and community warfare teams. additionally for those that are interested in meta's and min-maxing their loadouts there are several community members and websites devoted to getting the most out of your ride....but all this is for the experienced warrior, not the wide-eyed noob.
As a new player what can you expect? The short answer: To lose, a LOT.
The games learning curve can be (frustratingly, at times) steep. PGI has done better recenly by instituting a tutorial with teaches you the basics of moving and firing, and a few of the core concepts. it also provides you with few minigames to hlp build requisit skills (I personally enjoy the live fire gauntlet). Other reviewers have noted the grind required to get mechs and some seem to imply, or outright say that purchased mechs are better. This is simply not the case.  Completing the tutorial nets some decent cash, enough to buy a stock Medium or smaller Heavy mech. After a few matches you earn enough money to swap out some weapons or somesuch. I suggesting waiting though. Save those C-bills until you have played several matches in a variety of free to play Chassis to find one you like, then commit (purchase) to that chassis to master it. F2P chassis cannot be customised, but owned chassis can.
"Hero" Mechs are special variants with unique paint jobs, and loadouts. Hero mechs provide a Bonus to C-bills earned (30%). They are otherwise statistically identical to other mechs of the same chassis type.
Getting into a squad is the best thing you can do as a new player, and my only regret is that I didn't join one sooner. Most squads are willing to take fresh from the farm noobs and train them, so don't be shy or afraid to shop around for a good fit.

I've played over 10,000 matches of this game between aug 2012 and today but have rarely played it in the last 6 months.  This is a great and unique shooter.  It mostly feels like you're driving a tank or heavy machinery.  The game is about customization too.  When you finally own your own mechs, it is a lot of fun buying weapons and upgrades and making your build as unique or efficient as you can.  The weapons are pretty well balanced at this point.  There have been problems however with game balance for the first 2 years.  It seems like every time a weapon system became to powerful they would nerf the heck out of it 6 months later.  The fighting in the game is not like a traditional shooter because you have armor distributed throughout your mech and arms and legs and other parts of mechs can be destroyed which is part of the strategy to fighting.  Sometimes for example, you want to take out a shoulder where a weapon is mounted or shoot at the legs to take away the enemys ability to move.  The graphics are well done in my opinion.  They have actually recently gotten better.  The gameplay is solid with few crashes.  Overall the behaviour of players is pretty good too.
There is a con however.  While the game is free to play, playing as a new player is a very punishing experience.  As a new player you will not initially own your own mech.  You are given a handful of mechs with preconfigurations that are not optimal to go and fight against players who have the benefit of customizing and leveling thier mechs.  This means they probably can fire thier weapons with more heat efficiency, move faster, and even turn and aim faster.  Not from skill mind you, it is programmed into the game.    After you have been sufficiently hazed, you then have enough cbills to buy your own mech.  Hopefully you choose a good one because after that grinding for cbills can be extremely time consuming.  If you are a crazy person, or just don't care about being at a disadvantage, you will eventually get more mechs and it wont be so bad.  This is how PGI gets money from this game.  They are counting on you paying money at some point in order to keep your sanity and they charge a premium for every ounce of sanity.
Overall I've spent $60 founders package and another $30 MC and consider it totally worth it.  I've had a lot of fun and made some friends and hundreds of hours of entertainment.  Despite how new players are punished I recommend trying the game out for free.  You might get hooked.

A wonderful and worthy game in the line of Dungeon Keeper 2 and War for the Overworld.  A great sequel.
Dungeons 2 was a lot of great fun, with varied and fun to play races, a dungeon keeper gameplay that was solid and fun, and an interesting way of interacting with the overworld.  Dungeons 3 does everything a good sequel does:  The last game, but better.  Now all three races are combined into one big evil race, combined with a new "general" character, Thalya.  Each one having their own "mini economy" in the dungeon as well adds some neat spice and creates a variety of rooms without things getting needlessly bogged down.
Kevan Brighting, the man who did the voices for the Stanley Parable, returns as the narrator as well, which is a big plus.  He lends a lot of great, casual fun to the silly comedy of this game, and does the jokes even better this time around.
The humor is the same silly hit-or-miss nerd and meme culture fun that it was last time, with casual fourth wall breaks, and a general silly, relaxed tone to the whole narrative.  The game is silly, it knows it's silly, and has no problem making fun of itself the entire way through.  From a running "boats" gag, to all sorts of obscure to not obscure nerd culture references, just playing the game had a big, dumb grin plastered on my face.  It's a very relaxed, easygoing, and laid back comedy that knows it's not always side splitting, and that fact is a-ok and only helps the game more.  Even when it messes up, or you just don't get the joke at all, it's just so well delivered and playfully written it'll put a grin on your face.
The gameplay is much improved, with much more focus on what your creatures should be doing.  And when they have nothing to do, they still are active in the dungeon.  You'll see them pass in the halls, and stop to have little conversations, only to move on and keep doing what they're doing.  Overworld combat also feels more responsive and easy to understand, even when it's the final stages and it's "My huge zerg versus enemy fort" I can still see what's going on through clear damage numbers, clear abilities per creature, and helpful side pop-ups that let me know if a creature is dead, or if many have died recently in the current skirmish.  Spells are also helpful and fun, some being more powerful than others, but all having their use here and there.
Research and evilty resource creates an incentive to not just sit in your dungeon for days on end powering up, then crushing the whole map in a huge zerg.  Going out and claiming the islands makes you stronger faster through research, and heros will also occasionally attack those islands, giving a little further incentive to be active on the overworld as well as the underworld.
If the dungeon keeper series was your cup of tea, or you enjoy Sim-ish games, give it a go.  And if not, it wouldn't hurt to give it a try and see if this is up your alley.  It's a fun, relaxed experience that'll make you feel pretty good in general, giggle or laugh more than a few times, and genuinely make you glad you bought it.
