Unfortunately the ABXY buttons are below the thumbpad, instead of above. This is contrary to every other modern day controller. Muscle memory prevents the use of the controller without extreme reconditioning if you're already used to using, say, an Xbox or Playstation controller.

+ touchpads work like a charm
+ gyro aim gives a lot of precision, but has some learning curve to it
+ easy to reconfigure within the game via Steam Overlay
+ very large number of configuration options
+ comes with community config sharing
+ haptic feedback on the touchpads, but it's a little weak (you hear it more then you feel it)
+ more buttons then a Xbox360 pad
+ in-game HUD that shows button labels and actions (good for learning, when native in-game HUD is wrong)
- lots of little inconsistencies in how the touchpads and other features are used, even within Steam itself (e.g. Big Picture mode doesn't use them at all)
- LB/RB buttons a little fat and hard to press
- bumpers a little hard to press (they double as battery cover)
- not much range on the trigger
- no rumble
- analog stick and face buttons a little hard to reach (thumb stretch like on Playstation)
- software still somewhat unfinished with featured hidden behind "Coming soon" buttons
- only configurable in Big Picture (desktop config is in beta)
- shiny plastic on the front
- no compartment to store the wireless dongle
- no labels on the buttons, except for ABXY
- requires Steam to run, doesn't come with normal standalone drivers
- mouse emulation doesn't work in all situations (e.g. it stops working when upgrading AMD graphics drivers)
~ powered by 2x AA batteries
Overall I am very happy with the controller. It might not replace the Xbox360 controller in all situations, but it's certainly much better for situation where camera control/aiming is important. The amount of configurability also makes it the perfect controller for old DOS games and other classics that would be hard to make to work with a Xbox360 gamepad. Worth to mention however that regular DOSBOX games from GOG do currently not work properly at the moment, as the Steam Overlay doesn't integrate properly, some ported/updated games like System Shock Enhanced do however work great. So while the software still feels a little incomplete and sometimes buggy, it is already extremely powerful and relatively easy to use, especially since it allows you to remap controls in the game.
The biggest frustration so far are all the little inconsistencies in how the controller is used. There doesn't seem to be a well established best-practice yet. Sometimes you need to confirm an option with a full right trigger pull, sometimes you need only a soft right trigger pull, sometimes it's A, sometimes it's trackpad-click, etc. Sometimes you have gyro aim, sometimes you don't. Scrolling works differently all over the place. It all varies from game to game, even within Valves own content. This will probably reduce with time, but it's a minor frustrating when coming from a Xbox360 gamepad where everything was relatively standardized across games.
I did some measurements of the activation force required for the buttons and the lb/rb are indeed stiffer than what you find on an Xbox360 gamepad (measurements were performed with a kitchen scale):
Steam Controller:
face buttons: 150g
analog click: 1000g
trigger click: 200g
bumper: 350g
lb/rb: 350g
trackpad click: 500g
Xbox360 Gamepad (old one from first-gen Xbox360):
face button: 150g
analog click: 900g
trigger: 200g
lb/rb: 170g
Complete trash until we get some kind of DirectInput or XInput support, do not buy if you play non-steam games or console emulators.

This is not a controller for everyone, and not a controller for every game. It works great for slower paced games, where twitch reactions are non existent. Puzzle games, story driven adventure games, and similar will play well, but action games and shooters will take some getting used to or will just not work very well (Mostly because the touchpad works about as well as a laptop touchpad, only with less surface space).
Sadly I cannot recommend this because xbox controllers work fine, and are more suited to almost every kind of game than this controller.

I am glad that it seems like with every installment the series keeps getting better. This time, it was a really nice eulogy for Sega as a console maker and the Dreamcast specifically.
The game uses the usual fighting system and adds a few things on top (Next forms, parts breaking, combat traits) without being too loaded. Outside battle, you still have a lot to do in the cities, shops, with the scouts, the dungeons and the world map. The story is slightly better this time around, the humour also seems to be improved. I really liked the OST, although they reused many tracks. The Japanese voice acting is excellent. Graphics are fine, too - nothing too fancy, but solid for this kind of colorful JRPG.
On the downside, the itemization pacing seems a bit off. You lose access to the investment option for a good amount of your game, but it is vital for improvements and even a key item. A rand around a lot with the same weapons and processors to suddenly drowns in dozens of new ones when the game opened up again. Accessories and clothes still don't have stats (for a few exceptions). But this is just a small criticism here.
All in all, I enjoyed playing this game a lot. Probably even more than any of the predecessors. If you like round-based JRPGs, meta humour (especially regarding videogames, character stereotypes and storytelling) and can stand the occasional fan service (nothing too revealing, they also poke fun at themselves for that, too), this might be you game. If you didn't like the series before, however, this game probably won't change that.

I've played a whole slew of Neptunia games before and this is definitely a worthy entry.  All the characters are their usual quirky selves.  The 4th wall gets shattered, and rebuilt for the sole purpose of shattering it again.  There's a ton of meta references.  And the new characters are cool, especially Uzume (no she didn't slip me any credits to say that).  Basically, everything you enjoy from previous titles.
There were a few small changes made: some good and some bad.  I liked that they tied the weapons to their own combos, and combo traits to ensure crits, because it causes you to think about what style works best for you and realize not every new weapon is necesarily better for you.  I enjoy the strategy part of a game, and this added to it.  Not just picking out the newest weapon because this time it may not be better for you.
The investment system was fine although forgettable and I didnt really find a need to develop items much at all.
Difficulty-wise, it's usually not difficult (except optional dungeons), but there were some situations in the main dungeons where if you fought a certain enemy it was pretty much a game over, and every enemy will actively chase you and outrun you.  Wasn't too thrilled about that.  I don't mind difficulty, but some consistency would have been nice.
The new share system was a mixed bag for me.  Shares going down from being attacked did not make sense to me because taking damage in RPGs is a given and should not be penalized.  You could also game the system through scouts and investment, but at least it would negate the damage issue.
Scouts seems like a mixed bag.  They are both necessary and not.  They help you find new dungeons, items, and enemies, which can help you unlock quests, but the luck dependency can make this a chore, and makes quest hunting less prevalent than previous games.  Better than the Stella dungeons though, in my opinion.
My biggest issue though is the route building, which was pointless, but also having to traverse the entire world over and over again, instead of  teleporting.  I HATED going to Lowee and then back to Planeptune all the time, because you would get randomly jumped by usually very weak enemies, like Dogoos, leading to very pointless fights that should not even be there, sometimes a dozen times per trip.  And then I had one time when I got jumped by a enemy so powerful it one-shotted my entire party, leading to a very frustrating game over.  Really wish that system goes out or gets an overhaul.
Still though, very very enjoyable and I'm glad I spent 50+ hours on this.

I just finished playing the story mode for this new instalment of the ultimate series and I've been a fan of the franchise since its Narutimate Accel days (keeping it OG ^^).
This game stays true to its colors and improves its mechanics by introducing interchangable characters dynamically during battle. The fights are fast paced, flashy and easy to get a hold on. The roster is propably the largest they've put out there which is always a good thing.
I actually liked the part where they seperated the roaming part from the campaign. It made sense considering where we are in terms of story since 3, and offers the choice of replayability of favourite missions. The story mode as it is though has some strong moments and some really poor ones where you just want to move on. Lastly the game could use more fully animated cutscenes instead of the image afterimage kind we get (mostly in the first chapter of the story).
Be warned the story covers all things manga with pinpoint accuracy so spoiler alert is in order for the series fans. This game reaches the end of the series
Gameplay is as fast as always. Removing the choice system from Revolutions was a smart move in my opinion because it felt like it limited the powers of each character, while on previous titles they were full on. Additionaly the removal of instant awakenings surely helped with balancing issues the team seemed to have with them (I'm looking at you Minato ninja 3 edition). Again the fact that you control 3 players instead of one and two supports is really fun and it is handled extremely well. Wall run and jutsu clash make a welcome return (only in story mode unfortunately). Removing the choice of your supports being aggresive,defensive or supportish (I guess), finds my neutral to be honest.
On to the problems.
While its services are quite optimized for console experience, I'm afraid that it lacks to impress its pc competition.
I'll cover some of the issues below
Now that last one is the one that furstrates me the most. In order to make generic or playstation controllers to work you have to install emulators and other similar applications. In contrast lets say to Rocket League which you just plug in any generic controller (like in my case a Speedlink) and it registers perfectly. It is dissapointing to say the least, that this is the extend of polish this game had at release (hoping future patches will fix the issues at hand).
As for the on-line parts of the game, from personal experience, all of the ultimate ninja storm games (wether it was me playing in a console or pc, or in different places of the world) none of them could establish a solid connection, with my opponents unless they were in the same country. A shame that unfortunately plagues most fighting games. Problem with this is the lack of dedicated servers, although I suppose that technique costs a lot of money for the company. Nevertheless, these problems discourage on-line play in an on-line era for gaming.
I still recommend this game because it is tons of fun to play with friends, but with the conditions that the buyer knows exactly what problems he will face and how to solve them. Fans of the franchise will find enjoyment in this title, newcomers on the other hand will have a hard time.

This instance of the DOOM series proves that the mid to late 1990's style of first person shooter does not get old if it is made the proper way and on top of that it avoids several bad characteristics of modern games. The term, "keep it simple, stupid!", fits well to describe this game. In addition a few words on several aspects of the game:
Graphics are sweet! Enemies and weapons are well-designed, level of detail is adequate, textures are fine, lighting is great. Unfortunately, there is no upscaling, just downscaling, which comes in handy when playing on low-spec hardware. Speaking of which: DOOM offers you to use Vulkan API, which allows you to play the game on REALLY weak hardware. Youtube user LowSpecGaming released a video on this, running DOOM with a GTX 640 which is way below minimum requirements.
Sound: Voices are well done, except for Olivia Pierce's. She seems a little lifeless (could be intended, but still, she sounds a little off). Some kind of easter egg: UAC features Rugrats.
Music is the definition for "spot-on". Not as catchy as the original DOOM soundtrack, but nothing beats Fear Factory-like New Metal when releasing DOOM guy upon a horde of demons. Mick Gordon surpasses himself.
Story is the same as in every DOOM game: A big corporation opened a portal to hell on Mars and you are there to save the day. It is not that deep but has enough plot to provide a setup for each level and allows for a sequel. "Keep it simple...", all the way.
Levels are designed as they were in said era: Tubular, showing traces of a labyrinth, requiring you to activate switches or pick up items in order to progress. To loosen straight progressing, optional secrets can be discovered. Again:
"Keep it simple...". From the eighth level on, there is no way to return to earlier parts of the level to search for secrets or collect items, which makes optional challenges tedious. The eight level itself is a bummer as it has
an annoying first person platforming section. I'm not aware of any game to get this right and it left a bitter taste for following levels.
Enemies vary from cannon fodder to nearly overpowered bullet sponges. All have different attack styles (close combat, ranged attacks, aerial attacks, charging) and require you to keep moving while using the fitting weapon.
Their AI is not strong, meaning they will engage you without hesitating but since they represent mindless demons and DOOM is about shooting up demons, this just fits. Boss fights can be tedious and usually do not require more than spending all your ammunition while dodging.
Controls can only be described as precise. Mouse & Keyboard are highly responsive as they should be, especially in a PC version of a first person shooter. Controller input works fine, if you prefer this way of playing, you won't be let down.
I am very pleased by this fact, as controls in recent PC games, often ported from consoles, have so often been neglected and range from sluggish (GTA V) to p*ss poor (Watch_Dogs).
Gameplay is a dream! No automatic health recovery, no cover mechanics, no idiotically placed auto saving. Just run, gun, pick up items, watch your step and if you do not succeed, try again. Movement appears slow from time to time but
never sluggish. Compared with other current games I would even call it fast-paced. This game's autosaving works surprisingly well. In case of death you will  have to pick up ammunition and armor again as well as fight your way back to
the place you died. However, you won't have to revisit secret locations, pick up upgrade items, or redo challenges, so no time consuming replay of hidden passages is required. Placement of  checkpoints is okay, as far as I have seen, you won't be respawned into a horde of overpowered enemies.
I cannot judge multiplayer as I'm out for a singleplayer experience. A quick look into its options showed that there is an upgrade-based inventory which killed the last bit of interest in this mode. At least with Update 6.66 all weapons
and items were made available for everyone.
I genuinely enjoyed playing DOOM so much that I started it again on a higher difficulty right after finishing it. I think this is noteworthy as a) DOOM does not allow for variation in storyline and b) singleplayer modes of recent titles
often lack the ability to motivate you to play it again. I personally had this experience only with few games (Unreal, Half Life, Half Life 2, Deus Ex, Painkiller, and GTA V)  and I am glad that there is a new one to be added to this list. My final verdict on DOOM: A game done right, worth every bit!

Firstly I really enjoy this game, yes it has issues with framerates and hardware optimization. I've been playing the game since the founders package became available for sale back in 2012, the balance has come a long way since the days of AC20 lobbing and the LRM-apocalyse... One of the more recent balance changes that happened was ECM nerf, which makes sense because lore ECM isn't a giant null-sig bubble that can effectively hide your whole team from lock-ons... unless the enemy team is rolling UAVs, targeting lasers, and/or NARCs. The game has a lot going for it and I hope that the move to steam will bring out this game's fullest potential... A token campaign would be really nice. ;)
Pros:
- Giant Stompy Robots fighting other giant stompy robots
- The customization is strong, meta builds exist but aren't entirely necessary.
- Most mechs feel very different; even within the weight class.
- Lots of chassis to choose from.
- Solid lore, something many F2P games lack.
- Team play wins games, tonnage isn't everything.
Cons:
- Content releases can be few and far between.
- Pay walls can happen early on in the game; I'm looking at you mech-bays.
- Hardware optimization is definitely lacking; AMD cpu users you might not get over 40 fps.
- Community warfare is almost inaccessible if you don't have an organized team.
- Content prices are very high for a F2P game; $30-$220 if you don't want to grind the game to death to get the mechs.
- Maps are limited and not all of them are great for the current state of the game.
Hopes for changes the surge of steam users may bring:
- Lower prices for future content.
- New maps more regularly.
- Faster queue times.
- More community events.

I have played this game since its closed beta days and currently have over 4500 matches under my belt.  The game had  fairly rocky begining but over tha last year and a half development has really sped up and focused on whats important.  The developers have had a lot more community outreach and made multiple attempt to better balance and refine their game.  They spent months re-creating many of the maps that the game launched with, but were out of date.  Hitboxes have been altered and the game is in a living state of flux as improves every month.  Patches occur like clockwork, 2x per month and new content is added fairly regularly.
The gameplay itself is solid and the as a f2p there is grind.  The learning curve for new players is rough, but the community is very mature and help is offered on nearly every forum to impart and advance player skills.  You can spend some money if you wish to reduce grind, or to add more mechbays, but for the most part the only required investment is time.
I recommend that all new players hold on to their earnings from the academy and the first 25 matches before buying their first mech.  Community Warfare/ Faction play is something to avoid untill you've mastered 4-8 chassis and have around 100 matches under your belt.  It is a much longer duration game mode with no skill level matching, meaning that success is dependant on having fully customized mechs and excellent skills/ team work.  Consider joining a group or waiting until the next huge content update that supports more casual play before dipping your toes in there.
I recommend most new pilots start in mediums wich offer the following benefits:
middle of the tonnage spectrum topping out at 55 tons.
most powerful jump jets- most agile
decent armor, but not too tanky
a wide variety of chassis and variants that support a great number of play styles.
Centurions, shadow hawks, enforcers, and hunchbacks are all mechs I suggest
Good luck to you and I hope to see you on the battlefield.

BEFORE READING THIS REVIEW, PLEASE NOTE: If you haven't used an Xbox controller, or other controller, extensively, please disregard the text in between this and the list of pros as the text in between is not applicable to you. You can see all of the pros the controller has to offer down below, I tried my absolute best to review it!
I am someone who has used an Xbox controller extensively - on PC as well as Xbox for 10+ years now... I would think there are many people out there like me who are intrigued in the Steam controller and what it has to offer.
I can see the Steam controller being fantastic and amazing, however after using it for 2-3 hours, I still felt lost and out of place. I simply could not transition from the feel and familiarity of the Xbox controller. Also, if it means anything, I really don't have that big of an issue going from Xbox to a Playstation or Gamecube controller. This was not the case here.
Every time I went to move the camera, I would move it too far, or too little, or slightly in a direction perpendicular to what I meant (Yes, I messed with the sensitivity a lot to try and fix this).
The buttons didn't feel right, the left analog stick is significantly smaller, and there are literally 2-3 times as many buttons in total.
The biggest change, and what I absolutely had 0 progress on in 2-3 hours, was the change from a Right Analog stick to the 'mouse pad', and the positioning of that 'mouse pad' and the 4 main buttons swapping.
Once again I want to stress that if you are not familiar to the point of no return on a controller already, I think this controller would be awesome.
It has several PROS:
-Amazing customization
-Unique, cool, enjoyable look and feel
-Sounds, also customizable.
-Freedom to map any button to anything you want
-Can be a mouse and a keyboard both in and out of games
-Plethora of buttons at your disposal:
------A,B,X,Y,
------Start/Menu, Select/Back
------Power button/Steam button (Brings up steam overlay when in game, big picture when out of game)
------Two triggers (Both of which are ALSO buttons if you push them down all the way)
------Two bumpers (In between the top of the controller face and the triggers)
------Two 'paddles' (On the back side of the controller, on each side)
------D-Pad, which also acts has buttons on the top, middle, bottom and sides of it when pressed down
------'Mouse pad' (Basically like a touchpad on a laptop, but much better, also can be pressed down)

Bought the last copy in stock from a local store when I first saw them on sale, bought a second online immediately upon seeing another sale, and am seriously considering replacing every 360 controller I own with these (even though the 360 controllers work fine & are more familiar to most guests.)
I’m unaware of if/when a console ever updates the firmware of its controllers.  By contrast, Valve seems to have put (and continue to be putting) more effort into adding features onto these things than their marketing people can keep up with.  Neither I nor most of the reviews I read/watched prior to purchasing had any notion that there’s a gyroscope sensor in it, but by now there are people using it as an alternative to the wiimote in emulators.  Pre-release, everyone expected touchpads to be a middle ground of usability between worthless joysticks and the gold standard of the mouse, but instead users are finding that the couch replacement for the mouse is to use the touchpad & gyro in highly-customizable & intuitive combinations of gross & fine movement.
Speaking of customizable, overall customizability here isn’t just good, it’s nigh-overwhelming: a single moving part may have more options than the entire pages of options from multiple console games combined.  I can name HOTAS setups costing half a grand that may very well have fewer tweaks & settings than this thing.  The learning curve can seem intimidating at first, but it’s worth it to be able to have the option of the couch for otherwise desk-only games.  And it’s also satisfying to streamline games that already had controllers in mind to a level of efficiency and comfort that make them arguably playable by a wrist amputee.
Try one out at your first opportunity, and instead of basing your opinion on 30 seconds of twiddling through a game using whatever profile someone already loaded for you, try meddling with the controller configuration to get a feel for what’s possible with it in all kinds of games.
Why I bought this I will never know.
If you're willing to suffer the learning curve and have the patience for configuration, this controller is unique and highly rewarding.

Abandoned: Chestnut Lodge Asylum was the very first HOG I played nearly 4 years ago, and it made such an impression on me that I’ve been a fan of the genre ever since.  Despite its age, the title holds up very well with an interesting story, beautifully atmospheric artwork and rewarding adventure-light gameplay.
Every night you find yourself frantically trying to escape that dark place, your dream ending the same time and time again – plummeting to your death.  It is only when you read a newspaper story detailing a very similar death at an asylum that looks eerily like the one of your dreams that you realize there may be more to your nightmares than you originally believed.  Determined to find the truth, you decide to investigate this asylum and discover what answers it holds of your past and the nightmares that plague you.  Although the story isn’t the most original fair, the mystery is interesting and creepy enough to keep you searching for answers, even if you’re likely to figure things out early on.
The game plays more like old school point-and-click adventures than recent entries in the genre, especially on Expert difficulty.  While there are indeed a lot of hidden object scenes, you’ll find your inventory loaded with items, some of which may not have a use for quite a while.  There is also a bit of backtracking as you wander around trying to figure out what to do next.  This may prove irritating for players who prefer a map with quick travel, but I didn’t feel it was too troublesome as the game area is rather small (perhaps 30 screens total) and relegated to the asylum and its surrounding grounds.
The biggest challenge may be in the hidden object scenes themselves.  As was common in older HOGs, there are A LOT of random items in each scene, and unfortunately, the muted colors in the artwork make some of them very hard to locate.  Quite often items blend in so well that you’ll find yourself stumped for what feels like hours looking for that dang pen that just happens to be nestled within the crease of a windowsill that is the exact same color.  Normally, this isn’t such a huge issue, but it makes finishing all achievements in one play through fairly difficult.  I also came across a couple of typos which made finding said items a tad more challenging than they should be (hummer instead of hammer was particularly fun), as well as oddly named items that required some mental gymnastics to figure out.
Despite my issues with the HOS’s, the touch of realism in the artwork is a welcome reprieve from the cartoony aesthetic of modern HOGs.  I’ve always felt there is elegance in decay, and the asylum is an excellent example of that.  The dash of realism painted into each scene adds much to the atmosphere and provides us with beautifully decrepit areas to explore.  The artistry is phenomenal with creatively-designed rooms telling their stories through the details they hold.  If only the game were twice as big, I’d have been in heaven.
Abandoned may not be as flashy as more recent hidden object games, but it’s a title that deserves to be experienced even if only for its gorgeously atmospheric art.  A few annoyances are easily overlooked for what is one of the better HOGs of yesteryear.  If you’re even mildly interested, don’t hesitate to check it out.  The price is worth it for the amount of enjoyment you’re sure to receive from this old school gem.
Bottom Line: Highly recommended to all hidden object fans.

This, like many HO games, has a recommendation with a "get it on sale" caveat.  There are many, many better games out there, but this one is perfectly passable if you've exhausted many of the other options.
Plot is a little lackluster in terms of depth but it does really do well with the creepy factor, especially later in the game, and also especially because the deserted asylum setting, although hackneyed, never fails to give us chills.  There is no real bona fide horror involved, unless you're like me and find clowns and dolls absolutely terrifying.  You'll see what I mean if you play.
Art/graphics are decent in the stillshots and quite nice in the cutscenes (taking into account the age of the game and general quality of HO game animation).  The HO scenes themselves are challenging, with items really blending in sometimes.  Minigames are less frequent and are the usual fare, but are still entertaining.
The one major complaint I have with this game is the very badly done object naming for the HO scenes.  Other than blatant misspellings (I spent forever trying to figure out what a "hummer" was until I accidentally clicked on a "hammer" and it counted), some of the object names are so patently bizarre that I don't even understand where they came from.  A couple examples:  a milkshake being called a "milk cocktail" (WTAF?) and "yarn with spokes" that baffled me until I realized the "spokes" were actually knitting needles.  This sort of thing makes me absolutely crazy and seemed to get worse as the game progressed, as if quality control went out for lunch partway through, got swallowed by tigers, and never made it back.
The game would have benefited from a map system and what I call the Zoom-Zoom option, which is being able to jump directly to a particular location without endless back and forth, and there was a LOT of back and forth.  The progression of the game wasn't always intuitive either, so the more modern map function of "here are the places which have objectives remaining" would have been very helpful rather than making the player wander around the whole area looking for something they may have missed or a new HO scene that opened up.
So overall, I did enjoy the game with a few exceptions, and if you've exhausted the generally-excellent Artifex Mundi catalog and are looking for another decent game, this one will do you just fine, especially if you can nail a good sale and you aren't too picky about the little things.

This game was very good.  The story itself was interesting and had a nice twist.  The setting was eerie throughout without the annoying jump scares.  Most of the gameplay is hidden object of course but it wasn't overwhelming, and there were puzzles mixed in with figuring out what to do next so it didn't seem to drag.  The only downside were some of the items were not named correctly.  They were similar so you can figure it out but not the same.  For example a shovel is not a trowel and vice versa.  Didn't happen every hidden object scene but when it did it was only once per scene so not too terrible.

Story: Reoccurring nightmares bring a young woman full of questions to the abandoned Chestnut Lodge Asylum after seeing a news report concerning yet another mysterious death at the place she recognizes from her nightmares.  During the course of play the answers about the mysterious deaths and her own reoccuring nightmares are revealed.
Gameplay: Creepy (just another dark and stormy night and that whispering voice), slightly scary (a mystery boy, a terrified policeman, and six skeletons in very odd places) and full of mystery (Why, oh Why is any of this happening, that age old question).  I kept expecting jump scares but that just might be because I played Enigmatis lately, or from the initial and later nightmare scenes.
The game plays in 3D causing the screen elements to move and the entire screen to move side to side (unless the gamer adjusts it to widescreen.)  Adds to the creepy atmosphere and the internal fear guage of the unknown.  Just a warning if playing in this 3D mode, check the side edges of your screen for new areas and hidden object find items.  (I do believe there are complaints over this from the easily annoyed and the less exploratory gamers).
This is a true hidden object game, with hidden object finds nearly exclusive as the puzzle elements and plot movers meaning the inventory reward item.  They are a bit on the challenging side, with at least one very well hidden find.  Also the developers used at least one obscure, if not very obscure clue per hidden object scene.  For example calling a grater a grinder, or a spool of thread a cotton reel. (That one made me smile even as I said "jerks".)
There are few actual puzzles in this game comparatively speaking, making the true puzzling aspects of this game how to do something, like open locked doors, slide across a wire or just exactly what purpose that television has.  Some of the actual puzzles found in this game are rarely used by any game developer, which makes them fun and challenging.
A few words about achievements: The bulk of the achievements (22 of 27 in fact) come from finding the morphing/shifting objects.  These morphing/shifting objects in a few cases can be quite the challenge to find.  I had to look up four, two I knew were in the scene but could not find, the other two were really well hidden and I missed them completely.  Finding those objects is a challenge all by itself.
This game plays well for all level of player, novice to expert.  One final note in this game all achievements can be completed in a single play through.  Well almost the final note I forgot there is no game map. (I forget about maps since I rarely use one or there are penalties for map use.)

I don't even have to finish the game to know that this is a 100% recommendable game.
First off, don't let the cute, anime styling’s turn you away. The game is a solid Metroidvania game as well as a surprisingly well integrated bullet hell. Each boss has multiple bullet patterns to memorize and throw your controller at when you are trying to go for the no damage achievements. Also, the price, whether on sale or not, you get more than enough gameplay. Just look at the play times on some of the other reviews. Hell, look at mine.
Next, as with all good non-linear games, there are many ways to get to certain points without the “necessary” items. Hell, there are multiple achievements for bypassing story points.
For the controls, I’m using a cheap third party 360 controller. The gamepad is customizable and quite responsive (ex. Jumping is pressure sensitive). It’s taking me some time to get the bullet hell down with the controller, but I’ve pretty much got it down.
The best thing is that the devs are still very active in solidifying the main game as well as continually adding more gameplay options and content. That alone makes it worth the price.
With all this, I can place this game in my top Metroidvania games. And this is without my love of cute. So don’t ignore it just because of the anime.

This game is beautifully made, with a great story that stays in the background, without saturating the gameplay at all. It looks amazing, and is probably one of the best optimized games that have been released (ran fine with i3 4130t, 750ti and 4gb RAM). Enemies are varied and boss fights are extremely satisfying. The violence and gore is top-notch, and all the guns are as powerful you want them to be. This is not a game about ammo conservation or hiding behind cover, you will have to spamming every weapong in order to beat the levels. While it may have been a tad repetitive, the campaign was absolutely amazing. However, for me it stops there. The multiplayer is like Quake in many ways, just slower-paced (which is definetly not a good thing). It is unoriginal and the weapon choices are quite minimal, making it an unenjoyable experience for me. I also kept being disconnected from numerous matches, probably because of the lack of servers in Oceania. Snapmap kept crashing while loading, but I won't mark the game down as it's most likely an issue on my end. In conclusion, I recommend buying DOOM on a sale because of the amazing campaign, but the multiplayer leaves a lot to be desired.

I played this game from closed beta. Many fun times where had, it felt like a reasonably good battletech game, there was only a handfull of mechs, there was no Double heatsinks basically 3025 tech. When wanting to play a match it was easy to get a drop in, click launch and wham you were in and playing.
If you wanted to play with friends you could group up and easily get into a match. There was repair and rearm mechanic which was a good way to govern people running munchkin builds.
Over time numerous changes were made that made this game less and less fun, until finally I was forced to stop playing with the introduction of cockpit glass, since then I never went back.
Now with the introduction of steam I thought I would be fair and have another crack at this game I used to like playing, however sadly it just does not have it. It is not what I would expect from a mechwarrior game, it is very shallow, limited repetive gameplay. The tier system is not a true ranking system and the only goal in the game is to pokemech so you can collect them all.
The mech chassis are mostly just skins, and lack real variety or flavour, you have a few key loadouts replicated multiple times with just a different look. Since I last played it looks like they introduced the quirk system, this attempts to provide some unique flavour to mechs, but is more complicated then it needs to be and you need to play spreadsheetwarrior to be able to make sense of it. If mech customization was a bit more restricted I feel the balance would have been more natural then the artifiial quirk system that was introduced.
Since the lack of repair and rearm munchkin builds became prolific, and continue to do so to this day, there is no consequence to running the most expensive kit in your assault mech. Every other F2p games introduce a repair mechanic and it works quite well as a natural balance mechanic, ala World of warships, World of tanks ,Warthunder and Armored Warfare and it manages to work quite well but PGI could not make it work.
The graphics looked great back in Closed beta and were amazing, nowdays they are very hohum, the mech Models up to a certain point look pretty decent, but looking at some of the more recent releases, it looks like they are just calling it in doing the Bare minimum to pump out mech packs. The textures and effects are very dated looking now. Whether that is the age showing , or as Ihave heard they have dumbed the quality down because they couldn't make the game run optimally on higher settings I don't know.
The community is polar opposites generally, you have black knights who hate the game with a passion, and the white knights who love the game like it was brought to us by the messiah. In my eyes both are wrong and the game is just meh.
I may try a few more sync drops with friends that still club pugs over the next few days as that is the only way to get matches going quick enough, but taking the game as it stands today I find it a very shallow and meaningless game, unable to easily and quickly drop with friends for ♥♥♥♥♥ and giggles anymore.
The beauty of it being F2P is you can try it out and make your own decision as to whether you want grind away or pay to skip.

As a founder and player of this game since it was able to be played, I have mixed but overall positive feelings about the game.
The actual gameplay can be great. It is a tense tactical shooter where death means something (1 life per round in the main mode) and where team work is essential for victory. The game prods you towards teamwork too, with organisation into 3 lances of 4 per side, and VOIP which is used much more sensibly than in most games.
Besides the quick action mode there is a faction warfare mode, still in development and a little simple in current form. You pick 4 mechs with a weight limit and battle over objectives to eventually gain (or keep) control of the planet, with games often taking 30 minutes. There's a dynamic star map with planets taken over by factions, and individual player units can have their clan tag showing on worlds they take which is cool.
The downside is all from the F2P nature of the game. It can take a long time to earn money to buy mechs, then earn more to upgrade them to be competitive (although you'll get cadet bonuses for your first games to at least buy and outfit one decent mech - read some guides so you don't stuff it up). You can spend money to get 'premium time' to speed up the grind or just pay money for mechs outright. The price of single mechs ranges from around $10 - $15 on average although you can pay up to $30 for some single mechs, which is more than you pay for whole games that offer as much fun as this game overall. My feedback for PGI is: You'd probably sell twice as much if your prices were halved, so the net result would be the same but players much happier.
PGI also release packs of mechs regularly which represent better 'value' than buying individual mechs. Usually for around US$60 you can get several different mechs with 3 variants of each. You can see how most regular players of this game will be looking at spending several hundred dollars over time if they want a taste of new content as it comes out. On the plus side new mechs are released all the time for those who like variety, or on the other hand there's no reason you can't pick one mech, get it how you like, and never spend another cent.
Overall - fun game that rewards time spent learning how to build mechs and play well, but the very high prices or the grind to earn cbills might leave a bad taste in your mouth.

I have played this game since closed beta, and a Legendary Founder for the game. I have seen this game change very much since those days. Ever since IGP went bankrupt and the license has been under PGI control, they have done a lot to make the game so much more. From Faction Warfare, to a robust tutorial system, to a future PVE campaign.
This game is not Call of Duty, this is not Rambo rampage, this is MechWarrior. The combat is slower paced, and team oriented. Running around solo, trying to be superman will get you killed. Stick with your team, focus fire, provide cover fire and try to move from cover to cover.
Don't be scared by the price of mechs and mech packs, every single mech (except for hero mechs) can be earned for free by simply playing the game and grinding cbills. There is no 'Pay to Win' mech, buying mechs with cash does not give you a mech thats superior to a standard mech bought with cbills. The only difference between a standard mechs, champion and Hero mechs is that champion mechs earn 30% mroe xp (that stacks with premium time), and Hero mechs {designated by parenthesis like (F), (L), (I), (S), etc} earn 30% more cbills (which stacks with premium time). But you can get standard versions of the same mechs without the bonuses.
Not to mention that almost every month PGI has an event where you can usually earn free cbills, MC, mech bays and sometimes even mechs for free. And you can earn free mech bays for doing faction warfare. [Warning if you are a brand new player, I do not recommend doing faction warfare until you have 4 full mechs that are decently skilled)
This game will give back to you what you put back into, whether its just a couple quick drops for after hard day, or you are binge-playing over the weekend to get event rewards, The more you play, the better your understanding of the maps and mechs will do you will. Torso twisting, focus firing, cover from LRM swarms, This game will take time to get good at, and putting skills into mechs will make your mechs play better, which will in turn make you play better.
Dont be afraid to ask for help, the community thats been here for over 3 years has no problem helping out new players, but for more indepth answers to your questions, go to the MWO forums. There is only so much people can answer in the games chat.

Okay, after doing a little work on my Rig; this is slightly more playable. From a technical standpoint at least.
What is still utterly galling, is the fact that matchmaking... well, it doesn't exist. Or, rather, it's so loosely applied that it might as well not. I'm level six, 'kay? Fair enough. Don't play it that often, not all that good, whatever, but; that shouldn't be an issue. Any game half way worth it's merit would have a matchmaking system that could pair me with other such players.
What happens instead, is that I end up paired with players who evidently do nothing except play this game. The fact that another player's level isn't made clear to you is rather suspicious. In any event, the players you come up against, will, 9/10 times, be signficantly higher levelled, with far better gear, and far more experience.
(inb4 noob, play game more, shut up etc; I have a real life, some of us have to.)
Perhaps it's due to the small player base, I don't know; but if Loadout ever wants to make it big with anyone other than elite gamers, it needs to get it's♥♥♥♥♥♥together with regards matchmaking.
Also; it's worth noting that this game is terrible for abuse. Not so much verbal abuse, or bullying, or whatever; since it's damn hard to send out a message when you're trying to avoid twenty missiles at once, but there's plenty of cheating, and it's really, really annoying; especially when the reporting system doesn't actually work.
::::EDIT::::
I first played this about six months back, and it started to wear thin with repeated crashes, the most galling of which occur the moment a match finishes. So, you spend half an hour rocket jumping around a highly nondescript map; trying not to go blind from frequent screen tearing and hopeless lagging; only for your hard earned rewards to be swept away the moment the match finishes.
So, that in mind; I uninstalled, and moved on, hoping the devs would get their act together, and at least patch up performance problems.
Six months later, in a misguided fit of nostalgia, I came back, hoping there'd been improvements. There haven't.
It still lags.
It still drags.
It still crashes the moment a match ends.
Now. That sucks. That REALLY sucks.
The annoying thing is though, this could be a really cool game. The graphic style, character designs, and the massive customisability options are awesome. I can run around as a delightfully plump woman, virtually naked, firing bullets everywhere! What's more do you need?
Well, actually; a little stability and support would be good.
Likewise, there's some serious rebalancing work that needs doing. This game is noob toob central. Sure, you can build dozens of different types of guns (don't beleive the game's blurb when it says billions of weapon customisation options, there's probably a few hundred, at the absolute most) people, by and large, only ever use one or two types. Games rapidly devolve into a rocket slinging fest, and it gets really, really boring, really really fast. It's overpowered for both you, and your foes.
However, despite my ♥♥♥♥♥y tirade (and complaints from elsewhere) it seems unlikely that the devs will do anything to fix this game. They harp on incessantly about PS4 releases, and a SP campaign, but what about fixing the motor before you polish the bodywork?
Overall... probably 3/10, and then, only because I can run round as a pudgy cutie with a delightfully unkempt bikini line and a chaingun.

This aspect defines the entire game and poses the main difference to other games. The Tribes series was always centered around the gamemode "Capture the Flag" and offers fast and frantic battles, where aiming is as important as maneuvering the terrain:
It's difficult to describe this movement mechanic with words, so take a look at it in the following video. Attention! Playing Tribes requires some skill, therefore always remember: practice makes perfect!
There are 9 different classes (light to heavy) with class-specific weapons, items, perks and killstreaks. Most weapons shoot explosive rounds, which are quite useful for highspeed battles. The light classes are the fastest on the battlefield and are designed for attack maneuvers, while the heavy classes are mostly designed for defending your flag / base / domination-spot. There are also 3 different vehicles that can be bought with points (from kills and objectives) on some maps. The video below shows some weapons in action:
Tribes Ascend features multiple gamemodes including:
- Capture the Flag
CTF-gamemode with bases. Both teams have a base with turrets, radar, vehicle station and a generator. These "structures" can be destroyed to get an advantage when stealing the enemy's flag (there's also an engineer class to repair them).
- Deathmatch and Team Deathmatch
DM and TDM games with highspeed pursuits. In TDM the first dead player drops a flag and the team that carries the flag gets double points for kills.
- Dominition
Capture and defend spots.

Rabi-Ribi is yet another game that I was hesitant to buy.  At first glance, it looks like an anime style fan service fest.  While there isn't anything wrong with fan service, it's undeniable that it can be used to sell sub par products.  Another factor that made me hold back on purchasing it was the graphics.  It's not ugly, but it's far from the prettiest platformer I've ever played.  It made me further wonder if it wasn't primarily about fan service.  Well, I spent some time researching the game and it seemed to be well received by just about everyone. I gave it a try, and today I can say that I'm happy I didn't miss this game.
First and foremost I'll go ahead and confirm that the game has a fair amount of fan service as well as not so subtle innuendo.  Fortunately, Rabi-Ribi is carried by its strong and creative gameplay.  If you really dislike anime style fan service you might want to avoid Rabi-Ribi.  I think you would be doing yourself a disservice, but I have no doubt that these may be deal breaking traits for some individuals.
The basic story is that Erina wakes up one day and discovers that she has been transformed from a rabbit into a human.  Most of the story follows Erina's adventures exploring Rabi-Rabi Island and attempting to figure out what happened.  Overall, it's nothing remarkable, but there are some humorous moments.  There is a rather large number of characters, but the vast majority of them serve as little more than excuses to have boss fights.  This may sound negative, but in all actuality it's where the game really shines.
Boss fights in Rabi-Ribi are unlike any I've ever seen in an action platformer before.  It is almost like a mixture of a fighting game combo system mixed with shmup style bullet dodging.  As you explore each area you can encounter a wide variety of items that will enhance your combat skills, mobility, and stats.  During boss battles you shoot and do melee combos while your foe moves around and fires danmaku style patterns at you.  Not unlike ships in many shmups, Erina's hitbox is significantly smaller than her sprite, which makes it easier to dodge complicated patterns.  If you have experience playing shmups it will be very familiar to you.  During battle you have a combo meter that ranks your performance in battle.  If you avoid damage and keep your combo meter high the game will reward you with temporary stat bonuses.  Also similar to shmups is that there appears to be some sort of rank system (dynamic difficulty) via the levels of bosses.  Admittedly I don't know all the intricacies of it, but one clear way it manifests is through badges.
Badges are one of the many item types you find throughout the island.  They bestow beneficial effects including stat bonuses, damage reduction, and occasionally alter the way attacks work.  The more badges you equip, the greater the level of bosses.  This means you can wear many and face higher level bosses or alternatively use them selectively in order to lower their level while keeping specific bonuses.  As interesting as the dynamic difficulty system is, Rabi-Ribi is not without a couple flaws.
The open world and large amount of freedom leads to a very nonlinear game.  The player is free to fight bosses in many different orders and even skip nearly every item in the entire game if they so choose.  The developers have even added an achievement in for one of the sequence breaks.  The lack of a linear path allows for a lot of creative play, but unfortunately there were a few parts of it that were handled somewhat inelegantly.  Rather than having an impassible physical barrier, there are a few places in the game you simply can't enter until the appropriate time.  The characters will stop and say something along the lines of, “I don't think we should go this way.”  In the end it's not a big deal, but I think there could have been a better way to do it.  The only other issue of note I encountered was consistent FPS drops in two situations.  One of them happened intermittently during the ending credits and the other happened every time I loaded the game, though pausing and unpausing seemed to immediately resolve it.  My computer far exceeds the requirements and fortunately I never experienced  FPS drops at any other times so it seemed a little strange.  I've heard of others having FPS issues as well though so I suggest making sure your system meets the recommended requirements.
Other than that, there isn't anything negative I have to say about the game.  In fact, Rabi-Ribi is one of the most entertaining action platformers I've played in quite some time.  It has a surprisingly large amount of content and offers enough difficulty options to be provide a challenge for players of many skill levels.  As much as I enjoyed this game, I must admit it's probably not for everyone.  If you are staunchly against the art style and themes, or if you are frustrated by bullet hell patterns, this game might not be the best choice.  I'd highly recommend this game to anyone looking for an action platformer that focuses more on an interesting combat system than precision platforming.  Hopefully the developers create a sequel and/or DLC expansion.

To get it out of the way, I love this game!

The combat system in this game might seem relatively simple at first, you have a mellee attack button, a magic button and a special ability button. The depth for the combat comes in the form of attack combo's and your ability to avoid incoming attacks in a bullet hell style encounter. As you deal damage you recieve a rank that starts low, E, and eventually works its way through to A, then S, SS, SSS and, finally, MAX. As this goes up the amount of damage you do on attacks starts to rise as well, and as far as I'm aware, the damage bonus you can hit doesn't have a cap.
You will later also unlock items which change up your combo's, like an item which will allow you to do a sliding attack that  hits like a truck or the ability to continue your attack combo a little longer by chaining a couple of air attacks at the end of your combo.
The boss fights are what really makes this game and whilst they can start of relatively simple the challenge does ramp up, especially on the higher difficulties. I've never felt like any two bosses are the same and since I have played on a higher difficulty It feels like I have a lot of learning to do on any bossfight before I can actually take the boss down.
I loved the games OST, my favorites were the tracks; Unfamiliar Place, Warp Destination, M.R and Full on Combat.
The game does have post game content which I'm still trying to work my way through, The post game bosses are brutal man!
Finally, I'm in two minds about the story, it was hardly the greatest of plotlines, but on the other hand, this is literally a game about bunnygirls, fairy's and catgirls living on an island without any men at all. In fact the first male character you talk to is referred to as a woman because no one knows what a man is!
TLDR;
+ Combat
+ Movement
+ Exploration
+ OST
+ Post launch support
+ Character progression/upgrades
~ Storyline

Good turn based strategy game.  Graphics are a little simple but gameplay is solid and challenging.

It is a very good turn based strategy game, with high individualization factor.
playable maps from very small (perfect for 1v1) to pretty big (8v8)
Like Civ you have more options to win a game. These are Scientific, Economic, Diplomatic, Supremacy, Wonder, Expansion and last but not least Score victory. So it is up to you what strategy to use. Maps are like points (represent starsystems) connected with each other, to indicate how your fleets can travel from system to system.
There are four research-trees: galactic warfare, exploration & expansion, diplomacy & trading, and applied sciences. You can mix those trees together as you wish. E.g. You want a big ship from the exploration & expansion tree to use/carry all your weapon systems from the military tree.
You can also individually decide what exploitation should be used on each planet. Also it is possible to individually create ship-classes and  decide what weapon-, defense- , and utility systems they carry. The game also offers hero characters which can be assigned to either a star-system (as politician/researcher/economist) or to a fleet as Admiral (bonuses possible to: utility, attack power, defense power, and/or siege power).... So much depth
But that shouldn't shock you as the UI is kept very simple.
All in all it is a well elaborated sci-fi strategy game which can be compared to a mix of Civ and HoI in the setting of later future after humanity started its expansion in space.

It's not for everyone.
Is it easy to use,no.
Is it worth the hassle to learn how to use it? HELL YEAH.
The best controller *Option Wise*
Waste of money if you want a plug in and play system. You're much better off with an xbox controller.

-Can be really helpful for games that are not very good with mouse and keyboard, like Rocket League.
-Has tons of alternative buttons and widgets to make you feel comfortable with the steam controller in your own hands.
-Has a feature where you can browse custom controller configurations made by other people, which is probably one of the most unique things about the steam controller.
-Mouse and keyboard can be better for some games like CS:GO and TF2.
-Some games do not work with the steam controller AT ALL, for example Awesomenauts.

The Steam Controller is easily one of the best avalable on the market. It's fully customizable controls make it perfect for any game. You can control every aspect, from what buttons do what to changing how each control functions (re-map the joystick as a d-pad, emulate mouse movement with the pads, etc.) to even changing entire control schemes with a button press on the fly. If you can think of a way to use the controller, you can probably do it.
This controller makes gaming on the couch much easier as well. You no longer have to use 3rd party software to interprate controller commands as keyboard buttton press or mouse movements. You also won't have to use one of those wireless keyboard trackpad combo things that just never seemed to feel good to me. Playing mouse-heavy games is a breeze on your couch.
The controller also feels great in your hands. It was definetly meant to be used by adults, as the touch pads are pretty massive. This manages to make it feel comfy in your hands, and it's big enough that you won't have to worrk about your hands bumping into each other (this was a big problem I had when using a 360 controller, it just felt too small).
Although the controller excells on the couch, there are still some applications were it won't work the best. So far I've found FPS games to be nearly impossible to play. My aiming isn't as easy,smooth,or fast as if I were to just use a mouse. I feel like this controller was never meant to replace mouse & keyboard, but rather to make couch gaming easier.
I'd definetly reccomend picking this up if you play a lot of games on your couch, or they are interface heavy games like strategy games. For FPSs or other similar games where a mix of quick and precise mouse movments are needed, and you want to improve your gameplay, your better off sticking with the mouse. Hell, I'd actually still reccomend it just for the experience. This controller is really like nothing else currently on the market.

Thing is shaped weird - it's concave, the handles point up at your palms, i bend my thumbs now to compensate (and so the tips of them are touching the sensors instead of my fingers)
Button placement - I don't like them being to the left of my "analog stick" - wondering if I'm going to get used to it.
- certain browsers in windows don't seem to recognize my mouse clicks with it.

The sensation made my skin crawl at first, and my ears even flinched at the noise they make reminding me of that almost painful but not quite sound of friction on a plastic or leather like surface.   I'm used to it now.  Really the sound of them makes my ears tingle in a weird way.. but I can ignore it mostly.
- I think that if they didn't curve the handles up, they could've made room for a 2nd analog stick, allowing it to function as a normal xinput controller with out the need for launching through steam (and providing even more options).

Despite that.. and while I'm hoping Valve will eventually release a software package similar to logitech or some other peripheral manufacturer (only better) so that it's easier to use with non-steam games I'm in love with the Controller and hope more developers will consider its capabilities in the future of PC gaming.

I'd still go mouse +kb for competitive multiplayer FPS anyday, however, for single player action - this thing is amazing.  I have the touch pad set as a trackball for turning/spinning and then with the press of my left trigger the controller's gyros/accelorometer's kick in and I'm amazed with how accurate it is in mouse mode. If I can master utilizing both I'm almost so impressed with the motion sensor accuracy it COULD replace m+kb for all my fps. low ingame sensitivity, higher sensitivity in the controller settings.

- 4 extra buttons that you won't find on an xbox controller (and trust me..those grip buttons are nice)

reading some reviews that say it's poor quality, I know this thing is new to me, but because it's wireless I haven't dropped it like I have all my other controllers.  It doesn't feel like poor quality in my hands, and I'm probably going to be as gentle with it as I can possibly be, as your ability to be gentle matters alot with controller gameplay. So here is the deal with MWO.  Its NOT a tabletop game.  Its more of a shooter at this point with a huge selection of chassis and loadouts.  Depending on the chasis and loadout depends on how you play.  Its a huge cooperative/teamwork game.  If you dont play with your teammates you die.  Your team dies and you all look like noobs.  Its very unforgiving in this regard.
There is really no endgame at this point and as I am sure you have seen in some of the reviews it was promised to be much much more but it is not there yet.  They have been implementing new content at a higher pace recently and the balance and tweaks have been generally good.  The 3 different gameplays of Skirmish, Conquest, and Assault really do not vary much as it usually just turns into an all out brawl at the end.  Community Warfare is fun but intense and absolutly REQUIRES teamwork as you end up going against coordinated opposing teams that absolutly dominate uncoordinated teams.  However, some of the funnest, heart pounding, got the shakes gameplay has come from CW as it is very...well,,intense.
So if you are wanting an RPG style shooter this is not it at the moment.  If you are looking for a good well rounded stompy robot game then this is it.  Literally endless options on how to tweak your mechs and customizations.  Serious fun team play and solo play.  Find yourself a good group of friends to play with or a friendly unit to drop with and you will enjoy this game.
btw I have been playing MWO with
(SoR) for 3 years now and we can help point you in the right direction if you want.

AdVenture Capitalist is a clicker game where you have to click on investments to get them to earn money.
When you have enough money, you can hire a manager, who will automatically keep your investments ticking over for you (or should that be "clicking over"?); and when you get enough action happening, you will attract some angel investors (who can be sacrificed in a game reset, in order to significantly increase your profits when you do it all over again).
You can earn Mega-Bucks and Gold Bars, which can be used to increase the speed of investments and the like.
Or you can purchase them to make the game go faster (that's where the developers make their money).
You can operate businesses on Earth, the Moon, and on Mars.
It takes ages to beat each planet.
As an indicator, it took me 14 months to finish all three planets (that's without spending any money on the game).
Sometimes, for a bit of fun, the developers throw in some time-limited extra events.
I can recommend AdVenture Capitalist as a clicker game, but on that basis alone.
If you're not into clicker games, then don't bother.

Rabi-Ribi is up there as one of the best metroidvanias I've experienced, and has proven based off of other high ratings and mine to be one of the best metroidvanias in 2016, which says something about the others that have been churned out. The gameplay definitely keeps you on your toes, the difficulty levels are wide enough that any skill level can enjoy the game, the soundtrack is subperb. The only thing holding this back from being a complete cult classic in about 10 years is the weeaboo primary demographic and the par-on-average storytelling.
________________________________
The story is nothing special. You play Erina, a bunny rabbit that was turned into a girl for some unknown reason. You get transported to another world, filled with magic, called Rabi-Rabi Island. It's here where you set out to find your Master and find out what is even happening. Story is pretty cliche and doesn't throw in a lot of twists, but you'll find some depth in there.
The writing is par on average. There's some really interesting jokes and comments the characters make, but otherwise it's rather predictable. Won't blame Sekai Project for being like this - They've mostly written Visual Novels, one of their popular ones being Nekopara. Still, might've been a good idea to study a little further into storytelling that metroidvanias really like.
The character design has a pretty clear demographic - Men. There's plenty of scantily-clad girls in here, with some bordering on even being a bit TOO small-looking to wear such. The cutscenes like to play with men's crotches too. At least the characters, and surprisingly cultures, are diverse. You'll find plenty of personalities, so if you don't mind the girls baring their middriffs often, I don't think girls can't enjoy this, either.
________________________________
The game's sound effects are good, but they aren't out of the ball park. What you hear is what you get - a
hurt sound effect, a
attack sound effect, a
magic sound effect. The sound effects aren't what you will remember, it's the
. The music is average for a japanese indie game dev team - in which that means that it's pretty [gaben] amazing. There's a wide variety of different instruments, tempos, and keys that make each level's soundtrack unique. My favorite has to be the final boss themes, but in terms of stage, the Starting Forest - Night theme is pretty relaxing.
________________________________
This is one of the biggest parts of the game's positive qualities. The pauses could have a little more difficulty in them, even for higher difficulty levels, but that doesn't hurt the pauses in any way. They help build up for the main parts of the gameplay - the bosses, and oh boy, aren't there plenty. If it's a major character, you will fight them. Don't worry, you WILL fight them. And yes, you will fight yourself, too. The bosses, of course, are also the main part of any bullet-curtain game, which this game takes plenty of inspiration from, so guess what you will be having to deal with when you face these bosses? Dodging pretty patterns of deadly pellets. Or bullets. Or lasers. Or both.
That said, you get all of the tools needed to handle such bosses. First off, unlike a lot of bullet hells, you have a close-quarters weapon - your hammer. It deals a LOT of damage, and has plenty of combos to go off of. Then you have your partner, a barely-clothed fairy named Ribbon. She's your bullet-hell-style damage dealer, having the ability to throw out damaging projectiles, let that be yellow beams that penetrate enemies, or homing green projectiles that heal half a hit-point per hit. Oh, and if you hit them enough, you can summon a massive super-attack that also gives you a benefit, like extra defense or health regen, or extra attack power. There's plenty of strategies for this game.
There are some left-in skips and secrets from the beta that allows for some sequence breaking, though most of it won't be too much of an issue. Almost every game-breaking sequence break is patched up. With that in mind, there's some nice speedrunning capabilities in this game, and there's also some achievements for it. There might be some secret techniques too...?
________________________________
This game is an excellent example of a metroidvania paced right, and even better, a good example of metroidvania crossed with another game style in general. If you like metroidvanias, this is your introduction to bullet-curtain games like Touhou and many others. Those who like bullet-curtain games - welcome to Metroidvanias. As well, for those who like a challenge, this game's difficulty will keep you on your toes. Best part: So far, all of the content updates have been FREE. So the devs aren't being jerks about the game. Might be a seller for you. Have fun, otaku nerds. :P

However, as you see yourself clocking more and more hours, you realise that there's more than just bunnygirls involved (even though that's the one of the best parts). Some people might find the story to be rather "cheap" or "cliché", but I found it to be deep and enjoyable at the same time
, so much that I completed the game twice. As you gather more and more people to your town, you'll realise how nice the characters are, each one has a distinc personality, which makes the story even more enjoyable (
). Another thing to mention is the non linearity of the story, which means you can proceed with the game however you want, go beat the bosses in any order you want, making this game's replayability potential so high.
The grafics are actually one of this game's charm. This colorful pixel madness is what you need to break that monotony of ultra-realistic graphics, plus the artstyle which is also great.
As for the gameplay, the best definition for it is that: "If a metroidvania and a bullet hell had a baby, that'd be Rabi-Ribi". If you're a fan of one of these genres, you should definitely give it a go and if you're fan of both genres, how haven't you purchased this gem yet?
At first, the game seems way too straight forward, as many people might go for the lower difficulties in their first run, leaving the game with a possible "bad first impression". Fear not mate, you'll soon see yourself crying blood and almost having an aneurism as you try to beat the bosses on the most advanced difficulties. After clocking this many hours into this game, I can still barely beat bosses on the last difficulty.
Oh  yeah, how can I say all that without mentioning the boss fights, which in my opinion is the best part of the game and together with the soundtrack (which is absolutely fenomenal) is what keeps me coming back to this game after so many hours. Each boss feels unique to play against and the feeling of finally beating them on higher difficulties is just so rewarding.
After finishing the game, you have options of speedrunning the game or just beating the bosses, which makes the replayability of this game really high.
If after all this reading you're still not sure, just have a look at all other reviews and you'll realise that what I'm telling is actually true.
TL;DR

You know why you're here: for that quality metroidvania shootemup bunny and cat girl action. Weebs and normies alike will love it. Your parents will acknowledge your passion for games and will never bother you again if you introduce them to Rabi-Ribi.

10 Second Ninja turns even the most casual gamers into perfection seeking machines with its addictive yet cruel take on speed runs. Never has solely completing a level felt so unsatisfying and unfulfilling as it does here.
The concept of 10 Second Ninja is simple, Robot Hitler has raised an army of robots and you are tasked to stop him. Using only a katana and ninja stars (you only get 3!) you are charged in clearing a map of the evil Nazi robots as quickly as physically possible. As the name suggests the overall time you are able to take per map is a slim 10 seconds, although you soon realise that completing the level is merely the beginning of your quest.
At the end of each zone you get a "boss fight" with Robot Hitler himself! Hitler will use his mouth lasers to try and kill you whilst you do your best to not only dodge them but to avoid the obstacles in the environment whilst going in for the kill. This little mini game at the end of each zone is a nice little break as it plays out a little differently to what you are used to with the previous levels.
10 Second Ninja not only gives you a completion time per level, it is also accompanied with a star rating system. Achieving the full three stars seems easy at first as the basic levels allow you to over perform with their simplistic layouts and easily avoided obstacles, however as you progress the game begins to really test you and you begin to be relieved at mere completion.
Although entertaining at first the game itself can become incredibly annoying to play and after a while you start to develop a strong hatred against those blasted Nazi robots! Controversially however I would say this is also one of it's biggest appeals. The taunting of seeing how painfully close you are to maximum stars provides you the drive you need to perform over and over again, shaving those precious seconds off your time. Maybe, just maybe, if you jump here and throw there you can grab that elusive third star!
Considering how much you end up listening to the background tracks they never get monotonous and annoying which is a flaw that so many similar titles have endured. The music is fun and light hearted that when coupled with the sound effects offers a friendly environment to perform mass Nazi robot murder. In fact I only have one gripe audio wise and that is within the cut scenes. I feel that they really would have benefited from a voice over, maybe a Siri-esc style voice for Hitler to add to it's comedic value. The only issue with that of course is you always have to bear in mind that Indie games never come with a big budget and voice actors are expensive!

This is quite possibly one of the best Early Access games out there. Do you like the themes of FTL: Faster Than Light? The base building of the newer X-coms? How about the tactical turn based combo building combat of old school RPGS? Then you will love this game. The basic premise is that a derelict "Pre-Cursor" Space station, the namesake Halcyon 6 was discorved at the edge of the human realm and you are stationed there. Stuff happens and the rest of human kind is plunged into a cataclysmic event and you, the now commandor of the Halcyon 6 space station must unlock it's secrets and use them to your advatage to make a push against the Chruul, as well as fending off pirates, and other species who all want control of this powerful relic.

Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is Massive Damage, Inc.’s debut title on Steam.  In the Spring of 2015 Massive Damage, based in Toronto, Canada, successfully raised $187,000 to develop the game through its Kickstarter. The  team originally asked for less than a quarter of that – a modest $40,000 – with gamers eager to see the type of game that they envisioned. The game has now entered the Steam Early Access Program. It is a retro-styled sci-fi strategy RPG that utilizes a blend of base building, exploration and JRPG style combat. The game features capital starships and prototypical officer style rankings. The storyline focuses upon an unknown alien force that is set on destroying the universe and the planet Earth. It is up to you as the newly appointed Commander of a derelict starbase to save the New Terran Federation from its vicious new rival.
Massive Damage are onto a significant winner with Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander. While drawing inspiration from the likes of XCOM, FTL and other games they are creating a title that is distinctly their own design. This game should find itself deeply embedded among the most recommended games on Steam when it is retail ready.

I am a kickstarter backer and I watched this game develop for a while now. I played it some months ago. It was unplayable, now I tried again and can't resist in writing a review.
