example: I discovered a leecher hive when clearing some station space. I was able to kill them and build a propulsion lab. In the lab was an option to clear a leecher hive. I did and after I killed the leechers again my propulsion lab was gone and i was no longer able to build another one....
another example: I finished a mission and got a special commander as reward. on second later i had to read the same story again. after that I had two times this special commander...
These are just two examples. There are hundreds of bugs like this. This game needs a major repolish of code. It's far to soon to release it on early access...
But when it's one day finished it still has potential to be a good game.. the artwork and atmosphere is just awesome...

Well, so i got this game in its early access, at that time there was nearly nothing to what the game is now, their was balancing problem, no content, repetite micromanagment. All of it, gone.
The devs are active in the comments and review and clearly love their game. I used to have this game has not reccomended, and honestly i stand by that, back in early access this game was nothing compared to what it is now. The devs managed to get the game out of early access quickly without rushing at, a rare trait on steam, and in all honesty transformed a bland micromanagment game into a full fledged, fully working, fun game.
Very glad i could change this reveiw and very glad the devs listended to the points i, and other put forward, and instead of censoring it, embraced it.
Saying that though, their are some flaws with this game, so dont get it if:
-You are expecting deep diplomacy, its very straightforward unfortunately
-You do not like micromanagment of any sort, it is in this game and neccisary (with the 1.0.0.4. patch they actualy added a building which now collects recources for you, in other words they FIXED one of the most annoying parts of the game, AGAIN. )
-You like turn based combat with real time strategy, although your ships go areas in real time the actaul combat system is turn based.
-You like games where whoever has the biggest stick wins, the game has status effects that can be taken advantage of to do extra damage, so just because your move does more damage it might not be the right move to use.
-You are unlucky/hate RNG game, Luck is important in this game, from the success of critical hits, whether you will succeded with your plans, or just if you will have your fleet ready before the next attack.
In any case this has turned into a great game that after it has come out of EA has changed from a not reccomended to a fully reccomended game, so thanks devs for listening to the people!

This game is like mustard:
-There are people who hate it while others who love it. It all depends on what you personally enjoy.
- It takes a while to get used to so dont get discouraged if it leaves a bad taste after a while for it does get better with  repetition and experience. (steep learning curve)
Pros:
- It's free so you wont lose anything if you give it a try.
- No pay to win through added steroids and costly rare seeds.
- Many and continued improvements throughout the years
- Enjoyable and clean game play
- Plays best when accompanied by other helpful entities (TEAMWORK and friends)
- Many play styles to choose from like up close and personal or support (I like my mustard off to the side)
- Occasional free items through eating contests
- Many varieties to choose from (mech variants)
- Friendly community of enthusiasts
Cons:
- Lack of teamwork will make the game sour and spoil the experiance
- Stains carpet
- Pay for branding (colors/camo/aesthetics)

I never asked for this. Quite literally, because when I played Deus Ex: Human Revolution for the first time in 2012, I had no idea what to expect. I saw a few minutes of gameplay on YouTube and I ended up buying it because it looked like a "fun futuristic shooter", not knowing what kind of game it really is. It's a cyberpunk action role-playing game that takes place in 2027 Detroit, where the protagonist Adam Jensen escapes death and gets augmented as a last lifesaving resort. After returning to the job, he sets out for answers that will take him all across the world and unravels a global conspiracy. I'm not going to tread into spoiler territory, but it's a game with a heavy narrative that never lets go. The atmosphere, the freedom of choice en the ever-growing story arch; everything is in great balance.
+ Excellent level design. You can see its brilliance after subsequent playthroughs, because you rarely get to see or use them in one go. It really adds to the replay value.
+ A futuristic and very convincing world of two faces, corruption and deceit.
+ Conspiracies, conspiracies, conspiracies.
+ Absolutely great soundtrack and an even better cyberpunk atmosphere.
+ Heavy focus on narrative, great story that keeps interesting until the very end. Good length as well (~40 hours with all side quests).
+ A few nods here and there to the original, fun to see.
+ Good AI. Not fantastic by any means, but it made stealth (and probably combat as well?) not too easy.
+ The gameplay encourages you to adapt and experiment with new things. A lot of different options for both stealth and combat.
+ Oh yes, have I mentioned conspiracies?.
+ Pacifist/no-alarm runs are very addictive to do.
- Mediocre facial animations and NPC voice acting is questionable.
- Could do with just a little less holding hands, compared to the original Deus Ex.
- Choices don't seem to have a lot of big consequences, as opposed to the original Deus Ex.
- Boss fights could be better (but still, it's a lot better than they were in the vanilla version).
- The Missing Link DLC being integrated to the main story messes up the pacing greatly in those respective parts.
It sounds weird, but if you can somehow get your hands on the vanilla Deus Ex: Human Revolution (the Steam codes in the physical game box), I'd suggest getting that instead of the Director's Cut. Sure, the vanilla had pretty terrible boss fights, but you could easily cheese yourself through them (for example spamming your Stun Darts), but at least the pacing was great. With the Director's Cut on the other hand, it pretty much forces you to replay an entire segment that has very little to do with the overarching story. And I'd much rather have a few minutes of bad boss fights (which were easily cheesed) than the pacing getting messed up for several hours.
Despite that, since the Director's Cut is the only one available now on Steam, I still recommend it. The vanilla game is a great and more than worthy entry to the Deus Ex series and it's my personal game of the last generation. It's even one of my all-time favourites in general. Here's hoping Mankind Divided can be even better!

I've played MWO couple of years ago, when there were only Inner Sphere mechs, and not a lot of them, no Community Warfare, and mechanics were very different. Got bored after a week and gave it up.
I've came back 4 months ago, following friends' interest in the game, and this time instead of joining random battles and getting tired of the game, I've read some guides, push-farmed my first Community Warfare drop-deck (4 mechs), joined a big and active unit, and still having a blast so far; making new friends, having fun, actually enjoying the game.
So, is the game good / interesting / worth a try? Yes.
Is it a " Battletech lore masterpiece"? Not even close.
It's a MMO, based off Battletech universe, with everything that comes with those two things.
There is a very strong and active community of players, but also a very steep learning curve, with "veteran players" not pulling any punches. And to boot it up - a lot of the active players also very critical of the game, despite playing it. And there are a LOT of bitterness from former players as well.
So, both a pro and a con.

Developers did introduce various mechanics to ease it up for new players, by making separate match-making ques for solo-players and for groups, and also according to their "mastery rank", which adjusts accordingly with one's experience and how well they play as well.
The game is constantly updated, with various changes, not too fast to become a blur of constant instability, but fast enough not to get too stagnated and boring... in theory.
New content, and especially events - every week or two.
On the other hand - most of the new content just cosmetics: new mechs, sometimes redone maps etc. Mechs just recently got re-balanced, and not for the first time, but a lot of people feel, that changes could be far more substantial.
The map for the Community Warfare (territorial wars) was reset recently, opening new possibilities etc - but no actual changes to mechanics of the wars there. Which make quite a lot of people sad...
Would I recommend people to try it? Yes... but:
After trying it out, finishing the tutorial and getting some games in various trial-mechs behind your belt and pocketing all the newbie-freebies - read manuals, get some non-trial mechs (remember, that your own mechs you can refit - and for Inner Sphere, green by default, you can change the engines and what kind of armor and structure to use, and for Clan, gray by default, you can change arms/shoulders/legs, to get different weapon-slots and bonuses), learn to play in those, and then look for a unit. The game is fun when you're with a unit, and not fun at all when solo.
Then the learning curve won't be as brutal. And then you'd be able to judge the game for what it is and if you personally enjoy the game, and not feel frustrated at the starting learning curve and judge the curve instead of the game.
Unlike some other "match-games where one team of armored vehicles fight another team", where they lure you in with easy and fast progression at "low-tiers", and then stomp some huge grind on top of ya on later "tiers", MWO doesn't have vehicle tiers or levels. Mechs differ in classes, but anyone can get any mech they wish at any point. The prices don't change either (it'll cost exactly the same for a newbie as for a veteran). So, they bite when you just start playing, and they are easy when you've been playing for a while.
New players get it rather hard, because despite the huge tutorial and first-games pays off - it's barely enough to get you some mechs, depending on what you went for and without reading guides - one can easily spoil everything for oneself.
On the other hand, once you did that first proper drop-deck to go join Community Warfare (I'd recommend mix of mediums and heavies to begin with - lights, despite being extremely fun, require fast reaction and some knowledge of tactics and maps to be good, and assaults... are very situational, despite being brutal in right hands), and manage to find yourself in a team, that accepts new players but also do organized drops that win games - getting new mechs isn't hard. After a while (after 5 weeks of playing in my case) an evening or two worth of playing would get you a heavy mech. That's when getting mech-bays (slots) will become more important, than getting money to buy those mechs =]
P.S. yes, you can play it for free, without paying. Resisting the urge to "boost it up just a bit" may be hard, if you can pay, but if you cannot or just have a strong will combined with patience - it's very playable without any cash put into the game. Especially since often enough various "extras", including premium time, are parts of prizes for various challenges in events, that happen every week or two.

I'm glad I didn't. This game is a First Person/ Third Person -ish RPG. And while that may sound weird, it isn't. The game seamlessly blends combat with third person takedowns while also keeping core RPG mechanics reminiscent of Mass Effect or The Witcher games.
The story starts off slow but becomes grand in scale with the fate of the entire world resting upon the shoulders of our main character, Adam Jensen. One of the things that is so good about this game is that there are no black or white choices. You choices affect those around you and will come back to haunt you once the glory is over. Helping some means sacrificing others and this game captures the very essence of the trails someone who hold the fate of the world in his hands would face.
The gameplay could use a bit of tweaking and improvement. I almost played the entire game with stealth as getting killed is very easy. There was also a lot of backtracking and long, exhausting trudges through cities. Not to mention you can’t really run properly or for long.
All in all. An extremely enjoyable and underrated game that is sure to get you thinking about the ideas and philosophies it presents. The gameplay is not extraordinary or that polished but is still very enjoyable, especially later in the game as you unlock more of your awesome abilities.

In Bully you play as Jimmy Hopkins, 15 year old problem teen who right at the begginning of the game is being left at Bullworth Academy boarding school by his mother and new step father who are about to leave for their honeymoon.
When Jimmy first arrives at Bullworth he quickly learns he's at the bottom of the foodchain in the school and sets out to literally beat up each Cliques leaders to earn their respect.
The game controls and plays very similarly to GTA with some differences.
Jimmy is expected by teachers and prefects which act as the "police" within the school  grounds to attend classes on weekdays and go to bed on curfew.
Nothing stops you from skipping class or staying up late, but if you get caught it can mean detention.
Each class has its own minigame which gets harder each time you pass, and in the post-game you unlock some new classes you couldn't do at the start of the year.
Combat is very similar to that of GTAIV, but heavily improved upon. There are many moves and techniques Jimmy can learn such as sweeping under someones legs to knock them over or uppercuts.
When using a grapple on another student Jimmy is able to "bully" them in various ways.
Overall I'd say this is one of Rockstars best releases to date, and one of the few games released by them that I still fully enjoy.
If you enjoy GTA you're pretty much guaranteed to enjoy this.

AdVenture Capitalist is addicting!  Virtually no graphics, and the music is a constant loop, but the gameplay makes up for it!  Just as addicting as Civilization!

AdVenture Capitalist is a clicker game where you have to click on investments to get them to earn money.
When you have enough money, you can hire a manager, who will automatically keep your investments ticking over for you (or should that be "clicking over"?); and when you get enough action happening, you will attract some angel investors (who can be sacrificed in a game reset, in order to significantly increase your profits when you do it all over again).
You can earn Mega-Bucks and Gold Bars, which can be used to increase the speed of investments and the like.
Or you can purchase them to make the game go faster (that's where the developers make their money).
You can operate businesses on Earth, the Moon, and on Mars.
It takes ages to beat each planet.
As an indicator, it took me 14 months to finish all three planets (that's without spending any money on the game).
Sometimes, for a bit of fun, the developers throw in some time-limited extra events.
I can recommend AdVenture Capitalist as a clicker game, but on that basis alone.
If you're not into clicker games, then don't bother.

Now, if you're reading this, is probably beacause you are thinking of buying the game, but you're not confident enough if it's going to be a good choice or not.
So let me convince you on why you
this game.
Not sure where should I even begin with this g
ame, underrated is definitely the best description to be given.
I do understand that at first glimpse the game doesn't look appealing at all, almost looking like a childish game, especially because of its theme.
However, as you see yourself clocking more and more hours, you realise that there's more than just bunnygirls involved (even though that's the one of the best parts). Some people might find the story to be rather "cheap" or "cliché", but I found it to be deep and enjoyable at the same time
, so much that I completed the game twice. As you gather more and more people to your town, you'll realise how nice the characters are, each one has a distinc personality, which makes the story even more enjoyable (
). Another thing to mention is the non linearity of the story, which means you can proceed with the game however you want, go beat the bosses in any order you want, making this game's replayability potential so high.
The grafics are actually one of this game's charm. This colorful pixel madness is what you need to break that monotony of ultra-realistic graphics, plus the artstyle which is also great.
As for the gameplay, the best definition for it is that: "If a metroidvania and a bullet hell had a baby, that'd be Rabi-Ribi". If you're a fan of one of these genres, you should definitely give it a go and if you're fan of both genres, how haven't you purchased this gem yet?
At first, the game seems way too straight forward, as many people might go for the lower difficulties in their first run, leaving the game with a possible "bad first impression". Fear not mate, you'll soon see yourself crying blood and almost having an aneurism as you try to beat the bosses on the most advanced difficulties. After clocking this many hours into this game, I can still barely beat bosses on the last difficulty.
Oh  yeah, how can I say all that without mentioning the boss fights, which in my opinion is the best part of the game and together with the soundtrack (which is absolutely fenomenal) is what keeps me coming back to this game after so many hours. Each boss feels unique to play against and the feeling of finally beating them on higher difficulties is just so rewarding.
After finishing the game, you have options of speedrunning the game or just beating the bosses, which makes the replayability of this game really high.
If after all this reading you're still not sure, just have a look at all other reviews and you'll realise that what I'm telling is actually true.
TL;DR

You know why you're here: for that quality metroidvania shootemup bunny and cat girl action. Weebs and normies alike will love it. Your parents will acknowledge your passion for games and will never bother you again if you introduce them to Rabi-Ribi.

The Good: Fast paced satisfying gunplay. Every weapon is useful and feels great to use. Your impact during combat makes you feel like a nigh unstoppable badass even on higher difficulties. DOOM is one of the better games to come out in recent years where you can just drop in and focus on the simple things, such as introducing hordes of enemies to your bullet collection.
The Bad: Horrible level design. You frequently will end up having no idea where to go next or what the game wants of you. The compass is useless and the map more confusing than helpful. This results in long pauses inbetween ripping and tearing that dramatically drags down the pace of the game. Your adrenaline-fueled rampage will be put on hold as you circle around the same level four times trying to find the door or pathway that leads to your next bout of carnage. These frequent stops and starts will get old quickly. The lack of direction is in no way helped by the fact that the levels are all the same drab brown colors and industrial machinery which makes every corner of the level look identical to every other corner of the level.
As an added bonus I've died more times by falling out of a level than by demons. Nearly every level has huge swaths that are platforming nightmares with instant death for missing a jump and also sections where there are random holes and ledges with no railings that lead to your death. In and of itself this is not so bad, and one could argue I just need to pay more attention, but the game encourages constant movement during combat which means you will often be set upon by demons only to strafe off a random ledge into oblivion while your sights are focused on the enemy. Personally, I expected to shoot at demons, not play Super Mario.

Fun part of this game is about planning and composing your fleet to your playstyle. Are you a healer? who prefer to stay as long as possible in the battlefield, taking out your enemies little by little, or a nuker? ignoring the defense and just blast your enemies away? or a disabler? disable your enemies so they have no opportunities to fight back?... there are many playstyles within this game and I found it fun.

Halcyon 6 is a fun strategy game. Reminds me a lot of FTL. However, this is not FTL. There are a few gripes I have about this game, but they are not game-breaking. Simple little things that wear on you over time, which affects the re-playability.
What I like:
-Fleet control: build and send fleets out to fight or retrieve resources. Select a ship, make it a "fleet" and send it off. Very simple, and intuitive. It's like the map screen on Mass Effect.
-Combat: pick some guys who work well together. Use their powers to exploit the enemies. You're always planning your next move.
-Base construction: Want better ships and stuff? start clearing out your star base and construct some power stations.
-Story: I haven't beaten the game, but I am very happy with how the story is going. The dialog is my favorite. It's snappy and quirky.
-Music: This is kinda a mixed bag. I like the music. It's fun and sci-fi-y. Resembles a mix of Mass Effect and Faster than Light.
What I don't like
-Music: 7 times out of 10, the music does not fit the theme of what's going on. There are tracks playing over eachother in different situations (like, while building a ship, the main music is playing while the ship building music is playing). It's distracting and repetitive.
-Gameplay: This game can get very repetitive and tedious. Sending ships here and there and then back. Losing colonies to the Tyranid-like aliens. Constantly trying to fend off the Tyranids. Sending teams into the base to try and make it bigger. Fighting the same enemeis over and over and over again.
-Story: So far, none of my responses in dialoge have rendered much of a consequence. I'm not really engaged in the story, and I really don't care too much about what's goin on.
Overall, This game is worth waiting for a sale. I'd spend no more than $10

The Steam Controller is a wild technical experiment meant to bridge the gap between standard console controllers and KEYB / Mouse PC gamers.  Imagine the standard 7th / 8th generation 16-button controller with your bumper shoulder buttons, dual-stage triggers, analog pressure, etc.  Now invert the ergonomic design, add two high resolution trackpads with haptic feedback, two paddle buttons in the back and a high accuracy and low latency gyroscope for motion control.  Now make everything customizable, to include virtual buttons on the trackpads and you have one foreign beast.  Like many of the early adopters, we were at a loss as to how utilize the controller.  We imagine it was akin to handing a modern Dual-Shock controller to someone of the Atari 2600 generation.  However, thanks to user-generated per game controller configurations, we are slowly beginning to enjoy the Steam Controller.  Once you are in Steam Big Picture, the controller receives firmware updates, custom start-up sounds and downloadable configurations based on the game being played.  You can tweak your own controls or adopt top rated configurations.  The controller can last 80 hours on two AA batteries.  The downside is that these controller configurations only work on games or programs launched from Steam (although users have found some work arounds).

I purchased my steam controller as a bundle with Dark Souls III, and right from the get-go I was impressed. The touchpads definitely take some getting used to, but they give a feeling of precision I've never had with a controller, which was nice for a game as challenging as Dark Souls III. All of the buttons felt like they took a reasonable amount of force to actuate, and all felt pretty satisfying to press (especially the triggers). I do take issue with the bumper buttons, however. They take a significantly higher amount of force to press than any other buttons, and every time I do they make a very strange noise. It almost feels like I'm damaging them every time I press them.
Software support is pretty good, they're updating it regularly too which is great. It could definitely use some tweaks, the UI suffers from being "overly simple". As in, lots of menus or options are hidden behind other menus to give a more streamlined look, but in practice it's just annoying. No real major problems though.
I'll edit this review over time to mention how the controller ages, but for now, this is the best experience I've had with a controller. My previous controllers were a gamecube controller, a Mad Katz (I regret that purchase to this day), and a few different xbox 360 controllers.
Honestly, if you already have an xbox 360 controller that's in decent working order, I don't know if it's worth it to purchase the  Steam controller. My xbox controller broke, which lead me to purchase this one. I will say I prefer my Steam controller, but not so much so that I would've bought it even if I still had a working xbox controller.
All in all, good product. Buy if you don't already have a controller, maybe wait a bit if you already do own a controller.

The highly anticipated follow up to "the best pc game ever made" and "the worst sequel ever made" is Deus Ex 3 or Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The story focuses on Adam Jensen, a man forced to deal with augmentations on account of his past and present endeavours. In the first Deus Ex the story focuses on JC Denton, a man forced to deal with augmentations based on the time and place he was born. This dynamic offers a more interesting style of storytelling and presents a series of different connections that can be made within the Deus Ex Universe. Human Revolution revolves around the famous quote turned meme " I never asked for this" which although many claim "sums up" Adam's character, it may or may not in some cases. Something that this game did very well was offer players the choice to flesh out Adam's character in their own way. Often with games that focus on non-linear storytelling their biggest downfall falls into the fact that dialogue options are usually very black and white. While I am a big fan of the Mass Effect series, we notice that those games take advantage of the paragon and renegade system. Although that system is not bad, it doesn't leave a lot of room open for player involvement. This game allows the player to grow, learn, and adapt to the obstacles pressed upon you by society partly based on the immersive and breathtaking environments. Simultaneously, you can become your own person: conform, oppress, comfort; a lot of different ways to approach people.
Deus Ex 1, Invisible War, and Human Revolution are all 20 years apart so clearly there needs to be some change in direction. DX1 is a government controlled future influenced by private corporations, ideas and philosophies. Human Revolution perfectly sets up the world leading to Deus Ex 1 and leaves lots of room for Mankind Divided to step in. The game plays like a Deus Ex game. It tackles that perfect style of non-linear gameplay where you don't have to go on one path. Instead, you can crawl in through a vent, go through the front door, take a side door, avoid the area completely, crawl above, and much more. This style of non-linear gameplay was started with Deus Ex 1;  here it is definitely present and based on the improvements to the augmentation and inventory system, we have ourselves the definitive Deus Ex experience.
Overall, I reccomend this game based on it's nearly flawless level design with only a few issues shown during later levels where the gameplay is forced to slow down. It's less of an issue with level design and more with AI placement, however it is extremely rare. The gameplay is perfected here and does not get repetitive based on the non-linear approach you may take. Many complain about the boss fights throwing you out of the immersion of the titles stronger aspects, however, the fights themselves (in the director's cut) are well rounded and not overly simple. I recognize flaws with the bosses, however I feel that people are forgetting that boss fights existed in some manner on Deus Ex 1 along with Invisible War, if you compare that to this title's ability as a sequel, you see a better result here. The game is difficult and fair unlike many modern shooters. Human Revolution immerses you in the story and allows you to build your own character, while it is not confirmed if your save will carry over to Mankind Divided, Human Revolution set up it's sequel with a line of perfection that I look forward to more than any other title in 2016.
Play this game, play Deus Ex 1; you won't regret it.

Do you like composing your own unique race, building vast empires, playing the complex game of politics, and waging war with obscenely customizable fleets of ships?  I know I do, and Endless Space pushes all those buttons just right.
There are so many options that the game can seem intimidating at first, but the UI is incredibly user-friendly and easy to navigate while the game comes in varied difficulty from granny mode to juggernaut levels of play.  You're not going to understand the whole game at a glance, so if you're looking for something no more mentally challenging than an FPS, this is not the game for you.  However, once you do grasp it, it provides you with the tools to play the game in new and creative ways every single time.
Since its original creation this game has been updated and expanded(mostly free of charge) into something far superior to the original product.  Critics rightly pointed out the flawed combat, semi-bland universe, and wildly unbalanced starting situations in multiplayer.  However, every single one of these problems has been thoroughly handled by the devs at Amplitude.  The universe is still not top of the line in terms of interesting story-telling, but the combat has been fleshed out to an absurd level and the unfair luck of the early game has been almost entirely eliminated.
In short, if you like 4X strategy games, get this one.  It's currently the most solid one on the market due to the horribly botched coding of Civ 5.  If you don't like them, don't bother, this game is 4X to the core with nothing particularly unusual to offer a player who doesn't care for the genre.

AdVenture Capitalist is addicting!  Virtually no graphics, and the music is a constant loop, but the gameplay makes up for it!  Just as addicting as Civilization!

AdVenture Capitalist is a clicker game where you have to click on investments to get them to earn money.
When you have enough money, you can hire a manager, who will automatically keep your investments ticking over for you (or should that be "clicking over"?); and when you get enough action happening, you will attract some angel investors (who can be sacrificed in a game reset, in order to significantly increase your profits when you do it all over again).
You can earn Mega-Bucks and Gold Bars, which can be used to increase the speed of investments and the like.
Or you can purchase them to make the game go faster (that's where the developers make their money).
You can operate businesses on Earth, the Moon, and on Mars.
It takes ages to beat each planet.
As an indicator, it took me 14 months to finish all three planets (that's without spending any money on the game).
Sometimes, for a bit of fun, the developers throw in some time-limited extra events.
I can recommend AdVenture Capitalist as a clicker game, but on that basis alone.
If you're not into clicker games, then don't bother.

I've been playing since the last days of open Beta, and the game is in the best state it's ever been.
That said, there's still a LOT of room for improvement.
The Good: With a coordinated team that knows what they're doing, the game is fun as hell. The mech models look pretty great. For a few brief, shining moments the game can occasionally be the "mech simulator/Thinking Man's Shooter" that its hyped up to be, but those moments are few and far between.
The Bad: The meta is heavily skewed towards massive burst damage that turns the "thinking man's shooter" into "is that an enem- where'd all my armor and components go?". The gamemodes available are Team Deathmatch, Team Deathmach with lights running around to capture zones, Team Deathmatch that sometimes ends in before anyone gets any kills because lights with capture modules ran to the otherside of the map, and Queue Warrior Online, also called "How I learned to hate the Clans and get stomped by 12-mans". The weapon balance is constantly in flux, but rarely in ways that make sense. Rather than simply tweaking values, the devs prefer to add in "ghost" features that are never adequately explained and usually just make the balance issues worse.
The Worse: Know this before you start investing time and money:
The developers have a long history of being out of touch with the reality of the game. They've blatantly lied to players more times than I can count and see the player base as little more than wallets to be sucked dry. The game's pricing system may well go down in history as the worst ever.
All that said, the game is currently the best Mechwarrior game in the market (because development on the Living Legends mod for Crysis "conveniently" stopped around the time this game started up)

Firstly- this is not a review on the developer. Just a review on the game itself. If you want dev drama, look elsewhere.
The simplest way to put MechWarrior: Online is... it delivers some but not all of what you want in a MechWarrior game.
And so much of it is subjective.
It delivers enough to be a fun, relatively high quality mech shooter using fairly refined yet arguably simplified MechWarrior mechanics. It caters more towards the modern F2P competitive shooter crowd than previous MW games, and is more of a shooter than it is a sim.
On those grounds alone, then yes, I recommend the game. Especially if you're a BT fan in any way- it's free, you're not losing anything by giving it a shot. It isn't all that you want in a MechWarrior game... but it's enough for now.

Well, I started the game looking forward to another mainline Neptunia game...and was rather rapidly disappointed.
The bad:
The series has never been some grand source of storytelling but in the past it has been enjoyable and entertaining; with VII I found myself utterly uninterested in the story until maybe the last quarter of the game and even then it didn't come close to garnering the interest that the Rebirth games got from me.
Compounding the issues with the storyline were a few elements of the gameplay. I utterly detested the introduction of route building as having to connect locations with a route, and then follow the routes to get anywhere served only to waste time...especially with the random battles you would get into along the way. Simply getting anywhere for the story, never mind grinding rapidly became an annoying experience.
Lesser irritations included the game deciding the equipment on your characters whenever new characters entered the party, which wouldn't have been too bad a problem if it weren't for how often characters enter and leave (also the game would sometimes seem to change equipment setups even with characters that didn't leave the party). The investment system may have been interesting in concept but in practice it just meant grinding more credits.
We also had the new characters: Uzume/Orange Heart was ok; Adult Neptune failed to add anything (she actually at times made me dislike her) and the Gold Third (C-Sha, S-Sha, E-Sha and B-Sha) I pretty much entirely disliked.
There's also all the characters dropped from this game such as Plutia/Iris Heart, but even more surprisingly Falcom, Mages., MarvelousAQL and Broccoli. Sure, they weren't main characters but they were still staples of the series.
Mixed impressions:
The battle system revamp, while small was a step forward in trying to get players to do more than hit a single button. The dungeons had more interesting designs, though this was coupled with some annoyances in traversing them (best exemplified by the Golden Summit in Leanbox and especially with parts of Neplunker).
The Good:
The music for the game was easily the best of the series. Neptunia banter (pretty much the usual here, though I didn't think it was quite as good).
Summary:
I've seen a lot of people hold up Megadimension Neptunia VII as the best of the series, and quite frankly I can't see it. This was the first time I actually struggled to bring myself to finish one of the mainline Neptunia games and the only time with them that upon getting my first ending for the game I was like "Well, game finished, I'm done, time to move on to the next entry in my backlog."
If I was to recommend a Neptunia game, it'd be Rebirth 3 or 1. In fact, I might actually recommend Rebirth 2 over this (and I never would have thought I'd recommend 2 over any mainline Neptunia games before). Megadimension Neptunia VII I honestly feel I can safely say is the worst of the mainline Neptunia games. I hope that Idea Factory can get back to the feel of the Rebirth games, as even with their faults, I vastly prefer all 3 of them to this.

Play for maybe 30 minutes and you'll notice a pattern that the game follows that even a bacteria could figure it out. You guessed it: Enter room, fight a bunch of monsters, leave and enter different room, fight a bunch of monsters, rinse and repeat.
The real reason why this game won't be remembered or respected as Doom 1 & 2 is because it doesn't have any modding... and no, Snapmap doesn't count. You're really limited to what you can do in Snapmap that it's just a gimmick that they added to create the illusion of modding. Over 20 years later and people still make mods for Doom 1 & 2 and will probably still continue to do so; while Doom 2016 will just be like that one cool movie you watched years ago and don't really care much to watch again.
Sure the game looks fantastic but unlike what a lot of dinguses out there in the world think, graphics aren't what makes a game "good".

I have a few things to say about the game so I'll do a Pros vs Cons list first.
Fast paced
Pretty tight controls
Easy to pick up, difficult to master
CHALLENGING

Now I consider myself to be a veteran when it comes to platforming games like this. I have completed n, Meat Boy, Super Meat Boy, I wanna Be The Guy/Boshy all in their entirety, as well as a slew of other action platformer games. And I easily consider 10 Second Ninja to be up there as one of my favorites. It's a game with a realtively simple concept: Kill all robots on the map using either a close range sword or long range shuriken projectiles, all without dieing in as little time as possible. Easy enough to understand, but the level the game is played at makes it a deceptively difficult. The timing for a lot of the levels requires near perfect jumps and accuracy to get 3 star ratings on, and posting higher leaderboard scores requires near
accuracy and timing. There is a real challenge here hidden behind the easy to understand controls and mechanics. If you enjoy a good challenge in your platformers, don't skip this game. While not masochistic by any means, any self-respecting action platformer fan needs this game under their belt.
Now the controls for this game are also pretty good, with great response time. My only gripe with some of the controls comes from slight issues like corner bumping. Landing too far off the edge on the corner will not let you stand on the ledge, however a second mid-air jump can still be performed after falling off even if both jumps were used prior to landing, meaning the game registers that you have hit the ground already. In a game where pixel perfect accuracy comes into play, this might get a tad annoying on some levels, though it is a bit difficult to notice. It can also be difficult to gauge throwing shurikens along the ground as the hitbox for it is a bit strange. This is really a non issue, but sometimes a shuriken will hit the wall at a corner, and other times it will slide across the ground as you wanted it to. I say it is a non issue because honestly, it comes down to how precise you are when throwing it in the first place, so it becomes more of an issue of
rather than the game registering the hitbox badly. So in reality, its just a small visual gripe rather than an actual game issue. Otherwise, the controls are incredibly responsive and tight. A real pleasure to play as the game feels like its actually listening to what you tell it to do.
The sound design, while not much to note, is effective and aestheticly pleasing. No over the top speaker destroying sound bytes, just simple, effective sound design. Love it.
Now I listed 3 cons, however this boils down to really just one, and perhaps more of a reccomendation for future development. My only real con with this game is the current $10 price tag, for a pretty short game that can be completed in one sitting. No end game content, no unlockables, which means the only thing keeping you playing the game after beating the final level is getting better personal times, and ranking up on leaderboards. And with the few levels provided, should be quite a bit of replayability, though I would still say the game lacks girth. However, this issue would be remedied entirely by a user level repository, and obviously the ability to make your own levels. Now do I think the price tag is too steep? Not at all. I have payed more for less before, and given how awesome this game is, it is well worth it. More of a passing thought rather than a real issue to be fair.
As for any lacking features, it really boils down to adding in a level builder for users (Steam workshop integration would be awesome, a la Battleblock Theatre) and possibly adding in individual level leaderboards, though I could see how that would just be more confusing given that times come down to differences in 100th of a second resulting in long lists of the exact same time on down the leaderboard.
So in conclusion to my lengthy review of a rather short and simple game, I would absolutely reccomend the game to anyone, completley ignoring any small cons I might have found. Action platformer fans, if you don't already have it, get it. The games length and price is no excuse to not take part in the robo-nazi slaughterfest by the hands of a twitchy ninja. You are the only hope little man, save us from those Evil mecha-nazis. I heard they hate kittens!

Now the dead rising franchise always confused me about it's fans and this game. I find Dead Rising 1 and 2 very annoying because you never have any freedom, I always feel confined and like I am unable to do anything I want to in Dead Rising 2, and I haven't played 1 but I expect it to be the same way. Dead Rising 2 makes me feel annoyed and suffocated. You have a very annoying daughter that needs zombrex every 5 seconds, and then you have a 72h limit but 1 hour feels like 1 minute. You die easily, the game feels like it's made for speedrunners or hardcore gamers because I feel like I am being pushed. Then you have the weapon crafting where you have to lug 1 - 4(?) items back to some place so you can use that for a while, but you start out with little inventory space, so you can't create those and even if you did have materials I doubt you'd have the blueprints so you'd have to get the blueprints, search for the items for 2 hours, google for them just to find they're on the otherside of the map.
But this is Dead Rising 3 not 2. The game in my opinion fixes all these problems. I didn't mention the map felt way too big with very little in it. Now in Dead Rising 3 you are a mechanic named Nick Ramos, you are in the city of "Los Perdidos". Now there are 4 islands connecting to eachother through the highway. Now before the game starts you are going to have to do some techinical work. The game is locked at 30fps for some reason, and starting the game up is very slow. I will tell you how to uncap this at the bottom for more room to breathe. The game doesn't run very well I think, I have a PC system that is better than a X360 but I'm not sure if it's on par with a XBONE or PS4. But I get a good 40 - 60 fps now I haven't played far into the game I'm on the last chapter and the story is going ok, the game is getting extremly annoying but I prevailed, I've done multipul Phsyco quests and I've just given up on the stupid companion fetch quests. The start is kinda good, you start off in a checkpoint/prison area tunnel thing. And you see a plane crash over you on the other side, so the controls are heavily made for a mouse + keyboard, but both a M+K and controller have issues, the controller has camera problems that are fixed by using a mouse I think, but I feel like the M+K controls are delayed by a couple miliseconds. And there is a extremly annoying mouse smoothing like feel, now when you start you will check the controls and find a "chase cam" TURN THAT OFF it will not fix the mouse smoothing feel completely but it will help immensely. No that the controls are do-able (forgot to mention change the aim button in melee to Q, makes throwing things and aiming with a flashlight much easier) you go through the area, find a gun, and etc till you're out of the tunnel. And you find a pretty cool sight, a entire plane strewn about the freeway with about 1000 zombies in the way and I must admit that was a pretty epic sight. But we go through the area and get to the place and blah blah blah we go through the rest of the tutorial. I do not want to spoil the game, so I'm gonna stop. There is a new system called Safehouses and they're fun, now something about this game. There is no normal retail/downloadable copy, you can only get the Apocalypse version, and I'm going to tell you, once you reach that weapons locker, the game. gets. fun. You have a barrage of toys, a minigun, duel machine pistols which you will use 24/7, a chainsaw attached to a autoshotgun, and this is where the community hates the game. In the others you work for your crappy weapons that last 3 zombies. In this, you start out a god, and you stay a god. Pick up something once and it goes right to your weapons locker, pickup a brick a mile away from a safehouse? You'll find a infinite supply there, find a piece of clothing? You'll find a infinite supply there, and guess what, the same applies to combo/super combo weapons. That's right, infinite paddle saws, infinite shredders, infinte toys! This game is not for die hard Dead Rising fans, this is a game for a audience that doesn't want to work for crappy weapons, this is a game for a audience that want to feel like death among mortals. You can cut down 16 zombies with a single swipe of a combo, you will feel like Rambo with a autoshotgun attached to a chainsaw, you will feel like death with the fire reaper. If you want a hardcore Dead Rising game, then go get any other, if you want a load of endless fun, get this game, ignore those. I doubt this review will be well received or even make it higher than 10 likes, but I just want you to see this. Get this game.

Now onto uncapping the game
So if you bought the game make sure it's downloaded and run it atleast once to make sure it's capped. Now go into your Dead Rising 3.exe folder (C: > Program Filesx86 > Steam > Steamapps > common > deadrising3) But this may be different for W7 or W10 users, just get to where steam installed deadrising3.exe usually found in your "common" folder in steamapps. Now that you're in the deadrising3 game folder you should be seeing the .exe for the game, now create a new text document in the folder and copy + paste the line
gmpcr_unlock_frame_rate=TRUE
Now save the document and rename it to user.ini and if you did it correctly then open the game up and the first thing you should see is the game running high above 30fps and that is your go that it works. I hope this helped.

I've played Storm 3 and Revolution, and really enjoyed playing both of those with friends.  The gameplay mechanics are improved and there's a great deal of added depth and complexity for players who wish to play competitively.
However, I cannot find a single scrap within myself to recommend this game to an average consumer.
STORY/SINGLEPLAYER:
It's grossly full of laziness and poor effort.  The cutscenes are literally stills straight from the anime.  The fights are braindead simple, as the AI is designed so that a child mashing a single button can beat the entire campaign.  This may seem besides the main point, as story modes are often neglected in fighting games so that the emphasis of the developers is on delivering a rich multiplayer experience.  However, that front does not deliver either.
MULTIPLAYER:
One word: lag.  It's chockful of it.  The lag you'll experience is horrendous to the point where you'll find it difficult to input any commands unless you're mashing the button.  For some bizarre reason, it's also tied to FPS, so if you're playing against someone with 10 FPS, for example, while you're playing at 30 FPS, you'll experience massive stutter that will legimately make the match unplayable.  There is no specatating in this game, so you won't even be able to view anyone else's match online.  The ranking system is a joke, as anyone can disconnect from a losing game without penalty.  The developers have also not improved the amateurish setup of online play since Storm 3 so random disconnects trying to get into a game are still a problem.
I will continue playing this game solely because I like playing the local multiplayer with pals.  If you don't have anyone to play with locally, don't buy this game.  The netcode is brutally awful and makes for an extremely uncompetitive and unreliable environment.
All modern fighting games need a strong online multiplayer foundation.  It's a necessity, not an option.  Without having that foundation, Storm 4 will never possess the reliable playerbase and the longevity that other fighting games currently have.

I am not going to lie. I am very upset with how this game turned out. The ninja storm story has always been the main seeling point of the game. The combat has always been mediocre at best, and is pretty bland. The story however was exciting and fun. However; it brings me to much shame to say that the story in ninja storm 4 is just terrible. Most of the funny and interesting cutscenes were removed and replaced with still images from the anime with a voice over, which is just god awful. The story was rushed, missing almost half of the content from the manga and the anime, and just about every major and epic thing from the kaguya arc was squeezed into two battles. The final battles with madara and kaguya take up just one small chapter and they have left out a lot of things that were important to the series. An example of one is narutos most powerful attack, the 9 tailed beast rassengan barrage that he uses on kaguya. It was scraped from the game completely. There are also a few mechanical issues with the game. One of the ones i noticed most was the audio issue with the story mode. Sometimes there are massive frame rate drops but that isnt very common and you wont always notice it.
So now that thats out of the way, heres a pro and con list for you guys who like it simple.
Pro list:
> great combat (best in the series
> many characters
> cool attacks
> a few really cool boss battles
> adventure mode for added game time after story is done
> online works well
> final battle is really well done and almost makes up for all the flaws from the story mode (almost)
> lots of collectables and items to unlock
Con list:
> story mode was nerfed
> audio issues with story
> still images with voice overs replace cutscenes
> kaguya arc was nerfed and misses most of the epic moments
> a few really forced, boring and awful boss battles
> AI is a nightmare in story mode
> massive frame rate drop in certain parts of the game
> story mode is short (took me 5 hours after skipping a few cutscenes. as opposed to the 10+ hours from the previous games)
All and all, its a fun game for a few hours. Because of the story mode being how it is i cant recommend the game if you are playing for that reason. If you want a game you can play with some friends then go for it, but wait for a sale

It's ok... it's just one of those single player shooters that you play once or a couple of times, and then forget about until the rest of time.
Combat is simple yet it looks okay. Good variety of guns and they each have their own addons and upgrades. While it's possible to play the entire game using only one weapon, there is an ammo limit that does make you switch. However there is a simple way to work around that.
Movement in this game is so slow and is actually a downgrade from Doom 1 & 2. It's so generic that it just becomes a chore to get from objective 1 to objective 2. Play for maybe 30 minutes and you'll notice a pattern that the game follows that even a bacteria could figure it out. You guessed it: Enter room, fight a bunch of monsters, leave and enter different room, fight a bunch of monsters, rinse and repeat.
The real reason why this game won't be remembered or respected as Doom 1 & 2 is because it doesn't have any modding... and no, Snapmap doesn't count. You're really limited to what you can do in Snapmap that it's just a gimmick that they added to create the illusion of modding. Over 20 years later and people still make mods for Doom 1 & 2 and will probably still continue to do so; while Doom 2016 will just be like that one cool movie you watched years ago and don't really care much to watch again.
Sure the game looks fantastic but unlike what a lot of dinguses out there in the world think, graphics aren't what makes a game "good".

Purely as a singleplayer experience, this game is absolutely magical, and worthy of the legacy of DOOM. I have played, and replayed this game on PS4 to the point of earning the platinum trophy and I bought it on PC to test out my new rig. It goes without saying that I enjoyed this game immesely. From the varied levels, to the bosses, to the guns. This game does it all very well. The only real complaint I can level against this game is the gun sounds aren't as meaty as they deserve to be. Listen to the gun sounds of the original DOOM to understand where I am coming from. The chunkiness of the reports from the original guns are still to this day the best in the genre. From the slick boom of the Shotgun, to the loud clacks of the chaingun, to the whizz of the rockets. They should have taken more from the originals soundscape and tried to improve me. The guns sound so weak. They don't sound bad. They give you enough auditory information that you know what you're shooting, but it feels phoned in.

Wow, what a refreshing shooter.
I enjoy the fact that you win by trading damage over the duration of the match, as opposed to the twitchy reflexes required in CSGO or CoD.  Positioning accounts for so much here, and random headhots are SO MUCH rarer than in CSGO (yeah, I meant to hit you in the head with my P90 spray from 50 yards away...).
I played a bit before MWO went to steam, and I like the virtually unlimited customizability for your mechs.  Take some long range missiles to soften up enemies from a safe distance, or pack on the lasers and autocannons to shred your enemies from closer in.
Seems pretty grindy to start up though.  Either put in some cash to get some starter mechs or mech bays, or be prepared for a moderate grind to get up to speed.  Also, it's more expensive than other micro-transaction-based games, but I think that's because Battletech is an old universe, so many of the players are older and have jobs, thus are willing to fork out some cash.  If you enjoy the game though, then it's worth it.
Oh, FYI, NEVER SELL AN ENGINE!  You're probably just going to rebuy it when you finally figure out what's going on later, but you'll be down a few million CBills.
I absolutely recommend this game.  Very different pacing from other shooters. It rewards patience and good decisions.  Win over several minutes, not in a frantic 10-second shootout.

EDIT 11 Nov 2017:
After playing this game for several years and enjoing the game  I can no longer recommend this game. The only thing that is being added to the game is mechs that developers can sell while all system critical components are either degrade (like group matchmaking) or get stale (bad UI that never gets worked on).
I might jump on to do a game or two from time to time but it is obvious now that the game is dying its slow and painfull death. Which is a shame because there is so much that can be done with MechWarrior.
---
Of course, being a free to play title there would always be people complaining about monetization options available, however those in no way required for a game to be competitive and that is most important. if you don't like some, what one can see as overprised, offering just dont get it.., in the end everyone are able to get the SAME chasis with in game money, nothing here is locked behind a pay wall.
Now, the game itself while being simpler in terms of damage model and mission objectives compared to the good old signle-player MechWarrior games we all remember and love, it would be unfair to compare those to the multiplayer title in this franchise. Simply because, being multiplayer requiers different design goals and has a bunch of tech limitations that need to be considered. You have to look at this game with a fresh set of expectations.
Having said all that, the gameplay is solid... its highly tactical, it demands attention to enemy as well as your own team movement, requires you to constantly think, evaluate and choose carefully where you run and which point on the enemy mech you shoot and only then will you be successful.
With understanding of the underlying mechanisms, weapon loadouts and chasis abilities comes a deeper realization of your own camabilities and a great amount of satisfaction when you are able to pull off a succesful manuever in your beat up cicada and bring down an almost fresh thunderbolt surving long enough for your team to take things from there. And in now way, any amount of premium time or a hero mech of the opponent will helo him if you are able to execute correct manuevers and shot the part of the enemy mech that counts.
Currently, there is nothing quite like MechWarrior online on the market. It deserves its own place in every battletech fan's library.
At this moment, there are still a number of issues that I would like to see improved, however I have no doubt that a relatively small Piranha games team will get on it eventually considering a steady stream of updates to the game.
For example, some time ago, some maps were god aweful to play on and now we have a completely reworked iterations of those that are very difficult to recognise, with added are and reworked land features completely removing stalemate behaviour when you drop on them.
Overall, the game is quite good. It brings more satisfaction as you learn your way through, find your favourite chasis and join other groups of players.

Is it really free to play?  Is it pay to win?  It IS free to play.  If you want to speed the grind along faster, you can pay.  You do not gain any measurable play advantage by using real money.  The best mechs in the game are FREE(using in game currency, not real $).
You will read some negative reviews.  IMHO, they fit into the following:  1) Crusty MWO veterans who are bitter about something from 3 years ago.  2) Short attention span players who aren't willing to put in more than 10 minutes to learn the game.  3)  People that don't like the idea of  big stompy robots fighting other big stompy robots.
I have played this game extensively for over 2 years, and I keep coming back.  It's addicting and a ton of fun.  See you on the battlefield!

I was more than a little bit disappointed when I got the completed Steam version. Lach and crew claimed that the art would be updated and improved back in the Desura days, and it never was. Compared to the old Desura version, it is still the same writing, same character art, same backgrounds, same CGs, etc.
Only difference is there's several new characters, all with the same old style, and their own disturbing lack of story choices.
Speaking of the story, it is so scattershot that they had to create 2 new characters with linear paths to try and wrap it up.
I wouldn't have as many complaints if it weren't for the current price tag of $24.99 usd.
For the quality of the art and writing, I'd say wait until it's on sale for 75% off.

One of the creative minds behind Castles in Sky in now back with a frantic mixture of nazi robots, spikes and ninjas. The lose plot revolves around a robot Hitler and a ninja having to destroy robots with a big sword. It’s not likely to win best screenplay but then sometimes you just want to jump around and hit things.
A platform game mixed with a heavy puzzle element, the main gameplay gimmick is that you only have ten second with which to complete each stage. The timer only starts after you make your first move which means you can spend some time surveying the single screen style levels in an attempt to work out the best route to victory.
Your Ninja has a couple of skills to help along the way. You can use three shurikens in each level and also double jump. You’ll need to work out the best enemies to hit with throwing stars in advance as it can be the difference between victory and defeat if you use them in the wrong place. Shurikens can also be used to set off icicle falls, which in turn can crush robots for you.
You’ll need to complete levels as quickly as possible as well as you're awarded between one to three stars upon completion. You’ll start out completely mystified as to how you get the two or three star ratings but as you progress it all becomes clearer. Getting three stars on levels does require almost Jedi like reflexes though.
The levels themselves are a mixture of floating platforms, spikes and collapsing stones. More obstacles and enemies are added as the game progresses and you also have to contend with some good old fashioned ice stages as well. Everything is there for a reason and that reason is for you to plan your assault and deal with the robots as quickly as possible.
The star system does create a problem however, as you are required to collect a certain amount before taking on each areas boss. In our view the requirement is set a touch too high and we can see players hitting a complete dead end at times. In a game all about speed and momentum the need to better a high score and get higher amounts of stars is high enough without the enforced star barrier at the end of each level. It’s about the only misstep in what is a compact and focused game.
The boss fights themselves have the same ten second time limit and you also have your shurikens removed. They prove to be good fun and not a massive stumbling block to progression. They are simply designed as a different sort of puzzle to work out and work well to break up the regular levels.
Overall, 10 Second Ninja is a strong debut for the developer. There’s a hints of Kung Fu Rabbit and N+ (among other things), but the game also has its own distinct personality. It’s a fast, slick and fun game and one that will provide bite sized chunks of twitch gameplay. It achieves pretty much everything it sets out to and is certainly a game that we’ll come back to again and again.
Overall 8/10

This ain't a spectacular PC port I found; it's locked at 30 frames unless modded, moving the camera with a mouse is a bit of a pain, and some bugs exist. Sometimes the sound would get too high or too low, some graphics may not work as they're supposed to (like shadows not appearing as they should, night time suddenly getting brighter or darker), and a few missions may get bugged to the point where you can't complete it without maybe trying again.
Like in GTA: Vice City and San Andreas the storyline is about the protag's rise to power and some person betraying or using them. It's interesting to say the least if the storytelling I think isn't the best.
Just like most of 'em GTA games it's sandboxy, only the world you get to walk in is enclosed to just a small town with a relatively fancy school. Your weapons are only juvenile contraptions, you can't use general automobiles, and you've only got hand-to-hand combat to rely on for messing with other kids and maybe adults since a good majority of the weapons you get are mainly for screwing around with others. General stereotypical bully stuff.
The town likes to look populated by having NPCs walk around but my problem with that is that there isn't much variety in NPCs at all from the adults to the students, there's a real good chance that every NPC will be familiar very shortly.
You've got a "trouble meter" on you which works a bit like GTA's wanted star system only it goes down a alot faster here but at the same time is incredibly easy to raise as well since you can get in trouble without even knowing at times. Because you're 15 you can get chased by any authority figure easily for not attending classes when you should be, not following dress codes on school grounds, breaking curfew, etc. etc.
The dress code deal kind of ruins the fun a bit for wearing what you want. Because most story missions are in school you can't just simply wear whatever and not get in a bit of trouble needing you to run from authority for a short while each time they spot you.
Practically all the classes you attend are just minigames and you pass a subject by attending and passing the class for the day (beating its minigame). You're supposed to attend classes twice a day (or don't) and I don't know if there's an actual schedule for what class you attend next as you're just to follow the icon on the minimap when class starts and there's a small variety of what you attend.
I think there's supposed to be a focus on running around and screwing around in the world but I honestly couldn't find much entertainment in that so I just stuck with doing story missions and going to classes when prompted. There are some collectibles and small jobs you can do for extra money and other nifty things but I didn't see much needed use for what I earn aside from learning new combos after easily collecting a very small number of items for someone.
The game ain't too bad but it seriously could have been a lot better.

In my opinion the best 4x game since GalCiv II.
There are 10 factions with unique techs, shipdesign and raceutilities (like cloning, locust swarm,...) in the main game and one more in the DLC. Each of them plays different and uses a very balanced concept of fighting for their goals. Like in common 4x games there are warlike, economic, diplomatic and scientific races which all try to reach their prefered kind of victory condition. But here all of them are also able to defend themself which increases the difficulty of the game even against peaceful neighbours.
The game itself plays like the most known 4x games where you have to colonise planets, build lot of improvements on your systems and finally create a fleet to defend your worlds. Each part of this is well balanced and keeps interesting even in late game. The Heroes which improve your fleets or systems with unique boni increase the impact of your choices and add an important and interesting point while playing.
The shipbattles are a little bit more tricky then in older 4x games because it isn't all about numbers. The battle runs in timebased turns where you could give a main order to your ships (like focus first ship, spread fire ect.) but you do not directly controll your ships (like you did in Armada2526). The fight will be simulated with your orders. The battle card system (tactical options for each turn like sabotage, weapon overload) are hard to understand during the first game but after some time you learn what is important in which turn.
The biggest advantage of Endless Space is the battle grafic which is amazing and unchallenged in classic 4x games. The overview grafic is also absolutly okay and after some time even the interface that may be confusing during the first turns becomes absolutly useful. The soundtracks fits well in a spacegame and give you the right feeling while playing.
People who like 4x games and could handle to lose against an AI should buy this really amazing game. And yes, the AI is really hard and you will need some time to handle the game even on easy or normal. But for patient players that take the time to learn it will be a game for many, many hours.

I've played this game a couple hundred hours since it was in beta.  I'm glad this is on Steam now because I've had problems with the standalone client when trying to move between hard drives or updating operating system.
I would describe it like a cross between an FPS and tank battle sims.  You can shoot and destroy individual components on enemy mechs which destroys any weapons or loadout items stored in them. There are a few things you can buy which give advantage like special consumables or specific mechs which let you earn currency faster (but they mostly aren't top tier mechs), but honestly it doesn't make enough of a difference to detract from gameplay and doing well without them is no issue if you have a good loadout
Heavy mechs have the best balance of firepower and mobility and are the most popular.  Assault mechs have the most firepower and armor but have awful mobility. For new players medium mechs might be best to get used to the controls (my personal fav mech is a specific medium mech with a ton of hardpoints that makes it like a glass cannon). Light mechs are the hardest to use but can be gamechanging in the hands of a veteran for component sniping, taking down damaged or overextended mechs and point capturing.
Different weapons include hitscan lasers of various range and type, ballistic cannons, railguns for sniping, close and long range missiles, electronic warfare.
If you're new google the smurfy mechlab to play test loadouts and look up Meta Mechs for mech tier lists and some good loadouts to get you started. Also look up theB33f on youtube for some funny MWO vids

Got this badboy for a day and my first impressions are good. You will have to get used to the controller. It feels "weird" at first.
The Good:
* Cutomization, You can basically do anything you want with the controller. (Settings wise)
* Triggers are nice and linear with a crisp "click" at the end.
* Both touchpads work flawlessly, definately prefer them over regular analog sticks in most games. Default settings are terrible though.
* Downloading user created configs is simple. Simply browse them click "A" to import them and its done.
* All buttons on the controller give nice feedback and are not mushy
The Bad:
* Glossy plastic in some places. Really Valve?!
* Controller "feels" kind cheap.
* Buttons "may" be too low for ppl with short thumbs. (A friend of mine has VERY short thumbs and he was complaining about the buttons)
* If you have huge hands this controller will be too small for you (Just like the xbox and ps4 controller)
* I personally don't like to use the right trackpad as a "analog stick" I prefer to set it to "mouse" because I feel that I'm more "accurate". The default state isn't perfect, but I'm sure that can be dealt with by tweaking the settings

The focus on survival of your ships and their commanders (and their crew of course... though many will be lost on regular expeditions after the first few ingame weeks. lol), make this one feel something along the line of Star Trek meets X-Com.
Even this early on it's a good time. Personally it seem very stable for me (never crashed), nor did I encounter any game ending bugs. Worth noting as well that it also seems to be quite well balanced as far as difficulty is concerned.
I am looking forward to see this game evolve as it develops (hopefully), but it's already very much worth the purchase fee.

I used to be pretty good at the original game back in the day
At the time it was rather unique, a bit of a twist of Space Invaders with some ricocheting 'bubble' madness that offered a suprisingly good challenge. My friends and I sunk a lot of fun-filled hours into it on my Amiga 500
. Fast forward almost 30 years
the latest incarnation,
has set my nostalgia meter running.
Core mechanics remain essentially the same as they were, but there are a few more modes, ball effects, weapons & boss fights to spice things up.
It does 'kinda' feel as I remember. Sound effects, music & graphics do work well to rekindle that retro feeling & it still has that balancing act between firing your grapple or dodging, & the timing & calculating ahead to pop the bouncing bubbles as efficiently
as you can. A good test of your coordination skills. I can't say it's as engaging or replayable as my childhood remembers though, but there is enough content for a few good hours or more to clock the Tour mode, plus a bit more with multiplayer, Score & Panic modes.
Tour mode becomes very challenging
in later levels, often pushing you to the last second even after multiple attempts, but my favorite mode would have to be the Panic mode. It cuts out all the
story BS & gets you straight into the action in increasingly difficult challenges. The 99 levels are structured in waves, providing an almost constant stream of attack balls to pop.
It gets hard!
To add to the
panic, this mode also gets increasingly faster. This works really well, making the game play more fluid & frantic!
Score mode is locked behind Tour mode completion, but offers the added hardcore challenge of only three lives. I've try tried to find a multiplayer game on several occasions but have not been success to date. It can be played with friends in local coop though if you want to kick it old school
.
So to answer the question, did
burst my nostalgia bubble?
It strikes the delicate balance of being close enough to the original concept to be familiar, but also fresh enough bringing a new lick of paint, modes & other enhancements to the table. A quality remake that doesn't compromise the Pang legacy.

Don't let the 'bullet hell' tag scare you off, this game is nowhere near as difficult as a CAVE game, even on its harder difficulties. However, this game does require memorization of patterns so if you don't like that sort of thing this game is probably not the game for you.
In my experiance the game sort of cycles between gathering tons of items and fighting bosses. The item collection feels sort-of like an old collectathon game in that there are quite a few items in the game to collect, most of which are hidden or have some small challenge you have to beat to get them. The bosses are the centerpieces of the game that break up item collection, they attack with danmaku-esqe patterns that are generally very pretty. Your combat abilities seem to fall into three categories:
1) CQC with the hammer, which almost always resolves into doing the same few combos
2) ranged fighting with Ribbon which gives you a number of unique shot types to work with and is usually more fun than CQC
3) bomb-type attacks in the form of the amulet and super carrot (amulet being a defensive bomb with high invincibility but low damage, super carrot being an offensive bomb with short invincibility but high damage)
Overall I think the gameplay is quite fun.
There are also extra modes like speedrun mode and boss rush (and extra boss rushes with NPC characters in the DLC) which are exactly what you would expect. Also about a billion achievements ranging from boss rush to speedrun to low item% run to sequence breaking.
The game has been known to lag and crash for seemingly no reason sometimes on some computers, so that is something you should probably take into account if you are playing on a toaster.

The game's fun hi concept - combine Metroidvania style exploration with Touhou style bullet hell shooting - would alone make Rabi-Ribi worthy of a look.  But unlike many games that rely on a novel hook to obscure shortcomings in the implementation, every aspect of this game has a polish usually only lavished on sequels.  From the level design, to the play control, to the progression of new ability acquisition, everything here is positively brimming with an attention to detail that is always focused on the player's enjoyment.
The only reasons not to be in love with this game are purely matters of subjective taste.  The presentation is positively saturated in an aesthetic that is so unironically cute and pleasant that it may come off as quite bland to some.  It's a little similar to the flavor of many Nintendo games in this way, albeit with a more otaku-centric slant.  But, like Nintendo games, this intentionally harmless aesthetic serves to prevent stylistic elements from distracting from the excellent gameplay on display.
Best metroidvania on Steam!

The game itself is absolutely amazing. Out of all the Storm games this one is probably my favorite. I'm glad they did away with choosing between having Ult, Awakening, and Sealing from Revolution. Having everything all together plus the new linked secret techniques is very nice compared to Revolutions system of just picking the teams that link up and your ult is changed to their combo. This way you don't see it often but, when you do it is spectacular.
I haven't gotten that far into the game yet but, all the modes I have played are enjoyable. Especially the main combat, they kept everything that was good with Revolutions system and added on to it. Now as for the horde battles, it could do with some better camera mechanics or at the very least a lock on system. Other than this, the rail running system they have is fun and the giant battles are impressively done if a little slow but, it's giant monsters/susanoos/etc. so what can you expect.
Now on to technical issues with the game.
- As others stated it is locked at 30fps. (Which isn't a bad thing at all.)
- As it is, a new release, there are bound to be problems.
- The only issue I have run into that I could not fix was that some voice audio, from the story cutscenes from what I've seen, would only play through the left speaker.
Which honestly wasn't a problem to me. Other than that it works and plays like a charm.
I run a very high-end system though so for those that have the option, try playing it on console if your afraid your computer can't run it.
