It's ok... it's just one of those single player shooters that you play once or a couple of times, and then forget about until the rest of time.
Combat is simple yet it looks okay. Good variety of guns and they each have their own addons and upgrades. While it's possible to play the entire game using only one weapon, there is an ammo limit that does make you switch. However there is a simple way to work around that.
Movement in this game is so slow and is actually a downgrade from Doom 1 & 2. It's so generic that it just becomes a chore to get from objective 1 to objective 2. Play for maybe 30 minutes and you'll notice a pattern that the game follows that even a bacteria could figure it out. You guessed it: Enter room, fight a bunch of monsters, leave and enter different room, fight a bunch of monsters, rinse and repeat.
The real reason why this game won't be remembered or respected as Doom 1 & 2 is because it doesn't have any modding... and no, Snapmap doesn't count. You're really limited to what you can do in Snapmap that it's just a gimmick that they added to create the illusion of modding. Over 20 years later and people still make mods for Doom 1 & 2 and will probably still continue to do so; while Doom 2016 will just be like that one cool movie you watched years ago and don't really care much to watch again.
Sure the game looks fantastic but unlike what a lot of dinguses out there in the world think, graphics aren't what makes a game "good".

A turn-based space 4x strategy game set on a grand scale of galactic proportions. Intended to be more of a sandbox start where the stage is set with back-story, races and factions, but it is up to you to define the story after that. While lacking some of the charm and character of a game like Civilization 5, where the characters were very immersive and the feeling of writing history compelled you on. Endless Space, while comparable to Civ 5 and other space strategy games, is not trying to be a copy but a beast of its own. The game also runs fairly well on machines built from crumpets, like mine, 100% 7 year old genuine golden machine right here.
The games strength lies in the screen you will be spending a lot of time with, getting to know, making tea for and so on; the galaxy view, also FIDS is a guy you will have to get friendly with, get to know FIDS real well – FIDS stands for Food, Industry, Dust and Science; optimizing these will be important. The interface on the default view and the leaves that stemming from the branches connected to the galaxy interface are simple and relatively easy to navigate; the economy is rather solid, with many resources to monopolize and exploit, – my favourites being Bluecap Mold and Hydromiel - with resources set on low it can create some interesting situations. Managing and growing your empire is can be done easily, but to keep an empire at its optimal level some loving care to keep it in check and sound engineering ideas  are required to achieve a lovely, green and flowering empire. You can also zoom in and out of the galaxy view and into systems which you will find at helpful and the planets vivid colours pleasing to the eye.
Hero’s can be important to your strategy too due to their boosting abilities and a variety of roles they can fill either in administration or fleet command, however they are not essential pieces to make keep your empire spinning – just be sure to pick them up and assign them to tasks if you can.
Expansion is a very good thing and is a big part of the games early stage. Systems contain planets usually of varying tiers with nice planets being tier one and smelly gas planets + floating rocks being the highest tier, needless to say tier ones are better. You should probably colonise lots of systems as quickly as possible... but not too many at a pace your empire cannot keep up with... that could end very badly and happiness will snowball out of control very quickly; also keep an eye on the happiness of the populous, try to avoid planets with really bad happiness modifiers early on unless you have a good reason to colonise that system – such as a good happiness modifiers outweighing the bad one or a burning desire for that system. Initially colonised systems become outposts and over time will become colonies, colonies are better in many ways, for one they have an influence ring which is good for you but bad for your enemies systems if it swallows it whole; during their outpost state they can still be attacked without war being declared so you might want to defend them from the unforgiving galaxy until they mature. Also be sure to have each system doing something, even if it’s just Industry to Dust conversion, wasted turns don’t come back.
Research, is a bit like a big expanding circle, you can plough through in one direction if you wanted to but before long you will have to turn back and follow up the other branches for important and relevant technologies; in game terms, N-Way Fusion Plants & Isolation Shields in the Applied Sciences tree is important early on while Applied Casmir Affect in the Exploration & Expansion tree is very good for early expansion, there are techs in the Diplomacy & Trading tree that is important to happiness and keeping yourself protected is always imperative to your survival so the Galactic Warfare tree will be visited regularly.
The somewhat unusual combat system has a somewhat offhanded approach to it. The cinematic battle sequences while pretty and enjoyable to watch lacks some of the interactivity people are used to, where normally you needed to rely on positioning and particular manoeuvres in battle; however instead you rely more on the way you have set up your fleet beforehand which is assisted by a cards which designate actions your fleet can perform, whether or not a heroic Admiral is in the fleet and fleet targeting options during the battle. These battles can be auto-resolved if you wish; you can also invade systems with a number of methods such as a general siege, bombing or sending in the troops – of course you can turn to place to ashes after if you wanted to. The battles are not grand and truly epic but are enjoyable and perform their role rather well. Ships are arranged into fleets, which can be managed from the fleet tab on the galaxy screen, are custom built from hull designs, while the general blueprints are not yours to play with, the toys you attach to it are. Good ship design is essential to defend yourself from hungry Cravers or invade some helpless Sophons on an isolated system; while some understanding of the combat system and understanding how to achieve your design goal is crucial for success, designing the ships in question is quite easy once you know where to find shipyard is.
Amplitude while being a small - French – studio, have put a lot of love into its first game, they have also allowed the community to get involved in a number of occasions to help make decisions for the future of the game through the Games2Gether system and forums and are updating the game regularly with content and fixes. Visit the Amplitude forums if you have any questions about Endless Space; discuss the game, query problems or related waffles on your mind. You can also check out their other upcoming* games Endless legend – another strategy game - and Dungeons of The Endless – a rouge-like-dungeon-delving game – if they snatch your interest and run of with it. So, lead your empire to victory in the deep darkness of space, through the vibrant jungles, across desolate barren landscapes, scorching hot sand dunes and towering metropolises. Explore, Expand, Exploit, Exterminate my good friend.

How To Enjoy This Game:
See game for the first time, dismiss it as garbage.
See game for the second time by showing it to a friend, friend laughs it off.
Go look at game again because you get really bored one day.
Go back to the page again and actually watch the video on the store page.
Fully realize just how sub-par the game is.
Return to store page to read reviews.
Continue returning to store page because you now secretly want to see if the reviews are right.
Keep going back to look at the video and screenshots, debating whether or not you should buy it.
Convince yourself that this is quite literally the worst game ever created and that you will contract real world diseases by playing it.
Decide It can't actually be THAT bad.
Finally buy it.
Install it.
Boot it up.
Realize the soundtrack is pretty good.
Realize people weren't lying about the art style.
Cringe a little at some of the writing.
Keep playing.
Realize that there's probably worse games out there.
Realize that you didn't contract any real world diseases.
Go back to play it at two in the morning after all of your friends go to sleep.
Finally come to terms with the fact that you WANT to finish the game.
You like it.
You don't know why.
You just do.
TL;DR
Convince yourself that this game will cause you physical harm with how bad it is, and when you get something better than that you will be satisfied. Applies to any game, really.

I absolutely love this game, is the best Dead Rising I've played so far, the other titles have their own charm, but this one is just better in every way to my eyes. Are you in for some outstanding and ridiculous combo weapons? Hell, this game has a lot of them and they are all super fun to use. Survivors no longer have to be escorted to any safe house, they all help you instead (and don't worry, A.I isn't as broken as previous titles). Don't wanna be followed by them? no problem, there is a bunch of safe houses around Los Perdidos for you to either drop them or switch to other better survivors you rescued.
The city you play in has a pretty decent size for you to explore and have fun, as most ranged weapons you find and make require some space to be useful, melee weapons on the other hand are very fun to use when in close range, my favorite combo weapon has to be the "Ultimate Shout" as it clears a huge area of zombies in a single shout.
Story in this game is actually pretty good in my opinion, better than the previous titles? I wouldn't compare them, but it does have those twists you get to see in the previous stories, enough to make you feel like you are playing a Dead Rising game. Voice acting, specifically in terms of expression, is nicely well done, a nice improvement from the previous games, facial expressions in this one adds a lot too along with the very nice graphics it has.
If you liked the previous Dead Rising games then there is no doubt you'll like this one as well, and I believe you would still like it even if you are completely new to the series, you'll spend a decent amount of time on this if you play the main campaign and the DLC short campaigns that come with it, you'll spend even more time if you try to complete collectables and/or do every side quest like I do.
Dead Rising 3 is 70% off by the time I'm typing this review, you should definitely consider giving it a try.

This ain't a spectacular PC port I found; it's locked at 30 frames unless modded, moving the camera with a mouse is a bit of a pain, and some bugs exist. Sometimes the sound would get too high or too low, some graphics may not work as they're supposed to (like shadows not appearing as they should, night time suddenly getting brighter or darker), and a few missions may get bugged to the point where you can't complete it without maybe trying again.
Like in GTA: Vice City and San Andreas the storyline is about the protag's rise to power and some person betraying or using them. It's interesting to say the least if the storytelling I think isn't the best.
Just like most of 'em GTA games it's sandboxy, only the world you get to walk in is enclosed to just a small town with a relatively fancy school. Your weapons are only juvenile contraptions, you can't use general automobiles, and you've only got hand-to-hand combat to rely on for messing with other kids and maybe adults since a good majority of the weapons you get are mainly for screwing around with others. General stereotypical bully stuff.
The town likes to look populated by having NPCs walk around but my problem with that is that there isn't much variety in NPCs at all from the adults to the students, there's a real good chance that every NPC will be familiar very shortly.
You've got a "trouble meter" on you which works a bit like GTA's wanted star system only it goes down a alot faster here but at the same time is incredibly easy to raise as well since you can get in trouble without even knowing at times. Because you're 15 you can get chased by any authority figure easily for not attending classes when you should be, not following dress codes on school grounds, breaking curfew, etc. etc.
The dress code deal kind of ruins the fun a bit for wearing what you want. Because most story missions are in school you can't just simply wear whatever and not get in a bit of trouble needing you to run from authority for a short while each time they spot you.
Practically all the classes you attend are just minigames and you pass a subject by attending and passing the class for the day (beating its minigame). You're supposed to attend classes twice a day (or don't) and I don't know if there's an actual schedule for what class you attend next as you're just to follow the icon on the minimap when class starts and there's a small variety of what you attend.
I think there's supposed to be a focus on running around and screwing around in the world but I honestly couldn't find much entertainment in that so I just stuck with doing story missions and going to classes when prompted. There are some collectibles and small jobs you can do for extra money and other nifty things but I didn't see much needed use for what I earn aside from learning new combos after easily collecting a very small number of items for someone.
The game ain't too bad but it seriously could have been a lot better.

I do recommend this game heavily - VERY heavily.
HOWEVER, I do believe that unless you are an avid fan of the Naruto franchise, or REALLY like the Ultimate Ninja games, you should DEFINITELY wait on buying this one until it's patched up a bit and whatnot.
And here's why:
The game suffers from poor optimization in the absolute weirdest of ways. The actual gameplay runs PERFECTLY for me (I'm running it with 16gb RAM, i7, GTX 980 Ti) on the highest settings and the game is actually fairly pretty. However, the menu interfaces (and, to a lesser extent, most of the on-screen QTE prompts) lag significantly, and can often just not receive the button command the first time you push it, causing a lot of frustrated button bashing. Luckily enough, this isn't a very big problem with the QTEs as you can fail any of them and not be penalized, and the threshold to unlock secret events is so low that an inebriated sloth can manage it, even with these issues.
Other than that though?
This baby's a treat.
The roster is HUGE. Sure, of the 100ish characters playable from the start (plus a few extras unlocked later in the game and, for those who preordered, a couple MORE from Naruto: The Last), about 8-12 are Naruto and Sasuke variants. If each of these characters (Which then have their own occasional subvariants that can be accessed as skinswaps, though these don't count towards the character count) seem like clones, however, you're sorely mistaken. The only reason they're split is because 1) it'd be hell to have to dig through 40 Naruto skins/move-variants and 2) each of them has their own specific movesets, from basic attacks to special jutsu and awakenings. This probably made it easier to code them as different characters.
The combat feels the most fun and balanced it's ever been (There are exceptions but really, get over it if you think Part 1 Sasuke should be able to fight Sage of The Six Paths Madaara without a challenge), and mechanics like a Burst-system as a counter to being pinned into a combo or being knocked by a chakra-dash, the ability to switch player-character in Team Battles at will, and vastly varied movesets and skills allows each fight to be fun, refreshing, and just new enough to stave off monotany.
The Story mode ditches the Adventure Mode aspects of past games' campaigns, instead focusing on the plot from where Naruto and Obito begin to fight/Where Sasuke revives Orochimaru and the Hokage, with interspersed sidestories and flashbacks where appropriate, all the way to the very end. This is done via a few types of battles, punctuated with cutscenes. The battles are mostly Free Battles, which is just a simple one-round fight where you and your opponent have the normal 2 health bars. After this is Boss Battles, which are essentially Free Battles where the enemy has multiple health bars, and may have special attacks. Then there's larger scale battles where you freely move, and you try to kill as many enemies as possible in a big rumble (these are quite rare), and Dramatic Battles, which are typically just Boss Battles but with the QTE-cutscene portions as well. This sounds dull, however many of the more iconic and exciting battles have special conditions, or are recreated as excitingly as possible, including a giant game of Kid Icarus using the Uchiha power of the Susanoo, and a smackdown battle royale between the 10 tails and the giant summons of Saskue, Naruto, and Sakura.
Also included is Adventure Mode, which is a fun little extra side diversion that takes place after the events of the main story. I honestly haven't delved further than a few minutes into this, but it immediately brought back Storm 2/Storm 3 memories, which was quite nice.
All in all, a must have for any fan of the franchise or the line of games, but I STRONGLY suggest waiting for it if you're a bit more casually inclined.

Doom 2016 is the Dark Souls of Hell Based Shooters That Take Place on Mars.
The reason Doom 2016 is similar to Dark Souls is the difficulty that it may present and the disturbing imagery.
In Doom 2016 you take control of the iconic Doomguy donning his new and improved Praetor Suit. The Praetor Suit gives multiple abilities including a double jump and the ability to
. Without this vital suit your character is just a man that got excavated from the depths of hell on a bloody quest for revenge.
On your adventure you have many tools in your arsenal from the amazing rocket launcher to the iconic Doom II double-barrel shotgun. Yet the main gimmick to this entry in the series is the glory kill, which can be used to kill an enemy with low health as well as gaining health yourself. This feature promotes fighting fiercly and staying near your enemies instead of hiding behind cover. The glory kill is also used as a mechanic for platforming. If you are around 10 feet away from your enemie and perform a glory kill it will proppel you to the enemie. There is a moment in the campain in which there is a jump you cannot clearalone  but there is a stationary Imp on the other side. So you shoot the Imp until the glory kill is available, double jump across, and then try to glory kill the Imp. It is rarely used in a sense like that in the game but presents many ways you can you the mechanics in the game to your benefit.
It is a very fun Action FPS that really makes you remember the original Doom style where you just run around and Rip And Tear.
I give Doom 2016 a Dark Souls II/Souls-Like Games. I would suggest waiting for a sale, I would say that it is not worth the $30 price tag but if you can get it for $20 or less it should be on your watch list.
Heartbreaking that Eric Harris and Dylan Klebold did not survive the attack to enjoy this latest Doom.

DOOM has been one of the best video games I’ve played this year.
The gameplay definitely reminds me of the original doom while giving a new spin on the 1993 release with a new modern AAA game feel, the enemies are crazy fast-paced while you are more of a normal speed.
The reward and leveling system is great and the difficulty isn’t too hard but still challenging and fun, The Secrets and Mission Challenges are also amazing and give the game a nice replayability, with the option to replay any single mission once you have completed the game.
The graphics are wonderful but the game is definitely not too graphically intense making most machines easily able to run it. As I stated before you are slower than in the original doom but the gameplay and movement is still a crazy action-packed masterpiece where you are constantly running and gunning at tons of different types of demons.
The Multiplayer, on the other hand, is not necessarily bad but is definitely nothing special and is quite forgettable, with lots of other games releasing with great multiplayer these days I definitely don’t think DOOM’s stands out in any way.
In conclusion, the single-player campaign is lovely and the main reason you should buy this game. The multiplayer is not as bad as many people claim it to be, but nothing to ride home about. I would definitely recommend DOOM to anyone I know, especially considering its frequent 50% off sales.

Before playing this game I questioned how well you could merge two completely different genres, a Metroidvania and a Bullet Hell. The answer I got blew me away, the boss battles are some of the best I've ever seen in the Metroidvania genre. I hold both Metroid and Castlevania to high acclaim but if there was one compliant I had for both of these series it would be that the bosses are too easy, with this game each boss is a challenge that will have you on edge throughout the battle.
It starts off quite easy but the difficulty ramps up as you progress, the bosses present a fair challenge should you not be trigger happy and analyse their attack patterns (though for one or two of them I think they could have telegraphed their attacks better). The game also starts off with a basic move set but increases to have such variety that is rarely seen in the genre, the combos you can perform in battle are so satisfying.
Though you may look at the price and think its a little expensive for a game in this genre but believe me its well worth the price, even without being in a sale. It could take you close to 20 hours to beat it but it comes with a wealth of content that there's still plenty to do after you beat it. That's also not going into the 100+ achievements this game has, so it has plenty of replayability to it. A nice little bonus is the short manga that you can read in the game that pokes fun at the game and its characters.
If you're put off by the 'lewd' art then don't worry, there isn't much sexual content in this game. If a scene does feature this it's more for comedy than for eroticism. It's a beautiful game with an equally brilliant soundtrack, I honestly recommend buying the artbook and soundtrack.
This game has garnered high praise and reviews for a reason, well worth checking out for anyone looking to buy a 2D platformer on steam.

Adventure Capitalist is a game all about Capitalism. (And Making loads of money)
Completing this game without cheating is almost imposible. Is there even an end to this game! I don't know. Eventually, you start to get so much money that it becomes pointless because no matter how much money you have, you will always need more to progress, going as far to the moon and mars just to have more. I believe that this game is more simbolic rather than just a grind game. I believe this game perfectly represents the evils of capitalism. There is no end to the game because, no matter how much money you have, you will ALWAYS need more.
Caring on this subject, you also get angel investors in the game. They help you earn more money at the cost of a reset. Later on, however, you can SACRIFICE your angels to boost your profits! I dunno about you, but that sounds a lot like selling your soul to the devil for wealth. It's a stretch, but I think this is true and makes complete sense.
I believe reviewing the game in this way shines a bright light on this otherwise boring, redundant game. Which again, could represent what capitalism is like, boring and redundant. If I were to review this game purly on the core game mechanics, this game would have a TERRIBLE rating! But, I wanted to search deeper to see if this game really held any merit at all other than a grind game. And with this being said, I believe this game is not terrible, but also not super fun to play. (Unless you hack the game) I would definetly recommend this game to a friend, and I would also want to look deeper into this game like I did while typing this review to really see this games true merit.

Review of Endless Space
Pros:
-Relatively easy to learn compared to other 4X space games (i.e. stream-lined mechanics); tutorial itself is weak though so learning with friends help a lot
-Great visuals
-Good game length for 4X space game (ranges from 1 to 4 hours, depending on number of players, map size, and aggression of each player)
-Diverse number of races and makes good use of the hero system
-Gameplay itself is pretty good in terms of economy, expansion, and various aspects of "empire building"
Cons:
-Mediocre combat system; uses a combat card system, pretty hands-off but it's better than full auto-resolve or micro-managing every battle
-Diplomacy system is rather simple
-Mediocre AI (if you only play single player, then you'll have much less enjoyment than if you play with your friends)
-Increasing difficulty of AI just gives them "cheat" advantages
-Some bugs that cause game crashes; however, it is mitigated by auto-saves so this isn't too bad
-Other misc bugs can cause the need for loading of your auto-save
Overall 7.5/10. Would give it an 8.5 if it didn't have those annoying bugs and better AI. Recommend playing if you have friends that also enjoy 4X space games.

Okay, I never give negative reviews, and I like this game, but there are so many issues with it that the bad outweighs the good.
Here we go:
1. The game doesn't recognise controllers on many PCs. The devs are aware of this and are working on a fix, but to release a game based on twitch reflexes like this and have the controller support that bugged is a complete mistake on their part.
2. The game eats memory like I eat Chinese food at a buffet. Why is a game that looks like a Flash game from 2005 using 400MB of RAM? Why does it stutter and lag on my computer? My computer can run Super Meatboy just fine, but this game has to be dropped to the lowest resolution in windowed mode to run smoothly. On better computers, this is probably not an issue, but a game like this should be able to run well on a computer from 4 years ago - heck, it should be able to run well on a computer from 10 years ago.
3. This game is not worth 7.99€. The amount of levels is staggeringly low. I've played the game for 2 hours and am almost at 100% on all the levels except the locked bonus stage. Either the devs thought people would struggle more to get through stages that it would take longer, or they honestly thought the game has enough content to justify 7.99€. It does not.
I get that the devs are independant, probably don't have a lot of money, and are trying to make some money to work on bigger projects, I totally understand and respect that, but as a consumer, 7.99€ is not a price I would pay for a game this short with so many problems. The devs say they're trying to fix things, and if the issues go away I will gladly change the review to positive (even despite the shortness), but until then, I'd have to advise people to not buy this game.

Is it perfect? No. Has it provided me with hours of mech stomping fun? Yes! I have been playing this game since it came out of beta a couple years ago and am still enjoying it...more now actually than I have in the past as PGI has made some good strides recently.
At it's heart, MWO is a mech shooter that does a good job being a fun game to stomp around in Battletech IP mechs. They have done a good job making the core game fun to play. There is a huge variety of mechs and weapons to choose from, and they have been making efforts in recent months to better balance mechs so that less mechs are total trash and less mechs are just clearly OP.
I started playing about the time that the game came out of beta, and there have certainly been a lot of ups and downs. But recently, PGI has done a good job making the game more balanced, adding in features, and generally just improving the game and moving it forward. Granted, the pace of change is pretty slow, but it being a niche free-to-play game, that is understandable.
The Faction Play still needs a lot of help, as it is very much a 12-man group seal clubbing space. If on the off chance you get to play in a random group vs. another random group though it can be pretty fun and fairly even. In general I would stay away from this mode though until they fix that.
Playing in the solo queue, and even sometimes in the group queue now can be fun and result in close games, so the new matchmaker they have put in seems to be doing a decent job balancing out matches.
Recently, PGI has held frequent in game events, which has helped people that are free to play acquire mechs, in game money (c-bills), and real world funded money (MC), in a fun (and faster) way. I think this is good for the overall health of the game as it helps new players also get into the game more easily. In game earnings have also been recently bumped to help new players out. There is a pretty big learning curve though, so you will definitely need to invest time to learn the game before you start seeing yourself be effective in games.
The game is definitely NOT pay-to-win, but rather more a pay-for-early-access to new mechs / pay-for-cosmetics / pay-for-less-grind model, which is a good thing. All of the top tier mechs can be obtained without spending a penny, but be prepared to then invest significant time playing and grinding out c-bills. I choose to buy the mech packs that I like because it supports the game I enjoy, and to be honest is a fairly good deal considering everything you get and the loyalty rewards PGI has also been handing out each year.
Outside of PVP arena type matches, there is not much of a persistent world to care much about (star map with some names and factions claiming them, but no real impact), so this is something they really should focus on next, in addition to a coop PVE mode for folks that enjoy those kind of missions. There's certainly more potential out there that hasn't been harnessed yet for this game and the IP in general.
Overall, I would definitely recommend that people try this game if you like mech games and slower paced FPS games. It is probably will not appeal to more twitchy fps gamers though. But the Rainbow Six type of slower gameplay crowd may find it enjoyable, and the people that like driving big stompy robots may also enjoy this game. But it's free, download it and give it a try and see if you like it.

I've been a huge Battletech / Mechwarrior fan since I was a youngster in the mid 90's.  Played the snot out of MW2 especially.  The game is a hoot to play, with an emphasis on simulation (far more than FPS) and teamwork.
Be prepared for a large learning curve. And be prepared to spend a couple weeks playing to actually be able to fluidly execute what you've learned. But if you're like me, that was half the reason the game sounded interesting. I got hooked because I was finally able to play an old gem from the past with others who have shared the same passion for it (Which is kind of rare. I still only know 1 other person in my life that knows what Mechwarrior is. Which is sad)
I've played for about 4 months now or so, and there were quite the debacles in years past regarding development that I was lucky enough to miss. But since then as other reviews have stated, lots of changes have been taking place, and the community is very active and growing
I have yet to spend any money, but I also like the feeling knowing I earned my mechs. I had to fight for them. Some people would prefer to buy them, and thats okay. Skill and Teamwork is what's important here.  My Thunderbolts and Watchful Cicadas have put the, as some would say "OP Timberwolves" in the ground where the clanners belongs.
Is it perfect? No. But damnit, its fun to play. No other game quite like it, and certainly no other Mechwarrior at this day and age, and thats just fine - Because I quite like this one actually.
NEWBIE TIP:  Dont spend any of your C-bills from your cadet bonus until you feel very comfortable knowing what play style you want.  2 youtube channels to investigate for tips: Kanajashi, Nogutsnogalaxy
Also scope out
to see what the latest builds, trends, and guides are. Updated damn near weekly.

What makes the PC different from Consoles is adaptability and openness.  As more games have been conceived on console first, many developers have been sub-contracting out the PC port.  Sadly, the devs sub-contracted have often thought half-heartedly about how to manage the result, and there is not much in the way of analog hardware for the PC.
The Steam controller manages brilliantly to capture PC adaptability, by allowing the each input group to be considered individually, as emulating a controller, a mouse, or a keyboard, or even combinations thereof, like A for mouse click, X and Y for gamepad buttons, and B for the F key.  It's framework is used my me in less than 10% of my games, in most games I use it as a gamepad or I put it aside, but in games like Black Desert Online, GTA V, Star Trek Online, Civilization, and also some japanese adventure games, controlling VLC, using Second Life and GIMP (though not accurately), this controller's changing layout and Action Sets mean I can have it do just what I want, when I want it.
There are gamers that have made use of the gyro for general aiming, strapping it to their head for turning and looking up and down, and a second controller for actual gameplay.  There are people who are taking it apart to use in other form factors, like (bulky) wiimotes and mouse units.  This controller is a very useful piece of gear, and works well with my reprogrammable Razer Synapse gear, a keyboard and a 16-button mouse.
Cons: don't know about longevity yet, but I'mma use it till it breaks, and it's lasted longer so far than some Logitech gear of the same cost.  Also, having to be in Big Picture mode to change the config is annoying, but part of the concept I guess.

The smallest baloons are still too big which hinders small manouvers and that "saved by hairlenght" factor. Although there are some good levels, the level design might be better. Definitely overrated, but still not bad. It's enjoyable, strengths would be its simplicity is easy to pick up and play, weaknesses would be the lack of real depth to the gameplay makes it feel repetitive over time. You might love the gameplay enough to warrant a purchase but I would wait for a sale.
The strengths of the game is the graphics, the violence, and the music. The game's soundtrack is really unique, not many matches its style. The graphics is really well done as well, very easy on the eyes and even the up close and personal attacks feel rewarding. The violence the game has makes you feel like you're in a metal music montage, some melee attacks consisting of you just smashing the skull of a demon with a stomp. It's satisfying and the learning curve is very accessible.
The weaknesses is replayability and content. The replay value, as you will see from about two thirds of the reviews here, is you will get about twenty to thirty hours out of this game. This is good amount of hours, but I feel simple fixes could make it even longer. It is a matter of preference, but I don't like personally mechanics like the chainsaw giving you ammo and melee attacks giving you health, it makes it feel like the game has one correct playstyle and that's just rushing through enemies. It's fun for the first while, but then evetually you just want to kill enemies off with your arsenal, being forced to melee attack ALL enemies just gets stale for me.
The multiplayer is disappointing as well. It could have stolen a mode like Call of Duty Zombies or Killing Floor, but it did something else that more than half of the players just don't feel is special because it isn't; it's generic in nature. Skulltag games back in the day, for example, had invasion modes, where are they here?
This game overall is a positive experience, just don't get hyped up for it and you'll be pleased.

Halcyon 6 is a turn-based strategy game heavily inspired by games like X-COM, Civilization, and FTL.
Federation gets wiped out by weird fleshy aliens and you are put in command of its last space station.
To survive, you'll need to do a whole lot of things in a turn-based manner.
After you'd hired a couple of officers and built a couple of ships for them, you can send them off into space.
You'll start with exploring the nearest planets and stations to gather resources. But just gathering won't be enough - you'll also need to protect those planets and stations from aliens who'll try to destroy them. You can, of course, always close them down and just rescue the crew, but then you won't get those precious resources.
The time on the map works the same way it did in XCOM games - enemies move whenever you do. So you'll have to decide very carefully on where to fly next.
Oh, and don't send them too far away - your space station will get attacked sooner rather than later and you will have to defend it!
And you'll also need to expand your station. First, clean out the rabble, then build something in new clean room (very much XCOM-like).
There's also a tech tree with a variety of unlocks and upgrades that include new rooms for the base and new ships. And more boring stuff like cheaper repairs, etc.
You'll also encounter different factions and races. They'll have quests and amusing dialogues. And you can kill them all if you so desire.
And yes, combat is going to be your primary activity.
It's also turn-based, but this time, it's closer to FTL (or maybe even Final Fantasy), rather than XCOM.
You'll have your fleet against enemy fleet, both can have up to 3 ships.
Ships take a turn to execute one action - shoot, buff, debuff, heal, etc.
Mostly, the battles are all about synergy between your ships skills - if you exploit weaknesses (debuffs) applied by previous ships, you can get insanely huge crits. And the longer you play, the more important that synergy becomes. I found it to be pretty cool.
From my time of playing it, I haven't encountered any serious issues.
There are some minor annoyances in UI (that no doubt will be ironed out eventually) and I also had a few glitches, but that's about it - pretty solid v0.1 :)

Before I delve too deeply into this review, I first want to say that I don't recommend this game because of the quality, but because of the lacking updates, the cash shop prices, and the current population of the game.
This is a grand embodiment of your typical fast paced arena shooter. The gameplay encourages both high amounts of verticality and versitility. If games like Doom, Quake, or Unreal Tournament strike your fancy, then this is for you. The real cream of the game rests in the weapon crafting system, where you can craft virtually any weapon that suits your playstyle.
The game doesn't seem like it's being updated very frequently. I first staretd playing Loadout about a year ago. The amount of content that's been released during that time has been lacking to say the least. No new weapons have been added from the default Ball, Rifle, Laser, and Rocket types. Very very few attachments have been added. There are a couple new levels, and a couple reskinned levels that have been added. No new characters, and very very little has been added to the cosmetic shop. The population of the game is arguably dwindling. It's not uncommon to be paired off against the same player time and time again throughout the course of a few hours of gaming.
The cost of cash shop items are atrocious and is not very wallet friendly. Currently, 600 spacebux costs $1, and 16000 costs $20. It costs 2000 spacebux to buy 1 gunslot, and 6000 spacebux for 1 loadout. The amount of gunslots you get as a player isn't half bad, since they give you 9 slots for free, which you have to unlock by leveling up. However, they only give you 3 free loadouts, and each loadout allows you to use only 2 weapons at a time. Vanity items to customize your character typically costs between 2000 spacebux to 8000 spacebux for a singular item, such as shirts, pants, accessories, hats, masks, etc.
Given the steep prices of the cash shop, the lack of content updates, and the dwindling population, I cannot in good faith recommend this game. I honestly feel that if the game were updated more frequely, or the cash shop prices were to come down, that Loadout would have a fighting chance. But, personally, this game does little to encourage me to keep coming back to it. Loadout is great for a short term fix, or when you aren't in the mood to play any of your usual games. But simply put, there are other games that I would much rather commit to, both short term and long term.

This is a great game for fans of Battletech and the original Mechwarrior games. The learning curve is steep though so do the tutorial and get a 5 million C-bill (the in game currency) reward. That's enough to buy your own mech, but I would recommend holding off until you have run a few actual missions. They have a tier system so when you start you will be in tier 5 and will be playing against others who are in that tier. As you get better you will move up the tiers and tier 1 is the level where the best of the best play. Listen to the advice given to you by team mates and use the voice coms to communicate with your team. When you are ready to buy your first mech, you should have some idea what you enjoy playing and can then customize it to your liking. I would reccomend a medium or heavy mech for beginers because they are a bit more forgiving. Lights require fast thinking and a good knowledge of the maps to pilot well. Assaults are very slow and need to be aggressive in leading the charge and using their armor to soak up fire to allow the rest of the team to advance. Stick with your team, and don't wander off. And most of all have fun.

Review from someone playing since Open Beta:
In its current state: 7.5 / 10
This game is good and fun, not balls-to-the-wall astonishingly amazing, but it has the potential to reach those levels.
Fact is, at the moment, this is the only Battletech game we've got, and It's a damn decent one.
** A word of warning about the bad reviews: Many of these are salty old players who have not taken ANY time to re-examine the current state of the game** /end warning
----Visual/Audio------
Audio - 8/10  Sound design could be a bit beefier, I'm actually a fan of the audio that USED to be in the game (weapon SFX and stuff). I've always been hoping for dynamic music that changes based upon your situation, but that's a pipedream. What we have now is pretty good nonetheless.
Visuals - 7/10 I'm not someone who cares about the highest quality textures, details, etc... BUT they could be better, plus the game is poorly optimized. I find it hard to believe the reccommended specs on the Store Page. The game used to look much better, search for screenshots, but performance was worse.
------Gameplay------
Teamwork is key in this game, afterall, there is no FFA. If you lonewolf expexting to kill lots of things, you'll be dissappointed. Use voip, use chat, move with your team.
This is slower than Hawken, and certainly much different from your average resoawn-die-respawn-die twitch shooters. It really is a "thinking man's shooter" You have to think who to shoot, when to shoot, where to shoot on them, IF you even SHOULD shoot, have situational awareness, be aware of heat, weapon mounts, target locks, friendly location...the list goes on.
Teamwork is key in this game, afterall, there is no FFA. If you lonewolf expexting to kill lots of things, you'll be dissappointed. Use voip, use chat, move with your team.
All in all: blasting mechs feels fun.
------The Grind--------
Certainly not a grindy as other F2P games out there, but there is still a grind. That being said, it is now MUCH better than it used to be, with increased ingame rewards, and Faction Play paying out much more than it used to. Grinding for mechs becomes addicting (for me anyway).
------Pricing--------
Yes, DLC, MC, and mech packs (for real money) are expensive. They have been, and I don't think that will change. The main reason people spend money on this game is because they have cash to burn, or people like me, who want to see the Battletech IP survive to fight another day.
It is good to know that Steam DLC can go on sale.
All in all, if you are a fan of Battletech, or big stompy robots, you owe it to yourself to give this game a try. I like it, you might too.

I hate console controllers, with few exceptions. The few I've liked were usually extremely simple, like the original NES controller, which is great for simple games like 2D platformers. For complex games, like Civilization or Tribes: Ascend, I've always preferred keyboard and mouse. I STILL prefer keyboard and mouse when sitting at my computer.
But now, when I'm sitting in front of my TV and I want to play some of the more party, casual-oriented games I have on my HTPC, nothing really beats the Steam Controller for ease of use and adaptability. I also have an Xbox 360 controller, a PS3 controller, and some older gamepads - none of them allow me to use the mouse in any serious way, and none of them have button design that doesn't lead to muscle strain for me over time. The steam controller effortlessly switches me between controlling the game, controlling the steam interface, and controlling the windows or linux desktop environment with equal ease - all while keeping my fingers and especially thumbs from wearing out or feeling like they're fighting the controller to get the degree of control I want. Moreover, while I'm usually a wired-control kind of guy, the steam controller's wireless connection converted me - it's effortless and introduces absolutely no wonkiness to the controls. Beautiful to experience in action.
This is the controller that made living room gaming possible for me. It's true that it doesn't really make it possible to enjoy a serious FPS (though I get by in FPS-oriented games like Sir, You Are Being Hunted just fine), and it's also true that you won't really be able to type to friends in more than five word sentences without getting annoyed (I just keep a small wireless keyboard nearby for that), but strategy games, artillery games (worms), platformers, isometric twin-stick shooters, some roguelikes, 3rd-person games (Tomb Raider et al), and probably some other genres I'm not thinking of right now have all worked beautifully for me with this controller. I'm currently working out a way to make it usable for simulator games like War Thunder - I think I've hit on the genius of making the underside paddles forward and backward throttle, which frees up everything above for the maneuvering and targeting even while moving.
Here's the thing that most people who want a controller do not get or enjoy about this controller - it's insanely customizable. It is the embodiment of PC gaming in a controller's body. Every single control surface on it is tweakable and assignable - almost every single game I've played with it that seemed clunky at first was fixable by searching for premade button assignments that people have made (when you save your button config it's visible to everyone else, who can also try it out), or else muddling through the process of making my own, which is a whole other learning experience. Just last week I found out it has a gyroscope I can assign to move my characters in broad strokes, then have aim control switch to the "mousepad" for fine movement just by touching it. Super useful!
This controller is exactly what the Steam Machine concept is - a mostly misunderstood tool that fits right between PC gaming and console gaming, filling in that gap to bring us all closer together. Yeah, I drank the koolaid. It was delicious.

I started playing this game in early 2013 after the beta got moved to full release, but it took me quite a few matches of getting stomped to realize how epically awesome this game really was.  I started to learn that this was unlike any other FPS that I had ever played, as the time to kill seemed never ending(at least for the Mechs that I was trying to kill)!  The movement was a little wonky because these things are literally walking tanks, being able to turn your torso independently of the legs.  This led to some pretty embarrassing moments crashing into walls, mountains, teammates, etc.. while trying to retreat.  Fortunately this community is amazing and will help you through it once they know you are a rookie(By the way we call you rookies instead of n00bs, which should already make you feel a little more welcome).   They have even added a fresh shiny new tutorial/training mode which is GREAT.  It comes with a massive influx of c-bills, which you can use to buy your first mech right off the bat.   If you are itching for some PvP, I suggest playing some of the trial mechs until you find the role that fits you before you buy first Mech.  Once you do, you will have full access to the Mechlab, where you can create whatever kind of build with it that you like!  Your first 25 matches also come with a "cadet bonus", which totals another $5,000,000 c-bills or so.   The cost of Mechs goes hand in hand with tonnage, so if you want a heavy/assualt.. best to get that tutorial and all your cadet bonuses in before making a purchase.
Like most F2P games, there is a built in real money currency called MC(mechwarrior credits).  I went months before I finally dropped some real money on a MC pack, but only because I wanted a Hero Mech(which is no better than any other Mech, just a fancy paintjob with c-bill/XP bonuses) and some other stupid vanity stuff like cockpit items.  Some people spend ridiculous amounts of money to have newly released Mechs for a small window of a few months, before they eventually go on sale for c-bills just like everything else.  The only thing is the Mechbays required to expand your new collection of stompy robots can only be obtained with MC, but they are often very easy to come by as a reward in PGI's very frequent weekend events/tournaments.   You can buy mechs for MC if you don't feel like grinding for the c-bills.. which would be kinda dumb in my book.  Grinding for c-bills is a fun and enjoyable experience, as every battle is tactical and unique in its own way.  You also need to "master" your Mechs if you want to get the most out of them, which is a grind in itself.. but well worth it!
P2W does not exist with this game, as it is more paying for colors, camo, shiny Hero Mechs, etc..  You won't even know what to do with MC until you love this game to the point where you "must have" some silly cosmetic item.   Once you get it and say, "damn, now my Mech REALLY looks badass.."
Then you know the investment was well worth it.
10/10  -- TL;DR: Learning curve is steep, but unlike a vast majority of games.. Our community is willing to teach you the ways of the MECH.  Jump in with both feet; you will love it!  Don't let the real-money MC currency scare you.. It is 99% for cosmetic/vanity items.

Played this game on and off for a few years. It has a steep learning curve, but once you figure it out, it's loads of fun.
The customization of mechs is also pretty top  notch. Where you choose to put weapons matters greatly to your type of mech, and how you want to play. Want to be a small mech, with large gun? You can! Be careful though, because your small mech can't carry nearly as many rounds as a large bulky one. Now where do you want to store that ammo? Legs? the Arm? Torso? No arms? Put it in a pod. But be careful, because that ammo can detonate when you get hit there.
Want more armor? stack it up, but be careful again, it'll limit your storage and weight. There's mechs, items, equipment, and builds for every type of player. Missile mechs, bruisers, heavy cannons, light skirmishers, scouts, snipers, and everything in between.
Maybe you desire to be more of a small support, annoying bee. You can!

I have used this controller for hundreds of hours of use for several different genres of games. For turn-based strategy like XCOM, it's great. The complaints about the build quality seem a little weird to me, the thing works fine under normal use. The buttons aren't incredible, but it gets the job done.
My problem is that after hundreds of hours of use, in the end the track pad portion of the pad just doesn't work that well for precision movements. As a result, playing anything that requires precision movements will just end up frustrating you when you miss a shot or something that you would've nailed had you been using a normal controller or a standard keyboard/mouse setup. After dying in MGSV from one last guy after two hours of sneaking because you couldn't move the controller in small enough intervals while also being sensitive to turn at a reasonable rate, you will be amazed at how awesome games are when played with a mouse and keyboard. Mouse and keyboard are still superior to this, the only reason I ever use this is for controlling my home theater system. It will never be a truly equivalent replacement of dual joystick controllers OR mouse & keyboard. However, if you play turn-based strategy on the big screen, it works great, so keep that in mind. 5/10 (not quite perfected, but good nonetheless in certain applications)

So far the Main games I have focused on getting the controls right for the game are Witcher 3 Dota (even though I think Dota's mouse and Keyboard is gonna ultimatley the only way I play that game) and CS: GO (same belief for this one as I have for Dota) I dabbled a bit with Darksiders II, Risk of Rain and Dawn of War Soul Storm.
With Dawn of War I only spent a little bit of time with it, I actually realize now that I never tried it after learning about the ability to disable the trackball feature and before  I figured out how to adjust the sensitivity (it was the first game I attempted).
Darksiders for the most part was already good in my book considering I had played that game most of the way through on the 360 before hand so I was already familiar with it's controls, however I may adjust a few things here and there.
Risk of Rain doesn't have a copious amount of controls and again it's mostly got the same layout as it did for the xbox gamepad so I'm fine with it's default lay out.
The Witcher, now this was my favorite, and I think the final experience to make me feel like I didn't waste my money on a cool but extremely unneccessary idea. That's because, I barely changed anything. Well that and the fact that you can't really customize the controls for Witcher on the Gamepad. But with the steam controller all you have to do is map the function of a Key, a mouse button, or a gamepad button, to your desired steam controller button. The default Witcher scheme as a whole was pretty bad in my opinion but when I switched maybe just six buttons (which in comparison to how many you can configure yes that wasn't very much) I made the D-Pad into the four consumeable Item touch menu, where i could utalize the four items easily. On the xbox game pad (or on the consoles in general) there were only two Consumable buttons that were set. Which leaves Drawing/sheathing my swords. Well I hated the Idea of sprinting with A and being unable to move the camera around, so I made A button functions map to R-Grip (sprint interact roll), B button functions from L-Grip (Jump, Dodge, dismount), well what do my face buttons do now? Well X and Y are still attack (even though I was tempted to make the attack buttons R-button and R-Trigger like Dark Souls just for the hell of it) but now A draws my steel sword and B draws my silver sword.
And that's why I love this controller already. I can make any game I want have the Dark Souls control Scheme if I wanted regardless of practicallity. I can imagine handing this config to a friend and have them say "this doesn't work you lunatic" and then have them change it to a config that makes no sense to anyone else but them and still play just as well. This thing is smart, it's brilliant. Old games that aren't controller supported you can still configure to this controller which like I said with the LoK games makes it a lot better.
Not to mention The steam controller can be both wired and wireless. Runs on double AA batteries (have read in other reviews that rechargeable batteries are slightly bigger and won't come out of the controller without using a screwdriver so just use normal double A's or the cord even)
It's not perfect though. Reportedly this controller lasts a few months before breaking (read a review that compared it's physical quality to a kinder surprise toy and those are people who recommend this controller) I just got it so I'll have to wait and see. Also you have to use BigPicture Mode in order to use the configurations. The Config menu it self is run in the in-game BigPicture overlay. I personally once I opened big picture am now having my games blink every once in a while and by that I mean the screen goes black for 2 seconds then comes back. Sometimes, it does this repeatedly blink blink blink for like 10 seconds total. Now I can't say the problem with my video/game is directly related to the controller (in fact I'm pretty much certain it sin't) but last I checked there was a reason I don't really hear about people enjoying bigpicture mode or actually using it frequently. But other then that I really don't have any complaints about the controller.
Overall it's a good device, a really good one even, but for some it's not gonna be practical whether you've never been interested in gamepad/controllers in teh first place, or because you don't have the time/patience (and maybe not even the creativity) to learn the ins and outs of the controller and come up with and learn the config possibilties for each game you have and want to play with this controller. Regardless of that I think most should look into it at the very least and see if you can try it out a friends or something.
Anway have a good day and game like you've never gamed before. VAE VICTUS!

The moment I opened the steam store to check on the reviews of this game, GOSH they are so darn horrible. I immediately regretted my money spent even without playing the game yet. It took a while for a 31GB game to install and to imagine that its gonna suck so hard. Expected a 31GB worth of disappointment...
When I entered the game, NOTHING WENT WRONG FOR ME. It look hell of suspicious that the ENTIRE STEAM COMMUNITY is RANTING about this game and I was really gonna expect something bad happening to me. I went through the settings and play around. NOTHING WENT WRONG AGAIN!
I played with an AI using the mainstreamed heroes. With so much graphical power, there is still NOTHING WRONG ABOUT THE GAME! I was starting to con·tem·plate what went wrong with the massive negative reviews.
The story brings your back to the ending of Full Burst 3. And I can say the mode is so amazing that its easy to know what timeline is the Naruto story at. It is idiotproof and easy to understand, provided you watched the animations or played the previous series.
A lot of people love the free roam and quest system of Naruto, they are a classic that needs to be in every game. So far there is no disappointments here and everything is as expected from the great Naruto series. But nothing really new to mention in particular.
The interface of the free battle is easy to understand, but the partner selection with their support type is not self explainatory. You have to experiment through multiple battles to know what type a support character can do. Its bringing back the old Attack/Balanced/Defense mechanism but fixing it to a single character. The character customization is shorten down from Revolution.
I give commendation for the user friendliness in the lobby for guiding the players on what to do. But the game has serious lag balance issues between both players. The host will have the rightful ping and the opponenet will need to match his latency, which causes serious disruptance in gameplay. You must be lucky to face an opponent with a good ping.
Playing hours into the game, I realise that this is still one of the game worth buying. And I realised that every other issue that people does have, is their computers. Its true that there are a couple of settings you have to do before playing a 31GB game, its not simply just playing. Here is my spec that runs it at smooth criminal rate even at a period of 8 hours continuously.
Intel Core i7-4790 CPU @ 3.60Hz
16 GB RAM
64 bits Windows 7
NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970
If you are running anything higher than mine, read up the internet or forums and guides. There shouldn't be an issue for this matter. But if you are anything VIRTUALLY WAYYYYY lower computer specs than mine, you obviously know that this is a gigantic game of 31GB and not some old pc game right? Consider upgrading your computer.
My final conclusion is that all reviews are more of a personal issue running the game rather than the game having bugs or errors. I played with the amount of time into the game and I have ZERO issues with anything. Its one of the BEST buys I had even at full retail price. Remarkable

So there is a lot of hate on this game because it touches on the whole what defines your gender topic. But people just need to treat this as a game, with another what if situation and enjoy the story for what it is. It's a long, semi-choice driven visual novel that has decent graphics (all things considered) And for me, a lot of fun to play through each of the character's stories, some even multiple times.
There is also hate on the game for the graphics, but really, I loved them. The backgrounds were recycled for the entire game, but each of the characters had a set number of poses and costumes. And they all worked when they were used. I enjoyed the art style quite a bit and had a lot of fun playing through the game.
If there were a single problem I had with the game it would be the final two chapters of the story. I won't spoil the plot, but it felt rushed, and while I know that the developer had tried to tie up all the loose ends of the story and make sure it somewhat fit. I would have personally felt better not having all the main characters having a what happened in the end senario built into the end of the story, it kind of makes the choices of partners, and endings you can have in the individual ones less exciting and fun.
Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game and it left me with the feeling of reading a good book and  would recommend it to anyone looking to spend an hour or so having a bit of fun with the story.

What this game is:
Gender Bender DNA Twister Extreme is a light-hearted story about a science experiment gone wrong that transforms several people into the opposite sex. It also covers the consequences and aftermath of the accident in several of the newer characters.
Pros:
1. Funny, witty, silly, and occaisionally hits the mark on the emotional or profound.
2. Likeable characters
3. A soundtrack that grows on you after a while and is well utilitized during Dan's story
Cons:
1. Typos in the text. After 12 characters and multiple releases, this shouldn't be happening. Especially in the older content.
2. Incorrect name plates for characters involved in their own storylines and appearing in stories prior to their own. I'd really like to see this get fixed on account that it's distracting and a spoiler.
3. Character selection is not grouped or organized by plot timeline. While it's nice to be able to pick any character that looks interesting, there's a definite order for them to be played in for the plot to make sense. At the very least the loading screen should start up on Dina or Lynn since either of them play out the baseline story.
Conclusion:
GBDNATE is a fun little bit of entertainment. It doesn't try to dive into the deep emotional and physical hardships transpeople experience everyday. At the same time it doesn't minimize them either. It simply does two things- It tries to answer the question what if this happened. And conveys the simple message that identity, gender or otherwise, is a part of a person's mind and heart- not their body.

Anarcho-capitalism is a political philosophy that advocates the elimination of the state in favor of self-ownership, private property, and free markets. Anarcho-capitalists hold that, in the absence of statute (law by centralized decrees and legislation), society tends to contractually self-regulate and civilize through the discipline of the free market (in what its proponents describe as a "voluntary society").[2][3]
In an anarcho-capitalist society, law enforcement, courts, and all other security services would be operated by privately funded competitors rather than centrally through compulsory taxation. Money, along with all other goods and services, would be privately and competitively provided in an open market. Therefore, personal and economic activities under anarcho-capitalism would be regulated by victim-based dispute resolution organizations under tort and contract law, rather than by statute through centrally determined punishment under political monopolies.[4]
Various theorists have espoused legal philosophies similar to anarcho-capitalism. The first person to use the term, however, was Murray Rothbard, who in the mid-20th century synthesized elements from the Austrian School of economics, classical liberalism, and 19th-century American individualist anarchists Lysander Spooner and Benjamin Tucker (while rejecting their labor theory of value and the norms they derived from it).[5] A Rothbardian anarcho-capitalist society would operate under a mutually agreed-upon libertarian "legal code which would be generally accepted, and which the courts would pledge themselves to follow."[6] This pact would recognize self-ownership and the non-aggression principle (NAP), although methods of enforcement vary.
Anarcho-capitalists are distinguished from minarchists, who advocate a small night-watchman state limited to the function of individual protection, and other anarchists who may seek to prohibit or regulate the accumulation of property and the flow of capital.
Anarcho-capitalists argue for a society based on the voluntary trade of private property and services (in sum, all relationships not caused by threats or violence, including exchanges of money, consumer goods, land, and capital goods) in order to minimize conflict while maximizing individual liberty and prosperity. However, they also recognize charity and communal arrangements as part of the same voluntary ethic.[7] Though anarcho-capitalists are known for asserting a right to private (individualized or joint non-public) property, some propose that non-state public or community property can also exist in an anarcho-capitalist society.[8] For them, what is important is that it is acquired and transferred without help or hindrance from the compulsory state. Anarcho-capitalist libertarians believe that the only just, and/or most economically beneficial, way to acquire property is through voluntary trade, gift, or labor-based original appropriation, rather than through aggression or fraud.[9]
Anarcho-capitalists see free-market capitalism as the basis for a free and prosperous society. Murray Rothbard said that the difference between free-market capitalism and "state capitalism" is the difference between "peaceful, voluntary exchange" and a collusive partnership between business and government that uses coercion to subvert the free market[10] (Rothbard is credited with coining the term "anarcho-capitalism").[11][12] "Capitalism", as anarcho-capitalists employ the term, is not to be confused with state monopoly capitalism, crony capitalism, corporatism, or contemporary mixed economies, wherein market incentives and disincentives may be altered by state action.[13] They therefore reject the state, seeing it as an entity which steals property (through taxation and expropriation), initiates aggression, has a compulsory monopoly on the use of force, uses its coercive powers to benefit some businesses and individuals at the expense of others, creates artificial monopolies, restricts trade, and restricts personal freedoms via drug laws, compulsory education, conscription, laws on food and morality, and the like.
Many anarchists view capitalism as an inherently authoritarian and hierarchical system, and seek the expropriation of private property.[14] There is disagreement between these left anarchists and laissez-faire anarcho-capitalists,[15] as the former generally rejects anarcho-capitalism as a form of anarchism and considers anarcho-capitalism an oxymoron,[16][17][18] while the latter holds that such expropriation is counterproductive to order, and would require a state.[4] On the Nolan chart, anarcho-capitalists are located at the northernmost apex of the libertarian quadrant – since they reject state involvement in both economic and personal affairs.[19]
Laissez-faire anarchists argue that the state relies on initiating force because force can be used against those who have not stolen private property, vandalized private property, assaulted anyone, or committed fraud. Many also argue that subsidized monopolies tend to be corrupt and inefficient. Anarchist theorist Rothbard argued that all government services, including defense, are inefficient because they lack a market-based pricing mechanism regulated by the voluntary decisions of consumers purchasing services that fulfill their highest-priority needs and by investors seeking the most profitable enterprises to invest in.[20] Many anarchists also argue that private defense and court agencies would have to have a good reputation in order to stay in business. Furthermore, Linda and Morris Tannehill argue that no coercive monopoly of force can arise on a truly free market and that a government's citizenry can't desert them in favor of a competent protection and defense agency.[21]
Rothbard bases his philosophy on natural law grounds and also provides economic explanations of why he thinks anarcho-capitalism is preferable on pragmatic grounds as well. David D. Friedman says he is not an absolutist rights theorist but is also "not a utilitarian", however, he does believe that "utilitarian arguments are usually the best way to defend libertarian views".[22] Peter Leeson argues that "the case for anarchy derives its strength from empirical evidence, not theory".[23] Hans-Hermann Hoppe, meanwhile, uses "argumentation ethics" for his foundation of "private property anarchism",[24] which is closer to Rothbard's natural law approach.
I define anarchist society as one where there is no legal possibility for coercive aggression against the person or property of any individual. Anarchists oppose the State because it has its very being in such aggression, namely, the expropriation of private property through taxation, the coercive exclusion of other providers of defense service from its territory, and all of the other depredations and coercions that are built upon these twin foci of invasions of individual rights.
— Rothbard in Society and State

So when this piece of niffty hardware was announced I seam to recall having no analog stick and the face buttons formed around the steam button. I liked the look of that model better but after playing a bunch of games with the current model I have to admit it works better this way.
Anyway when I first saw this version of the controller I was pretty annoyed and figured I wasn't gonna bother buying. I honestly didn't think the damn thing would be comfortable in my hands.... man I was absolutely wrong about that. For starters I refuse to play witcher 3 with the mouse and keyboard and I refuse to play it with the default controller scheme it had. Thank valve for the amount of customization you can do to this thing.
Honestly I'm still testing to see if I could actually play FPS games with it and so far it's a hard no. Honestly I thought the most use I'd get from this controller would be playing RTS games and other top down games like Diablo clones (Grim Dawn or Torchlight) but where the button commands are fine I actaully find it hard to adjust the touch-pad well enough to be more accurate then a mouse. I actually think it's more plausible to play an FPS or TPS then a RTS or Moba with it.
However I am gonna give it time and keep trying before I decide on whether or not it's possible. Regardless there are some games that have so many commands in them that a keyboard will always be able to out class a controller including this one but I do enjoy using the Steam controller for 2D side scrollers like Rogue Legacy and Risk of Rain, as well as Third Person Action adventure RPG games again like Witcher 3, Darksiders and Castlevania. A reminder I'm only stating what I'm used to with this controller so far there are probably those who can play top down games and FPS/TPS games expertly with this controller. I only got it the same day I wrote this review but I spent all day messing with it and the customization for plenty of games. The next few I want to tackle are Soul Reaver 2 (cause the gamepad AND Keyboard controls for the LoK games are terrible) Exanima and really any of the 2D side scrollers that actually utilizes the mouse to aim like Apotheon, Axiom Verge, or even Terraria.
So far the Main games I have focused on getting the controls right for the game are Witcher 3 Dota (even though I think Dota's mouse and Keyboard is gonna ultimatley the only way I play that game) and CS: GO (same belief for this one as I have for Dota) I dabbled a bit with Darksiders II, Risk of Rain and Dawn of War Soul Storm.
With Dawn of War I only spent a little bit of time with it, I actually realize now that I never tried it after learning about the ability to disable the trackball feature and before  I figured out how to adjust the sensitivity (it was the first game I attempted).
Darksiders for the most part was already good in my book considering I had played that game most of the way through on the 360 before hand so I was already familiar with it's controls, however I may adjust a few things here and there.
Risk of Rain doesn't have a copious amount of controls and again it's mostly got the same layout as it did for the xbox gamepad so I'm fine with it's default lay out.
The Witcher, now this was my favorite, and I think the final experience to make me feel like I didn't waste my money on a cool but extremely unneccessary idea. That's because, I barely changed anything. Well that and the fact that you can't really customize the controls for Witcher on the Gamepad. But with the steam controller all you have to do is map the function of a Key, a mouse button, or a gamepad button, to your desired steam controller button. The default Witcher scheme as a whole was pretty bad in my opinion but when I switched maybe just six buttons (which in comparison to how many you can configure yes that wasn't very much) I made the D-Pad into the four consumeable Item touch menu, where i could utalize the four items easily. On the xbox game pad (or on the consoles in general) there were only two Consumable buttons that were set. Which leaves Drawing/sheathing my swords. Well I hated the Idea of sprinting with A and being unable to move the camera around, so I made A button functions map to R-Grip (sprint interact roll), B button functions from L-Grip (Jump, Dodge, dismount), well what do my face buttons do now? Well X and Y are still attack (even though I was tempted to make the attack buttons R-button and R-Trigger like Dark Souls just for the hell of it) but now A draws my steel sword and B draws my silver sword.
And that's why I love this controller already. I can make any game I want have the Dark Souls control Scheme if I wanted regardless of practicallity. I can imagine handing this config to a friend and have them say "this doesn't work you lunatic" and then have them change it to a config that makes no sense to anyone else but them and still play just as well. This thing is smart, it's brilliant. Old games that aren't controller supported you can still configure to this controller which like I said with the LoK games makes it a lot better.
Not to mention The steam controller can be both wired and wireless. Runs on double AA batteries (have read in other reviews that rechargeable batteries are slightly bigger and won't come out of the controller without using a screwdriver so just use normal double A's or the cord even)
It's not perfect though. Reportedly this controller lasts a few months before breaking (read a review that compared it's physical quality to a kinder surprise toy and those are people who recommend this controller) I just got it so I'll have to wait and see. Also you have to use BigPicture Mode in order to use the configurations. The Config menu it self is run in the in-game BigPicture overlay. I personally once I opened big picture am now having my games blink every once in a while and by that I mean the screen goes black for 2 seconds then comes back. Sometimes, it does this repeatedly blink blink blink for like 10 seconds total. Now I can't say the problem with my video/game is directly related to the controller (in fact I'm pretty much certain it sin't) but last I checked there was a reason I don't really hear about people enjoying bigpicture mode or actually using it frequently. But other then that I really don't have any complaints about the controller.
Overall it's a good device, a really good one even, but for some it's not gonna be practical whether you've never been interested in gamepad/controllers in teh first place, or because you don't have the time/patience (and maybe not even the creativity) to learn the ins and outs of the controller and come up with and learn the config possibilties for each game you have and want to play with this controller. Regardless of that I think most should look into it at the very least and see if you can try it out a friends or something.
Anway have a good day and game like you've never gamed before. VAE VICTUS!

I've had the steam controller since December 2015 - It's an amazing piece of kit
I have only used my XB1 controller once since getting it, and there is no going back.
With the Steam Controller there is a definite learning curve,
If you purchase the controller.
Expect to hate it for the first few hours of play at least. You will absolutely SUCK at EVERYTHING.
But PERSIST through this, be willing to learn the controller.
You will have years of muscle memory from old style gamepads to unlearn. and this takes time. but the reward is worth it.
It is incredibly customisable, Be willing to spend some time making profiles which feel right to you and the payoff is amazing.
There are a lot of community profiles out there for almost every game, even games with no gamepad support.
I will never use stick for movement / aiming again, the touchpads are infinitely more sensitive and precise.
If you play FPS with the gamepad, combine the Touchpads with Gyro for micro adjustments and you have almost mouse level precision from your couch
Controller is perfect for all genres of game. I have used it for
Witcher 3,
Rocket League,
GTA V,
Pillars of Eternity,
Metro 2033 & Last Light
Black Ops III,
