Its important when you read these reviews to understand 2 important timelines related to the development for MWO
The IGP Era and the Post IGP Era.  Basically IGP was the publisher that picked up MWO when PGI first pitched the game.  They were a publisher that was on the rocks and ended up going belly up a year or so after MWO went open beta.  This is important to note because alot of the negativity surrounding this game (including its reviews from game sites such as IGN/Gamespot), was largely due to IGP's death grip over the development team.  Once they went under and PGI purchased the publishing rights for themselves the game got noticable better and continues to improve to date.
As for the game itself, if you were a fan of any of the previous mechwarrior titles or a mech simulator fan at all, youll likely enjoy your time with MWO.  If your someone who likes to try out alot of the free to play games such as War Thunder and Wold of Tanks, youll likely have a good time.  Its not the most user freindly game when starting out as there is lots to learn, but youll with some practice that it can be rewarding.
Where this game really shines is when your working with a group of freinds or dropping with clan members.  Team work is what gives this game an edge over other games in this small genre. The community warefare system can also be an exciting mechanic if you are playing with a premade group, however pugging it is not very fun.
In terms of the monetary system its not bad.  All weapons and mech chassis are availible for the in-game currency, there are some hero varaints that are real life money only, but truth be told there is maybe 1-3 out of a selection of 20 that are "better" then what you can buy in game without spending money.  And usually its only a minor upgrade (1 extra energy slot for example).  So in terms of pay to win, not really a factor, or at least no where near on parr with something like WOT and their golden ammo.  Realistically a hero mech facing against a regular variant of the same chassis will be a very close fight and usually comes down to techniques used in the fight.  Beyond that theres the usual cosmetic purchases.
All in all, as a game id give MWO a 7,5/10 and as a mech simulator id give it a 8/10.  In summary it costs you nothing to try, and if your into simulator games youll have a good time.  Still plenty of room for improvement but its come a long way since the beta and ive had a good time while spending very little on the game.

For those that already own the original release of the game and want to know if the upgrade is worth it: I highly suggest picking it up the next time it's part of one of Steam's holiday sales. The extra battery, redone boss fights, and occasional automatic hacker contribute a surprising amount towards making the game experience smoother overall.
Now for the actual review of the game itself. TL;DR, the game is essentially cyberpunk
by way of
,with
and
mixed in.
DX:HR sees you playing as Adam Jensen, the head of security for Sarif Industries. In a world where biomechanical Augmentations are creating an ever-expanding rift between those that can afford the enhancements (and anti-rejection drugs) and those that cannot, Sarif Industries is on the cusp of a breakthrough that could bring an end to this segregation once and for all. ... and then the place is ransacked by terrorist mercenaries, destroying Sarif's progress and nearly killing Adam. Adam is forced to have almost his entire body replaced with biomechanical parts in order to survive, and he uses this technology to hunt down the mercs, and eventually, the global conspiracy that hired them.
Generally speaking, the story does a very good job of conveying what it wants to convey in a meaningful manner. The characters are all extremely well written, the plot progression is believable around 97% of the time, and the voice acting is... passable. The game tries to bring up ethical ambiguity regarding augmentation and really wants the player to sit down and think about these things. Usually, this works out well enough - but when the subject starts becoming the main focus of the endgame, it starts to become extremely grating.
The development team put a very heavy emphasis on visual storytelling. Anything that isn't a sewer or a labatory hallway (and there are a whole lot of those) is
... or, well, horrific, depending on where you are in the game. The point I'm trying to make is that the visuals, while cluttered and packed with all kinds of details, still (usually) manages to pick out and show you all of the important items that you need to see. Adam Jensen's posh apartment is a prime example of the attention to detail that went in to the game. One of my only major complaints with the visuals is that the cutscenes are rendered in 720p and do not scale up to 1080p very well.
The game's soundtrack is... well, there might as well not even be a soundtrack. That's how forgettable it is. By itself, this is merely a minor annoyance. When compared to the original game's incredible soundtrack, it's actively disappointing. It honestly makes me feel like some kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ soundtrack elitist.
The game's sound design seems to switch between working flawlessly and not working at all fairly randomly. The crunch from using a lethal takedown sounds every bit as lethal as it looks, but then you throw a refigerator at the wall and it makes the sound of a baseball dropping into a plastic bin. The equally sporadic volume of these sounds makes it difficult to tell what sounds enemies will hear and what ones they won't.
Speaking of which, lets actually talk about the gameplay. The core of the gameplay revolves making your way through hostile enemy territory to some kind of goal point through various means - hiding behind obstacles, crawling through vents, temporarily turning invisible, hacking doors and turrets, silently taking out enemies one-by-one... or, if you prefer, you can go in guns-a-blazing and stick a tranquilizer (or bullets if you perfer) into anyone stupid enough to turn their guns towards you. The game supports both playstyles and any variations thereof.
The core mechanics actually work pretty damn well: you'll feel like a badass for sneaking through an entire complex of hardened soldiers without them seeing you once, and you'll feel like a badass for constantly scoring long-range headshots with a mere pistol (the gunplay feels fantastic, BTW). You are rewarded for locating secret passages and for neutralizing enemies. You can find secret item caches or just loot your enemy's unconcious and\or dead bodies. Even within enemy territory, there will be places where you can sell extra loot and purchase more ammo or healing items.
The level designs also work to reflect these multiple gameplay approaches - nearly every area in the game has ample cover, alternate paths, and interractible objects, allowing you to hide from suspicious enemies or take cover from hostile ones. Most of the time, you're going to know exactly where you are going, though when you're exploring the city hub areas (especially in China) expect to get turned around many, many times. Thankfully, there are only two of these hubs in the game, and they stop appearing about two-thirds of the way into the game.
By completing various tasks and earning experience points, you will earn Praxis, which can be spent on upgrading your augmentations. This ranges from the seemingly mundane (lift heavy objects) to the highly practical (fall from any height, temporarily track NPCs through walls) to the downright badass (turn invisible, shoot bombs in every direction). There are even upgrades for the minigames, such as hacking or conversation boss fights.
There are a few not-quite-random gameplay changes to be aware of. First off, there's hacking. You will end up hacking a
of stuff in this game: computers, guard robots, doors, lasers, alarm triggers, and occasionally bombs. In this game, hacking is best described as a real-time strategy minigame, where you have to weigh the risks of capturing nodes versus how likely the antivirus software is to catch you if you capture said node. It actually works fairly well as a strange reflection of how the core gameplay can turn from stealth to action in an instant. That being said, the randomness that this minigame relies on can often be total bullcrap, even with nodes that only have a 10% chance of alarming the antivirus.
Secondly, you have the so-called conversational boss battles (or "Social Conflicts"). Certain important characters will need to be buttered up (or perhaps, put down) in order for them to give Adam vital information. The process is simple: listen to what they have to say, and pick the best counterpoint from a pool of responses. Unfortunately, these "puzzles" can very easily fall flat if you're not some kind of psychoanalyst extroardinaire. The summary of each response you can chose is written very ambiguously, and the perceptions of each individual user can affect what response they will percieve as the most logical choice. Ironic, considering the different perceptions of a common occurance are a prime theme in this game.
Since we're on the subject of variable gameplay, I should probably mention this before someone yells at me: the very final area of the game does replace the game's surprisingly intelligent and lethal armed opponents with "Left 4 Dead Zombie" style enemies. Going from bullets to fists does not exactly increase the opponent's damage output, if you know what I'm saying.
Finally, there's the subject of the boss fights. For the sake of simplicity, lets just say there are four and a half boss fights in the game. In the original release of the game, the boss fights all
. Thankfully, Director's Cut has redesigned the boss arenas so that alternatives to the "Call of Duty" shootout can be achieved, usually in the form of hacking turrets into shooting the boss. While they're still not exactly highlights, they're actually quite enjoyable, especially when you sic a pack of miniature tanks on their gloating, egotistical asses.
In summary, Deus Ex: Human Revolution is an overall enjoyable experience with a mostly solid story, extremely detailed visuals, and very fun gameplay. Just be wary of the generic soundtrack and lacklustre endgame.

Deus Ex: HR is a slightly older game (~2011) that tackles the question of makind's future and human augmentation. Set in 2027 across various locations including Detroit and Hengsha, it shows a possible future for humanity. Poverty, gangs, and protesters ranging from anti-augmentation "purists" to environmentalists all paint a sharp contrast to the scientific progress, the wealthy few who can affort augmentations, and corporations that have replaced governments.
The main protagonist, an ex-SWAT chief security guard with a voice similar to the sound of sandpaper, feels a bit forced, as if he were only here to let the story develop. After mercenaries attack his workplace at Sarif Industries, his life is saved by augmentations, and he becomes a one-man army. His boss sends him on missions where he either sneaks by everyone to steal important information or shoots everyone down and steals important information. As you may have guessed, this is a mix between a stealth and an FPS game. Stealth as in the Thief series' 2014 reboot, entitled Thief, and FPS as in games where you gun everyone down.
To make the gameplay work, you are given a choice on how you want to get to your objective -- the pewpewpew approach, the stealthy one-by-one takedown approach and the sneak by everyone through the vents approach are the main three ways of dealing with situations. Sometimes, an approach (especially the latter two) will require you to upgrade your character with augmentations. The upgrade system works, though some features are completely redundant, as your approaches may not require that augmentation (which is perfectly normal for this kind of upgrade system), or the character can already do what the upgrade enables him to do (such as some of the hacking-oriented augmentations).
I can't really find anything to complain about. The story was interesting, though at times a bit forced, and the lack of a definitive antagonist just makes the game feel messy
. Pritchard and David Sarif are both c*nts in their own ways, and character movement during dialogues is glitchy, repetitive, and unnatural. But that's all that's wrong with the game, and those are minor details that don't take away from the experience.
tl;dr: I liked the game and have played it twice (only once through Steam). I've often seen it on sale, and one playthrough is worth at least 20 hours if you don't rush everything, pick the more peaceful approaches, and complete a few side missions.

With a decent amount of hours sunk into the game I decided to write my review.
First of all, Rabi-Ribi is a metroidvania mixed with bullethell.  and it does this so extremely well you're surprised it isn't more common.
In the game you take on the role of Erina, a bunny girl with a massive hammer, and her partner ribbon, a magical fairy.
Together you explore Rabi-Ribi island finding helpers to aid you in solving the mysteries going on.
the island consists of numerous areas, each filled with their own unique mobs, boss battles, hidden secrets and collectables. All making sure you'll never get bored exploring.
The boss battles are where the bullethell element comes in. Each boss comes with a range of unique attacks. A type of bullethell-style attack that you need to dodge in order to get your damage in.
The attacks are nicely thought out. They make you learn (and on the more challenging difficulty levels master) the movement ingame. The creator also did a fine job in making the attacks feel like they belong to a boss by keeping them in the theme of said boss.
If a boss proves to challenging or you feel the game isn't quite in line with your playstyle. You can go for a little 'custimization' with the badges you find across the map. Each badges comes with a change to your stats or a buff. A nice, simple system to make your life a little easier. The game also has other systems in place to make sure people not familiar with the bullethellgenre don't get overwhelmed. Of course in the harder difficulties these dissapear and get replaced by a lot more bullet.
All in all, Rabi-Ribi is a cute, fun, challenging game with a lot of replayability that's worth every penny.

Explore the zombie-infested city of Los Perdidos, and find a way to escape before a military strike wipes the entire city, and everyone in it, off the map.
Dead Rising 3 is a tpp zombie massacre simulator. It follows the Dead Rising formula, by chance you end up as one of the survivors of the zombie apocalypse and you must fight to survive zombie hordes and non-zombie maniacs, and get out alive. It has a specific structure where most of the mission have specific timeframes, miss the timeframe and the mission is gone. It's not as bad as it sounds tho as these timeframes in DR3 are quite generous, so as much as there is not much time to just sightsee there is time to complete all the mandatory and optional missions.
The game itself is fun as usual. There are hordes of zombies and lots of ways to free them from this place of existence. The combo weapons are fun as usual and exterminating hordes of zombies using max level combo weapons is extremely satisfying. The PC edition includes all the dlcs, each dlc is a side story to the main storyline, which means 35-40hrs of reckless zombie murdering.
For me DR3:AE is the best franchise installment by far (haven't played DR4 yet). You're still time constrained but there is enough time to do everything, included dlc content removes the time constraints so you can just roam and kill zombies. And killing zombies en masse is what Dead Rising does perfectly. The story is crazy, but well written and fun. If you like zombie games then give this one a try.

This is a game that changed it all for me.
I thought Neptunia games were just some kind of fanservice grindfests, which they admittedly to a certain degree are, but they are also more than that.
In this game you travel between dimensions and meet fun and interesting characters. The story seems simple at first, but it quickly gets more interesting and addicting, and towards the end when you think you know the ending, you don't. It pulls the rug from under you and surprises you by just being a great story.
Its just wonderful how they managed to make a story that connects everything so well together.
Other than that this game is filled with anime and gaming tropes, and it references both mediums a lot. 4th wall is broken constantly and the fun, lovable *bubbly* characters just bring a smile to my face every time I see them.
Gameplay is a bit repetetive, but its nothing new if you have played JRPGs before. It looks like one, and it plays like one. Grinding might be needed at times.
The DLC are all worth it somehow(?) Now that's a surprise!
This game made me understand why I love video games and anime better than anything before... and I never thought a Neptunia game would do that.
Don't underestimate or overlook this game. Its great.

Honestly, this game isn't nearly as bad as many here are making it out to be.
If you're debating whether or not this is for you: This game is in no way even trying to be a realistic representation of being transgender. This is a fetish game, and one that's appealing to a very niche audience. If you're looking for a game about the life of transgender individuals, this isn't it; if you're looking for a normal-ish porn game, this isn't it, I would reccomend Huniepop though.
However, if transformation fetishes apply to you, be it breast expansion, animal transformation or gender swapping, this game is most certainly for you.
While it isn't cheap and the artwork doesn't even come close to standing up to a game such as Huniepop, it is actually fairly amusing for a visual novel. A lot of people I see talking about it ask why you wouldn't just on deviantart to find this; and to that, I challenge you to find anything nearly as vast or complete. Many of the characters have more than 5 endings to find. I can think of very few artists who have written stories retaining to these fetishes that would even come close to half of the stories this game tells.
While I certainly don't think it has the enjoyment factor of something like Huniepop which can also just be played for fun, I do think that it has plenty to offer. If it appeals to your weirder side like it does mine, get it, otherwise it simply wasn't intended for you and you can avoid it entirely.

I have not touched the online portion of the game but there's some points i'd like to discuss.
-The game is good, far better than the last game revolution and a wonderful finale to the Storm series as a whole.
-While playing this game, I have experienced the best looking Naruto Storm game to date. It may not get 4K resolution but every boss fight was a visual spectacle and surprisingly accurate to the manga (some changes but nothing to complain about.
- This is the shortest story mode so far. It covers the entirety of the final battle of the series. That's not a bad thing, it doesn't re-tread old ground and doesn't space out the bosses. There is an adventure mode where you can play old battles from the series (not boss battles) but that's mostly for some non-canon fun and some battles with twists on them. (including enemies with wildly increased stats as well as attacks that poison you)
- Gameplay has been the same with some new features. From revolution, the choosing of drive, ultimate attack, and awakening types are gone with the traditional fighting style gaining the new feature of switching your lead character in the middle of combat. This allows for crazier combos and the ability to switch up your fighting style in a flash. (using a puppet-user to keep opponents far away and switching to a melee fighter when they're up close is super fun)
I loved this series (excluding generations and revolution) and naruto is one of my favorite mangas. This is not a bad game. This is not the best game ever. If you love naruto or love this fighting game style, buy this game.
Final Verdict: 8/10 Great

Doom 2016 is the Dark Souls of Hell Based Shooters That Take Place on Mars.
The reason Doom 2016 is similar to Dark Souls is the difficulty that it may present and the disturbing imagery.
In Doom 2016 you take control of the iconic Doomguy donning his new and improved Praetor Suit. The Praetor Suit gives multiple abilities including a double jump and the ability to
. Without this vital suit your character is just a man that got excavated from the depths of hell on a bloody quest for revenge.
On your adventure you have many tools in your arsenal from the amazing rocket launcher to the iconic Doom II double-barrel shotgun. Yet the main gimmick to this entry in the series is the glory kill, which can be used to kill an enemy with low health as well as gaining health yourself. This feature promotes fighting fiercly and staying near your enemies instead of hiding behind cover. The glory kill is also used as a mechanic for platforming. If you are around 10 feet away from your enemie and perform a glory kill it will proppel you to the enemie. There is a moment in the campain in which there is a jump you cannot clearalone  but there is a stationary Imp on the other side. So you shoot the Imp until the glory kill is available, double jump across, and then try to glory kill the Imp. It is rarely used in a sense like that in the game but presents many ways you can you the mechanics in the game to your benefit.
It is a very fun Action FPS that really makes you remember the original Doom style where you just run around and Rip And Tear.
I give Doom 2016 a Dark Souls II/Souls-Like Games. I would suggest waiting for a sale, I would say that it is not worth the $30 price tag but if you can get it for $20 or less it should be on your watch list.

DOOM has been one of the best video games I’ve played this year.
The gameplay definitely reminds me of the original doom while giving a new spin on the 1993 release with a new modern AAA game feel, the enemies are crazy fast-paced while you are more of a normal speed.
The reward and leveling system is great and the difficulty isn’t too hard but still challenging and fun, The Secrets and Mission Challenges are also amazing and give the game a nice replayability, with the option to replay any single mission once you have completed the game.
The graphics are wonderful but the game is definitely not too graphically intense making most machines easily able to run it. As I stated before you are slower than in the original doom but the gameplay and movement is still a crazy action-packed masterpiece where you are constantly running and gunning at tons of different types of demons.
The Multiplayer, on the other hand, is not necessarily bad but is definitely nothing special and is quite forgettable, with lots of other games releasing with great multiplayer these days I definitely don’t think DOOM’s stands out in any way.
In conclusion, the single-player campaign is lovely and the main reason you should buy this game. The multiplayer is not as bad as many people claim it to be, but nothing to ride home about. I would definitely recommend DOOM to anyone I know, especially considering its frequent 50% off sales.

I'll try to keep this brief -
As a Founder from back in 2011/2012 I've played a lot of MWO ever since. I've also played a lot of Mechwarrior dating back to the 90's (Mechwarrior 2: 31st Century Combat) and I can safely say this is the best core 'mech combat I've ever played. They have the feel down and the graphics and art assets are beautiful. Battlemechs have never looked or felt better.
Despite some publisher gimmicks (IGP has since dissolved and is no longer running things) PGI has continued to improve MWO at an accelerated pace and if you like giant stompy 'mechs you will enjoy the core combat.
If there are any negatives I'd sum them up by saying that this game is very likely not going to expand much past an arena 'mech shooter, as much as I wanted it to be something like Mechwarrior EvE Online (in terms of economy and depth) I just don't think that's going to happen.
Even so, I'm ok with that and the 'mech combat itself is pretty deep in that you can customize everything under the sun and again, it's very enjoyabe to play. I'd recommend this game easily if you like the concept or are intrigued and enjoy a 'thinking man's shooter'. Or just plain like blowing stuff up, because in MWO, lots of thing blow up and blow up beautifully.

Gameplay: Controlling Nick is way smoother than controlling Frank or Chuck, and overall, the game feels a lot more action-oriented. The ability to craft weapons (and save the game) anywhere is super convenient, and the addition of combo vehicles is a fun and helpful change in this newly fully open world game.

Bottom line: they finally figured out how to make Dead Rising fun!

TL;DR: 8/10 nep game, definitely get it if you're a fan of the series but it's also a good rpg for newcomers.
Now.. some reviews are saying this is "more of the same", but it really isn't. If you're coming from the Re;Birth games, know that there are some fundamental differences between this game and them. I'm on my second playthrough at the moment to get another ending, the first took about 60 hours. I'll list the pros and cons now:
PROS
+ Improved graphics. Didn't think I'd ever say that about a Neptunia game, but there you have it. You'll notice the improvements right away when you take control of Nep for the first time.
+ New cool enemies. They made a bunch of new monsters to keep things fresh.
+ There are fewer dungeons, but each is now massive compared to the previous games. Some have up to 4 different areas.
+ Improved battle gameplay. EXE gauge is back but balanced. It charges way faster but is depleted after every fight. EXE moves are now better balanced and considerably weaker, sometimes it's better to just use a skill or a normal combo instead of an EXE.
+ Combos have changed. There's no easy way to explain this, but the combos you build will depend on your weapon. You can't repeat the same move, and each of them has a certain condition that if met, will land a sure critical hit. Choosing weapons is not just about stats and area of attack anymore.
+ The controller vibrates with attacks, making them pretty satysfying.
+ Formation skills. Like EXEs, they aren't particularly strong but now you need to make an actual formation to use them (line, triangle or square) and the move will hit every enemy caught inside.
+ Scout system. Some may dislike this, some my like it. Instead of Stella's Dungeon, now you have multiple Scouts that you can send everywhere to get items for you and provide bonuses while you're in the dungeon they were deployed to. For example, if you want to grind for credits you can send every Scout with a Credits UP bonus to a dungeon you like and then go grind there. The Scouts will also find new dungeons, unlock new monsters in dungeons and bring back new scouts.
+ More challenging than the previous games.
+ A new epic type of boss battle. Not too difficult, but looks awesome!
+ New fun characters. I don't think anyone can dislike Steamax.
+ Great story. Lots of mysteries that you'll piece back together at the end.
CONS
- Routes and route building. In my opinion, a major flaw in this game's design. Now instead of just selecting from the map the dungeon or city you want to go, they are now connected by routes that your character will need to traverse to get from one place to another. This process may trigger random encounters and can take quite a bit of time if you want to go from a dungeon in Leanbox to another near Lowee, for example. It's extremely annoying and time consuming for no good reason.
- Party building. This may or may not be a small story spoiler, so read at your own risk.
- Investment. You can now invest in cities to unlock new plans, items for sale and events. Compared to the previous games where you would find this stuff while exploring.. this is a big money sink.
- There are fewer plans, from what I can tell. I ended up only making a few (6 or so) because for some reason the materials seemed very hard to come by.
- The Scouts can be bothersome to manage. You need to be in a city to get their report, not from the menu like Stella's Dungeon. Also minor (and expected) story spoiler:
- Characters won't level up if they aren't in the main fighting party. Some of them have the "Learning" ability that lets them do so, but most don't.
- Lily rank seems to increase very slowly when coupling. But now it also increases very quickly between all the four front row characters. So before coupling a pair, you might want to let them fight side by side first.
Overall this is a great addition to the Neptunia series. There are some mechanics that could be improved, but this is a mostly fresh game, different from what we're used to. I'm extremely happy that Idea Factory and Compile Heart came this far with Nep games. Now we wait for Cyber Dimension 4 GO!

I have not touched the online portion of the game but there's some points i'd like to discuss.
-The game is good, far better than the last game revolution and a wonderful finale to the Storm series as a whole.
-While playing this game, I have experienced the best looking Naruto Storm game to date. It may not get 4K resolution but every boss fight was a visual spectacle and surprisingly accurate to the manga (some changes but nothing to complain about.
- This is the shortest story mode so far. It covers the entirety of the final battle of the series. That's not a bad thing, it doesn't re-tread old ground and doesn't space out the bosses. There is an adventure mode where you can play old battles from the series (not boss battles) but that's mostly for some non-canon fun and some battles with twists on them. (including enemies with wildly increased stats as well as attacks that poison you)
- Gameplay has been the same with some new features. From revolution, the choosing of drive, ultimate attack, and awakening types are gone with the traditional fighting style gaining the new feature of switching your lead character in the middle of combat. This allows for crazier combos and the ability to switch up your fighting style in a flash. (using a puppet-user to keep opponents far away and switching to a melee fighter when they're up close is super fun)
I loved this series (excluding generations and revolution) and naruto is one of my favorite mangas. This is not a bad game. This is not the best game ever. If you love naruto or love this fighting game style, buy this game.
Final Verdict: 8/10 Great

Before I start, yes the game is locked to 30 fps, everyone knows this by now. As for the other problems, I seem to be a lucky one in this scenario, I've played for nearly 4 hours straight (3.8 according to Steam) and have not run into a single crash or even hitch/lag spike. The game ran at a completely solid 30 fps the whole time for me and never dipped below, and that includes the menu screens. The game runs great for me, only flaw still being the crappy 30fps cap. The way I look at it is, no matter what, at least on my computer, it runs flat out better then the console versions. So I am happy with the purchase, and if they patch in a 60 fps boost, even better.
As for gameplay, if you've played Storm 3, it's essentially the same gameplay, though now there is "armor breaking" similar to Soul Calibur. It's a very "basic" fighting game to the point where someone who is not very good at fighting games will actually feel like they are doing well. Of course it's one of those "easy to learn, hard to master" scenarios, but it still feels rewarding to new players none the less.
And as a final note, I will just say, to me, the visuals are just flat out GORGEOUS.

The rage is real with this one. When you think you got 3 stars it knocks you down with a .02 until next star at the end of the level, but feels so gratifying when all 3 pop up for you. Really tests how fast you can move while still being accurate with shurikens. Levels are really well designed, yet challenging enough that a 3 star run will take many tries. Boss levels are great and the added story with cut scenes are filled with great humor.

Extremely short levels that are simple to beat but very difficult to master. The game design is perfect at mitigating frustration; the controls are spot-on, restarts are instant and easily performed, and you can go back and replay levels for more stars (3 star ranking per level) at your leisure. You might swear as you restart but it's never truly enraging.
It's much like Mighty Switch Force in that it's bite-sized speedrunning requiring very precise actions to finish (though shorter and more precise and action packed than MSF).
A short game, but one that will take a bit longer to 3 star all levels, and it's a heck of a lot of fun; great deal of excitement-per-second. Leaderboards are a natural "endgame" for those inclined.

So, after tearing apart the Steam Link for the hunk of junk it seems to be, what does it's older brother, the Steam Controller, have to offer? The answer: much more than the black box over there. Though, it still seems to suffer a case of Valve-Is-Kinda-Bad-At-Hardware-Itis (yes, I know -itis stands for "inflammation", but what else would you use for a made-up disease?), however, at the very least, it's redeemable in various ways.
- A Valve made controller, so it's made with Steam in mind
- Very comfortable and large. Would fit well into big handed people
- Customizable button assignment
- Cute little start-up and shut down sounds that can be customized. :3
- The mousepads are smooth, making finger sliding on them not a pain
- The buttons are placed in a way that you don't need to controt your thumbs in weird ways to reach them
- Battery replacement is a hassle since the batteries get really cosy in there once you insert them
- The letter buttons are rather small
- Some older games, like Suguri, can not register the Steam Controller as a controller for some reason
- Doesn't feel very durable, but I wouldn't know since it hasn't broken (yet)
- Typing with it is annyoing, especially in games
- The mousepads make a weird static, radioactive sound, and there seems to be no way to turn that off
- You must be in Big Picture to use the Steam Controller (to it's fullest, at least)
- No second joystick, or D-Pad (technically)
- Has a bit of a learning curve to it, which is odd for a controller
- That price wow that is huge for a controller
To be honest, a normal controller makes a better controller, and a normal mouse makes a better mouse, but if you want a best of both worlds kind of deal, this is about your best option. It's not perfect at either job, but it is good at both of them. Think of the Steam Controller as Frankenstein's Monster in a more child-friendly interpretation: clunky, awkward, kinda ugly, and an abomination to nature, but admirable and reliable, just don't expect him to be the best at his jobs. He's good, but there are better alternatives out there. Still, there's something good in there about him, so you should accept him for what he is and what he's good for.
Does exactly what it is ment to do, and very well. I use this instead of my Xbox 360 controller as my main controller.

About me: I'm 38 and was a console gamer most of my life (xbox 360 was my last console) and had to use my xbox 360 controller to play controller-friendly games or use software to try to emulate a keyboard + mouse.

Pros
Flexibility: you can configure the games the way you want to play them
Options: you can use batteries (2 AA) or connect any cellphone USB cable
Community-built/developer-built configurations or even templates
Works well for big-handed guys like me
You can add non-steam games or emulators and use the controller with non-steam games
Battery life is long (using the alcaline batteries that come with it)
Cons
It is harder to use it if you are used to an xbox 360 controller

Excellent f2p game.  The best mechs in the game aren't locked out and can be freely bought using ingame currency you earn through playing.  There are hero mechs which can only be bought using premium currency only and the Stalker mech Misery is often used as an example of a p2w mech by cynics but it isn't actually that strong or popular.  All the new mechs that have been released recently are balanced quite well without being op.
The only thing that really hinders a pure f2per's progress in MWO are the mechbays.  You have to use premium currency to buy those if you wish to play the pokemech game and catch them all.  Fortunately there are often weekend events that give you lots of free stuff including mech bays, mc, or cbills.
My favourite part of MWO is the unit aspect.  That's the part that really hooked me.  Finding the right set of people to play with and winning tough fights with them.  You can always try to lonewolf it but you can only carry the pugs so hard for a time.
To test out the new player experience, I started an alt account and had a complete drop deck ready for Faction Play within a month, fully kitted with modules.  So the grind is pretty easy compared to other f2p out there.
My best advice for a new player is to check out the community guides, visit /r/outreachhpg on reddit, and to look at the mwo streams on twitch.  The learning curve is steep but there's lots of information out there to help.

I've been playing for about 8 months; I recommend the game and want to set realistic expectations.
This is a game that has a lot of depth. That also means it has a very steep learning curve. I started playing because friends were playing it, and it took me some time to appreciate the game.
This isn't a twitch-based shooter. Gameplay and mechs move much more slowly than what you might be used to in an FPS. This allows time to set up strategies and respond, and you aren't likely to go from 100% to death in only seconds (same with enemies), but it may feel too slow to some.
As a free to play game, you don't need to spend anything, but you'll have to play a lot to get what you want. This is alleviated by somewhat regular weekend events that offer rewards for playing.
Clan mechs have been balanced to be only as good as Inner Sphere mechs (not perfectly, but that's the aim). Clan mechs still have superior equipment, but Inner Sphere mechs have much stronger quirks to make up for it. If you're a lore purist and hate that idea, this probably isn't the game for you. If balance is more important to you, as it is to me, you can play Clan mechs and get the Clan flavor but not have an absurd advantage over Inner Sphere mechs.
There's a lot to love about this game. There are definitely things to hate about this game. I agree with the direction it's headed. I recommend it.

Exec summary:
Pros: Really good tactical shooter. Established canon/lore behind the Battletech game. Very passionate (fervent) player base, many good, some not as much.
Cons: Mech pack prices for real world dollars are high. Quite easy to spend more than retail game shelf price to buy a couple of mechs.
Long time fan of the games with Mechwarrior 2 my first (gifted) retail purchase of a CD-ROM game in 1995.
I'd been hanging for a Battletech, in-cockpit mech game since MW4 and was really excited to hear this was coming out. After touching the game briefly in 2012, then again at the start of 2015, I've spent the past 3 months solidly, read: obsessively, playing MWO Mercs and am having a blast. Roped two friends in who are long time gamers and are old enough to know better also.
The game has(had) a steep learning curve that PGI have now done a lot of good work to correct through the in-game tutorials. Additionally, the creation of a tier 5 for new players should help all those new to the game get accustomed to how it plays without being demolished by the veteran players.
As general advice, play the tutorial, play through all cadet bonus missiones and then play for another few days before making your first mech purchase. The immediate desire will be to get something as beefy as you can, but this may not work in your favour. The Medium class are a good jack of all trades class with some really good mechs available that hit hard and can run fast enough to escape some bad in-game decisions (which you will make initially).
The in game  currency is c-bills which are earned freely by completing games. The more you do in a game, the more cbills you win. This includes assisting and defending your team, scouting enemies, capturing objectives, etc. C-bills are used for purchasing both mechs and also all upgrades to them. Upgrading or fitting out your mech to make it yours is what sets this game apart from many others. Those familiar with the mech bay concept in previous titles will be right at home with the ability to swap out your engines, change your armour type and quantity, the weapon load out on your mech and much more. C-bill earnings are relatively slow, so spend wisely, but don't be afraid to make purchases. Sometimes changing out that engine to drop speed so you can add in that AC/20 can make all the difference to your success with the mech, which in turn earns you more cbills.
Customising your mech's exterior and other fluffy stuff can only be done with Merc Credits (MC) which are purchased with real money. They do add to the appeal of the mech and don't be surprised if you find yourself spending more on the fluff than you initially expect as your experience and mech collections grow.
There is a pretty involved skill tree in game for both the "pilot" and the mech you are piloting. Check out some of the great tutorials on the official forum at
to learn this side of the game. At a high level, you earn XP for every mech variant you pilot and earn General XP (GXP) for your character/account. The GXP is earned very slowly comparative to mech XP and is used to unlock weapon range and cooldown modules and many other things to help give you an advantage on the field. Once you have unlocked a module, you then have to purchase it to equip it to your mech, so bear that in mind. Mech XP on the other hand you use to unlock attributes on the mech you are piloting. These include faster torso twist speeds, better cooling, faster accel and deceleration and others. A mech that has been fully skilled up to Master level will outperform an identical configured mech that is not levelled, therefore giving you an advantage (pilot skills not considered).
The two game types include Faction Play, also known as Community Warfare, and Quick Play. Faction Play is best left till you have a few mechs of your own that you are fairly proficient with and are comfortable piloting. It is a harder game mode with generally more experienced opponents and greater chance of playing against fully organised teams. Speaking of, this is a team game so use Voice comms in game if you can. Call targets, try and help your team with information to help coordinate the defence or offence more effectively. Play with friends if you can, or make friends in game or through steam so you can play some coordinated matches. It will make a big difference to your experience in game.
Long time players will say this game is easy to learn but hard to master. You will learn your play style and what mechs suit, or adapt your play style to the mech you are piloting. It is a solid game that gives you a lot for very little. Alternatively if you have high disposable income it is a game that gives you little for a lot, with real world dollar, mech pack prices quite high.
Pros: Really good tactical shooter. Established canon/lore behind the Battletech game. Very passionate (fervent) player base, many good, some not as much. Mechs. Customisation of mechs. Faction Play rewarding and open to further expansion.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut is a breath of fresh air, especially after the disappointing sequel to one of my favourite games of all time, Deus Ex. Invisible War was a mess. BUT, Human Revolution rejuvenated the franchise after returning to the core roots and pillars of gameplay which were founded in the original. Stealth, action, meaningful choice and consequence events, and of course many other role playing elements. Adam Jensen, ex-SWAT and military, is an awesome protagonist, and is easily one of the franchises best characters, just as JC Denton was in the first game. Augmentations are back, and are as awesome as ever. These give Adam a slick feel, especially as time progresses, and allows endless possibilities with character development. Augmentations give the player new avenues into approaching objectives which allows the game to feel more open ended and replayable.
5th time playing it myself (1st time on PC), and I was still discovering new and rewarding approaches to tackle my objectives. The dialogue system, which is very similar to Mass Effect, works extremely well in giving the player more choice and is intricately designed, much like the new hacking system. As far as the story goes, it absolutely works with the themes of the game. Conspiracies, secret organisations and of course...
. And not to mention, the writing in the game is impeccable. One of the best scripts I've seen in a video game.
The "Directors Cut" tag has added quite a few benefits over the original, the most noticeable being the New Game+ mode which was widely requested by fans for a long time. It's here and it absolutely works. Being able to continue on from where the game ended and keeping all augmentations just makes the game more enjoyable and also a little bit easier, allowing the "Give me Deus Ex" difficulty to be quite manageable, as it is very tough (1 or 2 hits and its "See ya later, Frank"). Only weapons and other inventory items will have been discarded if New Game+ is activated, which is not a very big hassle as it would have made the game way too easy, and that is not at all good for a game like this. The new "Directors Cut" also adds developer commentary which is quite insightful as it delves deeper into how different aspects of the game were considered and made.
In conclusion, Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut is one of last generation’s best games, in MY OPINION. The rewarding gameplay, multiple approaches to objectives, and just the sheer amount of replayability along with the engaging and well written 20+ hour storyline makes for an extremely enjoyable and immersive experience, especially for fans of the franchise, like myself. The only downsides, which I haven't yet mentioned have to be that the game only rewards one approach of gameplay,
, which is actually fine because ultimately this is how Deus Ex should be played, and it’s the way I played it. The other disappointment is in the boss fights. Although the "Directors Cut" added more flexibility to these encounters, they still lacked in the multiple approach department, especially
, which isn't very much like Deus Ex. Lastly, the inclusion of the "Missing Link" DLC, adds to the games total play time, but nothing more as it is quite a disappointment. The "Missing Link" should not have been embedded into the main game, as it seems rather forced due to the tedious objectives that need to be completed in a constricted hub, which ultimately results in rather stale and boring gameplay. All in all, I wish I could go over everything, but this was a short review. Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Directors Cut is one hell of a game and can easily be respected as one of the series' best. Hardcore fan or newcomer, this game should be played by anyone who enjoys lasting and rewarding RPG's. Having played the PC and console version, the PC version is far superior.

DXHR is a tactical first person stealth shooter with several RPG elements. Like the original, DXHR encourages player choice with many branching paths all of which lead you to your objective. You could blast your way through guards, hack into and shut down the security, or simply hop in an air duct and avoid everything. However, the choices arent balanced which leads to one of the only issues the game faces. There is no incentive to fighting the bad guys. While there is choice, the game does lead towards the stealth option which has you crawling through ducts and sneaking around the perimeter of the map. However, that doesn't make the game any less satisfying. Avoiding all guards and cameras is every bit as fun as gunning through a room full of guards.
Another stregnth of the game is the preogression system. The augmentations are all useful and unique. Each one will give you a very useful tool against your enemies and as a result, the progression system is as rewarding as it could be.
DXHR also benefits from a engaging and well written story which is aided by a superb soundtrack and top-notch voice acting. The story has you, Adam Jensen, traveling around the world in search of the people who led an attack on the Sarif Industries lab months earlier. The narrative never lets up and will keep you searching for the truth all the way through. The entire game oozes atmosphere and style in every aspect, and the narrative is no different as it maintains a sense of mystery and conspiracy for the full 25 hour playtime.
DXHR is a great game, and is one of the best acion RPG's in years. The A+ gameplay is just part of this as the game suceeds in every aspect. This is a great game, and a worthy prequel to the fantatsic original.

Okay, let's do this thing. I'm somewhat ashamed that I bought this game. This does coincide with my interests, and I felt like supporting an indie dev. It also got endorsements from a few webcomics I read, which also lead me to take an interest in it. If it were five or ten dollars, I would feel less ashamed, since I wouldn't feel quite so ripped off. In a world where Chroma Squad is 15 bucks, this game is a hard sell. I am not a troll and I am not a hater; in fact, I am somebody who is probably the EXACT TARGET AUDIENCE of this game.
Now, I'll admit that I haven't played all of the paths. I stayed away from the anthro-heavy arcs because that isn't an interest of mine. I played through Dina, Yael, Dan, Nadine, and dabbled with a couple of the others.
Positives-
* Um... er... Dan's cute. I feel sorry for Yael. I could feel something for THOSE two characters.
* I'm REASONABLY sure I don't have cancer afterwards.
Okay, now that we've gotten the nice things to say out of the way, let's get to the meat of this. This is not a good game. This is not a good story. This is not good porn. It tries to be all three of these things and largely fails.
First, let's look at Gender Bender DNA Twister Extreme as a game. Now, I'm not going to get into the "are visual novels games" argument. I'll accept here that a visual novel qualifies as a game because it's at least somewhat interactive (you make choices and there are branching paths). The number of choices are fairly limited and a couple (I think specifically of Yael choosing to slack off or not before the accident) are pointless and have no impact. I love alternate universe stuff and thinking about what might have been, but none of these endings were worth the effort to make save states to see how things play out. The differences are either insignificant or horrifying. This is more of a game than, say, Sakura Spirits (watch the Game Grumps playthrough of that, it's hilarious), but I didn't feel engaged. This is because of...
The story. Oh Lord, the story. This game actually has a surprisingly in depth story, as the playable characters weave in and out of each others' paths. And that story, for me, crashes and burns because of the character Dina. (It would be on life support if she wasn't the horror that she is, but she kills it). Dina is selfish. She wanted to be a woman with enormous jugs, so she decided to make a serum to make that happen. Fair enough. The accident at the start of the game that forcibly transgendered everyone was unintentional. Fair enough. Dina's actions afterwards are horrible, however. She promises to help work on a cure. She instead works on something to make her more buxom. She tests that buxomizing formula on a character who wants nothing more than to turn back to normal on the theory that "big boobs are awesome, and Yael's a jerk anyway, so forcibly altering his body further is AOK." She enjoys messing with people, has no responsibility, no EMPATHY for the people whose lives she ruined and is never punished for any of this. She doesn't even lose her job and in fact becomes stinking rich. The game clearly wants me to think that she's a funny character. She is not. I hate her and everything she stands for. The rest of the cast are more or less "insert body type fetish here." Short and Busty? Dan. Sorta regular looking brunette? Yael. And so on and so on.
I mentioned earlier that the branching paths often ended up being horrifying. The game does not regard them as horrifying. The game regards them as funny or sexy. However, paths where a character loses everything they have and is forced to transform into a half human creature and be objectified all day to make a living is horrifying to me. Paths where a character makes it QUITE clear that they have no interest in making already large boobs larger and is then forced into it by someone who claims to love them is horrifying to me. Sure, the characters accept this, but they do not feel like human characters. Everyone is EXTREMELY blase about everything that happens to them. The characters I actually sorta liked were Yael and Dan, and that's because I thought that their reactions to the whole thing (being miserable, at least to start) made SENSE. The game also has numerous romantic pairings. These relationships are rapid and forced but we're supposed to take them as being extremely romantic because... shut up, that's why! Clearly these characters who have been women for a week are able to make lifelong romantic decisions with people they've often JUST met! Because that's healthy! If I were transgender, I'd be insulted by how seamless and easy this game makes the whole thing seem.
Now, you'd be justified in saying to me, "You fool, you're obsessing over nonsense like gameplay and story when clearly this is just mindless smut based on a transformation fetish! You're just supposed to turn off your brain and be turned on!" Well, (despite some comments I saw in the Steam forum to the contrary), that is exactly what this is supposed to be, though there's no law saying that your porno needs to have a character as hateful as Dina. Well, the art really gets in the way of that. I'm no artist and I couldn't do better. I fully recognize this. But the character models are often inconsistent from shot to shot. There are sexy ideas utterly ruined by the execution, as I think to myself, "Is that Yael? I can't be sure... yeah, that's the same jacket, I suppose." Especially jarring are the stylistic shifts you see in images where it ISN'T the character's "talking" body with a different outfit thrown on.
The art has been described as amateurish and wannabe anime. I can't disagree with this. If this game was still in alpha and the images were placeholders along the lines of "pants to be darkened," it'd be acceptable. If this were a free beta with the promise of future improvements, it'd be acceptable. I've seen no evidence of any future improvement in the art in the materials I've read. This game costs more than Final Fantasy VII (a primitive looking game with infinitely more style than this one) on Steam. There is no excuse. There are also a lot of head scratching artistic decisions. Characters like Dan and Ben are always feeling themselves up in public in scenes where they really SHOULDN'T be, based on the dialogue, just because the artist didn't draw another placeholder shot. The anthropomorphic characters are horrifying to look at because of how the hair is drawn. The ultrabusty characters are horrifying to look at, eliciting sympathy rather than attraction. Even with perfect line art, these decisions would still make the game hard to look at.
In closing, notice how many times I used the word horrifying in this? Yeah, there's a reason for that. It is. I could see someone having a good laugh at the whole thing, but for me, I just come away feeling bad for myself for even giving this a second glance. Also, anyone trying to fool themselves that this isn't a borderline hentai is in denial.
TL/DR: Do not buy. I wish I had a physical copy of the game so I could burn it.

The easy way to describe this game is "pretty much Civ in space". It would not be 100% correct, but it would be close enough to get my point across. This game is a 4X game, and a good one at that.
The main difference from the aforementioned Civ (aside from the whole thing being set in space) is probably in the combat. When combat occurs in Civ, you have the two units face off against the other, the one with the highest combat score after applying bonuses wins, and the other one takes more damage. Here the battles are fought fleet vs fleet, rather than ship vs ship, but that is just the beginning. Before a combat, three orders are given, which are then carried out during the battle, giving various bonuses and possibly countering the opponent's orders. This way, a technically inferior fleet may still have a chance if used correctly.
There is also the hero system, which allows you to recruit heroes to assign either as governors of star systems or as commanders of fleets, giving various bonuses.
Then there is the fact that the factions are so different, offering very diverse playstyles as well as visuals.
All in all, this is the best Space 4X I've played since GalCiv2.

Don't get me wrong, I love DOOM and ID software but this game was just... underwhelming. First of all, I absolutely adore the new graphics and the music, but only one hour in I can see where ID and Bethesda failed.
Guns like the Shotgun and Plasma rifle are pathetically weak - with even the weakest enemies being bullet sponges - taking multiple point-blank shots to the head and still surviving. Combat is less fast-paced and more focused on longevity and ammo preservation, with the same engagements repeating over and over again. The game seems to rely on Melee functionality being more powerful than guns, rendering some weapons defunct, leaving the player with only one strategy to play - Shoot, punch them in the face and continue to the next one. Sometimes a grenade or burst fire is added in to spice things up, but everything else just becomes stale and repetitive. Sometimes the game grinds right down to a halt as the linear map design stops and turns into a platformer. The game becomes really frustrating with the addition of the climbing mechanic. Not only do I have to search left and right when I get stuck, but I have to worry about up and down, too. Though it does add some interesting possibilities for secrets and combat manoeuvrability.
When it comes to story, I was pleasantly surprised by the addition of a Human antagonist, though the story still seems a little underwhelming compared to the previous games. The length of the game is appreciated, though.
The Graphics and Sounds are astonishing however, with the accurate portrayal of Weapons in accordance with their power. Each crunch and splatter reverberates satisfyingly in High quality surround-sound. A welcome addition.
All in all, the game is definitely engaging. Although the gunplay is a bit iffy and the glory kills look like I'm stomping on a wet sponge, there's definitely an experience to be had, just don't expect any similarity to the previous game, as new DOOM takes the series into a whole new (Somewhat unprecedented) direction.

When playing games that are designed for gamepads the Steam Controller is a mixed bag.  Sometimes the remappable controls and extra functions allow a player to do great things, but sometimes it's basically a slightly worse Xbox pad.
When playing games that were not designed for gamepads is where this thing shines.  If you can't make it work with the Steam Controller you won't be able to make it work with any other gamepad either.

The Steam Controller is designed to replace mouse & keyboard for users playing PC games on a different monitor.
I purchased a Steam Controller to fill a single desire:
This controller was not designed to replace current, console controllers.  I feel it was designed with the following decision points:
1)  Compliment the Steam Box's market entry into living room / group based entertainment.
2)  Act as a substitute for mouse+keyboard (m+k).
3)  Outperform other controllers with aiming precision through use of the touch pads.
4)  Have an interface with unprecedented customization that can be changed on the fly.
The Steam Controller has successfully met each of these goals.  However, I made the mistake of not evaluating this purchase based on my own needs.  I loved the idea of this controller having full support from Steam and having the customization options that a PC environment provides.  Unfortunately, when evaluated to the controller's execution, my needs were incompatible.
I do not have a fancy living room or large, non-PC monitor.  I strictly do everything from the confines of my home-office.  I enjoy using a traditional Windows-looking Windows setting (95/98/XP/7)... god forbid this day and age.
I love m+k.  I have not a single drop of desire to replace it.  For FPS or any first person game, I will be playing on PC using m+k.  For retro, 2D, platforming, or any adventure games, I prefer using a traditional, but modern controller such as Sony's DualShock or Microsoft's XBox 360 designs.
My hands are above-average size for Caucasians.  I will not say "large" or "huge"; they are not that.  Compared to a 6'5 athlete, they're not big.  Compared to a 5'0-5'5 jockey, they're big.  I cannot fathom how anyone with average or below average size hands will want to use this.  The Steam Controller's layout of the XYAB buttons are too close to center of the pad.  My thumb cannot comfortably reach the X button without shifting across the pad.  The top Left and Right shoulder (L1 &R1)  buttons are not designed well.  There is no grip- your fingers will slip down to the LR trigger (L2&R2) buttons constantly.  The L1R1 buttons also require a considerably strong click motion with little button movement.  Compared to a controller where you feel the button move down; this will inhibit a bit of gameplay ability as the user does not feel the confirmation of the press.
Big Picture is meant to be utilized on a non PC monitor.  It is designed for a non m+k user to interact with Steam.  Menu placement is what it is- not similar to PC Steam.  You will need to play around with it.  That said, if you are on a PC, why on earth would you turn this interface on?  Trying to alt-tab out of Big Picture is a mess and trying to accomplish any PC-related tasks is an unnecessary mess.
To customize your Steam Controller, you need to be in Big Picture.  You can still play games with your Steam Controller without it, but any keybind settings or button configurations are not assessable without it.  As of early June 2016, additional button configuration options have been added.  You can now set how buttons react when performing various types of button presses.  The user creates these activator commands on how a button press functions depending on the type of input, such as Regular Presses, Long Presses, and Released Presses.  While an excellent, excellent, excellent customization feature- the instructions on what each option does are completely non-existent.  There are no tutorials or meaningful examples to teach the user what each option does or how long a time delay range is.  Example:
For the average user, including myself, maybe an explanation of what the flying hell the word "haptics" means would be nice?  Maybe an example of what high haptics would be like, or low haptics, or, Jesus, how about limp haptics?  Should I see my doctor if I notice my haptics is limp?  Does it go limp?  I don't know.  I don't know what the word "haptics" means.
The button sliders for time delays:  there's no numbers.  There's no dancing dot showing time.  How in ♥♥♥♥♥ name am I supposed to know what the time changes are in this slider?  It doesn't make sense.  For a controller designed to be used by some person in their living room, away from a m+k setting, it doesn't make sense.  Why are there no examples?
____________
The Steam Controller is worth investigating if you plan on playing FPS or PC-designed games away from a traditional m+k environment.  Unfortunately, I will not be recommending it.  I don't feel it is shoddy.  The controller was designed under specific goals and I believe those goals were met.  Unfortunately for me, that is not what I want in a controller.

I want to start off with saying this is my first Dungeons game.  I am a big Blizzard fan overall, I have played every Warcraft game starting back on DOS, and this is the first game similar I have played that gives me the same kind of feeling I got playing Warcraft 2 or Warcraft 3, whilie making fun with those games.  Obviously the creators are fans of Blizzard and this game is a fun way of being creative while creating something similar but their own.
Overall it is fun, however it is somewhat limited by very few gameplay modes, once you beat the campaign, it doesn't feel like there is much left to do.  Skirmish mode is lacking in features, and I have yet to play the multiplayer aspect of the game, however I see great potential of them releasing more content to correct the bland feeling left over once you finish the initial game.
Skirmish would benifit from having more modes, and more map features, for instance, most of the overworld maps only have a few enemy camps that send troops, and the hero portals inside the dungeons are limited to one portal and one entrance.  If you like building up the dungeon and benefitiing from the use of traps and mazes, there isn't much point in replaying if you can easily kill the enemies with a few ice crushers before they even become a threat.  They implement diamon mines in all underworld areas, but having unlimited gold is pointless when your dungeon can easily be protected by just a few well placed traps once you are built up.
Perhaps new enemies like sappers that can destroy doors and traps, or even drill tanks that can carve out walls for invading enemies would be something to expand the danger in defending your dungeon after a certain level.  Or even have camp respawning in the overworld that increase level on endless.
More map variation would be nice as well.  It is always the same terrain after the campain is over.
Great game, I look forward to content DLC preferably in the form of more campaigns, but I am more likely to spend my free time playing Starcraft 2.

BUGS

This game, had potential.
The main flaw is literally the F2P model. Obviously they have to make money somehow, but all we end up with is a TF2 style game with lots of pointless classes that u have to level (and then comes the requirement to pay to compete). The game in my opinion would be better with a single class, the pathfinder as it's fun and requires skill to use and can complete all the different objectives in the game, such as flag defense and offense.
The addition of generators and turrets that need repairing is really not that useful. The tech spends most time repairing (it takes 30+ seconds to repair) but it takes 5 seconds to destroy by the "infiltrator" (aka spy) class which can remain hidden for a fair time. So, it takes the tech 1 min 30+ to repair what took the spy class 15 seconds. Eventually you feel it's not worth the effort anymore. Sometimes you can spent ages having a battle with the spy or 2, not even getting outside of the generator room the entire game.
The heavy class, can sit outside the range of the turrets and destroy them from long range, obsoleting the point of turrets. Another flaw that makes the tech slightly redundant.
The soldier class has a thumper (aka a sort of grenade launcher) and IIRC a machine gun, making it way stronger than the pathfinder, at least at lower levels.
The problem with all the other classes is they are too imba and don't require skill. Unfortunately you can find yourself being pummelled by someone who has a weapon with a higher dispersal or a rapid fire weapon, such as SMGs or even chain guns (machine guns).
There is in fact, no need to go faster in this game because the strongest and most imba classes are the slower ones!
This game will never become big because the "levelling" element makes it unsuitable for competitive play and the lack of a level playing field, where the difference is in the players skill.

I’ve given this game a good chance, getting through several story-lines with multiple characters, and I can honestly say that it has captivated me into wanting to play more. Alot of it is fan service, I will admit, but the amount of individual scenes, characters, personalities, and stories that manage to link up to one-another in some fashion is to me mind boggling.
I recommend this game to anyone who does have even minor interests in gender transformation, anthropomorphic transformation, chest expansion, or same sex romances/multiple romances. Also, I highly recommend this for someone who loves a complex story tree that branches out into so many different avenue but still manages to keep the overall story intact.
Yes, I will admit that the art and stories are not on par with that of Nekopara or If My Heart Had Wings, but it is a very close second to me. Though the story is leagues ahead from such trash as the Sakura Spirit/Angles...
Give the Gender Bender a whirl, I believe in time you’ll come to enjoy the transformation as much as the characters. I look forward to the Rose story arch and hope to see more for this developer in the future. Awesome job guy!
As a P.S. to those who are interested (or care), I’m a woman and I still enjoy this game. It’s nice to think of guys being able to see the world from our point of view.
Edit 1: It has been a long while since I have played as I was waiting for the Russell update, then life happened and I was pleasantly surprised  by the addition of Aleanne.
First, let me say that the game does get better as you play it! Not only in story, but in art as well. You can see the artist improve with each new update and I find it prenominal. Like watching an artists progression only through a story telling media.
I will admit that it would be nice to see the entire game redone to fit the new and improved work, but that would be asking for an almost complete overhaul every time the game is updated. Not feasible in the slightest with the pittance that is being charged for this game.
Second, I hate to say that Aleanne is a little disappointing; with a story that feels rushed and a good deal of typos and incongruities, it’s not as captivating as the previous. But then I assume it would be hard to follow up after Russell, which is a really fun pit of story/puzzle.
Regardless, this bit of negative does not tarnish the game as a whole. It is still a wonderful game that will captivate and keep you going for a lot longer than most of the story games out there. I still highly recommend this game and look forward to the Scarlett update and any others that may follow. Keep going Dev, you’re doing amazingly despite what a few haters may think!

I love this game.  I saw the videos, when it was first being introduced and didn't think my old PC would handle it. I planned to get it once I've upgraded. A year later, I'm still using my old LGA775 PC with 3ghz q9650 oc'ed at 3.7ghz and 8gb of ram.  I bought a GTX960 4GB ssc GPU to run my older games and then I saw that DOOM 2016 was available to play for free, one weekend.
I said, what the heck and after spending a day and a half downlading it, I boot the game up, expecting myself to laugh for a possibly super choppy experience.  Whatdaya know Joe?  The game ran BEAUTIFULLY on it's default settings (which was a mix of medium to high settings, with textures set on ultra thanks to my 4gb gpu) and I WAS JUST BLOWN AWAY.
Fast, furious and pure rock and roll! I felt like a kid again!
The single player campaign is action packed fun, with amazing visuals (even at med settings, this game looks fantastic!), speed that took getting used to, wild demons and bad♥♥♥♥♥weaponry.
I finished the game recently and can now say, that the experience was great from start to finish.  I'm a big fan of the multiplayer mode as well and though it's not a perfect mode, I've had a lot of fun with it.
The Snap Maps mode, which is a creator zone, where fans can create their own maps and share them with the gaming community, deserves way more love than its getting now, because it is enriched with great features to keep you coming back to DOOM, even after you've achieved everything in the campaign and MP modes.
Bottom line is, no game is perfect. But there's always that one game that you know you love so much, despite any of its drawbacks. For me, it's DOOM 2016.  I definitely recommend it.

A counter point to the majority of negative reviews.  Name me a company that has never, and I mean never, failed to deliver on every promise they make and I'll show you an elephant riding in a Miata with Elvis.  That being said, I myself was a founder way back when, played it off and on.  Recently I've been playing it everyday and I'll tell you this, the game today is far more superior to the one I helped fund.
The graphics are well done and don't cause meltdowns in older computers.  The sound quality is very good, turn up your base and fire an AC20, if that doesnt get you hard....
The community, much like any other game has its elitest players, it's angry players, its laid back players and its clueless players.  The game now seperates these people into different tiers.  IF you are new you start in tier 5, it places you in games with others from your tier and occasionally a few people from a tier above you so you're not going to get roflstomped by someone who is in Redbull beast mode.  As you get better your experience goes up and you eventually make it to the next tier, but, there is nothing saying you have to.
People have claimed the game is a P2W.  Yes the "hero" mechs do have the occasional perk that makes it slightly better than the standard variants but they never outshine everything on the battlefield.  People talk about the (G) variant of some mechs, ones that costed I want to say $500 dollars or something like that, these mechs arent much better than their standard models either, the just look like giant Oscar awards (they're gold in colour). The first 25 games you play you get a lot of free C-Bills (standard MWO currency) even if you lose, you end up with enough to nearly buy any mech and with the introduction of the new tutorial system, you learn and earn as well.  There is nothing that says you have to spend real money to be competative.
MC (Mechwarrior Currency) is the premium currency.  You can use it to buy mechs, a wide variety of camo patterns and a very large selection of colours for said camo.  You can also buy premium time with it as well as consumables (Artillery strikes, UAVs etc. etc. etc.)  Premium time gives you 30% boost on your C-Bill earnings for a match as well as XP and GXP (general XP)  Again, you don't have to buy MC if you don't want to, you will still make money and XP, it just takes a wee bit longer depending on how well you matches go.
To all you jaded players, PGI dropped the ball a few times, no one is arguing that.  To lambast a game though that many of you freely admit you don't play anymore is just petty, childish if you will.  To the new players considering trying it, give it a go.  There are trial mechs you can use for every weight class as well as both Clan and Inner Sphere (IS) chassis.  The worst that could happen is you either become addicted to the game or you uninstall it.
Balanced free to play. Strategic learning curve. Worth the grind. Make purchases after you learn on the trial Mechs. Odds are you will earn a couple before you package up.

There's a very good chance you already know what this game is about, so I'm gonna keep it short and assume you know what I'm talking about.
So basically Megadimension Neptunia VII has two major areas worth discussing, and those would be the gameplay and the art/plot/voice acting/character design/music.
The gameplay is more or less what you'd expect, standard jrpg turn based battles, but they changed a lot of things. EXE bar charges quicker but resets every battle, the map is connected by roads, you can invest, send scouts around, play neplunker, they removed that thing that tells you where the items drop, there are epic as ♥♥♥♥ battles against giant enemies, you can break body parts --- The list would be very long. Some of those changes are good, some aren't, and you're gonna find many complaints about said elements, but let me tell you something.
It doesn't really matter if they are good or bad. The fact that they are there is to make you feel you're playing something new, to make you understand that they didn't just copypaste RE;Birth 3. And I believe it worked: the game feels fresh, even if it's basically the same Neptunia game in the end.
As for the second area, well, it's AMAZING. The music is a masterpiece, the plot is meh (not bad, but not that exciting either), new characters are awesome (Uzume is such a great one I couldn't believe it), the art and animation is really funny and greatly improved, and the voice acting is the stuff of legends. You know how there are some characters that are not that interesting like Ram or Nepgear? Well forget all that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ because they now have GREAT lines and are voiced in a way that you can't do anything else but love them.
Something I was a little disappointed with was the video quality for the video sequences. They feel weird, the colors are strange looking, IDK.
Also there are some new drawings for characters like Vert and Noire, they are not at an angle but stare directly at you, and they look a little puffy and silly. The others are good, but those two are way worse.
Overall, yes, definitely buy this game. It's the most fun I've had since a very long time.
And it has Nep Nep in it, so that should be enough by itself.
