What I like best about H6 is the tone. It's a mixture of horror and humor that is very well balanced to keep you laughing while at the same time just constantly uneasy. The character descriptions are especially good; whoever is writing those deserves a raise. Interacting with other factions diplomatically is a real treat. Do yourself a favor and really read all the text presented at you as you play. At any given point you realize you're in a blend of scifi parody and terrifying dystopia where technology is your last best hope for humanity but also incredibly dangerous. In that sense, I am reminded of XCOM, and the base-building and research gameplay reminds me of it as well. Other reviewers talking about FTL are right on the money, too, both in artistic style and game theme.
The story is compelling, but the game also has a wonderful soundtrack to really get you in the mood. It evokes a retro era while being unmistakably scifi with an epic scale. I'm a Kickstarter backer, and honestly the reward I am most looking forward to getting is a download of the soundtrack.
The game is currently in Early Access, so it should go without saying there are still bugs and balance issues, but the developers are addressing these quickly. I've been impressed with their professionalism and enthusiasm. The game is not yet content-complete, but it'll get there, and it promises to be highly moddable in the future. They've made a lot of tweaks to gameplay and the UI based on feedback, and I'm confident they're a talented and dedicated team.

If it sounds like a game you might be interested in, you'll probably really love it. There are other games out there with similar gameplay elements, though I feel there's some useful innovations here. The quality of art, writing, and music are what really make this game shine.

Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is a space strategy game from Massive Damage. Artefacts of an ancient, highly advanced civilization have been left scattered throughout occupied space. Halcyon 6, a derelict starbase, is one such artefact. Now in the hands of the Human Federation, Halcyon 6 is yours to command and restore, but with several factions around you, including a mysterious alien force, it’s going to be difficult to restore the base and protect nearby human settlements.
Visually, Halcyon 6 is fantastic. The pixel graphics are awesome, the menus and UI are great too. The design, though, is what really makes the visual side of things shine. The different factions are all well thought out and they look awesome, plus the different factions all have their own ships which are also very well designed.
Halcyon 6’s gameplay consists of several different elements which come together to create one game. Firstly, we have base building a la XCOM. You clear out rooms on the starbase which can then be used to house anything from power generators to ship hangars. Then we have a research tree similar to the one in Civilization: Beyond Earth (though Halcyon 6’s actually makes sense) through which you can unlock new ships, new rooms as well as improve fuel usage etc. Research is carried out instantly but it costs Materials and Dark Matter (two of the three resources in the game, they’re also used to build new ships and rooms though ships and rooms also require a certain number of humans to work on them, more humans can be found at colonies from which you can evacuate them). Fuel is the third resource which is consumed by fleets when you send them out. The game’s hints of FTL come from the different factions and the overall feel and the game’s design. The similarities also extend to the map which is a reasonably large portion of space filled with different sectors. When you send out a fleet and they move around the map is when time moves (though you can also unpause the game to hurry along any construction). Enemies and neutral or friendly ships can only move when time is unpaused so pausing the game can be used as a way to assess what’s going on and plan for any incoming attacks.
Combat is turn-based and can be up to 3v3 ships (though if you move to a sector with multiple groups on enemies you’ll have to fight one after the other). You have three different ship classes, each with a corresponding crew member class, there’s: Science, Engineering and Tactical. Each class has specific skills that you can unlock (and level up with your character) and each ship has three default skills as well which also improve when you level up. Skills usually inflict damage on a single target (though there are group attacks as well as buff skills for yourself/team) and they also inflict, exploit or inflict on-self different effects (usually a mixture of the three). Inflicting something generally deals damage over time or has some kind of status effect, for example you can disable a ship for a number of turns or damage the hull which deals a certain amount of damage over a number of turns. Other skills will then exploit these effects to create combos which deal considerably more damage than usual. For example, one of my Science ships can disable sensors which can then be exploited by my Tactical ships to deal considerably more damage than usual. To be effective in combat (and not get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you) you’ll need to use these combos as much as possible. Inflict on-self will inflict a negative (occasionally positive) status effect on you. Combat can be very challenging so it’s important to make sure you’re prepared before you can and attack something, especially as you can’t save/quit once you’ve entered combat (though you can at any other time).
When you unlock a new crew member slot, you’ll be able to choose between the three classes for what you want. Each crew member has specific ship and ground combat skills that they can unlock later when they level up. Ground combat works in the same way as space combat and occurs when enemies are found after clearing out a room. Your crew members earn experience, and in turn level up, by surviving combat and they’ll sometimes earn bonuses such as a damage increase against certain factions as well.
Halycon 6 does have a story and it plays out in a similar way to XCOM. Like with XCOM, you can pick and choose when you want to progress with the story of the currently available first act (act two and three will be added later). The other factions will become more powerful over time but rushing in can be just as bad as taking too long. The story progresses through main missions and side missions. Side missions usually consist of simply protecting a human colony from a fleet of pirates or aliens but there are other tasks you’ll have to complete too, such as defending your starbase from an attacker (incredibly important since the humans on-board will gradually die while you’re being attacked). There are a couple of different storylines running through it so you may receive several main missions at once which usually require a couple of extra steps than a side mission. I won’t go into any more details to avoid spoilers though I will say that the first act already offers quite a lot which is obviously stretched out by the fact you can go through it at your own pace.
Completing missions awards you with valuable resources and this is one of the three ways you can get resources in the game. You can also visit human colonies that have resource extraction facilities (fuel, materials and dark matter) which will collect a certain amount of resources for you to collect, once you’ve collected them the colony will begin producing more. The starbase also produces resources though it does this incredibly slowly to begin with, you’ll need to complete research for this to be a viable means of collecting the amount of resources you need. Just like in XCOM and FTL, resource management is INCREDIBLY important. Run out of fuel and you can’t send your fleet out. Run out of dark matter, you can’t repair your ships. Run out of dark matter and materials you can’t build anything new. Run out of everything…well you’re just screwed.
Just a couple more things to wrap up. The game is pretty difficult to begin with and you’ll probably die quite quickly but once you’ve got the hang of things it’s a manageable difficulty. The soundtrack is excellent. Controls are basic, you don’t have to use anything other than your mouse but there are also helpful hotkeys. And lastly, despite being an Early Access game I didn’t encounter any bugs while playing it.
Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is an excellent, well designed, space strategy game with great gameplay, a good amount of content (with more to come) and an interesting story. If you’re a fan of strategy games you’ll definitely like this, even in its Early Access state.

The traps might also need to be a bit weaker (or they could add a trap resistance stat for multiplayer only).Oh and no regen on the dungeonheart (in deathmatch if it became a thing). There was a time when Dungeon Keeper was a thing and everyone was happy about that. Developed by serial success artists, Bullfrog, Dungeon Keeper made you the bad guy, trapped you underground and released floods of do-gooders to pinch your gold and slaughter your troops. So you diligently mined out rooms, produced traps and bulked up your army of goblins, spiders and ghosts to thwart them. Many hours were lost to malicious chuckling, a sequel was produced and loved by all, and evil overlords destroyed all that was good worldwide. Then EA came along and ruined a good thing, as EA are wont to do. The series and the genre it championed were forgotten about for decades, until an awful mobile port dripping with beloved EA staples like microtransactions came along to be derided by a sneering fanbase.
While the founding title was cut down in its prime by a mixture of corporate greed and general incompetence (I’m not bitter), other titles have taken up the mantle from time to time to try to appeal to Keeper’s now nomadic fanbase. Games like Craft the World, Evil Genius and War for the Overworld are all worth a mention, but so too is the Dungeon series. The initial release was a clumsy but honest tribute to Bullfrog’s fallen juggernaut that did little more than clumsily ape its inspiration. The second release tried to do more, by allowing your rampaging hoards to leave the murky underground and reign chaos on the world above. The third game offers more of the same.
It would be a disservice to suggest that Dungeons III is just the second game with a few new maps lobbed in (especially when Dungeons II has that rarest of things; genuinely good DLC campaign extensions that do just that without the need for a sequel). There are changes afoot. For one, there is a much greater number and variety of missions that often go above and beyond just having you patiently build an unstoppable force and roll over everything when the time’s right. One early mission pits you against a fortified town filled with formidable gluttons. The only way to break their defences is to routinely hijack their food shipments until you starve them out and can put them to the sword. Another asks you to collect various ingredients from both the under and overworld to sacrifice so that you can summon a new demon ally. Another introduces a day/night cycle that has you under siege from hardy foes by day, but sees them exhausted at night, allowing you to creep around relatively unchallenged while they slumber and you destroy all their stuff.
Trying to juggle both aspects of the experience was a staple of the previous Dungeons game, but only up to an extent. Now the two halves are more symbiotic and feel much more like a whole.
In Dungeons II, you were free to lurk in your lair, building up your army and slaughtering the occasional band of heroes who journeyed into your depths in the name of goodness until you wanted to venture out. Some of that remains the same: the construction of your lair and the smooth management of your numerous facilities continues to be the foundation of a worthwhile army of evilness. You still need a constant supply of mined gold to pay wages or make purchases. Your troops need to be housed, fed and maintained. Want to start building traps to chip away at would-be defenders? You’ll need the machinery to produce it and the manpower to put it all in place. Want to start using the corpses of your enemies to animate a few zombies? You’ll need a graveyard for that.

Endless Space is endless fun! A game with both windows and osx support, Endless space is your standard galactic empire building "turn based" strategy game. It is pretty in presentation and relatively straightforward to get into, although it falls short in content. It offers a large variety of faction customization options and play styles although the game simply boils down to galactic conquest. The story and single player experience is virtually non-existent, and as such it is a game probably better played online. It is a moderately active community at the time of writing this, however it should be noted that games take several hours to complete and often players leaving or the game crashing can be a frustrating experience. Returning to the gameplay it is about planetary colonization, expansion, resource management and of course combat. The former is all quite self explanatory and is a little difficult to optimize without spending a couple hours of trial and error, the latter being the combat takes place in ship engagements in which your ships fight and you give orders in a series of phases, ultimately it is the orders that matter and the combat is essentially just a cutscene displaying the results of your combat selections. Overall a decent game, it is definitely a very niche game so unless you are familiar to this style of galactic conquest games it or are interested in seeing what they are all about, it is not for you. If that is your thing however Endless Space is a decent entry in the genre.

Many negative reviews are bashing the game for poor performance.  During my playthrough of the game there were a couple frame drops mostly when there was a lot happening on the screen, which has been the case for almost all Storm games. In addition, many reviews are reviewing the game on performance alone with little to no playtime.  This Storm game itteration was made to be more graphically intensive, which it is. However, I don't even have a high end PC and I am able to run the game perfectly fine.  So people claiming that the game is not running on an up to date graphics card and processor, I find it very hard to believe.   I am by no means saying the game couldn't use some optimization.  It can, but I also think people need to understand that the minimum requirements might not be good enough for this game.
If you are still sceptical about purchasing the game because of mixed reviews, I will almost gurantee the negative reviews will be flushed out by those who have finsihed the game, and also those who are aware of what their computers can handle in the next couple of months after release.

Dead Rising 3 is actually a really good game in my opinion.
Better than the first one? Yes and no.
Better than the second? Yes and no but mostly yes in my opinion.
Better than the fourth one? Totally.
So what makes it better than the previous ones?
- Better gameplay overall.
- Good pace, not too fast nor too slow unlike the previous ones which are kind of too slow in my opinion, keeping in mind that Dead Rising isn't a fast paced game, I personally think that this one is just right.
- Better textures of course.
- Skills, even though I prefer the system from the first one where you would get one randomly when leveling up, what's good about this one? The quantity of skills, they look pretty cool, you can always set the difficulty higher if you find it too easy but let's be honest, Dead Rising never were hard games anyway.
- More content overall.
- Better (and also good) music.
What's better in the previous ones?
- Better characters
- Better psychos
- There are other things but I can't remember them all right now.
Cons:
- Map is kind of boring, I mean, lot of roads are blocked, it's not as open as the previous ones which had more freedom.
- Mouse acceleration... Why? Seriously, why? What's the idea behind it? The person who decided that must be braindead, no but seriously, you can't aim at all and it just feel weird, I would really love to know why they do that and how does some people like it this way, at least, there's a fix online, it's not perfect, it will still feel like a console game but it's better than nothing am I right?
- 30 fps locked... Once again, the same as mouse acceleration, why is it even there? cinematics? Why not adding a slider in the settings for the people who wants to lock their fps?  Don't get me wrong, I do lock my fps to 60 because there isn't no purpose in locking it higher since my monitor hz is 60, if it would be 144, I'd lock it at 144, and above 144, it is useless, you'll just overheat your pc and it will eat energy for nothing, but locking it at 30 is seriously dumb, anyway, there's also a fix, a working one, just find it on google.
- Small map, first Dead Rising map is really good but very small, second Dead Rising map was also very small and I honestly did not like it that much not because it was bad but it needed more of a outside world pretty much like in the first game, Dead Rising 3 map is good, nothing epic, just good, but very small.
- There's lot of weapons but there are combos from the original that are not in this game, not a disaster but would have been cool to find all of them again.
7.8/10 - Honestly, not everyone may think that the game is good nor that it deserves at least 7.8/10 but honestly, I do like it.

Don't get me wrong, I love DOOM and ID software but this game was just... underwhelming. First of all, I absolutely adore the new graphics and the music, but only one hour in I can see where ID and Bethesda failed.
Guns like the Shotgun and Plasma rifle are pathetically weak - with even the weakest enemies being bullet sponges - taking multiple point-blank shots to the head and still surviving. Combat is less fast-paced and more focused on longevity and ammo preservation, with the same engagements repeating over and over again. The game seems to rely on Melee functionality being more powerful than guns, rendering some weapons defunct, leaving the player with only one strategy to play - Shoot, punch them in the face and continue to the next one. Sometimes a grenade or burst fire is added in to spice things up, but everything else just becomes stale and repetitive. Sometimes the game grinds right down to a halt as the linear map design stops and turns into a platformer. The game becomes really frustrating with the addition of the climbing mechanic. Not only do I have to search left and right when I get stuck, but I have to worry about up and down, too. Though it does add some interesting possibilities for secrets and combat manoeuvrability.
When it comes to story, I was pleasantly surprised by the addition of a Human antagonist, though the story still seems a little underwhelming compared to the previous games. The length of the game is appreciated, though.
The Graphics and Sounds are astonishing however, with the accurate portrayal of Weapons in accordance with their power. Each crunch and splatter reverberates satisfyingly in High quality surround-sound. A welcome addition.
All in all, the game is definitely engaging. Although the gunplay is a bit iffy and the glory kills look like I'm stomping on a wet sponge, there's definitely an experience to be had, just don't expect any similarity to the previous game, as new DOOM takes the series into a whole new (Somewhat unprecedented) direction.

That game is a fine example of a great idea, which is unfortunately poorly executed. I mean, first it really looks like a promising game. You can get to unlock some stores, invest some money to improve your income, get a loan if you need etc. Then, when you click to unpause, you realize where you've just got yourself into...
Well, how could I describe it in a practical manner? I guess that the best way, it would be to call it a "micro-management fest". That's because you actually gotta click on every single store that you have every day, in order to collect the cash that you make. At the beginning, it's no big deal, but just wait a lil' while and you'll see what madness it is. Oh, and if one reason isn't more than enough, you also have to click often to upgrade your stores as they level up (increasing stock and quality of items). So, pick up these two chaotic ingredients, blend them up and now you have a cocktail from hell. Of course, we can't forget to put a cherry inside of it: This game is one of those notorious achievements spammers. That by itself isn't really a big issue, except that the developers should have never inserted the damn buttons that you have to click on all the time, precisely at the right corner of the screen.
Ok, what else... There're also some broken achievements. That's because there're some you can only unlock after building a certain combination of stores. No matter how many times you try, they simply won't work. This game should also be known as one of those "FPS killers", because depending on how big your mall is, things will become really sluggish, and that can definitely wear on your patience (kinda like adding insult to injury). Hmm, there're some glitches too. I've seen some customers walking on air for whatever reason; there were times where I couldn't build an elevator (at all), and there were also some stores that wouldn't fit where you've clicked (they'd always skip to the next block).
Now that we're through all this, then what about the overall aspects? The graphics are ok, I guess. My only complaint is that the stores seem dead, as there's no movement going on, other than the costumers walking in front of them. There're no sound effects, and there's only one song available, which isn't really a bad thing, but it naturally gets annoying after listening to it for a long period of time. The game doesn't provide you any campaign mode, so my only guess is that you can say that you've truly finished this game, after you've successfully managed to unlock every possible achievement. As mentioned earlier, the gameplay itself could really use some improvement.
Well, for now this is my opinion. I doubt that the gameplay mechanics of having to click all the time will ever change, but I think that at least the broken achievements could be fixed. Just to finish, I hope that the next games from that company will be better, because their premise is surely interesting.

is a seemingly attractive indie strategy/management game which is entertaining for a while but is unfortunately full of flaws that don't let the game live up to its full potential.
Check out this review and many others on Save or Quit:
This game tries to mimic similar successful titles, Project Highrise being just one example. Your goal is to get as much money as possible by building a shopping mall and evolving it as you get more customers and more money.
The concept is fun and the game looks like fun at first but soon enough, it becomes obvious that there are countless problems that ruin the whole experience. Let's start at the beginning. As soon as I started the game ... it crashed. "No problem," I said to myself. "this can happen sometimes." Sure enough, the game started normally next time. However, a few hours later I started browsing the community forum and it seems like this has been happening to a whole bunch of people. I tried starting the game multiple times and it still crashes about 20% of the time for some reason.
The tutorial is somehow helpful, but it is sadly filled with grammatical errors, typos, and other things. Here's an example: "If you will upgrade stock, then your store will can to sell more products." Luckily, the tutorial is more or less the only thing you will have to read in this game.
The graphics are overall quite good-looking. The main menu is beautiful, the stores and the environment are also okay. The animations don't quite hit the spot, though. People buy things like this: 1. walk to the store, 2. touch the store for a millisecond and 3. walk away immediately. You don't see people spending their time around the mall and shopping like they're supposed to. They just come and go and they're not particularly slow at doing that. Another animation issue is the lack of the day-turning-to-night-and-vice-versa transition animation. When the daytime "times out", the bright background instantly switches into the dark one.
Since I'm already talking about time, here's another thing I noticed. I'm sure you know that all similar management games have time control buttons which allow you to speed up the time to ensure you can waste your whole weekend more effectively. This game has that too, but that is not the problem. The problem is the pause button. When you pause it, the time stops - no surprise there. However, when you resume the game, the time doesn't start running normally, it just fast forwards to the time the game would reach had the pause button not been pressed. "But that's good," I hear you say, "at least the game got you plenty of money in the meantime and you don't have to take loans and stuff!" Well, no. You see, although you lose a lot of in-game time, your other stats don't actually change. In that time, no customers arrived and entrusted you with their hard-earned money.
There is another issue regarding time in this game, but it invokes giggles instead of rage. One in-game day lasts two minutes in real life and progresses the in-game clock by one week. For some reason. I don't understand what is the point of having the day and night cycle if you're not gonna stick by it.
The issues do not end here, sadly. I really can't understand why I have to collect money myself. Every once in a while, a certain store will inform you that it is now time to collect the money and that you have 30 seconds to do so. No other similar game does this and it's for a good reason: it's annoying and it's dumb. Also, as you get visited by your beloved customers, you earn the so-called "rating", which is a sort of customer satisfaction. You can then
the rating (goodbye, logic) to buy store blueprints.
This game also features a store upgrade system, which allows you to, you guessed it, upgrade your stores. This sounds good and it is, in fact, crucial if you want to succeed in this game. Why? Because without the upgrades, some stores have as little as
pieces of their product in stock. "Want to buy some bread, buddy? Well, that's bad luck, five people came before you already." Ridiculous. And that's not the only weird thing with Mall Empire's stock system. Even restrooms and parks are limited in how many people they can serve per day.
This weird system brings up a very interesting question: how on earth do you earn any money if you can only sell five loaves of bread per day? Here's the obvious solution: you raise its damn price. I had a nice long laugh after I noticed something when I upgraded the restrooms: a single usage of the toilet brought me
. Those better be some gold-plated toilets for that price.
The controls are no better, too. You can't zoom in or out, which can be a problem once your establishment consists of more than five floors. Moving the camera with your mouse for some reason also lags the customers (the FPS did not drop one bit, however) while the time counter ticks down seconds like usual, which in theory reduces your daily profits. When placing stores into your mall, you may also have issues with stores that take up more space. When I was trying to place the bar, I somehow placed it
some of the existing infrastructures. This prevented me from collecting money from the covered up areas. I could destroy the bar in order to reveal the stores beneath, but I would lose $350k (this game does not refund your money when you destroy stores. Of course.).
Although this is not a full list of everything that is wrong with this game, I will only mention one other thing: the achievements. There are 400 of them and they were obviously integrated into the game to attract achievement hunters. Nothing wrong with that, we cannot argue the principle of supply and demand. However, the achievements are screwed up in a number of different ways. Firstly, you get the "build" achievement when you buy a blueprint for a store and the "buy a blueprint" achievement when you build a store. Furthermore, the achievements which you are supposed to get when you reach a certain amount of gained profit in a month work the same as the achievements for total earnings, but with one little difference: you get the achievement for total earnings 1-2 minutes
the "in a month" achievement.
I do also want to say that I love the music in this game. It's funky.
There are a lot of things that make this game bad, but for some weird enough reason, I still played it for about two hours straight. I couldn't stop. Do I recommend it? Not really, no. This is the poor man's version of Project Highrise and I do mean poor man's. Both games go on sale quite often and if you feel like managing some buildings, you should only buy this game if you're a bit desperate and you're as broke as you'll ever be. I'm not saying you won't enjoy this game - for a few hours, you probably will. I did. But still, do yourself a favor and buy some other game with a decent level of quality.

I really hope Valve is getting on this, because at this point you're better off sticking to a 360, XB1, or PS4 controller.

The controller is something to get use to. If you are thinking of buying it here are some things to help you out.
~~ Points of Interest: ~~~~~~~~~~
- Customize it for each game: Using it standard out of the box for all the games may not be so helpful for your gaming experience. Take the time to tweak and gear it to your desired configuration and settings.
- Do not start off with a Multiplayer FPS: you might make yourself or others annoyed trying to get the hang of it in such a game. Try a strategy game, puzzle, side scroller... heck fallouts a good one to try and get an understanding of the controller in. Basically try games that let you have the time to learn and enjoy learning in.
- You can practically use this in place of your mouse and keyboard: If your hand is tired of the keyboard and mouse you can switch to the controller. It was weird at first, but becomes easier. The right touchpad becomes the mouse cursor and when you click down the joystick twice when in areas to type, a keyboard pops up that you can type with. The left and right touchpads become 1/2 of the keyboard and the triggers for left anf right are for selecting on their respective sides.
- Some features of using the controller as a mouse and keyboard get turned off if Steam is not open... ya... I could not scroll using the left touch-d-pad (its a touchpad and a d-pad....not sure what they call it). So have steam turned on to be able to have full functional use.
~~ Note: ~~~~~~~~~~
~~ I honestly keep 2 different controllers on my desk, the Steam controller and an old 360 controller. I still play a tad weird on multiplayer FPS games, with my left hand on the 360 controller and my right on the mouse. The 360 controller lets me move better and the mouse lets me aim finer. The steam controller was, in my mind, going to replace my odd way of playing; but I have not found the magical setup I need to play these types of games to my liking. Who knows, maybe someone has a configuration that will work for me that I can copy. ~~
~~ What I think: ~~~~~~~~~~
SO.... DO I RECOMEND IT? Is probably what your asking. Its a decent piece of hardware, with more updates likely coming in the future. So heck, yeah get it. Its pretty good for most other games and for those times when you want to be lazy and lay in bed instead of sitting at a computer. Also I have 2 AA in both my 360 controller and my Steam controller, both new. And the 360 controller is starting to run out of power. So longer battery life on the Steam controller.

For those that don’t know a company known as ‘Killjoy’, a while ago now, submitted a very low substandard piece of work onto the Steam store and sold it for around $5.00 known as ‘Air Control’. Eventually as social media caught onto this fact, that not only was it a badly programmed vagrant cash grab, but that the game itself contained many cases of copyright infringement which the developer himself just stole without gaining approval. Hence the company known as ‘Killjoy’ eventually became known as a scam artist.
This tarnished reputation originally was evaded by the company changing their name to ‘Iron Game Studios’ and again another quick cash grab full of glitches and meaningless copyright infringement dribble was released onto the Steam Store, but not all consumers are dumbbells and soon many began to realise that this raw programming piece of sewage was from the exact same scammers of ‘Air Control’.
Eventually after a massive backlash exposing this fact, it’s interesting to note that the reputable publisher Kiss LTD (
) took a noble measure of immediate action removing it not only swiftly from the Steam store, but also from any other retailer, they made a formal apology that this violation somehow got through their scrutiny process and offered a refund for a period of time to anyone who bought this falsely marketed product. Since then you can bet Kiss Ltd have tightened the reins to make sure this kind of thing never happens again?
However it’s interesting to note that even to this day many question if the developer (
) is really a scammer or more just a delusional programming wannabe. For one thing, regardless of the sheer volume of glitches and bugs, one can’t ignore the amount of work that ‘did’ go into this press ‘w’ simulator. 30 levels of different landscapes, decorated with many animated versions of fish. One quickly therefore asks were they the work of the developer? Or are they also a copyright infringement? How much of this product was truly his?
What further makes this a puzzling thing is that the game starts off with a begging statement requesting that you meditate and imagine what life would be like as a fish. Whatever inspirational message the developer is trying to get across soon becomes lost as you begin to laughingly experience levels where a clown fish is experiencing flashbacks of her children being burnt as she swims along, and a questionable level where your clownfish seems to be on LSD.
The music which is supposed to be relaxing you into some type of Zen trance, instead is piercing your eardrums with a heavenly choir that sounds like they’ve just sat on a hot poker. There is no in game volume control other than to turn the damn thing off. Even the clown fish you control eventually swims into an Angler fish and snuffs himself for which I assume was an act of mercy in trying to get out of the game. Alas you’re not so lucky and for no apparent reason whatsoever get to control other fish in the following levels again where the only objective is to press ‘w’ until you trigger the next cut scene. This isn’t always the case though, for instance one scene does not trigger any cuts, and instead you can swim endlessly into the blue beyond for 6 hrs straight or more if you wish to experience a migration scene across the whole Atlantic.
What really gets my panties in a knot, is that the developer of the game even spent time translating this noble message of imagine what life would be like as a fish in more languages than what is even currently translated on the United Nations Website. Seriously! I KID YOU NOT! This guy REALLY wanted to get this message of ‘Let’s have some fish empathy!!!’ out there. I really wouldn’t be surprised if he hasn’t started door knocking by now asking people, ‘Have you ever wondered what life would be like if you were a fish?’ and let’s face it there’s probably many out there with a Christian fish symbol who might be tempted here…
Ironically many who wanted it originally completely scaled from the Steam store and now it is, a number of those avid game collectors would now love to hook themselves a copy, all because of its downstream antics and history. I concur and understand why some are truly vexed about the game. Was he delusional? Was he a scammer? Was he both? My personal beliefs is that he was definitely a very ‘fishy’ person.

I was expecting something indepth and realistic; but what I got was a low quality arrangement of coral and anemone I could pass right through ruining the illusion of them being real, fish that looked like toys you would find in a dollar store, and a movement system that didn't let you dive nor take into account the direction you faced while you moved. I was very dissapointed in the quality and the content. Do not buy!

Endless Space is simplistic enough to let you focus on strategy without getting bogged down by the details. If you want to take your game further, Endless Space has the depth and complexity to get pretty intense. It's a great entry into the 4X genre outside of Civ while still having worthwhile gameplay for experienced players.
You can build your own ship designs/specializations and issue your own battle commands which you can improve with heroes. It's fairly straightfoward but it adds a fun, small dimension of play without making turns go on forever. You can also build your own race using the art templates and abilities toolbox and if you want to use mods that option is there although there is no steamworks support currentlly. Also doesn't support more than one mod active at a time from my experience. I'd highly reccommend trying out some of the mods they offer some fun improvements to the game.
While there isn't a whole lot of story on it's own, which may disappoint some, it makes a great template of a game if you enjoy creating your own story about your empire. Also allows you to focus more on the gameplay.
Endless Space has a solid amount of replayability. The galaxy seed generator produces a pretty unique experience for every galaxy I've ever played on. Win strategies are pretty diversified but I find myself using a bit of everything to win. Some strategies are harder than others though.
Playing online is enjoyable but I wouldn't try it with more than 3 or 4 other people as turns get significantly longer after 75-100 turns into a game and even moreso at 200-250.
Endless Space is a great entry into 4X. It offers good replayability and fun unit/squadron customization while still being true to the genre.

My earlier review was too long for Steam, so here’s the abridged version.
GBDNATE purports to be a Visual Novel about a couple of researchers who devise a serum that changes the gender of anyone exposed to it. A lab accident occurs, hilarity (in theory) then ensues, and all of the exposed people have to cope with the ramifications of the gender swap.
What The Ad Copy Leads You To Believe: This is a zany, gender-bender comedy extravaganza along the lines of Ranma 1/2 that portrays the hilarity of a diverse cast of characters having to adjust ‘to wearing a bra in the morning’ (per the devs). That said, the title is also allegedly sensitive to the many difficulties transgendered individuals face in modern society.
What The Title Actually Is: The extended, misogynistic, self-insert fetish fanwank of two boys who wish they were hot lesbians, and whose comprehension of gender issues and cultural sensitivity lies slightly below that of Chris Brown.
How Much Have I Played: Every route of every character thus far released, from Yael to their latest character, Nadine.
As someone on the discussion boards pointed out, a Visual Novel needs to have: Art, Story and Gameplay. GBDNATE is wanting in all three categories.
The ART in GBDNATE has been called “anime style”, and that style is fairly common for VNs. The style itself would work, if not for problems with:
Basic Anatomy - Even by anime standards, the characters’ proportions are grotesque. Hands and feet are awkwardly avoided or poorly drawn. Character poses (especially Steph) would require breaking the character’s spine.
Clothing - The artist doesn’t seem to know how cloth hangs on the human body, nor how light shines on it. He also thinks every woman dresses like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Perspective - Backgrounds defy the rules of perspective drawing, and the characters (who are flatly drawn) appear simultaneously in front of and behind other objects.
Eye Bubbles - The characters’ eyes look more like lizard eyes than eyes with light reflections.
I’d encourage anyone who wants to see the art to look at the screenshots or download the demo.
The STORY in GBDNATE is not one story where you play the character you want. GBDNATE is implemented as separate (8 now, 13 total planned) stories that have some events (the explosion) in common, but otherwise contain too many inconsistencies to be deemed a perspective shift.
The first seven routes have none of the Setup / Conflict / Resolution narrative structure of a VN at all, so they read as “stuff happens until it stops”. The eighth route (Nadine) is the only route with a coherent narrative.
The characters in GBDNATE are flat and largely indistinguishable. Yael and Nadine are the most coherent characters; Lynn and Dina are the developers’ Mary Sues (with all the problems thus engendered), while the rest of the characters are forgettable. They all talk and think with the same narrative voice, despite differences in age, gender, education, social standing and anything else.
Good character ensemble humor comes from the interplay of different, well-defined personalities (think Rumiko Takahashi or Seinfeld), but since the characters are poorly (often inconsistently) defined, there’s no humor in their interaction. They’re just lifeless boob joke generators, and nothing more.
With no humor, a fanwank title like GBDNATE should at least have a titilation factor, but all the sex scenes are rendered as follows:  
…
 …… 
………
  “Was it good for you?”
  Unless one finds ellipses to be erotic, there’s no titillation to be had in GBDNATE. The characters masturbate more than they connect with each other anyway (Yael actually sets a flag for this, sadly).
In terms of the writing, the developers are violating the first rule of writing: “Write what you know”. Anyone with genuine experience in the sciences, technology, the law, sex or anything else will find much to bang their head on the desk over.
Nadine’s route was especially bad. It strayed into the realms of science, computer hacking & security, legality, criminal investigations, corporate business culture, investing, and a variety of other fields in which the developers clearly have no knowledge or experience. Even the background art will make any computer-savvy player twitch.
Mechanically, the writing is just not good. Tenses drift, continuity errors abound in all routes, there are plenty of spelling and grammar errors - it’s a hot mess. It’s not as hilariously bad as “My Immortal”, but it’s definitely a distraction in a format that relies on writing to convey 95% of the content.
Nadine’s route was the worst offender in this category as well. My impression was that someone had spell-checked the hell out of it, but nobody ever sat down to proofread it with a red pen. Again, in a text-centric medium, solid editing is just as important as basic code testing.
GAMEPLAY: Up until Nadine’s route, there is none. The first seven routes are nothing more than Choose Your Adventure novels (with very few choices). By making a choice, you choose which path the narrative goes down. What few choices you get often have no bearing on the content to which they lead, which means that making a single choice of “Stay At Work” leads inexorably to the Lesbian Catgirl Ending of that route. Things like sexual orientation are determined by getting haircuts and eating nachos.
There are no skills to master, there are no meaningful status flags to set, there is no endgame to navigate, there are no deductions to make. In the first seven routes, there simply is no gameplay at all.
They tried to change this in the Nadine route (which ends with a watered-down Phoenix Wright knockoff), but the only real “gameplay” here is in asking a few common sense questions in the right order. At no point is any information from the rest of the game required to navigate the endgame, and it’s quite possible to reach the optimal ending having never seen the rest of the story that leads up to it.
Still, as badly executed and derivative as it was, I’ll give them credit for the attempt. It’s a positive sign that after over a year of being told that their title has no gameplay, they actually gave it a try in one route.
CODE QUALITY: While not normally relevant in a review, I do have a couple of comments because of two factors:
The developers didn’t write their own VN engine; they’re using a free one called RenPy.
The developers are charging premium dollars ($25 as of this writing) for their title.
Given that the developers are charging premium dollars for a title that’s just a script running on someone else’s engine, it better be a pretty amazing script.
Thing is, it’s not.  GBDNATE is an absolutely appalling pile of spaghetti code that a) would not be accepted in a Comp101 class, and b) taps into almost none of the RenPy engine’s capabilities.
There are far more robust RenPy games available for free on the RenPy website. There are far more robust RenPy games right here on Steam for far less money. GBDNATE simply is not implemented well, nor is it worthy of the ridiculous price tag hung upon it.
FINAL SUMMARY:
GBDNATE is a bad title, plain and simple.
Do I recommend it? Well, if you share the developers’ fetishes, I’ll recommend that you download the free demo. If you like that, you’ll probably like the rest of it enough to buy it if they ever put a realistic price on it: say, $6.99 (the price of a trade paperback). It’s not worth any more than that, in my opinion.
I’ve been asked by several people if GBDNATE is a “so bad it’s good” title. In my opinion, it’s not. It’s just dull and tediously bad, with mediocre art and way too many 5th grade boob jokes.

Blockland may look like a Minecraft or Roblox clone at first glance to some people,but it really isn't and it in itself is much more than that. So BL is a building game first made in 2004 in the V0002 state, the retail version was then released in 2007 with the latest version being V21. Have you've ever played with LEGO's as a kid or built something with them? Did you ever have fun with them? If yes, then Blockland is the game for you. The game allows you to build with a virtually unlimted amount of bricks (There's a 256,000 brick limt,but you can set your own limt on your own server). It also even features an in-game eventing system that allows you to do cool stuff with your bricks like make a door that open and closes or a light switch. The modding community is also pretty good with a good number of brick packs, vehicles, colorsets, music, and etc. The community itself isn't the best, but there really isn't a perfect community out there anyway. You may meet some bad players here and there,but if you stay away from the bad side of the community you'll be fine. The graphics are very blocky and legolike giving a very nice look especially for a old 2003 engine.There are shaders in the game,but they look very jaggy and bad and they're also very poorly optimized at it too.If you want to there are modifications that can help you make the shadows look smoother,but you'll need a great PC to get it done. I would really recomend this game to anybody if you like building games and don't worry you'll really get your money's worth, I've spent at least about 400hrs (With my old blid and steam blid combined) on the game and haven't stopped yet.
Note: When you first get the game I would highly recommend getting RTB.

A prominent example of two steps forward, one step back.  On the surface, it seems like it makes a lot of user friendly improvements and expands the game world in ways that should make the game better.  But it turns out a lot of them are counter intuitive.
Sure, being able to craft items anywhere is great.  But being able to select items from the weapons locker and have them handed to you, rather than having to find them in the world, means that there's much less emphasis on improvising than in the previous games in the series.
Also this is the point where Dead Rising's careful balance between absudity and horror goes right out the window.  The previous two games were firmly in the goofy B-movie camp.  But 3's protagonist Nick Ramos is taking the zombie apocalypse 100% serious.  He looks at the camera with his sad brown eyes while horrible things happen to him and his friends.  And then he puts on an afro and a latex fetish outfit and kills 50,000 zombies with an RC helicopter.
It's not bad.  It's just not as good as it could have been.

This is just a personal opinion from my own experience. I only gave it a thumbs down because I was literally falling asleep from playing it. I may sound like a heretic since most people gave it a thumbs up. Perhaps it's the early alpha stage, but there is something about this game feels rather boring.
Graphic:
I love the art style. The presentation of the game is beautiful, and I can tell the developers gave a lot of loves and careful attentions to each pixel. The UI is simple to navigate and easy to the eyes. Job well done.
Story:
As the gaming age is constantly evolving, story writers are exploring non-linear storytelling style and there are untouched areas to be discover. Some game does it well, and some does it poorly. How does this game fair? At this alpha stage, it's rather boring. Yes, there are random encounters and events. However, just random event does not always make a good non-linear storytelling. For example in this game: some pirates appeared in a local sector and requires your decision to dispatch a fleet to eradicate them. However, there is no time restriction, so you are to do so whenever you are please. As an audience, there is no sense of urgency. My decision does not matter because I will eventually go fight them; it could be 2 days or 30 days later. These current random events are either fight these enemies or don't fight these enemies. I honestly hope there are further improvements. Give us the options to make a real decision and not a false illusion. Another example: we first encountered some pirates and they straight up declare war against Halcyon 6. The developer completely miss the opportunity to give these pirates a cunning personality trait such as persuasion, trading crews with you which later backstab your base and stealing tech from you, trading for their own profit gain, giving you a false sense of protection against the Cruul race, selling you faulty weaponries that you later discover during a combat and etc. These would broaden the non-linear story. But instead, we are the bad guys, therefore, we must fight. We then met the Cruul race and they straight up declare war against mankind. I can understand we need mortal enemies. But the current events are rather straight forward and boring when my decisions are either fight or don't fight; go there or don't go there. It feels so restricted.
Game play:
Base building can be fun. There is nothing wrong if this is done well. However, the 3 vs. 3 combat, some people will find this nostalgic and charming. Perhaps some younger audiences who didn't grow up with JRPG will find this refreshing. Very unfortunately, this is nothing new, nor unique, thus I find it outdated for anyone who played a fair amount of JRPG. I honestly think the developers restricted themselves on the current combat system. You probably saw many reviewers with a thumbs up saying the combat is repetitive. They are not joking. Just because we have fleet officers with different traits and status effects from ships, it doesn't always make the game complex, nor engaging.
Since the current story and gameplay both fail my expectancy. Reluctantly, I can't recommend it at this moment. However, it is only alpha, perhaps changes will be make and I may retract my statements.

Besides a platform level that keeps getting me mad (hence the opening), and a couple of ones where the performances drop to abysmal levels and forced me to lower my graphics, the game is a damn solid shooter.
Killing demons is a deeply satisfying experience, and the story, while not exactly original, is well delivered (I enjoyed especially how they managed to stitch together this game with the previous ones btw).
The sound compartment is great, and the graphics is as good as your GPU can manage, though even with my RX550 on medium/low, it looks glorious. Trying it on Ultra on the (few) levels whre that doesn't cause a performance drop, made my jaw fall from delight.
The game also shows quite some love from the developers: they didn't just made a perfunctory reboot to cash (hurry up and grab doom 3 BFG edition if you want that... ugh... :p), but created a game that stand on its own against contemporary shooters.
While the game mechanics are disarmingly simple (walk around shooting demons, get locked into a room full of them, clean it, rinse and repeat...), the game as a whole will sure delight (and wink at) fans of the original serie, but will not disappoint the newcomers.
Highly recommended!

Saw this game available on Chrono.gg for $2.50 and saw that the reviews were mostly positive, so I decided to take a punt.
What a complete waste of $2.50.
There's really nothing here that resembles strategy or even gameplay, for the most part. You buy store blueprints with a "heart" currency, build new stores with money, sell products to gain money and hearts, rinse and repeat.
There doesn't seem to be anything more to it other than the relentless clicking. To collect money from the stores you have to click on the store (which has a 4x4 pixel icon on it if there's money to be collected), then click on a menu icon to collect its money. As stores sell goods they'll level up, get a 4x4 upgrade icon and then need to be clicked on and upgraded by clicking on the menu bar, putting 5 points into two mysterious stats using tiny, tiny buttons, then click the close button on the upgrade window, then click the close button on the next "You have successfully upgraded your store with these exact stats that appeared on the previous menu" window.
The whole experience is a miserable UI disaster that would be far more comfortable in a touch-based interface, but which would *still* be terrible even then. It would just be *less* terrible.
The developers seem to have abandoned the game back in April, and probably aren't coming back; I don't think there's anything worth saving/patching here anyway. Not without totally redesigning the game from the ground up.
The soundtrack is pretty sweet though, I'll give them that much.
But yeah, the only reason to write this review is to try and counter the ridiculous number of positive reviews this game has. This is not a positive-review game. It's a terrible, terrible game, and you should not buy it.

For $2.50 (where it's currently on Chrono.gg for) I'd certainly say it's worth it. I've only just started but I can already see a lot of potential. First, it's not a very in-depth game (at the moment, I can't say that that is what the indie developers final goal is by any means), so if it's depth you're looking for I think you might want to look elsewhere until the game gets further in development. That being said, it fits with the style of the game, that style being minimalistic. It's a very minimalistic game and I think that's great for a game of this Tycoon genre.
On the topic of development, the developers are keeping the fans updated which is important in this day and age where indie development isn't always trustworthy due to games like No Man's Sky. Being updated on the content that gets added fairly frequently is a great thing to hear from developers and regardless of how this game turns out I'd be glad to keep an eye on what these developers do in the future, because I can trust them.
Back on the topic of the game I think it's great for people just wanting to relax. I mentioned how it's not very in-depth at the moment, and that's because, from what I understand of the game, the stores you choose don't make much of a difference, I mean, even the rest areas cost the customers. That makes me feel that, as it is, so far, the game seems like it's more of a build your own dream mall, than an actual tycoon. I don't mind that at all in my opinion, but I'm also looking forward to any future changes the devs make. I still think it's almost certainly worth the $2.50 on Chrono.gg at the moment.
I also mentioned the minimalistic style of it. I have played games like this before, I loved them and was happy when I was gifted this because it looked like it would play like those games where you build a hotel and decide what goes where and such. But....this is a let down...
The game pauses when you click off the game so if you want it to run in the background, too bad you will not get any gain at all.
The pause button in-game does pause the game but soon as you press play again it speeds up how many days/nights you would of missed to begin with making it pointless as a pause button!
You have to click your shops to get the money and after a while this gets boring, specially when you have many shops and you NEED to scroll across the screen to check if a shop needs money collecting. You can scroll with arrow keys but it is PAINFULLY slow that I question why even have it there. The mouse scroll is much faster.
If you don't feel like collecting from your shops, there is an "auto-collect". Good, you can semi-afk while reading a book (though why you would use your computer just to run this boring game and not use it for more fun things is beyond me) HOWEVER. It only collects 50% of what you would of gotten if you collected it yourself.
You can rank up your store if certain parts are met, such as enough shops or customers. But this is where auto-collect is more of a death sentence. Some of the items you buy, such as advertising, is daily. Which means if you bought the 10k one, you lose 10k everyday. WHY! Why not just let it be a one time thing and let me re-buy it if I wanted more customers? why force the money out of our pockets over something that seems to be a one time thing like the other upgrades were? that is stupid and misleading as well. No where does it state it is daily, this is why my money kept being drained like hell and heck the increased customers did nothing of use for me anyway.
Lastly, some of the placeables do not work. When I want to make a new floor, it won't let me. So I place a hallway down which is 10x more. Still nothing.
If a hallway DOES place down it is only 1 room! while the floor which is marked at 10k (is actually 100k nice typo developers) fills the next entire row. So what the hell? Why have a floor and hallway if both do the same thing but one just makes 1 room, just get rid of it. While you are at it, bloody make sure it works. I don't want to be clicking 5 times just to hope it places an actual floor down. Heck on some save-files I could not place a new floor at all, so I had to start a new game and lose my progress, this has happened TWICE! Wonderful, thank you.

Ultimate Ninja Storm 4 is the best Naruto game to date. The biggest cast of characters, new mechanics, etc. make for a great game.
Negatives first though:
-FPS lock. Can't go over 30FPS, but that's not a totally huge deal. Yes 60 would be better, but 30 ain't bad.
- 15 GB of cutscenes. All the full-motion story cutscenes are pre-rendered using the in-game engine and all have a soft, fuzzy look to them along with low anti-aliasing. It means you've got a fuzzy looking story while gameplay is bright and crisp. Not only is it a huge visual downgrade, but that's also a lot of extra hard drive space. The scenes aren't anything incredible so why they didn't just use in-game cut scenes is just baffling to me.
- Too many slideshows. There are plenty of cutscenes that aren't even animated and just use stills from the anime with some motion applied. It's lazy and, if they were going to go this route, why not just include all the actual animation from the series?
- Some bugs persist such as story mode dialogue audio only coming from the left channel, some crashing due to regular Windows processes, etc.
Positive time!
- Biggest cast of characters in any Naruto game. If you have a fan favorite, you can probably play them here.
- No longer are ultimate jutsu, awakening, and drive styles separated.
- Leader change system makes for fun combos and switching up of combat. It feels very fresh and fun.
- Love NUNS games? It's more of the same, just tweaked and improved all around.
- Replay story at whatever chapter you like. No need to start a new game.
I'd recommend it, for sure. Great game all around and sure to please Naruto fans. CC2 did a great job and, should they patch the issues, it'll be amazing.

I unironically LOVE this game, it's truly one of my favorites. People think I'm crazy because of the anime themed junk thrown in, but that adds to the comedy factor of it. It brings a whole new feeling to metroidvanias along with bullet hells, like the original Metroid or the GameCube renditions and all the Touhou games. Remember those ugly space pirates you encountered and those soul-sucking flying jelly headcrabs? Replace that with laser shooting snowflakes and anime chicks that want to do the diddly with you; it's just really fun to play, silly, and overall light-hearted
. On several occasions, I almost punched my monitor because of stress, however.
Pros:
-Amazing effects for a game that uses pixel graphics
-Highly detailed sprites
-New spin on metroidvanias and bullet hells
-Very big map with locations to explore and items to uncover
-A schwanzus-longus sized easter egg that took me like two hours to finish because I suck
-Each boss and enemy type has its own intricate attack pattern(s)
-Amazing soundtrack; I sometimes hum the official theme since it's so catchy.
Cons:
-You can't play this on your mother's notebook PC
This game is actually really well designed and a lot of work was put into the effects. There were some parts that were absolutely unbearable like the Spectral Cavern which gave me (not even kidding) more than a second of input latency when I wanted to play this on the go with my handy dandy laptop. I ended up having to wait for later to play it at home.
-Not for the weak!
This game is HARD. When I first started the game, I set the difficulty to normal and by golly I sure was glad I didn't set it to hard. Usually I would set games to the max difficulty like FPS games for a fun, yet challenging experience, but this is not the game to do it. Eventually, I couldn't even get past the sixth(?) boss. And this is on normal! I ended up having to set the game difficulty to easy because I was a stupid pleb. I don't even know how you pros do it. Damn Touhou-maniacs. Jesus Christ, it was still hard as hell on easy. I had to use "questionable methods" in order to actually finish the game.
Oh yeah, the devs are still active. They're still adding updates time to time, implementing more achievements and secrets for the players to find. Hell yeah! Their last update was October 27, where they added a free Halloween DLC for all and more (my review was written November 9). Almost a whole year of full support, thanks devs! There's also community comics that are being made and added for users to view. Oh right, following up on the easter eggs thing, there's even Chocola and Vanilla from Nekopara added into the game as characters. Cat and bunny lovers rejoice?
Overall, this game was a rollercoaster of fun to play through. 50 hours of my life wasted, collecting items, upgrading stuff, retrying more than 5 times on each boss. It almost feels worth it (which it was), until I play some of it again and then want to break something. There were only very slight things I didn't like, so whatevs.
I really recommend this game. Toss aside your opinions about 2D chicks, people, and give this game a try! It will definitely be worth your time.

Hi-Rez had a dedicated, passionate community that was willing to look past the fact that Hi-Rez is unable to fix  even gamebreaking severe bugs (of which there are many) that have existed for months, and they squandered it. This just goes to show you that the only thing more broken than their game is Hi-Rez themselves.

Another great game by Rockstar! From the creators of GTA V (Most of my friends didn't realise until I told them it was a Rockstar Game) It is actually a good PC port! Imagine GTA IV but instead you are a kid in a boarding school and you can explore the surrounding town. It's all the insanity of a Rockstar game. Slingshots, beating up nerds, Carnivals, Preps, Jocks, Chemistry class, it has everything! It's full of sterotyped cliques that you remember from your long passed school days!

Pros:
Another excellent Rockstar sandbox game, worth the price. Give this a go if you like GTA. I also recommend it for those who like GTA games but often find the story missions too difficult. Bully's missions are a lot easier than those found in most GTA games. There's a lot to do outside of the main story too, with countless side-missions, minigames, secrets and unlockables to find. The game's soundtrack is awesome, by the way, composed by Shawn Lee. If you play this game for more than ten minutes the music will have already been stuck in your head.
Cons:
If you're playing this on Windows 10 you may encounter crashes a fair few times, there are steps that can be taken to minimise the frequency of these crashes. I took these steps but I couldn't eradicate the crashes completely, I may have missed something however. Also, the game is locked at 30 FPS if you're worried about that. It can be brought up to 60 FPS with some tinkering if you like, I didn't mind it all that much. Another issue I had was the audio, outside of cutscenes I thought the characters' voices were too quiet and they were overpowered by the music, even though I had the speech option at max.
To sum up, Bully is a unique, funny game with a great story, a fantastic soundtrack, a ton of side missions, a lot of pranks to pull and a lot of characters to interact with. The few technical problems I mentioned are outweighed by this game's qualities.

I used to use a Sony PS3 controller for all my gamepad gaming, but it didn't take me more than a few hours to adjust to the Steam Controller. It's just as comfortable to hold and easy to use as the promotion video implies, and once you get used to it, the simplicity is astounding. Surprisingly, I don't find myself missing the feel of the traditional directional buttons, a second joystick or even the smaller design of the Sony gamepad. And for those of you that also prefer the Sony controller's functionality, don't worry, the Steam Controller also has customisable tilt sensors.
The synergy between Steam and the controller itself is great - the interface for remapping button functions is simple and elegant, as well as infinitely potent, and with a little messing around you can easily customise each button to your liking on a per-game basis, with options for turbo or toggle of any button as well as alternate functions for single-press, double-tap, holding and releasing each button. You can also remap the gamepad buttons to keyboard keys and the touchpads to your mouse, so you can use it to play games that don't support a gamepad. And don't think you have to set up a control scheme for every game - the first time you launch each game with the controller, Steam will ask you to choose a preset control layout, giving you additional options posted by the community which are usually perfect.
I own a Novint Falcon, so I know the potential immersion that Haptic Feedback can bring, especially in VR. The Steam Controller's Haptic Feedback does it's job well, and is customisable alongside the controls for any need. I found myself using it both to let me feel the kick of a gunshot as I pull the trigger, as well as a low pulse signalling a button i'm holding is repeating in Turbo mode like I told it to.
The controller is either wired or wireless and takes 2xAA batteries, which are included in the box (the GOOD brand, too) and the wireless signal is good enough for me to use the controller seamlessly in the next room across, through the wall. The batteries fit snugly inside the handles, one at either side, which makes the controller feel lighter when you hold it in one hand.
The pads on the back are incredibly useful; you'll never understand how much easier playing with a gamepad is when you have that one important button available to be pressed instantly at any moment without having to play twister with your fingers to press other buttons at the same time.
Even typing with the touchpads is as fluid as the promotional video shows, admittedly after a little fumbling at first. The Steam Controller's potential in your hands is limited only by your imagination, but while I prefer it to a keyboard any day, it will never beat the speed and precision of a mouse. It's designed for comfort and simplicity, and it does it's job in that regard better than you could imagine, but I do not recommend this for competitive play. While it's entirely possible to play games like Counter-Strike and even DotA smoothly with the Steam Controller, your performance will suffer compared to a keyboard and mouse.
All in all, that promotional video doesn't lie; it's not bull hyped up to get you to buy it - it really works, just like that! If you're the kind of gamer who admires comfort or sometimes wants to take a break from leaning over your keyboard and just sit back and relax while you play, the Steam Controller definitely is for you.

This controller is an innovative concept, and I think there's a lot of potential, but right now it's not worth the money. There's really two problems, and I think both stem from this controller being such a new and unique concept.
The bigger of the two issues is the software support. Not many games make good use of this controller. I tried about 5 games with it (granted, none were shooters, but there were platformers and racing games in the mix) and only one used either of the touchpads at all. Even that one game only used the left one, and simply treated it like an 8-way directional pad. This isn't really the controller's fault, but still, it's a pretty big disappointment.
Problem number two is that the focus of this controller is clearly the touchpads. Not necessarily an issue in itself, except they are so huge that the control stick and A/B/X/Y buttons are really out of the way. Still easily reachable with your thumbs, but your hands quickly get sore when using them. Which is a big deal, since (at least right now) the touchpads don't work for most games.
One neat feature is that the touchpads work as a mouse and scroll wheel when not in a game.
One other not so great issue is that when I tried it with a friend's Steam Link, it was only recognized as a keyboard, so the touchpads didn't work at all and the control stick acted like arrow keys. Such a shame.
If I could suggest one thing to make this controller better, it would be to swap the locations of the stick/A/B/X/Y with those of the touchpads. And maybe shrink the touchpads a tad bit. If they did that and this got better game support, this would be fantastic.

It's great for what it does i.e. giving you options to play games "more casually", "on your couch", or however you want to name it; games, that would otherwise be rather hard to play in such environment. So - I recommend it just for that. Options are good, and it gives you a-PLENTY, sometimes maybe even too many, if your game doesn't already have a community-prepared control scheme.
HOWEVER, sadly, I *don't* recommend it as your FIRST AND ONLY controller, unless you only care about the abovementioned scenario.
Some games really are designed with controllers in mind, and you're doing yourself a disservice not having such tool in your arsenal, even if you're a PC gamer. Sadly, I can't really "feel" (at least initially?) the Steam controller replacing something like your standard dual stick XBox or PS controllers.
The trackpads are amazing at pretending to be trackballs or mouse wheels, the haptic feedback is something to behold. It works great at driving Windows and some slower paced mouse driven games. Also the great enabler for many games is option for customized  onscreen popup menus which may fill in for many, many more buttons than a normal controller would give you.
But, the trackpads don't really do a good job at pretending to be a stick, and even the normal mouse mode, I expected something like a laptop touchpad - I've been playing on laptops for years! Alas, I simply cannot find the speed and precision of a normal laptop touchpad on those Steam controller trackpads... And, even though I am not accustomed to trackballs at all, Steam controller trackpads do a better job for me when trackball mode is on (guess that's why they're named like that... focused more on pretending to be a trackball rather than a touchpad)! This is perhaps my biggest dissapointment with this controller. Maybe that's something that would come with time, but I had no trouble picking up dual joystick controllers for the first time. Of course a stick will never be as accurate as mouse (even though I've seen some 10 year old kids doing magic with those), but on those trackpads I did expect the accuracy I find on a laptop touchpad! (not a trackball replacement...)
Other things I don't like is the placement of XYBA buttons; very small and far in. It only serves to reinforce my opinion that it doesn't do a good job at replacing a standard XBox-like/PS-like controller...
Also, bumpers are too hard and too loud-clicky to my taste (though seeing as some people are crazy about loud mechanical keyboards, that may not be an issue to you... but in a bumper heavy game you will be heard; trackpads clicking is also a rather loud sound, but not as much)
On the other hand I like the triggers very much, they have linear press detection, but also a soft silent click at the end (there's also configurable trigger point that may come earlier, with haptic rumble). It works great to to either have a direct action, or if pressed gently at first, a modified action (like a quick shot or aimed shot). But I've read some comments that actually don't like the triggers... So, another preference based stuff.
And, to make it clear, I *do* like the trackpads, just in all modes other than non-trackball mouse or stick.
So, again, it is great for many games that would otherwise be unplayable with a controller; however, for games that *have* dedicated controller support, a standard controller seems a better way to go
The controller is comfortable, extremely customizable, and battery life last pretty long. I would recommend this to anyone who has their Pc in the living room or bedroom.
