I just want to say that Halcyon 6 is probably one of the cleanest Early Access games I have ever played. This shiny Strategy RPG takes an X-Com type approach to Space command. This just might be the “Star Trek” game that we’ve all been looking for and it isn’t even finished yet.
The title revolves around the shattered Terran leadership that has just been overrun by a dangerous invading alien race. Long story short. Everyone else is dead except the Commander and their remaining crew members. The remaining Terrans find Halcyon 6, a Starbase at the fringe of Terran space with unknown ability. It’s basically the last refuge of power for the remaining humans and they have to protect it at all cost.

Halcyon 6 is similar to Babylon 5 or Deep Space Nine. Many gamers will find it similar to a combination of games like XCom, Masters of Orion, and etcetera. You’ll have to clear Halcyon 6 out by sending an officer down to open rooms for new research facilities. There are also various talent trees to reduce the cost of skills, create new ships, and improve base functions.
Halcyon 6 will act as a safe haven for crewmembers but it must also be protected from advancing alien attacks. The Terrans lost most of their power while still holding onto the most coveted space station in the galaxy. They have to rebuild their status by completing quests for allies. This will earn them a favorable reputation with some and hatred among others.
Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander goes out of its way to create a living world filled with danger and exploration. Enemies are around every corner but so are friendly extra-terrestrials in need of help. There are a ton of random events that can happen as the days pass. From simple things like explosions on the ship that can kill crewmembers, or finding highly volatile feces that can be used as fuel.
This isn’t a roguelike but that doesn’t mean that an encounter will play out as it did in the last play through. Each decision is randomized and it could either benefit the player or ruin their lives instead. In a small way, Halcyon 6 also takes a few cues from Oregon Trail.
The title leans heavily on comedy as its main story point. It has rare moments of seriousness during major storylines, but for the most part it creates a wacky set of alien lifeforms to interact with. The game prides itself on its zany nature and its obvious parody of familiar Sci-fi characters. It’s a welcome amount of fun to a genre filled with tough guy themes.
Let’s talk about the combat and the overall experience a bit. Surprisingly, the game uses traditional turn-based combat from most JRPG’s. It has a heavy emphasis on using vulnerabilities and exploits as its main means of battle. The fights are split between ground and space combat but they both share the turn-based combo structure.
This is a good thing because as the days pass the engagements with enemies will increase. The more days that pass the more frantic the state of the galaxy. It’s fine that the warfare is simplistic because of the large amount of enemies encountered.
Halcyon 6 is very much a sandbox game at heart. As Commander we will spend most of our time scouring nearby star systems for allies and resources. Not soon after we’ll spend a good chunk of our time defending those allies from many a dangerous foe. Our crew will level up from engaging the enemy and acquire new and devastating abilities in the process.
This is a title that uses a pixelated cartoonish stylishness that creates a bright and colorful galaxy. It’s incredibly well animated combat sequences are vibrant and often larger than life. From the heavily detailed galaxy map to the distinctly different lifeforms that appear on the view screen of the bridge.  Halcyon 6 creates a unique experience for every wannabe Captain in the gaming world.
The music is something you’d expect from a space geared title. That’s not to say it’s bad but I didn’t find it particularly remarkable either. The attack sounds on the other hand at as helpful cues and are distinct and stimulating. The game is utterly and completely devoid of voice work, but that’s not a downside and more of a warning. You are going to be reading a lot of text.
Right now Halcyon 6: Starbase Commander is one of the best Early Access titles I’ve ever played. Halcyon 6 is the lightest 4X out there, which makes it enjoyable for someone like myself who utterly detests that genre. It’s flush with content and strangely lacking in the glitches and bugs department for what’s essentially an Alpha release. I don’t recommend many Early Access titles, but this one is absolutely worthy of the support required to finish development.

I remember many years ago, playing through DR 1 and hating the fact that the missions were timebased, and often severely confusing the first time you went to complete them (I failed a few simply because I didn't leave the area and return). DR 2 fixed a lot of these issues and made the game more enjoyable in that way, BUT they added another timed mission, meaning I had even less time to do what I played the friggin game for: kill zombies.
Dead Rising 3 got rid of every annoying thing the previous games had, made the zombies actually able to tank a hit from the weaker weapons, added new features with actual customizable vehicles, and overall, made killing hordes of zombies a ridiculously fun thing. It also gave far more options on what one could do with their character, and added something worthwhile to the story, which thusfar was far too lighthearted for a zombie game.
Now that I've written this review and heard just how horrid the fourth game was (which apparently is a prequel instead of a continuation of the story), I am going back into the game to play again ^.^

Dead Rising 3 is an interesting game.  On one hand, the story is kinda♥♥♥♥♥even by Dead Rising's standards (which were never that high to begin with).  I'm not exactly expecting Shakespear here, but a lot of the dialogue in this game is very awkward in how it links together.  The overall plot is okay but it's the execution here that's off - there were many moments where I thought a few extra words would have made a moment a lot more meaningful.
But the good part of DR3 is the gameplay, and boy does it come through.  The combo weapon system from 2 has been heavily refined along with a new levelup system that allows you to pick what powers you gain as you level - including the ability to use certain categories of weapons as "wild cards".  Let's say you want to make a Defiler - normally you'd combine a Fire Axe with a Sledgehammer, but if you pick the Blunt weapon perk you can replace the Sledgehammer with any blunt weapon in the game - baseball bats, 2x4s, even a chair.
I cannot tell you how much I love this feature, as it cuts out one of the most tedious parts of DR2 - hunting for the right gear and rote memorization of item locations.  Now you can just whip♥♥♥♥♥♥up on the fly if you grab the right perks, so building your favorite weapons and getting back into the action is a lot faster.  Survivors have also been significantly improved and you no longer have to cart them back to a safehouse - most will simply leave when rescued, though a few side missions give followers you can recruit at Safe Houses.
One change you may love or hate is the elimination of time limits on main story missions - you have 6 days of in game time to finish everything but only side missions have strict timers.  I felt a lot less pressure in this game to finish everything as soon as it popped up - probably an intentional decision, given that this game has a bunch of collectibles to find.  Speaking of which, blueprints are now found instead of being earned through levels - another decision you may love or hate depending on how much you enjoy hunting♥♥♥♥♥♥down.
I personally found the game very satisfying overall.  Just make sure your expectations for the story are set pretty low.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a cliche-ridden mess. But it's a cliche-ridden mess with really solid gameplay. And even its story, as much as it will often just make you roll your eyes, has some charm to it. Controller support is also top notch; I honestly think it plays better on controller than mouse and keyboard--which is very unusual of an FPS.
Playing this game feels like a solving the puzzle, where the end goal is clear but there are many ways to get to it. For that reason, I enjoy it, and for that reason, I recommend it.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a much better game than I dared to hope for. As it is Eidos Montréal's first game, I was scared they couldn't pull a new Deus Ex off. I couldn't have been more wrong.
The first thing you'll immediately notice is how the atmosphere of the world is just right. It is completely believeable, immersive and Deus Ex. The story pulls you in right away and won't let go until you're finished with it. The visuals of this game are amazing, nailing the futuristic look but with an original twist. The worldbuilding effort has been immense: there's so much to dive into.
Next you'll notice how well the game plays. I've always loved stealth games and this one has that down so well. Unfortunately, the gameplay isn't balanced perfectly. Some of the augmentations are worthless, whereas some are highly useful in every encounter the game throws at you. Do some research beforehand if you don't want to waste your points. Many people have reported that combat playthroughs don't feel as rewarding as stealth runs, but I feel it's good that the game rewards carefulness and a strategic approach.
Voice acting is well done. I initially thought Adam's voice actor sounded 'forced', but that's how his voice really sounds like, and now I couldn't imagine any other voice for him.
A word of warning, though: don't chase the harder achievements like Pacifist or Foxiest of the Hounds on your first playthrough. It will distract you from the great storyline and take three times as long to finish the game. Finish the story first.
In closing, this is one of those rare games I'm willing to play through more than once. I'm eagerly waiting for the sequel, Deus Ex: Mankind Divided.

Deus Ex as a series has since its inception in 2000 been synonymous with its commitment to player choice. Though the freedom it proposed to offer only extended as far as the game had been designed to allow (as does every game by their very nature), its strength was in concealing these limits well enough that your actions still felt independent.
Human Revolution (and its Director’s Cut, which is what I will be reviewing and has been my first exposure to the game) intends to carry this torch forward, but rather than simply revive a franchise that has been dormant since the less positively received Invisible War in 2003, Human Revolution presents itself as a fresh start and a chance to redefine Deus Ex. In the process they’ve created a game that often feels ready to fall apart at a moment’s notice, but is uniquely fascinating in that despite all its faults Human Revolution still seems to accomplish virtually everything it intended to.
What Human Revolution does best is keep the player in the dark without telegraphing this with obvious plot holes or unavailable mechanics. As Adam Jensen, previous head of security for Serif industries brought back to life through an experimental human augmentation surgery, I felt from the very beginning sufficiently capable for what the game threw at me. I was informed, technologically and physically superior to my enemies, and clear as to what my role was in all of this.
Human Revolution manages to keep this up an astoundingly long time, keeping its narrative tightly concealed even when it seems to be spilling open before you. This is largely accomplished through Human Revolution ultimately being less about individuals, but organizations and ideas. The comically evil villains teased at the beginning of the game are quickly eclipsed by motives and plans far bigger and more radical than their mundane attempts at intimidation which are little more than a front. Human Revolution is a game with big aspirations that excels at asking complex, difficult questions with the intelligence they require and a lack of simple solutions to choose between.
Transhumanist and metaphysical debate as to the ethical implications of humanity accelerating its own evolution are at the center of all of this, but rather than creating two sides characterized by extreme extrapolations of their ideologies for the player to choose between, Human Revolution intentionally muddies the water so as to require the player to come to their own conclusions as to whose (if anyone’s) side they should choose. The ideas it presents are complicated and logical in a way that is rarely seen in games, which more often fall back to black and white views of morality even as they assume to be more intelligent than a collection of tired, easy clichés.
Human Revolution never falls into this trap, going so far as to omit many of the gaming’s standard illustrations of choice and consequence to avoid simplifying itself for the sake of convenience. There are no morality bars which swell and dip with each conversation, no side quests locked out by binary choices or indicators informing you that your decisions have consequences. In this way Human Revolution feels refreshingly unhindered by the freedom that ironically tends to lock games down, allowing you to approach situations and conversations on whatever terms you feel appropriate, and then requiring you to deal with whatever happens later.
Upgrades in the form of unlocked augments serve as a much more reserved skill tree than we have grown used to seeing, but rather than narrowing your options for growth Human Revolution has gone to great lengths to trim its progression system down to its most meaningful components. Skill points came very slowly throughout the game, but each time I received one it presented an important choice that had the potential to extensively alter my style of play. I found myself paying a great deal of attention with how I spent each of my points, giving me a greater attachment to my play style and a more noticeable sense of improvement than I initially expected.
Whether I was smooth talking a guard to let me by or opting to slip in through an air duct, my actions created natural ripples which often extended further than I even realized. This feeling that I was a part of a world which reacted and changed depending on how I interacted with it, made Human Revolution exceedingly engaging and surprising. It’s rare for me to feel like I’m inhabiting an actual developed world when I play a game, but no matter how long I spent with Human Revolution I rarely saw the edges where that illusion breaks and I’m reminded that these are just images on a screen.
Unfortunately though that means when those edges do appear, they’re that much more jarring and disappointing, even more so in this case as when Human Revolution fails it does so in ways you can’t unsee and which don’t go away. Bugs and glitches abound, from spotty hit detection to excessive clipping to instances of guards seeing/not seeing me when they should/shouldn’t to weird animation hiccups and general issues in presentation. More pressing than technical breakdowns though is how disconnected enemies felt from their environment. Repetitive patrol patterns and alert cooldown timers I could deal with, but looking at enemies standing above a stairwell unsure how to proceed, or having them crouch idly outside a vent I had just crawled into rather than proceed in after me made it hard to view my adversaries as people rather than models running on scripts with some very narrow parameters.
Human Revolution makes up a lot of the slack created by its incapable patrols with level designs I loved exploiting and experimenting within, often discovering routes where I least expected it and feeling incredibly clever each time I found a new solution to a problem I’d been stuck at. This is stripped away completely though in each of the games widely criticized boss fights, which amount to giant warts on a better game than they deserve to be a part of. They’re boring, simple, allow effectively no room to experiment, and are typically so easy as to make me wish they had simply been replaced with a cutscene that would at least have taken less time.
The worst offender in regards to wasting your time however isn’t a boss fight (or not entirely, that is), but the mini campaign originally released as DLC, The Missing Link. In the Director’s Cut this is integrated directly into the story as you play, but it is so abundantly clear it wasn’t originally a part of the game that you’d never mistake it for anything but an underwhelming add-on unceremoniously popping up at a pivotal point in Human Revolution proper. It’s a very tedious, meandering mission which essentially resets your progress in the game up to that point and takes several hours before it’s even clear why you should care about what’s going on, at which point it’s very nearly over.
There are so many rough edges to Deus Ex: Human Revolution that it would be easy to pick it apart bit by bit as half-baked and overambitious. Doing so though would miss what makes it so impressive and interesting. It’s a game with so many layers, of interconnected systems and the  dynamics that crop up between them, that even when one element breaks down it is held up by everything working together with it to create an experience that feels so uncharacteristically AAA. Human Revolution takes a lot of big risks with its design, not all of which work and some will likely fail to resonate with certain players, but its willingness to commit to itself feels inspired in a way I haven’t felt from a big budget game in quite some time.

MechWarrior Online is a Team Deathmatch shooter with BattleMechs. Not more and nothing less.
It's not "MechWarrior 5", meaning there's no single player campaign, no background story, no lore (in-game).
If you can accept that, MWO is a fun game to play.
There's quite a few negative reviews, and then there's positive reviews, and both sides are actually valid. As good as the game is, development is quite slow, other than some new mechs, there's few updates to game modes or maps.
And better don't get a veteran/founder player started on the things that were promised ...and never delivered.
Balance between the Inner Sphere and Clans is actually very good (currently). Must be since both sides claim the other to be overpowered ;)
For the matter of Pay-to-Win, you can buy every mech with real money if you like, but there's absolutly no requirement to do so. The Champion and Hero mechs can only be bought with real money. Champion mechs are just standard variants with a bonus to experience earned, Hero mechs have a custom paintjob and a slightly different weapon loadout than the standard variants and get a bonus to in-game currency earned (C-Bills).
In terms of performance those 'Hero' 'Mechs aren't better than the ones you can buy for C-Bills. Many are actually worse ;)
Buy them if you like the game and want to support the Devs.
A few hints for new players:
1) Go to the MechWarrior Academy, the in game training program. Not only does it show you how things work, but it rewards a sum of C-Bills, the in-game currency.
2) While the Inner Sphere 'Mechs are cheaper in the store, most of them require upgrades that need to be bought with C-Bills, usually adding another 2+ Million to the cost of the 'Mech itself. Clan 'Mechs are fully upgraded from the start.

Since only 5 individuals found this review helpful, I shall elaborate.
I've now been playing this game for one year. It took me a good while to finally engage and appreciate this game.
There are a lot of individuals who will either bash the game, or bless it. I have no knowledge of battle tech game lore, and perhaps because of that I am not irritated by the decisions made by "PGI". I will agree that there are a lot of aspects of the game which were quite awful at some point. The vast majority of these issues have since been addressed. Over the year that I've played the game I would say that PGI has done an over all decent job in fixing and adding to the game.
I don't really want to continue with the politics or any other irrelevant back stories.
Looking at the game itself and the gameplay. It's a niche game but can be incredibly satisfying. I perhaps enjoy it so much because of the metagame. I would say a lot of individuals perhaps hate the metagame because, "it creates a lack of variety and renders some mechs OP in comparison to others". Personally, I disagree with these claims. There certainly are super cookie cutter builds, and yes there are some mech builds that are optimal for certain mechs (because of quirks), however I've found that almost all the "cookie cutter" builds posted online aren't perfect. This being said, with some creativity and careful planning, there are still a lot of better builds that can be made and tailored to your liking while still being competitive.
(-I should warn that there are a good number of mechs that are actual garbage!-)
However the variety in mechs is amazing!
Being able to optimize these builds for my play style has resulted in even higher damage outputs in comparison to said "cookie cutter" builds.
I don't want to sound patronizing, but as a player you must be able to think outside the box in your builds, but also also pilot your mech efficiently in order to be successful and enjoy the game.
You will find that a large portion of the individuals complaining about the game are those who aren't successful in battle (and I feel bad for them).
In summary, I wouldn't allow the opinion of others to sway you from trying out a free to play game.
I would also strongly recommend not spending any money in this game until you've spent many hours and bought several mechs with in game currency only. Also spend a good amount of time researching before purchasing your first crucial mech. The first mech you purchase will most likely decide if you continue to play the game or not.
I would say spend some time in game, and generate some genuine opinions for your self. Don't be discouraged by the learning curve, I remember what it was like.
Best of luck.

I’ve played MWO for many, many, many hundreds of hours and I am happy that it wasn’t on Steam before becase seeing how much time I dumped into it could rip my brain apart.
Or remind me that I really want to try out the new Mechs.
It‘s about 50/50.
This game isn’t as close to your average MMO arena game as you might think. There is no tier nonsence like in WoT, no „YOU MUST HAVE THIS TO BE COMPETITIVE!!1!“ Mechs. There are many machines with their advantages and disadvantages, most weapon setups can be made to work (except for perhaps boating flamers). Balancing is constantly happening and if anything overperforms too much it gets adjusted. Also unlike in WOT you can’t really loose in-game currency in bad matches, you still get some rewards so playing with the heaviest Mechs has gameplay drawbacks, not monetary ones.
Common features with similar games? You are limited by number of Mechbays. Those are your general garage slots. The thing is, there are many events throughout the year and rewards where you can get these really easy. If you play the game you can have anything from the premium content (colors for Mechs, mechbays, hero Mechs and so on) without having to pay anything. Also there is nothing like gold ammo in WoT which ruins the game for many, keeping MWO as away from Pay-2-Win as possible.
Another similarity to WoT is how the devs make money. You can buy premium time, sure, but it isn’t really worth it. You can buy Mechbays and so on but these can be acquired in other way too. What makes PGI money is selling Mech packs. Look at
page and you will see what I am talking about. Every once in a while new set of Mechs is released and you can pay for it in advance, which will get you the Mechs and other freebies. These Mech packs are relatively expensive compared to other stuff but in time this turned out to work best for both MWO community and the dev team. What these packs get you is an early access because all these Mechs are released for everyone for free in like a month or so, only showing that you really don’t have to spend anything on this game to have it all.
Hope you enjoy this game as I do. It is a thinking mans shooter with impressive graphics and if you are in a market for one you should check it out.

Gender Bender DNA Twister Extreme Hyper Turbo Tournament Edition The Movie The Game featuring Dante from the Devil May Cry series is a visual novel fetish game. If you are expecting this game to be a commentary on anything or an interesting look at a different perspective, for example someone transitioning between genders, then do not play this game.
At its core, DNA Twister is a visual novel game which decides to give the player several shallow characters rather than one or two indepth paths like you would find in Japanese visual novels. I suppose you could draw a comparison to an CYOA novel, but it lacks the same feel as that kind of game. I will fully admit I read the bare minimum of text in this game because the writing in this game is really bad. Everything is stupid and cheesy but lacks self awareness. For example, the scientists who made the drug that makes you become a sexy woman work for a company called Abbadon. The writing just feels sophmoric, shallow and at some points blatantly insulting.
I considered writing more indepth on the story but I feel that it would be disingenious as this game is clearly not made for me. I do not have a huge passion for webcomics and I do not have a transformation fetish or gender bending one, and most of my comments would be on how stupid the characters are, which is a moot point. I will say, if you do love webcomics and have a laundry list of fetishes or you are Bulgarian, then seek professional help and buy this game
The art is bad, but I suppose that goes without saying. The phrase "deviantArt" gets thrown around a lot, but frankly, the art in this game is embarassing. The women stand at impossible angles, destroying their spines. Their bodies have long, weird stomachs with too small hips and giant balloon sized breasts. Perhaps it'd be best to describe the art as beloning to a bad webcomic? Really, that's what this game feels like.
One final thing I want to address is how gross this game made me feel at times. Now, before you assume I'm going to take some sort of moral high ground and condemn it for sexualizing women or something, I am not. I do not particularly find the T&A appealing, but that's my own view on sexuality and aesthetics. What left me feeling gross is the childish, and very stupid message the game shoves down your throat. It's not, as one might expect, "Wouldn't it be cool to see what life was like if you were the opposite gender?" where maybe the characters get to experience the good and the bad of being a woman, or something. You know, freaky friday style trials and tribulations that cause them to grow and better understand themselves and the female gender? DNA Twister, obviously, does not do this. What it does do is give the message "Everything would be better if you were a girl!" which to me is really unnerving.
All but one of the characters (from when I last played at least) was totally fine with being a girl. They totally embraced sexy clothing and in multiple characters' paths they spend entire nights masturbating (I am not kidding). It's this eye rolling drek that makes the whole thing feel like it was written by a 15 year old who loves boobies. The worst of it comes at the end of the fetish monster Dina (my pebbles) story where she talks to the one character unhappy with being a woman. The dialog essentially boils down to:
"I don't want to be a woman forever Dina!" "Fred, I know you say that, but deep down you actually want to be a woman." "Wow Dina you really changed my views on this."
That left me slackjawed in awe of how oblivious the writer(s?) of this game are.
Other highlights include: Black character grows straight, white people hair upon becoming a woman. Horrific breast expansion. Tons of implied masturbation. And an epic quest of self discovery.
In conclusion, this game is really good. Buy it now folks!
PS: As an aside, the devs were helpful and polite when it came to getting my key onto steam and did so fast so there's that.

For the impatient readers: Pick the demo and carefully choose which character route you want to play first. If you don’t like it at all, drop it. If you kind of like it, you can check out more routes. If the characters are really interesting and you laughed a lot, this is probably a game you want.
Ok, first off, the time you can see (7.6 hrs played) is only for the latest route.
I did play the other routes, but the game wasn't available on Steam when those came out.
Another "disclaimer": This game has "Gender Bender" in its title. As you might guess, that's the sort of "audience" for this game. If you do not like “Gender Bender” at all, this game probably isn’t for you.
I haven't looked at all "Gender Bender" material out there, but unless it's outright porn, most of it is a comedy. Ranma 1/2 comes to mind.
In short, the "Gender Bender" genre in general tends to mix comedy with fanservice, a lot. Usually, there is romance involved as well.
I view this game as a comedy as well. Yes, characters can have large breasts and they do wear ridiculous outfits.
Out of all the 7 currently playable characters:
2 wanted the change before it happened. (Derek and Liam. They're in charge of the lab)
4 were male and resisted the change, usually for at least a week. (Yael, Ben, Dan, Zeke)
1 was female and also resisted the change initially. (Stephanie)
In general, most of them change their opinion during the first week due to all the craziness that happens.
Usually the other "transformed" characters are the reason for the craziness, thus adding more and more "crazy" like a snowball effect.
In short, the characters may not be the most rational humans on earth. They just start "rolling with it" at some point.
For recommendations, I'd suggest to always play the newest available character. Making this game is a learning experience for the two devs that are making this. The demo does not contain the "newest available character".
It should be obvious for any Early Access Game, but if you are on the fence about it, you should wait until the game is "complete".
My "score" (since people apparently care about those) would be 5/5. I think the game exactly achieves what the target "audience" wants from it. This game isn't trying to be philosophical or ponder moral issues. This game is trying to provide you with some lighthearted fun most of the time.
The demo will contain 7 characters to choose from while the "full version" will have 13 characters.
It is likely that the "early character routes" (e.g. Yael) will be "brought up to standard" once all the other routes are done.
Edit: The "full demo" will have 7 playable characters, not 6.

Initially being unsure about this buying this game I first played the demo version of this on Desura. The next 3 Dan, Steph and Zeke progress this story forwards.
This game reminded me the simpler times, of chose your own adventure books, day of the tentical and Leisure Suit Larry in the land of the lounge lizard. At the moment all paths are unlocked in GBDNATE, and playing one story, does not effect any others, I suspect this is a product of how the game has had to be writen one character at a time, after all this is only an Alpha, nothing to stop the developers locking characters and paths, until other ones have been discovered, this however would be best done once all of the 13 character stories have been written. It took me about 25 hours to run through all the character paths, the game has a nice skip function where you can forward through sections you have already seen. However currently it cannot do this where sections are indentical but accessed through different paths.
There seems much debate if this game is "suitable" for steam. Personally I think not every game needs to be the latest shot them up, where the only difference is the arena, models for monsters and allowing people to pay real money to dress up your doll (oops sorry character!). All a game needs to be is something that is an amusing diversion for a number of hours, I have paid alot more for other games (such as X Rebirth) that have taken alot more developement hours and far more graphics eye candy, but yet been utterly boring to play. The story in GBDNATE grabbled me from the start, and made me laugh alot, even though I am not into furries!
If you don't like anime or don't like laugh at rediculous situations and prefer to spend your time blowing things up then this game is not for you. However the good news is there are plenty of identical clone first person shoters for you to pick from.
All we need now GBDNATE to be a proper steam game is Badges and Achievements!

I've been playing Loadout since closed beta, April 2013. Here are some of my thoughts on the game.
+ The gameplay is fun, fast-paced, visceral and incredibly satisfying. Kills are accompanied by an extremely satisfying "splat", and there are some great medals, like "Valar Morghulis", which is rewarded when you kill everyone on the enemy team at least once.
+ The art style is solid. Loadout is an extremely gory and violent game, which I suppose lends to the satisfying nature of the gameplay. There is nothing more fun than blowing off an arm or a leg with your sniper rifle, or reducing your enemy to a crawling torso with explosives, and Loadout lets you do both of those things and more. There are a wide variety of death animations, and they're all extremely satisfying.
+ The weapon building system is a great idea, and is implemented very well. You get to choose the type of weapon (rifle, beam weapon, launcher, etc.), and then customise it with different components, such as stocks, scopes, barrels, triggers and clips. You can also choose what your weapon's payload will be -- essentially what it shoots. At the moment you can choose from Slug (normal ammunition with no special effects), Pyro (incendiary ammo), Tesla (electrical ammo), Health (ammo which heals and overheals your teammates when you shoot them), and the Juice (which buffs your allies when you shoot them). There is a 6th payload in development -- Cryo, which is ice-based, although that has been in the works since early beta and there's still no sign of it, so don't hold your breath.
+ Gameplay is very movement-focused -- your characters run super fast and jump super high, and you can roll as well. Jumping off the edge of a cliff or ledge will propel you higher into the air than normal, as will jumping immediately after a dodge. There is no stamina sytem, so you are free to jump around to your heart's content.
+ The game runs very well -- I get 60+ FPS on my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop, with drops down to 30-40 when there's a lot of action going on.
- The payment model is incredibly poorly-implemented (pay money to unlock new weapon components, loadout slots and weapon slots, or grind an unreasonably long time to unlock them instead), and is essentially pay to win. It is incredibly difficult to create a half-decent gun without grinding for several dozen hours, and even then there are parts that are direct upgrades over others (e.g. Dampening Stock ---> Advanced Dampening Stock). This is a real shame, since it's a tremendous waste of the ingenious weapon building system.
- The game's population seems to be at an all time low and shrinking, which means finding a game can be a lengthy process. If someone leaves a match they will be replaced by bots, but bots have superhuman accuracy and probably cheat too.
Final Verdict: I'd recommend Loadout if you're just looking for a fun, fast-paced shooter to kill a couple of hours. Otherwise, I don't suggest getting too invested in the game, as it seems to be on its last legs.

If you're a fan of any 4X strategy games, you owe it to yourself to play this. The streamlined interface, and the deceptively complex micromanagement make this game compelling and intuitive from the first turn to the last. Several design decisions may seem awkward at first, such as the movement phase not actually ocurring between any singular turn but at any point during anyone's turn. However, this minor decision and many like it (I.E. starting in a "cold war" instead of peace with newly met factions) add quite a lot of depth and decision making to a genre that normally severely lacks, in both departments, even though it thrives on each. This is ESPECIALLY true in multiplayer. While the AI is quite good on higher difficulties, nothing beats the chess standoffs that can occur in the functional (surprise! Multiplayer in a 4X game that works!) and fun 8 player galaxy spanning matches.
Don't even get me started on the sound design. The music is top notch and I recommend any fan of ambient yet groovin jams to actually purchase the OST for this game. Music aside even, the little boops and blips as you navigate through the menus are satisfying and even gratifying, I personally dig the "you completed a research" jingle.
Every game has it's faults, though.
The space battles, however, lack in the sound department. The guns and lasers and explosions just don't have that "oomf" you'd expect. It's strange when pressing an "ok" button makes a more satisfying sound than having your fleet blow up a moon sized battlecruiser with space lasers.
The combat, also, I feel lacks a bit. Everything is automated with battle cards being selected. Where some counter others and have certain effects on your ships. While you can design your own ships in terms of the modules that they contain, the ships don't end up all being too dissimilar from eachother. This does work within the formula of the game, and I'm sure the inclusion of multiplayer might have something to do with it, but I would have preferred a turn based tactical battlescape ala Master of Orion 2.
The Disharmony expansion is also a must. Not because the new race is particularly cool, (Neat concept, very difficult to play as.) but because there are many minor tweaks that have been performed throughout the game, from UI changes to ship design and tech tree additions. It somehow makes the game even MORE polished.
Speaking of polish, I don't think I'd encountered a single bug in my play time with this game. It's almost eerie.
So yeah. Buy this game if you like 4X games. If you don't, I honestly don't see this changing your mind. It's like a really good hamburger. Yes that hamburger is delicious, but if you're a vegetarian it's not going to appeal to you. 8.6/10

If you like guns this game is fun, addictive, and educational (and if you aren't trying to play for score, throw some music on, it's pretty relaxing). It's really interesting to see the differences and similarities between various designs from different ages and cultures--I have a newfound respect for Russian guns and a newfound hatred for German guns (why use two parts to do a job when you can use eighteen parts to do the same thing instead!), being able to trace design elements on the Desert Eagle back to the Jericho and then the CZ-75, how Ruger's copy of the Colt SAA is in many ways more complicated, etc. All of this is pretty interesting to me.
But then again I'm a nerd about these things.
I like the "operation" mode too, where you can see how the gun functions using varying levels of transparency and slow motion. It's all fantastically polished, especially being free to play.
Not perfect though. As another reviewer mentioned, while the game requires you to remove and install parts in the proper order and shows animations of the various screws and pins, it leaves something to be desired as far as the actual method goes-- there's a difference between clicking on a 1911's recoil spring vs. slipping and sending the spring and plug across the room when you turn the barrel bushing, for example. So in its current form the educational aspects are limited, but I see a lot of potential there.
All in all, though, it's a heck of a lotta fun.

As a player since closed beta the ride has been bumpy but MechWarrior is the only game that I keep coming back to. It may not be perfect but it's come a long way since its first debut. MechWarrior online is the only modern First Person game of its kind: big stompy robots, big weapons and lots of wub wub.
The game is a lot of fun, it has a higher time to kill than any other game(although for a MechWarrior game I'd love it to be longer), a lot of variety in the mech chassis choices and even more in the customisable loadouts you can choose.
Those not familiar with the series may find the learning curve a tiny bit steep but wrecking other Mechs is one of the most rewarding things you can get in a game and when you land on a team that works together, you can have a load of fun.
I highly recommend this game to everyone.

Played this for about a year and a half before the glaring issues eventually forced myself and my friends to quit. To start expect a heavy pay to win experience or at best a pay to not grind three weeks for a standard mech. Also expect to be charged ridiculous amounts of cash to obtain hero mechs or even just mechbays or colors/patterns. Seriously it's in the neighborhood of $30+ PER MECH. Don't even think about the bundles and such as you'll get very little for $100+. Just standard mechs you can buy in game a little faster and MAYBE a bonus mech with a slight cbill boost.
Once you get into the game expect two things. Fun stompy mech action and complete and utter bs metabuilds. In my time it went from LRMs for a brief period to PPC/Gauss builds. The PPC/Gauss was the worst because it was instant pinpoint HIGH damage. You'd wait 5-10 minutes for a match and die in seconds if you weren't in a light or assault class. Unless you got lucky matchmaking wise and the other team wasn't loaded with 5-6 metabuilds and you'd get a decent match. After the forced mech setup for matchmaking requiring x of each class it got a little more even in matches but the wait times went skyhigh. Eventually the high alpha BS and long wait times drove myself and my friends to stop playing.
The company also has issues. One of the WORST I've ever dealt with. I understand Niko left a bit ago but still damn. They also can't balance their way out of a paper bag. Things get buffed WAY too far or not remotely enough and stay that way for months if not years. It took them six months or so to even start to nerf the high alpha metagame and even then it was weak nerfs that did very little curb it. Not even the bizarre ghost heat changes ever successfully killed it. The highest alpha to a side torso or center torso is the only real way to fight with any real success.
I will admit before the issues started piling up and things with the company got worse it was a blast. It really captures the stompy mech action quite well. However the magic is long gone so if you play do it without wasting money like I did. Get in, do a couple rounds for some fun, and get out when the lopsided matches get to be too much. The trial/standard mechs work well enough for light play. As long as you don't invest too much time or money it's a perfectly fine game to play a match or two on occassion.
EDIT - It seems they fixed up the wait times at some point. So it's faster to get into a game. The rest still stands.

I am a humble fan, I see Nep I buy.
But is the lattest game in series is still good? Is Nep still pudding? And does IF and Compa still have something to provide for those who love Gameindustri? Well, let's go through pros and cons:
Pros
1) Story: VII puts a spin on a traditional formula of Neptunia games. Where previous were following chapter by chapter scheme, this time game separated in three diffrent stories, all connected by a global plot. Each story follows a certan charecter and her story in one of three dimensions (later in the game you can travel between them). Without giving away too much spoilers, let's just say that plots are quite entertaining, espechially for those who played this series for a while.
2) Humor: Since VII provides new structure to plot telling, new charecters and refrences modern gameing as well as Dreamcast rise and fall... It does amazing job with making fun of todays console wars, trends and directions at wich gameindustry rolls, as well as simply being Neptastic in it's usuall well known way, After all most of us play this series for good laughs and this game provides them.
3) Combat: Best in series. This time it's not a simpel as get best weapon, set best combos and just spam those or use all the best SP moves. This time, each weapon have a certan ammount of slots for combos, and many of them connect to each other in diffrent ways for crit hits, so you will have to chose between weapon with low dmg but a lot of combo slots, or strong dmg weapon wich hold less. But overall it's not far fetched from previous games, just a little tweak that makes combat more intresting. Another change was done to EXE meter, unlike Neptunia 1 and 2 -- you can't fill it in diffrent battles and later use to your advantage in tough fight, and unlike Neptunia VI it came back: still it's same good old EXE meter, when heroes or enemies  takes damage it will be filled, and player can use it to transform, unleash a devistating drive attack or use it for coordination. What is coordination? Well if you remember, in previous games, heroines could do double-overdrives, now player have ability to execute a moves with 3 or 4 heroines, if they present and set on field.
Finaly we have so called Dark CPU bosses. Battles with them are diffrent from standart, but not much, you simply can not harm them with weapon and left with SP moves and coordination attacks, but the epicness is overwhelming.
4) Music and Sound: Amazing! Although some of trecks in OST are remakes of other games, and while it's understandable with Spelunky (to which there's a two dungeons as a huge nod) then with Guilty Gear or Phantom Break (and correct me if I am wrong, but isn't "Whirlpool of Insanity" kinda sound like one of God Eater themes?) it feels outta place. Still even remakes are awesome.
Neutral
1) DLC: By themself it's same old same old, a wee bit of overpowered equip and some charecters. However DLC charecters do have their events, dialogues and they feel like they should've been in the game from the start. Although they wont provide anything story related, it's still feels like a sort of scam... Not mad, simply dissapointed at you IF and Compa.
2) Random encounters on a world map. Random encounters on a world map Carl! Random encounters on a world map in modern JRPG! Well in NG+ you can turn them off, still very annoying, though not fatal and hey if you like 'em -- good for you.
3) Endings. With no spoilers, ♥♥♥♥ Normal Ending! ♥♥♥♥ it! ♥♥♥♥ it! Not very dark (this honor still belongs to Neptunia 2 and conquest ending) but my god it's sad, be aware. True ending is better, but it still fells quite depressing... I thought I played Neptunia not Tales of! But with all honesty, they both are strong endings and I put them in neutral section mostly because of subjective view.
Cons
1) Short
2) Auto-equip
3) Many boring dungeons and enemy variety
4) Hunting for secret treaures still sucks
5) Scouts (just play and you will know the pain)
Final verdict? 8 Neps out of 10. Great for those who played previous games and likes them.

Just when you thought that Neptune couldn't possibly add any more anime tropes, they added more anime tropes (absolute madmen). As the latest installment in the series, Neptune V2 introduces even more new characters to its already massive cast, knowing full well that all we want are more waifus.
1) Your favourite waifu gets more attention.
The story is structured in 3 arcs, with three separate conflicts that all tie together at the end. For the majority of the game, your party will only consist of 3-4 characters lead by one of the CPUs, and you waifu will likely get her own story at some point in the game. The consequence of this segmentation is that if you don't like one of the characters, you'll be forced to play her story.
2) Gameplay is much better from previous installments.
The new combo mechanic is great, and smaller party sizes really makes you appreciate the stronger characters (Rom & Ram OP). You shouldn't have to grind at any point in the game since there are a lot of ways to boost your defense. (Idea chips). The removal of DPS checks also meant that you just have to max out your defense to beat the bosses (by DPS check I meant enemy regen at end of turn, so if you can't out DPS the regen you are pretty much done).
3) New characters fill even more anime tropes.
We now have yandere, furyou, lolicon, dame otaku, etc. (Yes some male tropes too). Do know that not all of the above characters are fully developed, and some are just side characters. If you are like me though, more waifus are always better. The price you pay, though, is the lack of previous characters. (Plutia > Uzume)
There's some annoying details here and there, but overall Neptune V2 is a great waifu simulator. Because levels give you so much stats in this game, you can level your favourite waifu and actually feel like she's carrying the team (best grill confirmed). If you have not played this series at all, but want to get into it, I suggest the following play order: rebirth 1  -> rebirth 3 (V1) - > V2.

I'm not sure I'll be able to put my feelings for this game in words as eloquently as some of the other reviews here, but I'll do my best.
I would like to start off by saying that I have, at the very least, 2000 hours logged into this game pre-steam. Blockland is the first game I ever bought, almost 6 years ago. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ Back then, it was still $20, and I can tell you now that I would have paid five times that amount back then if I knew how much I would have loved it.
Other people have already explained the building system and the events system, so I won't really talk about those. What I would like to talk about, however, is the add-on creation system. Don't get me wrong, I truly enjoy building and eventing, but I wouldn't keep coming back to this game as often as I do if there weren't any add-ons. Not even just using add-ons though. More than that: creating them, changing them, collaborating on them. Even though some of the coding may be limited by the engine in this game, it more than makes up for this by flattening the learning curve for making your own mods. In my honest opinion, there are way more possibilities for creativity because of this. Because more people are making add-ons, there is a lot more diversity and plenty of originality when it comes to gamemodes, server mods, etc.
The reason why I said "at the very least, 2000 hours", is because of all the time I've spent in text editors, writing code. That's actually the reason why you won't see many hours played on my steam account for Blockland, I'm in the midst of making a big gamemode (look for it, people of the future). This game is where I learned how to do basic logic constructions and other similar things for writing code. The language is called "torquescript", and it's pretty similar to C in most ways. It's incredibly easy to learn because of the syntax checker (to catch any mistakes you make), and because you can instantly see the result of your code ingame. Because of my previous experience with coding, I've been able to pick up visual basic and C almost instantly. For my job, I was able to program a z-axis camera mount using C# and also to make a protocol for an x-y motion system using a custom compiler for visual basic. I've included these in my resume, and next year when I leave for college there's no doubt in my mind that I will continue using code. In fact, it's very likely that my experience with code will have helped me get in the school of my choice (already accepted to one of my top choices).
While I know this isn't necessarily something that everyone will experience if they play the game, I know I just wanted to share my story. Know that even if you have no interest in modding, Blockland has something for you. I've never seen, heard, or smelled of a game that could truly have "endless possibilities". That is, except for Blockland.

An awesome game from start to finish, I don't know why I waited so long to play this.. Definitely one of the best first person shooters I have ever played. This is really what Doom is supposed to be, playing this made me realize what Doom 3 was lacking..
The pacing in this game is practically perfect, It never once feels dull at any moment during the campaign - alternating between quieter exploration sections and all out carnage old school fast paced Doom/Quake/UT style combat. This version of Doom more than any other FPS I have played requires you to really think on your feet and keep moving at all times during combat. Different enemies and areas provide unique challenges - as well as every gun performing very differently with strengths and weaknesses. "Glory kills" make the combat in this game unique and a little easier but even the default "Hurt Me Plenty" difficult gets VERY hard at times especially in the second half of the game, although I never once died thinking to myself "That was BS." The game is brutal, fair and above all fun.
The graphics are incredible and the level design is excellent. Every chapter is layed out very differently, has a unique feel to them and is very memorable. Plenty of eye candy and secret areas/easter eggs in the levels as well. Lots of variety in the ways you choose to upgrade your suit and weapons that definitely affect gameplay quite a bit. I wish more FPS games would focus on making a great campaign like this that is memorable, challenging and fun. The multiplayer is awesome as well from what I played so far, definitely better than the current state of Quake: Champions. Even just based on the campaign I would give this game a 10/10.

I absolutely recommend this product. This is not a technical review more a dummy's perspective.
For those of you who have not yet bought this controller and have been reading that the xbox controller is better I implore you to ignore that myopic viewpoint.
Firstly let me say I had a madcatz c.t.r.l.r which was absolutely awful and was thinking of getting myself an xbox controller but I had some steam credit so I thought I would give the Steam Contoller a try. I went in partially unsure of what I would be getting myself into but the best advice I read was that you should keep an open mind and not think of this as even in the same category as your generic xbox controller or even as a keyboard and mouse.
Imagine the buttons on the xbox controller, if You count them up and then times them by something let's say x5 you still wouldn't have the amount of individual controls available that the Steam Controller has.
Right... no more comparing cos they are not the same.
For example I am currently creating a configuration for DCS with the steam controller. With ease I can start up the SU-25 fly it, operate the navigation and the weapons systems without ever needing the keyboard and mouse. I can zoom in and look around whilst flying and apply precise aircraft trim. Admittedly it has taken me about 5 or so hours to configure it so far and it's not exactly how I  want it yet but the possibilities are endless.
At first when you get the controller it might seem a litle daunting and getting to grips with the configuration software can be a bit of a pain but when you understand all the functions and how to set up modifiers you realise just how special a piece of kit this controller is.
One of the drawbacks is the way you operate the controller through Steam Big Picture. I was really looking forward to trying out the Steam Edition of FSX but the way the menu operates serperately from when you hit "fly now", Steam doesn' register it and so you may have trouble assigning axis.
One other tip is to run Steam and Steam Overlay as Administrator.
In terms of configs, lets look at the left d-pad. You can press it like a normal d-pad and click it. You can tap it in four directions (like a mouse pad) and tap/double tap the centre, You can use it like a mouse or left/right joystick. you can rotate it clockwise/anti-clockwise. You can have it operate an onscreen-menu with more custom controls. You can have it operate as a modifier for the GYRO. [[That's all just the Left D-Pad which you can have dfferent per config set]].
I have yet to come across a product that so breaks down the contexts of multiple peripherals and merges it into one revolutionary new tool.
ps. Delivery is a bit on the slow side.
I like it alot, i was expecting just a controller what i got was something much much more. Its versatility is unmatched.

So there are these basic steps you need to go through after you receive the controller:
1. Connect controller to PC
2. Start your favorite game
3. Configure controller for the game
4. Play the game with your lovely new controller
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 at least a dozen times to perfect your config
6. Give yp and find a community-made config
7. Feel the modding spirit inside you and start re-tweaking the community mod
8. Decide it's as good as it gets
9. Profit!?
The Steam Controller is really amazing (once its properly configured for your game).
If you play anything that involves aiming, REMEMBER THE GYRO!!

I’m going to give this a positive review because the price is slated to be “less than four dollars” according to the developer.
Mall Empire is the developer’s first game and it shows. While the game is by no means unplayable it doesn’t have much in the way of strategy or management that I was personally looking for in a mall tycoon style game.
I would liken the game more towards the clicker genre rather than tycoon or management simulators.
The game involves you placing a variety of different shops and rooms in your mall, gaining money by clicking on each individual shop when a small icon pops up, then using that money to buy more shops.
That’s pretty much the extent of the game. You can do a few more tasks such as buying advertising to increase the amount of people that visit, but this doesn’t seem to be needed.
Within the first 20 minutes I was able to keep accumulating more and more money to the point where it didn’t seem like there was much of a challenge involved.
By the time I got to even the second story of my mall, the game became very difficult to manage in that I had to constantly look and click on every shop each minute to claim my money from it. The money you gain from shops is on a timer, so if you miss that timer you simply don’t get the money from the shop.
The help system and tutorial for the game gives you the bare minimum information needed to understand what to do. There is a lack of tooltips when you hover over anything, so you don’t necessarily know what everything does.
There are a few minor, but not game-breaking glitches in the game that include blueprints for stores that I have already bought still showing up in menus and some other similar things.
The developer is obviously foreign, so sentences and grammar are often in broken english. I would highly recommend they have someone who uses english as a first language to go over and redo the writing throughout the game.
All that being said, the price being so low combined with the game being simple, but playable mean that I can still say that if you are looking for a very basic mall creation or clicker game to spend a bit of time on while you do other things, you may find some enjoyment out of it.
I also hope that my video and written review will help the developer update the game to fix issues and include more features for either this or their future projects.

I had no idea Halcyon 6 was even in the making and, to be honest, I'm glad I didn't. Coming home from work to check the featured list and finding this elegant package waiting for me was a pure delight.
Halcyon 6 is the synthesis of titles such as FTL (though I don't entirely agree with that comparison given how different the mechanics are at present) and a three-party turn-based RPG such as Final Fantasy.
Alongside the combat mechanics which are beautifully rendered in a colorful and approachable palette is the strategy section between missions where you manufacture and make improvements to ships, your officers in command of said ships,the Halcyon 6 base itself, and patrol your local system keeping the peace.
It's a great example of how less is more. H6 uses a substantially less complicated interface and economy than that of it's 4x's counterparts to allow for accessible and genuinely fun gaming while maintaining a similar level of complexity and challenge. The art of managing your vessels in order to strike a balance between preservation of current resources while scouring potential planets for resources is challenging though and still in need of balancing.
The ships are a treat to behold and each one is borrows from awesomely cheesed up TV series such as Star Trek while being uniquely singular and beholden to the universe the game takes place in.

Interaction with other species is more on the comical side of things in the same way the ios game Star Command is (which was also a Kickstarter backed title). They share a few similarities in aesthetics but H6, despite the various comparisons with equally fantastic games such as FTL, manages to stand apart from such titles with a unique, fun, and stimulating degree of challenge and reward.

I recommend this to anyone that liked the previous game, Dungeons 2, and those who haven't tried the previous one, but think a more light-hearted dungeon management game with lots of fourth wall breaking and (bad) jokes could be fun.
This review is only really based on the single-player campaign, since that is usually my focus in games, and what I enjoy playing.
The game is very similar to the previous one in its cartoony style and tone, so it obviously isn't for people, who wants a more serious and dark game. The reference-loving narrator returns from the previous title, along with this game's main character the Dark Elf Talia, who competes to see who can shatter the precious fouth wall the most.
Minor Story spoiler:
A lot of the creatures from the previous game returns, but instead of playing as three different factions, you are now combined into one faction, with three creatures from horde, three demons, and three undead. Each faction also has a "task" in your overall dungeon. Demons creates and need mana as well as torture heroes, the horde creates trap and has training equipment, and the undead can resurrect. And one Elite creature from each sub-faction. In the story of the game the focus is far more on Talia than it is the creatures. Which does lead to a more focused story-line, but I kinda enjoy maps in this kind of games where the goal is to recruit a certain race to your side. There are maps for the elite, but I would have liked for the more common creatures too, but seeing as the story is meant to be a new campaign after the ultimate Evil's conquest in the first game, it wouldn't make so much sense, I guess, to recruit creatures like the naga/goblin who are already loyal since they are returning from the previous game.
This time most creatures can't be upgraded other than rising in level, but I feel they do a good job balancing each other and serving different purposes, and there aren't any completely worthless creatures in the later levels.
I really like that converted heroes aren't just converted, but they actually change their design/colors to visualize the change, and show that they have properly fallen into evil.
Not sure if I prefer this one or the previous one, but they are both very solid Dungeon Management games, and I am glad I bought it and played it.
End note for achievement hunters: The achievements are very easy to keep track of. There are 60 achievement, 3 for each campaign map/level, one of which is completing the map, and the achievements are shown before you begin the map.

If you need help, folks will gladly step up and give you pointers, with many units inviting new players to team up with them over a few matches to learn alongside them.   It's a good place to play, and I hope you enjoy this thing!   I go under the callsign FlyingMonkey - hit me up!

The third installment in the Deus Ex game series is a prequel to the first game.  The premise is that you're Adam Jensen, a bionic security guard given top of the line mechanical enhancements.  These enhancements function as your "character growth", allowing you to become a better hacker, gun slinger, stealth fighter, tank, or any other plethora of fun upgrades.  It's a cool system that's been refined across several Deus Ex games, and it works perfectly.  Graphically the game is very stylized, with the world having tints of gold to it everywhere, making the game immersive in its own way.
The downsides are fairly minor.  In every previous Deus Ex game, it was possible to finish the game without ever taking a life.  In this game, there are a few boss fights, all of which require you to kill your opponent.  This takes away from the novelty of never killing anyone in a combat-oriented game.  The storyline stops in the middle to do a side story that was DLC for the original game, and which was released in a package deal for the Director's Cut.  In it, you're stripped of your biomodifications and forced to finish the side story before you can come back to the main tale.  This disrupts the pacing quite a bit, but the side story is still fun.  Finally, the game is fairly linear, with several side quests in addition to the main goal of each area.  However, you can't really go backwards or choose where the next area is.
All in all, this does not take away from any of the game's charm, however.  It's still fun to play through it without setting off alarms, or without killing, or by killing absolutely everything.  It's a polished game that's fun to play several times through.
Definitely recommend.  This is one of those priceless games that I keep coming back to over and over again.

text: The prequal to Deus Ex is pretty much what everyone hoped for; a good Deus Ex game.  The game takes place in 2027, so it's a lot easiar to see this future becoming true.  While Deus Ex was about humanity creating an A.I that was pretty much a god, Human Revolution is about the ethics of human augmentation.  You play as Adam Jensen, a man who got his upgrades unwillingly after an orginization attacks the company he works for and takes their science team.  What follows in an epic globe trotting adventure that'll take you from Detroit, to Hengsha, to Montreal, then Singapore, and ending in Antarctica.  Back again are the selection of augmentation upgrades that will help you take on your foes easier, now with a lot more focus on them.  You can still play it your way, however, it's been boiled down to "kill or don't kill".  You only have guns now, no melee for some reason.  The game is not held back by that, however.  You also have a lot more control over the character you play as, Adam.  He can go from a good guy, to a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with a capital "D" in a second, and it's fun to watch.  All in all, I recomend this game to anyone who liked the first one.

First of all, let's have a short resume of what this game is...
Megadimension Neptunia VII is the fourth part of this franchise's "main story" and the sequel to the events of Victory generation. The story follows the adventures of the CPUs of Gamindustry, Neptune, Noire, Vert and Blanc as they once again struggle to save their nations from total destruction. What made this game different from the earlier release is the fact that it's not one, but three different games merged into one, and it takes place in three different dimensions as well.
Pros:
Improved gameplay- One of the most notable features about this game is the improved gameplay mechanics and new elements such as the investment or the combos that, unlike earlier releases, won't let you spam the same attack over and over again, making you actually stop and think about what sort of combination of attacks you want. There's also the offensvie and deffensive stat boost granted by the support characters on the back that help you make your main four do more damage or become more resilient, and the challenges that will definitely make your favorite girls have an edge over the rest.
A more serious, yet still funny story- Unlike earlier games, Megadimension follows a darker and more serious story, which is something many people (me included) found suprisingly pleasant.
Don't worry about things getting too gloomy, though, because the protag of protagonists always makes sure to shove in one of her meta jokes and constantly keep you laughing like she always does. And the other CPUs won't fall behind in making you laugh either.
Amazing soundtrack- One thing everyone can agree on with this game is that the soundtrack for this game was probably one of the best in the whole franchise. With calm and soothing tones that help you feel like you're just having a casual walk or battle songs that will make sure to pump you up for the upcoming battles.
Monsters that look like real monsters- Remember those walking eggplants? Or the console shapped animals and pacman-like ghosts wandering around the dungeons? Well, you won't be seeing any of that here.
Instead of the usually cute and comical monsters, this game introduces a new batch of enemies that look a lot more like proper monsters. From giant mutant turtles and gundamn-looking robots to demons and even giants taller than a skyscraper. No more fluffy dogoos and weird horse-bird hybrids, now you're dealing with the real deal.
New characters- Yet again, there's a whole new cast of characters, both ally and foe alike. And some of them ae just as erratic and hilarious as our all-time favorite girls
Cons:
unsatisfying treasures- In the dungeons, you can get hidden treasures for fulfilling certain requirements. Unfortunately, though, these treasures can be rather unsatisfying or even dissapointing in comparison to the effort needed to fulfill some of these requirements.
Unnecessarily difficult coliseum- One of the things many of us loved about the Nep games was the coliseum, an extra area aside from the story where you were free to choose from a list of pre-made battles and could fight to your heart's content without worrying about getting the game over screen even if you got defeated. And besides from having all sorts of amusing battles, you could always use it as a  quick way to farm some healing items or credits and do quick leveling. Unfortunately, this is not the case with Megadimension.
This time, the arena fights aren't very enjoyable. Enemies, even those in the lower lv requirements can be quite a pain to fight, and it's after reaching lv 200 when things get really annoying when fights used to start getting challenging at around lv 500 to 700 in earlier games. Most enemies take incredibly little damage or require a specific type of attack to even take damage at all (Dark Black, for example, won't take a single point of damage from anything except ice attacks, and even then her massive pool of health makes the fight painfully long and monotone) requiring you to be much more of a strategist than before, which is something not everyone enjoys
Another detail is the rewards being a one-time only reward. Things like rare accesories and weapons I get it if I can only get them once, but healing items and idea chips are something that could help a lot if they could be farmed, even if it's just to sell them for extra credits.
Missing costumes and processors- One thing I couldn't help but notice after searching through every dungeon, quest and arena fight was that, while the CPU candidates had their maid, cosplay and idol costumes available, Neptune and the others didn't. And I'm not talking about DLC costumes here, I'm talking about the school and idol uniforms. Costumes that were always available without DLCs since Re;Birth 1. And yet, they're nowhere to be found
And the core processors that appeared in Re;Birth 1 and 3 seem to be missing as well despite all their processor parts being available.
I don't know if this was a mistake or something done on purpose, but that's just not okay.
Level grinding is frustrating- Along with some of the most unpleasant things found in this game, probably the second one to bother me the most was the insane EXP requirements. Reaching a high enough level to beat the game isn't that hard, and reaching level 99 is easy if you know about the big metal dogoo, but it's after hitting lv 99 when things get complicated, and it doesn't take long for them to get crazy either.
Unlike before, the arena isn't really a choice for grinding for max level. So the big metal dogoo, which gives 10 million EXP per kill, quickly becomes the fastest way to grind. Getting to it isn't that hard once you get used to the dungeon, but what's really frustrating is the amount of times you need to fight it. Which rounds up around hundreds, if not thousands of times. And this process can be quite brain-numbing.
Now I'm not one to judge how others do their game design, but when the fastest method to reach max level is having to kill the same enemy thousands of times (around 3000 if the discussions page is right) then i think it's time to take a moment and think things through a little bit more.
Conclusion:
In all and all, Megadimension Neptunia VII is still a great game. It may have taken some bad decisions (Some of which could be fixed rather easily), but it improved over earlier releases in many ways and has by far one of the best stories in the franchise along with a clasic meta sense of humor that will appeal to both old-time fans and newcomers. If you're a Nep fan, then this game is a must-have, and even if you're not, then give it a shot, you won't regret it.

A sequel to the third Neptunia game, this continues the story from the 2nd and 3rd game. Compared to past games, this one takes on a much darker tone in comparison to the rather bright scenery seen in the Hyper Dimension and Mega Dimesion; Zero Dimension has a more apocalyptic feel to it.
Gameplay remains somewhat the same, being a turn-based RPG, but with a few changes.
First off, it would seem like the damage system has been changed a bit. When comparing damage from older games to this one, there's a rather significant drop in damage, more than 50% when attacking at similar levels. A new addition is the parts system when fighting enemies which provides opportunities to shift battles in your favor. A major addition to the battle system is the introduction of Dark CPU battles, which takes place on floating islands surrounding said Dark CPU. This slightly changes the battle mechanics, disabling the use of regular attacks and some skills, instead relying available skills and positioning.
Storywise, this still follows the events of the previous games (aside from the first one) where several years have passed. Of course, this also follows the previous games in that multiple endings are available depending on what you do in the story. That aside, this game still finds room to crack jokes and references just like the previous games.
The soundtrack has many recycled ones, mainly during dialogs, but also has new ones to reflect the darker tone of this game. This also includes the random battles, which change depending on which dimension you're currently in, from the usual upbeat tone found in previous games (since the difference between Hyper and Mega Dimension was mainly time) to a slightly serious tone found in Zero Dimension. Boss battles use entirely new soundtracks, no longer using the ones from the previous three games while also reflecting the current progression in the story (generic boss battles do use the same one though).
This game also introduces more characters that reference various companies similar to IF and Compa from the previous games. Returning characters include the ever infamous Arfoire, the Compa-smitten Warechu, the lecturing Histoire, Financier (who initially appeared in Re;Birth1 and has returned with a similar role), and more. The game will also reference characters from the previous games.
The only complaint that I had was the change in the game's engine. Since this is NOT a remake and a direct port, performance drops are noticable.
Overall, the game has quite a story to it, and for those who are new to the series, it is recommended to start from the second game (Re;Birth2) as the story is canon from there (the first game is not related to the events of the games after that), otherwise, newcomers will not get the references throughout the story.

Wow.  What a game.  For an action platformer this is without question one of the best in the genre.  TL;DR Awesome game.  Better than Salt and Sanctuary.  Better than La-Mulana.  Closest thing to Symphony of the Night on steam.  Ok so what makes it so good?
Pros
- Crisp and responsive controls.  This is the most important aspect the game nails it.  Attacking feels like a fighting game.  Hammer combo -> drill -> air dash ->  hammer roll during which game atuo zooms in for max impact feels awesome.  The anime style boss pause before unleashing super attack is great too.
- Every game in this genre basically involves you dodging glowing stuff gets thrown at you.  Learn the patterns and the openings.  This game is no different, but does away with needlessly fancy animations or gimmicky mechanics and this is a plus.  Boss attacks comically make no sense lol and is basically just random laser and balls of death in increasing complex patterns....and its awesome!  The difficulty levels is toned so well that anyone, by learning the fight over and over, can eventually win.  Learn which attacks can be dodged, and which ones cannot, and take advantage of invicibility frames from super attacks, etc.  With enough skill (ie. not gear or stat check) you can defeat bosses that outlevel you, and when this happens it feels so rewarding and satisfying.
- there is an rpg element as well, with character customisation by choosing from a pool of various passive abilities that you collect.
- Levels are expansive and the full map is huge. Typical of metroidvania games, levels often contain areas that you will need to revisit after acquiring the appropriate skills elsewhere in the game.  There are also generous amounts of hidden items/upgrades to find on the maps that greatly encourages exploring.
- visuals are clean, the BGMs are fantastic, no pc performance issues, large replayability with various difficulty level and modes.
Cons
- Story/writing/dialogues  - its cutesy anime stuff that I dont care much for, but that's just a personal preference.  Don't expect any deep or engaging plot.  Some characters are interesting and on occassions some funny dialogue.  it doesn't take itself too seriously ie. there was a npc in a niche corner of a level that told you "there really is nothing hidden in this room!"  Lol that just made me search it even harder... XD
- Some dialogue texts are missing in traditional chinese setting.  You see placeholder numbers like "7852" instead of text.
Overall this is an incredible game and criminally under advertised.  If you are reading this because you are already somewhat interested, no need to hesitate it is definitly worth the purchase.
