I saw the trailer and I knew this game was going to be great. It's up there as one of my all time favourites along with Wings of Vi and Cave Story.
* The Gameplay itself is certainly the greatest strength of the game by far. Controls are extremely solid with a controller. The pacing is great, The difficulty curve is perfect; it starts off simple but continues to throw challenges at you that will always keep you on your toes and leads to some of the hardest encounters Ive experienced in a game, expect to die when learning a boss.
Like most metroidvania games, you can progress in a wide variety of ways. There are a ton of secrets and collectables throughout the world. There are over 40 bosses and if you complete the main story and post game and collect every item there is over 40 hours of gameplay.
* The music is 10/10. Seriously, buy the soundtrack. (imo top track is Sudden Death).
* The Art and Sprites are beautiful.
* 6 difficulty settings. Casual, Novice, Normal and Hard are available from the start. Hell and Bunny Extinction are unlocked via beating the game on harder difficuties.
* Several Boss Rush modes for those who want a next level of challenge or to compete against others for a great score on the ladder.
* Tons of Achievements that are fun and challenging to earn.
* The devs continue to add more content to the game. It received a free Halloween patch that contained a fair amount of content and a very fun boss and a paid DLC that I have written a seperate review for.
However, as much as I love this game it does have its flaws.
* The story is one of the games few weak points. When I picked it up I didnt expect much of a story to begin with, but it was very vague about a a few things as you progress and learn more about the world you are playing in and doesnt really explain why certain things occur, Though with the latest DLC it does explain a few things a little better and gives a little closure.
* Fair amount of fanservice. This can be a pro for some people but it wasnt for me, there were a few moments in the game that made me cringe a little bit, but it wasnt a big deal though.
* Bosses later in the game can scale out of control, after around chapter 4 some bosses were 10+ minute long endurance tests because they have so much health (and that is with keeping up Max damage combo up), however please take into account I jumped into this game on it's hardest difficulty that is available to you on it's first playthrough (Hard) and may not apply on easier difficulties.

An extremely nicely designed DX game. The story is sort of up there, not as good as DX1, but arguably more interesting than DX2.
Major gripe: nonsensical architecture that serves the gameplay more than design. Buildings without proper entry points. Random Airduct Syndrome. You get the feeling the persons involved with level design used to work on some death-match maps or something. This theme is so consistent that it makes completely different areas feel strangely similar.
Lesser gripe: Apparently this 'more advanced' edition of the game is in a more buggy state than the original. There are some missing texture and crashes in fixed locations. Interestingly, ENB graphics software only works on the regular version, not the Director's Cut. If you don't know what that is, it's probably best not to set yourself up for an additional disappointment.
Least gripe: The story lacks some kind of carrot. DX1 had the nanotech virus, DX2 had that crazy nanotech weapon that levelled cities. DX3 has some.. civil unrest? Okay, it turns out there is a big carrot, but you don't learn about the seriousness of it until you have played 3/4th of the game. Simply put, the story could have used more direction. At times it makes me want to skip through dialogue, which is a rare sin for me to commit.
Verdict: 6.5
I recommend this game only if you see it seriously on sale somewhere. Consider getting the regular version, if you can.

You could pay attention to the numbers of industry, monies, science, foods, and the population generating them. You could calculate out the economies, consider how much of that economy's being taxed into your coffers, and compare the potential earnings vs building and hero upkeep and optimize every unit of monies spent. You could calculate weapon accuracies vs combat phase vs build cost vs weapon type defense vs damage output and optimize every weapon and defensive choice against the build and maintenance cost of each ship, compared to fleet size, fleet bonuses, and admiral benefits. You could explore bartering your goods and strategic and tactical and technological and planetary resources with other nations for their own technologies, and then resell those technologies to every other nation for any other benefit, potentially buying the fleet you need to defend yourself with. You could calculate optimal research paths despite your species-class-specific changes to the tech-tree for your current goal, while loving that the game's so well crafted that there is no generic optimal research path; it's always a path for your current goal. You could terraform every planet, mitigating planetary anomalies like dangerous flora or fractured tectonic plates, and create paradises for your people as you research transcendence, build an Endless Empire, conquer your foes, or create a galactic alliance. Knowing every number, you still may have pirates converge, random events cut at you, and faulty choices undermine you until the razor-sharp AI cuts you down in a most enjoyable fashion.
Or you can think of a race you'd like to play, customize the hundred options to generate it, and just make choices based on the general feel of that choice. You'll still be playing to your species' strengths despite not studying the numbers. You'll still have a wonderful gaming experience, reacting to multiple fleets jumping into your local cluster of stars and building trade routes to the most distant of species. And, depending on the difficulty level, pirate activity, random events, and personal choices, you may not be squashed like a bug by the sharp AI.
It's just elegant. It's beautifully crafted. It's balanced. Its inundated with flavor. It's highly recommended.

Cool idea, but the hardware components aren't as well chosen/designed as those in controllers released with consoles 10 years ago.
While it is super configurable, that can lead to way too much set up time just to play a game, and in some cases I can't build a configuration that feels right so I end up tweaking over and over again, never mind "Tune once". The software
doesn't properly describe certain options, leaving just an ID of the description, like "ControllerBinding_TouchMenuButtonType_Description".
First person games that play nice with both joystick and mouse are very few and far between (Bioshock Infinite comes to mind). That is to be blamed on the gaming industry's preference these days for weak ports rather than actually taking advantage of our hardware, but it still works against this controller. The fake mouse-like joystick is a poor replication, still herky-jerky and hobbled by all the things games try to do with that camera stick to work with the strange idea of pushing the camera around until it is where you want (with a joystick) rather than directly moving the camera where you want it (with a mouse or trackpad).
I still use it exclusively because I have gotten very use to everything it adds, and I will definitely buy a new revision if they made a point to engineer the hardware for actual gaming use, rather than the tossed together proof-of-concept of this first revision.

This is my main controller now and I think it's great, but it's not yet a replacement for a mouse and keyboard when it comes to FPS'.
Positives: The buttons, especially the triggers, feel stern and clicky and are very satisfying to press.
-The controller feels well-built and solid with a nice weight.
-Tons of customization options and specific game profiles allow you to greatly adjust controls and settings so that every game feels just right.
-Extra buttons on the grips of the controller allow customization that isn't available on most pads
-Touchpads are of good quality and can be used to surf the internet from your coach, if you are feeling lazy.
-You can pick the sounds the controller makes when turned on/off. It doesn't sound like much, but it's a nice little touch and I always enjoy hearing them.
-The thumbstick feels very good and is textured very well.
Negatives: I think Valve would be smart to make a higher-end version with super-sensitive trackpads. The current version is good, but I think it could be better if they want to make it a legit replacement for the mouse.
-It uses batteries instead of recharging.
-Small-handed people might have issues, as the grips on this controller are huge. I could see many people not feeling quite-comfortable holding it.
-If these were available for use with consoles, I think it would be a better fit than PC because if you have a PC, you will probably prefer using the norm for shooters. I could see the trackpads being better than thumbsticks if you get used to and adapt to them, but the time it takes makes it not worth it, at least not yet.
TL;DR: I love this controller, despite some shortcomings. If you are looking for a new controller for non-FPS games, this is one of the best.

I saw the trailer and I knew this game was going to be great. It's up there as one of my all time favourites along with Wings of Vi and Cave Story.
* The Gameplay itself is certainly the greatest strength of the game by far. Controls are extremely solid with a controller. The pacing is great, The difficulty curve is perfect; it starts off simple but continues to throw challenges at you that will always keep you on your toes and leads to some of the hardest encounters Ive experienced in a game, expect to die when learning a boss.
Like most metroidvania games, you can progress in a wide variety of ways. There are a ton of secrets and collectables throughout the world. There are over 40 bosses and if you complete the main story and post game and collect every item there is over 40 hours of gameplay.
* The music is 10/10. Seriously, buy the soundtrack. (imo top track is Sudden Death).
* The Art and Sprites are beautiful.
* 6 difficulty settings. Casual, Novice, Normal and Hard are available from the start. Hell and Bunny Extinction are unlocked via beating the game on harder difficuties.
* Several Boss Rush modes for those who want a next level of challenge or to compete against others for a great score on the ladder.
* Tons of Achievements that are fun and challenging to earn.
* The devs continue to add more content to the game. It received a free Halloween patch that contained a fair amount of content and a very fun boss and a paid DLC that I have written a seperate review for.
However, as much as I love this game it does have its flaws.
* The story is one of the games few weak points. When I picked it up I didnt expect much of a story to begin with, but it was very vague about a a few things as you progress and learn more about the world you are playing in and doesnt really explain why certain things occur, Though with the latest DLC it does explain a few things a little better and gives a little closure.
* Fair amount of fanservice. This can be a pro for some people but it wasnt for me, there were a few moments in the game that made me cringe a little bit, but it wasnt a big deal though.
* Bosses later in the game can scale out of control, after around chapter 4 some bosses were 10+ minute long endurance tests because they have so much health (and that is with keeping up Max damage combo up), however please take into account I jumped into this game on it's hardest difficulty that is available to you on it's first playthrough (Hard) and may not apply on easier difficulties.

The first time I heard about Rabi-Ribi it was off of a recommendations thread on NeoGaf. Honestly, I thought it looked like a Sakura Spirits knockoff aesthetically mixed with Maple Story. With regard to the aesthetic, I still feel like it looks too much like an anime game for the actual kind of game that it is. However, the underlying game is PHENOMINAL. if you love 2d DIFFICULT brawlers in the vein of wings of vi, castlevania SOTN, momodora 4, then you'll love this game.
Honestly, it's very similar to wings of vi in that the game has very difficult and punishing boss fights that are a mix of getting damage (through both ranged shooting ala megaman x and close combat fighting ala WoV or SOTN) in while avoiding bullet hells. There's a pretty important distinction to be made with regard to the combat though, as in Rabi-Ribi you can only melee if your feet are on the ground (as far as i am in the game anyways). This might, and did to me, seem like a bad thing becuase it limits just how much freedom you have in attacking. However, it's alleviated by the fact that you can get your first 2 attacks in while moving (out of your♥♥♥♥♥♥combo) allowing you to attack while still dodging, making boss fights pretty hectic but still rewarding.
The game somewhat has a leveling system as well, but from what I can see it's mostly "buy this item to increase damage by 5x" or "buy this item to increase stamina be 10%" etc etc, which you'll also find in the world similar to a metroid game with its missle/etank capactity upgrades. There are upgrades for abilities that I just haven't unlocked yet (for example there's an air dash that has upgrade items, not sure what the upgrades do for it, maybe reduced timer or more invincibility frames?).  If it's a big selling point you should look up the upgrades to see if they're interesting and meaningful to you.
There's also a rating system in the game that as far as I can tell amounts to "do a lot of damage without getting hit and we'll give you a higher rating," similar to devil may cry somewhat. However, where it differs from DMC is the higher your rating, the more bonuses you get. So if you get to D rating, you'll have 5% extra damage, C = 10%, etc, incentivizing you to play perfectly to clear boss phases faster. Also similar to DMC, there are consumables to heal you in battle if that's your thing, but in Rabi-Ribi you have to stand in place for like 3 seconds to consume the item, which given the bullet hell nature of boss fights can be pretty unrealistic.
I think i have sufficiently broken out why this game is a mechanically superior 2d brawler, so let's go on to the rest of the game. There are additional modes that you can play, the most notable one being a boss rush mode that is locked until you beat the game I believe. It's cool that the devs decided to include this because the bosses are definitely the best part of the game.
The pixel art graphics are pretty cool, but in my opinion they don't hold up when compared to superior games like momodora 4. However, they're still clean and cute. Dialogue is.... there.. ha... the music is pretty dope during boss fights though, there are a lot of people that really love some tracks! A lot of the different "Zones" of the game give me a serious maple story vibe, but oh well..
Honestly, the bosses are what make the game so damn good.. the rest of the game is okay, but the bosses make it 110% worth playing through if you like this kind of game.

This is gonna be a long review. Tl;dr:
Where do we begin?
So I came across this game while surfing a gaming blog. Not too much description given, but it seemed to be the type of game that I liked, so I decided to give it a try. Two things surprised me when I first viewed the store page; first being that it was tagged to be of the "Bullet Hell" genre, and that the total price of the game, with all DLCs, came to thirty dollars. I was expecting an indie title with 10~20 hour playtime, then maybe extra for grinding achievements. Nevertheless, I did trust the blogger and we had a lot of shared interests. I was suspecting that I probably overpaid for a game that would keep me occupied for a couple of days, but I wasn't short on money or anything so I just went with it.
So I started up the game, and the first thing that came up was the difficulty choice. Now anyone who has played games for a while knows that 'normal' means easy, 'hard' means normal, and any extra difficulties are the ones that are likely to give you any real challenge. I'm also the type that goes for the highest dificulty first. So understandably, I was annoyed when I saw it had two
difficulties above hard  (I mean, like, the heroine is a bunnygirl. How hard can it be?). I started my first save in hard, pondering if I should put up with two more runthroughs of the game.
The first few minutes went exactly as I had expected; a few bosses that would've been hard to lose should I have been playing with my feet, dialog that pops up everytime you try to do anything, the stuff you expect from indie games of the genre. I finished the prologue with no difficulties at all, although I was starting to realise how expansive the map was, with areas I could not yet venture into due to the lack of gear. This actually seemed like a drawback at the time, because I'm a very linear and straightforward gamer. I don't like revisiting old areas with new gears to find secrets and loot, and I was considering looking into a guide should it ever become a problem for me getting the achievements.
And then it all changed. Just a few screens outside of town, I encountered the next boss. Expecting another easy victory, I headed into the fight...
And I died.
And then I died again.
And again.
I thought it was just me taking the game too lightly, or just an outlier boss that had difficulty above average. Maybe it was just me getting used to this weird cross of Bullet Hell and Platformer. Next boss.




So at this point, I was getting the idea that something was off, but I was mostly enjoying the newfound challenge. With high expectations, I entered my next boss battle.

Never had I ever thought that an innocent looking platformer would strain me to this extent (Although I did mess up on the progression; this boss should have been fought much later). I was now filled with determination to beat this game no matter what it takes, on the highest difficulty to boot; but to even start that run, I would have to complete two whole runthroughs. The difficulty of this 'hard' seemed more fitting to be something like 'hell' (Which, incidentaly, is the next difficulty up in this game), and I was both excited and fearful of what challenges the higher difficulties may bring.
But it turns out that I had enough to worry about on my own difficulty. Whenever I faced a boss that I thought would be impossible to top, the next would be a few times harder. I would be absolutely destroyed for the first ten or so tries, not being able to remove even a fifth of its health, then be destroyed again as it unleashes more and more moves as the fight progresses. Every boss left me feeling like I've seen the worst that this game can throw at me; the next would prove that the challenge I've faced so far is nothing. My most memorable moment of the main game is the final four-stage bossfight, which had me desperately hanging on with no healing items, as I had used all of them on the first part. The introduction of every new part brought absolute despair, yet at the same time strengthening my resolve to beat the game, knowing that I was only centimeters off now.
And then came the post game. While called that, excluding the final chapter (Which has a quite distinct 'extra' feel to it), the post game doesn't really feel like an extra at all, instead following the natural sequence of the main game. Anyway, at this point I was slightly disappointed that beating the main game did not give me access to the higher difficulty, as I wanted to start the highest difficulty run as soon as possible. I decided to finish the extra difficulty as soon as possible. After all, how hard could it be, after I just endured the four consecutive tortures that is the final boss?
The first boss of the post game was a challenge I almost lost hope on. Even after what seemed like an endless number of tries, I could not even get her below half health. Once I become used to one move, the next would be the end of me. With slow and painstaking progress, I finally defeated her, now terrified of what the next boss would have in store for me. Well, it turns out that even getting to her would be a problem on it's own; the non-boss stages have become just as hard, if not even harder than the boss stages. To be honest, I was slightly disappointed with the second post game boss in terms of difficulty, as the flight stages and the regeneration granted by them made it too easy. However, the she has some of the hardest and most interesting patterns in the game.
Then we come to the true final boss. The map where the fight occurs is a hell to navigate; without giving you any spoilers, it will test the player's movement accuracy to the maximum. Just in case you were feeling that the game was getting easier, with all the upgraded gear and whatnot, the final boss decides to strip you of all these privileges; Again, without spoiling too much, the fight will test the player on every aspect of skill that they have learnt throughout the game, and has a truckload of different moves, all with very different methods to avoid. The difficulty is legendary; I have tried so many times to defeat this boss, that I can now recite all of its patterns, from all phases, in order.
And now here I am, back to where I started. I've just finished the prologue on my Hell run, which I can currently say looks to be a good 2~3 times harder than the Hard difficulty, as well as started a new game + run for my hard run. I have also seen the special extra bosses that the game had generously prepared for me; for all three of them, my initial reaction was
and
, but I believe I'll be able to defeat them someday.
So where to now? Is it the extra bosses, the new Hell and even higher Bunny Extinction difficulties, the Boss Rushes I've unlocked or perfect boss clear achievements that I shall complete next? Only one thing is sure for me: I have over a hundred hours of playtime on this game so far, and I'll take however long it takes me to defeat everything, unlock all achievements and ultimately compelete the game. So, after a time, every single one of us gets bored and wants to just load up a game and shoot...
. It doesn't really matter what, just something. And that's where someone loads up TF2, someone else Tribes and some people even Quake. And there's this weird sort that loads up Loadout.
Loadout is a third-person multiplayer shooter that bases itslef off some pretty simple, yet well-executed ideas. Simply put, it's a straightforward shooter with weapon custamization on a higher level then... most games, really. You build your completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapon, you pick your unbeliavably stupid look, jump into a map and go shoot people while listening to a narrator talking about the progress of your match in a completely out-of-place voice. And you have fun doing stuff until you get bored of doing the same thing over and over again, and get back to other games, only to come back for more later. And on the occasion of playing enough games, you get to buy more modules so you can build even more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons that do wierder stuff. Simple on paper, ain't it? Well, simplicity is powerful.
In fact, turns out this is really fun. There's plenty of maps, gamemodes and equipment possibilities to keep you interested and provide some basic complexity, while on the other hand you get to play a solid twitch shooter. The gameplay is action-packed, gory, ridiculous and full of funny moments. It never fails to deliver, but can feel slightly frustrating at first, simply because of how crazy it gets.
However, you'll soon realise that rifle that they gave you right off the bat is not exactly what you're looking for. So you start up the weapon editor, give your new badass gun a name and start piecing it togheter from to you available modules. The first choice is the most impacting one: What is your weapon type? The game splits the weapons into four catagories: Rifle, Laser, Rocket and Pulse. Each of them has some unique characteristics and modules, be it Laser's graceful accuarcy, Pulse's damage, Rifle's rate of fire or the simple explosive mayhem of Rocket. This doesn't wrap up the idea though, next coming is your weapon's modules. these differ for all of the types, and affect EVERYTHING, be it firing mode, damage, clip size or ammo type. You can go for standart high-damage sniper rifle, or be a bit unconventional and try to make a napalm mortar. Hell, why not make a Tesla LMG? Or a Bolt-action Shotgun?
This system is surprisingly fun, while only very slightly limiting in the matter of requiring you to pay for it with playtime or money. All of the equipment is available for the free currency AKA Blutes, with only little needed to get the module into your weapon. However, the experience system on the weapons rewards you for playing with your favourite modules and leveling them up in order to make them more effective. These upgrades are rather costly, though, and provide only minor bonuses. And to end that up not only you're carrying your superb gun with you - you've got TWO, and an ability, be that a Frag grenade, personal shield or a fake explosive medikit. Yes, it's a thing.
And if you'r easking me how they make money out of this game, I don't know. There's a cosmetic items store, but nobody forces you to use it, and there are boosters for XP and Blutes, but you don't need them if you find the game fun.
After all, you won't rehgret trying it out. It's worth it. And by 'it' I mean download time, because that's everything it's worth.

The idea to mix a "lite" game with a beefier strategy title is a great one, but tricky to pull off, and this game suffers as much from the weaknesses of both approaches as it benefits from theirs strengths in this combination. It has too much going on to catch that relaxing/superstreamlined "lite" feeling of FTL or Battlestation Harbinger, etc., and it's too light to really be compelling as a strategy title. I liked the game and was on the fence about returning it as I got closer to the 2 hr refund limit, but I also was afraid I had seen much of what there was to see, and things started feeling pretty repetitive and gameplay varied but somewhat flat.
One example is combat: It's fairly tactical as attacks inflict states (hull breach, sensors down) which can then be exploited by other attacks. But from what I could see, most states didn't have any character beyond this rock-paper-scissors aspect, so it feels a bit too gamey after awhile. With the only real combat options being choosing attacks/buffs and targets, it gets a bit repetitive fairly quickly.
Again, it's a solid title, but it didn't work for me.

As most people know, JRPGs sink or swim based on the quality of their writing and characters, so that's where I'll start my review:
Jim Valvano said "if you laught, you think, and you cry, that's a full day," and the writers went the extra mile to make their audience laugh, cry, and think, all in the same playthrough. Don't worry, the game is still a comedy, and you'll still be laughing all the way through, but the narrative also goes to dark places, and there was a scene that genuinelly freaked me out. As a matter of fact, from the moment the playable part of the game starts, it's non-stop foreshadowning that "oh God, this can only end in tears." In addition, the story pays several nods to the iterative experience that were the previous games/dimensions, which makes the experience feel even bigger.
The new character (Uzume Tenoboushi) is endearing and will win you over rather quick. The best parts of the writing, however, were probably Nepgear and Uni. The writers seem to have learned their lesson from the Sisters Generation fiasco, and this time they turned the little sisters into a great complement to the story: Gear is a decent Straight Man in the middle of the circus (and her deprotagonization is still occasionally played for laughs, but without bordering on being mean as it happened in Victory). Uni this time distinguishes herself from her sister in that, while Noire is the dependable public figure, Uni is the dependable person willing to make the hard choices softer-hearted people won't, in addition to possessing a wisdom that shines at times.
Graphically speaking, Compile Heart seasoned their usual copypasta stew with enough new game assets to make it feel fresh (and they needed to, considering this game originally debuted on the PS4) as well as to keep it from being bullied by the other PS4 games after the 2K transition. The music is adequate, and conveys the narrative's theme of foreboding by toning down some of the more cheerful tunes, but still nothing to write home about (as it's usually the case with Neptunia games). There is a memorable track (namely, the one for fighting the dark CPUs), but sadly not enough to make me feel I should buy the soundtrack. The controls are basically more of the same thing, and if you're playing with a Steam Controller (as I did) you'll need to create your own control scheme as the default scheme will NOT work (look for the one I uploaded, that will get you through, and customize as needed if you want).
Warning: The game cheats in that the new game+' second playthrough is basically mandatory. To get the True Ending, you must (among other things) have each nation end their segment with shares of 60% or more in the Neptunia G part, and without the extra money from your first playthrough, getting 60% in the Planeptune part is impossible (furthermore, Planeptunes' shares somehow drain during the other nations' parts, making it even harder to make the mark). Also, you won't be able to complete the Neplunker levels without Flag Items you only receive upon start a new game+. Still, the experience is enjoyable enough and I'm fairly certain you'll want to do that second playthrough
The best Neptunia game so far, and basically the "ultimate" one... which is both good and bad, because narrative-wise, that means that, under Neptunia's current formula, there's nowhere else they can go from here. Furthermore, it somehow feels like the series' conclusion once you take all factors into consideration. If the franchise is to keep thriving, it will need to break its mold and move to terra incognita (which is exactly what Four Goddesses Online feel like). Only time will tell whether Neptunia manages to succeed where most franchises have failed and are then been accused of jumping the shark.

The H+ option which appears to let you keep the upgrades you got the first time you play the game through (if you play the director's cut version a second time) is a good option for increasing replayability even further. This game did not seem too repetitious even though I played the original version not that long ago. But aside from an increase in the number of graphical glitches, it has the same failings as the original: Endings chosen largely according to which button you press...main character's romantic interest left completely unresolved....endings that consist of non-option options. (there's no way to simply shut off the evil signal at the end and not broadcast any propaganda message without killing yourself and everyone in the base? Silly.) but it is still a good game and the director's cut can be a nice excuse to play through the whole game a second time.

Endless Space is a space based, turn based 4x title in the vein of titles such as Masters of Orion and Galactic Civilization.
Endless space gives this genre a breath of fresh air, with beautiful graphics and a sleek UI, the game is great but it does lack some of the depth that Masters of Orion offered and some of the customisation that Galactic Civilization had. However despite this the game is immensely enjoyable, with a good diversity of races, traits, ships, tech and so forth and well paced game play even in multiplayer.
However if you do plan to pick up the title, I would urge you to pick up the Disharmony DLC also, this expands the game quite a bit but also gives you access to some of the add-ons that have been released including the most recent of these The Search for Auriga.
If you are into the 4x Genre or have been craving for something worth playing since Masters of Orion 2 then this might be the title you have been looking for. The price point is a little high for some and I would agree, however if you pick this title up on sale then it is worth every penny.

An awesome game from start to finish, I don't know why I waited so long to play this.. Definitely one of the best first person shooters I have ever played. This is really what Doom is supposed to be, playing this made me realize what Doom 3 was lacking..
The pacing in this game is practically perfect, It never once feels dull at any moment during the campaign - alternating between quieter exploration sections and all out carnage old school fast paced Doom/Quake/UT style combat. This version of Doom more than any other FPS I have played requires you to really think on your feet and keep moving at all times during combat. Different enemies and areas provide unique challenges - as well as every gun performing very differently with strengths and weaknesses. "Glory kills" make the combat in this game unique and a little easier but even the default "Hurt Me Plenty" difficult gets VERY hard at times especially in the second half of the game, although I never once died thinking to myself "That was BS." The game is brutal, fair and above all fun.
The graphics are incredible and the level design is excellent. Every chapter is layed out very differently, has a unique feel to them and is very memorable. Plenty of eye candy and secret areas/easter eggs in the levels as well. Lots of variety in the ways you choose to upgrade your suit and weapons that definitely affect gameplay quite a bit. I wish more FPS games would focus on making a great campaign like this that is memorable, challenging and fun. The multiplayer is awesome as well from what I played so far, definitely better than the current state of Quake: Champions. Even just based on the campaign I would give this game a 10/10.

Ill keep this relatively simple
Pros:
-Relatively open ended gameplay, you arent shoehorned into doing story missions, though you are forced to fight the main antagonists if you want any chance of survival. this shouldnt matter given that youll be flying around looking for a fight to lvl up and collect resources anyways.

Fantastic game, has had it's ups and downs in development, yet it always bounces back better than before. Give the game a try, and play at LEAST 25 matches before deciding if you want to keep playing or not because this gives you all the rewards for being a new player. Shuffle through the different trial mechs during these games, as this will help pin down your best play style. Each mech plays differently. To help minimize frustration as you learn;
Tips and tricks:
-Lrms have a minimum range of 180m (unless they are clan-tech)
-When playing lights always keep moving.
-3rd person hurts you in major ways.
-Be aware of things like your armor paper doll. Even when you think you are safe someone could be shooting you in the back.
-When you see an enemy mech press "R" this locks onto the target and transmits data to your team. It also helps in picking already damaged parts of a mech to shoot at.
-Avoid running off, and stick with the team. Stragglers often meet untimely demises.
-Don't be the first one in line when in combat. Frontline units are the first to die.
-Spreading damage across your mech is key; twist your body while not firing in combat, as you become a better pilot this   will be more natural. Choosing a shoulder/arm to always show is also helpful when one side has less weapons.
Hope this helped. Good luck, and have fun!

A good deathmatch game for those who enjoyed the mech combat side of previous mechwarrior titles. It offers the best online mech vs. mech combat of any game so far but it is not without its flaws. If you are looking for a deep campaign system with role-playing and long-term strategic planning then you should probably look elsewhere. However if you enjoy good old giant stompy robots blowing the %#!@ out of each other in arena settings then this  probably a good game to try for free, especially if you have played other similar titles such as World of Tanks or Armored Warfare.
• The most deep and detailed mech combat system of any online mech game.  It is very fun once you understand what you are doing and it's the primary reason so many players stayed through the bugs and flaws of the original game.
• There is a huge range of mechs and a very deep customization system that offers a lot of options for tinkerers and collectors.
• The game should feel familiar and easy to pick up for those who have played games like World of Tanks.  In addition the grind and financial aspects of the game are considerably less.
• The game rewards skill. Paying money can save you time and give you more mechbays, but it will not give you any significant advantage over other players.
• The first mechwarrior title since 1989 that has actually included the original 3025 battlemechs.
• Despite considerable changes from the tabletop, it is the closest any mechwarrior title (to this date) has been to replicating its feel and tactics.
• In comparison with other online games, the community tends to be more mature and friendly on average.
• You can play on any of the worldwide servers (North America, Europe, Southeast Asia / Oceania) with the same account.
• Despite the grind being considerably less than other similar titles, it is still present.
• The game runs on cryengine3  which is not the most stable or efficient of online platforms.
• The game still has a number of minor bugs and balance issues to be fixed and the developers are often slow to react to this.
• Outside of arena battles the game doesn't offer much of a campaign mode. The community warfare mode (still in beta at the time of this review) is fun for short periods but it hasn't been developed nearly enough to be considered a fully functional feature.
• Because it is a heavily skill focused game, the game also punishes making bad decisions. This can make it more difficult for people who just want to play casually and not worry about using their best mechs all the time.
• The game uses an inefficient matchmaking system that results in longer wait times than necessary.

For those new to mechwarrior, allow me to provide an introduction.
These are not ultra fast, missile dodging anime style mecha.  These are big slow stompy deathbots that will get hit by hundreds of missiles, get annoyed and fire back.  Fast kills are rare, instant kills are extremely rare.
A battlemech is a 20-100 ton battle machine.  Each section of the mech has it's own independant health, and you can lose most of them without dying.  For example, if you are running a standard type engine you can lose both arms, one leg, your left torso and your right torso and still keep fighting.
You get to customize everything.  We're not talking putting skins on your guns, we're talking what guns do you want to carry where, how many rounds for each, how many heat sinks to keep the machine from getting to hot?  What size engine?  How much armor on your left leg, right leg, left arm, right arm, head, left torso, right torso, center torso, left tear torso, right rear torso, center rear torso?  - oh yeah, you get to paint everything too if you still care.
Teamwork is the deciding factor in matches, the nature of the machines and how they move and take damage means that even the most skilled player can't overcome a team that abandons them to the enemy.  Putting your team in a bad spot will lose the match even if you are better shots than they are.  This is chess with more layers of complexity.
Play intergalactic war.  There are 10 factions vying for control of the universe, pick one and start claiming entire planets in their name as you fight your way across the galaxy.
Now that you have the basics, here's the details on how this game has been.  I joined in closed beta and have been an active player the entire time, including all the massive meltdowns caused by actions of the publisher.  These incidents are incrediby public and easy to look up.  Yes, they earned a bad rep.
However, the game itself is quite fun.  It is not pay to win - the cash only mechs are not inherently better.  Different, but not better than the ones you can get for free.  If anything this game is only pay not to grind, which is fine.
Honest final recommendation?  If you are tired of fast action, actually want to see who is shooting you, and want to actually fight the other guy give this a shot.  If you like it, then put in a few bucks for a pack of mechs, skip a ton of grinding and enjoy yourself.  Also, join a team.  If you don't join a team, you will get constantly stomped in the community warfare mode.  Cannot stress this enough - no team, don't join CW.

Definitely a worthwhile play, although it's a very different game genre from most out there. I highly recommend it, but remember it has a high learning curve. It also isn't pay to win and way more team based than anything. Grind is heavy but paying is only for cosmetics and convienience.

For the first time in the series, the story is so lame and boring that it was hard to gather the enthusiasm to continue. It was a series of nonsensical and irrelevant things strung together to fill screen time.
From the utter irritation of the game constantly switching/removing your equipment (gasp!) to dropping the Plutia/Iris Heart character from the last game because she was too gross, it's one bummer after another. The new characters are awful, especially Uzume/Orange Heart. Dreamcast CPU  - she was as lame as the real Dreamcast console, indeed. The other new characters (with inexplicable names like C-Cha, S-Sha, E-Sha and B-Sha (!!!)) are as annoying as they are ugly to look at. If you like anyone but Neptune and Nepgear after this game, you're a bigger fan than I am. This is a letdown of massive proportions for all the wrong reasons. Also, it does the worst Neptunia trope of all time ALL THE TIME: "Oh, this is a different time/dimension/whatever, so I don't know you." Every character re-meets every character constantly. It's insufferable. Nice way to throw away all the character relationships from previous games or AN HOUR AGO.
PROS: Voice acting (Melissa Fahn as Neptune is *amazing*). Great game performance and framerate. Lots of options. Lots to see and do if you like that. Music is great. Battle system is the same as before: turn-based and fast.
CONS: Story. New characters. Level design. Missing the danger/conflict from previous games and making everything into an unfunny joke. Strangely rife with spelling/grammar mistakes (lying/laying, its/its) that I don't recall in previous games.

So where to start. Doom is one of the best first person shooters I have ever played, in almost every way possible.
The story is very simple, "demons everywhere, kill them all and fast!" Atleast thats what the common player is told, there is a very detailed story hidden in the collectables scatterd around the game, for example where the energy came from why humans need it and other little things. Or if you realy dont care for first person shooter storys just ignore it and keep shooting the demons, and have tones of fun doing it!
As for the first person shooting part of this FPS its is very smooth and feels amazing. Every shot feels like your shooting a gun, not a pea out of a straw, which may I add is super satisfying. The animations of the guns, the switch of gun mods and the secondary abilities animation is spectacular on every level. The look and almost the feel of the animations is heavy and powerfull.
Now as for the multiplayer, this is not why you should buy this game. It has almost no one playing it and was not the main centre of attetion for the development team at all. And it shows, because the campain is amazing.
As for the length of the game, its is a normal length campain if you intend on only playing it once. To get the full DOOM experiance you need to play the campain muliple times, on every difficulty, and set yourself little challenges such as only using the shotgun, or if your a god, only use the pistol on ultra-nightmare difficulty.
All in all this game is F***ing insane and is worth your time and money.

I remember first playing this on the XBox360.  I pre-ordered the game because it looked like a blast.  I thought of it as a more safe version of GTA.  Being an Achievement addict, my first couple hours in the game involved running back and forth giving wedgies to everyone, beating up anyone, and throwing all sorts of junk everywhere and making everyone cry...and honestly, I think that fit with the main character's attitude at the start.
Playing the game, I was delighted to see all the simplified stereotypes of people in school.  Who really needs individuality when you have a clique?  And we are the one boy who stands above all of it.  It was an amazing journey just trying to survive and not get kicked out of Bullworth Academy, while at the same time doing a Lot of messed up stuff I never did in school which would get anyone arrested now.  I enjoyed seeing Jimmy forced to be as much of the "good guy" as he could be while at the same time setting off just enough trouble not to get kicked out of school.
The formula for success was good enough to me.  It sort of fit into my own 15-year-old mindset of how growing up worked.  Get in good with the various cliques while not being a part of any.  Date your way up the ladder; you can't always start with the popular girl.  Before you know it, you're a star and everyone loves you!  Jimmy finds out it doesn't work like that, though.
Yeah, this isn't a complete review or anything.  The bottom line is "GTA without guns, carjacking or hookers, in school."  If you like GTA, you'll probably like this...unless you prefer guns, carjacking and hookers...  If you're not into shooting up a strip mall, this is your game.  The story shows the rise, fall, and rise again of Jimmy Hopkins as he struggles to keep his head above the water in the middle of chaos.  And I have to say, the ending was insane.  When you first meet Gary, you know there's going to be some trouble.  I'm amazed the principal was so worried about Jimmy messing up he never saw psycho Gary coming...poor guy.
This game is worth buying at any price, and playing to completion.

As a kid i was always taking apart my toys because i wanted to know what was inside and how they worked and then putting them back together again, something that didn't always work out that well. Though it was more out of curiousity it does help you to understand things better and why they do what they do.
Guns have been something else I've always been interested in, especially in how they work and where their life taking power comes from. And taking them apart and putting them back together again is actually a must, not only for maintenance purposes but also to understand them. Unfortunately it isn't that easy to get your hands on let's say an M4 (in the Netherlands at least), let alone have the money to spend on it, so stumbling on this little yet very in-depth and detailed interactive guide was a very welcome surprise.
World of Guns has a lot to offer the weapon enthusiasts among us. It not only lets you take them apart piece by piece but it also shows you how the pieces work together which you can view in X-ray vision or by cutting away different parts of a weapon. Next to that you'll also be able to read up on information and history of any weapon in particular by means of simple yet effective integrated links to the interwebs, check out the attachments of certain weapons and what they do, and you'll be able to give most guns a test run on numerous shooting ranges.
All in all this is a very complete package for it's asking price (Free if you are willing to put in the effort!) and will come as close to handling firearms as a non-specialist/criminal like you and me can. And if you do ever manage to get your hands on a real model of one of the weapons you have studied thoroughly in World of Guns than you will have no problem taking it apart and putting it back together in working condition again. That is probably the best compliment i can give to this little piece of software.

My biggest problem I've noticed is planning my moves in advance and my brain betraying me and turning when I am still on a straight path. Harder levels go faster and faster. It gets to the point where you aren't really "thinking" and just react. I'll beat a level and be amazed I completed it as it was like a blur. This is definitely hard and is a specialized type of "fun" that requires a deeper appreciation. The music in this game is fair, but the subtle beat and noises you generate from moving become quite hypnotic at times (really surreal).
I have a hard time understanding how anyone could argue that this isn't worth $3. How many hours of gameplay do you want for that much money? Worst case scenario, this is the game you put on when friends come over and have them have a go at it. Laughing at their pitiful attempts should be priceless.

Fun at first but it got repetitive quick.
I ended up requesting a refund due to it simply not being fun. It got boring quickly, and coupled with the dull music, it didn't keep me interested, and simply annoyed me. The menu's are well made, and it's glitch free, I'll give it that, but the repetitive dullness of it made me unable to stand it for enough time to invalidate the refund.
My advice to the dev would be to make the music more interesting. For a rhythm based game, it's incredibly important, so having it be this minimal really takes away from it. If it had more to it then I could endure it, as generally I enjoy tough games, but this one is boring.
EDIT!
The developer received the criticism very well, and went on to fix several of my criticisms! This game is looking to go in good directions!
